title: Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik: We must fight the roots of violence against women
content:
Writer Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik spoke to ANF on the occasion of 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, highlighting the direct relationship between the women's struggle and social peace, as well as the connection between male violence and state violence. Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik discussed women's struggle to become active subjects in the process of bringing Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan's Call for Peace and Democratic Society of 27 February 2025 into society, as well as the struggle that must be waged against policies of impunity.




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik said that the Women's Initiative I Need Peace, of which she is a member, was established to bring Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan's Call for Peace and Democratic Society of 27 February 2025 into society and discuss how women could become active subjects in this process. She stated that, as efforts to build social support for peace continue, state violence against women throughout the 40 years of war remains one of the most urgent issues they face.




'Male domination persists under every ruling system'




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik said that women were discussing not only the future but also the past, summarizing the historical transformation of male domination as follows: "Femicide and male violence against women, which continue to exist in human life, have been the most visible manifestations of male domination since its emergence. At the same time, we know that male domination has become a system in its own right, infiltrating and becoming embedded in every dimension of economic, social and political life, regardless of the system in place, and maintaining its existence under every ruling order. This is the reality from which we proceed."




'The same reality lies behind domestic violence and state violence'




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik stated that the state is the structure that governs on behalf of the ruling powers in today's world, pointing out that the same state structure stands behind violence, protects male perpetrators through the judiciary and grants reductions in their sentences.




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik recalled that women's bodies and sexuality were targeted through sexual torture and massacres during the 40 years of war, saying, "The same reality lies behind the violence directed at a woman murdered by her husband at home or shot in the street by her ex-husband, and the sexual aggression women encounter at the hands of state police officers, soldiers, village guards or counterterrorism units. And we women are still struggling against this as one of our most fundamental issues."




'Musa Orhan's acquittal is a major cause for outrage'




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik strongly condemned the acquittal of Specialist Sergeant Musa Orhan in the case in which he was tried on charges of aggravated sexual assault, emphasizing that a policy of impunity had been implemented despite Ipek Er explicitly identifying the perpetrator in a letter before taking her own life. She recalled that women, journalists, filmmakers and writers who protested against this situation had been punished. Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik said, "While state officials are treated with extraordinary privilege, a murderer like Musa Orhan can be acquitted. There is no more striking example that illustrates the situation so clearly. Above all, this is a major cause for outrage."




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik stressed that this situation must occupy a central place in the upcoming 25 November mobilizations against violence against women. She called for all femicides covered up by the state to become a central focus of the struggle, particularly the Gülistan Doku case, which she said had been covered up by a network responsible for murder operating around the governor's office.




'Making people compete over their suffering is a state policy'




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik said that an end to the conflicts would mean that massacres, torture and rape would cease and that this reality would become publicly acknowledged. She also stated that peace would lift the nationalist barriers obstructing class struggle. Pointing out that the 2027 budget had once again been prepared as a "war budget", with no allocation for women, Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik assessed the process as follows: "We need to stand side by side. Making people compete over their suffering is a state policy. When the Call for Peace and Democratic Society was made, those waging the war immediately came forward and asked, 'What will happen to our martyrs and veterans?' Yet this is precisely where both the sharpest edge of oppression and the key to resolving the problems lie. A door has opened, and that door is open to everyone. We must recognize this and organize a strategic approach and sphere of activity that will open that door wider."




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik stated that people could discuss everything in their daily lives, yet the Kurdish question could not be openly discussed by its name. She emphasized that everyone must take responsibility without delay at a time when Alevi, Kurdish and Yazidi identities remain unrecognized and a uniform Sunni-Turkish identity is imposed.




'Turkey does not implement ECtHR rulings'




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik said that Turkey's government was pursuing an anti-democratic and fascist practice of power, refusing to implement rulings of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) and disregarding court decisions even while exploiting the 12 September Constitution.




She said: "We can see just how anti-democratic Turkey is, with a government that has come to power by exploiting even the 12 September Constitution and refuses to implement court rulings. Turkey is a country that does not implement ECtHR rulings. At a time when imperialist policies around the world are organizing new wars and armament, the People's Leader of the Kurdish Freedom Movement, which has exposed the reality behind all this corruption, is still being held in prison, having been brought there through a conspiracy in the first place. We are confronted with repression and violence that refuse to lift the isolation despite ECtHR rulings."




'

We can develop a powerful struggle against violence'




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik recalled that 25 November emerged from the revolutionary resistance of the Mirabal sisters against state violence in Latin America and concluded: "The meaning of 25 November has expanded considerably in Turkey; state violence and patriarchal violence have merged. This is a very important phenomenon. If we properly understand its significance, we can develop a very powerful struggle against violence from the women's front. However, the women's movement must also make confronting the sources of this violence an essential part of its agenda."

title: Pascal Torre: Doubts will persist until Abdullah Öcalan is freed
content:
The discussions surrounding a democratic solution to the Kurdish question continue as part of the process initiated by Abdullah Öcalan's Call for Peace and Democratic Society. The legal and political steps that the Turkish state must take, as well as the responsibilities of the international community, remain on the agenda. Despite the decision by the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) to dissolve itself, the continued imprisonment of Öcalan, the situation of political prisoners and the lack of concrete steps towards recognizing the political and cultural rights of the Kurdish people remain central issues in discussions about the future of the process.




Pascal Torre, co-chair of the France-Kurdistan Association and a historian, spoke to ANF about the Peace and Democratic Society Process, the importance of Abdullah Öcalan's freedom for lasting peace and Europe's responsibilities in this process.




Torre emphasized that lasting peace is only possible through democratization and criticized the Turkish state's security-oriented approach to the process. He said that Öcalan's freedom is crucial for advancing peace negotiations and implementing any potential agreement. Torre also criticized the silence of France and the European Union, arguing that the Council of Europe must adopt a more determined stance towards Turkey.




Torre stressed that Öcalan's release would be an important indication of Turkey's commitment to peace, saying, "As long as Abdullah Öcalan is not released, doubts will persist about Turkey's willingness to bring this process to a conclusion."




The interview with historian Pascal Torre follows:




Efforts to find a democratic solution to the Kurdish question continue following Abdullah Öcalan

's call on 27 February 2025. How do you assess the process at its current stage? What do you think are the fundamental conditions for achieving lasting peace?




This is an extremely important process and, if it succeeds, although we are still quite far from that, it could mark the beginning of a new era. However, I would like to point out that this process is not entirely new. The Kurdish Movement and Abdullah Öcalan have been putting forward various proposals aimed at achieving lasting peace for many years.




Nevertheless, I believe that extremely important ideological and strategic innovations have taken place within the Kurdish movement. These innovations stem primarily from the conditions of armed struggle. But they also stem, above all, from the clearly expressed political will to find a solution, which has existed for a long time.




Secondly, there is the international situation, which is influencing this process today. So yes, this process could represent an extremely important development. However, to understand what is happening today, I believe we need to return to several fundamental points.




The political and cultural rights of the Kurds have not been recognized for decades. This lies at the root of the problems facing the Kurdish people as a whole. Through their struggle and at enormous cost, the Kurds have managed to overcome their marginalized position and become important actors in the states where they live and across the region. It is necessary to emphasize once again the extremely important role played by the PKK in this regard. However, as Abdullah Öcalan has stated, the PKK's historical mission has now come to an end.




'There can be no peace without democratization'




For many years, the PKK provided a guarantee for the Kurdish people. Today, however, it may be regarded as a source of vulnerability. As Abdullah Öcalan rightly stated, the era of non-state armed organizations is now over. The enormous political gains achieved by the Kurdish people through great struggles must now be transformed into institutional influence that will ensure the recognition of their rights and, above all, the fundamental democratization of Turkey.




These two issues cannot be considered separately. There can be no peace without democratization. In my view, this is the entire significance of Abdullah Öcalan's extremely important call. This call also responds to the fundamental issues of our time.




As you have pointed out, despite this peace process, Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan remains imprisoned, and there has been no fundamental change in his legal situation. Do you think lasting peace can truly be built without guaranteeing the necessary conditions for Abdullah Öcalan's freedom and participation in the process?




I would like to address two or three points here. Today, Abdullah Öcalan is a central figure in the negotiations taking place in the country. The first point that deserves particular attention is that Abdullah Öcalan possesses unprecedented political authority, and this authority must be utilized.




The second issue is this: How can peace negotiations be conducted while their principal interlocutor remains in prison? This is undoubtedly a significant obstacle. The third point, which I consider decisive, is this: If a lasting peace agreement is reached, although we are still quite far from that, who could better guarantee its implementation on the ground than Abdullah Öcalan? However, he cannot do this from prison.




In my view, the most decisive argument is that Abdullah Öcalan's continued imprisonment, despite the beginning of negotiations, demonstrates that the Kurdish people are not being recognized. This is because the Turkish state's response is a policing response.




What I mean is that Abdullah Öcalan's current situation clearly illustrates the dialogue of the deaf that has continued for two years, with neither side listening to the other. The Turkish state approaches the peace process solely from a security perspective and reduces the issue to the fight against "terrorism". It therefore continues its policy of police and military repression against the Kurdish Movement. We have also seen this in the removal of mayors from office.




'The Turkish state must take concrete political steps'




Although some things are slightly different today, the fact that hundreds of political prisoners, including Selahattin Demirtaş, remain imprisoned demonstrates that the Turkish government rejects the idea of democratization and recognition of the Kurdish people's rights. On the other side, the Kurds insist that this peace process must lead to recognition of their political and cultural rights.




The two sides are therefore not meeting on common ground. Abdullah Öcalan expresses this with great political intelligence, and this deserves particular emphasis. Abdullah Öcalan is saying that there is a dialogue of the deaf between the parties, that they are not listening to one another. He says that the weapons must fall silent for the parties to hear each other. However, the Turkish state must also take concrete political steps following two years of negotiations and struggle. So far, nothing has happened. This is precisely where the problem lies.




What can international experiences such as Northern Ireland, South Africa and Colombia teach us about peace processes?




Many peace processes have been initiated around the world. We can look at South Africa, Northern Ireland, Colombia and other examples. Despite past tensions between the parties, mutual trust is necessary for a peace process to begin. Both sides must also have the will to make progress.




Today, it is clear that the will to move forward exists, at least for now, on the Kurdish side. There is a serious asymmetry in the discussions taking place. As long as there are people like Erdoğan who present the end of armed struggle in Turkey as a victory intended to win the support of Islamist-conservative voters or extreme nationalists, no decisions can be made. A parliamentary commission was convened. The commission discussed the return of PKK fighters to civilian life, the release of thousands of political prisoners and the termination of thousands of entirely unjust judicial proceedings against Kurdish activists. Yet nothing has materialized.




In Colombia, Northern Ireland and South Africa, however, there was a shared will between the parties when negotiations began. Of course, that will depended on the balance of power, but there was a common determination to achieve results. Here, by contrast, we are left with the impression that the Turkish state has provided no response for two years.




The international situation should also prompt serious reflection. We are living through a period in which the Middle East is shaken by wars and violence, Israel is destabilizing and fragmenting the Middle East, Trump's aggressive policies are evident, and violence against the Kurds in Rojava continues despite the agreement that was signed. The Kurds, meanwhile, are proposing democratization and political stability. This is an extremely important achievement that many political leaders should reflect upon today. The Kurds carry a message: a message of peace. In a Middle East marked by constant wars, this message deserves serious consideration. That is precisely why the Kurds must be supported internationally.




'Europe's silence is a serious mistake'




First of all, the Kurds enjoy very broad support. The Kurdish people's struggle inspires great admiration. We cannot say, for example, that France has done nothing in Rojava. Nevertheless, when it comes to the peace process initiated by the Kurds in Turkey, a diplomacy of silence is being pursued. The French government and the European Union have made no statements on the matter. Yet if France and the European Union want to play a role, that role should be to ensure the implementation of international law and encourage the resolution of conflicts. Instead, France and the European Union remain silent in the face of this process. This is a very serious mistake. As France-Kurdistan, we are trying to mobilize various forces to support the process that has been initiated. And there are quite a number of such forces.




Despite the PKK's decision to dissolve itself, we see that the European Union and France continue to classify the PKK as a terrorist organization. Does this position constitute an obstacle to the peace process?




Of course. First and foremost, the PKK has announced its dissolution. Therefore, it no longer makes any sense to continue classifying the PKK as a "terrorist organization". The Kurds have fully committed themselves to a democratic and peaceful path. This is today's political reality, and the governments of France and Europe must take this reality into account. France and the European Union constantly declare their commitment to human rights and democratic policies. Yet those who defend these policies today receive no support whatsoever. This is absolutely unacceptable. A series of initiatives must therefore be undertaken.




For example, as France-Kurdistan, we are currently campaigning for the release of Abdullah Öcalan and all prisoners. We are also closely following the situation of singer Nûdem Durak. Nûdem Durak was imprisoned simply for singing in Kurdish.




I would also like to emphasize that, within a peace process, particularly one based on an inclusive policy, recognition of the Kurdish language would be an important element of both progress and peace. We therefore demand the release of Nûdem Durak and all Kurdish activists currently imprisoned. France and the European Union must also take action in this direction.




Unfortunately, this is not the situation in Turkey at present. France, meanwhile, gives greater priority to other issues, which are not necessarily of secondary importance. If we want to resolve the question of peace in the Middle East today, we must resolve the Palestinian question and the Kurdish question. It is not that complicated. These are two fundamental issues. And the Kurds are currently undertaking extremely important initiatives to build lasting peace. As you know, the Greek philosopher Aristotle said: "To build peace is to build the coexistence of peoples in the city."




'

The Kurds represent a modern understanding of peace'




The Kurds today represent this positive understanding of peace, in which peace does not simply mean the absence of war. It is a modern understanding of peace, one that recognizes otherness, accepts differences and lays the foundations for a more humane society. And it is precisely this more humane society that we need today.




The experiences developed by the Kurds in municipalities in Turkey and in Rojava have demonstrated their capacity to develop innovative democratic solutions. These experiences can sometimes serve as alternative models to the authoritarian, dictatorial and even fascist regimes we see in the region. We therefore have very strong reasons to support this peace process. And that support, as you rightly emphasized earlier, also includes Abdullah Öcalan's freedom.




You recently signed an international appeal calling for the release of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan within the framework of the "Right to Hope". In 2014, the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) ruled against Turkey over the aggravated life sentence imposed on Abdullah Öcalan. However, more than 12 years later, the judgment has still not been fully implemented. How do you explain this situation, and what concrete steps do you expect from the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe at its meetings in December?




As you know if Europe wants to maintain its existence, it must ensure respect for international and European law. At a time when international law is being trampled upon around the world, this is also where Europe's strength lies.




International law today provides a framework of principles. In other words, many peoples around the world rely on international law to defend their rights. Therefore, international and European law must now pave the way for the immediate release of Abdullah Öcalan and Selahattin Demirtaş.




Unfortunately, Turkey is currently violating both international and European law. Moreover, Turkey is a member of the Council of Europe. A determined stance must therefore be adopted towards Turkey. We are capable of doing this in relation to other countries. Turkey also has extremely strong economic relations with the European Union.




'Öcalan's freedom will demonstrate the will for peace'




Action can also be taken in this area, and Turkey can be told: "Honor your commitments, respect European Union law and European law. Immediately release political prisoners who should not be in prison under any circumstances. These people have been victims of trials that have become a caricature of justice."




Then there is Abdullah Öcalan, who is at the center of this process. His release would be an extremely positive indication of the will to bring the process to a conclusion. However, as long as Abdullah Öcalan is not released, doubts will persist about Turkey's willingness to bring this process to a conclusion. At the same time, there are many democratic and progressive forces. We can see this around the world today. Progressive forces have achieved victories in Serbia, Brazil and many other countries. Democratic voices from around the world can therefore be raised to support peace and democracy in Turkey. This is also the message conveyed by the Kurds.

title: Tracing the footsteps of martyrs in Qendîl - I
content:
The absence of someone who has not been heard from for years remains a constant presence in the lives of those left behind. Families continue living, sometimes with the hope that their loved one will return one day, sometimes with an old photograph, and sometimes with unanswered questions. Not hearing from someone for years and learning that they are no longer alive do not evoke the same feelings. As time passes, children grow up, parents grow old, and some die without ever receiving the news they have been waiting for. The name of the missing person continues to live on in conversations, memories and the possibility that they might one day return. Whenever the possibility of peace begins to be discussed again, hopes that those who have been missing for so long might return also grow stronger.




The recent announcements of martyrdom came at such a time. Condolence gatherings were held in different cities, photographs kept for years were brought out, and the lives of the martyrs were recounted. Some families had already heard of their loved ones' martyrdom and had been waiting for official confirmation. Others received the news for the first time after years of uncertainty. Some wanted to understand the reasons for the delay. Others wanted to know about their loved ones' final days, where and with whom they had lost their lives, and whether they had a grave.




We spoke to Munzur Diyar, a member of the Martyrs' Studies Committee, in Qendîl (Qandil) about the establishment of the martyrs' cemeteries, the reasons why announcements of martyrdom were delayed and efforts to reach families. Before explaining how information about martyrs is collected and how families are contacted, Diyar takes us back to 1983. He traces the history of the martyrs' cemeteries in Qendîl to Mehmet Karasungur.







'We have come to collect what we entrusted to you'




At that time, Qendîl was an area where different Kurdish organizations were present. Karasungur was holding discussions with these organizations when he was martyred in an attack on 2 May 1983.




The Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) began to become familiar with Qendîl during this period, and the area's significance grew following Karasungur's martyrdom. Following his death, Karasungur's body was entrusted to a villager named Sheikh Omar, who lived in the area.Those who handed over the body told him, "We are entrusting him to you. One day we will come back for him." Sheikh Omar, however, did not really believe them. He had previously encountered different organizations and seen bodies left behind. He thought that no one would return this time either. Fourteen years passed. In 1997, PKK members who arrived in Qendîl visited Sheikh Omarone night and asked about the body that had been entrusted to him years earlier: "We have come to collect what we entrusted to you."




The first martyrs' cemetery in Şehit Harun




Diyar says that the fact that the promise was remembered years later had a profound impact on the villagers. However, it was not immediately possible to retrieve the body. Several more years passed because of the fighting and security conditions in the area. In 2003, Karasungur's remains were taken from the grave in the villager's garden and transferred to one of the martyrs' cemeteries in Qendîl. In 2006, they were moved to the present central cemetery. The first martyrs' cemetery in Qendîl was established in 2001 in an area known as Şehit Harun. The Şehit Harun Martyrs' Cemetery was later renamed the Şehit Gulan-Şehit Simko Martyrs' Cemetery. As units stationed in different areas continued burying their fallen members where they were based, seven separate martyrs' cemeteries gradually emerged. When family visits increased in 2004 and 2005, reaching these cemeteries became increasingly difficult. Among those wishing to visit their children's graves were elderly mothers and fathers. Some cemeteries required a walk of one or two hours along mountain paths. 




Hundreds of guerrillas worked on the cemetery




A decision was therefore made to bring the graves together in one location. Hundreds of guerrillas worked on the construction of the Mehmet Karasungur Martyrs' Cemetery. Vehicles and construction machinery were limited at the time. Groups arrived to prepare graves and build paths before returning to other areas. Some of those who participated in the construction were martyred in subsequent years and buried in the very cemetery they had helped build.




Buried in the grave he had prepared 




One of them was Kendal, an Arab PKK member from Reqa. Kendal worked on the cemetery's construction for approximately two years. One day, he prepared a grave for a friend he knew personally. Because of their close relationship, he prepared it, in Diyar's words, "with great care and attention." However, the body of his friend, who was martyred in Silêmanî (Sulaymaniyah), was taken to Mexmûr (Makhmur), where his family lived. The grave remained empty. During the airstrikes in December 2007, Kendal was assigned before his martyrdom, he told his friends, "If there is an airstrike and I am martyred, my grave is already prepared." He was martyred in the first attack. His friends buried Kendal in the grave he had prepared himself.




'All of Kurdistan is here'







The graves standing side by side in the Mehmet Karasungur Martyrs' Cemetery also bring together different periods of the PKK's history. From the earliest members to those martyred in recent years, this history is reflected in the life stories of those buried there. Ibrahim Bilgin, who was martyred alongside Karasungur, is also buried there. Originally from Sivas, Bilgin was among the first and youngest people to join the PKK in Ankara. He was part of the first groups to travel to Lebanon and later joined the groups that went to the mountains. He came to Qendîl with Karasungur during preparations to move north and was martyred in the same attack in 1983. Diyar does not explain the significance of the cemetery solely through this historical continuity. It also contains the graves of people from all four parts of Kurdistan, as well as those who joined the movement from the Caucasus and the Kurdish diaspora. Tahir Aliyev, who came from Kazakhstan to join the PKK and was martyred in an avalanche, is among them. "All of Kurdistan has come together in the Mehmet Karasungur Martyrs' Cemetery. There are martyrs from all four parts. All of Kurdistan is here."




Karasungur, Altun and Kaytan together




The cemetery continues to expand as new remains are brought there. Diyar says that approximately 70 guerrillas whose martyrdom was recently announced and who died in Qendîl are buried there. Remains from other areas are also being transferred whenever conditions permit. However, not all remains are brought to Qendîl. There is also a martyrs' cemetery in Asos, while a new cemetery is being prepared in Gare. The remains of Ali Haydar Kaytan, recently brought from Gare, were also buried in the Mehmet Karasungur Martyrs' Cemetery. Diyar says that the presence of Karasungur and Rıza Altun, there was a factor in the decision to bring Kaytan to the same cemetery.




'The martyrs' cemeteries are the history of the revolution'







The cemeteries were also affected by airstrikes in subsequent years. Until 2015, although some surrounding areas had been bombed, the cemetery itself had not been directly targeted. The scope of the attacks changed in the following period. Diyar regards the attacks on the cemeteries as part of an effort to erase the PKK's historical memory: "Our martyrs are the memory of this revolution, our history. They targeted that memory directly. They wanted to create a history of their own over that memory, as though it belonged to them. Not only were the martyrs' cemeteries bombed, but there is also a Turkish military base next to every cemetery. Nevertheless, we persist in trying to keep this memory alive."




Records buried underground







An airstrike in 2017 damaged the museum where the martyrs' personal belongings were kept, as well as the guesthouses. Alongside repairs, the committee's responsibilities included protecting photographs, personal belongings and written records. The keeping of records about martyrs in Qendîl predates the establishment of the cemeteries. Diyar traces the history of this work to the commemorations and written accounts that began following the martyrdom of Haki Karer. Initially, the work was carried out mainly through the press, but it took different forms over time. At the end of 2002, a group of volunteers began collecting old testimonies and records. The work subsequently continued within different institutions.




The Martyrs' Studies Committee, established in 2014, brought research, archiving, cemetery maintenance and the preparation of life stories together under one structure. Initially, the committee had 35 members, but its numbers gradually declined because of the intensifying war, airstrikes and the martyrdom of its members. Kasım Engin, one of the leading figures in this work, was among those martyred. After 2018, the committee was forced to continue its work with just five or six people. Preserving the records proved at least as difficult as collecting them. Some archives kept in the mountains, in areas where fighting continued, were lost, while others fell into the hands of the state. "To protect these archives, you put them underground, you bury them. The comrades who do this are martyred, and the archives are lost in this way. We had an archival system, but records were lost because of the conditions. There are still many comrades we need to find."




Why were announcements of martyrdom delayed?




Reaching families has been one of the difficulties faced by the committee from the beginning. In the 1990s, announcements of martyrdom were largely made through Serxwebûn. Some families whose relatives' photographs and life stories had been published in the magazine told the committee, when they contacted it years later, that they had never seen those publications. It was not possible for the magazine, which was published in Europe, to reach every family.




The reasons for delays over the past decade were different. Changing conditions of warfare made communication increasingly difficult, not only with families but also between guerrillas themselves. Diyar distinguishes the harsh conditions of the 1990s from those of the recent period: "We fought under very difficult conditions in the 1990s as well. We went hungry and thirsty. But back then, an operation would take place, we would fight, and the operation would end. We could still maintain our own organization in the area. The war of the past ten years was not like that. It was a war in which we were constantly tracked and monitored, both from the air and on the ground. The slightest movement, the slightest image, could lead to martyrdom."




'Many comrades were martyred'




Surveillance carried out using unmanned aerial vehicles and armed drones, camera traps installed on the ground and the detection of signals from communication devices had largely eliminated previously used methods of communication. Moving from one area to another had become difficult for guerrillas, and even moving within the same camp was increasingly dangerous. "When reconnaissance aircraft were overhead, it was impossible to move from one squad to another. If you stepped outside the shelters and your image was captured, you could come under attack."




Previously, radios had made it possible to contact different areas and obtain information about the condition of units and the losses they had suffered. However, attacks carried out by tracking signals from communication devices eliminated this possibility as well. Messages were therefore sent through guerrillas who carried written notes between different areas. "We wanted to communicate through a system of notes without using technology. We tried to do this through couriers. Many comrades were martyred while selflessly trying to carry information to other areas. We had comrades who took that risk and travelled back and forth under conditions in which they were being monitored every hour of every day."




A ten-day journey became a month-long journey







The time required to travel from one place to another in the mountains no longer depended solely on the distance. Sometimes it was necessary to wait without moving for hours, or even half a day. "The journey from here to Behdînan normally takes four or five days. You walk for four or five days, but the technology used by the enemy prevents you from moving. Sometimes you have to remain motionless for hours, even half a day, to avoid being recorded. When these delays accumulate, a five-day journey becomes ten days. A ten-day journey becomes a month."




Under these conditions, even areas close to one another could go for months without exchanging information. Although Botan and Behdînan (Badinan) are closely connected geographically, news of a guerrilla martyred in Botan sometimes reached Qendîl six months later. There were also periods when no information could be obtained from Serhat for six or seven months. Verifying incoming information posed another problem. Under such limited communication conditions, incorrect reports about a guerrilla's martyrdom could also arrive. "Sometimes we would announce a comrade's martyrdom, only to discover that they were alive. Even the limited information we received could be wrong."




Such uncertainty made confirming the information received even more important. The delays in announcing recent martyrdoms were caused not only by the inability to obtain information for months but also by concerns about announcing incorrect news. Once a martyrdom was confirmed, the information had to be communicated to the family first. The committee tried, as far as possible, not to make public announcements before contacting the families. "Even if we receive the news, we cannot simply broadcast it on television. We do not think it is right for families to learn of their loved ones' martyrdom from television."




'It should have continued for months'




The most recent announcements of martyrdom had initially been planned to take place over seven or eight months. Rather than announcing names at short intervals, the intention was to devote separate attention to each guerrilla's life. "We wanted to tell society about the lives of these comrades individually, not through three-day condolence gatherings, but by covering their stories in the press over several months." However, the announcements proceeded faster than planned. Diyar says they believe the state's attitude may have played a role in this. He also acknowledges shortcomings within their own institutions: "There were also mistakes on our part. The institutions responsible for making the announcements and contacting families in the area made mistakes. They rushed too much and spread the announcements too widely. If things had been handled in a more controlled way, the plan could have been implemented."




'It was difficult for us too'




Expectations of peace were also growing during this period. At a time when families who had waited for years were hoping to reunite with their loved ones, the committee was uncertain how announcements of martyrdom dating back to previous years would be received. "To tell the truth, we did not expect this level of solidarity and commitment. In fact, we expected a reaction. There is an ongoing process. Everyone is waiting for peace, hoping that their child will come home. We thought that receiving news of martyrdom while holding on to that hope would provoke a reaction. We were preparing for that as well. But our people proved us wrong once again."




The intensity of the announcements was also deeply felt in Qendîl. Photographs of martyred guerrillas were broadcast on television throughout the day. The impact on the guerrillas was similar to that experienced by the families. "To be honest, it was difficult for us too. Sometimes we could not even watch television."




Families still waiting for answers







The committee is now continuing its work, particularly on records dating back to the 1990s. The real names of some guerrillas who joined the PKK during that period, or the areas where they were last stationed, remain unknown. Code names remembered by veteran guerrillas are compared with information and photographs provided by families. The fact that many guerrillas used the same code names makes the research even more difficult. Families are therefore asked to send as many photographs as possible. There are also plans to use technologies capable of estimating how a person's face might have changed with age based on childhood photographs.




'Clarifying the fate of martyrs from before 2000 is our main task'




In recent years, television programmes announcing martyrdoms have also raised the expectations of families who lost relatives in the 1990s. "Many families' requests concern the 1990s. We understand that. But I hope families will also understand our situation. In the 1990s, we did not have so many media outlets. Announcements on television became more common, particularly after 2010. Naturally, when families see these programmes, they also want to see the martyrs of the 1990s remembered. Through this work, we want to respond both to the families' requests and to their criticism. Clarifying the fate of our martyrs from before 2000 will be one of our main tasks and responsibilities."




'

Commemorations should become a tradition'




Another plan of the committee is to organize regular commemorations for the martyrs. They want the lives of guerrillas to be recounted again, even if their martyrdom has already been announced. Diyar gives Lice as an example. The idea is to commemorate guerrillas from Lice who were martyred in April at an annual gathering held in Lice during the same month. "Our aim is to make commemorations of martyrs a tradition rather than a one-off event."




The questions of families who receive news of their loved ones' martyrdom do not end there. Where are their loved ones' remains? Is there a grave? How were they buried? Bodies carried for days, graves whose occupants could not be identified, and families who came searching for traces of their loved ones years later form the second part of Diyar's account.




Tomorrow: Searching for the missing in Qendîl




Source: Yeni Özgür Politika / Rengin Azizoğlu

author: CNT Valladolid
title: Fuego al orden colonial: racismos, cuidados, trabajo y derechos
content:
Tengo mu poco dinero

pero no me quita el sueño.

Con dos duros me mantengo,

de mi libertad soy dueño.




El día 22 de octubre, dentro de las jornadas de inauguración del nuevo local de CNT en Valladolid, tuvimos una mesa redonda sobre ‘¿Qué sociedad queremos construir? Racismos, cuidados, trabajo y derechos’. En ella compartieron desde mesa sus conocimientos y experiencias sobre estos temas las siguientes personas, a las que agradecemos su generosidad:







Pastora Filigrana, investigadora y autora de 

El pueblo gitano contra el Sistema-Mundo

 (Akal, 2020)




Gabriela Poblet, investigadora y autora de 

Criadas de la globalización

 (Icaria, 2024)




Mónica Gortyare, activista de Articulación Antirracista de Madrid y  de Asamblea Regularización Ya de Madrid







Como en otras de estas jornadas, la mesa fue ocasión de abrir unos cuantos melones, que afectan no sólo a qué sociedad queremos, sino a qué movimientos sociales queremos pertenecer y qué mejorar dentro (y fuera) de nuestro sindicato. Pues como sindicato actuamos dentro de unas fronteras que causan desde hace años la muerte de miles de personas que quieren cruzarlas, donde se niegan o regatean derechos a quienes las cruzan, y dentro de una sociedad incapaz de superar la histórica persecución y exclusión del pueblo gitano, pero no siempre parece que nos afecte.




Muertes y discriminaciones ocurren bajo una indiferencia social a la que quizás somos menos ajenos de lo que pensamos, por sesgos, inercias y privilegios que tendríamos que revisar. Porque aunque como sindicato queramos ser de toda la clase trabajadora, es evidente que hay una buena parte de ella, la gitana, la migrada y la racializada, que no forma parte aún del mismo. No se trata de preguntarnos cómo conseguir más afiliades, sino de cómo apoyar y respaldar la lucha de los colectivos racializados que ya existen, que ya militan y que ya tienen fuertes redes de apoyo tejidas. Porque si no estamos todes, no hacemos nada.













Pastora Filigrana, desde su experiencia personal, su trabajo profesional y activista como abogada de trabajadoras migrantes del campo, puso sobre la mesa que el racismo no es una actitud o un prejuicio, sino un criterio estructural de distribución de la riqueza en el sistema-mundo, que despoja a unes y les hace instrumentos del bienestar y el enriquecimiento de otres -igual que lo es el patriarcado-. En este contexto, el antirracismo desde un sindicato no es una concesión solidaria, sino un elemento fundamental para ser inclusivo e interseccional.




Todas las intervenciones subrayaron que no es cosa de recursos o de puertas abiertas, sino de ser conscientes de que bajo el chantaje de la ley de extranjería hay miles de personas excluidas que arriesgan por manifestarse o movilizarse contra los convenios que se les aplican, fraudulentos cuando existen. También se trazó un paralelismo con las antiguas leyes antigitanas, que muestran cómo la legislación ha sido históricamente una herramienta de racismo institucional para limitar derechos, restringir el acceso al trabajo y mantener al pueblo gitano en una situación de exclusión.













Gabriela Poblet empezó su intervención recordando que la colonización no es una cosa de hace siglos, sino que sigue activa en fenómenos como los corralitos de los países de la llamada “América latina”, que evaporan los ingresos de todas las clases populares de un país por el ataque contra los bancos locales de los oligopolios financieros. Un método de esclavización a escala masiva no tan visible como las galeras de siglos pasados, pero igual de abusivo, pues somete a miles y miles al chantaje de la precariedad.




Son estos fenómenos los que incentivan que poblaciones migrantes acaben ocupando trabajos precarizados que no hace tanto eran cubiertos por las poblaciones rurales de los propios países del norte global, también sometidos a un proceso de vaciamiento no hace tantos años.




Es preciso referirse sin eufemismo ni coartadas paternales a estos trabajos de criada u otros a los que se ven empujadas muchas mujeres sin derechos laborales para mantener los privilegios de la población blanca adinerada que puede pagarse ese tráfico, y que no forma una patronal propiamente dicha -incluso amparando la explotación en el derecho a la intimidad de un hogar-.




Las medidas parciales que pueden atenuar esa explotación son ambivalentes -la mediación de los gobiernos para la contratación de esos servicios sería en el fondo una subvención a las clases contratantes-. La perspectiva última debería ser la abolición de unos trabajos donde unas se esloman para el bienestar de otras, si bien esperar a que llegue «el gran día» puede suponer desentenderse de las estrategias de supervivencia de esas trabajadoras hasta que se abra nuestro horizonte final. Es necesario afinar para conjugar ambas dimensiones. Se mencionó desde la audiencia la experiencia del convenio de porteros de fincas urbanas, que logró imponerse desde la acción directa a la miriada de patronales domésticas.













Como puso sobre la mesa Mónica Gortyare, la experiencia de quienes salen adelante bajo leyes como las de extranjería, leyes que deciden qué cuerpos pueden vivir y qué cuerpos no, no siempre son atendidas desde los movimientos blancos. La indiferencia de sindicatos mayoritarios o no tan mayoritarios hacia iniciativas como la ILP por la regularización, iniciativa legislativa popular que debe su aprobación a un esforzado trabajo militante de hormiga, es una prueba de esto, pero no la única.




Aún así, es muy significativo que se preveyese que la ley iba a beneficiar a medio millón de trabajadores sin regularizar -un tercio menores-, y que las burocracias del Estado se hayan visto desbordadas por más de un millón de solicitudes no prevista, por la salida a la luz de una realidad ignorada por haberse mirado hacia otro lado o priorizado otros intereses.




Ceuta ha sido la prueba reciente de que la población migrante se percibe como un enemigo, enviando al ejército -que, como además se subrayó, no tiene el cargo para ejercer las supuestas labores que están llevando a cabo de “protección a la ciudadanía”- a controlarla y agredirla sin que se provoque un escándalo y una actuación en consecuencia.




Todo esto revela un orden colonial hacia el que no cabe otra actitud que prenderle fuego. Pero para articular una lucha en este sentido, no basta con ofrecer unas estructuras sindicales que no han sido construidas desde las necesidades de quienes sobreviven a la persecución y la exclusión. La política de alianzas respetuosas con otros saberes y experiencias -y por lo tanto, ser conscientes del lugar de privilegio que ocupamos- es en este contexto tan necesaria como el esfuerzo por ser más integradoras. Hay formas de resistencia que no sólo no son respetadas, sino criminalizadas o ridiculizadas, pero son experiencia de resistir desde donde parece imposible.




Esta mesa redonda nos puso ante desafíos que un sindicato que se pretende alternativo debería estar dispuesto a afrontar, con fórmulas que vayan más allá de los caminos trillados en los que nos estancamos tantas veces. Podríamos tener un espejo en las estrategias de supervivencia del pueblo gitano, en resistencia durante siglos a leyes que castigaban con violencia sus formas de vida, su cultura, su organización comunitaria y su autonomía económica, para, declaradamente, reducirlo a bolsa de trabajadores sedentarios en los sectores más penosos.




La sala del nuevo local se llenó para compartir estas reflexiones y denuncias, dando lugar a un debate que continuó en la cena militante posterior -abrir un sindicato con cocina tiene estas ventajas- y en los corrillos. Que sea para bien.
















La entrada 

Fuego al orden colonial: racismos, cuidados, trabajo y derechos

 apareció primero en 

CNT Valladolid

.

Fuego al orden colonial: racismos, cuidados, trabajo y derechos

 se publicó primero en 

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

title: ¡Despotorre en Valladolid¡ Arriba el despotorre, abajo el facherio
content:
El fin de fiesta de las jornadas de inauguración del nuevo local de CNT en Valladolid fue la energía rebelde y contagiosa del espectáculo Despotorre, de las cómicas feministas y antifascistas Ane Lindane y Raquel Torres. Estuvieron con nosotras el sábado 24 de octubre, justo en medio de los preparativos de la huelga general del 11 de noviembre por la vivienda; y aunque no hace falta que nos den animo para luchar contra los usureros de la vivienda y sus aliados, podemos decir que este espectáculo sería suficiente para  inspirarnos ánimo de sobra.




Llenamos el local con la primera actuación en #Valladolid de estas cómicas, agotándose las reservas a los veinte minutos de ofrecerse públicamente. Casos como este o el de ‘No hay olvido ni sueño: carne viva’, que esa misma tarde enfrentaba el boicot made in fachadolid con absoluto éxito, demuestran que en la ciudad hay audiencia con demanda de actividades de arte combativo. ¡A ver si pronto Ane y Raquel pueden volver a Valladolid para más gente y con la tarima que merecen!




DESPOTORRE es un show de comedia salido directamente de nuestros mismísimos… corazones. Unidas en una visión feminista de la comedia y libres e irreverentes en el humor dan forma a éste espectáculo que no deja indiferente a nadie, sobre todo a los que no estén acostumbrados a ver a dos mujeres haciendo chistes, explicando por qué el machismo estriñe o lo difícil que es alcanzar los cánones físicos impuestos, pero sin parar de hacer reír al público. Durante casi 80 minutos puedes olvidarte de todo lo que te inquieta, te atormenta o te perturba, relajarte y dedicarte exclusivamente en reír –

 Así lo definen su espectáculo este pedazo no sólo de artistas, sino también de compañeras.




Compañeras que últimamente están sufriendo el intento de amedrantamiento de los empresarios de la vergüenza ajena made in Valladolid “Abogados Cristianos”, mediante querellas que pretenden censurarlas. Aprovechamos la ocasión para indicar nuestra solidaridad con las despotorres que están plantando cara a estos representantes de lo que toda la sociedad debe superar cuanto antes.




Ane y Raquel dijeron en sus redes que las agasajamos con nuestras risas durante el espectáculo. Ni que decir tiene que esas risas fueron absolutamente sinceras.




Compas, siempre en vuestro equipo, siempre antifascistas, siempre transfeministas.

title: Anarchist Parenting
content:
Author: 

An Anarchist FAQ




PDF File Size:

 381 KB




Download PDF




The Anarchist FAQ presents a compelling vision of parenting based on freedom, mutual respect and trust in children’s natural capacity for self-regulation, challenging the authoritarian assumptions embedded in conventional family structures. Its strongest contribution is connecting the personal and political, arguing that raising children without coercion, punishment or imposed moralism is itself a form of anarchist practice. It places freedom, mutual respect and autonomy at the heart of parenting. It challenges us to reject the authoritarian structures of the traditional family and recognise that raising free, confident and independent children is an essential part of building a free society.




Source:

 An Anarchist FAQ found at 

https://ananarchistfaq.anarcho-copy.org/




Read more

: Anarchist Parenting




Anarchist Parenting




 An Anarchist FAQ




 










Introduction:

 What methods of child rearing do anarchists advocate?




Part 1:

 What are the main obstacles to raising free children?




Part 2: 

What are some examples of libertarian child-rearing methods?




Part 3:

 If children have nothing to fear, how can they be good?




Part 4:

 But how will a free child ever learn unselfishness?




Part 5:

 Isn’t “libertarian child-rearing” just another name for spoiling the child?




Part 6: 

What is the anarchist position on teenage sexual liberation?




Part 7:

 But isn’t this concern with sexual liberation just a distraction from revolution?







Introduction: 

What methods of child rearing do anarchists advocate?




Anarchists have long been aware of the importance of child rearing and education. We are aware that child rearing should aim to develop 

“a well-rounded individuality”

 and not 

“a patient work slave, professional automaton, tax-paying citizen, or righteous moralist.”

 In this section of the FAQ [see 

here

] we will discuss anarchist approaches to child rearing bearing in mind 

“that it is through the channel of the child that the development of the mature man [or woman] must go, and that the present ideas of . . . educating or training . . . are such as to stifle the natural growth of the child.”

 [Emma Goldman, 

Red Emma Speaks

, p. 132 and p. 131]




If one accepts the thesis that the authoritarian family is the breeding ground for both individual psychological problems and political reaction, it follows that anarchists should try to develop ways of raising children that will not psychologically cripple them but instead enable them to accept freedom and responsibility while developing natural self-regulation. We will refer to children raised in such a way as 

“free children.”




Work in this field is still in its infancy (no pun intended). Wilhelm Reich was the main pioneer in this field (an excellent, short introduction to his ideas can be found in Maurice Brinton’s 

The Irrational in Politics

). In 

Children of the Future

, Reich made numerous suggestions, based on his research and clinical experience, for parents, psychologists, and educators striving to develop libertarian methods of child rearing (although he did not use the term “libertarian”).




In this and the following sections we will summarise Reich’s main ideas as well as those of other libertarian psychologists and educators who have been influenced by him, such as A.S. Neill and Alexander Lowen. We will examine the theoretical principles involved in raising free children and will illustrate their practical application with concrete examples. Finally, we will examine the anarchist approach to the problems of adolescence.




Such an approach to child rearing is based upon the insight that children 

“do not constitute anyone’s property: they are neither the property of the parents nor even of society. They belong only to their own future freedom.”

 [Michael Bakunin, 

The Political Philosophy of Bakunin

, p. 327] As such, what happens to a child when they are growing up 

shapes

 the person they become and the society they live in. The key question for people interested in freedom is whether 

“the child [is] to be considered as an individuality, or as an object to be moulded according to the whims and fancies of those about it?”

 [Emma Goldman, 

Op. Cit.

, p. 131] Libertarian child rearing is the means by which the individuality of the child is respected and developed.




This is in stark contrast to standard capitalist claim that children are the 

property

 of their parents. If we accept that children 

are

 the property of their parents then we are implicitly stating that a child’s formative years are spent in slavery, hardly a relationship which will promote the individuality and freedom of the child or the wider society. Little wonder that most anarchists reject such assertions. Instead we argue that the 

“rights of the parents shall be confined to loving their children and exercising over them . . . authority [that] does not run counter to their morality, their mental development, or their future freedom.”

 Being someone’s property (i.e. slave) runs counter to all these and 

“it follows that society, the whole future of which depends upon adequate education and upbringing of children . . . has not only the right but also the duty to watch over them.”

 Hence child rearing should be 

part

 of society, a communal process by which children learn what it means to be an individual by being respected as one by others: 

“real freedom — that is, the full awareness and the realisation thereof in every individual, pre-eminently based upon a feeling of one’s dignity and upon the genuine respect for someone else’s freedom and dignity, i.e. upon justice — such freedom can develop in children only through the rational development of their minds, character and will.”

 [Bakunin, 

Op. Cit.

, p. 327]




We wish to re-iterate again that a great deal of work remains to be done in this field. Therefore, our comments should be regarded merely as tentative bases for further reflection and research by those involved with raising and educating children. There is, and cannot be, any “rule book” for raising free children, because to follow an inflexible rule book is to ignore the fact that each child and their environment is unique and therefore demands unique responses from their parents. Hence the principles of libertarian child rearing to which we will refer should not be thought of as rules, but rather, as experimental hypotheses to be tested by parents within their own situation by applying their intelligence and deriving their own individual conclusions.




Bringing up children must be like education, and based on similar principles, namely 

“upon the free growth and development of the innate forces and tendencies of the child. In this way alone can we hope for the free individual and eventually also for a free community, which shall make interference and coercion of human growth impossible.”

 [Goldman, 

Op. Cit.

, p. 139] Indeed, child rearing and education 

cannot

 be separated as life itself is an education and so must share the same principles and be viewed as a process of 

“development and exploration, rather than as one of repressing a child’s instincts and inculcating obedience and discipline.”

 [Martha A. Ackelsberg, 

Free Women of Spain

, p. 166]




Moreover, the role of parental example is very important to raising free children. Children often learn by mimicking their parents — children do what their parents do, not as they say. If their mother and father lie to each other, scream, fight and so on, then the child will probably do so as well. Children’s behaviour does not come out thin air, they are a product of the environment they are brought up in. Children can only be encouraged by example, not by threats and commands. So how parents act can be an obstacle to the development of a free child. Parents must do more than just 

say

 the right things, but also act as anarchists in order to produce free children.




The sad fact is that most modern people have lost the ability to raise free children, and regaining this ability will be a long process of trial and error as well as 

parent

 education in which it is to be hoped that each succeeding generation will learn from the failures and successes of their predecessors and so improve. In the best-case scenario, over the course of a few generations the number of progressive parents will continue to grow and raise ever freer children, who in turn will become even more progressive parents themselves, thus gradually changing mass psychology in a libertarian direction. Such changes 

can

 come about very fast, as can be seen from various communes all over the world where society is organised according to libertarian principles. As Reich put it:




“We have learned that instead of a jump into the realm of the Children of the Future, we can hope for no more than a steady advance, in which the healthy new overlaps the sick old structure, with the new slowly outgrowing the old.”




Children of the Future

,


pp. 38-39




By means of freedom-based child rearing and education, along with other methods of consciousness raising, as well as encouraging resistance to the existing social order anarchists hope to prepare the psychological foundation for a social paradigm shift, from authoritarian to libertarian institutions and values. And indeed, a gradual cultural evolution toward increasing freedom does seem to exist. For example, as A.S. Neill suggested there is 

“a slow trend to freedom, sexual and otherwise. In my boyhood, a woman went bathing wearing stockings and a long dress. Today, women show legs and bodies. Children are getting more freedom with every generation. Today, only a few lunatics put cayenne pepper on a baby’s thumb to stop sucking. Today, only a few countries beat their children in school.”

 [

Summerhill

, p. 115]




Most anarchists believe that we must practice what we preach and so the anarchist revolution begins at home. As anarchists raise their own children in capitalist society and/or are involved in the raising and education of the children of other parents, we can practice in part libertarian principles even before the revolution. As such, we think it is important to discuss libertarian child rearing.




Part 1:

 What are the main obstacles to raising free children?




The biggest obstacle is the training and character of most parents, physicians, and educators. Individuals within a hierarchical society create psychological walls/defences around themselves and these will obviously have an effect both on the mental and physical state of the individual and so their capacity for living a free life and experiencing pleasure. Such parents then try (often unconsciously) to stifle the life-energy in children. There are, for example, the child’s natural vocal expressions (shouting, screaming, bellowing, crying, etc.) and natural body motility. As Reich noted:




“Small children go through a phase of development characterised by vigorous activity of the voice musculature. The joy the infant derives from loud noises (crying, shrieking, and forming a variety of sounds) is regarded by many parents as pathological aggressiveness. The children are accordingly admonished not to scream, to be ‘still,’ etc. The impulses of the voice apparatus are inhibited, its musculature becomes chronically contracted, and the child becomes quiet, ‘well-brought-up,’ and withdrawn. The effect of such mistreatment is soon manifested in eating disturbances, general apathy, pallor of the face, etc. Speech disturbances and retardation of speech development are presumably caused in this manner. In the adult we see the effects of such mistreatment in the form of spasms of the throat. The automatic constrictions of the glottis and the deep throat musculature, with subsequent inhibition of the aggressive impulses of the head and neck, seems to be particularly characteristic.”




Children of the Future

,

p. 128




“Clinical experience has taught us,”

 Reich concluded, 

“that small children must be allowed to ‘shout themselves out’ when the shouting is inspired by pleasure. This might be disagreeable to some parents, but questions of education must be decided 

exclusively in the interests of the child,

 not in those of the adults.”




Op. Cit.

,

p. 128




Besides deadening life energy in the body, such stifling also inhibits the anxiety generated by the presence of anti-social, cruel, and perverse impulses within the psyche — for example, destructiveness, sadism, greed, power hunger, brutality, etc. (impulses referred to by Reich as 

“secondary”

 drives). In other words, this reduces our ability to empathise with others and so the internal ethical guidelines we all develop are blunted, making us more likely to express such secondary, anti-social, drives. So, ironically, these secondary drives result from the 

suppression of the primary drives

 and the sensations of pleasure associated with them. These secondary drives develop because the only emotional expressions that can get through a person’s defences are distorted, harsh, and/or mechanical. In other words, compulsive morality (i.e. acting according to externally imposed rules) becomes necessary to control the secondary drives 

which compulsion itself creates.

 By such processes, authoritarian child-rearing becomes self-justifying:




“Psychoanalysts have failed to distinguish between primary natural and secondary perverse, cruel drives, and they are continuously killing nature in the new-born while they try to extinguish the ‘brutish little animal.’ They are completely ignorant of the fact that it is 

exactly this killing of the natural principle which creates the secondary perverse and cruel nature,

 human nature so called, and that these artificial cultural creations in turn make compulsive moralism and brutal laws necessary.”




Reich, 

Op. Cit.

,

p. 17-18




Moralism, however, can never get at the root of the problem of secondary drives, but in fact only increases the pressure of crime and guilt. The real solution is to let children develop what Reich calls 

natural self-regulation.

 This can be done only by not subjecting them to punishment, coercion, threats, moralistic lectures and admonitions, withdrawal of love, etc. in an attempt to inhibit their spontaneous expression of natural life-impulses. The systematic development of the emphatic tendencies of the young infant is the best way to “socialise” and restrict activities that are harmful to the others. As A.S. Neill pointed out 

“self-regulation implies a belief in the goodness of human nature; a belief that there is not, and never was, original sin.”

 [

Summerhill

, p. 103]




According to Neill, children who are given freedom from birth and not forced to conform to parental expectations spontaneously learn how to keep themselves clean and develop social qualities like courtesy, common sense, an interest in learning, respect for the rights of others, and so forth. However, once the child has been armoured through authoritarian methods intended to 

force

 it to develop such qualities, it becomes out of touch with its living core and therefore no longer able to develop self-regulation. In this stage it becomes harder and harder for the pro-social emotions to shape the developing mode of life of the new member of society. At that point, when the secondary drives develop, parental authoritarianism becomes a 

necessity.




This oppression produces an inability to tolerate freedom. The vast majority of people develop this 

automatically

 from the way they are raised and is what makes the whole subject of bringing up children of crucial importance to anarchists. Reich concluded that if parents do not suppress nature in the first place, then no anti-social drives will be created and no authoritarianism will be required to suppress them: 

“

What you so desperately and vainly try to achieve by way of compulsion and admonition is there in the new-born infant ready to live and function. Let it grow as nature requires, and change our institutions accordingly

.”

 [

Op. Cit.

, p. 47] So in order to raise psychologically healthy children, parents need to acquire self-knowledge, particularly of how internal conflicts develop in family relationships, and to free themselves as much as possible from neurotic forms of behaviour. The difficulty of parents acquiring such self-knowledge and sufficiently de-conditioning themselves is obviously another obstacle to raising self-regulated children.




However, the greatest obstacle is the fact that twisting mechanisms set in so very early in life, i.e. soon after birth. Hence it is important for parents to obtain a thorough knowledge of what rigid suppressions are and how they function, so that from the beginning they can prevent (or at least decrease) them from forming in their children. Finally, Reich cautioned that it is crucial to avoid any mixing of concepts: 

“One cannot mix a bit of self-regulation with a bit of moral demand. Either we trust nature as basically decent and self-regulatory or we do not, and then there is only one way, that of training by compulsion. It is essential to grasp the fact that the two ways of upbringing do not go together.”

 [

Op. Cit.

, p. 46]




Part 2:

 What are some examples of libertarian child-rearing methods?




According to Reich, the problems of parenting a free child actually begin before conception, with the need for a prospective mother to free herself as much as possible from chronic muscular tensions. It has been found in many studies that not only the physical health of the mother can influence the foetus. Various psychological stresses influence the chemical and hormonal environment, affecting the foetus.




Immediately after birth it is important for the mother to establish contact with her child. This means, basically, constant loving attention to the baby, expressed by plenty of holding, cuddling, playing, etc., and especially by breast feeding. By such 

“orgonotic”

 contact (to use Reich’s term), the mother is able to establish the initial emotional bonding with the new born, and a non-verbal understanding of the child’s needs. This is only possible, however, if she is in touch with her own emotional and cognitive internal processes: 

“

Orgonotic contact is the most essential experiential and emotional element in the interrelationship between mother and child,

 particularly prenatally and during the first days and weeks of life. The future fate of the child depends on it. It seems to be the core of the new-born infant’s emotional development.”

 [

Children of the Future

, p. 99] It is important for the father to establish orgonotic contact as well.

Part 3:

 If children have nothing to fear, how can they be good?




Obedience that is based on fear of punishment, this-worldly or other-worldly, is not really goodness, it is merely cowardice. Nor can it be inspired by hope of reward, such as praise or the promise of heaven, which is simply bribery. If children are given as much freedom as possible from the day of birth, if parents respect them as individuals and give a positive example as well as not being forced to conform to parental expectations, they will spontaneously learn the basic principles of social behaviour, such as cleanliness, courtesy, and so forth. But they must be allowed to develop them 

at their own speed,

Can a child really be taught to keep themselves clean without being punished for getting dirty? According to many psychologists, it is not only possible but 

vitally important

“When the mother says 

naughty

dirty

Summerhill

Similarly, sceptics will probably question how children can be induced to eat a healthy diet without threats of punishment. The answer can be discovered by a simple experiment: set out on the table all kinds of foods, from sweets and ice cream to whole wheat bread, lettuce, sprouts, and so on, and allow the child complete freedom to choose what is desired or to eat nothing at all if he or she is not hungry. Parents will find that the average child will begin choosing a balanced diet after about a week, after the desire for prohibited or restricted foods has been satisfied. This is an example of what can be called “trusting nature.” That the question of how to “train” a child to eat properly should even be an issue says volumes about how little the concept of freedom for children is accepted or even understood, in our society. The disciplinarian argument that that children must be
