author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Iqaluit observes Remembrance Day at cadet hall
content:
The cadet hall in Iqaluit was overflowing with about 300 people during the Royal Legion’s Remembrance Day ceremony Wednesday morning.




The annual event began around 11 a.m. in both English and Inuktitut.




“Canada as a nation owes an everlasting debt of gratitude to the men and women who have served and continue to serve their country, in times of war and peace,” said legion Branch 168 president John Graham,  the master of ceremonies.




The day began with a march that included police, veterans and community members. It began at the RCMP building on Sivumugiaq Street and ended at the hall.




RCMP chaplain Paul Hitz spoke about sharing gratitude for those who served.




“It is also a day to express our gratitude to those who serve today, the members of our Canadian Armed Forces, including our Canadian Rangers who stand guard over the ideals we as Canadians cherish,” he said. “Lest we forget.”




Hitz also acknowledged the youth who joined the ceremony and highlighted the significance of their presence.
















Remembrance Day wreaths were laid at the cadet hall in Iqaluit on Wednesday during the Royal Canadian Legion’s annual Remembrance Day ceremony. (Photo by Lilli Akpaleepaik)




“To the youth among us, many of whom cannot yet imagine the realities of war, this day matters too. May your hearts and minds be stirred by what we place before you today,” he said.




Nunavut’s deputy Commissioner Lew Philip and RCMP Staff Sgt. Abdelmalek Mezdour laid the first wreath. Nunavut MP Lori Idlout and Premier John Main followed.




Iqalummiut laid wreaths for loved ones who served. Cadets placed wreaths purchased by Canadian North, Arctic Survival Store, Baffin Building Systems and Nunavut Animal Rescue.




Just before Graham’s closing remarks, David Hoyt, an Iqaluit cadet flight sergeant, recited Lt.-Col. John McCrae’s 

In Flanders Fields

.

author: cnt.es
title: 11N: Sigamos uniendo las luchas de la clase trabajadora
content:
Imagen

: 12:55h. Piquete informativo anticapitalista por el centro económico de Valencia | Fuente: CNT




Leer en

Castellano

Català

Euskera

Galego

Asturianu







Castellano

Sigamos uniendo las luchas de la clase trabajadora




¡Compañeras! ¡Compañeros! Hoy hemos parado y salido a la calle porque los derechos no se piden, ¡se toman y se defienden!




Si echamos la vista atrás: ni la jornada de ocho horas, ni las vacaciones pagadas, ni la protección frente al despido fueron concesiones; conseguimos esos derechos gracias a las huelgas, a las cajas de resistencia, a décadas de organización colectiva y a la generosidad y esfuerzo de todas las compañeras y compañeros que pelearon por un mundo mejor para la clase trabajadora.




Y por eso mismo estamos hoy aquí, organizadas y utilizando la herramienta que siempre nos ha funcionado, la huelga: para decir basta a que, después de sacrificar nuestro tiempo y vida a cambio de un salario, no podamos ni pagar un techo bajo el que vivir.




La huelga es algo más que una movilización, es una protesta que interrumpe la producción, que duele y pone nerviosa a la patronal cuando la ven reflejada en sus cuentas. La huelga va más allá de grandes manifestaciones, rebasa las calles y entra en los centros de trabajo; la huelga demuestra que somos nosotras las que hacemos funcionar la economía, y que la podemos parar ante la injusticia del acaparamiento del fruto de nuestro trabajo por parte del capital.




Nos pagan salarios de miseria que no alcanzan, se llevan otra mordida con alquileres imposibles, nos desahucian y cortan los suministros si encima no los podemos pagar, seguimos teniendo la misma jornada laboral que hace más de 100 años y después de una vida entera trabajando no nos queda ni la certeza de podernos jubilar. Y todo esto tiene unos responsables, unas causas comunes que debemos enfrentar. No podemos conformarnos con pedir precios más bajos. ¡En la CNT queremos lo que por justicia social nos pertenece!: salarios y pensiones dignos, reducción de la jornada sin reducir el salario, y trabajo y casa para todas. En estas exigencias está lo que nos une a quienes solo vivimos de nuestro trabajo. Y esta huelga lo está demostrando.




Sin embargo, también sabemos que no todas podemos parar. Hay compañeras migradas sin papeles, atrapadas por una Ley de Extranjería que exige un contrato que no se puede conseguir sin ellos, que arriesgan mucho más que un día de sueldo. También hay trabajadoras con contratos tan frágiles que ejercer su derecho equivale a perder el empleo, falsas autónomas sin amparo alguno, trabajadoras de los cuidados y del hogar sin convenio ni interlocutor, personas atrapadas en contratas y subcontratas que nunca ven a su verdadero patrón, y quienes temen las represalias de empresas que han hecho de la amenaza una forma de gestionar las relaciones laborales. El hecho de que no puedan parar es la prueba de que la precariedad está diseñada para que defender los derechos salga caro. Las que sí hemos podido parar en esta huelga la hacemos también suya. El apoyo mutuo es la base de nuestra lucha, el sindicalismo de clase y combativo no deja a nadie atrás.




Desde la CNT entendemos además que, en esta disputa, el Estado no es una institución neutral ni un simple instrumento de la patronal: es una institución con intereses propios. Estos, a veces, coinciden con los de las clases dominantes y, en otras ocasiones, parecen estar a nuestro favor. Pero no podemos dejar que la patronal y el Estado jueguen con nuestros derechos a su antojo. No podemos permitir que cojan nuestras exigencias y nos las devuelvan diezmadas e irreconocibles.




No podemos permitir, tampoco, que pretendan dividirnos dejando a las trabajadoras migradas sin derechos. No vamos a conformarnos con sus migajas, lo queremos todo para todas, y ese todo solo lo podemos conseguir unidas, mediante la acción directa y en organizaciones propias de clase, independientes de gobiernos, instituciones y partidos.




Para la CNT, la huelga de hoy es un punto de partida: un paro de 24 horas es insuficiente, pero es un comienzo. Mañana, las que hemos parado y las que no hemos podido, tenemos que seguir encontrándonos; hacernos fuertes en nuestros centros de trabajo mediante las secciones sindicales y las asambleas de trabajadoras, y en los barrios y pueblos con las redes de solidaridad de las vecinas. Los sindicatos somos el nexo de unión, el punto de encuentro de todas nuestras luchas. La forma en la que se ha organizado esta huelga, de abajo a arriba, muestra que la horizontalidad, las asambleas y el apoyo mutuo son la clave. Nos sostenemos las unas a las otras, denunciamos y perdemos un día de salario por nosotras y por todas las que no pueden y para que, precisamente, en un futuro sí puedan. Canalizamos y organizamos nuestra rabia juntas contra quienes nos oprimen. Esta huelga, decíamos, es un punto de partida, pero también es histórica. ¡Esto es imparable, compañeras y compañeros! Queda mucho trabajo por hacer, pero el futuro que podemos alcanzar juntas es esperanzador. 

La huelga es nuestra herramienta. La solidaridad, nuestra fuerza. La organización, nuestro camino.




¡Fuerza, compañeras y compañeros!







Català

Continuem unint les lluites de la classe treballadora




Companyes! Companys! Avui hem parat i sortit al carrer perquè els drets no es demanen, es prenen i es defensen!




Si mirem enrere: ni la jornada de vuit hores, ni les vacances pagades, ni la protecció davant de l’acomiadament van ser concessions; aconseguim aquests drets gràcies a les vagues, a les caixes de resistència, a dècades d’organització col·lectiva i a la generositat i esforç de totes les companyes i companys que van lluitar per un món millor per a la classe treballadora.




I per això mateix estem avui aquí, organitzades i utilitzant l’eina que sempre ens ha funcionat, la vaga: per a dir prou al fet que, després de sacrificar el nostre temps i vida a canvi d’un salari, no podem ni pagar un sostre sota el que viure.




La vaga és una mica més que una mobilització, és una protesta que interromp la producció, que fa mal i posa nerviosa a la patronal quan la veuen reflectida als seus comptes. La vaga va més enllà de grans manifestacions, inunda els carrers i entra en els centres de treball; la vaga demostra que som nosaltres les que fem funcionar l’economia, i que la podem parar davant la injustícia de l’acaparament del fruit del nostre treball per part del capital.




Ens paguen salaris de misèria, ens roben amb lloguers impossibles, ens desnonen i tallen els subministraments si no els podem pagar, continuem tenint la mateixa jornada laboral que fa més de 100 anys i després d’una vida sencera treballant no ens queda ni la certesa de poder-nos jubilar. I tot això té uns responsables, unes causes comunes que hem d’enfrontar. No podem conformar-nos amb demanar preus més baixos. A la CNT volem el que per justícia social ens pertany!: salaris i pensions dignes, reducció de la jornada sense reduir el salari, i treball i casa per a totes. En aquestes exigències està el que ens uneix als qui només vivim del nostre treball. I aquesta vaga ho està demostrant.




No obstant això, també sabem que no totes podem parar. Hi ha companyes migrades sense papers, atrapades per una Llei d’Estrangeria que exigeix un contracte que no es pot aconseguir sense ells, que arrisquen molt més que un dia de sou. També hi ha treballadores amb contractes tan fràgils que exercir el seu dret equival a perdre l’ocupació, falses autònomes sense cap empara, treballadores de les cures i de la llar sense conveni ni interlocutor, persones atrapades en contractes i subcontractes que mai veuen al seu veritable patró, i els qui temen les represàlies d’empreses que han fet de l’amenaça una manera de gestionar les relacions laborals. El fet que no puguin parar és la prova que la precarietat està dissenyada perquè defensar els drets surti car. Les que sí que hem pogut parar en aquesta vaga la fem també seva. El suport mutu és la base de la nostra lluita, el sindicalisme de classe i combatiu no deixa a ningú enrere.




Des de la CNT entenem a més que, en aquesta disputa, l’Estat no és una institució neutral ni un simple instrument de la patronal: és una institució amb interessos propis. Aquests, a vegades, coincideixen amb els de les classes dominants i, en altres ocasions, semblen estar a favor nostre. Però no podem deixar que la patronal i l’Estat juguin amb els nostres drets al seu gust. No podem permetre que agafin les nostres exigències i ens les retornin trocejades i irreconeixibles.




No podem permetre, tampoc, que pretenguin dividir-nos deixant a les treballadores migrades sense drets. No ens conformarem amb les seves engrunes, ho volem tot per a totes, i aquest tot només el podem aconseguir unides, mitjançant l’acció directa i en organitzacions pròpies de classe, independents de governs, institucions i partits.




Per a la CNT, la vaga d’avui és un punt de partida: una aturada de 24 hores és insuficient, però és un inici. Demà, les que hem parat i les que no hem pogut, hem de continuar trobant-nos; fer-nos fortes en els nostres centres de treball mitjançant les seccions sindicals i les assemblees de treballadores, i als barris i pobles amb les xarxes de solidaritat de les veïnes. Els sindicats som el nexe d’unió, el punt de trobada de totes les nostres lluites. La forma en la qual s’ha organitzat aquesta vaga, de baix a dalt, mostra que l’horitzontalitat, les assemblees i el suport mutu són la clau. Ens sostenim les unes a les altres, denunciem i perdem un dia de salari per nosaltres i per totes les que no poden i perquè, precisament, en un futur sí que puguin. Canalitzem i organitzem la nostra ràbia juntes contra els qui ens oprimeixen. Aquesta vaga, dèiem, és un punt de partida, però també és històrica. Això és imparable, companyes i companys! Queda molta feina per fer, però el futur que podem aconseguir juntes és esperançador. 

La vaga és la nostra eina. La solidaritat, la nostra força. L’organització, el nostre camí.




Força, companyes i companys!







Euskera

Langile klasearen borrokak batzen jarrai dezagun




Lagunok! Gaur greba egin dugu eta kalera atera gara, eskubideak ez direlako eskatzen: eskuratu eta defendatu egiten dira!




Atzera begiratzen badugu, zortzi orduko lanaldia, ordaindutako oporrak eta kaleratzearen aurkako babesa ez ziren opariak izan. Eskubide horiek grebei, erresistentzia-kutxei, hamarkadetan egindako antolakuntza kolektiboari esker lortu genituen. Baita langile klasearentzat mundu hobe baten alde borrokatu ziren lagun guztien eskuzabaltasunari eta ahaleginari esker.




Horregatik gaur hemen gaude ere, antolatuta eta beti funtzionatu digun tresna erabiliz: greba. Gure denbora eta bizitza soldata baten truke sakrifikatu ondoren, bizitoki bat ere ordaindu ezin dugula esateko.




Greba mobilizazio bat baino askoz gehiago da: ekoizpena eteten duen protesta da. Patronalari min egiten diona eta urduri jartzen duena, haren kontuetan islatzen denean. Greba manifestazio handietatik harago doa, kaleak gainditu eta lantokietan sartzen da. Ekonomia guk geuk funtzionatzea ahalbidetzen dugula erakusten du grebak. Ekonomia geldiarazteko gaitasuna dugula ere erakusten du, kapitalak gure lanaren fruitua bereganatzearen bidegabekeriaren aurrean.




Miseriazko soldatak ordaintzen dizkigute, nahikoak ez direnak; ordaindu ezin daitezkeen alokairuen bidez beste hozkada bat kentzen digute; etxegabetu egiten gaituzte eta hornidurak mozten dizkigute, horiek ere ordaindu ezin baditugu. Duela 100 urte baino gehiagoko lanaldi bera izaten jarraitzen dugu, eta bizitza osoa lanean eman ondoren, ez dugu ziurtasunik ere erretiroa hartu ahal izango dugun jakiteko. Eta horrek guztiak baditu arduradunak, baditu aurre egin behar diegun kausa komunak. Ezin gara prezio merkeagoak eskatzera mugatu. CNTn justizia sozialagatik dagokiguna nahi dugu: soldata eta pentsio duinak, soldata murriztu gabe lanaldia laburtzea, eta guztiontzako lana eta etxebizitza. Eskakizun horiek dira gure lanetik soilik bizi garen guztiok batzen gaituztenak. Eta greba hau hori erakusten ari da.




Hala ere, badakigu denok ezin dugula greba egin. Paperik gabeko emakume migratzaileak ditugu, Atzerritartasun Legeak harrapatuta. Lege horrek lortu ezin den kontratua eskatzen du paperik gabe, eta emakume horiek askoz gehiago dute arriskuan egun bateko soldata baino. Badira, halaber, kontratu hain prekarioak dituzten langileak, ezen beren greba-eskubidea erabiltzeak lana galtzea ekar baitezake; babesik gabeko autonomo faltsuak; hitzarmenik eta solaskiderik gabeko zaintza- eta etxeko langileak; nagusi erreala inoiz ikusten ez duten kontrata eta azpikontrata sistemetan harrapatutako pertsonak; eta mehatxua lan-harremanak kudeatzeko modu bihurtu duten enpresen errepresalien beldur direnak. Greba egin ezin izatea prekarietatea eskubideak defendatzea garesti ateratzeko diseinatuta dagoenaren froga da. Greba honetan lanuztea egin ahal izan dugunok geurea egiten dugu haien borroka ere. Elkarri laguntzea da gure borrokaren oinarria; klase-sindikalgintza borrokalariak ez du inor atzean uzten.




CNTtik ulertzen dugu, gainera, gatazka honetan Estatua ez dela erakunde neutrala, ezta patronalaren tresna hutsa ere: bere interes propioak dituen erakundea da. Interes horiek, batzuetan, klase menderatzaileen interesekin bat egiten dute, eta beste batzuetan gure alde daudela dirudite. Baina ezin dugu onartu patronalak eta Estatuak gure eskubideekin nahi dutena egitea. Ezin dugu onartu gure eskakizunak hartu eta murriztuta eta ezagutzerik ere ez moduan itzultzea.




Ezin dugu onartu, ezta ere, gu zatitu nahi izatea, emakume langile migratzaileak eskubiderik gabe utzita. Ez gara haien apurrekin konformatuko: dena nahi dugu guztiontzat. Eta dena elkarrekin soilik lor dezakegu, ekintza zuzenaren bidez eta gobernu, erakunde eta alderdiengandik independenteak diren klase-antolakunde propioetan.




CNTrentzat, gaurko greba abiapuntua da: 24 orduko lanuztea ez da nahikoa, baina hasiera bat da. Bihar, greba egin dugunok eta egin ezin izan dutenek elkartzen jarraitu behar dugu; gure lantokietan antolakuntza indartu behar dugu, sail sindikalen eta langile-batzarren bidez, eta auzo eta herrietan, auzokideen elkartasun-sareen bidez. Sindikatuek gure borroka guztien arteko lotura osatzen dugu, elkargunea gara. Greba hau behetik gora antolatu izanak erakusten du horizontaltasuna, asanbladak eta elkarri laguntzea direla gakoak. Elkarri eusten diogu, guk eta ezin duten guztiek egun bateko soldata salatzen eta galtzen dugu eta, hain zuzen ere, etorkizunean bai izan dezaten. Gure amorrua elkarrekin bideratzen eta antolatzen dugu, zapaltzen gaituztenen aurka. Gure ustez, greba hau abiapuntu bat da, baina historikoa ere bada. Hau geldiezina da, lagunok! Lan asko dago egiteko, baina elkarrekin lor dezakegun etorkizuna itxaropentsua da. 

Greba da gure tresna. Elkartasuna, gure indarra. Antolakuntza, gure bidea.




Indarra, lagunok!







Galego

Sigamos unindo as loitas da clase traballadora




Compañeiras! Compañeiros! Hoxe paramos e saímos á rúa porque os dereitos non se piden: tómanse e deféndense!




Se botamos a vista atrás: nin a xornada de oito horas, nin as vacacións pagadas, nin a protección fronte ao despedimento foron concesións; conseguimos eses dereitos grazas ás folgas, ás caixas de resistencia, a décadas de organización colectiva e á xenerosidade e esforzo de todas as compañeiras e compañeiros que pelexaron por un mundo mellor para a clase traballadora.




E por iso mesmo estamos hoxe aquí, organizadas e utilizando a ferramenta que sempre nos funcionou, a folga: para dicir basta a que, despois de sacrificar o noso tempo e vida a cambio dun salario, non poidamos nin pagar un teito baixo o que vivir.




A folga é algo máis que unha mobilización, é unha protesta que interrompe a produción, que doe e pon nerviosa á patronal cando a ven reflectida nas súas contas. A folga vai máis alá das grandes manifestacións, rebasa as rúas e entra nos centros de traballo; a folga demostra que somos nós as que facemos funcionar a economía, e que a podemos parar ante a inxustiza do acaparamento do froito do noso traballo por parte do capital.




Págannos salarios de miseria que non alcanzan, lévannos outra mordida con alugueres imposibles, desafiúzannos e córtannos os subministros se ademais non os podemos pagar, seguimos tendo a mesma xornada laboral que hai máis de 100 anos e despois dunha vida enteira traballando non nos queda nin a certeza de podermos xubilarnos. E todo isto ten unhas responsables, unhas causas comúns que debemos enfrontar. Non podemos conformarnos con pedir prezos máis baixos. Na CNT queremos o que por xustiza social nos pertence!: salarios e pensións dignos, redución da xornada sen reducir o salario, e traballo e casa para todas. Nestas esixencias está o que nos une a quen só vivimos do noso traballo. E esta folga estano demostrando.




Porén, tamén sabemos que non todas podemos parar. Hai compañeiras migradas sen papeis, atrapadas por unha Lei de Estranxeiría que esixe un contrato que non se pode conseguir sen eles, que arriscan moito máis que un día de soldo. Tamén hai traballadoras con contratos tan fráxiles que exercer o seu dereito equivale a perder o emprego, falsas autónomas sen amparo ningún, traballadoras dos coidados e do fogar sen convenio nin interlocutor, persoas atrapadas en contratas e subcontratas que nunca ven o seu verdadeiro patrón, e as que temen as represalias das empresas que fixeron da ameaza unha forma de xestionar as relacións laborais. O feito de que non poidan parar é a proba de que a precariedade está deseñada para que defender os dereitos saia caro. As que si puidemos parar nesta folga facémola tamén súa. O apoio mutuo é a base da nosa loita, o sindicalismo de clase e combativo non deixa a ninguén atrás.




Desde a CNT entendemos ademais que, nesta disputa, o Estado non é unha institución neutral nin un simple instrumento da patronal: é unha institución con intereses propios. Estes, ás veces, coinciden cos das clases dominantes e, noutras ocasións, parecen estar ao noso favor. Pero non podemos deixar que a patronal e o Estado xoguen cos nosos dereitos ao seu antollo. Non podemos permitir que collan as nosas esixencias e nos as devolvan diezmadas e irrecoñecibles.




Non podemos permitir, tampouco, que pretendan dividirnos deixando as traballadoras migradas sen dereitos. Non imos conformarnos coas súas migallas, querémolo todo para todas, e ese todo só o podemos conseguir unidas, mediante a acción directa e en organizacións propias de clase, independentes de gobernos, institucións e partidos.




Para a CNT, a folga de hoxe é un punto de partida: un paro de 24 horas é insuficiente, pero é un comezo. Mañá, as que paramos e as que non puidemos, temos que seguir atopándonos; facernos fortes nos nosos centros de traballo mediante as seccións sindicais e as asembleas de traballadoras, e nos barrios e pobos coas redes de solidariedade das veciñas. Os sindicatos somos o nexo de unión, o punto de encontro de todas as nosas loitas. A forma na que se organizou esta folga, de abaixo a arriba, mostra que a horizontalidade, as asembleas e o apoio mutuo son a clave. Sostémonos as unhas ás outras, denunciamos e perdemos un día de salario por nós e por todas as que non poden e para que, precisamente, nun futuro si poidan. Canalizamos e organizamos a nosa rabia xuntas contra quen nos oprime. Esta folga, diciamos, é un punto de partida, pero tamén é histórica. Isto é imparábel, compañeiras e compañeiros! Queda moito traballo por facer, pero o futuro que podemos alcanzar xuntas é esperanzador.

 A folga é a nosa ferramenta. A solidariedade, a nosa forza. A organización, o noso camiño.




Forza, compañeiras e compañeiros!







Asturianu




¡Compañeres!¡Compañeros! Güei paremos y salimos a la cai porque los derechos nun se piden, ¡tómense y deféndense !




Si echamos la vista atraá: nin la xornada d’ocho hores, nin les vacaciones pagues, nin la protección frente al despidu foron concesiones; consiguimos esos derechos gracies a les fuelgues, a les caxes de resistencia , a décades d’organización colectivo y a l’arrogancia y esfuerzu de toles compañeres y compañeros que llucharon por un mundu meyor pa la clase trabayadora .




Y por eso mesmo tamos güei equí , organizaes y usando la ferramienta que siempres nos furruló , la fuelga : pa dicir que valió yá a que , depués de sacrificar el nuesu tiempu y vida por cuenta d’un salariu, nun podamos nin pagar un techu sol que vivir.




La fuelga ye daqué más qu’una movilización, ye una protesta qu’apara la producción, que duel y pon nervioso a la patronal cuando la ven reflexada nes sos cuentes. La fuelga va más allá de grandes manifestaciones, perpasa les cais y entra nos centros de trabayu ; la fuelga amuesa que somos nós les que facemos funcionar la economía , y que podemos parar énte la inxusticia del acaparamientu del frutu del nuesu trabayu por parte del capital.




Páguenmos salarios de miseria que nun algamen, lleven otru taragañu con arriendos imposibles, desagóspienmos y cortenmos los suministros si enriba nun podemos pagar, siguimos teniendo la mesma xornada llaboral de fai más de 100 años y depués d’una vida entera trabayando nun mos queda nin la certidume de poder xubilamos. Y too esto tien unos responsables, unes causes comunes que tenemos d’enfrentar. Nun podemos conformanos con pidir precios más baxos. ¡Na CNT queremos lo que por xusticia social nos pertenez: salarios y pensiones dignos, amenorgamientu de la xornada ensin amenorgar el salariu , y trabayu y casa pa toes. Nestes esixencies ta lo que nos xune a quien namái vivimos del nuesu trabayu . Y esta fuelga ta demostrándolo.




Sicasí , tamién sabemos que non toes podemos parar. Hai compañeres migraes ensin papeles, atrapaes por una Llei d’Extranxería qu’esixe un contratu que nun se puede consiguir ensin ellos, qu’arriesguen muncho más qu’un día de sueldu . Tamién hai trabayadores con contratos tan fráxiles qu’exercer el so derechu equival a perder l’empléu, falses autónomes ensin amparu nengún , trabayadores de cuidaos y del llar ensin conveniu nin interlocutor, persones atrapaes en contrates y subcontrates que nunca ven al so verdaderu patrón, y quien tarrecen les represalies d’empreses que fixeron de l’amenaza una forma de xestionar les relaciones llaborales. El fechu de que nun puedan parar ye la prueba de que la precariedá ta diseñada pa que defender los derechos salga caru . Les que sí pudimos parar nesta fuelga facémosla tamien de so. El sofitu mutuu ye la base de la nuesa llucha , el sindicalismu de clase y combativu nun dexa a naide atras.




Dende la CNT entendemos amás que , nesta disputa , l’Estáu nun ye una institución neutral nin un simple preséu de la patronal: ye una institución con intereses propios. Estos, dacuando , coinciden colos de les clases dominantes y, n’otres ocasiones, paecen tar al nuesu favor. Pero nun podemos dexar que la patronal y l’Estáu xueguen colos nuesos derechos al so antoxu . Nun podemos dexar que cueyan les nueses esixencies y nos les devuelvan recortaes ya irreconocibles.




Nun podemos dexar, tampoco , que pretendan dividimos dexando a les trabayadores migraes ensin derechos. nun vamos conformamos coles sos migayes, querémoslo too pa toes, y esi tou namái vamos poder algamalu xuníes, por aciu l’acción directa y n’organizaciones propies de clase , independientes de gobiernos, instituciones y partíos.




Pa la CNT, la fuelga de güei ye un puntu de partida : un paru de 24 hores ye insuficiente , pero ye un empiezu . Mañana , les que paremos y les que nun pudimos, tenemos que siguir atopándomos; facemos fuertes nos nuesos centros de trabayu por aciu les secciones sindicales y les asamblees de trabayadores, y nos barrios y pueblos coles redes de solidaridá de les vecines. Los sindicatos somos el nexu d’unión, el puntu d’alcuentru de toles nueses lluches. La forma na que s’entamó esta fuelga , de baxo p’arriiba , amuesa que la horizontalidá , les asamblees y el sofitu mutuu son la clave . Sofitámonos les unes a les otres, denunciamos y perdemos un día salariu por nós y por toles que nun pueden y pa que, precisamente , nun futuru sí puedan. Canalizamos y organizamos la nuesa rabia xuntes contra quien nos prime. Esta fuelga , dicíamos, ye un puntu partida , pero tamién ye histórica . ¡Esto ye imparable, compañeres y compañeros! Queda muncho trabayu por facer, pero’l futuru que podemos algamar xuntes ye esperanzador. 

La fuelga ye la nuesa ferramienta . La solidaridá , la nuesa fuerza . La organización, el nuesu camín. 




¡Fuerza , compañeres y compañeros!




La entrada 

11N: Sigamos uniendo las luchas de la clase trabajadora

 se publicó primero en 

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

author: David Venn
title: QIA considers ‘next steps’ after NIRB recommends hydro plant move forward without review
content:
The Qikiqtani Inuit Association is “considering its next steps” after the Nunavut Impact Review Board recommended that Iqaluit’s proposed hydro project move forward without a public review.




“Our priority remains ensuring that the development of new energy infrastructure advances alongside the protection of Inuit rights,” reads a statement from QIA spokesperson Markoosie Qaunirq, issued Tuesday.




The $500-million Iqaluit Nukkiksautiit Hydro Project, currently in its preliminary design phase, is proposed by Nunavut Nukkiksautiit Corp., a subsidiary of Qikiqtaaluk Corp., which is the QIA’s development arm.




If approved, it will lead to the construction of a hydroelectric plant able to produce up to 30 megawatts on the Kuugaaluk River, about 60 kilometres northeast of the city. It will also include a 7,136-hectare reservoir and a 66-kilometre access road.




NNC president Harry Flaherty has said the plant could replace 15 million litres of diesel fuel imported every year to generate electricity.




In November 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney named it a “nation-building” project to fast-track approvals. That move meant construction could begin in 2028 — two years earlier than originally anticipated.




On Nov. 4, the Nunavut Impact Review Board published its screening decision report, which determined a review of the proposal was unnecessary, and notified Minister of Arctic and Northern Affairs Rebecca Chartrand, who has the final say, of its decision. The board examines the social and economic impact of proposed developments and advises the federal government on whether the minister should allow the project to proceed.
















The board’s reasoning was that potential adverse effects can be addressed through terms and conditions and that the project does not “involve technological innovations for which the effects are unknown,” according to the screening report.




But QIA had argued that the effectiveness of mitigation efforts was uncertain, particularly for fish habitat, wildlife movement, permafrost conditions and harvesting.




Chartrand has 150 days to respond.




In the meantime, the Inuit association is planning its own community engagement events in Iqaluit and Pangnirtung, the release said.




Qaunirq did not respond to a request for comment, nor did the review board.

author: Carla Habif
title: How Brazilians pulled off Lula’s surprise win
content:
This article 

How Brazilians pulled off Lula’s surprise win

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







On Oct. 25, Brazilians made history by resisting hopelessness and achieving, for the first time since the return to democracy in 1985, a comeback in the runoff of a presidential election. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection by more than 4 million votes after losing the first round to opponent Flávio Bolsonaro by over 2 million votes.




Lula, a former metalworker and union leader who co-founded the left-wing Workers’ Party, 

was seeking his fourth term as president. Flávio, by contrast, was the candidate of the far-right Liberal Party and was running as the successor to his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally who was 

convicted and imprisoned for attempting a coup d’état

.




The first round suggested that Flávio and his party were on track to gain an enormous amount of power. The party won 

more seats in Congress than any other

 

—

 nearly a quarter of the lower house and more than a third of the Senate — which, together with other right-wing parties, 

gave the right a majority in both houses

.




Two days after the vote, 

Flávio said he would use that majority to “change the Constitution” and “re-democratize” the country. Asked what he meant, he 

proposed

 limiting the powers of Supreme Court justices, lowering the age of criminal responsibility and ending presidential reelection, and he left open the possibility of extending the presidential term from four to five years.




“I really think the desperation and fear after the first round changed everything. There was a need to act with more urgency, and this desire to organize.”





In addition, whoever won in October would be able to 

appoint up to four of the 11 justices of the federal Supreme Court

, 

the same court that convicted Jair Bolsonaro. A Flávio victory would have given the far right control over all three branches of government, amid the advance of the far right in Latin America and the United States.




As a result, after the first-round results came in on 

the night of Oct. 4, the mood among Lula’s supporters was one of deep discouragement and fear. But this fear quickly turned into forms of popular organizing that were diverse, complementary and consistently nonviolent — and they changed the course of the race. The mobilizations included a large-scale effort by politicians, activists, content creators and ordinary supporters to organize and amplify pro-Lula content on social media, and an equally massive occupation of the country’s streets in peaceful demonstrations.




Students took center stage in the street mobilizations, with thousands turning out for protests such as one 

led by the National Union of Students, or UNE, at the Candelária

 church in Rio de Janeiro, and one led by UNE and the University of Brasília’s student council on the Esplanade of Ministries in Brasília. People in the streets and on social media acted together and complemented each other.




Beyond protests and online activism, people organized to make sure that those who had not voted in the first round would go to the polls, including elderly people and those who live far from their polling places. They also got off the internet and talked in person with undecided voters who had not yet made up their minds, a process that had a name: vira voto, or flip the vote.




For Gabriel Rochlin, 

a director, actor and teacher who took part in a vira voto group in Rio de Janeiro, this was a way to get out of the social media bubble. “The work of vira voto has a lot to do with breaking through the algorithm,” he said. “The street has this real quality of not having an algorithm that separates people: you’re going to meet people you would never meet on your feed.” He saw the fear engendered by the first round as the turning point: “I really think the desperation and fear after the first round changed everything. There was a need to act with more urgency, and this desire to organize.”




From demoralization to esperançar




Given the collective feeling of fear and hopelessness after the first round of voting, the first challenge was to shift the mood of the left. It was on Oct. 5, the day after the results, that popular mobilization began in earnest.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










“When we got hit with the news that Flávio had more votes, there was a kind of desperation,” said Nayara Ruiz, a social media strategist with 

280,000 followers on Instagram

. “A huge shock, a feeling of fear, and a replay in our heads of 

2018 [when Jair Bolsonaro was elected].” At first, Ruiz recorded a video about that fear. “And while I was editing it, I started to feel really bad. And I said: I’m not going to post this video, this is not the path I need to take.” She came across a news story about how online fandoms dedicated to Brazilian and international musical artists like 

Taylor Swift, BTS and Anitta were putting their networks at the service of Lula’s campaign. “The moment I saw that, I said: ‘That’s it, I have to talk about this, about esperançar.’”




“Esperançar,” was a term used by Brazilian educator Paulo Freire to mean “hope in action,” as opposed to “esperar,” which in Portuguese means both to hope and to wait.




Ruiz then recorded 

a video

 talking about the fandoms and about esperançar, and why it matters for organizing. She explained that esperançar demands three things: seeing a possible future, understanding that there is a path to that future, and feeling that you can do something to make that path a reality. She wanted to show that there was a path to defeat Flávio if people came together.




The video was 

viewed 5 million times, the most of any she had posted, and brought her 40,000 new followers, Ruiz said. It was one of many videos and posts in the days after the first-round vote that spoke to people’s discouragement and helped turn it into a willingness to act.




Social media activism may have been one of the left’s most innovative strategies in this campaign. A WhatsApp channel called Exército do Lula, or Lula’s Army, was created by André Janones, a federal congressman from the state of Minas Gerais. What set it apart was its scale and its structure. It quickly grew from 

50,000

 

to 

more than 10 million followers

 in less than three weeks, in a country where WhatsApp had been the far right’s most effective tool since Jair Bolsonaro’s 2018 campaign.




“We learned together, we mobilized together, we practiced esperançar together, we believed together, and Lula’s Army was a place that brought all of that together.”




The channel’s growth came as the Lula campaign charged that Meta, which owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp, had limited the reach of Lula’s posts and favored Flávio’s. (

Leaked communications from inside Meta

 supported this, and Meta acknowledged “technical problems” with the Lula campaign’s paid promotions, but denied any bias.) For Lula’s Army, the WhatsApp channel had the advantage of delivering messages directly to its followers without an algorithm throttling their reach.




Rather than relying on a few official accounts to broadcast the Lula campaign’s message, it turned millions of ordinary supporters into active participants. It also gamified the organizing for the second round. Because voting is compulsory in Brazil, the goal was less to get out the vote than to reduce abstention and win over undecided voters. Through frequent audio messages, videos and texts, Janones handed out missions to participants, calling on them to share content, boost posts, promote hashtags, invite new members and amplify messages supporting the campaign. Everyone was given a rank and could advance up the ladder by completing these tasks. Janones “promoted” Ruiz from soldier to captain of the Army in a 

lighthearted video

 because of the explainer videos she made about the channel.




She believes one of the initiative’s contributions was fostering a kind of political digital literacy among supporters. Janones taught the channel’s followers how platform algorithms work, so that messages from Lula and critical information about Flávio would rank higher on social media. Until then, the far right had dominated social media, partly because of the high engagement its posts generated. Participants in Lula’s Army came to understand that part of that engagement came precisely from their reacting to far-right content that bothered them.




Previous Coverage

 

How a strong messaging strategy helped defeat Brazil’s Bolsonaro




Janones’ strategic directive to Lula’s supporters was that they should stop interacting with opponents’ posts and concentrate their collective strength on producing and circulating their own content. To that end, participants were instructed to watch videos to the end, and to like, comment on, save and share posts, using the platforms’ different features to expand their reach.




“Maybe Lula wouldn’t have won without this, without the Army, without this feeling that swept over people, without the sense that we weren’t fighting alone,” Ruiz said. “We learned together, we mobilized together, we practiced esperançar together, we believed together, and Lula’s Army was a place that brought all of that together.”




Ruiz credits Janones with turning that collective energy into a coordinated effort. “Janones calls himself a general, but I also see him very much as a conductor who led an orchestra that was disorganized, who tuned the instruments and managed to set the rhythm and organize the whole mobilization that took place and that is now being replicated around the world,” Ruiz said.




Taking to the streets




Social media also played an important role in spreading the word about and organizing the occupation of the streets during the weeks before the runoff. In the three weeks between Oct. 4 and Oct. 25, 

massive peaceful protests

 brought together hundreds of thousands of demonstrators across the country. 

These 

protests featured politicians, renowned Brazilian musicians

 like Chico Buarque, Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil, and grassroots artistic groups. Together, the iconic faces and grassroots artists helped bring in a very broad diversity of people.




“As we saw the big street protests, the power we had, not only inside the university but also in the streets, on social media too, it started creating a movement of hope.”





University students played a fundamental role in this occupation of the streets. They were the ones who kicked things off on Oct. 5, and throughout the three weeks between the first and second round of voting, they were a major force calling people to the protests, often organizing through their own social media.




The 

first street protest of the runoff campaign took place in Niterói

 in the state of Rio de Janeiro on Oct. 5, organized by students from Fluminense Federal University. Those students set an example, according to Gabriel Shpielman, a mathematics student and activist with the Rebellious Youth Union. “I think if that hadn’t happened on the first day, it would have been totally different,” he said.




Student mobilization quickly spread to other universities, including the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, or PUC-Rio, which also began organizing the day after the first round. Shpielman and a classmate created an Instagram profile and called on students at the university to attend an assembly, from which the 

PUC-Rio Antifascista

 movement was born. Around 200 students packed the auditorium, heard from a representative of the National Union of Students 

a

nd decided to go together to the protest in downtown Rio the following day.




According to Shpielman, this helped “put people in the position of seeing themselves building the comeback.” For him, it was in this experience with their collective strength that fear gave way to organizing: “At first it reflected despair, but as we saw the big street protests, the power we had, not only inside the university but also in the streets, on social media too, it started creating a movement of hope.”




The call for student protest started by word of mouth, in classrooms and WhatsApp groups, and gained reach through PUC-Rio Antifascista’s Instagram account. The account shared collaborative posts — Instagram posts that appear on several accounts at once — with other accounts, like 

Protesto Estudantil

 (a page run by high school students from Colégio Pedro II), 

the PUC-Rio Graduate Students’ Association, and with public figures such as Dani Balbi, Anielle Franco, Wagner Moura and Chico Buarque.




Students march in a rally for Lula at PUC-Rio on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Tatiana Chain)




Shpielman called the process cyclical: The more visibility PUC-Rio Antifascista gained, the more partnerships it secured, and those partnerships increased its visibility. The page has now reached over 30,000 followers. Even so, for him, social media was at the service of the streets. “What really turned the election around were the streets, the protests,” he said. “Social media reflected that mobilization. It’s so much better to see a protest with a million people than a page with 10 million people.”




Getting voters to the polls




Another point of concern in the first round was the abstention rate, which was the highest since 1998: Over 

21 percent

 of eligible voters, or 33.4 million people, simply didn’t vote. In light of this, much of civil society’s mobilization sought to make sure people went to vote. This took place through 

crowdfunding drives

 to arrange transportation for those living far from their polling places, ride-sharing initiatives, providing information for undecided voters in the streets and vira voto campaigns.




Diego Zuculin is one of the founders of 

Casa Marighella

, a cultural and artistic production company and organization in São Paulo that put all of its work on hold to get out the vote. After the first-round results, “everyone looked at each other and said: ‘Wow, we’re screwed. What are we going to do?’,” Zuculin said. The next morning, the team decided “almost everything could be postponed in the face of the end of democracy.”




The first idea was simple: He would offer his own car to neighbors whose grandparents had no way to get to the polls, and a friend would offer his motorcycle. They soon realized that many people were probably thinking the same thing and decided to create a platform connecting those who could offer rides on election day with those who needed them. That’s how 

Carona Solidária

, or Solidarity Ride, was born.




The team developed the first version of the platform in-house in two or three days. As word spread, partner collectives, artists, tech people and lawyers joined to help with legal issues and with outreach. The platform circulated on Instagram and WhatsApp, and in a second phase, the group reached out to journalists and pages in Brazil’s North region, where there were still few ride offers.




“The heart of vira voto is its humanity. It’s a place for building bonds, for looking people in the eye.”




“We had an idea, we put it to work, then it went to social media and it spread across all of Brazil,” Zuculin said. 

A total of 22,000 rides were offered, in every state and the Federal District, and the real reach was even greater. “Some people told us: ‘I registered two people, but I took two, and on the way back I took three more, and then five more.’ One person posted a video saying they drove 13 people, another 15, and only registered one or two.”




He also says that the reasons users gave when requesting a ride — such as a distant polling place, no nearby buses, advanced age or having to work on election day — could serve as a basis for public policy. In the second round, abstention fell to 

19.22 percent

, the lowest for a runoff since 2006, the result of an effort of which, Zuculin acknowledges, Carona Solidária was only one part.




Complementing these efforts, numerous vira voto campaigns took place across the country, in which people organized in groups to go out on the streets and talk to voters, especially those who were undecided or planning to abstain. Lula himself issued this call 

in a video posted on Oct. 7

: “Come on, everyone, to the streets, let’s talk to people.” 




In Rio de Janeiro, the local WhatsApp group that Gabriel Rochlin belonged to started with fewer than 10 people and ended with 60. Over two and a half weeks, according to the group’s own count, they flipped 181 votes. “Thinking of vira voto as collective action gives you a much greater sense of accomplishment,” he said. The group set up at Largo do Machado square and in front of the Catete Palace because, according to Rochlin, Workers’ Party congressman-elect Marcelo Freixo had indicated that there were many undecided voters there. WhatsApp was used to organize the actions and to make sure volunteers were always together and in safe places, given the risk of violence.
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













In their conversations, they used QR codes linking to informational materials, such as 

videos from Revelando

, an investigative documentary series launched in September by the Brazilian podcast Calma Urgente in which well-known Brazilian figures voiced criticisms of Flávio. They also 

encouraged people to search Google for information about Flávio

, something that Lula’s Army also urged voters to do. More than the information, however, Rochlin believes that “the heart of vira voto is its humanity. It’s a place for building bonds, for looking people in the eye.”




Oct. 25, the day of the runoff vote, went down in history. Brazilians achieved the unprecedented: They overturned the first-round result, elected Lula and halted the far right’s advance in just three weeks. The internet was flooded with powerful images — streets completely packed with peaceful demonstrations by Lula voters, the elderly voting, people journeying long distances to cast their votes, and entire Indigenous communities traveling to reach their polling places.




Ultimately, the movement to reelect Lula succeeded through a diverse range of civil resistance tactics. Right away, Lula supporters saw that to contain the far right’s advance, it was necessary to occupy the streets, deluge social media and create support structures so that people would vote and could reach the polls. They also saw the importance of mass participation: People from a broad range of social groups — of different ages, genders, social classes and regions of Brazil — acted together. 

In “

Why Civil Resistance Works

,” Erica Chenoweth and Maria J. Stephan 

identify mass participation like this as one of the key factors explaining why civil resistance is more likely to succeed than armed struggle.




But one insight runs through all these actions: People need esperançar, the capacity to transform fear into action. Millions organized and, following Paulo Freire’s advice, resisted when it felt hopeless. The far right, which has been advancing in many parts of the world, constantly uses hopelessness as a tool. Brazil’s civil mobilizations shows that esperançar is political, capable of acting as an engine of organization, social action and transformation.




This article 

How Brazilians pulled off Lula’s surprise win

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.

title: Çanakkale Emek, Barış ve Demokrasi Platformu: İşçilerin yaşam hakkı sermayenin kâr hırsından değerlidir
content:
Çanakkale Emek, Barış ve Demokrasi Güçleri HABAŞ’ta 19 işçinin hayatını kaybettiği ve pek çok işçinin yaralandığı patlamaya karşı bugün İskele Meydanında eylem ve basın açıklaması yaptı. Açıklamada iş cinayetlerine dikkat çekilirken Çanakkale de Dardanel işçilerinin ücretlerinin ödenmemesine de tepki gösterildi. Açıklamayı Eğitim Sen Şube Başkanı İnal Akoğlu okudu.

İşçilerin bir kez daha alınmayan iş güvenliği önlemlerinin, denetimsizliğin ve sermayenin kâr hırsının bedelini canlarıyla ödediğini söyleyen Akoğlu, “Bugün burada yalnızca acımızı paylaşmak için değil, bu katliamın sorumlularından hesap sormak için bulunuyoruz. HABAŞ’ta yaşananlar sıradan bir iş kazası olarak değerlendirilemez. İlk bulgular, bakım çalışmaları sırasında tavan vincinin düşmesi ve gaz hattının zarar görmesiyle patlamanın meydana geldiğine işaret etmektedir. Ancak asıl sorgulanması gereken, böyle bir facianın yaşanmasına hangi ihmallerin, hangi denetimsizliklerin ve hangi çalışma koşullarının zemin hazırladığıdır. Üstelik aynı fabrikada son üç hafta içerisinde, 21 Ekim ve 5 Kasım tarihlerinde iki işçinin daha yaşamını yitirdiği açıklanmıştır. Daha önce yaşanan ölümlere rağmen gerekli önlemler alınmamış, etkin denetim sağlanmamışsa bunun adı ihmal değil, göz göre göre gelen bir işçi katliamıdır” ifadelerini kullandı.

Türkiye’de işçi ölümlerinin ve emek sömürüsünün artık münferit olaylar olmaktan çıktığını vurgulayan Akoğlu, “Madenlerde, fabrikalarda, inşaatlarda, tersanelerde emekçiler çalışırken ölmekte; farklı işkollarında çalışan milyonlarca emekçi ise güvencesizlik, düşük ücret, ücret gaspı ve ağır çalışma koşullarıyla karşı karşıya bırakılmaktadır. Her facianın ardından aynı açıklamalar yapılmakta, soruşturmalar başlatılmakta, sorumluların hesap vereceği söylenmekte; ancak işçilerin yaşamına mal olan ve emeğini değersizleştiren düzen değişmemektedir” şeklinde konuştu.

İş güvenliğinin yalnızca işverenlerin iyi niyetine bırakılamayacağının altını çizen Akoğlu, “Devletin denetim sorumluluğu, işverenin yükümlülükleri ve çalışanların yaşam hakkı tartışmasız biçimde güvence altına alınmalıdır.

Buradan açıkça ifade ediyoruz. İşçiler çalışırken ölmek zorunda değildir. İş cinayetleri kader değildir. Çanakkale’de yaşananlar da emekçilerin karşı karşıya bırakıldığı tablonun başka bir yüzünü göstermektedir. İlimizde faaliyet gösteren Dardanel fabrikasında çalışan işçilerin ücretlerini zamanında alamaması, emekçilerin en temel haklarından biri olan ücret hakkının dahi güvencesiz bırakıldığını ortaya koymaktadır. İşçinin emeğinin karşılığını alamaması, geçimini sağlayamaması ve ailesinin ihtiyaçlarını karşılayamaz hale getirilmesi kabul edilemez. Ücret, işverenin lütfu değil, işçinin alın terinin ve emeğinin karşılığıdır. HABAŞ’ta işçiler yaşamını yitirirken, Çanakkale’de işçiler emeklerinin karşılığını almak için mücadele etmek zorunda bırakılmaktadır. Farklı biçimlerde ortaya çıksa da her iki tabloyu yaratan anlayış aynıdır: Emeği ucuzlatan, işçiyi güvencesizleştiren ve sermayenin çıkarlarını emekçinin yaşamının önüne koyan düzen. Buradan Dardanel yönetimine de çağrımızdır: İşçilerin birikmiş ücret alacakları derhal ve eksiksiz ödenmeli, emekçilerin ekonomik ve sosyal hakları güvence altına alınmalıdır” dedi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: "Я не преступник, а заложник". История осужденного по обвинению в подготовке теракта анархиста Алексея Григорьева
content: В феврале 2025 года суд приговорил 27-летнего анархиста из Оренбургской области Алексея Григорьева к 20 годам заключения. Его обвинили в попытке вступить в легион "Свобода России" и намерении поджечь по заданию украинских спецслужб релейный шкаф в Новотроицке. Во время следствия и суда он заявлял о пытках с применением тока. С марта 2026 года Григорьев отбывает наказание в Верхнеуральской тюрьме — по его словам, у него резко ухудшилось здоровье после избиений во время этапирования.

title: İspanya: Kiracıların isyanı genel greve dönüştü
content:
İspanya'da kiracı derneklerinin başlattığı barınma hakkı mücadelesi, ülkenin iki büyük sendika konfederasyonu CCOO ve UGT'nin katılımıyla 24 saatlik genel greve dönüştü. “Ücretler. Konut. Fiyatlar.” sloganıyla düzenlenen grev, sanayi tesislerinde üretimi durdurdu, ulaşımı aksattı ve onlarca kentte gösterilerle sürdü.




Madrid, Barselona ve diğer kentlerde grev gözcülerine yönelik polis müdahaleleri yaşandı. İçişleri Bakanlığı'nın gün içindeki verilerine göre 42 kişi gözaltına alındı.




Madrid'deki Mercamadrid toptancı halinde polisin biber gazı kullanmasının ardından en az 13 kişi sağlık ekiplerinin yardımına ihtiyaç duydu. Sendikalar müdahaleleri grev hakkının ihlali olarak nitelendirerek sorumlular hakkında hukuki girişim başlatacaklarını açıkladı.




Fabrikalarda üretim durdu, ulaşım aksadı




CCOO ve UGT, grevin özellikle otomotiv, limanlar, enerji ve ulaşım sektörlerinde etkili olduğunu bildirdi.




Sendikaların açıkladığı oranlara göre otomotiv ve deniz ve hava limanlarında iş bırakma yüzde 90'a, et üretiminde yüzde 85'e, çöp toplama işlerinde yüzde 82'ye, enerji sektöründe ise yüzde 75'e ulaştı.




Barselona yakınlarındaki SEAT Martorell fabrikasında üretim durdu. Navarra'daki Volkswagen tesislerinde de geniş çaplı iş bırakıldı. 




Tren seferleri olağan kapasitenin yüzde 50 ila 75'iyle sürdürüldü. Havalimanlarında 234 uçuş iptal edildi. Barselona'da metro ve otobüs seferleri sınırlandırıldı. Katalonya'da otoyollar, sanayi bölgeleri ve tren istasyonları çevresinde grev gözcüleri toplandı.




Eğitim kurumlarında da iş bırakma görüldü. Ancak perakende ticaret, küçük işletmeler ve bazı kamu hizmetlerinde katılım daha sınırlı kaldı.




Sendikalar grevin başarılı olduğunu açıklarken, işveren örgütleri katılımın düşük kaldığını savundu. Kiracılar Sendikası yaklaşık 4 milyon kişinin greve katıldığı öngörüsünü paylaştı. 




“Polisin görevi grev hakkını güvence altına almak”




CCOO Genel Sekreteri Unai Sordo, Mercamadrid'deki polis müdahalesini eleştirdi:







“Bu tam bir skandal. Yaşadıklarımızın cezai ve her türlü sorumluluğunun hesabını soracağız.”







UGT Genel Sekreteri Pepe Álvarez de polisin grev hakkını güvence altına almakla yükümlü olduğunu söyledi.




Polis, bazı göstericilerin yolları ve işyerlerinin girişlerini kapattığını bildirdi. Barselona'da lastiklerin yakıldığı barikatlar kuruldu; çeşitli kentlerde göstericilerle polis arasında arbede yaşandı.




“36 yaşındayım, hâlâ kendi başıma bir eve çıkamıyorum”




Genel grevin kaynağı, İspanya'da giderek ağırlaşan konut krizi. 




Madrid'de bir hastanenin bilgi işlem bölümünde çalışan 36 yaşındaki Jesús González, Reuters'a barınma sorununu kendi yaşamından hareketle anlattı:







“36 yaşındayım ve hâlâ kendi başıma bir eve çıkamıyorum.”







Ülkede ortalama kiralar son 10 yılda neredeyse iki katına çıktı. İspanya Gençlik Konseyi'nin hesaplamalarına göre ortalama aylık kira, genç bir çalışanın ortalama ücretinin neredeyse tamamına denk geliyor. 




Barselonalı 45 yaşındaki işçi Carlos Ferrer de Associated Press'e yaptığı açıklamada genel grevin gerekçesini şöyle anlattı:







“Yetkililerin bir şeyler yapması için yurttaşların baskısını hissetmeleri gerekiyor.”







Kiracı örgütleri kira artışlarının sınırlandırılmasını, sözleşmelerin otomatik yenilenmesini, tahliyelerin önlenmesini ve konut spekülasyonunun durdurulmasını istiyor.




Maricarmen'in tahliyesinden genel greve




Greve giden süreç, Madrid'de 87 yaşındaki Maricarmen Abascal'ın evinden zorla tahliye edilmesi ve ardından hayatını kaybetmesi üzerine büyüyen protestolarla hızlandı.




Kiracı örgütleri, hükümetin konut krizine karşı hazırladığı bazı önlemlerin 2 Ekim'de parlamentoda sağ partilerin oylarıyla reddedilmesinin ardından düzenlenen kitlesel gösterilerde genel grev çağrısını yükseltti.




Kiracılar Sendikası sözcüsü Alicia del Río, 11 Kasım'da şöyle konuştu:







“Maricarmen'in tahliyesiyle 40 gün önce başlayan öfke büyümeyi sürdürdü ve şimdi kentlerimizin sokaklarına taştı.”







Del Río, konutların yatırım ve rant aracı haline getirilmesine karşı mücadele ettiklerini belirtti:







“Evler, rantiyeci azınlığa hizmet etmek için değil, içinde yaşamak içindir.”







Kiracı örgütleri sendikaları harekete geçirdi




11 Kasım grevinin ayırt edici yanı, çağrının başlangıçta işçi sendikalarından değil, kiracı örgütlerinden gelmesiydi.




Kiracılar Sendikası, büyük konfederasyonlar katılmasa da küçük sendikalarla birlikte genel greve gideceğini duyurmuştu. CGT gibi örgütler çağrıya erken destek verdi. CCOO ve UGT ise 5 Ekim'de greve katılma kararı aldı.




Böylece konut hareketi, büyük sendikaların işyerlerindeki örgütlenmesiyle birleşti.




El País'e göre CCOO ve UGT'nin toplam 228 bin işyeri temsilcisi bulunuyor. Grev öncesinde yaklaşık 4.500 işyeri komitesi ve sendika birimi eyleme destek açıkladı.




Kiracılar Sendikası sözcüsü Sandra Mora da RTVE'ye 100'den fazla kentte ve mahallelerde 1.130 grev komitesi oluşturulduğunu söyledi.




UGT Genel Sekreteri Pepe Álvarez, konut krizinin ücret mücadelesiyle ilişkisini şöyle ifade etti:







“Ülkemizde hiçbir ücret konut fiyatlarına yetişemiyor.”







CCOO Genel Sekreteri Sordo ise konut sorununu İspanya toplumunun en büyük ayrışmalarından biri olarak niteledi:







“Konut, bu ülkenin büyük fay hattıdır.”







29 Kasım seçimleri öncesinde sağ sendikaları tehdit ediyor




Grev, İspanya'da 29 Kasım'da yapılacak erken genel seçimlerin 18 gün öncesinde gerçekleşti.




Muhafazakâr Halk Partisi (PP) ve aşırı sağcı Vox, sendikaları hükümet lehine siyasi faaliyet yürütmekle suçladı. PP lideri Alberto Núñez Feijóo, grevi sendikaların demokrasi dönemindeki en büyük tarihsel hatalarından biri olarak nitelendirdi.




Vox lideri Santiago Abascal ise grevin yasal olmaması gerektiğini savundu; iktidarın değişmesi durumunda sendikaların bugünkü tutumlarını unutmayacaklarını söyledi.




Sendika yöneticileri ise, grev hazırlıklarının seçim kararı alınmadan önce başladığını hatırlattı. UGT Genel Sekreteri Álvarez, taleplerinin yalnızca merkezi hükümete değil, bölgesel ve yerel yönetimlere ve işverenlere de yöneldiğini belirtti:







“Halk Partisi de Sosyalist Parti de bizi dinlemek zorunda, çünkü sokaklar güçlü biçimde konuşuyor. Çok ciddi bir konut sorunu var.”







İspanya'da seçim kampanyasının ortasında gerçekleşen, 2012'den bu yana büyük sendikaların birlikte düzenlediği ülke çapındaki ilk genel grevd, kiracı örgütleri konutların rant aracı olmaktan çıkarılmasını, sendikalar ise ücretlerin barınma ve geçim giderlerini karşılayabilecek düzeye yükseltilmesini seçim gündeminin başına yerleştirdiler.




(AEK)

author: Unknown
title: “How Has Serving Impacted You?” : Veterans of the US Military in Their Own Words
content:
What is it like to serve in the United States military? If only it were possible for those who are considering enlisting to learn the unvarnished truth. In 2019, a viral 

tweet

 from the official US Army twitter account unexpectedly drew over 11,000 candid replies in the course of 48 hours. These responses offer a rare window into the real experiences of servicemembers and veterans. We present a selection of them here for the benefit of anyone who is thinking about joining the military.




This is a document of an 

earlier era

 of social media, captured here before it 

vanishes

. You can obtain a book collecting the first twenty-four hours of responses 

here

.







Just before Memorial Day in 2019, the United States Army made a strategic blunder almost on par with invading Vietnam. They posted this inquiry on their official Twitter account:













In response, veterans and their family and friends posted thousands upon thousands of tweets recounting broken promises and broken people. They described cancer, PTSD, domestic abuse, unpaid college and housing loans, Gulf War syndrome, insomnia, sexual abuse, poverty, Agent Orange, racism, nightmare disorder, unemployment, burying loved ones, misogyny, orphaned children, burn pit syndrome, homelessness, debilitating injuries, divorce, alcoholism, disappearances, a Veterans Affairs department that was unwilling or unable to help, and suicide, suicide, suicide.








































































































































The United States military is one of the largest concentrations of power in the world. With 

tens of thousands

 of missiles, 

millions

 of firearms, and over 

5000

 nuclear weapons—about 40% of all the nuclear weapons in the world—the US military can hold the entire world hostage.





































The US military is also the largest employer in the United States, 

employing

 almost 2,900,000 workers—roughly 17 out of every 2000 people. If we add private military contractors like Blackwater (250,000 workers), the employees of non-combat support companies like Halliburton who build military infrastructure, provide food, and the like (150,000-250,000), US-based war manufacturers like Lockheed Martin and Boeing (1,500,000), and 

veterans

 who receive disability or pension payments (2,000,000), we find that roughly 1 out of every 50 Americans is economically dependent on US militarism.




As in all industries, without this workforce, the military would grind to a halt. It especially depends on regular transfusions of young blood—young people sold stories about adventure, duty, and upward mobility.





































If we were to ask new recruits why they joined, we’d 

likely

 hear a mix of narratives about gaining strength, seeing the world, paying for college, serving God and country, learning life skills, continuing a family tradition, escaping poverty or an unsafe home, obtaining housing, having fun, and protecting loved ones. Most people join the military because they think it will benefit them or because they believe they are serving a higher calling.














































Some recruits get to live out their dreams. Some leave instability, danger, or deprivation for a more structured and economically stable life; some even gain a sense of belonging. If they’re lucky, they serve their time without incident, then move on to free college tuition, a no-down-payment housing loan, health insurance, and a free meal at Golden Corral once a year.














































But thousands of veterans’ dreams become nightmares. The promises of recruiters, family members, and Hollywood movies offer a gamble at best—a roll of the dice that 

frequently

 ends with being harmed physically, psychologically, and sexually. Military service can lead to 

substance abuse

, 

homelessness

, and 

suicide

. It can also end in unspeakable acts of violence against others, whether those be the declared enemies of the United States, noncombatants, or veterans’ own loved ones.























































It is striking how many of these responses speak of being hoodwinked out of college, housing loans, and medical care—how many describe the pain of family members lost to PTSD, alcoholism, or suicide after witnessing or committing atrocities.














































American media bombards us with war propaganda. Almost every video game spreads the myth that combat makes us stronger: more powerful weapons, tougher armor, a bigger health bar, greater fortunes. Hollywood promises that the hero can weather any fight—or, if he can’t, his death will be meaningful and glorious.




Statistically speaking, the more we are exposed to combat, the more likely we are to be severely harmed, both physically and 

mentally

. This is true for both 

servicemembers

 and 

civilians

. As for the families we want to protect, at least 

one out of every three

 veterans brings the war home to their family through domestic abuse. Veterans are 

two to four times

 more likely to harm their families than their civilian counterparts.














































After massive troop and draftee 

resistance

 during the late 1960s and early 1970s, the US government ended selective compulsory military service (known as “the draft”). The military transitioned to a volunteer force, which means 

depending on

 recruits from families with a military tradition, working-class and impoverished enlistees, and whomever else recruiters can trick.




As one commenter pointed out,













How many people would give recruiters the time of day if they led with the truth?




“How would you like an 

11-20% chance

 of having debilitating PTSD? Or say, a 

7-11% chance

 of severe physical disability? A 32-50% chance you’ll 

physically

 or 

sexually

 abuse your family? If you’re a woman, I can promise you at least a 

25-50% chance

 that another service member will assault you. Or perhaps you’d like to become one of 

over 32,000 homeless veterans

?”




“But if you want to 

assault civilians

 in another country—to 

kill them and 

mutilate

 their bodies

—the likelihood of you getting in trouble will be 

almost zero.”














































If the benefits are bait to lure the young, the desperate, and the bored, what about the narratives that draw those who seek a higher calling?




Almost every war America has fought in the last hundred years has not achieved its stated goals. Supposedly, the US military invaded Iraq to bring stability, peace, and democracy to the region; in fact, it brought years of civil war and death. Most US citizens still cannot name the current Iraqi head of state or describe the political situation in Iraq. Twenty years of fighting in Afghanistan and Vietnam resulted in the Taliban and Việt Cộng acquiring more power than they started with. The Korean War has technically never ended; pick your poison—the poverty and hunger of a communist dictatorship or the sterility, inequality, and exploitation of the modern capitalist world.




We are told that World War II was fought to end authoritarianism and establish global peace. Yet fascism proper remained in power Spain and Portugal, while explicitly white supremacist governments retained control in places like South Africa—and the US government maintained supportive relations with all of them. In the wake of the war, humanity faced the threat of nuclear annihilation in a new Cold War. The military-industrial complex became one of the most powerful forces in society, and all kinds of violent and humiliating forms of oppression continued to exist in the victorious countries as well as the defeated ones.




But at least the Great War—the war fought to end all wars—brought lasting peace to the world. Right?























































War is a racket.

 The rich and powerful use those below them as cannon fodder as they maneuver to acquire more wealth and power. In 2003, the oil reserves of Iraq were the third largest in the world. Shortly after the US invasion and toppling of Saddam Hussein’s government, the reserves were privatized and contracted to Western companies, generating windfall profits for a few lucky capitalists.




A popular anti-war chant at the time exhorted, 

“ExxonMobil, BP, Shell, take your war and go to hell!”























































While militarists justified the War on Terror with rhetoric about fighting evildoers, the Bush administration sought to establish footholds on various continents in order to maintain military dominance throughout the world. One of the reasons the 

Afghan War

 lasted as long as it did is that the military industry prolonged it for profit. The United States government spent 

over $21,000,000,000,000

 on the War on Terror.




Weapons manufacturers made a killing. During the years 2020-2024 alone—in other words, well after the Iraq and Afghanistan wars were over—$771 billion
in Pentagon contracts 

went to

 Lockheed Martin ($313
billion), RTX (formerly Raytheon, $145 billion), Boeing ($115 billion), General Dynamics ($116 billion), and Northrop Grumman ($81 billion).
































































Even if we set aside the question of how the US government came to have $21 trillion at its disposal in the first place—think about what that $21 trillion spent on the War on Terror could have been used for instead. What do you need to live a happy, fulfilling life? What do the peoples of Iraq and Afghanistan and Vietnam need? How much healthcare and education could have been provided? Genuine healthcare, not what the VA and the for-profit hospitals crank out or deny. And real education—skills people need and want for life, knowledge based on our passions—not the traps that pass for schools in America, one part daycare and one part prison.




But thank goodness the US government didn’t go to the peoples of Iraq and Afghanistan and meet their needs. 

Fundamentalist extremism would surely have ballooned in popularity after that!























































It is not surprising that the US government and the warmongers didn’t meet the needs of the people they claimed to be liberating. They need new terrorists, or at least the threat of new terrorists, to keep up the racket. Without the fear of outsiders menacing America, how would they arrange trillions for war?





































We could tally up who profited on the Vietnam War or World War I with similar results. The protests and revolutions that broke out around the world during and after both of those wars indicate how millions of people understood what those wars were truly about. They showed successive generations that militarism, capitalism, nationalism, and authoritarianism only benefit those at the top.
































































Militarism always preys on the young and vulnerable, luring them with tales of heroism, riches, and duty. The young and desperate will serve their countries until they realize that their countries do not serve them.




No governments ever have. None ever will.





































The public can no longer view all of the replies to “How has serving impacted you?” The website still claims to retain 8.7k of them, but they are not accessible. In part, this is because people deleting their accounts, whether out of boredom with the platform or because they don’t want to support Elon Musk’s embrace of techno-fascism.




The X algorithm promotes conservative and extreme-right content, suppresses news from traditional corporate media outlets, and promotes “independent” but usually conservative or far-right influencers. When Elon Musk bought Twitter, he immediately 

purged

 high-profile accounts belonging to anarchists, anti-fascists, and far-left users. All of these are obstacles to using what remains of the platform under his ownership.





































In reaction to the neoconservatives in the Bush administration who led the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, many American conservatives shifted toward paleo-conservatism during the years-running Iraq and Afghanistan Wars. Some even became openly critical of war. Many believed that, in casting votes for Donald Trump, they were electing a politician who would keep the United States out of wars. But wherever there is nationalism, wherever state power is concentrated in the hands of an aspiring autocrat, 

war is never far behind

.




The answers to “How has serving impacted you?” comprise an interracial, multi-generational, gender-inclusive condemnation of the US military that cuts across the political spectrum. This is more of a liability to X’s brand of techno-fascism than an asset. Elon Musk’s platform has not buried them entirely, yet, but it’s not the sort of thing that he and his underlings would want people to easily and completely access. In view of that, it is unusual that so many damning tweets remain—a testament to how dangerous it is to trust your life to the military. It is worth documenting them before they disappear.




If you or your family members are currently serving in the US military, please contact the GI Rights Hotline at 1-877-447-4487 or just go AWOL. There is no need to stay in the service of a violent front for weapons and defense corporations. There’s no reason to die for their benefit, and there’s absolutely no excuse to become complicit in what the US government has done to to the people of Afghanistan, Iraq, and Iran.
