author: Archipelago Anarchist Archive
title: Archipelago Anarchist Archive, Perpustakaan Anarkis, and Anarsip: Jurnal Arsip & Perpustakaan Anti-otoritarian (A Brief Introduction)
content:
Initiatives in anarchist archiving, librarianship, and journals of archives & libraries in Indonesia

The Archipelago Anarchist Archive (AAA) is an informal, alternative archives and library initiative established in 2024 with the aim of preserving and distributing anti-authoritarian materials. AAA is driven by a number of anarchist archivists and librarians from various cities in Indonesia.

The materials that AAA focuses on are those produced in, and related to, the archipelago (known as Indonesia), whether in Indonesian or in non-Indonesian languages. These materials can take the form of texts, photographs, audio, video, and so on. All of AAA's digital archive collections can be accessed through the Internet Archive.

Link to the Archipelago Anarchist Archive collection: https://archive.org/details/@archipelago-anti-authoritarian-archive

Perpustakaan Anarkis (Anarchist Library) is an preservation and distribution project for anti-authoritarian materials based on plain text. Plain text was chosen because it makes it easier for authors and translators to distribute their work, easier for publishers to reproduce it, and easier for those who wish to archive it[1]. Perpustakaan Anarkis understands anti-authoritarianism in a flexible manner, though not without limits. Therefore, it can be said that Perpustakaan Anarkis accepts and includes both anarchist materials (from all tendencies, except anarcho-capitalism and anarcho-nationalism) and materials that can enrich anarchism, such as avant-garde(ism) that challenges not only the boundaries of art but also the state and centralized power, libertarian Marxism, autonomism, democratic confederalism, and so on. In addition, Perpustakaan Anarkis also accepts and includes reportage from the front lines (confrontation) and the home front (care) of flashpoints of popular struggle and resistance, labor strikes, and so on.

Because in anarchism, decentralization and prefiguration are important. And by practicing decentralization and prefiguration, we (and us all) no longer need to wait to act and be overly dependent on a single central point.

Besides anarcho-capitalism and anarcho-nationalism, Perpustakaan Anarkis is also not intended for authoritarian Marxists, misanthropic individuals, extractive technologism (automation that subordinates), avant-garde(ism) that leads to fascism, and other authoritarian tendencies and centralized power.

[1] Authors and translators can distribute their works without the hassle of layout, editing, cover design, and other technical work. Conversely, publishers no longer need to go through the trouble of dealing with writing and translation. And archivists—in addition to finding archiving easier—will receive various versions of the work.

Link to the Perpustakaan Anarkis collection: https://id.anarchistlibraries.net/special/index

Anarsip: Jurnal Arsip & Perpustakaan Anti-otoritarian (Anarsip: Journal of Anti-authoritarian Archives & Libraries) (published periodically, every 6 months) is a space for theorizing–practicing–theorizing–practicing anarchist archives and librarianship. Because we believe that anarchist archives and librarianship should not stop at merely the definition of "managed by, and archiving materials of, anarchist(s) and/or anti-authoritarian [movements and ideas]," but also means using methods, practicing ways of working, and thinking in an anarchist and/or anti-authoritarian manner. If the Situationist International said "to be avant-garde is to move in step with reality" (Internationale Situationiste #8); then we say "to be anarchist archiving and librarianship is to move in step with reality and anarchism."

Link to follow the developments of Anarsip: https://id.anarchistlibraries.net/special/anarsip-jurnal-arsip-perpustakaan-anti-otoritarian

Archipelago Anarchist Archive (AAA) adalah inisiatif pengarsipan dan perpustakaan informal nan alternatif yang didirikan pada tahun 2024 dengan tujuan mempreservasi sekaligus mendistribusi materi-materi anti-otoritarian. AAA digerakkan oleh sejumlah arsiparis dan pustakawan anarkis yang berasal dari berbagai kota di Indonesia.

Adapun materi-materi yang menjadi fokus dari AAA adalah materi-materi yang diproduksi di, dan yang berkaitan dengan, wilayah kepulauan (yang kini disebut sebagai Indonesia) baik itu yang berbahasa Indonesia maupun yang berbahasa non-indonesia. Dan materi-materi tersebut bisa berupa teks, foto, audio, video, dan lain sebagainya. Semua koleksi arsip digital AAA bisa diakses melalui Internet Archive.

Tautan menuju koleksi Archipelago Anarchist Archive: https://archive.org/details/@archipelago-anti-authoritarian-archive

Perpustakaan Anarkis adalah proyek pengarsipan sekaligus pendistribusian materi-materi anti-otoritarian berbasis teks polos (plain text). Teks polos dipilih, karena dapat memudahkan penulis dan penerjemah untuk mendistribusikan karyanya, memudahkan penerbit untuk mereproduksinya, dan memudahkan pihak-pihak yang ingin mengarsipkannya[1]. Perpustakaan Anarkis memahami anti-otoritarianisme secara luwes, meski bukan berarti tak terbatas. Karenanya, dapat dikatakan: Perpustakaan Anarkis menerima dan memasukkan baik itu materi-materi anarkisme (dari segala kecenderungan, kecuali anarko-kapitalisme dan anarko-nasionalisme), maupun materi-materi yang dapat memperkaya anarkisme seperti avant-garde(isme) yang tidak hanya menentang batasan seni tetapi juga negara dan kekuasaan tersentral, marxisme-libertarian, otonomisme, konfederalisme demokratis, dan seterusnya. Selain itu, Perpustakaan Anarkis juga menerima dan memasukkan materi-materi reportase dari garis depan (konfrontasi) maupun garis belakang (perawatan) titik-titik api perjuangan dan perlawanan warga, pemogokan buruh, dan lain-lain.

Karena dalam anarkisme, desentralisasi dan prefigurasi itu penting. Dan dengan mempraktikkan desentralisasi dan prefigurasi, kami (dan kita) tidak perlu lagi menunggu untuk bertindak dan terlalu bergantung pada satu titik sentral.

Selain kepada anarko-kapitalisme dan anarko-nasionalisme, Perpustakaan Anarkis juga tidak ditujukan kepada para marxis-otoriter, individu misantropis, teknologiisme yang mengekstraksi (otomatisasi yang mensubordinasi), avant-garde(isme) yang mengarah pada fasisme, dan kecenderungan otoriter serta kekuasaan tersentral lainnya.

[1] Penulis dan penerjemah dapat mendistribusikan karya-karyanya tanpa perlu repot-repot melakukan penataan letak, penyuntingan, merancang sampul, dan kerja-kerja teknis lainnya. Sebaliknya, para penerbit tidak lagi perlu bersusah payah mengurusi penulisan dan penerjemahan karya. Dan para pengarsip—selain menjadi lebih mudah dalam mengarsipkan—akan menerima beragam versi dari karya tersebut.

Tautan menuju koleksi Perpustakaan Anarkis: https://id.anarchistlibraries.net/special/index

Anarsip: Jurnal Arsip & Perpustakaan Anti-otoritarian (terbit berkala, setiap 6 bulan) adalah wadah untuk menteorisasi-praktik-teorisasi-praktik pengarsipan dan perpustakaan anarkis. Karena kami percaya, pengarsipan dan perpustakaan anarkis tidak boleh berhenti sekadar pada definisi "dikelola oleh, dan mengarsipkan materi, anarkis(me) dan/atau anti-otoritarian", tetapi juga berarti menggunakan metode, mempraktikkan cara kerja, dan berpikir secara anarkis(me) dan/atau anti-otoritarian. Jika Situasionist International mengatakan "untuk menjadi avant-garde berarti bergerak beriringan dengan realitas" (Internationale Situationiste #8); maka kami mengatakan "untuk menjadi pengarsipan dan perpustakaan anarkis berarti bergerak beriringan dengan realitas dan anarkisme".

Tautan untuk mengikuti perkembangan Anarsip: Jurnal Arsip & Perpustakaan Anti-otoritarian: https://id.anarchistlibraries.net/special/anarsip-jurnal-arsip-perpustakaan-anti-otoritarian

author: S. Baum
title: Justice Department Official Who Led Attacks on Gender-Affirming Care Resigns
content:
Brett Shumate is the fourth DOJ official to resign since the midterms after leading investigations that pressured hospitals to end care for trans minors.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Brett Shumate has become the fourth Department of Justice official to join the post-election exodus from the agency following Republicans’ crushing midterm defeat — marking the end of the tenure of a man who helped grease the wheels of the anti-trans machine.

“The rats are fleeing the sinking ship,” Alejandra Caraballo, a lawyer and trans rights scholar, posted on Bluesky, alongside news that Shumate, the Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Division, was resigning.

Under Shumate’s leadership, the DOJ aggressively targeted providers of gender-affirming care, subpoenaing patient records and waging False Claims Act investigations to intimidate hospitals. This caused some major hospitals to end care for trans minors and pay millions in settlements to the government. He was also instrumental in defending these actions in court against claims they were unlawful government overreach.

No hospital or clinic has been successfully sued because it provides evidence-based medicine, but some of them signed agreements with the DOJ to stave off the worst of federal threats: the demand that providers hand over identifiable patient data about thousands of transgender children and their families. Not all of these investigations or deals have been public.

Still, hospitals shut down their gender-affirming care programs for trans youth, leaving care deserts across the country. Lower courts condemned the government’s ploy, with one Boston judge calling it “a fishing expedition.” In a similar Rhode Island case, another judge said the DOJ — under Shumate’s leadership at the time — “has proven unworthy of this trust at every point in this case.”

In June 2025, Shumate issued a memo directing Civil Division employees to prioritize attacks on gender-affirming care, courtesy of the whims of President Donald Trump and then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, who was ousted in April. Shumate’s memo announced the Civil Division will “prioritize investigations of doctors, hospitals, pharmaceutical companies, and other appropriate entities” that ostensibly violate Trump’s declarations about transgender youth care. “In addition, the Civil Division will aggressively pursue claims under the False Claims Act against health care providers that bill the federal government for impermissible services.”

This largely included providers of wholly legal gender-affirming care, even in blue states — such as Children’s Hospital Los Angeles in California and Mount Sinai Hospital in New York. There is no federal ban on gender-affirming care.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, in announcing Shumate’s departure on X, praised him for “shutter[ing] dozens of clinics” for gender-affirming care.

The DOJ also saw the departure of Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division, and whose firm previously represented “ex-trans” activist Chloe Cole in her lawsuit against Kaiser Permanente for providing gender-affirming care.

Jason Reding Quiñones, U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, and John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for the National Security Division, also resigned. The department is also reeling from general attrition of staff throughout. The DOJ is not likely to stop pursuing political targets, including trans people and their caretakers and doctors, but if nothing else, the turmoil at the DOJ is liable to make it less effective. Under Trump, “a drastically diminished Justice Department workforce is struggling to keep up with its civil side caseloads,” The Hill found.

“A series of charts, apparently inadvertently shared and then recalled, show how the number of attorneys within the civil division has plummeted under the Trump administration.” This may slow down some of the destructive efforts by the DOJ — going after lawful gender-affirming care providers, defending the government from lawsuits over human rights violations. But others question how this might shape the department politically as new hires grow increasingly conservative and less qualified or willing to defy unlawful orders. Other important targets of the DOJ, such as those guilty of terrorism or white-collar crime, may also benefit from less competence in oversight.

A replacement for Shumate has not yet been announced.

This piece was republished with permission from Erin In The Morning.

title: Helau! Kontoerhalt der Roten Hilfe bei der Sparkasse Göttingen!
content:
Helau! Kontoerhalt der Roten Hilfe bei der Sparkasse Göttingen!




Elf Monate hat es gedauert bis nun im Hauptsacheverfahren das Konto der Roten Hilfe bei der Sparkasse Göttingen erhalten werden konnte. Heute am 11.11.26 ist die Entscheidung des Landgerichts Göttingen nun rechtskräftig. Wir hatten gegen die Kündigung durch die Sparkasse Göttingen Klage eingelegt und konnte diese in zwei Instanzen im Eilverfahren vor Gericht gewinnen. Dabei konnte das 

OLG

 Braunschweig keine Begründung für eine Kontokündigung feststellt.

Die Göttinger Sparkasse ließ es dennoch auf ein 

Hauptsacheverfahren ankommen und kassierte vor Gericht eine Niederlage

. In dem Urteil wird festgestellt, dass der erhöhte Aufwand zur Prüfung aufgrund einer Beobachtung der Roten Hilfe durch den Verfassungsschutz sowie die mutmaßliche Unterstützung einer von der 

US

-Regierung auf eine Terrorliste gesetzten und konstruierten »Antifa Ost« nicht ausreicht, um das Konto zu kündigen.

Der 

Hinweisbeschluss des 

OLG

 Braunschweig vom 15.07.2026 findet sich 

u. a.

 auf der Seite der Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte

Für uns bedeutet das:

Die Konten der Roten Hilfe sind gesichert und eine existenzgefährdende Bedrohung für den Verein wurde abgewendet.

Doch Druck gibt es weiterhin, auf Linke und linke Bewegungen und damit auch auf die Rote Hilfe. Dagegen braucht es solidarische Gegenwehr.

Wir stehen weiter solidarisch an eurer Seite und leisten Antirepressionsarbeit.

author: Joshua Carroll
title: Ex-Met Police Boss Works As Paid Advisor for Palantir
content:
A former head of the Metropolitan police, who was ousted amid scandals over misogyny and racism in the force, is now working as a paid advisor for spytech firm Palantir, the 

Bureau of Investigative Journalism has revealed

. 




Cressida Dick resigned as the force’s commissioner in 2022 after London mayor Sadiq Khan publicly said he had lost confidence in her, a move seen as effectively sacking the senior officer. 




In September 2025 she joined Palantir, the Bureau reported on Tuesday, becoming the latest of a number of high-profile public figures taking up work for the firm. 




Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson 

became the firm’s newest senior vice president

 in September this year, while former Conservative defence minister Leo Docherty 

joined the firm

 in February 2025.  




Palantir has supplied technology to the Israeli military throughout its genocide in Gaza and has worked with ICE amid its campaign of 

abductions and killings

 in the US. 




Palantir told the Bureau that Dick’s role was to advise the firm “on how our software could help improve the delivery of services in the public sector, drawing on more than 40 years of public service in a variety of roles.”




Dick told the outlet: “My role is limited to providing advice on the ways in which products such as theirs may assist public sector services. I do not and have not ever lobbied or advocated for Palantir with any organisation or individual in any sector, nor have I ever introduced Palantir to any contact of mine.”




In 2005, Dick was in charge of the operation during which police shot and killed Jean Charles de Menezes after mistaking him for a suspect in the 7/7 bombings. 




Earlier this week, 

the Citizens reported

 that Palantir had won a five-year contract with Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire police forces worth £10m. Palantir also has a £9m contract to oversee the firearms licensing system for all of the UK’s police forces.




“It never ceases to amaze me how willing people are to pay money to Palantir for the shoddy goods that they deliver,” Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat MP, told the Bureau. “They think themselves the best in the world but they are just not that good – and keep on hiring people to bend ears to get them in via the back door.”

author: Jake Johnson
title: Democratic Lawmakers Demand Removal of Provisions Deepening US-Israel Military Ties
content:
The group of 12 Democratic senators says the proposed legislation would give Israel greater leverage over US weapons and technology.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is considering a bid for Senate majority leader against Sen. Chuck Schumer, led a group of Democratic lawmakers on Tuesday in demanding that congressional leaders scrap a bipartisan effort to more closely integrate the American and Israeli militaries, warning the initiative would threaten U.S. national security and risk further complicity in Israeli atrocities.

In a letter to Democratic and Republican congressional leaders, Van Hollen (D-Md.) and 11 other members of the Senate Democratic caucus demanded exclusion of three specific provisions from the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), warning they would “constrain the administration’s ability to independently determine how best to protect U.S. national security and would lock in long-term commitments despite our serious concerns with the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and other parts of the region.” Schumer did not sign the new letter.

Two of the provisions raised in the letter — Section 1217 of the Senate-passed NDAA and Section 219 of the House version of the bill — would establish a “United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative” aimed at accelerating “bilateral defense technology research, development, testing, evaluation, coordination, and industrial cooperation.”

Lawmakers from both chambers must reconcile the differences between the House and Senate NDAAs before final passage, creating another opportunity for opponents of US-Israel military integration to strip out the provisions.

The senators warned in their Tuesday letter that the “agreements and projects these provisions envision threaten U.S. national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology.”

“Should these provisions be enacted, it would further increase Israel’s leverage over the United States through some of the most sensitive technologies in warfare. That is not in the U.S. interest,” the lawmakers wrote. “If enacted, these agreements would create long-term dependencies by embedding Israeli technology into the U.S. defense industrial base that could make future policy changes costly or difficult to implement.”

“We do not share, let alone co-produce, many of these sensitive technologies even with our closest partners, including NATO or other treaty allies,” they added. “To do so in this instance would be unwise, especially as the government of Israel continues to pursue policies in Gaza, the West Bank, and other parts of the region that are inconsistent with US interests and values.”

The lawmakers also warned against passage of Section 618 of the Fiscal Year 2027 Intelligence Authorization Act (IAA), which would require the executive branch to “expand and enhance intelligence sharing with the government of Israel.” The IAA is usually included in the NDAA.

“The provision would tie the president’s hands from limiting intelligence sharing with Israel, even when doing so may be necessary to protect US national security,” the senators wrote. “That would be irresponsible and especially troubling given public reports that the Defense Intelligence Agency recently raised the counterintelligence threat from Israel to its highest level.”

The senators’ letter came a week after President Donald Trump declared on the day of the midterm elections that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reached an agreement to end the roughly $4 billion in military assistance that the U.S. provides to Israel each year.

“This is where Section 219 of the NDAA comes in,” Drop Site reporter Julian Andreone wrote in response to the president’s announcement, referring to the military integration provision. “They’re going to transfer all of the aid behind closed doors and cut it from the appropriations process.”

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) argued in a social media post earlier this week that removal of the military integration language from the NDAA “needs to be a top priority” in the lame-duck session of Congress.

“I am pushing every Democrat and our leadership to get Section 219 out of our defense bill,” Khanna said.

Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $47,000 in the next 8 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

title: Τέλος ενός κόσμου: Ευρωπαϊκοί ξεσηκωμοί, αμερικάνικοι σεισμοί!
content:
Σκίτσο της Σόνιας Μητραλιά




Του Γ

ιώργου Μητραλιά




Υπάρχουν -σπάνιες- στιγμές στις οποίες η ιστορία της ανθρωπότητας επιταχύνεται σε βαθμό που να προκαλεί ίλιγγο. Και αυτό ακριβώς συμβαίνει σε αυτό το ανεπανάληπτο φθινόπωρο του 2026, που βλέπει τους τυράννους να τρέμουν, ακόμα και να καταρρέουν κάτω από τα ταυτόχρονα πλήγματα των λαών που εξεγείρονται σε μια ντουζίνα χώρες, κυρίως στην Ευρώπη αλλά και πέρα από αυτήν. Είναι σαν να παρακολουθούμε την επανάληψη της πολύ μακρινής «Άνοιξης των Λαών» του 1848, με τη (σημαντική) διαφορά ότι σήμερα το επίκεντρο αυτών των λαϊκών σεισμών βρίσκεται στην απέναντι ακτή του Ατλαντικού, στις Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες της Αμερικής.




Ας μιλήσουμε λοιπόν για τις Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες και τον ιστορικό σεισμό που συνιστούν τα αποτελέσματα των πολυδιαφημισμένων ενδιάμεσων εκλογών τους. Τελικά, αν υπάρχει κάτι που προκαλεί έκπληξη, αυτό δεν είναι τόσο 

η συντριπτική ήττα

 των Ρεπουμπλικάνων (1), όσο μάλλον η έκταση του θριάμβου των αντιπάλων του Τραμπισμού. Πράγματι, ενώ οι δημοσκοπήσεις προέβλεπαν την πιθανή εκλογή ενός Δημοκρατικού ακόμη και στο Κάνσας μετά από 94 χρόνια (!), σχεδόν κανείς, με εξαίρεση τον ίδιο τον ενδιαφερόμενο, δεν πίστευε στην εκλογή ενός Αφροαμερικανού στο Μισισιπή μετά από… 150 χρόνια, μετά από ενάμιση ολάκερο αιώνα! Τι συνέβη, λοιπόν, και φτάσαμε σε μια τέτοια ιστορική ανατροπή;




Η απάντηση σε αυτό το ερώτημα, που έχει κρίσιμη σημασία για την συνέχεια των γεγονότων, δίνεται από την πολύ σοβαρή και αξιόπιστη 

δημοσκόπηση

 του CNN (2) αμέσως μετά το κλείσιμο των καλπών. Και το πρώτο πράγμα που μας δείχνει αυτή η δημοσκόπηση είναι ότι η πλειοψηφία εκείνων που ψήφισαν υπέρ των Δημοκρατικών υποψηφίων δεν αυτοπροσδιορίζονται ως… Δημοκρατικοί. Πράγματι, το 35% αυτών αυτοπροσδιορίζεται ως «ανεξάρτητοι» και το 23% ως «Δημοκράτες Σοσιαλιστές (DSA)». Πράγμα που σημαίνει ότι το 58% των δημοκρατικών ψηφοφόρων απορρίπτει το Δημοκρατικό Κόμμα και ψηφίζει υπέρ του μόνο και μόνο επειδή θέλει να απαλλαγεί από τους Ρεπουμπλικάνους του Τραμπ! Με αυτά λοιπόν τα δεδομένα, το ερώτημα που προκύπτει είναι ποιο είναι το κύριο κίνητρό τους όταν επιλέγουν μια τέτοια πολιτική στάση. Η απάντηση της δημοσκόπησης του CNN διαψεύδει κατηγορηματικά όλα όσα λέγονται και γράφονται για το θέμα αυτό: το πρώτο (47%) κίνητρο των δημοκρατικών ψηφοφόρων ονομάζεται «

democracy

» και βρίσκεται πολύ μπροστά από το δεύτερο, που ονομάζεται «

economy

» (37%).




Συνοψίζοντας, οι Δημοκρατικοί ψηφοφόροι παρακινήθηκαν κυρίως να ψηφίσουν όπως ψήφισαν, όχι λόγω των –πολύ πραγματικών– υλικών προβλημάτων τους που απορρέουν από τις αποτυχίες της οικονομικής πολιτικής του Τραμπ, αλλά μάλλον λόγω της επιθυμίας τους να υπερασπιστούν όλα όσα αντιπροσωπεύει η «δημοκρατία», όπως δηλαδή τις δημοκρατικές και κοινωνικές ελευθερίες και δικαιώματα που απειλούνται άμεσα από τον Τραμπ και το αντιδημοκρατικό και φασιστοειδές καθεστώς του! Είναι λοιπόν αυτονόητο ότι ένα τέτοιο κίνητρο προδίδει την ύπαρξη μιας πολιτικής συνείδησης πολύ πιο προχωρημένης από εκείνη που περιορίζεται να αντιδρά (ακόμη και βίαια) στα υλικά προβλήματα της καθημερινής ζωής.




Κατά συνέπεια, δεν είναι τυχαίο ότι αυτή η δημοσκόπηση του CNN επιβεβαιώνει αυτό που τόσες άλλες είχαν διαπιστώσει προηγουμένως: δηλαδή, ότι ένας ολοένα και μεγαλύτερος αριθμός Αμερικανών πολιτών απορρίπτει τον καπιταλισμό και τάσσεται υπέρ του «σοσιαλισμού», ακόμα κι αν ο “σοσιαλισμός¨” του είναι κάτι συγκεχυμένο και όχι πολύ σαφές. Και αυτό εξηγεί με τη σειρά του, τη σημαντική επιτυχία των «σοσιαλιστών», ριζοσπαστικών προοδευτικών και λοιπών αριστερών υποψηφίων στις ενδιάμεσες εκλογές. Έτσι, οι DSA κατάφεραν να εκλέξουν μια συντρόφισσά τους δήμαρχο του Λος Άντζελες, με αποτέλεσμα οι δύο μεγαλύτερες πόλεις της χώρας, η Νέα Υόρκη και το Λος Άντζελες, καθώς και η διοικητική της πρωτεύουσα, η Ουάσιγκτον D.C., να έχουν πλέον δημάρχους των DSA! Και επιπλέον, οι DSA πέτυχαν να εκλέξουν 8 από τα μέλη τους στη Βουλή των Αντιπροσώπων, στα οποία θα πρέπει να προστεθούν τουλάχιστον άλλοι 6 επίσης νεοεκλεγμένοι βουλευτές, οι προεκλογικές εκστρατείες των οποίων υποστηρίχθηκαν ενεργά από τους DSA.




Ωστόσο, αν και αποτελούν τη μεγαλύτερη αριστερή οργάνωση της χώρας, οι Δημοκρατικοί Σοσιαλιστές της Αμερικής (DSA) απέχουν πολύ από το να οργανώνουν ή να εκπροσωπούν όλους τους σοσιαλιστές, τους προοδευτικούς ριζοσπάστες και λοιπούς αριστερούς, τόσο στην κοινωνία όσο και στο Κογκρέσο των Ηνωμένων Πολιτειών. Εξάλλου, πρέπει να αναμένεται ότι βοηθούσης της πολύ βαθιάς κοινωνικής και πολιτικής κρίσης, οι Αμερικανοί και, πρωτίστως, οι νέοι Αμερικανοί θα ριζοσπαστικοποιηθούν μαζικά, αυξάνοντας έτσι στο μέλλον τον αριθμό όσων αυτοπροσδιορίζονται «σοσιαλιστές» ή ακόμη και «επαναστάτες».




Όμως, τίποτα δεν γίνεται αυτόματα και πολλά θα εξαρτηθούν από το τι θα κάνει η αμερικανική αριστερά και κυρίως η ηγεσία της DSA και ο ίδιος ο Ζοχράν Μαμντάνι. Αντιμέτωπη με έναν Τραμπ που κάνει ό,τι μπορεί για να πείσει ακόμη και τους πιο αφελείς ή «μετριοπαθείς» ότι ετοιμάζεται να πολεμήσει μέχρι θανάτου για να παραμείνει στην εξουσία, η αμερικανική αριστερά έχει μόνο μία επιλογή: να μην καλλιεργήσει την παραμικρή αυταπάτη σχετικά με τις προθέσεις του Τραμπ και να εκμεταλλευτεί την ευνοϊκή συγκυρία που δημιούργησαν τα αποτελέσματα των ενδιάμεσων εκλογών για να περάσει στην επίθεση και να ικανοποιήσει, το συντομότερο δυνατό, το λαϊκό αίτημα να λογοδοτήσουν ο Τραμπ και οι δικοί του για τα εγκλήματά τους.




Επομένως, το να υποστηρίξει κανείς, όπως το υπαινίσσεται ο Μαμντάνι, την υποψηφιότητα για την ηγεσία του Δημοκρατικού Κόμματος καραμπινάτων συντηρητικών και συμφιλιωτών όπως ο Τζέφρις και ο Σούμερ, είναι κάτι περισσότερο από λάθος· είναι πραγματική αυτοκτονία για τη ριζοσπαστική αμερικανική αριστερά. Και αυτό επειδή ο Τζέφρις και ο Σούμερ καμώνονται πως δεν καταλαβαίνουν ότι η προαγωγή σε ένα είδος «πρωθυπουργού» αυτού που είναι αυθεντικός κλώνος του Γκέμπελς, του ρατσιστή και υπέρμαχου της λευκής υπεροχής Στίβεν Μίλερ, δεν αφήνει καμιά αμφιβολία για την πρόθεση του Τραμπ να σπείρει το χάος στη χώρα και στον κόσμο, χρησιμοποιώντας ό,τι υπάρχει και δεν υπάρχει από νεοναζιστικά και ρατσιστικά καθάρματα.




Αντίθετα, αντιδρώντας άμεσα στις προκλήσεις του Τραμπ και των οπαδών του με την κινητοποίηση των λαϊκών μαζών και προετοιμάζοντας τον λαό ενάντια στις κατασταλτικές, αν όχι δικτατορικές, προθέσεις του Τραμπ, η Αριστερά και πιο συγκεκριμένα οι Δημοκρατικοί Σοσιαλιστές θα μπορέσουν όχι μόνο να φράξουν το δρόμο στα αντιδημοκρατικά σχέδια του Τραμπ και να υπερασπιστούν τον λαό, αλλά και να στριμώξουν το κατεστημένο του Δημοκρατικού Κόμματος, που δεν έχει καμία διάθεση να κινητοποιήσει τις εργατικές μάζες και τη νεολαία. Κάνοντας όλα αυτά, η αμερικάνικη ριζοσπαστική αριστερά θα μπορέσει να μπει επικεφαλής της λαϊκής αντίστασης, να κερδίσει σε κύρος και, τελευταίο αλλά όχι λιγότερο σημαντικό, να εμπνεύσει και να συσπειρώσει γύρω της όλους εκείνους και εκείνες που θέλουν να παλέψουν ενάντια στον τραμπισμό και στα αντιδημοκρατικά και πραξικοπηματικά του σχέδια.




Η παρούσα ιστορική συγκυρία θα μπορούσε να χαρακτηριστεί ιδεώδης για να μπορέσει η αμερικανική ριζοσπαστική αριστερά να παίξει πρωταγωνιστικό ρόλο στη γιγάντια ταξική σύγκρουση που μόλις άρχισε. Απέναντι σε ένα στρατόπεδο της αντίδρασης διχασμένο και σε κρίση, σε ένα Ρεπουμπλικανικό Κόμμα που μετρά τις πληγές του και αναζητά αποδιοπομπαίους τράγους, και σε έναν αποδυναμωμένο, αμφισβητούμενο και ταπεινωμένο Τραμπ, η ριζοσπαστική αριστερά πρέπει να επιδείξει τώρα μέγιστη τόλμη και αποφασιστικότητα, έχοντας πάντα κατά νου ότι τα βλέμματα των καταπιεσμένων όλου του κόσμου είναι στραμμένα σε αυτήν…

author: Joshua Fechter
title: Texas Democrats Take Aim at Data Centers, Flock Cameras and Immigration Enforcement
content:
Democrats have taken control of the Texas House, but their proposals face resistance in the GOP-controlled Senate.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Riding high after their success in last week’s election, Democrats in the Texas Legislature unveiled an aggressive agenda Monday as bill filing opened for the 2027 session: Expand Medicaid. Boost the minimum wage. End tax breaks for data centers. Ban Flock cameras. Legalize marijuana.

Other ideas included undoing a state law that requires sheriffs to partner with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and forbidding border wall construction at state parks.

Democrats also filed proposals to end the state’s year-old school voucher program and boost per-pupil funding for public schools. They also eye building high-speed rail stretching from Dallas to San Antonio.

The 90th session of the Texas Legislature will convene Jan. 12 in a new era under a Democratic governor and divided Texas Legislature.

The opening of the bill-filing period marks the unofficial opening of the next legislative session. As of 5 p.m. Monday, more than 1,260 bills had been filed, with much more to come before bill filing ends March 12.

Most legislation will fall short of the governor’s desk, but Monday’s flurry offered an early glimpse of lawmakers’ priorities.

Democrats took majority control of the Texas House, but many of their proposals can expect heavy resistance in the Senate, where Republicans still hold the majority after last week’s midterm elections. And while Republicans took a drubbing in last week’s voting, bills filed Monday signaled they haven’t abandoned their priorities.

Republican lawmakers filed bills aimed at getting rid of property taxes, forbidding local governments from hiring lobbyists and making English the official language of the state of Texas.

There also were signs of common ground, particularly when it comes to tangling with data centers, wrangling property tax bills and enacting term limits for statewide officials.

First out of the gate Monday morning were House and Senate bills to expand access to Medicaid. Under Republicans, Texas has long held out on expanding Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act — which would send the state up to $10 billion a year and cover an additional 1 million Texans. Texas is the most populous state to not allow Medicaid expansion.

State Rep. John Bucy, D-Austin, filed a bill that would direct the Texas Health and Human Services Commission to file a federal plan to expand Medicaid. State Sen. Judith Zaffirini, D-Laredo, filed a companion bill in the Senate.

Bucy acknowledged that any move to expand Medicaid health insurance coverage would face pushback from the Texas Senate, where Republicans continue to hold a majority.

“We do think there’s going to be a lot of room to find compromise,” he said. “The House and the Senate need to find compromise to get things done for the people of Texas.

Medicaid in Texas mostly covers low-income children, new moms and older adults. It does not cover working-age adults who either earn too little to afford health insurance on their own or work for an employer that offers health insurance.

Rep. Jolanda Jones, D-Houston, filed a bill to require school officials to notify parents when there is not a full-time nurse or equivalent working on a public school campus during normal school hours. Currently, Texas does not require each public school to have a school nurse on campus.

On reproductive health, state Rep. Donna Howard filed an omnibus bill to repeal the state’s abortion ban and related statutes.

“The purpose here was to say, OK, we’ve had over a decade of restrictions on access to abortion healthcare, now we need to look at a reset,” Howard said. “Take it out. Let’s reset. Let’s talk about what can we do here that we can find some common ground on that makes more sense now that allows women to get the healthcare that they need.”

Howard’s bill would also repeal a 2023 state law passed that bans gender affirming healthcare for minors.

State Rep. Tom Oliverson, R-Cypress, filed several consumer-related healthcare bills, including one targeting penalties many Texans have complained about when they try to get medical treatment after getting a referral from a physician who is not in their insurance network.

Democrats and Republicans took aim at data center construction, signaling that tighter regulations will be central to next year’s efforts after the data center boom became a dominant campaign issue.

Proposals were filed to require data centers to share more information about their water usage, to bar data centers from receiving tax incentives and to give government entities more direct regulation over data center development.

The bills tackle key points of friction in communities worried that the facilities will drain local water resources and cause electricity rates to increase. State efforts to survey the facilities on their water use have seen low participation rates.

A bill by Zaffirini would require large data centers to share information about their water usage with the state Water Development Board.

The industry has also faced criticism for pursuing tax incentives. Lawmakers from both parties have expressed interest in repealing a state sales tax exemption for data centers, which The Texas Tribune reported in April has ballooned to more than $1 billion in annual revenue foregone by the state.

Democratic and Republican lawmakers filed a handful of bills to repeal the sales and use tax exemption for data centers.

A murkier subset of exemptions offered by local governments in the form of Chapter 380, 381 and 312 agreements allow data centers to negotiate tax abatements, rebates and direct infrastructure work from cities and counties seeking to lure economic development.

Zaffirini’s bill would bar data centers from pursuing those local tax incentives and prevent cities and counties from renewing those already in place.

Democrats also took aim at the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement and border wall construction.

A bill by Rep. Trey Martinez Fischer, D-San Antonio, would repeal a 2025 law that requires sheriffs who run or contract out operations of a jail to take part in a 287(g) partnership, which allows U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to deputize state and local law enforcement officers with certain immigration enforcement authorities. Sen. José Menéndez, another San Antonio Democrat, filed a similar bill.

The bills would let sheriffs terminate their agreements with ICE and would stop the comptroller’s office from awarding grants for these partnerships. The proposal would also dismiss any action from the attorney general’s office that sought to enforce the 2025 law.

There were 565 partnerships under the 287(g) program in Texas as of Nov. 4, ICE data shows.

A bill by state Rep. Eddie Morales Jr. of Eagle Pass would aim to bar the feds from building a border wall on state park property. Another by Morales would make it illegal for ICE agents to wear face coverings.

Martinez Fischer also proposed a state audit of Operation Lone Star, the state’s $11 billion border enforcement effort.

Lawmakers filed at least three bills seeking to rein in use of Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers, including legislation from Bucy that would ban the devices outright. State Rep. Brian Harrison, R-Midlothian, who filed bills in two prior sessions seeking to limit the devices’ use, also filed a bill limiting how police can use them.

Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against the spread of the AI-powered cameras, and told The Texas Tribune in September she supported a ban.

Lawmakers filed at least a dozen bills seeking to change how Texas — historically the country’s most prolific executioner — can use the death penalty. While most of the bills seek to limit or remove death sentences as an option in certain cases, three seek to expand charges that qualify for the death penalty, including in cases of sexual assault of minors and for politically motivated killings.

And the state would legalize, tax and regulate marijuana under bills filed by Bucy and Moody.

Democrats also made moves on the education front, filing several bills aimed at repealing the state’s $1 billion school voucher program — an idea likely to be met with significant opposition from Republican senators.

The voucher program — championed by outgoing Republicans Gov. Greg Abbott and Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick — launched this year and provides participating students with publicly funded vouchers for private schools or home schooling.

Meanwhile, bills from multiple Democrats aim to increase state funding for public schools. Last session, lawmakers approved an influx of dollars to schools that many education advocates said didn’t cover the cost of inflation since the last school finance overhaul in 2019.

Howard filed a long-sought proposal to raise the base amount of per-student funding the state provides to public schools, known as the basic allotment, and tying future increases in that base funding to inflation. Howard seeks to bump up the allotment of $6,215 per student to $7,500.

Other ideas would tweak how the state funds public schools. A proposal by Bucy would fund schools based on student enrollment, not average daily attendance. Only six states fund districts based on attendance, and the current attendance-based funding system leads Texas schools to lose out on money if kids aren’t showing up to class.

Bucy and Zaffirini filed identical bills that would require school districts to provide free full-day pre-K for all 4-year-olds. The state currently mandates free pre-K for 4-year-olds only if their families meet certain criteria, including if they are homeless, do not speak English, or have parents who are firefighters, first responders, teachers or members of the military.

When it comes to higher education, Democrats are again pushing to repeal Texas’ ban on diversity, equity and inclusion programs at public universities. One narrow proposal would exempt programs funded by private donations or federal money from the DEI ban.

Other bills focus on affordability, such as creating grants to help recent Texas high school graduates pay for community college or those from households earning less than $150,000 cover tuition and fees at four-year universities.

Other measures aim at making it easier to transfer more college courses so students could avoid repeating classes. Another would eliminate sales taxes on college textbooks for one week each in January and August.

Republicans, meanwhile, filed bills that would require public colleges and universities to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that students cheated or plagiarized before disciplining them, bar misconduct investigations without a sworn complaint and require universities to display class averages alongside students’ grades on transcripts.

Another proposal would let state lawmakers file complaints against universities with the state’s new higher education ombudsman office, a power currently reserved for students, faculty and staff.

Democrats also filed bills to raise the state’s minimum wage from $7.25 an hour, the rate set by the federal government. A pair of proposals from state Reps. Ana-María Rodríguez Ramos of Richardson and Armando Walle of Houston would raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour, while a proposal from Martinez Fischer would raise it to $17 an hour.

Texas is one of eight states that don’t allow residents to register to vote online, according to the National Conference on State Legislatures. A bill by Bucy would direct the Texas secretary of state to work with the Texas Department of Public Safety and Department of Information Resources to figure out a way to allow online voter registration.

Democrats will also seek to restrict who can purchase semi-automatic rifles. A bill by state Rep. Joe Moody of El Paso would raise the minimum age to buy certain semi-automatic rifles in Texas to 21.

And as Texans complain about worsening traffic congestion on the state’s highways, Democrats have signaled they’re looking at other ways to get around the state.

A Bucy bill would direct the Texas Department of Transportation to kickstart a high-speed rail line connecting Dallas, Waco, Austin and San Antonio along the congested Interstate 35 corridor. The state agency would have to enter a comprehensive development agreement with a private company to build, maintain and operate the line, which would have to reach speeds of at least 110 miles per hour. At the same time, the GOP’s Harrison filed a bill seeking to hamper high-speed rail construction.

Meanwhile, a proposal by Walle would dedicate state funds to public transportation, bike lanes and sidewalks — though voters would have to sign off because it would require amending the state constitution.

Texans have complained about the rising cost of homeowner and auto insurance. Under a proposal from Martinez Fischer, state insurance regulators would have to sign off on any rate increases that exceed 5%.

In an out-of-left-field swing, Democrats took aim at the amount of parking cities require homes and businesses to provide.

Homebuilders and housing experts have long argued that such requirements drive up the cost of housing, in part by forcing builders to construct parking where they may otherwise put more housing. Defenders of the requirements argue they prevent parking from spilling over onto neighboring streets.

Texas would get rid of all cities’ parking requirements under a proposal from state Sen. José Menéndez, a San Antonio Democrat. A separate bill from Walle would prevent cities from requiring bars to provide a certain amount of parking, a requirement critics have said encourages drunken driving.

Republicans remain in majority control of the Senate as Lt. Gov.-elect Vikki Goodwin, a Democrat, prepares to take office as part of a Democratic sweep of statewide offices in last week’s election.

Republican lawmakers, and some Democrats, offered a slew of proposals aimed at reining in property tax bills. Harrison of Waxahachie filed a longshot bill to abolish property taxes and create a joint committee on the abolishment of property taxes. Harrison and state Rep. Brent Money, R-Greenville, each proposed constitutional amendments to get rid of property taxes.

House Republicans have long sought to tighten the state’s appraisal cap, which limits how fast a home’s taxable value can rise each year. That cap stands at 10%. Under a bill by state Rep. Jared Patterson, R-Frisco, the cap would decrease to 3%. Tax policy experts on both sides of the aisle have warned that tightening the state’s appraisal cap wouldn’t result in lower tax bills and would have nasty side effects.

Democrats have their own property tax proposals. Texas gives direct property tax relief to homeowners, but doesn’t do so for the state’s renters. A proposal by state Rep. Salman Bhojani, a Euless Democrat, would change that.

Republicans in past sessions have unsuccessfully sought to forbid local governments from hiring lobbyists, a practice referred to as “taxpayer-funded lobbying.” That push faces an even tougher climb in a divided Legislature. Still, state Rep. Mike Olcott, R-Fort Worth, filed a bill to do just that.

Rep. Charlie Geren, R-Fort Worth, filed a House joint resolution that would allow voters to decide whether to legalize both casino gaming and sports wagering in Texas. Resolutions require two-thirds support in the House and Senate before voters can weigh in.

While a similar resolution passed the House in 2023, it failed in the Senate, where Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick has for years blocked efforts to expand gambling in Texas. While it is unclear what appetite the Republican-controlled Senate will have for legal wagering, Lt. Gov.-elect Vikki Goodwin voted for the failed 2023 measure when she served as a state representative.

Another Patterson proposal would prohibit Texans under age 16 from using social media platforms.

Efforts to set time limits on how long some statewide elected officials, including the governor and lieutenant governor, can serve saw bipartisan support, while several Republican bills also seek to limit the time of service in the Texas Legislature. Those proposals call for enshrining the limits in the Texas Constitution, which would require voter approval.

The Texas Tribune is a nonprofit, nonpartisan media organization that informs Texans — and engages with them — about public policy, politics, government and statewide issues.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $47,000 in the next 8 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

Oggi la resistenza dex abitanti di ZIA ADA, occupazione abitativa di piazza Miraglia, ha impedito il tentativo di sgombero di fronte a un dispiegamento di forze senza precedenti. 




Contro il progetto speculativo dell’Ordine dei Servi di Maria, determinato a lasciare le persone per strada senza alcun riguardo per le condizioni di fragilità sociale, pretendiamo soluzioni abitative dignitose per tuttx lx abitanti di ZIA ADA, che non strappino le persone dai propri quartieri e dalle proprie reti sociali. La Napoli ormai diventata città vetrina non ha bisogno di ulteriori strutture ricettive o di studentati privati a costi insostenibili, ma di politiche abitative reali e concrete, oltre la monocoltura turistica e al di fuori di ogni speculazione elettorale. Ogni occupazione sarà una barricata, piazza Miraglia non si sgombera!

ospita 30 famiglie

author: Alex Cuadros
title: Bill Gates’ $29B Stake in Landfill Company Tied to Major Methane Emissions
content:
Gates has called on businesses to fight climate change. But his own investments tell a different story.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

In November 2015, world leaders descended on Paris to negotiate a historic agreement to limit global warming. But on the summit’s opening day, attention turned to a private citizen slouched awkwardly in a chair on stage: Bill Gates.

Gates, with his characteristic flop of sandy hair, grinned impishly as President Barack Obama called him a “visionary” and a “driving force” behind a pair of pledges that both saw as key to the larger agreement. First the world’s largest economies would double their spending on research into clean-energy technologies. Then investors like Gates would back the startups that emerged. The Microsoft cofounder had already enlisted two dozen other billionaires to join the effort.

For Gates, who’d become increasingly consumed by this unprecedented threat to human well-being, the moment marked his arrival as a leading figure in the fight against climate change.

“If we back over 50 different breakthrough approaches, we know that several of those will give us the solution that we need,” Gates said during his own speech. He would invest at least $2 billion of his own money in companies developing geothermal wells, new kinds of nuclear reactors and machines that pull carbon from the air, to name just a few.

With much less fanfare, however, Gates has put more than double that amount into a very dirty, old-school industry. At the time of the Paris summit, he was already the dominant shareholder of America’s No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services. He has since increased his stake to 38% of the company, a position worth $29 billion.

While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see landfills as a crucial climate issue. They’re responsible for as much as a fifth of the country’s emissions of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate pollution as 3 million gasoline-burning cars each year, according to its own reports.

One might imagine that a landfill operator with Gates as its largest shareholder — and with three people closely linked to Gates on its board — would lead the way in tackling those emissions. Even after seemingly softening his stance on global warming in a controversial blog post last year, Gates remains one of the world’s most prominent voices on the issue. As he did in his bestselling 2021 book “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” he continues to advocate for cutting emissions, and he has called on his fellow business leaders to do their part.

Gates, though, has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor. Republic has even lobbied against policies that could make the wider industry cleaner, including by keeping organic waste out of landfills in the first place.

“It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic’s behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company profits,” said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at the University of Colorado, Boulder.

As for whether he should, in her words, “put his money where his mouth is,” Lipton said, “you can leave it to the reader to make the moral judgment.”

Gates didn’t respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments, and ProPublica couldn’t find any public comments he’s made about them. But the bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the owner of 5% of Republic’s shares — “It’s ‘Garbage In’ for Gates,” the New York Post headline read — the company’s stock price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows.

In those early days, Gates hadn’t yet awakened to the threat of global warming. It was a different time. Microsoft Windows ran on more than 80% of personal computers. Gates was the world’s richest person, and his bespectacled face graced the cover of Time magazine twice that year. He was simultaneously criticized for what a federal judge determined to be Microsoft’s monopolistic practices and admired for establishing what was soon to become the world’s largest charitable foundation.

A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an interview he gave to Fortune that year. To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said he’d given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets.

Republic’s then-chairman, billionaire Wayne Huizenga, had flown Larson by helicopter to his private golf course in Florida, according to the article. It’s unclear if Huizenga pitched Republic there, but it fit the remit. America would always produce trash, ensuring a steady stream of revenue. After that initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates’ stake in Republic over the years that followed. Larson would also acquire a small chunk of Republic’s main competitor, Waste Management — which Huizenga also once led — on behalf of the Gates Foundation.

It was only in 2006, when he asked two climate scientists to educate him, that Gates started to grasp the potentially “catastrophic” effects of greenhouse gases, he later wrote. But he also saw that the poorest people in the world needed more energy to improve their lot. The solution, he concluded, was something climate activists often underplay: innovation that could make clean energy cheap enough to naturally displace fossil fuels. That was the idea behind Breakthrough Energy, the initiative he launched in Paris in 2015.

Around the same time, methane began to emerge as a focus of climate action. The gas can trap 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide in the near term, and it’s responsible for one-third of the global warming we experience today, according to the United Nations Environment Programme. But it also breaks down much more quickly, turning into CO2 and water vapor in about a decade — which means that cutting methane emissions now would reduce that warming within our lifetimes. This is especially urgent, scientists say, as the climate approaches tipping points that could doom rainforests, coral reefs and ice sheets.

In speeches and interviews, Gates has sometimes warned about methane, but usually from agricultural sources (“cow farts,” in his words). He has rarely mentioned landfills, even after Larson — who still runs Gates’ investment office, Cascade Asset Management — joined Republic’s board in 2009. Gates’ stake in the company, though, was a relatively small portion of his own net worth until fairly recently. And as Larson put it to Fortune, “I’ll call Bill about something I’m buying if he needs to know, but Bill might not have any idea what Cascade owns.” (Gates’ Republic holdings are publicly disclosed in securities filings.)

Elsewhere in Gatesworld, people started to home in on the climate threat posed by landfills. The root of the issue is that landfills store buried trash — and when organic waste decomposes underground, in the absence of oxygen, it generates methane. The Gates Foundation has funded research and advocacy aimed at solving that problem, and Breakthrough has backed at least two early-stage companies developing their own solutions. One, Windfall Bio, uses microbes to digest methane into fertilizer. Its product was actually tested last year at a Republic landfill in California, where the pink liquid was sprinkled on the soil covering the top layer of trash.

Windfall said the test worked, substantially reducing emissions, but the startup reportedly ceased operations after a Department of Energy grant was canceled. (Windfall didn’t respond to emailed requests for comment.)

On the surface, Republic has pursued a path consistent with Gates’ mission. In 2019, it became the first U.S. landfill operator to sign up for the Science Based Targets Initiative, promising to cut its emissions by 35% by 2030. Not that this was charity. Republic’s “climate leadership” became part of its pitch for garbage-collection contracts in progressive cities and counties. The company also won placements on stock indexes for businesses that meet certain environmental, social and governance criteria, attracting sustainability-minded investors.

Still, a fundamental tension remained — one at the heart of Gates’ vision. As Republic’s then-CEO Donald Slager put it on a 2017 call with investors, “You can’t have sustainability without profitability.”

Each day, Americans throw away melon rinds, salmon skins and half-eaten drumsticks, paper towels, cheese that was too funky and eggs a day past their sell-by date. They discard greasy pizza boxes with crusts still rattling around inside and unthinkable amounts of leftover Chinese takeout. Not to mention the occasional dead pet.

Most of that trash — 240 million tons a year, enough to bury Manhattan under 100 feet of refuse — is hauled to one of the country’s 1,400 active landfills, where hulking vehicles with spiked wheels crush it into thin layers. At the end of each day, bulldozers typically spread soil on top, and for almost everyone who produced that trash, it will forever remain out of sight and out of mind.

People who live near landfills, though, describe smelling rotten cabbage, rotten eggs and rotten fish, as well as ammonia and skunk. Or as a neighbor to one Republic landfill put it: “I started smelling this stench like burning diapers. … It was foul.” Some describe burning throats, burning eyes, headaches and nausea. And while methane itself has no scent, those odors indicate that the gas is being released, studies show.

Still, modern landfills are an undeniable improvement over what came before. Open dumping and burning remained widespread until the 1970s. It was only in the ’90s that federal regulators started requiring operators to collect leachate (garbage juice, which can contaminate groundwater) and, at larger facilities, landfill gas (which is typically about half methane and half carbon dioxide but can also contain carcinogens like benzene).

Industry experts often compare landfills to living, breathing creatures. Underground trash inevitably shifts and settles, making it difficult to keep that gas from escaping. Managing such a beast is costly, which helps to explain why smaller operations have increasingly given way to corporations like Republic, which can turn a profit through economies of scale.

Republic declined to make executives available for interviews or to allow ProPublica to visit a landfill. But in May 2022 — around the same time Gates was lobbying for the passage of President Joe Biden’s historic climate bill — the company invited the Houston Chronicle to its local McCarty Road Landfill. Opened a half century earlier, the facility had passed through two corporate owners before being swallowed up by Republic, and now it was the site of a very Gatesian kind of project.

On the day of the visit, gulls circled hungrily as workers in neon vests gave a tour of the gas-collection system. Like at most other large landfills in the country, wells had been drilled deep into the trash below — five hundred of them in total. The top of each well sprouted from the grassy slopes in the form of a stubby black pipe fitted with a valve for adjusting the flow of underground gas. The workers also showed off large, bright blue, snail-shaped “blowers” — machines that suck that gas into a network of pipelines, then push it to the clanking, humming on-site plant that turns it into a salable product.

Most landfills that are required to collect gas simply burn it off. But they can also process it into “renewable natural gas,” which is functionally equivalent to the version pumped by oil companies. In part because this reuses the carbon from decomposing waste, it’s generally considered more climate-friendly. It also turns an environmental liability into a source of revenue — exactly the kind of win-win that Gates has long championed.

Yet the technology is no guarantee that the climate is being protected. In fact, it may be just the opposite.

In September 2024, the Environmental Protection Agency issued an “enforcement alert” saying that landfills across the country were “violating monitoring and maintenance requirements.” While the EPA didn’t name the operators, ProPublica obtained the corresponding spreadsheet through a public records request, and a fifth of the facilities targeted belong to Republic.

McCarty, far from being a model landfill, was among the worst offenders. It would soon earn Republic a formal “finding of violation” for allegedly failing to detect “exceedances” — methane escaping at levels above federal limits — for years on end. The EPA also noted repeated failures to address flooded wells, gullies formed by erosion and trash peeking through the surface of the landfill. Despite Republic’s economic incentive to capture methane, EPA inspectors found evidence of “poor maintenance” and “careless operation” of the gas-collection system as well.

And McCarty is hardly an outlier. Recent studies suggest that landfills with renewable natural gas facilities can actually emit more methane than those that only burn off the gas or use it to generate electricity. One possible explanation is that methane concentrations can vary across different parts of a landfill. According to researchers at Carbon Mapper, a NASA partner that measures emissions from various industries, some operators may prioritize collecting gas with higher methane content, which is cheaper to process — allowing more of the remaining methane to leak out.

Republic spokesperson Rob Litt declined to comment on whether that happened at McCarty, but said in a statement, “We employ hundreds of environmental managers and engineers. … If issues are identified, we work to resolve them.”

“Protecting the environment is part of Republic Services’ business,” he added.

The issues aren’t exclusive to landfills with natural gas facilities. Since 2020, EPA inspectors have used handheld methane detectors to sweep at least 39 of Republic’s roughly 200 landfills, according to inspection reports obtained by ProPublica. Including the issues at McCarty, they documented more than 1,400 problem spots — ranging from animal burrows to choked-off wells — spewing excessive amounts of methane.

In some cases, methane could be seen bubbling up through dark, fetid leachate pools. In others, so much methane was being released — with concentrations between 100 and 300 times the federal limit — that it was an explosion hazard.

Around the time of the Houston Chronicle visit, Republic’s CEO, a former McKinsey consultant named Jon Vander Ark, was promoting a new slogan: “Sustainability in action.” Meanwhile, though, Republic was quietly shying away from true climate leadership.

In 2021, two years after Republic signed on to the Science Based Targets Initiative, the SBTI made its minimum climate goal much more ambitious. Waste Management (where the Gates Foundation owns a small minority of the shares) would soon adopt it.

This was just months after Gates published “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” in which he exhorted private companies “to embrace the harder steps” toward solving global warming. Republic staff calculated that the new SBTI target could require more than $1 billion in additional spending on gas wells and other improvements, according to a former employee. Though that is less than half of what Republic has spent on dividends for Gates alone, it would leave less money for the company to redistribute to him and other shareholders. Republic has also spent more than $8 billion buying its own stock in the open market, ProPublica’s analysis shows, likely boosting the value of shares held by investors.

The matter was finally presented to the board around the second half of 2024, this person said. By then the board included Larson, Gates’ longtime investment manager — whose “insight into sustainability issues” is cited in company filings — and three other people with business ties to Gates (one has since left). While that is only four board members among a total of 13, Gates’ dominant shareholding means that, “as a practical matter, on any matter that gets voted on, he will almost certainly control the outcome,” said Lipton, the corporate-governance expert.

Republic never made the leap, and now it walks an awkward line. It continues to tout its affiliation with the SBTI while saying, in a note buried deep in one of its many sustainability reports, that the more ambitious target is “not an immediate strategic priority.”

Per SBTI rules, Republic has until the end of this year to submit an updated target. But when ProPublica asked if it would, the spokesperson said only, “We are reviewing our goals.” He declined to comment on the estimated cost or the board discussions.

There is, though, an even larger issue with Republic’s climate claims.

In line with its existing SBTI goal, Republic says it has already cut its landfill emissions by 20% since 2017. But that figure isn’t based on actual measurements of methane escaping from its facilities. According to the method cited in its sustainability reports, Republic instead typically measures the methane collected by its wells. Then it extrapolates how much it’s failing to collect — and how much is being emitted — based on the characteristics of each facility.

This method is based on an industry study that, as the EPA has noted, excluded data from gas-collection systems that were “not working well.” The EPA’s own reporting rules allow the same basic approach, which can cause companies collecting less gas due to a “malfunction or inefficiency” to “erroneously report decreasing emissions,” according to a 2025 study using satellite data by researchers at Harvard, NASA and Carbon Mapper. The researchers specifically examined two Republic landfills, and at one of them, the company reported declining emissions to the EPA even though satellite measurements showed they had risen over a four-year period.

The reporting gaps can be enormous. A study led by Hannah Nesser, now at Georgetown, found Republic facilities to be the No. 1 and No. 2 emitters among the roughly 70 large U.S. landfills the researchers observed over the course of 2019. The first, the National Serv-All Landfill in Indiana, was found to be releasing an astounding 13 times as much methane as what the company reported to the EPA. And that pattern repeated to varying degrees across three-quarters of the Republic landfills in the study. (McCarty wasn’t in the study, but according to measurements by Carbon Mapper, it emits more than twice what the company has reported.)

In response to questions about these studies, the Republic spokesperson said, “We stand by the sustainability results we’ve achieved.”

He also pointed to a letter from the National Waste and Recycling Association, a major trade group, questioning the accuracy of satellite measurements. It is a tactic from the playbook of another major climate polluter, the oil and gas industry, said Katherine Blauvelt of Full Circle Future, which advocates for cleaning up landfills.

“Satellites, peer-reviewed research studies and EPA inspectors on the ground all keep finding the same thing: unchecked and underreported methane emissions,” she said. “There’s a fire alarm going off and instead of getting out the extinguisher, the waste industry is blaming the smoke detector.”

Last year, Gates published a blog post criticizing the “doomsday view” of global warming — a striking shift for someone who’d once warned of the failing ecosystems, mass migration and soaring mortality that could result from hotter temperatures. That led climate skeptics, including President Donald Trump, to say that Gates had admitted he was wrong. But Gates called that a “gigantic misreading.” While he believed more lives could be saved by improving global health, where he’d decided to shift his resources, he remained a “climate activist,” he told one audience.

Gates has tried to lead by example. In 2019, he sold his shares in oil and gas companies because, he later wrote, “I don’t want to profit if their stock prices go up because we don’t develop zero-carbon alternatives.” He kept flying by private jet, but he “offset” those emissions by buying credits from a company that removes carbon from the air. He has also called on other business leaders to “make sure that they’re not holding back” climate policies, even if those policies could cut into profits.

Republic has actively worked against such policies — and yet Gates, according to securities filings, has never sold a share.

In the final year of the Biden administration, the EPA announced a plan to update its landfill gas rules, which have changed little since the ’90s. Among other potential changes, the agency asked for comments on the newer technologies, such as satellites and drones, that research has found to be effective in monitoring and controlling methane pollution.

Some landfill operators were already experimenting with these innovations. But they wanted almost all of it to remain voluntary, according to a joint statement from the National Waste and Recycling Association and the Solid Waste Association of North America, both of which have Republic executives on their boards.

“We do not believe that any of these technologies are sufficiently developed,” the industry groups said, adding that the various innovations were “not cost-effective,” “reliable” or “transparent.”

The Republic spokesperson declined to comment on whether that lobbying goes against its climate commitments.

“A lot of the issue comes down to the profit of the corporate landfill operators and their resistance to do things that will eat into that,” said Darin Schroeder of the Clean Air Task Force, a climate advocacy group.

Gates’ press representatives didn’t respond to questions about whether he’s aware of the issues at Republic — or whether he has independently investigated the source of a fifth of his fortune. But ProPublica interviewed multiple former employees at Breakthrough Energy, Gates’ clean-tech investment arm, who all spoke on condition of anonymity. They each said they hadn’t even heard about his landfill holdings.

“I agree there’s a bit of a conundrum there,” said one high-ranking staffer who was laid off last year. But this person added, “Based on my time with him, I think he’s very serious about climate change. This isn’t a vanity thing for him.”

“My theory is that he probably doesn’t have much involvement in those investments,” said another laid-off staffer.

Gates’ investment managers, at least, can’t claim total ignorance. Larson and Thomas Handley, a Cascade senior adviser, both participate actively in Republic’s board discussions, according to a fellow director who spoke on the condition of anonymity to share details of those private discussions. The board also receives regular management briefings, including “high level” reports on the company’s lobbying and litigation over “practices we could do better,” this director said. (Larson didn’t return phone messages left by ProPublica at his office, and Cascade didn’t respond to a question about his and Handley’s involvement in Republic.)

It’s unclear if Gates himself ever learned of those reports. But he appears to have an even larger blind spot on the issue. The waste industry doesn’t fit neatly into his view of climate change as a problem to be solved mainly through technological breakthroughs. Innovations can help, but the root of the problem is the inescapable fact that, when organic waste decomposes in the absence of oxygen, methane is produced.

Properly managing the waste we’ve already buried is only the first step, said Riley Duren, the former NASA engineer who founded Carbon Mapper. “In parallel,” he said, “reduce food waste. Full stop. Then divert organic waste away from landfills to prevent future emissions.”

This isn’t a utopian fantasy. Germany started phasing out the landfilling of biodegradable waste in 1993, and its landfill methane emissions have plunged by more than 90%. (That compares to a decline of 40% in the U.S. over roughly the same period.) Within the U.S., California now requires food scraps and yard trimmings to be collected for composting or other uses, and state regulators found that the economic, climate and health benefits would ultimately outweigh the costs.

In its glossy sustainability reports, Republic says that “organics recycling plays an important role in our operations.” And in California, with its mandatory collection rules, the company processed close to a million tons of organic waste last year, much of that at composting facilities.

But that remains a small fraction of its business. Speaking to a different kind of audience — investors — Republic has described landfilling, along with dumpster collection, as its most profitable segments. So when the EPA floated a federal organics-diversion policy in 2024, the company, along with the rest of the landfill industry, opposed this, too. Their response invoked an argument often used by opponents to regulation: It should be left to the states to decide.

“It’s like you’ve got a mousetrap, and it catches mice,” said Robert Bullard, a Texas Southern University professor widely seen as the father of the environmental justice movement. “You’ve got a landfill, and it makes money — big money. So why tinker with it?”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. author: Simon Childs
title: Millions of Workers Shut Down Spain With First General Strike in 14 Years
content:
Spanish workers braved stormy weather to go on general strike in protest against the country’s housing crisis on Wednesday.




Unions reported 90% turnouts among dockworkers and carmakers, as millions downed tools three weeks before a snap general election. There were 

“total stoppages”

 at Volkswagen’s factory in Navarre and SEAT’s in Barcelona, organisers said.




Around 85% of meat industry workers, 82% of waste collection employees and 75% from the energy sector are also taking part, they added. In healthcare and ⁠social services roughly 38% are striking while 35% of postal service workers have also joined.




The 24-hour strike, Spain’s first in 14 years, is backed by the country’s two biggest unions, UGT and CCOO, as well as tenants’ associations fighting rising rents and evictions.




“We won’t stop until we transform this country’s housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the rentier minority,” said Alicia del Rio of the Madrid Tenants’ Union.




Mass protest marches were planned for Wednesday afternoon despite the expected arrival of two storms, Charles and Bruna.




Unions pointed to a 10% drop in electricity demand across the country, saying it shows that activity in energy-intensive industries such as steel processing had come to a halt.




Barcelona’s metro is only running during peak commuting hours. Protesters swarmed Madrid’s municipal bus depot in an attempt to stop busses from moving and dragged wheelie bins into roads in order to stop traffic. Shops in Barcelona were closed in anticipation of unrest.




The CCOO union 

said on X

 that 13 people in Madrid needed medical attention after police fired pepper spray at picketers. “It’s a disgrace that workers are being prevented from exercising their right to strike,” the union said.




Spain has witnessed weeks of protests over housing, sparked by the eviction and subsequent death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal. 




The country  has a deficit of 750,000 homes, which is set to grow to over a million by 2028. The average rental price of a home – €1,176 – is equivalent to 98.7% of the average young person’s monthly salary, according to the Youth Council of Spain.




The protests have led Spain’s government to call a snap election on 29 November, after it was unable to pass housing reforms in the legislature, where it lacks an outright majority. 




With the far-right ahead in the polls, Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party prime minister Pedro Sanchez is hoping to mobilise his base around the housing crisis despite criticism from protesters that his government has failed to address the issue for years. 




A train c that killed dozens on the high speed line south from Madrid last month – the country’s fourth deadly train crash this year –  has also damaged confidence in Sanchez’s government.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Six hopefuls in running for Kitikmeot Inuit Association president
content:
Six candidates have put their name forward in the Kitikmeot Inuit Association’s presidential election.




The organization that manages lands in trust for Kitikmeot Inuit will elect its president, a vice-president and three regional board of directors on Dec. 14.




Two other Inuit organizations, Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. and Qikiqtani Inuit Association, will also host their 

leadership elections

 the same day.




The KIA presidential nominees are Jeannie Ehaloak, Rosabelle Klengenberg and Lawrence Otokiak from Cambridge Bay; Simon Komangat and Raymond Quqshuun Sr. from Gjoa Haven; and David Audlatak Nivingalok from Kugluktuk, according to a news release from the organization.




Since late June, Nivingalok has served as acting president after KIA announced former president James Eetoolook had to take leave “for personal matters.”




James Aiyout, Abel Aqqaq, David Aqqaq, and Ashoona Iroqiut hope to be elected to the board to represent Taloyoak.




Kugluktuk and Kugaaruk have one person running for their community’s spot on the board of directors: Leah Kadlun put her name forward for the Kugluktuk seat, and Tars Angutingunirk put his name forward to represent Kugaaruk.
















The nomination period for KIA’s social and cultural vice-president position has been extended until Friday.




Successful candidates will hold onto their roles until 2030.
