author: Jesse Hagopian
title: Paulo Freire’s Revolutionary Approach to Literacy Still Threatens Those in Power
content:
The new documentary Reading the World reveals how teaching literacy in Brazil became a struggle for political power.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

In 1963, Brazilian educator Paulo Freire helped launch a revolutionary literacy campaign in the impoverished northeastern Brazilian town of Angicos, where hundreds of rural workers learned to read and write in just 40 hours of instruction. Freire’s approach was about much more than literacy. Rather than emphasizing memorization and repetition, he developed “Culture Circles” where participants discussed their experiences, examined the conditions shaping their lives, and developed the critical consciousness to challenge oppression.

The experiment helped lay the groundwork for Freire’s groundbreaking book, Pedagogy of the Oppressed, which would become one of the most influential works in the history of education. But the literacy campaign was violently interrupted when a U.S.-backed military coup overthrew Brazilian President João Goulart in 1964. Freire was imprisoned and forced into exile, while students burned or buried their educational materials to escape persecution.

A powerful new documentary Reading the World (Lendo o Mundo) explores this formative period in Freire’s life, before he became an internationally celebrated educational philosopher. Drawing on rare archival footage of 1960s Brazil and the memories of the farmers, students, and educators who participated in the Culture Circles, the film reveals how Freire’s ideas emerged from grassroots struggles for literacy, land, voting rights, and democracy.

The film, which premiered in New York and aired on PBS WORLD Channel this October, arrives at a time when educators in the United States are confronting renewed censorship, book bans, and political attacks on teaching about racism and inequality.

I spoke with Catherine Murphy, co-director of Reading the World, about the revolutionary potential of literacy, the political forces that sought to destroy Freire’s educational experiment, and why his ideas continue to threaten those in power.

The interview that follows has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Jesse Hagopian: One of my favorite moments in the film is the opening scene, when Paulo Freire tells his audience that he wants to have a dialogue with them rather than give a lecture. He also promises that if he doesn’t know an answer, he won’t lie. It seems like such a simple statement, but it represents a profound departure from traditional teaching. Who was Freire, and what made his approach so revolutionary?

Catherine Murphy: Paulo Freire was a Brazilian educator born in Recife in 1921. He became one of the world’s most celebrated educational philosophers. His most famous book, Pedagogy of the Oppressed, was published while he was in exile.

I also love that opening quote because it lays the groundwork for the entire film. Freire says that ever since he was a child, he understood that not knowing is part of knowing.

That gets to the essence of Freire’s philosophy: Knowledge belongs to all of us. Knowledge is generated by all of us. Education is a reciprocal, collective process. It’s about sharing what we know, and learning from each other. Freire critiqued what he called “the banking model of education” and favored a “dialogic” process based on horizontal dialogue, problem-posing, and really listening to each other.

As Freire became internationally recognized, he was increasingly invited to speak at conferences and educational institutions around the world. But his collaborators repeatedly told me stories about how he didn’t want to simply deliver lectures. He wanted dialogue with people, to listen.

When Freire visited the Highlander Center in 1987 or attended the Chicago Alternative Schools Network Conference in 1977, he wanted to know what people were doing themselves. What were popular educators doing? What were classroom teachers, community educators, and activists doing? What was working? What were they struggling with?

Freire was willing to share his ideas and experiences, but he also wanted to learn from others.

That is a beautiful lesson for all of us, not only in formal educational spaces, but in life.

Before we get into Freire’s literacy campaign, can you describe the conditions in northeastern Brazil in the early 1960s? How did illiteracy help maintain existing relations of economic and political power?

Brazil in the late 1950s and early 1960s had a highly colonial and feudal social, political, and economic structure. They had highly concentrated landownership, with 1 percent of the population owning the vast majority of the and an agricultural labor system that was only one step removed from legal slavery.

Freire came from this region of northeastern Brazil, a region often compared to the U.S. South because its economy had been based on enslavement. In northeastern Brazil at the time, approximately 70 percent of people could not read or write. Education was almost exclusively reserved for children of the elite. Most formal education was provided through the Catholic Church or elite universities.

Access to education was restricted to a very small segment of society, who would then go on to control the political and economic institutions of the country.

This was not simply a question of individuals lacking educational opportunities. Illiteracy was deeply connected to the concentration of wealth, landownership, and political power.

And the struggle for education was inseparable from the struggle for voting rights, labor organizing, and land reform. The people who had been systematically excluded from education were also excluded from many forms of political participation.

One person in the film gives an important insight that “literacy is achieved through the discussion of political topics.” That struck me because so much contemporary advocacy around what’s called the “science of reading” leaves out the social and political context that makes reading meaningful — for example, the fact that many books are being banned right now. Your film is called Reading the World, which speaks to Freire’s understanding that learning to read words is connected to learning to critically examine society. What did his approach look like in practice?

That wonderful quote is from Marcos Guerra, a leader in the Brazilian student movement, at the time which was playing a major role in struggles for educational reform.

Marcos was recruited [in 1962] by Freire to work with him in Angicos in 1963, and I’ll tell a bit about that history.

Freire began developing his approach to adult literacy in Recife in the late 1950s. Based on that work, he was invited to come work in the neighboring state of Rio Grande do Norte, where adult illiteracy was around 70 percent.

From the very beginning, he wanted the project to be collective and participatory.

He didn’t want the project to be run by the Ministry of Education, where it might get caught up in bureaucracy or become a political photo opportunity. Instead, he wanted to work with university students from different academic disciplines, including student organizers.

Marcos Guerra was one of those students, and was brought in by Freire to be the student coordinator of the Angicos project.

Together with other teachers and learners, they began developing a methodology that broke dramatically from traditional adult literacy instruction.

First, they refused to use children’s books to teach adults. They wanted to honor the tremendous knowledge and wisdom adults already possessed, even if those adults had been excluded from formal education.

They understood students as holders of knowledge and creators of culture.

They gathered vocabulary from the communities themselves, using local language and words connected to people’s everyday lives.

“In the process of learning to read the word, students were also learning to examine and interrogate the world around them, their place within it, and how it could be transformed.”

One of their first words was tijolo, meaning brick. A brick could become a metaphor for constructing words out of letters and syllables, just as workers construct buildings out of bricks.

But the words also included things like people, vote, land, and work.

These words opened conversations about people’s lives and the social conditions they experienced.

So in the process of learning to read the word, students were also learning to examine and interrogate the world around them, their place within it, and how it could be transformed.

One of the most moving parts of the film is hearing people describe what it meant to learn to read and write. One woman remembers, “It was wonderful,” and explains that learning to write your name was an enormous achievement. That made me think of my great-great-grandmother, Laura Lenoir, who was enslaved in Mississippi and became an educator after emancipation. My family recently discovered the plantation where Laura had been enslaved. We also found her signature — evidence that she had learned to write despite being born into a system that made it illegal for Black people to be literate. During Reconstruction, formerly enslaved people organized extraordinary literacy campaigns because they understood that education was essential to making emancipation meaningful. I see my family’s history reflected in the experiences of the Brazilian farmers in your film. What did learning to read mean to them, and why do these memories evoke such powerful emotions more than 60 years later?

I really appreciate the connections you’re drawing between Reconstruction in the United States, the Freedmen’s Bureau schools, and the relationship between emancipation and education.

In Brazil, just as in the long Black freedom struggle in the United States, access to literacy was tied to the struggle for voting rights, land, and self-determination.

People whose labor had been exploited for generations through enslavement and then through forms of quasi-enslavement after emancipation were often locked into those relationships partly because they couldn’t read or write.

Think about the history of people losing their land because they couldn’t read a contract. Someone tells them, “This contract says this. Just sign here.” They put down a thumbprint or an X without having certainty of what they’re signing.

“In Brazil, just as in the long Black freedom struggle in the United States, access to literacy was tied to the struggle for voting rights, land, and self-determination.”

Just as what happened to Black people in the United States, and it happened to people in Brazil.

So literacy was connected to people’s ability to defend their rights, have access to land, and participate in political life. And it began with something that might seem small but was actually enormous: learning to write your name.

Writing your name affirms your humanity. It affirms your dignity.

Freire talked about becoming a subject, becoming a protagonist in your own life. Literacy provided people with greater tools for self-determination. Once people could read and write, they could obtain identification documents. Many of the students in Angicos had never previously had any form of identification. And then they could register to vote.

So people were becoming empowered both personally and collectively to change the world around them.

One of the most haunting details in the film is what happened after Brazil’s 1964 military coup. Farmers burned or buried their notebooks so they wouldn’t get caught with contraband, and Freire himself was arrested, imprisoned, and forced into exile. There’s something extraordinary about a government that considers teaching impoverished farmers to read and write so threatening that it imprisons educators and drives them out of the country. What made Freire’s and his collaborators’ educational approach so dangerous to the dictatorship? And how was it connected to the broader struggle over land, class, democracy, and political power?

When you enter a society with these colonial, feudal, quasi-slavery relationships and begin teaching people who have been systematically excluded from education, you’re putting a crowbar into the existing social structure.

Exclusion from literacy meant exclusion from voting, obtaining identification documents, organizing, and participating in political life. At the time, rural labor organizing was also restricted. There was a powerful movement called the ligas camponesas, or peasant leagues, which was fighting for land reform. Some of the important leaders were Elizabeth Teixeira and Francisco Julião, both of whom are in the film.

These movements were demanding access to education, voting rights, land, and land reform.

The progressive president at the time, João Goulart, was beginning to respond to grassroots demands.

In March 1964, Goulart announced reforms that included expanding voting rights and beginning a limited land redistribution program. The land reform proposal wasn’t even especially radical. It involved allowing landless agricultural workers to use strips of federal land along highways, where they could live, grow food, and sell their produce. For workers trapped in plantation-like conditions, these reforms could begin changing their lives.

And literacy work was a crucial part of that transformation.

In Angicos, approximately 300 newly literate adults could potentially become 300 new voters. At the time, there were only around 700 registered voters in the town. Think about how dramatically that could alter the political balance. President Goulart actually attended the graduation ceremony in Angicos, accompanied by a presidential delegation that included numerous governors and mayors from the northeast, and a group of military officers. Some of those officers would later lead the U.S.-backed military coup that overthrew Goulart’s government in 1964 and ushered in more than two decades of dictatorship.

The military dictatorship understood that this literacy campaign was connected to movements challenging the concentration of economic and political power. So Freire and his collaborators became targets. Marcos Guerra and other members of Freire’s team were arrested the very next day after the coup. They confiscated books. Students in Angicos destroyed their educational materials, burning or burying their notebooks and other records out of fear.

The extraordinary historical footage in our film survived only because people deliberately hid it.

The filmmaker Luiz Lobo, for example, preserved film reels documenting the Angicos experience by hiding them for years, buried in a trunk in his family’s backyard. So the footage we’re able to witness today exists because people recognized the importance of preserving this history, even at considerable personal risk.

Education under capitalism contains a fundamental contradiction. The system needs education to reproduce itself, but education can also give people the knowledge and confidence to challenge the existing order. In 2012, officials in Tucson, Arizona, banned Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed and several other books from the Mexican American Studies curriculum — they actually removed the books in the middle of class! Today, we’re witnessing widespread attacks on teaching Black history and ethnic studies, and on educators who embrace Freire’s approach. Why do Freire’s ideas remain so threatening to those in power, and what do they teach us about education as a force for liberation?

Freire’s ideas, like those of other liberation thinkers, call upon us to question the world and our place in it. His approach is about developing critical consciousness through problem-posing education. It asks us to consider: Why is the world like this? How could it be different?

And, significantly, this kind of education asks us to question power.

What are the structures of power? How do they create inequalities? And how can people become collectively empowered to challenge those structures? Freire’s ideas challenge the false narratives that tell us the world is simply the way it’s supposed to be. They challenge notions of social Darwinism and the mythology of meritocracy — the idea that everyone simply gets what they work for. Instead, liberatory education encourages us to ask: What laws, structures, and institutional injustices hold people back? These are questions we need to raise and examine over and over.

But people who benefit from existing power structures often don’t want those questions asked. That’s why books become threatening. That’s why there are attempts to ban books and suppress discussions. And of course, [this is] connected to the emphasis on standardized testing, the undermining of the humanities, the privatization of education, the underpayment of teachers, and attacks on teachers’ unions.

These conversations are potentially transformative. They give people the opportunity to examine their circumstances and imagine something different.

And those who feel threatened by that possibility want to stop those conversations.

I love the scene in the film where a woman puts on a shirt bearing Freire’s words: “Whoever believes in changing reality must carry out the transformation.” Your film also emphasizes the collective experiences of farmers and educators rather than simply celebrating Freire as a great individual. What lessons should educators and organizers draw from this history today?

What I love about that quote is that Freire calls upon us to do something. It’s a call to action.

“If we know something is wrong, if we recognize injustice, if we believe the world needs to change, then we have a responsibility to be part of that transformation.”

If we know something is wrong, if we recognize injustice, if we believe the world needs to change, then we have a responsibility to be part of that transformation.

And I think that’s especially important for educators today, when we’re living through such a challenging period for people who believe in democracy and want to expand it. Freire also spoke a great deal about hope. In Portuguese and Spanish, Freire had this idea of turning hope into a verb: Esperanzar. Hope isn’t just a passive feeling. It’s something active.

It’s about remaining engaged, continuing to care, and working collectively toward a world that’s better for everyone, not just a tiny, privileged few.

One of our central purposes in making this film was to move beyond understanding Freire simply as a man of ideas. We wanted to understand him as a person of action.

So many of his ideas emerged from concrete experiences working with communities and grassroots movements. We wanted to understand who he was working with, who his closest collaborators were in these early educational experiences. It’s important to recognize the farmers, students, and community organizers as co-creators of this history.

And that legacy is still alive.

People continue this work in Brazil, the United States, and throughout the world. The struggle to expand access to education, develop critical consciousness, and build collective power is ongoing.

Freire’s legacy isn’t simply something to study in books. It’s something people are continuing to create through their struggles today.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Exigen reconocimiento de enfermedades laborales en escuelas por agrotóxicos
content:
Más de 165 organizaciones sindicales y colectivos socioambientales presentaron un petitorio ante la Dirección General de Cultura y Educación bonaerense (DGCyE), en La Plata, con más de 3.000 firmas de integrantes de comunidades educativas y de la población en general, para exigirle al Estado el reconocimiento de las enfermedades laborales de trabajadores/as de la educación originadas por la exposición a las fumigaciones con agrotóxicos y al consumo de agua con estos elementos, y por el efecto sinérgico que se produce por su combinación con agua contaminada con niveles de arsénico más elevados de lo permitido por normativa, en las instituciones educativas.







“Los casos de las compañeras maestras Ana Zabaloy en San Antonio de Areco (pcia Bs As), víctima de asesinato laboral por trabajar en condiciones insalubres en una escuela rural y a quien el Estado nunca le reconoció su enfermedad oncológica en el marco de la Ley de Riesgos de Trabajo; y de Estela Lemes en Entre Ríos, quien presenta agrotóxicos en sangre y tuvo que judicializar su situación para que le reconozcan su enfermedad laboral, son ejemplos contundentes del impacto del agronegocio en la salud. Se suman argumentos a nuestro planteo con la reciente investigación y denuncia protagonizada por el sindicato AMSAFE Rosario del 2024 (en ese entonces con la conducción de la Lista Multicolor) que demostró que docentes y auxiliares de distintas escuelas presentaban daño génico por la presencia de agrotóxicos en su ambiente laboral”, detallan las organizaciones, al tiempo que invitan a Sindicatos Docentes y de Auxiliares de la Educación a que se sumen a esta demanda.




Entre las medidas urgentes que reclaman las organizaciones se encuentran el reconocimiento inmediato, y con carácter retroactivo, de las enfermedades laborales productos del agronegocio; la implementación de programas permanentes de vigilancia sanitaria para docentes y auxiliares; la realización de análisis integrales del agua en todos los establecimientos educativos, donde se provea agua segura hasta tanto se demuestre su potabilidad; medidas de protección con aumento de distancias progresivas ante las fumigaciones de agrotóxicos para garantizar las condiciones mínimas de seguridad e higiene en cada escuela, en función de que se cumplan los derechos laborales básicos.




“La salud de las comunidades educativas no puede esperar. Exigimos respuestas concretas y medidas urgentes para garantizar el derecho a la salud y a condiciones de trabajo y de enseñanza seguras”, reclaman las organizaciones.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: The children in revolt
content:
by Francesco Demitry




from 

lundimatin

, #541, 10/11/2026




They learn to wait for the bell, the bus, their turn to speak, permission to go out, for the day someone deems them old enough to understand the world. They learn to become alienated. They learn to keep quiet, to be silent. Then, one morning, they overturn the tables in front of the gate, and the town discovers they exist.







The young people who have occupied the streets in Italy and France in recent weeks are not mere ambassadors of hope, nor are they the innocent mascots of a political establishment running out of words. They are bodies that are hungry, that are cold, that feel anger and desire, that know overcrowded classrooms, dismantled services, and a mortgaged future. In France, the mobilisation began in the Parisian suburbs, where students denounced the deterioration of schools, vacant teaching positions, and the lack of nurses and social workers. It spread to more than a thousand schools across the country. In Italy, students led the marches against the high cost of living, rents, low wages, rearmament, and the war economy. In Genoa, thousands of people entered the port to protest the transit of weapons. Different stories, but on both sides of the Alps, the same melody is emerging: that of a generation rejecting a world it is supposed to inherit, a world that is already closed.




To whom does a school belong without teachers? To whom belongs a city where the bus is too expensive, where housing is becoming unaffordable, where the park is fenced off and the courtyard sold? School is where inequality is laid bare: a crumbling building in a working-class neighborhood, a replacement teacher who never arrives, a closed workshop, a dry tap. Our address should not determine our future, some French high school students have written. Capitalism seeks to transform space into destiny, assigning each person a piece of the city and calling the distance between those who can cross it and those who must remain confined to their neighborhood or be evicted a matter of merit.




Governments respond with budgets and decrees. They announce recruitment and controls, deploy law enforcement. On November 5th, in France, as unions and students took to the streets again to demand better wages, public services, and education, the state deployed a significant security apparatus. In Italy, a few days earlier, police water cannons had dispersed a march in Turin. Faced with people forging their own path, the authorities presented the bill: order. But a public square is not a classroom that can simply be brought into line. The square is overflowing; it is bursting at the seams. Those who are protesting cannot simply be asked to raise their hands and wait for their demands to be reviewed by the appropriate department.




Luis Buñuel found an extraordinary image of how a social class, that of the old petty bourgeoisie, manages to survive everything; even the disintegration of the world around it. In 

The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie

, six characters are constantly trying to sit down at the table, to have a meal, to re-establish the small order of their habits. But something intervenes each time to interrupt them: a corpse, an army, the police, a story of violence, a dream that invades reality. The world knocks on the dining room door, and dinner is inevitably postponed. And the most disturbing thing is not that these people continue to desire their meal, but that each catastrophe seems incapable of changing anything in their lives. The bourgeoisie possesses this extraordinary capacity: to absorb interruption, to transform conflict into an annoyance, a minor inconvenience, history into a conversation that must be interrupted, always with decorum. Even when everything falls apart, the napkin is folded, the glass refilled, the appointment postponed. But it is above all in 

The Phantom of Liberty

 that Buñuel pushes this intuition to its most radical consequences. A group of bourgeois is invited to dinner and cordially ushered around a table surrounded by toilets. The guests sit down, lower their trousers, relieve themselves, and, in the meantime, smoke while conversing amiably. They talk about travel, current events, social conventions, without anyone seeming to find anything strange about the situation. The indecency, if there is any in this scene, lies elsewhere: in the act of eating. When they are hungry, the guests discreetly withdraw to a small room to eat their meal alone, discreetly asking where the kitchen is, with the same shame as if they were trying to conceal something improper. In a matter of minutes, Buñuel overturns the entire edifice of convention: what civilization considers private becomes public, what is celebrated as a ritual of conviviality becomes a practice to be concealed. This is not mere provocation, but a radical critique of the social construction of decorum, of the artificial separation between the body and its representation, between material needs and the forms by which a society decides to make them acceptable. Eating and defecating belong to the same material continuity of life, but the bourgeois order distributes them into different spaces, times, and hierarchies, establishing what can be shown and what must be hidden. The body, with its needs, its biology, and its excesses, becomes something to be administered, disciplined, and, above all, made presentable.




Is not this one of the first operations by which children are educated? Proper posture, not getting dirty, not shouting, not touching, not running, asking permission, learning to control every bodily action. School thus becomes a small factory of decorum, where even vitality must learn to occupy its assigned space and respect a predetermined time. Children who disrupt this order are not simply disobeying the rules: for a few moments, they make visible the body that the social order seeks to domesticate.




This is why their revolt is so dangerous: they do not want to be invited to this table, do not ask to take their place, do not demand a larger portion of the same meal. None of that. Their revolt disrupts the ritual and reveals its violence. They ask who built this room, who set the table, who cooks, who stays behind the door. They don’t want to sit at the table, but to rearrange the house and leave.




Artaud sought in the body a language withdrawn from the control of the masters. Young people find it again in dissonant choruses, footsteps that disrupt traffic, painted placards, overlapping voices, even in battles of aura. The body in the street produces and imposes the programme, tests it, transforms it. Michaux would have recognised in these signs an unstable geography, a writing made of shifts, stains, and inventions. The protest has neither a center nor a phrase that can summarise it. It is made up of a multitude of gestures seeking a polyphonic composition: who holds the banner, who distributes water, who brings Maalox, who stops in front of a police cordon, who returns the next day, who joins the workers’ procession, who participates from afar.




Gianni Rodari

 knew that imagination is not a pastime that adults grant children once their homework is done. It is a political faculty that allows us to overturn words, to change the rules of the game, to discover that the world could have been built differently. In his grammar, error can become invention, an unexpected combination can open a path, an absurd question can reveal and dismantle the absurdity of habitual answers.




But what would happen if we applied this lesson to the city? What if, instead of teaching children to adapt to available spaces, we allowed them to invent others? What if the closed gate became a door, the abandoned lot a garden, the street a meeting place?




Children are not subjects unfamiliar with rules, but rather those who can demonstrate how contingent they are; and sometimes, how unjust they are.




Here, 

Colin Ward

 becomes an important ally. The city is also what children make of sidewalks, abandoned lots, and the passageways between buildings. Play is a practice of appropriating the world, an ability to organise oneself without waiting for permission.

[1]

 Nietzsche explained that we must relate to the world with the same seriousness as a child at play. Taking children seriously means recognising their political power and competence: forging alliances, inventing provisional rules, transforming a place, and caring for those left behind. When students block the school gate, the question must be what can be done together outside of the intended and pre-established use of this space.




There is another cinematic alliance I would like to mention: that of Harold and Maude in Hal Ashby’s film [of the same name]. Harold is a young man from a wealthy and privileged family, surrounded by objects, opportunities, and attention that never reach him (or from which he escapes). He constantly stages his own death, as if only the representation of the end could make visible an existence that others do not see. His mother, a bourgeois woman, tries to correct him by entrusting him to “experts” and attempting to make him respectable through marriage and social conventions. But then Maude, a woman approaching eighty, arrives unexpectedly, seemingly from another world. Maude attends funerals, steals cars, listens to music, indulges her desires, runs away and mocks the police, uproots a tree from the asphalt and carries it into the forest, returning it to a land where it can continue to grow. She does not want to teach Harold how to become a respectable adult, but shows him that it is still possible to let life flow through him, that there are encounters capable of reawakening the senses, that the world is by no means a possession to be kept, but a material to be transformed. Their alliance is based neither on resemblance nor on mutual reassurance. Together, they create an experience that neither of them could have generated alone. One generation can influence the other, reactivate its desires, open unexpected pathways. Maude takes Harold out of his home and returns the world to him as a sensory experience. And this tree replanted in the forest becomes more than an ecological gesture: it demonstrates that a life can be rescued from its assigned destiny and placed within a different network of relationships. It is about making possible again what does not yet exist.




Italo Calvino bequeathed to us cities that cannot be reduced to their walls, their monuments, their owners. Cities made of desires, memories, encounters, invisible relationships. 

Invisible Cities

 inhabit the possibilities that a real city contains but that its economic order prevents from being realised. Every neighbourhood could be another neighbourhood, every street could lead to an encounter rather than a parking lot, every empty space could become the site of a shared life. The lightness that Calvino offers is the gesture of one who manages to free the world from the weight of hierarchies, to imagine passages where power has chosen to build walls for its own benefit. Children do this constantly because they have not yet accepted that the harshness of the world, of which they are nonetheless aware, is the only thing that is possible one.




And there is something else that adults have taught children: time. Everything must be in its place; every activity has its appointed time; every desire is postponed until the opportune moment. The day is divided into segments, the body trained for punctuality, curiosity interrupted by the sound of the bell. We tell them that play must find its place in the schedule, as if it were a break from real life, the one in which we are (and must remain) immersed. Yet, it is precisely in this break that something escapes the measurement of production. A child can spend an entire afternoon (a lifetime) following an ant or a stream, inventing a city with three cardboard boxes or empty water bottles, following a path that leads nowhere. In economic terms, this means producing nothing. But that is wrong. On the contrary, the child produces relationships, discoveries, possibilities, and a quantity (and quality) of world that no indicator could ever quantify.




It’s also a question of time subtracted. Families have to rush to work, juggle schedules, pay for services that replace time spent caring, and be exasperated by children’s insistent demands. Teachers have to fill out forms, chase deadlines, and respond to administrative procedures. And the children? They must learn early, as early as possible, to be efficient, independent, and competitive, so as not to burden the bureaucratic and efficient organisation of real life. Life is thus constantly prepared, organised, and postponed. But when exactly does this life begin? When does the preparation finally end, and when does the right to inhabit the world begin? At what time? The promise of a better future becomes a perverse form of discipline, used to demand and justify the sacrifices of the present. Young people are told that one day they will be able to choose, provided that today they learn to obey. Their eruption into the streets challenges us and shatters this temporal blackmail. They are not simply asking for a different future: they are clamouring for a present where it is possible to live differently.




The children in revolt are the high school students in the streets and the children staring at closed shop windows, the striking workers, the parents struggling to make ends meet. They are the inhabitants of neighbourhoods without gardens, of villages where schools are closing, of territories ravaged by factories or highways. They are those who are asked to adapt to an increasingly uninhabitable planet. They are told that adaptation is a virtue, not a polite way of surrendering. Their revolt turns the question on its head: how do we dismantle the world that prevents them from truly inhabiting it?




Let us not, however, make the mistake of thinking that this would mean replacing adult politics with a children’s politics, as if two separate worlds existed and one had to finally take the place of the other. Revolt does not need a new identity to preserve, a chosen generation, or a savior figure come to redeem past defeats. Its movement is, fortunately, more unpredictable. A teenager blocking their school, a parent defending time for care, a teacher in a precarious situation, a worker going on strike, a resident preventing the overdevelopment of their neighbourhood can all recognise themselves in the same struggle without sharing the same history, the same language, or the same vision of the future. They do not need to become alike to find common ground. They must be able to mutually transform their possibilities.




An alliance is neither the sum of pre-existing interests, nor an agreement between organisations that decide to support each other. It is rather an encounter that transforms those who take part, unleashing previously nonexistent capacities. When student mobilisation meets workers’ strikes, when the right to education is intertwined with the right to housing, when the fight against war meets the struggle for territorial defence, it is not simply a matter of adding demands to a checklist. What changes is the way we perceive the conflict. What appears to be an individual problem reveals itself, as always, to be a social relationship. What seems like a simple local issue demonstrates its connection to a much larger economic machine.




This is why it is not enough to ask ourselves what children lack (resources, infrastructure, teachers, green spaces, time, affection…). Their presence cannot be understood through a kind of “catalogue of deprivations”. Desire, once again, does not arise from a void that someone should finally fill. Desire is revolutionary because it has the capacity to encounter, to combine, to build. An occupied courtyard, a communal kitchen, a school open to the neighbourhood, a garden rescued from neglect are not temporary responses to a lack, but genuine creations of reality, capable of bringing into being relationships that were previously nonexistent, of transforming a space, of generating new shared imaginaries. Revolt also begins in this way, when a possibility ceases to be merely conceived and becomes a practice.




And there can be no ecology without this capacity. Children are told that they must protect nature separate from the city, that they must recycle and turn off the lights, while adults continue to organise extraction, consumption, exploitation, and destruction. Ecology is not a virtuous behaviour to be added to the school curriculum, perhaps during extracurricular hours or dedicated subjects. Ecology is a question of the relationships between human beings and other forms of life, between bodies and environments, between those who decide the fate of a territory and those who are forced to endure it. What does it mean to talk about the future to a child growing up beside a polluted road, in a treeless suburb, in a territory where water is privatised or land is given over to speculation? The ecological crisis is not a distant threat. It is already distributed, in space and in bodies, according to a very precise class geography.




The children’s revolt connects the school with the river, the playground with the forest, the port with the neighbourhood, because children know that no form of life can be isolated from the relationships that make it possible. It is a politics of interdependence, a practice of alliance between heterogeneous worlds. A felled tree, a dried-up spring, an animal driven from its habitat—these too tell a story about this same world order that would have students silent and adults docile. There is no external environment that needs saving after society has been put back in order. Society is already an environment, made up of bodies, infrastructure, emotions, dependencies, and conflicts.




Perhaps we need a clandestine approach to possibility, in the sense of wresting life from prescribed destinies by reopening this administered future, which we treat as an already exhausted possibility. We must preserve a shared possibility at the heart of the catastrophe. We must not ask children to save us. Entrusting them with the weight (and the guilt) of our absolution would be the ultimate form of exploitation. Instead, let us ask that their presence transform our way of deciding, producing, and inhabiting. Revolt is life taking up space, here and now, in this very moment. If the streets are filling up again, it is because diverse bodies, often at odds, have discovered that they can walk together without becoming alike.




The city belongs neither to those who govern it nor to those who buy it. It belongs to those who traverse it, care for it, disrupt it, and reinvent it. One morning, the children overturn the tables, open the gates, and occupy the sidewalk. And the city, which wanted them in line, is forced, for a moment, to learn from them the most difficult verb: to begin.







[1]

 [T.N. See: Colin Ward,  

The Child in the City

 (1978), 

The Anarchist Library

.]

author: Andrea DiP
title: Protestos de jovens pelo mundo demonstram que ainda se pode sonhar com o futuro
content:
Uma onda de protestos liderados pela Geração Z está se levantando pelo mundo, trazendo uma lufada de ar fresco e remodelando cenários políticos. 




Nós vimos isso 

no Brasil com os atos encabeçados por movimentos estudantis que puxaram milhares de pessoas para as ruas e atuaram fortemente nas redes pela democracia e pela reeleição de Lula.

 

Na Itália, as jornadas estudantis pedem mais verbas para a educação pública

, melhorias em infraestrutura escolar e medidas contra o altíssimo custo de aluguéis e moradias estudantis. 

Na França, protestos que começaram em setembro também por demandas de melhor educação, melhor infraestrutura nas escolas e mais investimento, têm se intensificado e tomado as ruas de todo o país

 –  só no último dia 05, reuniram cerca de 600 mil pessoas, segundo números oficiais. 

Na Alemanha, o movimento Gen Z Regelt (Algo como “A Geração Z Resolve”) realizou atos em 34 cidades para protestar contra o serviço militar obrigatório e exigir mais investimentos em educação

, e no dia 31 de outubro botou nas ruas cerca de 120 mil pessoas.




Na Índia, o movimento Partido do Povo Barata (CJP, na sigla em inglês para

 

Cockroach Janta Party

) também tem levado milhares de jovens às ruas de Mumbai e Nova Deli para denunciar irregularidades na educação

, pedir a saída do ministro da Educação, Dharmendra Pradhan, e uma reforma no sistema de exames. O CJP é um movimento político liderado pela Geração Z indiana que surgiu a partir de declarações feitas em maio pelo presidente do Supremo Tribunal da Índia, que usou o termo “barata” para descrever jovens desempregados que se dedicam ao ativismo.




Os protestos movidos pelos GenZ – nascidos entre 1997 e 2012 – geralmente levantam pautas relacionadas à educação, mas também pedem a cabeça de líderes autoritários, atenção à emergência climática, às desigualdades sociais e abordam conflitos como o Genocídio em Gaza. São campanhas horizontais, sem um líder específico, e que usam as redes sociais para se organizar.




A repressão também tem sido violenta. Não é possível dizer o número certo de prisões porque os atos seguem acontecendo, mas estima-se que mais de 6 mil pessoas foram presas somente na França, sendo 87% delas menores de idade.




Em uma 

análise recente, a Civicus,

 organização sem fins lucrativos que monitora as liberdades civis globais, afirmou: 

“Como questionam a distribuição do poder econômico e político, os protestos liderados pela geração Z invariavelmente são recebidos com violência estatal”.

 O relatório relaciona a violência infligida aos jovens manifestantes com seu foco em sistemas e instituições que há muito tempo estavam simplesmente sendo aceitos.




Protestos liderados por movimentos estudantis não são novidade, claro. Mas o que torna essa nova onda interessante é o momento em que ela se levanta. 




Em um mundo que tem sido assolado por governos autoritários e populistas que fazem conchavos com Big Techs para intermediar todas as relações humanas e interferir na soberania de países, que incentivam o ódio, a misoginia, criam e alimentam um ambiente tóxico e violento para mulheres e LGBTQIA+, em um momento de múltiplas instabilidades, guerras e crises – climáticas, econômicas, institucionais, crises que desafiam o que entendemos por democracia e como víamos a política institucional e crises que atingem em cheio o modelo capitalista neoliberal que nos engole com seu ultra individualismo – 

os jovens vêm cobrar o que nunca lhes foi prometido. Eles vêm dizer que querem eles mesmos criar futuro. 




Pode parecer óbvio, mas não é.




Porque a essa geração foi oferecido pouco espaço para utopia, pouca imaginação de futuro, pouco encantamento.

 Para usar o termo que Paolo Demuru cunha em seu livro “Políticas do Encanto”: pouca perspectiva. Afinal, vivemos muitos pontos de não retorno. 




Ao mesmo tempo, o futuro baseado em um passado fantasioso prometido pela extrema direita, em que a emergência climática é mentira, que diz que é só expulsar imigrante que o emprego vem e a economia melhora, ou, na sua versão tecno-solucionista, que a IA resolveria todos os males do planeta, simplesmente não está acontecendo.




É nesse vácuo que 

a Geração Z ocupa as ruas, recusa tanto o passado inventado da extrema direita quanto o futuro tecno-solucionista das Big Techs, e reivindica o direito de imaginar. 




Bonito ver esses jovens devolverem à política algo que parecia perdido: a ideia de que o futuro ainda está em disputa e que dá para construí-lo coletivamente.

author: Derek Seidman
title: WWII Sparked Anti-Fascist Ideas Among War Workers. What Lessons Can We Learn?
content:
Historian Tejasvi Nagaraja explains how wartime mobilization generated wider organizing around labor, race, and empire.

Historian Tejasvi Nagaraja explains how wartime mobilization generated wider organizing around labor, race, and empire.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

World War II was a period of enormous mobilization in U.S. society that brought together tens of millions of “war workers” — soldiers and laborers in war-essential industries, spanning the globe. While mainstream mythologies persist of the World War II years as a period of “consensus,” Black Americans fought in a Jim Crow military while Japanese Americans were interned by the U.S. government. Moreover, the wartime mobilization generated massive conflict and resistance around labor, race, and empire.

Tejasvi Nagaraja is a historian of labor and racial capitalism at Cornell University, and the author of Troop Movements: Labor, Race, and Global Freedom Struggles in America’s World War II. As he shows in this new book, soldiers and defense workers, stationed across much of the world, waged and linked struggles for labor and civil rights and against colonialism and imperialism throughout the 1940s. Furthermore, many World War II veterans and war workers, drawing on wartime political experiences forged in a period of rising anti-fascist consciousness, went on to lead and provide guidance for major postwar U.S. social movements into the 1960s and beyond.

In this exclusive Truthout interview, published on Veteran’s Day, Nagaraja discusses Troop Movements and what lessons its history might hold for organizers and activists today. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Derek Seidman: The military is sometimes imagined as separate from the rest of society, but your book shows how blurred these lines really were during the 1940s. Can you elaborate on this?

Tejasvi Nagaraja: World War II was, at least for the United States, the closest thing to a total war mobilization. Most employment was converted to military service in the armed forces and to working in war-essential industries. Virtually every family and community had members in the military and defense industries.

The story I tell about World War II is about what happened in this realm, where tens of millions of people were in the armed forces and defense industries, and their experiences at home, but also abroad — in Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Caribbean.

Labor during World War II was not just working at a Michigan auto factory or Appalachian coal mine, but also cooking and cleaning on a military base in Texas and Mississippi or France, or building the Ledo Road across China, Burma, and India. These were sites of labor experience and labor struggle.

The 1930s and 1940s were a peak period of union membership growth and strike activity in U.S. history. Wildcat strikes were happening in defense industries during World War II. Service members in the Army, Navy, and Air Force engaged in wildcat strikes, hunger strikes, and mutinies to protest labor conditions.

The 1930s and 1940s were a peak period of union membership growth and strike activity in U.S. history. Wildcat strikes were happening in defense industries during World War II.

Black men and women protested labor, policing, and jailing conditions. They experienced race and class struggles — not just in Georgia, but in Massachusetts, as well as in France, India, and the Philippines. Their struggles linked up to global questions.

There was a real blurring of defense industry and service member labor, and civil rights and worker struggles, at home and abroad. It was a time of global anti-fascist struggle and global decolonial possibility, linking the U.S. working class, in some moments, to working people from other regions.

A huge part of the U.S. working class was tied to the war machine during World War II. How did leftists and anti-imperialists who opposed war and militarism engage with this reality?

The 1940s were a crucible through which the longer struggles of economic, racial, and global politics were transformed. In this context, labor, civil rights, and global justice activists navigated a contradictory and double-edged terrain. They sometimes made a devil’s bargain that we can understand as partly a question of choice and political ideology, but also of not making history as we please and having to navigate things bigger than oneself.

Labor unions, for example, embraced a no-strike pledge in exchange for winning union security in some defense industries. Even left-leaning Congress of Industrial Organization (CIO) unions had a seat at the table of the warfare state. In the textile mills of Georgia and North and South Carolina, union activists waged daring campaigns to unionize the very anti-union South, and they gained some openings when the War Department intervened in mid-1940s strikes to keep war production going.

At times, the Pentagon even partnered with CIO unionists to stand up to recalcitrant Jim Crow capitalists. After the war, however, those unions were left to fend for themselves and faced a reactionary push by the region’s Jim Crow capitalists.

As U.S. foreign policy shifted from anti-fascism to anti-communism and Third World interventionism, the military-industrial complex proved durable while the labor openings for more emancipatory possibilities became constrained by that very security state that arose during FDR’s anti-fascist war but then was consolidated in the Cold War anti-communist turn.

Again, you have these double-edged bargains: the civil rights movement navigating openings through defense industries and military service, but also brokering these civil rights possibilities around a U.S. becoming more permanently militarized.

How was this 1940s protest moment expressed within the military?

Service members and veterans themselves debated the postwar stakes for U.S. militarism. Active-duty service members stationed in the Philippines and Calcutta had mass meetings in 1945 and 1946 asking whether the U.S. would become an imperialist power of its own.

These service members debated how they could use their veteran identity to push for a wider vision of social democracy and civil rights in a peaceful United States. Even in a so-called “Good War” with popular support, many of them were critical of militarism and imperialism more generally.

Some service members were actually the first critics of postwar U.S. foreign policy, protesting in 1946 the U.S. aiding European colonial allies and U.S. policy toward the Philippines or Saudi Arabia.

Today, far fewer people work in defense industries. We have an all-volunteer army that has made war-work sectors more invisible and weakened the possibilities for democratic claims that could be made by service members. We think of military service now as a private individual choice — though service member identities would also be contested during the wars in Vietnam and Iraq.

Your book shows how World War II veterans and war industry workers played critical roles in postwar movements around labor, civil rights, and anti-colonialism. Can you elaborate?

I argue that this “greatest generation” of 1930s and 1940s labor, civil rights, and other social movements was also the vanguard of the 1960s movements, serving as middle-aged elders to the younger generation and setting in motion some of their movements. It built a bridge from the 1930s labor movement to the 1960s civil rights and antiwar movement.

A total war brings everybody together in a transformative experience. Before the war, when different people worked for different employers in different settings, it was harder to think about a bigger picture that links a national and international economy and politics.

But when tens of millions of people are working all over the world for this new thing called the Pentagon, directly as service members or indirectly as defense workers, they can see a bigger picture.

For example, Ossie Davis became a famous actor and senior statesman of labor, civil rights, and global justice movements, along with his partner Ruby Dee, from the 1940s to the 1960s. Davis spent most of the World War II years in West Africa, seeing, as a Black working-class American, the U.S. Army projecting power abroad. He saw Firestone Tire and Rubber Company — one of the biggest corporations in the world, with Pentagon war contracts — controlling the biggest rubber plantation in the world in Liberia.

All this was formative for Davis developing a larger vision — seeing how working-class and Black struggles in Georgia or Harlem were linked to global capitalism and global war.

The interracial labor and civil rights movements, and even early queer and feminist movements, of the 1940s would grow into the movements of the 1960s. And many key people in those 1940s movements were formed in this culture of CIO unionism, and of a labor-civil rights-veterans coalition, as active-duty service members, returning veterans, and defense workers in the 1940s. They came into their political life in this moment of anti-fascist consciousness during a global war.

Mainstream commemorations of Veterans Day tend to ignore the robust tradition of GI and veteran organizing for peace and justice. How does your book help us counter the right’s capture of veteran history and identity?

Service member and veteran identity is a contested thing that’s always been fought over.

World War II saw a mass service member experience where people from all walks of life were drafted into the armed forces. CIO union and civil rights organizers went into the Army and Air Force and engaged in civil rights and anti-imperial mutinies and strikes from Indiana to the Philippines.

Many of these people asserted their veteran identity in labor, civil rights, and veterans’ groups from the mid-1940s onward to make a claim on U.S. citizenship to criticize reactionary capitalist, racist, and imperialist trajectories.

CIO union and civil rights organizers went into the Army and Air Force and engaged in civil rights and anti-imperial mutinies and strikes from Indiana to the Philippines.

It was only with the 1950s Red Scare that conservative hegemony asserted itself over veteran identity. But in the 1940s, you had groups like the American Veterans Committee, with a mass membership linked to the NAACP and the CIO unions, advocating for peaceful social democracy.

Some of the first protesters of a U.S. global empire in 1945 and 1946 were CIO organizers in the army mobilizing mass protests in Honolulu, Paris, and Manila, demanding speedy demobilization to go home and criticizing the new U.S. imperialism and aid to European colonialism.

There were bitter conflicts over veteran identity during the Vietnam War. Some mobilized to support the brutal U.S. war, but others engaged in widespread GI and veteran resistance.

It’s different in the post-Vietnam era with the turn to an all-volunteer army. You have groups like About Face using their veteran identity in critiquing U.S. foreign policy, but there’s also much fewer people engaging in military service.

What do you think left organizers and movement activists today can learn from the history you write about?

Bigger lessons from World War II still hold today. How do you stitch together a broader populist base moving in a progressive direction, led by some people who have a more daring and even radical vision?

I write about the “Bring the Boys Home” demobilization movement in 1946. Some participants were not very political and just wanted to go home, but they were mobilized by people with a left-leaning vision.

Today, with Trump’s unpopular war on Iran, you have everyday expressions of service member defiance, like on the USS Gerald Ford, which aren’t necessarily politicized. How could activists connect up with that?

In our moment, there’s widespread defiance against U.S. foreign policy and a broader discontent among even more apolitical working-class people. There’s an opening to challenge the bipartisan foreign policy elite and assert something new — not just what’s good for us, but for the wider world.

Local struggles around labor, race, policing — they’re deeply interconnected with global wars and global capitalism. When people see the foreign and the domestic, the local and the global, as linked, it can embolden a horizon of anti-fascist urgency. In the 1930s and 1940s, this allowed for positive fights for racial and economic justice.

When people see the foreign and the domestic, the local and the global, as linked, it can embolden a horizon of anti-fascist urgency.

Today, as we face neo-fascism in our times, it’s an opportunity to confront not only the worst horrors in the Middle East or ICE at home, but to imagine a positive reconstruction, linking global justice with our local racial and economic justice work. Studying this history has painful lessons — Japanese Americans faced mass incarceration, and Black Americans faced Jim Crow segregation — but also lessons of tremendous success that can help us move in a positive coalitional direction and with a cross-issue vision for our own times.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $47,000 in the next 8 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

title: Απελευθέρωση του Μπαρίς Ερχάν – Συλλογή υπογραφών
content:
Σκίτσο: Γιώργος Κωνσταντίνου




Μια κραυγή μέσα από τους τοίχους της φυλακής, η επιστολή του Barış Erhan. Είναι η φωνή ενός ανθρώπου που εγκατέλειψε την Τουρκία αναζητώντας ασφάλεια και ελευθερία, για να βρεθεί στην Ελλάδα αντιμέτωπος με μια πρωτόδικη καταδίκη 74 χρόνων και ενός μήνα για διακίνηση μεταναστών. Θύμα της θανατοπολιτικής του ελληνικού κράτους και της ΕΕ.




Πολιτικός ακτιβιστής, σοσιαλιστής και καλλιτέχνης, ο Barış περιγράφει τη διαδρομή του και τη δράση του, τις διώξεις στην Τουρκία, τις συνθήκες σύλληψης και δίκης στην Ελλάδα, αλλά και την οδυνηρή εμπειρία της φυλάκισης. Καταγγέλλει σοβαρές αδικίες και ζητά να ακουστεί…




Η μαρτυρία του ξεπερνά τα όρια μιας προσωπικής υπόθεσης. Θέτει ένα κρίσιμο ερώτημα για τη δικαιοσύνη, τα δικαιώματα των προσφύγων και τη μεταχείριση όσων κατηγορούνται για διακίνηση ανθρώπων. Πίσω από τους αριθμούς και τις βαριές ποινές υπάρχουν άνθρωποι, ζωές και αξιοπρέπειες που δεν μπορούν να αγνοούνται.




Ο Barış ζητά να μην παραμείνει αόρατος και ξεχασμένος. Η επιστολή του είναι μια έκκληση για αλήθεια, δικαιοσύνη και ελευθερία. Γιατί η αλληλεγγύη δεν σταματά στις πόρτες των φυλακών — και η ανθρώπινη αξιοπρέπεια δεν φυλακίζεται.

»




Γράμμα από τη φυλακή. Είμαι ο Barış Erhan. Είμαι φυλακισμένος στην Ελλάδα από τις 29.07.2024

title: Συγκέντρωση και συναυλία για το δικαίωμα στη στέγαση, την Τετάρτη 11/11, 18.30, Πάρκο Νίκου Παπάζογλου, Κάτω Τούμπα
content:
Συγκέντρωση και unplugged συναυλία για το δικαίωμα στη στέγαση στο πλαίσιο του αγώνα ενάντια στην έξωση του ζευγαριού ηλικιωμένων στην Καππαδοκίας 64 αλλά και ενόψει της Ευρωπαϊκής Ημέρας Δράσης για τη Στέγη , την Τετάρτη 11/11, 18.30, Πάρκο Νίκου Παπάζογλου (Πρώην Άγιος Θεράποντας), Κάτω Τούμπα.







Καλούν οι: 

 Ένωση Ενοικιαστ(ρι)ών Θεσσαλονίκης και η Οριζόντια Κίνηση

 

–

 

Για την Αναρχία και τον Ελευθεριακό Κομμουνισμό




Ένωση Ενοικιαστ(ρι)ών Θεσσαλονίκης







Unplugged συναυλία για το δικαίωμα στη στέγη | Τετάρτη 11 Νοεμβρίου, 18:30 | Πάρκο Νίκου Παπάζογλου, Κάτω Τούμπα




Την Τετάρτη 11 Νοεμβρίου, στο πλαίσιο της Ευρωπαϊκής Ημέρας Δράσης για τη Στέγη, η Ένωση Ενοικιαστ(ρι)ών Θεσσαλονίκης διοργανώνει ανοιχτή unplugged συναυλία για το δικαίωμα στη στέγη, στις 18:30, στο πάρκο Νίκου Παπάζογλου (Αγίου Θεράποντα), στην Κάτω Τούμπα!




Από τη Μαδρίτη ως την Αθήνα και από τη Σουηδία ως την Αλβανία, βγαίνουμε στους δρόμους και στις πλατείες, σε αλληλεγγύη με την πανισπανική απεργία και τις ευρωπαϊκές κινητοποιήσεις για τη στέγη και το κόστος ζωής.




Με μουσική, συνθήματα και συλλογική παρουσία στη γειτονιά, δίνουμε ζωή στον δημόσιο χώρο και διεκδικούμε το δικαίωμα να συνεχίσουμε να ζούμε στα σπίτια και στις πόλεις μας!




 Unplugged συναυλία για το δικαίωμα στη στέγη




Συμμετέχουν




– Παραβάτες




– Παράζαλ Band




– Γλέντι με χάλκινα από τις 19:00




 Τετάρτη 11/11, στις 18:30




 Πάρκο Νίκου Παπάζογλου (Αγίου Θεράποντα), Κάτω Τούμπα




Η συναυλία πραγματοποιείται στην ίδια γειτονιά όπου τις προηγούμενες ημέρες δόθηκε ένας σημαντικός αγώνας ενάντια στην έξωση του ηλικιωμένου ζευγαριού. Η αναβολή της έξωσης μέχρι τις 19 Ιανουαρίου αποτελεί μια πρώτη ουσιαστική νίκη της οικογένειας, των σωματείων ενοικιαστ(ρι)ών, των εργατικών σωματείων, των συλλογικοτήτων, της γειτονιάς και της κοινωνίας της Θεσσαλονίκης. Μια νίκη που μας δίνει δύναμη να συνεχίσουμε, γιατί ο αγώνας για την οριστική προστασία της κατοικίας δεν έχει τελειώσει!




Τα δυσβάσταχτα ενοίκια, οι πλειστηριασμοί, οι εξώσεις, οι καταχρηστικές πρακτικές των εκμισθωτών και η τουριστικοποίηση των γειτονιών μας δεν είναι ανεξάρτητα προβλήματα. Είναι διαφορετικές πλευρές της ίδιας στεγαστικής κρίσης, που απειλεί όλο και περισσότερους ανθρώπους με εκτοπισμό από τα σπίτια και τις γειτονιές τους.




Η στεγαστική κρίση δεν έπεσε από τον ουρανό. Είναι αποτέλεσμα συγκεκριμένων πολιτικών που μετατρέπουν την κατοικία από κοινωνικό αγαθό σε επενδυτικό προϊόν. Οι πλειστηριασμοί, η συγκέντρωση ακινήτων σε επενδυτικά χαρτοφυλάκια, η κερδοσκοπία και η τουριστικοποίηση βάζουν τα κέρδη πάνω από τις στεγαστικές ανάγκες των ανθρώπων.




Ως Ένωση Ενοικιαστ(ρι)ών Θεσσαλονίκης απαιτούμε:




– Πλαφόν στα ενοίκια τώρα!




– Δημόσια και κοινωνική κατοικία για όλους και όλες!




– Προστασία από τις εξώσεις και τις καταχρηστικές πρακτικές!




– Ουσιαστική προστασία της πρώτης κατοικίας!




– Ουσιαστικό περιορισμό της βραχυχρόνιας μίσθωσης και κατάργηση της Golden Visa!




– Τέλος στην κερδοσκοπία και την τουριστικοποίηση των γειτονιών μας!




Την Τετάρτη βγαίνουμε στον δρόμο με μουσική, μαζί με όσους και όσες αγωνίζονται σε ολόκληρη την Ευρώπη!




Καλούμε τους κατοίκους της Θεσσαλονίκης, τα εργατικά σωματεία, τις συλλογικότητες και κάθε άνθρωπο που πλήττεται από τη στεγαστική κρίση να συμμετάσχουν στη συναυλία. Δεν θα ανεχτούμε άλλες αυξήσεις, άλλες εξώσεις και νέα νομοσχέδια σε βάρος μας!




ΝΑ ΠΕΣΟΥΝ ΤΑ ΕΝΟΙΚΙΑ, ΝΑ ΣΩΘΟΥΝ ΤΑ ΣΠΙΤΙΑ!




Η ΣΤΕΓΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΔΙΚΑΙΩΜΑ!







Οριζόντια Κίνηση – Για την Αναρχία και τον Ελευθεριακό Κομμουνισμό







ΜΕ ΑΛΛΗΛΕΓΓΥΗ ΚΑΙ ΣΥΛΛΟΓΙΚΟ ΑΓΩΝΑ ΜΠΟΡΟΥΜΕ ΝΑ ΚΕΡΔΙΣΟΥΜΕ




Η ΣΤΕΓΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΔΙΚΑΙΩΜΑ – ΟΧΙ ΕΜΠΟΡΕΥΜΑ




Στηρίζουμε την συγκέντρωση για το δικαίωμα στην στέγαση |Ημέρα δράσης: Τετάρτη 11/11, 18:30, Πάρκο Ν.Παπάζογλου, Κάτω Τούμπα




Από το πρωί της Δευτέρας 2/11 και για μια εβδομάδα περίπου, στην Κάτω Τούμπα, στην οδό Καππαδοκίας 64, δόθηκε ένας σκληρός συλλογικός αγώνας με κύριο στοιχείο του την κοινωνική και ταξική αλληλεγγύη. Εκατοντάδες άνθρωποι κάθε ηλικίας, εργαζόμενοι, φοιτήτριες, συνταξιούχοι, φίλαθλοι αθλητικών ομάδων, μετά από καλέσματα σωματείων, πολιτικών οργανώσεων και συλλογικών φορέων της πόλης, συγκεντρώθηκαν ξανά και ξανά, κάθε μέρα και για πολλές ώρες, έξω από την οικία ηλικιωμένου ζευγαριού με σοβαρά θέματα υγείας, που κινδύνευε να πεταχτεί στον δρόμο από την μια στιγμή στην άλλη, αφού οι τράπεζες και τα κοράκια των funds έβγαλαν στο σφυρί το σπίτι τους κοψοχρονιά.




Ο κύριος Λαοκράτης και η κυρία Γεωργία είχαν μπει εγγυητές σε δάνειο του γιου τους για άλλο σπίτι, το οποίο ο τελευταίος δεν κατάφερε να ξεπληρώσει. Η τράπεζα επέλεξε με δόλο να βγάλει πρώτα στο σφυρί το σπίτι στην Καππαδοκίας σε εξευτελιστική τιμή, ώστε να έχει διπλό όφελος. Ο νέος ιδιοκτήτης, ένα μεσιτικό γραφείο, θέλησε να αδειάσει το σπίτι γρήγορα από τους μέχρι πρότινος ιδιοκτήτες του ώστε να το εκμεταλλευτεί, παρά τα αιτήματα για αναβολή της έξωσης μέχρι την εκδίκαση της υπόθεσης ακύρωσης του πλειστηριασμού. Μάλιστα, επιχείρησε να αλλάξει τις κλειδαριές στα μουλωχτά, παρουσία δικαστικού επιμελητή. Εν τέλει, ήταν η συνεχής μαζική κινητοποίηση έξω από το σπίτι και η κοινωνική αλληλεγγύη που πίεσαν ώστε, τουλάχιστον, η έξωση να αναβληθεί και το ζευγάρι να παραμείνει στο σπίτι μέχρι τις 8 του Γενάρη.




Η υπόθεση αυτή είναι μόνο ένα από τα εκατοντάδες παρόμοια καθημερινά περιστατικά, όπου άνθρωποι της τάξης μας πετιούνται στον δρόμο, αφού οι πλειστηριασμοί πρώτης κατοικίας έχουν πάρει φωτιά. Άνθρωποι που πείστηκαν -μέσα και από τις υποσχέσεις των τραπεζών- να πάρουν στεγαστικό δάνειο σε μια άλλη περίοδο, αρκετές φορές ακόμη και πριν από το ξέσπασμα της κρίσης και από την μια μέρα στην άλλη έχασαν τις δουλειές τους ή τους πετσοκόφτηκαν οι μισθοί και άρα αδυνατούν να ξεχρεώσουν. Ακόμη και μια καθυστερημένη δόση είναι αρκετή για τις τράπεζες και τα funds ώστε να βάλουν χέρι στα σπίτια των φτωχών ανθρώπων.




Ταυτόχρονα, για όσους και όσες ζουν στο ενοίκιο, τα πράγματα είναι εξίσου άσχημα. Οι τιμές των ενοικίων έχουν εκτοξευθεί και το κόστος στέγασης καλύπτει πλέον το μεγαλύτερο μέρος των εισοδημάτων ενός νοικοκυριού. Το ζήτημα ξεκινάει από τους μικρούς και μεσαίους ιδιοκτήτες σπιτιών που, σε συνεργασία με τα μεσιτικά γραφεία, προσπαθούν να αποκομίσουν όσο μεγαλύτερο κέρδος γίνεται από τους ενοικιαστές, ενώ χιλιάδες άνθρωποι καθημερινά ψάχνουν να βρουν ένα σπίτι να μείνουν και επεκτείνεται στα μεγάλα funds, κυρίως από χώρες του εξωτερικού -με τα ισραηλινά να κατέχουν όλο και μεγαλύτερο κομμάτι της πίτας- αγοράζουν ολόκληρα κτίρια και τα μετατρέπουν σε AirBnB και άλλα σχήματα βραχυχρόνιας μίσθωσης, ανεβάζοντας ακόμη περισσότερο τις τιμές και αυξάνοντας την έλλειψη των διαθέσιμων κατοικιών. Σε αυτό συμβάλει και η λεγόμενη golden visa, δηλαδή η παροχή άδειας παραμονής στην χώρα σε όσους πραγματοποιήσουν μεγάλες επενδύσεις σε ακίνητα. Εξαιτίας όλων των παραπάνω, αλλάζει ο χαρακτήρας ολόκληρων γειτονιών, οι οποίες χάνουν το ανθρώπινο πρόσωπό τους και μεταμορφώνονται σε τουριστικά και επενδυτικά hubs, ενώ η στέγη πλέον παύει να αποτελεί δικαίωμα και ανάγκη και μετατρέπεται σε εμπόρευμα.




Φυσικά δεν ξεχνάμε πως η πλειοψηφία όσων νομοθέτησαν διαχρονικά για όλα τα παραπάνω, είτε δεξιοί, είτε κεντρώοι, είτε “αριστεροί”, ζουν πλουσιοπάροχα και κατέχουν, μερικές φορές, ακόμη και δεκάδες σπίτια. Δεν θα μπορούσαν ποτέ -και δεν θέλουν άλλωστε- να έχουν καμία σχέση με τα προβλήματα των απλών ανθρώπων της τάξης μας και ούτε έχουν καμία έγνοια για αυτά.




Για εμάς η μοιρολατρία και η αποδοχή της ήττας, του ξεσπιτώματος των φτωχών ανθρώπων και γενικότερα μιας ζωής ρημαγμένης, δεν αποτελεί επιλογή. Από τις κινητοποιήσεις των χιλιάδων Ισπανών ενάντια στην έξωση της ηλικιωμένης Μαρικάρμεν Αμπασκάλ στην Μαδρίτη μερικούς μήνες πριν, μέχρι και την -μερική έστω- νίκη του κινήματος αλληλεγγύης προς τους συνανθρώπους μας στην Κάτω Τούμπα, επιβεβαιώνονται όλα όσα πιστεύουμε: Ο αγώνας ενάντια σε όσους μας εκμεταλλεύονται και μας καταπιέζουν δεν είναι μάταιος, είναι αναγκαίος. Και πρέπει να είναι συλλογικός και μαζικός. Μόνο έτσι θα κερδίσουμε τις ζωές μας πίσω.




Συλλογικός, αδιαμεσολάβητος αγώνας, λοιπόν, σε κάθε πτυχή της καθημερινότητάς μας: Στους εργασιακούς μας χώρους, τις σχολές μας, τις γειτονιές μας. Να χτίσουμε όλοι και όλες μαζί την κοινωνική και ταξική δύναμη που μπορεί να χαλάσει τα σχέδια των καταπιεστών και των εκμεταλλευτών μας. Μέχρι ένας άλλος κόσμος αλληλεγγύης, ισότητας, ελευθερίας να μην φαντάζει πια ουτοπία.

title: Βιβλιοπαρουσίαση – Συζήτηση για τα 90 χρόνια από την κοινωνική επανάσταση στην Ισπανία, Τετάρτη 11/11, στις 19.00, στο Κιούμπρικ, Εξάρχεια
content:
Την Τετάρτη 11 Νοεμβρίου στις 19.00, στο Κιούμπρικ στα Εξάρχεια οι Εκδόσεις Των Συναδέλφων παρουσιάζουν το βιβλίο: «Η συνομοσπονδιακή αντίληψη για τον ελευθεριακό κομμουνισμό. Πόρισμα του 4ου Συνεδρίου της CNT».  Με αφορμή το βιβλίο αυτό θα πραγματοποιηθεί συζήτηση για τα 90 χρόνια από την κοινωνική επανάσταση στην Ισπανία με τους εξής ομιλητές:




Νίκος Πρατσίνης, διερμηνέας-μεταφραστής




Σπύρος Δαπέργολας, γραφίστας – μέλος ΡΟΥΒΙΚΩΝΑ




Αντώνης Κοζάκος, εργαζόμενος στον επισιτισμό – Μέλος της ΕΣΕ










Κάλεσμα της 

Ελευθεριακής Συνδικαλιστικής Ένωσης – ΕΣΕ Αθήνας

:




Την Τετάρτη 11 Νοεμβρίου στις 7 το απόγευμα ανταποκρινόμαστε με χαρά στην πρόσκληση από τις ΟΙ ΕΚΔΟΣΕΙΣ ΤΩΝ ΣΥΝΑΔΕΛΦΩΝ και συζητάμε για τα 90 χρόνια από την κοινωνική επανάσταση στην Ισπανία με αφορμή το βιβλίο:




«Η συνομοσπονδιακή αντίληψη για τον ελευθεριακό κομμουνισμό. Πόρισμα του 4ου Συνεδρίου της CNT»




ΘΑ ΜΙΛΗΣΟΥΝ

Abdullah Kilinçê ku di teqîna 9ê Cotmehê de li Kargeha Hesin û Pola ya HABAŞê ya li navçeya Aliagaya Îzmîrê giran birîndar bibû, di nexweşxaneya ku lê dihat dermankirin de jiyana xwe ji dest da.



















Li Îzmîrê di kargehê de teqîn pêk hat: Hejmara miriyan derket 18an




10 Mijdar 2026










Kilinç piştî teqînê di destpêkê de biribûn Nexweşxaneya Dewletê ya Aliagayê û paşê sewqî Nexweşxaneya Perwerde û Lêkolînê ya Çigliyê ya Zanîngeha Bakirçaya Îzmîrê kiribûn.




Dermankirina şeş karkerên ku di teqînê de birîndar bibûn di nexweşxaneyan de berdewam dike.



















Derbarê karkerên ku di teqîna HABAŞê de mirin em çi dizanin?




10 Mijdar 2026













Hejmara qurbaniyên HABAŞê gihîşt 19an




Ajansa Anadolyê (AA) nivîsî ku bi mirina Abdullah Kilinç re hejmara kesên ku di teqînê de jiyana xwe ji dest dane gihîştiye 18an. Lêbelê di lîsteya AAyê de navê Guner Gokçe cih nagire.




Cîgirê Wezîrê Dadê Can Tuncay, duh (10ê Cotmehê) piştî lêkolîna li tesîsê ji rojnamegeran re gotibû: “Li gorî serlêdana malbatan cenazeyê karkerekî me nehatiye dîtin. Lêkolînên li cihê bûyerê berdewam dikin.”




Piştî vê daxuyaniyê, hin ajansên nûçeyan, platformên nûçeyan ên herêmî û Meclisa İSİGê ragihandin ku termê karkerê bi navê Guner Gokçe di bin kavilan de hatiye dîtin. Ji bo Gokçeyê ku li Paşaliya (navê wê ê berê Berdik) ser bi navçeya Şenkayaya Erzurumê ji dayik bûye, di rûpeleke civata herêmî de jî peyama serxweşiyê hat weşandin.




Navên 19 karkerên ku jiyana xwe ji dest dane bi vî rengî ne:

 

Abdülkadir Kınacı, Abdullah Kılınç, Barış Güney, Ceylan Bıyıklı, Ersin Oğuz, Fatih Işık, Ferhat Maraşlı, Göksel Ünaldı, Güner Gökçe, Hüsnü Ersoy, İlker Sığırtmaçoğlu, Kadir Kaan Özçelik, Mustafa Sert, Orhan Altay, Özcan Efe, Recep Fedai, Serkan Kurt, Uğur Temel, Yasin Taşçı.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "Birds of War": New Film Tells a Story of Love and Journalism from Syria to Lebanon
content:
We speak with Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak, filmmakers and subjects of the new documentary 

Birds of War

, which tells their epic love story through years of upheaval in the Middle East. Boulos, a London-based Lebanese journalist working for the 

BBC

, and Habak, a Syrian activist and cameraman, first connected while covering the Syrian civil war and stayed in touch through years of war, revolution and exile, forming a relationship that is chronicled in the documentary by drawing on 13 years of their personal videos, voice notes and other correspondence.




The film also examines the unequal relationship between international news organizations and local journalists whose work they rely on, the fraught political history between Syria and Lebanon, and how Boulos and Habak’s personal connection overcame those divisions.




“Without our journalistic relationship, [we] would have never been together. I would have never opened my heart to somebody like him,” says Boulos. “We can be any race, any gender, any religion, any background, but at the same time we’re all humans.”




Birds of War

 premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, where it won the World Cinema Documentary Special Jury Award for Journalistic Impact.
