author: James Moore
title: Be More Human: Why Mental Health Care is Broken and What We Can Do to Fix It: An Interview with Sir Norman Lamb
content:
H

ello, this is James and welcome to the Mad in America podcast. This week, we are asking why people with mental health conditions die 15-20 years earlier than people without. Why does the UK spend £100 million every year placing patients far from home? How did the question, ‘What matters to you?’ transform mental health care in Norway? Can mental healthcare be more compassionate?




Sir Norman Lamb asks these questions, and more, in his book 

Be More Human

, published by Jessica Kingsley Publishers. Sir Norman is a former Health Minister, an NHS trust chair, and a dedicated mental health campaigner who was knighted in 2019 for his public and political service. He has seen the cracks in the system up close. In his book, he sets out to answer these questions, and many others, uncovering the reasons why our mental health services are failing. He shares eye-opening stories from patients who have been let down, but also inspiring tales from trailblazers who are shaking things up with creative, community-first solutions.




In this interview, we talk about how his personal and professional experiences led to him wanting to lift the lid on the UK’s mental health system. We also discuss how personal accounts of mistreatment and abuse motivated him to think differently about the human element so often missing from mental healthcare. Finally, we discuss novel, community-based alternatives that offer dignity, compassion and hope.




The transcript below has been edited for length and clarity. Listen to the audio of the interview here.







James Moore: Sir Norman, welcome. Thank you so much for joining me for the Mad in America podcast. It’s an honour to get to talk to you and to delve into your recently published book, 

Be More Human

, published by Jessica Kingsley Publishers in August this year.




Before we kick off, I have to say that upon reading the book, I found that it’s one of those books that stays with you long after you finish it. We’ll come on to talk about some of the details, but the personal stories shared, the lived experience accounts, particularly resonate. Welcome, first of all.




Norman Lamb:

 Thank you, James. You can drop the Sir bit. I’m happy just to be Norman, but it’s really good to talk to you; great that we’ve got this opportunity.




Moore: First, I’d like to talk a little bit about you and your entry into this world. You’re someone with wide-ranging experience across government. You’ve been a Liberal Democrat member of parliament for Norfolk. You’ve held positions in science and technology and business and skills departments. 

More recently, you’ve spent time in the Department of Health and Social Care and also, perhaps very importantly, been Chair of mental health services at South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust. 




How was it that those experiences came together to you wanting to put a spotlight on mental health services and how they can be made more compassionate?




Lamb:

 Yes, it’s been an interesting journey, James, because if you scroll back to the late ’90s, early 2000s, I hadn’t really focused much on mental health. It hadn’t touched me in any particular way. Then I was elected to parliament in 2001, and as a member of parliament in North Norfolk, I wanted to be available to constituents to take up their concerns. I became aware of a lot of people coming to see me with their own stories about the mental health system and how, in their terms, they felt it was failing them in various ways: awful waiting lists, awful use of coercion and institutionalisation. Those stories leave a mark on you.




Then we were hit personally in our own family. Our oldest son, Archie, when he was 15, was diagnosed with obsessive-compulsive disorder. We managed to get a referral to the Mental Health Trust at a moment when we were fairly desperate. He was in quite a bad way, and we were told that we would have to wait up to six months for anything to happen.




When you’re a family in despair and really anxious about a child, being told you’ve got to wait up to six months is sort of hopeless, really. I’m acutely conscious that for many people nowadays, it could be a year waiting. We did what any family would do if they’re able to. We paid for care, and in a way, there’s the injustice because most people can’t do that. They are literally just left waiting.




I sort of concluded that a service that leaves people waiting so long when they’re desperate is not really a service at all in any meaningful sense, and everyone preaches the importance of early intervention in mental health. Yet the system seemed to be delivering intervention at the latest possible moment, often when people were already in crisis.




Then scroll forward to 2012: I became a minister in the Department of Health, and you get a whole lot more stories, people coming to talk to you, wanting to influence you, and it’s a profound privilege for people to be willing to tell you their very personal stories. Sometimes about dreadful loss through suicide, but often just other failings of a system that is under acute strain, but failing too many people.




I left the department in 2015, after the General Election that year, and a couple of months after that, my elder sister, Catherine, who’d been in a state of acute depression after the death of our mother, made one or two attempts on her life and was admitted to a fairly dismal unit up in the north of England. She was in there for about 10 weeks. She was a voluntary patient. But despite being a voluntary patient, she was locked up with everybody else.




After her period in there, she was discharged back home. But some months later, she ended up taking her own life, and so our family had to cope with that tragedy, leaving two adult children who’d already lost their dad to bowel cancer. I suppose it left me thinking that a lot of money was spent on her. Those 10 weeks in an inpatient unit will have cost a lot of money. It’s effectively incarceration. But what good did it do? If someone loses their life after being discharged, and that’s an acutely risky period, we know that from data across the system, was there not a better way of using money to be more ambitious for someone?




In a way, it led me on a voyage of discovery to find more effective approaches that were more humane, kinder, more generous, more ambitious for people. That was in a period before I became Chair of the South London and Maudsley, which was in 2020. But the five years I had there sort of reinforced all of my views about a system that was under acute strain, despite enormous numbers of people doing their very best and often achieving amazing things, despite the system, not because of it.




So, this is not a criticism of people working in mental health. It’s a criticism of a systemic problem that I think has to be confronted. It’s sort of like a relic from a Victorian era that is too often cruel and inhuman, and should not be tolerated. We sort of end up tolerating the intolerable.




So, it’s a rather long answer, James, but that’s the story that led to me wanting to write a book to make my case, as it were, for change. I wanted it ultimately to be an optimistic, ambitious book. I offer a critique of a system that I think is failing. I enable people to tell their stories in the book about their experiences of the system, often harrowing and shocking. But then in part two of the book, I put the spotlight on a whole load of enlightened examples of beautiful practices and approaches that are humane, generous, kind, but also more effective at keeping people safe, and giving people the chance of a good life that the rest of us perhaps take for granted.




Moore: Norman, I’m so sorry to hear about Catherine.




Lamb:

 Well, the book is in memory of Catherine, James, and I wanted it, in a way, to be a legacy for her. I want something good to come out of that tragic loss.




Moore: And I hope that Archie is doing better too now.




Lamb:

 Archie’s doing great, and that’s another important point I want to make, James, because I think often when young people experience mental distress or ill health, it’s easy for them to believe that this is almost like a life sentence, that their life will be defined by this. But actually, so often, there is an opportunity to get to a better place, to achieve some sort of recovery, to be able to enjoy life.




Archie is a good example of that. He’s now running a record label. He still experiences some anxiety, but he’s thriving as a human being, married with children. It’s a sort of success story, and there could be so many success stories. I suppose I want everybody involved in mental health, in whatever respect, whether it’s working in a service or whether it’s a family member, to actually have some hope and some optimism that not always, but so often, there are opportunities to enable people to get to a better place.




Moore: The book certainly does that, and particularly the latter half where you talk about so many fantastic examples from around the world of how we can approach distress in a more compassionate way. The book covers a lot of ground, and you ask some very fundamental questions about how we approach distress.




One thing that stood out to me was how diagnoses are made and the impact they can have. The book isn’t just about diagnosis; it’s much wider than that, but diagnosis is perhaps the entry point for many people into this system.




I was particularly struck by Birgit Valla’s chapter. She describes a Norwegian service where diagnosis is optional rather than a prerequisite for treatment. For those who don’t know, Mad in America has several global affiliated sites. One of those is 

Mad in Norway

, and Birgit is one of the founders.




It was pretty clear from reading that chapter that a diagnosis can help some people make sense of their experiences, but other people can find it limiting or even harmful. Almost every day at Mad in America and across our network of sites, we publish stories of people who have felt that their diagnosis made their difficulties seem insurmountable or lifelong.




Given that psychiatric diagnoses are often based upon symptoms rather than established biological causes, how can we strike a balance between offering a diagnosis as a useful tool while recognising it’s not always an explanation and can sometimes constrain treatment choices and options?




Lamb:

 I think it’s such an important point you make. I mean, before I get on to Birgit and the way she ran her service in Norway, I learned so much, doing the research for this book, discovering wonderful approaches like hers in Norway. But one thing that struck me when interviewing people who had their own experience of the mental health system was how people would describe how they’d been given one different diagnosis after another, and how disorienting and confusing that must be.




One amazing woman, 

Rai Waddingham

, describes in her story this succession of different diagnoses. I asked her what that meant to her, and she said, well, it’s just the lens through which different people see me. But for the person concerned to be told one thing and then told another and then be given the label, perhaps of borderline personality disorder. They might suddenly discover that when you’ve got that label, the way you’re treated in the system gets worse because somehow you’re seen as a difficult person and somehow responsible yourself for your own actions, putting to one side or ignoring a life story which might get you to that place. You start to think this system is doing people damage, not helping them heal.




Now, it’s important to offer the caveat, as you did with diagnosis, that some people talk to me and they tell me that they’ve been really helped by the mental health system, often because they’ve been linked up with someone who really cares, who builds a relationship with them, and who aids their journey of healing. But for too many people, the story is one of trauma, and diagnosis is sometimes part of that experience.




Then you interview someone like Birgit Valla in Norway, and you hear that Birgit, from the inside, concludes early on in her career that the system isn’t working for the people she’s trying to help and that a different approach is needed. We really need to listen to those people who, from the inside, as a professional, are realising that something is not working. She sets up this service where she’s determined not to rush to diagnosis, not to rush to medication, but just to say, look, we’re here to help. Open the doors, ask people what matters to them, and build a relationship with people and jointly problem-solve.




I suppose what I’d say to you is if you can help resolve someone’s issues that are causing them acute distress and enable them to move on in their life without resorting to a diagnosis which can end up defining you, then surely, we can all agree that helping someone move on and rebuild their life after some joint work addressing the issues that are in their head or the causes of those issues that are in their head, surely that’s just a good thing. Can’t we all agree on that? Then when you hear from Birgit that in 10 years leading this service, she didn’t diagnose anyone. It’s just a wonderful example of how we can rethink how we do things.




And she had no waiting lists; we’ve become sort of conditioned in this country to believe that waiting lists are just an unfortunate necessity. They just are part of a system that’s overloaded with need. You then discover when you talk to people like Birgit, or you go to Trieste and you talk to the amazing Roberto Mezzina, that actually waiting lists are not necessary.




You can rethink things in a way that just enables people with open access to see someone immediately when they need help, not putting them on an awful, impersonal waiting list ignored for six months or a year or whatever it might be with potentially awful catastrophic consequences.




Moore: Birgit’s service was incredibly successful, but it was also seen as quite risky by the authorities, wasn’t it? It was investigated, and the authorities struggled with the concept that anybody could do anything differently than diagnose and provide drugs.




Lamb:

 The extraordinary thing, James, is that the Norwegian system gave people a right to a diagnosis. Now, I’m sure those people, those legislators who originally introduced that, were doing it for what they felt was a really good reason to ensure that people got help when they needed it and so forth. But, of course, that right to a diagnosis ended up with Birgit’s service facing potential closure because they weren’t routinely giving people a diagnosis.




She was faced with the loss of that amazing service until various parliamentarians stepped in late to save it, and new guidance was issued to allow it to continue, and now it’s spread to lots of places in Norway.




James, you’ll forgive me for trying to encourage people to get the book, but just reading the story about this, I mean, she calls it a help centre. That’s what they’ve become known as in Norway. I think people will find it absolutely fascinating, along with all of these other examples.




There’s a common thread that runs through almost all of the examples I give in part two, and that is the importance of relationships. If we stand back and think about it, this is not rocket science. We all, as human beings, are what our relationships are like. We are social beings, but we are ignoring the importance of relationships or treating someone as an island, separate from society, as psychiatry too often traditionally has done. I say that, being very clear that lots of psychiatrists have been very influential to me, people who completely get it and who recognise that their role is part of a much bigger picture.




Roberto Mezzina is a psychiatrist. He’s a wonderful human being who I have enormous respect for, a principled man. But the old-fashioned view of treating someone in isolation from the people that they have relationships with seems to me to be a flawed approach, and also treating them in a way where the professional keeps a professional distance from people. This is another thing that I found acutely fascinating. This principle spreads much further than mental health services.




There is a culture in a lot of public services that people working in the service have been sort of conditioned to believe that sometimes, for their own protection, they must keep a professional distance. Purposefully not establishing any sort of relationship with the person that they’re trying to help, keeping professional distance, not engaging, not getting to understand and know the person, not offering any vulnerability yourself. Actually, the very opposite of that is so much more helpful to the person seeking help, but actually also so much more rewarding for the professional.




Moore: I certainly would echo, Norman, that people should go out and read the book because there are so many fabulous examples. We’ve mentioned that part one is a kind of a diagnosis of the problems, and then part two is about how other people do things differently.




I got a distinct sense from reading that in part one, almost every example given, almost every personal story, was us trying to fit a person into a system that had very little to offer them outside standard approaches. But in part two, where you talk about alternatives, it’s about fitting a service to the person coming in, meeting them where they are, finding out where they’re from, finding out their social and cultural context, perhaps. It was incredibly refreshing to read.




Lamb:

 I’m glad you saw it in that light, and I think you’re totally right. The current system that I describe in part one is inflexible and not person-centred. I mean, we often use that expression, but it’s too often pretty meaningless.




I think another interesting aspect of the system, and this comes out in Liam’s story in the book—it’s an extraordinary story of someone who’d had a difficult childhood with a mother who experienced really significant mental ill health. Liam ends up in the mental health system, has such an awful traumatic experience that he literally escapes and gets abroad, gets away from the U.K. to escape the mental health system and lives an itinerant life in continental Europe for two or three years just to keep away from the system.




He returns because he’s heard, wrongly, I think probably you and I would agree, that a new generation of antidepressants may be more effective, and he wants to get hold of them to help him. He goes to see his GP, and he describes how he purposefully didn’t reveal to the GP what was going on in his head because he knew that if he did that he would be back into the system again, locked up in a dismal unit. What do we learn from that? We learn that we create incentives not to disclose, not to open up. Indeed, incentives to keep away from the system.




When you look at the disproportionate use of coercion in terms of the black community, you look at some of the horrific stories of lost life and damage to people in the Black community who’ve experienced the mental health system. The story told by Aji Lewis, who lost her son, Seni Lewis, a young Black student who lost his life after being admitted as a voluntary patient when he was in a bad place. He ends up with police being called to the unit on the first night there, restrained face down on the ground for half an hour by several police officers. There are echoes here of George Floyd. It happened before George Floyd, but he ends up a week later with a life support machine being switched off.




Now, when a community gets to hear of stories like that, what’s the incentive to engage with mental health services? Then we look at the data, and we know that Black teenagers are less likely to seek early help than their white counterparts. Well, is that surprising? I don’t think so. You then have a sort of loss of trust between the community and a mental health service, which is deeply unhelpful.




Then you compare it with Trieste in Northern Italy, where there’s a community mental health centre. Everyone knows where it is. The doors are open, long hours. There are six beds for anybody who’s worried about falling into a crisis. They can go there for a few days just to stabilise themselves in a kind therapeutic environment. But it’s the same people there, and there is continuity of support. There’s a friendly welcome, and anyone can go. You don’t need a referral from your GP. The contrast is enormous. What I found quite troubling was how a number of senior psychiatrists, including academic psychiatrists, would say to me, “Oh, Trieste works in Trieste, but it doesn’t work here.” Why is that? Have you been there? No.




A very different approach dismissed without properly examining it, without ever visiting or talking to the people there. I’ve been there three times now, and that sort of dismissive attitude is so much greater in London: we can’t do that here. Well, I would say in riposte that a young Black man in Lewisham has just the same right to be treated with dignity and respect as any person in Trieste in Italy. There are some universal principles at stake here about the way we treat human beings, which don’t depend on ethnicity or on location or on circumstance, but are universal, and we’ve lost sight of that. People who would often, I think, describe themselves as being progressive individuals end up in a position where they are refusing to contemplate change in a way that feels reactionary.




But what I found immensely positive at the Maudsley was that there were so many people who saw the need for change and then who embraced the opportunity to trial a new model of care based on the principles from Trieste and then found that attendances at A&E started to go down. Admissions to hospitals started to go down because this more humane approach was more effective for people.




Moore: It’s a good time then to move on to how do we achieve change and what are some of the obstacles? As we’ve said, anyone who wants to change the mental health system is inevitably met with a response like “We’d love to do better, but there’s no alternative to diagnosis and drugs.” But as your book so clearly shows, there are plenty of successful alternatives, many of them built on very simple principles of dialogue and community. Many of them are much less expensive to administer than a medical setting. Perhaps it’s partly just about having the courage to admit that maybe a biomedical focus is just too narrow.




The way that we take people in distress away from their communities, hundreds of miles away, we take them away from any support system and then are surprised somehow when they become even more distressed, which leads to more diagnosis and more drugs and so on.




I wanted to ask for your thoughts on why change is so hard to achieve and how we can start to open up to the idea that we need a more compassionate, perhaps less biology-led response to distress and trauma.




Lamb:

 Well, I hope that this book will encourage people at the top in government. I’ve given a copy to the Minister responsible for mental health. I’ve given a copy to the Prime Minister. I would love government to lead the case for change. The centre of government in the U.K. can’t dictate a change of culture, but they can lead the conversation and encourage a change of culture within services and promote alternatives that might demonstrate much better outcomes. But at the same time they can encourage government to think afresh, and incidentally, James, to recognise that a different, more humane approach doesn’t cost more. If anything, it costs less than if you have a system that’s based very much on heavy medication and institutionalisation, and a lot of these inpatient wards are akin to being in prison. People have often described it to me as being like in prison or being incarcerated.




That costs a lot of money. We spend about 50% of our clinical budget in the NHS on inpatient care. That’s what it’s called, inpatient care. But in many respects, it’s akin to incarceration. Everybody in England is locked up, whether they’re voluntary patients or detained under the Mental Health Act. That in itself is really shocking, it seems to me.




The use of restraints remains endemic in the system, and you’re more likely, if you’re Black, to experience this sort of coercion. I want government to lead the charge on making the change, and they would see that they could achieve better outcomes for no more expenditure. You may have to spend some money on affecting the change, moving from one approach to another, investing in things like 24/7 community mental health centres. But you could do public-private collaborations and so on. But I also want a grassroots revolution. I want to get the message out to anybody who’s interested in mental health, as indeed we all ought to be, because every family is touched by it in some way or other.




I want to get the message out that we can all have an impact in our communities and in the organisations that we work in. We can all play a part in helping to prevent distress in the first place, because that’s one of the key themes in my book: that we pay so little attention to preventing distress. We allow people to fall into crisis, and then the system is overwhelmed. What a ridiculous way to behave. So much better, surely, to invest in preventing people from falling into distress in the first place. But I think every person working in a public service, not just in mental health services, who reads this book might reflect that they could do things differently.




I’m not claiming personal credit for this, because it was the editor who came up with the title of the book. I described my argument to him, and he said, “What about being more human?” I thought that encapsulated it perfectly. But you could almost describe it as a sort of call to our age, because in so many ways, we have an angry public space now and an enormous risk of an accelerating loss of humanity, and a reminder to everyone that we need to be more human to recognise the vital importance of human relationships and building trust between us in communities and in organisations. Then a grassroots revolution could change things fundamentally. I want change from the top down, but also from the bottom up.




Moore: The way I feel about this is that I think there’s a demystification of mental health that needs to happen. I think while it remains in the medical realm and you need to see a very expensive specialist who knows about broken brains and chemical imbalances and so on, that just puts people at arm’s length from the help they need, quite often. Having mental health challenges is one of the most normal things that can happen to a person, to a greater or lesser extent.




There are clearly some severely ill people who need specialist help, but there are also many people who can benefit from community-led interventions rather than being taken out of their community.




Just to give you an example, Norman, where I live in South Wales, we have a local community café. I have to give them a shout-out because they do brilliant work. It’s called 

Rogiet Community Junction

, and it’s a mental health intervention. It was never set up that way; no one really views it that way. But every time you walk past it, the local community, especially older people, are in there chatting, meeting new people, making connections. That is demonstrably good for their mental health. I do think we need to try and wrest control back from biology and connect with this on a human level, and your book does that so well.




Lamb: Well, thank you. I’ll join you in that shout-out to that community café, and what we need to remember is that there are thousands of those wonderful community-based groups all over the place doing this work. If the statutory formal service could learn from what is all around them, but so often ignored, then things could change radically.




Your description of the help that people get from engaging in those sorts of things reminds me also of Rai Waddingham. I’ve mentioned her before, but she describes this harrowing journey through the mental health system.




She’s someone who had very difficult experiences in childhood and teenage years, including abuse, and none of the things that happened to her in the mental health system really helped her. What actually helped her was this amazing thing called the 

Hearing Voices Network

, where people who hear voices come together to engage with each other and to normalise the hearing of voices. They discover that you don’t necessarily have to eradicate the voice to move on and to start to enjoy life again. You can take back control, to coin a phrase from our political past in this country. The power of how she benefited from others with lived experience, after all of that specialist intervention, which had labelled her in different ways so unhelpfully, I thought that was incredibly powerful.




The only other aspect which we haven’t touched on is the fact that a lot of the same issues apply to people with a learning disability and people who have been diagnosed as autistic. Alexis’ story in the book is probably the most shocking of all.




As a minister between 2012 and 2015, I had to deal with the aftermath of a very shocking expose of abuse in a private hospital called 

Winterbourne View

. The government response to that was to say that there are far too many people with a learning disability or who are autistic, or both, who are in institutional care. Some of these people are literally kept in solitary confinement, which surely is a human rights abuse. Some of them are fed through hatches in doorways.




We set a clear ambition that we should substantially reduce the number of people in institutional care. The shocking thing is that the numbers have come down, but they haven’t come down nearly far enough. Again, what we’ve recognised is that institutional care costs a lot of money, and we could be giving these people the chance of a good life in the community with support if we only had brave leadership.




I think it’s really important to recognise that a lot of the characteristics of our mental health system also end up having awful impacts on people with a learning disability and autistic people. Autistic people are often misunderstood in inpatient services, and Alexis’ story in part one of the book describes how the one thing that keeps her sane is running miles every day. She has to do this. Then she’s locked up in an inpatient unit. She can’t run because there’s no outside space, and this idea that the people who are acutely unwell for whatever reason are denied access to fresh air, to open space, to beauty and nature, I find just extraordinary. It’s a very stupid thing to do, and yet we routinely do it.




Even the old asylums that we rightly got rid of had access to open space. Today, we deny people even that in these units. It’s really important to recognise that this assault on people’s human rights applies also to people with a learning disability and to autistic people.




Moore: Again, you just get a distinct sense of people being forced into a system that isn’t flexible enough to cope with differing needs of different groups of people. You also get a sense of almost fear, I guess, to let in this different thinking, these new ideas. If psychiatry and the system let in more of these people, if the learning was from the people with lived experience more, the learning needs to be as much in the other direction, I think.




Lamb:

 Exactly right.




Moore: Well, Norman, I have to say, the book is such an important read. I’d encourage everyone to go out and get a copy. The personal stories in particular are so powerful and leave such an impact. We know that after many years of providing a voice for people with lived experience on Mad in America, it’s the personal stories that tell us whether we’re doing a good job or not, and it’s clear that we’re not doing a good job.




Lamb:

 Absolutely.




Moore: As we said at the start, we have to recognise there are many compassionate and caring people working within a system, but the system itself constrains and limits so much what they can and can’t do. But it’s so refreshing to read in your book that there are so many good alternatives out there that we could learn from. We need to be brave enough to perhaps shut up and listen a bit more.




Lamb:

 Absolutely right, James. Thank you for everything you do on this podcast and more broadly on Mad in America and other countries’ equivalent systems. You’re giving a voice to people who are often not heard, and you’re exposing evidence that often is not seen or heard. You’re doing really important work, and I’m very grateful for it.




***

author: Kerry Smith
title: Socialist Alliance: Funding cuts to Villamanta throw people with disability on scrap heap
content:
Brenden Grull, Socialist Alliance spokesperson and candidate for Geelong, has called for funding cuts to Villamanta, Geelong’s Disability Rights Legal Service, to be reversed.

The community-based service, which is housed in Geelong West but works across Victoria, fights for the rights of people with disability-related justice issues. It has been operating since 1990.

The Department of Health and Ageing said on November 10 that it would be cutting approximately 30% of Villamanta’s total funding and around 50% of its core funding.

“It is almost unbelievable that as the demand for disability advocacy increases and in defiance of the Disability Royal Commission’s recommendations to recognise independent advocacy as a vital safeguard for people with disability that Villamanta’s funds are being cut so significantly,” Grull told Green Left.

“I understand that the decision will have an immediate impact; it will lead to substantial job losses. I presume that this is part of the federal government’s cuts to NDIS services.

“It is particularly shocking when independent reviews have recognised that Villamanta is a leader in best-practice disability advocacy and community legal support.”

Grull said the cuts will “only cause more pain and suffering for clients and workers”. He said as cost of living pressures rise for everyone, these cuts show federal Labor’s “diminishing commitment” to community-based organisations.

“Labor’s preference is for dodgy providers from the private sector.”

Grull said Socialist Alliance backs Villamanta’s campaign to get the funding cuts reversed and to protect access to independent disability advocacy.

“We support the reintroduction of publicly-funded disability services to fix gaps in the National Disability Insurance Scheme. Villamanta has our 100% support and we will be doing everything in our power to help restore its funding.”

author: Mag
title: Racial Profiling
content:
Dossier




„

Als racial profiling (auch „ethnisches Profiling“ genannt) bezeichnet man das Handeln von Polizei-, Sicherheits-, Einwanderungs- und Zollbeamten, wenn dieses auf allgemeinen Kriterien wie Rasse, ethnischer Zugehörigkeit, Religion und nationaler Herkunft einer Person basiert. Kritiker fordern, dass sich Verdachtsmomente nur auf das Personenverhalten und auf objektive Beweise gründen sollten. Das racial profiling wird dem institutionellen Rassismus zugeordnet. Der Ausdruck entstammt der US-amerikanischen Kriminalistik

…“ (Wikipedia) – auch in Deutschland wird es ausgeübt! Siehe dazu:







Racial-Profiling-Vorwürfe: Die Frankfurter Polizei kontrolliert nach Plünderungen auf der Zeil am 31. Oktober gezielt migrantisch gelesene junge Männer 







Racial Profiling: Polizei durchsucht in Frankfurt migrantisch gelesene Personen




„

Die Frankfurter Polizei kontrolliert offenbar gezielt migrantisch gelesene junge Männer, durchsucht deren Handys und fotografiert die Kontrollierten. Den Vorwurf, rassistische Kontrollen durchzuführen, bestreitet sie.




Die hessische Polizei hat in den letzten Tagen fast 1000 Personenkontrollen auf der Frankfurter Einkaufsmeile Zeil durchgeführt und dabei offenbar auch Handys durchsucht. Laut Medienberichten nimmt die Polizei dabei gezielt männliche, migrantisch gelesene Jugendliche und junge Erwachsene ins Visier. Als Grund für die Aktion gibt der hessische Innenminister Roman Poseck (CDU) die Ausschreitungen vom 31. Oktober an. Poseck hatte im Nachgang des Ereignisses vor allem ein „migrantisches Milieu“ für die Ausschreitungen verantwortlich gemacht, diese Äußerung war von verschiedener Seite als rassistisch kritisiert worden.


Unbeeindruckt von der Kritik gibt es nun offenbar vermehrt Kontrollen gegen migrantisch gelesene Jugendliche und Erwachsene. Einem Bericht der Frankfurter Rundschau zufolge hat die Polizei bei diesen Kontrollen Mobiltelefone und in diesen die Mediengalerien durchsucht, offenbar um Bilder von den Krawallen zu finden. (…)


In einem Bericht der Hessenschau ist davon die Rede, dass die Polizei kontrollierte Personen gegen deren Willen fotografierte.




Anwalt hält Maßnahmen für rechtswidrig




Der Frankfurter Rechtsanwalt Johannes Koch hält die Maßnahmen gegenüber der Frankfurter Rundschau für rechtswidrig. Personenkontrollen bräuchten immer eine gesetzliche Legitimation, sagte er dem Medium. Die „freiwilligen Handykontrollen“ hält der Anwalt für Makulatur. „Durch die Bedrohungskulisse bin ich der Meinung, dass eine freie Willensbildung nicht möglich war“, zitiert die FR den Anwalt

…“ 

Beitrag von Markus Reuter vom 10. November 2026 in Netzpolitik

 




Racial-Profiling-Vorwürfe gegen Frankfurter Polizei




„Seit den Plünderungen auf der Zeil kontrolliert die Polizei dort verstärkt junge migrantisch gelesene Männer. Racial-Profiling-Vowürfe weist die Polizei zurück.


Wer in der vergangenen Woche in Frankfurt auf der Zeil unterwegs war, wird eine erhöhte Polizeipräsenz beobachtet haben. Laut Hessens Innenminister Roman Poseck (CDU) waren von Montag bis Samstag rund 400 Polizist:innen im Einsatz. Die Besondere Aufbauorganisation (BAO) Zeil ist seitdem nicht mehr nur freitags und samstags im Einsatz. Sie sollen 945 Personen und 169 Fahrzeuge kontrolliert sowie 31 Strafanzeigen gestellt haben. 334 Ordnungswidrigkeiten sollen auch festgestellt worden sein. Sicherheitsdiskurse versprechen Schutz, Ordnung und Verlässlichkeit. In der Praxis bedeuten sie für viele Menschen aber vor allem eins: häufiger kontrolliert zu werden, schneller verdächtigt zu werden und in Begegnungen mit der Polizei nicht als Bürger*innen, sondern als potenzielle Gefahr gelesen zu werden. Genau hier setzt die Debatte um Racial Profiling an. Sie beschreibt nicht nur einzelne Fehlentscheidungen, sondern ein Muster, in dem Aussehen, zugeschriebene Herkunft und stereotype Erwartungen darüber mitentscheiden, wer kontrolliert, beobachtet oder hart behandelt wird.


Diese Debatte ist in Deutschland alt, aber sie ist noch immer nicht erledigt. Schon 2020 wurde ein Forschungsprojekt zu Racial Profiling bei der Polizei gestoppt, obwohl Betroffene und zivilgesellschaftliche Organisationen seit Jahren auf diskriminierende Polizeikontrollen hinweisen. Das zeigt ein Grundproblem: Der Staat erklärt das Thema zwar oft für geregelt, untersucht es aber nur begrenzt. Für Betroffene ist genau diese Lücke entscheidend, weil fehlende Forschung auch fehlende Anerkennung bedeutet.




Racial Profiling im Alltag




Racial Profiling meint, dass Menschen nicht wegen konkreten Verhaltens, sondern wegen zugeschriebener Merkmale kontrolliert oder verdächtigt werden. Besonders betroffen sind Menschen, die als „fremd“ wahrgenommen werden, etwa wegen Hautfarbe, Kopfbedeckung oder anderer äußerer Merkmale. Die SVR-Analyse auf Basis des Integrationsbarometers 2022 zeigt, dass solche Personen von Polizeikontrollen etwa doppelt so häufig betroffen sind wie Menschen, die nicht als fremd wahrgenommen werden: 8,3 Prozent gegenüber 4,4 Prozent. Noch stärker betroffen sind junge Männer zwischen 15 und 34 Jahren, die als phänotypisch anders wahrgenommen werden. Bei ihnen lag die Wahrscheinlichkeit einer Polizeikontrolle bei 18,4 Prozent, verglichen mit 11,9 Prozent bei Vergleichspersonen ohne solche äußeren Merkmale. Das ist wichtig, weil es zeigt, dass es hier nicht nur um subjektive Eindrücke geht, sondern um messbare Ungleichheiten im Polizeikontakt. (…)




Sicherheitslogik und Vorurteil




Die heutige Polizeipraxis ist nicht nur durch Gesetze geprägt, sondern auch durch Erwartungen und Routinen. Eine Studie aus Niedersachsen zeigt, dass Polizeibeamt*innen bei Kontrollen und Lageeinschätzungen häufig auf ethnische Marker und stereotype Annahmen zurückgreifen. Dabei werden bestimmte Gruppen schneller mit Kriminalität, Aggression oder Unkooperativität verbunden. Genau hier wird sichtbar, wie Sicherheitslogik und Vorurteil ineinandergreifen können. Besonders problematisch ist, dass solche Muster oft als „praktische Erfahrung“ getarnt werden. Dann heißt es nicht offen, jemand werde wegen Hautfarbe oder Herkunft verdächtigt, sondern man spreche eben von „Einschätzungen“, „Gefahrenlagen“ oder „Erfahrung im Dienst“. Doch gerade diese Sprache verschleiert, dass vermeintlich objektive Sicherheitsurteile häufig von rassifizierten Zuschreibungen mitgeprägt sind

„

Die Gewalt gegen rassialisierte Personen an den Staatsgrenzen hat in den letzten Jahren zugenommen. Dies ist von Aktivist*innen häufig erfolgreich angeprangert worden

.




Begegnungen mit der Polizei sind folgenreich, sowohl auf persönlicher als auch auf gesellschaftlicher Ebene. Die einen erleben die Polizei als Schutz und Hilfe. Dies kann das Vertrauen in eine funktionierende, demokratisch legitimierte Polizei stärken. Andere wiederum machen die Erfahrung, von der Polizei kriminalisiert oder nicht ernst genommen zu werden. Dies kann sich negativ auf die gesellschaftliche Teilhabe und das Vertrauen in den Staat auswirken. (…) Ein etwa 30-jähriger Mann, der aus Afghanistan geflohen ist und nun in Deutschland in einer Grossstadt lebt, verlässt mit seinem aus dem Iran geflüchteten Freund den Hauptbahnhof. Dort werden sie von der Polizei für eine Identitätskontrolle angehalten. Mein Interviewpartner erzählt, dass sein Freund aufgrund von Gewalterfahrungen mit der Polizei im Iran grosse Angst davor hat. Er erzählt: „Ich werde diesen Tag nie vergessen, weil er zitterte. Und ich habe [der Polizei] gesagt: ‚Bitte, wir müssen gehen’“. Der Polizist antwortet mit einem knappen „Nein“, woraufhin mein Interviewpartner den Polizisten fragt: „Was haben wir getan?“. Daraufhin herrscht zunächst Stille und der Polizist antwortet: „Ich habe dir gesagt, nicht reden“. Er bittet die Polizist*innen, schnell weitergehen zu dürfen. Die Polizisten reagieren jedoch nicht auf diese Bitte und zeigen keinerlei Empathie. (…) Rassifizierte Differenz kann also nicht nur durch polizeiliche Aktivität und das übermässige Polizieren bestimmter Gruppen (…), etwa durch Racial Profiling, hergestellt werden, sondern auch durch In-Aktivität. (…) Rassismus zeigt sich nicht nur durch übermässige polizeiliche Aktivität wie Racial Profiling, sondern auch durch polizeiliche In-Aktivität, wenn betroffenen Personen Schutz und Hilfe verwehrt werden. Dies erweitert den Blick für rassistische Praktiken, die vermeintlich weniger offensichtlich oder spektakulär sind. Zudem ermöglicht dies ein tieferes Verständnis dafür, wie unterschiedliche Formen der Diskriminierung intersektional zusammenwirken. Im Rahmen meiner Forschung habe ich den Fokus bewusst auf das Wissen von Rassismus betroffenen Personen gelegt. Bei der Wahl dieses Fokus habe ich mich insbesondere von zwei Gründen leiten lassen. Erstens sind gelebte Erfahrungen nicht ausschliesslich individuell, sondern strukturell bedingt. Das heisst, wenn nicht-weisse Personen im Alltag von der Polizei rassistisch behandelt werden, spiegelt dies ein Geflecht von Erfahrungen wider, das von gesellschaftlichen Machtverhältnissen durchzogen ist. Dieses Erfahrungswissen bildet eine wesentliche Grundlage, um gesellschaftliche Differenzordnungen und eben auch Rassismus besser zu verstehen. Zweitens stellt dieses Wissen von Rassismus Betroffenen ein Gegennarrativ zur hegemonialen Erzählung der Polizei dar. Die Erfahrungen von Rassismus betroffenen Personen mit der Polizei sind sowohl im gesellschaftlichen als auch im wissenschaftlichen Diskurs nach wie vor unterrepräsentiert; wenngleich spätestens durch die Black-Lives-Matter Proteste im Sommer 2020 ein Wandel erkennbar ist. Dieser Perspektivwechsel, weg von der der Polizei und anderen sicherheitsnahen Akteur*innen, die oftmals im Fokus solcher Untersuchungen stehen, kann dazu beitragen, die ungleiche Deutungsmacht zwischen Polizei und Bürger*innen, und hierbei insbesondere marginalisierte Stimmen, abzubauen. Dies kann zu einer Infragestellung vermeintlicher Normalitäten führen. Gesellschaftspolitisch ist dies wichtig, weil die Polizei eine enorm machtvolle Institution ist, die zu oft unhinterfragt bleibt bzw. zu wenig kritisch begleitet wird. Dies ist jedoch essenziell für eine demokratische Gesellschaft.“

„Sogenanntes Racial Profiling ist im Hamburger Stadtteil St. Pauli insbesondere in der Gegend der Hafenstrasse seit Jahren ein Problem. Erst im November 2020 hatte Barakat H., ein aus Togo stammender junger Mann vor dem Verwaltungsgericht Hamburg Recht bekommen. Er war in den Jahren zuvor auf dem Nachhauseweg unzählige Male kontrolliert worden. Zwei Kontrollen, gegen die er symbolisch Anzeige erstattete, wurden von den Richtern als verfassungswidriges Racial Profiling angesehen. Eigentlich sollte die Polizei auf Grundlage der Entscheidung des Verwaltungsgerichts seither nicht mehr anlasslos Personalien prüfen. Anwohner der Hafenstraße beschreiben jedoch, dass seit gut zwei Monaten die Kontrollen ganz im Gegenteil extrem zugenommen haben. Täglich würden nichtweiße Menschen von Polizeiaufgeboten in Uniform und in Zivil kontrolliert, oftmals regelrecht gejagt. Zweimal im vergangenen Monat sei zudem der Garten eines Hausprojekts mit Drogenhunden durchwühlt worden. »Insbesondere betroffen sind unsere gambischen Nachbarn, die in einem Garten einen Rückzugsraum haben. Racial Profiling ist struktureller Rassismus? Auch. Und auch: Erlebter Polizei-Rassismus  


„… 

Das hat zwar auch mit dem Rassismus der Polizist_innen zu tun, rassistischer Polizeigewalt liegt aber vor allem ein strukturelles Problem zugrunde, dass über die (rassistischen) Einstellungen individueller Polizist_innen hinaus geht. Gesetzliche Regelungen wie § 22 Abs. 1a BPolG und § 23 Abs. 1 Nr. 3 BPolG, sind die Rechtsgrundlage für Racial Profiling, sie ermöglichen verdachtsunabhängige Kontrollen und Befragungen. Vor allem der Phararagraph 22 Abs. 1 erlaubt der Bundespolizei lediglich eine Befragung von Reisenden in Zügen, Bahnhöfen und Flughäfen und nur in tatsächlichen Verdachtsmomenten auch eine Identitätsfeststellung. Die Realität sieht jedoch so aus, dass vor allem Schwarze Menschen unmittelbar aufgefordert werden sich auszuweisen. Dies stellt einen klaren Verstoß gegen das Gleichbehandlungsgesetz dar und wurde entsprechend von mehren Verwaltungsgerichten entsprechend untersagt. Die Kampagne „Ban Racial Profiling: Gefährliche Orte abschaffen“, an der die ISD maßgeblich und initiativ beteiligt ist, wird durch viele antirassistische, migrantische sowie Schwarze Organisationen getragen und wendet sich gegen die polizeiliche Praxis, einige Gebiete zu „kriminalitätsbelasteten Orten“ zu erklären. An diesen Orten ist die Polizei mit Sonderrechten ausgestattet, und das hat zur Folge, dass migrantische und nicht-weiße und vor allem Schwarze Menschen gezielt kontrolliert werden. Die Abschaffung dieser völlig intransparenten Einstufungen ist das vornehmliche Ziel..

.“ – aus dem 

Beitrag „Schwarze Perspektiven auf institutionellen Rassismus“ von Bafta Sarbo und Tahir Della (Initiative Schwarze Menschen in Deutschland Bund e.V. – ISD) bereits 2018 bei berlin rechtsaußen

 

, aus dem beide Dimensionen polizeistaatlichen Rassismus deutlich werden










Racial Profiling – Oberverwaltungsgericht NRW erklärt Personenkontrolle am Bahnhof Bochum für rechtswidrig  


„

Am heutigen Dienstag, dem 7. August 2018, verhandelte das Oberverwaltungsgericht des Landes Nordrhein-Westfalen in Münster einen Fall von ‚racial profiling‘ (Az. 5 A 294/16). Ein Schwarzer Deutscher war am Bahnhof Bochum einer verdachtsunabhängigen Personenkontrolle unterzogen worden. Er fühlte sich rassistisch diskriminiert und legte Klage gegen die Bundespolizei ein. Die Verhandlung endete mit einem Erfolg des Klägers und der Aufhebung des erstinstanzlich zum Teil klageabweisenden Urteils. Das Gericht verurteilte die Kontrolle des Klägers als Diskriminierungsverstoß. (…) Bei der Verhandlung wurde durch das Oberverwaltungsgericht klargestellt, dass die Hautfarbe auch als lediglich ein Kriterium unter mehreren grundsätzlich keine Rolle bei der Auswahl der zu kontrollierenden Person spielen darf. Deswegen war die Kontrolle des Klägers als nicht verfassungsgemäß einzustufen. Der Kläger äußerte: „Ich bin sehr froh über die heutige Entscheidung. Zwar glaube ich nicht, dass derartige Kontrollen nun aufhören, das Urteil ist jedoch ein großer Schritt in die richtige Richtung.“ Der Anwalt Sven Adam schätzt ein: „Mit dem heutigen Urteil hat das OVG deutlich gemacht, dass das Verbot rassistischer Diskriminierung bei Polizeikontrollen streng beachtet werden muss. Deswegen hat die Bundespolizei heute verloren und das ist erfreulich. Wenn das Gericht allerdings – wenngleich unter strengen Voraussetzungen – Ausnahmen von diesem Verbot andeutet, werden wir in weiteren Verfahren auch gegen solche Ausnahmen kämpfen, damit Kontrollen anhand der Hautfarbe aufhören.“ (…) Seit 2011 wurden vermehrt Klagen bei Verwaltungsgerichten verhandelt, die die Praxis des ‚racial profiling’ hinterfragen. Die gerichtliche Einschätzung geht zunehmend dahin, solche  verdachtsunabhängigen Personenkontrollen, aufgrund der Hautfarbe – auch wenn dies nur ein Kriterium unter mehreren darstellt – als nicht mit dem Gleichbehandlungsgrundsatz des Grundgesetzes (Art. 3 Abs. 3 GG) vereinbar, einzustufen

.“ 

Pressemitteilung vom 07.08.2018 von und bei der Anwaltskanzlei Sven Adam

 

 – wir gratulieren zum Urteil!










[Polizeikontrollen und Racial Profiling] 2,3 Prozent Trefferquote: Bundespolizei kontrolliert fast nur Unschuldige – Trotz geringer Trefferquote will Bundesregierung verdachtsunabhängige Kontrollen nicht abschaffen  




„… Fast 2,3 Millionen Mal hat die Bundespolizei im vergangenen Jahr Personen kontrolliert. Dabei hat sie nur wenige Gesetzesverstöße und Straftaten aufgedeckt. Um bei Polizeikontrollen Racial Profiling – Kontrollen nur oder hauptsächlich aufgrund der Hautfarbe – zu verhindern, fordern EU, Betroffenenvertreter und auch deutsche Gerichte, konkretere Vorgaben für Polizisten, wann und wie Reisende und Verdächtige kontrolliert werden können. Doch dazu sieht die Bundesregierung keinerlei Veranlassung. Das zeigt die Antwort auf eine Anfrage der Linkspartei-Abgeordneten Ulla Jelpke, die dem »nd« vorliegt. (…) Die meisten entdeckten Verstöße beziehen sich auf das Aufenthaltsgesetz, im vergangenen Jahr waren das 41 509. Damit liegt die Trefferquote beim Aufspüren von Verstößen gegen das Aufenthaltsgesetz bei unter zwei Prozent. Die Innenpolitikerin Jelpke fordert deswegen die Abschaffung verdachtsunabhängiger Kontrollen. Der »mageren Ausbeute« der Kontrollen stünden »gravierende Grundrechtseingriffe« gegenüber. (…) »In keinem einzigen Fall ist die Bundespolizei bisher bereit, einzugestehen, dass eine Kontrolle rassistisch motiviert war«, kritisiert Jelpke. Die Bundespolizei verweigere sich »hartnäckig einer Auseinandersetzung mit Rassismus in den eigenen Reihen« „

 

Beitrag von Moritz Wichmann unter Mitarbeit von Fabian Hillebrand vom 18. Mai 2018 bei neues Deutschland online 










[Audiointerview] Millionenfache, oft rassistische Polizeikontrollen z.B. in Zügen im Dreiländereck waren rechtswidrig  


„

Der Baden-Württembergische Verwaltungsgerichtshof hat am heutigen Mittwoch ein wegweisendes Urteil gegen das sogenannte racial-profiling bekanntgegeben, also gegen Kontrollen einzig aufgrund der Hautfarbe. Ein Deutscher mit dunkler Hautfarbe war während einer Geschäftsreise im Zug zwischen Baden-Baden und Offenburg von Bundespolizeibeamten einer sogenannten „verdachtsunabhängigen“ Personenkontrolle unterzogen worden. Außer ihm waren im Sichtfeld des Betroffenen keine weiteren Personen kontrolliert worden. Er klagte gegen die Polizeikontrolle. Vor dem Verwaltungsgericht Stuttgart hatte die Polizei sich zur Begründung der Kontrolle auf die sogenannte Schleierfahndung gestützt. Doch das Gericht stufte diese Rechtsgrundlage im Bundespolizeigesetz als europarechtswidrig ein. Und das sah nun in der Berufungsverhandlung auch der Baden-Württembergische Verwaltungsgerichtshof so. Über die Bedeutung des Urteils haben wir mit dem Anwalt des Klägers, dem Göttinger Rechtsanwalt Sven Adam gesprochen, der immer wieder erfolgreich Klagen gegen racial profiling führt.“

 

Interview von Fabian vom RDL mit Sven Adam vom 21. Februar 2018 beim Audioportal Freier Radios

 

 

 (Audiolänge: 10:27 Min.). Siehe dazu auch: 

Teilerfolg gegen Racial Profiling. Gerichtsentscheidung könnte helfen, rassistische Praxis weiter zurückzudrängen

. 

Artikel von Moritz Wichmann vom 23.02.2018 beim ND online 










Wie man gefährliche Orte schafft – und abschafft  


„

Vor einer Woche veröffentlichte das Berliner Polizeipräsidium auf Wunsch der Berliner Koalition zehn der sog. kriminalitätsbelasteten Orte (kbOs). Die Brisanz der Berichte von Betroffenen über Racial Profiling an diesen Orten bleibt bestehen. Zahlreiche antirassistische Berliner Organisationen und Initiativen haben sich daher zusammengetan, um die Landesregierung mit einer gemeinsamen Kampagne daran zu erinnern, Racial Profiling abzuschaffen und die polizeiliche Befugnis zur anlass- und verdachtsunabhängigen Kontrolle an den kbOs zurückzunehmen

“  – aus dem 

Beitrag „Ban! Racial Profiling. Gefährliche Orte abschaffen“ am 16. Juni 2017 bei linksunten.indymedia

 

, worin auch noch angekündigt wird: „

Neben einer Pressekampagne werden wir eine Postkartenaktion starten um unsere Wut den Verantwortlichen auf den Schreibtisch zu bringen und zu zeigen, dass wir viele sind. Auch ein rechtliches Gutachten ist geplant, um den Druck zu erhöhen. Denn egal ob »gefährlicher Ort« oder »kriminalitätsbelasteter Ort«: Racial Profling bleibt Rassismus und der muss gestoppt werden!

“ und auf Webseiten mit weiteren Informationen verwiesen wird.










Sicherheitsfalle: Racial Profiling


„

Aber auch viele Menschen, die nicht blond und blauäugig sind, sind Deutsche. Ein rassistisches Konzept von Nationalität ist noch immer tief in den Köpfen verankert. Wie dramatisch die Blindheit ist, die aus diesem Scheuklappendenken entsteht, wurde deutlich, als die NSU-Morde ans Licht der Öffentlichkeit kamen. Die einseitigen Ermittlungen führten dazu, dass die Täter unter den Migranten gesucht wurden, statt deutsche Nationalisten und Rassisten zu verdächtigen. Offene Ermittlungen ohne Vorurteile hätten viele Morde verhindern können. Nicht zu unterschätzen ist auch, welche Wirkungen solche Kontrollen haben. Sie bestätigen der Umwelt, dass schwarze Menschen und People of Colour verdächtig sind…

“ 

Beitrag von Elke Steven in der SoZ Nr 2/2017 










Januar 2017: 

Nach dem Anschlag in Berlin werden Flüchtlinge als Sündenböcke missbraucht: Überwachung treibt die Radikalisierung voran










Siehe auch das Dossier von 2016: 

Auch nach Köln: Gegen Sexismus und Rassismus!










My Right is your right: Demoaufruf zum Globalen Tag gegen Rassismus (21. März 2015)










Polizei und Rassismus. Über einen unschönen, aber unvermeidlichen Zusammenhang


„… 

Polizeirassismus hat Gründe: Der gesetzliche Auftrag zur Sortierung der Bevölkerung in staatlich anerkannte Rechtspersonen mit Aufenthaltstiteln einerseits und unerwünschte, d. h. »illegale« Ausländer andererseits übersetzt sich in der Praxis der polizeilichen Durchsetzung notwendigerweise in einen ethnischen Selektions- und Verdächtigungsprozess. Polizisten müssen das staatlich gewünschte Sortieren anhand von äußeren Merkmalen verinnerlichen, wollen sie ihre Aufgabe »vor Ort« erfolgreich bewältigen. Bereits hier zeigt sich, dass die beliebte Forderung nach einer Trennung von gesetzgeberischem Auftrag und ethnisch diskriminierendem Verhalten für Polizisten praktisch unmöglich ist. Kein Wunder, dass Polizisten dabei die feinen Unterschiede zwischen dem rechtsstaatlich gebotenen Verdacht gegen Ausländer und der geächteten Vorverurteilung von Menschen aufgrund von Rasse, Religion und Herkunft nicht immer ganz sauber auseinanderhalten. Die Übergänge von der vorurteilsfreien und möglichst humanen Durchsetzung der auf Abschottung, Abschreckung und Abschiebung orientierten Flüchtlingspolitik über die Übersetzung derselben in ein Feindbild vom Asylsuchenden bis hin zu den Abgründen rassistischer Misshandlungen sind keinesfalls zufällig, aber auch nicht zwangsläufig. Rassismus bei der Polizei ist eine Déformation professionelle und folglich auch kein speziell deutsches Phänomen. Den Rassismus bei der deutschen Polizei gibt es deshalb auch ohne die »ewig gestrigen Kollegen« aus alten Zeiten, die der frühen Bundesrepublik bei der Durchsetzung der demokratischen und freien Ordnung des westdeutschen Kapitalismus gedient hatten. In ihr nämlich hat er seine aktuelle Grundlage!…“

 

Artikel von Arian Schiffer-Nasserie

, zuerst erschienen in der Jungen Welt vom 7. November 2014. Wir danken dem Autor!










Polizei-Kontrolle: Das Ende von Racial Profiling


„

Eine groteske Kontrolle dunkelhäutiger Deutscher in einer Regionalbahn fordert eine richterliche Klarstellung heraus. Das Verwaltungsgericht Koblenz belehrt im Urteil die Bundespolizei, was eigentlich Einreise bedeutet. Die Folgen des Richtspruchs sind weitreichend – wenn er rechtskräftig wird…

“ 

Artikel von Joachim F. Tornau in der  fr online vom 7. November 2014

 

. Aus dem Text: „…

Verdachtsunabhängige Kontrollen sind in Deutschland grundsätzlich nur unter sehr eingeschränkten Bedingungen zulässig. Paragraf 22, Absatz 1a, des Bundespolizeigesetzes erlaubt jedoch das „Befragen“ von Bahnreisenden, wenn es dem Kampf gegen illegale Migration dient. So weit, so pauschal – und so umstritten, weil vor allem Menschen ins Visier geraten, die für die Streifenbeamten nicht „deutsch“ genug aussehen. Das Koblenzer Verwaltungsgericht aber verweist nun auf einen anderen, bislang kaum beachteten Passus des Paragrafen: Es darf nur in Zügen kontrolliert werden, von denen, wie es im Gesetzestext heißt, „auf Grund von Lageerkenntnissen oder grenzpolizeilicher Erfahrung anzunehmen ist, dass diese zur unerlaubten Einreise genutzt werden“. Und nach Ansicht des Gerichts kann davon bei einer fernab jeder Grenze verkehrenden Regionalbahn ganz offensichtlich nicht die Rede sein

…“










Neue Verfahren gegen die Bundespolizei zu „racial profiling“ in Zügen und Bahnhöfen


“

Das so genannte „racial profiling“, die Kontrolle von Menschen anhand äußerer Merkmale wie der Hautfarbe und anderer Zuschreibungen, wird die deutsche Justiz weiterhin beschäftigen. Erst im Oktober 2012 hatte des Oberverwaltungsgericht (OVG) Rheinland Pfalz mit einer Entscheidung europaweit für Aufsehen gesorgt, nach der die Kontrolle eines Studenten einzig wegen seiner „Hautfarbe“ nicht mit dem Gleichheitsgrundsatz des Grundgesetzes vereinbar ist. Nun sind vor den Verwaltungsgerichten Stuttgart und Köln zwei neue Verfahren gegen die Bundespolizei anhängig – auch hier war wieder die „Hautfarbe“ der Kläger der Grund für die Kontrollen

…” 

RAV- Pressemitteilung vom 18.12.13

title: Çiğdem Doğu: AKP's delaying tactics pose serious risks
content:
Kurdistan Women's Communities (KJK) Executive Council member Çiğdem Doğu appeared on a special program broadcast by Medya Haber television, where she discussed the Peace and Democratic Society Process initiated by Leader Apo (Abdullah Öcalan) and violence against women.




Çiğdem Doğu emphasized that the Peace and Democratic Society Process cannot be reduced to disarmament alone, arguing that a democratic solution to the Kurdish question and the democratization of Turkey must be addressed together. She stressed the importance of recognizing Leader Apo's role as coordinator of peace and political participation, saying that transparency, mutual dialogue and concrete steps are essential for building social support for peace.




Çiğdem Doğu also called on women to take action ahead of November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. She emphasized that violence against women cannot be explained as a series of isolated incidents but is produced by the male-dominated system. She stressed that women must go beyond resisting violence by building free lives, organizing themselves and developing self-defense mechanisms. Çiğdem Doğu said that women must establish control over their lives in economic, social, cultural and physical spheres, calling for November to be dedicated to the struggle for women's freedom under the slogan, "Now is the time for women, now is the time for women's self-defense."




Çiğdem Doğu also discussed the youth movements emerging in different countries, describing them as expressions of significant social opposition to the existing political system. Citing the student movement in Serbia, she said that young people no longer accept the capitalist way of life or the existing order and have the potential to bring about profound change by joining forces with society.




Abdullah Öcalan took a step by initiating the Peace and Democratic Society Process and assumed full responsibility. However, the Turkish state has yet to take any concrete steps in response. There has been discussion in certain circles, but nothing tangible has emerged. Let me also mention that reports suggest Öcalan has been moved to a new location. Yet the Turkish state has made no official announcement concerning Öcalan's coordinating role. Could you provide some information about this?




Before answering, I would like to mention that we have entered November, and the anniversary of November 27 is approaching. On this occasion, I congratulate President Apo on the anniversary of November 27 and extend my congratulations to our people. Throughout our history of struggle, we have lost thousands of martyrs and martyred comrades. Each of these martyrs played an enormously significant role in affirming the existence of the Kurdish people and opening the path toward freedom and a free life. They opened this path for us and showed us the way. On the occasion of November 27, I commemorate all our martyrs with love, respect and gratitude.




November 25 is also approaching. From the Mirabal sisters to Rosa Luxemburg, our comrades Sakine Cansız (Sara) and Evîn Goyî, and all the women comrades who were martyred throughout the years of war, these deaths and massacres resulted from attacks produced by the male-dominated system. There are also women murdered in social life as a result of this murderous, hierarchical system and the violent masculinity it produces. Hundreds of thousands, even millions of women have been killed. The struggle against this violence and the creation of a life in which women can live freely constitute a fundamental responsibility and obligation for our women's struggle. I therefore commemorate all women who have been murdered.




Turning to your question, there is certainly a process underway, and it is being widely discussed. Some say that everything is progressing smoothly. We also assess the situation. In reality, the process is largely standing still. It is not progressing as smoothly as some claim. There are difficulties and steps that have not been taken. We can therefore speak of an existing process, but how effectively and healthily it is advancing remains highly questionable. From our movement's perspective, it is a process that is not functioning or moving forward. It has not collapsed, but neither is it actively progressing.




Are they deliberately dragging out the process?




Yes, the process is being prolonged. But this delay poses a very serious danger. You asked about reports that Leader Apo has been moved to a new location. As far as we know, this is true. However, special warfare is also being conducted around this development. Ümit Özdağ recently made a statement claiming that Leader Apo had actually been freed but that the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government was having difficulty announcing it. Of course, this is not the case. There is a new location, but it remains a continuation of imprisonment. It is not a situation in which Leader Apo has been freed and can move around freely. Leader Apo must be free within the framework of this process, able to work freely and live freely.




This is essential for the process to advance and reach a healthy conclusion. As a movement, this is our fundamental position. A process in which Leader Apo is not free, cannot work and cannot participate more actively and effectively has no conditions for progress. The objective conditions for advancement cannot be established under such circumstances. The political significance of moving to a new location must therefore be understood in this context. A committee has been established. Its formation was officially announced, although its name was changed and it was described as a disarmament committee. Leader Apo called it the Peace and Political Participation Committee. The central issue under discussion is Leader Apo's role as the Coordinator of Peace and Political Participation within this committee.




The new location can only have meaning in this context, because Leader Apo fundamentally needs to be free. Its significance can only lie in enabling Leader Apo to work and participate actively as the committee's coordinator. There is talk of the "law of fraternity" in this peace process. For the process to advance in a healthy manner, it is extremely important that Leader Apo be able to assume an official, publicly recognized and effective role within this committee. Leader Apo must be able to meet journalists, academics, politicians and other individuals who can contribute to the Peace and Democratic Society Process. There must be opportunities for discussion and dialogue. An environment must be created in which Leader Apo's ideas, views, approach and strategy can reach the broadest possible sections of society and become widely understood. Yet none of these steps have been taken.




Would it not be better for Turkish society if Abdullah Öcalan could meet journalists, answer their questions and explain the paradigm of fraternity, allowing the democratic nation paradigm to become a reality for the peoples of Turkey and Kurdistan? Should the Turkish state not take more open and concrete steps?




Of course, it would be much better. As Leader Apo has repeatedly emphasized, we have experienced 50 years of struggle and a very difficult period of war. Naturally, mutual prejudices and fears have developed. This applies to both sides, to the Kurdish people and to the peoples of Turkey. There is therefore an urgent need to transform this atmosphere. How can that happen? We believe that the government's and state's approach must become much more visible and concrete. Creating such an atmosphere is important for building social support for peace. Fears must be overcome, we must get to know one another better, and relations must become more transparent. How much can the two sides communicate with each other? How effectively can they explain their concerns and circumstances? What is our strategy? What, for example, does a democratic republic strategy mean?




I sincerely believe that Leader Apo should be able to meet journalists and representatives of different sections of society. Leader Apo's views should be freely and openly communicated throughout society. Leader Apo must be able to address the Turkish public. I believe that the peoples of Turkey will understand the Kurdish People's Leader. They will understand what Leader Apo means and what a democratic republic represents. When we speak of a democratic nation, we are not seeking to divide Turkey. We do not want to partition this country. Yet this accusation has been attached to us. The definition of terrorism has largely been framed around allegations of separatism.




What harm could a democratic nation, a democratic republic or a democratic society cause anyone? What harm could they cause the peoples of Turkey, a woman, a man, a family or a young person living in Afyon, Edirne, Sinop, Antalya or any village or city in Turkey?




'Peace will harm no one'




Not only would these ideas cause no harm, but they would also create an environment in which shared life, democratic coexistence and living together would strengthen Turkey and its peoples. Mutual prejudices and fears would gradually disappear, and the distance between communities would diminish. We believe this. That is why the move to a new location must be accompanied by these steps as a matter of urgency. There is no reason to fear democracy. Why should anyone fear peace? It is something worth seriously considering. Why would anyone be afraid of peace? There was a situation of conflict, and a period of war emerged from those circumstances. The Kurds were denied recognition. The struggle arose as a necessity to overcome that denial.




Leader Apo has explained this repeatedly and continues to do so. Yes, there was a war, and we have reached this point. Now is the time for peace. Now is the time for fraternity. Yet we continue to see approaches that resist this perspective, particularly in the media and among certain politicians. There is also fear within the ruling AKP government. The answer to why the process is not advancing must largely be sought here. There is fear. What would be lost if peace were achieved? What could the Turkish state possibly lose through peace? On the contrary, it would gain much more. There would be significant gains for the state economically and politically, as well as opportunities to develop a more democratic culture of coexistence and political life among the peoples.




For example, there is frequent talk of a "regional ownership strategy" or the "Turkey Century" vision. These are objectives that the AKP government has presented as part of its political vision. But how can a Turkish state that has not resolved the most fundamental problem within its own country develop a regional strategy? Is it possible to pursue a regional strategy based solely on security concerns and particular interests? To use their terminology, there is a "terrorism" problem, and the approach is simply to disarm those involved and consider the matter settled. This is an extremely superficial, narrow and dangerous approach. If you do not resolve a problem, it will continue to reappear, grow and eventually produce different consequences.




Are the contradictions within the AKP not also contributing to the growth of this problem? The AKP has been unable to resolve its own internal contradictions, and there has been a major financial scandal within the party.




There are certainly very serious problems produced by the war, both inside and outside the AKP. Under the banners of nationalism, patriotism and declarations of love for the homeland, countless massacres have been committed. That is one dimension. Another dimension is the creation of enormous opportunities for profiteering. We see companies operating within the state, the government and political structures. The alliances and relationships between political actors and companies have created extensive opportunities for profit. How did this happen? If there had been genuine peace, healthy state administration and effective oversight mechanisms, would such enormous opportunities for profiteering have emerged? A political environment has developed in which even the little bread remaining in the hands of the people is taken away and stolen. We cannot consider this independently of the war. Of course, this is also a characteristic of the capitalist system itself. But the system has become even more corrupt as capital has used the war to expand its opportunities for profit.




There is no oversight within the state or government institutions. Nobody supervises anybody else. Such oversight does not serve their interests, and nobody holds them accountable. The institutions responsible for oversight should be investigating these matters. But the judiciary and many other state institutions have become paralyzed, producing serious consequences. The situation within the AKP reflects this reality. Similar consequences are emerging in different sectors. If there were peace, if the Kurdish people and the peoples of Turkey could come together within a democratic political environment, and if this atmosphere of hostility and the politics built upon it disappeared, corruption, profiteering and moral decay could certainly be prevented.




Why am I saying all this? Because we are currently in such a process, and problems are erupting. Imagine a person with an infected wound. You say, "I will heal this wound." You open it, but you neither operate on it nor treat it. The wound remains open, becomes exposed to more germs and grows increasingly infected. 




That is the situation we face. There are unhealthy approaches within the opposition, and there are problems emerging within the AKP. Rather than adopting the superficial approach of disarmament, we must carry out a proper, radical operation by democratizing the system and identifying the problem for what it is. This is the Kurdish question. It is a question of democratization, of Turkey's democratization. We must name it and undertake this operation together. The result would be a healthier and more democratic Turkey. Leader Apo has a historic role to play here. Nobody should portray Leader Apo as an enemy. Nobody should approach Leader Apo through special warfare or hostile characterizations. The Kurdish question does not concern Turkey alone. It is a multilayered issue.




'Democracy will benefit everyone'




The Kurdish question concerns Rojava and Syria. It concerns Başûr (Southern Kurdistan) and Iraq. It directly concerns Rojhilat (Eastern Kurdistan) and Iran. It has a very broad sphere of influence and involves multiple dimensions. The continued refusal to recognize Leader Apo's role and mission in resolving such a complex, multilayered question, attempts to trivialize that role or even portray Leader Apo as an enemy, are profoundly misguided. Such an approach carries the danger of losing a historic opportunity. Everyone must therefore recognize Leader Apo's role as Coordinator of Peace and Political Participation. This role must be acknowledged as an open, official and legitimate reality. Such recognition would also contribute to genuine normalization. I believe that everyone who understands and becomes familiar with Leader Apo's views will agree with this. It is therefore important to open the way for the process in this manner. Steps must be accelerated. The healthiest approach is not simply to say that the process is progressing well, but to advance it through concrete action.




Democracy will benefit everyone. Peace will benefit everyone. There should be no fear of democracy, peace or a solution. If a new republic is to emerge, it will be through overcoming our fears. The opposition should not fear this. Neither should ordinary people, workers or laborers. It is possible to develop such a process together. But as I have said, we can achieve this only by overcoming our fears and expanding the areas in which we come together. Leader Apo's role is extremely important in this respect.




We hope the state overcomes its fears. I do not believe that workers or Turkish society are afraid.




Special warfare creates precisely that perception!

title: ISIG: At Least 193 workers killed in workplace incidents in October
content:
The report published by the Workers’ Health and Safety Observatory (ISIG) said that at least 193 workers died in workplace fatalities during October and provided data on the causes of these deaths.




According to the report, 22 percent of workplace fatalities were caused by crushing and building collapses, 18 percent by traffic accidents, and 16 percent by falls from height.




The report states that 15 of the workers who lost their lives in October were women and 178 were men. It also records the deaths of nine child workers and 25 refugee and migrant workers in workplace fatalities.




In its September Workplace Fatality Report, ISIG stated that at least 226 workers had lost their lives in workplace fatalities across Turkey. The same figure of at least 226 worker deaths was also reported in its August report.




Meanwhile, ISIG's Child Workplace Fatality Report, covering the period from September 2025 to August 2026, recorded the deaths of 95 children in workplace fatalities.
