title: Spring named after Martyr Zinar
content:
A spring flowing down the slopes of the Pirîz region in the mountains of Kurdistan not only brings life to its surroundings but also preserves the memory of the friendship between local villagers and guerrilla Zinar. Used by local residents as a source of drinking water and by travellers as a place to rest, the spring became known as “Kanîya Şehîd Zinar” (Martyr Zinar’s Spring) following Zinar’s death as a martyr. He had devoted considerable effort to protecting and maintaining it.




With their natural caves, steep cliffs and cold-water springs, every corner of the mountains of Kurdistan holds its own story. Among the hidden natural wonders high in the mountains, springs play an important role in sustaining the lives of both people and other living creatures.







 







Various species of plants grow around Martyr Zinar’s Spring. As the water nourishes the surrounding vegetation, greenery spreads throughout the valley, turning the area into a resting place for travellers as well. Those crossing the mountain roads stop by the spring to catch their breath and cool off with a bowl of cold water.




Despite the harsh natural conditions and airstrikes in the area, the spring continues to flow, also meeting the water needs of nearby villagers. The cleaning and maintenance of this water source, which holds an important place in local life, is carried out through the collective efforts of those who use it. Villagers clean the spring and maintain its surroundings at regular intervals.




A friendship forged by the spring




One of those who devoted their efforts to protecting the spring was the young guerrilla fighter Zinar. Whenever villagers came to clean the spring, Zinar would help them and take part in building its stone walls. His care for the water source and participation in collective work helped forge a strong friendship between him and the local community.




Believing that a life of freedom could only be achieved through collective labour and struggle, Zinar saw taking part in the maintenance of the spring as an expression of this way of life. Working alongside the villagers, he contributed to protecting a water source that everyone could benefit from.




Villagers gave the spring Zinar's name




After Zinar fell as a martyr, the villagers named the spring after him so that his labour and sacrifice would not be forgotten. In this way, the water source they had worked together to maintain became a place where Zinar’s memory would live on.




Today, villagers continue to collect water from the spring, while travellers still stop there to rest. Nourishing the surrounding plants and bringing life to the valley, the spring also preserves the memory of the shared labour and friendship between Zinar and the villagers.

title: Climate change can be prevented through the struggle against capitalism
content:
The 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) is being held in Turkey to discuss ecological destruction and climate change. Environmental movements are organizing an alternative gathering and protest demonstrations in response.




Turkey currently ranks among the countries causing the greatest destruction of nature worldwide. Almost no city or district has been spared from environmental destruction. Nature is being deliberately devastated, particularly in Kurdistan. The Turkish state has built dozens of dams to separate guerrilla areas from one another and destroyed forests in areas where guerrillas operate. It has eliminated the living spaces of villages under the pretext of mineral exploration. The areas where dams have been constructed are among humanity's earliest settlements. This has also been another dimension of the cultural genocide carried out against the Kurdish people.




Policies of ecological destruction are also being implemented throughout Turkey. Streams that provide essential water supplies to villages in the Black Sea region have been destroyed. Forests have been devastated, and water sources poisoned in many places, particularly in the Kaz Mountains. The Justice and Development Party (AKP) government has launched unprecedented attacks on nature to enrich companies close to it. The AKP, which describes itself as Islamist, has turned hostility toward nature into a political policy to generate profits for its supporters. Money has become the AKP's only religion. Those benefiting most from profiteering in Turkey today are AKP members. The AKP can boast of making its supporters wealthy. Almost all those involved in investment fund fraud are AKP supporters, while many of the victims are also AKP members. Such a government thinks of nothing other than money and profit. AKP members have become people who swallow everything whole. In short, the AKP, which claimed to have come to power to fight corruption, has established an entirely corrupt system.




Marx said that capitalists would cut down a tree if they could not sell its shade. This is precisely the mentality of the AKP government. There is virtually nothing left in Turkey that the AKP has not sold. Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek's greatest talent is his constant search for new sources of revenue. With such a mentality, even the air will eventually be sold.




Now this government, which is so hostile to nature, is organizing COP31. It has even enlisted Tarkan in an attempt to deceive the world. The AKP has become skilled at deceiving both its own people and the international community. The reality of the AKP is that it blames others for the wrongs it commits. Erdoğan, in particular, has become an expert at this. He can tell all kinds of lies without the slightest embarrassment. Through COP31, he will explain how much Turkey supposedly cares about nature. He will probably point to the few public gardens he has had built as evidence of his environmental credentials. Perhaps he will even boast about how environmentally conscious his wife is.




The AKP government's assault on nature is a clear example of an authoritarian state's practices. It acts as though it can say, "I am the state, and I can turn nature upside down wherever I want." Yet nature is humanity's living environment. Settlements were established in particular places because those areas were suitable for human life. Settlements that have existed for thousands of years are being forcibly destroyed by an authoritarian state. No power has the right to make decisions concerning nature without the consent of the people. Yet this authoritarian state destroys people's living environments without their consent. From this perspective, holding COP31 in Turkey is deeply ironic.




Capitalist modernist forces around the world are hostile to nature. Industrialism, which is inherently destructive to nature, is being legitimized. Capitalist modernist forces attack nature from the air, land and sea, only to shed crocodile tears afterward. They conceal their true nature by organizing conferences on eliminating the factors that damage the climate. Capitalist powers destroy nature while competing with one another, then hold meetings to discuss how to prevent air pollution. This is the extent of the hypocrisy and dishonesty of capitalists.




Once everything becomes permissible in the pursuit of wealth and profit, nature is polluted and the climate is altered to a degree that threatens humanity's future. The mentality that considers the destruction of nature acceptable for profit and production must therefore be eliminated. Capitalist modernist forces will not do this. The destruction of nature can only be stopped by mobilizing all sections of society outside these capitalist modernist forces.




All humanity is currently under threat. Capitalism creates this threat in multiple dimensions. Neither air pollution nor climate change can be prevented without opposing capitalism.




Turkey is hosting COP31 to conceal its hostility toward nature. The conference serves no other purpose for Turkey. Perhaps those speaking there are delivering their speeches while standing on one leg! Nothing could be more hypocritical than those who destroy nature presenting themselves as its defenders.




Source: Yeni Yaşam newspaper

title: Incekara: Determination of young people proves that resistance is possible
content:
Protests launched by high school students in Paris against poor educational conditions have had a domino effect, spreading across France and to other countries. What began as a protest over education has developed into broader opposition to the system, encompassing the rising cost of living, declining wages and the housing crisis. These developments have also drawn attention to Turkey, where exploitation and inequality are even more deeply entrenched. University students took to the streets in Istanbul on the anniversary of the establishment of the Council of Higher Education (YÖK), an institution created in the aftermath of the fascist military coup of September 12, 1980. Students protested against the government's increasingly repressive measures. Demonstrations in Beyazıt Square and Beşiktaş were particularly marked by anger over a directive issued by the Ministry of Interior concerning universities in September. Istanbul University student Yasin Incekara spoke to ANF and said, "The determination shown by young people during the March 19 protests demonstrated that it is possible to resist the repressive regime being established in Turkey and showed how these blockades can be broken."




'Young people face similar forms of repression worldwide'




Yasin Incekara, a second-year sociology student at Istanbul University, said that young people taking to the streets across Europe and other parts of the world reflected the problems they share. Incekara emphasized that although Europe is often portrayed as a prosperous society, young people there also struggle with poverty and the problems created by the capitalist system. He said, "Over the past few months, we have seen young people taking to the streets against poverty, the lack of a future and repressive policies, not only in the Middle East but also in Europe, which is presented as prosperous. The youth uprising that has emerged particularly in France shows that young people face similar forms of repression not only in Turkey but in many parts of the world."




'March 19 showed young people's determination to seek freedom'




Incekara said that although resistance in Turkey has been weaker than in other countries, the March 19 protests demonstrated how young people could break through the restrictions being imposed on them. He described the March 19 protests and subsequent developments as evidence of young people's determination to pursue freedom in the face of oppression. Incekara said, "Through their determination to demand freedom against oppression, young people demonstrated during the March 19 protests that it is possible to resist the repressive regime being established in Turkey and showed how these blockades can be broken."




'Repressive directives seek to label revolutionary students as terrorists'




Incekara said that the authorities had intensified repression through various mechanisms in response to the determination shown by young people in their struggle. He pointed to the 17-article directive sent to universities by the Ministry of Interior in September, which he described as fascist, as the latest example. He argued that the directive sought to label students involved in progressive and revolutionary activities at universities as "terrorists." Incekara said: "The directive explicitly refers to providing private security personnel at universities with training similar to that given to police officers, as well as intensifying efforts to recruit informants and pressure students into becoming collaborators. It also opens the way for officers from the Anti-Terrorism Branch to set up information stands at universities under the pretext of awareness-raising and preventive activities, allowing them to conduct intelligence operations. Through these stands, the police aim to criminalize students involved in political struggle in the eyes of newly enrolled students, portraying them as marginal groups associated with terrorism and manipulating newcomers with warnings to 'stay away from them.' Of course, this does not reflect reality. If there is any group seeking to spread terror today, it is the capitalist state and the police themselves."




'Families are also pressured to inform on their children'




Incekara continued: "Just recently, a comrade from the Federation of Socialist Youth Associations was unlawfully abducted by police in Ankara. Our comrades from the Revolutionary Youth Union have also been receiving threatening phone calls from police officers. The police do not stop there. They directly contact our comrades' families. They call our families and attempt to portray our activities as being connected to terrorism. At the same time, they pressure families to act as informants by asking questions such as, 'Who are your children meeting? What are they doing?' These methods impose a profound humiliation on both families and revolutionary young people. We recently held a press conference at the Taksim branch of the Human Rights Association (IHD) to expose these practices, including summonses to the Vatan Police Headquarters. Our comrades have been forcibly summoned for questioning, subjected to pressure to become informants and faced numerous similar practices. Over the past three weeks, police have called eight of our comrades as well as their families. They particularly target families because they know that one of the first obstacles a revolutionary young person may encounter when deciding to struggle is opposition from their own family. The state is aware of this and attempts to exert pressure through family members. Last year, the family of our fellow student Ilayda Zorlu, who was studying at Karadeniz Technical University, was contacted by police because she had participated in International Working Women's Day activities on March 8. She subsequently lost her life under suspicious circumstances after being shot with a bullet from her father's service weapon. Her father was a police officer. That same year, our comrades who protested Ilayda's suspicious death outside the Süreyya Opera House in Kadıköy were detained and subjected to torture. I was also detained and tortured for delivering a political speech at my university protesting the loss of Ilayda Zorlu's life at such a young age. I am now facing trial and a possible five-year prison sentence."




'State student grants effectively tell us to die'




Incekara also drew attention to the economic difficulties facing university students, emphasizing that grants provided by the Credit and Dormitories Institution (KYK) fall far short of covering their basic needs. He said that he was forced to take on casual jobs to support himself. Incekara also said: "The little over 4,000 Turkish lira provided by the state today is essentially the capitalist state's way of telling young people: 'You might as well die. We do not care that you are condemned to misery, poverty and a future without prospects. Do whatever you want.' Young people are being driven to suicide because they cannot sustain their lives at university and are struggling with poverty. People living in state-run student dormitories, or struggling in their everyday lives, are reaching a point where they see no way out other than death. It is hardly surprising that the system promotes such profound hopelessness at a time when people, particularly young people, are being condemned to poverty and deprived of a future. But there are certainly things we can do against this. We must strengthen the struggle for freedom and a future. We must expand organized resistance. As young people, we must come together on campuses and wherever struggles are taking place. We must strengthen solidarity. We must demonstrate that liberation lies in a revolutionary way of life and in organized struggle. Without solidarity among ourselves, the capitalist system can easily condemn us to poverty and throw us into prison. We face various forms of repression precisely because we struggle for education in our mother tongue, against poverty and deprivation, and for our rights to free, quality education, housing and adequate nutrition. Our universities are being placed under siege through government-appointed trustees, fascist directives and the constant presence of police officers. Meanwhile, children forced to work in Vocational Education Centers (MESEM) are being killed in workplace accidents. When we speak out against this, we face further repression from the capitalist state."




'There has been a setback, but it can be overcome'




Incekara said that the recent decline in the youth movement and broader social opposition could not be explained solely by their own shortcomings. He argued that imperialist capitalist states around the world were attempting to create an atmosphere of fear and intimidation. He recalled that the fascist military coup of September 12, 1980, had sought to suppress social opposition and the progressive revolutionary movement. He said that the establishment of the Council of Higher Education following the coup was part of the same policies. Incekara described the Council of Higher Education as a project designed by the military junta to suppress the revolutionary democratic movements and progressive revolutionary youth whose influence had been growing both inside and outside universities.




Incekara said: Of course, there has been a setback. We are talking about the generation of Sinan, Mahir, Ibrahim and Deniz, who drove the US Sixth Fleet into the sea, carried out punitive actions against American imperialism and Zionists, and set fire to the official car of Komer, who was known as the 'Butcher of Vietnam.' Of course, compared with that period, there has been a decline. But this is not something that cannot be overcome. It certainly will be overcome. As I said at the beginning, we saw this during the March 19 protests. We witnessed people who have never known any government other than the Justice and Development Party (AKP) throughout their lives standing up against this ever-increasing oppression. We saw people pouring into the streets, resisting police barricades and fighting back against torture. This is undoubtedly valuable, and we must repeatedly examine what these developments mean for our struggle today."




'We need a movement that goes beyond the limits of the system'




Incekara recalled that the protests launched by young people living in the suburbs of Paris, demanding better educational conditions, more teachers and smaller class sizes, had gradually expanded with the participation of workers and other laboring sections of society. He emphasized the importance of connecting the youth movement with the demands of different social groups and argued that a similar approach was needed in Turkey. Incekara said: "Today, revolutionary leadership must be capable of guiding young people and working-class masses. There must be a political center. The issue is not simply the removal of the AKP government. Developments in Serbia demonstrate something important. The system is capable of skillfully exploiting such situations. Young people struggling for their rights in Serbia are once again being directed toward elections and attempts are being made to channel their movement into the ballot box. The situation in Turkey is not very different. The attitude of the Republican People's Party (CHP) during the March 19 protests, when it sought to neutralize the actions of young people, was clear for everyone to see. We need a mass movement capable of going beyond the limits of the existing system and uniting around the goal of revolution against that system. We need a generation of young people whose demands go much further and who are capable of building a life worthy of human dignity. Of course, this does not mean that we should disregard present conditions or abandon organizing around immediate demands. It is certainly important for a young person to organize around the problems they experience at university or in a state-run student dormitory and to ignite the spirit of resistance through those demands. However, our responsibility as progressive and revolutionary people is to take these demands further and enable people to struggle collectively against capitalism, imperialism, capital and neoliberal policies."

title: Συγκέντρωση για το δικαίωμα στη στέγαση, την Τετάρτη 11/11, 18.00, στην πλατεία Κλαυθμώνος
content:
Την Τετάρτη 11/11, στις 18.00, στην πλατεία Κλαυθμώνος, οργανώσεις και τοπικές πρωτοβουλίες καλούν σε συγκέντρωση για το δικαίωμα στη στέγαση, διαδηλώνοντας ενάντια στις εξώσεις, τις πολιτικές των funds και τις αυξήσεις των ενοικίων. Την ίδια μέρα πραγματοποιείται γενική απεργία στην Ισπανία με βασικό αίτημα το δικαίωμα στη στέγη ενώ παρόμοιοι αγώνες αρχίζουν να πραγματοποιούνται και σε άλλες χώρες στην Ευρώπη δομώντας ένα πανευρωπαικό αγώνα για την στέγαση.




Αφίσες/Καλέσματα:




Γειτονιές για το Δικαίωμα στη Στέγη







ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΙΒΗΡΙΚΗ ΧΕΡΣΟΝΗΣΟ ΜΕΧΡΙ ΤΗΝ ΕΛΛΑΔΑ, ΒΓΑΙΝΟΥΜΕ ΣΤΟΥΣ ΔΡΟΜΟΥΣ!




Τα ενοίκια ανεβαίνουν, οι εξώσεις και οι πλειστηριασμοί απειλούν όλο και περισσότερους ανθρώπους, οι γειτονιές μας αλλάζουν και η κατοικία μετατρέπεται ολοένα και περισσότερο από δικαίωμα και βασικό αγαθό σε εμπόρευμα και πεδίο κερδοσκοπίας.




Το τελευταίο διάστημα, η επίθεση στο δικαίωμα στην κατοικία κλιμακώνεται. Κάθε λίγο γινόμαστε μάρτυρες μιας νέας περίπτωσης όπου οι περίφημοι «επενδυτές» προσπαθούν να υφαρπάξουν σπίτια και να τα μετατρέψουν σε επενδυτικές αποδόσεις. Στις γειτονιές, στα χωριά και στις πόλεις μας, το αυτονόητο δικαίωμα στη στέγη και την αξιοπρεπή ζωή βρίσκεται υπό συνεχή πίεση, στο όνομα του υπερκέρδους και της μετατροπής ολόκληρων περιοχών σε θεματικά πάρκα για τουρίστες.




Όμως, τίποτα από όλα αυτά δεν συμβαίνει σε κενό. Αποτελούν μέρος ενός συνολικότερου αναπτυξιακού μοντέλου που προωθεί η ίδια η κυβέρνηση, ξεπουλώντας τη γη και την κατοικία και επιχειρώντας να μετατρέψει τη χώρα σε ένα Ελ Ντοράντο του επενδυτικού real estate. Τελευταία πράξη αυτής της προσπάθειας είναι το νομοσχέδιο «Ενίσχυση εποπτείας των υπό διαχείριση απαιτήσεων από δάνεια και πιστώσεις», όπου, παρά τον τίτλο του, στην ουσία δίνεται η δυνατότητα στα funds και στους servicers να λειτουργούν πλήρως ανεξέλεγκτα.




Απέναντι σε αυτή την επίθεση, όμως, οι τοπικές κοινωνίες και οι κοινότητες μας δεν μένουν με σταυρωμένα τα χέρια. Οργανώνονται, βρίσκει η μία την άλλη και δίνουν δεκάδες μικρές και μεγάλες μάχες. Αυτές οι διεκδικήσεις δείχνουν ότι η Ελλάδα έχει μπει για τα καλά στη μάχη για την κατοικία και ότι μόνο η συλλογική διεκδίκηση μπορεί να νικήσει.




Όμως δεν είμαστε μόνες/οι.




Στην Ισπανία ο κόσμος ξεσηκώθηκε για να υπερασπιστεί το σπίτι της Μαρικάρμεν και, μέσα από αυτή τη μάχη, να υπερασπιστεί τα σπίτια όλων. Στην Πορτογαλία, αντίστοιχα, όλο και περισσότεροι άνθρωποι οργανώνονται και παλεύουν για το δικαίωμα στην κατοικία.




Στις 11 Νοεμβρίου, ημέρα πανευρωπαϊκής διεκδίκησης του δικαιώματος στην κατοικία, δίνουμε ραντεβού στις 18:00 στην πλατεία Κλαυθμώνος. Ενώνουμε τις φωνές μας με όσους και όσες αγωνίζονται σε όλη την Ευρώπη για το δικαίωμα να ζούμε στις πόλεις και τις γειτονιές μας.




Διεκδικούμε:




• Πλαφόν στα ενοίκια




• Απαγόρευση πλειστηριασμών πρώτης κατοικίας & πώλησης κόκκινων δανείων με προσημείωση της πρώτης κατοικίας




• Κατάργηση της Golden Visa




• Φρένο στο Airbnb




• Δημόσια και αξιοπρεπή κοινωνική κατοικία




• Στήριξη εγχειρημάτων συλλογικής και συνεταιριστικής, μη κερδοσκοπικής κατοικίας




• Δημιουργία επαρκούς φοιτητικής στέγης




• Φρένο στις εξώσεις




• Καμία εκκένωση καταλήψεων στέγης




• Κανένας άνθρωπος στον δρόμο




Μας πετάνε στον δρόμο. Βγαίνουμε στους δρόμους!







Κατάληψη Στέγης Προσφύγων/Μεταναστών Νοταρά 26




Στηρίζουμε τα καλέσματα για το δικαίωμα στη στέγαση ενάντια στα ψηλά ενοικία, στο gentrification, στα airbnb, στα funds κοράκια, στις εξώσεις, κλπ.




Στηρίζουμε την γενική απεργία για το στεγαστικό στην Ισπανία που προκυρήχθηκε την ίδια μέρα.




Νίκη στον αγώνα των κατοίκων ενάντια στους εκμισθωτές, τους επενδυτές και τους επιχειρηματίες του real estate!




Συγκέντρωση-πορεία αυτή την Τετάρτη 11/11 στην Πλατεία Κλαυθμώνος, στις 18.00!













Κοινότητα Κατειλημμένων Προσφυγικών







ΚΑΛΕΣΜΑ ΤΗΣ ΚΟΙΝΟΤΗΤΑΣ ΚΑΤΕΙΛΗΜΜΕΝΩΝ ΠΡΟΣΦΥΓΙΚΩΝ ΣΤΗΝ ΚΙΝΗΤΟΠΟΙΗΣΗ ΓΙΑ ΤΗ ΣΤΕΓΑΣΗ ΣΤΙΣ 11 ΝΟΕΜΒΡΗ

Τους τελευταίους μήνες, σε πολλές χώρες της Ευρώπης και ιδιαίτερα στον ευρωπαϊκό Νότο, αναπτύσσονται σημαντικοί αγώνες με επίκεντρο το ζήτημα της στέγης. Στην Ισπανία, την Καταλονία και την Ιταλία, χιλιάδες άνθρωποι βγαίνουν στους δρόμους δυναμικά, αντιστέκονται στις εξώσεις και διεκδικούν το δικαίωμα της κοινωνικής βάσης στη στέγη.

Για εμάς, ως Κοινότητα Κατειλημμένων Προσφυγικών, που συγκροτεί μια μορφή κοινωνικής στέγης με ριζοσπαστικούς όρους, η διεκδίκηση της στέγης -στην περίπτωσή μας μέσω της κατάληψης- δεν αφορά απλώς την εξασφάλιση ενός χώρου κατοικίας. Αποτελεί μια διαδικασία επανοικειοποίησης βασικών δικαιωμάτων που έχουν αφαιρεθεί από την κοινωνία, μέσα από βίαιες και κοινωνιοκτόνες πολιτικές προς όφελος του κεφαλαίου. Πολιτικές που υποτιμούν την ίδια την αξία της ανθρώπινης ύπαρξης και μετατρέπουν ακόμη και τους στοιχειώδεις όρους επιβίωσης σε αντικείμενο διαπραγμάτευσης και κερδοφορίας.

Η στεγαστική κρίση, η οποία πλήττει ολόκληρη την Ευρώπη, στην Ελλάδα έχει λάβει ανεξέλεγκτες διαστάσεις, επηρεάζοντας πάνω από τον μισό πληθυσμό της χώρας. Δεν πρόκειται για ένα μεμονωμένο φαινόμενο, αλλά για το αποτέλεσμα της λειτουργίας του κρατικοκαπιταλιστικού συστήματος και των πολιτικών του: του ακραίου νεοφιλελευθερισμού και της χρηματικοποίησης των πιο βασικών κοινωνικών αγαθών, της τουριστικοποίησης και του εξευγενισμού των γειτονιών, καθώς και της επιθετικής δραστηριότητας των αρπακτικών ταμείων και των ολιγαρχών.

Η στεγαστική κρίση δεν περιορίζεται στην αδυναμία εξασφάλισης ενός σπιτιού. Οι εξώσεις, οι πλειστηριασμοί και τα απλησίαστα ενοίκια αποτελούν εκφάνσεις μιας ευρύτερης επίθεσης απέναντι στην κοινωνία, διαπερνώντας συνολικά τους όρους της ανθρώπινης επιβίωσης και στερώντας από τους ανθρώπους τη δυνατότητα να καλύψουν βασικές τους ανάγκες. Έρχεται έτσι να συμπληρώσει ένα ευρύτερο τοπίο κρατικής καταστολής, νεοφιλελεύθερων πολιτικών ανεξέλεγκτης κερδοφορίας του κεφαλαίου και ολοκληρωτικών πρακτικών κοινωνικού ελέγχου.

Γι’ αυτό και η συλλογική διεκδίκηση της στέγης είναι κάτι πολύ περισσότερο από τη διεκδίκηση ενός σπιτιού. Είναι πράξη αυτοάμυνας απέναντι στις επιθετικές πολιτικές κράτους και κεφαλαίου. Είναι αγώνας για ζωή και αξιοπρέπεια. Οι κινητοποιήσεις που αναπτύσσονται στις χώρες του ευρωπαϊκού νότου αναδεικνύουν το στεγαστικό ως ένα βαθιά πολιτικό ζήτημα, συνδέοντάς το με το σύνολο των προβλημάτων που αντιμετωπίζουν οι άνθρωποι από τα κάτω στην καθημερινότητά τους. Η τροφή, η στέγη, το νερό, το ρεύμα, η υγεία και η παιδεία δεν αποτελούν ξεχωριστά πεδία διεκδίκησης, αλλά αλληλένδετες όψεις της ίδιας πραγματικότητας. Στο επίκεντρο αυτών των αγώνων βρίσκεται, τελικά, η ανάγκη να επαναπροσδιοριστεί η χρήση όλων αυτών των αγαθών, ώστε να υπηρετούν τις κοινωνικές ανάγκες και όχι την κερδοφορία.

Η συλλογική διεκδίκηση της στέγης, ακριβώς επειδή αφορά έναν τόσο πυρηνικό στοιχείο της ανθρώπινης ύπαρξης, μπορεί να αποτελέσει αφετηρία για τη συγκρότηση ή την επανασύσταση των κοινοτήτων: για την οικοδόμηση, δηλαδή, ενός τρόπου συλλογικής ζωής που κράτος και καπιταλισμός επιχειρούν διαρκώς να αποδιαρθρώσουν και να εξαφανίσουν. Σήμερα, η συγκρότηση κοινοτήτων δεν αποτελεί μόνο μια απάντηση στη στεγαστική κρίση, στη βάση της αλληλεγγύης και της συλλογικής κάλυψης των αναγκών μας. Αποτελεί ταυτόχρονα μια αναγκαία μορφή κοινωνικής αυτοάμυνας απέναντι στον ολοκληρωτισμό και στον πόλεμο που διεξάγεται ενάντια στις κοινωνίες.

Ως Κοινότητα, ως κέντρο αγώνα και ως κίνημα αλληλεγγύης, ερχόμαστε από την εμπειρία των αγώνων του προηγούμενου διαστήματος -με αιχμή τον πολύμηνο αγώνα που δώσαμε τους τελευταίους μήνες για την υπεράσπιση της ύπαρξης της Κοινότητας, του παραδείγματός της και της ίδιας της ζωής-, μέσα από τους οποίους αναδείχθηκαν όλες αυτές οι διαστάσεις της ανθρώπινης ύπαρξης. Οι διεκδικήσεις για τη στέγη, την επιβίωση, την αξιοπρέπεια και τη συλλογική ζωή συναντήθηκαν και συμπυκνώθηκαν σε έναν κοινό αγώνα. Η απεργία πείνας αποτέλεσε την αιχμή αυτής της προσπάθειας και συνέβαλε στη συγκρότηση ενός ευρύτερου μετώπου στήριξης της Κοινότητας, φέρνοντας στο προσκήνιο ζητήματα που ξεπερνούν τα όρια της ίδιας της υπόθεσης των Προσφυγικών. Το κίνημα που αναπτύχθηκε πέτυχε μια σημαντική νίκη, ανοίγοντας τον δρόμο και δημιουργώντας προοπτικές για νέες νίκες της κοινωνίας και των κινημάτων.

Μέσα σε αυτή τη συνθήκη, θεωρούμε σημαντικό να συνδεθούμε με το κίνημα για τη στέγαση που αναπτύσσεται στην Ευρώπη, να συναντηθούμε στους δρόμους και να συμβάλουμε από κοινού στο άνοιγμα ενός κεντρικού αγώνα γύρω από αυτά τα ζητήματα. Να συμμετάσχουμε στις κινητοποιήσεις που έχουν οριστεί ως ορόσημα σε ευρωπαϊκό επίπεδο, με στόχο τη συγκρότηση ενός ευρύτερου μετώπου για τη στέγη και για όλα όσα συνδέονται με αυτή: τα ενοίκια, τους πλειστηριασμούς, τις εξώσεις, αλλά και την επανοικειοποίηση της χρήσης των άδειων σπιτιών προς όφελος της κοινωνίας. Σε αυτή την κατεύθυνση, η 11η Νοέμβρη μπορεί να αποτελέσει την πρώτη κοινή συνάντηση και συντονισμένη δράση όλων όσοι πλήττονται και οραματίζονται και αγωνίζονται για έναν άλλον κόσμο.

Καλούμε στις 11 Νοέμβρη, στις 18:00, στην πλατεία Κλαυθμώνος, σε συγκέντρωση και κινητοποίηση για να ενώσουμε τις φωνές μας και τους αγώνες μας με τις υπόλοιπες δυνάμεις της Ευρώπης για το ζήτημα της στέγης και να διεκδικήσουμε συλλογικά το δικαίωμα όλων σε μια ζωή με αξιοπρέπεια.







Αναρχοσυνδικαλιστική Πρωτοβουλία Ροσινάντε







#ΑΠΕΡΓΙΑ_25Ν




Η ΣΤΕΓΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΔΙΚΑΙΩΜΑ, ΟΧΙ ΕΜΠΟΡΕΥΜΑ!




Η απεργία στην Ισπανία στις 11 Νοέμβρη θα αποτελέσει το φάρο για ενα πανευρωπαΪκό κίνημα για το δικαίωμα στη στέγη. Η υπόθεση της Μαρί-Κάρμεν ήρθε σε μια συγκυρία πανευρωπαικής στεγαστικής κρίσης, κυρίως στον ευρωπαΪκό νότο, οπου η τουριστικοποίηση των μεγάλων αστικών κέντρων και νησιών έχει φτάσει στο απροχώρητο. Μεγάλες εταιρείες Real Estate, funds και services ελέγχουν όλο και μεγαλύτερο ποσοστό των ακινήτων. Η στέγη, η οποία είναι πανανθρώπινο δικαίωμα, εδώ και χρόνια αποτελεί πεδίο κερδοφορίας για το Κεφάλαιο και πλέον η πολιτική αυτή βρίσκεται στην κορύφωσή της.




Στην Ελλάδα, το Κεφάλαιο του Real Estate, εκμεταλλευόμενο τις ευνοϊκές συνθήκες για αυτό που άφησε η κρίση του ’09, μέσω κυρίως των πλειστηριασμών πρώτης κατοικίας, έχει μαζέψει ήδη ένα τεράστιο κομμάτι της αγοράς ακινήτων, το οποιο ειναι ετοιμο να ριξει στην αγορά και να θησαυρίσει απ αυτο. Ειδικότερα, στις περιοχές πέριξ των κέντρων των πόλεων η βραχυχρόνια μίσθωση είναι ένα φαινόμενο που τα τελευταία χρόνια κάνει όλο και λιγότερο βιώσιμες τις περιοχές αυτες για τους μόνιμους κατοίκους. Λιγότερα σπίτια προς μακροχρόνια μίσθωση σημαίνει αυτόματα αυξηση των τιμών των ενοικίων, λόγω της φυσης της αγορας, χωρίς αυτό βέβαια να αντικατοπτρίζεται και να μπορεί να στηριχθεί απο τους πενιχρούς μισθούς μας.




Προφανώς οι μεταναστευτικοί και προσφυγικοί πληθυσμοί δεν έμειναν έξω από το στόχαστρο της κυβέρνησης και της όλο και πιο ακροδεξιάς πολιτικής της. Μετά τις πρόσφατες δηλώσεις Χρυσοχοϊδη οπου στοχοποιεί προσφυγες και μετανάστες που διαμένουν σε μεγάλους αριθμούς στο ίδιο σπίτι για οποιαδήποτε εγκληματική δραστηριότητα στην περιοχή, η επιτροπή κατοίκων Αγίου Παντελεήμονα, Βικτώριας, η οποία στην περίοδο ανόδου της Χρυσής Αυγής είχε δείξει τα χρώματα της, σε συνεργασία με το ΑΤ Αγιου Παντελεημονα ξεκινήσανε καμπάνια για τον διωγμό από τα σπίτια τους. Με λίγα λόγια η στέγαση έγινε δούρειος ίππος για τη διάχυση φασιστικού δηλητηρίου.




Όμως, ο κόσμος της εργασίας δεν στέκεται αμέτοχος σε αυτό το πογκρομ του Κεφαλαίου απέναντι στο δικαίωμα της στέγασης. Η μαζική πορεία στην περιοχή της Κυψέλης στις 3 Οκτώβρη, η νίκη στον αγώνα της Κοινότητας Κατειλημμένων Προσφυγικών της λεωφόρου Αλεξάνδρας, που διασφάλισε την κατοικία εκατοντάδων ανθρώπων, οι μαζικές συγκεντρώσεις κατά του πλειστηριασμού πρώτης κατοικίας ηλικιωμένου ζευγαριού στην περιοχή της Κάτω Τούμπας στη Θεσσαλονίκη, καθώς και πρωτοβουλίες που ξεπηδούν και μαζικοποιούνται σε κάθε γειτονιά, κάνουν ξεκάθαρο πως ο αγώνας μας για το δικαίωμα στη στέγαση τώρα αρχίζει.




Στηριζουμε τη μικροφωνική συγκέντρωση του Σωματείου Βάσης Ενοικιαστών Αθήνας την Κυριακή 8/11 στις 12.00 στην πλατεία Βικτωρίας και την συγκέντρωση για το δικαίωμα στη στέγη στην Πλατεία Κλαυθμώνος την Τετάρτη 11/11 στις 18.00.




ΑΠΑΙΤΟΥΜΕ:




– Πτώση των ενοικίων, αυξήσεις στους μισθούς.




– Προστασία των ενοικιαστών/ριών από τις αυξήσεις και τις εξώσεις. Θεσμοθέτηση πλαφόν ενοικίου.




– Κατάργηση των ηλεκτρονικών πλειστηριασμών. Κούρεμα δανείων.




– Εργατική, κοινωνική, φοιτητική κατοικία για την κάλυψη όλων των αναγκών.




– Να γεμίσουν τα άδεια σπίτια! Στην Ελλάδα σήμερα υπάρχουν περισσότερες από 600.000 άδειες κατοικίες. Είναι αδιανόητο να υπάρχουν άνθρωποι που είναι άστεγοι ή ζουν σε απαράδεκτες στεγαστικές συνθήκες.




– Πάγωμα της βραχυχρόνιας μίσθωσης.




ΑΛΛΗΛΕΓΓΥΗ ΣΤΗΝ ΓΕΝΙΚΗ ΑΠΕΡΓΙΑ 11Ν ΣΤΗΝ ΙΣΠΑΝΙΑ




¡SOLIDARIDAD CON LA HUELGA GENERAL 11N!







Αναμέτρηση – ΑΠΟ – Ξεκίνημα -Μετάβαση




Τα σπίτια είναι για να ζούμε, όχι για να πλουτίζουν!




Όλοι και όλες στη διαδήλωση για το δικαίωμα στη στέγη,




Αθήνα: Τετάρτη 11 Νοέμβρη, πλατεία Κλαυθμώνος













Εργατοϋπαλληλικό Κέντρο Αθήνας







ΣΥΛΛΑΛΗΤΗΡΙΟ “ΣΤΕΓΗ ΓΙΑ ΟΛΟΥΣ” 11 ΝΟΕΜΒΡΗ










Το Εργατικό Κέντρο Αθήνας στηρίζει το συλλαλητήριο που πραγματοποιεί η Πρωτοβουλία Αγώνα «Κατοικία για όλους», για το ζήτημα της στέγης, στις 11 Νοέμβρη, στην πλατεία Κλαυθμώνος και ώρα 6μ.μ., ημέρα Γενικής Απεργίας στην Ισπανία για το θέμα αυτό.










Γιατί το δικαίωμα στην αξιοπρεπή κατοικία για όλους ως κοινωνικό αγαθό, και όχι εμπόρευμα, είναι αδιαπραγμάτευτο. Γιατί πρέπει να μπει ένα τέλος στην ανεξέλεγκτη εκτόξευση των ενοικίων, στους πλειστηριασμούς των κατοικιών και τις αρπαγές από τις Τράπεζες, τα funds και τους servicers. Γιατί πρέπει να ανασυγκροτηθεί ο Οργανισμός Εργατικής Κατοικίας ώστε να ξεκινήσει ένα μαζικό πρόγραμμα εργατικής, κοινωνικής και φοιτητικής κατοικίας.










Το ΕΚΑ καλεί τα σωματεία μέλη τους να συμμετάσχουν στο συλλαλητήριο ώστε όλοι μαζί να υπερασπιστούμε το δικαίωμα στην κατοικία για όλους.













Σωματείο Συνταξιούχων “Η Συσπείρωση”




Πανευρωπαϊκή Ημέρα Δράσης για το Δικαίωμα στην Στέγη – ΤΕΤΑΡΤΗ 11 Νοεμβρίου, Πλατεία Κλαυθμώνος 18:00




Η Πρωτοβουλία μας συντάσσεται, καλεί και συμμετέχει




Πανευρωπαϊκή ημέρα δράσης με αφετηρία κυρίως την Ισπανία και συμμετοχή από άλλες χώρες:




Ισπανία: Γενική απεργία 24 ωρών (Huelga General / Huelga por la vivienda) που έχουν προκηρύξει τα μεγάλα συνδικάτα CCOO και UGT, μαζί με CGT, CNT και τα συνδικάτα ενοικιαστών (Sindicato de Inquilinas).




Τα βασικά αιτήματα, είναι προσιτή κατοικία, αύξηση μισθών, έλεγχος των τιμών και μέτρα κατά των εξώσεων.




Η κινητοποίηση ενισχύθηκε μετά την έξωση και τον θάνατο της ηλικιωμένης Maricarmen Abascal.




Ελλάδα (Αθήνα):




Συγκέντρωση την Τετάρτη 11 Νοεμβρίου στις 18:00 στην Πλατεία Κλαυθμώνος. Συμμετέχουν συνδικάτα, φοιτητικοί σύλλογοι και κινήσεις για τη στέγαση. Το σύνθημα είναι “Κανένας άνθρωπος χωρίς κατοικία”.




Ο Δήμος Αθηναίων ενέκρινε ομόφωνο ψήφισμα στήριξης, με εισήγηση του δημάρχου Χάρη Δούκα.




Αναφέρονται επίσης δράσεις ή οργανωτικές κινήσεις στο Βερολίνο, στην Πορτογαλία και σε άλλες ευρωπαϊκές χώρες, καθώς και συντονισμός μεταξύ οργανώσεων από διάφορα κράτη.




Η στεγαστική κρίση (αυξήσεις ενοικίων, έλλειψη κοινωνικής κατοικίας, πλειστηριασμοί κ.λπ.) είναι το κεντρικό θέμα σε όλη την Ευρώπη αυτή την περίοδο.




Η Πρωτοβουλία “Η ΔΙΚΑΙΩΣΗ”, συντάσσεται, καλεί και συμμετέχει και με το αίτημα για την σύσταση Εξεταστικής Επιτροπής, σύμφωνα με την δική της πρόταση που κατέθεσε ο ΣΥ.ΡΙΖ.Α. και αναμένεται να έρθει σε ψηφοφορία εντός του Νοεμβρίου

author: cnt.es
title: La huelga general del 11N transcurre con normalidad generalizada, con incidencias en varios puntos del Estado
content:
Imagen

: 07:30h. Piquete informativo en el Poligono do Tambre (Compostela) | Fuente: CNT







CNT denuncia que, en algunas localidades, los cuerpos policiales están impidiendo a los comités de huelga ejercer su labor de comprobación del cumplimiento de los servicios mínimos, obstaculizando así el legítimo ejercicio de las funciones que corresponden a la representación de las personas trabajadoras durante la huelga.







La huelga general convocada este 11 de noviembre está teniendo un seguimiento e incidencia desigual en los distintos territorios, con una situación de relativa normalidad generalizada, aunque con actuaciones destacadas de los piquetes informativos y algunos incidentes policiales.




Todo esto, después del establecimiento de servicios mínimos abusivos, como ha ocurrido en Madrid, donde el Tribunal Supremo ha anulado los servicios mínimos establecidos por la Comunidad para esta huelga.




En varios puntos, sobre todo en Valencia y Cataluña, se han producido cortes de tráfico en los accesos a la ciudad o a los polígonos industriales, en una acciones conjuntas de los comités de huelga de barrio, sindicatos de vivienda y CNT.




La situación más tensa se ha vivido en Zamora, donde durante el primer piquete en el servicio de autobuses se han producido agresiones policiales, con un compañero detenido y varias personas identificadas. En Madrid, también se ha producido una detención durante las actuaciones de los piquetes.




CNT continuará informando del desarrollo de la jornada y de las incidencias que se produzcan en los distintos territorios.

author: ROAPE
title: A demand that can be checked
content:
Africa is not poor. Africa is drained. What changed for the generation that filled Nairobi’s streets in 2024 was not courage but the ability to prove it.




I was raised inside a sentence. Before I could find my grandparents’ country on a map, I had been handed a verdict: it was poor. The word arrived with the settled cadence of fact, and it lodged so early that I mistook it for a thing I had discovered rather than a thing I had been given.




What broke the sentence was not a feeling. It was a number. The continent I had been taught to grieve over is not a debtor to the world. It is a creditor. More wealth leaves it each year than arrives. I had accepted that poverty the way one accepts weather. Weather has no author. A transaction has two parties.




A generation is now doing the arithmetic in public, and it has begun to ask who the other party is.




That question travels further than the ledger. It begins as arithmetic: whose wealth leaves, and by what route. It becomes politics the moment enough people can do that arithmetic at once, which is what happened in Nairobi in June 2024. And it arrives, finally, at the governments that have taken up the same grievance and answered it by making the arithmetic impossible to check. Nairobi and Ouagadougou are not two subjects. They are the same demand at two different stages of what happens when it is made.




The lie and the ledger




Across most of the colonized continent, a child was taught a single proposition: Africa is poor, as though penury were a fact of the soil rather than a condition imposed on it. The word arrived early and without cease, in the textbook, the telethon, the appeal letter. Poor Africa. It was the first sentence the world pronounced over its people, and it was a falsehood, an inversion so total that once seen, it cannot be unseen.




One fact undoes it. In 2015, a high-level panel convened jointly by the African Union and the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, chaired by Thabo Mbeki, reported that 

Africa loses on the order of fifty billion United States dollars each year to illicit financial flows

. The money is spirited out through trade misinvoicing, transfer mispricing, and outright theft, most of it effected by multinational corporations. Mbeki stated the arithmetic without embellishment: “The continent is losing an estimated US $50 billion a year through illicit capital outflows. This amount of money is larger in volume than the assistance the continent receives annually.”




The panel’s estimate rested on trade misinvoicing alone, the gap between customs records for the same shipment on each side of a border. A later UNCTAD accounting used a broader methodology, adding capital flight and criminal proceeds to the same trade data. It put the annual loss at 

$88.6 billion, 3.7 percent of Africa’s GDP, with a cumulative total of $836 billion between 2000 and 2015

.




The abstraction “illicit financial flows” conceals how ordinary the theft is: not the suitcase of cash but the routine of commercial mispricing. A subsidiary in Lusaka or Kinshasa sells its ore to a related company abroad at a fraction of market value. The profit settles in a low-tax jurisdiction while the producing country records a loss on wealth that was demonstrably its own. Each transaction is individually deniable, papered with defensible transfer prices, so a systematic drain presents itself as a thousand unrelated, lawful-looking transfers. Estimates built on mirrored trade statistics are themselves debated among economists, and the panel’s figure is best read as an order of magnitude rather than a ledger line.




The poverty, then, is real but not native. It is manufactured: the classic paradox of plenty, in which the ground beneath the poorest villages holds the minerals the wealthy world cannot function without, and the wealth flows outward rather than up. Africa is not poor; Africa is drained. The entire moral theatre of the preceding century – the rescue, the aid, the loan – has depended upon the colonized believing the first sentence rather than the second. This is coloniality in its economic register: the extractive periphery maintained long after the flag has changed, its dispossession renamed as assistance.




The paradox of plenty




To speak of a resource curse risks the fatalism the inversion is meant to dispel: the suggestion that mineral wealth simply ruins whatever it touches, a law of nature no one need answer for. 

Terry Lynn Karl’s study of oil booms and petro-states

 shows the paradox of plenty is a property of the institutions that form around a resource, not of the resource itself. It is a political-economic trap, engineered and maintained, not a destiny written into the ore.




Where a state’s revenue comes from renting out extraction rather than taxing its citizens’ labor, the architecture of accountability inverts: government depends on the buyer rather than the people, and answers to whoever holds the concession rather than whoever holds the vote. Incentives that might have built roads, schools, and factories redirect toward capturing a rent that requires none of that.




Transposed to the continent at large, this relocates the curse from the mineral, and from the African, to the relation: the arrangement by which extraction’s proceeds flow outward while its costs remain behind. A cobalt seam under a Congolese village is not a misfortune; the arrangement by which that cobalt leaves the country barely valued, its worth realized in a refinery, a battery, and a share price located everywhere but there, is a design. Manufactured poverty is the correct term because manufacture implies a maker, a process that could have been made otherwise and can yet be unmade.




The Democratic Republic of the Congo furnishes the starkest illustration. Its mines produce roughly three-quarters of the world’s cobalt, and its soil holds about half of known reserves, the mineral without which the batteries of the energy transition cannot be built. Yet the country ranks persistently among the poorest on earth, its artisanal miners among the least compensated participants in one of the most valuable supply chains in the world.




This is not irony; it is mechanism. The cobalt is cheap at the pit and dear at the point of sale because its value is deliberately realized elsewhere, in the refining and the branding the extractive arrangement is designed to keep abroad. The poverty of the Congolese miner is the success of a structure engineered to ensure the cobalt would not enrich him.




The engineering, and the fight over it, can be dated and named. The 2018 revision of the country’s mining code declared cobalt a strategic substance and raised the royalty on it to ten percent, resisted at every step by the international miners it taxed. The refining, where the value concentrates, remains overwhelmingly abroad, above all in China




Artisanal cobalt miners in the DR Congo (Wikimedia Commons, 2020)




And the Congolese have never lacked their own historians of the arrangement: Georges Nzongola-Ntalaja’s people’s history runs the line from Leopold’s concession state to the present, a study in how a territory was organized to hold wealth for other people to collect, and its population counted as the expense of holding it.




A generation has now learned to say the second sentence out loud: not poor, but drained.




The generation built to see it




Every generation before the present one received the lie, and most were made to live inside it. The difference now is not courage, and it is not will; earlier generations rose repeatedly, in the anti-austerity riots of the 1980s, the democratization wave of the early 1990s, Kenya’s own Saba Saba movement of 1990, all without a smartphone among them.




I am of that generation. I was at the University of Nairobi in 1990, and Saba Saba is not a date I looked up. Most of my contemporaries from that campus have children in their twenties now, which means the crowd that filled the streets in June 2024 is, in the plainest sense, ours. What changed is the cost of finding one another and of knowing that others know: one cannot audit a ledger one is never shown, and one cannot rise alone against a room that pretends the ledger does not exist.




The world our parents inhabited was one in which the story of Africa was composed and broadcast elsewhere, delivered to its own people already finished. To dissent, one first had to discover, in libraries that did not stock the relevant books and against newspapers that did not print the relevant numbers. Epistemic erasure operated at the level of everyday access: not the burning of an archive but the quiet management of what a people may come to know about itself.




That scarcity has ended. Gen Z, born into the century of the phone, is among the most educated generations in the continent’s history and the first raised inside something approaching information liberty. A nineteen-year-old in Nairobi, Lagos, or Ouagadougou can, within an afternoon, set the official account of her country’s poverty beside the figures of the Mbeki panel and the history of the loan that mortgaged her future before her birth. The veil our parents needed a lifetime to lift, she lifts before noon, on a shared platform, in real time, alongside millions performing the same arithmetic.




The collective dimension is constitutive, and it turns on a threshold. Below it, a discovery is a sensation, and it dies when the next one arrives. Above it, the discovery trends, and it reaches millions. A fact discovered alone can be doubted or dismissed by an authority that controls the room; a fact discovered simultaneously by millions, each able to see the others discovering it, acquires a different kind of solidity. The infrastructure built to monetize attention has become an instrument of collective epistemic labor, and it is that labor the old management of knowledge cannot survive.




Consider the young Kenyan history creators now easy to find on Instagram and TikTok, a documented cohort teaching their country’s history from the sources that matter most: books written or narrated by Kenyans who lived the events, read with scrutiny. The first of them reached print through the recording and shaping hand of an American anthropologist, and the memoir corpus is fought-over memory, marked by post-independence politics, not a pure archive awaiting retrieval.




They hold up 

Mau Mau from Within

, Karari Njama’s account, himself of the movement, of the Kenya Land and Freedom Army, co-produced with Donald Barnett; 

The Swords of Kirinyaga

, Kahinga Wachanga’s memoir of the same war; and 

Kenya’s Freedom Struggle: The Dedan Kimathi Papers

, gathered by the historian Maina wa Kinyatti. They set these against the colonial counter-account, Fred Majdalany’s 

State of Emergency

, “the full story of Mau Mau” narrated from above.




They carry their phone cameras to the sites themselves, the detention-camp grounds, the museum at Nyeri, posting the remnants still standing where the official story insisted there was nothing to see. On the camps they reach for 

Imperial Reckoning

, Caroline Elkins’s Pulitzer Prize–winning reconstruction of the detention system Britain built and then tried to burn out of its own records. Its death-toll estimates remain sharply contested by historians who confirmed the system’s brutality while rejecting the largest numbers. David Anderson’s parallel history of the Emergency’s gallows stands beside it. They do not refuse external scholarship; they conscript it, reaching for a Western historian’s work precisely where it corroborates their people’s testimony and convicts the empire out of its own archives.




I have my voice; don’t you dare claim to represent it

 is not a slogan the Mau Mau borrowed; it is a thing they did, in print, from within. A generation of creators now carries that refusal onto the feed: not merely consuming the data of extraction but producing the counter-history from their own people’s writing. The platforms that elsewhere turn suffering into spectacle are converted here into a schoolroom the empire never authorized.




Kenya in June 2024 is the emblem. When the government advanced a finance bill stacking new taxes on an already-straitened population, it was the young, not the parties or the unions, who rose first. Organized horizontally and largely without leaders, they filled the streets and, for a moment, the parliament itself. Analysts now track the episode as the leading edge of a continent-wide wave, “Africa’s Gen Z awakening,” a politics digital, Pan-African in sympathy, and constitutively unwilling to be spoken for.




The police answered the protests with live fire: 

the national human rights commission counted at least sixty dead

 across the June and July 2024 wave. The president declined to sign the bill the day after Parliament was breached, saying the people had spoken; by December, a substantial part of its revenue substance had returned in amendment acts passed under quieter skies. Through the following months the commission documented dozens of abductions of critics, many seized over posts, some never returned.




In June 2025 a young teacher and blogger, Albert Ojwang, died in a police cell after being arrested over a post about a senior officer. The anniversary protests that month, and the Saba Saba demonstrations of July 7, 2025, were met with the deadliest force yet: 

thirty-eight killed on that single day by the commission’s count

, and 

one hundred and fifteen across the year of protest by the tallies reported since

.




The movement, leaderless by design, has strained under what leaderless movements strain under: the difficulty of converting a street’s veto into a durable politics. Its members now argue among themselves about registration drives, further protest, and exhaustion. None of this cancels June 2024; it prices it. An awakened voice met force, lost ground, and has not yet been converted into power. That question is still open. What the record forbids is only the pretence that the breach of parliament was a conclusion.




What the young in Nairobi said, on their placards and in their hashtags, is on the record: 

reject

, Reject Finance Bill 2024, Occupy Parliament, a grammar of refusal aimed at their own government’s arithmetic. What they did not say is on the record too: the demand was not for more aid, a softer loan, a kinder donor. To ask for more aid would be to accept the first sentence and plead for its consequences to fall more lightly; to refuse the finance bill was to reject the arithmetic that made the citizen, rather than the outflow, the object of the state’s extraction. Once a population knows itself to be drained rather than poor, the demand shifts from mercy to accounting, which is far more dangerous, because it can be checked.




The youth and the junta




The second objection presses the same charge harder. This time it is aimed at me. I have braided two movements together, and they are not one. To celebrate Sahelian “sovereignty,” the critic says, is to whitewash a coup.




The charge is largely correct. On one side stand the Gen Z youth movements, in Kenya and Nigeria, bottom-up, digital, democratic, and directed at their own governments. On the other stand the Sahel’s sovereigntists, in Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger. Their economic refusals are real, and they are specific. They are led by military governments that seized power in coups




Assimi Goïta shortly before proclaiming himself head of the ruling junta in Mali following the 2020 coup (Wikimedia Commons, 2020).




The test is not an electoral calendar. That is the West’s favorite yardstick, and the easiest to fail on somebody else’s behalf. The test is whether a Sahelian can tell his own government it is wrong and still be free the next morning. On that test the young in Nairobi and the juntas in the Sahel are not doing the same thing.




The credit side must be entered with the same specificity, or the audit is not one. 

Mali adopted a mining code in August 2023

 that raises the Malian share of a project from a maximum of twenty percent to thirty-five, ends a set of tax exemptions, and was projected by its own government to add some five hundred billion CFA francs a year.




Burkina Faso 

completed the transfer of five gold assets to a state company, SOPAMIB

, in June 2025. It had broken ground on its first gold refinery, designed for a hundred and fifty tonnes a year, in November 2023. Traoré put the reason in his own words: “We will no longer be refining our gold abroad but have it refined. And we will know what the real value of the raw gold that comes out of our mines is.”




Niger moved in June 2025 to nationalize Somaïr

, where Orano held 63.4 percent against the state’s 36.6, and reassigned the permits to a state entity. The three governments left ECOWAS together in January 2025, with a joint force and a common biometric passport. They are the same act the Congo performed in 2018, and they earn the same credit.




They are also recent, unfinished, and taken by governments no one is permitted to question. Each will be judged by whether it survives the war and outlives the men who ordered it. That judgment requires a press, and the press is the thing being conscripted.




Benin ran the same experiment without a coup. The country exported almost all its raw cotton to Bangladesh until 2020. The Glo-Djigbé zone now turns some forty thousand tonnes of it into seven to ten million garments a year, and 

the African Development Bank recorded the current-account deficit falling from 6.2 percent of GDP to 5.7

 between 2024 and 2025. That is the cobalt argument answered by a government that holds elections.




Then the other ledger. In December 2025, soldiers announced they had removed then President of Benin Talon, and were beaten within hours by loyalist units, by Nigerian air strikes, and by French troops clearing the ground afterward. Romuald Wadagni, the finance minister who built the Glo-Djigbé zone, won the presidency four months later with 94.27 percent. The main opposition party fielded no candidate. Observers called the vote neither free nor fair.




No one called any of that a coup. The test is the same in Cotonou, Benin as in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, and Cotonou fails the second half of it too. A voter in Benin had no way to ask it in April. A journalist in Burkina Faso was conscripted for asking it in print. 

Why, and who says, and on whose authority.




The coups rode a war, and the war did not begin in the Sahel. Mali’s north had risen three times before 2012, most recently in 1990 and 2006, each time against a state that left it unemployed, unrepresented, and largely ungoverned. What changed in 2011 was armament. NATO’s intervention collapsed the Libyan state, and Tuareg fighters came south carrying the largest arsenal northern Mali had ever seen. They founded the MNLA that October.




By April 2012, the rebellion they began had been captured by Ansar Dine and its jihadist allies, and a sovereignty claim had become a sharia claim. France then fought there for a decade, through Serval and Barkhane, and withdrew without defeating what its own earlier intervention had helped to arm. An argument that refuses to call African poverty natural cannot then treat an African war as weather.




That is the charge against Paris, and it is sustained. It does not acquit Ouagadougou or Bamako. The insurgency was the stated justification of junta rule, and on that stated mission the record since is damning.




In the three years after Burkina Faso’s second 2022 coup, civilian deaths at the hands of militant groups nearly doubled against the pre-coup period, and deaths at the hands of the state’s own forces and allied militias rose faster still. Independent analysts assess that the army operates freely in as little as a third of the country.




Human Rights Watch has documented massacre after massacre attributed to the security forces and their auxiliaries: 

at least 156 civilians at Karma in April 2023

; 

223 at Nondin and Soro in February 2024, including at least 56 children

; 

at least 130 Fulani civilians near Solenzo in March 2025

. In Mali, the UN found at least 500 killed at Moura in 2022 in an operation by Malian forces and their Russian partners.




The dead of these operations are disproportionately Fulani, a largely pastoralist people collectively silhouetted as jihadist by the counterinsurgency’s own categories. Suspicion by category is being run here at its most lethal setting, by African states, against African civilians. The rule against it does not change nationality at the border. Gold retained in a war economy funds the war, and the condition of being answerable at home is precisely what a junta forecloses. Nothing in the resource-sovereignty case survives contact with a massacre it declines to mention.




Ask the Sahelian press, since it is Sahelian. On 24 March 2024 Burkina Faso’s government conscripted four journalists into the army, among them Guezouma Sanogo and Boukari Ouoba of the national journalists’ association and Luc Pagbelguem of BF1, after they criticized restrictions on speech. Kalifara Séré went the same way for questioning a photograph of the head of state. Serge Oulon and Adama Bayala were conscripted and have not come back. A sweeping emergency law supplies the mechanism.




These are not French proxies. They are Burkinabè reporters, and the state silencing them is Burkinabè too. The Nigerien political scientist Rahmane Idrissa, writing from inside the region’s own argument rather than from Paris, traces Niger’s coup to the hollowing of its domestic institutions rather than to foreign hands alone, and doubts the soldiers will give the state back. The demand that African resources serve Africans is not weakened by asking which Africans, and who is permitted to answer.




The line between the two is real, and the generation it describes does not all stand on one side of it. Afrobarometer’s surveys complicate the picture: about two-thirds of Africans prefer democracy to any alternative, yet a slim majority would tolerate a military intervention when elected leaders abuse power, and the tolerance runs highest, at 56 percent, among the young. The adulation of Burkina Faso’s Ibrahim Traoré across African and diaspora social media is a documented phenomenon, not a fringe.




It is also, in documented part, manufactured: fact-checkers have traced hundreds of AI-generated videos glorifying Traoré, synthetic celebrities singing his praises to tens of millions of views, an organized propaganda ecosystem whose volume must not be mistaken for a measured public. Some of the same generation that filled Nairobi’s streets demanding accountability cheers a captain in Ouagadougou who answers to no electorate.




What unites them is narrower but real: a generational refusal of the neocolonial economic order, the insistence that African resources must serve Africans and that the loan is not fate. The vehicles diverge sharply, and the divergence is exactly democracy: whether the people in whose name the resources are reclaimed are themselves in the room. Economic sovereignty can be honoured; the suspension of a people’s voice cannot, and must be refused in the Sahel for the same reason it must be refused everywhere else.




To celebrate a government’s gold while ignoring its silenced press would do to the Sahelian people the very thing the refusal forbids: speak for them while they are kept from speaking for themselves. A junta that reclaims the mineral and confiscates the microphone completes only half of the decolonial task, and betrays the other half, the half that would have let its own people tell it when it was wrong.




Return to the ledger. The fifty billion is not an injury that happened once. It is a procedure that runs, and a procedure can be interrupted by anyone who can see it working. That is what the generation in Nairobi discovered. Not that they had been wronged, which they had always known, but that the wrong was itemised, dated and attributable, and that a demand built on an itemised wrong is harder to refuse than a plea. It is why they asked for accounting rather than mercy, and why the state answered with live fire rather than argument.




The Sahel’s governments make the same claim against the same drain, and the gold they have reclaimed is real. But they have removed the thing that gave the claim its force. A demand that cannot be checked is only an assertion, and an assertion made on a people’s behalf by men they are not permitted to question is the old arrangement wearing a new flag. Africa is not poor; Africa is drained. Whether that sentence becomes a reckoning or merely a better slogan turns on one question, and it is the same question in Nairobi, in Cotonou and in Ouagadougou. Who is permitted to check?

A demand that can be checked

author: TGEU
title: Trans Murder Monitoring 2026 shows that every 32 hours, a trans person was murdered
content:
TGEU’s Trans Murder Monitoring (TMM) has recorded 273 trans and gender diverse people murdered worldwide over the past year, on average, one murder reported every 32 hours. Murders were reported across 35 countries, the second-highest number since the monitoring began, and for the first time in Romania and Cameroon. In total, TMM has now recorded over 5,500 murders globally since data collection began in 2009. 




TGEU – Trans Europe and Central Asia publishes the annual update of its global Trans Murder Monitoring project in the lead-up to Trans Awareness Week, ending with the Trans Day of Remembrance (TDoR) on 20 November. 




The TMM project counts only reported murders, and monitoring work is getting harder. The total number of reported murders is under 300 for only the second time in a decade, but the violence has not eased. Shrinking civic space, media and state-backed hostility towards trans people, and cuts to funding make it less likely that a murder is reported and recorded. 




Read in:

 

Portuguese

 ┃

Spanish

┃ 

Russian




Key findings







273 trans and gender diverse people were reported murdered

 between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026 – 

one murder every 32 hours

.




35 different countries

 reported a murder – 

the second highest ever

. Only in 2024 was the number of reporting countries higher (38).




One in three victims were sex workers (

32%

), who remain the most targeted group

 of all known occupations. 




Echoing the patterns of previous years, 

almost all reported murders (95%) were feminicides

 (victims were trans women or transfeminine people), and 

three-quarters (75%) of victims were Black or Brown trans people.




The age profile of murder victims appears to be shifting 

slightly older

. More than one third (35%) were aged 

31-40

 in 2026, while one in five (21%) victims were aged 

19-25

 – consistently the largest age group in the first decade of TMM. One in twenty (5%) victims in the past year were 

minors under the age of 18

.




Seven out of ten (

69%)

 

murders occurred in Latin America and the Caribbean

. Brazil leads the list once again, accounting for one in three (32%) of the global total. Numbers continued to fall in 

Mexico

, with the lowest reported murders (29) since 2011. However, 2026 saw the highest-ever total in 

Argentina

 (16) and the second-highest total in 

Ecuador

 (16) since TMM began.




The number of reported murders in 

Asia

 (32) fell after last year’s all-time high (51). This year’s total is 

likely an undercount

 – some monitoring partners in Asia reported no capacity to provide data this year, citing lack of resources and even electricity.




13 murders were reported in Europe, 

the highest total since 2023

 – as many as 2024 and 2025 combined. The 

majority of victims were international migrants

.




One in ten murders were recorded in the 

United States

 (29), a similar level to 2025 (31).




Two in five (40%) reported murders were 

shootings

, while a quarter (24%) were 

stabbings

. Three in ten (30%) of murders occurred on the 

street

, and one quarter (25%) occurred in the victim’s own 

home

.




Of known perpetrators, one in four (25%) were a current or former partner, lover or spouse. Other commonly reported perpetrators were organised hate groups/gangs (15%), strangers (14%), police/military/army (12%) and sex work clients (8%).




A 

perpetrator was

 

arrested

 in only one in five murders (21%) where local authorities documented a response.










Intersectional violence




Year after year, the same demographic of trans people are murdered. Almost all reported victims (95%) were trans women or transfeminine people. Sex workers, who make up one in three victims, remain the most targeted group of all known occupations, and three in four victims were Black or Brown trans people.




This is what intersecting oppression looks like in practice. Misogyny, transphobia, racism, xenophobia and whorephobia compound one another, and those at their crossroads are the ones most at risk. 




“As a Black trans woman and a refugee, I live with the constant fear of losing my life. While others go about their daily lives with a sense of safety, Black trans women must remain vigilant, always watching our backs. Our safety is never guaranteed.




These murders are not just numbers in a report; they are our friends, colleagues, siblings, parents, and members of our communities. As these killings increase year after year, we demand more than sympathy: we demand justice, proper investigations, and accountability for every life taken. Black trans women deserve the right to live safely, freely, and with dignity.”




– Purity Tumukwasibwe, TGEU Board member  







Most reported murders: Latin America and the Caribbean




Behind the global total, the violence is not evenly spread. Seven in ten of this year’s reported murders took place in Latin America and the Caribbean, and Brazil again accounts for one in three murders worldwide.




The concentration reflects the scale of violence, and it also reflects documentation. Latin America has a long-established movement of trans and feminist organisations that monitor and report feminicides. As a result, more murders reach the record than in regions where that infrastructure is thin. The figures are also raw counts, not adjusted for population size, so they show where murders are reported, not where a trans person is at greatest risk. 




Within the region, the picture moves in different directions. Some countries appear to be on a downward trajectory (e.g. Mexico), while others have reached the highest annual total since our monitoring began (e.g. Argentina). A lower national figure should not be read as a safer country without looking closely at each context, as one of our monitoring partners points out:




‘We must not show any signs of celebration [over the decline in recorded murders]; rather, we must scrutinise current trends, including those in each individual country.’

 




– Rocío Suárez, Centro de Apoyo a las Identidades Trans A.C., Mexico







Our region: Europe and Central Asia




In Europe, 13 murders were reported this year. That is as many as in 2024 and 2025 combined. Most victims were international migrants; almost all were trans women or transfeminine people, and a third were sex workers. The pattern is clear: those at the intersection of multiple forms of marginalisation are the most at risk. 




Many people come to Europe in search of a life in which they can be themselves and be safe. For the migrants among these victims, that search ended in murder. The pattern points to the combined effect of xenophobia, racism and transphobia, which leaves trans migrants without protection and among the most exposed to harm. This comes amid a growing far-right and anti-gender backlash across Europe, translating into increasingly hostile rhetoric, restrictive legislation and political attacks on the rights of migrants and trans people.




In Central Asia, no murders were reported to us this year. This should not be read as an absence of violence. It more likely reflects a lack of safety for trans people in the region, forced to remain as invisible as possible, while their relatives may not disclose their trans identity after death. With activists facing overwhelming challenges and limited resources for monitoring, murders often go uncounted. One of the victims killed in Europe this year was a migrant from Central Asia, which echoes a wider story of trans people leaving the region to build a life where they can live more openly.




“Laws that target the rights of migrants and asylum seekers—especially racialised people from the Global South—and criminalise sex work are State tools that enable the murder of trans migrant women and trans sex workers. We must keep fighting back against these laws and building caring, strong and resistant communities. Fascism and fortresses will fall only through our collective struggles and through allyships with those at the margins and with colonised peoples.”




–  Tayri Fadil, TGEU Board member 







Who is behind trans murders?




Where the perpetrator was known, one in five murders (19%) was committed by a partner, lover or spouse.  Almost a quarter of this year’s murders (25%) took place in the victim’s own home. It is a pattern that echoes previous years: in a society hostile to trans people, even one’s own home is not a safe place.




Organised hate groups and gangs (15%) and strangers (14%) were also commonly reported. Together, these patterns point to violence that reaches trans people everywhere: in their relationships, in their communities, and on the street.




In 12% of cases where the perpetrator was known, the person responsible was a member of the police, military, or army: 13 murders, up from five last year. Nine trans people were murdered or died in suspicious circumstances in prisons or police stations, compared with four last year. These are state institutions, and deaths inside them are violence committed or allowed by the state.




These figures raise hard questions about who is protected, and who is not. Trans people are exposed to hostility, profiling and abuse by state actors, and those with a duty to uphold the law are among those responsible for taking trans lives. When transphobia and transmisogyny shape how these institutions operate, trans people are left more exposed.




When local authorities responded, a perpetrator was arrested in only one in five cases (21%). Judicial processes take time, and some cases move slowly through the system. However, many murders of trans people are not investigated at all; others are investigated without urgency, or are not recorded for what they are. Bias in how murders are investigated and ruled on, including the dismissal of anti-trans motives, means those responsible are less likely to be held to account. For families and communities, the absence of justice can be another loss.




“Every year we witness the predictable result of the systemic hate and repression of trans lives. While remembering our lives, I want to also name who kills us: family members, partners, clients, police, and the institutions that let them. It’s time they answer for it.”




– Isa Nico Borrelli, TGEU Board Chair







Demographic trends




The pattern of who is most at risk has not changed. One in three victims were sex workers, the most targeted group of all known occupations. Almost all (95%) were trans women or transfeminine people, and 76% were Black or Brown trans people.




Recorded victims appear to be getting slightly older, with one in three aged 31 to 40, while one in twenty were minors. Furthermore, reported murders in Asia fell from last year’s all-time high of 51 to 32. This is likely an undercount: some monitoring partners in the region lacked the capacity to provide data this year, citing a lack of electricity and funding.







Recommendations 




TGEU calls on  governments and institutions to:







Repeal laws and policies that criminalise or restrict trans identities, legal gender recognition, trans specific healthcare, and the public expression of trans and gender diverse identities.




End the criminalisation of sex work in full and guarantee labour rights and protections for trans and gender-diverse sex workers.




Harmonise and adopt hate crime and anti-discrimination laws that explicitly protect trans people in employment, education, and other areas, and work towards a shared understanding of what counts as illegal hate speech.




Ensure prison placement decisions are based on self-determination, irrespective of legal gender recognition status, and include the wishes and welfare of the trans person concerned.




Back trans human rights defenders and civil society organisations by relieving financial pressures, safeguarding their security, and allowing them to keep organising and advocating for their rights without fear.




Train professionals to respond appropriately to anti-trans violence, including police forces, with particular attention to those facing intersecting forms of discrimination, including Black trans women and sex workers.




For EU countries, ensure fully trans-inclusive and timely transposition and implementation of the EU Directive on combating violence against women and domestic violence.










TGEU’s research partners 







Asociación de Derechos Humanos Cozumel Trans (Honduras)




Asociación Silueta X (Ecuador)




Association Unity (Togo)




Caribe afirmativo (Colombia)




Centro de Apoyo a las Identidades Trans (Mexico)




HOPE – Have Only Positive Expectations (Pakistan)




Horizon Burkina (Burkina Faso)




Jaringan Transgender Indonesia (Indonesia)




Jinsiangu (Kenya)




LakanBini Trans Network (The Philippines)




Mawjoudin (Tunisia)




Observatorio de Feminicidios Ensenada (Mexico)




Observatorio de violaciones a derechos humanos de personas LGTBIQ+ en Nicaragua (Nicaragua)




OTRANS Guatemala (Guatemala)




Qıy Vaar (Azerbaijan)




Qorras (Lebanon)




Queer Art and Action (India)




Rede Trans Brasil (Brazil)




Samabhabona (India)




STRAP – The Society of Trans Women of the Philippines (The Philippines)




Trans Lives Matter (United Kingdom)




Tranz Network Uganda (Uganda)










Note on the term feminicide




TMM uses 

feminicide

 rather than 

femicide

 as it better reflects the structural and political causes of violence against women and girls. Coined by Marcela Lagarde in Latin America, the term highlights state responsibility and the systemic failures of prevention, protection, and accountability that enable such murders.




More information







Look at the 

global map

 of all reported murders (Jan 2008 – Sep 2026; EN, ES, RU, PT)
