title: 6emîn Festîvala Fîlman a Rojava a Navneteweyî dest pê dike
content:
Bernameya 6emîn Festîvala Fîlman a Navneteweyî ya Rojava ya ku dê bi dirûşma “Çîrokên Hevpar, Sînemaya Azad” diyar bû.  Festîval roja 13ê Mijdarê li Navenda Mihemed Şêxo bi fîlma “Heval Kekê Min” dest pê dike.




Festîval dê di navbera 13 û 20ê Mijdarê de sînemager û sînemahezan bîne ba hev. Di nîşandana li Navenda Mihemed Şêxo de, li gel pênc fîlmên di beşa “Ji Rojava” de, kurtefîlmên bi kurdî, belgefîlm û fîlmên navneteweyî jî dê werin nîşandan. Panel û atolye jî dê li TEV-ÇAND, Sîne Jîn û Hunergeha Welat werin lidarxistin.




Bernameya Festîvalê wiha ye:




13ê Mijdarê




17.00 – Di vekirina festîvalê de MA Music dê konserekê bide û Narin Dance jî dê nîşandana dansê pêşkêş bike.




19.00 – Fîlmê vekirinê “Heval Kekê Min” ê ku derhêneriya wê Haşim Aydemir kiriye dê bi sînemahizan re werin ba hev.




14ê Mijdarê




10.00-12.00 – Belgeselçêker û karkerê kûrguyê Sasha Ayoub, dê li Sîne Jînê behsa xebatên Stories Film Labê bike ku sînemagerên serbixwe yên li Sûriyeyê projeyên xwe tê de pêş dixin. Di rûniştinê de fîlmên ku di çarçoveya bernameyê de hatine hilbijartin dê werin nîşandan.




11.00 – Nîşandanên rojê dê bi fîlmê “The Country Judge” dest pê bikin. Di bernameyê de fîlmên kurt ên kurdî “House of The Moon” û “Dorpêç” û belgesela “The Wedding of the Pirs” jî cih digirin.




15.00-17.00 – Derhênerê dîmenê Cemil Kızıldag, dê li TEV-ÇANDê li ser zimanê dîtbarî yê sînemayê perwerdehiyê bide.




15ê Mijdarê




09.00-13.00 – Atolyeya sê rojî ya li ser bikaranîna ronahiyê ya di sînemayê de ya derhênerê dîmen û ronahiyê Jafar Amin Al-Betar, dê li Hunergeha Welat dest pê bike. Atolye dê di 16 û 17ê Mijdarê de jî di heman saetan de berdewam bike.




09.00-13.00 – Belgeselçêker Guevara Namer, dê li Sîne Jînê pêvajoya çêkirina belgeselê û ezmûnên xebatê yên di qada navneteweyî de binirxîne. Rûniştina duyem a atolyeyê dê di 16ê Mijdarê de were lidarxistin.




11.00 û 11.50 – Du fîlmên yekem ên beşa “Ji Rojava” yên bi navên “Rêwiyên Ser Riya Agir” û “Keziyên Berxwedanê” dê werin nîşandan.




15.00 – Derhênera fîlma “Berbû” Sêvînaz Evdikê, dê li TEV-ÇANDê behsa Festîvala Fîlman a Jinan a Nûjîyan bike. Di heman saetê de li Navenda Mihemed Şêxo belgesela “Kî me ez?” dê were nîşandan.




18.00 û 19.10 – Bi rêzê ve belgeselên “04.17 Adiyaman” û “Pêlên Kurdan” dê bi sînemahizan re werin ba hev. Piştî her du nîşandanan jî dê rûniştina pirs û bersivan were lidarxistin.




16ê Mijdarê




11.00 – Fîlmê “To Fetch a Pail of Water” dê were nîşandan. Di saet 15.00an de jî belgesela “Under the Flags the Sun” dê bi sînemahizan re were ba hev.




15.00-17.00 – Di panela li TEV-ÇANDê de çêkirina fîlman a kolektîf a ku Komîna Fîlm a Rojava ji sala 2015an û vir ve berdewam dike dê were nirxandin. Di panela ku dê ji aliyê Mirzan Bekir ve wre birêvebirin de, ji damezrînerên komînê Diyar Hesso û Şêro Hindê û sêwirînerê deng Coni Docolomansky ê ku di fîlmên “Kobanê” û “Berbû” de xebitiye dê wekî axaftvan beşdar bibin.




17ê Mijdarê




10.00-13.00 – Senarîst Onder Çakar, dê li Sîne Jînê atolyeyekî li ser mijara, ‘Karakterê sereke yê fîlmekî ji qonaxa ramanê çawa derbasî senaryoyê dibe’ pêk bîne.




12.00 û 12.30 – Di beşa “Ji Rojava” de fîlmên “Youthful Wrinkle” û “Nameya Dawî” dê werin nîşandan.




15.00-17.00 – Di panela li TEV-ÇANDê de derhênerê fîlmên “Kuf” û “Kronoloji” Ali Aydin, dê beşdarî panela bi sernavê “Di sînemayê de pirsgirêka Kurd” bibe. Panel dê ji aliyê Berfîn Hezil ve were birêvebirin.




18ê Mijdarê




10.00-13.00 – Li Sîne Jînê fîlmê Ghasan Halawani ê bi navê “Erased, Ascent of the Invisible” dê were nîşandan.




12.25 – Fîlmê 5emîn ê bijareya “Ji Rojava” ê bi navê “Decision” dê were nîşandan.




15.00-17.00 – Li TEV-ÇANDê pirsa “Çima îro li Sûriyeyê xebatên çandî girîng in?” dê were nîqaşkirin. Di panela ku dê ji aliyê Ciwan Tetter ve were birêvebirin de Boushra Adi, Khoshman Qado û Muhammad Hajj Hussein dê beşdar bibin.




Nîşandanên din ên rojê – Ji bijareya fîlmên kurt ên kurdî fîlmên “Gazelle” û “Limo Knew Everything” û fîlmê ku Soudade Kaadan derhêneriya wê kiriye ê bi navê “Nezouh” dê bi sînemahizan re werin ba hev.




19ê Mijdarê




09.00-13.00 – Derhêner Leena Manimekalai, dê li Sîne Jînê li gel nîşandana fîlmê “Maadathy – An Unfairy Tale”, ezmûna xwe ya çêkirina fîlman a bi civakan re parve bike.




15.00-17.00 – Ji derhênerên fîlmê “Silvered Water, Syria Self-Portrait” Ossama Mohammed, dê li TEV-ÇANDê behsa çêkirina sînemayê ya di şert û mercên dîktatoriyê de bike.




17.25 û 17.45 – Ji bijareya fîlmên kurt ên Kurdî fîlmên “Ishaq” û “Fountain” dê werin nîşandan. Di saet 18.15an de jî fîlmê “As We Breathe” dê bi sînemahizan re were ba hev.




20ê Mijdarê




09.00-13.00 – Derhêner û Nivîskar Liwaa Yazji, dê li Sîne Jînê li ser derbaskirina projeyên fîlman a ji qonaxa ramanê ber bi senaryoyê ve atolyeyekê pêk bîne.




10.00-13.00 – Derhêner Soudade Kaadan, dê li Hunergeha Welat behsa senaryo û pêvajoya çêkirina fîlmê “Aziza” bike.




14.00-16.00 – Fîlmê derhênerê Lubnanî Maroun Baghdadi ê bi navê “Ninety” dê li TEV-ÇANDê were nîşandan.




17.00 – Di bernameya girtinê ya li Navenda Mihemed Şêxo de Hunermend Adnan Karim dê konserekê bide.




19.00 – Festîval dê bi merasîma xelatdayînê bi dawî bibe.




(AY)

author: John Mullen
title: France: The brass band and the revolution
content:
For the third time in a week, there were major strikes in education and mass demonstrations across France, on November 10.

More than a million people took to the streets in more than 200 towns and cities, on November 5, in support of school students and to demand wage rises, more jobs and an end to cuts in public service budgets. Health workers, dockers, teachers, journalists, municipal staff, train drivers, bank workers and many others joined the one-day strike.

Two days later, hundreds of thousands marched again.

Student assemblies attracted more than a thousand participants at many universities, including Marseille, Rennes, Bordeaux and Paris-Cité.

In some towns, notably Rennes and Bordeaux, and in sectors such as university staff and healthcare, general assemblies of workers (known as interpros or coordinations) are taking the lead in organising the struggle, hoping to overcome the horrific inertia of the national union leaderships.

High school student representatives walked out of a government consultation session on university admissions policy, held in Paris on Monday November 9, when they discovered that ministers had invited fascist MPs to take part.

There are three strands to the present revolt.

First, highschool and university students are in their sixth week of blockades, and are not giving up despite the police beating thousands and mutilating dozens.

Secondly, the Yellow Vest networks are back, and they worry the government because they seem leaderless and prefer wildcat demos.

Most importantly, there is the workers’ movement, which holds, in strike action, our most powerful weapon, but which is held back by catastrophic national leadership from a band of professional “Bordeaux and sandwiches” negotiators.

On the demonstrations, people wave thousands upon thousands of home-made cardboard placards, with slogans from the bawdy to the philosophical, quoting poets, rappers or constitutional documents.

My favourites include: “Let’s do a poo on the fascists!”, “You thirst for power, we thirst for beauty!”, “Class struggle begins in high school!”, “Looters in hoodies make you angry? Looters in suits are your government !”, “Plan A: protest in a dignified manner. Plan B: smash everything up.”, “Have you forgotten how we became a democracy?” and “This is getting expensive in cardboard!”.

The now traditional demo song rings out across the country: “For the honour of the workers, and to build a better world! Although Macron doesn’t like it, here we are!”

Brass bands and orchestras are present everywhere, following a call from the New World Orchestra, who were tear-gassed while playing in mid-October. They have popularised a new demo song: “I’ve two great loves: the brass band and the revolution! Long live blockades and sabotage, occupations and wildcat demos!” Groups of thousands were filmed singing this and dancing.

Last week, a new opinion poll found that 57% of the population approves of the movement, and 88% consider the demands concerning purchasing power and the cost of living legitimate, while 75% approve of the students’ demands. This is impressive, given the massive government propaganda campaign against the revolt.

With such support, even the mainstream media feel obliged to feature interviews with inspiring high schoolers, explaining their demands in detail, even if the channels rapidly return to their preferred fare — interviews with headmasters, police and shopkeepers upset by the movement, and political experts who want to discuss supposed personality clashes between left politicians.

This crisis is not going to go away. Emmanuel Macron’s minority government must push its national budget through before Christmas. Massive tax cuts for the rich mean they are short of money, so their initial proposal is for €50 billion in budget cuts. The international bankers are breathing down their necks, already charging France more than neighbouring countries to borrow money.

The situation is extremely fluid. The government met with unions and bosses on November 9, and then declared that the national minimum monthly wage would be raised — by €24. The CGT union demand is for a €150 rise. Later this week a decision will be announced about public sector wages. Public servants have lost 20% of their purchasing power since 2010, and nearly a million are on the minimum wage.

The national union leaders are following their habitual hymn sheet of “days of action”. The dynamism of Thursday’s social explosion should have convinced them to call more action immediately, but they waited “to see the results of the negotiation”, which were, of course, pathetic.

Monday’s talks with the unions took place behind closed doors — they should have been live streamed. We could do with rallies outside the weekly meetings of the leaders of the six different union confederations, to help them concentrate.

Not all the union leaders are identical. The more radical, like Sophie Binet of the CGT confederation, say they would like to see strikes spread further, while the CFDT is not calling for more strikes right now. But all generally move very slowly, in practice.

The movements are enthusiastically supported by the radical left organisation La France Insoumise (France in Revolt). The result has been that FI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélénchon has gained a couple of percent in the opinion polls. It is unheard of to have such a huge movement within a few months of presidential elections, and the stakes are very high indeed. More mass strikes have been called by some union leaders for the 17th. We need to go further.

[John Mullen is a revolutionary socialist living in the Paris region and a supporter of the France Insoumise.]

author: Kerry Smith
title: Students organise nationwide rallies against artificial intelligence
content:
A student-led national day of action against artificial intelligence (AI) and mega data centres was held on November 10. The rallies were called by Students for AI Regulation (SAR), a group of high school and university students, and supported by the Tomorrow Movement.

SAR said students are “terrified of the impact AI is going to have on our future”. “It’s easy to wallow in AI news and climate disasters but … we must act now!”

Speakers at the Gadigal Country/Sydney rally highlighted successful campaigns against AI data centres in Arncliffe, Lane Cove and the Blue Mountains, and called on people to join the December 5 statewide rally against data centres.

Paddy Gibson from Stop the Cooks River AI Project said defeating the project was an important win for people power. He said the fight is not over, as the community wants to stop the developer Stockland’s other plans for the former Kogarah Golf Club site.

Gibson said students and staff at universities and schools are raising important anti-AI demands and cited the National Tertiary Education Union’s push to include AI protection clauses in enterprise agreements.

Robin, a student at the University of New South Wales, high school teacher and campaigner with Students Hate AI, said it was being forced on teachers and students.

Isaac Nellist from Sydney Students for Climate detailed the climate impacts of mega data centres, including their use of vast amounts of electricity and water, and thereby helping the continued expansion of coal and gas mining projects.

“The huge amount of money being invested into AI and AI infrastructure around the world is money that should be going into addressing the existential threat of climate change, and the countless other social issues that we are facing.”

He said data centres were being used to “accelerate militarism and war, drive down wages and workers rights and replace artists and steal their work”, while driving inflation and pushing up the cost-of-living.

“AI is a key part of the AUKUS pillar two agreement, which further ties Australia to the US military … and we are seeing the devastating impacts of AI-enabled warfare in Gaza and Iran.

“The good news is that communities are fighting back, we know data centres are massively unpopular and when communities organise and fight back, they win.”

About 80 people joined the Naarm/Melbourne rally at the State Library of Victoria. Jacob Andrewartha, childcare worker and Socialist Alliance candidate for Pascoe Vale, said AI is a “technology that represents the destruction of the environment and an attack on our democratic rights”.

He said AI was being used in surveillance and by government agencies. “There isn’t a convincing case for why we should use AI … What does it have to offer? Worse artistic works? Polluting social media?

“Young people are rejecting this technology, despite the massive investment from big tech capitalists.”

Rallies were also held in Garamilla/Darwin, Nipaluna/Hobart, Kaurna Yerta/Adelaide, Kanamaluka/Launceston, Magan-djin/Brisbane and Kabi Kabi Country/Sunshine Coast.

author: Shannia Cabuello
title: Artists, Ayta sing vs Pax Silica
content:
Photo by Shannia Angel Cabuello

Artists and other advocates amplified their opposition against a US-led initiative through song.

On November 6, an artist group launched the anti-Pax Silica anthem “Get Off Our Lands” in a solidarity night filled with protest songs.

Produced by the Concerned Artists of the Philippines (CAP), the song was accompanied by a documentary music video featuring the Ayta community in Sitio Kalangitan, whose ancestral lands and natural resources are threatened by displacement and plunder.

Through the song, CAP aimed to expose the false promises behind the Pax Silica and to condemn those in power who allowed it.

Cultural performances and solidarity messages completed the program as part of the Trump Out campaign and the ‘12 Days of Protests’, building up the major protest actions on November 16 and 17.

Ayta elders also attended the solidarity night and expressed their strong rejection of Pax Silica, chanting “Ako Labay Ya Pax Silica!” (I don’t like Pax Silica!).

They led a community dance ritual to drive away “bad spirits,” which they associate with the Pax Silica Initiative and the impending visit of US President Donald Trump for the ASEAN Summit.

Ayta Chieftain Nelson De Guzman countered the statement of Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) President Joshua Bingcang that no Indigenous community would be affected by the Pax Silica Initiative. He said that no proper consultation was conducted within their community.

“They learned that they were being driven away from their land even before they knew about the project,” said Sandiwa Network project coordinator Gina Cambronero.

“The Pax Silica will kill our future. We nurtured our lands. We cannot allow foreigners to claim it,” said Ayta Indigenous woman Tessie Sanchez.

Sanchez told Bulatlat that planting rice, taro, and sweet potato helped support her seven children. She feared that the signing of the agreement could dry their water sources and take away their farmlands.

“The ruling class used the term pax which meant peace. But is there peace in it? They use it as instruments for deception,” Cambronero said.

“We just want peace in our tribe and in our land,” De Guzman said in the song’s documentary music video.

Around 20,000 peasants and 15,000 Ayta could be reportedly displaced once its Artificial Intelligence hub was established on the 1,620 hectares of land in Tarlac.

The anthem started by introducing the Philippines as a friendly Southeast Asian country that shares its homeland to everyone, even to foreign ones.

The music video explained that Ferdinand Marcos Jr. volunteered to give the agricultural and ancestral lands in Tarlac to the United States to establish an Economic Security Zone.

CAP said that the establishment of an Artificial Intelligence hub in Tarlac and the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) in Subic Bay, Clark, Manila and Batangas that claims of job creation and economic security are false promises. The group said that it only “prioritizes corporate profits and militarization, fueling war for the US benefit.”

“In the past years, we have always been at a disadvantage with US relations. There are already several trade agreements that only lead to our losses,” said Attorney Rey Cortez of National Union of People’s Lawyers (NUPL).

Cortez added in a solidarity message that it only allowed for the United States to mine the country’s lands and determine how to exploit its resources. He described the government’s marketing of the country’s environment and sovereignty as unconstitutional, as only the Filipinos are allowed to explore the Philippines’ critical minerals.

“Development should not be measured by the number of investments, infrastructure, and technology advancements. Its effect on the people, community, and environment must also be analysed,” said College of Social Work and Community Development Dean and CAP member Justin Nicolas.

Arthur Cadungon of CAP and writer of Get Off Our Lands said that the anthem is not just for the fight against the Pax Silica Initiative, but also a song of protest against the reclamation of Manila Bay, Laguna Lake, and Pasig River Expressway (PAREX).

“An example of this is the Laguna Lake, which before sources at least 40% of protein food sources like mussels and freshwater fish tilapia,” said Environmental Advocates group Nilad coordinator Samantha Yzabel.

She added that fishing has become difficult for the communities near Laguna Lake as the destruction of ecosystems and pollution worsens. She also stressed that the Manila Bay and Pasig River are being destroyed, while communities continue to be displaced and deprived of livelihood.

Cadungon dedicated the song to the trees that were cut along the Quirino highway, and for the Filipinos who were drowned by flood and were neglected by the people in power.

“This is also a fight with the courageous people of the Kasibu community in Nueva Vizcaya, around the nation, and other countries that are being stripped bare by imperialists,” Cadungon said.

Artists and cultural workers strengthened their rejection of the Pax Silica that facilitates the use of Artificial Intelligence saying that it undermines human creativity.

“Trump’s visit means taking away my workforce. It means building of AI hubs that would replace years of artist’s struggle in honing their crafts,” handcrafter Aila Bathan said.

Just like the Ayta Indigenous Peoples and communities in Central Luzon, Bathan said that Pax Silica means death of their lives and livelihoods.

“True prosperity promotes people’s dignity, strengthens communities, nurtures the environment, and advocates for overall well-being,” said Dean Nicolas, calling on the Filipinos to be critical and stand firm for social justice.

CAP Secretary-General Edge Ungayuren emphasized that once farmers that cultivate the lands are threatened, even ordinary Filipinos are affected. “We believe that we must take a stand in this issue because it would kill our lands, bodies of water, farmers, and Indigenous Peoples. Our culture is rooted in our lands and bodies of water. If these will be gone, our culture will also be gone,”

CAP urged artists, cultural workers, and the public to use their art and the anti-Pax Silica anthem to take their resistance on the streets and get imperialists off the nation’s land. (AMU, DAA)

author: Rachel Evans
title: Anti-racists counter protest far-right ‘Australia Marches’ rally
content:
About 300 people joined the “No to Racism: Migrants and Refugees Are Welcome” rally at Sydney Town Hall on November 8. It was organised by the Refugee Action Collective Sydney (RAC) to counter the far-right Australian Marches rally against migration.

The far-right rally, which featured speakers from One Nation, Libertarian MP John Ruddick and other right-wing influencers, rallied at the Royal Botanic Garden and drew about 500 people.

Speakers at the counter-protest included Lynda-June Coe, Wiradjuri and Badu Island woman and NSW Greens upper house candidate; Nour Salman from Australia Palestine Advocacy Network; Ishita Chakrabarty from Hindus for Human Rights; Bidjigal/Gweagal activist Jordan Ryan-Hennessy; Ann El Khoury, from University of Sydney Staff for Palestine; Beau Lyon from Action for Public Housing’ and Anisa, a Somali refugee who was held in the Naoero detention centre.

Chakrabarty spoke about the racism faced by Indian migrants and linked One Nation and the Australia Marches rally to the far-right Narendra Modi government in India.

Ian Rintoul from RAC, who chaired the rally, said the United States midterm elections were a huge blow to the racist politics of US President Donald Trump, but said anti-racist campaigners still need to get organised.

“The tragedy is that the racist policies of Australia Marches and One Nation are being fueled by anti-migration and anti-refugee policies of the Labor government,” Rintoul said.

“Labor is linking migration with the housing crisis; cutting the numbers of international students; has introduced fees that will make it harder for refugees to seek asylum in Australia and is implementing an ICE-like compliance force to round up people on temporary visas.”

Lyon said those in power are pushing racism to distract from the real cause of the housing crisis, the for-profit housing system.

“Migrants are not responsible for the housing or cost of living crisis,” Rintoul said.

author: labor4pal
title: The U.S. government is escalating its attack on Palestine activism in Michigan (Mondoweiss)
content:
Four more pro-Palestine activists have been indicted on “conspiracy” charges stemming from protests at the University of Michigan, bringing the total to 12. The defendants now face sentences ranging from five years to several decades.

By Yarden Azoulay Katz and Adi Saleem November 10, 2026

FBI agent stopping and searching a vehicle in Ann Arbor, MI as part of the crackdown on new defendants, October 29, 2026.

The U.S. government is expanding its assault on Palestine solidarity activism in Michigan. Last summer, the FBI conducted raids against pro-Palestine activists connected to the University of Michigan. The defendants, known as the Michigan 8, were indicted by the Department of Justice on “conspiracy” charges, specifically “conspiracy to transmit threats in interstate and foreign commerce” and “conspiracy to intimidate a witness.” On Thursday, October 29, the FBI raided the home of activists in the same circle. The next day, the government unsealed a superseding indictment that adds four more defendants to the case, turning the Michigan 8 into the Michigan 12.

The four new defendants are all recent graduates of the University of Michigan with ties to campus Palestine activism. Like the initial eight defendants, they are charged with conspiracy and potentially face long prison sentences, from five years to several decades.

The federal government’s new indictment doubles down on previous allegations of “antisemitism.” In a press release announcing the indictment, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan Jerome F. Gorgon, Jr. claims the defendants aimed “to terrorize our Jewish community” and even compares them to Hitler and the biblical Pharaoh. The government again portrays the defendants as “terrorists” because of their alleged support for Palestinian resistance groups, despite never charging any defendant with “terrorism,” “hate crimes,” or even “vandalism.”

As part of this attack, the government filed an emergency motion to detain one of the initial eight defendants (who had been released on bond) all the way until trial. In recent months, FBI agents have also made visits to the homes of several Palestine activists in southeast Michigan.

This new wave of repression and propaganda is intended to send chills through the Palestine solidarity movement and sway public opinion against the defendants. But community supporters, family, and friends of the Michigan 12 are continuing to fight back.

On October 29, Henry David Mackeen-Shapiro (who goes by Drin Shapiro) was heading home from the Detroit public school where he teaches. Shapiro was stopped by FBI agents who had their guns pointed at him, with about six police vehicles present. They arrested him and seized his car and phone.

Around an hour later, about fifteen FBI agents arrived at Shapiro’s home. They knocked on the door, announcing they had a search warrant but refusing to show it, according to one person who was present for the entire raid. Those inside the house decided to open the door to avoid having the agents break through it (as they have done in the June 2026 and April 2025 raids on local Palestine activists). As the search began, two agents were stationed outside, pointing their rifles at the house windows, while another agent with a rifle guarded the door.

The agents conducting the search made clear to those present that if they stay in the house, they must remain put and not follow the agents. The agents soon received a message on their radio devices asking them to turn off their body cameras; they later confirmed to the residents that they have done so. The agents refused additional requests to show a warrant, only leaving it on the kitchen table when the search was over. The warrant instructs the agents to seize devices that may contain communications with several other Michigan 12 defendants (the agents took Shapiro’s computer).https://archive.org/embed/fbiagents-seizing-materials-drin-shapiro-home-oct-29-2026

FBI agents exiting defendants’ Detroit home after the raid, carrying a box with seized materials, October 29, 2026. Video by the Michigan 12 defense effort.

“It was a really unjust process,” a person present during the raid said. “I was not told what was happening, I was not told my rights, and I was not shown a warrant.” That the agents turned off their body cameras made it obvious the government is acting with “a total lack of transparency,” they added.

Shapiro spent the night in jail and was arraigned the next day in Detroit federal court, where he was released on $10,000 unsecured bond with similar conditions to those of his co-defendants, including restrictions on travel and wearing a GPS ankle monitor for which he must cover the costs.

On the day of the Detroit home raid, FBI agents searched Ann Arbor for a newly indicted defendant in the case, Aaron VonBargen. The agents ended up detaining and searching VonBargen’s younger sibling, Eric Ming VonBargen. “As I was walking to my car after class, multiple unmarked vehicles cornered me and about a dozen FBI agents proceeded to search and detain me. It wasn’t until minutes in that they asked for my name, and only then did they realized I was not my sibling, who is several years older,” VonBargen said in a November 3 statement published by the Michigan 12 defense effort. “By the time I was released, my car and backpack were already thrown apart.” The following morning, Eric’s sibling, Aaron VonBargen, turned themselves in. They were also released on unsecured bond with similar conditions to Shapiro’s.

The agent who detained Eric Ming VanBargen has been attending multiple court proceedings in the Michigan 12 case. The authors witnessed him sitting next to and speaking with Ryan Cavanaugh, a Sergeant Detective with the University of Michigan Police (UMPD) who has a long record of going after local Palestine solidarity activists. Cavanaugh has also been speaking in court with the government’s attorney, and UMPD, which participated in the June 2026 raid on the initial eight defendants, alongside the FBI. While the University of Michigan has officially remained silent regarding the case, it is clearly aiding the Trump administration’s crackdown.

Following the raid on Shapiro’s home, on November 2, U.S. Attorney Maggie Smith filed an emergency motion to revoke the bond of Zainab Hakim, one of the original eight defendants, and jail her until the trial. The November 2 motion alleges that Hakim, who was present during the raid and lives with Shapiro (who is her boyfriend), damaged his computer to prevent seizure. Yet the government also used the motion to promote bigger allegations of antisemitism, revealing the absurdity of their case.

The motion attacks a statement made by the judge on the case, Judith E. Levy, who had stated in a September 2026 bond hearing that there is nothing to suggest Hakim is anti-Jewish. “There’s nothing that’s happened over the last two months or maybe last year or anytime I’ve seen, there’s nothing in the indictment, there’s nothing in any of this material that would indicate that that’s the case,” concluded Levy, who is Jewish and the daughter of a child survivor of the Nazi Holocaust.

To argue against Levy’s conclusion, U.S. Attorney Smith – who wears a large cross necklace to court – presented what are allegedly encrypted messages between Hakim, who is Muslim, and her co-defendant Shapiro, who is Jewish. The two appear to be discussing chants that could be used at protests against the genocide in Palestine. Smith claims that this is merely one example of Hakim and Shapiro’s “many conversations regarding their antisemitic feelings,” and supposedly evidence of their risk to the “Jewish community.”

It’d be hard to make up a more ridiculous scenario: a Christian prosecutor with strongly Zionist views arguing against the Jewish judge’s call that there’s no trace of antisemitism by showing that a Muslim woman and her Jewish boyfriend are resisting Zionism together. The only “antisemitic” thing here is the government’s premise that the Zionist organizations aiding it (such as the Jewish Federation of Detroit) speak for all Jews – and that the safety of Jews requires the settler-colonial brutality of Israel.

In the October 30 press release announcing the new indictment, Smith’s superior, U.S. Attorney Jerome F. Gorgon, Jr., also framed the case as a heroic mission to defend Jews:

“These alleged attempts to terrorize our Jewish community and government officials are nothing new. From Pharaoh to Hitler to Hamas, those who terrorize Jews have been the bad guys. As Americans, our job is to fight the bad guys.”

On November 3, the initial eight defendants were re-arraigned in Judge Levy’s courtroom based on the superseding indictment, which resulted in the same bond conditions.

In the same court session, Judge Levy also considered defendant Ahmet Korkaya’s motion to remove the curfew and GPS ankle monitoring from his bond conditions. U.S. Attorney Smith argued against the motion, again invoking Jewish safety. “I can tell you, and as the Court knows, [that] being a member of the Jewish community automatically puts them on edge and at risk [of the defendant],” Smith said. Judge Levy was not persuaded and granted Korkaya’s motion, citing the Bail Reform Act, which calls for “the least restrictive” conditions to be used when possible. Smith asked for 48 hours to appeal the decision, which the court granted, but the government abandoned the appeal and the requested bond conditions were removed.

During proceedings, an attorney for one of the Michigan 12 argued that Gorgon’s press release is an unethical attempt by the government to influence public opinion before the trial begins. Judge Levy agreed that the statement is “very concerning” and asked Smith’s office to consider “taking this [press release] off the government’s website” or at least “retracting this statement about Hitler and Pharaoh.”

The Michigan 12 defense effort and community members have continued to fight the charges. On October 30, 2026, Drin Shapiro and Aaron VonBargen were arraigned in a courtroom packed with supporters, signaling to everyone that the defendants do not stand alone. Most court proceedings so far have been well attended by supporters, who often had to be redirected to court overflow rooms.

During the November 3 proceedings, a large crowd also gathered for a rally outside the Ann Arbor federal court. Community members raised the Palestinian flag, served food, and prepared gift bags and cards for the defendants. A hearing on the government’s motion to revoke defendant Zainab Hakim’s bond is scheduled for November 18 and is also expected to be packed with Michigan 12 supporters.

Michigan Democratic Party politicians, however, have not shown much support for the defendants so far. Representative Rashida Tlaib and Amir Makled, a lawyer who had represented student activists criminalized over Palestine and was recently elected to the University of Michigan Board of Regents, have said little about the case. One of the defendants had worked on the campaign of Abdul El-Sayed, the recent winner of the Michigan senate race, but after the June 2026 FBI raid, a spokesperson for El-Sayed distanced themselves from her.

The Michigan 12 case resembles other cases where the government is using “conspiracy” charges to criminalize social movements, like the case of the Minnesota 15 anti-ICE organizers. All this repression is linked: U.S. Attorney Gorgon, who oversees the Michigan 12 case, also brought charges of “using interstate communications to transmit a threat” against those making anti-ICE comments online in Michigan. This is why organizers across defense campaigns have been joining forces. It’s essential to strengthen these grassroots efforts, given the powers we are up against.

author: Rizomatica
title: Sobre la propuesta de modificación al artículo 13 de la ley indigena 19.253
content:
La propuesta de modificación al artículo 13 de la ley 19.253 impulsada en el gobierno anterior a través de la denominada Comisión para la Paz y Entendimiento, fue una iniciativa transversal de la clase Política que incluyó a personeros de todo el espectro político Chileno como propuesta para el desarrollo en materia indígena.




Está propuesta ha sido fomentada por el actual gobierno de tinte ultraderechista con la finalidad de instalarla cómo política pública para el pueblo mapuche. Prueba de ello es que hace pocos días se reunieron en Temuco diversos personeros del gobierno con la finalidad de promover una consulta para dar implementación a esta medida.




El artículo 13 de la ley 19.253 es la normativa que regula y contiene restricciones respecto del dominio y uso de los terrenos indígenas. Este artículo contiene una protección exigida por el interés nacional del cual son sujetos los terrenos indígenas que impide que estos sean sometidos a enajenaciones, embargos, gravámenes, ni ser adquiridas por prescripción, salvo entre comunidades o personas de una misma etnia.




En términos generales, hasta ahora, el artículo 13 ha sido una salvaguarda para el dominio de la tierra indígena en manos de los pueblos originarios, por cuánto la ley en este aspecto tiene un carácter imperativo y obligatorio de protección.




No obstante aquello, esto no ha significado una protección completa ya que a través de diversos artilugios legales se han registrado casos en que a pesar de sus diversas prohibiciones, si se ha logrado enajenar (

vender

) terrenos indígenas a personas no mapuche. Esto ha sido en virtud de vacíos contenidos en la normativa que dejan espacios a artilugios legales que diversos abogados han utilizado para realizar esas ventas en vulneración al espíritu de la ley.




Un caso emblemático a este respecto fue el mediático caso de la venta realizada por la viuda chilena de un mapuche después de su muerte en la comuna de Pucón al ex subsecretario Ubilla durante el gobierno del expresidente Piñera.




Está venta de un terreno indígena a un chileno dejó de manifiesto lo frágil de la ley respecto de la real protección a los terrenos indígenas cuando hay intereses económicos importantes de por medio. Esta venta se pudo realizar en el contexto de lo que en derecho civil se conoce como liquidación de una sociedad conyugal y adjudicación por disolución de esta.




Volviendo a la propuesta de modificación al artículo 13, lo que preocupa es el aparente sentido inocuo de dicha medida, ya que directamente no habla de 

enajenación

 o 

venta

 de un terreno indígena a una persona o entidad no mapuche, sino que el énfasis ha sido puesto en la posibilidad de 

arrendamiento

 de un terreno indígena a personas 

no indígenas

 o 

personas

 

jurídicas

 de diversa índole.




Está situación es más compleja de lo que parece a simple vista porque abre una posibilidad de vulneraciones difíciles de prever a futuro.




Lo que señala la propuesta de modificación es que los terrenos indígenas podrán ser arrendados a cualquier persona no indígena o persona jurídica por un plazo de hasta 10 años y 25 años con consulta al órgano técnico encargado en materia indígena que es la Conadi.




El argumento para esto, es que en las condiciones actuales de restricción que contiene la propiedad indígena ha sido muy difícil incorporar estos terrenos a los beneficios que contempla la ley y a diversas medidas administrativas de los órganos y servicios del Estado en materia de fomento productivo, acceso a vivienda, acceso a crédito, transferencia tecnológica y oportunidades de desarrollo en general. En la visión de los promotores de esta iniciativa se sostiene que esto ha sido el principal elemento de tope que han tenido los mapuche para hacer productivas sus tierras e incorporarlas eficientemente al circuito productivo de la economía local y regional.




Para ello se propone bajar el nivel de restricciones que contiene la ley en materia de protección y permitir arriendos en condiciones de mercado actuales y competitivos.




Esto en teoría significaría regular de forma más eficiente situaciones de arriendo irregular que hoy pudiesen existir y por otra parte mejorar los promedios de los valores de los precios de arriendo para el arrendador y conceder garantías tanto de tiempo como de condiciones jurídicas que permitan al arrendatario realizar una labor productiva con seguridad en un tiempo acorde a dicha inversión, pudiendo ser por un lapso de hasta 25 años.




Lo preocupante de esta iniciativa es que nada dice sobre qué tipo de actividades puede realizar el arrendatario sobre dicho terreno ni de quien regulará esa situación.




Esto es bastante complejo porque, en materia de derechos ambientales, en Chile en general eso es una situación de difícil control aunque exista institucionalidad para ello y más aún cuando este gobierno parece supeditar dicha situación a una visión de carácter más bien economicista que proteccionista, desde el punto de vista ambiental. En lo concreto perfectamente un arrendatario puede utilizar el terreno en una actividad productiva contaminante de cualquier índole o destructiva del medio ambiente y la propuesta nada señala de como se regulará eso, ya sea para prevenir, sancionar o reparar dichos actos.




La tierra indígena debe ser entendida no solo en términos individuales, sino colectivos. De acuerdo al convenio 169 de la OIT “los gobiernos deberán respetar la importancia especial que para las culturas y valores espirituales de los pueblos interesados reviste su relación con sus tierras y territorios o con ambos, según los casos, que ocupan o utilizan de alguna manera y en particular los aspectos colectivos de esa relación”. Si los contratos de arriendo se rigen por el Derecho Privado, los términos de este contrato dependerán únicamente de la voluntad de arrendador y arrendatario, eliminando de forma inconstitucional toda posibilidad de considerar al colectivo que habita dicho territorio, por lo demás debe considerarse que quien impone las cláusulas de un contrato generalmente es la parte con mayor poder económico, por lo que abrir el derecho privado a materias con protección jurídica especial supone restringir arbitrariamente la voz del indígena frente a quien puede imponer cláusulas contractuales.




Al quedar esto en una zona gris evidentemente se queda sometido una vez más a interpretaciones tendenciosas de los infaltables operadores jurídicos cuyas acciones puedan ir en desmedro de los propietarios indígenas en virtud de cláusulas abusivas que por desconocimiento o mala fe del arrendatario derive a situaciones de conflictos jurídicos latentes dónde la historia nos señala claramente quienes históricamente han salido perjudicados.




Respecto de la operatividad del mecanismo, es importante saber qué ocurriría por ejemplo con la cláusula de 

tácita reconducción

 que opera en el arriendo de predios rústicos dónde si nada dicen los contratantes se puede seguir arrendando después de cumplido los plazos estipulados en el contrato si de manera tacita manifiestan intención de continuar con el arriendo; aquí se abre una situación gris amparada en un resquicio legal que podría significar una renovación de contrato y quizás una situación de usurpación avalada legalmente como lo fueron los arrendamientos a 99 años, situación injusta pero amparada por los tribunales que significó el despojo por la vía legal de una cantidad importante del territorio mapuche.




Otra inquietud a resolver sería saber que ocurriría si el arrendatario haciendo uso de las facultades legales que le confiere el contrato alega que de parte del arrendador hay incumpliendo de contrato o algún perjuicio atribuido al propietario indígena y alega indemnización de perjuicios y aquel no pudiese pagarlo, ¿Cuál sería la compensación que reclamaría el arrendatario?




Por otro lado, si se rebaja el nivel de restricciones respecto del uso del terreno y se permite legalmente el arrendamiento a instituciones jurídicas no mapuches, ¿que impediría que sobre ese terreno se permitiera constituir gravámenes como la hipoteca?




Si bien estas son situaciones hipotéticas, son altamente probables de ocurrir con esta arremetida legal.




Lo que preocupa en el fondo es develar cuál es el espíritu que motiva la propuesta de modificación a la ley, la intencionalidad que hay detrás de la aparente propuesta de mejorar las rentas de los arriendos y mejorar las condiciones de vida de los propietarios mapuche.




A este respecto señalar que es un anzuelo bastante fácil de morder para gente mapuche que tienen propiedades rurales y que por diversos motivos como trabajo, estudio, enfermedades incapacitantes o cualquier otro, no pueden producirlas eficientemente. En este sentido, esta iniciativa pareciera ser conveniente para aquel que ya lleva una vida desligada del ámbito rural, resultando ser esta una medida como anillo al dedo, pero que conlleva un contrasentido con el espíritu que dio origen a la ley y que contiene las principales salvaguardas de protección a las tierras mapuches. Aquí se abre una vez más la delgada pero peligrosa línea del desarraigo del territorio de las nuevas generaciones que solo verían a éste como una fuente de ingresos económicos y no cómo el sustrato y vinculo cultural que conlleva el ejercicio de la vida comunitaria que tanto ha costado mantenerla y que constantemente se ve amenazada por diversas influencias y por otra parte se evidencia claramente una intención de 

vulneración

 al 

dominio

 

sociopolítico

 del territorio mapuche.




Si de verdad se quiere mejorar el acceso a capacitación del propietario mapuche, aumentar la transferencia tecnológica, promover iniciativas económicas indígenas, acceder en mejores condiciones a los instrumentos de fomento productivo, 

¿porque entonces no se aumenta el presupuesto economico en la ley de presupuesto para inyectar recurso permanente y fresco para desarrollar los componentes necesarios para un desarrollo integral y pertinente a través de programas eficientes y focalizados ?




Si hubiese voluntad, se apuntaría en ese sentido más allá de estar proponiendo modificar la ley, ya que si el espíritu fuese lo señalado en el párrafo anterior entonces no sería necesario modificación alguna, sino que dar cumplimiento al articulo 23 de la ley indígena que establece mecanismos y herramientas de desarrollo para los pueblos indígenas, en relación a los artículos 24, 25, 26 del mismo cuerpo legal.




De la mano de esto ¿Porque no se regula de mejor manera el uso del suelo en el Wallmapu? impidiendo que se instalen y se profundicen actividades productivas extractivistas, contaminantes que perjudican directamente los ecosistemas y calidad de vida de quienes lo habitan traduciéndose en marginalización y precarización social y económica.




El tema central entonces no radica en la modificación de la ley, sino en la voluntad de inyectar recursos para su efectiva implementación y desarrollo, incluido recursos para el fondo de tierras, de la mano de una propuesta politica seria de devolución del territorio mapuche.




La estrategia de fondo es generar políticas públicas eficientes con la participación de los actores pertinentes, con la voz de aquellos a quienes se dirigen las medidas y no tomarlas entre cuatro paredes a nivel central con actores que solo representan a una casta política desconectada de la realidad y cruzada por intereses partidistas e ideológicos mezquinos que tanto mal le han hecho a la sociedad en general en todos los gobiernos de turno y en todos los ámbitos del acontecer social, político y económico del país.




Pareciera ser que la intención es desmantelar la poca legislación existente que de alguna manera ha servido para dar cierta protección al derecho que tienen los mapuche sobre una mínima parte de su territorio.







Por: Álvaro Millalen

Radio Kurruf

author: Kodao Productions
title: Angry farmers dump rotten vegetables at DA
content:
Vegetable farmers from the Cordillera dumped rotten vegetables at Department of Agriculture’s (DA) main office in Quezon City on Tuesday, protesting the agency’s failure to solve the worsening crisis faced by local food producers.




The protesters said plummeting farm gate prices and continuously rising costs of agricultural inputs have forced many farmers in the upland region to refuse farming or selling their produce at bottom level prices.




Farmers led by the Kanatengan Network, Apit Tako, the Cordillera Peoples Alliance (CPA), and KATRIBU are demanding fair floor prices, affordable agricultural inputs, sufficient subsidies, improved farm-to-market roads, measures against vegetable importation and smuggling, and an end to usurious lending and excessive land rental costs.




“The rotten vegetables thrown at the agency were the very same produce that farmers could no longer sell amid intensifying competition with imported vegetables, plummeting farm gate prices, and continuously rising costs of agricultural inputs,” KATRIBU in a statement said.




The Indigenous Peoples’ group said the agriculture department allowed local farmers struggling to recover production costs and earn a decent livelihood.




“Instead of strengthening domestic agricultural production through genuine agrarian reform, adequate government support, and the development of local industries, the Marcos Jr. administration continues to allow agricultural importation and smuggling to undermine Filipino farmers. Local producers are left competing with cheaper imported vegetables while receiving inadequate support to sustain their own production,” the group said.




On Tuesday, the Bureau of Customs announced a planned investigation of a P524.27 million worth of reportedly smuggled agricultural products found in a warehouse in Valenzuela City last October 17. Tons of red onions, beans and legumes, ginger and carrots, as well as peanut products were allowed to pass through customs inspection and were seized outside port premises.




While Cordillera farmers complain of diving farm gate prices, meanwhile, retail prices for their produce have risen in lowland wet markets.




The Philippine Statistics Authority reported the following selling prices in Mimaropa region this week:

title: Declaración publica Lof Pillumallin Autónomo y Coordinadora Arauco Malleco
content:
«Marimari pu peñi pu lamgen, a los lof en resistencia y a toda la gente consciente de la digna lucha mapuche. Cómo lof en recuperación Pillumallin autónomo y Coordinadora Arauco Malleco, venimos a expresar lo siguiente:




Kiñe: El día sábado 07 de noviembre del presente año, llevamos a cabo un txawun Palin, dónde asistieron diferentes comunidades de wallmapu, logrando así una jornada familiar llena de nutxam hacia nuestros ppm y nuestros lamgen caídos en el weichan, cómo también un gran palikantun en honor a ellos.




Epu: En nuestro txawün palin también reivindicamos a nuestro peñi/lamgen Álvaro Quinchanao Hueche yem, weichafe de nuestra organización a quien conocimos apoyando y acompañando en distintos procesos de recuperación territorial, incluyendo el nuestro, así como en distintas actividades propias de la militancia mapuche como siembras, construcción de ruka e instancias espirituales.




Hoy a casi 6 meses de su partida queremos reivindicar la figura de nuestro weichafe como una persona profundamente humana que brindó su vida para cuidar y aportar al proyecto de reconstrucción nacional tanto desde su rol como weichafe así como en su vida personal donde pudimos dar fé de su integridad, su feyentun y apego a los valores del mapuche gen. A pesar de que el winka quiera reducir su persona y su convicción política y espiritual a la imagen de terrorista.

Nuestro peñi/lamgen dejó una profunda huella por su compromiso y entrega a su pueblo, legado que nosotros continuaremos reivindicando en el weichan y en cada recuperación territorial, su memoria, entrega y vida no serán en vano, sino que vivirá en cada militante de la causa mapuche autónomista, tal como él lo eligió en su vida.




Küla: Que el segundo objetivo de nuestro txawun Palin era reivindicar y visibilizar la causa de nuestros peñi/ lamgen ppm Jorge Caniupil Coña, Juan Carlos Mardones Saez, Luis Menares Chanilao y Pelentaro Llaitul Pezoa, quienes están agrupados en la denominada Causa Lautaro, por la que recientemente el día 4 de Octubre recibimos la negativa respuesta del sistema judicial de la Nulidad de sentencia en la corte de Apelaciones de Temuco, ratificando así la condena de nuestros weichafe a 14 y 16 años de cárcel. Los cuales este 22 de noviembre cumplen ya 4 años secuestrados por el Estado de $hile.

De esta manera se puede demostrar como el poder judicial una vez más se ensaña con nuestros ppmcamche, con sus políticas racistas hacia nuestros weichafe.




Meli: Así también queremos demostrar nuestro descontento del actuar racista, discriminatorio y clara persecución política por parte de Gendarmería, el poder judicial y el estado $hileno hacia nuestro Peñi/ lamgen Lonko Daniel Canio. A quien una vez más se le han negado sus derechos como ppm, en este caso su correspondiente Libertad Condicional, nuestro Lonko lleva ya 11 años y medio cumplidos de su condena, tiempo más que suficiente para otorgarle el derecho a su salida y «Beneficios» cómo es la salida a un CET. Recordar también que no es el primer atropello por parte de Gendarmería que recibe nuestro peñi/ lamgen Lonko Daniel Canio Tralcal, ya que el año pasado se le negó la salida para el eluwun de su ñuke, coartandolo de despedirla y de su cultura como mapuche.




Así queremos enviar newen a todos nuestros peñi/lamgen que resisten al estado que nos persigue, nos encarcela y mata por recuperar nuestro territorio, nuestro feyentun, kewün ka mogen.

Un abrazo fraterno a nuestros ppm camche, y a todos los lof en recuperación, a las reñma que resisten junto a sus pichikeche para que siga brotando nuestra semilla, para nuestros nuevos choyün. También para los seres queridos del weichafeyem Kincha.




Desde nuestro lof en recuperación le decimos con la frente en alto, que mientras existan Presos políticos mapuche, mientras el winka y el yanakona siga usufructuando con nuestra mapu, mientras exista despojo territorial, seguiremos luchando.




Petu mogeleiñ tufachi mapu mew

Petu muleiñ weichan mew




Libertad a todos los PPM secuestrados en las distintas cárceles de wallmapu por la digna causa mapuche.

Fuera Forestales, extractivistas y latifundistas de territorio Mapuche!».

author: none
title: Why Alex Contompasis deserves Executive Clemency
content:
More than five years have passed since January 6, 2021, a date forever linked with one of the most divisive moments in modern American history.

by Don Ritter (The Saratogian)







While the nation’s attention focused on the attack on the United States Capitol in Washington, D.C., another violent confrontation unfolded hundreds of miles away outside the New York State Capitol in Albany during a “Stop the Steal” rally. It was there that Albany resident Alex Contompasis became involved in a violent altercation that ultimately resulted in his conviction and a lengthy prison sentence.




Today, a striking contradiction exists. Nearly all of the individuals convicted of federal crimes arising from the January 6 events at the U.S. Capitol have been released after President Donald Trump issued sweeping pardons and commutations in January 2025. Yet Alex Contompasis remains incarcerated in New York State. 




Whether one agrees with his politics is not the issue. The real question is whether justice has been served and whether executive clemency is appropriate. Supporters argue that Contompasis believed he was defending himself and others during a rapidly escalating confrontation involving members of the Proud Boys and counter-protesters. They contend that the circumstances were chaotic, emotions were high, and decisions had to be made in seconds rather than after hours of legal analysis. Advocates have continued to campaign for clemency, arguing that his sentence is disproportionate and that his case raises broader questions about New York’s self-defense laws.




The courts, however, viewed the evidence differently. An Albany County jury convicted Contompasis, and in 2025, the Appellate Division unanimously upheld his conviction, concluding that the evidence supported the verdict and rejecting his self-defense arguments. Still, executive clemency exists precisely because the legal system recognizes that mercy may sometimes be appropriate even after a lawful conviction.One of the strongest arguments for clemency is consistency. The federal government chose to extend extraordinary mercy to those convicted of offenses connected to the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, including individuals convicted of assaulting police officers and other serious crimes. Whether one




supported or opposed those pardons, they fundamentally changed the landscape of January 6 justice. Against that backdrop, Contompasis’ continued imprisonment appears, to many observers, increasingly difficult to reconcile. Executive clemency is not a declaration that someone was legally innocent. It is an acknowledgment that mercy, fairness, rehabilitation, or broader public interests justify reducing or ending a sentence. Governors and presidents have exercised this authority throughout American history.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul has granted numerous pardons and commutations during her administration after reviewing evidence of rehabilitation and other equitable considerations. If executive clemency is intended to recognize cases deserving individualized consideration, then supporters argue that




Alex Contompasis deserves that consideration as well.Reasonable people can disagree about what happened outside the State Capitol that day. They can disagree about whether Contompasis acted reasonably, whether he overreacted, or whether the jury reached the correct verdict. Those debates will likely continue for years. But clemency is not about retrying a criminal




case. Instead, it asks whether continued imprisonment still serves the interests of justice.If New York believes in redemption, proportionality, and individualized review, then Contompasis’ petition deserves careful consideration. His supporters argue that enough time has passed, that he no longer presents a danger to society, and that continued incarceration accomplishes little beyond extending punishment.




Others will disagree and believe the seriousness of the assault warrants completion of the sentence.




Ultimately, clemency is an act of executive judgment, not judicial review. It allows elected leaders to balance justice with mercy when extraordinary circumstances warrant. Whether Governor Hochul ultimately agrees is her decision alone. Under New York law, she has constitutional authority to grant pardons and commutations after reviewing the facts of each individual case.As New York continues to reflect on the divisions exposed on January 6, it may also be time to ask whether mercy has been applied consistently. If nearly every federally convicted January 6 defendant has now received clemency or release, supporters argue that Alex Contompasis should at least receive the same careful consideration under New York’s clemency process. I have known Alex since he was a young man, and I have known the family for more than 50 years, a family that has contributed to the arts and business community of Albany. This was not some out-of-state radical who came to Albany to start trouble.




Justice should always be even-handed. Mercy should not depend solely on which government prosecuted the case or on the politics surrounding it. Regardless of one’s view of Alex Contompasis, his application for executive clemency deserves a thorough, fair, and impartial review.




Is this an American Justice System or an American Injustice System?




Sign petition for Alex:

https://www.change.org/p/show-your-support-for-alex-stokes




Write

Alexander Contompasis 22-B-5028 

Sing Sing Correctional Facility 

354 Hunter Street 

Ossining, New York 10562

title: Sara’s clown show at the Senate
content:
The Nov. 9 and 10 impeachment trial sessions of Sara Zimmerman Duterte Carpio turned out to be poorly choreographed, with the defense witnesses apparently unprepared to handle questions from the prosecution, with two of them suffering from instant amnesia and can’t recall joining an all-expenses paid excursion to China the previous year. One, Davao City assessor Jaime Adalin, even tried to be funny by tagging a question “irrelevant,” and drew guffaws from the gallery.




However, he could determine a property of Sara’s husband, Manases Carpio, is listed in Sara’s SALNs even without seeing the coordinates, or the meters and bounds, of the asset. His testimony runs afoul of the testimony of two property registrars who said Carpio’s landholdings were not reflected in Duterte’s SALN. Davao City Register of Deeds IV Kathy Florence Baldonado testified that Carpio had acquired a 379-sq-m lot in Juna Subdivision, Matina Crossing, Talomo, Davao City, which was not declared in her SALN.




Samal Deputy Register of Deeds III Marco Pineda testified that Carpio bought a 751-sq-m lot in Matanos for P3,453,849 on March 15, 2018. Pineda said no entry in Duterte’s SALN matched the deed of absolute sale for that property. However, when shown images of a building from Google Maps with the sign “Prime Bistro,” Adalin admitted he wasn’t sure. He can’t remember the China journey and couldn’t be certain that it was the property which he said was included in Sara’s SALNs. On Nov. 10, the defense presented its second witness, Samal City Assessor Engr. John Kenneth Enumerables, who will testify on property records linked to Atty. Manases Carpio.




Presiding officer Sen. Chiz Escudero said senators might be confused with the location of the Carpio property in the deed of sale since it says the property is located in Barangay San Isidro but the TCT shows the lot is in Barangay Matanos. Enumerables says it is a small matter, a mere technical description. Sen. Panfilo Lacson said Matanos is actually located in Barangay Pangubatan, which Enumerables confirmed. Prosecutor Prosecutor Benjamon Tolosa Jr. noted that the deed of Absolute Sale for the property was executed on March 2018, while Duterte’s 2025 SALN showed the property was acquired in 2013. Enumerables acknowledged the discrepancy and said he is not certain if the property in the TCT is the same property in the SALN.




If Adalin performed badly for the defense, Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan snatched the bragging rights for the day’s worst dodger. Bajan claimed she wasn’t friends with Sara Zimmerman Suterte Carpio when she was appointed city accountant in 2026. Apparently, prosecutor Mae Divinagracia argued, Sara trusted Bajan so much that she appointed her chairperson of the City Audit and Transition Teams for Barangays in 2018, and as member of the Investigating Committee of Davao City in 2020.




Divinagracia asked Bajan if the accounting firm she worked for was registered in 2023 with the Securities and Exchange Commission in (SEC). Bajan could not answer at first, but later said “yes” after getting some signal from the defense, prompting the prosecutor to ask the court to stop her from getting coached. Bajan also hesitated when asked by Divinagracia to confirm if the signature appearing in the original Articles of Partnership of the accounting firm she worked with was hers, and she dithered and said she cannot remember the 2003 documents of Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co., causing uproar among the senators who told her pointblank that it was unacceptable that she could not answer such a simple question. Still, Bajan said the signature was similar as hers but insisted she cannot recall signing the document that contains her tax account number. Sensing that she is not being truthful, Escudero, Sens. Bam Aquino and Francis Pangilinan warned her that she is in “danger zone,” which could lead to a contempt citation or even a case of perjury.




Divinagracia noted that the firm Elises and Ciudadano is the same Elises and Ciudadano which is the external auditor of GenCorp Industries Inc., Metro City Chow Foods, and Great Jolly Times, all of which are businesses in which Sara and her hubby own shares of stock. Pangilinan points out that the address of Bajan’s former accounting firm – Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co. – in Davao City is the same address of the auditing firm of GenCorp and Metro City Chow. Bajan also denied knowing anything about GenCorp, Pikimong Pikimong and other companies related to Duterte and Carpio. Bajan also could not answer categorically Sen. Risa Hontiveros who asked her if she ever certified or signed a disbursement voucher for a company related to the Dutertes. All she said was that there were no names in the supporting documents, consistent with the “I don’t know” excuse crafted by the defense. Yet, she admitted touring Shanghai and Beijing like Adalin.




Bajan’s evasive tactics only created more problems for her and Sara as they inevitably showed she was trying to protect Sara. Moreover, it just might be true that her former accounting fire may be doing work for Cale88 Foods, the company that Carpio controlled and profited immensely from “selling” a product made by two people to China, Hong Kong and other destinations notorious for money laundering. Before the Sara impeachment trial, Carpio mysteriously disappeared from the ownership structure of Cale88 Foods, his 47.5% equity gone in a jiffy. Corporate records also showed that the firm was not buying bananas. One likely theory is that Cale88 Foods was a shell company for foreign interests engaged in disinformation campaigns, like China’s using operatives in Mindanao to attack the Philippine position on the 2016 award of the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) that knocked out China’s “historical rights” to maritime features in the South China Sea. #

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: First Nations Bank CEO says federal budget is a ‘generational’ opportunity for First Nations
content:
First Nations Bank of Canada (FNBC) president and CEO Bill Lomax says the federal budget offers a rare opening for First Nations to move from consultation into genuine ownership of the infrastructure and energy projects that will define Canada’s economy for decades.




Lomax framed the scale of planned investments in transportation, energy and electricity infrastructure as “a generational opportunity for First Nations to play a leading role in building Canada’s future.”




“When First Nations move beyond participation to become owners, we create lasting economic opportunities, build wealth for future generations and strengthen Canada’s economy as a whole. When First Nations succeed, Canada succeeds,” Lomax said in a statement following the budget. 




“But we need to think beyond consultation, employment and contracting opportunities. While these remain important, First Nations must also be recognized as business partners and owners, with the ability to build businesses, acquire equity and participate directly in the long-term economic benefits these projects generate.”




The FNBC is Canada’s only Indigenous-owned chartered bank, founded in 1996, operates 22 branches and service centres across six provinces and three territories, manages more than $1.6 billion in assets, and through its subsidiary FNB Trust, administers approximately $5.5 billion.




The federal budget, tabled Nov. 5, commits more than $50 billion over 10 years to Indigenous programs and services. The largest single piece is $32 billion over a decade for First Nations housing and on-reserve infrastructure. 




That includes the new First Nations On-Reserve Infrastructure Program, backed by $18.5 billion for infrastructure and $11 billion for housing that aims to maintain, renovate and build thousands of homes over 10 years. 




“This budget is an opportunity to invest in who we are,” Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty told APTN News in an interview Tuesday. “It’s an opportunity to better define who we are. It’s an opportunity to have a strategic approach to what our financial position is going to be, and I think the greatest opportunity of all is to demonstrate to Canadians the fiscal impact that Indigenous people have on the Canadian economy.”




Indigenous Services Canada Minister Mandy Gull Masty at a news conference on Parliament Hill in May. Photo: APTN.







The budget also introduces the new Canada Growth Incentive (CGI) for Canadian entrepreneurs, investors and employees, which is also open to Indigenous business people. The goal of the CGI is to keep investment money in Canada. 




It offers a new capital gains tax exemption for “Canadian builders” of up to $15 million earned from the Canadian businesses they invested in. 

To benefit, Canadians will have to reinvest and keep their money in Canada and Canadian businesses.  




“The Canada Growth Incentive (CGI) will be one of the most significant incentives to attract and retain builders here in Canada by creating the path for entrepreneurs, investors, and employees to reinvest in Canada,” the budget said. “This represents a level shift in the attractiveness of firms, large and small, to invest-and reinvest-in Canada, and deliver lasting prosperity for all Canadians.”  




The budget is also promising money for education, health, child welfare, policing and emergency management. 




The budget also outlines the government’s support for the Indigenous Loan Program that loans money to First Nations for projects. 




“I hope everybody listening or reading our interviews about the budget understands that I’m here to spend money; come to me with your proposals. I’m going to do everything I can to meet the needs, so work with me,” said Gull Masty. 




 Where’s the money?




Aaron Pete, chief of Chawathil First Nation in British Columbia, told APTN that he’s taking a cautious approach to the budget because the money “rarely finds its way to First Nation communities in a constructive way.” 




Chief of Chawathil First Nation Aaron Pete. Photo From aaronpete.com,







“It [the budget] sounds promising, but again, my concern is that it gets stuck in Ottawa and doesn’t actually reach these communities,” he said. 




Pete was a councillor in 2022 and became chief in 2025. He has a podcast where politicians of all stripes are invited to share their opinions on the state of the country and First Nations politics. 




He acknowledged that many of the government’s stated priorities — clean running water, higher-quality infrastructure and support for First Nations — are the right ones, but flagged ongoing concerns.




“My big overarching concern that I continue to have is how Indigenous Services Canada has a very Ottawa-centric approach,” he said. “There are restrictions on how provinces use [money] and they have to go to Ottawa for approval on budget spending. I think there should be more regional support so they can make decisions on a case-by-case basis.




He said the government does have other programs that help First Nations financially, but isn’t sure everyone is getting assistance. 




“We have the

 

First Nations Finance Authority

, we have the

 

First Nations Financial Management Board

, and we have the

 

First Nations Tax Commission

. There are experts in this area out there,” said Pete. 




“Is that knowledge, is that capacity reaching the most vulnerable First Nations that are still far behind the poverty line and need that support?”




Major Projects ‘designated in the national interest’




Another way the government is bringing in First Nations to participate in the economy is through its proposed infrastructure projects. 




It set up a 

Major Projects Office

 based in Calgary to oversee the development of the projects that are heavy in fossil fuels and gas. 




Currently, three projects- Roberts Bank Terminal Expansion Project, LNG Canada Phase 2 in B.C., and the Pacific Link Pipeline from Alberta to Vancouver have been designated as “projects of national interest.” 




Canada said it approached approximately 130 First Nations along the Pacific Link pipeline route and offered them a chance to invest in the project. 




First Nation leaders complained the federal government came with little information about the project. It’s still not clear what the final investments or arrangements will be.




Pete said he’s optimistic about the shift toward economic partnership with Canada in major projects. 




“We have moved a long way within First Nation communities and Indigenous communities more broadly to where we get to even be considered for equity ownership for an opportunity like this. Our ancestors were just trying to have a voice on where it would be placed and the impacts on the environment,” he said. 




“To be able to reap financial benefits from something like this is a huge change. And I just hope that everybody is processing how monumental that is. Imagine if we had had some equity ownership in CN Rail or CP Rail. That is unthinkable. But the amount of revenue we would have produced had we been equity owners in that would have been incomprehensible.




“Our ancestors fought for us to have a seat at the table. And now we have one. And we get to reap some of the financial benefits from major projects moving forward. That’s a big deal from my perspective. And that should be celebrated.”







Read More: 




Mississaugas of the Credit invests $15M million to become shareholder in First Nations Bank of Canada




Budget 2026 delivers $32B to First Nations, but Métis, Inuit largely left out







He also noted progress in the consultation process itself. 




“With the major projects office being required to consult First Nations communities, First Nations get to play an instrumental role in shaping where the pipelines end up going. And that’s, again, a huge change of pace, even since the TMX pipeline, so the conversations have advanced so significantly that now we’re being consulted well before the project is finalized. 




“They’re seeking our input on a planned project. And that’s another major step.”

First Nations Bank CEO says federal budget is a ‘generational’ opportunity for First Nations

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: From the battlefield to barriers at home: Remembering Indigenous veterans in Yellowknife
content:
One by one, veterans, cadets, Elders and community leaders line up for a smudge to mark the beginning of Yellowknife’s 

Indigenous Veterans Day ceremony

.




For the first time, the annual gathering incorporates traditional practice and offers participants a moment to ground themselves, reflect and honour First Nations, Inuit and Métis people who served in Canada’s military.




Retired chief warrant officer Richard Francoeur says the day provides Indigenous veterans recognition for their service and sacrifices.




“There are so many people from the Indigenous communities that went into wars that a lot of people weren’t aware of,” Francoeur told 

APTN News.




He says Indigenous people have served in conflicts throughout Canada’s military history, including the First and Second World Wars, as well as NATO and United Nations operations.




Indigenous Veterans Day is recognized across Canada on Nov. 8.




A Métis veteran lays a wreath at the memorial in Yellowknife’s Lakeview Cemetery paying respects to those who served. Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.







Returning home 




During the Yellowknife ceremony, attendees heard how some Indigenous veterans returned home to a country that did not recognize their service on equal terms.




Many faced racism and prejudice and were denied the same veterans benefits, land grants and reintegration support available to non-Indigenous veterans.




A reflection shared during the ceremony described the difficult choice some veterans faced between their military identities and their Indigenous identities.




“Many were forced to choose between their identities as soldiers or their identities as Indigenous peoples and often experienced barriers from receiving veterans benefits,” Framcoeur said.




Indigenous soldiers also brought skills from their communities onto the frontlines. The ceremony recognized their knowledge of tracking, marksmanship and the land, along with the use of Indigenous language such as Cree, which helped encode military communications during the Second World War.




The ceremony also recognized the 80 veterans buried at Yellowknife’s Lakeview Cemetery, many of them Indigenous.


Organizers paid tribute specifically to two Métis soldiers from the Northwest Territories who died during the First World War.




Private George McKenzie, from Fort Resolution, died on active service on Nov. 9, 1918.




Private Frank McPherson, from Fort Simpson, died three days earlier, on Nov. 6, 1918.




The ceremony included two minutes of silence, an Act of Remembrance and readings by cadets from Yellowknife.




Cadets line up to take part in Yellowknife’s Indigenous Veterans Day ceremony. For the first time, the annual ceremony incorporated the traditional practice of smudge. Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.







Cadets help keep the stories alive




The history was not lost on the younger generation.




Blake Ohokannoak, a cadet with 2837 Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry said he hopes people continue to share the stories.




“I think more Canadians should know about the discrimination they face while serving and after serving,” he said.




Ohokannoak, who is Inuit, has been involved with cadets for four years. He says his interest in the program started with his father, who was a commanding officer with the Cambridge Bay Cadets.




Jason Meyer has been a cadet with the 825 Yellowknife Royal Canadian Elks for a year. His father was a member of the Canadian Rangers in Nunavut.




Meyer said attending the ceremony is personal for him.




“I’m Inuit, so I come every year that I can, so I can honour those who served,” he said.




The cadets also help maintain the Field of Honour and take part in the annual remembrance activities, including placing candles in honour of Indigenous veterans.

From the battlefield to barriers at home: Remembering Indigenous veterans in Yellowknife

 appeared first on 

APTN News

.
