title: Aisha Wahab’s Victory Shows What Afghan Women Can Achieve. The Taliban Is Denying Afghanistan That Future.
content:
Last week, amid the many historic firsts and important victories in the midterm elections, Afghan American Aisha Wahab won her first full term representing California’s 14th District.

Wahab’s victory is a powerful reminder of what women can accomplish when given the opportunity to lead. Her commitment to public service reflects the talent, determination, and leadership Afghan women bring to their communities and to the world.

At a time when women and girls in Afghanistan are systematically excluded from public life, her achievement is also a reminder of what Afghanistan is losing by denying its women the opportunity to serve, lead, and shape their country’s future.

The contrast could not be more striking.

Wahab’s achievement should not be exceptional. Women’s leadership should be the norm, not the exception. Yet women’s opportunities to lead are still too often denied, obstructed, or dismissed.

Afghan women are just as capable of serving their communities, shaping policy, and holding public office as women anywhere in the world. They have the knowledge, ambition, and commitment. What they need is the opportunity.

The Taliban has made that opportunity impossible for women and girls in Afghanistan. Since returning to power in August 2021, it has barred girls from education beyond the sixth grade, excluded women from universities and most employment, and systematically erased women from public life by issuing over 160 decrees. These restrictions are not simply a collection of discriminatory policies. They are part of a system designed to deny women autonomy, human rights, and participation in society. In other words, it’s a system of gender apartheid.

And Afghanistan is paying the price.

When women are excluded from public service, the country loses leaders who could work for its people. When women are denied education, the country loses future teachers, doctors, scientists, advocates, and policymakers. When women are forced out of the workforce, families, communities, and the national economy suffer. The Taliban’s oppression of women is not only a violation of their rights; it is an assault on Afghanistan’s future.

Aisha Wahab’s victory makes visible what the Taliban seeks to suppress: Afghan women’s capacity to lead, contribute, and shape the world around them.

Her story is a reminder that women’s rights have never been a question of capability or merit. They are a matter of policy, equality and opportunity. The barriers are not a reflection of what women can achieve, but of the systems designed to deny them the chance.

The world must not forget the women and girls of Afghanistan. Their exclusion must not become normalized, and their struggle must not fade from the global agenda. Leaders, governments and institutions must continue to demand an end to the Taliban’s system of gender apartheid and stand for Afghan women’s fundamental rights to education, employment, and full participation in society.

An Afghanistan that excludes its women cannot fulfill its potential. And a world that celebrates women’s achievements while forgetting those denied the chance to achieve is failing them too.

author: Qassam Muaddi
title: What Will a New Israeli Government Actually Mean for Palestinians?
content:
The Arab vote made it possible to oust Netanyahu for the first time in nearly two decades.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Israel might be coming closer to resolving its political impasse following last month’s elections, as Israeli President Yitzhak Herzog officially tasked Gadi Eisenkot, the main rival of Benjamin Netanyahu, with forming a government.

Netanyahu, who ran with the hopes of staying in power, lost seven of the 54 seats won by the camp under his leadership. On Thursday, the Ashkenazi Haredi ultra-Orthodox party, Yehodot HaTorah, announced that it would no longer support Netanyahu, effectively reducing his camp to 46 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament. Yehodot HaTorah decided not to nominate any candidate for prime minister during the consultations that the Israeli president concluded on Thursday with different parties, before deciding to tap Eisenkot to form a government. The Haredi party’s decision came as a response to Netanyahu not delivering on his promise to the Haredi community to put their exemption from the military draft into law.

On the other hand, Arab-Palestinian parties allied in the Joint List have stated that they will nominate Gadi Eisenkot, thereby contributing to the majority needed to form a government, provided that Eisenkot’s other allies, especially Avigdor Liberman, who refuses to ally with Arab parties, maintain their support.

Netanyahu might be in his final days as head of the Israeli government, after 18 years and six governments in office. He might also be facing an investigation by a commission over the security failure on October 7, and charges in Israeli courts for his ongoing corruption cases. However, although significant for Israeli politics, how much difference would such a change mean for the Palestinian people, and for the region?

The scene could have looked very different, as it did after the 2015 and 2022 elections, with Netanyahu easily achieving a majority and staying in power. The difference, this time, is the massive turnout of Palestinian citizens of Israel, descendants of the minority who weren’t expelled in 1948, who represent around 2 million people today, and a fifth of Israel’s population. Two weeks ago, for the first time in Israel’s history, their 80% turnout gave the two main Arab lists 19 seats in the Knesset, blocking both Netanyahu and Eisenkot from reaching the 61-seat majority required to form a government.

This development didn’t come in a vacuum. In the past three years, the world witnessed an unrestrained display of what has been Israel’s policy towards the Palestinian people since 1948. But what Palestinians witnessed was even more crude. In Gaza, Palestinians lived the genocide in their own flesh. Outside of Gaza, Palestinians were forced to watch what the Israeli war machine did to their own people in Gaza, with threats of unprecedented repression if they spoke out. In other words, they were forced to normalize these new levels of brutality and accept them as the new norm. For Palestinian citizens of Israel, this was particularly consequential. In the years before October 2023, Palestinian mobilization within Israel was on the rise, with citizens protesting home demolitions, the expulsion of Bedouin communities in the Negev, the state’s indifference towards organized crime in Arab communities, the events of Sheik Jarrah and Jerusalem, and also in Gaza. That mobilization was forced into silence.

The past three years also saw a very aggressive and explicit affirmation of the most anti-Arab racist tendencies. This included resolutions voted on in the Knesset, such as the resolution rejecting any Palestinian statehood west of the Jordan River, passed in July 2024, and the rhetoric of politicians and the media calling for the expulsion and extermination of Gaza, or calling for the “transfer” of Arabs in Israel by ministers like Bezalel Smotrich. The Palestinian community needed some kind of response to remind Israel that they are present and part of the country. This is, in part, what their massive turnout in the recent Israeli elections was about.

But it was also more than just making a point or sending a message. After all, the Palestinian vote put its weight behind the immediate project of ousting Netanyahu, which could only come through a government headed by Gadi Eisenkot, which makes it imperative to ask: what do Palestinians in general, and Palestinian citizens of Israel more specifically, expect from an Eisenkot government?

Palestinian leaders in Israel have made it clear, time and time again, that they don’t expect an Eisenkot government to be one of peace. Palestinians don’t expect a new government in Israel to end the occupation, allow the reconstruction of Gaza, or reverse the annexation of the West Bank. This conclusion is based on Palestinians’ knowledge of the components of the Eisenkot camp.

Eisenkot himself is the former chief of staff of the Israeli army between 2015 and 2019, during which years he directed the occupation and the blockade of Gaza. Before that, he built a career in the military and left his mark on the Israeli army’s doctrine. In 2008, Eisenkot articulated and theorized the Israeli army’s strategy followed in the 2006 war on Lebanon, and the subsequent wars on Gaza, which became known as the ‘Dahiya Doctrine,’ named after the southern suburb of Lebanon’s capital, Beirut. In an interview, Eisenkot explained that the destruction and harm caused to civilian infrastructure in Dahiya would be replicated in future conflicts. He stated that villages that were used to fire missiles at Israel would be treated as military targets with disproportionate force, and revealed that this was an approved plan, rather than a mere recommendation.

Eisenkot’s first ally is Naftali Bennet, a far-right politician who emerged from the ranks of the Likud before forming his own party. It was Bennet who brought Smotrich to the Knesset on the ‘Jewish Home’ party’s list in 2015. In 2013, he declared, “I’ve already killed a lot of Arabs in my life – and there is no problem with that,” and later said that he had meant only “Arab terrorists”. He stated that captured “terrorists” should be killed rather than imprisoned. Bennet also supported the “shoot-to-kill” policy against Palestinian protesters crossing the fence into Israel during the Great March of Return.

The other ally is Avigdor Lieberman, who leads the Yisrael Beiteinu far-right party representing Russian-origin Jewish Israelis. Lieberman has been known for his extremist positions, notably against Palestinian citizens of Israel. Since 2004, he has been calling for “transferring” the Arab population to the Palestinian Authority’s jurisdiction as part of a territory and population swap, which would allow Israel to have more land with fewer Arabs. Most recently, he has been the major obstacle in Eisenkot’s camp to forming a government with Arab support, even if Arab parties didn’t join the government itself.

The third ally in Eisenkot’s camp is Yair Golan, leading The Democrats party. A remnant of the old Israeli left, Golan opposes uncontrolled settlement expansion in the West Bank and has pledged to dismantle illegal settler outposts. He remains, however, supportive of state-led settlements in the West Bank through the established settlement blocs, which he has considered “part of Israel”. Golan represents the old school approach to Palestinian governance as a partner in controlling Palestinians, while maintaining strategic elements of the occupation, like control over the borders, natural resources, and all of Jerusalem, while allowing Palestinians to have limited autonomy over civil affairs. All the leaders of the opposition to Netanyahu have rejected a Palestinian state and, therefore, by consequence, the internationally celebrated two-state solution.

The allies in the Eisenkot camp have two things in common: they are all opposed to Netanyahu as a person, and they are for strong state institutions, as opposed to ideologically driven fanaticism taking the lead on the state’s policy and agenda. This is, in part, because the extremist takeover means a destabilization of Israel’s old, established system and society, as religious fanaticism can only rise through an escalation of internal social divisions.

Netanyahu’s power has relied on the rise of the religious, disenfranchised sectors of Israeli society. This includes West Bank settlers, particularly those who settle in the West Bank for ideological reasons, while accepting the least comfortable living conditions, and spearheading the expansion movement through rogue outposts and violent attacks on Palestinians. This Netanyahu support base also includes the large parts of the religious Sephardic, eastern Jewish population, who has been mostly kept out of key roles in state institutions for decades. Altogether this fusion of social groups has created a kind of sub-identity in Israel that no longer identifies with the traditional, secular, state-centered, modern model of Israel which has been led by Ashkenazi, secular, middle to upper class elites.

Netanyahu empowered fanatic settlers, providing them with unlimited protection and support. He also enabled them to control key institutions like the Israeli army’s ‘civil administration’ of the West Bank by placing Smotrich in a key position in the Ministry of Defense to control the entire occupation policy. But the controversial aspect of this change in Israel is not the fact that new people have control in institutions, but that their policy is based on ideological agendas developed outside of the state framework. In other words, ideological groups that have operated outside of the state were now given access to state institutions.

These fanatic sectors, carrying a messianic agenda, overlap with the parts of Israeli society that have felt marginalized for most of Israel’s history by centers of power, particularly the Supreme Court. Netanyahu’s push to make the Supreme Court unable to check the government’s decisions and to allow the government to name members of the court represented the peak of these changes, as the Supreme Court has been seen as a stronghold of the secular, Ashkenazi establishment. Netanyahu played on these divisions, jeopardizing the established institutional rules of Israel’s political, legal, and social life.

The other side of Israeli politics aims to restore institutional order and stability while avoiding social divisions rather than exploiting them, which means adopting a pragmatic approach, even in deciding when to go to war. In general, this means managing the so-called ‘conflict’ with the Palestinian people, but before anything else, it means ousting Netanyahu and his populist allies

Arab turnout in massive numbers impacted the way the vote-to-seat ratio is calculated, taking away seats from both main camps and thus blocking Netanyahu’s usual way, as in past elections, to form a new government again and stay in power. This means the Arab vote made it possible to oust Netanyahu for the first time in nearly two decades. Netanyahu’s main allies would also be ousted in this scenario, like Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, who have pioneered some of the cruelest policies against Palestinians everywhere.

However, the opposition’s reluctance to ally with Arab parties, which should be the obvious choice for an alliance running on ousting Netanyahu, indicates that, despite its more pragmatic tone, the alternative to Netanyahu shares the same anti-Palestinian tendency.

The most hardline anti-Palestinian ally of Eisenkot has been Lieberman, who expressed his willingness to negotiate with Haredis as an alternative to accepting support from Arab parties. Although this is a show of Liberman’s hostility to Arabs, it also means that the reforms promised by the opposition would also depend on the issue of drafting, or not drafting, Haredis into the Israeli army.

If Israel is going to make any de-escalation on all its fronts, it would do so on its own terms, without the influence of any party that identifies as Arab or Palestinian. This means that the general direction of Israeli policy wouldn’t change. Palestinians expect that a new Israeli government would allow some or all of the Palestinian Authority’s customs and restore some of the Palestinian workers’ permits. For Gaza, the new Israeli government is expected to allow more humanitarian aid in and, at most, stop the daily strikes. This being said, Eisenkot has promised to “dismantle Hamas” in the first 18 months of his government, which could indicate a new round of bombing.

In Lebanon, a new Israeli government might lower its military presence, and it could even stop trying to get the US to resume war with Iran. In general, the highest hopes are that an Israeli government without Netanyahu and his allies would seek to lower the divisions and restore some stability in Israel, which means that it would need to de-escalate on all fronts, without ending or changing its policy of occupation, which it maintained even in the most optimistic years of the Oslo peace talks.

Seen from the outside, it seems that the change is not substantial, and that’s because it isn’t, even when the changes are entirely hypothetical and uncertain. Palestinians are aware of it, and Palestinian citizens of Israel were aware of it going into elections last week, deciding to bet on a change in the leadership of the Israeli government.

However, in the immediate context, given the time and place, this decision makes sense for many reasons. First, after the horrors of the last three years, and the crackdown on Palestinians in Israel who had been outspoken in the years prior to October 2023, the Palestinian community in Israel had to rally a collective response. A response both to the genocide and to the overwhelming rise of anti-Palestinian and racist sentiment in Israeli society. A way to remind Israelis that two million Arab Palestinians are part of the country and must be taken into account.

The opposition is still Zionist, and occupation is the core of its security doctrine. But the Arab turnout made possible the ousting of a specific trend of Zionism, which has been, for many years, on a mission to decisively and brutally destroy Palestine as a political and social entity, and destroy and control Israel’s surroundings as much as possible.

For Palestinians within and outside of Israel proper, especially in Gaza, the West Bank, and Jerusalem, this means that the priority is to oust the government with such an agenda. For them, it means they could, though not certainly, have a chance of not being directly expelled and exterminated over the coming four years. A chance that they would go back to some kind of long-term, structural oppression. And even though it remains only a probability, for those sitting under the immediate threat of bombs, bulldozers, and settlers’ guns, with the rest of the world showing an uneasy indifference, such a small chance can make a big difference.

title: Bakan Bak’tan kredi ve burslara ilişkin açıklama: “Sıkıntı yok, halledeceğiz”
content:
AKP Samsun Milletvekili Mehmet Muş başkanlığında toplanan TBMM Plan ve Bütçe Komisyonu'nda Gençlik ve Spor Bakanlığı ile bağlı kuruluşlarının 2027 yılı bütçesi, 2025 yılı kesin hesabı ve Sayıştay raporlarının görüşmeleri tamamlandı. Gençlik ve Spor Bakanı Osman Aşkın Bak, milletvekillerinin değerlendirmelerinin ardından soruları yanıtladı.

Bak, eski milli sporcuların futbol müsabakalarını ücretsiz izleyebilmesine yönelik talebine ilişkin, mevcut yönetmelikte bu konuda düzenleme bulunduğunu, ancak güncelleme yapacaklarını belirtti. Stadyumların kulüpler tarafından işletilmesi nedeniyle uygulamada bazı sorunlar yaşandığını ifade eden Bak, ilgili kulüplerle görüşerek talebi sisteme yerleştirmeyi planladıklarını söyledi.

KYK yurtlarının kapasitesine ilişkin eleştirilere yanıt veren Bak, yurt kapasitesini 1 milyona çıkardıklarını belirtti. Yurt yatırımlarının sürdüğünü ifade eden Bak, 2026 yılı sonuna kadar yapım ve kiralama yoluyla 29 yurdun tamamlanacağını, bunların toplam kapasitesinin 31 bin olacağını söyledi.

İnşaatı devam eden 21 yurdun 25 bin kişilik kapasite sağlayacağını belirten Bak, ihale aşamasında da yaklaşık 32 yurt bulunduğunu ve bunların tamamlanmasıyla 34 bin kişilik kapasite daha oluşturulacağını kaydetti.

Yurt başvurularının yüzde 96'sının karşılandığını ifade eden Bak, öğrencilerin aylık bin 300 ila bin 450 lira arasında değişen ücretlerle barındığını, sabah kahvaltısı ve akşam yemeğinin ücretsiz verildiğini söyledi. Yurtlardaki denetimlere ilişkin de bilgi veren Bak, mutfaklara kamera yerleştirildiğini, öğrencilerin denetim süreçlerine ve öğrenci temsilcilikleri aracılığıyla yönetime dahil edildiğini belirtti.

Adana Sarıçam'da bin kişilik, Ankara Beştepe'de 2 bin 500 kişilik yurt inşaatlarının sürdüğünü aktaran Bak, Antalya Konyaaltı'nda 2 bin 667 kişilik yurdun yüzde 82 seviyesine ulaştığını, Finike'de de yurt inşaatlarının devam ettiğini söyledi. Tekirdağ'da yeni yurt yatırımı bulunduğunu, Çorlu, Ergene, Malkara ve diğer ilçelerde gençlik merkezlerinin hizmet verdiğini de sözlerine ekledi.

Öğrenci burs ve kredilerine ilişkin değerlendirmelerde de bulunan Bak, 4 bin lira olan burs miktarının 2026-2027 döneminde artırılacağını söyledi. Yaklaşık 650 bin öğrenciye karşılıksız burs verildiğini, 800-850 bin öğrenciye ise kredi sağlandığını belirten Bak, 2022 yılında yaklaşık 22 milyar liralık öğrenci kredi borcunun silindiğini hatırlattı.

Kredi geri ödemelerinin öğrencinin eğitimini tamamlamasının ardından başladığını, mezuniyet sonrasında işe girene kadar iki yıl boyunca ödeme talep edilmediğini ifade eden Bak, tahsilat işlemlerinin Hazine ve Maliye Bakanlığı tarafından yürütüldüğünü söyledi.

Bak, "Sıkıntı yok. Bütçe yapıyoruz. Merak etmeyin. Bütçe içerisinde kaydırma yaparak halledeceğiz" ifadesini kullandı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: Evrensel'in HABAŞ gerçeğini katliamdan önce ortaya koyan haberleri TBMM gündeminde
content:
İzmir'in Aliağa ilçesindeki HABAŞ Demir Çelik Fabrikası'nda meydana gelen patlamada 18 işçinin yaşamını yitirmesi üzerine TBMM'de Yeni Yol, CHP, DEM Parti ve Yeni Parti gruplarının verdiği Meclis araştırma önergeleri, AKP ve MHP'nin oylarıyla reddedilirken milletvekilleri konuşmalarında sık sık Evrensel'in HABAŞ haberlerine atıf yaptı. Bazı milletvekilleri Evrensel'in İzmir bürosunun HABAŞ patronu hakkında attığı manşetin ardından kurşunlandığını hatırlattı, bazı milletvekilleri ise Çalışma Bakanlığının "gerekli denetimler yapıldı" açıklamasına Evrensel haberlerinde yer alan bilgilerle tepki gösterdi ve aslında şirketin kendi kendini ihbar ettiğini ortaya koyan "HABAŞ patronu katliamın geleceğini biliyordu" haberimizdeki bilgileri aktardı.

Konuşmasında Türkiye'nin dört bir yanında işçilerin yaşadığı sorunlara değinen DEM Parti İstanbul Milletvekili Cengiz Çiçek, "Bu ülkeyi patronlar kulübü yönetiyor. Evrensel gazetesi, ilgili şirketle ilgili manşet yaptığında gazete kurşunlandı" dedi.

Yeni Parti Ankara Milletvekili Gamze Taşcıer ise Çalışma Bakanı'nın HABAŞ'taki denetimlerde ciddi bir sorun bulunmadığı yönündeki açıklamasına karşın Evrensel'in daha önce yayımladığı haberleri gündeme getirerek "Oysa daha bir buçuk yıl önce Evrensel gazetesi bu fabrikayla ilgili haberleri manşete taşımıştı ve çok uzağa gitmeye gerek yok, şirketin kendi raporunda bile kendini ihbar ettiği çok açık bir şekilde gözüküyor ancak ciddiye alan bir Bakanlık yok" dedi.

Taşcıer, şirketin verilerine dayanarak ağır iş kazalarının bir yılda yüzde 56, taşeron işçilerin geçirdiği kazaların yüzde 120 arttığını söyledi. İş güvenliği eğitiminin 66 bin saatten 9 bin saate düştüğünü ve şirket raporunda haftalık çalışma süresinin 61 saat olarak yer aldığını belirterek “Çalışma Bakanlığı neyi denetledi?” diye sordu.

DEM Parti İstanbul Milletvekili Kezban Konukçu da HABAŞ’ın kayıp günlü iş kazası sayısının 2024’te 109’dan 2025’te 146’ya çıktığını belirterek Bakanlığın denetimlerini eleştirdi. Konukçu, "HABAŞ patronu Mehmet Rüştü Başaran 2025’te işçilerin ücretlerini yüzde 33 düşürerek 4,7 milyar lira kazanç sağlamıştı. Bunu haber yaptığı için Evrensel gazetesi silahlı saldırıya maruz kalmıştı yani organize suç örgütü olarak çalışan bir kuvvet görüyoruz karşımızda; iktidarından patronuna, yargısına kadar ve yer altı örgütüne kadar işçiler ölsün, patronlar kâr etsin diye çalışıyorsunuz" ifadelerini kullandı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Attacks Massie After Lawmaker Files Impeachment Articles Against Hegseth
content:
The president falsely claimed that Hegseth is “the most popular” military official in the country.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump made a surprise appearance at a White House press briefing on Monday, attacking Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) following the lawmaker’s submission of articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Massie is “a sick, sick guy. There’s something wrong with him, actually,” Trump said during the presser. “Now he’s after Pete Hegseth. He doesn’t like Hegseth, but really, what has Hegseth done?”

“He shouldn’t be taking up the time of Congress, or the Senate or anything that he’s doing. The guy’s a stone-cold loser,” Trump added.

The president told the press that he didn’t watch Massie’s announcement of the impeachment articles. He also didn’t respond to any of the charges the lawmaker is leveling against Hegseth, instead focusing on belittling Massie’s character.

Earlier in the day, Massie filed eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, which included accusations that the defense secretary engaged in unlawful war or military actions, ignored statutes designed to minimize civilian casualties, and suppressed the free speech rights of members of Congress.

“Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation,” Massie’s impeachment articles stated, adding that Hegseth “has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to civilians, the lawful conduct of United States military operations, the integrity and credibility of the United States Armed Forces, and the Constitution if allowed to remain in office.”

Trump continued his attacks against Massie on Truth Social on Monday night.

“Defeated Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, a total loser, is trying to Impeach perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country, Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth,” Trump wrote.

“Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached,” the president added.

On Tuesday morning, following a press conference in which Hegseth attempted to defend himself against Massie’s impeachment efforts, Trump again attacked Massie.

“Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” Trump wrote.

Despite Trump’s characterization of Hegseth as “popular,” several polls indicate that the American public is upset with him and wants him out of his position of power.

According to an Economist/YouGov poll conducted in September, 51 percent of Americans support impeaching Hegseth for “starting a war with Iran without authorization from Congress,” while only 34 percent are opposed to the idea. A Quinnipiac University survey from that same month found that only 34 percent of Americans give Hegseth a positive job approval rating, while 57 percent disapprove.

That same poll found that, unlike Trump, most Americans are not confident in Hegseth’s ability to lead the U.S. military, with 56 percent expressing that view and only 39 percent saying they have confidence in him.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $50,000 in the next 9 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Unknown
title: Giresun’da “temizlik personeli ameliyatlara girdi” iddiasına adli ve idari soruşturma
content:
Giresun İl Sağlık Müdürlüğü, kentte özel bir hastanede temizlik personelinin ameliyatlara girdiği yönünde basına ve sosyal medyaya yansıyan iddialar üzerine adli ve idari soruşturma başlatıldığını bildirdi. Müdürlük, Sağlık Bakanlığının iddiaların araştırılması için müfettiş görevlendirdiğini duyurdu.

Zafer Partisi Giresun İl Başkanı Mesut Aydın, Özel Giresun Ada Hastanesi’nde temizlik görevlisi veya yardımcı personel olarak çalıştığını öne sürdüğü S.T.’nin, tıbbi eğitim ve yetkisi bulunmadan ameliyatlara katılarak hastalara cerrahi müdahalede bulunduğu iddiasıyla Cumhurbaşkanlığı İletişim Merkezine (CİMER) başvurmuştu. Aydın, fotoğraf ve video kayıtlarına dayandırdığı başvurusunda ameliyat kayıtlarının ve geçmiş operasyonların incelenmesini istemişti.

Giresun İl Sağlık Müdürlüğü, iddialara ilişkin yayımladığı açıklamada şu ifadelere yer verdi:

“Bazı basın yayın organları ve sosyal medyada yer alan; Giresun’da özel bir hastanede bir temizlik personelinin ameliyatlara girdiği yönündeki iddialar üzerine, adli ve idari soruşturma başlatılmış olup Bakanlığımızca konuyla ilgili müfettiş görevlendirilmiştir. Kamuoyunun bilgisine saygıyla duyurulur.”

Hastanenin Başhekimi Dr. Cenap Damcı, daha önce yaptığı açıklamada iddiaları reddetmiş, söz konusu kişinin ameliyathanede yardımcı personel olarak görev yaptığını belirtmişti. Hastanede görev yapan Genel Cerrahi Uzmanı Op. Dr. Korhan Arslan da kamuoyuyla paylaşılan görüntülerdeki ameliyatları kendisinin gerçekleştirdiğini açıklamıştı.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Kuujjuaq festival organizer hopes to spark conversation about Inuit identity
content:
For organizer Saali Kuata, the Path to 100 Festival offers an opportunity to move beyond commemorating the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement. It allows for Inuit to examine how it has shaped their communities.




Art can start that conversation.




“Art is just another language that we can use that can transcend language,” said Kuata, Avataq Cultural Institute program director, in an interview.




The Path to 100 festival celebrates the 50th anniversary of the JBNQA and takes place at the Katittavik Theatre in Kuujjuaq from Sunday to Wednesday. It features an art exhibition, performances and workshops, as well as discussions about cultural identity, futurism and economic development.




The governments of Quebec and Canada, as well as representatives for Nunavik Inuit and Crees of Eeyou Istchee, signed the the JBNQA on Nov. 11, 1975. It led to 

the creation

 of a school board, a regional government and health-care system in Nunavik.




The festival’s name, Path to 100, reflects a long-term vision for Inuit.




That means Inuit having greater control over the decisions that affect their communities while protecting their cultural identity and rights.
















“If we want a sustainable future, we have to put our feet down and determine for ourselves, as we have done before, that nothing goes without us,” he said.




Kuata said he worries that as more Inuit adopt English and participate in the western education system and economy, they risk losing touch with what makes their culture unique.




“We find ourselves attaching our identity and our language to the common culture,” he said.




Besides throat singing, drawing, carving and printmaking workshops, the festival also had performances.




Singer Niivi Snowball, child of musician Etua Snowball, performed on Monday night and dedicated the song 

No Pride in Genocide

 to Etua, who was in the audience.




“My writing style is so heavily influenced by him,” Snowball told the audience. “The way he writes music, this heavy-hitting, unapologetically political way of writing his songs influenced me without me even realizing.”
















Before performing the song, which addresses suicide and the impacts of colonization, Niivi Snowball urged Inuit to reject the idea that death is their only way out.




“I want you to know that this is not our fault,” Snowball said. “The government, colonization wants us to think that the only way out is to die. But we are strong, and we can fight against it.”

title: Başsavcılıktan Kaşif Kozinoğlu'nun adli tıp raporuna itiraz
content:
Silivri Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı, 2011 yılında tutuklu bulunduğu Silivri Cezaevi’nde yaşamını yitiren eski Milli İstihbarat Teşkilatı (MİT) Dış Operasyonlar Daire Başkanı Kaşif Kozinoğlu’nun ölümüne ilişkin Adli Tıp Kurumu 1. İhtisas Kurulu tarafından hazırlanan rapora itiraz etti.

Başsavcılık, rapordaki tespitlerin ayrıntılı biçimde değerlendirilmesi amacıyla Adli Tıp Genel Kurulundan yeni rapor hazırlanmasını talep etti. Adli Tıp Kurumunun 3 Kasım 2026 tarihli raporunda, Kozinoğlu’nun kalp hastalığı nedeniyle hayatını kaybettiği, zehirlenme veya travmatik etki sonucu öldüğüne ilişkin tıbbi delil bulunmadığı belirtilmişti.

title: GENAR Başkanı Aktaş: "Yolsuzluğa karışan AKP’li siyasetçi ve idareciler hesap versin"
content:
GENAR Araştırma'nın sahibi İhsan Aktaş, 8 Kasım'da Yeni Şafak'ta yayımlanan "Bu millet AK Parti'den ne istiyor?" başlıklı makalesinde, Türkiye'yi sarsan "fon krizi"ni "AKP yönetiminin içinden kaynaklanan bir sorun" olarak tanımladı. Aktaş, yolsuzluklara karışan iş insanlarının yanı sıra kamu görevlileriyle onları koruyan siyasetçilerin de hesap vermesini istedi.




"AKP 3 puan kaybetti"




Aktaş'ın değerlendirmeleri, GENAR'ın ekim araştırmasında AKP'nin "fon krizi" sonrasında kendi araştırmalarında yaklaşık 3 puan oy kaybettiğinin ortaya çıkmasının ardından geldi.




Aktaş, 18 Ekim'deki ilk yazısında "fon krizinin AK Parti'nin oylarını yüzde 36 bandından yüzde 33,7'ye düşürdüğünü" açıklamış, kaybın sınırlı kalmasını ise "muhalefetin dağınıklığı"na bağlamıştı.




Ancak üç hafta sonra meseleye yalnızca seçim sonuçları açısından yaklaşmadı. 8 Kasım tarihli 

yazısında

 krizin kaynağını doğrudan iktidarın yönetim mekanizmasında aradı.




"Dış güçler değil, iktidarın içindeki ilişkiler"




Aktaş, yazısının büyük bölümünü AKP'nin tarihsel misyonunu ve Erdoğan'ın uluslararası önemini savunmaya ayırdıktan sonra sözü "fon krizi"ne getirdi. 




Krizin kaynağının yabancı güçler, darbeciler veya eski vesayet kurumları olmadığını vurgulayan Aktaş, iş insanları, imza yetkisi bulunan kamu görevlileri ve onları koruyan siyasetçiler üzerinden ortaya çıkan tabloyu şöyle tanımladı:







"Doğrudan AK Parti yönetiminin iç travmasıdır."







Bu ifade, başta Erdoğan olmak üzere AKP yetkililerinin sorunu "dış güçler"e bağladıkları bir saldırıyla açıklama teşebbüslerini benimsemeyişiyle dikkat çekiyor.




Aktaş, krize karışan herkesin hukuken hesap vermesini, denetim ve yönetim mekanizmalarının yeniden düzenlenmesini, AK Parti'nin kuruluş dönemindeki reformcu siyasi kimliğinin güçlendirilmesini istedi:







Bu işe bulaşan dolandırıcı, amir, memur, siyasetçi kim varsa hukuk karşısında hesabını vermeli ve milletin sisteme olan güveni yenilenmelidir.







Ancak sorumluluğu Erdoğan'ın liderliğinden ayrı tuttu. Sistem eleştirilerinin Cumhurbaşkanı'na yöneltilmiş eleştiriler gibi gösterilmesine karşı çıkarak liderlik ile yönetim mekanizması arasında kesin bir ayrım yaptı:







"Lider bir misyondur, bir ruhtur."







Buna karşılık sistemi, aksayan parçaları değiştirilmesi gereken teknik bir aygıt olarak tanımladı.




Üç haftada üç yazı: Anketten sistem eleştirisine




Aktaş'ın 8 Kasım'daki değerlendirmesi, 18 Ekim'de GENAR'ın sonuçlarını açıklamasıyla başlayan tartışmanın üçüncü halkası.




18 Ekim'de yayımladığı "AK Parti seçmeni olana razı olmadı fakat partisini terk etmedi" başlıklı yazısında, AKP'nin oy kaybını kabul etmiş ancak seçmenin bütünüyle partiden kopmadığı görüşünü savunmuştu.




GENAR'ın Ekim 2026 araştırmasındaki başlıca oy oranları şöyleydi:

Ankette AKP ile CHP'den ayrılanların kurduğu Yeni Parti arasındaki fark 10,4 puan olarak ölçüldü. DEM Parti 9,5 puanla üçüncü sırada yer alırken CHP yüzde 7,5'e geriledi.




Aktaş, AKP'nin oy kaybını muhalefetin yeniden yapılanma süreciyle birlikte değerlendirdi. Yeni Parti'nin henüz kurumsallaşmasını tamamlamadığını, CHP'nin yeniden örgütlenmeye çalıştığını, DEM Parti'nin de Demokratik Cumhuriyet Hareketi'ne dönüşme sürecinde olduğunu belirtti.




Böylece iktidarın uğradığı siyasi zararı kabul ederken, muhalefetin bu kaybı kendi lehine değerlendiremediğini savundu.




Seçmenin yüzde 20'si "fon krizi"nden etkilenebilir




Aktaş, 1 Kasım'daki “Fon krizi AK Parti'nin reformcu kimliğini geri çağırabilir mi?” başlıklı yazısında 18 Ekim araştırmasından yeni bulgular da paylaştı.




Buna göre fon krizinden haberdar olanların oranı yaklaşık yüzde 60'tı. Aktaş, seçmenlerin yaklaşık yüzde 20'sinin oy verme davranışının krizden etkilenebileceğini belirtti. Bu etkinin Cumhur İttifakı seçmenlerini de kapsadığını vurguladı.




Aktaş'ın aktardığı rakamlar, seçmenin bir bölümünün kriz karşısında tutum değiştirebileceğine işaret ediyor. Ancak yüzde 20, gerçekleşmiş bir oy kaybını değil, davranışının etkilenebileceği varsayılan seçmenleri ifade ediyor.




Araştırmanın örneklem büyüklüğü, saha tarihleri ve soruların tam dağılımı açıklanmadı. 




Aktaş aynı yazısında, Cumhurbaşkanlığı Hükümet Sistemi'nin merkezinde oluşan bürokrasinin reform tartışmalarını engellediğini savundu.




Önerileri arasında müsteşarlık sisteminin geri getirilmesi, kritik bürokratik görevlerde çoklu denetim mekanizmalarının kurulması ve vatandaş şikâyetlerinin sonuçlandırılmasını sağlayacak düzenlemeler bulunuyordu.




Siyasi sorumluluğun sınırı nereden geçiyor? 




Aktaş'ın üç yazısı birlikte değerlendirildiğinde ortaya çıkan belirgin siyasi yaklaşımda AKP'nin oy kaybettiği kabul ediliyor, krizin kaynağının dışarıda değil, parti ve devlet yönetiminin içinde bulunduğu saptanıyor, ancak Erdoğan'ın siyasi liderliği bu eleştirinin dışında tutuluyor.




Fon soruşturması yalnızca özel şirketlerin faaliyetleriyle sınırlı kalmadı. SPK'nin 131 yatırım fonunu tasfiye listesine almasının ardından kamu kurumlarının denetim sorumlulukları, Borsa İstanbul ve Takasbank yöneticileri hakkındaki soruşturmalar ve siyasi koruma iddiaları da tartışma konusu oldu.




Bu yaklaşım, AKP'nin ve rejimin krizin yükünden kurtulması için sorumluluğun nereye kadar uzanacağı sorusunun Beştepe dışında her düzey olabileceğini ima ediyor ancak doğrudan bir öneride bulunmuyor. 




AKP seçmeni için yeni bir siyasi konum mu?




Aktaş'ın 8 Kasım yazısının sonunda vardığı sonuç da dikkat çekici.




Aktaş, AKP tabanının eleştirilerini partiden kopuşun değil, partiye yönelik beklentilerinin bir ifadesi olarak yorumluyor. Seçmenin Erdoğan'ı ve partiyi terk etmek yerine yönetimin düzeltilmesini istediğini savunuyor.




Bu görüşünü, seçmenin başka bir siyasi örgütlenmeye sahip olmadığı iddiasıyla destekliyor:







"Bu milletin başka bir partisi yok."







Oysa GENAR'ın kendi araştırması, AKP'nin oy kaybettiğini ve CHP'den ayrılan Yeni Parti'nin yüzde 23,3'e ulaştığını gösteriyor.




Aktaş rejimde reform öneriyor




GENAR'ın ekim araştırmasıyla ortaya koyduğu yaklaşık 3 puanlık kayıp ile Aktaş'ın kasımdaki müdahalerinin AKP kamuoyundaki huzursuzluk kapsamında ortaya koyduğu öneri, kullanılan dilin ihtiyatlılığı ve ölçülülüğüne karşın partinin 24 yıllık iktidarı boyunca gündeme hiç gelmediği kadar radikal: Erdoğan'ın liderliği tartışmaya açılmadan rejimde reform. 




(AEK)

author: Admin101
title: Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago
content:
We’re thrilled to announce the formation of three new Locals of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN)! From the Texas Hill Country, to the Great Lakes, to the Northeast, our organization is growing deeper roots and expanding our capacity to organize, struggle, and build popular power in communities across the country.




As you will read below, each new local grows out of its members’ deep involvement in the popular struggles of their neighborhoods, workplaces, and broader communities. What follows are brief introductions in their members’ own words — including their contact info and social media handles.




Austin, TX




The Austin Local has officially re-formed! Our members are primarily focused on labor and tenant organizing, as well as rapid response to ICE. We are also making preparations for an open reading group to discuss 

BRRN’s Program

.




We welcome those with interest to contact us. 




Email:

 austin@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:

 

@blackrose_atx




Chicago, IL




The Chicago local is back! Our logo honors the Haymarket Martyrs Memorial — a symbol of the organizers who made anarchism a powerful current in immigrant and women workers’ struggles of their time, as well as the place we gathered for our first event all together as a local. 




We carry their memory with us alongside others as we work in the social movements where we are rooted. These include tenant struggles on the South and Northwest sides, as well as labor organizing in the Chicago Teachers Union. author: Mike Ludwig
title: “Green Economic Populism” Candidates Won 39 Out of 56 Races for Congress
content:
Support for climate action tied to the economy was also visible in the results of state-level ballot initiatives.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The dominant narrative about the Democratic sweep of the midterm elections has focused on President Donald Trump’s brash ineptitude and voters fed up with the costs of living amid reports of corruption emanating from the White House. The climate crisis appeared to take a backseat to concerns about rising energy prices driven by data center build-out and inflation linked to the U.S.-Israel war on Iran, but experts say an emerging class of Democrats successfully fused momentum behind economic populism with the need for climate action to win over voters.

“Voters rewarded economic populists who tied that message to climate, and I think there is a lot of appetite and movement in that direction,” said Patrick Bigger, research director at the Climate and Community Institute (CCI), in an interview with Truthout.

In surveys, potential voters ranked climate change behind most other concerns, with the economy, health care, and the war on Iran consistently topping the list. However, Bigger said victories for Democrats such as Senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine suggest that voters are making connections between an economy rigged by elites and environmental concerns such as fossil fuel extraction and noise pollution from data centers.

“We had Troy Jackson in Maine talking about heat pumps and cost of fuel oil, and Abdul El-Sayed talking about reining in Michigan’s utility companies and data centers,” Bigger told Truthout. “How our economy is being organized and its link to the natural world, that is very much front of mind even if people don’t say they’re voting on climate specifically.”

Bigger is the co-author of a new report tracking the success of midterm candidates that embedded messages about climate action within a broader populist economic agenda, reflecting what CCI calls “Green Economic Populism.” The report finds that the 2026 candidates aligned most strongly with Green Economic Populism — virtually all of them Democrats — won 39 out of 56 races for Congress, including six of the seven Senate seats that were up for grabs.

Multiple green populist-aligned candidates also won state and local races or defeated moderates in primary races, most notably Angie Nixon of south Florida, a progressive who won a Democratic congressional primary by tying climate to broken housing insurance markets, according to the report. Nixon narrowly lost to Republican Ashley Moody, and the progressive’s supporters complained that she received little support from the Democratic Party.

According to the CCI report, these candidates offered policy platforms that drew connections between the climate crisis and the rising cost of living by identifying many of the same culprits driving both, including energy utilities, fossil fuel companies, corporate landlords, AI companies, and data center developers. Candidates such Democrat Claire Valdez, the first Native American woman to win a U.S. House seat from New York, and Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, argued that one way to lower costs is to “take back power from the elite” and invest in cheap clean power and green infrastructure built by union labor.

”Our polling shows that people link these costs of living crisis to the climate crisis,” Bigger said.

Other incoming House members who ran on a green economic populist platform include Democrats Angela Gonzales-Torres of California, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Patty Garcia of Illinois, Will Lawrence of Michigan, and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania, according to the report. Incumbent green populist Democrats returning to Congress after fending off GOP challengers include Rep. Ro Khanna of California, Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Rep. Adelita Grijalva of Arizona, among others.

Climate and energy policy remains a challenge for Democrats. On November 9, the Senate voted 73-25 to advance a permitting “reform” bill that split the Democratic caucus, with Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) arguing Democrats should negotiate a new deal once they take the majority.

“I cannot support a bill that relies on a handshake promise from the same administration that’s spent the last two years waging a war on new clean energy projects to hold up its end of the bargain, and continues to do so even after negotiating the reform proposal,” Wyden said in a statement.

The bill would speed up permitting for transmission lines needed for clean energy infrastructure but also defang bedrock environmental laws that communities rely on to challenge polluters and fossil fuel projects.

While CCI does not comment on pending legislation, Bigger suggested policy makers could speed up permitting for clean energy projects by properly funding the federal agencies responsible, which have suffered from deep staffing and budget cuts under Trump.

“If you are wanting to get more renewables on the grid, get more transmission on the grid, accelerate the clean energy build-out in any shape or form — you have to staff the requisite agencies to do that permitting,” Bigger said. “Gutting the Endangered Species Act instead of rebuilding staff at the Bureau of Land Management seems like a stupid way to do it.”

Support for green economic populism — and frustration with industrial and Silicon Valley elites — was also visible in the results of state-level ballot initiatives. Of the 56 ballot measures related to climate and energy tracked by CCI, including proposals for prohibiting electric utilities from using profits to influence politicians, 21 initiatives restricting the industry passed while 10 pro-industry initiatives failed.

The backlash to the AI industry and data center build-out is profound: According to Bigger, 45 out of 46 local data center measures in the midterms went against developers, and 30 of 31 ballot measures that seek to impose restrictions passed while all 15 pro-development measures failed.

Green economic populism has been brewing at the nexus of the climate action and labor movements for the past two decades, with environmental justice activists and union members finding common cause in a “just transition” away from reliance on climate-warming oil and gas. This coalition shaped federal policy under the Biden administration, which pushed to expand clean energy infrastructure and pledged to address environmental racism.

However, much of the limited progress made under President Joe Biden was quickly reversed by Trump and the current GOP majority in Congress. Frustrated with Trump and Republicans, voters handed Democrats a solid majority for 2027.

Founded in 2006 by the Sierra Club and United Steelworkers, the BlueGreen Alliance promotes job-creating policies that fuse worker power with environmental justice. As midterm election results revealed a “blue tsunami” last week, BlueGreen Alliance Executive Director Jason Walsh said that creating opportunity for workers while addressing environmental challenges is not just good policy, it’s good politics.

“Across our coalition, we’re seeing those concerns come together around good-paying union jobs, affordable energy, and healthier communities,” said Walsh in an email. “In this election, union households demonstrated strong support for Democrats who won majorities in the House and Senate.”

Beyond Congress, Bigger is encouraged by Democrats winning state and local elections, including races for governor in Ohio, Texas, and Pennsylvania — three states where fracking has exploded over the past two decades, providing the oil and gas industry with serious political leverage. The midterm results are a signal that the industry’s political and economic dominance in these states may be fading as the ruling class faces a backlash from voters.

“There is cool stuff happening not just at the federal level, but across the country,” Bigger said.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

author: Indo
title: On “Sultat al-Majalis”
content:
Rather interesting text on the Arab Council Communist group “Sultat al-Majalis” formed by Lafif Lakhdar and Mustapha Khayati. Originally published in "Al-Hewar Al-Mutamadin, Issue 8699, 6th May 2026”. Can be found here.

The Arab Communist Grouping, which published the magazine Sultat al-Majalis (The Power of Workers’ Councils), was a revolutionary organization that adopted the ideas of council communism, drawing inspiration from the experiences of workers’ councils in Europe. The group was active in the early 1970s and consisted of intellectuals and workers of Maghrebi (North African) origin living in France. Its members were influenced by the events of May 1968 in France and by the left-wing critique of the existing socialist regimes of the time.

The group focused on the idea that revolution should be led by workers’ councils elected directly by the workers themselves. It rejected the traditional Leninist party model and centralized bureaucratic authority. It regarded Soviet communism, as well as its Chinese Maoist counterpart, as systems that had nothing to do with socialism. In its view, both were forms of state capitalism, owned and controlled by a new class known as the bureaucracy, which, like the bourgeoisie, was hostile to the working class and its independent movement.

The organization also launched a scathing critique of existing Arab regimes, whether self-proclaimed progressive or conservative, as well as all Palestinian organizations and the very idea of a Palestinian revolution, insofar as it remained detached from an all-encompassing Arab revolution aimed at overthrowing the existing state structures across the various Arab countries.

The first and only issue of Sultat al-Majalis was published in January 1974. Its purpose was to promote awareness of the self-organization of workers and peasants, free from the tutelage of political parties. The magazine included translations of texts by leading international theorists of council communism, articles analyzing the Arab-Israeli conflict from a class-based perspective that rejected nationalism, and studies of Arab labor movements.

Despite its limited organizational base, the group had a notable intellectual influence in independent left-wing circles and helped introduce concepts of workers’ self-management. It remains one of the distinctive experiments in the history of the Arab Left, representing an attempt to offer a third alternative outside the frameworks of Arab nationalism and official communism aligned with Moscow.

The group operated clandestinely, which meant that some of its contributors wrote under pseudonyms while others remained behind the scenes. Its initial core included young university graduates from Beirut who had been influenced by the global New Left movement but chose to work under the umbrella of the group in order to distinguish themselves from the official communist parties and the Organization of Communist Action in Lebanon.

The relationship between Lafif Lakhdar (1934–2013) and Mustapha Khayati was central to the establishment of this tendency. In his writings, Lafif Lakhdar confirmed that he and Mustapha Khayati had overseen the publication of Sultat al-Majalis.

Mustapha Khayati was a Tunisian activist and intellectual, a prominent member of the Situationist International in France, and the author of the famous pamphlet On the Poverty of Student Life. Khayati brought Situationist thought and the critique of the “Society of the Spectacle” into the Arab context, an influence that was reflected in the pages of Sultat al-Majalis.

Lafif Lakhdar was a radical left-wing Tunisian intellectual and one of the most outspoken critics of state capitalism in the Soviet Union and the Arab regimes. He argued that the genuine alternative lay in the “power of workers’ councils,” exercising self-management. This position formed the central ideological identity of the group.

The magazine served as a platform through which Khayati and Lakhdar translated unorthodox Marxist texts and analyzed Arab conflicts from an internationalist perspective.

Regarding the joint activities of three members of the group in early 1970, before its formal establishment, the Palestinian journalist Bilal al-Hassan wrote the following in an article discussing the book Nayef Hawatmeh Speaks, published in Beirut in 1997:

“... After the name of the Democratic Front [for the Liberation of Palestine] became widely known, along with its Marxist orientation, large numbers of Arab and foreign Marxists and communists began joining its ranks.

Among the most prominent figures who joined the Front at the time were three individuals distinguished by their extensive Marxist knowledge and familiarity with the European critical debate on Soviet Marxism: Lafif Lakhdar (Tunisia), Mustapha Khayati (Tunisia), and Hakima Barada (Morocco).

These three engaged extensively with the Democratic Front and spent time with its cadres and fighters in their military bases. They also proposed establishing a school for cadres, developed its educational curriculum, and participated in the educational process.

The three adopted the Marxism of Rosa Luxemburg as the foundation for educating the Front's cadres. They explained the theory of popular councils to these cadres at length, with their explanations ultimately leading to a critique of Lenin's theory of the party.

This experiment came to an end only when a member of the leadership visited the school and raised the issue before the Political Bureau, criticizing and warning against it.

These examples make it clear that what was known as the Marxism of the Democratic Front was subject to competing ideological currents, reflecting a state of intellectual disarray within the Front, concealed beneath an exceptionally vibrant and energetic political environment...”

(Al-Safir, Lebanese newspaper, February 24, 1998.)

In April 2026, in response to a request from an editor at the electronic website Matzpen, Mustapha Khayati provided the following details about the prominent activists in the group:

“The Sultat al-Majalis group consisted of a small circle of intellectuals who worked for a living. We had nothing beyond what we earned through our own labor.

Here are the names of our comrades:

Hakima Barada: A student working toward her doctorate. I used to share with her what I earned from writing for some obscure encyclopedias. She came from a well-known family that had fallen on hard times, forcing her brothers and sisters to find work in various service-sector occupations.

Kamal Lhbabi: An architect who refused to practice his profession even for a single day. Instead, he learned the craft of pottery and continued working as a potter until he developed kidney failure, from which he still suffers. He was born in 1946 and, like Hakima, was Moroccan.

Saleh al-Mathlouthi: At the time of Sultat al-Majalis, he was teaching in French secondary schools after graduating from the Faculty of Law. He is the father of the singer Emel Mathlouthi, known for her revolutionary songs in three languages: Arabic, French, and English.

Mohamed Chaïrat: At the time, he was working in factories. He later became an Arabic-language teacher and translator. He passed away several years ago.

Najib Ayad: A fellow factory worker alongside Chaïrat. He fled Tunisia with him during the Bourguiba era, subsequently completed his education, and returned to Tunisia under Ben Ali, where he worked at one of its universities. He was the cause of a disagreement between Lafif and me. He was the first among us to pass away.

That, in brief, was the Sultat al-Majalis contingent.

After years of estrangement, I met Lafif in Cairo while I was working as the director of a library at a French research center. We greeted one another warmly, bringing the estrangement to an end and restoring our friendship, although it was never quite what it had been before.

The group ceased to exist in 1976, and the revolutionary tide came to an end as well. Hakima and I returned to Morocco, where I stayed for ten years before moving to Aix-en-Provence to teach the history of political thought in the Islamic world.”

This is Mustapha Khayati's account.

Because of their ideological affinity, connections developed in Europe between members of the Sultat al-Majalis group and the Israeli socialist organization Matzpen.

During the October 1973 War, the two organizations signed a joint statement, which was published in both Sultat al-Majalis and Matzpen magazines.

The magazine Sultat al-Majalis also published an article by Lakhdar calling for dialogue with Matzpen.

In early May 1976, revolutionary socialists from several Arab countries and Israel, including members of both Matzpen and the Sultat al-Majalis groups, met and issued a joint appeal addressed to Arab and Israeli workers and revolutionary youth. It was entitled:

“No to War, Yes to Proletarian Revolution!”

Matzpen published the appeal in its bulletin, From Our Struggle Against Zionism and for Socialism.

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Administration Seeks to Strip 6.3 Million More People of SNAP Food Aid
content:
The proposed rule change comes as 34 percent of Americans report that they are suffering from food insecurity.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

A proposed rule change by the Department of Agriculture (USDA) seeks to limit eligibility standards for some households with low incomes when it comes to automatic enrollment into the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), sometimes referred to as the food stamps program.

Currently, any household that receives cash or in-kind assistance from the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program is automatically enrolled into SNAP. The USDA proposal would change that, requiring individuals who receive TANF assistance to apply for SNAP separately.

The administration claims that cuts would occur “because their income or resources exceed the Federal statutory limits.” USDA’s draft proposal states that more than $44 billion would be saved by the changes, but admits that the cuts would kick 6.3 million people off of the program in its first year.

The formal notice was published on Monday. It requires a 30-day comment period before it can be fully implemented.

The changes to SNAP would follow similar cuts that were made last year, when Republicans and President Donald Trump passed the “One Big Beautiful Bill” Act into law. In the year after that act was passed, 5.1 million people lost SNAP eligibility, amounting to a 13 percent decrease in total participation and dropping enrollment numbers for the program to the lowest levels seen in almost two decades.

The new rule would be even more drastic, dropping participation by 17.6 percent from its current numbers.

Major cuts to SNAP have long been a goal of conservatives — indeed, changes to the program, like those being proposed this week by the Trump administration, were part of Project 2025, the Heritage Foundation-backed blueprint for how Trump should govern that was published during the 2024 presidential campaign.

Trump has claimed that he had nothing to do with Project 2025, but his administration has implemented over 55 percent of its published objectives so far, and two-thirds of his first round of executive orders were taken directly from the document.

The SNAP changes, if the administration does indeed move forward with them, come at a time when more Americans are becoming food insecure. According to one survey, more than a third of consumers (34 percent) reported that they have skipped meals or cut meal sizes for financial reasons over the past year — an 11 percent increase from the previous year’s rates.

Relief doesn’t appear to be coming anytime soon, as the latest federal inflation report, published Tuesday morning, indicates that costs on most goods continue to increase, despite Trump’s claims last week that “inflation is solved.”

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Democrats Demand Admin Stop Shredding Records Related to Trump’s DC Projects
content:
Reports find that the Interior Department has been routinely shredding official documents.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

House Democrats are demanding that key federal agencies and corporations retain their records after receiving a whistleblower report that the Trump administration is shredding records related to the president’s expensive, scandal-ridden construction projects around Washington, D.C.

CNN reports that administration officials are rushing to shred key paperwork before Democrats take charge of Congress in January. Democrats have pledged to conduct a wide variety of hearings and investigations into Trump administration actions, and are planning a “high-profile hearing on one or several projects early in the new Congress,” CNN reported.

President Donald Trump’s plans to build a massive arch and revamp the East Potomac golf course are two major areas of focus because Democrats believe they may be able to stop construction before it starts. The Trump administration, on the other hand, is trying to move as fast as possible on the president’s arch, golf course, Lafayette Square, and Tidal Basin projects before the new Congress is sworn in on January 3.

Huffman said the Democrats “have standing to go to court if we have to” over the projects, per CNN. “We’ll have tools to be able to stop a lot of it.”

The Interior Department has denied reports that it is violating federal records preservation requirements.

The Democratic push against the records deletions is more wide-ranging than just Trump’s D.C. projects, however.

On Monday, the House Natural Resources Committee’s top Democrat, Rep. Jared Huffman (California), sent letters to 36 federal agencies and corporate donors ordering them to preserve records and communications related to the committee’s investigation of the Trump administration and corporations that have donated to Trump’s projects. The records requests require a certification from recipients, and include requirements to recover lost records that may have been deleted.

“For two years, this administration has stonewalled us and kept the American people in the dark while Democrats have fought tirelessly to daylight and stop their corruption,” said Huffman in a statement. “I am sending a message to President Trump and his allies: our investigations will continue full steam ahead. And to every agency official and corporate executive receiving these letters: save everything.”

The committee, which oversees federal lands, is slated to take the lead on the investigations into the projects. It’s also working with the powerful House Oversight and House Judiciary committees on other as-yet unspecified investigations into the Trump administration.

Agencies that received letters from the Democrats include the Department of Agriculture, Department of Interior, and Department of Commerce. Non-governmental recipients include military contractors like Boeing, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Oracle, and Palantir, as well as other entities like ExxonMobil, Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), and UnitedHealth Group.

Huffman’s office cited a report from August by Politico that found that the Interior Department has “devolved into secrecy” and hemorrhaged staff under Doug Burgum. The agency, which oversees federal lands and agencies like the National Parks Service, has blocked over 100 projects being undertaken at national parks while working to help fast-track Trump’s D.C. projects, even sometimes against court orders.

That report found that Interior Department officials have “routinely shredded official documents and use disappearing Signal messages — even for mundane scheduling matters — to avoid communications being preserved, as is required by the Federal Records Act.”

Burgum has created an environment of paranoia, apparently asking for the installation of a second sensitive compartmented information facility (SCIF) in the building. A SCIF is a unit used to house and access classified government information, typically used by the Department of Defense.

“They’re terrified of written records,” one former Interior Department official told Politico.

author: David Swanson
title: World BEYOND War Education Director Visits Romania, Bulgaria, and Belgium to Discuss Peace, Security, and Youth Participation
content:
By Phill Gittins, World BEYOND War, November 2026




From October 26 to November 4, 2026, World BEYOND War’s Education Director, Dr. Phill Gittins, visited Romania, Bulgaria, and Belgium to meet with peace activists, speak with students and educators, and join discussions on peace, security, and youth participation.




Romania: Chapter Members and University Students




On October 28 in Bucharest, Phill met with Hans Hedrich and George Epurescu of the 

World BEYOND War Romania Chapter

. They discussed local peace and anti-war organizing and ways to stay connected.




Later that day, Phill gave a presentation and joined a discussion with an international group of master’s students at the 

University of Bucharest’s Faculty of Political Science

, hosted by Associate Professor Luciana Alexandra Ghica. Drawing on WBW’s forthcoming book, 

From the War System to a Global Peace System

, he explored different approaches to security, alternatives to war and militarism, and the role of civil society in building peace.

























Phill Gittins with Hans Hedrich and George Epurescu of the World BEYOND War Romania Chapter in Bucharest




Phill Gittins speaking with students at the University of Bucharest.
















Bulgaria: Peace Education and Practical Action




On October 30, Phill spoke at 

Sofia University

 with Bulgarian and international students, doctoral researchers, and faculty members. The presentation drew further on the forthcoming book and led to a lively discussion about non-military defense, including how countries facing armed aggression might protect themselves without relying solely on military force.




Afterwards, Phill spoke with Professor Tatyana Dronzina and Dr. Denitsa Hinkova who expressed interest in possible collaboration, including a summer school for young leaders from Central and Eastern Europe. The idea is to combine peace education, dialogue, and practical training with support for participants to develop projects afterwards.




That afternoon, Phill met with Denitza Vidolova of the 

Sofia Platform Foundation

 to learn about its work in civic and history education, including helping teachers address Bulgaria’s communist past and polarizing issues.




While in Sofia, Phill also caught up with 

Veronika Botsova

, who served as President of Rotaract Europe during the 2023–2024 term and previously collaborated with World BEYOND War on its 

Peace Education and Action for Impact (PEAI)

 programme.




























Students and colleagues at Sofia University.




Phill Gittins with Denitza Vidolova of the Sofia Platform Foundation.




Phill Gittins with Veronika Botsova in Sofia.
















Belgium: Youth Participation and Dialogue




The final stop was Brussels, where Phill contributed to the 

Voices of Change Final Conference at the European Parliament

 on November 3. The Erasmus+-supported event, delivered by 

World Scouting

 and the 

Erasmus Student Network

 (ESN), brought together young people, youth organizations, civil society representatives, and policymakers to discuss democracy, participation, and peacebuilding.




In a fishbowl discussion titled 

“Neutral or silent?”

, Phill considered when neutrality protects dialogue and when it becomes silence in the face of injustice. As he put it: “We are clearly not neutral about war and militarism. We have a position. But having a position does not mean closing down dialogue.”




Conversations with participants from Georgia and Ukraine raised further questions about whether non-military defense could protect societies facing armed threats. The exchanges were challenging but friendly, showing how experiences of war and insecurity shape different views of what keeps people safe.




Phill also spoke with ESN and WOSM representatives about possible contributions to future regional and international student gatherings, including peace education workshops.
















Meeting Erasmus Student Network representatives.





Voices of Change Final Conference at the European Parliament.





Participants at the Voices of Change conference.













The visit was also a chance to reconnect with 

Donna-Marie Fry

, a WBW Advisory Board member and longtime contributor to its education courses, and Belén Luna Sanz, who took part in a peace education program Phill led in Bolivia in 2014 and now works in digital policy.




Many thanks to everyone who hosted the visits, joined the discussions, and shared their ideas.














Phill Gittins with Donna Marie Fry in Brussels.







Phill Gittins with Belén Luna Sanz in Brussels.

World BEYOND War Education Director Visits Romania, Bulgaria, and Belgium to Discuss Peace, Security, and Youth Participation

 appeared first on 

World BEYOND War
