title: Iraqi Martyrs Foundation: 85 mass graves have been opened in Shengal
content:
More than twelve years after the genocide committed by the so-called Islamic State (ISIS) against the Yazidi population of Shengal, efforts to exhume and identify the victims continue. According to Iraq’s Martyrs Foundation, 90 mass graves have been discovered so far. Of these, 85 have been fully excavated, with the recovery of human remains and documentation completed. In total, the remains of around 700 people have been recovered.




Abdulilah Naili, head of the foundation, told the Iraqi daily newspaper Al-Sabah that 300 victims had been identified and their remains returned to their families. Identification was carried out through forensic DNA analysis. Genetic samples obtained from the mass graves were compared with blood samples collected from relatives during regular search and identification campaigns.




More mass graves may be discovered




According to Naili, work on the five remaining burial sites is expected to be completed within the coming months. This will mark the conclusion of investigations into the mass graves currently documented by the foundation. However, he said, it would not mean that the crimes had been fully investigated. Previously unknown burial sites could still be discovered during construction and reconstruction work in Shengal.




These figures differ from those published in late October by the Ministry of Martyrs and Anfal Affairs of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI). According to the ministry, 78 mass graves had been opened at that time, and the remains of 857 people had been recovered. Preparations for further exhumations were also announced. The respective statements do not explain the discrepancies between the figures reported by the two authorities.




Psychosocial support for families




The Iraqi Martyrs Foundation also stated that it had established a specialized unit to assist victims’ relatives. Psychologists and social workers are expected to support families receiving the remains of their murdered loved ones after years of uncertainty.




On August 3, 2014, ISIS launched an assault on Shengal and committed genocide against the Yazidi population. Thousands of people were murdered, while women and children were abducted and enslaved. Many families are still waiting to learn the fate of their loved ones.

title: Kurdish organizations in Switzerland deny any links to criminal groups
content:
The Democratic Kurdish Council of Switzerland (CDK-S) and the Association of Kurdish Women in Switzerland (YJK-S) have firmly denied any links to criminal groups that publicly portray themselves as part of the Kurdish freedom movement. Their statement follows an investigation published on November 4 by Swiss public broadcaster SRF into alleged mafia-style networks with links to Basel and international operations. Subsequent media coverage repeatedly associated the groups in question with the Kurdish freedom movement and organizations affiliated with it.




In a joint statement on Tuesday, the two Kurdish umbrella organizations criticized the media for sometimes accepting the self-portrayals of criminal groups without sufficiently verifying their actual organizational ties. CDK-S and YJK-S specifically rejected allegations of cooperation with the group known as “Tolhildan” and other similar structures.




“No institutional ties whatsoever”




“We state unequivocally: We have no institutional ties whatsoever to Tolhildan or any other gang structures. These groups’ claims of affiliation with the Kurdish freedom movement cannot be regarded as evidence of any relationship with our organizations. We reject the misuse of our institutions’ names and symbols, or the values of our people’s struggle for freedom, to lend legitimacy to such groups.”




The organizations emphasized that the use of Kurdish symbols or references to political causes did not constitute evidence of actual organizational affiliation.




Warning against the recruitment of young people




The umbrella organizations expressed particular concern over attempts to recruit young people into criminal activities by appealing to their Kurdish identity and patriotic convictions. They called on Kurdish youth in particular to stay away from such groups and neither support nor participate in their activities.




“We must remain vigilant and resolute in the face of attempts to exploit Kurdish identity, patriotic sentiments and the shared values of our people to recruit young people. Our youth belong in spaces where free thought, solidarity, culture and democratic social struggle flourish.”




The organizations announced that they would use democratic and legal means to counter the spread of intimidation, violence and criminal networks of dependency. They stressed that the social achievements of the Kurdish community must not be exploited to advance private or criminal interests.




Criticism of unverified claims in the media




At the same time, CDK-S and YJK-S appealed to the media’s journalistic responsibility. They emphasized the need to distinguish claims through which criminal groups seek to portray themselves as politically legitimate from independently verified facts.




“We call on the media to distinguish between these groups’ self-proclaimed affiliations and verified information, to take into account the statements of our organizations, and to avoid sweeping associations of our people or democratic institutions with criminal organizations.”




In conclusion, the umbrella organizations called on families, young people and civil society organizations to work together to strengthen safe spaces for cultural activities, solidarity and democratic participation. The aim is to enable young people in particular to organize independently of criminal networks and participate actively in society.

title: Hatimoğulları: This is not the first workplace killing at HABAŞ
content:
Tülay Hatimoğulları, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), leveled serious accusations against the company and the relevant state authorities following the devastating explosion at the HABAŞ steel plant in Aliağa. The explosion at the iron and steel plant, located approximately 60 kilometers north of Izmir, killed 18 workers and injured another 18. Hatimoğulları described the disaster as a “workplace killing” and blamed years of failures in occupational safety measures.




After visiting the injured workers in hospital, Hatimoğulları traveled to the plant on Tuesday with a delegation. Speaking outside the factory, she stated that this was by no means the first fatal incident at HABAŞ. She recalled that eleven workers had lost their lives at the plant over the past ten years alone. She said there were serious indications that essential safety measures had not been implemented for a long time.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/0a66ee8f_20261110152022_2026-11-10-izmir-tulay-hatimogullari-dem-parti-es-genel-baskani-habas-is-cinayeti-aciklama-1.mp4










Two fatal incidents within just a few weeks




The explosion occurred on Monday morning while the plant was in operation. According to initial information from the Izmir Governor’s Office, an overhead crane broke loose during a casting operation and fell into an industrial furnace. The resulting explosion triggered a fire, sending thick clouds of smoke rising above the plant.




It was the third fatal incident within just a few weeks. In October, temporary worker Hakan Doğan fell from a height of approximately eight meters and lost his life. On November 5, 20-year-old temporary worker Eyüp Eğinli died when an explosion occurred while a tire on a piece of industrial machinery was being inflated. Including the victims of the latest disaster, a total of 20 workers have lost their lives at HABAŞ within a short period.




Hatimoğulları stressed that these deaths demonstrated the need for a comprehensive investigation into working conditions and the responsibility of the company’s management. She recalled previous court proceedings in which HABAŞ had been found to bear 70 percent of the responsibility for fatal workplace accidents. Those responsible had been sentenced to two years and six months in prison but had nevertheless been able to continue working at the company.




Call for the resignation of ministers and regulatory officials




The DEM Party Co-Chair therefore directed her criticism not only at the company’s management but also at the state authorities responsible for overseeing occupational health and safety. Despite repeated fatalities, she said, sufficient action was apparently not taken.




“The Minister of Labor and Social Security, the Director General of Occupational Health and Safety, the Minister of Industry and Technology, and the head of the supervisory and inspection authority, all of whom bear responsibility, must resign immediately. They must not remain in office for a single day longer,” Hatimoğulları declared.




The public prosecutor’s office has since launched an investigation into the explosion. According to Turkish Deputy Justice Minister Can Tuncay, arrest warrants have been issued for eleven individuals, including HABAŞ Chairman Mehmet Rüştü Başaran. Investigators are examining whether technical defects, inadequate maintenance or violations of safety regulations contributed to the disaster.




Criticism of continued production after the explosion




Meral Danış Beştaş, Co-Spokesperson of the Peoples’ Democratic Congress (HDK), also criticized the treatment of workers. She noted that while the search for victims was still underway at the plant, workers in another section of the factory were required to continue working. Beştaş described this as reflecting an attitude in which economic interests took precedence over the protection of human life, even in the face of numerous fatalities.




Beştaş called for a nationwide period of mourning to draw attention to the scale of the disaster and the continuing loss of life in workplace accidents. Hatimoğulları and Beştaş extended their condolences to the families of the workers who lost their lives and wished the injured a speedy recovery.




HABAŞ exports steel to Israel




The HABAŞ Group has also faced criticism over its trade relations with Israel. According to available information, the company has continued exporting high-quality steel to Israel since 2024. These business relations have become politically controversial, particularly in light of Israel’s war in the Gaza Strip and the Turkish government’s announced suspension of trade with Israel.

title: DEM Party calls for climate justice instead of new profit opportunities as COP31 opens in Antalya
content:
At the start of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, the Ecology Commission of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) called for a fundamental transformation of international climate and energy policies. The commission argued that the climate crisis could not be overcome through market-based mechanisms but instead required a democratic and socially just restructuring of society’s systems of production and ways of life.




In a statement on Tuesday, the commission blamed the capitalist model of production and consumption for the ongoing destruction of the environment.




“Policies focused on unlimited economic growth, the exploitation of natural resources, deforestation and dependence on fossil fuels are exacerbating the crisis. Existing international climate agreements have failed to bring about binding changes. Instead, official climate negotiations have been reduced to market mechanisms and emissions trading.”




Criticism of Turkey’s energy policies




The DEM Party sees a fundamental contradiction between Turkey’s role as host of COP31 and its actual energy policies. Although Ankara is hosting the international climate conference, it still lacks a concrete and binding roadmap for phasing out fossil fuels, the party said, adding that the country continues to rely on coal and natural gas.




“The consequences of the climate crisis are distributed highly unequally across society. People living in poverty, workers, women, children, Indigenous peoples and local communities are particularly affected.”




The statement further noted that droughts, floods, forest fires, and water and food crises were exacerbating existing inequalities and forcing increasing numbers of people to flee their homes.




Energy transition under democratic control




As an alternative, the Ecology Commission called for a just and carefully planned phase-out of fossil fuels, democratic control over energy supplies and the protection of food sovereignty. According to the party, environmentally destructive projects must be halted.




“At the same time, those states and economic actors that have historically contributed the most to the climate crisis must fulfill their obligation to repay their climate debt,” the party demanded.




The commission stressed that climate justice could only be achieved if the social groups directly affected were able to participate in decisions concerning the necessary changes. These groups, it said, include local communities, farmers, workers, women, young people and environmental movements.




“The solution to the climate crisis does not lie in market mechanisms that create new profit opportunities for capital, but in building a democratic, egalitarian and ecological way of life that exists in harmony with nature and places society’s needs at its center,” the statement underlined.




Participation in the Peoples’ Climate Summit




The DEM Party announced that it would closely scrutinize the COP31 negotiations and actively participate in the preparations and events of the “Peoples’ Climate Summit.” The summit aims to provide a platform for social movements and communities affected by the climate crisis to develop their own demands and alternatives to the official negotiations.




“We will intensify our struggle for a future that places people rather than capital, life rather than markets, and ecological and social justice rather than profit at its center,” the Ecology Commission declared.

title: PEN conference in Amed calls for recognition of the Kurdish identity, language and culture
content:
The international “Language and Peace” conference, held on November 6 and 7 in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır), has published its final declaration. Participants called for constitutional and legal guarantees of linguistic and cultural rights, recognition of Kurdish identity and the release of political prisoners. They also emphasized the responsibility of writers and intellectuals to stand up for truth, justice and lasting democratic peace.




Organized by PEN International, the Kurdish PEN Center and the municipal administrations of Amed, Sur, Yenişehir, Bağlar and Kayapınar, the conference was held under the theme “The Role of Literature, Language and Intellectuals in Processes of Dialogue, Peace and Equality.” The two days of discussions focused on the conditions necessary for social coexistence based on equal rights and recognition of different identities.




'Peace must not be reduced to disarmament'




In their final declaration, participants welcomed the ongoing efforts to achieve a peaceful resolution of the Kurdish question. They described calls for peace and corresponding political steps as necessary and positive developments. However, they emphasized that such efforts could only lead to lasting results if accompanied by legal guarantees and social change.




“For peace to be built on strong and lasting foundations, cultural and linguistic rights must be recognized, and conditions that enable freedom must be established,” the declaration stated.




The final declaration stressed that peace must not be defined solely in terms of laying down arms. Rather, it must encompass social equality and recognition of the political, social, economic, cultural and human rights of all people. According to the participants, coexistence within a common state and constitutional framework must also be based on equal rights, equal opportunities and free dialogue within society.




Call for recognition of Kurdish as a language of education and official use




One of the conference’s central demands concerns the legal status of the Kurdish language. Participants called for recognition of Kurdish identity, language and culture, as well as the establishment of the necessary conditions for their free development. This includes legal provisions guaranteeing the right to education in one’s mother tongue and ensuring the official use of Kurdish.




Linguistic equality must not be limited to symbolic recognition but must be reflected in the education system and public life, said the final declaration, which also rejected all forms of forced assimilation. In a society based on equality, it said, no one should be compelled to abandon their cultural identity or conform to another identity.




'Freedom for writers and political prisoners'




Alongside linguistic rights, the conference emphasized freedom of opinion and expression as a fundamental prerequisite for democratic peace. Particular significance was attached to the symbol of the “empty chair,” which PEN uses to draw attention to writers who are imprisoned, persecuted or prevented from freely expressing their views.




The empty chair serves as a painful reminder of the ongoing attacks on freedom of thought and human freedom, the declaration stated. PEN International and the Kurdish PEN Center therefore called for the immediate and unconditional release of all imprisoned writers, journalists and political prisoners.




“As long as critical thinkers and writers remain behind bars, no peace initiative can attain moral or democratic legitimacy,” the organizations declared.




'Literature becomes the voice of those who have been silenced'




The final declaration also emphasized the particular social responsibility of literature and culture. “Where political institutions reach their limits, literature can connect directly with people, bring experiences to light and foster mutual understanding. Literature becomes the voice of those who remain silent or whose voices have been forcibly silenced,” the declaration stated.




Participants reaffirmed their conviction that literature and culture are not merely secondary elements of political peace efforts but among their fundamental prerequisites.




“As writers and PEN representatives, we wholeheartedly believe that literature and culture are essential components of peacebuilding. We pledge never to place our pens in the service of conflict, hatred or chauvinism. Instead, we will use them with unwavering determination in the service of truth, justice and the universal recognition of our shared humanity.”




In conclusion, the conference called on the state and political decision-makers to initiate a sincere and comprehensive dialogue based on equality and constitutional guarantees. It also urged civil society initiatives to participate with courage and foresight in efforts to achieve genuine, constitutionally guaranteed and lasting peace.

author: Carlos Pérez
title: “Esto no para”: Una perspectiva de base sobre la huelga indefinida por la educación pública en Madrid
content:
“Esto no para”: Una perspectiva de base sobre la huelga indefinida por la educación pública en Madrid




Desde el 14 de octubre, las docentes de Madrid, España, se encuentran en huelga indefinida en defensa de la educación pública. Tras años de deterioro de las condiciones laborales y una organización sistemática de las bases, las docentes han inundado las calles de la capital española en una movilización masiva que ha vinculado la lucha por la educación pública con la reciente revuelta en torno a la vivienda.




La lucha conjunta por la vivienda y la educación pública en España se encamina ahora hacia una huelga general el 11 de noviembre, en medio de un levantamiento más amplio que se extiende por toda Europa.




Carlos Pérez, maestro de estudios sociales en Carolina del Norte y miembro de la junta directiva de Labor Notes habló con María, profesora de secundaria de historia y geografía en Madrid y militante de Menos Lectivas, una de las principales fuerzas de base detrás de la huelga.




Pérez: Los docentes de la escuela pública en Madrid mantienen una huelga indefinida desde el 14 de octubre. ¿Cuáles son los motivos principales que les llevaron a usted y a otros docentes a convocar una huelga, y cuáles son sus reivindicaciones?




María:

 En la Comunidad de Madrid venimos arrastrando recortes en la educación pública desde el año 2011. Estos han ido deteriorando el estado de las aulas y la calidad educativa de los estudiantes madrileños. 




La falta de recursos y de personal, la cantidad de alumnos en el aula, el aumento de horas lectivas (horas de clase directa en el aula) y la falta de mantenimiento y construcción de infraestructuras nos han dejado un escenario en el que impartir clase es muy complicado. Las docentes no llegamos a atender a todos nuestros estudiantes y hemos decidido plantarnos ante el maltrato institucional que sufrimos tanto nosotras como nuestro alumnado.




En mi caso, he dado clase a aulas de bachillerato con 33 alumnos, he tenido que buscar un aula donde meter a mis alumnos cada día durante un mes de lluvias intensas porque las aulas tenían unas goteras que provocan que estuviesen constantemente mojadas; mis alumnos con necesidades educativas (autismo o dificultades de audición y lenguaje) no han sido atendidos por las profesionales que hacían falta porque no había ni integradora social ni profesora específica para ellos, y por supuesto trabajo una cantidad de horas extra ingentes y no están remuneradas ni reconocidas. 




Por eso reivindicamos y exigimos a la Comunidad de Madrid que reduzca las horas lectivas; reducir los ratios entre las docentes y alumnos; acabar con la segregación, dado que la Comunidad de Madrid es la región de España más segregada en educación; aumentar el salario para equiparlo a las necesidades económicas actuales; reducir la burocracia, entre otras cosas. 




Menos Lectivas, una plataforma de base que agrupa a varios sindicatos, ha sido uno de los principales impulsores de la huelga. ¿Qué es Menos Lectivas y qué papel ha desempeñado en este conflicto?




Menos Lectivas nace en el 2023, inspirada por colectivos como Labor Notes en los EEUU, con la intención de organizar a las trabajadoras de la educación desde los centros de trabajo y devolver el poder sindical a las trabajadoras. Desde entonces hemos construido nuestro movimiento a través de asambleas de centro. 




En estos años previos a la huelga indefinida se han convocado huelgas, manifestaciones y concentraciones que han servido para que cada vez el movimiento fuese más grande y, sobre todo, tuviésemos legitimidad institucional — tanto con los trabajadores que nos ven como un agente de lucha válido porque se sienten parte de él gracias a las asambleas, como para el resto de sindicatos, los medios de comunicación y en última instancia los gobiernos — para decidir cómo, cuándo y dónde queríamos luchar por el derecho a la educación y nuestros derechos laborales.




Desde los inicios sabíamos que la huelga indefinida sería la última herramienta de lucha sindical si nuestras demandas no eran escuchadas por la Comunidad de Madrid y, el pasado junio, se decidió en asamblea que las docentes iríamos a la huelga indefinida. Siendo ya un conjunto de asambleas con legitimidad el resto de sindicatos que no formaban parte de Menos Lectivas tuvieron que sentarse con nosotras en el Comité de Huelga a negociar la constitución de una mesa de negociación y las condiciones de la huelga. Este hito ya es un éxito, consiguiendo que el poder vuelva a las trabajadoras y salga de los despachos.




¿Cómo ha sido recibida la huelga por parte del alumnado y sus familias?




Tanto las familias como el alumnado están de acuerdo con nuestras reivindicaciones. En última instancia, son los principales beneficiarios de las mejoras que consigamos. Nos sentimos muy apoyadas por ellos y son una parte esencial de la lucha.




Los estudiantes organizados han convocado también huelga indefinida a través de distintos partidos y organizaciones políticas como el Sindicato de Estudiantes o la Organización Estudiantil Socialista. Están presentes en todas las acciones que hacemos en las calles y forman una parte importante de la lucha por la educación. 




Las familias, por su parte, se organizan en asociaciones de familias en cada uno de los centros educativos y en los barrios y ayudan a sostener las cajas de resistencia. Además, han convocado una concentración propia para hacerle ver a la Consejera de Educación que esta lucha no es exclusiva de las docentes, si no también de las familias.




Dado que la huelga es indefinida, ¿qué tipo de tácticas han empleado para mantener la participación colectiva y la presión? 




Estamos en la calle constantemente, concentraciones, manifestaciones, performances, asambleas y ocupando el espacio suficiente como para que los medios se hagan eco de nuestras reivindicaciones. 




Es importante que toda la ciudadanía nos vea y nos escuche para que sean conscientes de la realidad de las aulas. En cuanto son conscientes de ella, se unen a la lucha, como mencioné con los estudiantes y sus familias.




Esta huelga tiene lugar bajo el gobierno progresista de Pedro Sánchez, del Partido Socialista Obrero Español (PSOE). ¿Cómo ha respondido el gobierno de Sánchez ante la huelga?




El pasado 5 de octubre el presidente del Gobierno convocó elecciones generales en España, por lo que está huelga ha entrado dentro de su campaña electoral. No les ha quedado otra que mostrar su apoyo a las docentes madrileñas. 




Sin embargo, en los 8 años que el PSOE lleva gobernando en España, no han hecho nada por mejorar las condiciones del profesorado ni del alumnado. Desde el gobierno se limpian las manos y argumentan que las competencias en Educación son de las Comunidades Autónomas pero el Ministerio de Educación y el Gobierno Central son responsables tanto de las condiciones de los trabajadores como de la educación de todos los españoles. 




Además, la Delegación de Gobierno, que pertenece y dirige al Gobierno central y que controla la Policía Nacional, no está dando explicaciones sobre las brutales cargas policiales que hemos sufrido, tanto los docentes como los alumnos, durante las manifestaciones y concentraciones de este último mes.




La huelga en la enseñanza pública coincide con un movimiento masivo en torno a la vivienda, tanto en Madrid como en otros lugares. ¿Hasta qué punto están vinculadas ambas luchas?




Menos Lectivas siempre ha estado muy unida con el Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid. Hace un año se empezó a desarrollar el protocolo “Sin vivienda no hay educación” en distintos institutos de la Comunidad de Madrid con el fin de que las familias y alumnado que tuviesen una situación de vivienda precaria o se fuesen a enfrentar a un desahucio supiesen cómo actuar y pudiésemos atajarlo no solo desde el sindicato sino también desde los centros educativos. 




Lo que refleja esta situación es que la socialdemocracia supeditada al neoliberalismo no está garantizando que los trabajadores tengan sus necesidades básicas cubiertas y este hecho está provocando una oleada de protestas y huelgas en toda Europa. España no es una excepción.. El maltrato de los servicios públicos, como educación o sanidad, y la mala gestión del problema de la vivienda en España están siendo el talón de Aquiles del “gobierno más progresista de la historia”.




¿Qué logros han obtenido ya gracias a la huelga y qué lecciones están surgiendo a medida que esta avanza?




En el momento en el que se hace esta entrevista, la consejera de educación de la Comunidad de Madrid se sigue negando a negociar con el comité de huelga. Llevamos ya más de dos semanas de huelga. 




Pero sabemos que hemos conseguido dotar de fuerza a las trabajadoras para luchar por una mejora en sus condiciones laborales. Hemos conseguido devolver el foco a las aulas y mostrar cuál es la realidad de la educación pública, mostrando que el gobierno de la Comunidad de Madrid no tiene ninguna intención de sostenerla. Hemos conseguido organizarnos y vamos a conseguir ganar. Esto no para.

author: Carlos Pérez
title: ‘This Isn’t Stopping’: A Rank-And-File Perspective on the Indefinite Strike for Public Education in Madrid
content:
Since October 14, teachers in Madrid, Spain, have been on an indefinite strike in defense of public education. After years of deteriorating conditions and systematic rank-and-file organizing, teachers have flooded the streets of Spain’s capital in a mass mobilization that has linked the fight for public education with the recent revolt around housing. 




The shared struggle for housing and public education in Spain is now heading toward a general strike on November 11 in the midst of a broader uprising spreading throughout Europe. 




Carlos Pérez, a North Carolina high school social studies teacher and Labor Notes board member, spoke with María, a secondary school teacher of history and geography in Madrid and a member of 

Menos Lectivas

 (a group whose name means “Fewer Teaching Hours”), one of the leading rank-and-file forces behind the strike. 




Pérez: Public school teachers in Madrid have been on an indefinite strike since October 14. What are the main issues that drove you and other teachers to call for a strike and what are your demands?




María:

 In the Community of Madrid, we have been dealing with cuts to public education since 2011. These have led to the deterioration of classroom conditions and the quality of education for students in the region.




A lack of resources and staff, high student-to-teacher ratios, an increase in direct teaching hours, and a failure to maintain or build necessary infrastructure have created a situation where teaching has become extremely difficult. We, as educators, are unable to adequately attend to all our students, and we have decided to take a stand against the institutional mistreatment that both we and our students are subjected to. 




In my case, I’ve taught high school classes with 33 students; I had to find a classroom to accommodate my students every day for a month of heavy rain because the classrooms had leaks that kept them constantly wet; my students with special educational needs (autism or hearing and speech difficulties) were not supported by the necessary professionals because there was neither a social integration specialist nor a teacher specifically assigned to them; and of course, I work an enormous amount of unpaid and unrecognized overtime.




This is why we are demanding that the Community of Madrid reduce the number of instructional hours; lower the teacher-to-student ratios; end segregation, given that the Community of Madrid is the most segregated region in Spain in terms of education; increase salaries to bring them in line with current economic needs; and reduce bureaucracy, among other things.




Menos Lectivas

, a rank-and-file formation that includes several unions, has been a driving force behind the strike. What is Menos Lectivas and what role has it played in the strike?




Menos Lectivas

 was founded in 2023, inspired by groups like Labor Notes in the United States, with the goal of organizing education workers from within their workplaces and returning union power to the workers themselves. Since then, we have built our movement through assemblies held at individual workplaces.




In the years leading up to the indefinite strike, we organized strikes, demonstrations, and rallies. These actions helped the movement grow and, crucially, provided us with the institutional legitimacy—both with the workers, who view us as a legitimate force for struggle because they feel part of it through our assemblies, and with other unions, the media, and ultimately the government—to decide how, when, and where we would fight for the right to education and for our own labor rights.




From the outset, we knew that an indefinite strike would be our ultimate tool for union struggle if our demands went unheeded by the Community of Madrid. Last June, it was decided in an assembly that we, the teachers, would launch an indefinite strike.




Given that these assemblies held clear legitimacy, the other unions that were not part of 

Menos Lectivas

 had no choice but to sit down with us on the Strike Committee to negotiate the establishment of a formal negotiating table and the terms of the strike.. This milestone is already a success; it has shifted power back into the hands of the workers, taking it out of the administrative offices.




How has the strike been received by students and their families?




Both families and students support our demands. Ultimately, they are the primary beneficiaries of the improvements we achieve. We feel very well supported by them, and they are an essential part of the struggle.




Organized students have also called for an indefinite strike, acting through various political parties and organizations such as the 

Sindicato de Estudiantes

 (Students’ Union) and the 

Organización Estudiantil Socialista

 (Socialist Student Organization). They are present at all our street actions and play a significant role in the struggle for education.




Families, meanwhile, are organizing themselves into associations, both within individual educational institutions and across neighborhoods, and are helping to support strike funds. They have also organized a demonstration of their own to show the Minister of Education that this struggle is not limited to teachers, but also involves families.




Given that the strike is indefinite, what kind of tactics have you all used to maintain collective participation and pressure?




We are constantly out in the streets—holding rallies, demonstrations, performances, and assemblies—occupying enough space to ensure that the media takes note of our demands.




It is important for the public to see and hear us, so that they become aware of the reality inside our classrooms. Once they are aware of it, they join the struggle, as I mentioned with students and their families..




This strike is taking place under the progressive government of Pedro Sanchez from the Spanish Socialist Workers Party (

Partido Socialista Obrero Español

, PSOE). How has Sánchez’s government responded to the strike?




On October 5, the Prime Minister called for general elections in Spain, meaning this strike has now become part of an electoral campaign. They had no choice but to express their support for the teachers in Madrid.




However, throughout the eight years that the PSOE has been in power in Spain, they have done nothing to improve conditions for either teaching staff or students. The government washes its hands of the matter, arguing that jurisdiction over education lies with the Autonomous Communities; yet, the Ministry of Education and the central government remain responsible for both the working conditions of staff and the education of all Spaniards.




Also, the Government Delegation—which is part of and directed by the central government, and which oversees the National Police—has offered no explanation for the brutal police crackdowns that both teachers and students have endured during the demonstrations and rallies held over the past month.




The strike in public education is taking place during a mass uprising around housing in and beyond Madrid. To what extent have these two struggles been linked?




Menos Lectivas

 has always maintained a close relationship with the Madrid Tenants’ Union (

Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid

). A year ago, a shared plan titled “No Housing, No Education” was launched in various secondary schools across the Community of Madrid. Its purpose was to ensure that families and students facing precarious housing situations or the threat of eviction would know how to respond, allowing us to address these issues not only through the union but also in our schools.




This situation reveals that social democracy, subordinated to neoliberalism, is failing to ensure that workers’ basic needs are met, which is fueling a wave of protests and strikes across Europe. Spain is no exception.. The neglect of public services, such as education and health care, combined with the mismanagement of the housing crisis in Spain, has become the Achilles' heel of what has been described as the “most progressive government in history.”




What gains have you already seen from the strike and what lessons are already emerging as the strike advances?




At the time of this interview, the Madrid regional government’s Minister of Education continues to refuse to negotiate with the strike committee. We are now more than two weeks into the strike.




Yet, we know that we have succeeded in giving strength to the workers in their fight for better working conditions. We have managed to shift the focus back to the classrooms and reveal the reality of public education, demonstrating that the Madrid regional government has no intention of supporting education. We have succeeded in organizing ourselves and we are going to win. This isn’t stopping.

author: Lovin Kobusingye
title: Africa Can’t Build a Blue Economy Without the Women Who Bring Its Fish to Market
content:
Before dawn, wherever Africa has a coast or a lake, women wait on the shore for the boats. When the catch lands, our work begins. We smoke, dry, salt or ferment the fish, using skills passed down for generations, and carry it to market. We are more than a quarter of the 

12.3 million people

 who work in Africa’s fisheries, and 

58 percent

 of its fish processors.




In July, African ministers meeting in Luanda promised women, youth and local communities at least 

40 percent representation

 in blue economy advisory bodies and financing programmes. The African Union Commission has been tasked with drafting the roadmap to deliver it. Unless that roadmap names women fish processors and traders, and removes the rules that keep us from credit, the promise will pass us by.







 




Many countries still count fisheries only by what happens in the water, so the millions of women who process and trade the catch barely register. But if you are invisible, you receive invisible budgets, invisible investments and invisible policies.




I am one of these women. I run a fish-processing business in Uganda, where our lakes yield more than half a million tonnes of fish a year, more than any other African country’s inland waters. I also represent a network of women fish processors and traders across 46 African countries, and though we are proud of the work we do, we know we can do even more.




We feed our children with the day’s catch. We keep our culture and cuisine alive in the markets, from the sun-dried mukene of Uganda’s lakes to Senegal’s ceebu jën. And we are the first to notice when fish grow smaller, the waters turn muddy or catches suddenly fall.







Massive fishing vessels and bottom trawlers from around the world are scooping up fish off our coasts, and illegal fishing alone may cost West Africa 

up to $9.4 billion a year

. The 

UN Food and Agriculture Organization

projects that if emissions stay high and climate change continues to escalate, most African countries will lose fish this century, with the steepest losses in tropical waters like ours. Inland, pollution, mining runoff and dams threaten our lakes. Along the coasts, mangroves are shrinking, leaving fewer places for fish to breed.




This matters far beyond the shore. Africa has only 

9.1 kilograms of fish

 per person a year, less than half the world average, and 

supply must grow 67 percent

 by 2050 just to match the population growth.




But where we have a say, we can reverse the damage. In The Gambia, women oyster harvesters of the 

TRY Oyster Women’s Association

 won exclusive rights to manage their fishery in 2012, a first for a women’s group in Africa. They restored mangroves and introduced an eight-month seasonal closure, protecting both breeding grounds and the coastline. 

Ghana’s Densu Delta oyster pickers

 copied the model and have managed their fishery the same way since 2020. If we have more of a say, we can replicate these successes.




We have the solutions. Estimates of the catch lost after landing in African small-scale fisheries commonly run from 

15 to 50 percent

. 

On Lake Victoria

, simple raised drying racks have cut those losses by about 15 percent, and solar tent dryers by about 25 percent.




These fixes are cheap, but they still need capital. 

Africa’s blue economy

 already generates close to $300 billion a year, and money is flowing into ports, fishing technology and offshore wind. Little of it reaches the women who process and trade fish. That is the blue economy’s missing piece.







Leaders must break down one of the biggest barriers women face when seeking credit: land titles. Banks ask for them, and few women fish processors have them, because land in many of our communities passes through men. Lenders call that risk. We call it a rule written without us. Our savings groups lend and repay every day; lenders could accept group guarantees, stored stock or mobile-money records instead of title deeds.




The 

Luanda Declaration

 offers a path, but its 40 percent target for representation is shared among women, youth and local communities. It could be met without a single woman who smokes or sells fish. The roadmap must name women fish processors and traders as a distinct group, ensure that access to the national blue funds promised by 2027 is not dependent on land titles, and count us, by sex, in the new blue economy accounts across the entire value chain. By the Declaration’s mid-term review in 2028, ministers should be able to say how many of us those funds have reached. AWFISHNET’s chapters stand ready to help map who to count and co-design fund eligibility.




From sardinella and anchovies in West Africa to Nile perch and tilapia in Lake Victoria to sardine and hake in South Africa, the fish are there, and so are the women who know them best. Treat us as partners and invest in us, and Africa gains allies for conservation, nutrition and prosperity at once.







The post 

Africa Can’t Build a Blue Economy Without the Women Who Bring Its Fish to Market

 appeared first on 

African Arguments

.

author: Randi Beers
title: Expect office, road closures Wednesday for Remembrance Day
content:
Parts of downtown Iqaluit will be closed to traffic Wednesday morning to allow for a Remembrance Day ceremony and march to take place.




The closures will affect parts of Sivumugiaq Street and Mivvik Street starting at 9:30 a.m. until approximately 12 p.m., the City of Iqaluit announced Monday in a public service announcement.




“The closure is necessary to ensure the safety of participants and the public while the march is underway,” said the announcement.




The march, which starts at the RCMP detachment and ends at the cadet hall, is scheduled to start at 10:30 a.m.




Remembrance Day ceremonies are also planned in Rankin Inlet at the Singiituq Complex, from 10:30 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. and Cambridge Bay’s community hall at 10:30.




Government offices across the territory will also be closed to mark the day.




Remembrance Day is observed every year on Nov. 11 to honour armed forces members who have died in the line of duty.

author: Roderick Long
title: C4SS Panelists on the Intellectual Legacy of Don Lavoie
content:
There will be a Molinari/C4SS presence at the 10th annual PPE Society meeting, 12-14 November 2026, at the Westin New Orleans (100 Iberville St.).













I’ve organised a panel on “The Intellectual Legacy of Don Lavoie.” We’re in the very first session of the conference: Thursday, 12 November 2026, 9:00-10:30 a.m. (Central time) in River Room II.













The panel features Cory Massimino (C4SS) on “National Economic Planning: What is Right?” and Nathan Goodman (Mercatus; co-authoring with Molly Rovinski and Karla Segovia) on “Immigration Restrictions as Non-Comprehensive Planning.” Zak Woodman was also scheduled to speak at the panel, on “Ratcheting Up State Power: The Knowledge Problem, the Power Problem, and Legibility,” but will probably not be able to make it.













(This is not to be confused with the panel on the same topic at last month’s Mercatus Markets & Society conference, organised by Nathan Goodman and featuring Jason Byas, Akiva Malamet, and again Cory Massimino.)













Jason Byas, currently in his first year as Assistant Professor in Philosophy and Political Economy at Tulane, is also on the program; he’ll be speaking in a panel on “Anarchism as a Practical Philosophy,” Friday, 13 November 2026, 9:00-10:30 a.m. (Central time) in the Salon Room. Jason’s fellow panelists are Jesse Spafford, Jessica Flanigan, and Billy Christmas.

author: Administrador
title: DI COSA SI TRATTA. COSA SÌ E COSA NO
content:
Attenzione a chi accompagna le Familias Buscadoras:

A.- Abbiamo rilevato una serie di confusioni, affermazioni infondate e tentativi di manipolazione riguardo agli obiettivi, alle date, ai luoghi e alle attività della delegazione della Commissione Sexta Zapatista per questi mesi di dicembre e per la prima settimana di gennaio del 2027.

Si parla e si diffondono notizie errate su un presunto incontro nazionale tra le famiglie delle persone scomparse, Familias Buscadoras, e la delegazione zapatista presso la cosiddetta “Glorieta de los Desaparecidos” il 6 dicembre, nonché su altre attività pubbliche della Commissione Sexta Zapatista in altri luoghi e in altre date.

Questo non è vero, compagne e sorelle buscadoras. Forse chi si riunisce in quel luogo o in altri, considerandoli punti di riferimento per la propria giusta lotta, terrà davvero un incontro, ma noi non vi parteciperemo.

Non solo perché “l’invito” che abbiamo ricevuto da loro denota ignoranza, malafede e maleducazione. Non si invita nessuno insultandolo. A tempo debito ne parleremo più approfonditamente. Ma anche perché non partecipiamo a raduni di massa con le familias buscadoras.

I gruppi, i collettivi e le familias buscadoras che si riuniscono nelle piazze o in qualsiasi altro luogo, possono incontrarci IN PRIVATO, gruppo per gruppo, presso la sede della delegazione a Città del Messico e nelle sedi che saranno rese note, registrandosi tramite il Frayba, nella data e nell’ora che preferiscono, se lo desiderano.

B.- Sentite, sia voi che noi, i popoli zapatisti, sappiamo che esistono non solo differenze, ma anche vere e proprie rivalità e controversie, persino tra i collettivi delle buscadoras, tra le reti e i movimenti. Si arriva persino a cercare di porre il veto su certi collettivi e a decidere chi può e chi non può incontrare la delegazione zapatista. Forse è per questo che cresce il numero delle familias buscadoras che non fanno parte di nessun gruppo o collettivo e che ci contattano direttamente.

Non vogliamo giudicare nessuno. Non vogliamo dire quale strategia sia giusta o sbagliata, quale sia legittima e quale no, quale sia buona e quale cattiva.

Riteniamo che chiunque cerchi la verità e la giustizia e abbia l’obiettivo di ritrovare la persona cara scomparsa a causa di una sparizione forzata possa e debba percorrere tutte le strade e bussare a tutte le porte per alleviare il proprio dolore.

Sia che conducano ricerche sul campo con piccone e pala; sia che si rivolgano alle autorità giudiziarie locali, statali e federali; sia che vogliano incontrare il capo dell’esecutivo federale o la sua piramide di funzionari; sia che organizzino campagne internazionali e nazionali; sia che riescano solo ad affiggere le foto dei loro cari scomparsi nelle strade e nei quartieri; sia che si rivolgano alle organizzazioni non governative per i diritti umani; sia che richiedano il sostegno di specialisti nella ricerca delle persone scomparse e nell’analisi dei resti umani; sia che ricorrano a marce, comizi, sit-in, occupazioni di edifici e blocchi di strade e autostrade; sia che preghino; sia che si lancino maledizioni; sia che si faccia tutto quanto sopra.

E sempre con la memoria come motore.

Qualunque cosa decidiate e facciate, è una decisione che spetta a voi, a coloro che portano quel dolore e provano quell’angoscia, e a nessun altro.

Quindi non vi diremo cosa fare né lo faremo al posto vostro. Vogliamo conoscervi, ascoltarvi, abbracciarvi.

Né intendiamo dire quale rete o gruppo sia migliore dell’altro.

C.- Per questo motivo il nostro percorso non privilegia né manifestazioni di massa, né eventi mediatici, né assemblee generali, né la creazione di alleanze, fronti o iniziative simili, né una nuova organizzazione che riunisca o includa tutti i collettivi e le familias buscadoras, o parte di essi.

Non discuteremo né dibatteremo nemmeno sul numero delle persone scomparse, che siano 135 mila o di più o di meno, perché quelle cifre hanno un nome, una storia, una tragedia, un dolore e un dovere: quello di cercare chi si ama, chi manca e, non di rado, chi è sangue del proprio sangue.

D.- L’obiettivo principale di questa iniziativa è quello di ascoltare ogni famiglia o gruppo di familias buscadoras che desideri raccontarci la propria storia e, soprattutto, la storia della persona scomparsa.

Perché noi abbiamo visto e ascoltato il loro cammino, i loro sforzi, i loro sacrifici, il loro non arrendersi nella ricerca, il loro non svendere il loro caro assente, il loro non cedere nella memoria.

E vi chiediamo: se lo desiderate, se ne avete la possibilità e se ritenete che ciò possa aiutarvi nel vostro eroico lavoro, raccontateci questa storia.

E.- Finora, gli unici eventi pubblici a cui parteciperemo come delegazione zapatista sono:

– 19 dicembre. Sede della Sección 9 CNTE. 10:00 am. Con i membri del Coordinamento Nazionale dei Lavoratori dell’Istruzione. E quello che faremo sarà chiedere loro di aiutarci a diffondere i volantini di ricerca in tutte le scuole in cui lavorano, in tutto il Paese. E di coinvolgere altre insegnanti, anche se non fanno parte della CNTE.

– Lo stesso sabato 19 dicembre, nel pomeriggio, la marcia “Tutte le lotte e una richiesta comune: verità e giustizia per chi non c’è più”. In quell’occasione chiederemo alle organizzazioni sociali, ai movimenti, ai partiti politici non istituzionali, alle organizzazioni studentesche, ai sindacati, alle ONG, ai gruppi, ai collettivi, agli artisti, agli studenti, agli insegnanti, alle lavoratrici, agli autisti, alle famiglie e ai singoli cittadini, che, pur rimanendo fedeli a se stessi e senza rinunciare alle loro lotte e rivendicazioni, sostengano la diffusione delle schede di ricerca e delle denunce dei movimenti per la giustizia e la verità riguardo alle morti non naturali e alle incarcerazioni ingiuste di persone di ogni età, colore, razza e ceto sociale.

In sintesi, chiediamo a tutte, a tutti e a todoas di unirsi alla ricerca della verità e della giustizia.

F.- Partiamo quindi con l’intento di far sì che l’intero Paese si unisca alla vostra lotta. Trasformare il Messico in una geografia dotata di memoria, in una geografia che cerca incessantemente, in ogni angolo.

Dalle montagne del Sudest Messicano.

author: Anita Wadhwani
title: After Elections, CoreCivic Urges ICE to “Move Quickly” on Finalizing Contracts
content:
The company netted $1.3 billion in its most recent quarter from the sales of four immigration jails to DHS.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The CEO of Brentwood-based CoreCivic is urging Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials to act with speed in inking contracts for immigration detention centers after Democrats scored big wins in last week’s elections.

“We would urge the ICE administration to move quickly,” President and CEO Lucibeth Mayberry said during a quarterly earnings call on Thursday. “They have a need for capacity. We have the capacity. There’s no reason to wait.”

The private prison and immigration detention center operator netted $1.3 billion in its most recent quarter from the sales of four detention centers to the Department of Homeland Security as the second Trump administration ramped up immigrant detentions nationwide. The sales helped bolster the publicly-traded company’s better-than-predicted profits in the third quarter of this year.

Mayberry said the company is hoping to sell more.

“We continue to have discussions with ICE about the potential acquisition of additional CoreCivic detention facilities,” she said, noting the discussions remain preliminary. “However, we do believe additional facility acquisitions continue to be a key element of ICE’s detention strategy.”

Historic Democratic victories on Nov. 3 could put a damper on future ICE deals after members of the newly-elected Democratic majority in the U.S. House and Senate are sworn into office in January. Democratic candidates across the country campaigned on reining in controversial ICE enforcement tactics that have led to unprecedented numbers of immigrants being detained.

Democrats have pledged scrutiny, investigations and accountability for ICE’s enforcement tactics, which have resulted in tens of thousands of immigrants with no criminal backgrounds held in detention centers, the arrests of U.S. citizens and the deaths of two Americans.

CoreCivic has drawn scrutiny for its own role in the administration’s immigration crackdown, with reports about poor and unsafe conditions at its detention centers and new questions about its sales.

A recent investigation by a Minneapolis television news station showed CoreCivic offered to sell a shuttered prison in Appleton, Minn. to the State of Minnesota for $75 million in 2025. A year later, ICE paid $485.6 million for the facility, which is to be used as an immigration detention center. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison has called for a Congressional investigation into the sale.

ICE, however, remains the highest-funded law enforcement agency in the nation, boosted over the past two years by more than $240 billion in appropriations to the agency and the U.S. Border Patrol by a GOP-controlled Congress. President Donald Trump, in the days since his party suffered big losses in the election, has offered mixed signals about plans for the agency going forward.

Trump on Sunday said his administration’s aggressive detention deportation policy may have been “too tough” and contributed to the GOP election losses during an interview with “60 Minutes” on Sunday. However, the president also promoted the architect of his immigration policy, Stephen Miller, as his Chief of Staff. And key administration leaders have signaled the administration will stay the course on its immigration detention and deportation plans.

“Deportations will continue,” Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin wrote on X a day after the midterm elections.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $50,000 in the next 9 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Julia Conley
title: In Letter, 600,000-Member Machinists Union Urges Schumer to Step Aside
content:
The “elections sent a clear message: Working people are demanding change,” wrote IAM Union’s international president.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s bid to continue leading the Democratic Party when it takes control of the US Senate in January continued to falter Monday night as a key machinists’ union asked the New York senator to step aside and allow “a new generation to lead Senate Democrats.”

In a letter, Brian Bryant, international president of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM Union) thanked Schumer for “many years of leadership, friendship, and unwavering commitment to working people” before telling him that “after thoughtful discussions,” the IAM Union Executive Council had opted not to support Schumer’s push to remain as the Senate leader.

“With the utmost respect and appreciation for your service, we respectfully urge you not to seek another term as Senate Democratic leader,” Bryant wrote. “We also encourage all returning and newly elected Democratic senators to join together through a fair and open process to select a consensus leader who can unite the party, build on your legacy and carry forward a bold vision for working people.”

Schumer losing support of unions now. Big development. https://t.co/dvG1MNMefz

The letter came hours after Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) told reporters that he was considering a challenge to Schumer, after initially saying he was not interested in running for the Senate majority leader post following the party’s electoral sweep last week.

Candidates who won Senate seats include several outspoken proponents of Medicare for All, such as Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.), Troy Jackson (D-Maine), and Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.), and others who centered in their campaigns the need to decisively take on billionaires and worsening economic inequality.

A decision by Schumer to step aside in favor of “new leadership,” said Bryant, would allow the party to “turn this moment into lasting progress.”

He wrote that the party must push to pass the Protecting the Right to Organize (PRO) Act, restore collective bargaining rights to all federal workers, reinstate Affordable Care Act and give “every American the healthcare they need, and pass ”meaningful rail safety legislation.“

“Our country is at a critical crossroads and a moment of extraordinary opportunity. This week’s elections sent a clear message: Working people are demanding change,” said Bryant. “The IAM Union’s Workers vs. Billionaires movement reflects a growing desire for an economy and political system that puts working families ahead of wealthy special interests. We have a tremendous opportunity to build on this momentum, but doing so will require fresh ideas, new energy, and a new generation of leadership.”

Bryant’s message made clear that “it’s time” for Schumer to step aside, said author and commentator Don Winslow.

“The Democratic Party will make a catastrophic mistake if they lock out all of these voters for a man who has been in political office for 51 years,” said Winslow.

The letter came after Schumer’s support among senior Democrats appeared to crack on Monday, with Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) telling reporters, “We need a conversation about leadership going forward because we need new energy and ideas.”

But later that evening, the senator said that he expected Schumer to become Senate majority leader and plans to back him.

Van Hollen, who has reportedly received a steady stream of phone calls since last week from voters calling on him to take the helm of the party in the Senate, reiterated Monday evening that he believes there should be “a full caucus discussion” about the path forward.

BREAKING: Senator Chris Van Hollen is now considering a run against Chuck Schumer for the Senate’s next Majority Leader. This is amazing. Voters want generational change. Let’s give it to them. pic.twitter.com/xS5LuykauM

“I am in listening mode,” he said of the possibility that he could challenge Schumer. “There are clearly lots of people around the country and a number of our members, quite a few of our members, who want to have this discussion… I haven’t closed the door.”

He also told Semafor: “I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, but in particular to new members who have just come off the campaign trail. So what I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation.”

Van Hollen also met Monday with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who has not endorsed Schumer.

On Monday afternoon, Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), who is also facing calls from newly elected progressive lawmakers to step aside in his push to become House speaker, released a statement saying that “Democrats are united and ready to lead.”

But several representatives-elect, including Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) and Adam Hamawy (D-NJ) suggested that even if Jeffries secures the top post in the House, he will have to contend with many new members of Congress who will be pushing for far-reaching action.

“It’s about the agenda, an agenda that actually reflects the priorities of the American people,” said Kiros. “We might have different ideas about how to accomplish certain things but we all agree that we have to reduce costs for working families, we all agree that we have to root out corruption in government, we all agree that our foreign policy has to reflect our values. And in order for us to be able to do that we need an agenda that’s bold enough to meet that vision. And so what we’re demanding is an agenda, it’s not about the individual.”

“We, as progressives, want to build,” she added. “We want to accomplish things, we want to work together with this caucus to actually get work done, and we haven’t had that conversation yet.”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $50,000 in the next 9 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.
