author: Agência Mural
title: Construção: filhos de pedreiros que migraram para São Paulo buscam novas profissões
content:
Antônio Pedro de Lima, 54, e Naldo José Leite Lima, 50, têm algumas coisas em comum. Moradores de 

Paraisópolis

, na zona sul de São Paulo, os dois chegaram à capital vindos do Nordeste em busca de trabalho e de uma vida melhor.




Começaram na construção civil como ajudantes de pedreiro, não concluíram o ensino fundamental e passaram boa parte da vida em uma profissão marcada pelo esforço físico. Ambos também são pais: Naldo tem três filhos e Antônio, quatro. Nenhum dos filhos, porém, quis seguir o mesmo caminho profissional.




A diferença está nas oportunidades. Quando chegaram a São Paulo, Antônio e Naldo encontraram na construção civil uma das poucas possibilidades de trabalho. Os filhos cresceram com acesso à educação, cursos e projetos sociais que ampliaram as opções de profissão.
















Breno ao lado do pai, Antônio, que trabalhou na construção civil para sustentar a família




O tema virou polêmica este ano, quando um empresário da construção civil reclamou da 

falta de mão de obra

.




Antônio veio de Murici, em Alagoas, em 1994, aos 22 anos. Chegou à cidade com uma promessa de trabalho que o irmão havia conseguido para ele. Na República, região central, começou fazendo manutenção em um hotel, lixando paredes e pintando. Depois, foi trabalhar em 

Itaquera

 como ajudante de pedreiro. Foi ali que aprendeu o ofício que marcaria sua trajetória.










 




Com seis meses eu já sabia de muita coisa. Foi quando comecei a pegar esses conhecimentos e a levantar minha casa em Paraisópolis”




Antônio

 

pedreiro

 










Foi com o trabalho de pedreiro que Antônio sustentou os quatro filhos, entre eles Breno Tenório, 26, publicitário. Ainda criança, Breno percebia os efeitos da rotina do pai.




“Quando a gente é criança, não consegue traduzir muito essas coisas. Mas sempre senti a ausência dele em casa. Via meu pai chegando cansado e via meu pai saindo de madrugada, ainda escuro. Eu pensava: ‘Imagina como é difícil sair de casa às quatro ou cinco da manhã’”, lembra o publicitário.




A mesma realidade atravessou a trajetória de Naldo. Paraibano, ele chegou a São Paulo em 1995, aos 19 anos, para trabalhar na construção civil, em um emprego conseguido por primos. Iniciou a jornada como ajudante e aprendeu o ofício na prática. Foram mais de dez anos dedicados às obras, período em que também aprendeu pintura, encanamento e elétrica.
















Gustavo Lira e o pai, Naldo, que trabalhou como pedreiro e atualmente é eletricista




“Quando comecei, não entendia de nada, mas fui aprendendo como ajudante. Era muito puxado. Porque a maioria das pessoas que vieram do Nordeste na minha época não tinha serviço além de coisas pesadas. Lá também é pesado o serviço, só que era diferente. Era agricultura, na roça”, relembra.




Durante os anos de obra, tijolos, concreto, pedras e sacos de materiais fizeram parte da rotina.










 




Carreguei muito tijolo, concreto, encher laje na mão. Você carrega pedra, carrega cimento, saco de 50 quilos praticamente. Não é fácil, exige muito do corpo da gente”




Naldo

 

eletricista

 










O filho, Gustavo Lira, 26, diretor de fotografia, cresceu vendo os efeitos dessa rotina.




“Meu pai chegava cansado, só tinha tempo de tomar banho, jantar e dormir para acordar cedo de novo. Durante anos, sempre vivi essa cena”, compartilha o jovem.




Outros caminhos




Breno acompanhou o pai levantar cada cômodo da casa da família. Mesmo assim, nunca se interessou pelo ofício. Quando criança, chegou a ajudar algumas vezes a carregar tijolos, mas logo corria para longe do trabalho pesado.




“Sempre corri, nunca quis ficar carregando peso não”, recorda, aos risos, enquanto conversa com o pai.




Com o tempo, Breno passou a enxergar que a escolha profissional também estava ligada às oportunidades que cada geração teve. Para ele, trabalhos essenciais para o funcionamento das cidades continuam concentrados entre populações mais pobres e migrantes, enquanto outros grupos têm mais possibilidades de escolha.
















Breno, publicitário, afirma que busca oferecer uma vida melhor ao pai




Ele encontrou outro caminho por meio da educação. Antes de chegar à faculdade de publicidade, participou de cursos gratuitos de teatro e informática e de diferentes projetos sociais, que considera fundamentais para ampliar suas oportunidades.




Hoje, formado e trabalhando na comunicação, olha para a trajetória do pai, que continua atuando de forma autônoma na construção civil. Antônio teve carteira assinada apenas uma vez, em 1999. Para Breno, o custo desse trabalho não pode ser medido apenas pelo salário.




“E qual que é o lucro que a gente gera disso? Sendo que, em paralelo, a gente perde tempo com a nossa família, perde qualidade de vida”, afirma.




Gustavo tem uma percepção semelhante. Ele diz não conhecer jovens de sua geração que desejem seguir a profissão do pai e atribui essa escolha, em parte, ao que viu dentro de casa.




“Acompanhando meu pai, hoje vejo ele com problemas na coluna, dores. Ele paga com a saúde dele a troco de pouco salário recebido. O valor pago não paga a situação que ele se encontra hoje”, comenta.
















Gustavo, diretor de fotografia trabalha com cinema e sonha em aposentar o pai




Assim como Breno, Gustavo participou de cursos e projetos sociais ainda adolescente. As oportunidades ajudaram a construir a trajetória na direção de fotografia e, para ele, foram fundamentais para encontrar uma opção de carreira diferente da do pai.




As marcas do trabalho




A construção civil deixou marcas no corpo dos dois. Naldo hoje trabalha como eletricista, função que aprendeu durante os anos nas obras. A experiência permitiu que desenvolvesse conhecimentos em pintura, encanamento e elétrica e encontrasse outros ramos de trabalho. As dores, porém, permaneceram.




“Sinto uma dor no joelho, para dobrar, para subir uma escada, e na lombar das costas, imagino que seja por ter carregado tanto peso nesses anos todos”, comenta.




A mudança de profissão também não eliminou o esforço físico. Como eletricista, ele continua carregando materiais, cabos e montando estruturas.




No caso de Antônio, os problemas também estão relacionados aos anos nas obras. A exposição constante à poeira, segundo ele, afetou os pulmões. Em exames, chegou a identificar uma mancha escura que precisou de acompanhamento médico.




Ele também carrega as marcas de acidentes de trabalho. Em um deles, estava sobre um andaime quando a estrutura desabou. Cerca de três metros e meio de blocos caíram sobre ele. Antônio sofreu ferimentos nas costas e na cabeça, levou doze pontos e ainda carrega as marcas do acidente.




A coluna também se tornou uma das principais fontes de dor. Depois de passar horas agachado para colocar cerâmicas, ele diz sentir os efeitos do esforço físico.




Profissionais da construção civil estão desaparecendo?




Os dados do Novo Caged, do Ministério do Trabalho e Emprego, mostram uma mudança no perfil do mercado da construção civil em São Paulo.




As vagas de entrada, como ajudante de obras civis, tiveram saldo positivo de 1.878 postos em 2025. Já as funções especializadas, que exigem anos de experiência prática, perderam 1.895 postos.




Entre os trabalhadores de estruturas de alvenaria — categoria que reúne a função de pedreiro propriamente dita — o saldo foi negativo em 739 vagas. Profissionais de acabamento também terminaram o ano no negativo, com 141 postos a menos.







Uma escolha que os pais desejavam




Para Antônio e Naldo, a redução no número de jovens interessados em seguir a construção civil não é necessariamente um problema. É também o resultado de uma geração que passou a ter oportunidades que eles próprios não tiveram.




“Hoje os jovens não querem ser pedreiros porque têm muitas possibilidades de estudo, né? E é pesado esse trabalho. No meu tempo eu fui porque não tinha a oportunidade de estudar, mas eles estão certos de estudar e querer outros rumos”, afirma Antônio.




Naldo compartilha da mesma visão. Ele diz que nunca quis que os filhos precisassem enfrentar a rotina que marcou sua trajetória.







“Eu nunca tive intenção de que eles trabalhassem com isso, porque é difícil. Sempre tentei dar o melhor para eles, mas preferi que estudassem, porque não tive estudo e sofri muito por isso. Ser sem estudo aqui em São Paulo era complicado. Ainda é.”




Breno, porém, vê a própria trajetória como algo que também traz responsabilidade. Em eventos, viagens ou restaurantes, muitas vezes pensa que o pai passou a vida trabalhando para construir coisas para outras pessoas e talvez nunca tenha tido acesso a muitas dessas experiências.




“Não quero vencer sozinho. Acho que o meu maior sonho é conseguir proporcionar para os meus pais coisas que eles não tiveram oportunidade de viver. Não porque eles peçam isso, mas porque sinto que eles merecem.”




Gustavo também começou cedo a pensar em como ajudar a família. Ainda criança, percebia as dificuldades financeiras e evitava aumentar os gastos dos pais.




“Sempre entendi a pobreza desde pequeno. Quando era pequeno, não pedia dinheiro para os meus pais, porque sabia que eles não tinham. Catei latinha porque queria ter minha grana.”




Hoje, com uma profissão construída a partir das oportunidades que encontrou fora da construção civil, ele tem um objetivo que considera um dos maiores sonhos: conseguir proporcionar uma aposentadoria ao pai.




“Um dos meus sonhos é poder proporcionar uma aposentadoria para o meu pai, para que ele não precise se matar de trabalhar. Quero poder dar uma vida digna para ele, para que aproveite o resto da vida, possa descansar, porque ele começou a trabalhar muito cedo.”

author: Trevor Ngwane
title: African Labour and Liberation
content:
African Labour and Liberation

 brings together the experiences of workers, trade unions and labour movements across the continent to ask what they can tell us about work, power and liberation today. We assembled this collection because of the surprisingly few recent accounts of the emergence of a class politics on the continent. Labour is central to understanding the present political economy of Africa.  More than 90 percent of Africa’s 500 million workers work in informal and precarious jobs in a labour force that will grow rapidly in the next three decades.




The social and political mobilization of workers in multifarious contexts across the continent is imperative to improving their socio-economic conditions. It is necessary to situate Africa’s workers at the centre. This collection starts from the premise that labour struggles are essential to improving the conditions of work and stamping out poverty and inequality that confront most African workers today and form the basis for building new forms of collective power.




This heterodox collec­tion finds six primary patterns prevalent in the struggle for working-class liberation in the post-independence era.




1. Most governments in Africa are comprador-bureaucratic regimes beholden to foreign capital and imperialists’ interests to protect and maintain unequal exchange of trade and the attenuation of demands by the masses for national control over natural resources and production. Comprador-bureaucratic regimes remain loyal to their post-colonial powers and pay fleeting attention to national sustainability, the rights of women, natu­ral ecology, and the ever-growing needs of the masses for health care, education, housing, infrastructure, water, and electricity.




Government legislation to defend popular interests that have been enacted by national assemblies are rarely fully implemented and are likely to be opposed by international banks and lenders, predominantly from the West through structural adjustment programs that undermine evanescent attempts to ameliorate the most significant challenges.




2. Diverse workers’ movements form to resist t the comprador-bureaucratic political economies which formed in the colonial era which most often extract surplus value from workers and natural resources from the continent  through what  Arghiri Emmanuel  identified as 

unequal exchange of trade

, and despoiling, and plundering African nations. Control is maintained by local elites attached to state power who are beneficiaries of rentier capitalism. These national elites have welcomed Western powers to establish military bases osten­sibly to establish peace and order.




In most instances, the emergence of violence and disorder were generated by Western military intervention. However, as Samir Amin shows, workers and peasants drive the enduring imperative for the formation of national projects for popular sovereignty, which are often imperfect and challenged by imperialists seeking to maintain the unequal exchange of trade.




3. African states are ruled by comprador state-centric bureaucratic elites who maintain rentier capitalism as the primary source of revenue rather than investing in productive technology. The historical pattern is opposition to the redistribution of wealth and income to the masses.




This process, in which bureaucratic elements seek to transform themselves – sometimes successful sometimes not, but nearly always drawing links to imperial­ism and thereby fusing the bureaucratic and comprador elements – can be seen nearly everywhere. Unquestionably, compliant and often corrupt political elites provide the patina of legitimacy for all practical purposes, for the expansion of inequality.




4. In Africa, racial justice must include an anti-imperialist per­spective which acknowledges the legacy of European colonialism and the protracted nature of imperialism which sustains racial subordina­tion. Markedly, South Africa, a semi-peripheral mineral-rich state, did not redistribute wealth and property with the end of political apartheid and the development of a superficially democratic state. Black South Africans, composing over 80 percent of the country’s 65 million popu­lation, remain marginalized through the 1994 accords, which did not include a redistribution of wealth and resources – causing higher levels of poverty and inequality and impeding the working class from improv­ing its living standards.




5. Women constitute a large proportion of the African labour force, while also being disproportionately concentrated in precarious and insecure forms of work. Their labour is central to the reproduction of the economy, both through their participation in vital productive sectors and through forms of unpaid and underpaid labour that sustain households and communities.




Two women selling okpa at the Eke Awka Market in Awka, Anambra State, Nigeria (Wikimedia Commons, 2026)




This is particularly significant on a continent where, despite rapid urbanisation, more than half of the population continues to live in rural areas. Women are central to subsistence production and food sovereignty, while their role as primary caregivers places them at the centre of social reproduction. Any account of labour and liberation must therefore attend not only to women’s position within waged employment, but also to the often invisible labour through which they reproduce life, sustain communities and secure livelihoods.




6. The rural and urban economy, which is dominated by precarious employment, is also produced and amplified by climate uncertainty primarily instigated by Western consumption. A formula for social justice must include eco-socialist perspectives, ecological concerns and the extent to which these have been and are addressed by African labour movements. We attach importance to trade unions as sites of radical democracy and decolonial politics.




However, there is also significant invention and development that has taken place within African trade unions in different times and places that must be accentuated. We believe that trade unions and working-class organisa­tions must be tested, from case to case, rather than asserted, because of the proliferation of African trade unions which have developed forms of organisations and struggle that are necessary, novel, innovative and effective.




Taken together, enduring patterns of labour resistance demonstrate the enduring centrality of workers and popular movements to struggles for political and economic transformation and anti-imperialism. The histories gathered in 

African Labour and Liberation

 show that labour is not only understood simply through the workplace or trade union but must be situated within the anti-imperialist contestation over natural resources and the unceasing struggle to achieve, genuine popular sovereignty.




Concomitantly, these histories reveal that existing workers’ organisations on the continent are not uniform or even the vehicle for advancing the interests of the masses who are living under informal and precarious conditions. Across contexts, workers and their class allies have developed distinct modes of organising, resisting and building collective power.




African Labour and Liberation

 foregrounds histories of differentiated movements that resist enduring forms of domination and lay the groundwork for new terrains of conflict in opposition to internal oppression and imperialist domination. Far from being peripheral to the history of labour, they are central to understanding how working people have confronted exploitation and sought to reshape the societies in which they live.




–




This article was first published by 

ROAPE

.




The post 

African Labour and Liberation

 first appeared on 

The Elephant

.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Makabayan rejects Trump’s visit; Bayan condemns Imeldific welcome for US president
content:
The Makabayan Coalition filed a resolution at the House of Representatives (HOR) opposing US President Donald Trump’s visit to the Philippines to attend the upcoming 2026 ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations) Summit.




The anti-imperialist bloc filed House Resolution No. 1593 on Tuesday “expressing the sense of the [HOR] to oppose the welcoming of…Trump” who they said is expected to sign the Pax Silica Initiative, “among other lopsided agreements between the US and the Philippines.”




House Assistant Minority Leader and Kabataan Partylist Rep. Atty. Renee Co said: “A convicted warmongering racist, rapist, pedophile loser should not at all be welcome to step foot on our lands.”




“The American people have themselves rejected Trump. Why should we be forced to accept him here? This administration has no reason to welcome the primary imperialist oppressor of our nation,” Co said.




Co added that because of Trump, hundreds of thousands of people are being killed in various countries and oil prices are skyrocketing worldwide, including the Philippines. Because of Trump, the Filipino people are suffering even more under the mounting burdens he has imposed, she said.




Makabayan condemned Philippine government’s “all-out on spending and preparations” for Trump’s visit.




Imeldific welcome




Meanwhile, Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) condemned Ferdinand Marcos Jr. government’s “Imeldific” cleanup drive to hide poverty from foreigners during the ASEAN summit.




Bayan said government’s cosmetic “cleanup drive” to drive out street vendors and urban poor residents from areas where ASEAN Summit dignitaries will pass through is a whitewash meant to hide the Filipino people’s deepening poverty.




“No amount of fresh paint, swept sidewalks, or hidden human beings can erase the hunger, joblessness, and misery that this government has failed to address,” Bayan said.




“We condemn the Marcos Jr. administration’s shameless attempt to prettify Manila for the cameras of foreign leaders while the poor are treated as eyesores to be swept away. The poverty of the people cannot be hidden by a cleanup drive,” the group added.




Bayan secretary general Raymond Palatino called on affected vendors and the urban poor to join the protest actions being organized for Trump’s visit. # 

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

author: Jordan Humphreys
title: The “two souls” of the Spanish general strike
content:
A 24-hour general strike is set to take place across the Spanish state on 11 November, sparked by recent struggles over housing. In the lead-up to the general strike, 

Red Flag

’s 

Jordan Humphreys

 spoke to Germán 

P. Montañés

, a member of the revolutionary organisation Anticapitalistas, about the unfolding situation.

Red Flag

:

 Rising rents and house prices are affecting people across the globe. Why has it become such a flashpoint in the Spanish state in particular? What is the housing situation like there?

Germán

 

P. Montañés:

 Housing in the Spanish state has been a structural problem for a long time. One of the most visible impacts of the 2008 financial crisis was a wave of mortgage evictions. Today, mortgage-related evictions are less common, but renting has become much more widespread.

Even so, renting remains less common in Spain than in cities like Berlin or New York, where tenant voting blocs have played a major political role. In Spain, home ownership is the norm even among much of the working class. This stems from a strategy popularised during the dictatorship—echoing Margaret Thatcher’s later policies in the UK—summarised by a government minister’s famous quote: “I want a country of homeowners, not proletarians”. This high level of home ownership has somewhat cushioned the crisis; without it, the social situation likely would have collapsed much sooner.

Still, the crisis remains severe for two main groups: young people, who are locked out of home ownership and forced to pay exorbitant rents; and low-income workers and migrants, who face the worst housing instability.

The modern housing movement began around 2008 with anti-eviction campaigns such as the Plataforma de Afectados por la Hipoteca (PAH). Later, tenants’ unions emerged from these struggles—founded in 2017 in hubs like Madrid and Barcelona, and expanding across the Spanish state over the past few years.

A major tipping point occurred in late September, when police evicted 87-year-old María del Carmen (Maricarmen) Abascal from her home in Madrid. She had lived there for nearly 50 years under a rent-controlled agreement, but after an investment fund bought the building, her rent drastically increased. On the fourth attempt, police successfully removed her. This high-profile eviction sparked widespread outrage across the country. In response to the growing public backlash, the prime minister brought the general elections forward to 29 November.

RF

: 

Could you give us a better idea about the tenants’ unions—what kind of organisations are they, and what relationship do they have with the revolutionary left?

GPM:

 The emergence of tenant unions reflects the limits of the previous housing movement, which focused almost exclusively on stopping evictions. The problem with focusing on evictions is that the movement arrives far too late: by the time a family is facing removal, the police are already at the door.

The founding principle of the tenants’ unions was to adapt the most effective elements of trade unions to housing—arriving early to conflicts and organising people sooner. Rather than a diffuse social movement, housing activism needed a formal union. Members pay a monthly contribution, providing a financial base that allows staff to work full time and maintains an ongoing presence.

They also drew heavily on US labour tactics, focusing on entire buildings or properties owned by the same investment fund or landlord family to intervene long before eviction day.

They’ve been very successful recently in Madrid. Around September, they had about 2,000 to 3,000 members, and over the last two months of conflict, that number doubled to roughly 6,000. To clarify: these are financial members, not dedicated militants—there are perhaps 100 to 150 core militants—but the growth is significant.

The mainstream political left has no militant presence inside these spaces and does not control them; it tries to exert influence from the outside through government institutions and political pressure.

The revolutionary left isn’t broadly present either, though our organisation is the only one with a real foothold inside the unions. Our influence extends beyond raw numbers: we’ve maintained a dialogue with the union leadership for ten years. While the leaders come from autonomist or anarchist traditions, key militants in leadership positions allow us to maintain a solid presence. Our goal is to build a revolutionary current inside the tenants’ unions to counter progressive institutional pressure and steer them toward radical goals.

RF

: 

One of the most striking aspects of the housing protests has been the encampments, particularly in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol. What role did these camps play in the struggle?

GPM:

 Encampments are a very common tactic in Spain—from university encampments for Palestine to the current housing actions.

The recent encampment was crucial because it sustained momentum and provided a long-term vision. A single demonstration after Maricarmen’s eviction would have fizzled out. Of course, encampments bring challenges—you know when to start one, but never when to end it, and coordinating unorganised individuals can be tricky. But it sustained the movement.

This encampment differed significantly from the 2011 

Indignados

 occupation in Puerta del Sol, which was driven by an anti-political sentiment—the belief that being explicitly left-leaning or bringing party banners would alienate the public.

In contrast, this new encampment was structured and managed by militant organisations—primarily the tenants’ unions, alongside our organisation and others from the revolutionary left. Not only were political organisations present, but there was a collective consensus that we 

should

 be there. Today, growing the movement relies on maintaining clear, radical demands rather than moderating them (though as anti-capitalists, we don't always agree with the tenants’ union’s direction or negotiations with the government).

RF

: 

Why do you think that shift away from 2011’s “anti-politics” occurred?

Germán:

 A few factors contributed. First, political organisations like ours have consistently shown up in strikes, social movements, and local struggles, earning respect through active participation over time. Second, the tenants’ unions led the encampment with a framework that respects political organisations and shares space with them. Finally, public perception is different because we aren't a parliamentary party—if we held seats in parliament, people might have viewed our presence very differently.

RF

: 

It seems like people were raising the need for a general strike early on?

GPM:

 Tenants’ unions have been demanding a housing general strike from the major trade unions for two or three years because rising buying and rental prices demand it—prices that have only increased under eight years of progressive governments.

The major trade unions traditionally focus on social peace, class collaboration, and tripartite negotiations with the government and employer associations. They were never going to call a general strike against a progressive government—they refused to do so for eight years. So why agree to it now?

The push toward this general strike essentially has two “souls”:

The first is radical, stemming from widespread disappointment with the progressive government’s housing policies and the strategic leadership of the tenants’ unions.

The second soul belongs to the two major trade unions, who believe they can leverage this strike in two ways. Firstly, they see an electoral advantage. They want to help the progressive government win the upcoming elections by co-opting the movement’s momentum, claiming housing reforms failed only because parliament is controlled by the right. That argument lands because it’s partially true—parliament is right-leaning now. However, six years ago when the progressive coalition took power with a left-leaning majority, it also failed to act. The Socialist Party is an institutional party, and real estate capital—developers, mortgage lenders, and banks—is a pillar of Spanish capitalism that the Socialist Party will not touch.

Secondly, the major unions recognise that a right-wing or far-right coalition is the most likely outcome of the November elections. Expecting attacks on organised labour, they are using the strike to reposition themselves as defenders of working-class rights and rebuild public trust.

Given these competing motivations, it remains uncertain how committed the major unions are to executing the strike. One of the two major federations has historical ties to the communist movement, and its militants are actively organising on the ground, while the other may have called the strike on paper without intending to mobilise.

As anti-capitalists, we believe this strike has real potential. Less than 20 percent of the working class in Spain is unionised, so we may not shut down every factory. But we can disrupt normal commercial life across the country.

Political events can serve reformists and revolutionaries simultaneously. A battle for leadership is taking place inside the strike movement between reformist and revolutionary tendencies, and we intend to win it. While the strike’s core demands are too radical for the progressive government to adopt, strengthening our organisations and the tenants’ unions through this strike represents a win regardless of the election outcome.

Finally, a crucial aspect of this strike is that it has been called jointly by all trade unions across the Spanish state. While the two major unions—CCOO (Workers’ Commissions) and UGT (General Union of Workers)—dominate regions like Madrid, Andalusia, and Castile, independent nationalist unions lead in Catalonia, Galicia, and the Basque Country. Usually, nationalist unions schedule strikes on separate dates. In this case, every single union has called for the strike on the exact same day, which is remarkably rare.

title: Un message
content:
Un cinétract de Nasri Sayegh & Mama Ganuush

« Leurs prisons ne sont pas assez grandes pour accueillir tous les insurgé.es de ce pays. »

Version sous-titrée en français d’un court métrage documentaire qui donne la parole aux personnes palestiniennes queer en exil.

Un film de Nasri Sayegh & Mama Ganuush Production : TheHalaCollective.com Durée : 5:18

Plus d’information sur mamaganuush.com

Par Sarah Kilani et Thomas Moreau

Must We Lie to Please the Critics?

Social Conditions and Character.

Anarchists, Wise and Otherwise.

We find ourselves in a world of conflicting ideas, and every person who has individuality enough developed to be more, in human life, than a domestic animal or lifeless machine, must align himself with others who hold the same opinions, whether he will or not, and then he is in the view of others, and perhaps in his own view, labeled with the name of the idea he holds. So we find that nearly every person is labeled, and some persons have a number of labels.

Finding that we must be something—must hold to certain ideas and work for certain ends—if we work at all, or amount to any more in human life than an ox, or an ax, it very naturally follows that we will adopt and work for the prevalence of such ideas as will bring us the greatest happiness, now or bye and bye. That is why I am an Anarchist. I am convinced that to work for the realization of the Anarchist ideal will bring me more satisfaction than an adherence to, or working for, any other ideal would bring me.

But every one should be able and willing to give a reason for the “faith that is within him,” and I will try and do so.

I find myself in a world of sunshine and shade; of joy and sorrow; of happiness and woe. All around me I see fellow beings; beings that are constituted very much as I am, have similar desires, hopes and aspirations. I find that they are constantly trying to gratify these desires; to realize their hopes and attain to that for which they aspire. I find further that they can do these things only by exploiting inorganic nature, and by assisting each other. I find that as things are now, these beings instead of mutually assisting each other are constantly striving to injure each other, not because they take delight in the suffering of a fellow, but because they see no other way of satisfying their desires and aspirations. They think this state of affairs wrong, and are constantly clamoring for a change, but have not yet learned the great fundamental fact of human solidarity—of our interdependence.

Long have the various members of the human family sought to adjust themselves to environment, and of late have begun to endeavor to adjust the environment to suit themselves. All mankind craves for freedom, but most of the people have sought to gain freedom by subjugating others, or by restricting all alike. They have not learned that they cannot be free while they are holding others, or while they seek to restrict the freedom of others. No one desires to be injured, and yet no one can be secure from injury as long as he injures others. We all wish to be free from injury. I crave for freedom. I see that others want the same condition, and I know that my freedom can be made secure only by the freedom of all others. I know of no other ideal but Anarchy that, if really would secure freedom to me and to all others, therefore I am an Anarchist.

I long for plenty; for a sufficiency of the material necessities of life to make it possible for me to satisfy all my physical cravings, and I know that all others want the same thing. I see that the Earth yields abundantly; that it is possible for human beings to produce all the material necessities required to satisfy their physical cravings, and that if they would stop restricting and interfering with each other and turn their attention to production and mutual assistance, they could have every material comfort they desire. Anarchy is the only theory that, if put into practice, would secure this abundance and at the same time secure full liberty. Consequently I am an Anarchist.

I love my fellows, some of them at least, and pity those who suffer. I desire association with my fellow humans, and crave their friendship. I have a horror of violence and of the shedding of blood. I find that, as a rule, the other members of the human family are influenced by the same emotions, and I see that these emotions are warped and stifled by the conditions by which we are surrounded. I realize that Anarchy would be a condition that would tend to develop these emotions, and to eliminate the emotions of hatred, revenge, jealousy and envy, by disuse: That in Anarchy association would rest upon mutual attraction, that all such hindering barriers as class distinction, rank, title or wealth would not exist, and so I am an Anarchist.

I love the beautiful. It gives me joy to see gorgeous sunsets, towering mountains, picturesque scenes. It increases my happiness to see bright cheery faces, happy people and comfort. I take great delight in works of art, in poetry and music. I do not enjoy these things alone. I wish to share my joy with others. As things are today the ability to enjoy these things is crowded or crushed out of most people, and I must have my enjoyment of them constantly marred by the lonesomeness I feel when trying to communicate my joy to those I love, or with whom I associate. I know that many who have great artistic power; who could add much to the world’s stock of art, poetry and music, are prevented from so doing by the hard necessities that surround them, and I see that Anarchy would remove the stifling conditions that kill the appreciation of the beautiful and prevent the development of the artistic. I am, for these reasons, an Anarchist.

All this and much more goes to make up the reasons for my adherence to, and advocacy of Anarchy.

Again the anniversary of the Paris Commune is approaching. All around the world, wherever modern industrialism has gone, this anniversary will be celebrated. Much has been written concerning this great popular uprising, most of which has been of a derogatory character, but some truthful and commendary.

The uprising of the people of Paris against official corruption, in time of siege and general distress, is one of the brightest pages in the history of France, and has been a source of encouragement to the oppressed of every country. The lover of liberty, and the admirer of heroism and devotion may never weary of contemplating and discoursing on the events of the Commune, and the personalities of those who figured most conspicuously in it. How grand a relief to the stinking and cowardly action of the rulers of France, was that splendid uprising of the “common herd,” when they swept the city clean of “boodle politicians,” and found themselves free.

How it shocked the thrones of Europe and sent a thrill of hope through the minds of the down-trodden of every nation. Ah, how near to the realization of the dream of all ages it came. Ever had the people prayed for deliverance from bondage, and from the domination of oppressors. Always hopeful of what the future would bring forth, they had watched and waited for deliverance, and now, oh glorious reality, freedom had triumphed in Paris—the people of Paris were free. Were they incapable of appreciating their freedom? Did they feel like a fish out of water or a bird that longs for its cage? Nay, they enjoyed their freedom; they were happy. They flung themselves into the new form of life with a will and the spectacle of women and children, as well as men, walking abroad at all hours of the day and night, unprotected by police or other “minions of the law,” and with no reason to fear, no robbery or other acts of violence occurring, was seen for the first and only time in history. Strange as it may seem, contradictory as it is to all authoritarian assertions to the contrary, Paris, during the Commune was absolutely without all those acts that the law is said to be made to prevent. Although besieged from without, violence was unknown within, and no community containing as many persons ever before or since existing that was as full of happiness and security.

But some men were foolish enough to think that all this must be made “legal.” That “administration” was necessary. A “Committee of Public Safety” was elected, and it assumed the right to manage the affairs of the Commune. In other words, a government was established. Then trouble began within, and the foe without found it easier to force an entrance into that city. That was their great mistake. What need had they of legal sanction or “administration?” Had they not just shaken off the oppression of law and its administration? But the habit of thinking that some law was necessary was too strong, and while the majority were enjoying their newly gained freedom, the minority were unwittingly preparing a deadfall that would eventually engulf them all.

How alarmed the “powers that be,” in the other nations were is shown by the fact that the Austrian government sent troops over to assist the French army in re-capturing the city, and the German army that had marched on to Paris and captured it from its governmental defenders, was held at Sedan in readiness to assist the French troops if need be. In fact every indication is that every government in Europe would willingly and freely have rendered the French government aid, if they had dared, to crush out what at first bid fair to be the initial step toward the abolition of political domination of all kinds. But would they have dared? The International Workmens Association had its ramifications in every nation, and the attention of the down-trodden was directed to this, the first great attempt to gain real liberty, and it would have been dangerous for other governments to attempt such a thing, could the Commune have retained its original revolutionary character and have opened up communication with the outside world.

So the radicals every year find it of advantage to come together and discuss the glories of the Commune, and consider how best to avoid the mistakes made in ‘71, in the event that such another opportunity to shake off the shackles of oppression should ever again present itself. What governments will do in the name of “law and order” is shown by the unparalleled butchery that accompanied the re-capture of the city by the government troops. Calling the Communards wolves, they played the part of hyenas, aye, of demons. In the name of “order” the commanders of the government troops caused the most henious and bloody tragedy in the annals of history to be enacted, and the woe that they created has lasted even to this day, and it throws a dark shadow over the lives of many of the noblest and beset persons in Paris.

Oh, the lesson that is taught by the Paris Commune! Can you not see it? It shows all to clearly to those who can comprehend, that with the passing of government goes crime and insecurity, and that all attempts at legality, at legislation, are but toying with a deadly monster. Let all who desire liberty learn a lesson: Refrain from legislating; from obeying the command of a military commander; from participating in any of the functions of government, and no more will the promise of freedom realized, be thwarted by such mistakes as were made by the Paris Commune.

In a recent number of The Firebrand a correspondent says that I want “too much variety”. It is certainly true that every New-Idealist may be called “a varietist of the extremest type”, as he holds that to be able to enjoy at all times the best and most agreeable complement to his own complex nature he needs a great variety of human beings. How much variety (if any) in sexual enjoyments this would naturally involve is dependent upon the particular qualities of the individual, and in many cases, alas, it would probably include no sexual intercourse whatever. For some men it seems extremely hard to understand that love’s joys include many things besides the sexual embrace. As I am convinced that my critic, in writing the above, thought only and exclusively of variety of partners for coition and that the majority of the readers understood it thus, I reject his interpretation as false and misleading and consider it wise to offer an explanation.

I want the abolition of any and all sexual contracts and defy the world to show the least advantage in such a contract. I advocate freedom in love, i. e. real freedom which is never to be sacrificed to any contract or “relation”, nor to such a monstrously absurd ideal as the prevailing love-ideal. This is the theory “in a nutshell”. To test its value I, of course, had to take into consideration all the conditions which could reasonably be expected to result from its general acceptance. My studies soon convinced me that a natural and inevitable consequence would be “variety in the sex-life of almost every healthy human being”. Hence I had to figure with this and was highly pleased to find that we have no reason to dread this, that our objection to such variety is based upon nothing but rank superstition, that this conviction “is, in fact, far more cheering than if we had to suppose that for each of us there were in this wide world but one true sexual mate, but one being who could be considered a beautiful complement to our sex-nature.” When I had reached this stage in my “emancipation,” I felt justified in giving this advice: Be free in love and never barter away in any manner this your most precious, inalienable right! Whatever this may bring you to, never fear, you have everything to gain and nothing to lose thereby! I hope that at least the majority of my readers will be clear-headed enough to understand that this is by no means equivalent to advocating variety in sex-association as a good thing per se. And now I wish to say to my worthy critic: Don’t be scared! All that we “want” of you is that you obtain for yourself and retain forever the right to say to partner, friend and foe, to Mrs. Grundy, Church and State, to each and every one in fact: “None of your business” whenever you are asked, how, when, where, with whom, or with how many you enjoy sexual pleasures. You might be a perfect New-Idealist, and still, under certain circumstances, happen to have the same partner for all your sexual co-enjoyments. If, however, this latter condition is due to the fact that you cautiously guard against “outside attractions” because you consider such “exclusiveness” purer, nobler, better, or healthier, then you are yet too superstitious to be called a New-Idealist. And, furthermore, if you desire to label a woman as being reserved for your sexual pleasures—no matter whether the label is a legal one or not, whether it reads “for life” or for a limited time (i. e. “until mutual love ceases”),—then you are very far from being a New-Idealist, even if you should desire to thus label a full dozen, or if your sexual record should bear the names of a whole army of women.

Another correspondent of The Firebrand thinks that I am “not out of the woods yet,” because I believe in “an inviolable contract.” The word “inviolable” is hardly in order here as it suggests the idea of enforcement by state, society or community by means of brute power, a thing in which I certainly do not believe. Leave out this word and I promptly plead guilty. Yes, I am forced to still believe in some binding contracts as long as the present economical conditions prevail. My opponent is perfectly correct in saying that every such a contract is enslaving to some extent, but it is equally true that under existing conditions not to enter into such may enslave me still more. To illustrate: I enter into a binding contract through which I secure for myself a steady income. Without this or a similar contract I would be obliged to steal or beg for my daily bread. In which manner do I gain the greater freedom? Or, suppose a man craves for a home. At present he cannot expect to gain this except through a binding contract which may enslave him to quite an extent for life,—and yet, every one who enjoys the benefits of a real home will agree with me that this may gain for him so many other liberties (by means of the security which it affords) that even in this case the net result will be a gain in his personal freedom. I hope as fervently as my opponent does that we may some time reach such conditions that we will not be forced again and again to sacrifice one liberty in order to again another, but I must remind him of the fact that my book is to offer suggestions for immediate action and that, therefore, I had to reckon with things as they are (economically) and not with the things as they ought to be. I promptly admit that it would be a great deal nicer for us men, if the women would offer us the benefits of a beautiful home and the joys, rights and privileges of fathership without binding our freedom in any way, without asking of us the promise to perform a lot of duties for a term of years or for life, but, as things are, I yet feel obliged to advise the women to “believe in” a good solid contract, yes, to make it pretty nearly “inviolable” by an intimate association of interests. This latter forms far stronger and far more reliable ties than the legal law, yet, I would no more blame a woman for adding to them a legal contract than I would blame an Anarchist for making any other business agreement, a sale or a purchase for instance, a legal one.

Another remark of the correspondent has caused me a good hearty laugh. “That’s all rubbish! You can’t evade my supervision!”—that’s just what Mrs. Grundy will say too, but very soon she will find out that she has made a great big fool of herself, and that all her carefully compiled dates and figures (which seemed to show up the poor victim as a vertiable Messalina) are in fact absolutely valueless for the “control of the sex relations” of a New-Idealist. As to my assertions referring to our position towards the legal law. I will say that any intelligent lawyer of the U.S. will promptly concede that they are correct. I do not offer this article as an argument for my theory. My only object in writing it was to fully explain a few points alluded to by my critics. These allusions are so misleading that they might prejudice many against the book and induce others to buy it who would be disappointed in not finding therein what they had expected. I am receiving hundreds of letters expressing objections, doubts, fears etc. and pretty soon I intend to publish in The Firebrand some discussions and controversies on far more important and more interesting phases of the subject than those treated to-day.

I am much pleased with the way you have defended Samuel P. Putnam against his own people. I have not read the article, but was told by one who had, that The Freethinker’s Magazine published at Buffalo, N. Y., had an editorial speaking very derogatorily of Mr. Putnam, saying he was a free lover and a disgrace to the cause of Liberalism.

Mr. Putnam had his faults, but they were those of a lion and not of an ass, and when a living ass attacks a dead lion, the louder he brays the more sensible people stop their ears. I have listened to a great many speakers in my day, but never but to one in which the words seemed coming from a soulless shell. I thought it was my fault and spoke to a friend, a materialist, of the effect this same Buffalo editor’s lecture had upon me, and I found that he was similarly impressed. So much for personalities, and I only brought them in to introduce that question of all questions, the sex question. Until there is Freedom for the holder of the creatory there can be freedom nowhere else. Liberals make a great mistake when they defend church morality, for by so doing they are really the supporters of church power.

Sex is the source, or channel, through which all life—I repeat, all life—is made manifest, and as without life there can be no power, it follows that sex is the fountain of all power. As before, I repeat— sex is the fountain of all power. Here we can meet on common ground. It makes no difference whether we believe in one, two, or a dozen states of existence, whether we believe that “death ends all” or not, science demonstrates that the two factors of sex are at the root of all life, and science further demonstrates that the finer forces are the most powerful, and that there can be no action without an elimination of some portion of that which acts and is acted upon, a fine, often invisible but potent force. Now, please, reader, note every step in this demonstration—I was going to say argument, but it is more that—please mark every step and weigh carefully each statement, for I shall show that church power is rooted in sex, consequently those who assay to oppose the church and at the same time sustain the standard of church sex-morality are really sustainers of the church.

In order to find why the church opposes the open and honest investigation of sex, we notice first the fact that the church secures its adherents by appealing to the emotions instead of to the reasoning powers. Now, if we can find what relation the emotions sustain to sex, we may readily tell the why of the law that makes it dangerous to investigate sex outside of church theory.

A. C. Thompson, a Kentucky Legislator, gives us the key note to the relation of sex to religion in an article to be found in the July Arena for 1895. He says, in arguing what is called “The age of consent” law:

“It not infrequently happens that when the first dawnings of sexual appetite make their appearance this natural desire is, under proper instruction, changed in character and becomes an acquired psychical habitude, religious emotion. “For it is a fact, and one capable of easy demonstration, that there is a close relation between religious emotion and sexual desire, the natural desire and the acquired emotion taking the places one of another, on occasions unconsciously and without volitional effort on the part of those in whom the transformation takes place.”

What an admission is here! Religious emotion unnatural sex action! But this writer continues:

“The young girl yearning for she knows not what, will in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred find perfect satisfaction in religious emotion.”

What more can we ask to show that sex is the basis of religion? But remember, please, that wherever there is action there is waste, a something set free that corresponds to the nature of the action or emotion. It follows, then, that when sex desire is transformed into religious emotion that in the action upon the desire which so transforms it, there is, there must be set free a fine element, a sex-aura, and what becomes of it? Is it not appropriated by those who so control these emotions as to absorb the desire?

But sex is life. Sex-aura is life-aura, and those who appropriate it grow strong in psychic power. No wonder the priest sways the people! Emotion, transformed sex-desire, in connection with servile worship curses the worshiper by weakening his life force, and so long as the manes are thus held Freedom is impossible.

I cannot half elaborate this question in a newspaper article, but I have said enough to show the importance of the sex question in connection with that of Freedom, and I hold that those who defy the church sex-code from principle, and stand by their acts, are doing more to hasten the day of universal freedom than are any other class of people, because they thus set free creative elements that vitalize life’s currents, or atmosphere with the very essense, or soul of freedom, they create a mental soil in which Freedom can grow.

There is, there can be no question of more importance than the sex question, because all other questions are involved in that, and the so-called church opponent who sneers at “free love” don’t know what he is doing.

We are in need of two copies of “The Speeches before the Court,” to use as “copy,” as we wish to get out a new edition of them.

The uselessness of legislation was nicely illustrated by the failure of the Oregon Legislature to organize. The deputy City Attorney remarked to me that it was a good thing; that they would have past some fool laws, and that there are too many laws now.

The Oregon National Guard (State Militia) has not been called out—except last spring at time of the fishermen’s strike—nor used at all, in thirteen or fourteen years, but lots of money has been spent in keeping the organization up. Now that there has been no appropriation made for its benefit what will the captains do? Will they continue to command, without pay, or will they leave the State defenseless, to be ravished by its enemies? The truth is they know that they do not preserve order, and that the State would be just as tranquil without them, but it gratifies their vanity to be called captain, and it suits them very well to live such a life of ease, at good pay.

Morrison I. Swift sent us a circular letter, addressed to the unemployed, calling on them to make themselves conspicuous on inauguration day (March 4th), and for all who can to be in sight in Washington, D. C. It reached us too late to appear in The Firebrand before that date.

The Legislature of South Dakota refused to make any appropriation for the militia, and the Oregon Legislature failed to make any such appropriation because of its failure to organize. It remains to be seen how these two states get through two years without spending a lot of money on military displays.

How many radicals are there who wish to live a life a little more in harmony with their ideals? By this I mean how many want to realize a little of the freedom and fraternity we love to talk about, now, without waiting for the revolution or the judgement day.

It is possible, as The Firebrand publishers have demonstrated, to carry on an undertaking and make a success of it, without constitution, by-laws, rules of order or other supposed necessities of association.

It is a perfectly feasable proposition to undertake the carrying out of any object, or purpose, or the accomplishment of any task, or the conduct of an industry on a purely communistic basis. If undertaken by those who are mentally free, and anyway congenial, there is no good reason why the life attendent thereon should not be far more happy than the life of the average person in the ordinary struggle for bread.

Where co-operative homes are undertaken it is well to have persons of various occupations connected therewith. A shoemaker, a barber, a tailor, a dresmaker and so on, in such a community will always prove of great advantage even if farming is the chief industry.

Do you want better conditions? Greater freedom? Then do what you can to help get it. Merely wishing for it will do but little to bring it about. Can you awaken the same desire in another, that will do much to hasten its realization.

There is much to do, and much joy to be realized in “bringing the lost sheep into the fold;” in setting an example of fearless opposition to established customs; in sowing the seeds of Anarchy, of peace, love and plenty.

There are two ways to propagandise, one in opposition to existing conditions because they are hateful: in creating discontent and unrest from an iconoclastic standpoint. Another way of propagating Anarchy is by pointing out how much more comfortable and happy we could all be in Anarchy. How all our wants can be supplied, our artistic tastes and longing for the beautiful and grand gratified, and contrasting that with what exists now.

J. Allen Evans, corresponding secretary of the Liberty Co-operative Association, at Hutsburg, Tenn., writes: “We now have our own school for the colony children, and a few pupils from the outside attending. Mrs. Gerauld has been installed as teacher. Mr. F. L. Avery, who went away from the colony to visit friends and spend Christmas, has returned and says there is no place like home. Comrade Beck, who went back to Brooklyn, N. Y., on account of homesickness, writes that he is coming home for keeps, just as soon as he can earn enough money to pay his fare to Hutsburg. He is as homesick to get back to Liberty as he was to return to the place of his nativity. Any friends of co-operation who feel disposed may lend a helping hand to Liberty co-operators by sending them garden seeds or bulbs, vines, cuttings, etc. Such favors will be greatly appreciated by them. We want a good blacksmith who is tired of hunting for a boss. A good mechanic of this kind can find a congenial home with the Liberty Co-operators if he can comply with the terms of membership.”

“A rose would smell as sweet called by any other name.” Great William assures us. So, a court house ring would act the same, whether called democrat, republican or “Union Bimetallic party, formed regardless of former party affiliation.”—[Harney Co. News.

Why, then, brother News dont you throw the whole mess of political corruption overboard and make a clear unmistakable demand for freedom? The politicians act the same in office, no matter what party ellects them.

At the banquet given by the Sons of the American Revoluion, Mr. W. H. Chapin of this city said:

“We do need that spirit of our forefathers—that unselfish devotion to and loyalty for our country’s good. The country is running wild. Anarchy and Socialism go stalking through it rampant. Even Portland supports an out-and-out anarchistic paper, that is rapidly increasing in size and circulation. Politics are disreputable. Honorable men, let them once enter the field, and get the breath of office, and they stoop to things undreampt of before, so as to gain their ends. The country places in office the men with the longest purses. The day before election the papers on all sides urge their respectable following to go to the polls early so as to avoid the desperate characters that take possession later and frighten away the timid citizens who would vote if not too much trouble.”

This was said in the presence of a number of politicians, and has caused much comment, but none of them deny its truthfulness. It is too well known to be denied, and indicates the decay of patriotism. Commercialism knows no national bounderies, and the commercial spirit is dominant. Everything is for sale: office, honor, glory, fame, comfort, luxury, love.(?) Consequently the long purse wins. It is as useless to try to win for patriotism against commercialism as to try to turn the course of events backward. Patriotism must disappear, and universal fraternity appear before the evils complained of can be overcome.

J. T., Brazil, Ind.—We are sorry to say it, but you are the only reader of The Firebrand in your town. We hope you’ll get us some more.

B. G., New York City.—The books are sent now and you will have seen the reason of the delay in the last weeks issue.

C. S.,—We are receiving many encouraging letters, but that is surely not sufficient to keep The Firebrand eight pages. If it were not for you and a few other comrades, we would hardly have been able to cover the expenses. We trust, though, that the comrades will appreciate our efforts and assist s as much as possible and not leave the greatest burden to relatively few comrades. Many thanks!

R. T., New York City.—We are always willing to argue with individuals that are honest and fair, but when they are intentionally lying and knowingly misrepresent facts, as the editor of the Age of Thought does, we prefer to ignore them. On the other hand, we could not find anything in his paper that would be worthy of consideration. He is simply “committing a double-headed tapeworm every week,” as one reader of Age of Thought writes us. The fact is that Mr. Fulton is retrogressing steadily.

To find the HOME OF THE FIREBRAND take the Oregon City car at cor. First & Alder Sts., and ride out to Sellwood. Get off at Spokane Ave. Walk two blocks toward the river, then turn to the right and walk one block.
