author: David Swanson
title: Talk World Radio: How the Unprovoked War Was Provoked
content:
Russian aggression and any militarism should not be justified by any provocations. Russian leader, suppressing voices of dissent and antimilitarism, in a long multi-track conflict where tragic mistakes were made on all sides (background ignored in this conversation) decided to escalate by brutally invading Ukraine, killing thousands of innocent civilians, ruining and blackouting cities, not resorting to international courts or other mechanisms of pacific conflict resolution according to UN Charter, not building nonviolent action and nonmilitary peace protection institutions.

It is pity that alternative journalism, similarly to mainstream journalism, seek whom to blame instead of seeking peaceful solutions towards justice and reconciliation. Truth must be told, but in narrative of reconciliation: there were nasty CIA operations in response to nasty operations of Russian military intelligence, methods of both sides are wrong, it is wrong that some actors of Ukrainian independence movement partnered (rather than become stooges of) U.S. military intelligence, Nazi links of some Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. actors are outrageous, but there was also always the will of Ukrainian people and genuine grievances that matter much more than any covert operations attempting to ride the wave. As Kinzer recognizes, Ukrainians and the United States had many reasons to feel unsafe provoked by Russia, Soviet Union, Russian Empire. Responding in kind, they sustained the vicious circle of violence. But there is no truth about escalation ladder, mutual harm and mutual provocations, there is only blame of one side and no vision of reconciliation of rival stories and modus vivendi. In my view, it is not how you tell truth to achieve genuine peace.

Truth is that we need no corporations and tools of death and pain in Russia, in Ukraine, in United States, all peoples have a right to peace on common planet. People need to support each other seeking universal peace by nonmilitary means.

We need nonviolent interventionism of peace crowds everywhere in the world, protesting against war at Red Square and calling to protest against military dictatorship everywhere else, not stay aside when brutal dictator subjugates neighboring people and his own people out of imperialist ambitions. Violent mass arrests of youth in Moscow imposing military mobilization are disgusting, similarly to Ukrainian busification.

All civilians of the planet shall stay for peace together to get rid of all armies of NATO and CSTO, Russia and Ukraine, Israel and Palestine, United States and China. We need nonviolent governance of the world, representing all peaceful peoples, able to decide to disband all armies and make it happen by nonviolent action. Not recognizing this and continuing to debate who is guilty, who provoked whom where everyone provoke everyone, mean we allow great powers to generate endless wars by their rivalries and provocations. Ukrainian Helsinki Group, created to advocate human rights after the Helsinki Accords, sought democratic transformations, peaceful coexistence of independent democratic Ukraine and Russia, and nuclear disarmament. Members of the group were repressed, but they managed to send from Gulag an open letter to world leaders in 1980 saying: “The war of ideologies gives rise to a senseless arms race, so the disarmament of hearts and souls is necessary.” Let’s remember this call and disarm the world together.

author: CMI Argentina
title: La Justicia de Milei: Urgencias políticas detrás de los fiscales crédulos que defienden a quienes deberían acusar
content:
Adorni encontró un defensor en Pollicita, como los Milei en Taiano. La ausencia de un vocero, la recesión y el “todos contra todos” en Casa Rosada. Rodrigo Sbarra, el antecedente gemelo de otro funcionario que se enriqueció sin darse cuenta y fue comprendido por el mismo fiscal.




Javier Milei, Manuel Adorni, Eduardo Taiano y Gerardo Pollicita




Por Sebastián Lacunza




El reacomodamiento de las piezas en el edificio de Comodoro Py ejecutado este año por los Hermanos Milei aporta una novedad sustancial: fiscales federales argumentan como si fueran abogados defensores de las personas a las que deben investigar.




No importa que los planteos esgrimidos por los acusados sean un insulto a la inteligencia de tan absurdos. Los fiscales aceptan el argumentario con candidez ilimitada y procuran cerrar la causa. Una condición: los imputados deben orbitar en los planetas del mileísmo y el macrismo.




La diferencia que se huele en estos meses con respecto a los largos años de impunidad de los que goza el entorno político y económico de Mauricio Macri radica en la celeridad del proceso y la nitidez de un fiscal y/o un juez dispuestos a inmolarse con su firma.




En los tiempos de dominio plenipotenciario de la trama compuesta por el PRO, el Grupo Clarín y la SIDE, los tribunales penales federales de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires alternaron la técnica estelar del adormecimiento con un ida y vuelta más movidito entre juzgados e instancias superiores, cambios de radicación del expediente y otros ardides procesales.




De esa manera, transcurrieron años hasta gestar un sobreseimiento a hurtadillas cerca de Año Nuevo, un Mundial, o en un cambio de Gobierno, o simplemente se optó por dejar que el expediente languideciera en un cajón, sin morir del todo. Ejemplos emblemáticos de esto último son las causas del soterramiento del ferrocarril Sarmiento, que tiene a Ángelo Calcaterra como uno de los grandes beneficiados por decisiones tomadas por su primo y Cristina en Casa Rosada, o el presunto fraude cometido por Sociedades Macri (Socma) en la gestión privada del Correo Argentino. Ambos expedientes llevan una eternidad en el edificio de Comodoro Py, lo que motivó alguna precipitación ansiosa de Macri que le terminó jugando en contra para dar vuelta la página definitivamente.




El mecano de Juan Bautista




El dato clave de 2026 es la coronación de Juan Bautista Mahiques y Santiago Viola como números 1 y 2 del Ministerio de Justicia. Pocos despachos de Comodoro Py se resisten al llamado del primero, un artífice de la Mesa Judicial del macrismo y representante de una familia multiempleada en el fuero federal. Su amigo Viola, en tanto, sobrelleva un currículum de operaciones de Inteligencia, otro factor de empoderamiento en el edificio de Retiro. Ese dúo heredado del corazón del macrismo y entronizado por Karina Milei fue el motor de la reciente aprobación en el Senado del pliego de 180 jueces y fiscales, 

y va por más

. Esos nombramientos habilitaron un toma y daca de enorme eficiencia para negociar sentencias.




El mecano armado por Mahiques y Viola eliminó riesgos y acortó plazos. Así aparecieron los otrora lentísimos Marcelo Martínez de Giorgi (juez) y Eduardo Taiano (fiscal) para tratar de borrar de un plumazo la causa por la presunta criptoestafa $LIBRA. Primero, limpiaron a los damnificados como querellantes para actuar sin interferencias. Tras cartón, a fines de octubre, los anestesistas más letales de Comodoro Py sostuvieron que la criptomoneda fue una inversión de riesgo similar a una apuesta en un casino —no un mecanismo de financiamiento de las pymes, como propagandeó el Presidente en X—, y el cúmulo de indicios sobre 

la remuneración de USD5 millones

 y la 

coordinación entre la gavilla

 de los 

cryptobros

 y 

los Hermanos Milei

 fue simplemente desestimado, sin explicaciones. La posibilidad de reapertura de la causa vía la reincorporación de los querellantes y la intervención de la Procuraduría de Investigaciones Administrativas (Fiscalía Anticorrupción) pende de un hilo.




 El empresario Hayden Davis, junto al presidente Javier Milei, socios intelectuales de la cripto $LIBRA. NA




En pocas semanas, una sala de la Cámara Federal (Llorens, Bertuzzi, Yadarola) gatilló varios fallos con beneficiarios cantados (causa espionaje ilegal bajo Macri, deuda con el FMI de 2018, negocios personales de Luis Caputo, vínculo de una hermana de Caputo en el financiamiento de grupúsculos violentos de ultraderecha), pero el segundo gran acto de un fiscal que actúa como un defensor de quien debería ser investigado acaba de ser puesto en escena por Gerardo Pollicita en beneficio de Manuel Adorni.




Pollicita, como Taiano




Pollicita, como Taiano, tiene una carrera de cuatro décadas en tribunales, lo que le da un amplio conocimiento en diferentes terminales. Como Taiano, tiene vínculos orgánicos con el macrismo. Además de su amistad con Juan Bautista Mahiques (“son íntimos”, relatan en el edificio de Retiro), integró años atrás la comisión de Seguridad de Boca Juniors, el club que bajo las presidencias de Macri y Daniel Angelici actuó como hub de conexiones que se extendieron a Comodoro Py. A diferencia de Taiano, poseedor de un rayo adormecedor de las causas precisas, Pollicita asoma hiperactivo apenas toma un expediente. Los resultados, no obstante, no difieren demasiado.




En el dictamen emitido el viernes, el fiscal de la investigación por el presunto enriquecimiento de Adorni adoptó por entero la explicación de que el exjefe de Gabinete de Milei invirtió en criptomonedas entre 2014 y 2018, y ello le dio un rédito extraordinario, hasta llegar a US$565.000. La única prueba que aportó Adorni meses atrás —luego de múltiples dilaciones— fue que poseía las claves de ocho billeteras cripto, ya vacías de fondos. Dijo que esas mismas billeteras son las que manejó en sus años como supuesto inversor, pero no lo pudo probar, porque no eran nominales.




Pollicita razonó que, como tampoco cuenta con elementos para asegurar que Adorni no poseía las billeteras virtuales una década atrás, la aparición de los $565.000 suena hipotéticamente factible; por lo tanto, cae la imputación de enriquecimiento ilícito, y a lo sumo se lo podría acusar de evasor, un delito subsanable con una multa.




Dictámenes como los de Pollicita y Taiano deberían ser estudiados en las universidades por muchas décadas. Son fiscales, deben investigar. Cuando se encuentran con cabos sueltos (desde las acciones de la gavilla de $LIBRA en Casa Rosada a la incapacidad de Adorni de dar una explicación mínimamente verosímil de cómo le apareció medio millón de dólares), deciden que no configuran de por sí una prueba del delito y cierran el expediente. Sin imputación del fiscal, el margen del juez de ir en camino contrario es muy acotado.




La modalidad del investigador que se ata de pies y manos y finge demencia implicó que Pollicita no se cuestionara por qué Adorni vivió en un modesto edificio de Parque Chacabuco durante una década, si tenía US$565.000 en un placard; cómo fue que, con un pasar discreto y un sueldo como vendedor de autos en una concesionaria, decidió volcar sus magros ahorros a comprar criptomonedas a desconocidos, de quienes no pudo aportar ningún dato; ni qué llevó al matrimonio Adorni-Angeletti a desatar en 2024 y 2025 un frenesí de adquisiciones: un departamento en Caballito de mucho más nivel que aquel en el que vivía, una casa en un country y una camioneta. Tampoco se preguntó cómo la pareja pudo afrontar esas compras mientras gastaba de US$10.000 a US$20.000 mensuales y sumaba viajes frecuentes, cuyo costo triplicaba su ingreso declarado, y traslados en aviones privados, etcétera.




Los US$565.000 seguían en el placard y Adorni solicitaba préstamos con intereses. Avanzado 2026, ya se había desatado la indignación colectiva por los gastos exorbitantes de un funcionario que estigmatizaba a críticos y opositores muchas veces con datos falsos, y Adorni seguía aferrado a la mentira de sus declaraciones juradas. Hasta hizo concurrir a un desencajado Milei y a todo el gabinete a una sesión especial de la Cámara de Diputados para seguir mintiendo. Los US$565.000 se impacientaban para salir a aclarar las cosas, mientras Pollicita ordenaba allanamientos y se valía de cuanta escribana pintoresca apareciera frente a cámaras para ordenar más medidas.




 Javier Milei, durante el Tedeum en la Catedral Metropolitana, con un manuel Adorni en la cuerda floja, el 25 de mayo de 2026 Sebastián Hipperdinger – Europa Press 




El mordaz Adorni de antaño lucía atribulado, sin hilvanar una idea que no lo perjudicara. Las pantallas de TN, LN+ y A24, aliadas de las llamaradas del jefe de Gabinete hasta poco antes, se volvieron hostiles. Su abogado penalista, Matías Ledesma, causaba intriga en funcionarios judiciales, porque no atinaba a solicitar ninguna medida ni a formular preguntas mientras cada testigo que aparecía develaba otro set de mentiras de Manu.




Hasta que Adorni renunció a horas del comienzo del Mundial y Pollicita entró en modo Taiano: tres meses de siesta. Finalmente, a horas del comienzo de una visita papal, el fiscal suscribió un texto que parece más propio de un defensor que de un acusador.




Una persona con acceso al expediente ve tantas lagunas en la explicación de las billeteras cripto, que buscan algún resquicio para tratar de reanimar una investigación herida de muerte. Otra fuente clave de Comodoro Py recuerda que, en el delito de enriquecimiento ilícito, es el imputado quien debe demostrar cómo accedió a sus bienes, y que hay antecedentes de peso, como los casos de Carlos Menem y Julio de Vido, en los que, ante la inacción de un fiscal, intervino la Procuraduría de Investigaciones Administrativas. Ese organismo estuvo hasta ahora bastante raleado de la investigación de Pollicita, pero podría actuar.




El pasado del fiscal brinda un antecedente gemelo que permite entender su último movimiento.




El antecedente Sbarra




El 21 de enero de 2020, transcurridas apenas cinco semanas de la asunción de Alberto Fernández en Casa Rosada, una funcionaria del Ministerio de Desarrollo Productivo halló un sobre con US$10.000 en un cajón. Rodrigo Sbarra, exsecretario de Coordinación del Ministerio de Producción durante la Presidencia de Macri, había ocupado ese escritorio hasta el 10 de diciembre de 2019.




Sbarra fue funcionario de Economía durante los Gobiernos de Néstor y Cristina Kirchner, y en 2012 se cruzó a la vereda del PRO en la Ciudad de Buenos Aires. A partir de 2015, fue una pieza clave de Francisco Cabrera en el Ministerio de Desarrollo Productivo.




La denuncia del hallazgo del sobre que hizo la Oficina Anticorrupción, a cargo entonces de Félix Crous, recaló en la fiscalía de Pollicita. A los US$10.000 que Sbarra se había olvidado en el cajón en un sobre con membrete de Nordelta —casualmente, el mismo monto que costó el vuelo de Adorni a Punta del Este que disparó la sospecha de enriquecimiento ilícito, 

revelado por este diario

—, el fiscal le sumó la incongruencia del avance patrimonial de Sbarra. En el lapso que fue del inicio al fin del mandato presidencial de Macri, el patrimonio declarado por el olvidadizo funcionario creció de $1,1 millones a $30 millones, unas cinco veces medido en dólares. El progreso significó depósitos en el exterior y un Mini Cooper.




Pollicita pareció ir a fondo y le imputó a Sbarra lavado de dinero.




Rodrigo Sbarra, registrado en el sitio oficial de la maratón de Nueva York, el 1 de noviembre de 2026




Tras el impulso inicial, la causa entró en letargo. El 13 de diciembre de 2023, tres días después de la asunción de Milei, el fiscal dictaminó a favor del sobreseimiento de Sbarra. El crédulo Pollicita adujo que los US$10.000 hallados en un cajón podían estar relacionados con la venta de una propiedad heredada (tal como Adorni justificó parte del capital inicial que lo llevó a comprar criptomonedas hace más de diez años), y que el progreso patrimonial pudo suponer evasión impositiva, pero no enriquecimiento (igual que Adorni). El juez federal Julián Ercolini confirmó el sobreseimiento el mismo día.




Con cuarenta años, todo un pasado como funcionario y toda una fortuna por delante, Sbarra quedó rehabilitado para la función pública apenas asumió Milei y pasó a ser uno de los ex PRO legados a la gestión ultra.




Primero ocupó un puesto en la vicejefatura de Gabinete y luego, en julio de 2026, pasó a ser viceministro de Salud, la cartera de Mario Lugones, verdadera caja de cristal por su reconocida transparencia. Sbarra quedó a cargo de lo que era la Agencia Nacional de Discapacidad, dependencia disuelta luego de que su extitular Diego Spagnuolo describiera en un audio cómo Karina Milei y los Menem le habían puesto interventores “para afanar” y llevarse, todos juntos, un 8% en coimas. A Sbarra le toca la tarea de perfeccionar esa oficina.




En semanas complicadas para el Soez, jaqueado por la recesión y el riesgo país, Sbarra no pareció especialmente afligido. Voló a Nueva York para participar el domingo pasado de la Maratón de esa ciudad. Demoró 4 horas y veinte minutos en recorrer los 42 kilómetros, registró el usuario de X Bartolomerulli. El registro oficial de la maratón 

ratifica la información

. “Fue por las suyas. Partió el viernes y regresó el lunes”, dijeron en el Ministerio de Salud ante la consulta de este medio.




Con Sbarra, Pollicita demoró cuatro años entre el ímpetu inicial y el desistimiento de la acusación. Con Adorni, apenas seis meses.




La celeridad para limpiar los cargos más graves contra el exjefe de Gabinete es una señal de que los tiempos políticos son otros, tanto como el margen de acción. En $LIBRA, como con Adorni, los fiscales liquidaron el pleito sin siquiera formular una imputación, y mucho menos solicitar una indagatoria.




“Todos contra todos” y sin vocero




En el mismo momento en que Adorni recibía la primera buena noticia de un año aciago, un funcionario del ala karinista describía un cuadro lúgubre para La Libertad Avanza: “Antes, la pelea con Santiago (Caputo) de alguna manera ordenaba al Gobierno. Había quilombo, pero se avanzaba a algún lado. Ahora hay un todos contra todos; ni Karina, ni los Menem, ni Santiago manejan a su gente como lo hacían; se sumó el Colo (Diego Santilli), presiona el PRO”.




La mirada optimista sobre la ola que trajo a Milei y el desprecio por sus adversarios prevaleció por mucho tiempo en el mundo oficialista, pero ya no. “La economía se enquilombó bastante antes de lo pensado, y tenemos que afrontar esta situación sin vocero”, se lamentó el funcionario, conocedor al detalle del paisaje de Casa Rosada.




El razonamiento expone la convicción generalizada en el Ejecutivo de que Adorni era el portavoz que necesitaba Milei, así como el ninguneo que concita la figura de Adrián Ravier, su reemplazante en los papeles. “Como la designación de Ravier fue por decisión de Milei, no va a saltar por una interna. Javier no se banca las internas, pero si decidió él, mucho no se discute”, sintetiza.




El Presidente ya hizo pública su indecorosa conducta de celebrar sobreseimientos urdidos en Comodoro Py como si fueran reivindicaciones del honor personal y de los suyos. ¿Se verá nuevamente a Adorni con el traje de funcionario y sus corrosivos estiletazos más temprano que tarde?




El Gobierno necesita rearmarse. Un agobio económico cada vez más profundo ocupa el lugar de los “mejores 18 meses de la historia” prenunciados por Caputo, mientras Milei sigue subsumido en su espiral de groserías y violencia, que ya no prenden ni siquiera en sus huestes (salvo en los fans que acudieron a las clases magistrales en la Universidad Di Tella, las escuelas ORT y un par de templos evangélicos).




A la preocupación por esa realidad se suma la convicción en el Gobierno de que Patricia Bullrich inició un camino con el objetivo ya no de plantearle cara a Milei y competir, sino de lograr una rendición de los Hermanos.




Es un elemento que transita los pronósticos en el campo de la derecha, dentro y fuera del Gobierno. Cada vez más voces con peso se animan a elucubrar un escenario en el que Milei se retire en 2027, con el incentivo de hacerlo por las buenas, como un Presidente que, desprendido de ambiciones, deja la posta con algo de capital político, y no humillado por una derrota en una primaria o envuelto en una deriva violenta y autoritaria propia del político despectivo con la democracia que es.

title: Why Fewer People Are Challenging Bad Patents
content:
The number of petitions being filed at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) has collapsed. That’s not reason for celebration. The PTAB is an important line of defense against low-quality software patents being used in lawsuits against people and companies.

The drop didn’t happen because suddenly patents have become higher quality. It’s simply because USPTO leadership is increasingly refusing to consider good challenges to patents, for reasons unrelated to the merits. The process has become so unreliable that many would-be patent challengers aren’t even trying.

Inter partes review (IPR) is a process that allows people to challenge patents at the Patent Office, rather than having to fight an expensive lawsuit in federal court. It’s one of the most important ways to get bad patents out of the system.

In the third quarter of 2026, July through September, only 97 IPR petitions were filed at the PTAB, compared to 327 petitions during the same period in 2025. Similarly, only 37 IPR petitions were filed in September 2026, compared to 129 petitions in December 2024—the last full month before the current USPTO leadership began reshaping how the Board handles patent challenges.

This dramatic decline shouldn’t just concern patent lawyers. EFF has fought bad patents because so many software and internet patents make claims to the basic tools of free expression online, like sending email, using online ads, or publishing web pages. When bad patents go unchallenged, they affect everyone who cares about the freedom to write new code and make new technology.

That’s why EFF has defended IPR since it came on the scene more than a decade ago. It provides a faster and less expensive way to challenge patents that should never have been granted. Congress created IPRs because the Patent Office makes mistakes. District court litigation is an extraordinarily expensive way to correct them. Without a meaningful administrative review process, bad patents remain powerful weapons in the hands of patent trolls and others seeking to extract settlements from companies that often did nothing wrong.

Now, USPTO leadership is dismantling that safeguard.

Since Congress created the IPR patent challenge process in 2012, the PTAB has always had some discretion in deciding which petitions deserve review. But institution rates today are much lower than their typical historical range.

Between fiscal years 2022 and 2024, the PTAB instituted between 66% and 68% of IPR petitions. In fiscal year 2026, which concluded in September 2026, the institution rate fell to 41%. And institution is only the first step of an IPR—it means the PTAB has agreed to hear the challenge, not that the challenger won, and the patent will be invalidated.

That decline helps explain why fewer petitions are being filed in the first place. Preparing an IPR petition takes substantial time and money. While cheaper than federal court, it’s still a complicated administrative process. Before filing, a challenger typically needs to search for prior art, hire experts, and develop detailed technical and legal arguments about why the patent never should have been granted.

Companies were willing to pay for IPRs because, historically, they could expect a predictable process. Petitions that met the statutory standard generally had a reasonable prospect of being heard and decided on the merits. But the USPTO has made it harder to get petitions heard and is throwing them out for reasons that have nothing to do with the merits of the challenges. Faced with these odds, many potential challengers aren’t filing at all.

When the PTAB decides to hear an IPR case, that means the petition has been “instituted”—but that has never meant that the petitioner will definitely win. It means the PTAB has determined the challenge warrants a full merits review, and the parties could expect the proceeding to continue toward a final written decision. But under the current USPTO leadership, that expectation has disappeared. The PTAB’s institution decisions are being repeatedly vacated by the Director.

USPTO Director John Squires has vacated at least 29 decisions granting institution of IPR proceedings, and subsequently denied the petitions, terminating those proceedings before a final written decision. These include cases that PTAB judges had already agreed to hear, as well as proceedings that Squires himself had previously allowed to proceed. This level of retroactive intervention is unprecedented.

In some cases, the parties had already invested substantial time and money litigating before the PTAB, only to have the proceeding terminated based on new reasoning by the Director’s office that arose after institution.

For example, in Revvo Technologies v. Cerebrum Sensor Technologies, the Director vacated an institution decision and remanded the case to the Board. The Board then instituted review again, but the Director reversed that decision. Using a new approach, the Director said that the petition had inconsistencies between claim construction positions taken before the PTAB and in district court. Since then, that decision has been cited as a basis for terminating several other instituted proceedings.

The result is another layer of uncertainty for people who want to challenge bad patents. Getting through the front door of an institution decision is much harder than it used to be—and now, even getting through that door doesn’t mean the PTAB will decide your challenge. Predictability is one of the things that made IPRs work.

Congress created IPRs in part because challenging a questionable patent in federal court is enormously expensive and risky. Patent examiners work under serious time constraints, and some patents that shouldn’t have been granted will inevitably issue. Not every patent dispute requires years of expensive district court litigation. Congress recognized that, and created an administrative process, staffed with experts more capable of correcting those mistakes.

That system has benefited the public. Since 2012, it has helped invalidate thousands of patent claims that never should have been issued. The IPR process has protected startups, software developers, nonprofits, and small businesses that otherwise would have faced crushing litigation costs simply for building products or offering services that use everyday internet technology.

EFF supports a balanced IPR system because it should be easier to fight against bogus patents that should never have been issued. The cost of fighting a patent can be a weapon in itself, and weak patents don't just burden large technology companies. Patent trolls routinely target small businesses and independent developers, and have gone after podcasters, retailers, and even coffee shops and nonprofits. These organizations have neither the resources nor the desire to spend years litigating over potentially invalid patents in federal court. IPR offers a chance to challenge those patents before litigation costs get out of control.

If we weaken the IPR system, bad patents become much harder and more expensive to challenge.

Some defenders of the current approach argue that lower institution rates reflect more balance in the patent system. But institution rates at the PTAB have plummeted from 68% to 41% in just two years—a nearly 40% decline. IPR petition filings have reached historic lows. And even proceedings that have already been instituted can now be terminated months later, without a decision on the merits.

These developments send a troubling message to members of the public who might want to use the PTAB: don't bother. The PTAB doesn’t need to institute every petition. But it does need to provide a process that is transparent, predictable, and fair. Right now, confidence in the system is disappearing.

If companies, individuals, and nonprofits conclude that IPRs aren’t worth pursuing, the consequences won't stop at the PTAB. More weak patents that never should have been granted will survive, and patent trolls will use them. That means more defendants facing expensive district court litigation or paying settlements driven by the cost of litigation.

That's not what Congress intended when it created IPRs. It should not become the PTAB's “new normal.”

author: The Canadian Press
title: Chiefs question motive behind Indian Act talks after meeting with Carney, premiers
content:
First Nations chiefs who attended a closed-door meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney and premiers last month say their concerns were overshadowed by Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew’s call for the abolition of the Indian Act.




One chief also criticized Carney’s tone as he responded to a comment about how the United States works with Indigenous people.




“We have to ask ourselves if this was a co-ordinated effort between Wab Kinew and the prime minister,” Treaty 8 First Nations Grand Chief Mercredi said of the talk about abolishing the Indian Act.




Chief Sheila North of Bunibonibee Cree Nation in northern Manitoba said it’s beginning to appear that way to her.




“I hope that wasn’t the case because that would mean they were disingenuous in what they wanted the outcomes [of the meeting] to be,” North said. “It was a complete waste of time if that’s the only outcome that they were hoping for.”




Treaty 8 First Nations Grand Chief Trevor Mercredi on the steps of the Alberta legislature Monday, Mar. 9, 2026. Photo: Alberta NDP Caucus







Chiefs gathered with Carney and most premiers in Ottawa in late October for their first meeting since the 2005 Kelowna Accord talks. First Nations leaders prepared for the meeting for months and even enlisted the help of former Indigenous Services deputy minister Gina Wilson to tailor their messages to government.




Chiefs said they wanted to use the gathering to discuss the federal government’s controversial major projects legislation, health services, policing and public safety and the Natural Resources Transfer Acts.




Those resource agreements were negotiated with the Prairie Provinces at a time when First Nations were barred by the Indian Act from hiring their own lawyers. Chiefs have said those agreements should be abolished or changed to ensure resource development projects meaningfully benefit their communities.




But the main topic to come out of the closed-door meeting was Kinew’s sudden call to abolish the Indian Act — something he acknowledged he didn’t consult on with chiefs beforehand.




The law, which dates from 1876, gives Ottawa sweeping power over First Nations communities and people, including the authority to decide who qualifies for status and what reserves can and can’t do. While there is a widespread consensus that the law is outdated and restrictive, there’s little agreement on what could or should replace it.




Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew speaks with media at the First Nations-First Ministers Meeting in Ottawa on Monday. Photo: Raven Brascoupe/APTN.







In an audio recording of the closed-door meeting obtained by The Canadian Press, Kinew referred to his own First Nations status card and said he would keep it until he dies or the Indian Act is abolished.




“The idea that we have a race-based identification in our country in 2026 is inconsistent, at the very least, with Canada being a leader for human rights and democracy around the world,” Kinew, who is Anishinaabe, told Carney, chiefs and premiers.




“Typically, prime ministers are around for about a decade. And if we don’t put it on the agenda for this prime minister, that means we’ll be back here in 2036 and I’ll still have my laminated plastic card …




“And to the chiefs who may be like, ‘He didn’t consult with us before he’s saying this,’ I just wanted to say I think this is consistent with what you’re bringing forward here.”




Kinew made similar remarks to media following the session.




In a closing press conference after the meeting with chiefs, Carney said he was “very open” to the idea of abolishing the Indian Act. He said it’s important that the call came from community members and not the federal government.




Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak told The Canadian Press Kinew and Carney were the only ones at the meeting who brought up eradicating the Indian Act.




Sheila North looks towards an eagle feather as she speaks during the All Candidates Forum on the first day of the annual Assembly of First Nations Special Chiefs Assembly (SCA) in Ottawa, in December. Photo: Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press.







North said members of the Liberal Indigenous caucus told chiefs shortly after the meeting wrapped they didn’t believe Carney fully understood the comments he made about the Indian Act and that they would speak to the prime minister about clarifying his stance.




“I think they were a little bit caught off-guard, based on some of the reaction we got from them afterwards,” North said.




Carney did clarify his stance the next day, saying the Indian Act could be reformed instead of abolished.




In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for Indigenous Services Canada did not say if the relevant ministers were told in advance that the prime minister would be commenting on the Indian Act. The spokesperson said those ministers were in the meeting with chiefs when the Indian Act was raised.




North said it was inappropriate for Kinew to divert attention from the issues the chiefs wanted to talk about.




Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and Yukon Premier Currie Dixon (left) listen to a chief deliver opening remarks at the First Nations and First Ministers’ meeting in Ottawa on Oct. 26. Photo: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press.







“He may be Anishinaabe, he may have a status card, but that was not his place as a sitting premier to be calling for that,” she said.




North said that when the controversial Natural Resources Transfer Acts were brought up during the meeting, Kinew left his seat and didn’t return until the subject had changed. The day prior, North said, Kinew told chiefs he wasn’t open to the idea of moving past those agreements.




The acts, known as NRTAs, signed in 1930, transferred control of Crown lands and the resources they hold to Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. First Nations did not have a say in the negotiations that led to the agreements, nor were they allowed to hire legal representation to challenge them.




Chiefs, including former national chief Matthew Coon Come, have called for negotiations to change those agreements to something that better reflects their rights.




The Canadian Press asked Kinew’s office if he is open to revisiting the NRTAs and if he discussed the Indian Act with Carney before the meeting, and requested his response to the chiefs’ criticisms. His office said it would not be commenting further on the matter




In a statement sent to The Canadian Press, the federal Crown-Indigenous Relations Department said Carney has made it clear First Nations must have a direct stake in Canada’s economic future, and the NRTAs do not prevent the negotiation of new resource revenue sharing agreements.




Mercredi said that while conversations about moving away from the Indian Act aren’t new, it seemed “a little bit offside” to bring the topic up at a meeting when chiefs really wanted to discuss the NRTAs.




Mercredi also questioned the format of the meeting, saying Carney only responded to a handful of chiefs “when he wanted to respond.”




“There was no real discussion around the issues that we’re facing,” Mercredi said. “There was really no positive outcome when it came to this meeting.”




Prime Minister Mark Carney listens to opening remarks during the First Nations and First Ministers’ meeting in Ottawa on Oct. 26. Photo: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press.







Another chief in the meeting took issue with the way Carney responded to their concerns.




Chief Rodger Redman of Standing Buffalo Dakota Nation in Saskatchewan said he told Carney in the meeting he thinks Indigenous people in the United States have a better relationship with their governments, and that they are generally left alone to govern their nations.




In a video of the interaction posted online, Carney asked if Redman was “seriously making that point.”




“Just look around this table. Imagine, imagine this in the United States, under a Democratic administration, a Republican administration. It doesn’t even enter their thinking to have this discussion,” Carney said, interrupting Redman’s remarks.




“It kind of got under his skin a bit and he went sideways on me,” Redman told The Canadian Press.




Redman said he thought it was a valid point to bring up, since the push to accelerate major project development in Canada — a push that some chiefs say threatens First Nations rights — is largely being driven by pressures in the Canada-U.S. trade relationship.




“How can you say that you’re being equal sitting at the table?” Redman told The Canadian Press. “What happened in that circus in Ottawa was just there for the photo ops. We weren’t there for the photo ops.”




In remarks to chiefs shortly after responding to Kinew’s comments, Carney said he “can’t sit here and hear that there will be no progress” on the issues chiefs brought forward.




“Part of a respectful dialogue is recognizing facts and where those facts fall short, and where there’s gaps. And, very importantly, where there are programs that don’t work and why they don’t work,” he said in the audio recording.

title: A QUÉ VAMOS. QUÉ SÍ Y QUÉ NO
content:
Atención Familias Buscadoras, sin o con colectivo: Atención quienes acompañan a familias buscadoras:

Éste es el primero de varios textos donde iremos aclarando algunas dudas que hemos recibido, responder a algunas ofensas e insultos, e irles dando a conocer poco a poco parte de la agenda de la delegación. Por favor les pedimos estar pendientes de éste y los siguientes escritos.

A.- Hemos detectado una serie de confusiones, malhabladas e intentos de manipulación sobre los objetivos, fechas, lugares y actividades de la delegación de la Comisión Sexta Zapatista para estos meses de diciembre, y la primera semana de enero del 2027.

Se habla y se malinforma de una supuesta reunión nacional entre familias buscadoras y la delegación zapatista en la llamada “Glorieta de los Desaparecidos” el 6 de diciembre, y de otras actividades públicas de la Comisión Sexta Zapatista en otros lugares y fechas.

Esto es falso, compañeras y hermanas buscadoras. Tal vez sí tengan una su reunión quienes se convocan en ése o en otros sitios como referentes a su justa lucha, pero nosotros no participaremos ahí.

No sólo porque la “invitación” que recibimos de ahí refleja ignorancia, mala fe y grosería. A nadie se le invita insultándolo. En su oportunidad explicaremos más sobre eso. También porque no vamos a reuniones masivas con familias buscadoras.

Los grupos, colectivos, colectivas y familias buscadoras que se reúnen en las glorietas o donde sea, pueden reunirse EN PRIVADO con nosotros, grupo por grupo, en la sede de la delegación en la Ciudad de México y en las sedes que se harán públicas, registrándose vía el Frayba, en la fecha y hora que les convenga, si así lo desean.

B.- Miren, ustedes y nosotros, los pueblos zapatistas, sabemos que tienen no sólo diferencias sino francas rivalidades y disputas, mismo entre colectivos de buscadoras, entre redes y movimientos. Incluso hasta llegar a tratar de vetar a ciertos colectivos y a decretar quién sí y quién no se reúne con la delegación zapatista. Tal vez por eso crece el número de familias buscadoras que no están en ningún grupo o colectivo, y que nos contactan directamente.

Nosotros no vamos a juzgar a nadie. No vamos a decir cuál estrategia es correcta o errónea, cuál es legítima y cuál no, cuál es buena y cuál es mala.

Consideramos que, quien busca verdad y justicia y tiene el objetivo de encontrar a quien le hace falta a causa de una desaparición forzada, puede y debe recorrer todos los caminos y tocar todas las puertas para aliviar su dolor.

Sea que hacen búsqueda de campo con pico y pala; sea que recurren a las instancias judiciales locales, estatales y federales; sea que quieren reunirse con la titular del ejecutivo federal o con su pirámide de funcionarios; sea que hacen campañas internacionales y nacionales; sea que sólo alcanzan a pegar las fotos de sus ausentes en sus calles y barrios, sea que recurren a Organizaciones No Gubernamentales de Derechos Humanos; sea que solicitan el apoyo de especialistas en búsqueda de desaparecidos y análisis de restos humanos; sea que recurren a marchas, mítines, plantones, tomas de edificios y bloqueos de calles y carreteras; sea rezar; sea maldecir; sea todo lo anterior.

Y siempre con la memoria como motor.

Sea lo que sea que decidan y hagan, es una decisión de ustedes, de quienes cargan ese dolor y sufren esa angustia, y de nadie más.

Entonces no vamos a decirles qué hacer ni a hacerlo por ustedes. Vamos a conocerlas, a escucharlas, a abrazarlas.

Ni vamos a decir cuál red o colectivo es mejor que el otro.

C.- Por eso nuestro viaje no privilegia actos de masas, ni mediáticos, ni asambleas generales ni creación de alianzas, frentes o cosas parecidas, ni una nueva organización que englobe o incluya a todos los colectivos y familias buscadoras, o a parte de ellas.

Tampoco vamos a discutir o a debatir el número de personas desaparecidas, si son 135 mil o son más o son menos, porque esos números tienen un nombre, una historia, una tragedia, un dolor, y un deber: el de buscar a quien se ama, a quien hace falta y, no pocas veces, a quien es sangre de su sangre.

D.- La principal intención de esta iniciativa es escuchar a cada familia o grupo de familias buscadoras que quiera contarnos su historia y, sobre todo, la historia de su ausente.

Porque nosotros hemos visto y escuchado su caminar, sus esfuerzos, sus sacrificios, si no rendirse en la búsqueda, su no vender a su ser ausente, su no claudicar en la memoria.

Y les pedimos, si es que quieren, pueden y creen que eso les ayuda en su heroica labor, nos cuenten esa historia.

E.- Hasta ahora, los únicos actos públicos en los que participaremos como delegación zapatista son:

.- 19 de diciembre. Local de la Sección 9 CNTE. 10:00 am. Con miembros de la Coordinadora Nacional de Trabajadores de la Educación. Y lo que haremos es pedirles su apoyo en la difusión de las fichas de búsqueda en todas las escuelas donde trabajan, en todo el país. Y que involucren a otras maestras y maestros, aunque no sean de la CNTE.

.- El mismo día, sábado 19 de diciembre, en horas de la tarde, la marcha “Todas las luchas y una demanda en común: verdad y justicia para las ausencias”. Ahí les pediremos a las organizaciones sociales, movimientos, partidos políticos no institucionales, organizaciones estudiantiles, sindicatos, ONG, grupos, colectivas y colectivos, artistas, estudiantes, maestros, empleadas, choferólogos, familias y personas individuales, que, sin dejar de ser lo que son y sin abandonar sus luchas y demandas, apoyen en la difusión de las fichas de búsqueda y de las denuncias de movimientos por justicia y verdad para las muertes no naturales y los encarcelamientos injustos de personas de todas las edades, colores, razas y estratos sociales.

En resumen, pedirles a todas, todos y todoas que se sumen a la búsqueda de verdad y justicia.

F.- Vamos también, entonces, con la intención de que todo el país se haga común en su lucha de ustedes. Convertir a México en una geografía con memoria, en una geografía que busca todo el tiempo y en todos los rincones.

Desde las montañas del Sureste Mexicano.

Capitán Insurgente Marcos. México, noviembre del 2026.

author: Brett Wilkins
title: Past 4 Years Have Been Hottest on Record, UN Meteorological Organization Finds
content:
The alarming climate report was released on the opening day of the COP31 climate conference.

The alarming climate report was released on the opening day of the COP31 climate conference.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The Earth is hurtling deeper into a climate emergency, with 2026 on track to be one of the four hottest years ever recorded, ocean temperatures and sea levels hitting record highs, and glacier melt accelerating at an alarming pace, according to a report released Monday by the World Meteorological Organization as the United Nations Climate Change Conference kicked off in Türkiye.

The WMO’s “State of the Climate” report “shows that the past 12 years have individually been the warmest on record, with the past four years being the top four,” according to a summary of the 25-page publication.

WMO further noted that “the global average surface temperature for January – September 2026 was about 1.47°C above the preindustrial average,” or right on the brink of the 1.5°C of warming beyond which scientists say the risks of catastrophic and potentially irreversible climate impacts increase substantially.

2026 is on track to be one of 4 warmest years on record, marked by exceptional global temperatures, melting ice, rising sea levels, and a very strong El Niño that will unleash more heat & extreme weather into 2027.New WMO #StateOfClimate #COP31 Update↪️ https://bit.ly/stateofclimateCOP31pr

UN scientists said last month that the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C this century is no longer achievable without an overshoot.

The 1.47°C figure “is likely to rise through the end of the year because of the warming effect of El Niño, which has been intensifying since August and is expected to be the strongest on record by December,” the report’s summary states. El Niño is the warm phase of a pattern in the Pacific Ocean whose impact on disrupts weather, ecosystems, and economies.

Earth’s energy imbalance is rising… The imbalance reached its highest level since monitoring began, as greenhouse gases trap unprecedented amounts of heat and upset the equilibrium between incoming energy from the sun and outgoing energy. The ocean absorbs 90% of this excess heat, and 2026 is on track to be the 10th successive year of record ocean warmth.

Sea level is the highest on record, and sea-surface temperatures hit monthly records during 2026. The long-term retreat of glaciers continuesv— the annual mass loss of ice in 2025 would have filled five Olympic pools every second of the year. Freshwater storage has been dwindling since 2014.

“Extreme weather has made headlines throughout 2026. Behind the headlines and the statistics in this report are people who suffered the loss of loved ones, threats to their health and safety, flooded homes, failed harvests, empty shelves, lack of water, and choking air,” WMO Secretary General Celeste Saulo said in the report.

“The past four years have been the warmest in the 177-year observational record, and the heat in the oceans is breaking records for the 10th year in a row,” she continued. “The ongoing El Niño is forecast to be one of the strongest on record, and the heat it releases from the ocean will continue to fuel high temperatures and extreme weather into 2027.”

“El Niño and indeed the state of the global climate in 2026 gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts,” Saulo added. “El Niño doesn’t add new heat to the planet. It releases heat from the ocean, which is the warmest ever measured. There is simply more heat available to release.”

Indeed, climate scientists are warning that the planet is closer than previously thought to tipping points leading to hellish feedback loops and a “hothouse Earth.”

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres responded to the WMO report in a statement, saying: “We have entered a new age of climate extremes. A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising. And those least responsible are suffering first and worst.”

“Leaders must get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels, and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need,” he added.

The “State of the Climate” report was released on the first day of the UN summit, or COP31, in Antalya, Türkiye. Advocacy groups warned that world leaders must commit to phase out fossil fuels, finance a just transition to a post-carbon economy, and protect vulnerable populations from worsening climate harms.

“No country can confront this crisis alone. Those who have contributed least to global warming are often suffering the greatest harms. COP31 must deliver collective action that reflects this profound injustice,” Marta Schaaf, Amnesty International’s program director for climate, environmental and social justice, and corporate accountability, said Monday.

“The world is not running out of climate warnings. It is running out of excuses,” she continued. “After more than 30 years of climate negotiations, governments can no longer hide behind promises of future action or avoid confronting their fossil fuel industry allies.”

“The climate crisis is not a failure of knowledge, but a failure of political courage,” Schaaf added. “It is time to break the stranglehold of corporate power over political decision-making and end the fossil fuel era before it ends us.”

Oil Change International global policy senior strategist Shady Khalil asserted that “we know what needs to happen. Governments must stop fossil fuel expansion, plan a fair phaseout of existing production, and invest public money in renewable energy and economic diversification.”

“Wealthy countries must move first and fastest and provide the finance needed to make this transition possible everywhere,” he added.

author: Ciudong Ng
title: Aggression Against Iran Has Been Bipartisan. Will Midterm Results Change That?
content:
The US and Israel repeatedly subverted Iranian sovereignty, threatened nuclear war, and destabilized the Middle East.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The Republican Party’s staggering losses in the November midterm elections have prompted speculation about the future of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, which is overwhelmingly unpopular with voters. Democratic leaders have portrayed President Donald Trump’s military offensive as an unconstitutional fiasco and an economic disaster driving inflation.

But their choreographed outrage conceals a long tradition of bipartisan support for aggression, which President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran denounced in his UN address this September. For decades, the United States and Israel have referred to Iranians as terrorists, “but we are the victims of terrorists,” Pezeshkian underscored. His speech outlined a record of hypocrisy: U.S. and Israeli officials talk about peace, but plot to assassinate political leaders and negotiators. Most notably, both states command nuclear arsenals, yet impose debilitating sanctions on Iran’s atomic energy program.

As Pezeshkian emphasizes, the war is the latest episode in a turbulent history of energy and imperial assertion that contradicts U.S.-Israeli claims about proliferation risks and regional security. During the Cold War, Western powers shattered Iran’s democracy, before consolidating a brutal petromonarchy to guarantee access to its oil reserves. While undercutting Iranian energy sovereignty, they allowed Israel to become a nuclear-armed occupier, spreading dirty weapons and armed conflicts across the Middle East. This tangled history of oil and atoms is essential to understanding the war’s causes and contradictions, as two rogue states with thermonuclear weapons attack Iran under the pretext of nonproliferation.

Since the nineteenth century, Western powers have attempted to curb Iran’s sovereignty or seize its vast energy reserves. By 1914, Great Britain controlled its oil industry, after extorting concessions from the Iranian government. Over the following decades, the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company (AIOC) turned its refinery in the southwestern city of Abadan into the main energy supplier for the British Empire. Winston Churchill called the gushing wells “a prize from fairyland.” Yet AIOC officials warped Iran’s economic development by handpicking politicians and shamelessly exploiting workers. British personnel at Abadan lived in segregated splendor with swimming pools and servants, while local laborers inhabited parched slums.

After World War II, Iran attempted to improve its contract with the AIOC in order to raise government revenue and living standards. But company officials refused to compromise. In April 1951, Mohammad Mosaddegh became prime minister and initiated a series of ambitious reforms, which included nationalizing the oil industry.

Privately, the U.S. government lambasted the AIOC for behaving like a “typical nineteenth-century colonial exploiter,” while dealing “ineptly and disastrously” with Iran. Secretary of State Dean Acheson was scathing: “Never had so few lost so much so stupidly and so fast.” Nevertheless, U.S. leaders colluded with Britain to undermine nationalization. They feared that Mosaddegh’s policy set a destabilizing precedent, sapping British imperial power, upending the Cold War balance, and compromising Western control over strategic resources.

“I fought the fascists and Nazis,” one CIA adviser ruminated. “My lesson was that we were becoming just like them.”

Posing as a mediator, the State Department pressed Iranian leaders to make concessions, yet privately conceded that Britain’s demands were unreasonable. British negotiators advocated paying “lip service” to the principle of nationalization, while “keeping effective power … in our hands.” Ratcheting up pressure, the United States and Britain organized an oil embargo to suffocate Iran’s economy. Officials also bribed dozens of legislators, who physically assaulted Mosaddegh’s allies in parliament. And they launched a global propaganda campaign, pumping what one British operative called “a steady supply of suitable poison” into the press.

Mosaddegh held out until August 1953, when the CIA and British intelligence orchestrated a coup. From the shadows, foreign agents helped disloyal officers and paid rioters take Tehran, before assaulting the prime minister’s house. After a blistering shootout, Mosaddegh and his allies fled across his rooftop as his home dissolved into rubble. He would spend three years in solitary confinement and the rest of his life under house arrest.

Pressing their advantage, U.S. leaders broke Britain’s energy monopoly after the coup, securing the right to market 40 percent of Iranian oil. CIA Director Allen Dulles, whose law firm represented the AIOC, supervised a transition to unabashed authoritarian rule under Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. The CIA bragged that it was “very active” in selecting parliamentary deputies, and the shah exclaimed to one American spymaster: “I owe my throne to God, my people, my army and to you!” Notoriously, U.S. agents helped establish the intelligence service, SAVAK, which tortured countless dissidents. “I fought the fascists and Nazis,” one CIA adviser ruminated. “My lesson was that we were becoming just like them.”

During the Mosaddegh administration, the United States and Britain portrayed Iran as a fanatical state tottering on disorder. Before international audiences, they fielded legal arguments opposing nationalization, claiming that Iranian leaders were hotheaded, breaking inviolable contracts, and flirting with communism. But the goal of U.S. and British stakeholders was always control: unfettered access to Iran’s bountiful oil and the suppression of demands for resource sovereignty across the Global South.

As Mosaddegh languished in prison, Israel launched a nuclear program that reflected the colonial double standards of Western energy policy. In July 1956, Egypt nationalized the Suez Canal, which French and British investors controlled. Outraged, Paris and London conspired with Tel Aviv to invade the Sinai Peninsula and retake the waterway. During secret talks, the diplomat Shimon Peres leveraged cooperation to secure French assistance for Israel’s atomic energy program. “I finalized,” Peres wrote in his memoirs, “an agreement for the building of a nuclear reactor at [the Israeli city of] Dimona.”

That October, the tripartite invasion of Egypt incensed both the Soviet Union and United States, which forced its Western allies to withdraw. Afterward, French Prime Minister Guy Mollet deepened his commitment to Israel’s nuclear program, portraying it as a consolation prize. “I owe them the bomb,” Mollet insisted. Within a decade, Western capital investment allowed Israel to join the nuclear club. Beersheba became a francophone enclave with 2,500 French citizens and Renault cars cruising its streets as guest workers constructed the Dimona plutonium plant.

Experts feared that the atom bomb would embolden Israeli aggression, undercut peace negotiations, and trigger a world war.

Meanwhile, both states exploited colonial Algeria as an arms range. Between 1960 and 1966, French authorities conducted nuclear tests in the Sahara, spreading radioactive fallout across North Africa while sharing their findings with Israeli observers and the Zionist state’s scientific establishment. The experiments spawned a toxic nightmare, reportedly poisoning 30,000 Algerians in 1962 alone.

Fearing nuclear weapons proliferation, U.S. President John F. Kennedy pressed Israeli leaders to accept inspections at Dimona. Yet Zionist activists succeeded in reducing them to a political charade. “I fought the strongest battle of my career to keep them from full inspection,” the lobbyist Abe Feinberg recalled. “I violently intervened … half a dozen times.” Under pressure, U.S. officials agreed to announce visits beforehand and forgo using their own testing equipment. Feinberg boasted that his political campaign turned inspections into “a scam job,” while secretly collecting funds for Israel’s nuclear weapons program from American Zionists.

In The Samson Option, journalist Seymour Hersh reveals that Israel went to extraordinary lengths to deceive inspectors. Before visits, the Israeli military covered paths and bunkers at Dimona with dirt and grass, relandscaping the complex to conceal its awesome scale. Officials also constructed a false control room with rigged computers, pretending to operate a modest 24-megawatt reactor. And an Israeli “cover up team” plugged information leaks. One member recalled scolding engineers who divulged secrets. “‘Listen, you mother-fucker, don’t answer that question,’” the official interjected in Hebrew. “The Americans would think I was translating.”

Privately, U.S. leaders suspected that Israel was building a bomb. Yet hostility toward the Arab powers, sympathy for Zionism, and electoral considerations encouraged them to tolerate its duplicity. Off the record, Kennedy was irate, confiding that Israeli “sons of bitches lie to me constantly about their nuclear capability.”

After acquiring nuclear capabilities, Tel Aviv invaded its Arab neighbors in June 1967, occupying the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza Strip, West Bank, and Golan Heights. Increasingly, the Pentagon regarded Israel as the world’s greatest proliferation threat. Experts feared that the atom bomb would embolden Israeli aggression, undercut peace negotiations, and trigger a world war. In his classic study, Israel and the Bomb, Avner Cohen unveiled a dangerous cycle, arguing that Washington boosted conventional arms shipments to reduce the appeal of nuclear weapons.

Anxieties peaked in 1968 when Secretary of Defense Clark Clifford sought Israel’s commitment to the Non-Proliferation Treaty in exchange for F-4 Phantom jets. After tense negotiations, the Israeli embassy again mobilized Feinberg to press President Lyndon B. Johnson’s hand. The maneuver worked. A tenacious lobbyist, Feinberg was also a major Democratic Party fundraiser with a direct line to Johnson, which he used to bypass the Pentagon.

“Clifford called Johnson and LBJ said, ‘Sell them anything they want,’” an aide to the senior U.S. negotiator claimed. He recalled that the secretary of defense was stunned, replying, “‘Mr. President, I don’t want to live in a world where the Israelis have nuclear weapons.’” Johnson simply told Clifford to not bother him anymore before hanging up.

Read together, the history of U.S. policy toward Iran and Israel offers surreal contrasts. Western empires crushed Mosaddegh’s attempt to achieve economic sovereignty, demolishing Iranian democracy in the process. Yet afterward, they helped Israel become a nuclear-armed occupier, while combating Arab nationalism. Repeatedly, they prioritized power over nonproliferation, opening a nuclear umbrella over the Middle East.

In October 1973, Clifford’s worst fears materialized, as Egypt and Syria launched a coordinated offensive to reclaim land that Israel had seized in 1967. Prime Minister Golda Meir’s government panicked, apparently mobilizing Israel’s nuclear arsenal. To calm Israel’s nerves, the U.S. government airlifted 22,318 tons of materiel to the Israeli military. According to Hersh’s reporting, Secretary of State Henry Kissinger told a colleague that Meir blackmailed him, implying that “if they didn’t get military equipment, and quickly, they might go nuclear.” As tempers flared, both Kissinger and Soviet leaders, who backed the Arab powers, engaged in nuclear brinkmanship, escalating the most dangerous standoff since the Cuban Missile Crisis.

Although averting Armageddon, American officials triggered an Arab energy embargo that boosted oil prices fourfold, upending the global economy and again elevating Iran’s strategic significance. Over the 1970s, the United States sold staggering quantities of high-tech weapons to the shah, in order to guarantee access to petroleum and “petrodollar recycling” — ensuring that oil-producing states reinvested the U.S. dollars flooding the region into Western banks and financial markets.

In particular, U.S. policymakers helped develop the monarch’s nuclear program, which became a symbol of his overbearing ego. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology established a special arrangement, which educated dozens of Iranian personnel and, consequently, helped raise the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran’s staff of scientists from 67 to 862 within three years. Pushing back, professors and students claimed that the agreement strengthened the shah’s “fascistic dictatorship” and organized a sit-in at the Nuclear Engineering Department in April 1975. One faculty member warned that MIT was potentially “training engineers to build bombs.”

Yet U.S. cooperation continued and was no outlier. Without exception, the European countries now spearheading sanctions against Tehran previously supported the shah’s drive for nuclear mastery, training scientists, building reactors, and selling sensitive technologies.

Until 1979, Israeli leaders also regarded Iran as an essential lifeline and helped build the shah’s military-industrial complex. At times, the monarchy was Israel’s sole oil supplier and a leading market for its defense exports. Revamping relations, Israeli military officers reportedly maintained regular contact with Iranian staff, and the shah helped them develop missiles capable of carrying nuclear warheads. Their relationship set a new pattern, as Israel helped authoritarian regimes build advanced weapons — including nuclear bombs — to secure hard currency. Prioritizing oil and petrodollars, Israeli leaders respected the shah’s ability to “stifle any resistance.” Any “change in this government will,” Ambassador Uri Lubrani stressed, “be to the detriment of our relations.”

Ultimately, U.S.-Israeli support for the shah backfired. In 1978, military and nuclear spending accelerated an economic crisis, which spiraled into a revolution. Israeli diplomats favored “extreme toughness” and “the establishment of a military regime” to crush protests. But it was too late: The shah fled Iran in January 1979. That same year, evidence emerged that Israel tested a nuclear bomb in the Atlantic, underscoring the failure and hypocrisy of U.S. nonproliferation policy.

In recent decades, American and Israeli officials have portrayed Iran as an existential menace bent on nuclear conquest. In 1992, Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin warned that Iran was only years away from procuring a nuclear bomb, a claim his successors have repeated ever since. For Tel Aviv, demonizing the Iranian government served two purposes: It justified sending unrivaled levels of U.S. military aid to Israel and diverted attention from the occupation of Palestine.

Following the 2003 invasion of Iraq, President George W. Bush’s administration declared Iran a member of the “axis of evil,” labeling it a proliferation threat while preparing for war. Senior officials were “literally levitating off the ground in pure excitement,” the EU diplomat Alastair Crooke recounted. They boasted that “‘only the wimps … went to Baghdad,’” but “real men” would attack Iran. Over the following decade, U.S. and Israeli policymakers laundered false intelligence, manipulated the International Atomic Energy Agency, and spread unsubstantiated claims about an Iranian bomb program to promote regime change.

For Tel Aviv, demonizing the Iranian government justified sending unrivaled levels of U.S. military aid to Israel and diverted attention from the occupation of Palestine.

Upon taking office in 2009, President Barack Obama maintained pressure through sanctions and cyberattacks. He also tolerated Israel’s assassination program against Iranian nuclear experts; in one case, an undercover operative murdered a scientist in front of his infant daughter. Notoriously, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took their propaganda campaign to the United Nations, where he brandished a poster of a cartoon explosive. Drawing a red line below the fuse, Netanyahu warned that Iran was approaching “the second stage of nuclear enrichment to make a bomb.”

To avert war, Obama concluded a nuclear agreement with Iran in 2015. But three years later, President Donald Trump arbitrarily scrapped the accord, initiating the latest wave of false accusations to justify unconditional support for Israel and a reinvigorated sanctions regime.

This February, U.S. and Israeli leaders finally launched a full-scale military offensive against Iran. With unintended irony, Trump has threatened to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” while insisting Iran threatens regional stability. Rehashing three-decade-old arguments, Netanyahu also asserts that the war is necessary to forestall disaster. “We have prevented Iran from carrying out a plan to annihilate us, and today they would have had … an atomic bomb to do so,” he informed a press summit.

That propaganda not only justifies the ongoing offensive but disfigures the historical record. Israel, not Iran, has thermonuclear weapons. The illegal offensive has killed thousands of civilians, upended the global economy, and undermined Republican dominance in Congress. The midterm election results represent a stinging repudiation of the war. But its implications remain unclear, as senior Democrats such as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries have asserted that Iran is “a bad actor” that “must be aggressively confronted.”

Since the 1950s, U.S. and Israeli leaders have repeatedly subverted Iranian sovereignty, threatened nuclear war, and destabilized the Middle East. As under Mosaddegh, Iran once again confronts unapologetic Western aggression, while fighting the latest incarnation of its colonial past.

title: IEC declares 2026 local elections free and fair as coalitions get set to run municipalities
content:
The Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) has declared the 2026 local government elections free and fair, with 14.9-million people having cast their ballots in an election that has left most municipal councils facing the prospect of coalition government.




The African National Congress (ANC) retained its position as the largest party nationally, securing 30.76% of the vote and 3,246 council seats. However, the result represents a significant decline in its electoral support and leaves the party needing to negotiate with other political formations in municipalities where it failed to secure an outright majority.




Announcing the results at the IEC results operations centre at Gallagher Estate on Sunday, IEC chairperson Mosotho Moepya said the elections had largely been conducted in a peaceful environment.




A total of 29.2-million voters were registered, with approximately 14.9-million participating. The national turnout was 52%, an increase of 6.1 percentage points from the 45.9% recorded in the 2021 local government elections.




The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second with 24.64% and 1,695 council seats, followed by the uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) with 9.76% and 785 seats. The Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) received 6.22% and 588 seats, while ActionSA secured 5.67% and 313 seats.




Moepya said the commission’s declaration was informed partly by findings from the 2026 Elections Satisfaction Survey conducted by the Human Sciences Research Council. The survey found that 90% of respondents regarded the elections as having integrity, 91% considered them free and fair, and 95% were satisfied with the services provided by the IEC.




Some voting stations experienced problems with voter management devices. Photo by Mzi Velapi




However, the commission acknowledged that the electoral process had not been without challenges.




In Douglas, Northern Cape, ballot papers were destroyed before counting could take place when political party supporters allegedly stormed the voting station at a community hall. The IEC ordered a revote in Ward 3 of the Siyancuma Local Municipality, saying the affected votes could not be counted since ballot papers had been destroyed. The commission approached the Electoral Court and registered a criminal case with the police.




Chief electoral officer, Sy Mamabolo outlined the scale of the election operation, which involved approximately 188,000 staff deployed across 23,696 voting stations.




The IEC printed more than 100-million ballot papers and deployed approximately 56,000 voter management devices to support voter verification and the administration of the elections.




Mamabolo said approximately 28-million ballot papers had to be superseded following a Constitutional Court order affecting candidate lists. The order affected 181 ANC candidates in six municipalities. The commission extended the same dispensation to other parties in similar circumstances to ensure equal treatment.




The IEC also introduced a virtual results operations centre, allowing political parties and candidates remote access to selected applications and reports during the results process.




Mamabolo said the commission would assess both the successes and shortcomings of the election operation. “Operational excellence is not a destination, but it is a continuous institutional commitment,” he said.

title: Антифашистская контрдемонстрация 11 ноября в Варшаве
content:
Анархическая группа «Прамень» призывает присоединиться к контрдемонстрации 11 ноября в Варшаве (pl. Unii Lubelskiej,14:00). Вот что пишут авторы призыва:

За последние пару лет правые популисты сильно продвинули антимигрантскую повестку в Польше. Чуть ли не ежедневно появляются новости об избиениях мигрант_ок. Фашистские патрули устраивают рейды на улицах городов. Люди боятся говорить на родном языке в публичных местах и часто сталкиваются с агрессией со стороны прохожих или на работе.

Государство же не только не защищает мигрант_ок, но и само последовательно ужесточает условия для легализации и пребывания на территории страны.

Популярность фашистской партии «Конфедерация» растёт с каждым годом, что наглядно показывает тенденцию в общественных настроениях.

11 ноября мы в очередной раз заявим о своей позиции. Пока десятки тысяч патриотов будут маршировать по центру Варшавы, мы традиционно выйдем на улицы со своей антифашистской повесткой и покажем, что не всё общество болеет коричневой лихорадкой.

Присоединяйся к чёрному блоку на контрдемонстрации 11 ноября!

author: CNT Galiza
title: La CNT inicia un conflicto contra la academia de inglés This Way
content:
Leer en

Castellano

Galego







Castellano

La CNT inicia un conflicto contra la academia de inglés This Way en Vigo: ¡Ese no es el camino!




Las academias y centros de formación de inglés siguen agravando la precariedad del sector, aprovechándose fraudulentamente del modelo de contrato indefinido. El caso más reciente se sitúa en Vigo, donde la CNT acaba de iniciar un conflicto sindical contra la empresa This Way.




La táctica de esta empresa es tan antigua como perversa: en lugar de respetar la ley y conceder a nuestra afiliada la baja temporal de verano para luego reincorporarla, optaron por despedirla directamente. Esta es una práctica habitual en un sector que convierte la estabilidad laboral en una quimera, jugando con la vida y el sustento de quienes se dedican a la enseñanza.




Desde la CNT no toleraremos que se siga despidiendo a docentes al llegar el verano para ahorrar costes, tratándolos como mercancía desechable. Los docentes son fundamentales para el desarrollo y el futuro de nuestra sociedad; su trabajo es esencial y merece condiciones dignas, un reconocimiento real y una garantía de estabilidad.




Este no es el primer conflicto al que nos enfrentamos en el ámbito de los centros de formación. Ya hemos librado batallas sindicales contra otras academias de inglés que intentaban imponer estos mismos abusos, y las hemos ganado.




Las y los trabajadores nos organizamos y las victorias se consiguen gracias a la unidad de todas y a la lucha sindical. Ante el abuso individual, la respuesta colectiva. No daremos un paso atrás hasta que se respeten los derechos de nuestros compañeros y se ponga fin a estas prácticas abusivas en el sector educativo.




Si tú también sufres el fraude de los contratos temporales, si te dejan en la calle al terminar el curso o si quieren hacerte creer que no hay nada que hacer, recuerda que la solidaridad es nuestra mejor arma. ¡Organízate con la CNT!







Galego

A CNT inicia conflito contra a academia de inglés This Way en Vigo: Ese non é o camiño!




As academias de inglés e os centros de formación continúan profundando na precarización do sector, aproveitándose de maneira fraudulenta da figura do contrato fixo-descontinuo. O último caso ten como escenario a cidade de Vigo, onde a CNT ven de iniciar un conflito sindical contra a empresa This Way.




A táctica desta empresa é tan vella como perversa: en lugar de respectar a lei e pasar á nosa afiliada ao período de inactividade estival para reincorporala despois do verán, decidiron directamente despedila. Trátase dunda práctica habitual nun sector que converte a estabilidade laboral nunha quimera, xogando coa vida e co pan de quen se dedica ao ensino.




Desde a CNT non imos tolerar que se siga desbotando ás docentes cando chega o verán para aforrar custos, tratando ao persoal como mercadoría de descarte. As profesoras son fundamentais para o desenvolvemento e o futuro da nosa sociedade; a seu labor é esencial e merece unhas condicións dignas, un recoñecemento real e a garantía de estabilidade.




Este non é o primeiro conflito que enfrontamos no ámbito dos centros de formación. Xa mantivemos batallas sindicais contra outras academias de inglés que pretendían impoñer estes mesmos abusos, e ganámolas.




As traballadoras nos organizamos e as vitorias conséguense grazas á unidade de todas e á loita sindical. Fronte ao abuso individual, a resposta colectiva. Non imos dar un paso atrás ata lograr que se respecten os dereitos da nosa compañeira e se poña fin a estas prácticas abusivas no sector do ensino.




Se ti tamén estás a sufrir a fraude dos contratos fixos-descontinuos, se che botan á rúa cando remata o curso ou se queren facerche crer que non hai nada que facer, lembra que a solidariedade é a nosa mellor arma. Organízate coa CNT!
