author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: John Amagoalik seeks funding to stay in Nunavut while case winds through court
content:
Lawyers for John Amagoalik are scheduled to appear in court Friday in the hope of securing emergency funding that would allow him to stay in his home while his lawsuit against the Nunavut government proceeds.




Last month, the retired politician filed an 

application for a judicial review

 in response to the Department of Health’s refusal to fund his medical care and housing in Iqaluit.




Amagoalik is revered by many as the “Father of Nunavut.” He dedicated decades of his life to advancing Inuit rights.




He had been living at the Embassy West long-term care home in Ottawa before returning to Iqaluit this summer. While his goal is to 

live his final days

 in the territory he helped create, his family says they can’t afford to make that happen without funding from Nunavut’s Health Department.




The department has stated this type of funding 

does not fall

 under its authority.




Nunavut Chief Justice Susan Cooper is scheduled to preside over Friday’s hearing, said Andrew Morrison, among the lawyers that represent Amagoalik. She’s set to decide whether to grant funding that would allow Amagoalik to remain in Nunavut during the judicial review process.




The hearing for a judicial review of the Health Department’s decision not to fund Amagoalik’s care will happen at a later date, Morrison said.
















“The government was willing to pay for his care in Ottawa,” he said in an interview Monday. “We don’t think that Inuit elders should have to have to chose between going south for their health and their homeland.”




Nunavut’s Health Department did not immediately respond when reached for comment.




Spokesperson Charmaine Deogracias has previously stated that the Health Department does not have the legislative authority to fund independently arranged private care and can not make exceptions in individual cases.

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Revives Election Fraud Claims Days After Pledging to Accept Midterms
content:
“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest?” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

President Donald Trump issued a Truth Social post on Monday morning casting doubts on the “honesty” of the 2026 midterm elections, less than one week after initially stating he would accept the results.

“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest?” Trump wrote in his latest missive about the midterms.

He went on to reprise grievances from past elections, in which he errantly claimed that results that came in later (often due to absentee ballots being counted after polls closed) were somehow suspicious.

“How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote,” Trump wrote. Contrary to Trump’s objections, polls widely predicted Democratic gains this midterm season.

Trump also expressed doubts about the security of voting machines, a familiar but debunked claim he frequently used to suggest that his 2020 presidential election loss was somehow rigged.

“It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!” Trump said.

Trump’s Monday morning post comes just six days after he told The New York Times that he would respect the results of the midterms, telling the publication he was “absolutely willing” to accept the outcome after Republicans were routed by Democrats in races determining control of both houses of Congress. Trump also said he was “look[ing] forward to working with” Democrats when they take office in January.

At multiple points over the past year — including in late October, just weeks before the elections took place — Trump said he would only accept the results of the midterms if he deemed them “honest.”

Trump’s initial statement declaring that he’d accept the results likely surprised millions of Americans. In polling conducted last month, 7 in 10 Americans said they didn’t believe the president would accept the results, while fewer than 3 in 10 respondents said they believed he would.

It’s unclear whether Trump is planning to demand that Republicans take action to address his false claims of “dishonesty” within the election results. One theory worrying political observers is that Trump and Republicans could attempt to demand that the House Clerk refuse to seat newly elected lawmakers in January, justifying the action by citing unfounded claims of election fraud. That move could create a constitutional crisis, as it would be unclear as to who would be in control of Congress, the outgoing session or the incoming one, and would likely require judicial intervention.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $50,000 in the next 10 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: By Clint Combs, Contributor
title: ICE Agent Falsely Accused Federal Defender of Helping Client Evade Arrest and Deportation
content:
Minneapolis, MN — It was supposed to be another routine court appearance.




Assistant Federal Defender Michael Deates and his Salvadoran client settled inside the Minneapolis courtroom on April 28. ICE Deportation Officer Michael O’Neal sat inside the gallery when he heard a familiar name: Ezequiel Portillo-Rodriguez.




He pulled out his government phone and then searched for the name. A Certificate of Nonexistence (CTNE) that he filed in April 2025 popped up. To O’Neal, this meant that there were no official records of Portillo-Rodriguez ever holding a visa, green card or U.S. citizenship. He texted agent Blake Willwerscheid, asking if he knew about the case. Willwersheid told him that Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Special Agent Brubaker was in charge of the case. A prosecutor later testified that this HSI Agent thought he was talking to an agent Witt in St. Paul.




Had O’Neal looked through court records he would have found something more relevant than a CTNE. On Sept. 2, 2025, Portillo-Rodriguez started his six-month stint inside the notorious Golden State Annex in McFarland, Ca. He filed an asylum claim while inside the private immigration jail run by GEO Group. Attorneys wrote that Portillo-Rodriguez had a “fear of persecution and torture” if he were deported back to El Salvador. Two weeks later an asylum officer denied this claim.




An immigration judge overturned that denial on November 7, 2025, finding his fears credible.




Portillo-Rodriguez filed a habeas corpus petition on Jan. 26, 2026. His attorney Deborah Czuba filed an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order on March 12. Four days later the government decided not to contest the review.




In California, U.S. District Judge Dale Drozd declared that the government had violated Portillo-Rodriguez’s Fifth Amendment Due Process rights by subjecting him to indefinite detention without a proper hearing.




On March 18, Judge Drozd issued an injunction releasing Portillo-Rodriguez and barring ICE from re-arresting him on immigration charges.




A month later, O’Neal was texting his boss, Supervisory Detention and Deportation Officer Nicholas Carey, looking for a green light to arrest Portillo-Rodriguez. He got no response while court was in session. Once the hearing adjourned, O’Neal cornered the prosecuting attorneys, asking if this was a case where Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) was barred from placing a detainer. The prosecutors told him they didn’t know.




O’Neal then approached U.S. Deputy Marshal Cassandra Stone, telling her he planned to take Portillo-Rodriguez into custody. Stone told him an arrest could be made at the U.S. Probation and Pretrial Services office. O’Neal claimed that Deates was standing close enough to eavesdrop.




“Deates was listening to the conversation I was having with Deputy Marshal Stone, made eye contact with me, then told his client Portillo-Rodriguez they needed to leave and follow him downstairs,” O’Neal wrote.




Deates denied this in his sworn declaration.




“I did not overhear, and had no knowledge at the time of, any conversation,” he wrote.




Deates and Portillo-Rodriguez walked downstairs to eat lunch at the Federal Defender’s Office. O’Neal rushed to the courthouse cellblock. He called Carey, demanding an immediate administrative warrant. Minutes later, Carey emailed a signed Form I-200 straight to O’Neal’s inbox.




The plainclothes task force scrambled to spring a familiar trap. O’Neal left the courtroom with Deputy Marshals Cassandra Stone and Gnika. Stone went to the Marshals Office to scan the live security video feeds, spotting Deates and his client in the public lobby.




By the time O’Neal and the marshals rushed down to the ground floor, the lobby was empty. The marshals searched the interior corridors while O’Neal glanced out a window. He caught sight of the pair walking along the sidewalk next to Minneapolis City Hall toward the light rail platform.




The three rushed outside before a red light stopped them at the intersection of 3rd Avenue and 4th Street. The light turned green. Trains departed in both directions. O’Neal saw Deates standing alone on the light rail platform. Portillo-Rodriguez was on his way back home to California.




After the failed trap, O’Neal contacted Special Agent Brubaker for an update. Brubaker informed him that Portillo-Rodriguez had been released in California on a habeas corpus petition.




The next day O’Neal sent a memo to Assistant ICE Field Officer Director Corey McMahon with the subject line “Aid and Abetting.”







“Aid and Abetting” written on the subject line on a memo sent by ICE agent Michael O’Neal to Corey McMahon claiming that Assistant Public Defender Matthew Deates committed a federal crime – 

page 39 of 54

 in exhibit document.







“Portillo-Rodriguez did not make his appointment with the U.S. Public Defenders Office and was aided and abetted from immigration arrest by Assistant Public Defender Matthew Deates,” O’Neal wrote.




O’Neal told McMahon that the hearing took place in front of former U.S. Magistrate Judge Raymond Erickson. That case was in front of U.S. Magistrate Judge David Schultz. Raymond retired in 2010.




No one knew of O’Neal’s mistakes for four months until prosecutors accidentally filed the memo as evidence in the 

Minnesota 15

 federal conspiracy case on Aug. 20. U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen and Assistant U.S. Attorney Tory Sailer wrote that the memo “does not reflect the position of the U.S. Attorney’s Office.”




Deates broke his silence on Oct. 1, 

filing a sworn affidavit

 demanding the U.S. government correct the record and clear his name.




“My professional reputation depends on the trust of this Court, opposing counsel, and my clients,” Deates wrote. “The O’Neal Memorandum’s accusations about me are false … The government’s … letter, which says nothing about the falsity of the accusations against me, does not correct the record.”




Supporters of the Minnesota 15 packed both an overflow room and Judge Schultz’s courtroom on Oct. 20. Some laughed at the revelations. Others shook their heads in disbelief.




See Unicorn Riot coverage of the Minnesota 15 conspiracy case.




Sailer told Schultz that the government possessed zero evidence linking Deates to criminal obstruction or aiding and abetting an escape. Schultz then asked about his client.




“If you take the facts that are disclosed in the O’Neal memo, is there a factual basis for asserting that Mr Portillo-Rodriguez evaded a lawful arrest?” Schultz asked.




Sailer called his position “unpopular,” saying “it does get into constitutional issues.”




“It’s not that it’s not popular. It’s ludicrous,” Schultz said.




“I don’t agree with that,” Sailer replied.




“Agent O’Neal can decide which orders of Article 3 are lawful?” Schultz asked. “INS [Immigration Naturalization Services] rules trump the California judge’s order?”




“I have my own personal views about this. The legal analysis I don’t think is clear,” Sailer said. “I’ve done this in Texas. Expedited removals happened all the time… I am just relaying that the executive has quite a bit of authority with regards to immigration matters.”




Sailer maintained that O’Neal detaining Portillo-Rodriguez on April 28 qualified as a legal arrest.




Yet, O’Neal carved out a critical admission at the end of his memo: “I contacted Special Agent Brubaker, I inquired about the case and she stated Portillo-Rodriguez had been in custody in California and released on a Habeas Corpus and made his way to Minnesota to attend an initial appearance. At no time prior to the incident had I been aware of that information.”




“If Agent O’Neal thought that it was somehow lawful for him to immediately arrest and deport Mr. Portillo-Rodriguez, then why in his memorandum made a point of saying I was unaware of the fact of a restraining order? Why would he cover his trail?” said Schultz.




“I couldn’t answer that,” said Sailer.




Kevin Riach told Schultz that he would cross-examine O’Neal if his name was tied to the Minnesota 15 case.




“It confirms that this entire investigation is being driven by people who have no idea what they’re doing,” Riach said. “The agents don’t even know the names of who they’re talking to. It’s like an ever-ending fountain of impeachment material.”




Riach’s client felt amused. Isaac Sant has described the case against the 15 as purely political and an attack on the working class.




“It is both humbling and a little embarrassing to learn that I was arrested by the dumbest cops alive,” Isaac Sant said.




Joshua Panduro Preston, co-counsel for Macalester Professor and Minnesota 15 defendant Erik Davis, said that Schultz berating the U.S. Attorney’s Office was justified and also unprecedented.




“We’re witnessing at this moment in time the judiciary asserting itself in a way it hasn’t done before. Historically, there’s been the presumption of regularity.” Preston said. “Now we’ve reached a point where all that trust is out the window and we see the court rake these prosecutors over the coals. I mean, that is not stuff you normally see.”




“The government has no plans to go forward with these ridiculous changes. The government is unwilling to say that Mr. Deates done nothing wrong. That is besmirching the reputation of one of the finest lawyers in this district,” Schultz said before turning to Deates. “On behalf of the United States: I apologize to you. This should not have happened.”

author: Amy Goodman
title: LA’s DSA Rep.-Elect Says She Won’t Back Hakeem Jeffries for House Speaker
content:
“As of right now, my vote is no,” Angela Gonzales-Torres says. “Over 100,000 Angelenos voted for courage.”

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The next Congress will include about 100 new lawmakers in the House of Representatives, the largest freshman wave in decades. That also includes six newly elected members of the Democratic Socialists of America, bringing the total number of DSA members in Congress to eight. One of the incoming DSA congressmembers will be California’s Angela Gonzales-Torres, who worked two other jobs while campaigning and was massively outspent by her opponent, incumbent Democratic Congressmember Jimmy Gomez.

In her first national TV interview, Gonzales-Torres tells Democracy Now! she will prioritize immigrant justice, Medicare for All and fighting corruption, when she is sworn in. She also explains why she has not yet committed to supporting Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker.

“As of right now, my vote is no,” she says. “Over 100,000 Angelenos voted for courage. They voted for change.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.

Newly elected members of Congress are in Washington, D.C., this week for orientation. The new class of Democrats will include the largest-ever incoming class of progressives, including six newly elected members of DSA, the Democratic Socialists of America. This will bring the total number of DSA members in Congress to eight, joining Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib.

On Tuesday, our next guest, Angela Gonzales-Torres of Los Angeles, defeated the sitting Democratic Congressmember Jimmy Gomez, who’s under investigation by the House Ethics Committee over sexual misconduct allegations, which he denies. Gonzales-Torres grew up in the district she’ll represent, in Highland Park. She was raised by a single mom after her father was deported, and her family relied on Section 8, SNAP and Medicaid. She ran a campaign focused on affordable housing, abolishing ICE, rooting out corruption in Congress. This is Angela Gonzales-Torres speaking after her election.

REP.-ELECT ANGELA GONZALES-TORRES: We took on corporate donors and corruption, and this apparent culture in Congress in which men appear to abuse their positions of power and abuse women. And I am sick of it. And so I’m ready for change, because Los Angeles doesn’t belong to AIPAC, right? Los Angeles doesn’t belong to crypto or big AI lobbies. And Los Angeles certainly doesn’t belong to corporate real estate developers. And so, it belongs to us.

AMY GOODMAN: During the primary, Gonzales-Torres was working two jobs — in education, supporting formerly incarcerated students; as an affordable housing advocate — also served as president of the Highland Park neighborhood.

For more, we go to Washington, D.C., where we’re joined by Congressmember-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres.

Thank you so much for being with us. It’s great to have you. You’re in D.C. right now for the incoming congressmembers’ orientation. Can you talk about what you plan to bring to Congress? What are your demands, Congressmember-elect?

REP.-ELECT ANGELA GONZALES-TORRES: Sure. I’m so happy to be here.

Yes, we are in D.C. now. They threw me right in here. Our election was Tuesday, and here we are, ready to hit the ground running and take this information back home and fight for working families like my own.

I am really focused on why I got into this race in the first place, which is that I grew up in this district that has some of the highest costs of incarceration. One of the largest jail systems on the face of the planet is actually in the middle of California’s 34th Congressional District. And we have some of the dirtiest air in all of L.A. County, some of the largest eviction notices issued in the entire city. And I am so proud to be now, hopefully soon, representing one of the largest immigrant populations in the country.

I am really hoping to bring this urgency. I really feel the urgency of this moment, and I’m looking forward to representing Los Angeles with the respect that we deserve.

AMY GOODMAN: And tell us more about your district. You’re right next to where Stephen Miller —

REP.-ELECT ANGELA GONZALES-TORRES: Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN: — grew up. As you are there in Washington for your first days for orientation, he has started —

REP.-ELECT ANGELA GONZALES-TORRES: Yes.

AMY GOODMAN: — his first day, the architect of the immigration crackdown, as the chief of staff of President Trump.

REP.-ELECT ANGELA GONZALES-TORRES: Yeah. First of all, Stephen Miller is a fearmonger. He is a fool. And we definitely saw this coming. I think the Trump administration knew that they were going to lose big this midterm, and I think that this is proof that they’re trying to double down on their cruel and corrupt agenda.

And the reason I got into this race as the daughter of a deportee, as someone that proudly works with formerly incarcerated and undocumented students, is because we are going to need to fight back. And so, while they are trying to lean in on fear, we are going to lean in on love and courage in this time of extreme cowardice. And I’m ready to get to work.

AMY GOODMAN: Can you talk about the race for the House leader, for the House speaker? I mean, you have —

REP.-ELECT ANGELA GONZALES-TORRES: Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN: — a real controversy brewing. In the Senate, it’s around Chuck Schumer, now the Democratic minority leader. In the House, it’s Hakeem Jeffries. And will you be endorsing him for House speaker? In our headlines just now, we talked about progressives demanding new leadership. An online petition urging Democratic Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries to remove himself from the running to become next House speaker has surpassed 1 million signatures, facing mounting opposition over his pro-Israel interests, continued acceptance of corporate PAC money, including from AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. Your thoughts?

REP.-ELECT ANGELA GONZALES-TORRES: As of right now, my vote is no. I know for sure that over 100,000 Angelenos voted for courage. They voted for change. And I think that what I don’t know is what Representative Hakeem Jeffries is offering my community and constituents of California’s 34th Congressional District for their vote. I think I know for sure that the incumbent would have rolled over and handed over the vote without keeping our community in mind, without one community conversation, and that is not the case anymore. Those days are behind us.

And so, respectfully, Representative Hakeem Jeffries will have to work for our vote. And again, we have not spoken yet. I just got here. This is my second day in D.C., and I’m really looking forward to the rest of orientation, learning as much as possible. But I’m really looking forward to getting back home and making sure my community feels heard.

AMY GOODMAN: Can you talk about your father being deported when you were a teenager? And talk about your own district more. You can talk about the critical issues one of the poorest districts in this country face, and the fact that you had, what, at least two jobs while you were running for Congress in order to support yourself.

REP.-ELECT ANGELA GONZALES-TORRES: Right. That is proof alone that anything is possible. We won the primary election while I was working two jobs, but also we had to stretch, you know, $200,000, which might sound like a lot to my neighbors and I, but in this political world, that was proof that anything is possible, and it’s possible not to sell out your community to corporate PACs and corporate donors.

And I think that, for me, the reason why I got into this race, again, is because I, for generations, have seen the same issues over and over and over again — largest eviction notices in the heart of Los Angeles, some of the dirtiest air in all of L.A. County. I mean, kids in East L.A. have lead found in their teeth, while we’re also trying to recover from the Lineage warehouse fire and an oil spill and ICE raids and the warmest year on record with no ACs in our public schools. It’s unacceptable.

And I think that being the — one of the poorest districts in the country, yet part of the fourth-largest economy in the world, I know that Angelenos are some of the hardest-working people you will ever meet. And I am here to represent them in the way that they deserve to be represented. So, we are looking forward to finally having in-person town halls to make sure that, you know, people know that even now in this transition period, they can go to Angela4Congress.com and leave a comment, especially for constituents of CA-34, to make sure that our office is prepared to meet people where they’re at.

AMY GOODMAN: And how do you fight for Medicare for All and abolishing ICE, two of the issues you ran on, as we wrap up this discussion?

REP.-ELECT ANGELA GONZALES-TORRES: Sure. I mean, fortunately, and I have to tell you, the energy here in D.C. is electric. I mean, the Progressive Caucus had a press conference yesterday alone, and you can feel that we are ready to actually fight for these bare minimum things that people should be guaranteed across the country. Medicare for All is bare minimum.

And I think that there’s certainly a difference between former elected officials, that would just co-sponsor or sign on to these bills, and those of us moving into Congress this January, that will actually fight for it and make sure that we’re doing everything that we can to let people know what abolish ICE even means, holding accountable those masked agents that are terrorizing our communities, redirecting those funds back into our districts. And really, it’s an energy that you can feel, and I’m really looking forward to carrying that through this transition, and certainly after we’re all sworn in.

AMY GOODMAN: And as you go off to your next meeting, I’m wondering how you feel in this first national TV broadcast to be standing in the Capitol Rotunda as an incoming congressmember from Los Angeles.

REP.-ELECT ANGELA GONZALES-TORRES: It’s incredible, honestly. Yeah, it’s really — I think, for me, this is exactly where we need to be, because that was a really hard past year and a half, and our community asked us to step up and throw our name in this race because they know I am in these fights already, this fight to get AIPAC and crypto and big AI funding out of our politics, certainly out of California’s Democratic Party. And it’s possible. We just proved that. And I’m really excited and proud that over 100,000 Angelenos made their voices very clear.

AMY GOODMAN: Well, I don’t want you to be late for one of your first meetings —

REP.-ELECT ANGELA GONZALES-TORRES: Thank you so much. Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN: — as congressmember-elect, Angela Gonzales-Torres, democratic socialist, elected to represent California’s 34th Congressional District in Los Angeles.

REP.-ELECT ANGELA GONZALES-TORRES: Yes.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to thank you so much for being with us, in her first national TV broadcast.

This is Democracy Now! Coming up, we look at the crackdown on press freedom in Egypt. We’ll speak with the editor-in-chief of the largest independent newspaper in Egypt, Mada Masr. She faces a criminal trial this week and possible prison. Stay with us.

author: Hend Salama Abo Helow
title: Israel Is Rapidly Turning the Yellow Line Into a Permanent Border in Gaza
content:
Israel is building an earthen wall along the line that marks the ever-expanding territory within Gaza that it controls.

Israel is building an earthen wall along the line that marks the ever-expanding territory within Gaza that it controls.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

During a creative and journalistic writing training program I joined in Gaza City to nurture the skills of emerging writers, one seat remained empty, session after session. It belonged to Sarah, whose name has been changed to protect her identity, and who never managed to escape the brunt of Israeli violence long enough to attend a single session.

Sarah currently lives with her family in a half-demolished home just a few meters from the “Yellow Line” — the ever-shifting, poorly demarcated boundary marked by yellow concrete blocks that is intended to separate areas under Israeli military control from the rest of the Gaza Strip.

Her family was forced to return there after enduring the grim realities of life in displacement camps. Caught between two impossible choices, Sarah lamented, “Venturing outside my home may cost me my life.”

When I reached out to her, curious to know why she had been unable to attend a writing program that remains a distant dream for hundreds of writers, she replied in a grieving voice: “I live beside the Yellow Line in the south, while the sessions are held in Gaza City, and the killing machine is waiting outside my home.”

She described the incessant rattling of drones overhead, the deafening echoes of explosions, the ever-present threat of being targeted by a quadcopter, and the anguished cries of grieving mothers, bereaved fathers, and frightened children.

“Together, these sounds, mingled with deep-seated fear, have turned even the most mundane activities indispensable to our survival into perilous undertakings.”

Meanwhile, the rumbling of bulldozers and the scraping of earth intruded upon Sarah’s daily life. From her window, she watched as a new earthen berm gradually took shape, rising higher and stretching farther with each passing day.

“The Yellow Line keeps creeping forward, while a new earthen berm rises day by day, obscuring our view of what lies beyond it,” Sarah said.

Citing satellite imagery supplied by Planet Labs PBC in July 2026, an Associated Press investigation revealed the construction of a new earthen barrier, resembling a physical border, along stretches of the Yellow Line — a supposedly temporary demarcation separating Israeli-controlled territory from the rest of Gaza pending further withdrawals under the U.S.-brokered ceasefire agreement — and in some places beyond it.

These tall sand embankments cut through demolished Palestinian communities, further entrenching Israel’s expanding area of control.

According to the investigation, the earthen berms have been constructed near Rafah, across Khan Younis, and stretch northward toward Gaza City. By July 2026, they extended for more than 23 kilometers (14 miles), equivalent to more than half the length of Gaza’s approximately 40-kilometer coastline.

These tall sand embankments cut through demolished Palestinian communities, further entrenching Israel’s expanding area of control. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, access-restricted areas had grown to encompass 65 percent of the Gaza Strip by June 2026. Meanwhile, Israeli forces continue clearing and demolishing Palestinian land and homes, in what humanitarian experts describe as a scorched-earth policy and ethnic cleansing.

“My neighborhood was once marked by greenhouses, towering green trees, and flourishing gardens. But it truly breaks my heart to scan the horizon and not catch sight of even a centimeter of greenery anymore,” Sarah said, her voice quivering. “My life is now colored only in grey and blood.”

It appears that Israel has been constructing this barrier since February 2026, justifying its construction on security grounds and equipping it with intelligence and technological assets. Yet this justification is flatly contradicted by the mounting death toll among Gazans near the Yellow Line and its designation as a killing zone for Palestinians attempting to check on their homes or salvage the remnants of their belongings.

“But where can we go?” Sarah told Truthout. “Here, the danger is escalating, and nowhere promises safety. Where else are we supposed to go?”

The continued expansion of the earthen berms has fueled growing concerns among Gazans that this supposedly temporary demarcation may morph into a permanent border.

For Abu Ammar Fares, a 68-year-old retired teacher who has witnessed firsthand some of the most defining turning points in Palestinian history — from the 1967 war and the Al-Aqsa Intifada to the successive wars and military offensives waged on Gaza — this growing fear carries the weight of decades of lived experience.

Yet Fares’s turmoil has only deepened since he fled his four-story home in eastern Al-Bureij refugee camp on October 7, 2023, a house that now lies in ruins beyond the Yellow Line.

“I desperately wished to return to my home, even if it lay in rubble. But the new earthen border has dashed my hopes,” he told Truthout.

The second phase of the U.S.-brokered ceasefire agreement, which was supposed to pave the way for Israel’s withdrawal toward Gaza’s borders according to the agreed-upon road map, remains stagnant. Israel continues its attacks and maintains its grip over large swathes of Gaza, while disputes over Hamas’s disarmament remain unresolved.

“I was cautiously hopeful about the agreement’s phased withdrawal when it was first proposed,” Fares remarked. “But what has unfolded on the ground is in stark contrast to what was promised. Instead of withdrawing, Israel is expanding its control beyond the Yellow Line by erecting more physical barriers and shifting the boundaries further into Gaza.”

Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir openly celebrated Israel’s expanding territorial control over Gaza, declaring, “Gaza is ours.”

As a result, Fares has been unable to find a way to check on the ruins of his home. “Getting close to the earthen berms and the Yellow Line is tantamount to throwing yourself into the jaws of death,” he said.

Like hundreds of thousands of other Palestinians whose homes and belongings lie beyond the newly constructed earthen embankments, Fares fears that Israel is quietly plundering their land.

“I don’t think any of us can call anything our own anymore beyond the Yellow Line,” he said.

He went on to recall what followed the 1967 war, from the construction of Israeli settlements to Israel robbing Palestinians of their belongings and seizing their lands.

“A similar scenario is being repeated,” Fares warned.

But for Kawthar Sader, a Palestinian lawyer, the expression “loss of property” is a misuse of terminology. She argues that it is more precise to say that Palestinians are being deprived of access to, possession of, and enjoyment of their property.

“The distinction between the two is fundamental. The former implies that the right has ceased to exist, while the latter means that the right remains intact. Our role is to preserve that right, keep it alive, and seek compensation for the damage resulting from deprivation of property rights,” she explained.

“I do not see the Yellow Line or the earthen berms as political borders, nor do they confer sovereignty or erase Palestinians’ ownership rights over their land,” Sader continued.

Yet the entrenchment of these physical barriers, coupled with statements from senior Israeli officials, has raised further concerns. Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir openly celebrated Israel’s expanding territorial control over Gaza, calling for the establishment of Israeli settlements throughout the enclave and declaring, “Gaza is ours.”

“From a legal standpoint, even if the ceasefire process remains stagnant, this does not give the Israeli military the green light to plunder Palestinian land or disregard international law,” Sader explained.

Under Article 53 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, the occupying power is prohibited from destroying private or public property unless such destruction is rendered absolutely necessary by military operations.

Sader stressed that the legal standard is not whether the destruction is politically beneficial, serves security interests, or is militarily convenient, but whether it is absolutely necessary for military operations.

“But if the destruction is willful, unjustified by military necessity, and carried out unlawfully and wantonly, Article 147 of the Fourth Geneva Convention serves as a litmus test,” she added.

That provision classifies extensive destruction and appropriation of property, when unjustified by military necessity and carried out unlawfully and wantonly, as a grave breach of international humanitarian law.

“This is precisely what we are witnessing in Israel’s actions in constructing the illegal earthen berms,” she argued.

Sader concluded that satellite imagery provides incriminating evidence of what she described as egregious acts committed by Israeli occupation forces.

“And this is where the battle to preserve our rights begins,” she stressed. “It does not begin merely with the removal of the earthen berms, but long before that, with the preservation of evidence.”

“Every property deed, every map, every official record, every satellite image, every certificate, every civil registry document, and every photograph of a home before it was reduced to rubble serves as evidence of Palestinians’ ownership of their land and their enduring ties to it. Palestinians must never relinquish their rights,” she added.

“Nothing is promising. One hour brings a glimmer of relief, and the very next brings the fear of genocide resuming,” Fares said.

His voice cracking, he added, “We are fed up with tomorrow. We are fed up with the status quo. We are fed up with all the agreements that have never materialized. For one hour, we allow ourselves to feel optimistic, while for the rest of the day, we remain constantly on edge.”

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

title: Seattle Event: Anarchists in the Labor Movement Panel and Discussion
content:
This event is co-sponsored by Black Rose/Rosa Negra

, 

Seattle Organized Anarchists

, and the 

Institute for Anarchist Studies

.




Anarchism emerged as a wing of the workers’ movements in the 19th century. What place do anarchists have in the contemporary labor movement?




Join us for a moderated panel and discussion with anarchists from around the Puget Sound currently engaged in the labor movement as rank-and-file workers, union staffers, and community organizers. 




How do anarchists organize in the workplace? What sets anarchists apart from other political tendencies in labor? How do anarchists relate to unions? And how can anarchists contribute to building workers power from below? 




When:

 Friday, December 4 • 6-8 PM




Where:

 Chinatown-International District, Seattle, WA (specific location details sent upon registration)







Registration is required to attend

!







Click here to register










About the Panelists







JOMO

 is a former healthcare worker and currently organizes with immigrant workers. They write at 

https://substack.com/@chinatowncommune1312













Jorge

 has been organizing in his workplaces for nearly 25 years. Across seven different industries, within four different unions, and in nonunion workplaces too. He has been an elected shop steward, served on contract negotiating committees, organized rank-and-file caucus efforts, and written for Labor Notes. He is a member of 

Black Rose Anarchist Federation/Federación Anarquista Rosa Negra (BRRN)

.













Taylo

r is an anarchist organizer and started organizing with the Seattle Solidarity Network (SeaSol) in the middle 00s. In SeaSol (and alongside many talented organizers) she organized for repeated worker and tenant empowerment through dozens of successful direct action pressure campaigns for stolen wages and stolen deposits, including her own. She is a proud IWW member and currently works as a staff organizer for one of the biggest unions in Washington State. In her staff-work she organizes and advocates for continued rank-and-file worker empowerment by sharing with workers many of the same tactics and strategies acquired through her time in SeaSol and the IWW.

author: Natalia Viana
title: As Big Techs saíram perdedoras das eleições nos EUA?
content:
Quer receber os textos desta coluna em primeira mão no seu e-mail? Assine a newsletter Xeque na Democracia, enviada toda segunda-feira, 12h. Para receber as próximas edições, 

inscreva-se aqui.







Foram pelo menos US$ 800 milhões. Juntos, os bilionários das Big Techs e Criptomoedas 

fazem

 parte dos 20 maiores doadores de campanhas para as eleições de meio de mandato nos EUA. Sozinho, Elon Musk doou quase meio bilhão de dólares. Os investidores Marc Andreessen e Ben Horowitz criaram seu próprio Super Pac – comitê de apoio eleitoral regado a dinheiro privado – chamado Leading the Future apenas para defender pouca regulação federal sobre a IA; arrecadaram US$ 100 milhões.  




Mesmo assim, a campanha eleitoral norte-americana foi repleta de promessas como essa, de Gina Hinojosa, que derrotou o governador republicano no Texas de maneira histórica – o estado não elegia um governador democrata desde 1988. 




“Quando eu for governadora vou propor uma moratória de todas as aprovações de data centers até os legisladores aprovarem leis que protegem os texanos, para dar aos texanos um assento na mesa para decidir se e como os data centers chegarão às suas comunidades”. Uma das suas propostas é fazer uma auditoria sobre os data centers que pediram autorização para usar a rede elétrica do Texas.   




Em especial, 

o embate em torno da construção de data centers tornou-se um dos principais temas de campanha em diferentes regiões dos EUA

. Três dos estados em que a cadeira do Senado mudou de republicano para democrata têm um problema de rápida expansão de data centers: além do Texas, Ohio e Iowa chegam a ter de duas a dez vezes o número médio de data centers por estado.  




Fato é que os eleitores não estão convencidos de que a construção de data centers vai beneficiar suas comunidades.

 E as pesquisas têm apontado para essa insatisfação. 




Uma pesquisa feita pela Ipsos com o Washington Post descobriu que 2/3 dos americanos se opõem à construção de novos data centers, enquanto 57% dizem que a IA é um mal para a sociedade e 67% desaprovam a política de “liberou geral” abraçada pelo governo Trump.




Além dos data centers, a percepção negativa da população quanto à IA, resultado das demissões massivas que já estão ocorrendo, fizeram com que, hoje, defender a desregulação tenha se tornado uma medida pouco popular. 




Portanto, os investimentos dos tech bros não renderam os votos esperados. Eles foram derrotados nas urnas. Parece que essas eleições marcaram a primeira vez que as Big Techs se tornaram uma pauta tóxica.  




Os resultados desta derrota foram sentidos na própria semana eleitoral. Com a resistência à construção desenfreada de infraestrutura necessária para a IA nos EUA, expressa em votos, a perspectiva de uma redução da corrida desenfreada derrubou as bolsas pelo mundo; Wall Street levou um tombo – perdeu 3 trilhões de valor em apenas um dia. A CEO da Meta já reconheceu que será mais difícil construir novos data centers, e a empresa deve se concentrar em ampliar a capacidade dos já existentes.   




Espera-se uma nova onda regulatória, impulsionada pelos democratas eleitos em diferentes estados e também no Congresso. 




Na Câmara dos Deputados, há um projeto de lei proposto por deputados democratas que prevê supervisão federal sobre modelos de IA mais poderosos e impedir que os estados tenham poder de fazer leis livremente. No Senado, um grupo bipartidário está articulando a criação de um padrão federal de segurança para inteligência artificial (IA) que permitiria ao governo federal proibir o lançamento de produtos considerados inseguros.     




O provável futuro presidente da Câmara dos Deputados, Hakeem Jeffries – que deve ser o primeiro negro a assumir o cargo – tem prometido que o Congresso tem que agir para criar uma regulação para a IA. 




“Nós queremos garantir que os empreendedores norte-americanos e empresas possam continuar liderando neste espaço e não ser superados pelo Partido Comunista Chinês. Mas, por outro lado, temos que garantir que o povo americano de fato goze dos benefícios da inteligência artificial sem ser sujeito às suas desvantagens muito reais, muito graves e perigosas”, afirmou em um evento de campanha.




Ele já disse que concorda com a ideia de uma moratória no desenvolvimento de IA, algo que já foi aprovado em diferentes estados. 




“É [um perigo] muito real, em que pese o que o Donald Trump diga sobre o assunto, e requer ação imediata de modo consistente com o que algumas das vozes mais proeminentes sobre IA no país estão dizendo, referente a desacelerar as coisas para proteger a saúde, a segurança e o bem estar do povo americano”. 




Hakeem prometeu, primeiro, revisar todos os Projetos de Lei atualmente no Congresso, antes de liderar um esforço por uma legislação federal. Segundo a imprensa, ele considera montar um comitê parlamentar para investigar e exigir depoimentos de executivos das empresas enquanto os deputados elaboram uma política mais abrangente – um dos principais problemas, que tem se tornado crescentemente perigoso e fora de controle, são os ciberataques liderados por ou conjuntamente com IA nos últimos meses.      




Do seu lado, as Big Techs já vêm se preparando para refrear a sanha regulatória dos democratas – com o bom e velho lobby. 




Quem começou foi a Meta, que substituiu o fervoroso republicano Joel Kaplan como chefe de políticas públicas globais e, ao mesmo tempo, contratou um democrata, Brian Rice, que chegou a ser assessor do ex-secretário de Estado John Kerry durante o governo de Barack Obama, para chefiar as relações governamentais com o governo dos EUA. A Open IA contratou a filha do senador democrata Chuck Schumer como chefe de relações governamentais. Já a Anthropic e a Nvidia contrataram ex-membros do governo de Barack Obama para chefiarem seus departamentos de lobby. 




Como o rechaço vai se desenrolar em novas leis para limitar o poder exacerbado das Big Techs e preservar algumas salvaguardas numa era em que a IA parece estar saindo do controle de vez, é algo que ainda veremos. Mas é importante escutar com cuidado as palavras dos democratas eleitos para observarmos que, como sempre, sua preocupação é com o público interno e não com os danos causados pela tecnologia fora do seu país (afinal, democratas acreditam tanto no excepcionalismo dos EUA quanto os republicanos). 




Mais do que sermos otimistas sobre o que pode vir em termos de regulação 

Made in USA

, a derrota das Big Techs nos EUA representa uma janela de oportunidade para que novas leis sejam aprovadas pelo mundo. Aqui no Brasil, deveríamos fazer valer essa rara oportunidade, que está afinada, aliás, com o recado que foi dado nas urnas no segundo turno das nossas eleições.

author: Sharon Lerner
title: Trump Admin Awarded $40M in Federal Contracts to Firm Linked to President’s Sons
content:
Donald Jr. and Eric Trump work as advisers for a firm that invested in the awardee’s parent company in February.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The Trump administration awarded a small biosecurity company nearly $40 million to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases just months after a firm linked to President Donald Trump’s elder sons invested in its parent company, according to records and interviews.

The contracts, one to screen for Ebola in several U.S. airports and the other to respond to disease outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo, are seven times the total value of government contracts the company had directly received before.

The company, XpresTest, has years of experience monitoring for COVID-19 and other diseases for the government at U.S. airports. That makes its parent, XWELL, an unusual hybrid, selling both spa treatments and biosecurity services. Last year, it made most of its money from waxing salons and airport spas that offer manicures, massages and “chakra beds.”

The contracts are the latest example of the president’s family benefiting financially from his administration’s actions. And the stakes for these deals are particularly high. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, an Ebola outbreak has killed more than 5,000 people this year, and the federal government is trying to stop the pathogen from coming to the U.S.

XpresTest has never worked with Ebola or provided biosecurity services abroad, let alone in the kind of volatile locales it’s now expected to work in. The CEO of its parent company, Ezra Ernst, said XpresTest won both contracts in a competitive bidding process and pointed to its years of experience doing screening for COVID-19 and other pathogens at American airports. But even he acknowledged that working internationally is “a new thing for us” and expressed uncertainty about being able to complete the work in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

“This is a risky contract. I’m not sure we can do it,” Ernst said in an interview.

Jeremy Konyndyk, who helped oversee the U.S. government’s response to a 2014 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, said there are some parallels between monitoring for COVID-19 and Ebola at airports, but he said it’s concerning that the government would award such a lucrative contract to a company that has no experience in Africa.

“There are countless organizations in the world that have decades of experience doing this work,” Konyndyk said. “I have to wonder why the hell they’re not going with someone who has actually done this before.”

Under previous administrations, the U.S. government addressed international disease outbreaks in partnership with the World Health Organization. But Trump withdrew from the group last year, dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development, which handled much of this work, and dramatically scaled back the global presence of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

At the same time, the State Department launched the America First Global Health Strategy, which calls for the U.S. to use aid to foreign countries to “promote American companies and American innovations abroad.” This March, the State Department announced it would be giving up to $4.5 billion in funding for various purposes, including responding to infectious disease outbreaks.

Under that program, XPresTest was awarded $20 million. Other funding went to better-known global aid nonprofits, including International Medical Corps, Save the Children and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, whose awards ranged from $25 million to $35 million.

The CDC also awarded XPresTest a contract, for $18.8 million.

In response to questions from ProPublica about XPresTest and its parent company, XWELL, the State Department noted the firm’s previous work screening for diseases at airports under a contract with the CDC and said its own award was made “through a competitive process that builds on this successful model.”

The CDC did not respond to a request for comment.

A spokesperson for the president’s sons Donald Jr. and Eric Trump said that they are “merely passive, minority investors in a fund that invested in this company,” and that they had no “involvement in or knowledge regarding the negotiation or procurement of any of its contracts, including any government contracts.”

“Both are private citizens who hold no government positions, broken no laws and who have every right to pursue lawful business and investment opportunities,” the spokesperson said.

The Trump sons’ connection to XWELL was established in February, when a fund called American Ventures invested in the company. The fund was launched by Dominari Holdings, a small financial firm with offices inside Trump Tower in New York. The leaders of Dominari hired the Trump sons as advisers after their father was elected to a second term and granted them a stake of more than 10% in Dominari.

Anthony Hayes, the CEO of Dominari Holdings, told ProPublica, “We have never seen or even heard of Don or Eric using their family name to influence the granting of a government contract.”

American Ventures has taken stakes in other companies that have benefited from Trump administration actions. The Florida-based drone company Powerus got a contract worth up to $90 million from the U.S. Air Force five months after the Trumps’ involvement was announced. Through American Ventures, Donald Jr. and Eric Trump also are acquiring a stake in a critical minerals group that has received U.S. government support to mine for tungsten in Kazakhstan. The Trumps have described themselves as passive investors who do not advocate for the companies they have stakes in before their father’s government.

XWELL was founded in 2006 as a line of airport-based spas that provided massages and facials. During the pandemic, the company, then known as XpresSpa Group, got $5.5 million from the CDC to offer travelers COVID-19 testing. It also collected waste from airplane toilets to check for new viral strains. It has done similar work for at least one other company that has received government contracts.

In January, XWELL announced that it was hiring a former senior adviser at the CDC who created and led the agency’s traveler surveillance program. The firm said the move was part of a plan to expand “its traveler-based pathogen surveillance capabilities to support international travel hubs and large-scale mass gathering events worldwide.”

The following month, American Ventures invested about $30 million in XWELL. The company had lost money the previous year. “We were so cash-strapped, close to bankrupt,” its CEO said.

Its valuation before the cash infusion was just $3 million. In exchange, American Ventures got a roughly 10% stake in the company to start, with an option to essentially print and sell millions of shares in the future.

Why American Ventures would invest so much in XWELL is unclear. In other cases, when the fund has invested in similar tiny publicly traded companies, some of those firms have moved into hot new sectors and drawn publicity for their connection to the Trumps, then Dominari has offloaded shares. In this case, there is no indication it has sold any of its stake yet.

In June, XpresTest was awarded the CDC contract for what a public notice about the grant said was “Ebola entry screening services.”

XpresTest then received the State Department grant for “rapid, effective, and coordinated outbreak response” to infectious disease threats in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in September, according to a government database. The company is also planning to work in Kenya and Morocco. XWELL’s website shows it is now hiring specialists in Ebola response training and biosecurity in the U.S.

In July, after XpresTest was awarded the CDC contract, XWELL announced plans to sell the subsidiary along with its line of spas to a private facial spa company. Ernst, the CEO, said the government contracts played a role in the $13 million sale price and will follow XpresTest to the new company.

That means XWELL, the company that the Trump-linked investment fund took a stake in, will benefit financially from the Trump administration contracts if the sale closes, even though it won’t be involved in doing the work for the government.

XWELL said in a public filing that the sale was part of an effort “to pursue a new direction in the national security sector.” Ernst said he didn’t know the exact plans but thought the parent company might be looking to work with the Department of Defense.

XWELL did not announce either of XpresTest’s biosecurity contracts, which recently became public in federal contracting disclosures. Public companies like XWELL are required to report so-called material events, developments that could affect their share price, such as a large government contract. XWELL has publicized previous work for the federal government, including a $2 million, eight-week pilot program for testing COVID-19 in 2021.

When asked why his firm didn’t announce the awards, Ernst gave various reasons, including the possibility that XPresTest might wind up not being able to do the work — either because of its own inexperience working internationally or because the Trump administration might suddenly shift priorities and only pay for a fraction of the contract.

“None of these contracts are guaranteed,” he said.

The biosecurity awards add to the questions about the Trump family’s enrichment during his second term. The Trump family’s business activities extend far beyond Dominari and American Ventures. The president himself has made more than $1 billion from cryptocurrency ventures whose value has ballooned as his administration has taken a friendly stance to the industry. And other companies backed by his sons Donald Jr. and Eric have received billions of dollars in federal deals. Earlier this year, ProPublica reported that the Pentagon granted a small North Carolina startup linked to Trump Jr. a $620 million loan after a top aide to the president intervened on the company’s behalf. The Pentagon denied preferential treatment, and a spokesperson for Trump Jr. said he played no role.

The Trumps’ financial ties to government deals and actions are expected to be a primary focus of Congress in the coming months after Democrats won control of both the Senate and the House in last week’s midterm elections.

“When the government is corrupted for personal gain over the public interest, Americans lose trust and taxpayer dollars are wasted,” Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, wrote in a letter to colleagues last week.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $50,000 in the next 10 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Sophia Cope
title: U.S. Supreme Court Deals Final Blow to Corporate Human Rights Accountability
content:
For the past two decades, the U.S. Supreme Court has been slowly weakening the Alien Tort Statute (ATS), a key human rights law that allows foreign nationals to sue persons or entities in civil court for harms resulting from violations of international law. The court’s recent ruling in Cisco Systems, Inc. v. Doe I dealt the law a final blow, foreclosing—absent new legislation by Congress—any future ability by plaintiffs to use the law to hold technology companies accountable for aiding and abetting human rights abuses. EFF filed multiple amicus briefs in the case, including most recently in the Supreme Court.

The ATS was passed by the very first Congress in 1789 and in just a few words gives U.S. federal courts jurisdiction to hear civil claims brought by foreign nationals against defendants who violated “the law of nations or a treaty of the United States." There has been a longstanding question about what counts as a valid civil claim under “the law of nations.”

In Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain (2004), the Supreme Court had noted three historical international law claims that the First Congress likely had in mind: violation of safe conducts, infringement of the rights of ambassadors, and piracy, collectively known as the Blackstone Three.

The Sosa court also held that federal courts may recognize other substantive causes of action under the ATS if they reflect international norms that are “specific, universal, and obligatory,” stating that this “door is still ajar subject to vigilant doorkeeping, and thus open to a narrow class of international norms today.”

Thus, the Sosa court recognized that the ATS could be used to bring claims related to historical violations of international law as well as select newer claims reflecting modern concepts of human rights.

In Cisco, the Supreme Court overruled the second Sosa holding. The majority held that the current case, a technology company aiding and abetting torture and other human rights abuses, was beyond the scope of the original three ATS claims and it was not for the court to create new ways of enforcing international law. The court said:

[W]e close the door that Sosa cracked to judicially created ATS liability. We do not disturb Sosa’s holding that the ATS is a jurisdictional statute; nor do we revisit its assumption that causes of action are available for torts corresponding to the Blackstone three. We conclude only that Sosa was overly optimistic in its prediction that there might be a narrow class of cases in which courts may create ATS actions without infringing on the prerogatives of the political branches. In truth, this class is a null set.

What result for this case? Cisco argues that the Ninth Circuit erred in holding that aiding-and-abetting liability exists under the ATS for the torts alleged by the plaintiffs. Cisco is correct. Courts cannot create new rights of action to remedy violations of international law, so there is necessarily no liability for aiding and abetting such violations. Plaintiffs’ ATS claims against Cisco must be dismissed.

The Supreme Court’s ending of the plaintiffs’ case against Cisco is hugely disappointing given that the case has been going on since 2011 and the Ninth Circuit in 2023 allowed the case to move forward in an excellent and well-reasoned opinion. The court held, in part:

We conclude that Plaintiffs’ allegations, accepted as true, are sufficient to state a plausible claim that Cisco provided essential technical assistance to the douzheng [violent struggle] of Falun Gong with awareness that the international law violations of torture, arbitrary detention, disappearance, and extrajudicial killing were substantially likely to take place.

The plaintiffs sued Cisco for the company’s role in building and deploying the “Golden Shield,” also referred to as “The Great Firewall of China”—a vast surveillance system that Cisco began building in the late 1990s and that the company customized to enable the Chinese government to target disfavored minorities, including members of the Falun Gong religion.

The thirteen plaintiffs—Falun Gong practitioners—alleged arrest, detention, and torture, including of themselves and family members, at least one of whom died by beating while being detained. The allegations were horrific: the plaintiffs were placed in forced labor camps, beaten with steel rods, shocked with electric batons, and endured sleep deprivation and violent force-feeding.

Importantly, the plaintiffs also alleged that their private emails, text messages, and other information—intercepted by the Golden Shield—were shown to them and used as part of their torture and forced conversion sessions, which included threats to their family members and others who had communicated with them.

And now, Cisco is off the hook for all of this.

As we argued in our amicus brief to the Supreme Court, a robust federal statute is necessary given that voluntary and informal mechanisms of corporate human rights accountability are inadequate.

The plaintiffs filed their lawsuit in 2011. The following year, in 2012, Cisco first published its Global Human Rights Policy. Since then, the company has never provided redress to the plaintiffs, despite its currently operative human rights policy stating:

Where we have identified that we have caused or contributed to an adverse human rights impact, we are committed to providing access to and cooperating in remediation for affected individuals, workers, and communities through legitimate processes.

What’s more, the Associated Press conducted an extensive 2025 investigation, which recently won the Pulitzer Prize, further mapping Cisco’s and other American tech companies’ involvement in creating China’s surveillance state over the past three decades. When questioned by the AP reporters, the companies dismissed any notion of human rights obligations and simply “said they adhere to relevant export controls, laws and regulations where they operate.”

In short, Cisco’s commitment to human rights is a fiction.

Given that the U.S. Supreme Court has effectively read the ATS into non-existence, Congress must now step up. While there might be other avenues for redress including under state law, there must also be a comprehensive federal human rights law allowing any plaintiff to hold American companies—especially technology companies—accountable for aiding and abetting human rights abuses, with knowledge or intent that those abuses would occur, and whether the victims suffered those abuses in the U.S. or in foreign countries.

The implications of this gap in U.S. human rights law are significant. As Prof. Harold Koh considered:

[T]he Justices should ask whether affording such immunity in Cisco would implicitly signal to U.S. companies that they could not be held liable for assisting the U.S. government in committing gross violations. Such violations could include constructing a mass surveillance system that may be used to surveil, persecute, retaliate against, and punish real and perceived opponents and constructing systems that autonomously commit war crimes.

American companies should not have a free pass to build out surveillance states (or other technologically sophisticated systems) that not only violate personal privacy or facilitate censorship, but that can also lead to real-world physical violence and even death.
