On 25 October, the “Student List” won a projected 140 of 250 seats in the Serbian parliament, defeating the ruling party that has been in power for 14 years. The electoral victory comes on the back of a student movement that began on 1 of November 2024, when a newly renovated canopy fell at the railway station in Novi Sad and killed sixteen people. Since then, people in Serbia have organised mass protests and assemblies.

We reached out to Klasna Solidarnost (Class Solirarity), founded in Belgrade in 2016, which grew out of an anarcho-syndicalist movement. Its members continue to participate in student occupations while critiquing electoral strategies. They are also active in antifascism, solidarity with Palestine, antimilitarism, support for workers, and the “Solidarna kuhinja” free kitchen, as well as political analysis and publications.

The mainstream media has presented the student movement as “decentralised” and highlighted the appointing of non-politicians to parliament; is this an accurate reflection of the movement now?

The appointment of non-politicians to parliament is one of the main talking points of the Student List. There were over 160 candidates with PhDs on the list, which was highlighted as a key reason why the new government should be “better” than the old one in which it turned out that even some ministers had fake PhD diplomas. The Student List basically has a technocratic structure and by what we’ve seen so far, it aims to create a “government of experts” which is perfectly in line with the dominant neoliberal ideology that convinces us that the society will be better as a whole if we have experts leading the government.

For us as anarchists, this of course is a fairy tale because we know how technocratic governments ended in countries like Italy and Greece in the last 10-15 years, where they simply ushered in the most brutal neoliberal reforms, bringing down the life standard of the working class even more than their predecessors. And this is actually one of the key elements that show us there probably won’t be much improvement in the working class’s life standard.

During the Student List’s electoral campaign, the focus was on defeating the political mafia regime of the SNS (Serbian Progressive Party), which had been in power for 14 years. The movement focused on the regime’s criminal acts and massive corruption scandals, but it barely mentioned any economic measures to improve the everyday lives of the working class.

Now that the SNS regime is finally gone, it remains to be seen what the economic policy of the new government will be, but from what we’ve heard so far, there isn’t any mention of substantial changes in the economic position of Serbia as a client-state of the European Union, and a partial economic partner of the US, China, and Russia.

How does it compare to former “decentralised” parliamentary movements such as Podemos in Spain?

It’s quite problematic for us that a decentralised, direct-democratic movement ended up fighting to replace one capitalist elite in power with another. Compared with Podemos, one key difference is that Podemos was explicitly a leftist movement addressing some of the working class’s pain points in Spain. Of course, as all leftist movements that participate in capitalist parliamentary politics, they ended up in reactionary politics, without introducing any benefits for the working class once they gained power.

The Student List, on the other hand, isn’t leftist in any way. It’s essentially a broad liberal right-wing candidate list, which may well split into different factions once the government is formed. In fact, given the major differences between candidates, it would be logical to see the Student List establish multiple political parties, ranging from extreme neoliberal to centre-right and conservative. There isn’t an even remotely left-wing current among the Student List candidates.

One of the key lessons from the history of the movement in Serbia for us as anarchists is that in the absence of a massive anarchist movement capable of effectively participating in the assemblies, the dominant, neoliberal ideology and its political forces were the ones who won, despite the movement being based on anarchist organising methods. The method isn’t enough if you don’t have a movement capable of articulating the ideology behind it. We saw how an anarchist organising method was abused to oust one pro-EU capitalist government and install another pro-EU capitalist government in power.

Can you tell us about decentralised organisation in Serbia in general: what are Zborovi and plenums? How widespread have these sorts of leaderless structures become?

Zborovi and plenums are the same thing, just in different contexts. Both words mean “direct-democratic assembly”. A plenum is a student assembly of a specific faculty, while a zbor is a people’s assembly, usually for a specific neighborhood or a small town.

The student movement that developed after the state murder in Novi Sad on November 1st 2024 was based on Blokadni kuvar (Occupation Cookbook), a short anarchist student book written by comrades in Zagreb, Croatia, after the massive student blockade wave in the country in 2009. That occupation wave was inspired by the first faculty occupations in Serbia in 2006 and 2007. At that time, there were close connections between politically active anarchists in Serbia and Croatia, which resulted in shared experiences, ultimately resulting in the birth of the Occupation Cookbook, which Serbian anarchists then republished in Belgrade in 2011, creating a blockade blueprint that can easily be distributed. Dozens of Occupation Cookbooks were distributed among students in November 2024, ultimately leading to the adoption of firm direct democracy among students. For coordination between faculty plenums, confederal direct democracy was adopted.

However, it was far from ideal. In fact, on many faculties, political interest groups, liberal NGOs and members of various political parties tried from the start to manipulate the direct democratic mechanics. While the radical left elements of the student assemblies fought the liberal right-wing parts of the movement as best as they could, in the end the liberal current won and essentially ousted any leftist elements of the movement by marginaliszing them.

People's assemblies had a critical role

From our perspective, the truly direct-democratic period of the student movement lasted between November 2024 and February 2025, when the liberal elements managed to consolidate power because initially they were disorganised and confused about direct democracy. They were used to hierarchical, authoritarian structures, and since plenums are leaderless, egalitarian structures, they couldn’t just corrupt prominent individuals. Their financial and infrastructural backing from individuals and political organisations keen on taking ruling power in Serbia enabled them to outplay the radical-left elements of the movement and impose complete liberal ideological and political hegemony.

Of course, anarchists continued participating in the movement’s activities that retained a progressive character, which is especially true for the zborovi. In spring 2025, the plenums published an open letter to the people of Serbia, calling on them to begin self-organising into people’s assemblies. Soon after, assemblies began popping up across Serbia. In major cities like Belgrade, there were more than a dozen assemblies across various neighbourhoods and inter-assembly coordination was established.

The people’s assemblies had a critical role in expanding the struggle from the faculties into the streets. In fact, the assemblies opened up a new frontier for people, because they suddenly realised they could be used to organise around local issues, such as local criminal landlords, infrastructure problems, ecological questions, and even antifascist events.

Even though the movement ended up focused on an electoral victory, we believe there is still potential for radicalisation, especially now that we’ll have a new capitalist government. As anarchists, we believe unavoidable disillusionment with the new government, from a working-class, anti-capitalist perspective, could catalyse radicalisation in both student and people’s assemblies.

The movement against the government in Serbia has faced intense repression by the state, including the use of a sonic weapon, mass arrests and hospitalisation, and intimidation at ballot boxes. How has the movement sustained itself in spite of this?

Yes, state repression was intense in some periods of the movement, but it was essentially non-existent during extended periods. The first blockade of the Faculty of Dramatic Arts in Belgrade was a reaction to an attack by SNS party members on a student protest. In the beginning, a common form of violence was the attack on student protests with cars, during which multiple students were injured by SNS regime supporters who rammed their cars into protests. In fact, the state chose to avoid any direct police repression up until one of the major protests on the 15th of March 2025, when apparently a sonic weapon was used on thousands of people in Belgrade during the 16 minutes of silence for the 16 victims of the state murder in Novi Sad. The state continues to deny the use of a sonic weapon to this day.

After that, the state entered a new period of relative silence, until the massive protest in Belgrade on the 28th of June 2025, after which riots broke out. This period lasted over a week, and that is when we witnessed mass police oppression, brutal beatings of protestors across Serbia, as well as coordination between police and fascist state thugs in civilian clothes who began systematically attacking protestors.

There was another wave of riots at the end of last summer when organised state-backed thugs began attacking student protests. However, after that wave, repression and state violence dramatically subsided, leading to a year of relative calm, both on the student movement’s side and the state’s activities to undermine it with violence. Both sides focused on an electoral campaign through a propaganda war.

So although these episodes of state repression have been violent, they were a very short period during the last two years. And even during the riots, the scale of state repression wasn’t even remotely comparable to the violence and repression horizontal movements experience in Western Europe, like the student movement in France during the past month, where we saw thousands of arrests, brutal violence, and even mutilation of protesters.

What does the fall of SNS mean for the repression (both by state and non-state actors) of anarchist organising in Serbia?

The anarchist movement wasn’t under much repression in Serbia during the SNS government’s time in power, in fact most of the repression against our movement happened during the previous government of the Democratic Party (DS), between 2009 and 2011 when anarchists in Serbia were being arrested for numerous acts of protests, including for organising a protest against the then largest-ever NATO conference in Europe, which was held in Belgrade.

During the SNS government, state repression was much more focused on the liberal opposition than on anarchists or other leftists. One reason is that liberal opposition parties challenged the SNS regime by seeking to take over political power, and they were correctly perceived as the main danger. Regarding non-state actors such as fascist and neonazi groups, there weren’t many problems with them in the previous period, and we don’t expect any in the future, however, we remain vigilant as always in order to firmly stand our ground and physically protect our members and events.

It remains to be seen how the new liberal right-wing government will treat the anarchist movement, especially since we plan to actively contribute to the movement’s radicalization by focusing on targeted critique of the new government’s moves.

Is there anything else you think our readers should know about the situation in Serbia, and do you have any ways they can support you?

The best way to support Klasna solidarnost is to share our publications online or translate and publish our articles about current developments in Serbia to spread the word about an anarchist perspective from inside the movement. When there’s such deep political turmoil in a region, it’s easy for observers elsewhere to jump to conclusions and assume things are more radical than they are. We’ve seen this from people abroad who think there’s some kind of “revolution” going on in Serbia, when in fact what happened was a government change driven by a truly grassroots direct-democratic movement, but no systematic, anticapitalist change.

The change is welcomed and necessary as a step toward building a radical, anticapitalist movement in Serbia, but it’s in no way a revolutionary change. It’s more of a shift within the liberal capitalist right-wing, supported by the EU, which used the grassroots movement as a tool for regime change.

We anticipate that the period ahead in Serbia will be extremely politically volatile, with many dangers as different interest groups fighting for power within the new government. For us anarchists, this is the time to return the movement to its radical, direct-democratic roots, now that electoral politics are out of the picture. It’s time to build alternative structures that won’t focus on parliamentary politics, but on systemic change that challenges the logic of the capitalist socioeconomic order.

author: Chris Walker
title: Massie Files 8 Articles of Impeachment Against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
content:
The articles charge Hegseth with waging illegal wars, engaging in extrajudicial killings, and suppressing free speech.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) has filed multiple articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and is forcing a vote on the measure as soon as this week.

Massie has leveled eight separate impeachment charges against Hegseth, accusing him of unlawful war or military actions in Iran, Yemen, and Venezuela; “ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties”; engaging in extrajudicial killings; and suppressing free speech rights.

The impeachment resolution makes several mentions of the fact that President Donald Trump never sought congressional authority to wage a war on Iran, and that subsequent War Powers Act deadlines expired without any consequences. (Indeed, the articles of impeachment suggest that the White House violated at least three different sections of that law.)

“Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation notwithstanding the absence of congressional authorization, an attack upon the United States giving rise to the national emergency contemplated by law, or an imminent threat requiring immediate defensive action, thereby substituting unlawful executive action for the constitutional and statutory judgment of Congress,” the document states.

The document concludes by declaring that Hegseth “has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to civilians, the lawful conduct of United States military operations, the integrity and credibility of the United States Armed Forces, and the Constitution if allowed to remain in office.”

An impeachment vote could happen as soon as this week. If a vote does happen, it’s likely the measure will move forward, as a number of Republican lawmakers will likely join the entire Democratic conference in voting to impeach the defense secretary.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) has voiced support for the measure. “I’m a hard yes,” he said when asked over the weekend about Massie’s impeachment plans.

Hegseth’s removal from office is a different story. It is unlikely that the current Senate will vote to remove Hegseth from his position — but it’s possible that Trump will demand his resignation before a Senate trial even occurs, seeking to distance himself from Hegseth in the wake of Republicans’ midterm losses, which have been widely attributed to voters’ frustrations with rising prices due to the Iran war.

While Trump has publicly said that he has no intention of giving Hegseth the boot, the president has reportedly been surveying members of the White House on whether Hegseth should be replaced. Notably, Trump made a similar comment regarding his former Chief of Staff Susie Wiles before she was forced to resign late last week.

Even pro-Iran war Republicans are skeptical of Hegseth, with one GOP lawmaker telling Axios that the Defense Secretary’s rhetoric has been “very damaging” in the party’s efforts to justify the war to the public ahead of the midterm elections.

Americans are largely supportive of impeaching Hegseth. In an Economist/YouGov poll conducted mid-September, 51 percent of Americans said they back impeaching Hegseth over the administration “starting a war with Iran without authorization by Congress.” Only 34 percent of Americans disagreed.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $50,000 in the next 10 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

title: فریدریش انگلس و نقد اقتصاد سیاسی   ِ   مارکس
content: مقالۀ «طرح‌واره‌ای برای نقد اقتصاد سیاسی» به قلم انگلس در سال۱۸۴۳ ، نقطۀ عزیمت اثر سترگی شد که مارکس چهار دهۀ پایانی عمر خویش را صرف نگارش آن کرد. با این حال، انگلس در هیچ‌یک از نوشته‌های متأخر خود، که مدعی بازنمایی و تبیین دیدگاه‌های مارکس بود، نتوانست آن ابعاد بنیادینی از اندیشۀ مارکس را دریابد که خودِ مارکس آن‌ها را حیاتی و اساسی می‌دانست. از آنجا که نوشته¬های انگلس تأثیری ژرف بر قرائت‌های بعدی از کتاب سرمایه بر جای گذاشته‌اند، اذعان به این غفلت و کاستی می‌تواند به ما یاری رساند تا مقصود و غایت واقعی مارکس را در پژوهش‌هایش بازشناسیم.

title: Aufruf zur Unterstützung unseres Kooperationspartners Tacheles e.V.
content:
„

Das Jahresende nähert sich, es ist Zeit einmal Bilanz zu ziehen. Der Verein Tacheles wurde im Februar 1994 aus einer Betroffeneninitiative von Sozialleistungsbeziehenden gegründet und existiert also seit fast 30 Jahren. Seitdem führen wir Sozial- und Existenzsicherungsberatung auf lokaler Ebene durch. Im letzten Jahr haben wir rund 1000 Beratungsanfragen vor Ort beraten. Außerdem bieten wir wöchentlich eine bundesweite Telefonberatung an, ebenso kollegiale Beratung in Vernetzung mit anderen Beratungsstrukturen. (…) Um diese Arbeit fortzusetzen, brauchen wir Solidarität und Unterstützung, und zwar EURE! Daher möchten und müssen wir dazu auffordern, unterstützt Tacheles. Wir brauchen Eure Spenden, um diese Arbeit auch im nächsten Jahr fortsetzen zu können. Der Verein ist auf Eure Unterstützung angewiesen, ohne würde es eng werden. Daher: wer sich an der Finanzierung beteiligen will und kann, findet hier die Möglichkeiten: 

https://tacheles-sozialhilfe.de/verein/spenden.html

 

…“ 

Aufruf vom 23.11.2023

 

 mehrfach bekräftigt, siehe nun den von 2026:







Spendenaufruf: Soziale Rechte massiv unter Druck – Tacheles braucht jetzt Eure Unterstützung! 

 


„

Wenn das Jobcenter nicht zahlt, fehlt das Geld für Lebensmittel. Wenn die Miete monatelang offenbleibt, droht der Verlust der Wohnung. Wenn Leistungen rechtswidrig verweigert werden, geraten Menschen in existenzielle Not. Dann braucht es schnelle, fachkundige und unabhängige Unterstützung. Dafür steht Tacheles seit bald 35 Jahren.


Die Verschärfungen im Sozialrecht erhöhen den Druck auf Leistungsberechtigte. Menschen werden verunsichert, unter Generalverdacht gestellt und mit dem Entzug ihrer Existenzgrundlage bedroht. Gerade jetzt braucht es eine Organisation, die sich einmischt, Behörden widerspricht und Betroffene bei der Durchsetzung ihrer Rechte unterstützt.


Wir beraten und unterstützen jedes Jahr Tausende Menschen: persönlich in Wuppertal, per E-Mail, in der bundesweiten Telefonberatung und durch direkte Vertretung gegenüber Sozialbehörden. Wir prüfen Bescheide, intervenieren bei ausbleibenden Leistungen und helfen, drohenden Wohnungs- und Energieverlust abzuwenden. Wir machen Missstände öffentlich und fordern Verantwortliche zum Handeln auf.


Unser Wissen steht auch allen zur Verfügung, die andere unterstützen 

(…) Wir erhalten keine öffentliche Förderung. Unsere Arbeit finanzieren wir ausschließlich durch Spenden und eigene Einnahmen, etwa aus Newsletteranzeigen und gewerblichen Verzeichniseinträgen. Vieles wird seit Jahrzehnten durch ehrenamtliches Engagement und Arbeit an der Belastungsgrenze möglich gemacht. Um diese Arbeit fortzusetzen, brauchen wir EURE finanzielle Unterstützung

…“ 

Aufruf vom 08.11.2026 von und bei Tacheles

 

 mit Spendenformular etc.




Spendenaufruf für Tacheles e.V. 2025: Gemeinsam gegen soziale Ausgrenzung!




„

Das Jahresende nähert sich und es ist trübe im Land.  Immer wieder erreichen uns Rückmeldungen von Menschen, die unsere Arbeit so wichtig finden und sich dafür  bedanken. Jetzt besteht die Möglichkeit, dies praktisch zu tun und dies mit einer Spende an den Verein Tacheles e.V. zu honorieren. (…) Der seit über 30 Jahren bestehende Verein ist ein bundesweit bekannter Leuchtturm für soziale Gerechtigkeit und Empowerment. All diese Tätigkeiten erfolgen ohne öffentliche Förderung. Tacheles finanziert sich ausschließlich durch Spenden sowie durch eigenwirtschaftliche Tätigkeiten wie Newsletteranzeigen oder gewerbliche Einträge im Adressverzeichnis. Auch die umfangreiche und hochqualifizierte Beratungsarbeit wird seit Jahrzehnten durch weitgehend ehrenamtliches Engagement und Selbstausbeutung getragen

…“ 

Spendenaufruf vom 09.11.2025 bei Tacheles

 

 – siehe mehr Informationen in







Thomé Newsletter 37/2025 – 09.11.2025

 

 und




Thomé Newsletter 38/2025 vom 16.11.2025

 










Aufruf zur Unterstützung von Tacheles 2024




„

Das Jahresende nähert sich, es ist Zeit einmal Bilanz zu ziehen. Der Verein Tacheles wurde im Februar 1994 aus einer Betroffeneninitiative von Sozialleistungsbeziehenden gegründet und existiert also seit über 30 Jahren. Seitdem führen wir Sozial- und Existenzsicherungsberatung auf lokaler Ebene durch. Im letzten Jahr haben wir rund 1000 Beratungsanfragen vor Ort beraten. Außerdem bieten wir wöchentlich eine bundesweite Telefonberatung an, ebenso kollegiale Beratung in Vernetzung mit anderen Beratungsstrukturen. Der Verein Tacheles konfrontiert außerdem die lokalen Behörden mit ihren Defiziten und Missständen und fordert Änderungen ein. (…)


Der Verein ist ein bundesweit bekannter Leuchtturm, der für den Einsatz für soziale Gerechtigkeit und Empowerment steht. All diese Tätigkeiten erfolgen ohne öffentliche Förderung. Tacheles finanziert sich durch Spenden und eigenwirtschaftliche Tätigkeiten, so Newsletteranzeigen und gewerbliche Einträge im Adressverzeichnis. Auch die umfangreiche und hochqualifizierte Beratungsarbeit wird seit Jahrzehnten durch Selbstausbeutung und weitgehend ehrenamtlich sichergestellt. Um diese Arbeit fortzusetzen, brauchen wir Solidarität und Unterstützung, und zwar EURE! Daher möchten und müssen wir dazu auffordern, unterstützt Tacheles. Wir brauchen Eure Spenden, um diese Arbeit auch im nächsten Jahr fortsetzen zu können. Der Verein ist auf Eure Unterstützung angewiesen, ohne würde es eng werden

…“ 

Aufruf vom 09.12.2024

 

 mit beeindruckender Tätigkeitsliste allein für das Jahr 2024 sowie verschiedenen Möglichkeiten zum Spenden




30 Jahre Tacheles e.V. – 30 Jahre Widerstand gegen Entrechtung, Armut und Rassismus: Feier am 24. August 2024 in Wuppertal




„

Seit drei Jahrzehnten kämpfen wir bei Tacheles dafür, eines Tages überflüssig zu sein. Doch unsere Arbeit ist heute wichtiger denn je! Soziale Standards und Teilhabemöglichkeiten, die hart erkämpft wurden, werden zunehmend abgebaut. Arme Menschen, Migrant*innen, Schutzsuchende und vermeintlich „andere“ werden in einer immer populistischeren Debatte diskriminiert. Einseitig geführte Diskussion und die zunehmende Polarisierung zwischen „Gut“ und „Böse“ vergiften das gesellschaftliche Klima und schwächen die letzten Reste unseres solidarischen Gemeinwesens. Erschreckend ist dabei, dass selbst Parteien, die sich demokratisch nennen, diesen Trend aktiv fördern. Dem setzen wir unseren entschlossenen Widerstand entgegen. Und dies nun schon seit 30 Jahren

 zur Feier samt Spenden-Verdoppelungsaktion der Bethe-Stiftung – wir gratulieren und erinnern an den Spendenaufruf!







Da hilft mir jemand – 30 Jahre Tacheles

Video von Medienprojekt Wuppertal vom 24.08.2024 bei youtube

25 Jahre Widerstand gegen Verarmung, Entrechtung und Rassismus – Tacheles e.V. wird 25 – und ist heute notwendiger denn je!

Diffamierungs– und Rufmordkampagne gegen Tacheles und Harald Thomé

author: Ben Smoke
title: US Firm Linked to Gaza Aid Site Massacres to Help With Burnham’s 10-Year Plan
content:
Andy Burnham’s government has hired a US consultancy firm that helped set up a group to run “aid” sites in Gaza where Israeli forces massacred starving civilians. 




Boston Consulting Group (BCG) will advise on Burnham’s his 10-year plan, the Times reported. The plan, which has yet to be published, has been billed as part of the prime minister’s pledge to end decades of neoliberalism in the UK. 




BCG last year had to 

publicly disavow its role

 in creating the notorious Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF), which operated four sites where

 

hundreds

 of people were killed

 while trying to get food in 2025, as Israel deliberately starved Gaza’s population.  




BCG, one of the ‘big three’ global consulting firms, was also involved last year in Donald Trump’s plan to turn Gaza into a riviera, which would effectively amount to ethnic cleansing. As part of those plans, it produced a financial model for a scenario where Palestinians were ethnically cleansed from Gaza. 




It built the model two months after Trump suggested emptying Gaza of its inhabitants, 

the Financial Times reported

.




“Aside from an obvious point that you don’t appoint companies like the Boston Consulting Group if you have any actual intention of ending 40 years of neoliberalism, Trump’s ‘Gaza Riviera’ blueprint is clear ethnic cleansing,” Green party leader Zack Polanski said in a statement. 




“The idea that Andy Burnham has invited these people into the heart of Downing Street shows contempt for the victims of the genocide. They must be removed from this project.” BCG previously employed Burnham’s chief of staff, James Purnell.




BCG said in a July 2025 statement that two of its partners “provided pro bono support to help establish an aid organisation intended to operate alongside other relief efforts” in Gaza. The partners “failed to disclose the full nature of the work. These individuals then carried out subsequent unauthorised work,” it added. “Their actions reflected a serious failure of judgment and adherence to our standards.”




The UK government said BCG is providing a single consultant for the 10-year plan and their support is limited to “specific specialist advice.”

title: Rankin Inlet taxi service shuts down after nearly 6 years
content:
After nearly six years of driving residents around Rankin Inlet, Silu’s Taxi has closed.




Owner Silu Autut announced the closure Nov. 5 on Facebook, saying the cost of keeping vehicles on the road had become too much to justify continuing the service.




“The breakdowns and the cost of maintenance kept adding up, especially with what the cost of living is nowadays, and the long hours do catch up at the end,” Autut said to Nunatsiaq News in an interview conducted over Facebook Messenger.




Silu’s Taxi opened in February 2021, after the start of the Covid-19 pandemic.




“I started it for the town, to make sure the town is taken care of, not just to make money,” Autut said. 




The taxi operated daily, starting at 8 a.m. and usually running until at least 10 p.m. 




On Fridays and Saturdays, service often continued until midnight.
















“Sometimes, in the cold winter months or in the rain, we would pick up people walking by with an amauti carrying their infants, just to get them out of the cold and home safe,” Autut said.




The business partnered with the Northern store and Kissarvik Co-op to deliver groceries to residents in isolation during the pandemic. During this time, t

he Kivalliq Inuit Association hired the company to deliver 

gift cards

 door-to-door.




The taxi company has also partnered with Slap Shot Canteen to donate pizza to students and staff at Leo Ussak Elementary School to celebrate their last day of classes.




By January 2022, the business had grown to seven drivers and a mechanic, Autut said. 




But operating a vehicle for more than 12 hours a day came with considerable expenses, he said, including fuel, insurance, maintenance and repairs.




“Especially in winter, the vehicle had to stay running throughout the days, and gas consumption was a lot too,” Autut said. 
















The company went through several vehicles over the years and experienced multiple breakdowns in the past year alone, he said. Not having a hoist in the garage for certain repairs also made major rebuilds more expensive.




Finding reliable drivers was another challenge, as the long hours took a toll on employees, Autut said.




Rankin Inlet still has another taxi company, Rankin Taxi. Autut said he hopes it continues to serve the community and that he will offer help when needed.




He said the response to the closure announcement on Facebook has been kind. 




“It is very hard to see some of the comments, as they relied heavily on the service we provided,” Autut said. 

“I hope someone steps up soon, so there can be more reliable service out there all day and night.”
















He now plans to focus on his other businesses in the community: Silu’s Shop, a small-engine repair business, and Angijut Ltd., an overland hauling company.




“We are so grateful for every person who called us, rode with us, and trusted us over the years,” Autut said. “We will miss all of you, and we will miss being out there for you, day and night.”

author: ROAPE
title: South Africa’s water crisis is about more than water
content:
Komani—formerly known as Queenstown—is a town in the Eastern Cape province, in the eastern part of South Africa. It is part of the Chris Hani District and serves as an important commercial and administrative centre for surrounding rural communities and smaller towns. Its current water crisis is therefore not simply a local inconvenience in a little-known South African town. It is a window into a much larger question facing many countries: what happens when ageing public infrastructure, unreliable energy supply, weak public finances, fragmented institutions and unequal historical development intersect?




South Africa is an upper-middle-income country with sophisticated water infrastructure, major dams, treatment works and publicly owned bulk-water institutions. Yet access to reliable water remains deeply unequal. The country’s democratic Constitution recognises access to sufficient water as a right, while the practical responsibility for getting water from national and regional systems to households is spread across several institutions. This distinction is important: a water crisis can occur even where there is water in dams and substantial treatment capacity, because the infrastructure and institutions required to move that water to households can fail.




Komani makes this problem tangible. During September 2026, residents, community organisations and technical personnel examined the local water system, including the treatment works, pumping arrangements, reservoirs and community experience of repeated interruptions. Their findings, set out below, should be read both as evidence about Komani and as a case study of a wider infrastructure problem. The purpose is not to present Komani as unique, but to show why water security has to be understood as a chain linking water sources, energy, treatment, bulk supply, municipal distribution, finance, maintenance and public accountability.




South Africa’s water crisis

 is usually narrated as a story about drought, ageing pipes, leaking infrastructure or municipalities that cannot deliver. Those explanations are not wrong, but they are incomplete. The more revealing question is what happens between the moment water exists in a dam and the moment it reaches a household tap. The answer is a chain: raw-water abstraction, pumping, treatment, electricity, storage, bulk conveyance, reservoirs, municipal distribution and maintenance. A failure at any critical point can turn available water into a dry tap.




The Komani water crisis makes this chain unusually visible. Community fieldwork undertaken between 15 and 17 September 2026 combined a technical visit to the Komani Water Treatment Plant with community testimony and a public mobilisation. The technical evidence identified electrical faults, damaged control panels, faulty generators and electricity interruptions affecting pumping to reservoirs. The community then connected these failures to their own experience of recurring water interruptions and called for reliable electricity alongside reliable water.




The national lesson is 

bigger than Komani

. South Africa has to stop discussing the water crisis as if water and electricity were two unrelated service-delivery sectors. Water systems are energy systems. Treatment plants, booster stations, transfer schemes and reservoir pumping require reliable electricity. The Department of Water and Sanitation’s own recent regulatory standards recognise this dependency by requiring water-service institutions to provide backup generation or alternative electricity sources for critical water and wastewater infrastructure.




The Komani numbers expose the difference between ‘water available’ and ‘water delivered’




The Komani field report records a reported pumping capacity of 360 litres per second for the newer treatment plant and 122 litres per second for the older plant — a combined nominal figure of 482 litres per second. If that rate were sustained continuously, it would correspond to about 41.6 megalitres (ML) per day. But this is a theoretical conversion, not a measurement of actual daily production.




The same fieldwork records Waterdown Dam at 189 litres per second and Xonxa Dam at approximately 180 litres per second. Bokolo Dam’s contribution was not confirmed. The two confirmed figures together amount to 369 litres per second, or about 31.9 ML/day. That gap is important: the system cannot be understood by looking only at treatment-plant nameplate capacity, because the upstream source-to-treatment pumping chain also has limits.




At the distribution end, the report records 90 litres per second to Finchams Neck, 160 litres per second to Mlungisi and approximately 90 litres per second to the Ezibeleni high- and low-level reservoirs — 340 litres per second in total, equivalent to about 29.4 ML/day.




The report explicitly warns that these figures were recorded during the field visit and require confirmation against official municipal engineering records.




That caveat is not a weakness. It is precisely what serious evidence-based water politics should look like. Communities should not have to rely on rumours about how much water exists, how much is being pumped, how much is treated, how much sits in reservoirs and how much actually enters distribution. These should be public operational data.

The 5 ML Berry Water Storage facility is another useful illustration. At a continuous outflow of 340 L/s, 5 million litres would correspond to only about 4.1 hours of flow at that combined rate. This does not mean Berry is the only storage available or that the system can only operate for that period. It demonstrates, however, why pumping interruptions can quickly become reservoir-level crises when storage, redundancy and refill times are limited.




Load reduction changes the meaning of a water outage




South Africa’s electricity debate has also changed. The country can no longer reduce the energy-water relationship to the old national 

load-shedding 

story. In 2026, the government has distinguished 

load reduction

 from load shedding: load reduction is a localised network-protection response where distribution networks are under severe stress, often associated with illegal connections, meter bypassing, tampering and vandalism. At its peak, the government reported about 971 feeders affecting roughly 1.69 million customers.




That distinction matters for water. A community may experience a power interruption even when the national electricity grid is stable. If the affected electricity network supplies a pump station, treatment works or reservoir, the water consequences can continue after the electricity interruption itself. The government’s own 

Gauteng water-security strategy 

notes that electricity outages disrupt water supply when pumping or treatment is affected, and that more recently many disruptions have arisen from municipal electricity-distribution breakdowns rather than national Eskom load shedding.




The Komani report does not establish that a particular episode of load reduction caused each local water interruption. It establishes something more basic and more defensible: the water system experienced electrical faults, damaged control panels, faulty generators and electricity interruptions affecting pumping. That evidence should trigger a joint water-energy investigation rather than another round of isolated explanations.




But electricity cannot become an excuse for failures inside the water system




The opposite mistake would be to blame every water crisis on electricity. South Africa’s water institutions have their own failures. The national water system is institutionally fragmented: the Department of Water and Sanitation is the national custodian and regulator; water boards provide bulk services; municipalities generally function as water-services authorities and may also act as providers; and other institutions manage catchments, infrastructure and regulation. DWS describes water boards as government-owned institutions that operate dams and bulk-water infrastructure and provide technical support to municipalities.




This means accountability must follow the water chain. If raw water is available but cannot be pumped, the electricity and pump systems must be examined. If water is treated but does not reach reservoirs, pumping, electrical controls and bulk conveyance must be examined. If reservoirs contain water but households remain dry, the municipal distribution network, pressure management, leaks, illegal connections and operational decisions must be examined. Blaming ‘the municipality’ or ‘the water board’ without locating the failure in this chain produces politics without diagnosis.




The water boards are not outside the crisis: they are part of the evidence




The condition of the water boards demonstrates why bulk-water governance cannot be treated as a technical footnote. DWS reported municipal debt to water boards rising from R7.96 billion in 2018 to R24.81 billion by January 2025 — more than tripling. DWS warned that this threatens the financial viability of water boards and, ultimately, their ability to continue supplying municipal customers.




Amatola Water’s 

2024/25 Integrated Annual Report 

provides an Eastern Cape example of the problem. It reports a R159.1 million deficit for 2024/25 and deficits in each of the preceding three financial years. It attributes the 2024/25 deficit partly to reduced production efficiency caused by infrastructure constraints, as well as higher bulk-water purchases, electricity and chemical costs.




The preceding Amatola Water annual report is even more explicit about the energy connection: it says load shedding during much of 2023/24 negatively affected assurance of water supply, including pumping capacity and pipe breaks, and records an approved alternative-energy strategy whose implementation depended on funding.




This is why the argument should not be reduced to ‘i

nept water boards versus bad municipalities

’. The deeper problem is an interlocking public infrastructure system in which municipalities struggle to pay bulk suppliers, bulk suppliers face cash-flow and production constraints, electricity costs and reliability affect pumping, and ageing infrastructure reduces operational resilience. DWS’s own 

institutional framework 

says water boards are supposed to provide bulk services to other water-service institutions; that makes their financial and operational health a matter of public water security, not simply corporate administration.




The tanker economy is the symptom; the infrastructure failure is the disease




Komani residents also raised a politically explosive question: whether repeated water interruptions and emergency tanker procurement can create an economy in which a crisis becomes a source of contracts. The field report records allegations that reliance on JoJo tanks and water trucks creates opportunities for politically connected businesses. It also carefully states that these are community allegations, not findings of an independent procurement investigation.




That distinction must be preserved. But the concern cannot be dismissed. The Auditor-General has independently identified serious risks in 

water tankering

. Its 

2025/26

 reporting records material irregularities involving water-tanker invoicing and a R4.6 million certificate of debt arising from overpayments for water-tankering services. It also reported a suspected fraud matter where evidence of actual water-tankering delivery could not be substantiated, with a likely loss of R1.6 million.




The point is not that every tanker contract is corrupt. Tankers are sometimes essential emergency infrastructure. The point is that a permanent emergency-water economy must be subjected to the same public scrutiny as any other major public expenditure. Who receives the contracts? What volumes are delivered? At what price per kilolitre? How many deliveries are verified? How long do emergency contracts remain active? Why has emergency procurement not been replaced by permanent infrastructure where the underlying problem is known?




The financial crisis is measurable too




The Auditor-General’s 

2024/25

 local-government findings show that water-sector failure is also a financial-management problem. Municipalities disclosed R14.73 billion in water losses, although the AG cautions that the real figure is likely higher because some municipalities did not disclose losses and others materially misstated them. In the same year, 98 municipalities — 41% — spent more than they generated in revenue, producing a combined deficit of R17.41 billion.




The procurement picture is equally serious. Of 10,830 municipal procurement awards audited in 2024/25, 216 municipalities — 85% — failed to comply with procurement and contract-management legislation; material non-compliance was found at 60% of municipalities.




These figures do not prove that the Komani crisis is caused by corruption. They do establish that corruption, procurement weakness, poor contract management and financial instability are systemic risks within the environment in which water services are delivered. Any serious water-recovery plan therefore has to combine engineering with public finance, procurement transparency and consequence management.




What a serious water recovery plan should measure




The answer is not another generic promise to ‘fix the water crisis’. South Africa needs a public water-and-energy performance dashboard that follows water from source to tap. At minimum, every crisis-affected system should publish:







Raw-water availability and dam/source abstraction volumes. (2) Actual treatment-plant production in ML/day, compared with design and operational capacity. (3) Electricity interruptions affecting each critical water asset, including duration and cause. (4) Pump availability, generator availability and fuel/backup-energy status. (5) Reservoir levels and inflow/outflow rates. (6) Bulk-water purchases and volumes actually received by municipalities. (7) Municipal water losses and non-revenue water. (8) Repair backlogs, procurement dates and contractor performance. (9) Water-tanker volumes, delivery points, prices, contracts and independent verification. (10) Municipal debt to water boards and the effect of arrears on bulk-water operations.







The Komani lesson: diagnose the whole system, not the loudest failure




The Komani fieldwork provides a useful model for how communities can interrogate the water crisis. First, establish the physical system. Second, collect the numbers. Third, identify where water is lost or stopped. Fourth, overlay electricity interruptions and equipment failures. Fifth, examine the financial and procurement decisions that determine whether known failures are repaired. Sixth, compare official explanations with the lived experience of residents.




That is also why the broader water-justice project should combine community research with engineers, hydrologists, economists, municipal-finance specialists and lawyers. The concept note underpinning the work correctly identifies infrastructure condition, maintenance, budgeting, water losses, governance, climate vulnerability, service delivery and legal obligations as interconnected areas of investigation.




The ultimate political question is simple: if South Africa has water in its dams, treatment capacity in its plants, public institutions responsible for bulk supply and municipalities responsible for distribution, why are millions of people still being asked to live with dry taps?




Komani suggests the answer is not one failure. It is a chain of failures. Electricity instability can stop pumps. Failed pumps can empty reservoirs. Ageing infrastructure can magnify every interruption. Weak maintenance can turn a repairable fault into a prolonged outage. Municipal debt can weaken bulk suppliers. Weak procurement can divert money from durable infrastructure. And permanent tanker dependence can normalise emergency governments instead of restoring public infrastructure.  It also points to the question of spatial apartheid economic planning. According to Masindi & Duncker, South Africa’s history of apartheid geospatial planning has resulted in many rural areas not having access to basic water supply and sanitation services.  We must formulate this this the following ways: The apartheid geospatial and economic planning has remained a challenge in   eradicating the historical geospatial inequalities and socio-economic disparities. This means, in places like Komani there has not been an investment to expand infrastructure to cater for the growing population.  This is clear when one takes into account the combined total volume of water pumbed by the dams, the population of Komani as well as the standard required liters per household.




The significance of Komani is therefore straightforward. This is not only a story about whether a South African municipality can keep its taps running. It is a case study in the vulnerability of essential public infrastructure when water, electricity, public finance and institutional accountability are treated as separate policy problems. Similar questions arise wherever communities depend on complex networks of pumps, treatment plants, reservoirs and public utilities: how much water exists, how much can the system actually move, who controls each stage, who pays for it, who is accountable when it fails, and whether emergency responses are becoming substitutes for long-term public investment.




South Africa therefore needs a different water policy: one that treats electricity reliability, water-board viability, municipal capacity, infrastructure maintenance and procurement accountability as one connected public-service question. The test of reform should not be how many emergency tankers are dispatched after taps run dry. It should be whether the system can reliably move measured volumes of safe water from source to household, every day, and whether the public can see the data proving that it does.

South Africa’s water crisis is about more than water

ROAPE

.
