Veja mais episódios desta série










Para começar eu queria ouvir a sua avaliação geral sobre a eleição de meio-mandato nos Estados Unidos, na qual os democratas retomaram o controle das duas casas no Congresso. Como você analisa esses resultados e os impactos para Donald Trump?




Acredito que estamos de frente, possivelmente, de um cenário mais interessante do que muitas pesquisas estavam antecipando às vésperas da eleição. Muitos analistas estavam também, talvez, um pouco céticos que poderia acontecer a retomada democrata, tanto do Senado quanto da Casa dos Representantes, além de vitórias significativas em diversos governos dos estados. É muito interessante interpretarmos esses dados em contraste com as eleições de 2024. Naquele momento, os resultados demonstraram uma guinada significativa do eleitorado americano para a direita, ou seja, cada vez mais pessoas votando nos republicanos, o que garantiu a partir de 2025 a possibilidade do Trump governar com relativo baixo atrito.




Para entendermos melhor: a composição da Casa dos Representantes e do Senado nos Estados Unidos serve como um contrapeso para o Executivo Federal, para a presidência. Quando o presidente e as casas estão alinhadas, dominadas pelo mesmo partido, isso reduz significativamente o atrito que o presidente pode encontrar para avançar questões políticas e pautas que ele considera interessantes. Nós vimos o efeito disso nos dois primeiros anos do mandato de Donald Trump. Comparando o governo de 2017 com o que começa em 2025, em 2025 percebia-se um governo muito mais desinibido e com decisões inclusive muito polêmicas, como a questão da imigração e da dimensão comercial internacional dos Estados Unidos.




Agora, essa vitória democrata que muito da mídia americana e dos analistas tem chamado de uma onda, ou agora com os resultados confirmados, de um ‘tsunami azul’, na verdade reequilibra, digamos assim, o jogo de forças dentro dos Estados Unidos. Também indica algumas tendências de mudança muito interessantes para as próximas eleições presidenciais, em 2028. É um cenário muito fascinante para pensarmos não apenas em termos analíticos – que a mim interessa pontualmente –, mas, sobretudo, a dimensão de uma certa vitalidade democrática, inclusive no contexto dos Estados Unidos.




Sobre Trump, assim que ele retornou à Casa Branca, em seu segundo mandato, assinou várias ordens executivas, as executive orders, que são decretos presidenciais que não exigem a aprovação prévia do Congresso, inclusive algumas bem polêmicas. Mesmo com a derrota nesse

 

midterm

, o resultado pode frear o Trump ou ele é capaz de seguir impondo suas pautas, mesmo sem apoio?




Uma das coisas que nós aprendemos nos últimos dez anos acompanhando a figura política do Donald Trump é que ele é um tanto imprevisível e isso nos coloca numa situação um tanto quanto delicada. Em um cenário mais normal – e eu não acho que o Trump nos apresenta um cenário normal necessariamente –, nós veríamos um presidente republicano bastante preocupado com esses resultados e o termômetro que eles indicam para as eleições de 2028. Ou seja, em um cenário normal, não apenas um presidente republicano, mas todo partido republicano já começaria a pensar em estratégias de mobilização para pelo menos se não virar esse quadro, retomar algum controle em termos legislativos e, claro, do Executivo Federal. Mas o Donald Trump é uma carta fora do baralho nesse sentido, porque apesar dele não poder concorrer a um terceiro mandato, como está bem colocado na 22ª emenda da Constituição norte-americana, ele já tem falado e, inclusive, na loja do MAGA já temos materiais de campanha “Trump 2028”.




Claro, podemos interpretar isso de muitas maneiras diferentes, inclusive apenas como um recurso de mobilização de base. Mas é verdade que o Trump fez dessas eleições de meio de termo de mandato muito a respeito dele e da performance dele como presidente, o que não é necessariamente comum, porque essas são eleições mais regionalizadas. Elas são para a Câmara, que é voto distrital, um voto muito local e que traduz as ansiedades mais imediatas do eleitorado estadunidense. Também é uma eleição para o Senado, que ainda assim representa uma dimensão estadual, ainda que de atuação federal, além dos governos estaduais. O Trump já vinha com índices de aprovação muito baixos e me parece que os resultados dessa eleição selaram isso, agora o que permanece em aberto é como ele responderá a esse resultado.




Em entrevista, ele estava declarando que iria aceitar os resultados da eleição como legítimo e trabalharia com a Câmara e com o Senado, com os democratas, ou seja, entendendo e afirmando que ele tem certeza que ambos conseguiriam trabalhar bem nesses próximos dois anos. Isso, a princípio, é uma sinalização para moderação, mas não sabemos se ele consegue se moderar durante muito tempo. Acho que isso permanece para observação. Entretanto, temos um outro elemento que precisamos começar a considerar, que é como o Partido Republicano deve se articular pós-Donald Trump?




Nós temos pensado uma série de discussões e disputas que já começaram e vão ficar mais públicas agora, a respeito da sucessão do Donald Trump. Claro, nós temos dois grandes nomes: Marco Rubio, secretário de Estado do Donald Trump, grande responsável por administrar algumas das dinâmicas de imigração e política externa do Trump, sobretudo com relação à América Latina, e temos entre outras figuras importantes, principalmente, J.D. Vance, que é o vice-presidente dos Estados Unidos e que tradicionalmente é a figura mais cotada para a sucessão.




Pensar a sucessão do Trump vai além de pensar só quem os republicanos vão escolher, e, passa por entender também como fica a disputa pelo legado do MAGA, de toda essa base eleitoral que foi radicalizada pela figura do Donald Trump e que permanece como um ativo político super importante no contexto dos Estados Unidos. Fica a questão se o MAGA precisa ser continuamente radicalizado para se manter ativo. E, nesse cenário, talvez vejamos uma radicalização e não uma moderação, e também como as disputas internas dentro do Partido Republicano vão moldar essa relação com os democratas e com um legislativo dominado pelos democratas nos próximos dois anos.




Com relação ao Brasil, a proximidade com as

 

midterms

 

fizeram com que o Trump, também, fosse mais cauteloso com relação à carta golpista do Flávio Bolsonaro? Qual a sua avaliação sobre o envolvimento dos Estados Unidos nas últimas eleições no Brasil e seus desdobramentos?




Nós não temos como contornar o fato de que houve não apenas uma grande influência, como também algumas tentativas de interferência efetiva dos Estados Unidos nas eleições brasileiras. Nós observamos que, desde 2025, o Trump presta cada vez mais atenção na América Latina, um pouco como parte da estratégia de política externa dele, e por isso temos falado de uma “Doutrina Donroe”. Aqui a ideia é recuperar um pouco a Doutrina Monroe de pensar a “América para os americanos” – americanos aqui entendidos como estadunidenses –, ou seja, isolar o espaço das Américas de influências extra-americanas, sejam elas europeias, como era o caso da 

Doutrina Monroe originalmente

, sejam elas asiáticas, como é o caso da doutrina Donald, em uma tentativa de frear o avanço da China sobre a América Latina. 




E isso resultou, para além de questões internacionais, numa influência muito profunda em eleições domésticas, e por isso que vemos essa onda de governos de direita radical ou de extrema direita sendo eleitos recentemente na América Latina: Colômbia, Peru, Chile, Argentina. Então, nós estávamos pensando e observando se o mesmo aconteceria com o Brasil. E eu relaciono as duas coisas, porque é óbvio e é inegável que governos de extrema direita na América Latina tornam a presença dos Estados Unidos de Donald Trump mais fácil. São governos que se alinham muito rapidamente, digamos assim, aos interesses estadunidenses e, assim, reduzem o atrito nas relações interamericanas e facilitam com que Trump avance as pautas dele de preservar o espaço das Américas como um espaço de domínio dos Estados Unidos.




Por isso, a vitória brasileira, a vitória do PT e do Lula nas eleições brasileiras foi tão significativa e importante. Mais do que representar um freio para essa onda, não podemos esquecer a dimensão, a importância e o peso que o Brasil ocupa nas relações do espaço das Américas. Somos um país muito grande, com uma população significativa, com recursos muito importantes e inserido de maneira importante nas relações internacionais. Então, precisamos ter essa dimensão que nós vimos um interesse pronunciado dos Estados Unidos na nossa eleição.




Agora, com relação pontualmente à família Bolsonaro e à carta golpista e a todas essas questões, eu acho que podemos fazer uma diferenciação. Digo isso porque o Trump nunca me pareceu pontualmente interessado nos Bolsonaros. Claro, ele recebeu, tem foto na Casa Branca, mas é um pouco do um misancene que ele faz com todo mundo.




Quem estava bastante ligado com os Bolsonaros é o Marco Rubio, que é um cara bastante radical que, digamos assim, tem uma posição muito peculiar dentro dos Estados Unidos, dentro do governo americano. Ele é filho de cubanos que fugiram de Cuba pós-revolução, então tem todo esse contexto dele ser um cara que esposa, se não um anticomunismo, um anti-esquerdismo bastante forte, e que daí, sim, me parece ter visto nos Bolsonaros um elemento-chave bastante interessante. Pontualmente percebo que toda essa articulação do Bolsonaro com o governo dos Estados Unidos está mais centrada na figura do Rubio do que do Trump. Então, nós precisamos pensar nessas dimensões. Se o Trump talvez foi um pouco mais cauteloso com relação às eleições brasileiras por causa disso? Acho que sim, mas eu me pergunto o quanto o Trump se ocupa, efetivamente, de pensar sobre o Brasil.




Acredito também que tem uma questão de uma performance pública importante, como todo aquele atraso em reconhecer o resultado das eleições brasileiras, mas elas foram reconhecidas. A embaixada norte-americana enviou uma carta para o Itamaraty dizendo que as eleições estão reconhecidas, mas a figura do Trump não foi a público congratular o Lula e tudo mais; não faz parte da performance dele como político. Mesmo assim, reforço que vale a pena pensar nessas duas dimensões e separar o que é o Trump e o que é Marco Rubio, porque isso nos permite ter um pouco mais de nuance para entender e, talvez, até investigar como essa questão se desenrola a partir de agora.




No sentido de que esse cenário das eleições apresentou uma série de desafios, não apenas para o Trump, mas para os republicanos de maneira geral, e principalmente para as lideranças republicanas que ainda têm ambição de seguir o caminho da política nos Estados Unidos. Talvez isso enfraqueça relativamente à posição dos Bolsonaros, porque americanos como Trump e como Rubio vão ter problemas maiores para se ocupar e mais imediatos dentro de seu contexto doméstico do que apoiar um candidato que perdeu as eleições no Brasil e está efetivamente elaborando uma posição um tanto esquisita, que complica a coisa toda.




Por outro lado, alguns analistas dos Estados Unidos estavam dizendo que o Trump pode dobrar a aposta agora nesses dois últimos anos: tentar radicalizar a pauta e se tornar mais agressivo com uma série de questões justamente por ter perdido as eleições de midterm. Eu acredito que é uma possibilidade, mas não sei se ele vai ter tanto espaço para fazer isso. Efetivamente, o domínio democrático nas duas casas significa que ele perde uma série de questões importantes e está sujeito a uma transparência maior. Além de perder a capacidade de nomear facilmente os cargos de âmbito ministerial, que nos Estados Unidos chamamos de secretarias, como o secretário de Estado ou de defesa.




Trump perde também um controle significativo sobre o orçamento nacional, porque isso está nas mãos da Câmara de Representantes, e ele fica sujeito a mais investigações por parte do legislativo. Acho que estamos olhando para um cenário em que o Trump talvez comece a considerar o que ele vai fazer a partir de 2028 e fico me perguntando quanto de energia ele tem, efetivamente, para continuar engajado numa política que está pouco receptiva às propostas que ele apresentou.

author: Yo-Ling Chen
title: “My Body Is My Own”: Collective Memory, Remembrance, and Dignity in Taiwan Transgender and Intersex History
content:
This article submission was originally published by 跨服TransServer’s trans co-created column, Trans Day Reader and is syndicated here on New Bloom Magazine’s website with 跨服TransServer’s permission. In the original article, TransServer writes the following introduction:

November is Transgender Awareness Month and November 8th is Intersex Day of Remembrance. For the author, November 8th carries the weight of intertwined histories of medical violence within transgender and intersex communities, as well as the responsibility of building solidarity across these communities. Choosing this day to begin HRT, Yo-Ling offers this Trans Day Reader as an act of intervention, grounding its significance within the Taiwanese context.

The medical establishment profoundly impacts intersex well-being, as medical authority often overshadows bodily autonomy for intersex people. At the same time, scholars shape collective memory by ghostwriting for historical subjects. Positioned with critique and reflexivity, this article revisits archives of Mr. Xie Jianshun’s gender transition under duress, but more importantly, his acts of resistance, which advance a politics of self-respect for Sinophone trans and intersex communities. In reaching a wider public, readers must recognize academic critique as an autonomous domain and respect the author’s embodied self-disclosure.

NOVEMBER 8TH is both my gender affirming hormone therapy anniversary day, as well as Intersex Day of Remembrance. There is a story and a set of political reasons for choosing this particular date to start hormones. I am a Taiwanese transgender activist, as well as an independent scholar of transgender studies and Taiwanese postwar trans history. The first recorded use of hormones for gender transition in Taiwan is from the 1950s and was far from “gender affirming.” May this Trans Day Reader entry be a reminder to us all that holding our own collective memory is a form of resistance, especially when our histories have been written by scholars profiting off of our suffering, distorting and reproducing the realities of medical and archival violence, and damaging the intertwined dignity of Sinophone trans and intersex peoples.

On August 14, 1953, doctors at No. 518 Hospital of the ROC Army (陸軍第518醫院) in Tainan discovered that a soldier named Xie Jianshun (謝尖順) had intersex characteristics. The doctors performed an exploratory laparotomy on August 20 to determine Xie’s “true biological sex” and decided that he was anatomically “female” due to his having a uterus, two ovaries, and fallopian tubes. Doctors subsequently decided for Xie that he should receive “sex change” procedures, which included further surgeries and feminizing hormone therapy, in order to become a woman. [1] Xie expressed a strong desire to continue living his life as a man, even going so far as to tell reporters on August 21, after undergoing exploratory laparotomy, that he would rather kill himself than become a woman (United Daily News, 1953/08/21). Indeed, throughout the course of medical treatment and afterwards, archival materials surrounding Xie’s gender transition consistently demonstrate Xie’s self-conceptualization as a man and deep discomfort being both misgendered as and medically transitioned into a woman.

When Xie was ordered to be moved from No. 518 Hospital in Tainan to No. 1 General Hospital in Taipei (陸海空軍第一總醫院) later in 1953 to receive further “sex change” procedures, he told reporters that “I have already decided not to go up to Taipei. Whoever wants me to go to Taipei is better off sending me two bullets. I would rather die than comply. Although I am a soldier for whom obedience is my duty, my body is my own. I have the freedom to decide what to do with my own body” (Min Sheng Daily, 1953/12/09). Despite his explicit refusal, he was relocated to Taipei in early 1954 to continue receiving “treatments.”

In the fall of 1955, doctors at No. 1 General Hospital in Taipei decided for Xie that in order for him to “be able to become a mother” and have “menstrual bleeding that is the same as regular women,” and also for the sake of “achieving an even more tremendous advancement in medical research,” they would specially purchase injectable estrogen for Xie (United Daily News, 1955/10/15). Regarding how Xie felt about being injected with estrogen, news reports record him sharing “the pain of having needles inserted into [his] body is only secondary; watching [his] body change day by day is what really causes [him] anxiety” (United Daily News, 1955/10/17). Under the “care” of the military hospital system in 1950s Taiwan as a soldier, Xie could only accept what was being done to his body and practice refusal in line with his understanding of himself as a man in small yet powerful moments—such as in his refusals to wear a qipao during his hospital stay, and his refusal wear women’s clothing and to allow others to refer to him as a woman or to call him “Miss Xie” after finally being discharged from No. 1 General Hospital to live and work at the Ta Tung Relief Institute for Women and Children (大同婦孺教養院) on September 16, 1958 (United Daily News, 1964/12/16).

Before being discharged, Ta Tung’s founding director Madam Huang-Lu Hsiao-chu (黃盧小珠女士) told reporters that Ta Tung was “preparing to assist [Xie] in reconstructing [his] psychology” to be in alignment with his re-assigned sex as a woman (United Daily News, 1958/09/04). While existing historical records do not detail how exactly Ta Tung, as an institution, sought to “reconstruct [Xie’s] psychology,” given the institution’s background as a Christian relief organization, it is reasonable to infer that techniques including talk therapy counseling and “spiritual guidance” sessions aimed at encouraging Xie to live his new life at Ta Tung as a woman. The scarce amount of archival materials we have during Xie’s time at Ta Tung shows that he “rejected ‘spiritual guidance’ from missionaries” (United Daily News, 1964/12/16). While it is unclear what exactly transpired during Xie’s stay at Ta Tung, what is clear is that in the last media report we have of him after over six years of stay, Xie is described as “depressed” and “negative,” “feeling that [his] sex change was a tragic event, and hence resenting the doctors who operated on [him]” (United Daily News, 1964/12/16).

Despite the abundance of archival instances of refusal to live as a woman and Xie’s unchanging understanding of himself as a man, in Sinophone trans historiography, scholars such as Howard Chiang claim that after a single debrief meeting on the afternoon of August 29th, 1953, where Xie was informed of his doctors’ plans to medically transition him into a woman, “Xie agreed to cooperate in all subsequent medical procedures that would bring about a full sex reassignment” (Chiang 2018, 246). Chiang, as well as Taiwanese scholar Angel Wang (王孝勇, 2020), have proceeded to use feminine pronouns to refer to Xie in their scholarship, as if consent under duress were sufficient to justify the reproduction of medical and archival violence in Sinophone trans historiography, and as if Xie’s own protestations to being medically transitioned throughout the archival traces he left behind were less important than the decision-making of medical authorities that had the ultimate say over Xie’s body and life.

It is impossible to observe Intersex Day of Remembrance in Taiwan without confronting the multiple layers of violence that Xie Jianshun endured, but nevertheless, found ways to defend his dignity as an intersex man throughout the many attempts of doctors, reporters, and institutions to physically and psychologically transform him into a woman he never wanted to become. At the same time, remembrance as resistance is not limited to a single day. As a Taiwanese trans activist organizing against the government’s long-standing insistence on medical authority to validate trans existence as a non-negotiable part of gender recognition, and as an independent scholar attempting to redress the historiographical violences committed by Taiwanese scholars in their telling of Xie’s story, every day is Intersex Day of Remembrance for me. Every day when I nourish my body with feminizing hormones in ways that are deeply gender affirming, I remember the fact that the introduction of estrogen use for gender transition in Taiwan was completely opposite to my experience.

Hormone anniversaries are usually joyous occasions to celebrate one’s gender transition milestones. While I do feel some joy today for myself, what I feel much more intensely is the need for Sinophone trans communities to learn about, remember, and learn from Xie Jianshun’s multiple acts of refusal. Our dignity must be defended, even and especially from those who claim to be in support of transgender liberation while unapologetically writing undignifying histories of Sinophone gender transition. May we remember, on our own terms, what the systems that oppress us have done, and the power that our collective memory can bring to Sinophone transgender movements that refuse compromise, co-optation, and confinement within existing structures of power.

[1] Explanatory note added by 跨服TranServer: The term “sex change” (變性) reflects the original phrasing of 1950s-1960s news and medical archives—language later critiqued for imposing pathologizing.

Chiang, Howard. After Eunuchs Science, Medicine, and the Transformation of Sex in Modern China. Columbia University Press, 2018.

“Dabing jiang biancheng xiaojie” 大兵將變成小姐 [Soldier to become a lady]. Lianhebao 聯合報, August 21, 1953.

“Xie Jianshun pa zuo shiyanpin jujue beishang jiaozhi” 謝尖順怕作實驗品 拒絕北上矯治 [Xie Jianshun afraid of being experimented on, refuses to go north for corrective treatment]. Min Sheng Daily 民聲日報, December 9, 1953.

“Xie Jianshun xiaojie gushi” 謝尖順小姐故事 [The Story of Miss Xie Jianshun]. Lianhebao 聯合報, October 15, 1955.

“Xie Jianshun xiaojie gushi” 謝尖順小姐故事 [The Story of Miss Xie Jianshun]. Lianhebao 聯合報, October 17, 1955.

“Xieshun feizhangfu youlei jin qingtan” 謝順非丈夫‧有淚今輕彈 [Xieshun is not a man: Today, tears fall]. Lianhebao 聯合報, December 16, 1964.

“Yishi chuangzao nüren wunian duding qiankun” 醫師創造女人 五年篤定乾坤 [Doctors create a woman after five years of grappling with universe]. Lianhebao 聯合報, September 4, 1958.

Wang, Hsiao-Yung 王孝勇. “‘Xie Jianshun shijian zhi meiti yuyikuangjia fenxi: ‘kuaxingbie guojiazhuyi de guandian” 「謝尖順事件」之媒體語藝框架分析：「跨性別國家主義」的觀點醫療專業、性別與國家：台灣助產士興衰的社會學分析 [A Rhetorical Framing Analysis of Media Discourse of the “HSIEH Chien Shun Event”]. Taiwan shehuixue yanjiu 台灣社會學研究 117(2020): 47-111.

author: Unknown
title: Üçlü zirve için APEC iddiası: ABD, Çin ve Rusya masaya oturacak mı?
content:
ABD, Rusya ve Çin’in masaya oturmasına ilişkin yeni bir gelişme yaşandı. ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, Rusya Devlet Başkanı Vladimir Putin ve Çin Devlet Başkanı Şi Cinping arasında olası bir görüşme planlanırken Çin Dışişleri Bakanlığı temaslarda bulunduğunu açıkladı.

Associated Press'in (AP) haberine göre, üç liderin Çin'in Shenzhen kentinde 18-19 Kasım tarihlerinde gerçekleştirilecek Asya-Pasifik Ekonomik İşbirliği (APEC) Zirvesi kapsamında bir araya gelmesi bekleniyor. Ancak görüşmenin yapılacağına ilişkin henüz kesin bir karar alınmadı.

CNN Türk'ten Mariye Ekinci'nin haberine göre Çin Dışişleri Bakanlığı Sözcüsü Mao Ning, sürece ilişkin değerlendirmelerde bulundu. 4 Kasım'da Pekin'de düzenlediği basın toplantısında üçlü zirve ihtimaline ilişkin açıklama yapan Mao Ning, Çin, ABD ve Rusya devlet başkanlarının olası buluşması konusunda ilgili taraflarla iletişimin sürdüğünü bildirdi.

Kremlin Sözcüsü Dmitriy Peskov da daha önce yaptığı açıklamada üç liderin bir araya gelmesi için çalışmalar yürütüldüğünü belirtmişti.

ABD Başkanı Donald Trump'ın Çin ziyareti sırasında Putin ve Şi Cinping ile nükleer silahların kontrolünü görüşmek istediği belirtiliyor.

Rusya'nın ise olası zirvede Ukrayna savaşını gündeme getireceği tahmin ediliyor. AP'ye değerlendirmelerde bulunan eski ABD Dışişleri Bakanlığı yetkilisi Danny Russel, böyle bir buluşmanın Rusya açısından diplomatik kazanım sağlayabileceğini belirtti. Stimson Center Çin Programı Direktörü Sun Yun ise Moskova'nın görüşmeyi, Washington ve Pekin'i Ukrayna konusundaki tutumuna yaklaştırmak için kullanabileceği değerlendirmesinde bulundu.

Bununla birlikte Ukrayna meselesinin üçlü zirvenin resmi gündemine alındığına ilişkin bir açıklama bulunmuyor.

Pekin, Washington ve Moskova arasındaki temasların önümüzdeki günlerde sürmesi bekleniyor.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Yo-Ling Chen
title: 「我的身體為我自己所有」：台灣跨性別與雙性人歷史中的集體記憶、紀念及尊嚴
content:
本篇投稿原刊於跨服TransServer之《跨日典》跨性別共創欄目，在此以《破土雜誌》官網做轉載。在原文中，跨服撰寫了本篇以下的引言：

每年11月是跨性別意識月，11月8日作爲紀念閒性人的日子，承載著跨性別與間性人/雙性人社群所經歷醫療暴力歷史的重量，同時也肩負著在這些社群之間建立團結的責任。有靈選擇這天開始用藥，以此紀念辭作為行動，也賦予其台灣語境的意涵。

醫療體制深刻影響著間性人/雙性人福祉，醫療權威蔓延至個體身體改造之決策，相關學者更進一步透過代筆當事人塑造集體記憶。本文帶著批判與反身性現身，重述謝尖順先生被迫進行性別轉換的檔案及其主體抗爭，向華語跨性別與雙性人社群發出自我尊重的倡議。本文面向廣泛社群的同時，讀者亦須理解學術批判作為獨立疆域的本質，並尊重作者的現身。

11月8日，既是我性別肯認荷爾蒙治療的用藥週年紀念日，又是雙性人紀念日。選擇這個日期開始用藥，有它背後的故事和政治原因。我是一名台灣跨性別倡議者，也是一名從事跨性別研究和台灣戰後跨性別歷史研究的獨立學者。台灣首例使用荷爾蒙進行性別轉換的記載來自於1950年代，且該案例與「性別肯認」相去甚遠。祝願這篇《跨日典》的篇章能提醒我們所有人：守護我們的集體記憶本身就是一種抵抗，尤其是當我們的歷史被一群消費我們的受苦、扭曲並複製醫療與檔案暴力現實，以至損害華語世界跨性別與雙性人集體尊嚴的學者書寫時。

1953年8月14日，台南陸軍第518醫院的醫師們發現，一名名為謝尖順的士兵具有雙性人特徵。醫師們於8月20日進行剖腹探查手術，以確定謝尖順所謂真正的「生理性別」，並判定其解剖結構屬「女性」，因他擁有子宮、兩側卵巢及輸卵管。隨後，醫師們決定，謝尖順該接受「變性」療程，包括後續手術及女性化荷爾蒙治療，以使他成為女性。[1] 期間謝尖順強烈表達了希望繼續以男性身份生活的堅持，甚至在8月21日剖腹探查手術後，向記者表示：「過了卅六個年頭的男子生活，再叫我變成一位女性，那麼我非要自殺不可」（《聯合日報》，1953年8月21日）。關於謝先生性別轉換的檔案資料一貫顯示，他始終將自己視為男性，並對被錯稱為女性以及經醫療介入「被變性」為女性感到極度不適。

1953年稍晚，謝先生接到命令，須從台南的第518醫院轉院至台北的陸海空軍第一總醫院接受進一步「變性」醫療處置，他向記者表示：「我的主張已經決定不上臺北。誰要我去，莫如送我兩粒花生米 (即兩粒子彈的意思)。我寧死不屈。我雖有軍人身分，以服從為天職，但我的身體為我自己所有。我有處理我自己身體之自由」（《民聲日報》，1953年12月9日）。然而，儘管他明確拒絕，仍於1954年初被轉送至台北，繼續接受「治療」。

1955年秋季，第一總醫院的醫師們，為了讓謝先生「能夠做母親」、「便 [他] 的月紅如一般的女性一樣」，並「為了在醫術研究上獲得更偉大的成就」，擅自專購雌激素注射劑給謝先生做實驗（《聯合日報》，1955年10月15日）。關於對注射雌激素的感受，記者訪問謝先生時，報導記載：「針插在體內的痛苦還在其次，眼看自己的身體，一天一天地在起變化， [他] 實在有點躭心」（《聯合日報》，1955年10月17日）。在1950年代台灣軍醫院體系的「照護」下，身為一名士兵，謝先生只能接受當局對其身體所施加的一切，並在那些微小卻充滿力量的時刻，依據他對自身身為男性的認知來實踐拒絕——例如他在住院期間拒絕穿旗袍，以及於1958年9月16日從第一總醫院出院、入住大同婦孺教養院生活工作後，他依然堅持「不願穿女裝，不願別人稱 [他] 小姐或女士」（《聯合報》，1964年12月16日）。

出院前，大同的創院院長黃盧小珠女士向記者表示：「我們現在準備協助 [他]，改造 [他] 的心理」，使其與重新指定的女性性別相符（《聯合日報》，1958年9月4日）。雖然現存史料並未詳細說明大同人員究竟如何試圖「改造他的心理」，但鑑於該機構身為基督教救濟組織的背景，可推斷其採用了包括談話治療諮商及「開導」之靈性領導方法，旨在鼓勵謝先生以女性身分在大同展開新生活。關於謝先生在大同期間的檔案資料極為稀少，但現有資料反映他「拒絕傳教士為 [他] 『開導』」（《聯合日報》，1964年12月16日）。雖然謝先生在大同期間究竟發生了什麼事尚不清楚，但可以確定的是，在他入住逾六年的最後一份媒體報導中，謝先生被描述為「精神抑鬱」且「消極」，並「感到變性是一件不幸的事，因此 [他] 厭惡為 [他] 動手術的醫生」（《聯合日報》，1964年12月16日）。

儘管史料中充斥著謝先生拒絕以女性身分生活、始終將自己視為男性的證據，但在華語世界跨性別史學研究中，姜學豪教授卻聲稱，在1953年8月29日下午單一場醫療協議會議中，謝先生被告知醫師們打算透過醫療手段將他「變性」為女性，在此之後， 「謝同意配合後續所有旨在實現完全變性的醫療程序」（Chiang 2018，246頁）。姜教授以及台灣學者王孝勇（2020）在有關謝尖順的學術研究中，皆延用女性代詞 ，彷彿在脅迫下獲得的同意，便足以為華語世界跨性別史中持續的醫療檔案暴力辯護；謝先生在檔案深處留下的抗議行動與反對聲明，其重量被視為遠低於醫療權威的決策，仿佛後者獨占了對個體身體與生命的最終決定權。

在台灣紀念雙性人紀念日時，不可不面對謝尖順所承受的多重暴力；以及確證他展現的主體抗爭，儘管醫生、記者和各類機構多次試圖在生理與心理層面將他「變性」為他從未想成為的女性，他仍設法捍衛身為雙性人男性的尊嚴。與此同時，「以追憶作為抵抗」並不限於單一日子。身為一名正在組織抗爭反對政府長期堅持借醫療權威來驗證跨性別者的存在、將此視為性別承認中不可協商的環節之台灣跨性別倡議者，同時，身為一名試圖修復台灣學者在敘述謝尖順故事時所犯下的史學暴力之獨立學者，每一天對我而言都是雙性人紀念日。每天當我透過雌性化荷爾蒙滋養身體，以深刻肯定自身性別認同的方式生活時，我都會憶起：在台灣，將雌激素應用於性別轉換的首例，與我的親身經歷截然相反。

荷爾蒙用藥週年日，通常是慶祝個人性別轉換里程碑的歡樂時刻。雖然今天我確實為自己感到些許慶悅，但我更強烈地感受到，華語世界的跨性別社群有必要了解、銘記並從謝尖順的種種拒絕中汲取教訓。我們的尊嚴必須被捍衛，即使——尤其是——面對那些自稱支持跨性別解放，卻在歷史書寫中毫不掩飾地踐踏個體尊嚴的華語世界性別轉換敘事者。 願我們能以自己的方式銘記：那些壓迫我們的體制曾做過什麼，以及我們的集體記憶能為華語世界跨性別運動帶來何種力量——這股力量將拒絕讓步、拒絕被收編，並拒絕被禁錮於現有的權力結構之中。

[1] 跨服TransServer 添加註釋：本文引述「變性」一詞係真實反映1950-1960年代新聞與醫療檔案，該用語後被批判為反映了醫療權威強加的病理化框架；當代用語「性別肯認」與「性別過渡」則被期待挑戰這一框架，強調基於個人自主意願與認同的性別實踐。儘管如此，當事人仍應保有選擇自身描述語言，且不受指責的權利。

Chiang, Howard. After Eunuchs Science, Medicine, and the Transformation of Sex in Modern China. Columbia University Press, 2018.

author: Unknown
title: Azerbaycan ziyareti sırasında Erdoğan'ın yerine Cevdet Yılmaz vekalet edecek
content:
Erdoğan'ın Azerbaycan ziyareti süresince Cumhurbaşkanlığı görevini 8 Kasım 2026 tarihli Resmî Gazete'de yayımlanan tezkereye göre, Cumhurbaşkanı Yardımcısı Cevdet Yılmaz üstlenecek. Vekâlet işlemi, Anayasa'nın 106'ncı maddesi uyarınca gerçekleştirilecek.

Cevdet Yılmaz, Erdoğan'ın yurda dönüşüne kadar Cumhurbaşkanlığı görevini yürütecek.

Azerbaycan’da okul ve kamu kurumlarındaki başörtüsü yasağına Türkiye'den tepki gösterilmesi üzerine iki ülke arasında gerilim yaşanmıştı. Azerbaycan Cumhurbaşkanı Aliyev krizin ardından Türkiye'de düzenlenen Türk Devletleri Teşkilatı'nın 13. Zirvesi'ne katılmamıştı. Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan'ın, Azerbaycan Cumhurbaşkanı İlham Aliyev’in daveti üzerine 8 Kasım 2026’da Karabağ’ı ziyaret edeceği açıklandı.

Gerilimin ardından Azerbaycan yönetimine tepki gösteren Cumhurbaşkanı Danışmanı Oktay Saral görevden alınmıştı. Azerbaycan yönetimi bazı isimlere ülkeye giriş yasağı getirmişti.

Cumhurbaşkanlığı İletişim Başkanı Burhanettin Duran, sosyal medya hesabından yaptığı açıklamada, Erdoğan'ın 8 Kasım 2026 (yarın) tarihinde Karabağ'ı ziyaret edeceğini duyurdu.

Duran, açıklamasında şu ifadeleri kullandı:

"Cumhurbaşkanımız Sayın Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Azerbaycan Cumhurbaşkanı Sayın İlham Aliyev’in davetine icabetle, 8 Kasım 2026 tarihinde Karabağ’ı ziyaret edeceklerdir."

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: Bursa otogarında 1 ton bozuk tavuk eti ele geçirildi
content:
Adana'dan otobüsle Bursa'ya getirilen yaklaşık 1 ton bozuk tavuk eti, belediye ekiplerince imha edildi.

Bursa Uluslararası ve Şehirlerarası Otobüs Terminaline 6 çuvalla gelen kişi, güvenlik görevlilerinin dikkatini çekti. Çuvallarda siyah poşetlere sarılarak ambalajlanmış bozuk tavuk etleri bulunduğunu fark eden güvenlik görevlileri, durumu Terminal Zabıta Amirliği, İl Tarım ve Orman Müdürlüğü ile polise bildirdi.

Ekipler, incelemenin ardından son kullanma tarihi geçmiş tavuk etlerinin imha edilmesine karar verdi.

Yaklaşık 1 ton tavuk eti ekiplerin gözetiminde imha edilirken, ürünleri getiren kişi hakkında işlem yapıldı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Police seize liquor, cash in Nunavik-Quebec investigation
content:
A man from Chambly, Que., and a woman from Kangiqsujuaq could face charges following a police investigation into the illegal possession and sale of alcohol.




The Sûreté du Québec’s Contraband Investigation Unit, working with the Nunavik Police Service, searched a property in Kangiqsujuaq on Wednesday. 




The investigation, which began in June, also led to a search in Chambly on Tuesday, after investigators determined the two cases were linked.




The searches resulted in the seizure of nearly eight litres of various alcoholic beverages and close to $12,000 in Canadian currency, according to a news release issued Thursday by the Quebec provincial police.




The individuals involved are a 34-year-old man from Chambly and a 32-year-old woman from Kangiqsujuaq. The news release did not provide their names. They could face charges related to illegal possession of alcohol and selling it without the required permits under Quebec’s Act respecting offences relating to alcoholic beverages.

author: Daron Letts
title: Dialogue about Inuit-specific housing funding underway, says Indigenous Services Minister
content:
Inuit-Nunangat’s share of billions of dollars in federal housing and infrastructure funding announced in 

Thursday

‘s budget

 remains undetermined, but that could change soon, Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty said Saturday in Iqaluit.




“I think that we’ll have greater clarity in the next few days,” Gull-Masty said during a news conference at the Inuusirvik Community Wellness Hub. It marked the start of a two-day visit to the territory, her first trip to the eastern Arctic. In addition to her role as Indigenous Services minister, Gull-Masty is the Liberal MP for Abitibi—Baie-James—Nunavik—Eeyou, the sprawling Quebec riding that includes Nunavik.




The Liberal government’s budget allocated $30 billion for First Nations housing and infrastructure as part of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s new commitment to eliminate homelessness within a decade.




But the budget did not mention comparable investments for Inuit communities.




However, discussions with Inuit organizations about how to fund housing and infrastructure in Inuit communities are ongoing, Gull-Masty said.




“It’s imperative that we take the time, that we take that space and really have that conversation to reflect the uniqueness of the North,” she said. “It’s important for us if we want to reach that target in the North that we shape it according to the realities of what it means to live here and deliver services.”




She met with representatives from Nunavut Tunngavik Inc., the organization that represents Inuit beneficiaries under the Nunavut Agreement, on Saturday.
















On Thursday, she met with Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami president Natan Obed, the head of the national organization for Inuit in Canada.




Gull-Masty said the dialogue about Inuit-specific funding for housing and infrastructure will continue later this year during a meeting of the Inuit-Crown Partnership Committee, a bilateral forum that brings together Inuit leaders and federal cabinet ministers to advance shared priorities.




Nunavut MP Lori Idlout and Iqaluit Mayor Solomon Awa also met with Gull-Masty on Saturday.




Idlout said she is confident Nunavut will be included in Carney’s commitment to eliminate homelessness across Canada within a decade.




“What this government will need to do is make sure that it works respectfully with the Inuit organizations to ensure that Nunavut’s needs are being met,” Idlout said.




Awa shares Idlout’s optimism.
















“It can be done if we work really hard,” he said.

author: CNT Madrid
title: 8 razones para parar en el sector de la prensa y la comunicación este 11-N
content:
Si trabajas en medios de comunicación escritos, en línea o en papel, en radios, en teles o en agencias de publicidad, diseño o cualquier ámbito de la comunicación te sobran los motivos para ir a la huelga este miércoles 11 de noviembre. Aquí la sección de trabajadoras de la Prensa y la Comunicación de la CNT de Madrid y la CGT y las trabajadoras en el sector de la comunicación del Sindicato de Artes Gráficas, Papel, Comunicación y Espectáculos de CGT Mad-Castilla-La Mancha-Ext te dan, al menos, ocho motivos más:




SALARIOS QUE CIERREN LAS HERIDAS ABIERTAS DESDE 2008 Y QUE ALIVIEN LA CRISIS DE ASEQUIBILIDAD DE LA VIDA Y LA VIVIENDA




Tras más de quince años de ERE, despidos y congelaciones, la profesión sigue sin recuperarse, agravando el encarecimiento general de la vida y, en concreto, los problemas para acceder a una vivienda digna que sufre toda la clase trabajadora. Entre los periodistas con contrato, cerca de la mitad cobra entre 1.000 y 2.000 euros netos al mes. Entre los autónomos, algo más de la mitad recibe menos de 100 euros por pieza. Exigimos subidas salariales que devuelvan el poder adquisitivo perdido y salarios mínimos del sector a la altura de la responsabilidad del oficio.




CONVENIOS VIVOS, NO CONVENIOS CADUCADOS




La patronal deja morir los convenios sectoriales, empezando por el de Prensa Diaria. Exigimos su renovación y actualización inmediata con tablas salariales al día. Exigimos también que se cumpla la obligatoriedad de los planes de igualdad en las empresas informativas.




REDACCIONES SIN BRECHAS




Las mujeres son mayoría en las redacciones, pero sólo 19 de los 100 medios con más audiencia de España estaban dirigidos por una mujer en 2025, dos menos que en 2024. Exigimos acabar con la brecha de género en salarios y ascensos. Exigimos reducir la distancia entre direcciones y jefaturas, de un lado, y redactoras, redactores, productoras, productores y personal técnico, del otro, que son quienes sostienen el día a día.




CADA HORA, REGISTRADA Y PAGADA




La actualidad no entiende de horarios, pero eso no puede ser excusa para el trabajo gratis. La mayoría de los periodistas trabaja más de 40 horas semanales, el máximo legal del Estatuto de los Trabajadore. Muchas veces trabajan más de 45 y de 50 horas… Exigimos un registro real de jornada y el reconocimiento de las horas extraordinarias, compensadas en dinero o en descanso. La dedicación especial que exige este oficio no puede salir gratis a las empresas.




INTELIGENCIA ARTIFICIAL AL SERVICIO DE LA INFORMACIÓN, NO CONTRA QUIENES LA HACEN




Exigimos que el uso de la IA se negocie y se regule en los convenios. No aceptaremos que la automatización sirva para sustituir a profesionales ni para recortar plantillas. Cada puesto que se pierde así degrada la calidad informativa y pone en riesgo el derecho de la ciudadanía a una información veraz.




SEGURIDAD FÍSICA Y ECONÓMICA GARANTIZADA POR CONVENIO




Exigimos que quien cubre conflictos, catástrofes, manifestaciones o cualquier información de riesgo tenga por convenio seguros, protocolos de protección, material adecuado y respaldo económico y jurídico. Esas garantías deben valer también para freelances y colaboradores, no solo para la plantilla.




TELETRABAJO Y CONCILIACIÓN COMO MODELO NATURAL DEL SECTOR




El periodismo ya se hace desde cualquier lugar. Exigimos que el teletrabajo y la jornada sean compatibles con el descanso y el cuidado de nuestros familiares. Y que sean un derecho regulado y compensado en los convenios, y no una concesión que la empresa da y quita a voluntad. Los gastos deben ir a cargo de la empresa y el derecho a la desconexión digital debe estar garantizado.




CONTRA LA PRECARIEDAD Y POR LA ESTABILIDAD EN EL EMPLEO




Que las becas no sustituyan puestos de trabajo: tener becarios es una práctica habitual en nuestro sector y su figura se ha convertido en caldo de cultivo para tener trabajadores y trabajadoras a bajo coste y de las que se pueda prescindir libremente. Algo similar ocurre con los falsos autónomos, personas obligadas a darse de alta como autónomo pero que en realidad dependen completamente de la empresa como cualquier otra en plantilla. Exigimos la desaparición del fraude y el respeto a la legalidad en el empleo.

8 razones para parar en el sector de la prensa y la comunicación este 11-N

 se publicó primero en 

Sindicato CNT de Madrid

.

author: CNT Aragón-Rioja
title: Inspección obliga a Cerma&Arriaxa a reducir la temperatura de sus naves tras una denuncia de CNT
content:
El pasado mes de octubre, Inspección de Trabajo y Seguridad Social ha requerido a Cerma y Arriaxa (principal empresa del sector del alumbrado, ingeniería y regulación del tráfico en Zaragoza) el acondicionamiento de sus naves para antes del verano de 2027, en las que la empresa deberá instalar equipos de climatización adecuados y realizar diversas mejoras.




Además se realizará un seguimiento durante julio y agosto, meses de máximo calor, para registrar temperatura y humedad y ver que las condiciones ambientales están dentro de los márgenes legales, con especial atención a las personas trabajadoras que, por sus circunstancias particulares, sean especialmente sensibles a las altas temperaturas.




Desde la Sección Sindical de CNT en Cerma y Arriaxa, que ya el pasado mes de abril 

conseguimos la retribución de más de 18mil euros de horas impagadas

 para 10 de nuestros afiliados en la empresa, celebramos la nueva victoria que significa para la plantilla de estas medidas de Prevención de Riesgos Laborales. En un escenario de cambio climático, donde las olas de calor son cada año más frecuentes, desde el sindicalismo debemos velar por la seguridad en cada puesto de trabajo.




Animamos a los trabajadores/as a afiliarse y organizarse, para conseguir éstas y otras mejoras en cada empresa, vigilando porque nuestra salud y dignidad se respeten en todo momento.




Si trabajas en Cerma y Arriaxa, cuenta con CNT.







La entrada 

INSPECCIÓN OBLIGA A CERMA & ARRIAXA A REDUCIR LA TEMPERATURA DE SUS NAVES TRAS UNA DENUNCIA DE CNT

 aparece primero en 

CNT Aragón-Rioja

.

title: The death of a scammer Tonggo Simangunsong
content:
Poipet, near the Thailand–Cambodia border. Credit: wattana / Shutterstock.com I t was the end of 2024. Almost five months after losing his job at a food and beverage company, thirty-nine-year-old Rasdy Fawzi told his wife, Kiki Tresia Ginting, that he was going to accept a job in Cambodia. Kiki was concerned, and for good reason. The man who’d offered him the job was part of a scam syndicate; the recruitment agency was unregistered and the work Fawzi would be undertaking was illegal. She’d heard stories of young Indonesians trapped in Cambodia, tortured and forced to work as scammers. “I worried and asked my husband about his safety if he worked there, but he said, ‘That’s okay, it’s fine, don’t worry’,” she recalls. Fawzi reassured her many times that his friend had been there, too, and he trusted him. He believed that he was too old for any company in Indonesia to want to hire him for the same role he’d had in mobile sales marketing with his previous employer. While going to Cambodia was risky, the salary offered would be more than enough to support their small family. It was an opportunity he didn’t want to pass up. In the end, there was nothing Kiki could do but let him go and pray for his safety. To read the rest of this article, and to access all Mekong Review content, please subscribe . title: When the tigers become rats Jake Adelstein
content:
Yakuza fan magazines like Jitsuwa Document were sold all over Japan until as late as 2018. Credit: Jake Adelstein Yakuza: A 400-Year History of the Japanese Underworld Andrew Rankin Basic Books: 2026 . E very few years, someone announces that the Japanese organised crime groups known as the yakuza are finished. Every few years, a book tries to explain what, exactly, has been dying. Many people still assume “the yakuza” are one monolithic criminal organisation ruling Japan from the shadows. That’s completely wrong. They are more than twenty separate criminal organisations. And they have never lived in the shadows. Andrew Rankin has probably written the best explanation yet of their unusual character: Japanese underworld analysts tend to regard the yakuza as a uniquely Japanese phenomenon, and so they dislike the term Japanese mafia. Criminologists in the West have defined a mafia as an organized crime group that specializes in protection: A mafia supplies and sells protection and aggressively tries to monopolize the supply of protection within specific fields of business, both legal and illegal. Understood in that way, the yakuza groups surely constitute a Japanese variety of mafia. There are some types of crimes that yakuza almost never commit, such as armed robbery, kidnapping for ransom, and murder for hire. Regarding protection rackets, however, yakuza ambition knows no bounds. At one time or another, the yakuza have penetrated almost every industry in Japan, from fish markets to geisha agencies, including pachinko parlors, garbage collecting, sumo wrestling, speedboat racing, property development, and pornography. title: Chronicler of insurgencies Kristian Odebjer
content:
Credit: Apirak Kosakijjawut I n October 1985, the Swedish writer Bertil Lintner, then thirty-two, crossed illegally from Indian Nagaland into Burma. A year-and-a-half later, he emerged in Xishuangbanna in Yunnan, China. He’d trekked with his wife, Hseng Noung Lintner, and infant daughter along 2,000 kilometres of Burmese jungle paths, crossing the Chindwin, Mali Hka, and Salween rivers. The aim of the journey was to report on little-known insurgency campaigns waged by groups like the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and the Communist Party of Burma (CPB). This was journalism undertaken by a writer prepared to immerse himself fully in order to tell an important story. The risks were real: on occasion, the family found themselves caught in the middle of active combat. Lintner’s reporting from the trail appeared in the Far Eastern Economic Review , a weekly news magazine. Published in English in 1990, the book Land of Jade: A Journey from India through Northern Burma to China —part travel diary, part eyewitness account—told the story of Burma’s ethnic conflicts through Lintner’s writing and Hseng Noung’s photographs. The book contains plenty of drama as the Lintners survive close calls with the Burmese army and battle serious disease. In the main, however, it is about the people of northern Burma. The family encounters a motley crew of characters: rebels, farmers, missionaries, and drug smugglers. Lintner’s empathy and curiosity lead the way as he forms a close rapport with his interlocutors. As they come alive on the page, the reader is transported to the misty hills of the “land of jade”. To read the rest of this article, and to access all Mekong Review content, please subscribe . author: Mekong Review 2
title: The ineligibles Thammika Songkaeo
content:
BTS at the 61st Annual Grammy Awards in 2019. Credit: Kathy Hutchins / Shutterstock.com W hen BTS, the K-pop boyband, refused to submit their music for consideration in the 2026 Grammy Awards, artists worldwide were filled with pride but also envy. Many know that to walk away from the table, one must first be invited to sit down. For artists outside the West, the Grammys, the Oscars, and major literary prizes represent something far more coercive than mere vanity. Art requires no institutional seal to be profound. The best art in the world is likely unknown to the mainstream. In late capitalism, however, discoverability has come to be a major factor in dictating an artist’s success. While BTS has enough clout to turn down the Grammys, many artists—operating in domestic ecosystems that lack the infrastructure for global marketing and distribution—know that major prizes do not merely recognise creative excellence but also manufacture further success: for instance, foreign-rights advances, festival marquee placement, and prime spots in retail outlets. BTS has been nominated at the Grammys before, but has never won. Their decision not to submit this year was a reaction to the introduction of a new Best Asian Pop Music Performance category. “We hope our music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language,” they said in a statement. This move has been supported by fans as a principled stance against the othering of Asian artists in Western markets but, in the context of major awards, it’s worth considering those who might never have been eligible in the first place. O rganic global reach may not be real. The visibility gap across artistic spheres does not stem from an uneven distribution of talent but from the cold arithmetic of wealth and operations. In creative capitalism, success builds success. Early structural visibility compounds exponentially, and the capacity to achieve such visibility is not evenly spread across the world. BTS did not conquer Western airwaves in an institutional vacuum. They emerged from a nation that had spent decades assembling a cultural export engine. The band worked hard but also had a system to benefit from, unlike artists in regions like Southeast Asia. Many Southeast Asian artists have no supportive infrastructure for boosting; in some cases, their own governments view them with indifference or active suspicion. Without the resources to amplify output, hard work alone is rarely enough to achieve breakout success. Yet, as the Grammys demonstrate, even a worldwide sensation like BTS can run into the glass ceiling of Western gatekeeping. If even BTS must fight to be truly equal, where does that leave the rest of us? W hile many focus on the ways non-anglophone literature can “go global” if picked up for translation, more thought needs to be given to something more quietly insidious: prizes. On the surface, literary prizes seem like wonderful megaphones. Often, one sees people celebrate a book they discovered because of a prize. However, at literary festivals internationally, I have watched serious bibliophiles and readers who consider themselves politically informed recoil in disbelief when confronted with the entry requirements of the world’s most celebrated literary prizes. The Booker Prize, for instance, mandates that a novel be written originally in English and published in the United Kingdom or Ireland by a recognised imprint. (Even if the parent company is British or Irish, only imprints registered in the UK or Ireland will be eligible to submit titles.) Although it does not name or market itself as this, the Booker Prize is, in practice, the UK and Ireland Book Prize for several reasons, starting with how gatekeeping exists from the most fundamental level of deciding what gets published in those countries in the first place. Many, many authors who have no associations with these countries discuss rejections they have received from UK or Irish publishers. A common denominator: they wrote about life outside of these places, chronicling local complexities. In other words, they were Asians writing about life in Asia, or Africans writing about life in Africa. Securing a UK or Irish publishing contract is an extraordinary anomaly for such writers. British and Irish publishers are accountable to their bottom lines, and as such mind what their (British and Irish) readership want, which is suspected to be something more obviously relatable. Learning of the Booker’s bottleneck, readers often ask: “What about the International Booker then?” The moniker suggests embrace, the word “international” connoting a warmer and more inclusive approach to global talent. In truth, its criteria impose an equally restrictive administrative sieve: the submission must have originally been written in a language other than English, translated into English, and published by a UK or Irish press. Here is where—if we can give the International Booker the benefit of the doubt that being published by a UK or Irish press does not immediately prompt expectations, conscious or otherwise, of some exoticisation—we face a reality many have not considered: many authors who are “international” write in English. For various reasons—colonial history, contemporary childhood upbringing, the multitude of places where English is still perceived as the language of opportunity—an increasing number of people are educated in and write in English. A postcolonial catch-22 cruelly surfaces in the International Booker’s eligibility criteria. Across large swaths of former colonies—such as India, Pakistan, and Singapore—English is the medium of national intellectual life, education, and literary expression. Ironically, writers who inherited the language of the empire are now excluded by one of the world’s most prestigious literary prizes . W hen anglophone institutions turn their attention towards the wider world, they rely heavily on a familiar compromise: the elevation of the diaspora. This is relatable, or at least ‘relevant’ , to the aforementioned publishers. Confronted with demands for racial and cultural diversity, gatekeepers routinely select artists who are first- or second-generation immigrants. The outputs of these creators frequently focus on the friction of immigration: generational estrangement, hyphenated identities, racial code-switching, and the melancholic excavation of an ancestral homeland. These narratives are vital, artistic contributions to the countries where their authors reside, but cannot be substitutes for the literature of non-diasporic writers, who inhabit an entirely distinct ontological universe. Anglophone publishers and institutions should not be able to pat themselves on the back for ticking the diversity box simply because they’ve included a few diaspora writers. In fact, it is highly morally and ethically wrong to see diasporic writers be celebrated in lieu of non-diasporic writers. The substitution never comes overtly, but through celebrations of diversity being achieved when a diasporic writer, with an immigration-related story that the West can relate to or sees its involvement in, has some spotlight, while the majority of the world could not contend in the first place. Whether or not these substitutions are done consciously or unconsciously by the industry, we, writers of the non-diaspora, cannot accept this, for our long-lost cousins should not substitute for us. It perpetuates a dynamic with the West where we only exist in relation to them. The ‘same kind of face’ does not mean the same stories or experiences. I n cities worldwide, literary and arts festivals design their programmes around headliners certified by metropolitan prizes. An author who lacks a Booker nomination or a film director without a Cannes premiere might struggle to pack an auditorium, regardless of their mastery. Event organisers, operating on lean municipal grants and ticket revenues, must trade in the universal currency of Western acclaim. The colonial relationship is replicated on home soil: domestic audiences learn to evaluate their own storytellers through the seal of approval granted by institutions thousands of miles away. To demand that artists in under-resourced regions ignore these dynamics and ‘focus purely on the craft’ is a romantic delusion. It demands an exhausting level of psychological fortitude, requiring an artist not only to produce serious work amid financial precarity, but to suppress the bitterness that comes from watching better-resourced works elevated by institutional engines—not for the sake of craft. The true loss belongs not only to the artists who fail to secure a place on an overseas prize roster, but also to our collective intellectual life. When the machinery of global validation systematically excludes many—quietly, sometimes under a guise of generosity—it ensures that our enjoyment of the arts is curated by a handful of metropolitan committees catering to their own domestic market anxieties and ability to relate to other humans. BTS can walk away from the Grammys because they already possess an alternative empire. For the rest of the world’s creators, there is nowhere to withdraw to. We remain trapped inside a cultural geography where the most urgent stories are precisely the ones the global clearinghouses were never built to amplify, and so maybe, even if feeling slighted, we would take the title of the ‘Best Asian’ something. Thammika Songkaeo is a 2022 National Geographic Explorer and the author of Stamford Hospital . The post

title: Chasing the burning pearl Angela Sim
content:
The fire dragon in flight. Credit: Yeo G.T. I n the pantheon of Chinese mythology, few symbols command as much awe as the dragon (龍). Majestic and unrestrained, it stands as the preeminent member of the four divine creatures, alongside the turtle (龟), phoenix (凤), and qilin (麒麟). Historically, the dragon was the ultimate emblem of the Son of Heaven. During the Ming dynasty, the five-clawed dragon adorned the  buzi  (補子), or rank badges, of the Emperor’s robes. These intricate badges weren’t merely decorative; they were markers of nobility and merit, awarded to those who performed exceptional service. Despite its omnipresence, the dragon remains a creature of pure myth, never witnessed by the human eye yet vividly rendered through the ages. It is a biological mosaic; a lion’s nose and tiger’s mouth paired with the ears of an ox and the shimmering eyes of a goldfish. Crowned with deer antlers and grounded by eagle claws, its energetic, snake-like body is shielded by the underbelly of a clam. To the Chinese world, this auspicious creature is more than legend; it is spiritual sustenance used to conquer nature and ward off evil. Whether dwelling in the depths of the water or the vastness of the sky, the dragon’s eleven distinct forms remain a powerful symbol of protection. In Singapore, this reverence finds its most vibrant expression in the dragon dance. Chasing the ‘pearl of wisdom’ to the thunderous beat of percussion, the dragon has been a harbinger of clement weather and bountiful harvests since the Han dynasty. Today, it remains a staple of the Lunar New Year and a blessing for new beginnings, bridging the gap between ancient ritual and contemporary celebration. author: Mekong Review 2
title: The state and the sin Rafly Gilang Pratama
content:
Calling themselves “boti hunters”, young men on motorcycles ride through dark alleys in Bogor targeting people they perceive to be queer. Credit: Dominic Kurniawan Suryaputra / Unsplash T he young men in the videos sounded as though they were having fun. It was well past midnight in Bogor, Indonesia’s “rain city”. The roads were mostly empty and the boys rode motorcycles, looking for people they perceived to be gay, effeminate, or transgender. They revved their engines as they rode through the streets, shouting: “Bersih-bersih boti!” “Clean up the boti!” They proudly called themselves “boti hunters”, turning boti , a slang term derived from ‘bottom’, into the name of their little vigilante enterprise. There’s something accidentally homoerotic about groups of young men spending their midnight hours patrolling pitch-black alleys thinking about nothing but bottoms—but then someone in the frame starts running for their life, and the joke dies. Accounts carrying variations of the “boti hunter” name soon appeared online. In the videos, the boys laugh and shout while they chase people through the streets, filming everything for a little bit of social media clout. I’ve heard those laughs before. I attended an elite, all-boys pesantren , an Islamic boarding school, in West Java. I entered primary school through a scholarship programme for yatim —children who had lost their fathers—and students from low-income families. By junior high, paying students from much wealthier families had joined us, many able to afford fees my family would have considered astronomical. We joked that the pesantren was a “holy jail”: we were cut off from almost everything beyond the compound, our school surrounded by high walls with barbed wire. Our contact with the outside world was limited to about thirty minutes of restricted internet use at the end of computer class, Sunday family visits, and newspaper clippings pinned to noticeboards around the campus. I remember how my friends and I were then. My roommates and I would steal (sorry!) the newspapers from the noticeboards and hoard the sports pages inside plastic binders. Our most prized trophy was a grainy image of Cristiano Ronaldo in his gloriously red Manchester United home kit. We loved the swagger, but mostly we loved that he belonged somewhere outside our cloistered world. One of my friends was from England—I called him “Brit Boy”—and some of the other kids would make fun of him for playing with us scholarship kids. Twelve-year-old boys can be cruel. Hundreds of us living together, without girls or much privacy, meant that we turned our attention towards one another. As a scholarship kid whose father died when I was two, I learnt to harden myself. I had little in the way of a monthly allowance, and I didn’t receive the care packages that arrived for some of the other boys. I couldn’t compare with the rich kids who went on holiday and came back to school wearing the same bright Nike or Adidas shoes that professional footballers wore. I had no interest in becoming easy prey, so I tried my best to keep my head down. One of the words we threw around was banci , a slur for boys thought to be too ‘feminine’. I had a friend who cared about his skin. We usually went straight to the mosque after our afternoon classes, carrying our bags with us at the end of the school day. One afternoon, he sat among us, putting something on his face. I don’t even remember what it was anymore, but that was enough. Suddenly, he was “banci” and the other boys were making fun of him. I laughed, too. I was scared of becoming the next boy people laughed at. At that age, drawing attention to myself felt like flying too close to the sun. Laughing along felt safer. D uring those years in school, we learnt the story of Prophet Lut and the destruction of Sodom. We heard frightening descriptions of stones, each engraved with a sinner’s name, falling from the sky, and the earth being overturned. We were taught that it was an azab, a divine punishment. By the age of nine, I had internalised the message that it was a sin for men to develop romantic relationships with other men, and that tolerating this sin would bring punishment upon everyone. It was only years later that I would encounter other interpretations of the story, including from progressive Muslim scholars, that centred coercion, sexual violence, and abuse of power. In our school, we were aware of kakak-adek-an —situations in which older boys developed conspicuously close attachments to younger boys, often the fair-skinned, smooth-faced ones. (We had a word for them, too: amrad , the unbearded youth.) Some of the kakak-adek-an relationships may have been exactly what they claimed to be—just an older boy looking out for a younger kid—but others are harder for me to remember so innocently. From time to time, there were stories of sexual abuse: we once heard that an older boy, who had been given authority over a dormitory room of younger students, had made those who were under his charge touch him after lights-out. His punishment was gruesome: positioned in the centre of the open courtyard, many of us were ordered to watch as he received twenty strokes of a rattan cane on the naked soles of his feet before he was expelled. A friend also once told me about being cornered by an older boy in an empty classroom after prayers. Most of the other boys were playing outside when this boy led him away. My friend said he was pressured to touch him, but somebody ran past the classroom and that disruption put a stop to everything. The story stuck in my mind; back then, I had no real way of separating abuse from sexuality. In my young mind, homosexuality and predation blurred together, because so many of the same-sex encounters that I remember being told about involved coercion or abuse. There were no examples of same-sex couples who had simply chosen each other. All I had, in that gated world behind barbed wire, were rattan strikes to the feet and stories of boys being assaulted and then silenced over bowls of bakso and mie ayam. It took me years to understand that abuse was about coercion and power, that it was not the same as homosexual love. W hen I was in Grade 10, I moved to another pesantren in Central Java, at the foot of Mount Merbabu. This second school is why my story is not a simple, clear-cut one of internalising hatred in religious establishments and later being liberated from conservatism. I found a tight-knit community in this second pesantren and still treasure much of what boarding-school life gave me. Some of the friendships I made there have lasted into adulthood, and my years in that school also gave me some of the ideas I later used to question my own prejudice. The previous school had shut us in, but I never saw this pesantren as another place to escape. I learnt how to live away from my mother, to live among people I had not chosen and yet still find my footing. I learnt that it was possible to end up anywhere on God’s green earth and still fit right in. So, when I eventually moved to Cluj-Napoca in Romania in my early twenties, the distance barely made me flinch. It was an adaptability that mattered in a predominantly white, Eastern Orthodox country where I was constantly the outsider. Cluj-Napoca, Romania. Credit: Motofily My pesantren years left me with religious concepts I use to this day, although not always in the way I was taught to use them. Two were hablum minallah , one’s relationship with God, and hablum minannas , one’s relationship with other people. Hablum minallah became increasingly private to me as I got older. Whatever bargain I have with God is difficult enough; it’s no one’s business to weigh in on something that’s only between us. Hablum minannas was trickier because it had to do with my interactions with other people. But by the time I boarded a plane for Europe in the winter of 2020, some of the beliefs I’d grown up with were already loosening their grip on me. One of the first openly queer people I became close to in Romania was a bisexual German woman. We dated for a month or two; she later married a woman back in her home country. Then there was another woman I dated. One afternoon, while on a bus, I noticed a rainbow pin on her very mainstream JanSport backpack. “Wait. Are you…?” “Yeah,” she replied. “Didn’t I tell you?” “No? But cool.” The bus kept going. There was nothing more that needed to be said. This was true of most of the queer people I met; unlike the horror stories I’d heard in my childhood, there was nothing frightening or threatening about their sexual orientation. People, whether queer or straight, went to class, partied too hard, missed buses and trams, fell in and out of relationships, and worried about their exams. Obviously, there was plenty of homophobia in Romania, too. Like in Indonesia, people teased and joked about being gay—as if it was something insulting or strange—and the government still does not recognise same-sex marriages or registered partnerships. In the 2026 Rainbow Map compiled by ILGA-Europe, an umbrella organisation of LGBTQ+ groups in Europe and Central Asia, Romania is the lowest-ranked European Union member state in terms of legal and policy practices relevant to LGBTQ+ people. But the ordinary lives of the queer people around me were a world away from the revulsion for queer people that my first pesantren had drummed into us. W hile in Romania, I also got a taste of what it felt like to be reduced to just one aspect of myself. Almost every Friday in Cluj, I would walk twenty minutes down to Hașdeu, a massive student complex. The mosque was housed in an Islamic community centre tucked just outside Pasteur, barely a three-minute walk from Piezișă, the city’s infamous student party street. Leaving my shoes at the door, I prayed in a carpeted room with other international students and foreigners, many Arab and North African. I kept up this routine for my first two years in Romania, but began to show up less in my third year. I didn’t pretend to be a saint. I checked if the university canteen’s sarmale (cabbage rolls) contained pork, but was never above grabbing a glass of mulled wine at the overpriced Christmas markets when the season rolled around. I wasn’t the most pious of Muslims, but no ustaz hunted me down to tell me that I was damned. Despite my changing relationship with Islam, Ramadan meant something to me beyond a set of religious rules. As the month approached, I told the woman with the JanSport backpack that I wanted to fast. She did not take it well. During the argument that followed, she eventually told me: “I’m not saying all Muslims are terrorists, but all terrorists are Muslims.” When I told her to get out of my apartment, she cried, as if I had been the one in the wrong. I hated that all the other things she knew about me suddenly mattered less than the fact that I was Muslim. It was a reminder that, just as I didn’t want to be reduced to just my religion, I had no business reducing someone else to just their sexual orientation. A verse I had recited since childhood began to sound different: “ Lakum diinukum wa liya diin (for you your religion, for me mine)”. I could keep my faith without expecting other people to live by it. My early relationship with Islam had been shaped by a carrot-and-stick system—there was constant judgment about whether I conformed to the rules or not. While Islam has given me things that I value, I don’t want my religion to simply be a box of dos and don’ts. I realised that it was unreasonable to demand that everyone adhere to my beliefs and standards; in any case, I’d stopped caring about policing how other people lived. It was never my place to sit in judgment of others. N ot long after I moved back to Indonesia, I met an old friend from my second pesantren at a coffee shop near the Romanian embassy in central Jakarta. We sat in the open-air smoking area and did what old classmates do: tried to work out who had married, who had had kids, who had disappeared. All the fun, juicy gossip. Nearly five years abroad had changed how I dressed. In Europe, I got used to walking outside in a sleeveless cotton vest, a necklace, and loose trousers without it even occurring to me that such an outfit might signal anything about my sexuality. “You look like a boti,” my friend suddenly said. “What makes me look like one?” He looked me over again, inspecting the ‘evidence’. I touched my necklace and asked if that was the problem. Then the vest. Or maybe the trousers? He laughed a little and said, “I don’t know. You just do.” Heh? Nothing came out of that offhand comment, but it wasn’t the last time someone made assumptions based on how I dressed, reminding me how quickly judgment and prejudice can manifest. Months later, something happened in Indonesia on a much larger scale. President Prabowo Subianto signed Presidential Regulation (Perpres) No. 111 of 2025. It laid out Indonesia’s general national defence policy for 2025 to 2029, and included a long list of non-military threats to the country. Terrorism and separatism appeared alongside radicalism, prohibited ideologies, narcotics, online gambling, illegal lending, and… “ penyebaran budaya Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Queer (LGBTQ) ”, which roughly translates to “the spread of LGBTQ culture”. My conservative education had insisted that queer relationships were sinful. But a threat ? That word carried a different weight. My mind went to Joshua Oppenheimer’s The Act of Killing and The Look of Silence , films about the anti-communist massacres of 1965 to 1966. Suharto’s New Order regime spent decades framing those killings as a justified defence of Indonesia against a communist threat. Looking at the new presidential regulation, I feared that Indonesians were once again being turned against their fellow citizens. The government has tried to have its cake and eat it, too, drawing a line between LGBTQ+ people and LGBTQ+ “culture”. In July 2026, Yusril Ihza Mahendra, the coordinating minister for law, human rights, immigration, and corrections, said Perpres 111 could not justify the persecution of queer Indonesians; the threat, he said, was the spread of LGBTQ+ “culture”, not the people themselves. That same month, the religious affairs ministry said it was preparing educational material for students as young as fourth graders to prevent the spread of such “culture”. I was around that age when homosexuality was presented to me as something frightening and shameful. That was when teachers told us the story of Prophet Lut; when it was heavily implied that same-sex relationships could only be harmful and abusive; when we began to police one another in our boarding school, ready to pounce on anything that seemed to diverge from what was expected of boys. That was when I learnt to laugh at another boy when he was singled out for being “banci”; I’d even thought that he deserved it. My own upbringing is proof that it’s not possible to denounce a “culture” without hurting the people associated with it. The videos from Bogor went viral on social media in mid-July and are still available online. Amnesty International Indonesia reported that at least ten trans women had been targeted there in a two-month period. In some cases, the attackers forced the victims to strip and tore their clothes. Through it all, the boys who called themselves “boti hunters” laughed. Where did they pick up these attitudes towards queer people? Whenever I think of this, I remember that a young Rafly would probably have laughed along, too. Rafly Gilang Pratama is an Indonesian journalist and writer based in Jakarta. He is a senior journalist and associate editor at Migrant Times , where he covers migration, labour, and human mobility across Asia. He previously lived and reported in Romania, and his work has appeared in Internazionale , Scena9 , Școala9 , and Romania Insider . The post

The state and the sin

Rafly Gilang Pratama

appeared first on Mekong Review .

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Ottawa’s International Inuit Day brings communities together
content:
Clyde River seamstress Sarah Kiliktee had never seen a traditional sealskin tent before she helped build one in Ottawa.




Kiliktee travelled south to teach members of Ottawa-based Isaruit Inuit Arts how to construct an ittaq, a traditional Inuit tent made from sealskins.




Pangnirtung singer-songwriter Joey Nowyuk performs in Inuktitut for a crowd at Isaruit Inuit Arts’ sixth annual International Inuit Day celebration at Annie Pootoogook Park in Ottawa on Saturday. (Photo by Nehaa Bimal)




The project began Oct. 26 and was completed 10 days later, just in time for Saturday’s International Inuit Day celebration at Annie Pootoogook Park in Ottawa’s Sandy Hill neighbourhood, near the University of Ottawa.







Twenty-five sealskins were stitched together to make the tent that was on display at the park for visitors to step inside.




Kiliktee said the group of nine seamstresses relied on Google Images for reference because sealskin tents are no longer commonly used. They repeatedly checked measurements and patched holes around the flippers and tails of the skins.




“This is our first time and it turned out good, so we’re happy with it,” she said.
















Kiliktee said she came to Ottawa specifically for the celebration and was scheduled to leave early Sunday morning.




Austin Joseph Lafreniere Kaufhold, left, and Khalid El-Masri stand in line for the traditional feast at the International Inuit Day celebration at Annie Pootoogook Park in Ottawa on Saturday. (Photo by Nehaa Bimal)




It was the sixth annual celebration, organized by Isaruit, and it brought together Inuit artists, performers, vendors and visitors for an afternoon of cultural activities and food.







The feast featured frozen caribou, or quaq, and beluga, or muktuk, as well as roasted caribou.







Among the vendors was Aupaluk Designs founder Eleanor Partridge, who is originally from Kuujjuaq, and now based in Ontario.







It was Partridge’s third time selling her work at the celebration, she said, adding that non-Inuit attendees often ask about her earrings, which feature miniature ulus, and what the traditional tool is used for.



















The event also attracted visitors from First Nations communities interested in learning about Inuit culture.







Khalid El-Masri, from Ochapowace Nation, a Cree First Nation in southern Saskatchewan, attended with 16 students from the Indigenous Leadership Opportunity Year at the Royal Military College of Canada in Kingston, Ont.




The program gives First Nations, Métis and Inuit students an opportunity to experience university-level education and military life.




El-Masri said the event offered an opportunity to learn about Indigenous cultures beyond his own.




“We’re all a bunch of different tribes, a bunch of different people. Each reservation practices something different,” El-Masri said. 
















“Inuit communities are, especially in this area, really underrepresented, so we’re coming down here to experience the Inuit way of life, try 

muktuk

 and hopefully speak to some elders,” he added.




The afternoon’s entertainment included musical performances in Inuktitut by Pangnirtung singer-songwriter Joey Nowyuk, Ottawa-based drum dancer Donovan Gordon Tootoo, originally from Rankin Inlet, and the Nunavut Sivuniksavut students’ performing group.
