title: Ken Knabb - The Relevance of Rexroth
content:
Author

: Ken Knabb

Title

: The Relevance of Rexroth

Date

: 1990

Notes

: Originally published in 1990, reprinted in 1998 in Public Secrets: Collected Skirmished of Ken Knabb

Source

: https://bopsecrets.org/PS/Rexroth.htm




Chapter 1: Life and Literature

Brief biography. What he was like in person. His poetry. Opposition to Pound, Eliot, and academia. Remarkable variety and liveliness of his essays. Views on Blake, Baudelaire, Whitman, Henry Miller, etc. 




Chapter 2: Magnanimity and Mysticism

Magnanimity as central theme of his life and works. Mystical experiences. Views on Taoism, Buddhism, Christianity, psychedelics, pseudosciences, D.H. Lawrence, Martin Buber, etc. 




Chapter 3: Society and Revolution

His opposition to Bolshevism. His anarchist perspectives and activities. Views on the Beats, the sixties counterculture, ecology, underground songs, etc. Ambiguity of his position as public social critic. Limits of his social analyses and of his notion of cultural subversion. 




Chapter 1: Life and Literature







 REXROTH (

before reading his poetry

): “Well, what would you like tonight, sex, mysticism, or revolution?” 










 WOMAN IN AUDIENCE: “What’s the difference?” 







 Kenneth Rexroth was born in Indiana in 1905, descended from a variety of abolitionists, socialists, anarchists, feminists and freethinkers. After an unusually enlightened upbringing he was orphaned at the age of twelve. He spent most of his teenage years in Chicago, where he worked as a newspaper reporter and helped run a jazz coffee house, mingling with the musicians, artists, writers, radicals and eccentrics who made up the bohemian world of the twenties. Almost totally self-educated (he had only five years of formal schooling), he read omnivorously, wrote poetry, did abstract painting, worked in avant-garde theater and began teaching himself several languages. In his late teens he hitched all over the country, spending summers in the Far West working as a cowboy cook and wrangler and at various farm and forestry jobs, and once worked his way to Paris and back. 




 He recounts these early adventures in 

An Autobiographical Novel

.

 The first impression you get is that it is mostly about other people — Louis Armstrong, Alexander Berkman, Clarence Darrow, Eugene Debs, Marcel Duchamp, Emma Goldman, D.H. Lawrence, Diego Rivera, Carl Sandburg, Edward Sapir, Sacco and Vanzetti all turn up briefly, along with an Indian woman who introduces him to sexual yoga, a member of the Bugs Moran gang who later retires to Hollywood as a consultant for gangster movies, a talkative poet who says he has belonged to “the three most gossipy organizations in modern life, the Anglo-Catholics, the Trotskyites, and the homosexuals,” and a multitude of others — anarchists, Communists, Wobblies, dadaists, surrealists, occultists, prostitutes, crooks, cops, judges, jailers, hoboes, hillbillies, lumberjacks, cowboys, Indians. . . . It’s a fascinating book, not only for its account of Rexroth’s own incredible range of experiences, but for its evocation of a radical-libertarian American subculture that passed away in the early years of the century and for its glimpses of the 1920s bohemianism that foreshadowed the later worldwide counterculture. “What I was witnessing was the development in a few places in Chicago, New York, and Paris of a culture pattern that was to spread all over the world. In another generation all professional people of any pretense to bohemianism in Sydney or Oslo did the things we did, but back in those days we all knew one another.” 




An Autobiographical Novel

 leaves off in 1927 [a later edition brings the story up to 1949], when Rexroth moved to San Francisco. (He said he liked it because it was accessible to the Western mountains, remote from New York cultural domination, and virtually the only major American city that was not settled by puritans but by “gamblers, prostitutes, rascals, and fortune seekers.”) In the thirties and forties he played an active role in a number of libertarian, civil rights and antiwar groups (during World War II he was a conscientious objector), and he was the leading spirit in the literary and cultural ferment that led to the postwar San Francisco Renaissance. During the fifties and sixties he wrote poems, plays, essays and social criticism, translated poetry from seven languages, presented book reviews and other programs over noncommercial radio KPFA, and pioneered the reading of poetry to jazz. 




 In 1968 he moved to Santa Barbara, California, where he taught courses in underground poetry and song. Apart from several extended visits to Japan, he lived there until his death in 1982. 







 * * * 







 I was fortunate enough to get to know him a little in the sixties, when I attended a class he was giving at San Francisco State College. He had been at odds with academia all his life (he called the universities “fog factories”), but by this time his stature was so undeniable and there was such a demand for “relevance” in education that he was allowed to create whatever course he wanted. His “class,” which was certainly more instructive than any other I ever took, consisted simply of open-ended discussions of anything and everything, along with occasional other activities such as group dramatic performances.

author: Unknown
title: Killing King Abacus - Parodie und Subversion: Notizen zu Rollen
content:
Katalog Liste aller Texte AutorInnen Themen Letzte Einträge Zur Bibliothek hinzufügen

Mehr Kontakt Material Sticker, Plakate, etc.

Rollen sind die wiederholbare Aufführung einer bestimmten Reihe von Machtbeziehungen. Der Anreiz dazu, eine Rolle zu spielen ist ein Stückchen Macht; selbst wenn man eine unterwürfige Rolle spielt muss es dafür irgendeine Art von Anreiz geben, selbst wenn es nur ein negativer Anreiz ist, die Vermeidung eines schlimmeren Schicksals. Zu sagen, dass Rollen Aufführungen sind, macht sie nicht unreal, Rollen sind reale Akte, Akte, die wiederholt werden, bis sie sich zu Gewohnheiten verfestigen. Rollen tauchen nicht einfach aus dem Nichts auf, sondern werden von Institutionen, wie der Familie, dem Arbeitsplatz, Unternehmen, Bürokratien, Schulen aufrechterhalten und halten im Gegenzug die Machtstrukturen diese Institutionen aufrecht. Es gibt objektive soziale Strukturen und Institutionen, die Rollen aufrechterhalten, was nicht bedeutet, dass diese in Stein gemeißelt wären. Es gibt subjektive Sehnsüchte diese Rollen zu unterlaufen und zu zerstören, was nicht bedeutet, dass dies einfach wäre oder dass die Subversion Erfolg haben wird. In der Spannung zwischen den Machtstrukturen und dem Verlangen zu rebellieren findet das Spiel der Subversion statt.

Ethnizität, Geschlecht und Klasse existierten schon vor dem Kapitalismus, allerdings in sehr unterschiedlicher Form. Ethnizität wurde vom Aufkommen des Nationalstaats drastisch verändert, Geschlechterrollen haben sich durch die Proletarisierung von Frauen verändert und es ist recht offensichtlich, dass der Aufstieg des Kapitalismus die Klassenstruktur verändert hat. Nichtsdestotrotz wurden Rollen, die auf Geschlecht, Ethnizität und Klasse basierten sowohl vor dem Aufstieg des Kapitalismus, wie auch danach von den Machtstrukturen dazu genutzt, um die Machtbeziehungen aufrechtzuerhalten. Nationalismus ist etwas, das die Menschen oft nicht historisieren, sie begreifen schlicht nicht, wie jung der Nationalstaat ist und dass dieser die bloße Vorstellung von kultureller Identität beeinträchtigt hat. Unser derzeitiges Konzept von Ethnizität (dieses Wort stammt von dem griechischen Wort für Nation) ist vom Nationalstaat geprägt. Einige glauben, dass Nationalismus in seiner derzeitigen Form schon lange vor dem Aufkommen des Nationalstaats existierte und andere glauben, dass das Patriarchat in der Vergangenheit in einer stärkeren Form existierte, die sich heute langsam auflöst. Patriarchat ist eines der offensichtlicheren Beispiele eines Prozesses, der die Rollen der Herrschaft und Unterwerfung schon lange vor dem Kapitalismus aufrecht erhielt. Ich würde argumentieren, dass einige Formen von Patriarchat tatsächlich abgenommen haben, aber das das Patriarchat im allgemeinen nicht verschwindet, sondern vielmehr vom Kapital in eine andere Form umgewandelt wurde, diejenigen Aspekte, die den Kapitalfluss und die Proletarisierung der Frauen einschränkten, wurden verändert. Patriarchat ist keine einzelne, globale monolithische Struktur; es ist kulturell und hat verschiedene Formen. Es beginnt in der Familie, breitet sich auf andere Institutionen aus und wird folglich in der gesamten Gesellschaft reproduziert. Kapitalismus reproduziert neue, mutierte Formen des Patriarchats, er bedient sich der Geschlechterunterschiede, ebenso wie er sich der Klassenunterschiede und ethnischen/rassischen Unterschieden bedient, um die Arbeitskraft im größtmöglichen Maße auszubeuten.

Wie können wir die Kategorien der Identität dazu nutzen, die Gesellschaft in der wir leben zu verstehen, ohne genau die Rollen zu reproduzieren, die wir überwinden wollen? Das ist trickreich, denn wenn wir die Kategorien, die Geschlecht, Rasse und Ethnizität beschreiben, einfach verwerfen, verlieren wir wichtige Werkzeuge, die wir benötigen, um zu verstehen, wie diese Gesellschaft funktioniert, wie diese Kategorien unsere Beziehungen beeinträchtigen und strukturieren. Auf der anderen Seite verfällt man leicht dazu, genau die Rollen aufrechtzuerhalten, die wir überwinden wollen. Das ist ein Problem, das oft in der Identitätspolitik auftaucht, die von einer identitären Kategorie ausgeht. Da solche Politiken auf identitären Kategorien basieren, die im Wesentlichen an Rollen gebunden sind, verfestigt man diese, wenn man nicht bewusst versucht, diese Rollen zu unterlaufen. Kürzlich bezog sich der Artikel „Stick it to the Manarchy“ auf Frauen und People of Color auf die selbe Weise wie auf Kategorien wie die Ältesten und Kinder, als ob weiblich oder nicht weiß zu sein eine Person weniger dazu befähigen würde, mit Demonstrationen und Riots umzugehen. Das Argument ist, dass People of Color härter verfolgt werden würden, was stimmt, und doch habe ich nie bemerkt, dass dies irgendjemand abgeschreckt hätte. Tatsächlich sind es meiner Erfahrung nach jene, die aus privilegierteren Hintergründen kommen, die mehr Angst vor solchen Situationen haben. Was ihr Grund dafür ist, Frauen in dieser Liste aufzuführen das habe ich nicht verstanden. In jedem Fall verfallen die Autoren in einen bevormundenden Tonfall, ungeachtet irgendwelcher gegenteiligen Absichten. Es gibt die Gefahr, dass die Diskussion über Geschlecht in einen bevormundenden Tonfall verfällt, der die Rolle von Frauen als Opfer aufrechterhält. Auf der anderen Seite bedeutet das nicht, dass wir die Diskussion über Sexismus, der sehr real ist, vermeiden sollten, oder dass sich Frauen nicht darüber beschweren sollten, übergangen zu werden, weil sie vermeiden wollen ein Bild der Frau als Opfer abzugeben. Wir können die Kategorien von Geschlecht, Rasse, Klasse und so weiter nur dann abwerfen, wenn wir auf den Ruinen dieser Gesellschaft tanzen und gelernt haben, uns ohne diese Rollen in einer klassenlosen, staatenlosen Gesellschaft aufeinander zu beziehen. Bis zu diesem Zeitpunkt können wir nur vortäuschen, dass wir alle gleich behandelt werden; Einfach den Tod dieser sozialen Trennungen zu behaupten, indem wir uns weigern, uns auf diese zu beziehen, erreicht nichts außer dem Verlust eines Mittels zur Konfrontation der Probleme, die sie erzeugen.

Rasse (bzw. Rassismus) basiert im Gegensatz zu Ethnizität auf der Erscheinung einer Person und nicht notwendigerweise auf ihrer Kultur. Ich behaupte nicht, dass Rasse etwas biologisches wäre, sie ist eine soziale Konstruktion. Es geht vielmehr darum, dass beispielsweise eine schwarze Person, die von Weißen aufgezogen wurde und die kulturell von weißen nicht unterscheidbar ist, noch immer Rassismus erfährt. Geschlecht ist allgemein rund um biologische Geschlechtsmerkmale strukturiert (man muss sein Aussehen drastisch verändern, um als Angehörige*r eines anderen Geschlechts behandelt zu werden); die von diesen Kategorien beschriebenen Merkmale sind teilweise bioloigisch (oder basieren auf der Annahme der Existenz einer bestimmten Biologie) und folglich ist es unmöglich, vollständig mit diesen Kategorien zu brechen, solange die gegenwärtige Gesellschaft besteht, da sie beeinflussen, wie Menschen dich behandeln, unabhängig davon wie du dich verhältst. Das heißt, Rasse und Geschlecht bestehen aus mehr als bloß Rollen.

Rollen sind sozial, weil sie Beziehungen sind, sie sind Aufführungen in denen es immer eine Interaktion mit dem Publikum gibt. Sie können nicht einfach auf einer individuellen Ebene durchbrochen werden; durch die Veränderung oder den Bruch mit einer Rolle verändert man notwendigerweise eine Beziehung. Allerdings bedeutet das nicht, dass sie nur kollektiv durchbrochen werden könnten, oder gar nur von der Gesellschaft als Ganzes. Rollen zu verändern bedeutet Beziehungen zu verändern und so eine Veränderung kann auf vielen Ebenen stattfinden, sie ist nicht ausschließlich eine Frage der kollektiven Veränderung. Es gibt unzählige Zwischenstufen zu sozialem Wandel, die zwischen Individuum und Kollektiv oder dem individuellen und dem gesellschaftlichen liegen. Wir müssen also nicht darauf warten, dass irgendein „kollektiver Bruch“ bevorzustehen scheint, um die Rollen zu überwinden, die unsere Beziehungen formen. Es ist vielmehr genau nicht das Warten, sondern damit zu beginnen diese Beziehungen jetzt in dem Grad, der nur möglich ist, zu untergraben, was einen Bruch schließlich sich auf die Gesellschaft als Ganze ausbreiten lassen wird. Ich beziehe mich dabei nicht auf einen kollektiven Bruch im Sinne eines homogenen, simultanen Bruchs mit Rollen, sondern einen facettenreichen Bruch, der sich durch die ganze Gesellschaft ausbreitet; das Konzept von rollenlosen Beziehungen impliziert notwendigerweise Vielfachheit, da ohne Rolle zu handeln bedeutet, ohne jene Machtbeziehungen zu handeln, die Homogenität erzeugen. Natürlich ist es nicht so einfach, es ist nicht nur eine Frage, ob alle versuchen, einen Wandel in ihren alltäglichen Leben zu erzeugen und dass sich dieser Wandel zur Revolution aufsummiert. Ein ausgedehnter Bruch mit Rollen impliziert auch einen ausgedehnten Bruch mit den Machtbeziehungen, die Rollen aufrechterhalten – in anderen Worten: Kapital und Staat müssen in all ihren Ausdrucksformen zerstört werden, den zahlreichen Mikro-Weisen auf die sie unsere Beziehungen infiltrieren ebenso wie ihren makroskopischen institutionellen Formen.

Mit einer Rolle zu brechen ist nichts, das sofort oder einfach erreicht werden könnte, oft muss man erst einen Prozesse der Untergrabung und Überdehnung von Rollen durchmachen, mit ihnen spielen, die Unnatürlichkeit von Rollen durch Parodie aufzeigen. Wie enthüllen wir die Unnatürlichkeit von Geschlecht, Rasse oder Nationalität? Parodie kann eine Rolle als unnatürlich enttarnen. Wenn jemend einer Geschlechterrolle nicht entspricht, wenn ein Mann weibliches Verhalten schlecht kopiert oder anders herum, dann können wir dazu gezwungen werden darüber nachzudenken, ob es ein ‚genuin‘ weibliches und männliches Verhalten gibt. Kopiert der Transvestit wahre Weiblichkeit oder Männlichkeit oder kopiert sie/er eine Kopie? Plötzlich wird alles verwirrend. Ist sie eine echte Frau? Gibt es soetwas überhaupt?

Wie organisieren wir uns auf eine qualitativ andere Weise ohne die Einschränkungen von Rollen? Wie würden wir uns organisieren, wenn die mächtigsten und repressivsten Strukturen, die unsere derzeitigen sozialen Rollen reproduzieren, nicht vorhanden wären? Es ist wichtig in der Lage dazu zu sein, sich so eine Situation vorzustellen und zu versuchen uns soweit irgendwie möglich im Hier und Jetzt anders zu organisieren, ohne die Rollen, die uns einschränken und die Staat-Kapital-Maschine aufrechterhalten.

title: İhtiyacımız tablet ve kulaklık mı?
content:
Haziran ayında yatırılacak prim iptal edilince sendika primden daha iyi bir hediye vereceklerini açıkladı. Temmuz ayının sonunda ise fabrika genelinde yapılan toplantıda yönetim Almanya’dan gelecek yöneticinin hediyeyi açıklayacağını söyledi. Toplantıda sürekli “Biz bir aileyiz” vurgusu yapılmıştı. Hediyenin ise ağustos ayındaki duruştan sonra açıklanacağı söylenmişti.

Ekim ayının son haftasında Almanya’dan gelen yönetici hediyeyi açıkladı: Tablet ve kulaklık. Dört aylık bekleyişin ardından açıklanan hediye ihtiyaç ve beklentimizi karşılamadı.

Vergilerle azalması yetmiyormuş gibi enflasyonla ve borçlarımızla birlikte ücretler ayın başında bitmeye başladı. Tablet bizim günlük yaşantımızı etkilemeyen bir hediye oldu.

Kasım ayının başında üretim iki otobüs azaldı. Günlük üretim 18’den 16’ya düştü. Bu ise işten çıkarmaların başlayacağını düşündürmeye başladı. Bir yandan haklarımızdaki azalma, primin verilmemesi, çok büyük bir hediye olacağı söylenirken tablet ve kulaklık verilmesine ek olarak üretimin de azalması aramızdaki tedirginliği büyütüyor.

Bizlerin talebi ve ihtiyacı olmayan cihazların hediye verilmesi yerine, günlük ihtiyaçlarımız göz önüne alınabilirdi. Herhangi bir temel ihtiyacımızı karşılayabileceğimiz bir hediye daha verimli olurdu.

Sadece aralarda gelip açıklama yapmaktan öteye hiçbir adımı olmayan sendikacılar hediye açıklanırken de tek söz söylemedi. Hediye meselesinde tartışmalara ne düzeyde katıldı neler konuşuldu bilmiyoruz. Üretim tekrar artacak mı işçilerin iş güvencesi olacak mı bir bilgi verilmiyor.

Bizim için en önemlisi iş güvenliğimizin sağlanması. Bunu nasıl sağlayabileceğimizin yollarını sendikayla birlikte bulmalıyız. Çünkü herkes bilir ki bir konu herkes tarafından konuşuluyorsa gerçekleşebilir. İşten çıkarmaların yaşanmaması ve işçilerin taleplerinin gerçekleşmesi için sendikayla birlikte hareket etmeliyiz. Birlikte düşünmeli birlikte çözüm üretmeliyiz.

MAN Türkiye, 2025 yılında üretimden satışlarını bir önceki yıla göre yüzde 92.7 artırarak 38.9 milyar liraya çıkardı. Şirket, İstanbul Sanayi Odasının (İSO) 500 büyük sanayi kuruluşu sıralamasında 2024’te 85’inci sıradayken 33 basamak yükselerek 52’nci oldu. Net satışları 20.2 milyar liradan 39 milyar liraya, ihracatı ise bir yılda yüzde 68.9 artarak 554.6 milyon dolardan 937 milyon dolara yükseldi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: Gerçekten harika bir çözüm!
content:
Fotoğraf: Şişecam Basın Bülteni

Merhaba Evrensel Gazetesi okurları. Ben Eskişehir Şişecam Fabrikasında çalışmakta olan Kristal İş Sendikasına üye bir işçiyim. İçinden geçtiğimiz süreç hakkında ve cam işçilerinin yaşam ve çalışma şartları hakkında bir şeyler yazmak istedim.

Eskişehir’de C fırını kapatılacak ve şubat ayına kadar uyutulacak. Patronun direktifleri yerine getiriliyor. Şişecam patronu. bizlerin ücretlerine göz dikmiş durumda. Ücretlerimizin piyasa ortalamasının çok üzerinde olduğunu ve böyle bir maliyet kalemi varken rekabet edemeyeceğini her fırsatta söylüyor.

Hadi oradan! Hangi yüksek ücretten bahsediyorsunuz? Aldığımız ücretler açıklanan yoksulluk sınırının altında. Bu hayat pahalılığında çarşıda, pazarda, kiraların karşısında aldığımız ücretlerle zor ayakta duruyoruz. Sabahtan akşama ya da akşamdan sabaha kadar camın o ağır kimyasal maddeleriyle, kulağı sağır eden gürültüsüyle, eklemleri kurutan çalışma şartlarıyla boğuşurken aldığımız ücretlerle insanca yaşayacak bir düzen kuramıyoruz.

İşçi evlerini gezin evlerde huzur yok. Ek iş gerçeği, sanal bahis gerçeği, eşini ve çocuklarını görememe gerçeği… Cam işçilerinin gerçekleri işte bunlar. Mesele sadece ücret mevzusu da değil. Patron bir kriz bahanesi ortaya atarak cam işçilerinin haklarını ve kazanımlarını tırpanlamak istiyor. Bu kadar açık bir konuyu bütün cam işçisi arkadaşlarım görmeli.

Şişecam patronu tüccar kafasıyla tabii ki böyle düşünecek. Asıl üzerine düşünmemiz gereken bu koşullarda biz işçiler ne yapıyoruz. Ancak biz uyursak bu zamana kadar kazandığımız ne varsa bir anda buhar olur ve ellerimizden uçar gider.

Geçtiğimiz günlerde Genel Başkan Bilal Çetintaş Eskişehir’e geldi, bizlerle görüştü. Bir sürü şey söyledi ama özetlersek şunu dedi; “Patron görüşme talep etti. 155 işçi fazlalık var çıkması lazım” dedi. Biz de onlara ‘İşten çıkartma bizim gündemimizde yok, başka türlü çözelim’ dedik. Ortaya çıkan çözüm ise “Doğrudan işten çıkarma olmayacak. İşçiler sırayla ücretsiz izne çıkacaklar” oldu. Gerçekten harika bir çözüm!

Pek çoğumuz yarın işsiz mi kalırız tedirginliği ile çalışıyor. Bence sendikalıyız ama örgütlü değiliz. Birlikte hareket etmiyoruz. Sendikacılar üzerinde baskı kurmuyoruz. Ne derlerse neredeyse kafa sallayıp geçiyoruz. Biz böyle dağınık ve örgütsüz olduktan sonra haklarımızın elden gitmesi kaçınılmaz olacak. O nedenle daha fazla da vakit kaybetmeden bir araya gelmenin yollarını aramalı ve bulmalıyız.

Şişecam’ın yatırımcı raporlarına göre, 2026 yılı parasal değerleriyle faiz, amortisman ve vergi öncesi kârı (FAVÖK) 2024’te 13.9 milyar TL’den 2025’te 23.9 milyar TL’ye, net dönem kârı ise 5.24 milyar TL’den 9.54 milyar TL’ye çıktı. 2026’nın ilk altı ayında FAVÖK 13.19 milyar TL, net kâr 1.16 milyar TL oldu. Şirket, 2025’te yatırım harcamalarını üç katına çıkarırken 2026’nın ilk yarısında 6 milyar TL yatırım yaptı. Mısır’da ortağı olduğu Saint-Gobain düz cam fabrikasında yaklaşık 200 milyon dolarlık yatırımla yeni üretim hattı açtı. Buna karşılık üretim maliyetleri içindeki konsolide işçilik payı 2024’te yüzde 17, 2025’te yüzde 19, 2026’nın ilk yarısında yüzde 20 oldu. Yani şirketin işçilik maliyetleri yıllık yüzde 1 bandından daha fazla yükselmedi.

author: Unknown
title: Reklam krizinin faturası kime kesiliyor?
content:
Irmak Su Timur [email protected]

Reklam gelirlerindeki düşüş nedeniyle televizyon dizilerinin yeni bölümleri erteleniyor, yeni dizilerin çok azı devam ediyor, yapımcılardan maliyetleri kısmaları isteniyor. Sektördeki kriz tartışması büyürken set emekçileri, yıllardır ücretlerini zamanında alamadıkları, uzun saatler çalıştırıldıkları ve sigortasız bırakıldıkları koşullarda çalışmaya devam ediyor.

Sektördeki sorunların yalnızca son dönemde yaşanan reklam daralmasıyla sınırlı olmadığını belirten Sine-Sen hukuk biriminden Kurgucu Haydar Yenmez ve Reji Koordinatörü Tuğçe Kaya, yıllardır devam eden hak ihlallerine dikkat çekti.

Film emekçilerinin en kronik sorunlarından birinin ücretlerin geriden ödenmesi olduğunu belirten Yenmez, işverenlerin bu durumu döviz kurundaki değişim, yüksek enflasyon ve kanalların ödemeleri 4-6 aylık çeklerle yapmasıyla açıklamaya çalıştığını söyledi. Yenmez, “Fakat yapımcının sorumluluğu, gerekli olan sermayeyi henüz işe başlamadan hazır etmektir. Dolayısıyla öne sürülen bu gerekçelerin kabul edilebilir tarafı yoktur” dedi.

Set emekçilerinin haftada 90 saate yakın çalıştırıldığını belirten Yenmez, sigorta primlerinin de gerçek ücretler üzerinden değil, asgari seviyeden gösterildiğini söyledi. Her bir set emekçisinin iki kişilik çalıştırıldığını ifade eden Yenmez, çekimlerin durduğu dönemlerde de işçilerin ücret alamadığını ifade etti.

Reklam gelirlerindeki düşüşün işçi ücretlerine yansıtılamayacağını vurgulayan Yenmez, “Alınan reytingler, reklam gelirleri ya da şirketin kârlılık oranı, sette veya stüdyoda alın teri döken emekçilerin kontrolünde olan bir durum değildir. Bu nedenle bugünlerde sıkça dillendirilen ‘Reklam gelirlerindeki düşüşün ücretlere yansıtılacağı’ söylemleri tamamen hukuk dışıdır” dedi.

Reji Koordinatörü Tuğçe Kaya da sektörde yıllardır yaşanan ödeme ve güvencesizlik sorununun artık kangrene dönüştüğünü söyledi. Bugün ‘en güvenilir’ yapımlarda bile ödeme sorunları yaşandığını anlatan Kaya, sektörde çalışanların her projeye ücretlerini alıp alamayacakları kaygısıyla başladığını belirtti.

Artan yapım maliyetlerinin kamera arkası emekçilerine yansıdığını söyleyen Kaya, oyuncuların bölüm başına kazançlarıyla set çalışanlarının ücretleri arasında büyük bir uçurum bulunduğuna dikkat çekti. Set emekçilerinin soğukta saatlerce çalıştığını, buna rağmen aldıkları ücretlerin kira, aidat, fatura ve temel ihtiyaçlarını karşılamaya yetmediğini belirten Kaya, iki yıl önce çalıştığı bir projede ücretini alamadığını, konuyla ilgili hukuki sürecin hâlâ devam ettiğini anlattı.

Kaya, sektörde aynı oyuncuların ve benzer hikayelerin tekrar edilmesinin yeni projelerin önünü kapattığını belirterek yeni yüzlere fırsat verilmesini de talep etti. Kaya, dizi sürelerinin azaltılmasını, oyuncular ve set emekçileri arasındaki ücret farkının yeniden değerlendirilmesini önerirken Yenmez ücretlerin zamanında ödenmesi, insani çalışma saatleri ve işçi sağlığı ve güvenliği koşullarının sağlanmasının temel talepleri olduğunu belirtti.

author: Unknown
title: ‘Her Şey Ortada’ vizyonda: Gerçek kimin hikâyesi, kimin kamerasında?
content:
Her Şey Ortada filminden bir sahne

Bir insanın anlattıklarına ne kadar güvenebiliriz? Peki ya o insanın hikayesini kayda alanlara? Kameranın karşısındaki kişi kadar kamerayı tutanların da anlatının bir parçası olduğu bir yerde, izlediğimiz şeyin ne kadarının hakikat, ne kadarının kurgu olduğunu nasıl ayırt edebiliriz? Nathan Fielder ve Lance Oppenheim’ın yönettiği Her Şey Ortada (You Can See Everything), tam da bu soruların peşinden gidiyor. Kurmaca ile belgesel arasında gidip gelen, ancak ağırlığını belgesel sinemadan yana koyan film, izleyiciyi sürekli bu iki alanın sınırında tutuyor. Bir noktadan sonra anlatılan hikayeden çok, hikayeyi kimin, nasıl ve hangi amaçla anlattığıyla ilgilenmeye başlıyoruz.

Her Şey Ortada filmi ne anlatıyor? Herkes Elizabeth Holmes'a inanmıştı, gerçek bambaşka çıktı

Yapımın merkezinde, yakın dönem teknoloji dünyasının en büyük dolandırıcılık vakalarından biriyle gündeme gelen Theranos’un kurucusu Elizabeth Holmes var. Holmes, parmak ucundan alınan birkaç damla kanla çok sayıda sağlık testini gerçekleştirebileceğini iddia ettiği teknolojisiyle Silikon Vadisi’nin en çok konuşulan girişimcilerinden birine dönüşmüştü. Ancak şirketin teknolojisinin vadedilen sonuçları vermediği ortaya çıktı. Yatırımcıları dolandırmaktan suçlu bulunan Holmes, 11 yıl 3 ay hapis cezasına çarptırıldı.

Yapım, Holmes’un cezaevine girmesine 34 gün kala başlıyor. Holmes, kendisinin ve ailesinin gündelik hayatını kayda almaları için Nathan Fielder ve ekibini evine davet ediyor. Başlangıçta bir portre çalışması gibi görünen anlatı, üç yıla yayılan çekim süreci içinde bambaşka bir yere evriliyor.

You Can See Everything adlı belgeselden bir sahne.

You Can See Everything adlı belgeselden bir sahne.

Belgesel sinemanın en temel meselelerinden biri, kameranın gerçekliği ne ölçüde kaydedebildiği, ne ölçüde dönüştürdüğüdür. Kamera yalnızca olup biteni kaydetmez; varlığıyla davranışları, ilişkileri ve anlatıyı da etkiler. Her Şey Ortada, bu meseleyi filmin merkezine yerleştiriyor. Holmes’u izlerken onun kendisini nasıl sunduğunu, Fielder’ın sorularına nasıl karşılık verdiğini ve kameranın varlığında nasıl bir kişiliğe büründüğünü düşünüyoruz. Fakat bir süre sonra aynı sorgulamayı yönetmen için de yapmaya başlıyoruz. Fielder’ın soruları ne kadar kendiliğinden? Onun şaşkınlığı, sessizliği ve müdahaleleri ne kadar gerçek?

Yapımın asıl başarısı, bu sorulara kolay yanıtlar vermemesinde. Holmes’un geçmişini ve Theranos skandalını biliyoruz. Buna rağmen karşımızdaki insanın anlattıklarını dinlerken, bir yandan da onun hangi noktada kendisini savunduğunu, hangi noktada gerçekten inandığı şeyleri dile getirdiğini anlamaya çalışıyoruz. Üstelik yalnızca Holmes’u değil, onu izleyen Fielder’ı da izliyoruz. Ardından kameranın ve kurgunun bu karşılaşmayı nasıl biçimlendirdiğini sorguluyoruz. Böylece seyirci, yalnızca hikayeyi takip eden kişi olmaktan çıkıyor; kendi izleme eyleminin de farkına varıyor.

Bu açıdan yapım, İranlı Yönetmen Abbas Kiarostami’nin sinemasını da hatırlatıyor. Özellikle Yakın Plan (Close-Up, 1990), gerçek ile kurmaca arasındaki sınırın nasıl geçirgenleşebileceğini gösteren en güçlü örneklerden biri. Ancak Kiarostami’nin yaklaşımı, Her Şey Ortada’dan farklı olarak kurmacaya daha yakın duruyor.

Kiarostami’nin Zeytin Ağaçları Altında ve Hayat Devam Ediyor filmlerinde de karşılaştığımız bu yaklaşım, Her Şey Ortada ile farklı bir noktada kesişiyor. Kiarostami gerçekliği kurmacanın olanaklarıyla yeniden kurarken, Fielder ve Oppenheim belgesel olarak başladıkları anlatının içinde kurmacanın ve performansın alanını giderek genişletiyor. Ancak Her Şey Ortada, Kiarostami’nin aksine, seyirciyi daha uzun süre belgesel gerçekliğinin içinde tutuyor; bu gerçekliğin ne zaman ve nasıl bir performansa dönüştüğünü anlamaya çalışmak da filmin temel gerilimlerinden birini oluşturuyor.

You Can See Everything adlı belgeselden bir sahne.

You Can See Everything adlı belgeselden bir sahne.

Anlatının bu denli ilginç bir sorgulamaya dönüşmesinde Nathan Fielder’ın yönetmen ve anlatının içindeki bir karakter olarak konumu belirleyici. Kanadalı Komedyen Fielder, özellikle Nathan for You ve HBO yapımı The Rehearsal ile tanınıyor.

Fielder’ın mizahı, çoğu zaman karşısındaki insanın söyledikleriyle ortaya çıkan çelişkiler arasındaki mesafeden besleniyor. Onun kamerası ve soruları, sıradan görünen durumları giderek tuhaflaştırıyor. Her Şey Ortada’da da bu yaklaşımı sürdürürken, alışık olduğumuz komedi anlayışını çok daha rahatsız edici bir zemine taşıyor.

Üstelik Fielder’ın Holmes’un hikayesini anlatmak üzere seçilmiş olması başlı başına bir ironi taşıyor. Kendisini absürt iş fikirleri ve ticari başarı vaatleri üzerinden tanıtan, iş dünyasının müşteriyi ve kazancı artırma arzusunu tiye alan bir komedyenin, Silikon Vadisi’nin en büyük dolandırıcılık vakalarından birinin merkezindeki insanla karşı karşıya gelmesi…

Lance Oppenheim’ın yönetmenlik yaklaşımı da bu karşılaşmayı görsel olarak destekliyor. Some Kind of Heaven ve Spermworld gibi belgeselleriyle tanınan Oppenheim, gündelik hayatın içindeki tuhaflıkları sinemasal bir anlatımla görünür kılmayı tercih ediyor. Fielder’ın rahatsız edici soruları ile Oppenheim’ın bu gözlemci kamerası bir araya geldiğinde, evin içindeki sıradan anlar bile bir gerilim sahnesine dönüşebiliyor.

Görsel: Her Şey Ortada (You Can See Everything) filminin fragmanından alınan ekran alıntısı

Görsel: Her Şey Ortada (You Can See Everything) filminin fragmanından alınan ekran alıntısı

Yapımın adındaki Her Şey Ortada iddiası da giderek daha fazla sorgulanır hale geliyor. Her şeyin kaydedildiği, her ayrıntının görülebildiği bir dünyada gerçekten her şeyi görebilir miyiz? Bir insanın evine girmek, gündelik hayatını izlemek, onunla saatlerce konuşmak, hakikate ulaşmak için yeterli mi? Yoksa kameranın karşısındaki kişi, kendisine yönelen bakışın farkında olduğu sürece bir performans sergilemeye devam mı ediyor?

Üstelik bu performans yalnızca Holmes’a ait değil. Fielder da sorularıyla, sessizlikleriyle ve tepkileriyle kendi karakterini kuruyor. İzleyici ise bu iki kişi arasındaki ilişkiye bakarken bir yandan da kendi merakının, şüphelerinin ve yargılarının farkına varıyor. Kimin yalan söylediğini bulmaya çalışırken, neyi gerçek kabul etmeye hazır olduğumuzu da sorguluyoruz.

Bir noktadan sonra filmin konusu geri plana çekiliyor. Yönetmen, özneyi izlerken kendisini de kadraja dahil ediyor; seyirci de bu ilişkinin dışında kalamıyor. Böylece izleyeni izleyen, onu da izleyen bir bakış ortaya çıkıyor.

Her Şey Ortada, belgesel sinemanın tarafsızlık iddiasını kolayca bir kenara bırakıp kendi araçlarını sorgulayan bir yapım. Çünkü karşımızda yalnızca kendisini anlatmaya çalışan bir kadın, onu anlamaya çalışan iki yönetmen ve bunları izleyen bir seyirci yok. Herkesin birbirini gözlediği, herkesin bir ölçüde performans sergilediği bir karşılaşma var. Ve belki de anlatının asıl meselesi tam burada: Her şeyin ortada olduğu bir yerde bile hakikatin neden bu kadar zor görünür olduğu.

author: Sharon Lerner
title: Trump Admin Giving $1M to Group Studying Crime Against White South Africans
content:
The new award comes after the administration cut human rights funding to nations in crisis.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

After slashing funding for programs that documented atrocities and protected human rights abroad, President Donald Trump’s State Department is now granting one of its first new human rights awards to a controversial South African organization that promotes the disputed notion that white farmers are a violently targeted, persecuted group, according to multiple sources knowledgeable about the funding.

The group expected to receive the nearly $1 million award, AfriForum, is a nonprofit that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners, a subset of South Africa’s white population. The organization says its members, who have a “God-given calling,” fight for Afrikaner interests and self-governance. The money will be used to “document hateful rhetoric and violent acts” against Afrikaners and other minority populations in the country.

The new award comes from a State Department bureau tasked with promoting democracy and human rights internationally. Until last year, those funds were mainly spent in poor and authoritarian nations — to fight corruption in the Democratic Republic of Congo, for example, or combat child exploitation and sexual abuse in Afghanistan. Since Trump returned to office, his appointees have transformed the bureau, gutting its staff, canceling programs and reorienting some of its funding toward conservative causes in Europe.

Samuel Samson, who was appointed as a deputy assistant secretary to the State Department bureau by Trump, has claimed the U.S. has a “civilizational” connection to Afrikaners, who descend primarily from Dutch migrants and predominantly speak Afrikaans. Samson, who has met with far-right leaders in Europe since joining the administration last year, has framed the U.S. government’s financial support for Afrikaners as grounded in “a common heritage, a common culture, a common way of life, shared history and ultimately a common anthropology.”

There’s a long shared political history between Afrikaner groups and white nationalists in the U.S., said Audie Klotz, a political science professor at Syracuse University who has studied those connections. But, she said, “There’s no heritage connection here. It’s pure scientific racism. In the history of U.S. immigration, there’s no direct connection between South Africa and the United States.”

AfriForum met with the Trump administration in February 2025 to plead for help. The group told officials that Afrikaners are subject to racial discrimination and murders that are more frequent and asked the administration to “act strongly against hate speech that incites violence” against them, according to a statement.

South Africa is plagued by high rates of violence, and some Afrikaners have been tortured and murdered. But independent researchers have found those killings represent a tiny fraction of murders across the country, whose victims are disproportionately people living in poor urban areas, where residents are predominantly Black. Official government statistics, and two formal inquiries into the matter, do not reveal a pattern of targeted violence against Afrikaners.

But Trump subscribes to the idea that white farmers face a “genocide” and has cited disproportionate violence against them as a reason for punishing Africa’s wealthiest nation. In February 2025, he issued an executive order that cut off hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to South Africa and welcomed Afrikaners to the U.S. as refugees. Since then, the administration has opened the doors to more than 16,000 white South Africans while halting virtually all other immigration. Officials recently told Congress they plan to invite as many as 17,500 Afrikaner refugees to the U.S. in 2027.

AfriForum did not respond to specific questions for this story but said that “our understanding is that the allocation has not yet been finalised. Should the allocation indeed be awarded to AfriForum, we will make a public announcement in this regard.”

The new award is the administration’s latest show of support for the Afrikaner cause. The white South African group governed the nation for decades under a brutal system of segregation known as apartheid, which kept the Black majority an impoverished underclass until the system was dismantled in 1994. Now, with Black South Africans governing the country, white people — of which Afrikaners are the majority — remain one of the wealthiest segments of the population.

The support has caused dismay among several former high-level diplomats, who spoke to ProPublica anonymously because they fear retribution from the administration.

Two former senior U.S. officials responsible for Africa policy said that they would never have met with AfriForum, let alone funded the group, because it was considered to be politically extreme and not credible. They described the organization as cherry-picking crime statistics to create a misleading narrative. “We would certainly not have funded what we would see as a racially incendiary initiative,” said one of the officials.

The decision to direct money toward the group comes after the Trump administration halted programs that advocated for the end of violence in African countries such as Sudan, where the Biden administration determined in 2025 that there was a genocide, calling it “the world’s largest humanitarian catastrophe.”

“It’s offensive to provide funding solely to this one group after we’ve cut off funding in countries undergoing real documented crises,” said David Jandura, who managed the Africa portfolio for the State Department’s human rights bureau for several years and lost his job during the mass layoffs in 2025.

Congress has also raised questions about how the award was made. A Senate aide to Democrats told ProPublica that despite repeated requests to State Department officials, they had not received a briefing outlining the recipients of funds earmarked for democracy and human rights, which they described as “highly unusual.”

“The Trump Administration proceeded with funding fringe right-wing causes internationally despite objections from Congress,” said Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, a New Hampshire Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, who described the lack of transparency as “unacceptable.”

In response to a series of questions about the AfriForum funding, a senior State Department official wrote in an email that the department does not comment on funding deliberations and that they routinely keep Congress informed of their actions, consulting extensively on this year’s programming. “The Administration has been clear about its concern about the abhorrent race-based discrimination and violence in South Africa,” the unnamed official wrote. “Human rights protections do not depend on a person’s income or ethnicity.”

In July, ProPublica revealed that the State Department originally intended to give the $1 million research award to Lex Libertas, a small organization founded last year by a former AfriForum executive named Ernst Roets. Trump officials later expanded the potential awardees to a small pool of handpicked organizations. The plan drew outrage from Congress over the content of the award as well as plans to bypass the typical competitive bidding process. After ProPublica’s reporting, the State Department released an open call for the funding opportunity, offering $986,500 to a nonprofit organization to “create a comprehensive record of violence affecting Afrikaner and other South African minority populations.” It’s this grant that is now being awarded to AfriForum.

Both AfriForum and Lex Libertas advocate for Afrikaner rights and have developed relationships with the Trump administration. Trump’s ambassador to South Africa, L. Brent Bozell III, visited AfriForum’s headquarters in September, praising the organization for its neighborhood watch programs while criticizing the South African government for not enacting policies requested by the Trump administration. AfriForum has also met with Trump officials in Washington, D.C., drawing public criticism from South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. And in September, Roets met with administration officials.

AfriForum was founded 20 years ago and, with some 300,000 members, claims to be the biggest civil rights organization in South Africa. It says it aims to “establish self-dependence and growing self-governance” and provides some local civic services, such as garbage collection and systems for reporting pot holes and broken traffic lights. The group has said it distances itself from “white supremacist and extremist groups” and that it disagrees with Trump’s assertion that white South African farmers are experiencing a “white genocide.” But it has also said the South African government is “targeting the continued existence of Afrikaners” through racial legislation and the downplaying of farm murders, among other things. Academics and former U.S. diplomats have repudiated some of the ideas the group promotes as racist.

It unsuccessfully challenged a ban on the “gratuitous display” of the national flag flown during apartheid, which a South African court has found to be a form of hate speech. And while the group’s leader, Kallie Kriel, has said apartheid “was wrong,” he has also said it did not constitute “a crime against humanity” as the U.N. has determined, on the grounds that not enough people were killed during that time.

AfriForum has been focusing on farm attacks since at least 2009. In 2018, during Trump’s first presidency, Kriel and Roets, who was then his deputy, met with government officials in Washington, D.C., about the issue, and Roets spoke about it with Tucker Carlson on Fox News, as the chyron below him announced in all caps, “White farmers brutally murdered every week in SouthAfrica.”

Additional research on crimes against white South Africans is an unnecessary and confusing use of U.S. taxpayer dollars, said Carolyn Holmes, a professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, who studies democracy in southern Africa. Holmes noted that AfriForum already produces annual reports on crimes against farming communities. “These data already exist,” she said. “You don’t need a new study. You don’t even need a far-right study, we have those.”

The U.S. support offers more than a financial boost to the organization. “For some time, AfriForum has been campaigning for recognition of their claim that white people face discrimination and persecution,” said Alex Dyzenhaus, a lecturer in international relations and African politics at the University of St. Andrews. “Before, they were only getting the Tucker Carlsons and the far right of the news ecosystem. Now they have the U.S. government on their side.”

The Trump administration has made the plight of white, rural South Africans a key foreign policy issue. In addition to the early executive order, Trump held a contentious meeting with Ramaphosa in the White House last year where Trump claimed white farmers were being executed. The administration has also considered an ad campaign focused on encouraging more Afrikaners to come to the U.S.

In September, Roets of Lex Libertas met with the White House to discuss what he sees as the crisis facing the Afrikaner community and, along with the New York Young Republican Club, placed 3,000 white crosses on the National Mall to commemorate South African farm murders.

Roets declined to answer specific questions from ProPublica but, in a text message, described the murders of several Afrikaners that he knew personally. He also wrote, “I see the suffering of black people in South Africa, I am deeply moved by it, and I spend every day of my life campaigning to make things better for us all.”

Appearing at a press conference for the Lex Libertas event, Samson, the State Department official, showcased the sharp shift the administration has made in U.S. relations with South Africa. While apartheid has been understood globally as a symbol of racist oppression, Samson described the current South African government as having discriminatory “race-based” policies and a cautionary tale for the rest of the world.

At the end of apartheid, in 1994, South Africa was a “flourishing, prosperous society,” Samson said. Since then, the country has gone to “ruin.” He blamed the fall on a “radical ideological leftist movement that wears human rights, that wears tolerance and inclusivity, as a skin suit to advance their Marxist communist worldview.”

Part of the Trump administration’s solution to this perceived crisis, he said, was to provide the research funding.

title: Mississippi Ballot Monitors Say They’re Being Shut Out of Vote Counting
content:
Volunteers say they are navigating confusion and obstacles while trying to ensure a transparent counting process.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

It took Natt Offiah an hour to realize he had arrived at the wrong location to monitor the provisional and absentee ballots in the Mississippi U.S. Senate race. He drove to Madison County Circuit Clerk’s Office on Wednesday, but the building was under construction.

After a phone call, Offiah, director of organizing for the People’s Advocacy Institute, and his colleague finally reached the temporary clerk’s office. They were redirected again, shared Offiah, still unable to locate officials.

At the next building, one woman said, “I haven’t seen them in an hour or so,” before directing the organizers down a hallway.

Offiah said he banged on the door, to no avail. The duo sat outside the room for 45 minutes before heading back to the front desk. A receptionist then told Offiah about two dozen staffers had left 15 minutes before his initial arrival.

No one could provide him any information on when they would return to continue counting votes.

“There is no standardized process for counting. Each county can pick and choose when they want to start counting. So, we’re running into this runaround issue,” Offiah said.

His experience mirrors the dozens of other volunteers who say they didn’t sign up for chaos and confusion, but to protect the democratic process. Some — who reported their concerns in group chats shared with Capital B — say they’ve been denied a seat to observe the process, while others struggle to find information.

With the nation’s close eye on Mississippi, advocates say it’s even more critical to ensure election officials “do the right thing.” Voters have been on edge since Election Day, waiting to see who will become the state’s next U.S. senator.

Despite no early voting or online registration, turnout and absentee ballots have surged. As of Nov. 6, Democrat Scott Colom leads Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by over 2,500 votes.

Yet, there are still thousands of mail-in and affidavit ballots outstanding.

Issues like voter ID laws and inoperable machines have fueled delays, said Lydia Grizzell, policy and advocacy manager of ACLU of Mississippi.

“It is appalling the number of issues that we’ve seen and we had on Election Day, and now we’re seeing the extension of that post-Election Day in a way that is not great,” she said.

The Mississippi secretary of state’s office did not address the monitors’ allegations of being shut out of the vote counting process, but told Capital B the public is entitled to be present for the counting of ballots, the process where election commissioners announce which affidavit ballots are accepted or rejected, according to state statute. This does not include the preliminary work commissioners do to determine a voter’s eligibility.

There is no uniform process on how officials conduct affidavit ballot counting. In some counties, where ACLU dispatched attorneys, election officials had a closed door process, Grizell added.

“The best thing that we can do is have people watching, witnessing, and doing their best to gather as much information as possible as to what is happening,” she said.

Volunteers across the state are being deployed in a widespread effort prompted by several grassroots organizations. The NAACP has also deployed national legal, policy, and field staff to the state to make sure every vote is counted.

Both candidates sent their own groups to monitor the process and assembled a group of lawyers who are prepared to take legal action if necessary. Lawyers for Hyde-Smith sent a letter to election commissioners requesting “immediate separation, secure custody and preservation of all affidavit ballots.” Following Hyde-Smith’s legal team’s response, Colom’s legal counsel sent a letter to all 82 counties, calling the GOP senator’s demand unlawful.

Ahead of the election, thousands of Mississippians were moved to inactive status because the secretary of state’s office paid $50,000 to use unverified data from credit bureau Experian to clean out voter rolls. Secretary of State Michael Watson told Mississippi Today that the rollout of the commercial data was “wildly successful.”

This unprecedented number of inactive voters led to more affidavit ballots, prolonging the count, Tarekegn said. These ballots must be “cured”, meaning to correct issues with voter identification or mail-in ballots, by Nov. 10.

Organizers also pointed out that Mississippi’s outdated voting system exacerbated the counting issues. With no early voting, most ballots come in on Election Day. This overwhelms the system. Still, Tarekegn praised Mississippians for the high turnout.

“Mississippi is one of the hardest, if not the hardest, state to vote in,” she said. “We’re truly talking about probably more than 90% of the people having to show up on Election Day between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. to cast their vote.”

On Election Day, Rachel Madden was the 20th person in line at her precinct in DeSoto County. After an hour’s wait, she was told she had been made inactive and needed to vote by affidavit.

“She just told me that my name wasn’t in the system, and I was like, ‘Well, that doesn’t make any sense,’” Madden said.

She hadn’t changed her address, so she was confused why she had been flagged as inactive. The poll worker assured her, “It’s not a big deal, you’re like the second person this has happened to,” she said.

She said she was instructed by the poll worker to go to the courthouse to “cure” her ballot after being given a form. She made the 25-minute drive to the courthouse, where the employee informed her she had been inactive since May by District 1 Election Commissioner Laura Edler because of Madden’s supposed move to nearby Memphis, Tennessee.

Madden says she never moved anywhere. Her address was corrected in the system and she received a new voter card.

She recalls she then called to ensure her ballot was accepted. She said that an employee told her they would not be taking any more calls about affidavit ballots for the next 10 days, which would put Madden outside the deadline of ballot curing.

“I was like, in 10 days, it’s not gonna matter,” Madden said. “Even in person that day, they were not helpful. If I had not insisted, I don’t think they would have done it. I just don’t think that’s fair or right.”

Edler did not speak to any individual’s standing, but told Capital B that when the commission receives a change of address from the secretary of state’s office, then the voter will be notified and must rectify the issue or remain inactive.

Ballot monitors say it’s also been difficult to do their jobs.

In DeSoto County, Kelly Jacobs, a local organizer, said District 4 Election Commissioner Sissie Ferguson prevented her from watching as election officials presorted ballots and checked names.

The day after the election, Jacobs said she stopped by the election’s commissioner office, but learned they had changed locations. She then traveled to the police department, which directed her to the new location.

After being barred from entry, Jacobs called an attorney, who affirmed her rights, but officials continued to block her from observing, she said, which she captured on video. Commenters on the video state that they were allowed access to observe vote counting in other counties.

On Nov. 5, around noon, the public was able to monitor the process, but by then, the process had already started, she said. Jacobs is not confident officials will follow the law.

“Why did I have to go and complain? If not for my complaint, they would still be all locked up [in the room],” she said. “There’s five election commissioners. Why would none of them know the open meetings law?”

Ferguson did not respond to Capital B’s request for comment. However, commissioner Edler said no one has been denied access. As of the afternoon of Nov. 6, she said there’s “a room full of people” who were actively watching the process.

In Lee County, about 100 miles away, a monitor reported that an official told them a count wouldn’t happen until “later this week or early next week,” according to a group chat shared with Capital B. Another volunteer was told it would occur on “Thursday morning” with no additional details.

Offiah, although still battling frustration and confusion, said he is looking forward to continuing the good work with the community.

“As a lifelong Mississippian, I am used to us living in a legacy of constantly fighting back, and this is just in alignment with our legacy,” he said. “And people ask folks from Mississippi, why do we live down here? Why do we stay out here with everything that we’re facing?”

He added: “But we’re fighters, and we won’t ever stop fighting.”

author: Jon Queally
title: Flooding in Gaza Destroys 70,000 Tents as Israel Continues to Block Aid
content:
The Palestinian Health Minister warned of “a catastrophic deterioration in health and environmental conditions” in Gaza.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The suffering of the people of Gaza went from horrific and beyond comprehension to something worse on Saturday after storm waters overnight destroyed tens of thousands of tents and flooded tens of thousands of people into further desperation, all while the US and Israeli governments continue to maintain a cruel blockade on life-saving supplies despite a fast-approaching winter and a military occupation with no end in sight.

“At least 70,000 tents have been flooded & blown away by the torrential downpour and tempestuous wind in Gaza since last night,” reported Palestinian journalist Abubaker Abed, citing statements from health and media officials. “Families are shelterless. Food prices are soaring. Children are starving and shivering with cold. Caravans and mobile homes must enter Gaza now to avert this cataclysm.”

Gaza’s Government Media Office on Saturday, holding Israel wholly responsible for the disaster, said initial losses from flooded and destroyed tents were estimated at $3 million and that dozens of walls of homes had collapsed, resulting in injuries, while the threat of broader building collapse remained a serious risk.

In a statement, Palestinian Health Minister Dr. Majed Abu Ramadan said, “What is happening in Gaza is not a passing winter crisis. I urgently call on the international community, the United Nations, and health, humanitarian, and relief organizations to intervene immediately to save the lives of hundreds of thousands of displaced people in the Gaza Strip, following the flooding of thousands of tents with rainwater and the absence of basic safe shelter conditions.”

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), about 950,000 displaced people in Gaza are living in areas exposed to flooding. Low-lying locations and sites near the coast are particularly vulnerable, with more than 400,000 people living in areas considered at high risk of flooding.

About 44,000 Palestinians are living in structurally unsafe buildings, while more than 4,000 buildings across the territory are estimated to require full or partial demolition due to damage caused by Israeli air strikes. About 294,250 families need shelter assistance ahead of winter, but the available supplies cover only 18 percent of their needs.

Ramadan further warned of “a catastrophic deterioration in health and environmental conditions, alongside growing risks of the spread of diseases and epidemics” if an emergency response was not rapidly and comprehensively deployed.

This is the worst morning ever. No one in Gaza City slept last night. The rain completely flooded the tents, soaking mattresses and destroying families' belongings. We are underwater. Thousands of families have been trying for hours to save what little they have left, with…

Video footage and eye witness accounts offered a heartbreaking picture of the suffering by those hit by the floods.

“We woke up and found ourselves surrounded by water,” a man named Mansour al-Sakni, 33, told the Middle East Eye. “The children were crying. I did not know what to do, and I started crying too.”

“We stood inside the tarpaulin shelter waiting for the rain to stop so we could try to push the water out of the room,” he said. “We are poor people in Gaza. We want to live. We do not want to die from the bombing or the cold. Enough. Have mercy on us.”

The territory’s civil defence service said it had received 1,500 distress calls from displaced residents. Three abandoned houses collapsed without causing injuries, it added.

At a tent encampment in Gaza City, some people tried to repair their tents, ⁠while others used sand to reinforce them and prevent water from entering. ⁠Some were busy getting their children out of flooded tents.

Olfat Magdoub, a Gaza resident, tried in vain to sweep water away from her tent.

“This is the first day of rain, and of course ⁠we are already flooded. What will happen if it rains again the next day? This is only the first day and ⁠we’re already overwhelmed,” said the woman.

“Two weeks ago when it rained, I swear to God, I spent four days sleeping on blankets spread on the floor because the rainwater had flooded the bedding. Same now, the mattresses are wet so we sleep on the ground.”

While the flooding devastated the people and families trapped by the blockade of life-saving aid and shelter, fresh ire was pointed at the US government for refusing to rebuke the Israeli government for its wanton disregard for human life and suffering.

On the ground in Gaza, the anguish of Palestinians, including children, was on display in videos of the devastation and ongoing catastrophe posted to social media:

🚨 CATASTROPHIC SCENES IN GAZA RIGHT NOW. Heavy rainfall is flooding displaced Palestinians’ tents, leaving families exposed to the harsh winter with no alternative shelter. This is their fourth winter since Israel destroyed their homes and continues to block essential… pic.twitter.com/NI7DRgCSMs

“How long are we supposed to live like this?” declares the young boy featured in the video. “I swear I don’t know what to do. Have mercy on us for God’s sake! For the sake of God, have mercy on us!”

Rain is worsening the suffering of Gaza’s children as water pours into homes damaged by Israeli bombardment, soaking bedding and clothes. With no shelter repair materials or tarpaulins available, families are left unable to protect their children from the flooding. pic.twitter.com/OzVMGHzssI

Children are particularly impacted by the rain water and vulnerable to the increasingly dangerous conditions imposed by the floods.

The image of a little girl in Gaza standing in the rain captures a stark, painful contrast: the innocence of childhood set against the harsh reality of life in Gaza. 🍉 The winter rain has transformed the scene into a tableau that blends spontaneous, childlike joy with profound… pic.twitter.com/YkTRt4RWJW

“What remains of Gaza’s homes is collapsing under heavy rain, amid the ongoing genocide and deafening silence,” said Ramy Abdul, chairman of the human rights groups Euro-Med Monitor.

“For the fourth consecutive year,” Abdul added, “Gaza remains under a suffocating Israeli siege that prevents even the recovery of victims’ bodies from beneath the rubble.”

author: Ashley Smith
title: As AI Threatens Tech Workers, Their Workplaces Become Sites of Class Struggle
content:
We must develop new modes of organizing that go beyond a narrow focus on labor law and shop floor issues.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A political and economic battle against today’s robber barons — the billionaire and trillionaire class of tech bosses — is unfolding on many fronts as tech workers agitate against these oligarchs’ complicity with the U.S. military, the cops, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and the Israeli occupation of Palestine.

In their new book, Against Tech Oligarchy: Workers Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry, JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine recount the emergence of the tech workers’ movement over the last two decades, from the political campaigns they have launched to the heroic strikes they have staged against companies like Kickstarter and The New York Times.

No armchair analysts, Tan and Redwine are tech worker leaders who have been at the heart of many of these fights. In this interview, they discuss the rise of the movement, the workers’ turn to unionization, and the oligarchs’ adoption of authoritarianism and austerity to crush it. And they draw lessons from this struggle not only for tech workers, but for the entire labor movement.

The interview that follows has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Ashley Smith: The tech workers’ movement was first spurred into action by the radicalization and social movements triggered by the Great Recession. Workers launched campaigns against their companies’ contracts with, for instance, the U.S. military and ICE. What strategies and tactics did workers use?

JS Tan: After the Great Recession, corporate America thought the tech sector was going to rejuvenate the U.S. economy. The tech bosses were aligned with the Democratic Party and embraced things like identity politics and put forth a progressive, democratic vision of the future.

But the industry’s workers realized that the tech sector was not living up to its mission statements and public pronouncements. They were making software for the U.S. military, ICE, and police. And their internal culture was rife with sexism and racism.

So, tech workers launched campaigns to expose their bosses’ hypocrisy. A good example of this is the Google workers’ campaign against the company’s Project Maven, which used AI to analyze military drone footage.

Workers mobilized their radical co-workers and went public with an open letter [to Google CEO Sundar Pichai] in The New York Times. That exposure forced the company to concede to their demand not to renew its Project Maven contract. Simplifying greatly, the tech movement as a whole adopted this strategy of mobilization behind open letters.

This provoked opposition from the tech oligarchy. It abandoned its California liberalism, which included opposition to Donald Trump in his first term, and instead largely backed him in his second term. What caused this political reorientation? How did it change their companies and treatment of workers?

Tan: In our book, we show how the battle in the tech industry led both workers and bosses to acquire class consciousness. It was a process of radicalization on both sides. Initially, the bosses expressed sympathy with the upsurge of tech worker activism, conceded to their workers’ demands, and implemented DEI [diversity, equity, and inclusion] initiatives.

But they got fed up with being told how to run their businesses and started retaliating against their workers for writing open letters, participating in walkouts, and starting union drives. Then, after the pandemic, the Federal Reserve Bank ended its zero-interest rate policy to combat the sharp rise in inflation.

Suddenly, the tech companies lost access to cheap credit and lost billions of dollars in market valuation. To restore their profit margins, they enacted mass layoffs (being asset-light businesses, employee salaries were their largest costs), return-to-work orders, and speed-ups of the remaining workforce.

Elon Musk’s takeover of Twitter is a paradigmatic example. He fired 80 percent of the workforce. He combined that with an ideological assault on the company, targeting teams that oversaw human rights, AI ethics, and content moderation — the teams he believed housed the most progressive, pro-union workers. Seeing this, other tech bosses followed suit, imposing a new normal of authoritarianism, austerity, and anti-wokeness.

In the face of the tech oligarchs’ new authoritarianism, the workers abandoned their old strategy of using open letters and instead started unionizing to protect their jobs and rights. They pursued what you call the union movement’s “Recognition Playbook.” What is that and what did it accomplish?

Clarissa Redwine: The Recognition Playbook is the dominant method for organizing unions with the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB). We made lists of everyone that works at a company, identified organic leaders, trained them to set up one-on-one conversations with co-workers, and systematically built toward a supermajority for a union.

After that, we filed for union elections with the NLRB — in some cases, won them — and then established a legally recognized union. Because this strategy required majority support, we switched from organizing against political issues like military contracts or systemic sexism to bread-and-butter economic demands.

“[Labor law] is not designed to enable class struggle but ensure class peace — a peace that only benefits the bosses.”

These issues, we believed, would build solidarity and unite the broadest section of the workforce behind a campaign for union recognition under the NLRB. Following the Recognition Playbook, tech workers organized several unions at Kickstarter and other companies.

This Recognition Playbook ran into real problems and workers faced diminishing returns. How did the bosses undermine new unions and how did they block the formation of others?

Redwine: The bosses used their own union busting playbook against tech workers. They fired the most visible organizers at Kickstarter, Google, and Amazon. In some cases, they went further. For example, Google fired not just core organizers of a Palestine action, but everyone involved, including bystanders that were just watching.

Tech bosses hired union-busting consultants. They claimed no venture capitalist would ever invest in a union company, putting their viability in jeopardy. When that didn’t work to intimidate organizers, they piled extra work on everyone.

After the end of the zero-interest rate policy, they generalized this crackdown to impose austerity measures, speed-ups, and layoffs on the entire tech workforce. One trick they used to get rid of people was return-to-office orders. At Grindr, for example, management demanded that workers return to the office furthest from them, basically forcing them to quit.

You analyze one of the biggest moments militancy: the tech workers’ strike at The New York Times. How did the company’s bosses neutralize the effectiveness of the strike? Why didn’t the rest of the unionized workforce join the strike?

Redwine: The bosses exploited the nature of tech work to neutralize the strike. A lot of tech workers are used to speed-ups to finish projects by a specific deadline. So, there’s ebbs and flows in the intensity of work and overall number of hours.

The New York Times bosses took advantage of that norm leading up to the strike that was set to take place on the eve of the 2024 presidential election. So, months before that, management asked their workers to prepare their platforms to withstand the surge of election coverage.

In retrospect, it should have been obvious that they were undermining the impact of the strike by setting up the platform to function without workers. But organizers didn’t see that at the time.

When they finally did walk out, the strike lasted about a week. Their picket line grew in size with more and more workers joining the picket line excited to be a part of a militant action. The solidarity was electric.

But the strike did not shut down the platform. It largely stayed up, and management didn’t offer anything new at the bargaining table. As a result, the strike was essentially a failure.

If the rest of the workforce (e.g., the newsroom) had struck, it would have made a huge difference. But they were legally barred by the no-strike pledge in their contracts. This is the norm for most unions between negotiating periods.

Moreover, existing labor law bars unions from engaging in solidarity strikes. It fundamentally constrains the power of our unions. To overcome these legal barriers, workers have to align their contracts, get rid of no-strike clauses, defy labor law, and exercise our power. Remember, most of the big breakthroughs in the union movement came from illegal strikes.

How has AI compounded the challenges of tech worker organizing? Does the new mass opposition to data center construction open up possibilities for organizing?

Tan: AI is dramatically changing the tech industry, creating new divisions between different groups of workers. The vast majority of tech workers will be negatively impacted by AI.

Many will lose their jobs and others will be de-skilled. As a result, a lot of tech workers are moving toward a new politics that’s class-conscious, concerned with affordability, and aware that their companies are sites of class struggle.

Another smaller group of AI engineers, who develop the frontier models and its surrounding ecosystem, are in a totally different position. The bosses covet their skills. As a result, they enjoy a tight labor market and have a great deal of leverage as individuals.

We need different strategies to organize these two groups of tech workers. We’re just beginning to think through how to do this on the new terrain of precarity and division created by austerity and AI.

Additionally, the movement against data centers will have contradictory impacts on different groups of workers. Most of the tech workforce that is being proletarianized will be sympathetic to this organizing.

But the construction workers and their building trades unions at this point are not sympathetic for obvious reasons. They are getting good jobs and contracts to build the data centers.

We have to develop new modes of organizing that are not constrained by the Recognition Playbook, labor law, and a narrow focus on shop floor issues. How can we build a strong coalition of workers, unions, and communities to overcome the divisions the bosses use to pit us against one another?

You point out one of the biggest limits of the Recognition Playbook: its strategy of delaying conflict with the bosses. Could you explain how it does this and how it poses problems for the labor movement?

Tan: The Recognition Playbook’s defers direct conflict with the boss until after organizers win a supermajority for a union election. This deferral does not prepare workers to organize job actions and strikes necessary to defeat the bosses.

Organizers aren’t getting practice in finding out where their leverage lies and therefore how to design a strike that actually works for the tech sector. In retrospect, this reliance on the Recognition Playbook has held back rather than advanced our organizing.

Redwine: The same applies to our reliance on labor law. It is not designed to enable class struggle but ensure class peace — a peace that only benefits the bosses. So, it has a chilling effect on militancy and has constrained workers’ exercise of our power. We need a new strategy to confront our bosses in this new epoch of austerity and precarity.
