author: Henry A. Giroux
title: Global Youth Rising Up Know There’s No Democracy Without Economic Justice
content:
Youth around the world are rising up against capitalism and for democracy.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Young people are taking to the streets across France, Italy, Belgium, India, Serbia, and Albania, refusing to surrender their futures to a capitalist system that has abandoned them or to a politics that Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor have described as “end times fascism.”

These protests are fueled by mounting anger over deteriorating schools, economic insecurity, unaffordable housing, political corruption, and a ruling class increasingly indifferent to the needs and voices of the young. As far right governments in Europe, the United States, and Latin America cancel out a future plagued by endless wars, climate catastrophe, staggering inequality, deepening poverty, and deteriorating public institutions, young people are rethinking the language of politics, resistance, and hope.

A 21-year-old student protesting in Milan captured this spirit of resistance in an interview with Reuters, declaring: “It’s vital to take part in people’s spontaneous movements born from an explosion of rage that made collective action possible.” She added, “I think the worst damage this ruling class has done to my generation is stealing even the ability to imagine a future, to dream.” Rather than address these grievances, governments have increasingly responded with curfews, protest bans, and brutal police repression, treating the democratic aspirations of young people as threats to be crushed rather than demands for justice to be heard.

These uprisings are driven by more than economic grievances. They express a growing refusal to accept the moral and political cruelty of a system that has declared the young disposable. At their core is a recognition that neoliberal capitalism has robbed an entire generation of the promise of a better future and that austerity is class warfare disguised as economic necessity. As reported in Rolling Stone, Mathys Le Coz Ndzié, a 17-year-old Parisian student, noted: “The current government hasn’t managed to give us a clear picture of the future, or the world we’re heading into. So we feel completely lost. … We haven’t been prepared for the world that’s coming. The one they’ve prepared us for no longer exists.” This war on youth is intensified by the destruction of social protections and the rise of governments that increasingly rely on surveillance, criminalization, and police repression to enforce obedience, especially among the poor and racially marginalized.

Yet out of these conditions of abandonment and repression, something more profound is emerging: a moral and political awakening rooted in the struggle for economic justice and a collective refusal to accept a world in which human dignity is sacrificed to private profit, democracy is hollowed out, and the very possibility of imagining and creating a different future is stolen from an entire generation.

Carlotta Magoga, writing in European Democracy Hub, is right in stating that, “From Serbia to Bangladesh and Senegal, young people are becoming a driving force for a more democratic world. … In search of alternative routes, they are developing new forms of civic engagement — through artistic protest, online campaigns and storytelling — and rewriting the rules of political participation.” Through their courageous presence in the streets, they are fashioning a form of activism “as a way to rethink how democracy works.”

For example, in France, students have challenged overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, and a university admissions system that reinforces class inequality. In Italy, students have joined workers in protests over low wages, unaffordable housing, deteriorating public services, and increased military spending. In Genoa, port workers and students have also protested the use of ports for arms shipments. In Serbia, where opposition to government corruption has been central, students have demanded investigations into public contracts, government spending, and the political control of public institutions. These movements do not all embrace an explicitly anti-capitalist agenda, but their demands expose conflicts over who controls public resources, whose interests governments serve, and how economic and political power is organized and maintained.

Capitalism, in one of its more disingenuous moments, celebrates youth rhetorically as the future but denies youth the resources to have a future. What governments fear about these revolts is that students are moving beyond demands to make capitalism more humane. Protests across Europe and beyond are challenging gangster capitalism as a political order marked by corruption, neoliberal austerity, authoritarianism, militarism, racism, and the concentration of wealth and political power in the hands of a financial elite. At the heart of this confrontation is a struggle over the moral and political values that will govern society and determine the fate of future generations.

Two radically opposed moral visions are confronting one another on the world stage. One is rooted in solidarity, justice, and democratic possibility; the other in greed, racial hatred, organized brutality, and authoritarian domination. What is at stake is the future of democracy and whether coming generations will inherit a world governed by human dignity or one surrendered to the cruelty of the powerful. This culture of moral depravity finds one of its most revealing expressions in the U.S. billionaire class, where technological achievement is increasingly invoked to excuse political and moral cruelty. In an October 20 article in The Dispatch, Marian L. Tupy asks: “Is Elon Musk Worth the Trouble?” His defense of Musk turns technological achievement into a moral alibi for authoritarian politics, reducing the suffering produced by the exercise of billionaire power to an unfortunate price of technological progress.

Missing from this calculus is any serious reckoning with Musk’s role in dismantling USAID, an assault on humanitarian assistance associated with catastrophic human suffering and potentially hundreds of thousands of deaths. Tupy’s invocation of Henry Ford is equally revealing. Ford’s antisemitism is reduced to an unfortunate character flaw, conveniently excused in the gratuitous celebration of industrial progress. This is the poisonous morality of gangster capitalism: technological progress divorced from justice, human suffering reduced to an acceptable cost, and billionaires shielded from moral accountability. The victims disappear while their powerful tormentors are celebrated. This is the moral rot of a political and economic order inhabited by the living dead, a world in which wealth and power can shield predators from accountability. The crimes of Jeffrey Epstein, who preyed on and trafficked underage girls for sexual exploitation, offer a chilling illustration of this culture of impunity. In this world of rapacious political zombies, wealth becomes a shield against accountability, and the victims of predatory power are condemned to silence.

This culture of cruelty and unapologetic viciousness also reaches into electoral politics. Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign released an ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, physician Amy Acton, denouncing her daughter as a liar. Acton has publicly described being removed from her mother’s custody at age 12 following sexual abuse by her stepfather. Her mother reportedly remained married to the accused man. Ramaswamy’s weaponization of Acton’s childhood suffering for political advantage reveals a political culture in which private trauma becomes electoral ammunition and cruelty becomes a badge of political power.

This politics of dehumanization is also evident in the racist rhetoric surrounding the November elections. At a campaign event in Michigan, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. declared: “There’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce — they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Field prize, they don’t win the Wolf Prize. They don’t produce literature.”

These examples are not isolated instances. They expose a political culture and pedagogical regime organized around fear, racial hatred, and the degradation of human life. The language of social justice and compassion is increasingly displaced by the discourse of fascist cruelty, in which conscience is treated as weakness, domination becomes the measure of political power, and human suffering is transformed into a public spectacle. This is how a culture of cruelty becomes the pedagogical foundation of authoritarian rule.

Against this culture of organized cruelty, young people are taking to the streets, transforming their anger into a collective struggle against the economic and political forces that have stolen their futures.Youth are rejecting the neoliberal fiction that individuals alone are responsible for their suffering. They are connecting private troubles to public injustices, building alliances with workers, teachers, and trade unions, and transforming anger into collective political agency.

These struggles remind us that culture is not merely a reflection of politics — it is a central site of contestation where consciousness is formed, identities are shaped, and political possibilities are either destroyed or brought into being. Schools, media, digital platforms, and public institutions are powerful pedagogical forces. They can manufacture ignorance, obedience, and political indifference, or nurture the critical consciousness, historical memory, and collective agency essential to resisting authoritarian power.

The United States cannot afford to regard these youth uprisings as distant spectacles. They offer a powerful indictment of the political and economic forces that are also destroying the foundations of U.S. democracy. Donald Trump’s response to the protests in France — referring to “people coming into the countries that hate the country” — reveals the fascist logic underlying his own war on youth, immigrants, and democratic dissent. Rather than acknowledge the legitimate grievances of young people protesting deteriorating schools, austerity, inequality, and the destruction of their futures, Trump has portrayed the unrest in France as the consequence of immigrants flooding Europe, claiming that France is being overrun by migrants who threaten Western civilization.

This is the poisonous logic of fascist politics: erase the social conditions that produce resistance, transform the oppressed into enemies, replace demands for justice with racial hatred, and turn legitimate protest into a pretext for massive police repression. Under the Trump regime, the assault on public and higher education, the criminalization of dissent, the erosion of social protections, and the concentration of wealth and power in the hands of a billionaire ruling class have become defining features of an increasingly fascist political order. Schools and universities are being transformed from institutions of critical inquiry and democratic possibility into laboratories of ideological conformity, corporate power, and political intimidation. Young people are being robbed not only of economic security but also of the public institutions, critical capacities, and collective hopes necessary to imagine a future beyond the brutality of gangster capitalism. What the United States needs is a generation unwilling to be schooled in obedience, stripped of historical memory, or taught to regard injustice as inevitable. It needs young people capable of challenging the machinery of authoritarian power and reclaiming education as a force for democratic resistance.

Democracy cannot be defended through appeals to civility, symbolic gestures, or concessions designed to contain popular anger while leaving existing structures of power intact.

The struggles unfolding across the globe offer a crucial lesson: Democracy cannot be defended through appeals to civility, symbolic gestures, or concessions designed to contain popular anger while leaving existing structures of power intact. It requires organized movements capable of uniting students, workers, educators, and communities in a sustained struggle for economic justice, human dignity, and democratic power. For too long, young people who have taken to the streets to challenge their political exclusion have been met with a mixture of admiration and condescension, celebrated for their idealism while their demands for fundamental change are dismissed, diluted, or met with brutal state repression.

In France, this assault on dissent has taken an especially vicious turn. The French Senate has approved legislation dubbed the “Rioters Pay” bill, which could impose financial penalties of up to €10,000 on protesters, including those who did not personally cause property damage, while threatening to seize welfare benefits from impoverished families and parents of minors. This is both an attempt to crush dissent through financial intimidation and an act of state terrorism that threatens to turn poverty into an instrument of political repression, imposing devastating economic hardships on students and families already struggling under a punitive, austerity-driven neoliberal state. Rather than address the injustices driving young people into the streets, the government is seeking to make resistance itself a source of economic impoverishment. The irony here is particularly vicious. While the French government has met with student leaders and promised to meet several of their demands — including abolishing the controversial university admissions system, increasing funding for teachers, and investing in improvements to public schools — these promises have yet to be translated into concrete action. What has moved forward, however, is the machinery of repression. In fact, Amnesty International France condemned the French government for adopting “authoritarian practices [that seek] to silence dissenting voices by restricting space for expression.” Promises of educational reform remain unfulfilled, while the state moves with unrelenting speed to punish those who have taken to the streets demanding justice.

Serbia offers a powerful rebuke to this politics of containment. Refusing to be pacified by cosmetic reforms, government reshuffling, or empty promises, student protesters transformed their outrage over corruption and authoritarian rule into a nationwide movement that ultimately defeated the ruling party of longtime right-wing leader Aleksandar Vučić in the October 25 election. Their victory demonstrates that young people need not settle for a place at the margins of a political system that has betrayed them. They can challenge the foundations of that system and turn collective resistance into a force capable of breaking the grip of entrenched power.

Democracy has no future if the young are merely permitted to protest … while those responsible for these injustices remain securely in power.

In France, too, student resistance has begun to yield results, forcing the government to promise to replace Parcoursup, the deeply unpopular university admissions platform, a limited but significant concession that demonstrates how collective struggle can compel those in power to retreat. India’s “Cockroach” movement over the summer has generated widespread unrest “contesting the Hindu-nationalist movement” led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, suggesting “that he is vulnerable.” These struggles offer a lesson that extends far beyond Serbia, France, and India: Democracy has no future if the young are merely permitted to protest against the destruction of their futures, the brutality of austerity, and the systematic assault on their dignity and rights, while those responsible for these injustices remain securely in power.

These uprisings are exposing a truth that neoliberal capitalism and its authoritarian defenders can no longer conceal: A system built on organized inequality, racial domination, dispossession, and the disposability of human life cannot be redeemed through cosmetic reforms or appeals to civility. Their struggle is not simply for a more humane capitalism, but against a system that has turned human life into a commodity, public goods into sources of private wealth, and democracy into a hollow ritual emptied of economic and political power. Frederick Douglass understood what is at stake when he declared: “If there is no struggle, there is no progress.” He added, “Power concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will.”

These young people are refusing the politics of resignation. They are insisting that a radical democracy must be fought for, that justice demands more than the redistribution of suffering, and that the future must be wrested from those who have made greed, violence, and domination the governing principles of society. Vuk Bačanović, writing about the Serbian student uprising, captures the spirit of resistance that now animates young people confronting authoritarian power across the globe. He writes: “At a time when democracy is retreating before the power of capital, authoritarian caprice, and a corrupt cynicism elevated to the status of statesmanlike wisdom, one generation has demonstrated that history has not ended, that obedience is not humanity’s destiny, and that no government is eternal.”

Their revolt carries a message that ruling elites and authoritarian regimes can neither dismiss nor silence: The task is not to make the machinery of capitalist oppression more tolerable, but to dismantle it and struggle for a world in which justice, equality, and human dignity are not empty promises but the very foundations of democratic life.

The challenge now is to transform these diverse uprisings into an international movement capable of sustaining their revolutionary energy, forging new forms of solidarity, and building the collective power necessary to bring an end to gangster capitalism and create a world in which democracy can breathe again.

author: Unknown
title: Constitutional Court orders retrial of Mazlum İçli after ten years in prison
content:
Mazlum İçli has already spent more than ten years of his life in prison. He was accused of involvement, at the age of 14, in the killing of four people during the Kobanê protests in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) in October 2014. He was sentenced to a total of 124 years and eight months in prison. However, evidence that could exonerate him was not adequately considered during the trial. Turkey’s Constitutional Court has now confirmed serious deficiencies in the reasoning behind the verdict and ordered a retrial. İçli’s defense team intends to seek his immediate release.




The ruling, issued on September 16, 2026, could mark a decisive turning point in a case that has been fraught with contradictions for years. At the heart of the case is the question of why İçli was convicted despite several witnesses confirming that he was attending a wedding in the district of Kulp, approximately 140 kilometers away, at the time of the alleged crime. Video footage and an expert report also support his alibi.




The Constitutional Court particularly criticized the criminal court’s failure to provide a reasoned assessment of conflicting expert reports. While one examination suggested that İçli might be identifiable in footage from the crime scene, another report by the same expert confirmed with a high degree of probability that he was present at the wedding. It remained unclear why the court had relied on the incriminating report while failing to give appropriate consideration to the exculpatory evidence.

author: Unknown
title: Women organize symposium on social memory and trauma in Amed
content:
A symposium titled “Speaking Out: Social Memory, Testimony and Trauma” began at the Ali Emiri Conference Hall in cooperation with Amed Metropolitan Municipality, the Trauma Studies Association, and the Forum for Social Peace and Freedom.




Speaking during a session titled “Waiting at Ground Zero: Trauma, Unresolved Grief and the Power of Testimony in Enforced Disappearances,” moderated by social worker İrfan Ekinci, Sebla Arcan, a member of the Human Rights Association’s (İHD) Commission on Disappearances in Custody, said, “A person experiencing trauma due to the disappearance of a loved one can neither move forward nor go back. They remain trapped in that moment.”




Highlighting the trauma caused by enforced disappearances, Arcan said, “The effects continue for two or three generations after an enforced disappearance. But other things are also passed down through generations in connection with enforced disappearances. A sense of justice, the determination to struggle, and the spirit of resistance are also transmitted. What is passed down from generation to generation is not only trauma and grief but also political consciousness.”




Emphasizing the importance of testimony, Sebla Arcan said, “Your account of what happened is denied. Some people come and take your child into custody, but when you go to inquire about their detention, the authorities deny it ever happened. Denial is the most severe form of state violence and the most profound form of trauma.”




İHD Women’s Secretary Handan Çoşkun spoke in a session titled “The Perception of Space and the Body in the Intergenerational Transmission of Grief: Sur.” Çoşkun said they had been conducting research since the 1990s into issues including the forced evacuation of villages, enforced disappearances, suicide, and numerous other subjects.




Speaking on the topic “Disenfranchised Grief: Unrecognized Suffering,” neuropsychologist Masum Aydın said, “Witnessing is fundamental to existence. We cannot become ‘us’ without the other.”




Participants then shared their testimonies and asked questions of the panelists.




The third session of the symposium was moderated by sociologist Didem Aydemir. TJA (Free Women’s Movement) activist and psychological counselor Esra Kahraman spoke on “Geography, Body and Mother Tongue: The Transmission of Memory and Healing Mechanisms among Displaced Kurdish Women in the Middle East,” while TJA activist Rojda Bedia Akkaya addressed “From Oppressed Lives to Collective Healing: The Historical Legacy of Resistance, Communal Life and Distinctive Coping Mechanisms of the Kurdish Women’s Movement.”




Referring to the Peace and Democratic Society Process, Esra Kahraman emphasized the importance they attached to the process and stated that confronting the past and ensuring justice were essential to building lasting peace.




Discussing their work with women who came to Amed following the attacks on Rojava, Kahraman said they had observed how women collectively resisted suffering and hardship.




Rojda Bedia Akkaya highlighted the struggle of Kurdish women and the methods they have developed.




The symposium will continue with presentations titled “What Remains in the Body: Rights Violations, Bodily Memory and the Conditions for Healing,” “Traumatic Silence and States of Subjecthood: From Perpetration to Involvement,” “Tracing the Unspoken: The Speaking Body,” and “Traces Left in Memory and Nature: Destruction and Possibilities for Healing.”

title: We Congratulate the Canadian Labour Congress On Its “Hot Cargo” Endorsement: A Response to the Canadian Jewish Labour Committee (Labour for Palestine-Canada)
content:
A post shared by Labour for Palestine (@labourforpalestine)

The Canadian Jewish Labour Committee (CJLC) claims that the May 2026 Canadian Labour Congress convention “explicitly rejected attempts to include “Hot Cargo” language” during resolution debate. This is inaccurate. No “hot cargo” resolution reached the convention floor and no amendment was brought forward to add “hot cargo” to the resolution that was passed, GEN-134.

The record must be corrected: the CJLC – an organization which has claimed a venerable title from Canada’s labour movement history, but which today serves the purpose of defending Israeli apartheid and genocide – has called on the Canadian Labour Congress to disregard its own constitutional process.

The convention floor clearly demonstrated support for Palestinian solidarity and the principles of trade unionism. A massive majority of delegates supported the amendment to GEN-134, calling on the CLC to cut ties with the Histadrut. When Resolution GEN-134 came to a vote, the overwhelming majority of delegates voted in favour of standing in solidarity with Palestinian workers and cutting ties with the Histadrut.

GEN-061 “Palestine” was submitted to the convention by more submitting bodies than any other resolution, by a wide margin. The decision of the resolutions committee to rule such a highly vetted resolution as non-concurrent was not reflective of the democratic principles that our union governance aspires to. The decision of the Canadian Council to pass this resolution reflects positively on their duty to consider the political concerns being raised by grassroots labour activists, who are listening and responding to the expectations of union members and Canadian workers.

Workers in Canada do not want to be complicit in Israeli genocide, nor do they believe our taxes or economic output should sustain a state which is in open contravention of international law and a source of population displacement and threats to international security.

The decision to enforce hot cargo, and to refuse goods, services and relationships with the Israeli apartheid state, will always be in the hands of the workers themselves. Labour for Palestine applauds the Canadian Labour Congress for declaring its support for workers who take the necessary action and show that Canadian unions remain a force for peace, justice and solidarity with the workers of the world.

author: Matt Simon
title: Extreme Flooding in US Southwest May Foreshadow a Disastrous El Niño Winter
content:
Historically, the phenomenon boosts precipitation in the southern US. This may be a glimpse at the pain to come.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The Southwest just got way too much of a good thing. Last weekend, a ferocious storm inundated communities and killed at least four people. Though precipitation is an essential component of Arizona’s desert climate, the state got two or three months’ worth of it in just a few days — far more than human infrastructure could handle all at once. Since September 20, an astonishing 28.84 inches of rain has fallen on Clovis, New Mexico, compared to its historical average of just 3.3 inches.

“This weekend was just adding more on the rough times that those communities in Southwest Colorado and Arizona and Utah and New Mexico have been having recently,” said Russ Schumacher, director of the Colorado Climate Center at Colorado State University, who’s also the state climatologist. “I think the El Niño connection is pretty clear.”

Indeed, that band of warm water in the Pacific could be priming much of the southern United States for a winter of increased precipitation, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s seasonal outlook. “Could an event like this have happened in a non-El Niño year?” asked Michael A. Crimmins, a climatologist at the University of Arizona. “It could have, but it would have been a lot harder to pull all of the ingredients together at the same time, and would have been a lot less likely.”

The looming problem this winter is heat, oddly enough. The unfolding El Niño is already the strongest on record, and it could get stronger still in the next few months. Although that amounts to just a handful of extra degrees in the Pacific, it injects a tremendous amount of energy into the atmosphere, scrambling weather the world over. The phenomenon is so influential, in fact, that it has helped cancel hurricanes over in the Atlantic, by messing with winds high up in the atmosphere. Accordingly, this year shattered the record for the latest first hurricane in a season by nearly a month. Normally by this time of year we’d have seen six of these cyclones, but 2026 has still only produced one.

The Southwest, though, gets no such relief from inclement weather. In addition to adding heat to the sky, the warmer waters of El Niño also increase atmospheric moisture. Even beyond the El Niño, temperatures in the Pacific have been running extra hot, which explains why the western part of the ocean has produced 10 hurricanes this season even as the Atlantic has remained quiet. (Overall, more than 90 percent of the excess heat that humans have pumped into the atmosphere has been absorbed by the oceans.)

All this warm water means more moisture for the weather patterns that have been moving into the Southwest over the last month. A separate system in late October, for instance, became one of the most extreme storms in Colorado’s history, pelting higher elevations with up to 8 inches of rain in four days, causing widespread destruction. “It’s just really extreme amounts of water vapor in the atmosphere that have been aimed into the Southwest in each of those storms,” Schumacher said.

This autumn precipitation primed Arizona, Colorado, and other Southwestern states for yet more destruction this past week. For one, rivers were already running high, then ran all the higher. And two, if soils are soaked, a follow-up bout of rain will run off and cause flooding. “We get the second storm, just a little bit after the first one, then everything was primed for even worse flooding this time around,” Schumacher said.

In mountainous terrain, this gets especially dangerous, as the topography funnels rainwater into raging torrents. “If you hike around the Southwest, you’re going to see out-of-place boulders all over the place,” Crimmins said. “Water put it there. Maybe it was 5,000 years ago or something like that, but water moves. We can have really epic flash flooding.”

The one silver lining here is that any increased precipitation from this El Niño could bring drought relief to much of the southern U.S., according to NOAA’s projections. Climate change is not only exacerbating these ongoing dry spells — hotter temperatures also increase evaporation from reservoirs. At the same time, populations are growing in the Southwest, meaning more people demanding more water.

With these factors conspiring, the Colorado River’s two largest reservoirs, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, are approaching the point of collapse. The potential for more rainfall this winter might help fill them, Schumacher said, but it can’t reverse the system’s precipitous decline. “It’s a long way to go to get even back to where we were a year ago,” he said. “Let alone when it was in good condition decades ago.”

The wildcard this year is snowpack: It’s still too early to tell, Schumacher said, how much snow will fall in Colorado. Whereas rainwater flows quickly into rivers, making it harder to store without overwhelming infrastructure — hence all the destructive flooding of late — snowpack slowly releases water as things thaw in the spring. With a record low snowpack earlier this year, Colorado is in desperate need of bountiful flakes in the months ahead.

Water agencies can’t change the weather, but they can at least change how they manage precipitation. Down in Arizona, cities like Tucson have been installing green infrastructure — basically dirt spaces that hydrate native plants — which slow down the flow of water, thus preventing flooding. “There’s really cool and clever ways of thinking about stormwater as a resource,” Crimmins said, “rather than a nuisance.”

author: Jessica Kutz
title: The Navajo Nation Just Elected Its First Woman President
content:
The Navajo Nation isn’t alone. The Seneca Nation of Indians also elected its first woman president this week.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Crystalyne Curley is set to become the first woman president of the Navajo Nation, the largest reservation by land mass in the country.

Curley, who also held the distinction of being the first woman to serve as the Nation’s council speaker — the head of its legislative branch —when she was voted by council members to fill that role in 2023, has worked on issues related to water rights, uranium contamination and voter rights.

In another first for tribal governments, the Seneca Nation of Indians in New York also elected its first woman president, Tina Abrams. She previously served two terms on the Nation’s council.

While Native women made history for their tribes in this election, it is not uncommon for women to hold top positions in tribal nations. Activist Wilma Mankiller was appointed as principal chief of the Cherokee Nation in 1985, the largest tribe in the country by tribal enrollment numbers. Though there is no official data on women’s representation in tribal governments, the nonprofit RepresentWomen found that in 2020 at least 78 tribal nations had reached or exceeded gender parity in their legislatures.

Curley’s campaign website lays out her vision as president, including prioritizing behavioral health services, affordable housing programs, workforce development and protecting Diné culture and sovereignty, among other initiatives.

Leading up to the election, Curley told Indian Country Today, a nonprofit news outlet, that she brings her perspective as a mom to the position. “I want to make sure that our children have a safe future, a safe home where they feel they’re proud of who they are,” she said.

By Navajo Nation election law, the results are considered unofficial for ten days after November 3rd. With an 1115 vote count difference between them, Curley’s opponent Justin Jones has not conceded and says he’ll launch a legal challenge over the results, according to the Navajo-Hopi Observer.

The Nation, which has the second largest number of enrolled tribal members nationwide, spans northeastern Arizona and parts of New Mexico and Utah.

author: Novara Media
title: Inside China’s Biotech Revolution
content:
In the Mao era, ‘barefoot doctors’ received just a few months of training before being sent out to straighten broken bones and administer vaccines. Now China’s researchers make world-class cancer drugs, cheap surgical robots and cutting edge brain-computer interfaces. Its doctors make AI-powered avatars of themselves to deal with ever more patients.




But China is growing old before it grows rich. Cancer, diabetes, Alzheimer’s and cardiovascular problems are ballooning. And its aging crisis is coming on faster because of the legacy of its one-child policy. How will China adapt?




Ruby Wang worked on the NHS Covid frontline before becoming Head of Health at the British Embassy in Beijing. And now she’s written 

The China Cure: The Rise of Biotech, AI Medicine and a Global Health Superpower

. She tells Richard Hames how China got from barefoot doctors to high-tech hospitals, what it learned from Covid, and what the NHS could learn from China.

author: Jon Queally
title: Petition Urging Dems to Reject Jeffries as House Speaker Passes 1M Signatures
content:
“The Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment,” reads the petition.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

An online petition that demanding that Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) not be the next Democratic Speaker of the House has hit one million signatories on Saturday as the clamor for a leadership change within the party explodes after historic midterm wins driven by populist demands.

As of this writing, the Change.org petition — titled “House Democrats: CHOOSE A NEW SPEAKER” — has 1,007,831 verified signatories, with the number rapidly rising.

While the final totals are not yet established, Democrats emerged from Tuesday’s elections with at least 254 seats in the next Congress, reclaiming the majority from the Republicans who currently can count on just 162 seats when new members are sworn in come January.

While Jeffries is clearly the presumptive choice for Democrats, and he formally put himself in the running on Wednesday with a letter to all members, outside progressives have voiced serious opposition given his failure to embrace many of the positions — including backing Medicare for All, taking on entrenched corporate power, and restricting military assistance to Israel over its genocide in Gaza — that have animated voters nationwide this election cycle.

We believe the Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment.

The Speaker has enormous influence over the direction of the House, including its legislative priorities and agenda. Before casting their votes, representatives should closely examine Jeffries’s public record, policy positions, campaign donor record and leadership … and listen to constituents who do not want him elevated to Speaker.

This is not a foregone conclusion. There is still time for other Democratic members of the House to step forward and seek the nomination for Speaker, someone whose priorities more closely reflect the voters who hope to elect the Democratic majority.

We are calling on every member of the incoming 120th Congress to vote against Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker in January 2027 and choose a different candidate.

Axios reported Friday that members of Congress have been “inundated” with calls urging them not to elect Jeffries and suggested that some of the hesitations are not just among progressives.

The outlet reporting interviewing “nearly a half-dozen incoming House Democrats in deeply red seats Thursday who declined to state a firm position one way or another on voting for him.”

Sign this petition if you want a new speaker of the house. https://t.co/G88VLySjsQ

As Corbin Trent, the former top aide to Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) who now runs a progressive organizing outfit called A Fight Worth Having, wrote in a column published at Common Dreams on Friday, “the Democratic leadership we have today is completely ill-suited for this moment. They do not have the vision for what it’s going to take to rebuild the trust the American people have lost in their government, their institutions, and the Democratic Party itself.”

“Democrats have spoken loudly and clearly that they want new leadership,” Trent said of the election. “Unfortunately, too many of the people in Washington aren’t listening.”

While the large Democratic majority in the House makes it easier for Jeffries to maneuver leading up to the leadership vote, and given that no challenger has stepped forward to take him on directly, the betting money is still safe that Jeffries will be the next Speaker of the House.

But the public push denouncing him as the wrong choice of leadership in a moment where Democratic voters are clearly demanding — and expecting — a much bolder agenda, the pressure may yet have an impact on his calculations.

author: Wütende Flintas*
title: Patriarchale Strukturen und Täterschutz in Hannover
content:
Wir sind wütende FLINTA*s aus Hannover. Wütend auf patriarchale Gewalt, auf Mackertum in linken Strukturen und auf diejenigen, die sich nach außen feministisch geben, während sie im eigenen Umfeld wegschauen. Und wir haben keine Lust mehr, dazu zu schweigen.




Am 18.10. veröffentlichte das Offene Antifa Café (OAC) Hannover gemeinsam mit dem „FLINTA Bündnis“ einen Aufruf zum gemeinsamen Bannermalen anlässlich des 25. November, dem internationalen Tag gegen patriarchale Gewalt.




Ein Aufruf, der uns fassungslos und wütend macht.




Denn während das OAC nach außen feministische Kämpfe unterstützt, erleben wir seit Jahren, wie in seinem Umfeld patriarchale Gewalt relativiert, Tätern der Rücken gestärkt und Betroffene im Stich gelassen werden.




Feminismus ist kein Banner, das mensch einmal im Jahr hochhält, um sich anschließend wieder mit den eigenen Mackern gutzustellen.




Aus Rücksicht auf die betroffenen FLINTA*s werden wir an dieser Stelle bewusst keine detaillierten Schilderungen der Gewalterfahrungen veröffentlichen. Ihre Geschichten gehören ihnen. Niemand ist verpflichtet, eigene Traumata öffentlich auszubreiten, damit patriarchale Gewalt endlich ernst genommen wird.




Was wir aber benennen wollen, ist der Umgang mit den Vorwürfen und den beschuldigten Personen.




In einem der uns bekannten Fälle wurde eine Person nach unserem Kenntnisstand wegen Gewalt gegen eine FLINTA* gerichtlich verurteilt. Trotzdem ist für uns bis heute keine klare Distanzierung des OAC von dieser Person erkennbar.




Wie weit die Solidarität mit Beschuldigten im Umfeld des OAC reicht, zeigte sich aus unserer Sicht auch am Rande der Demonstration „Nazizentren dichtmachen“. Nachdem Ordner*innen die betreffende Person von der Demonstration ausgeschlossen hatten, solidarisierten sich dem OAC nahestehende Personen unter Protest mit ihr und verließen anschließend gemeinsam die Demonstration.




Anstatt den Ausschluss zu respektieren, wurde öffentlich Solidarität mit der ausgeschlossenen Person gezeigt.




Was ist eine feministische Haltung wert, wenn sie genau dort aufhört, wo es um die eigenen Freunde und Genossen geht?




Für uns steht dieser Vorfall nicht isoliert. Seit Jahren bestehen enge Verbindungen zwischen dem OAC-Umfeld und einem Kreis von Graffiti-Malern, dessen Umgang mit patriarchalem Verhalten wir als zutiefst problematisch erleben. Gegen mehrere Personen aus diesem Umfeld wurden in den vergangenen Jahren Vorwürfe erhoben. Konsequenzen blieben nach unserer Wahrnehmung in vielen Fällen aus.




Es geht uns dabei nicht um eine vermeintliche moralische Reinheit linker Räume. Es geht um Verantwortung. Um die Frage, ob Betroffene ernst genommen werden oder ob persönliche Freundschaften, Szenezugehörigkeit und die eigene politische Reputation am Ende schwerer wiegen.




Patriarchale Gewalt ist kein Problem, das nur außerhalb unserer Strukturen existiert. Sie verschwindet nicht, weil Menschen sich Antifaschist*innen nennen, linke Parolen rufen oder feministische Sticker verkleben. Auch linke Räume sind durchzogen von patriarchalen Machtverhältnissen, Männerbünden und Schweigestrukturen.




Gerade deshalb ist es notwendig, das eigene Umfeld zu hinterfragen, statt Gewaltvorwürfe als unangenehme Störung des Szenealltags zu behandeln.




Wer feministische Kämpfe für sich beansprucht, muss sich auch dann mit patriarchaler Gewalt auseinandersetzen, wenn die Vorwürfe die eigenen Genossen betreffen.




Wir sind es leid, dass FLINTA*s in vermeintlich emanzipatorischen Räumen immer wieder selbst dafür kämpfen müssen, ernst genommen zu werden. Wir sind es leid, dass der Schutz Betroffener zur Verhandlungssache wird, sobald die beschuldigte Person gut vernetzt ist. Und wir sind es leid, dass diejenigen, die diese Widersprüche ansprechen, häufig mehr Widerstand erfahren als die Strukturen, die sie kritisieren.




Besonders bitter ist es, wenn wir uns nicht einmal bei einem Vorbereitungstreffen zum Tag gegen patriarchale Gewalt darauf verlassen können, dass die beteiligten Strukturen selbst eine konsequent antipatriarchale Haltung vertreten.




Der 25. November ist kein Tag für feministische Selbstdarstellung. Er ist ein Kampftag gegen patriarchale Gewalt. Ein Tag, an dem Betroffene und ihre Perspektiven im Mittelpunkt stehen sollten – nicht das Bedürfnis linker Gruppen, sich ein feministisches Image zu geben.




Antipatriarchale Praxis beginnt nicht beim Bannermalen. Sie beginnt dort, wo Solidarität unbequem wird.




Deshalb fordern wir:




* Das sofortige Ende der Zusammenarbeit zwischen dem FLINTA Bündnis und dem OAC Hannover.


* Den Ausschluss des OAC aus feministischen und linken Räumen, bis eine ernsthafte, betroffenenorientierte Aufarbeitung der kritisierten Vorgänge stattgefunden hat.


* Eine klare Distanzierung von patriarchaler Gewalt und dem Schutz gewaltausübender Personen sowie einen transparenten Umgang mit den erhobenen Vorwürfen.


* Konsequente Solidarität mit Betroffenen statt Loyalität gegenüber den eigenen Mackern.




Wir wollen keine weiteren leeren Bekenntnisse zum Feminismus. Wir wollen Strukturen, in denen Betroffene nicht fürchten müssen, auf die Freund*innen ihrer Täter zu treffen. Strukturen, in denen patriarchale Gewalt nicht aus falsch verstandener Solidarität verschwiegen wird. Strukturen, die Kritik zulassen und Verantwortung übernehmen.




Wer von Feminismus spricht, muss sich auch an feministischer Praxis messen lassen.




Keine Solidarität mit patriarchaler Gewalt!




Gegen Mackertum, Männerbünde und Täterschutz – auch und gerade in unseren eigenen Reihen!




Für einen konsequent antipatriarchalen, betroffenenorientierten und antiautoritären Feminismus!




Wütende FLINTAs aus Hannover*

author: Jakob Reimann
title: „Renn oder Brenn“ – Brandanschlag gegen propalästinensische Aktivistin Lisa K.
content:
Am Freitagabend [30.10.26] brannte es in der Wohnung von Lisa K. in Leipzig-Connewitz. In den Wochen zuvor wurden im Kiez Graffitis mit expliziten Morddrohungen gegen das Mitglied des FLINTA*-Teams des Fußballvereins Roter Stern Leipzig gesprüht. Im Vereinsvorstand haben proisraelische „Antideutsche“ erheblichen Einfluss. Eine Rekonstruktion der Ereignisse von etos.media-Redakteur Jakob Reimann.




UPDATE: In einer ursprünglichen Version des Artikels waren zwei Funktionäre des Vereins Roter Stern Leipzig mit Klarnamen genannt. Auf Wunsch der betroffenen Mitglieder des FLINTA*-Teams wurden diese entfernt.




Manchmal folgen Worten eben auch Taten. Am Freitagabend brannte es in einem Mehrfamilienhaus in der Wolfgang-Heinze-Straße in Leipzig-Connewitz. Die Wohnung im dritten Stock war zu dem Zeitpunkt leer – die Bewohnerin Lisa K. war nicht vor Ort. In den Wochen zuvor waren im Kiez Dutzende Graffitis mit Morddrohungen gegen die palästinasolidarische Aktivistin gesprüht worden: „Lisa K. renn oder brenn“, lautete eine davon.




Um 19.22 Uhr ging der Notruf bei der Leitstelle ein, berichtete die Leipziger Volkszeitung; 30 Minuten später wurde der Brand als gelöscht gemeldet. Die Feuerwehrleute mussten sich gewaltsam Zugang verschaffen. Bereits zuvor hatten die Bewohner das Haus verlassen. Verletzt wurde niemand. Mit Spezialfiltern musste der Rauch entfernt werden.




Die Kriminalpolizeiinspektion führe Ermittlungen wegen des Verdachts eines Branddelikts, erklärt ein Polizeisprecher gegenüber etos.media. Der oder die Täter müssten in die Wohnung eingebrochen sein und hätten in allen Räumen Brandbeschleuniger verteilt, erzählt Lisa K. im Gespräch. Fotos und Videos des Tatorts liegen der Redaktion vor, werden aus Achtung vor K.s Privatsphäre jedoch nicht veröffentlicht. Sie zeigen schwere Brandschäden im Eingangsbereich der Wohnung und in einem zweiten Raum. Die Einrichtung wurde in weiten Teilen zerstört und die Wohnung komplett verwüstet. Dies deutet neben Einbruch und schwerer Brandstiftung auch auf Vandalismus hin. Solidarische haben einen Hilfsfonds für Lisa K. eingerichtet.




Am frühen Sonntagmorgen brannte es in einem weiteren Haus in Connewitz, berichtete die Leipziger Volkszeitung. Ein Kinderwagen im Hausflur in der Bornaischen Straße wurde in Brand gesetzt. Auf der Fassade des Hauses stand ein Soli-Graffiti: „We stand with Lisa.“ Es wurde später von Unbekannten übermalt.




*„Stell dich dem Plenum“*




Dem Brandanschlag ging über Monate hinweg eine Reihe von Ereignissen voraus, die womöglich in direktem Zusammenhang mit der zerstörten Wohnung stehen. In der Nacht zum 17. September und in drei weiteren Nächten wurden insgesamt mehr als 80 Graffitis im Umfeld des Vereins und in Lisa K.s Connewitzer Kiez gesprüht. Sie enthielten gewaltverherrlichende, rassistische, frauenfeindliche und teils extrem verstörende Inhalte. Darunter waren zahlreiche Todeswünsche bis hin zu Morddrohungen:




– „Häng dich auf Lisa K.“


– „Lisa K. renn oder brenn“


– „Antisemiten raus aus dem RSL. Lisa K. nimm dir einen Strick“


– „Anti-Lisa Aktion Antisemiten raus aus dem RSL!“


– „Lieber 100 Nazis im Kiez als Lisa K.“


– „Lisa K. raus aus dem RSL“


– „Lisa K. stell dich dem Plenum“


– „Lisa K. töten!“


– „Lisa K. totknüppeln“


– „Lisa K. jagen!“


– „Lisa K. wir kriegen dich!“


– „Antisemiten töten. Lisa K. stell dich!“


– „Lisa K. raus aus dem Kiez!“


– „Bald 1 Raum Whng unter der Erde für Lisa K.“


– „Lisa K nach Gaza deportieren“


– „Vergewaltigung in Gaza für Lisa K.“


– …




Es werde „unter anderem wegen Sachbeschädigung und Bedrohung ermittelt“, erklärt ein Sprecher der Polizeidirektion auf Anfrage. Die verschiedenen Handschriften legen nahe, dass es sich um mehrere Täter handelt. „Lisa K. renn oder brenn“ impliziert eine Verbindung zum Brandanschlag. Der mehrfache Bezug zum Roten Stern lässt womöglich auf Personen aus dem RSL-Umfeld schließen, etwa die Aufforderung „Lisa K stell dich dem Plenum“.




Auf dem Plenum am 24. September habe die RSL-Sicherheitsbeauftragte laut mehreren Anwesenden mit Nachdruck erklärt, sie erwehre sich dagegen, dass die Person/en aus dem Verein stammt/en. Worauf sich diese Ansicht stützt, ließ sie offen. Eine diesbezügliche Presseanfrage an den RSL blieb unbeantwortet. „Dem Vorstand ist nicht bekannt, wer die Graffiti gesprüht hat“, heißt es in einer Stellungnahme vom 29. Oktober. „Hinweise darauf, dass Personen im Verein die Täter kennen und schützen, liegen uns, der Sicherheitsbeauftragten und auch anderen Personen im Verein nicht vor“, heißt es weiter. Angesichts der Zahl von 2.163 Vereinsmitgliedern (Stand 1. Januar) ist eine solche Aussage aus praktischen Erwägungen schwer zu treffen.




*Streit beim Roten Stern*




Lisa K. ist seit Sommer 2024 im Fußballverein Roter Stern Leipzig aktiv und ist zum aktuellen Saisonbeginn im Mai vom zweiten in das erste FLINTA*-Team, das sogenannte Team23, gewechselt. Nach Angaben mehrerer Vereinsmitglieder kam es in dem stark von den sogenannten Antideutschen geprägten Verein wiederholt zu Konflikten im Zusammenhang mit dem „Nahostkonflikt“, insbesondere um die Frage der Solidarität innerhalb des Vereins.




Eine Person habe bei einem Training im Januar ein FC-Palestina-Trikot getragen, auf dem die beiden Einsen der Rückennummer 11 in Form des Umrisses des historischen Palästinas dargestellt sind. Daraufhin sei es zu Anfeindungen durch proisraelische Vereinsmitglieder gekommen, da die Darstellung „eine Auslöschungsfantasie Israels“ vermittle und das Trikot „antisemitisch“ sei. Die Person nahm am 7. Oktober 2025 auch an einer von der antifaschistischen Gruppe Handala organisierten Demo teil und wird seitens des RSL sanktioniert.




Das Team23 wird nach Aussagen mehrerer Personen insbesondere von „antideutschen“ RSL-Mitgliedern angefeindet. Bei einem Spiel der Herrenmannschaft seien laut Lisa K. transfeindliche Aussagen gegen das FLINTA*-Team sowie Diffamierungen wie „Team der Judenhasser und Antisemiten“ geäußert worden. Die 27-jährige Lisa K. hat ein Elternteil aus Bangladesch und wurde als Woman of Color von „Antideutschen“ im Verein wiederholt rassistisch stereotypisiert, erzählt sie im Gespräch. Sie werde als hysterisch, emotional und unsachlich dargestellt – als „angry black woman“.




Am 10. September kam es im RSL-Plenum zu Streit. Das Team23 und zwei weitere FLINTA*-Teams wollten am kommenden Spieltag mit einem Kuchenstand Spenden zugunsten des „Lemon Tree Collective“ sammeln. Die NGO wurde von der Leipziger Journalistin Helen Fares gegründet und leistet humanitäre Arbeit in Gaza, Syrien und Ägypten. Gegen das Kollektiv, insbesondere gegen Fares, seien auf dem Plenum und in folgenden E-Mails Antisemitismusvorwürfe erhoben worden, berichten mehrere dort Anwesende. Gegen Fares wurden entsprechende Vorwürfe seit dem Frühjahr 2024 öffentlich geäußert, nachdem sie mit ihrer humanitären Arbeit in Gaza begann und sich für einen Boykott israelischer Waren und Dienstleistungen aussprach, „um nicht indirekt den Genozid am palästinensischen Volk zu finanzieren“, erklärt sie gegenüber etos.media.




Nachdem Lisa K. im Plenum die Hoffnung geäußert hatte, dass zumindest ein Minimalkonsens darüber bestehen sollte, dass in Gaza ein Genozid stattfinde, wurde gelacht. K. reagierte mit den Worten: „Adolf Hitler wäre stolz auf euch“ und „Ihr seid richtig gute Nachfahren eurer Nazi-Großeltern“.




*„Sieg Heil!“ gegen Antisemitismus*




Etwa eine Stunde nach dem Plenum ging Lisa K. mit ihrem Hund Gassi und traf in der Nähe der szenigen Connewitzer Fußballkneipe König Heinz auf einen Trainer mehrerer Teams beim RSL. In Richtung von Lisa K. habe der „Sieg Heil!“ gerufen und ihr den „Hitlergruß“ gezeigt. Auf K.s Nachfrage „Wie bitte?“ habe er den in der Zeit des deutschen Faschismus allgegenwärtigen Gruß Adolf Hitlers wiederholt, erzählt sie im Gespräch. Die faschistische Symbolik sei im Zusammenhang mit den von K. im Plenum erhobenen Vorwürfen verwendet worden.




Die nach § 86a StGB in der BRD verbotene „Sieg Heil!“-Äußerung räumt der Vereinsvorstand in seiner öffentlichen Erklärung vom 29. Oktober ein. Der Trainer wird darin als namenloses „Vereinsmitglied“ bezeichnet, ohne zu erwähnen, dass er hauptamtlich beim RSL tätig ist. „Einen Hitlergruß hat diese Person aber nachweislich nicht gezeigt“, heißt es vom Vorstand. Wie dieser „Nachweis“ aussehe, bleibt auf Anfrage unbeantwortet. Mehrere Vereinsmitglieder geben an, der Trainer habe später behauptet, er habe Lisa K. lediglich zugewunken. „Diese Person ist aktuell suspendiert. Ein Aufarbeitungsprozess wurde begonnen“, heißt es beim RSL weiter.




Laut dem Sitzungsprotokoll des RSL-Plenums vom 29. Oktober, das etos vorliegt, hat der Trainer bereits am Workshop „Überlastung im Ehrenamt“ teilgenommen und sich für „Anfang November“ zum Workshop „Positionen von Männern als verbündete Personen in Arbeitskontexten“ angemeldet. Der Zusammenhang dieser Seminare mit dem Zeigen faschistischer Symbolik erschließt sich nicht. Laut Plenumsprotokoll werde der Trainer seine „hauptamtliche Tätigkeit weitermachen“; er nehme „laut Aussagen gerade seine Überstunden“.




*Ideologische Irrwege*




„Der Rote Stern Leipzig ’99 ist ein antifaschistisches Sportprojekt“, beginnt das „Selbstverständnis“ des Vereins, der das öffentliche „Sieg Heil!“ eines führenden Mitglieds einräumte. Auch der dort formulierte Anspruch, „sich gegen jegliche Form von Diskriminierung wie Rassismus, Sexismus, Antisemitismus und Homophobie“ einzusetzen, scheint mit den geschilderten Vorfällen nur schwer in Einklang zu bringen zu sein.




Es bleibt ein „antifaschistischer“ Fußballverein, der an seinen selbst gesetzten Ansprüchen scheitert. Es bleibt die Gewalt in Westasien, die sich über ideologische Irrwege ihren Weg in die Kieze der Bundesrepublik bahnt. Lisa K. ist schwer mitgenommen von dem Angriff auf ihr Leben. „Laufen Sie nicht mehr ohne Pfefferspray alleine rum“, riet ihr ein Polizist. Auch bei Tageslicht traut sie sich in Connewitz kaum mehr auf die Straße, erzählt sie.

author: Solarpunk Magazine
title: Radical Hope From Gaza
content:
Subscribe to Solarpunk Magazine‘s free blog today!

RADICAL HOPE FROM GAZA: A COLLECTION OF ESSAYS BY AYA AL-HATTAB

An Introduction from the Editors-in-Chief of Solarpunk Magazine

What does it mean to hold on to hope when the world around you is being destroyed? What does it mean to imagine a better future when even the possibility of an ordinary tomorrow feels uncertain at best?

In this powerful six-part series, Palestinian writer and journalist Aya Al-Hattab takes us into the lived realities of Gaza, offering an intimate and deeply human perspective on war, occupation, displacement, loss, and the struggle to preserve hope. Through personal reflections, historical examination, and stories of everyday compassion, Al-Hattab reveals the profound consequences of violence on people, communities, animals, and the places they call home.

Throughout these essays, a central truth emerges: hope requires the courage to imagine a future beyond the suffering of the present, even when that future feels impossibly distant. Sometimes that hope takes the form of caring for a beloved animal, remembering a familiar street, or simply dreaming of a home filled with books and loved ones.

At Solarpunk Magazine, we believe imagining better futures is inseparable from confronting the injustices that prevent them. Aya’s writing reminds us why those futures are so important, and why the right to peace, dignity, freedom, and an ordinary life is worth fighting for.

We are deeply honored to share her words. We invite you to read these essays with open hearts, to bear witness, and to consider what radical hope demands of all of us.
