Als positive Selbstverwirklichungsmöglichkeit müssen sich Frauen ihre Sexualität erst wieder zurückerobern. Dies wird noch dadurch erschwert, daß gerade an der Sexualität die gesellschaftliche Verachtung der Frau festgemacht ist. Als extremstem Ausdruck in der Pornographie, der Vergewaltigung und in abgeschwächter Form in der sexistischen Werbung. Damit tagtäglich konfrontiert, eingebunden in Systeme von subtiler Gewaltandrohung gegenüber allen selbstbestimmten Befreiungsversuchen – und sei es nur der nächtliche Spaziergang ohne Begleitung – entwickeln Frauen vor allem Vermeidungsstrategien; werden immer neu durch Rückzugsgefechte lahmgelegt, am Vorausschreiten verhindert. Ein ganzheitlicher Lebensentwurf ist für Frauen quasi unmöglich. Was eine Frau vorfindet – sind Rollenstereotype, mit denen sie sich identifizieren kann, aus denen sie sich aussuchen kann, auf was sie sich günstigen Falls reduzieren will.

Wir stehen auf der Suche nach einer authentischen, offenen Weiblichkeit immer noch ganz am Anfang – vorschnelle Festlegungen locken von allen Seiten. Jeder Schritt ist mit Widerhaken versehen.

Das Gleiche betrifft natürlich auch die männliche Sexualität. Ich denke – aber hier müssen sich die Männer selbst klar werden und äußern – daß bei deren gesellschaftlicher Bewertung nach wie vor die Potenzfähigkeit im Vordergrund steht. Eine Sexualität, die auf der Verfügbarkeit und damit Verachtung des weiblichen Sexualpartners ausgelebt wird, kann ebenfalls nicht glücklich machen.

Dennoch – die Lage der beiden Geschlechter unterscheidet sich darin grundsätzlich, daß Männer (Homosexuelle ausgenommen) zur Erlangung eines sozialen Status nicht ihre Sexualität unterdrücken müssen. Während Frauen der ständigen Gefahr ausgesetzt sind, über die Identifizierung mit ihrer Sexualität als minderwertig gebrandmarkt zu werden. Gegen die psychologische Wirkung von Männerwitzen hilft eben keine berufliche Qualifikation!

Die Beschreibung des Sexismus bleibt in solcher Kürze natürlich recht thesenhaft. Sie ist m.E. aber die wichtigste notwendige Erweiterung, die der Anarchismus von der feministischen Analyse aufnehmen muß. Denn der anarchistische Freiheitsbegriff, seine Analyse von Herrschaft umfaßt ja bereits ausdrücklich beide Geschlechter und bezieht in seine theoretischen Entwürfe (vgl. Murray Bookchin) auch eine Kritik am herrschenden Verhältnis zur Natur mit ein.

Die feministische Forderung nach der Befreiung der Frauen, der Beseitigung der patriarchalischen Herrschaft, ist für den Anarchismus also nichts Neues! Seine These ist allerdings auch, daß eine Situation immer nur konkret auch von den konkret Betroffenen verändert werden kann. Deshalb ist ihm der Feminismus nicht einfach einzuverleiben, sondern er muß eine autonome, kämpferische Bewegung von Frauen bleiben. Daß der Feminismus, wie er sich in seinen aktuellen Diskussionen in der BRD darstellt, mit seinen zahlreichen, gegensätzlichen Flügeln auch von sich aus schon niemals im Anarchismus aufgeht, liegt auf der Hand. Er bedarf der anarchafeministischen Kritik. Wie ich mir diese konkret vorstelle, möchte ich am Beispiel der Diskussion um die Quotierung abschließend deutlich machen.

Hören wir zunächst Mechthild Jansen, Quotierungskämpferin und Herausgeberin von »›Halbe-Halbe‹ – der Streit um die Quotierung, Berlin 1986«:

»Die Forderung nach Quotierung symbolisiert einen Bruch zur gesamten bisherigen Funktionszuweisung für Frauen in der kapitalistischen Gesellschaft und einen Gegendruck gegen die Abwälzung der Krisenlasten, gegen Ausbeutung und Gewalt überhaupt. Die »quotierte« Frau ist das Gegenbild zur »flexiblen« Frau, nach der die neokonservative Politik ruft, um mit ihr die gesamte Gesellschaft zur flexiblen Reserve für höhere Profite zu degradieren.« (S. 8)

Nun Elisabeth Kiderlen in ihrer am 4.12.87 in der taz dokumentierten Rede (anläßlich ihrer Entgegennahme des Elisabeth-Selbert-Preises von der Hessischen Landesregierung):

»Quotierung war ein erster Schritt. Jetzt gilt es, sie zu ergänzen. Sie meinte ja nichts anderes als die Forcierung von Chancengleichheit, das Eindringen in männliche Berufe, die Möglichkeit für Karrieren, den Einstieg in die Politik. Das bedeutet aber auch Anpassung der weiblichen Lebensläufe an die der Männer, …« und das möchte sie so geändert sehen:

»Bei der Bewältigung der Arbeitslosigkeit wird schon jetzt implizit vom klassischen Modell eines weiblichen Lebenslaufs ausgegangen: Ausbildung, Beruf, Pause, Neueinstieg, Weiterbildung, Teilzeit. … Das Modell müßte offensiv verfochten werden.«

Der Widerspruch ist offensichtlich: laut Frau Jansen bedeutet die Quotierung eine Strategie gegen die Flexibilisierung der Ware »weibliche Arbeitskraft« – Frau Kiderlen möchte jedoch die Perspektive nach der errungenen Quotierung in Richtung einer Flexibilisierung für alle, – nicht mehr nur für Frauen! Das von ihr skizzierte Modell der Teilzeitarbeit entspricht genau dem momentanen ökonomischen Konzept der Hausfrauisierung der Lohnarbeit.

Was bei beiden völlig untergeht, ist die Frage nach den Inhalten der Arbeit. Ist es überhaupt wünschenswert, daß sich Frauen »halbe/halbe« in die Organisation der Welt einbinden wie sie sich heute darstellt? Zum einen werden sich die 50% Männer kaum von ihrem eingefahrenen Trott abhalten lassen – haben sie doch dazu die ganze historische Macht der Institutionen auf ihrer Seite. Zudem fehlt völlig eine radikale Institutionenkritik – wenn Kritik geäußert wird, dann werden Institutionen lediglich als »männlich« charakterisiert; was auch immer das heißen soll!?

Zum anderen wird sich die Art der Arbeit nur dadurch, daß sie nun von Frauen getan wird, kaum ändern. Sie bekommt allerdings vielleicht einen freundlicheren kosmetischen Anstrich – wieder wird also die »alte Weiblichkeit« ausgebeutet, von der wir doch wegwollen.

So formuliert auch Anita Heiliger von der KOFRA (Kommunikationszentrum für Frauen zur Arbeitssituation) München:

»Was wir brauchen sind … zunächst unzählige Möglichkeiten für Frauen, ihre Fähigkeiten und Möglichkeiten selbst zu entwickeln und zu praktizieren, nach ihren Interessen – statt halbe/halbe an dem teilzuhaben, was Männer geschaffen haben – dabei aber keinen Raum zu haben, eigenes zu entwickeln.« (Heft 10/11, 1987, S. 8)

Was durch solche reformerischen Vorhaben wie die Quotierungsforderung also allenfalls erreicht wird, ist ein Abrücken von der Utopie. Die Situation der Frauen, ihre Ausgangsmöglichkeiten werden zwar verbessert – die Frauen selbst andererseits aber gerade auf die patriarchalischen Strukturen vereidigt, die verändert werden sollen.

Diese Gefahr liegt immer dort, wo Frauenpolitik nicht mehr den Rahmen des bestehenden überschreiten will, sondern nur noch auf ihren anerkannten Platz darin pocht.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Prime minister announces $1B for housing, new hospital to ‘tackle’ homelessness in Winnipeg
content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney joined Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and the mayor of Winnipeg to announce a joint funding venture to build more than 2,000 new homes and an addictions treatment centre in the middle province’s capital.

The federal government will be allocating $1 billion overall, with $800 million going to the homes and the remaining $200 million going to the proposed Winnipeg Mental Health and Addictions Centre, as well as the refurbishment of similar facilities.

“There’s no simple answer,” Carney said. “This is a hard problem. And hard problems demand the humility to learn from previous well-intentioned efforts that have fallen short.”

Funds will also go to supporting local, grassroots organizations that are already involved in addressing the homelessness crisis, including End Homelessness Winnipeg, the North End Women’s Centre, and Chalmers Neighbourhood Renewal Corporation.

Carney said the partnership is one project in an “unprecedented” $30 billion allocation in the 2026 budget, with the end goal of ending homelessness in Canada in 10 years.

“Help works,” he said, which extends to housing and healthcare.

Alongside federal, provincial and municipal governments, funding for these Winnipeg-based projects will also be provided by First Nation governments such as the Southern Chiefs’ Organization (SCO), as well as private funders such as True North Sports and Entertainment, owner of the Winnipeg Jets and the primary investor in several major infrastructure projects downtown.

“It’s the first time in our country’s history where every level of government has come together to tackle homelessness,” Kinew said. “Including First Nations and Métis governments.”

“The reality is that a huge part of what we see is that [in the past] failed policies like residential schools left a disproportionate number of Indigenous people vulnerable to the ravages of addictions. And the only way for us to find a solution is to have the full participation and engagement of the leaders of those people.”

He said, “A challenge for Indigenous Peoples in Canada has never been that Indigenous Peoples don’t know the solutions. Absolutely we do. The challenge has been that we didn’t have access to the resources and to the decision-making tables to make that happen.”

Carney said that previous government and community efforts to address homelessness have been “inadequately resourced, poorly co-ordinated, and not sustained.”

He said it’s “imperative” that this new strategy succeeds.”

“In Canada, we know we’re not perfect, but we always strive to be good,” Carney said. “We do things because they’re right, not because they’re easy. Ending homelessness is hard; it’s good, and it’s right. And it will require more than compassion.

“It will require ambition, execution, and partnership amongst all levels of government with contributions from philanthropy and business,” Carney added.

There was no determined answer when it came to where most of the 2,000 planned units will be built, but the first 373 are currently being developed inside of Wehwehneh Bahgahkinahgohn, formerly known as the Hudson’s Bay Building, just down the street from the Manitoba Legislature.

The building was acquired by the SCO in 2022, and is scheduled to be complete in 2028. Funding is supported through a partnership with True North.

Jamil Mahmood, the executive director of Main Street Project, a major non-profit addictions treatment centre and homeless shelter, said that additional housing would be useful anywhere in the downtown core.

The organization’s emergency shelter on Main Street has been affected by several fires in 2026, beginning in January. The most recent was on Oct. 31.

Money from this announcement will help refurbish the building, which housed over 2,900 people in 2025, according to its annual report.

“We know that’s where people are, we know that’s where the resources are, so the more you can put housing up where resources are is great,” he said.

“I think over time we can definitely expand that … from the core area to different areas, but then you also need to move resources to those places,” he added. “So we believe a decentralized model would work over time, but right now we have resources downtown.”

Mahmood said “the big thing,” however, is the inclusion of wrap-around support on-site, and staff who can remain there to help.

“I think that helps a lot of people really feel more comfortable with this housing,” he said. “And also, the reverse option is people stay in encampments or they stay on street corners.”

End Homelessness Winnipeg, a non-profit that, through its data collection, determined that every one in four homeless people in Winnipeg is Indigenous, stated the announcement was a “significant opportunity for Winnipeg,” after the fact.

“We have an opportunity to move beyond managing homelessness and toward ending it,” CEO Jennifer Moore Rattray said in the statement. “Housing is medicine, but housing alone is not enough. We need prevention, mental wellness services and sustained community supports.”

Similar to Mahmood’s point, Moore Rattray also noted that “the solutions are already in our communities, led by people and organizations who know what works.

“This once-in-a-lifetime investment could give us the resources to bring those solutions to scale and create lasting change for the people we serve.”

The additional money going towards mental health care would be to help address the issues which may render someone homeless at their source, Carney said.

Now not everyone without a home needs health care, but most desperately do,” he said. “Nine in 10 people on the Winnipeg streets face a health challenge, most often addiction, mental illness or both. And for them, the emergency room becomes their only respite, but it’s a temporary respite. They’re treated, discharged, and then they go straight back onto the street. and the cycle begins again.”

As of Friday afternoon, the wait time at St. Boniface Hospital’s emergency room was 15 hours long, according to the Winnipeg Regional Health Authority.

He said having improved mental health care would decrease the number of people visiting emergency rooms as a last resort.

In Toronto, Carney added, emergency room visits went down 80 per cent because of the Fred Victor Dunn House, a four-storey apartment building with on-site social support for people who were previously homeless or struggling with addiction. A new mental health centre in Winnipeg would fill the same need.

Kinew described the centre as “a new health care campus” and said that Manitoba has needed to “do more” when it comes to mental health and addictions support, and not only for the homeless population.

“I want to be clear,” he added, “yes, there’s a lot of people we drive by on the street doing the fentanyl fold, but there’s people in the suburbs in a basement who are struggling right now, there’s people in rural communities who are struggling from the very same vices and very same disease, and this service is going to be there for everybody in Manitoba who wants recovery.”

Mark Chipman, the executive chairman of True North, had originally proposed the idea of a new hospital, according to Kinew.

Alongside Wehwehneh Bahgahkinahgohn, True North is also responsible for the $650 million redevelopment of Portage Place Shopping Mall, soon-to-be the site of a mixed-use True North Campus, which will include housing, health care centre, grocery store, and urban greenspaces.

Chipman said the number of people “with an acquired brain injury” due to toxic drugs “is staggering,” and the new centre will serve as “an entry point to stabilise them, and then find the correct supports for them.

“Every person’s got a different story, and then those supports are co-located and lined up,” he said.

Speaking at the podium, Chipman said he’s learned that “there are several ways to look at this [homelessness] crisis.

“You can look at the burden it places on our health care system, our social service network, our justice system, and the sheer human impact it has on those in our emergency rooms and our first responders. You can look at it through the effect it has on our community’s sense of safety and security,” he said.

The stop in Winnipeg was the first of several in a tour Carney is taking to promote the 2026 federal budget, according to the Canadian Press.

APTN also asked SCO Grand Chief Jerry Daniels for a comment, but a spokesperson said he is not speaking to media at this time.

Emma is a Red River Métis with family roots in St. Malo, Manitoba. She graduated from RRC Polytech’s Creative Communications program in 2023 and went on to serve as a community journalist and photographer for the Free Press Community Review until she joined APTN in 2026. Equipped with a strong sense of justice, she enjoys covering stories in the central prairies for a larger audience. Her work has also appeared in Manitoba Inc. Magazine, the Free Press, and RRC Polytech’s student paper, The Projector.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: International Inuit Day celebration set to return to Ottawa’s Annie Pootoogook Park
content:
Isaruit Inuit Arts, an Ottawa-based organization, will host its sixth annual International Inuit Day celebration Saturday at Annie Pootoogook Park in the Sandy Hill neighbourhood. 




The event runs from noon to 4:30 p.m. and will feature musical performances, a feast, family games and cultural activities. It is free and open to the public. 




Performers include Pangnirtung singer-songwriter Joey Nowyuk, Ottawa-based drum dancer Donovan Gordon Tootoo, who is originally from Rankin Inlet, and the Nunavut Sivuniksavut students’ performing group.




Inuit arts and crafts vendors will also sell their work at the event.




The schedule includes a qulliq lighting at 1:30 p.m., performances from 1:40 p.m., a feast at 2:30 p.m. and community games at 3:15 p.m. 




An Inuit cultural activity tent will offer a qulliq making activity and photo opportunities featuring Inuit clothing.




International Inuit Day, observed annually on Nov. 7, was established by the Inuit Circumpolar Council in 2006 to celebrate Inuit culture and amplify Inuit voices across the circumpolar world.
















The date honours Greenlander Eben Hopson Sr., founder of the first Inuit Circumpolar Conference in 1977.

author: Daron Letts
title: MLAs wrap up fall sitting
content:
The fall sitting of Nunavut’s legislative Assembly wrapped up Thursday, with MLAs passing into law seven bills they introduced, leaving four to be dealt with later. 




“Thank you, each and every one of you, for working hard for the two weeks of what we did,” said Speaker David Joanasie, the MLA for South Baffin, as he closed the session at the end of the day.




MLAs looked at 11 bills over the two weeks that that they sat, beginning on Oct. 22, including legislation to increase the student loan limit, changes to the membership of the board of inquiry that governs medical professionals, and an approval for capital expenditures.




Among the bills that were passed were:







Bill 15: an act to amend the Student Financial Assistant Act to double the limit of loans made to a person who is eligible to receive other loans to $300,000.




Bill 14: an amendment to the Medical Profession Act to update the membership composition of the Board of Inquiry, set out term limits for members of the Board of Inquiry, establish hearing panels, and modernize the law’s language. 




Bill 10: Appropriation (Capital) Act, a bill that authorizes capital expenditures for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2028.







The policymakers are scheduled to return to the Legislative Assembly in the new year on Feb. 27.

author: By Dingane Xaba, Unicorn Riot
title: Seven of the Minnesota 15 Defendants Speak on Indictments
content:
Minneapolis, MN — In June of 2026, 15 Minnesota-based activist organizers were 

indicted

 by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) on charges of conspiring to “impede or injure” federal officers during mass protests against the deadly deportation surge led by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). 




Unicorn Riot interviewed seven of the 

Minnesota 15

 — 

Isaac Sant

, 

Emmett Doyle

, 

Cam Kennedy

, 

Cal Robinet

, 

Gabriel Van De Water

, 

Treasure Thoreson

, and 

Mac Stewart

 — over the course of the Summer to hear about their involvement in the historic immigrant-defense movement that led to them becoming political 

targets of the federal government

.
















The indicted include teachers, professors, union workers, electricians, and wildlife managers, among other careers. All are Minnesota residents and most of them have a longtime experience in local community activism; a common thread that defense lawyers stress is the real reason for the indictments.




The 

prosecution claims

 that the accused were part of two local organizations known as Direct Action Minnesota (DAMN) and the Black Cat Workers Collective that “emphasize a violent, militant approach to politics and are highly critical of non violent peaceful protest.” This is according to Trump’s U.S. Attorney for Minnesota Daniel Rosen who announced the charges during a 

June 16 press conference

.




Rosen went on to claim that the defendants were being charged “not for what they said, but what they did,” and that his office will introduce “video and eyewitness accounts” as primary sources in court.




Federal Indictment on Minnesota 15 Peddles DOJ ‘Antifa’ Conspiracy Angle After Raids




Dragnet Surveillance 




Court documents from only a fraction of the government’s evidence already reveal that 

ICE is running Operation Puppet Master, likely the largest surveillance operation in U.S. history

. See 

Unicorn Riot’s deep-dive video

 on some of the initial court documents made public.




A large amount of 

encrypted text message data is also being disseminated by the prosecution team

 and expected to be used in court. Much if not all of this data appears to have been gleaned from undercover HSI agents who joined the myriad of public Signal text groups created by local community organizers to coordinate protests against the ICE-led 

Operation Metro Surge

. 




Government surveillance of the defendants extended beyond Minnesota as it was recently reported that Chicago-area cops assisted Homeland Security in monitoring a multi-state organizing tour attended by some of the defendants and sponsored by the Anarchist collective Crimethinc. The same report by Wired reveals that 

Homeland Security agents monitored other tour events in Michigan and Seattle

.




Mass surveillance utilizing artificial intelligence in facial recognition cameras has also been 

deployed against protesters

. A photo that defendant Isaac Sant uploaded to a Signal group depicting his wounds after being struck in the face by a crowd-control munition was used to build a dossier on him. Said photo was run through a Clearview AI search and falsely linked his identity to a completely unrelated person. It isn’t the first time that said technology has produced false results, increasing calls from privacy advocates to ban the technology all together.













Deep Dive: Minnesota 15 Case Reveals Range of Pervasive Surveillance
















DHS Facial Recognition Software Used Against Minnesota 15
















Government Says Terabytes of Signal Chats are Central to the Case Against Minnesota 15













What the Defendants Say




Out of the hundreds of thousands of people involved in anti-ICE protests, the government has taken particular aim against prominent local left-wing organizers it perceives as leaders of a grand political conspiracy against the state. 




One of the Minnesota 15 and a special education teacher, Treasure Thoreson, elaborated to UR: “I think this is meant to be chilling. Pretty much everyone who was arrested is someone involved in labor organizing … This was a threat to the federal government who does not want to see us getting along and supporting each other.”
















Emmett Doyle, also a co-defendant and a union organizer added, “the most powerful thing that people in Minneapolis did to oppose Operation Metro Surge was the general strike, and they [the government] needed to try to get rid of the people who they think helped organize it … I think that’s why they worked so hard to construct this narrative around what are actually quite normal protest activities.”
















Union electrician and Minnesota 15 defendant Cal Robinet said plainly that they felt the charges were “retaliation” from the government for their “political beliefs, for activities as union organizers and for existing as queer people in this world.”
















“This is a naked attempt to silence our voices, to squash dissent and to have a chilling effect on organizing here in the Twin Cities,” said Minnesota 15 defendant and healthcare worker Isaac Sant. 




“It’s about quelling dissent in Minneapolis. And it’s about coming after the movement that rose up against ICE during Metro Surge in December and January.”
















Charged in Anti-ICE Conspiracy, Two Minnesota Defendants Speak Out




The Raids




Out of the 15 defendants that the prosecution and 

the White House appears to have taken particular aim at, is Kyle Wagner

. He is the only defendant currently in federal prison for separate charges relating to a online dispute between him and far-right agitator Jayden Scott.




Wagner, who used his social media accounts to call for community defense, was apprehended by a large group of masked, and heavily armed federal agents, who were in turn 

confronted by a group of people who showed up in response to the raid on February 5 in south Minneapolis.

 He was subsequently granted bail by a pre-trail judge, but that decision was overturned by the sixth circuit at the direction of the DOJ. Wagner’s appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court for his immediate release 

was rejected earlier this month on unexplained grounds

.




Most of the defendants were arrested on June 16, the day the charges were announced, while Wagner was in jail two others turned themselves in days later. 




Kennedy, Doyle, Callum and Sant, in particular, recounted dramatic arrest scenes resembling something out of a movie.







“I woke up to the pounding cop knock, I rushed to grab some clothing, and I went to the front door, and there was just a rifle pointed right at my face. I opened up the door, and I was given a bunch of conflicting commands. And then they handcuffed me and they took me out barefoot into the rain. I had to walk down the broken glass alleyway barefoot until they got me into an SUV.”




Cameron Kennedy




Helicopters, armored convoys and swarms of masked federal officers in military tactical vests were also deployed for these particular arrests. 




A massive and expensive show of force that Kennedy says was more about theatrics than public safety, “they wanted to get this dramatic footage that cost taxpayers tens of millions of dollars in investigation. To my co-defendant’s house [Sant and Robinet], they sent two helicopters on top of a fleet of SUVs. This was a very expensive operation.”
















Kennedy says that his partner was also apprehended and that despite the surveillance, the feds apparently didn’t know they were a couple despite being together for over 11 years. 




Kennedy said they tried to get him to snitch on his co-defendants. “They loosened my cuffs and put them in front of me, started playing nice,” Kennedy said, “then they gave me a 10-minute PowerPoint presentation on some of the discovery that they were using. And this was all in an attempt to get me to turn over evidence on my friends. And then I told them I’m obviously not going to cooperate or talk without a lawyer, and I’m going to reserve my right to remain silent.” 




When asked how the indictments affected them personally, all said they had suffered some kind of psychological trauma and, or, material damage. 




Yet, many noted they were also encouraged that the government’s crackdown was an indication that their actions were having a positive impact in their ultimate goal to halt deportations.




Indeed, even Rosen, the head prosecutor himself, acknowledged that activists had been partially successful in achieving their goals stating, “DAMN members shut down federal operations at the Whipple building a government building just north of the Minnesota-St. Paul airport and the main hub for several federal agencies.”




Trial Timeline & Community Support




Recently, judges have lifted all of the no-contact orders that the defendants were straddled with, allowing the 15 to speak with each other as they await trial. Many of them are close friends and some are roommates.




An evidentiary hearing was held on Oct. 20 and subsequent hearings are expected to occur in coming months, but the sheer amount of evidence still being disseminated could possibly see the entire court process drag well into 2028.




Despite the considerable costs and uncertainty over the legal process, the defendants maintain an air of defiance and optimism, buoyed by considerable community support and absolute conviction that their actions were demonstrably legal and justifiable.




Co-defendant Mac Stewart echoed these sentiments, adding that “humans deal with chaos and tragedy pretty well when we lean into each other. It’s intrinsic to our DNA … So I just want to see more of that. As far as what the government can offer, I expect nothing besides more repression.”
















“The combination of being able to be in custody with my co-defendants and share in that moral support, and then be able to go home and receive the support of friends and family made a really big difference in my initial response to that situation, as jarring as it was.” added Van De Water.
















As the case reaches six months old, the support continues to grow. Kennedy along with defendant and professor Erik Davis have 

expressed gratitude for the additional support they’ve received from neighbors and coworkers

.




Numerous community groups have held solidarity events, fundraisers and rallies for the Minnesota 15 defendants. 




A 

benefit concert

 titled Abolish ICE is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 7 from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. at the Hook & Ladder in South Minneapolis. The concert will feature Nur-D, Isavela Lopez, Brandyn Lee Tulloch & Poetic Roots and emceed by Fanaka Nation.




Minnesota 15 Coverage

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Clyde River grieves hamlet councillor, victim of Iqaluit homicide
content:
Community members in Clyde River are grieving the death of Sandra Aipellee, who was the victim of what police say was a homicide in Iqaluit in October. She was a hamlet councillor, who had just been sworn in this summer.




Steven Aipellee, her brother, said she had been visiting Iqaluit with her partner when when she was fatally stabbed on Oct. 17.




“It’s unbelievable, that happening to the family,” he said in a phone interview from Clyde River on Friday. She had one sister and five brothers.




Nunavut RCMP had reported her death to the public on Oct. 19, but didn’t identify her then. Police 

charged

 32-year-old Christie Nutarariaq with second-degree murder. She was taken into custody and had a court appearance scheduled for Nov. 17, an RCMP news release said.




Steven Aipellee said police told the family that Sandra knew the accused.




He described his sister as a social person who looked out for those around her, and as a dedicated caregiver to her mother. She leaves behind three children, he said, one young girl and two teenage boys now being cared for by their grandmother.




“Sandra was kind to everyone,” her brother said. “She had love when she talked to people, whoever they were, children, elders or adults. A lot of people knew her.”
















On Oct. 19, flags at the hamlet office were lowered half mast in her honour, said Billy Palluq, the hamlet’s chief administrative officer.




“We were shocked and we’ve been saddened,” he said, saying she had joined council in early July.




She had recently earned a certificate from the Piqqusilirivvik Inuit cultural school, he said, and was an active member on the hamlet’s recreation committee.




“She was doing an excellent job,” he said.




Dr. Anna Banerji, a Toronto-based pediatrician, has since launched a Go Fund Me fundraiser in support of the family.




Banerji described Aipellee as part of her extended family, saying she was the aunt of her late adopted son Nathan, also from Clyde River. She said the money raised will go to supporting Aipellee’s three children.
















“Financially, it’s very difficult for them, plus emotionally very traumatic to lose your mother in such a tragic way,” she said in a phone interview from Toronto. “I know the cost of living is so high, and if there’s anything we can do to help to make it a little bit less difficult, then why shouldn’t we?”




The fundraiser has set a goal of raising $16,000, and has raised just over $2,000 as of Friday.

author: Unknown
title: The Hot Potato Changes Hands Again : On the 2026 Midterm Elections
content:
Ultimately, the Democrats are no more capable of addressing the root causes of popular anger than the Republicans. State power will continue to swing back and forth more and more wildly between different parties until our rulers consolidate an autocracy or we manage to effect revolutionary change.







As we anticipated 

in April

, the death knell of the Trump era has rung. Despite being 

historically unpopular

, Democratic politicians won a sweeping victory in the November 2026 midterm elections. Many are describing the rout as an “

extinction-level event

” for the Republican Party.




All this should feel familiar. Only two years ago, when Democrats lost the 2024 elections, pundits across the political spectrum rushed to declare the collapse of the Democratic Party. Summarizing a widespread perception, one 

expert

 claimed that







“Fundamental shifts are occurring in the body politic that have left Democrats on the wrong side of the popular vote, congressional races, and the country’s shifting demographics.”







Two years later, people are saying the same things about the Republican Party. The backlash against Republicans in this year’s election eclipses the gains they made in 2024. Yet the pendulum has been swinging wildly back and forth between parties for over a decade now—and it could be that the wildest swings have yet to come.




For all the talk of political polarization, loyalty to political parties is at its 

lowest

 in decades. Since at least 2016, anger at the status quo has been the most powerful force in politics; Democrats like Hillary Clinton and Joe Biden who attempted to present themselves as its defenders have learned that the hard way. Likewise, Donald Trump has only able to win elections when he is not in office. Whenever Trump represents the ruling order, he draws the same backlash that he once managed to channel.




Since 2014, we have argued that state power itself has become a hot potato that burns whoever holds it. In a globalized economy, in which governments can no longer mitigate the impact of capitalism on their citizens without investors taking their money elsewhere, no party is able to hold state power for long without losing credibility with voters. Similarly, the challenges of maintaining position as a waning imperial power inevitably undercut the legitimacy of whoever controls the state: just as the genocide in Gaza damaged the Biden administration’s support, Trump’s 

war with Iran

 has contributed to driving away voters.




Similar things are taking place all around the world. 

British politicians

 have also seen rapid reversals in fortune. The centrist parties that have long ruled Germany and France are in precipitous decline. One Latin American government after another has swung to the far right, but that hardly indicates a 

social consensus

 in favor of 

any political camp

.




Only countries under continuous autocratic rule, such as Russia, Belarus, China, and North Korea, are excepted from the hot potato pattern. Donald Trump has made no secret of his desire to establish a similar state of affairs in the United States. Yet even in Hungary, which Republicans took as a model for their illiberal aspirations, the long-running autocratic government ultimately lost control. The same has occurred in Poland and, more recently, Serbia. Wherever voters have an opportunity—however narrow—to demand change, they do so—however arbitrarily and capriciously.




With no prospect of improving life for his rank-and-file supporters, Trump’s solution was to 

inflict violence

 on their behalf, offering them the vicarious thrill of watching the state cause harm to others as an outlet for their frustration. 

Less bread, more circuses

.







 




Republicans and Democrats—trash and recycling.










It might have worked—if ordinary people had not courageously taken the streets to interfere. We owe Trump’s failure to those who assembled at 

Tesla dealerships

 in spring 2025, who 

rose up

 against federal agents and the National Guard that June, who confronted Immigration and Customs Enforcement mercenaries in 

Chicago

, 

Minnesota

, and elsewhere. As we previously saw in 

the movement against police and white supremacy

, when people take risks in solidarity with others, this makes it possible for more people to experience empathy where previously, they only felt dissociation and apathy.




The grassroots resistance that emerged in response to the Trump administration stands in stark contrast to the way that elite figures across the political spectrum immediately put themselves as Trump’s disposal. Tech billionaires from Silicon Valley flocked to his inauguration to throw themselves at his feet. Powerful 

law firms

, university administrations, and 

corporations

 subordinated themselves to his will. Heads of state from across the world groveled and toadied to Trump—regardless of how he 

treated

 them, no matter how absurd his 

demands

.




Throughout 2025, Democratic politicians confined themselves to expressing opposition in purely symbolic ways, if occasionally 

at great length

. Cowardly centrist Democrats had already 

embraced Trump’s anti-immigrant politics

 well before the 2024 election; after it, many of them 

actively participated

 in the Trump regime’s attacks on immigrants, seizing the opportunity to call for the Democratic Party to continue tacking 

rightward

.




The scale of subsequent 

resistance

 to ICE showed that this was not hard-nosed pragmatism, but political opportunism at the service of xenophobia. A 

poll

 at the beginning of March 2026 showed that only 39% of respondents opposed abolishing ICE, with fully 50% actively calling for its abolition. The disparity between these figures and the very small number of politicians prepared to consider abolishing ICE even today shows that Democratic politicians will openly defy their supporters’ wishes in order to continue to advance a reactionary agenda. As politicians, they do not simply answer to a constituency of voters, but above all to a clientele of capitalists.




Trump did his best to rig the system in his favor ahead of the 2026 elections, arranging for widespread gerrymandering, seeking to control the voting process, and attempting to put the pieces in place to contest the results. Billionaires backed him financially—Elon Musk singlehandedly spent half a billion dollars, a quarter of the entire Republican budget for the election, in an effort to put his thumb on the scales. In the end, the results were so conclusive that none of this mattered. As in 2016, 2020, and 2024, the majority of voters rejected the reigning party.




Yet because this will was expressed via voting, rather than through more direct means, the result simply hands power to another coterie of politicians who will not address the needs of those who elected them. The more secure the Democrats’ grip on power becomes, the less they will concern themselves with the wishes of the electorate. If anything, the 2026 election will only embolden the centrists within the party, as it put power in the hands of more moderate Democrats, especially in swing districts.




But those who imagine that the Democrats did so well in the 2026 election on their own merits are fooling themselves.




The core issue at the root of the hot potato pattern is that the existing political order cannot address the instability, disparities, and crises of a capitalist system that has concentrated most of the wealth of society in the hands of a few while inflicting grievous social, psychological, and ecological damage on the rest of us. No political party will initiate the kind of revolutionary transformation that will be required to shift to a more egalitarian and sustainable way of life; such change can only come from grassroots mobilization. As long as there is no widespread, powerful social movement that offers the prospect of addressing these problems through profound change, people will continue rejecting one government after another in increasing desperation.




Silicon Valley tech moguls—who backed Joe Biden in 2020 only to switch sides in 2024—are even less popular than Donald Trump. Hatred of tech billionaires, data centers, and Flock cameras cuts across political lines; like the war on Iran, it is one of the factors that caused many former Trump voters to stay home or vote for Democrats. Yet as they regain their hold on power, Democrats will be inclined to work more and more closely with capitalists and the tech industry, rhetoric about “oligarchy” notwithstanding.













If social movements die down again as they did in 2021 after Biden took office, this will bode ill for the future, opening the way for even more extreme far-right reactionaries to pretend that they represent the only alternative to an unendurable status quo. If the 

cycle

 that played out between the first and second Trump administrations repeats itself again, the third iteration of far-right reaction will be more horrific than we can possibly imagine.




For good or ill, it does not look like anyone will be able to delude themselves into believing in a “return to normal” any time soon. The 

accession

 of Stephen Miller, an avowed white supremacist, to White House Chief of Staff sets the stage for the Trump administration to conclude with a period of brutal, open conflict. The administration lacks the support to win an open power struggle with the rest of society, but has left itself no alternative. As one 

New York Times

 commentator put it, “The next two years could actually be pretty volatile.”




As long as Trump remains in power, the far right will be perceived as the hegemonic force against which social anger will gravitate. But we must not wait for Democratic politicians to stand up to the Trump administration; even if they did, at best, that would function to relegitimize the same state institutions that will once again be turned against us in the future—as we saw in the Democrats’s response to the 

failed coup

 of January 6, 2021.




We must set an example by continuing to resist the Trump administration—and, wherever necessary, Democratic local and state administrations as well—through grassroots 

direct action

. Rather than simply waging a defensive struggle, we must figure out how to take proactive steps towards 

a completely different way of life

 in the process. Otherwise, the far right will eventually benefit once again from the inevitable disillusionment with Democratic administrations.




In short: it’s good to see Trump losing control. But the pendulum will continue to swing back and forth between political parties in wilder and wilder oscillations until we make revolutionary changes in our society.

author: Ed Wanderley
title: Imposto do pecado: Governo alivia para indústrias e adia proteção popular, alma da reforma
content:
Após quase dois anos de espera, o governo federal enfim definiu as alíquotas do Imposto Seletivo (IS), mas, na prática, adiou a incidência das medidas de proteção à população que inspiraram parte da reforma tributária, ao desidratar o chamado “imposto do pecado”. Além disso, deixou para 2027 a definição do real impacto na indústria, além de colocar a questão, na prática, nas mãos de um Congresso Nacional onde a oposição tem maioria, o que, por enquanto, beneficia indústrias como a das bebidas açucaradas.




Desde janeiro de 2025, quando da publicação da Lei Complementar nº 214, o Ministério da Fazenda tinha que publicar as referências do substitutivo do Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados (IPI), que será zerado em janeiro. Na reforma tributária, cinco impostos, incluindo o IPI, foram condensados e apenas dois, para unificar as cobranças e modernizar o processo de forma mais transparente – uma demanda que vinha sendo discutida há três décadas. A 

Medida Provisória 1.399/26

 foi finalmente publicada nesta quarta-feira (4) e trouxe uma proposta de neutralidade fiscal provisória – em outras palavras, não é agora que as indústrias vão sofrer qualquer baque.




Gradativamente, os impostos no país estão sendo adequados para existirem apenas três. Os dois que afetam todos os setores já estão desenhados são o IBS, Imposto sobre Bens e Serviços (que reúne o que antes eram ICMS e ISS) e a CBS, Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (unificando PIS, Cofins e IPI).



















O último e mais polêmico elemento dessa tríade é o IS, que reúne indústrias cujos produtos representam custos sociais, ambientais ou à saúde pública – daí o nome “imposto do pecado”. Por que cigarros e refrigerantes estão lá? Porque causam doenças que aumentam a despesa com o Sistema Único de Saúde. Por que incluir veículos automotores? Dado a emissão de CO² e a necessidade de investir em transportes coletivos. E por aí vai.




O que o imposto do pecado muda no seu cotidiano? O exemplo máximo é o cigarro. Essa é uma indústria que mantém público mesmo tendo publicidade proibida e fumo em locais públicos restrito há anos. De toda forma, os números de fumantes caíram. Em outras palavras, o poder público dificulta o acesso. Você continua tendo liberdade para fumar, desde que arque com os custos disso. No caso da reforma tributária, esse custo incide sobre o que beneficia pouca gente e/ou prejudica milhares todos os anos.




A inspiração central do dispositivo é o de desincentivar o consumo de produtos que gerem custos elevados ou sejam prejudiciais ao próprio consumidor, dificultando o seu acesso, logo, o protegendo. Há quem discorde – e apresente o argumento da liberdade de escolha –, especialmente 

as próprias indústrias

, mas o IS passou e foi aprovado.




“Ele [o IS] vai incidir sobre exclusivamente sobre bebida alcoólica, refrigerante, bebida açucarada, tabaco, carro, embarcação. Então, são alguns poucos itens. Com o fim do IPI para a indústria como um todo, a indústria fica desonerada, e a gente passa a ter o imposto seletivo sobre esses poucos setores”, disse o ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, em entrevista coletiva nesta quinta (5).




A definição do imposto do pecado era bastante esperada porque definiria o nível de desestímulo aos produtos listados e poderia ajustar a versão final da reforma pelo legislativo, cuja influência do lobby industrial criou distorções tributárias, como a baixa distinção entre veículos automotores entre os de combustão e elétricos ou de produtos de consumo, como os refrigerantes produzidos na Zona Franca de Manaus, que poderiam pagar menos impostos que a água mineral, como 

já mostrou a 

Agência Pública

.



















Elas por elas?




Mas o que fez, na prática, o governo agora? Publicou uma lista com alíquotas baixas, para apenas equiparar o que a maior parte das indústrias já pagavam com o IPI, que será zerado a partir de janeiro e jogou o início da progressão tributária apenas para 2028. Os refrigerantes, por exemplo, ficaram limitados a 2,6% – na prática, não haverá progressão das taxas cobradas em 2027. Durigan, no entanto, negou adiar os efeitos da reforma tributária.







Para o cientista político e coordenador de advocacy da ACT Promoção da Saúde Marcello Baird, a alíquota de 2,6% sobre bebidas açucaradas iguala o mesmo 

patamar de tributação já praticado

 hoje sobre a indústria, o que beneficia os fabricantes desses produtos nocivos e a gente não consegue ter os impactos na redução de adoecimentos e mortes na população, em especial a mais vulnerável.




“Com isso, o governo está atrasando em um ano a implementação do imposto seletivo, o que é muito ruim do ponto de vista do que a reforma propõe em termos de impacto na saúde e no meio ambiente”, pontua, acrescentando que a sociedade civil vai se organizar para “lutar no Congresso para alterar a MP e fazer emendas para aumentar essas alíquotas já para o ano que vem”, o que depende dos parlamentares.




Baird lembra ainda da relação inversamente entre o IS, restrito a esses setores considerados nocivos, e a CBS, que afeta toda a economia. “A arrecadação tem que respeita o teto, da CBS mais o Seletivo. Quando um baixa o outro sobe. A CBS saiu o cálculo de 11,3% e todo o mercado chiou, com razão, é alta; mas se a gente aumenta de forma robusta o seletivo – como a comunidade internacional, em especial de saúde, sugere – a gente pode ver uma redução na CBS”, avalia.




“Zero ou 2,6% é praticamente a mesma coisa”, avalia o Roberto Luis Troster, ex-economista-chefe da Federação Brasileira de Bancos (Febraban) e da Associação Brasileira de Bancos (ABBC). “Você tem que achar uma forma de desestimular o consumo. Entendo que se você põe mais alto, com os sucos e outros produtos, você pode matar o setor, mas acho que faria sentido ser mais alto, mesmo sem estudo de calibragem”, opina.



















Em outra ponta, o economista destaca a decisão do governo quanto à mineração. A expectativa é que, em maio, as alíquotas definitivas sejam publicadas e a reforma prevê o IS para o setor. No entanto, até dezembro de 2027, os bens minerários extraídos terão tributação zero durante o período de transição da reforma. Para Troster, no entanto, o caminho mais socialmente justo seria multiplicar os impostos que eram cobrados a essa indústria, não zerar os tributos.










 




Ao tributar [mais], você, por um lado, estaria tirando competitividade do setor, inclusive no cenário internacional, tem isso. Mas deveria ser o dobro, triplo [do que já era praticado]. E por quê? Porque você está tirando da terra algo que não tem reposição. O minério que for embora, o ouro que for, foi. E o que está sendo feito para compensar isso? Você deveria estar olhando isso por outro ângulo, já que é necessário transformar uma geração de riqueza em outra.”




Roberto Luis Troster

 

Professor e ex-economista-chefe da Febraba

 










Por outro lado, não apenas as mineradoras se beneficiam da desoneração durante o período de transição. Também foram zerados impostos de veículos considerados sustentáveis, sem propulsão a combustão, incluindo até barcos e aeronaves e serão beneficiados parte da população que adquirirem veículos em geral, incluindo pessoas com transtorno do espectro autista (TEA), com deficiência (PCD), taxistas, caminhoneiros (veículos acima de 3,5 t) e as forças armadas ou de segurança.



















Atraso estratégico




Para ter início corretamente 2027, o governo federal precisaria ter publicado a MP até o início de outubro deste ano, para que os efeitos entrassem em vigor noventa dias depois, a partir de 1.º de janeiro – o que não foi feito tendo em vista a corrida eleitoral disputada e a dificuldade de tratar sobre o tema impostos.




O atraso terá um custo também estratégico: como só entra em vigor em fevereiro, e em janeiro o IPI é zerado, o governo federal precisou emitir uma Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC), que será submetida ao Congresso, buscando prorrogar o IPI pelos 30 dias de janeiro.




Agora, o governo conta com o Congresso, conquistado pela direita no próximo mandato, para aprovar as alíquotas “definitivas” do IS e colocou como prazo de envio de um projeto de lei com essas alíquotas até 31 de maio de 2027.

author: Andrés
title: Patricia Walsh deja abierto el camino para construir otro futuro
content:
Patricia Walsh en su escuela primaria




Llevaba más de una semana internada. La habían operado de un pulmón. Ayer a la mañana supe que había muerto. Patricia Walsh fue periodista, diputada, legisladora, dos veces candidata a presidente. Un cuadro político de peso que luchó por los derechos humanos y bregó todo lo que pudo por la unidad de la izquierda. «Bajaba a la calle a pelearse con la policía que estaba asediando a un pibito vendedor de paltas.» me relató 

su yerno 

hace unas horas, en el velorio. «

Ni un paso atrás, era su lema y tal cual, hasta el último día» agregó. «Me pidió disculpas por mover unas plantas que le había regalado, me dijo la última vez que estuve en su casa, es fea, no me gusta pero la salvé porque la habían tirado en un volquete, ¿podés creer?.», me contó el hermano del yerno. Lucidez y ternura, coraje y tosudez fueron las palabras que le arrancaron lágrimas a los y las presentes en el salón blanco del Congrrso, donde fue velada esta tarde. Su 

muerte nos toma por sorpresa, cuando el futuro todavía d

ura para siempre. Por Andrés Manrique, ANRed.







No imaginé que podía pasar esto. Pocas veces estuve cerca. Una tarde la iba a conocer, me pondría a conversar con ella. La muerte es un hecho para después. Y la de Patricia Walsh me deja con la culpa de poder haberlo hecho mucho mejor. Ojalá fuera culpa solamente, porque es más. Una mezcla de culpa e impotencia que busco aplastar con rabia para que no me gane la frustración.




¿Cómo ser la hermana de una mujer a la que el Estado persiguió hasta su muerte? ¿Cómo tolerar la figura de un padre, Rodolfo Walsh, cuadro, escritor y periodista fundamental de la historia Argentina, también asesinado y desaparecido por el aparato represivo del Estado?




Myriam Bregman despide a su colega y amiga íntima




¿Qué decía Patricia de la tibieza para la oposición de nuestra época? ¿Cómo continuaba sus luchas dentro de este generalizado clima de apatía? ¿Cómo hacer para dejar de administrar la miseria y pasar a la delantera? La de veces que se  habrá hecho estas preguntas desde sus variados roles y puestos políticos.




Patricia vivió la muerte de su hermana, Victoria. Leyó la carta que su padre Rodolfo escribió para ella al enterarse de su muerte. Vivió la muerte y desaparición de su padre. Leyó la carta que había dejado Rodolfo a la Junta Militar poco después de que las Fuerzas Armadas emboscaran a Victoria. Nunca recuperó el cuerpo del padre.







Patricia, además de referente de izquierda, legisladora, diputada, dos veces candidata a presidente. Además de hija y hermana, fue mamá y abuela. Compañera y suegra. Su entorno la quiso, la admiró y la admira. Su hija la recuerda con amor y humor negro: «Si no me hago problema, ¿que hago?», cuenta que decía. Sus compañeras se acuerdan con sentido orgullo de ella.




Patricia llenó de cariño y capricho a sus nietos. Peleó con las herramientas de la época. Fue autora y propulsora de la nulidad de las leyes de Obediencia Debida y Punto Final cuando todo el mundo le decía que una ley no podía anularse, contó Bregman emocionada hasta las lágrimas. Avanzó a fondo contra los militares culpables por delitos de lesa humanidad. En 2005, la Corte declaró la inconstitucionalidad de las normas. Desde entonces, más de 1250 represores fueron condenados. Pero ella murió sin poder enterrar a su padre.




Textos de su nieta dedicados a Patricia Walsh




Fue incansable militante de los derechos humanos, participó de Proyecto Sur y del MST. Buscó y persiguió hasta el último día a los asesinos de su hermana. Quería que le devolvieran la casa de San Vicente, en la que su padre se había recluido clandestinamente. Esa casa que los militares habían bombardeado, para luego cedérsela a una familia de policías. Por esas vueltas que tiene la justicia en este país, con sus demoras y atropellos, la expropiación para declararla sitio de memoria se firmó ayer mismo (05/11/26). Patricia tampoco llegó a conocer la noticia.




Al día de su muerte seguía detrás de los juicios de la calle Corro, donde había resistido su hermana María Victoria Walsh con cuatro compañeros de la dirección política de Montoneros, a 150 militares con armas pesadas, un tanque y un helicóptero. En mayo de este año había estado declarando en Comodoro Py contra el Estado, con una lucidez que te invito a ver aquí. 

Así declaró ella el pasado 19 de mayo de este año.




“Pudo haber elegido otros caminos sin ser deshonrosos, pero el que eligió era el más justo, el más generoso, el más razonado.”, le escribió Rodolfo Walsh a Vicky en la conocida carta de despedida, que reparte entre amigos. Posiblemente, algo similar le hubiera dejado por escrito a Patricia.




Fue velada en el Salón Blanco del Congreso este viernes 06v de noviembre, entre las 12.00 y las 14.00.




Y nos va a faltar.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Ottawa renews Inuit Child First Initiative funding, tops up Nutrition North
content:
The federal government is committing $575 million over five years to Inuit children’s services and more than $610 million over four years to northern food subsidies in this year’s federal budget.




The Liberal government released its budget for 2026-27, titled “Masters of our Destiny,” on Thursday.




It proposes renewing the Inuit Child First Initiative and transitioning it to Pirutsiagutiit, an Inuit-designed program developed with Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami and the four Inuit treaty organizations.




The $575-million commitment would begin in the 2027-28 fiscal year. Pirutsiagutiit is expected to begin April 1, 2027, and will be operated by the treaty organizations or their designates, according to ITK.




Launched in September 2018, the Inuit Child First Initiative provides health, social, educational and other support to Inuit children and youth. Funding for the program ran out in 2025 and it 

has received

 one-year top ups since then, with the 

promise to retool

 it.




ITK had requested $600 million over five years for Pirutsiagutiit in its pre-budget submission. 




The budget also proposes $610.3 million over four years, beginning in 2027-28, for Nutrition North Canada and associated initiatives. It includes another $118.1 million in 2031-32, followed by $117 million annually.
















Nutrition North subsidizes shipping costs for eligible food and essential goods in remote northern communities and supports harvesting and community food programs. 




It spent $163 million 

subsidizing nutritious food

 in 124 northern communities in the 2025-26 fiscal year, including in communities in Nunavut and Nunavik.




Ottawa also announced a $30-million top-up in February.




The funding comes as the government considers changes 

following a review

 led by former Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. president Aluki Kotierk.




She recommended 

expanding the subsidy

 to all items sold in eligible communities, rather than limiting it to products classified as nutritious. Her review also questioned whether retailers passed the full value of subsidies on to consumers.




The budget describes the new funding as an expansion and stabilization of Nutrition North and related initiatives.
















This approach to Nutrition North will “maintain the inefficiencies of the current program,” with no funding identified for reforms to address food insecurity in Inuit Nunangat, ITK said in a Nov. 5 news release.




ITK also criticized the lack of Inuit-specific housing and infrastructure funding, noting the budget allocates $30 billion for First Nations housing and infrastructure but does not mention comparable investments for Inuit communities.




“Aside from the welcome funding for Pirutsiagutiit, the broader sustainability of our communities is not reflected in this budget,” ITK President Natan Obed said in the release. “Building projects is not enough. The lack of investment in building healthy Inuit communities is a risk to this country.”




Conservative MP Billy Morin, the party’s shadow minister for Indigenous services, called the Nutrition North funding “a Band-Aid,” saying the program is not audited effectively.




“What a Conservative government would do is truly sit down with northerners, Inuit people and jurisdictions and groups and organizations and governments, to let it be defined more by them,” he said Friday in an interview.
















ITK’s pre-budget submission also called for a $7,500 refundable tax credit for low-income residents of Inuit Nunangat, legislation to establish Inuit Nunangat University, funding for a national Inuit identity card and Inuit-led justice services.




It also proposed a $1-billion fund for Inuit housing and infrastructure. Budget 2026 does not include specific commitments for those proposals.







Liberals MPs Mandy 

Gull-Masty, who represents the Nunavik region, and Nunavut’s Lori Idlout were not available for interviews about the budget, nor was NDP northern affairs critic Leah Gazan.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Pangnirtung’s Auyuittuq Lodge takes top tourism award
content:
Auyuittuq Lodge is Travel Nunavut’s business of the year.




The lodge, owned by Pangnirtung Inuit Co-operative Limited, was celebrated along with three other tourism-oriented businesses Tuesday evening at the Aqsarniit hotel in Iqaluit.




The event was part of Travel Nunavut’s annual conference and annual general meeting, which ran Monday to Wednesday. The three-day conference included workshops, panel discussions and networking opportunities for those in Nunavut’s travel industry.




Other recipients of this year’s awards were:







Terry Uyarak, Anu Outfitting of Igloolik — Outstanding Cultural Tourism award;




Crystal Noulaq-Lloyd, Aqsarniit Hotel and Conference Centre of Iqaluit — Individual Service award




Peter Kilabuk, Peter’s Outfitting and Expediting of Pangnirtung — Legacy award.

author: CNT Galiza
title: Nueva victoria para la CNT en La Galletería
content:
Leer en

Castellano

Galego







Castellano

Nueva victoria para la CNT en La Galletería: la acción directa y la presión sindical redoblan sus esfuerzos contra Álvaro Cernuda




La lucha en las calles, el apoyo mutuo y la acción directa demuestran una vez más ser las herramientas más eficaces para defender la dignidad de la clase trabajadora. Tras una campaña de presión y movilización impulsada por la CNT, logramos una importante victoria contra la empresa tras el despido injustificado de dos de nuestros compañeros.




El resultado de esta batalla sindical es contundente: los despidos fueron declarados infundados, se otorgó la indemnización correspondiente y uno de los trabajadores fue reincorporado. Este triunfo no surgió por arte de magia ni de buenas intenciones: se logró gracias a la presión constante del sindicato y su firme presencia en las calles.




Álvaro Cernuda, reincidente en abusos laborales y antiguo conocido de la CNT por conflictos anteriores, pretendía marcharse con un escándalo tras acumular un historial de impago de horas extras, falta de pago de preaviso y denegación de vacaciones pendientes. Pero la respuesta no se hizo esperar. Los piquetes sindicales frente a su negocio, La Galletería, en Ribadeo, denunciaron públicamente la injusticia y dejaron claro que ningún ataque contra los trabajadores queda impune.




Esta victoria confirma que los trabajadores nos organizamos y que las victorias se consiguen gracias a la unidad de todos y a la lucha sindical. Cuando llevamos la lucha a las calles, cuando practicamos la acción directa y cuando nos centramos en la solidaridad de clase, los empresarios tienen que ceder y reconocer nuestros derechos.




Ante los abusos laborales, las amenazas y la precariedad, la organización sindical es nuestro mejor escudo y nuestra mejor arma. Cuando nos unimos en el sindicato, el miedo cambia de bando.







Galego

Nova vitoria da CNT en La Galletería: a acción directa e a presión sindical dobregan de novo a Álvaro Cernuda




A loita na rúa, o apoio mutuo e a acción directa volven demostrar que son as ferramentas máis efectivas para defender a dignidade da clase traballadora. Tras unha campaña de presión e mobilización desenvolvida pola CNT, acadamos unha importante vitoria fronte ao empresario tras o despedimento inxustificado de dúas das nosas compañeiras.




O resultado desta batalla sindical é rotundo: logrouse a declaración de improcedencia dos despedimentos, a correspondente indemnización e a readmisión dunha das traballadoras. Este triunfo non caeu do ceo nin veu da man de despachos nin de boas palabras: acadouse grazas á presión constante do sindicato e á presenza firme nas rúas.




Álvaro Cernuda, reincidente nos abusos laborais e vello coñecido da CNT por conflitos anteriores, pretendía marchar de rositas tras acumular un historial de impagos de horas extras, non abonar os días de preaviso e negar o pagamento das vacacións pendentes. Pero a resposta non se fixo esperar. Os piquetes sindicais ás portas do seu negocio, La Galletería, en Ribadeo, sinalaron publicamente a inxustiza e deixaron claro que ningún ataque contra as traballadoras queda sen resposta.




Esta vitoria confirma que as traballadoras nos organizamos e as vitorias conséguense grazas á unidade de todas e á loita sindical. Cando levamos a loita á rúa, cando practicamos a acción directa e cando poñemos o foco na solidariedade de clase, a patronal ten que ceder e recoñecer os nosos dereitos.




Fronte aos abusos laborais, ás ameazas e á precarización, a organización no noso sindicato é o noso mellor escudo e a nosa mellor arma. Cando nos xuntamos no sindicato, o medo muda de bando.




La entrada 

Nueva victoria para la CNT en La Galletería

 se publicó primero en 

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Van Hollen, Khanna Launch Effort to Cut Trump Off From Funding His War on Iran
content:
The lawmakers say they’ll go as far as forcing Donald Trump to choose between ending the war and a government shutdown.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Progressive lawmakers are mounting a campaign to end the Trump administration’s war on Iran by cutting off funding for the effort and potentially forcing a government shutdown, after Democrats won a historic majority running against the unpopular conflict.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) are two figures leading the effort, which is akin to Congress’s efforts to end the Vietnam War, The Washington Sun reports.

The strategy would involve not just stripping funding for the war in existing legislation, but also adding stipulations barring appropriated funds from being used for war operations. This goes further than passing war powers resolutions, which the Trump administration would likely ignore. Analysts have said that the budget is one of the most powerful tools that lawmakers have to end the war.

With their sizable majority in both chambers of Congress, Democrats could force a showdown with President Donald Trump by forcing him to choose between ending his war or shutting down the government.

“I’m not planning to vote for anything that provides any funding to fuel the war in Iran,” Van Hollen said. “If the president wants to tell the country that he’s prepared to shut down the United States government in order to conduct an illegal and senseless war in Iran, that will be his choice.”

Some other Democrats have also voiced their support for the idea of using the power of the purse to end the war this week, including Rep. Adam Smith (D-Washington), the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, and Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Connecticut), the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee. Incoming Sen. Abdul El-Sayed (D-Michigan) has also said he would back such efforts.

Van Hollen and Khanna have said that the effort could be modeled after Congress’s effort to end the Vietnam War in 1973, when Congress overwhelmingly passed legislation that would cut off all funds for bombing Cambodia, Laos, or Vietnam unless explicitly authorized by Congress; that same year, Congress passed the War Powers Act over President Richard Nixon’s veto.

Khanna wrote in a post on X on Wednesday that he thinks lawmakers should “[s]upport a continuing resolution prohibiting the financing of any combat activities of the U.S. military in Iran. End the Iran war like we did for Vietnam.”

The two lawmakers both said the effort should be forced as soon as possible. Funding for the federal government is currently set to expire on December 11. Republicans will still control the House and Senate until the new class of lawmakers is sworn in in January, but even some Republicans — including President Donald Trump himself — have lamented that the war was one of the top contributors to the blue “tsunami” this week.

Meanwhile, one of the lame duck Congress’s tasks before January is to consider the Pentagon budget bill for next year. Previous versions of the bill have contained $70 billion for the Iran war.

“It would be a betrayal of the voters to be complicit in keeping the war going,” Van Hollen said.

The effort may be the first test for Democratic leaders Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) and Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-New York) as they vie to keep their leadership positions going into the new Congress.

Schumer, for his part, pledged in a news conference on Wednesday that “we are going to end the war,” adding: “The founding fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people.”

But both Schumer and Jeffries are vehemently pro-Israel and have previously, in their own ways, cheered the war.

This past June, Schumer criticized Trump’s signing of a deal with Iran to end the war as “the art of surrender.” Meanwhile, just a few days after the U.S. and Israel launched the war, Jeffries declined to rule out voting for a potential request from the Trump administration for Congress to grant more funding for the fighting.

author: Chris Walker
title: Muslim, Jewish Groups Warn “Right to Worship” Bill Could Undermine Free Speech
content:
“Protecting religious freedom must not come at the expense of other constitutional rights,” the groups explained.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Two religious organizations — one Jewish and one Muslim — are urging lawmakers to reject a bill that ostensibly aims to protect houses of worship but that would actually quell free speech rights.

“The Right to Worship Act,” sponsored by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and cosponsored by Republicans and Democrats alike, seeks to “protect” religious buildings and people inside them by limiting the First Amendment right to protest in nearby areas.

The bill prohibits activities within 100 feet of a house of worship that include actions that are “knowingly disrupting the scheduled religious service” or “impeding people from participating at [a] scheduled religious service.”

While the legislation limits protections to the period of time “beginning 1 hour before the start of and ending 1 hour after the conclusion of a scheduled religious service,” the ambiguous language of the bill could feasibly allow houses of worship to define almost any event as being “protected” from demonstrations happening nearby — for example, a church bake sale could be considered a “scheduled religious service” by some, as could a political event featuring a controversial speaker discussing religious topics.

“Offenders” could be fined $2,500 by the federal government for their first instance of violating the rules laid out in the bill, and up to $10,000 for subsequent violations. The bill also grants private individuals who feel that their religious rights have been violated the ability to sue for “damages” of up to $5,000 per violation.

While most sponsors of the bill are Republican, it does have bipartisan support. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) has signed on as a cosponsor, and 13 Democrats are cosponsors of the House version of the bill.

The Muslim Public Affairs Council (MPAC) and Bend the Arc: Jewish Action issued a joint statement urging lawmakers to reject the legislation, arguing that it sacrifices protections for one fundamental liberty to provide unnecessary protections for another.

“As Muslim and Jewish organizations, we understand the urgent need to protect houses of worship from threats, violence, intimidation, and physical obstruction,” the statement from the two groups explained. “Every person deserves to practice their faith freely and safely. However, protecting religious freedom must not come at the expense of other constitutional rights.”

The organizations argued that the broad language of the bill risks “chilling lawful speech, peaceful assembly, and political protest, including on public sidewalks and streets.”

“The legislation fails to adequately distinguish between genuine threats to religious exercise and constitutionally protected expression,” they said, adding:

Our communities know firsthand the consequences of religious hatred and discrimination. We reject the notion that protecting Muslim and Jewish Americans requires weakening the constitutional freedoms that safeguard us all.

The groups are calling on other members of Congress to reject the bill, and in the future, for lawmakers to only “pursue narrowly tailored protections that safeguard religious communities without restricting lawful expression.”

The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) has also condemned the bill, warning that it could limit speech protections for protests outside religious venues that are hosting Israeli settlement land sales, further promoting dispossession of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

In an explainer on the legislation published in September, CAIR labeled the bill as essentially an “Illegal Israeli Settlements Protection Act” that, if enacted into law, could be used to “discourage lawful demonstrations against events promoting Palestinian dispossession.”

“Existing federal law already prohibits force, threats of force, and physical obstruction directed at religious worship,” the organization said in a statement. “CAIR therefore questions the need for a new civil-liability regime that could be used to burden constitutionally protected advocacy and dissent.”

“Hosting a political or commercial event in a religious building should not shield that activity from public accountability,” CAIR added.
