author: Rory Mir
title: Google Forcing AI on Students Is BS
content:
Google is rightfully facing blowback for forcing K-12 schools to enable AI if they wanted to keep using Google search. The company quickly backtracked and decoupled and turned off the services by default, but made it clear search will continue to be just another AI chatbot. This mandate forces an ultimatum on educators: accept generative AI or de-google your school.




Students, teachers, and parents across the U.S. are now years into an argument about how schools should respond to the growth of AI-enabled tools. Google decided to skip this debate and take this choice from schools. In August it activated AI chatbot Gemini 

for 150 million K-12 students

 on Google Classroom, leaving educators 

scrambling to respond

. A few months later, Google introduced a new way to turn it off — but now administrators 

would also be turning off Google search

.




Google 

walked this back

 somewhat, clarifying that Gemini, Gemini notebook, and Search will have their own controls and will be off by default. But because of Google’s broader approach to force AI on all search users, this change is still an example of a tech monopolist pushing unwanted changes into the classroom.




Tying AI to Search




It’s no secret that the biggest companies in AI  are 

operating at a huge loss

, in the hope they can follow

 

Uber’s enshittification playbook

. Offer a cheap convenience 

at a major loss

 until old systems atrophy, then flip the script to reduce wages and raise consumer costs—whether that’s paying with cash or with data. 




This puts Google in the odd position of an incumbent, with around 

90% of search traffic

. It needs to not only make good on its own AI investment, but protect its dominance from new AI tools. It’s not just enough to offer its own AI mode, it needs to turn search into AI mode, while engaging in 

clumsy self-preferencing

 that is 

eating its own ad revenue

.




The problem with this approach is the public is split on AI, to put it mildly. Some users will welcome these changes, but the rest are stuck in an all-or-nothing bargain. Anyone concerned  

about the accuracy of AI overviews

 or their 

impact on click-through rates

 for 

online communities

 and 

small publishers

 can just 

deal with it

. The bet is any inconvenience in switching to an alternative is enough to keep you trapped.




Google can and should offer a way to disable AI overviews. Smaller services like DuckDuckGo* and Brave search have simple and persisting AI settings which don’t require login. These services also don't mince words and make a distinction between generated AI summaries, suspected AI results, and the backend use of AI to curate links. 




It’s not enough to point to 

opaque workarounds

, either. Adding “-ai” to your Google search will usually remove AI Overview, but so will “-unicorn”. This trick isn’t meant to be an AI off-switch, it’s a quirk of how AI Overview was implemented and can change at any time. These tricks also don’t generalize well to 

settings for system administrators

. Hacks might work for now, but everyone—including administrators—deserve clear set-and-forget controls for the tools they rely on.




Pushing AI on Schools




De-googling your life isn’t easy, and for schools it can be even more difficult. For decades Google has gone after schools to foster life-long Google users—resulting in many institutions being deeply entrenched in its ecosystem 

despite data privacy concerns

. That’s because schools face major 

switching costs

 when moving to a competitor. It takes more than flipping a setting—it means a lengthy contract process, staff retraining, and a cumbersome migration of past work. 




The difficulty of switching makes granular controls even more essential, particularly for a hot-button issue like generative AI. Few parents would send their kids to 

AI-driven schools

, but they may want their kids to learn tools like search as they exist outside of the classroom. However, many parents and teachers concerned with AI disrupting learning are pushing 

major school districts

 to implement temporary 

AI moratoriums

 for young students. These pauses are meant to make sure any introduction of AI 

fits the needs of students

 

and is done in a way that actually makes sure educators are prepared. 




But in either camp, this is a choice that must be made by schools, not Google. Teachers know more about what their students need than a trillion-dollar tech company, and this expertise should be respected in their own classrooms. 




Google’s self-preferencing and desperate attempt to eventually recoup on an AI money pit must be tempered with more fine-tune controls over generative AI. It’s in Google’s 

own interest

 to stop abusing its dominance to piss off users, advertisers, and school communities. It’s also Google’s 

responsibility

 as an adjudicated monopolist.




*DuckDuckGo is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

author: Mitch Perry
title: CAIR Ends Operations in Florida as “Domestic Terrorist” Designation Takes Effect
content:
Gov. Ron DeSantis has been attempting to put the Muslim civil rights organization out of business for nearly a year.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The Council on American Islamic Relations (CAIR) has suspended operations in Florida, the organization has announced.

It did so after a federal judge rejected an emergency request Wednesday by the Muslim civil rights organization to stop the state from designating the group and its state chapter as domestic terrorist organizations, allowing the designation to take effect while its legal challenge, litigated by the ACLU and the Southern Poverty Law Center, continues.

Federal Judge Allen C. Winsor of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida denied CAIR and CAIR Florida’s request to reverse the designation. In a ruling released Wednesday night, Windsor said the plaintiffs were unlikely to succeed at this stage on their claims that the designations under a new law (HB 1471) violates their due process and First Amendment rights.

The judge did issue a narrow form of preliminary relief, stating that Florida prosecutors cannot enforce the law against CAIR and CAIR Florida, their employees, or third parties with respect to provision of legal services to the groups.

That designation took effect Thursday. As a result, both groups say they have been forced to shut down their advocacy and operations in Florida.

“Today’s ruling is deeply disappointing and we are appealing it,” said Ashley Gorski, senior counsel with the ACLU’s National Security Project.

“Today’s decision upholds state officials’ sweeping power to punish American organizations they brand as ‘terrorist,’ without due process and in violation of the First Amendment. Florida officials have been relentless in seeking to silence our clients’ civil rights work and advocacy, damaging not only them but also their community. We cannot allow this dangerous and sweeping censorship regime to stand.”

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Attorney General James Uthmeier hailed the ruling Thursday. “Great win by our Solicitor General’s office and for the people of Florida!” Uthmeier wrote on X.

DeSantis and other members of the Florida Cabinet voted to designate CAIR and CAIR Florida as domestic terrorist organizations on Sept. 29. They contend the group operates as a front for Hamas and the Muslim Brotherhood.

Attorneys for CAIR have vehemently denied the allegation, contending its mission, “rooted in faith, is to enhance the public’s understanding of Islam, protect civil rights, promote justice and empower American Muslims.”

The designation in late September came months after DeSantis signed legislation approved by the Legislature earlier this year that gave five Florida executive officials — the head of domestic security (the commissioner of the Florida Department of Law Enforcement), the governor, and the three members of the state Cabinet — power to designate and eliminate groups operating in the United States without filing any legal charges or submitting their case to a jury.

The legislation prohibits any state agency, political subdivision, or public school district from expending or accepting state funds to support groups thus designated. It bans public schools or school districts from spending state or federal funds or maintaining programs on campus that “promote” a designated group.

The law also says any college or university must report information relating to the status of a student attending that school on a student visa if the student “promotes” a terrorist-designated organization. Students found to have promoted the group can be expelled.

The ACLU, the ACLU of Florida, and two other legal groups representing CAIR and CAIR Florida filed a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the legislation in July in the Northern District.

“As Florida chief of domestic security, I know there are imminent dangers to public health, safety, and welfare due to increasing risks from foreign and domestic terrorist groups,” then-FDLE Commissioner Mark Glass said on Sept. 11. Glass has since been replaced by Larry Keefe.

DeSantis has been attempting to put CAIR out of business for nearly a year. He issued an executive order in December designating CAIR and CAIR-Florida as terrorist organizations, directing state and local agencies to block them and their supporters from public contracts, funding, and benefits. After the groups sued, a federal judge issued a temporary injunction blocking the order in March.

Shortly afterwards, the Legislature passed and DeSantis signed HB 1471.

CAIR and CAIR-Florida say the impact on the communities they serve will be “immense.” They say they provide a range of pro bono legal services to Florida residents, including those who suffer government and workplace discrimination in violation of their civil rights, as well as those navigating the immigration system.

“CAIR-Florida categorically rejects Florida officials’ baseless designation of us,” said Hiba Rahim, executive director of CAIR-Florida, in a written statement. “Nevertheless, we are heartbroken that we have no choice but to close our doors to protect our staff and people of all faiths who support our work.”

author: Sharon Zhang
title: AIPAC Has Lost Over 30 of Its Midterm Races So Far, In Sign of Major Shift
content:
Roughly two-thirds of the spending by the once insuperable lobbying group this cycle went toward races they lost.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) has lost dozens of races in which it backed a candidate in this year’s midterm elections, accounting for nearly two-thirds of the spending by the once insuperable political lobbying group, in a sign of its waning influence.

Politico found in a report on Thursday that more than 30 of the group’s candidates lost their elections this week. This marks “defeat for AIPAC in over three-fourths of the competitive races that have been called so far where it backed an incumbent,” Politico reported.

This includes candidates like Republican Representatives Mike Lawler (New York), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pennsylvania), and Max Miller (Ohio), as well as Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who fell to progressive Israel critic Troy Jackson, and Mike Rogers in Michigan.

Collins has been a staunch defender of Israel in the Senate, and AIPAC was her biggest outside donor by a massive margin during the race. AIPAC gave $2.8 million supporting her race against Jackson, as data from OpenSecrets showed; the next-largest outside donor, investment firm KKR & Co., gave just a fraction of that, at $160,000.

AIPAC dumped even more money into the race against Michigan candidate Abdul El-Sayed, whose opposition to the U.S.-Israel relationship has been a hallmark of his campaign. AIPAC and its super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP), reportedly dropped up to $9 million supporting Rogers in the last weeks of the election. This came after AIPAC spent a whopping $30 million opposing El-Sayed and backing Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Michigan) in the primary.

The next largest target after El-Sayed was Daniel Biss, who won his election to the U.S. House in Illinois after UDP dumped $6.3 million against him. Biss explicitly ran on a platform opposing AIPAC and its influence.

These losses are staggering for a political group whose name was once synonymous with power in D.C. In fact, these results indicate that being affiliated with the group is becoming politically toxic, due in large part to the work of pro-Palestine advocates who spoke out against the group amid Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

AIPAC, perhaps concerned about losing donors, defended its record on X, arguing that it backed 245 candidates who won their races. But the contributions to these races represented only about a third of their spending in this cycle.

According to Responsible Statecraft, almost two-thirds of the money that AIPAC and UDP spent this cycle went toward losing candidates. Via UDP, AIPAC spent $84.1 million on elections — $55.3 million of which went toward races where their preferred candidate lost. This stands in sharp contrast to prior election cycles. In the 2022 midterm election, Responsible Statecraft found, 69 percent of UDP spending went toward races their candidate won. In 2024, their winning ratio was 87 percent.

AIPAC can still wield enormous power over Congress. In its first post-election post on social media on Wednesday, the lobbying group congratulated Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) and Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-New York) for the “resounding victories for their caucuses.” The lawmakers are currently poised to lead the House and Senate when the new Congress begins in January, and are two of Israel’s staunchest defenders in Congress and major allies of AIPAC.

But the sands are quickly shifting under their feet. Opposing Israel and AIPAC have become increasingly normalized positions for politicians as the public overwhelmingly rejects the U.S.-Israel relationship, with even candidates in deep red states running against the lobbying group.

NEW poll: A supermajority of Jewish Americans believe Israeli & AIPAC actions increase antisemitism. 80% say Israel’s actions in Gaza & the West Bank increase antisemitism in the US. 66% say AIPAC’s campaign spending against candidates critical of Israel increases antisemitism. pic.twitter.com/oIS1wUYSRi

In Mississippi, for instance, Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom pledged to never take AIPAC money. He is currently holding on to a narrow lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Mississippi) in their election, and, if he wins, will be the first Democratic senator elected from the state since 1989.

“I will never take a penny from AIPAC or Super PACs that don’t put Mississippi and America first,” Colom said in a post on social media last month. “This Senate seat belongs to the people of Mississippi. That’s who I’ll answer to.”

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: It Wasn’t Just Gas Prices. Anti-ICE Sentiment Fueled Republican Midterm Losses.
content:
Polling finds that Americans across racial and ethnic groups view ICE more unfavorably today than they did a year ago.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

While President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance blame Republicans’ losses in the midterm elections on their war on Iran — with Trump flippantly saying that the war “drove the gasoline up a little bit short term” — Tuesday’s results also represent a rejection of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.

In Texas, where Trump won a Latino majority in the presidential election in 2024, the midterms saw a reversal, with Latino votes playing a role in the victories of Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa. Polls show 6 in 10 Latino voters supporting Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton — and in South Texas, Talarico performed better than Democrats have since the 1930s.

Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-Texas) said that “we haven’t seen this huge a Latino voter surge before,” and stated that “the difference is ICE and the mass deportation campaign.” Talarico had spoken against the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, and against ICE’s tactics.

ACLU Texas polling prior to the midterm elections showed that 53 percent of residents in Texas border regions feel that immigration enforcement has made life harder, rather than making their communities safer. The polls also showed that 63 percent of those residents believe that ICE tactics “have gone too far.”

One resident surveyed in the poll — which spoke to 1,031 adults in El Paso and Rio Grande Valley counties — said that “ICE isn’t helping by deporting our hardworking immigrants regardless of their status. This whole region and country has been built on the backs of immigrants.” The resident had voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

In Maine, too, voters expressed that the ICE crackdown over the past year had pushed them to vote against Republican Sen. Susan Collins, with the ICE killing of Johan Sebastian Guerrero in July as a particular flashpoint. Residents asked why Collins had not done more to stop ICE’s violent raids — and why she instead voted for more funding for the agency.

Democrat Troy Jackson, on the other hand, has said that he will “fight to abolish ICE.” In his victory speech on Wednesday, he said: “Masked agents terrorizing our neighbors and ripping families apart should never be accepted in the United States of America.”

And in Minnesota, the site of ICE’s “Operation Metro Surge” at the beginning of the year, which saw federal agents murder Renee Good and Alex Pretti, the early Latino vote increased by 217 percent compared to 2022.

Polling by Pew Research Center in September and October found that a majority of Black (69 percent), Latino (67 percent), and Asian (66 percent) adults in the U.S. have a negative opinion of ICE, while 49 percent of white adults have an unfavorable view of the agency. Pew also found that Americans across racial and ethnic groups view ICE more unfavorably today than they did a year ago, with 56 percent of Americans saying they have a negative view of the agency overall. Only 35 percent say they view the agency favorably.

However, while voters demonstrated their rejection of ICE and Trump’s rule in Tuesday’s elections, it remains unclear if that will lead to sweeping policy changes. The mainstream Democratic Party position — touted by figures like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become Speaker of the House — is to call for reforms of ICE rather than the abolition of the agency. But human rights advocates have warned that reforms to ICE, like reforms to the police, will not quell the repression and brutality inherent to what is now the U.S.’s most well-funded law enforcement agency.

author: Paige Collings
title: Presenting 'Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures'
content:
What does the digital future look like? Who gets to imagine it, shape it, and make it real?




Building a freer, more inclusive digital age requires not only challenging systems of surveillance and control, but also making space for creativity, community, and radical imagination. 




That's why earlier this year with the 

queer arts collective

, we put out a 

call for submissions

 inviting people to explore the intersections of technology, identity, and digital liberation—whether that involved pointing the lens towards an underrepresented issue in digital justice efforts; sharing personal accounts of joy, pleasure, or sorrow under surveillance; or painting wide imaginations for our communities using technology for good instead of carcerality and doom.




And we’re excited to share that the project is now live! 

Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures

 explores a digital world that dreams wilder and exists louder. Seven artists share their visions of digital liberation, spanning from early internet-coded yearning to escapist steamy chat rooms and seed-laced battle suits for revolution. 




These essays and stories remind us that digital rights aren't just about the existence of technology and its deployment as existing in a vacuum, but instead about how tech tools are a way for people to express themselves freely, find communities, explore identities, and build spaces to exist and seek joy without fear. Too often, conversations about technology focus on innovation, efficiency, and the next big thing while overlooking the people and communities most affected by the systems being built. This project was an effort to break containment and make space for something different: a chance to imagine digital futures rooted in queer creativity, resistance, and possibility.




Together with the queer arts collective, we were excited to launch the magazine and celebrate the artists and ideas that brought it to life through our session at Mozilla Festival last week, ‘

Privacy x Queer Desire

,’ where we started out by co-curating a community privacy plan grounded in digital fairness before launching the magazine. 




If the stories in 

Encoding Queer Digital Futures

 teach us one thing, it’s that we don't have to accept the digital future handed to us by oppressive governments and tech companies. We already have pre-Big Tech internet experiences encoded in our fondest memories that can inform our dreams for something better, and together we can build a new reality.

here

author: El Surtidor
title: Como a quebra do banco Ueno, no Paraguai, acabou com o governo do presidente Santiago Peña
content:
Na terça-feira, 3 de novembro de 2026, quase 3 milhões de paraguaios — cerca de metade da população — acordaram sem poder usar o seu dinheiro.

 Às 3h24 da madrugada, o Banco Central do Paraguai (BCP) anunciou no X/Twitter o fechamento do Ueno Bank, banco digital ligado ao presidente Santiago Peña, por falta de solvência. As economias de milhares de famílias estavam depositadas ali, assim como 800 milhões de dólares em recursos públicos.




Naquele mesmo dia, o Ministério Público emitiu uma ordem de prisão contra oito dirigentes do banco, a partir de uma denúncia do Banco Central. 

O principal apontado é Federico Miguel Vázquez, primeiro vice-presidente do Ueno e fundador e acionista majoritário do Grupo Vázquez

 — um conglomerado de pelo menos 28 empresas que fazem parte de um suposto esquema de captação de recursos e fraude bancária. O empresário está sendo apelidado de “Vorcaro do Paraguai”, pelas semelhanças com o escândalo brasileiro do 

Banco Master

.




Na quarta-feira, 4 de novembro, o Ministério Público imputou a 27 dirigentes do grupo os crimes de conduta indevida em situações de crise e lesão de confiança, incluindo os oito primeiros. À tarde, deputados da oposição apresentaram o projeto de impeachment contra Peña e, nas ruas da capital, a polícia reprimiu manifestantes com balas de borracha, gás lacrimogêneo e caminhões-pipa.




Às 10h da manhã de quinta-feira, 5 de novembro, a Câmara dos Deputados deu início ao processo de impeachment para destituir o presidente. Mas, às 13h30, Peña renunciou antes que fosse afastado. O Senado tentou aceitar sua renúncia, mas prevaleceu a linha do impeachment, que continua nesta sexta-feira. Paralelamente, um juiz decidiu pela prisão preventiva dos oito dirigentes do Ueno.




Na mesma manhã de quinta-feira, senadores da oposição apresentaram uma denúncia contra Peña ao Ministério Público especializado em crimes econômicos, o mesmo que investiga os dirigentes do Ueno Bank. “Que ele seja indiciado e tenha seus bens confiscados. O dinheiro que roubaram precisa ser recuperado e usado para pagar as pessoas”, afirmou a senadora oposicionista Esperanza Martínez. A denúncia também inclui integrantes da diretoria do BCP, como Carlos Carvallo Spalding, que foi dirigente do Ueno Bank antes de assumir a presidência do Banco Central durante o governo Peña.




Se a investigação do Ministério Público comprovar os crimes atribuídos aos dirigentes do Ueno e do Grupo Vázquez, assim como a cumplicidade de Santiago Peña e de integrantes do BCP, esse caso será tão grave quanto ou maior que o do Banco Master, no Brasil

, ligado a 

Flávio Bolsonaro

 e que afetou quase 2 milhões de brasileiros. Há, além disso, um temor latente de aprofundamento de uma crise social e econômica, com diversas ramificações a médio e longo prazo.
















Miguel Vázquez, executivo do banco Ueno, está em prisão preventiva




As manobras que permitiram um esquema de fraude com recursos públicos




O crescimento do Ueno Bank e do Grupo Vázquez foi meteórico. Em menos de cinco anos, o grupo alcançou uma carteira de milhões de clientes. 

Mas esse aumento contou com o apoio do poder político a partir da chegada de Santiago Peña à presidência, em agosto de 2023.

 Desde então, diversas manobras legais e políticas permitiram a expansão desse grupo econômico:




Manipulação das normas do Instituto de Previdência Social em benefício do banco Ueno.




Três meses depois da posse de Peña, o jornal ABC Color denunciou que o conselho da instituição de seguridade social havia 

reduzido

 as exigências para que um banco pudesse receber seus recursos, o que permitiu que o Ueno se qualificasse. Um ano depois, também foi eliminado o limite patrimonial que o IPS podia depositar em um banco.




O Ueno ficou com cerca de 350 milhões de dólares do Fundo Comum de Aposentadorias e Pensões, aproximadamente 9% do dinheiro dos aposentados atuais e futuros. Agora, com o fechamento do banco, não se sabe qual será o destino desse dinheiro nem por quais mecanismos ele poderá ser recuperado.




Alteração da lei de conflitos de interesses e das portas giratórias




No final de 2023, o Congresso enfraqueceu a lei de conflitos de interesses, o que 

facilitou

 a nomeação de ex-funcionários do banco Ueno e do Banco Basa — do ex-presidente Horacio Cartes — para cargos estratégicos na economia, além da distribuição de licitações ao Grupo Vázquez, no qual Peña tinha ações.




O próprio Peña é um caso de porta giratória: foi integrante da diretoria do BCP, ministro da Fazenda no governo Cartes, posteriormente diretor do Banco Basa e, depois, presidente da República.




O crescimento acelerado




Em novembro de 2021, o Grupo Vázquez adquiriu a Financeira El Comercio, que estava havia mais de 40 anos no mercado. Um mês depois, com a aprovação do BCP, ela passou a se chamar Ueno. Na época, Carlos Carvallo Spalding era presidente da financeira e Federico Miguel Vázquez, seu CEO. 




Com a posse de Peña na Presidência, em 2023, Carvallo Spalding assumiu a presidência do BCP. Em novembro do mesmo ano, o BCP, sob o comando de Carvallo, autorizou o Ueno a começar a operar como banco.




As ações do presidente na Ueno Holding




Em 2019, Peña era acionista da Credicentro, uma financeira do Grupo Vázquez que, em 2022, passou a se chamar Ueno Holding. 

Em 2023, Peña quadruplicou sua participação acionária, chegando a ter 6 bilhões de guaranis na empresa (cerca de 1 milhão de dólares, na cotação atual)

, segundo publicou o 

El Surti

. 




Em março de 2025, após denúncias constantes na imprensa, o presidente anunciou a venda de suas ações.




Favorecimento do Grupo Vázquez em licitações públicas




De agosto de 2023 a agosto de 2026, o Grupo Vázquez venceu 145 licitações públicas, em um total de cerca de 40 milhões de dólares.




O El Surti 

revelou

, em 2024, que apenas a ITTI, empresa de tecnologia do grupo, já havia sido beneficiada com mais adjudicações do que o governo anterior. Entre elas, estavam o desenvolvimento do sistema de internet banking do Banco Nacional de Fomento e a conexão das bases de dados financeiros do Che Róga Porã, uma política pública de acesso à moradia.
















Os manifestantes afetados pelo fechamento do banco foram reprimidos pela polícia




As consequências da crise recaem sobre milhares de trabalhadores




Com a quebra do banco Ueno, as economias de 2,9 milhões que tinham contas no Ueno foram afetadas, entre eles, 32 mil aposentados.

 O governo decidiu recorrer a um fundo garantidor — mecanismo de proteção das economias bancárias previsto em lei — para devolver o dinheiro aos correntistas com depósitos de até 75 salários mínimos, aproximadamente 37 mil dólares.




Demissões em massa estão acontecendo no Grupo Vázquez e no Ueno Bank. Com o fechamento, o Grupo ficou sem capital. Todos os trabalhadores do banco e das empresas vinculadas recebiam seus salários por meio do Ueno. Ainda não há consenso, mas o número de afetados gira entre 4 mil e 6 mil trabalhadores. Entre eles, estão 200 profissionais da imprensa que ficaram desempregados e apresentaram uma ação coletiva contra o Grupo Vázquez.




Além disso, trabalhadores no exterior estão à deriva. A empresa ITTI, do Grupo Vázquez, tem uma filial na Argentina, com cerca de 800 contratados pela empresa Kaitel SRL. Eles também não sabem o que acontecerá com seus empregos ou com suas indenizações.
















O Ueno Bank possuía uma carteira de 2,9 milhões de clientes que repentinamente perderam o acesso às suas contas




Como foi articulado o sistema que concentrou recursos públicos em um grupo econômico




Entre 2025 e 2026, a diretoria do Ueno autorizou empréstimos milionários a empresas que pertenciam ao mesmo grupo econômico que controlava o banco. Os empréstimos foram concedidos sem garantias e em valores muito superiores à capacidade de pagamento dessas empresas. O dinheiro acabava em outras companhias do Grupo Vázquez.




Para o Ministério Público, a figura central é Federico Miguel Vázquez, que era, ao mesmo tempo, o beneficiário final do banco, seu vice-presidente e a pessoa que controlava as empresas que recebiam os recursos.




O controle do banco passava por uma cadeia de sociedades. O proprietário direto do Ueno Bank é a U Paraguay S.A., com 91,21% do capital, segundo a agência de classificação de risco FIX. Por sua vez, a U Paraguay pertence à U Holdings, uma sociedade que o Grupo Vázquez constituiu em Luxemburgo 45 dias depois de Santiago Peña assumir a Presidência do país. Nessa holding europeia, o Grupo Vázquez detinha 86,73% do capital, o banco OTP — o maior banco da Hungria — tinha 9,99%, e o restante pertencia a acionistas minoritários. Francisco Peña, irmão do presidente, tinha ações na sociedade de Luxemburgo.




Com a intervenção, a Justiça determinou o bloqueio preventivo de bens no valor de 70 milhões de dólares e 1,62 trilhão de guaranis pertencentes a dirigentes e às empresas U Paraguay, U Holdings e Grupo Vázquez.




Além dessa cadeia, existe a Ueno Holding, na qual Santiago Peña tinha ações. Entre seus acionistas estavam o Grupo Vázquez, a Ueno Seguros e a ITTI.




No centro do circuito financeiro está a ITTI, empresa de tecnologia do grupo. Seus acionistas eram o Grupo Vázquez, a Ueno Seguros e o próprio Ueno Bank, que detinham quase 17% da empresa: cerca de 68 bilhões de guaranis ou 11 milhões de dólares na cotação atual. O banco não apenas repassava dinheiro à ITTI por meio dos empréstimos, como também era seu sócio.




A ITTI desempenhava três funções. Primeiro, era proprietária, junto com o Grupo Vázquez, de várias empresas que solicitaram os empréstimos, das quais se desfez pouco antes ou pouco depois delas receberem os créditos. Segundo, era o principal destino do dinheiro. Terceiro, era a empresa que pagava as dívidas, direta ou indiretamente.




Segundo o Ministério Público, o esquema era circular. As dívidas não eram pagas com o que as empresas devedoras faturavam, mas com dinheiro proveniente de outras empresas do mesmo grupo

, principalmente da ITTI e das processadoras de pagamentos Red Digital, por vezes obtido por meio de novos saques a descoberto no próprio banco.




Segundo a acusação, o banco ocultou do órgão supervisor que havia ultrapassado os limites legais de crédito para partes relacionadas. Quando a Superintendência de Bancos insistiu, o Ueno vendeu uma carteira de 74,4 milhões de dólares a outra empresa vinculada, a Vinanzas S.A., que a pagou com recursos que, rastreados, vinham, em última instância, do próprio Ueno Bank.




O Ministério Público calcula que ainda restam cerca de 167 milhões de dólares e 343 bilhões de guaranis a receber, com poucas possibilidades de recuperação. Isso coloca em risco o dinheiro dos correntistas e os recursos públicos depositados no banco.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Latino Voters Just Remade the Political Map
content:
The midterms saw a landslide of Latinos vote for Democrats.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The midterms saw a landslide of Latinos vote for Democrats. In Texas, California, Kansas and Colorado, Latinos who had voted for Republicans just two years ago voted for Democrats in large numbers, helping secure Democratic control of both the House and the Senate. Latino lawmakers will make up about a fifth of the Democratic majority in the House. And in an historic victory, the two most populous states in the country, California and Texas, will soon be led by Democratic Latino governors.

“Texas has been suddenly transformed into a battleground state,” says Democracy Now! co-host Juan Gonzalez. “Texas has been the biggest and most important red state in the country for decades, and I’ve been predicting for years that it is the key link for achieving a realignment of national politics.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

The midterms saw a landslide of Latino voters towards Democrats in state after state. In Texas, California, Kansas and Colorado, Latinos who had voted for Republicans just two years ago swung to Democrats in huge numbers, helping secure Democratic control of both the House and the Senate.

Latino lawmakers will make up about a fifth of the Democratic majority in the House. And in historic victories, the two most populous states in the country, California and Texas, will soon be led by Latinx Democratic governors. On Tuesday night, Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa defeated the incumbent Republican Governor Greg Abbott with a margin of over 700,000 votes. This is a clip from her speech.

GOV.-ELECT GINA HINOJOSA: I am a daughter of the Rio Grande Valley, where the people embody the work ethic and values of our great state, where no one would have imagined that one day a little girl from the RGV would stand before you here as the next governor of the greatest state, Texas.

AMY GOODMAN: That was Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa speaking in Austin, Texas, right after she was declared the winner.

And this is California Governor-elect Xavier Becerra addressing supporters Tuesday night in Sacramento after he easily defeated Republican challenger Steve Hilton.

GOV.-ELECT XAVIER BECERRA: Ladies and gentlemen, you have now entered the Becerra era. Tonight, I have a message for all those who have been made to feel afraid. There’s a new sheriff in town, and he’s got a law degree and a union card. If anyone wants to come after California or any one Californian, they better be ready for a fight.

AMY GOODMAN: For more on the significance of these victories, we turn to Juan González, yes, co-host of Democracy Now!, author of, among other books, Harvest of Empire: A History of Latinos in America.

Juan, can you talk about this massive Latino victory across the country? What was expected? What wasn’t expected?

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Yeah, well, Amy, it’s been quite a week in U.S. politics, and I’ve been poring over the voting returns and the exit polls the past two days to glean a clearer sense of the trends and outcomes that maybe the major media may have missed, and not just about Latinos.

Let’s begin with the turnout, which I believe is always key. It tells you how motivated and mobilized people were. Well, nationally, the turnout was 63% of registered voters. Now, that’s high by historic standards for a midterm, because, remember, it’s always less voting in the midterms. But it’s still a lower rate than either the Biden midterm election of 2022 or the first Trump midterm elections of 2018. So, while some areas of the country may have had a historic turnout, across the country this was not the highest turnout of any midterm in recent years.

And the most notable shift occurred among white voters. They made up 73% of all ballots cast. That’s the same percentage that they made in 2022. But while they voted 58% for Republicans four years ago — and I’m comparing it midterm to midterm, not midterm to the presidential election — this time they split almost evenly between Republicans and Democrats. So you’re talking a huge shift among white voters away from the Republican Party and to the Democratic Party.

What about people of color, who represented 23% of the electorate? The turnout rate for Blacks and Latinos nationwide stayed about even, or even possibly dropped a little bit, compared to 2022. And both groups, though, shifted much more to Democrats than previously. Black voters nationwide went from about 86% to 90% this year, and Latinos moved from 60% Democratic to — it depends on who you look at. The national exit poll said it went to 64%. The New York Times voter trend says it went to 69%. But both groups shifted nationwide significantly toward Democrats.

But here’s the biggest surprise that no one has paid any attention to, is that what happened among Asian Americans. They not only doubled their share of the electorate — they went from 2% in 2022 to 4% in this year — but 71% of Asian Americans voted for Democrats. That’s a 13-point shift from what Asian Americans did in 2022. And I have to think that the wars in Gaza and Iran, the Trump administration’s banning of travel from many Asian and Middle Eastern countries, its constant belittling of that region’s countries and cultures, the deportation even of refugees from Afghanistan, all have dramatically transformed how Asian Americans view the two major political parties.

Now, there’s been a lot of attention to the Latino vote, and which I’ve been studying for decades, obviously, as you mentioned Harvest of Empire. But we have to begin with what I’ve always called the Brown Belt. That’s a vast area of six Western and Southwestern states where Latinos make up as much as 30% or more of the total population — talking about Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and California. And, of course, as you mentioned, in Texas and California, the first elected Latino governors in both of those states. But the most startling trends came at the congressional level.

Take northern Nevada, for example. Democrat and former social worker Teresa Benitez-Thompson defeated a Republican incumbent to become the first Democrat ever to win that state’s 2nd Congressional seat, a district that Trump won by 14 points in 2024. With her victory, all four of Nevada’s congressional districts are held — will be held by Democrats.

In southern Arizona, JoAnna Mendoza, a 20-year Navy and Marine Corps veteran, flipped another Republican seat. And meanwhile, an emergency room doctor, Dr. Amish Shah, a former state legislator, won the 1st Congressional District in another Republican seat with a large — a district with a large Latino population.

In Colorado, Democrat Manny Rutinel, a Latino attorney and former state legislator, defeated a Republican incumbent in a district in Denver’s northern suburbs with the highest percentage of Latino voters in the state.

Of course, Texas has been the biggest and most important red state in the country for decades, and I’ve been predicting for years that it is the key link for achieving a realignment of national politics. Remember those five [seats] that Trump ordered redrawn to elect more Republicans? Well, the voters didn’t cooperate. Democrats held on to four of those five seats. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen, two moderate congressmen, prevailed in their reelections. Democrat Leticia Gutierrez rode a wave of anti-mass deportation and anti-ICE sentiment to defeat her Republican opponent in the redrawn 9th District outside of Houston. That’s the seat that Al Green, the longtime congressman, used to hold. And in the San Antonio area, former Deputy Sheriff Johnny Garcia won in the newly created 35th District. And at the same time, Republicans lost two other seats in Texas to Latino Democrats. In West Texas, former educator Katy Padilla Stout won a congressional district that had been in Republican hands for the past six elections. That’s followed the resignation of Representative Tony Gonzales in the wake of sexual misconduct and the ethics scandal. And in the lone Rio Grande Valley seat held by Republicans, the famed Grammy-winning Tejano singer Bobby Pulido, who describes himself as a conservative Democrat but favors immigration reform, he defeated Republican Monica De La Cruz, who was thought to be a rising Republican star.

Now, here’s another surprise that no one’s paid attention to, maybe the biggest Texas bright spot that has escaped notice. I’m talking about the remarkable performance by Greg Casar, the chairman of the House Progressive Caucus. He’s also a democratic socialist and someone we have interviewed on Democracy Now! numerous times. He ran for reelection, but to a seat formerly held by Congressman Lloyd Doggett, after Republicans moved Casar’s hometown of Austin out of his district and into this reconfigured district, and Doggett agreed to retire. Well, Casar won that race as expected, but he did so in a super landslide. He amassed over 254,000 votes. That’s 70,000 more votes than any other congressional candidate got in Texas this year — for a socialist in Texas. By my calculations, Casar received the fifth-highest vote in the U.S. out of all of the candidates for the 435 House seats.

The bottom line is that Texas has been suddenly transformed into a battleground state. Republicans not only lost the governor’s seat, a U.S. Senate seat, other statewide races, several state House and Senate seats, but instead of winning five new congressional seats, they ended up with a net loss of one. If Democrats are able to consolidate some of those Texas gains in the coming years, national politics will never be the same. That’s why progressive organizers and fundraisers should be looking at Texas, like the civil rights movement of the 1950s regarded Mississippi and Georgia, as the place to send resources and train new leaders for the upcoming 2028 election.

Meanwhile, over in California, all five Republican districts that Democrats redrew ended up flipping to Democrats. Two of those five went to Latinos. Randy Villegas, a progressive community college professor, won a seat in the Central Valley in the 6th District, and Linda Sánchez prevailed in Orange County’s redrawn district.

And it’s not just the Brown Belt where Latinos had an impact. In Pennsylvania, where Democrats flipped four Republican seats, 73% of the state’s Latinos voted for Democrats, according to The New York Times. That’s a 26-point shift from the 2024 election. And it almost certainly fueled Democratic victories in two of those districts, where Latinos make up 15 to 25% of the population. That’s the 8th District, around Scranton, where the city’s Democratic Mayor Paige Cognetti won, and the 7th District, around Allentown, Bethlehem, where retired firefighter Bob Brooks ousted the Republican incumbent.

So, Democrats controlling Congress, however, does not offer any certainty that a new era of progressive government is dawning in Washington. We shouldn’t forget, for example, that South Texas Democrats have historically been more conservative than those in other parts of the country. So it remains to be seen how those Texas victories will ultimately affect legislation in the new Congress.

In addition, the country’s billionaire class will doubtless ramp up its torrent of cash donations directed at the new Democratic majority, hoping to buy off enough of them or foment sufficient infighting among them to kill or stall any substantive efforts at truly progressive legislation.

So much damage has already been perpetrated on American society by the lawlessness and corruption of the Trump era that it will take who knows how long to repair. To do so, progressives will need to contend not only with their — with the billionaire class and the corporate Democrats, who never tire of conspiring to control things, with Trump for the next two years and his MAGA faithful; they must also contend with their own ultra-left activists, who will increasingly demand no compromise by the new Democratic majority, as if this week’s election was some kind of revolutionary sea change, and not just a much welcome shift in the seesaw world of late-stage neoliberal capitalism, which is what I think it is.

AMY GOODMAN: Juan González, thanks so much for that analysis. Juan, of course, co-host on Democracy Now! and author of a number of books, including Harvest of Empire: A History of Latinos in America.

Coming up, we’ll be joined by Hasan Piker, the popular political left commentator and live-streamer, who had one of the biggest streaming broadcasts on election night, number two just after NBC, beating out the networks. He campaigned heavily in the last months with many progressives and DSA candidates. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: “Copper Kettle” by Stephanie Coleman and Nora Brown, performing at the Brooklyn Folk Festival. This year’s festival is this weekend, and Democracy Now! will be there.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

Truthout produces reporting you won’t see in the mainstream: journalism from the frontlines of global conflict, interviews with grassroots movement leaders, high-quality legal analysis and more.

author: David Swanson
title: World BEYOND War Asia Joins 2026 ASEAN Civil Society Conference / ASEAN People’s Forum (ACS/APF)
content:
Asia, Culture of Peace, East and Southeast Asia, Nonviolent Activism

By World BEYOND War Asia, November 6, 2026

World BEYOND War Asia joined other civil society organizations during the 2026 ASEAN Civil Society Conference / ASEAN People’s Forum (ACS/APF).

We hosted a Peace Solidarity Booth that featured activities like paper crane folding, color-your-own postcards, and a photo/video booth.

We also co-organized a Workshop on ASEAN Youth, Peace, and Security with organizations from Myanmar, Indonesia, Thailand, and Malaysia. We aim to produce a Youth Manifesto on Peace and Security.

Our Asia Organizer, Jhay de Jesus, hosted several portions/activities during the event.

We want to thank various organizations that we were able to work with during this momentous occasion.

Thank you to A New Burma, KONTRAS, SEM, Queers for Alternative Burma, The Happy Ripples, KILUSAN, Stop the War Coalition, and the rest of the organizers and participants of this year’s ACSC/APF for taking part in our peace advocacy.

And Thank you, Philippine NOC for including World BEYOND War be part of this endeavor.

More power to ACSC/APF! See you all again soon.

If you select to make a recurring contribution of at least $15 per month, you may select a thank-you gift. We thank our recurring donors on our website.

author: Ohood Nassar
title: “The Hall Turned Red”: Survivors Recount Israeli Strike on University in Gaza
content:
“I still remember the bombing, the sound of people screaming, and the sight of the injured,” said one student.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

At 10:15 am on October 25, 2026, an Israeli missile struck the courtyard in front of the female students’ lecture hall at Gaza’s Islamic University. Baraa Abu Hujeir, a 22-year-old English language student, was attending a linguistics lecture inside.

“We were in the linguistics lecture hall when we were suddenly hit by the blast. Stones scattered around us, and pieces of the windows, which were made of nylon and wood, flew toward us,” Abu Hujeir told me.

She confirmed that approximately 130 female students were inside the hall, along with their lecturer, Dr. Khader Khader.

Minutes before the strike, Abu Hujeir had been absorbed in the lecture despite the difficult conditions under which the university was attempting to continue teaching.

“I was excited, and the lecture was very interesting, despite the lack of resources. There was no electricity, no internet, and not even a blackboard,” she said.

Getting to the university was not easy for Abu Hujeir, who lives with her family in the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza. She spent around half an hour looking for transportation before making the 40-minute journey to the university.

During the lecture, she was reading the presentation slides on Dr. Khader’s laptop when everything suddenly changed.

“As I was reading the slides, the hall turned red, and stones scattered around us,” she said.

According to Abu Hujeir, there had been no warning before the explosion. As the blast rang out, the students began screaming. Dr. Khader’s laptop and Abu Hujeir’s own iPad were damaged.

But what frightened her most was seeing her classmate Salwa injured in the face: “Her face was covered in blood,” Abu Hujeir recalled.

At first, Abu Hujeir thought the missile had struck the lecture hall itself. She and the other students went outside to see what had happened and discovered that the missile had landed directly in front of the hall, approximately one meter away, according to her account.

Fear quickly spread among the students, especially when they began hearing calls for the university to be evacuated immediately amid concerns that it could be attacked again.

Dr. Khader, 80, was inside the linguistics lecture hall explaining the lesson when the strike transformed the room into a scene of panic and confusion.

After the explosion, he called for the university to be evacuated immediately. However, he refused to leave the hall until he had made sure that all the female students had evacuated safely.

Abu Hujeir says she tried to take his hand to help him leave, but he refused and told her, “You leave.”

As he prepared to evacuate, Dr. Khader saw that his car, which he had parked outside the entrance to the lecture hall, had been damaged by the strike. Its windows were shattered, and its tires were damaged. He stood looking at it sadly, tears in his eyes, repeating, “My car is gone.”

After leaving the hall, Abu Hujeir found more than six injured people outside, their bodies covered in blood. Among the injured was her 18-year-old classmate, Ahmed Nasser.

Nasser had been waiting on the steps outside the female students’ lecture hall for Dr. Khader so he could help him move to the male students’ lecture hall. During the war, Dr. Khader had sustained an injury to his foot that left him unable to move independently. He needed someone to hold his hand and assist him when walking.

But the explosion struck before Nasser could help his professor.

“At the moment of the attack, I was sitting on the steps outside the girls’ lecture hall, waiting for the doctor. When the explosion happened, I fell to the ground and couldn’t run,” Nasser told me.

His fear was compounded by his inability to move and his uncertainty about the extent of his injuries.

“I couldn’t run, so I was screaming and crying,” he said, his voice breaking. “I thought I had been paralyzed and would lose my ability to move.”

Nasser’s back was bleeding. His university classmates tried to provide first aid, using a piece of cloth to stop the bleeding before he was transferred to Al-Quds Hospital in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City. He had lost consciousness by the time he reached the hospital.

The first strike was not the end of the violence at the Islamic University that day. At 12:30 pm, a second strike hit members of the university’s security team who were still inside the campus in the university courtyard.

The Islamic University confirmed in a statement that the attack killed three security personnel: Sami Baroud, 52; Ashraf Dahlan, 47; and Shadi Abu Ataya, 41.

After these attacks, the university carried out minor repairs, mainly fixing the broken windows and damaged chairs. The university suspended classes for a few days and resumed operations on October 31.

According to a comprehensive assessment conducted by UNESCO, the Palestinian Ministry of Education and Higher Education, and the Arab World for Research and Development (AWRAD), approximately 95 percent of higher education campuses in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed since October 2023. Of the 38 campuses assessed, 22 were completely destroyed, and 14 sustained varying levels of damage. The destruction has not only deprived thousands of students of their right to education but has also devastated the academic infrastructure that generations of Palestinians worked to build.

A day that had begun with a university lecture had become a series of traumatic events marked by fear, injuries, and loss. The consequences continued long after the explosions had stopped.

Nasser was admitted to the intensive care unit, where he remained unconscious for two days. When he regained consciousness, doctors discovered two shrapnel fragments in his back. Doctors managed to remove the first fragment, but they have been unable to extract the second because it is extremely close to his spinal column, Nasser said.

He remains in the hospital, unable to move or resume his education, with no clear indication of when he will be able to return to his studies.

“I am now afraid that my condition will continue to deteriorate and that doctors may not be able to remove the shrapnel lodged near my spine,” he told me.

The impact of the attacks extended beyond physical injuries and the damage to the university and people’s belongings: Students and their professors have also been left struggling with the psychological effects of what happened.

Dr. Khader says he feels guilty toward his students because he was among those who insisted on resuming in-person classes at the Islamic University.

“During the attack, I felt immense fear because the missile landed just one meter away from us,” he said. “If the lecture hall itself had been hit, more than 100 people could have been killed.”

The lecture that Abu Hujei had been following so enthusiastically before the explosion is no longer just an academic subject — it has become inseparable from the memories of fear, blood, and the screams of her classmates. She says it remains the most difficult experience she has endured since the beginning of Israel’s war on Gaza.

“I still remember the bombing, the sound of people screaming, and the sight of the injured,” she said. “Whenever I open my linguistics textbook to read, I can’t concentrate. I remember the attack, feel my heart tighten, and immediately close the book.”

author: Mark Olalde
title: Trump Official Who Wants Data Centers on Public Lands Is Invested in AI Industry
content:
Other officials across the administration also stand to profit from the White House’s support for AI and data centers.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The Trump administration has likened the need to build out the nation’s artificial intelligence infrastructure to the Manhattan Project, the World War II effort that produced the world’s first atomic bomb.

The White House’s point person on the effort, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, has spoken of the “AI arms race” with China as an existential issue for the nation. “AI is manufacturing intelligence, and, if we don’t manufacture more intelligence than our adversaries, it affects every job, every company and every industry,” he said during his Senate confirmation hearing in January 2025.

But advancing the administration’s AI objectives also could benefit Burgum’s own finances.

Much of his wealth is held in Arthur Ventures, an investment firm he co-founded, according to his 2026 financial disclosure form, which has not been previously reported. Between $18.1 million and $64.4 million of those investments are in AI companies, according to an analysis of the companies’ marketing materials shared with ProPublica by public lands advocacy group Save Our Parks. (Government financial disclosure forms allow filers to report wide ranges instead of the specific value of their investments.)

Burgum made his fortune 25 years ago when he sold a software company to Microsoft and has remained heavily invested in technology. In the year before joining the administration, when he was North Dakota’s governor, he made between $2.1 million and $11 million in capital gains from AI-related investments, Save Our Parks’ analysis showed. In 2025, he sold millions of dollars of stocks and equity in AI companies, bringing in capital gains worth between $2.5 million and $15.1 million.

In the ethics agreement Burgum signed as part of his Senate confirmation, he agreed to resign from his positions at Arthur but not give up his financial interests there.

“Secretary Burgum has met his federal ethics and financial disclosure obligations,” a U.S. Department of the Interior spokesperson told ProPublica in a statement. “Any suggestion that his office decisions are driven by personal investments are false and completely unsupported.”

Officials across the Trump administration also stand to profit from the White House’s support for AI and data centers. For example, 380 of President Donald Trump’s political appointees or their spouses hold stocks or have other financial connections to Nvidia, which has become the world’s most valuable company thanks to the data center boom. More than 320 have ties to Alphabet, Google’s parent company, which plans to spend at least $195 billion this year building data centers and AI-related technology. And more than 240 are invested in or otherwise have financial ties to Meta Platforms, which is developing a “fleet” of data centers. This is according to an analysis of records added last week to the Trump Team Financials database developed by ProPublica to make accessible the financial disclosures of administration officials.

Federal officials’ activities are governed by a criminal statute that sets a high burden of proof for potential wrongdoing — for example, approving permits for a company in which they are substantially invested, multiple ethics professors and lawyers told ProPublica. They said that Burgum’s investments appear to be acceptable under this law.

But ethics rules that do not carry criminal penalties also apply, explained Cynthia Brown, senior ethics counsel with Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a government watchdog group. These rules, she said, “instruct officials not to work on anything that would create the appearance of a conflict of interest.” She said this would include Burgum’s support for data centers on federal land while holding investments in AI.

Richard Painter, a law professor at the University of Minnesota and President George W. Bush’s chief ethics lawyer, agreed that Burgum should avoid making decisions benefiting an industry in which he is heavily invested. “I, as the ethics lawyer, would insist he stay away from it,” Painter said. “In the Bush administration, the answer would’ve been ‘he has to recuse,’ I can guarantee you that.”

A review of recent Interior Department secretaries’ financial holdings suggests it’s common to have some potential conflicts, but Trump’s appointees are more heavily invested in the industries they oversee than their predecessors. Deb Haaland, President Joe Biden’s appointee, held no direct financial investments in companies the department regulated. President Barack Obama’s first appointee, Ken Salazar, listed ownership of his family’s ranch but few other investments. Obama’s second appointee, Sally Jewell, held stocks in oil and gas, which she agreed to divest as a condition of her confirmation.

Ryan Zinke and David Bernhardt served as Interior Department secretaries during Trump’s first term. The former was found by the agency’s Office of Inspector General to have improperly assisted a development in his hometown, while the latter had so many potential conflicts that he reportedly carried a card listing them. (Zinke said the OIG investigation was a political attack, while Bernhardt recused himself from several decisions in which there would have been clear conflicts.)

More recently, as the effort to build data centers has run headlong into broad public opposition, the current administration has offered federally managed public lands to them. Unlike local or state processes, where concerns about water use, power consumption and the lack of transparency around permitting have slowed or halted projects, the public has less ability to stop them on federal property. The Interior Department oversees most of this land.

A little-noticed U.S. Geological Survey report released earlier this year found at least 91.3 million acres of public lands managed by the Interior Department — an area comparable to Montana — could potentially host data centers.

The department’s mandate includes overseeing tribal affairs, managing national parks, regulating extractive industries like coal and operating dams across the West. Burgum, though, is spending significant time on other things. This includes meeting with representatives of companies such as Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet more than 20 times from January through November 2025, according to a compilation of his schedules shared with ProPublica by public interest watchdog group Public Citizen.

In response, several Democratic senators sent a letter to Burgum in October saying, “We demand that you immediately cease all efforts to hijack public lands for the development of data centers, and urge you to provide full transparency on your role in the DOI’s efforts to site data centers.”

Some of Burgum’s meetings have been previously unreported, including a June 2025 dinner with a high-ranking United Arab Emirates delegation in the wine room of the upscale Italian restaurant Cafe Milano in Washington’s Georgetown neighborhood. The small guest list included the United Arab Emirates’ AI lead, Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, as well as Amos Hochstein, a prominent American proponent of AI data centers via his investment firm TWG Global.

Several months later, Burgum signed a memorandum of understanding with the Emirati delegation, pledging to work together to deploy AI.

Neither the Emirati Embassy nor TWG Global responded to requests for comment.

The Interior Department spokesperson said that Burgum “is responsible for helping unleash American energy production and ensuring our nation has the resources and infrastructure necessary to lead the future. That mission requires engagement with industry leaders, stakeholders, and international partners.”

In an August Fox News appearance to promote the administration’s AI efforts, Burgum was asked about the network’s poll showing 70% of voters opposed data centers. He countered by alleging that “foreign influence” and “misinformation” had played a large role in fueling public opposition.

Jayson O’Neill, a spokesperson for Save Our Parks, said Burgum and others in the administration are out of touch with public concerns. “His almost myopic focus on artificial intelligence and the data center build-out at the expense of our public lands serves not only the globalist tech titans behind and within the Trump administration, but also him and the tens of millions of dollars of his own personal wealth invested in the industry.”

Across the administration, political appointees whose offices have AI business before them hold significant investments in the industry.

Steve Pearce is director of the Bureau of Land Management, the Interior Department agency that administers more land than any other entity in the country. The former New Mexico representative was confirmed over Democrats’ concerns that he favors selling public lands and that his career in oil and gas presents a conflict of interest involving an industry the agency regulates.

But public lands advocates say his AI investments now worry them. Pearce owned stock in Nvidia, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other AI-focused companies, according to his most recent publicly available financial disclosure, signed in October 2025. He also is invested in Titan Development, a real estate company that has managed several land acquisitions for data centers in the Southwest. (He pledged to divest many of his AI investments, but not Titan.)

An agency spokesperson pushed back on the concerns. “Director Pearce complies with all applicable federal ethics requirements and financial disclosure obligations,” the spokesperson said in a statement, adding that “conflating lawful disclosure of financial holdings with an actual conflict of interest ignores the federal ethics framework designed to identify and address precisely these questions.”

The BLM is reviewing permit applications for about 15 data centers and 17 associated infrastructure projects, including nuclear power plants and transmission wires, in Arizona, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Wyoming and Idaho. This is according to an agency spokesperson and its Mineral & Land Records System.

The project that was to be the first data center on BLM land, near Boulder City in southern Nevada, had earned a permit to build a solar plant, before changing its plans. The BLM approved the change in June without studying the potential environmental implications. (An Interior Department appeals board has since paused the project, sending it back to the agency for further review.)

Meanwhile, it remains unclear how much the public will benefit from data centers on BLM land. The foundational federal land management law was passed in 1976, so it does not envision data centers. Even so, the department said it is relying on this statute to permit data centers.

Businesses pay the government to use public land. Oil and gas drillers pay a royalty on each barrel they produce. Solar power plants pay a per-megawatt fee.

For data centers, the main charge appears set to be an “annual fair-market-value rent,” an Interior Department spokesperson said. But such rental fees can be quite low, so the economic benefit to the public won’t be known until the data centers are permitted.

Another key official with a land management agency who’s heavily invested in AI is Michael Boren. He first served as acting assistant secretary of the Interior Department before transitioning to U.S. Department of Agriculture undersecretary, where he oversees the Forest Service, second only to the BLM in the land area it stewards.

Among his many investments in AI companies, Boren reported between about $1.5 million and $6.1 million worth of financial interests in Elon Musk’s xAI, which has since been acquired by SpaceX. Additionally, he has up to $500,000 invested in Valar Atomics, which is pushing to build a data center complex called Project Beehive on thousands of acres of BLM land in Utah, complete with more than 450 small nuclear plants to power it.

“Undersecretary Boren has fully complied with all federal ethics laws and requirements and will continue to follow the advice of USDA’s excellent ethics attorneys,” an Agriculture Department spokesperson said in a statement.

Lee Zeldin, whom Trump appointed to head the Environmental Protection Agency, has also emerged as a major AI booster. He too has dabbled in AI investments. Zeldin’s financial disclosure forms reveal that in May 2025 he bought and sold up to $15,000 worth of shares of Datavault AI, a company selling AI-, data- and blockchain-based products.

“Administrator Zeldin followed every ethical rule to a tee in his disclosure without exception,” an EPA spokesperson said in a statement. The agency added that he was cleared by its ethics officials and that he has no obligation to explain such transactions.

The EPA under Zeldin has taken steps to minimize oversight of data centers and power plants built nearby to keep them running. This includes a rule the agency proposed in July to end a requirement that states gather public feedback as they consider air permits for certain facilities, including data centers.

In October, a group of Democratic senators sent a letter to Zeldin asking the EPA to withdraw the proposed rule. “The federal government should encourage transparency and public engagement around these projects, not make it easier to shroud their construction in secrecy,” they wrote.

Brandon Roberts contributed reporting.

author: Michael Arria
title: The GOP Wasn’t the Only Midterms Loser. Voters Slapped Data Centers With Limits.
content:
This week voters nationwide approved 40 out of the 41 ballot measures that had been proposed to rein in data centers.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

In recent months, thousands of Americans have flooded municipal government buildings to testify against the construction of AI data centers in their communities.

According to a May 2026 Gallup poll, 7 out of 10 people oppose the construction of data centers in their local area, citing grave concerns over their environmental impact, water consumption, noise, and potential health risks. A Blue Rose Research poll from December 2025 found that Americans would rather live near prisons or nuclear power plants than data centers.

“Overcoming this opposition stands as a major hurdle in the expansion of AI computing,” noted Gallup Senior Editor Jeffrey M. Jones. “The intensity of opposition means that proposed data centers are likely to spur grassroots activism from local residents as well as legal challenges.”

Many of those challenges have proven successful, as more than 500 jurisdictions have approved moratoriums or bans even before the midterms. That trend was extended during this week’s elections, where data center-related questions appeared on the ballot in 13 states: 40 out of 41 ballot measures placing restrictions on data centers were passed throughout the country.

Data center-related questions appeared on the ballot in 13 states.

In many cases, the results were not close: 77 percent of voters in Edgewater, Florida, approved a ban on new data centers, while 82 percent of voters in Alhambra, California, endorsed one. Ohio, which had more data center-related questions on its ballots than any other state, saw voters pass outright bans in 11 municipalities, while another seven approved further regulations on them.

“Tuesday’s election was a historically bad night for the Republican Party,” declared the Boston Globe. “It might have been even worse for big tech and their plans to spend trillions of dollars building AI data centers.”

Anger over data centers certainly wasn’t limited to local ballot questions. Polling suggests that it helped determine the results of major races amid the Democratic Party’s historic “blue wave.” Exit polling from NBC News reveals that 56 percent of voters identified data centers and AI as a “crucial or major factor” in their vote.

Chief among these contests was the Ohio Senate race, where incumbent Republican Sen. John Husted was ousted by Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown.

Husted was backed by powerful tech giants like Oracle’s Larry Ellison and Safra Catz; and a cryptocurrency PAC, funded by companies like Coinbase, spent $55 million trying to stomp out Brown’s challenge.

The Brown campaign consistently highlighted these ties during the campaign, running ads that referred to Husted as “the face of data centers in Ohio” and bankrolling billboards that directed voters to a website which details how Husted is the “chief reason” that 226 data centers exist in the state.

An internal National Republican Senatorial Committee memo, originally reported on by Axios, showed that Brown’s attacks were working and causing Republican anxiety over not just the Ohio race, but the GOP’s relationship with data centers more broadly.

“More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” it read. “If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one.”

56 percent of voters identified data centers and AI as a “crucial or major factor” in their vote.

In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned on a data center moratorium, ousted Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott. Abbott embraced guardrails on the facilities leading up to the election, but for years he welcomed their construction in the state and, in 2025, he declared Texas to be the “epicenter of AI development.”

“I think we will see the end to favorable tax breaks, and it’s clear that people like Greg Abbott were harmed by their history of giving those financial incentives to AI companies and data center developers,” Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist who works on AI, told WIRED.

Tech magnate and GOP mega-donor Elon Musk dumped $224 million into the Texas elections in a failed effort to keep it red. After the Democrats prevailed, Musk, who had plans to construct multiple data centers across his adopted home state, tweeted: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

Immediately after the election, Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) released a statement calling on incoming House members to make AI regulation a top priority and for AI company CEOs to testify before the chamber.

“The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics,” said Casar.

Georgia’s Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms and Ohio’s Governor-elect Amy Acton have also endorsed moratoriums, and Annie Andrews’s victory in South Carolina is another blow to the AI industry, which spent heavily in support of short-time incumbent Sen. Darline Graham.

Immediately after the election, Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Rep. Greg Casar released a statement calling on incoming House members to make AI regulation a top priority.

Like Flock cameras and support for Israel, data centers are an issue that cuts across party lines and upends our perception of partisanship. In May 2026, Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis signed SB 484, which “protects ratepayers, the environment, and local communities from harm caused by hyperscale data centers.”

“These are much-needed protections for taxpayers and our natural resources,” said DeSantis at the time.

Even President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly touted the benefits of data centers, has modified his stance in recent months, seemingly aware that much of his base is skeptical about further construction.

In a Truth Social post days before the election, Trump called on AI companies to pay impacted communities a “dividend” in exchange for a data center’s construction.

“I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck,” claimed the president, who provided no proof that this has ever happened.

Amid the growing resistance, tech companies have also shifted their approach.

Amazon has pledged to improve the environmental rating of its backup data center generators and to disclose more information about their water use. OpenAI has rebranded its data centers as “compute campuses.” Companies like Google have announced that they will stop requiring government officials to sign nondisclosure agreements in an effort to increase transparency within communities.

Sam Burleigh, who helped found an organization aimed at stopping an Amazon-backed data center project in Pennsylvania, told the Associated Press that such efforts are merely “propaganda.”

“What I see is them realizing they have more resistance than they ever dreamt of. And so now they have to find some way, some method to break through that resistance,” he explained.
