author: Rick Kuhn
title: Unemployment: a feature of capitalism, not a bug
content:
Today more than one in ten workers can’t find enough paid labour to live a decent life. And that’s only workers actively looking for a job or for more hours of employment. It doesn’t count those who have given up on finding a job, even though they want one, and survive thanks to friends, family or a measly government payment that isn’t an unemployment benefit.

In September

 the seasonally adjusted 

un

employment rate was 4.7 percent; 

under

employment was 6.3 percent. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, you’re not unemployed if you worked even an hour in the survey fortnight.

To get the Jobseeker Payment or Youth Allowance the un- and underemployed have to follow the Albanese government’s savage eligibility rules, inherited from its Liberal predecessors. If you earn more than a pitiful $75 a week, your payment starts to go down. You must follow the instructions of Workforce Australia and, if you’ve been directed to one, of an outsourced “employment services provider” agency, which profits from government funding.

That may mean applying for a certain number of jobs every “reporting period”, doing training they tell you to do, however meaningless courses about writing job applications or behaviour during an interview might be; or perform “work for the dole”, that would normally be done for much higher award wages. You have to “accept any offer of suitable paid work”, defined by the provider, whether the type of work or its location actually suits you or not.

If you’re single, without kids, the dole is 

currently

 

a princely $413 a week. Certainly in Sydney, you’d be very lucky if less than half of that went on renting a room. And if you’re young, that’s unfortunate: unemployed aged 21 or younger are penalised and get less money than those over 21. Apparently young people don’t need as much shelter, food, clothing, etc. as older people.

Both the unemployment and underemployment rates are rising.

Unemployment is not a bug in capitalism, but a feature. The threat of un- and underemployment – descending into what Marx called “

the industrial reserve army

”—disciplines workers fearful of losing their jobs. The higher the level of unemployment, other things being equal, the less likely they are to take risks by fighting to defend or improve their pay and conditions.

The extent of the reserve army of labour changes in the course of economic cycles: lower during booms, higher in slumps.

Many central banks, like the Reserve Bank of Australia, are bumping up interest rates to slow their countries’ economies down. Their goal is not increased unemployment; that’s a side effect. Their main target is the rate of inflation. High inflation—lack of stability in the purchasing power of money—makes calculations by capitalists about their activities and especially investments more difficult. 

In legislation

, the RBA has two goals: “price stability and the maintenance of full employment”. It says that “

[t]hese two objectives usually work together

”. In practice, the bank favours sacrificing jobs to keep a lid on inflation.

But today, high oil prices, due to the USA’s and Israel’s war on Iran, is the main driver of inflation. The RBA isn’t bumping up interest rates to discipline workers, although that’s a side-effect. Governor 

Michelle Bullock 

said at the end of September that “There is no wage price spiral going on in Australia. Rises in wages are not driving … cost pressures”.

In fact, it is workers who are mainly affected by inflation. Greg Jericho, in the 

Guardian

, has illustrated how workers’ real pay has been falling since 2021, compared with the Consumer Price Index by 7 percent; compared with the more appropriate Employee Living Cost Index, by more than 12 percent.

The hostility of most union officials to leading their members in serious struggles to defend, let alone restore or improve their living standards, is mainly to blame.

In his 1972 report 

Poverty in Australia

, Ronald Henderson, appointed by the Liberal government of Billy McMahon, calculated a poverty line, marking an “austere” standard of living below which people were in poverty. The Melbourne Institute of Economic Research frequently updates it. 

JobSeeker 

has consistently been below this line. Today that unemployment benefit is less than half the 

Henderson poverty line

. Using 50, let alone 60 percent of median 

household income

, common alternative international measures of poverty, the situation of people on JobSeeker is even worse.

Consequently, people on unemployment benefits are much more prone to illness and death. In 2022, the government’s own Australian Institute of Health and Welfare calculated that the death rate of people on unemployment benefits was five times 

higher

 than of those who weren’t on an unemployment, parenting or carer payment, or Disability Support Pension. The mortality rate of the unemployed fell dramatically during the COVID crisis, when Scott Morrison’s Liberal government made temporarily higher payments available, to avoid a revolt prompted by the 

sudden increase

 in unemployment by almost half to 7.5 percent.

In 1993, during the last severe recession in Australia, 

unemployment climbed

 to 10.9 percent. Recurrent economic crises are built into capitalism. Whether the next one is triggered by over-zealous action by the Reserve Bank, the collapse of the AI investment bubble or something else, the number of people living in poverty will skyrocket again, and a repeat of Morrison’s “generosity” to them, by a Labor, Liberal or One Nation government, is exceptionally unlikely.

author: Priya T.
title: Workers can overthrow capitalism
content:
Human beings are the most cooperative species that have ever existed. The expectation that we will live socially, with other people to help and guide us, is built into our biology. 

Compare a human baby with, say, crocodiles, which are born with as many as 60 teeth and use them to break through their eggshell, fending for themselves from their earliest moments. Or baby horses, who can walk within an hour of birth. Human babies can’t so much as lift their own heads

. 

Our evolutionary survival instinct is to 

cry

, the single purpose of which is to 

alert others

 to needs or distress. This interdependence continues, in various ways, throughout our lives.

The fact that humans are not designed to make it alone is why capitalism feels so deeply wrong to so many of us. It is not geared towards meeting people’s needs, and the values it promotes—individualism, competition and greed—run counter to the social and collective instincts that are crucial to our survival as a species. 

The enormous resources and technologies that capitalism brings into existence are not used to provide for people or distributed to meet need. Instead, they are bought and sold to generate wealth for the tiny minority who control them. This gap between how things are, and how they could and should be, is one of the features of the system that perpetually cause people to turn against it. And it is becoming increasingly obscene. 

At the same time as the super-rich are getting on commercial space flights—at $70 million a ticket—the majority of the world’s population have never set foot on a plane. While the ultra-wealthy pour resources into the pursuit of immortality 

for themselves, 

wasting millions on cryogenic chambers, organ replacement, blood transfusions and uploading themselves to the cloud, millions of children die from diarrhea-related illnesses every year, and 3.4 billion people live without proper sanitation. Twelve billionaires hold more wealth than half of humanity. Abundance exists, but it is hoarded away from the masses. 

The rich would like us to think they earned and therefore deserve this wealth; that they are compensated in proportion to what they contribute to society. Australia’s richest person Gina Rinehart wrote a column expressing this view for the industry publication 

Australian Resources and Investment 

in 2012: “If you’re jealous of those with more money, don’t just sit there and complain; do something to make more money yourself—spend less time drinking, or smoking, or socialising, and more time working.” 

Leaving aside that Rinehart seems to spend heaps of time drinking and socialising, including at expensive Italian hotels with One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, nobody really thinks that a mining executive works harder than a garbage truck driver or early childhood educator. But the reality is that on average Australian salaries, it would take these workers about 650,000 years of “more time working” to earn the $40 billion Rinehart is worth. 

The truth is that the ruling class amasses their wealth not by working harder than everyone else, but by getting 

other people to work for them

. Wealth is “created” when the value of the products other people produce is greater than what they are paid by their bosses in wages. This is called exploitation, and it is the basis of capital accumulation. 

Without the labour of workers, bosses wouldn’t have profits or power. Workers do the work to produce what we all need, while the “work” bosses do is to protect their control over this process, make it more profitable and manage the profits. This control gives bosses the ability to shape the lives of millions if not billions of other people—they decide what is made, who gets it and what it sells for. 

The majority, on the other hand, are oppressed: they are denied control over their own activity, as well as what happens to the products of their labour and, by extension, how their society is organised. This oppression is a prerequisite for exploitation—workers are conditioned from birth into accepting their subordinate place in society, and are expected to accept it throughout their working lives. Whether this is unadulterated, as in tyrannical dictatorships, or sanitised, as in parliamentary democracies, the underlying reality is the same. Bosses exercise dictatorial authority in the workplace. And their interests inform government policy. 

The majority of us get little to no say over what happens in our communities, despite living there. Nobody asks residents if they want data centres plonked in their neighbourhoods, for example, or a McDonalds on every shopping strip. Unless collective action forces the outcome to be different, politicians and corporations get to do whatever they want because they hold economic and political power. 

Workers can’t just opt out of this system. To survive, most people need to earn a wage, or depend on someone who does. The prospect of a life where you can’t pay for things is so terrible, that for most people, most of the time, it is preferable to make peace with exploitation and the accompanying lack of control. If the alternative is poverty, it can feel preferable to follow the unfair rules bosses lay down; to “suck it up” when life is unsatisfying and “get over it” when the world makes you sick and sad, and shrinks your dreams. 

The fact that nearly half of young people in Australia, according to a 2025 Headspace survey, reported experiencing high or very high psychological distress, speaks to a society that is broken. The future is especially bleak if you’re young. Some life goals previous generations might have taken for granted, like owning a home and having a stable job, are increasingly out of reach. Meanwhile, the future of the planet is in jeopardy and no-one in power cares enough to act, and tech experts are warning that AI, already widely resented, may soon wipe out our species. It is perfectly rational for young people to feel panic or despair watching all this. Rational, too, for this reality to make someone want to barricade their school. Or throw a trash can through a window.

Capitalism has brought the world to extremes of inequality and degraded the majority of people materially and morally. So is there hope? Yes, there is. 

Workers are not merely victims. At the same time as being exploited, oppressed and alienated, workers are cooperative, able to produce everything we need to survive, and potentially extremely powerful. And they don’t have a stake in the status quo. 

Billions of workers around the world are connected to each other through the labour process. Despite the ideology of individualism, workers are mutually dependent on each other, and, at a local and global level, are only able to produce the things we all need collectively. This means the ability to cooperate is built into working class life in a way it is not for bosses. And workers everywhere share not only the labour process, but also the antagonistic relationship with their bosses—bosses everywhere want workers to work harder for less to maximise profit, while workers want the opposite.

In fact, it is 

because 

workers are structurally united in this way that the system requires division and repression. The ruling class have a variety of tools at their disposal to maintain their social position, from the brute force of police and soldiers, to spreading hateful ideologies like racism through the media or politics. They need scapegoats and enforcement mechanisms because fundamentally, the capitalists’ wealth and privilege rests upon workers accepting their exploitation, and not realising the common interest they share with other workers. 

These containment measures can only be so effective, because capitalism repeatedly gives workers reasons to rebel. Workers can be compelled to resist out of frustration with a steady erosion of their rights, by attacks on their wages or conditions, a significant shock to society like a war or economic crisis, or through disgust with the moral depravity of capitalism. And because the system has an integrated purpose—profit making—when workers get angry about one issue, it often leads them to question other aspects of the system too. 

When workers stand together and start to take action, it shatters the optical illusions that make capitalism seem all-powerful. Instead of spending their days checking off tasks set by capitalist managers, in times of struggle workers take collective control over their workplaces, and start consciously directing the labour they already do, using the skills and knowledge they already possess. 

Democracy is essential to these sorts of working-class rebellions. Workers can only exercise their power collectively, which means it is essential that all participants feel invested in the struggle. This means everyone needs a voice and a say, and disagreements have to be debated out until a collective decision can be reached that people are happy to stick to. Dictating to others weakens the unity workers draw their strength from. 

For this reason, and contrary to the stereotypes, revolutions involve a lot more talking and debate than they do violent uprising. This sort of collective organising often centres around places and activities where people ordinarily gather; schools and universities, neighbourhoods, and, crucially, workplaces. 

Importantly at work, talk can translate into action. Workers have the practical, hands on, down-to-earth skills to bridge the gap between how the world is and how it should be. Electricians, forklift operators, delivery drivers and supermarket workers can not only come up with a plan for moving resources around to get food on every table, they could make it happen. Workers could distribute resources for human need and not profit if they performed their labour collectively and consciously. 

To do this on a larger scale, workers also need wider organising and coordinating bodies, which means more talking and discussion. This is crucial to the process of revolution: to succeed, workers must create their own institutions for governing the economy and society, rooted in their collective power and able to coordinate the conscious, democratic organisation of labour. Bodies like these have been repeatedly created in workers’ revolutions throughout history. 

When workers start to organise on this scale, it is an acute challenge to the existing order. The state, with its wide reach and ability to intimidate through organised violence, is mobilised to force workers back into their place. A revolution therefore needs to defend itself from the old order at the same time as it creates a new one, which means dismantling the capitalist state. 

None of this is easy. The capitalist class is very sensitive to any challenge to its power, while workers are not used to exercising theirs. And action has to be taken quickly and decisively when struggles erupt—workers are much more prone to losing their nerve than the capitalist class. Having a large current of organised revolutionaries prior to massive struggles breaking out, with a clear idea of what is needed to overthrow capitalism and establish workers’ power, is an indispensable tool. Such organisation needs to be built before revolutions begin; it is too late to get organised once things start to move. This is why Socialist Alternative argues we need to be organised today, not because revolution is imminent, but because building our forces in the less explosive times is necessary. 

A world run by workers has the potential to replace profit making with rational organisation: to go from a society in service of the wealthy to one that serves us all. No more deprivation alongside excess; no more reducing human beings to cogs in a machine. If the majority had real control over their labour, and real control over society, life could be lived in a completely different way. 

The potential for an equal society—for socialism—already exists in capitalism, even if it is not always obvious. Fulfilling this potential is not a straightforward task, but it is an important and necessary one.

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: Victorian Liberals flag free speech crackdown
content:
State Liberal leader Jess Wilson has used a book launch to make public her intent to ban protests and political phrases in Victoria if elected in November. 

Speaking

 in Caulfield at the launch of 

Bondi Terror

, written by a SkyNews host and Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive officer Alex Ryvchin, Wilson 

linked

 the movement for Palestine with the horrific violence in Bondi. “When governments, both at federal and state levels, allow hatred like ‘all Zionists are terrorists’, and ‘globalise the intifada’ to be spewed and normalised on our streets, at our universities, and online—Bondi is the result” she said. 

There is still no evidence that the Bondi shooters had ever attended a pro-Palestine protest or otherwise been part of the movement against Israel’s genocide, nor that they had set foot on a university campus or championed the slogan “globalise the intifada”. 

Nevertheless, Wilson told the crowd “Under my leadership, we will expand bans on speech that amounts to incitement to violence, like “Globalise the Intifada”. She also announced her intention to introduce move on laws and to require protests gain permits, so that “all Victorians can feel safe in the city they love”. Except presumably those wanting to exercise the democratic right to protest or use slogans that the government objects to. 

These measures have been demanded by sections of the business and the political right in Melbourne for some time. During the most acute phase of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, when weekly protests took place in Melbourne’s CBD, much anger was expressed at the supposed disruption to normal trade. Melbourne city mayor Nick Reece 

claimed

 he received “weekly phone calls from restaurateurs and city retailers telling me the protests are having a real, negative impact on their business”, particularly “Sunday yum cha”. Never mind there was not one documented case of a Palestine protester preventing someone having yum cha, even imaginary threats to small business bottom lines trump a genocide in the world of council and right-wing politics.  

Last year Brad Battin, the leader of the Liberals at the time, announced the Liberals would introduce a 

permit system

, following the Melbourne City council approval of a plan to request state and federal governments to restrict protest rights. Wilson has now recommitted the Liberals to this plan. 

Wilson and the Victorian Liberals are only the latest to get on the anti-free speech bandwagon. The Liberal Nation Party government in Queensland has already criminalised the phrases “From the river to the sea” and “Globalise the intifada”. Dozens of activists have been charged and are facing jail time because of these laws. An appeal to the High Court against the laws has been launched by pro-Palestine activists, based on the implied right to political communication in the Constitution. In October, the New South Wales Labor government 

joined

 the case on the side of the Queensland government, defending the Orwellian laws. This comes after Minns’ anti-protest laws were 

struck down

 as unconstitutional by the New South Wales Supreme Court. 

There is no sign of this offensive abating. Antisemitism envoy Jillian Segal in October released a 

report

 calling for exclusion zones for protests and bans on face coverings, explicitly declaring “progressive” antisemitism to be the “most pervasive” form of antisemitism. Segal is increasingly open about her purpose being to reframe opposition to Israel’s genocide in Gaza and support for the liberation of Palestinians as racism towards Jewish people and therefore unacceptable and unlawful. 

If the Victorian Liberals win in November, as is now looking 

increasingly likely

, we will have to launch vigorous campaigns to defend our rights to freedom of speech and the right to assembly.

author: Brian Hioe
title: What Do the US Midterms Mean for Taiwan?
content:
THE US MIDTERM elections resulted in a massive win for Democrats, who made historic gains and took control of both the House and Senate. Consequently, the win has been interpreted as a rebuke to Donald Trump’s presidency.

For its part, the Taiwanese government has sought to reassure that support for Taiwan is bipartisan and that it expects arms sales to continue. Nevertheless, one notes that Trump has himself suspended arms sales, out of an apparent desire to please Chinese president Xi Jinping in trade negotiations.

Analysts have suggested that Trump’s actions may be further constrained after the midterms. After all, Trump is now a lame duck, with two years left in his term. His ability to accomplish his agenda will become further limited with the House and Senate out of his control.

At the same time, Trump may seek to override institutions altogether, tapping into his base. Trump supporters were willing to invade the Capitol as part of an attempted insurrection on January 6, 2021, as part of an attempt to prevent the certification of the 2020 presidential election won by Joe Biden, and they may do so again.

It would not be out of character for Trump to try and dismantle institutions he views as opposed to him. If pushed into a corner and desperate, it is unclear what Trump or his supporters may attempt. Trump will be reaching the end of his second term, but Trump has suggested a desire to stay on, or some of his current allies may position themselves as a successor.

This could prove particularly dangerous for Taiwan. In particular, one notes actions before the midterm elections, such as Elon Musk suspending Starlink access for Ukrainian military forces, as well as negotiations between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Such negotiations seemed to be in return for oil access, with Trump hoping for a quick win to lower gas prices in the hopes that this would change the election outcome.

Evidently, this was for naught, with Trump’s last-minute actions failing to have any impact on the American electorate. Nevertheless, such actions point to the desperate moves that Trump and his allies might have as Trump nears the end of his presidency. Trump may, for example, try to come to some grand bargain with Xi Jinping that involves signing away Taiwan with the belief that this would rescue his presidency.

Taiwan should be wary of this possibility and seek collaboration with American counterparts to forestall this possibility, then, along with other global actors such as Ukraine that could also potentially be thrown under the bus by a desperate Trump. Indeed, the Democrats’ dominance of the House and Senate also means that Taiwan’s relationship with the Democratic Party will become increasingly important when it comes to the direction of future US-Taiwan policy.

author: Rindala Alajaji
title: Reflecting on Digital Rights Wins and Losses in Sacramento
content:
California’s 2026 legislative session has officially adjourned and it’s time to reflect on the wins and losses that have shaped Californians’ digital rights landscape this year. This was the second year of a two-year legislative session, which meant several bills 

resumed their legislative paths from 2025

.




EFF monitored nearly 100 bills in the state over the two-year session. These included proposed regulations on 3D printers, access to social media platforms, police, commercial, and workplace surveillance practices, AI, and other privacy concerns. While we saw some victories, alarming developments also raised serious concerns about the future of privacy protection in the state.




Celebrating Wins




Use of automated decision-making and surveillance in the workplace




Governor Newsom signed vital protections on the use of automated decision-making in the workplace and workplace surveillance tools, specifically 

No Robo Bosses

 (

SB 947

) and 

AB 1883

.




Championed by our 

labor partners

, 

SB 947

 limits how employers can use automated decision-making to fire or discipline workers, including provisions that ensure workers get vital information about automated decisions that affect them, and that an algorithm is not the only authority for these consequential decisions. Alongside it, 

AB 1883

 prohibits the use of workplace surveillance to predict emotions or collect neural data. This stops employers from using potentially biased, invasive, and exploitative forms of AI surveillance at the workplace, marking an important step toward creating workplaces that respect the privacy and autonomy of workers. We look forward to continuing to ensure that technology in California’s workplaces is deployed fairly, thoughtfully, and with respect for all workers.




Protecting against federal overreach




EFF was also grateful to see Governor Newsom sign 

SB 747

, which allows damages lawsuits against federal officials 

who violate the U.S. Constitution

. Victims of constitutional violations deserve a complete remedy and this law also helps deter constitutional violations in the first place. Gaps in current law often make it difficult to seek a damages remedy against federal officials who violate the U.S. Constitution. This bill makes it easier to bring such litigation. Federal law enforcement officials have violated our

 First Amendment right to record on-duty police

 and other newsworthy subjects, and also sometimes violate our Fourth Amendment right to be 

free from unreasonable searches of our phones and laptops

. When this happens, the people who suffer these violations should be able to 

sue these officials for damages

.




Additionally, EFF supported two bills (which are now state law) that clarify and extend California’s shield laws to protect patients, healthcare providers, and others involved in reproductive healthcare and gender-affirming care that is legal in California. After the 

overturn of Roe v. Wade

, California 

enacted

 

numerous shield laws

 to protect people who provide, receive, or help others obtain healthcare that is legal in California. These laws prohibit California agencies and certain companies from helping other states enforce laws that punish this care. Yet the 

federal government

 and coordinated efforts in 

other states

 still 

threaten access

 to these legally protected healthcare services. 

AB 1854

 addresses these threats by expanding coverage to more California businesses and individuals who receive legal demands, creating a notification process so the Attorney General can intervene to stop improper disclosures, and clarifying that law enforcement cannot arrest someone if the Governor refuses an extradition request. These protections serve as a necessary response to real and escalating tactics outside the state targeting lawful reproductive healthcare.




EFF also supported 

AB 1930

 to protect confidential medical records from politically motivated investigations into lawful healthcare, empowering the California Attorney General’s office to meaningfully intervene and respond to out-of-state subpoenas or requests for data regarding protected care.




Young people online




EFF is dedicated to protecting the rights of young people online. We supported a handful of bills on 

digital literacy and cybersecurity education

 that were signed into law, such as 

AB 2071

 on digital wellness instruction and 

AB 2298

 on cybersecurity in educational standards. Unlike 

blanket bans

, these bills address online safety through education rather than prohibition. Young people rely on the internet not just for entertainment, but for 

civic engagement

, 

education

, 

self-expression

, and

 community

—especially vulnerable youth who may 

lack support

 in their physical surroundings.




Real digital safety comes from preparation, not isolation. Research consistently shows that 

open, honest conversations

 about digital literacy and privacy with trusted adults are 

far more effective

 at protecting youth than restrictive censorship laws. Young people themselves recognize this need; in fact, 

AB 2071 was co-authored by a group of students

 actively seeking better resources to navigate their digital lives safely.




EFF and our allies were also able to 

stop the expansion of California’s dangerous age gating law

 from operating systems to browsers. The California legislature 

stepped back from their plan

 to expand the 2025 age-gating law and ultimately removed language from 

AB 1856

 that could have compounded serious threats to users’ speech, privacy, and security just to browse the internet, and positively, removed the burdens on open-source operating systems.




Real digital safety comes from preparation, not isolation




While EFF still believes the underlying law that AB 1856 amends, 

AB 1043, is unconstitutional

, we appreciate that the legislature did not 

expand this problematic age-gating framework

 to browsers. We were also pleased that an earlier amendment to AB 1856 

reduced the threat to the open-source community

 by exempting open-source operating systems. Given these changes, EFF 

removed its opposition

 to AB 1856, and thanks the author for listening to concerns from advocates and developers.




Mourning Losses




Updating California’s Information Practices Act (IPA)




EFF was 

proud to co-sponsor

 

AB 1337

 this session alongside our friends at Oakland Privacy and Assemblymember Chris Ward, who is also the chair of the legislative LGBTQ Caucus. The bill unfortunately failed to cross the finish line after stalling in the Senate.




AB 1337

 would have updated California's foundational 

Information Practices Act of 1977

 and extended its vital privacy safeguards present at the state agency level to counties and cities. Today, city and county governments collect vast amounts of sensitive personal data (from public health records such as vaccinations, to welfare assistance details, to license plate reader data) and administer programs that were likely not contemplated back in 1977. Yet the law has simply not kept up with modern data practices, and California still has no state law governing how local governments handle this information. While we could not build enough political progress to pass the bill this session, closing this local privacy gap remains an urgent need for California.




Social media ban




Another major setback was the passage (and 

subsequent signing

) of a 

social media ban

 for youth under the age of 16 (

AB 1709

).




Technology and the laws that regulate it should support and empower young people, but AB 1709 falls far short of this goal. Using technology is how we learn and build community in today’s world, but laws 

such as AB 1709

 cut young people off from 

essential information and experiences

. They also particularly harm those already facing increased challenges who find safety in supportive online communities that they cannot always access in the physical world.




Technology and the laws that regulate it should support and empower young people




Denying minors access to digital forums or stripping out basic tools needed to navigate them will not make young people safer or healthier in the AI age. Research shows 

social media bans are ineffectual

 while denying young people opportunities to develop their own voices, share their art, practice religion, or engage in politics. These laws also hurt all of us. Age-gating requirements 

force everyone to give up more personal information

. To verify who can pass through online gates, companies will collect even more data, 

concentrating power

 in corporate hands rather than protecting people. AB 1709 is also inconsistent with 

rights to free expression

, meaning California will spend resources 

defending a law that will likely get tied up in court

.




Gutting California’s Invasion of Privacy Act (CIPA) 




CIPA was originally intended to protect personal privacy against surveillance and included a private right of action so consumers could hold corporations accountable in court. This is why EFF and allied organizations spent the two-year session strongly opposing 

SB 690

—a bill we dubbed the "

Corporate Cover-Up Act

" for its attempt to weaken consumer protections in CIPA. Although SB 690 

was narrowed from its original draft

, we asked Governor Newsom to veto it because it strips away the law's private right of action—a vital tool for individuals fighting back against unlawful metadata surveillance. People deserve the right to decide whether to 

bring a lawsuit

, which remains one of the most effective ways to deter corporate abuse. Unfortunately, the Governor signed the bill and even urged the legislature 

to go further next year.

 It's especially alarming to see this disregard for accountability as the federal government and law enforcement agencies seek data from businesses or data brokers to target people based on political beliefs, religious affiliations, or health decisions.




We expect to see further attacks on CIPA next legislative session, as 

Governor Newsom’s signing statement

 called for “additional work in this area” and urged the legislature to “take this on next year to ensure a fair balance between protecting private information and preventing rapacious litigation."




Banning the sale of sensitive personal information




California also missed the opportunity to join other states in restricting the sale of sensitive data. We are deeply disappointed that Governor Newsom vetoed 

AB 1542

, which would have ensured sensitive personal information stays private by banning its sale outright. There's a 

nationwide movement

 to protect consumers by making intimate details off-limits for businesses to sell or share. From 

precise geolocation

 and genetic data to private messages, health records, sexual orientation, and immigration status, sensitive data reveals the most private aspects of our lives. Monetizing this information fuels financial scams, predatory pricing, and warrant-free government surveillance. By 

vetoing this bill

, California not only fails to lead but falls behind other states, by missing a critical opportunity to protect our most vulnerable communities.




3D printing 




The California legislature unfortunately also passed 

AB 2047

, which aimed to make every 3D printer come 

pre-loaded with censorship software

. It's a law that is trying to prevent an act that 

is already illegal in the state

, and 

just won't work

. It was part of a recent sweep of 

misguided state bills

 which purport to go after "ghost guns," but actually 

“enshittify” 3D printers

 by introducing privacy risks and a new way to restrict or upcharge users. Lawmakers even considered including misdemeanor charges that would have impacted people using alternative open-source programs. Fortunately an outpouring of opposition from makers and civil liberties advocates resulted in a bill so limited that, despite having passed and been signed into law, will not affect makers until ASTM International publishes a standard — something the 

organization had not been considering doing

.




Where California Missed the Mark




Consumer privacy




California lawmakers also missed key opportunities to curb commercial surveillance. EFF supported 

AB 2564

, which prohibits retailers from engaging in 

surveillance pricing

, the invasive practice that allows corporations to offer the same product to two different people at two different prices based on scrutiny of their personal data. Unfortunately, the bill stalled on the last day of session.




The legislature also failed to move 

AB 322

, which would have safeguarded the privacy of Californians by placing restrictions on the collection, use, and sale of location data. Last year, EFF 

published a rubric for comprehensive location privacy laws

, outlining baseline standards states should meet to shield individuals from pervasive location surveillance. Since then, states like Connecticut, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, and Virginia have 

enacted new consumer privacy restraints on geolocation data

. Yet, even as these states move the ball forward, most of their laws leave significant gaps that still must be filled. California failed to make that change and protect residents from location surveillance.




Automatic license plate readers




California lawmakers have lagged in 

enacting meaningful limits

 on automated license plate readers with all proposed ALPR regulation bills failing to pass since 2022. 

SB 1013

 initially appeared on track to pass with broad support, but ultimately stalled in the final days of the session.




EFF maintains 

high standards for ALPR legislation

, favoring 

full bans or, at minimum

, strict warrant requirements and brief data retention limits. While we remained neutral on earlier versions of SB 1013, EFF and our partners 

ultimately opposed the bill

 after late amendments compromised key privacy protections. The final draft would have doubled the current data retention period and allowed agencies to archive rather than delete data unrelated to active investigations—effectively shifting away from data minimization toward indefinite retention. (We saw 

San Francisco adopt a similar proposal this year

). We encourage California lawmakers to draw from 

our ALPR legislative agenda

 to enact robust safeguards or ban ALPR mass surveillance altogether.




Looking Ahead




Next session, we expect ALPR legislation to be top of mind as 

states across the country

 reckon with the harms the technology has caused. We will also be monitoring the results and action following the 

state’s audit into California’s fusion centers

. Following calls from advocates to address privacy abuses and a lack of transparency, the Joint Legislative Audit Committee 

approved Senator Sabrina Cervantes’ audit request

 in March 2026. This builds on our past experiences working with JLAC audits to expose law enforcement overreach—such as 

the state auditor's damning 2020 report on law enforcement’s use of automated license plate readers

 and our 

2016 push to fix the deeply flawed CalGang database

. The audit will examine the legal authority, governance, and funding of the centers, map out state and private data systems accessed by personnel, and review protocols for handling data breaches and unauthorized surveillance. This audit will mark the first comprehensive review of these facilities in 13 years and should be released by Summer 2027. We hope lawmakers use the findings to rein in these centers and their unauthorized surveillance.




Other “zombie bills” are also expected to return next year, including legislation regarding the use of copyrighted material to train AI systems. Throughout the two-year session, EFF raised serious concerns about 

AB 412

, a bill that would require AI developers to identify and disclose copyrighted works used in generative AI training. We argued that complying with such a mandate is 

practically impossible

, as it demands information that often does not exist and cannot realistically be obtained. While we are glad the legislature paused to consider the best approach rather than rushing this policy forward, we expect legislation targeting fair use and AI training to return next session.




More broadly on AI, 

vulnerabilities

 and 

security issues

 have dominated recent news cycles, and everyday Californians feel real anxiety about the risks of AI. We expect to see numerous bills addressing issues like 

existential risk and kill switches

, as 

Assembly

 and 

Senate

 privacy committees in California have held informational hearings on these topics over the last month.




We hope to work with legislators to address the threats of AI and ensure that technology supports rights, justice, freedom, and innovation for all people. Laws should always ensure that technology empowers rather than oppresses.

author: Hayley Tsukayama
title: Join EFF to Celebrate the Life of Aaron Swartz
content:
Join us to 

celebrate the legacy of Aaron Swartz

 on Nov. 8, 2026. With the organizers of 

Aaron Swartz Day

, we’re honoring his life with an in-person and remote hackathon. This event is supported by several organizations that carry on his work, including the Internet Archive—which is hosting the in-person event—the 

Freedom of the Press Foundation

, 

Creative Commons

 and the 

Free Law Project

.




Aaron Swartz was a 

digital rights champion

 who believed in the need for an open internet. His life was cut short in 2013, after federal prosecutors charged him under the 

Computer Fraud and Abuse Act

 (CFAA) for systematically downloading academic journal articles from the online database JSTOR. Facing the prospect of a long and unjust sentence, Aaron died by suicide at the age of 26.




EFF was proud to call Aaron a friend and ally. We continue to stand with programmers and developers engaged in cutting-edge exploration of technology through our 

Coders' Rights Project

.




Hackathon participants can contribute code, documentation, and design to several open-source and public-interest projects. These include 

Secure Drop

, 

Open Library

, 

Quantifying the Commons

, 

Onion Press

, and our own 

Atlas of Surveillance

.  EFF Director of State Affairs Hayley Tsukayama will also join hackathon participants at the Internet Archive at 11 a.m. for an Atlas of Surveillance on-boarding session.




Contributors across experience levels are welcome. The Aaron Swartz Day organizers are also open to adding new projects and workshops, so please contact them at 

aaronswartzday@gmail.com

 if you’d like to suggest a workshop or project—particularly open-source projects on Github that participants can continue to work on after the event. For more details on how to participate in-person or remotely, please visit the Aaron Swartz Day and International Hackathon page at 

www.aaronswartzday.org

.




Event Details







Date:

 Sunday, November 8, 2026




Time:

 10:00 AM – 5:00 PM PST




Social Lunch:

 1:00 PM – 3:00 PM PST




In-person Location:

 Internet Archive Headquarters, 300 Funston Ave, San Francisco, CA 94118




Admission:

 Free, but please 

RSVP here

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Search called off for missing Gjoa Haven elder
content:
This story was updated on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026, at 9:45 a.m. ET.




The Hamlet of Gjoa Haven has called off a search for an elder who went missing two weeks ago.




On the morning of Oct. 21, 84-year-old David Siksik left home on his Honda ATV without a satellite messenger device to set fishing nets at a lake about 32 kilometres north of the community.




He never returned home, though his son,

 Allen Siksik, still believes he might.




“I do have hope,” Siksik said in an interview Thursday. “I still have hope, thinking he is waiting in a cabin, but no one could find even the ATV.”




Over 13 days, searchers travelled by ATV within 100 kilometres of Gjoa Haven, the hamlet said in a Nov. 3 update on Facebook.




A Canadian Coast Guard helicopter and a Royal Canadian Air Force Hercules aircraft assisted. Community members organized ground searches, including trips to Peel Inlet, on the northern coast of King William Island.
















The neighbouring community of 

Taloyoak pitched in fuel, Siksik said. 




Siksik believes his father may never have reached their family’s cabin, which is near the lake that David Siksik was heading toward, as there were no footprints or ATV tracks nearby.




Some lakes in the area were not completely frozen, and Allen said his father may have gone through the ice.




“I was just aching from trying too hard. Every time I went out, I thought I would find my dad and take him home, and it seemed like we were getting closer to him but no one could find him,” Siksik said. 




The hamlet announced in a Facebook post on Tuesday that its search and rescue team, alongside David Siksik’s wife Alice Siksik, agreed to call off the search.







“We have no choice, and we accept it,” Allen said, adding that his father prepared him for tough situations in life. 

“He told me to be strong for my family and my loved ones.”
















Allen said his family is grateful for the community’s efforts, with some searchers overnighting on the land in stormy weather.




On Facebook, the hamlet said the search could continue this winter, with specialized equipment to look beneath the ice. Aerial searches are expected to resume in the spring if David Siksik is not found.




Hunters and fishers travelling anywhere on the island this winter can have half their fuel costs covered if they agree to watch for signs of David Siksik or his Honda, the hamlet’s post said.




Correction:

 This story has been updated to correct 

David Siksik’s age.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Quebec coroner looking into death of Inuk girl
content:
A Quebec coroner is investigating the death of a four-year-old Inuk girl who died while under the supervision of Montreal’s youth protection services.




The girl, whose mother is from Nunavik, died in a hospital on March 31, after a worker at Batshaw Youth and Family Centres failed to respond to a request for an urgent visit at her family home, according to reporting by 

Radio-Canada.




“We can confirm that an investigation into the causes and circumstances of this death is being conducted,” said Jake Lamotta Granato, a spokesperson for Quebec’s coroner’s office, in an email to Nunatsiaq News.




Coroner Steeve Poisson has been assigned to the case, Lamotta Granato said.




“At the end of his investigation, should he deem it appropriate, the coroner may also issue recommendations aimed at protecting human life and preventing deaths under similar circumstances,” he said.




In late July, Santé Québec, which oversees health and social services in the province, announced it had ordered its inspection office to investigate the quality of youth protection services offered under its agency for Ouest-de-l’Île-de-Montréal — Universitaire area, which has jurisdiction over Batshaw.




The announcement about the investigation came days after the Montreal Gazette revealed three youth under Batshaw’s care — including the four year old girl — had 

died suddenly in March

.
















In an email to Nunatsiaq News, Santé Québec declined to confirm the Gazette’s and Radio-Canada’s reporting, as well as what prompted the investigation request.




The investigation will look into service gaps and compliance issues and make recommendations for improving the quality of youth and family services, the organization stated in a July 28 news release.




Santé Québec’s Ouest-de-l’Île-de-Montréal – Universitaire social services agency, whose jurisdiction Batshaw operates in, also declined to comment, citing confidentiality.




Spokesperson Myriam Paquet said the agency is collaborating with investigators to ensure “circumstances surrounding these events can be examined in an independent and rigorous manner.”

author: Sharon Zhang
title: El-Sayed Backs Van Hollen for Senate Leader as Calls to Replace Schumer Grow
content:
Van Hollen has previously criticized Schumer for his weak leadership during Trump’s second term.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Incoming freshman senator Abdul El-Sayed says that he would support progressive Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) to replace Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-New York) as Democratic leader in the Senate, advocating for a rejection of Schumer’s stalwart centrist mode of operation after Democrats’ massive blue wave.

“I’ve been very clear. I think he’d be an amazing Senate majority leader. Of course, that’s a choice he has to make about whether or not he wants to pursue that,” said El-Sayed in an interview with CNN on Thursday. El-Sayed added that Van Hollen, who backed El-Sayed during his primary race, seems “quite interested in another goal politically,” likely referring to Van Hollen’s hints that he is running for president in 2028.

“A vote is a choice between two or more options,” El-Sayed said. “If we have another option, I’m going to look at that and say, ‘who is best placed to get us action to get money out of politics, put money in politics, pass Medicare for All?’”

Van Hollen, who has led the charge for Democrats to rethink their leadership for over a year, has demurred on running for Senate leader, suggesting several times that he is not planning to run because he’s “kicking the tires” on a 2028 presidential campaign. Still, Van Hollen is a favorite for the position among many progressives, who point to things like his stances on foreign policy and his trip to El Salvador to visit Kilmar Abrego García last year after García was deported by the Trump administration.

This week, Van Hollen was the first sitting senator to call for an open process to consider replacing Schumer — or, at least, extracting more concessions out of the centrist, vehemently pro-Israel lawmaker who has served as Democratic leader for a decade now.

“No one should be committing to anybody as the next Democratic leader without having that conversation,” said Van Hollen in an interview with Bloomberg, demanding “commitments” on a more aggressive agenda to combat President Donald Trump and deliver on economic promises.

Other candidates have yet to emerge, and some Democrats have already pledged to back Schumer in the election, which is slated for early December. However, a large portion of the incoming Democratic senator class has openly rejected Schumer as leader — including Troy Jackson of Maine, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, Adam Hamilton of Kansas, and Juliana Stratton of Illinois, almost all of whom flipped their seats.

At the same time, public support for Democratic leaders has cratered as they have largely declined to use their leverage in key moments to oppose Trump’s agenda. An NBC poll released earlier this week found that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) has an approval rating of a mere 18 percent among voters; a petition shared by actor and activist Mark Ruffalo encouraging House Democrats to replace Jeffries had over 600,000 signatures as of Thursday afternoon.

Schumer’s approval is even worse than Jeffries’s, at only 13 percent.

Schumer has been speaking as though he was already democratically chosen by the caucus. “The issue is not me. I’ll be reelected as majority leader, but the issue is focusing on the American people and what they want,” he said on Wednesday after being asked how he would deal with the incoming class of senators who ran on platforms calling for new leadership.

Van Hollen has rejected this framing, and says that he wants Democrats to come together as a caucus and decide on an agenda before considering who would be best to deliver that plan.

In a call with nationwide activist group Indivisible, the organizers of the “No Kings” protests, on Thursday, Van Hollen said that the new leader must not take “baby steps” or a “finger in the wind” type of action, but something that “responds to the size of the American peoples’ cries and votes” that delivered the Democrats their decisive majority this week.

Indivisible has been a vocal advocate for new Democratic leadership for months. In the wake of the election, the group has launched a campaign opposing a “Schumer coronation,” saying that Americans have “closed the door on an entire political era” that includes Schumer in a memo sent out Thursday.

“Any Democrat who is considering business as usual, or unwilling to fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action — is not qualified to lead the party at this moment,” the group wrote. “Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation.”

author: Ali Harb
title: Dispatch From Dearborn: How El-Sayed Flipped Precincts That Had Voted for Trump
content:
Voters who spurned the Democratic Party in 2024 turned out en masse to elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

As the sun set in Dearborn, Michigan — a city on Detroit’s western border that is often called the “capital of Arab America” — the sense of urgency to elect Abdul El-Sayed to the U.S. Senate was becoming palpable on an unseasonably warm November election day.

The lines of hijab-wearing women and curly-haired young men at the polling stations on November 3 kept growing longer. More cars clogged up the streets around the schools that were serving as election precincts in normally quiet neighborhoods.

“Today, our vote is our power,” said Fares Alshawhati, an Arab American truck driver who was urging voters outside of a polling location to back El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate.

Now, election data shows that Arab voters in Dearborn needed little convincing to elect El-Sayed. The progressive former public health official approached 100 percent support in some of the most predominantly Arab precincts in the city.

It was a stunning swing in a community that had all but abandoned the Democratic Party two years ago over Israel’s wars on Gaza and Lebanon.

In one precinct in Dearborn’s Southend neighborhood, which is home to a large Yemeni community, more than 97 percent of the voters — 927 out of 949 — cast their ballots for El-Sayed. Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers received less than 2 percent of the votes in the Southend.

In 2024, Republican President Donald Trump won the same precinct with nearly 53 percent of the votes. His Democratic opponent, then-Vice President Kamala Harris, finished a distant third behind Green Party candidate Jill Stein. Harris received less than 13 percent of the votes.

That’s an 84 percentage point shift from Harris to El-Sayed among voters in the same precinct in two years.

And such shifts did not only occur in this one precinct. Across Dearborn, voters swung by dozens of percentage points in a dizzying political whiplash in anger at Trump and his policies.

“The Republicans made a targeted choice to use Islamophobia as their core line of attack against Abdul, and it backfired tremendously.”

El-Sayed won Dearborn with 82 percent of the vote. In predominantly Arab precincts on the east side of the city, support for El-Sayed surpassed 94 percent.

“I think that shift is very healthy actually because it indicates that the community is not a monolith and also that the community is moving where the country’s best interest is,” said Chadi Abdulrazek, an Arab American political activist who was volunteering to help elect El-Sayed.

“Two years ago, we were deep in a genocide,” Abdulrazek told Truthout. “This community was bleeding. We were all hurt. We were all seeing our families being slaughtered. We were all in pain for a long period of time, and the Democratic Party failed to stop that genocide.”

He added that Trump came and made big promises about being a man of peace, and some Arab Americans decided to give him a chance.

“Eventually he failed and made things worse. I think it is actually very smart to see that the community and people across the country are shifting their perspective because they’re seeing what has happened in the past two years,” Abdulrazek said.

Arab American voters interviewed by Truthout in Michigan consistently cited three reasons for backing the Democrats in this election cycle: Trump lied to the community about his foreign policy; they support El-Sayed’s policies, such as Medicare for All; and they were turned off by Republicans’ embrace of Islamophobia.

In the lead-up to the election, many Arab voters criticized Trump for breaking his promises about pursuing peace in the Middle East and for starting yet another destructive war in the region, while also continuing to offer unconditional support to Israel, even as it intensified its abuses in Gaza and the West Bank and sought to annihilate South Lebanon.

El-Sayed’s platform of ending funding to Israel and investing in local priorities also aligned with the community’s agenda. And his being Arab and Muslim further boosted his standing.

El-Sayed’s campaign manager, Alia Kapasi, hailed his gains in the Arab community, releasing a statement on November 5 saying:

In 2024, the Democratic ticket performed poorly with Arab-American voters in Dearborn. Abdul didn’t just make up those losses, but ran up the score. Record-breaking turnout in Dearborn was nearly 5% above 2024 turnout. While Harris lost the city by 6%, Abdul won by more than 65%. In Dearborn, nearly 3,700 more voters voted in the Senate contest than in the race for Governor.”

Kapasi also paid a nod to El-Sayed’s dominant performance in neighboring Dearborn Heights, which is also home to a large Arab community.

In order to win the senatorial race, El-Sayed was forced to overcome extreme and persistent targeting for his Muslim identity: Rogers and Trump had made El-Sayed’s faith a focal point of their campaign in Michigan.

Trump repeatedly called the Democrat a “jihadist,” as Rogers falsely accused him of ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas, and Hezbollah.

Voters were flooded with misleading ads on the subject.

One Republican-funded video commercial featured a woman in a burqa and baselessly suggested that El-Sayed would impose Sharia law if elected, warning that under Islamic rules, women cannot leave the house without a guardian.

“We concluded that the best response is through the ballot box — that we must all come out and vote.”

In her November 5 statement, El-Sayed’s campaign manager, Kapasi, underscored the bigotry against him, saying: “The Republicans made a targeted choice to use Islamophobia as their core line of attack against Abdul, and it backfired tremendously with one of the key constituencies that won Trump the presidency in 2024.”

In 2024, Republicans had softened their tone on Arabs and Muslims, seeing an opening in a community that was furious at Democrats over then-President Joe Biden’s uncompromising support for Israel.

According to estimates by the Arab American Institute — which corrects for undercounting by the U.S. Census — Michigan is home to nearly 400,000 Arab residents. In a state of 10 million people, that bloc of voters can be decisive.

So back in 2024, Trump and his team decided to woo them.

He personally visited Dearborn, spoke of peace, and invited Arab American supporters and local Muslim imams to the stage in one of his rallies.

The Republican president ended up winning Dearborn that year, and his staunchly anti-immigrant adviser Stephen Miller thanked the city on election night.

The honeymoon, however, was short-lived.

On his first day in office in 2025, Trump revoked U.S. sanctions against violent Israeli settlers. Weeks later, he called for removing Gaza’s entire population from the Palestinian territory and turning it into the “Riviera of the Middle East.”

While some may have given Trump the benefit of the doubt, the war on Iran — which he launched jointly with Israel earlier this year — left few Arab Americans in Dearborn on his side.

Then came Trump and Rogers’ Islamophobic campaign against El-Sayed, which pushed what remained of the local community’s Republican voters to the Democratic camp.

“The Republican Party and Trump came to Dearborn and … gave us false promises. But they don’t know the Arab community. The Arab community doesn’t forget.”

Trump had especially angered the Yemeni voters who backed him in 2024 after revoking temporary protected status for Yemeni immigrants earlier this year. More recently, the U.S. president called Yemen and other developing nations “shithouse” countries.

Abdulrahman Barman, an activist in Dearborn, said the Yemeni community had discussed ways to respond to the president’s comment and decided not to release angry statements.

“We concluded that the best response is through the ballot box — that we must all come out and vote, so our response is direct and practical,” Barman said.

In the mostly Yemeni Southend neighbourhood, turnout comfortably surpassed 2024 levels despite presidential elections usually drawing out more voters than the midterms.

After the polls closed on November 3, dozens of Arab Americans flocked to an election results watch party at a banquet hall on the east side of the city.

Celebrations began even before the results started to trickle in. The high turnout was enough reason for joy.

“Two years ago, the Republican Party and Trump came to Dearborn and … they bamboozled the Arab community and gave us false promises,” journalist and activist Hussein Hachem told the crowd. “But they don’t know the Arab community. The Arab community doesn’t forget. Today, the Arab community in Michigan and across the nation gave Trump a slap in the face that he will never forget for the rest of his life.”

author: Orion Rummler
title: Meet the Transgender and Nonbinary Candidates Who Just Made History
content:
Six candidates won races in states that have never elected a trans person into their legislature before.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Six transgender and nonbinary candidates made history on Election Day by winning races in states that have never elected a trans person into their legislature before. These candidates will expand LGBTQ+ political power at a time when their rights are increasingly under attack nationwide. All races are called according to projections by Decision Desk HQ.

Bentley Hudgins will be Georgia’s first nonbinary and first Japanese-American lawmaker after winning their bid to represent State House District 90 in east Atlanta. They easily defeated their opponent, Republican Samantha Boston, in the deep-blue district.

Hudgins, a 33-year-old democratic socialist, spent the last three years advocating for LGBTQ+ rights in the Georgia statehouse through their work with the Human Rights Campaign. But LGBTQ+ issues were not core to their campaign: They ran on affordability, expanding healthcare access and broadly protecting civil rights. Those issues are personal for them. As they had told The 19th, Hudgins faced homelessness and barriers to accessing care for cluster headaches and seizures. They were diagnosed as legally deaf at 19, and had to have their eardrums rebuilt.

Many of Hudgins’ campaign goals, like raising the state minimum wage to $20 an hour or creating an earned income tax credit to give money to lower-income Georgia families, depend on whether Democrats gain enough leverage in the state House to influence policymaking. The party needs to gain 10 seats in the chamber to reach a majority — and as of Wednesday morning, that feat looks possible.

Joanna Whaley, a hospital chaplain, will be the first trans person elected to Michigan’s state legislature after winning her race for House District 2, outside Detroit. A former megachurch pastor who has spoken openly about surviving years of “conversion therapy” as a young adult, Whaley acknowledged after winning her primary in August that her victory was “a defining moment for state history,” but added that her campaign “has never been about history.”

She handily defeated her opponent, Republican Ron Kokinda, with 63 percent of the vote.

Whaley ran on securing fair wages for workers, supporting statewide job training programs and lowering the cost of utilities and medical debt. She was endorsed by U.S. Rep. Sarah McBride of Delaware, the only trans member of Congress, and Abdul El-Sayed, who became the nation’s first Muslim senator on Tuesday. She was also backed by progressive advocacy groups and Democrats in the state legislature.

Whaley’s primary was contentious at times. In April, her Democratic opponent, former Michigan state Rep. Frank Liberati, claimed Whaley had violated state campaign law by omitting her deadname, or the name she used before transitioning, from the affidavit of identity she submitted to run for office. A county clerk denied Liberati’s challenge to Whaley’s candidacy in May.

In an interview with The 19th on Wednesday, Whaley said she was grateful to voters who crossed party lines to support her campaign. She heard from some Republicans that she was the first Democrat they had ever voted for.

“Our community has been so wonderful. They are just the most kind, good-hearted people who didn’t care who I was — they cared that I wanted to work for them,” she said. “To have Republicans voting for me means the world, and to have people all across the political spectrum believing in what we can do has been really awesome.”

Allison Montgomery will be Alabama’s first trans lawmaker after winning her bid for state House District 25, defeating incumbent Republican Rep. Phillip Rigsby. A software engineer and lifelong Alabamian, Montgomery ran on broadening access to healthcare, strengthening workers’ rights and eliminating the state’s grocery tax.

“I know the headlines tomorrow are gonna be provocative and catchy, but let’s focus on the most important part of this victory: we showed that a truly grassroots campaign that stands on its policies and its principles has a real shot in Alabama,” Montgomery said in a statement on Tuesday after her race was called. “We the people are tired of attempts to distract us with culture war issues, whether we’re in a minority group or not. We the people know corporate interests use these issues to pit us against one another while they pick our pockets.”

She added: “I’m going to work especially hard for those who hate me, because they deserve a better Alabama as much as anyone.”

Jaelynn Scott will be Washington’s first trans state lawmaker — and the first out Black trans state lawmaker elected in the country — after winning her bid for state House District 37 in southeast Seattle. She easily defeated her opponent, independent Evon McCorkle, a college student, with 88 percent of the vote.

Scott, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, is the executive director of the Lavender Rights Project, a Black- and trans-led civil rights nonprofit based in Seattle. Her pitch to voters centered largely on affordability, universal healthcare and taxing large corporations and billionaires. In an interview with The 19th on election night, Scott said she plans to lead “with love and compassion and empathy.”

“It’s pretty surreal,” she said of her barrier-breaking win. “The fact is, people that look like me and have my identity in 2026 are used to being under attack — not leading. I think it was because of what’s happening to us, and really maybe even a bit of fear about what might happen to me and my community, that inspired me to run. I never thought we would get this far.”

Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford will be the first trans person elected to the Wisconsin state legislature after winning her race for state House District 76. She defeated her opponent, Republican Nina Chat, with more than 90 percent of the vote in the deep-blue district.

Martinez-Rutherford, a former food service worker, comedian and small business owner, made history in 2023 as the first trans woman elected to the Madison Common Council in the state capital. She’s spoken previously about experiencing housing and financial insecurity.

Martinez-Rutherford’s campaign centered largely on economic issues, promising to fight for a living wage tied to inflation, affordable housing and access to quality healthcare.

“I’m honored to have made history, but that’s the last thing on my mind,” she told The 19th in an interview Wednesday morning. “It wasn’t ever about history; it was just about making sure that people are taken care of.”

In a hyperlocal race that still breaks national barriers, Quinnie Perez is projected to win her seat on the Orange County Soil and Water Conservation District. This humble board lacks a budget and has little power, but Perez winning the position in Seat 1 makes her the first trans woman ever elected in Florida.

Perez ran on supporting farmworkers with fair wages and safe conditions, highlighting her family history as the daughter of Mexican farmworkers, as well as wetland restoration and building green infrastructure.

Several other transgender candidates still made history, although they didn’t win. They ran in deep-red, conservative districts, taking on difficult fights without any guarantee of success. Some were the first Democrats to run for their seats in decades, signaling a new energy to run for office among trans people even as their identities become increasingly politicized. Others have had their candidacies or ability to vote questioned by local authorities due to their gender identity.

After Bella Bautista decided to run for Georgia State House District 14, she went on to become the first trans woman to win a legislative primary in Georgia. Her race was a long shot: Her district hasn’t elected a Democratic state representative since 1996. She ran anyway.

She is the first Democrat to run for this seat since 2010 — and it put a target on her back. As she told The 19th, this campaign cost her privacy and peace, leaving her feeling isolated in her rural and heavily conservative district. But she said she was determined to challenge the status quo. Her campaign focused on affordability, protecting rural land and fighting data centers.

Bobby Robertson Jr., a trans woman and financial analyst, lost her race for Kansas House District 73. But she still broke barriers as the first Democrat to challenge this seat in 10 years.

She decided to run for office after the statehouse passed SB 244, a law that invalidated thousands of trans Kansans’ drivers licenses based on gender identity, over the governor’s veto. She wrote several letters to her state representative, Republican Rick Wilborn, explaining how the law would hurt her and her family. According to Mother Jones, she asked him to meet. She never got a response. So she decided to act.

Avery Rowland, another trans woman in Kansas, ran to represent House District 2, in the bottom-right corner of the state. According to a report by Kansas Reflector, a state GOP official questioned her eligibility to vote over the state law that targeted trans residents’ drivers licenses.

Arienne Childrey previously challenged Republican incumbent Angie King in Ohio’s House District 84 in 2024 and lost. She lost again this election cycle.

Trans Ohioans have seen overt efforts to keep them off of the ballot in the state. Childrey’s ability to run for office was challenged in 2024 because she omitted her deadname on petition paperwork. She had legally changed her name years ago and had no idea about the obscure Ohio elections law that brought her candidacy into question.

Aiden Swallow, a military veteran of nearly two decades, lost her bid for Arizona House District 19 to former Republican state Sen. David Gowan. Swallow previously ran for Congress in Arizona’s 6th district, but dropped out of that race last year to run for the statehouse.

In this race, she faced two Republicans on the ballot as well as another Democrat, Jackie Anderson, a retired emergency room nurse.

Swallow’s campaign took a hard line against President Donald Trump and the MAGA movement in a GOP-controlled district — and that stance was personal. She was kicked out of the military in 2025 due to Trump’s nationwide ban on trans service members, which was allowed to stay in place by the Supreme Court. She was removed from her military position without retirement benefits, according to her campaign website.

title: Raskin Says Democrats Aren’t Afraid to Impeach Trump for a Third Time
content:
Impeachment is a “major instrument of constitutional self-defense” against corrupt presidents, Raskin said.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, likely the next chair of the House Judiciary Committee, has expressed greater openness to impeaching President Donald Trump following his party’s “blue wave” of election victories earlier this week.

Although Raskin previously served as manager of the Trump impeachment that followed the January 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol by a mob of the president’s loyalists, he has been reserved in recent months about the possibility of a third Trump impeachment.

In April, for example, following renewed calls for Trump to be impeached after he issued genocidal threats against Iran, Raskin told Time magazine that such moves should not yet be pursued, describing the effort as politically unviable.

“For people to say we should just go ahead and impeach him simply denies this political reality: There is not a single Republican who has called for impeachment or indicated to us interest in impeachment at this point,” Raskin said at the time.

With Democrats attaining 54 seats in the Senate following the midterms (and potentially as many as 56 seats, pending two “too close to call” elections that are still being tabulated), that math changes. Trump’s diminished power due to Democratic gains in Congress could also result in some Republicans being more open to the idea of removing the president, depending on the specific charges against him, if a Senate trial occurs.

In an Election Day interview with The Baltimore Banner, Raskin indicated that impeachment was definitely on the table.

“We’re not afraid to impeach Donald Trump. We’ve done it twice,” Raskin said. “He has 50 percent of all the presidential impeachments in American history. It’s Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton, and two for Donald Trump.”

“It cannot be a fetish, but it also can’t be a taboo either,” Raskin went on. “It is one of the people’s major instruments of constitutional self-defense against a president who continues to act like a king or an emperor.”

The shift in Raskin’s stance comes as another top Democrat, Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, has also expressed a new outlook on impeachment.

After refusing to back the idea early this year, Smith, who is currently the ranking Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, told Time last week that he now believes impeachment isn’t just viable, but necessary.

“Trump has become beyond dangerous. He is just completely out of control in what he says and how he is governing,” Smith said. “I think we have to try [to impeach], even if it doesn’t succeed.”

Yet presumptive Speaker-elect Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) has dismissed efforts to hold Trump and other administration officials accountable. Speaking on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” program on Wednesday, Jeffries stated:

The American people don’t want us to get even; they want us to get things done on their behalf, because life is way too expensive.

While affordability ranks highest on most voters’ lists of priorities, accountability is not far behind, recent polling has shown.

In an Economist/YouGov survey conducted just before the elections, 26 percent of likely voters said that “presidential leadership,” “corruption and waste,” and “democracy and the rule of law” were their top issues.

Impeachment is also likely to be embraced by voters if Democrats pursue it. A Politico poll from October found that 54 percent of Americans believe there are already grounds for impeaching Trump, while only 33 percent disagreed.

title: ΓΑΛΛΙΑ. Υπό τον κλοιό 1,6 εκατομμυρίου απεργών η κυβέρνηση Μακρόν
content:
Η Γαλλία έζησε μία από τις μεγαλύτερες κινητοποιήσεις στην ιστορία της, καθώς υπολογίζεται ότι συμμετείχαν περισσότεροι από 1,6 εκατομμύριο διαδηλωτές, σύμφωνα με τους διοργανωτές. Τα γαλλικά συνδικάτα ένωσαν τις δυνάμεις τους στην πανεθνική απεργία της 5ης Νοεμβρίου στη Γαλλία για αυξήσεις στους μισθούς και για υποστήριξη του κινήματος διαμαρτυρίας των μαθητών, ασκώντας νέα πίεση στην πολιορκημένη κυβέρνηση του Μακρόν.  Σήμερα φοιτητές, εκπαιδευτικοί, εργαζόμενοι, εργατικά συνδικάτα και μέλη του κινήματος των Κίτρινων Γιλέκων ενώθηκαν για να απαιτήσουν αλλαγές.




Η απεργία διοργανώθηκε από την L’intersyndicale,  που εκπροσωπεί όλα τα κύρια συνδικάτα της Γαλλίας. Η εκπαίδευση, η υγειονομική περίθαλψη, οι δημόσιες συγκοινωνίες και άλλοι τομείς επηρεάστηκαν και πολλές υπηρεσίες παρέμειναν κλειστές.




Μετά από περισσότερο από ένα μήνα τακτικών και μεγάλων διαμαρτυριών σε όλη τη Γαλλία, μεγάλες συγκεντρώσεις πραγματοποιήθηκαν στο Παρίσι, τη Λυών και τη Μασσαλία. Η

CNT-Solidarité Ouvrière (
