title: Ernesto Castro - We Have Confused Thinking with Certificates of Belonging Long Enough
content:
Author

: Ernesto Castro

Title

: We Have Confused Thinking with Certificates of Belonging Long Enough

Subtitle

: An interview with the Spanish philosopher Ernesto Castro

Source

: Retrieved on 2026-11-05 from 

<mowmag.com/attualita/-nei-vetri-rotti-non-c-e-nessun-significato-politico-intervista-totale-a-ernesto-castro-la-star-della-filosofia-mai-tradotta-in-italia-citare-sorel-o-benjamin-non-trasforma-un-incendio-in-una-tesi-di-dottorato>




Introduction




 In Spain, Ernesto Castro is something of an anomaly: an academic philosopher who fills lecture halls, who has turned his classes into one of the most-watched philosophy channels in the Spanish-speaking world, and who despite this (or perhaps because of it) remains wary of his own popularity. Born in Madrid in 1990, he teaches Aesthetics at the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, where for years he has been building a philosophical system of his own, which he has named “generic naturalism.” He has not yet been translated into Italian, and that gap is worth filling. 




 His bibliography has a range that in Italy would seem almost suspicious. There are books of ontology, such as 

Realismo poscontinental

, in which he tries to end the old trench war between analytic and continental philosophy. There is 

El trap. Filosofía millennial para la crisis en España

 (2019), which used a musical genre despised by highbrow critics to read the forms of life, desires and contradictions of the generation that grew up inside the 2008 crisis. There are the political essays, from 

Ética, estética y política. Ensayos (y errores) de un metaindignado

 (2020) to 

Memorias y libelos del 15M

, an unsparing reckoning with a movement Castro lived from the inside, at twenty, in the squares of the 

indignados

. And there is a Platonic trilogy of philosophical novels, opened by 

Jantipa o Del morir

 (2022) and continued with 

Perictione o De la libertad

 (2023), an epistolary novel set in Paris in 1968. 




 Why talk about him now, and why in Italy? Because the squares are full again. From France to Spain, from Portugal to Belgium and all the way to Milan, a new wave of protest, driven by the cost of living, low wages and the housing crisis, has brought back onto the streets a generation that waves One Piece flags alongside red and Palestinian ones, that is rediscovering the communist vocabulary, and that at the same time lives in countries where the ballot box rewards the radical right. Castro is one of the few European thinkers who has already been through all of this: he has watched a street movement be born, become a party, enter institutions and disappoint many of its promises. He talks about it without nostalgia and without cynicism, and with a quality rare in public debate: a willingness to contradict even those who consider him one of their own. 




 There is also a more intimate, distinctly Italian reason. The radical thought our struggles produced, from Tronti’s 

operaismo

 to Negri’s autonomism, has been read, debated and often mythologized elsewhere. Hearing how it is judged by a Spanish philosopher trained on Manuel Sacristán, one who refuses to “inherit the obligation to always prove it right,” is a good way of looking at ourselves in the mirror. The answers that follow are an exercise in what Castro calls the training of attention, as opposed to the management of indignation: drawing distinctions where everyone else generalizes, and thinking precisely when it would be most comfortable to stop. 




The Interview




1. From 15M to 2026.




 You took part in the 

indignados

 movement and wrote about it in 

Memorias y libelos del 15M

. Today protests have spread to France, Italy, Belgium, Portugal and Spain, driven by the cost of living, low wages and the housing crisis. Is this a return of 15M or something different? And what should these squares learn from 15M’s passage from the street to the institutions, with its promises and its disappointments? 




 It’s best not to turn 15M into a generic name for any discontent that takes to the streets. I took part in it at twenty, and precisely for that reason I distrust its retrospective canonization. The most valuable thing about those squares was that you could argue with someone who didn’t share your premises and leave the conversation thinking something else. When a movement turns into an identity to be defended, that possibility begins to disappear. We had come together to talk, and we ended up fighting over who got to speak on behalf of everyone. 




 Nor do I accept, just like that, on trust, that Podemos was 15M come of age. Assembly democracy and electoral competition follow different logics. Many demands for institutional transformation were lost along the way, while the initial plurality narrowed until it became a new division into friends and enemies. We left the two-party system without leaving binary thinking. 




 To today’s protests I would say: don’t confuse the success of your spokespeople with the satisfaction of your demands. That someone moves from the banner to the parliamentary seat may be wonderful for their CV. For those who still can’t pay the rent, it all remains to be proven. And I would also say: don’t turn defeat into a comfortable identity. Being right against the whole world is not the same as having changed something. 




2. The aesthetics of protest.




 In 

El trap

 you read millennial precarity through a musical form. Today in Paris you see One Piece flags in the marches, next to red and Palestinian ones. Has pop culture become Gen Z’s political grammar? Is it a sign of powerlessness or a new form of collective imagination? 




...

title: Carcere e domiciliari per la manifestazione del 31 gennaio a Torino
content:
Questa mattina la Questura di Torino ha eseguito diverse misure cautelari inerenti il filone di indagini sulla manifestazione nazionale contro lo sgombero del centro sociale Askatasuna di Torino, del 31 gennaio 2026.




All’alba diversi compagni e compagne sono stati prelevati dalle loro abitazioni dalla Digos per eseguire le misure cautelari decise dal Giudice per le indagini preliminari. 

Due compagni sono stati portati in carcere, sette agli arresti domiciliari, sei si vedono applicato il divieto di dimora a Torino con obbligo di firma quotidiana e un ulteriore obbligo di firma quotidiana.




Tutto questo avviene dopo che, una decina di giorni fa, la prima fase dell’operazione giudiziaria aveva convocato una ventina di persone davanti al Giudice per gli interrogatori di “garanzia”.




Compagni e compagne da diverse città del paese sono stati colpiti da questa inchiesta con accuse talvolta anche molto gravi come il 

“tentato omicidio”

, nell’intento di criminalizzare poche persone per un corteo di più di 50 mila persone che erano scese in piazza per protestare contro la stretta repressiva del governo Meloni e la “punizione” che questo aveva voluto infliggere alla città di Torino, colpendo uno dei simboli delle lotte cittadine.

Il Gip avvalla quasi in toto le richieste della Procura torinese disponendo misure che colpiscono in maniera pesante le persone inquisite.

 Le accuse spaziano dalla resistenza a pubblico ufficiale e danneggiamento fino al tentato omicidio e la rapina. I reati smisurati che vengono contestati sono l’immagine plastica di come la le istituzioni vogliano trasformare il dissenso e il conflitto sociale in un problema di ordine pubblico. Viene sposata una lettura della manifestazione che non tiene conto della spontaneità della rabbia di quella giornata e cerca di rinchiuderla tutta all’interno del solito teorema di “un’oscura premeditazione” , arrivando a disporre i domiciliari anche per chi è accusato solo di essere stato presente vicino o sopra il furgone del corteo.




Le lotte che hanno seguito lo sgombero di Askatasuna si sono inserite in un contesto più ampio di opposizione al governo e di rifiuto del genocidio contro il popolo palestinese, di cui è tutt’ora complice. In questi mesi assistiamo ad una grande sollevazione sociale contro il carovita di guerra e i suoi responsabili, gli arresti di oggi rientrano nella strategia del manganello adottata dal Governo per punire chi protesta.

 Oggi però non sarà solo il primo passo concreto di una ingiusta e criminale operazione repressiva, ma l’inizio di un’iniziativa di solidarietà che dovrà saper sostenere chi è stato colpito nelle spese legali che dovrà affrontare e per non lasciarli soli. 

Il 31 gennaio c’eravamo tutti e tutte! Que viva Askatasuna!




Network Antagonista Torinese

title: Ten pociąg już odjechał. Lewica w konflikcie o TK. (komentarz)
content:
Kolejne starcie w walce o polityczną kontrolę nad Trybunałem Konstytucyjnym wprawia w wyraźne zakłopotanie lewicowy komentariat.







Od piątkowego wieczora, gdy pod ochroną policji delegaci obecnej władzy opanowali budynek TK lewicowe blogi zdominował przekaż “nie moje małpy, nie mój cyrk”, tezy o zastępczym konflikcie wywołanym przez cichy sojusz władzy i prawicowej opozycji, ubolewanie, że społeczne emocje nie skupiają się na “prawdziwych problemach.”




Jest zrozumiałe, że problem bezprawnych działań rządu czy wykorzystania zinstytucjonalizowanej przemocy by zmienić skład instytucji, powołanej do kontroli poczynań władzy metodą faktów dokonanych może być niekomfortowy dla zwolenników państwowego socjalizmu, widzących w zdobyciu władzy politycznej przez lewicę drogę do realizacji ideałów wolności i sprawiedliwości. W końcu to zagrożenie oligarchizacją i samoistnym przekształceniem każdej władzy w dyktaturę są jednymi z najważniejszych argumentów w krytyce etatyzmu, nie tylko tej anarchistycznej. Milczenie lewicy w chwili, gdy zagrożenie to staje się realne nie jest dowodem jej intelektualnej wyższości, lecz własnej niemocy i braku przekonujących odpowiedzi na pytania, stawiane przez rozwój politycznej sytuacji.







Anarchizm i socjalizm to nie “prawie to samo” 

. Od czasów sporu Bakunina z Marksem o konieczność powołania “państwa socjalistycznego” jako etapu budowy bez państwowego społeczeństwa anarchiści rozwijają własną krytykę hierarchicznej władzy, a kolejne, historyczne doświadczenia potwierdzają słuszność jej założeń. Z anarchistycznego punktu widzenia to, czego jesteśmy świadkami to po prostu kolejny przykład tego, jak władza ustanowiona dzięki społecznym protestom i społecznej mobilizacji w krótkim czasie zmienia się w oligarchię, zmierzającą do przejęcia wszelkich instytucji mogących ograniczać jej kompetencje i gwarantować choćby niewielki zakres kontroli jej poczynań aż do momentu, gdy jedynym ograniczeniem uprawnień rządu staje się jego własna wyobraźnia. Historycznie proces ten był udziałem wszystkich “socjalistycznych demokracji” jakie próbowano ustanowić w różnych okresach i różnych punktach świata. Dziś, na naszych oczach, dotyka zaś demokracji liberalnych – udowadniając że zasada rządów prawa, demokratyczny konsensus czy konstytucyjne bezpieczniki nie są w stanie powstrzymać rządu, zdeterminowanego by poszerzyć własne kompetencje poza te zapisane w prawie. Liberalne państwo i jego demokratyczne instytucje nie jest w stanie powstrzymać samego siebie przed demontażem liberalnego porządku, gdy staje on na drodze realizacji “sprawczości” władzy. Może to zrobić tylko społeczeństwo, o ile jest zorganizowane, świadome swoich interesów i zdeterminowane do działania.







To fakt, że realistyczny zakres politycznych wyborów sprowadza się dziś do wyboru między dżumą a cholerą. Bez względu na to, czy w obecnym konflikcie zwycięży “uśmiechnięta dyktatura” czy “nowy faszyzm” – nie przybliży to w żaden sposób realizacji anarchistycznych ideałów. Wciąż jednak w naszym interesie jest, by ktokolwiek wygra, nie był dość silny by rządzić bez stałego zabiegania o społeczne poparcie. By w sporze z władzą, ktokolwiek będzie ją sprawować, sprawczość była po stronie społeczeństwa. Nawet pozorowane, sprokurowane na potrzeby politycznego spektaklu konfrontacje są realne o tyle, o ile generują realne społeczne napięcia i definiują nowe linie społecznych podziałów. Stać z boku i krytykować je z wyżyn własnej, intelektualnej refleksji to przegrać walkę o społeczeństwo na starcie – to jak stać na peronie i czekać aż nadjedzie wagon z napisem “uprawniony, socjalny konflikt społeczny” w czasie, gdy pociąg społecznych emocji znika już za horyzontem.

author: Joshua Carroll
title: Home Office Unlawfully Blocks Gaza Children From Joining Families in UK
content:
The Home Office is refusing to allow mothers and their children trapped in Gaza to join family members in the UK, even after a judge said the government’s position is unlawful.




The two women, who have five children between them aged seven and under, were told to submit biometric information as part of a security check to obtain family reunification visas.




But the application centre where they would need to submit fingerprints and other information has been closed since the start of Israel’s genocide in October 2023.




On 30 September, a judge in the immigration and asylum chamber of the upper tribunal ruled that the Home Office, by refusing to waive the biometric requirement for these families, had unlawfully applied its unsafe journeys policy.




In her ruling, judge Fiona Lindsley said the mothers and children – who have been granted anonymity – “have too little food and are suffering from malnutrition. They dare not go to US aid collection points as they are aware that people have been killed by Israeli forces at these places.”




She said the children’s fathers, who are based in the UK, were also suffering severe psychological hardship. One has been diagnosed with PTSD due to his experiences in Gaza “coupled with the continuous threat” to the survival of his wife and children, she added.




The Home Office has appealed the judge’s decision and a hearing is set for 16 December. But the Greater Manchester Immigration Aid Unit (GMIAU), whic

h

 

represents the families,

 said th

at process will further delay reunification and put the families “in grave danger” in Gaza.




“The children are all traumatised,” said Decla Palmer, a lawyer from GMIAU. “They have gone to bed every night to the sound of bombs, suffering from nightmares, with rats and mice crawling around their tent. The mothers are completely exhausted and without hope.”




“Every day the families remain in Gaza, they are at risk of death,” said GMIAU.




Surgeons who have worked in Gaza have said Israeli forces

 deliberately and systematically

 kill children. Dutch newspaper Volkskrant last year 

published testimony from doctors

 who had encountered at least 114 children with multiple bullet wounds in the head and chest.




A Home Office spokesperson told Novara Media that “enrolment of biometrics enables comprehensive checks… to identify individuals who may pose a threat to national security, public safety or immigration controls.”




Ghassan Ghaben of the British Palestinian Committee, an advocacy group, said the government was applying a double standard against Gazan families.




“The UK has shown in other situations that, when there is the political will, rules can be adapted to the realities of war – and in this case, genocide,” he said. “The Ukraine Family Scheme recognised that ordinary immigration procedures were not appropriate in the circumstances and enabled people to reunite with their families.”




Since the Russian invasion in 2022, Ukrainians and their children have been able to live and work in Britain under special temporary humanitarian visas.




“Palestinians have been asking for a similarly practical response since 2023, yet the response has instead been to maintain or introduce even stricter barriers,” said Ghaben.




He added there was “a real contradiction” between the shift in rhetoric about Gaza from Andy Burnham’s Labour government and its treatment of the families. 




“The home secretary has recently announced the reopening of the UK Resettlement Scheme, and spoken about creating safe and legal routes for people fleeing persecution,” he said.




“Yet at the same time, the Home Office is continuing to fight against the reunification of Palestinian mothers and young children with their fathers who are already in the UK.”




During the genocide in Gaza, the UK has 

allowed weapons

 sales to Israel, flown spy flights over Gaza, allowed 

military planes to depart

 from its bases bound for Israel and 

refused to investigate British nationals

 who joined the Israeli military.




Home secretary Shabana Mahmood was accused last month of

 

giving people in Gaza “false hope”

 after announcing a new safe route to the UK for Palestinian refugees. The route only applies to those who have 

already escaped to Lebanon or Jordan

 and will benefit only a few hundred people a year.




Last year, the government suspended a programme that allowed people granted asylum in the UK to bring their family members over.

title: Why I Launched an Antidepressant Injury Petition
content:
Kim Witzak writes on 

Substack

 about her recently launched 

petition

 calling for better research, stronger warnings, and truly informed consent regarding antidepressants.




“After my husband Woody died by suicide five weeks after being prescribed Zoloft, we reported what happened directly to the top FDA officials. Like so many other families, I quickly learned how easily an individual experience can be dismissed because it isn’t considered proof. I was told Woody’s story was “just an anecdote.” That has stayed with me ever since.




The more experiences we bring together, the clearer the picture becomes—and the harder it becomes to ignore. Your voice matters.”

author: Isabel Seta
title: Como anda a democracia? Pergunte a um indígena – com Maíra Pankararu
content:
O 

Bom dia, fim do mundo

 da semana recebe Maíra Pankararu, advogada indígena que atuou no julgamento do Marco Temporal no Supremo Tribunal Federal e que compõe a 

Articulação dos Povos Indígenas do Brasil

 (APIB) e a Articulação Nacional das Mulheres Indígenas Guerreiras da Ancestralidade (ANMIGA).




Na conversa com Isabel Seta e Ricardo Terto, Maíra fala sobre a onda de violência contra indígenas ocorrida após as 

eleições

, em especial no Mato Grosso do Sul, e sobre as dificuldades enfrentadas por comunidades indígenas para exercer o direito ao voto. O episódio também aborda a participação indígena na democracia de forma mais ampla e como isso só é possível tendo o direito ao território assegurado, uma luta que é dos povos indígenas, mas é fundamental para toda a sociedade e para manter a floresta em pé. Ouça agora.







E MAIS:




No quadro “Se é pra falar de economia…”, Clara Marinho pede: demarcação já.

title: Προβληματισμοί για τη χάραξη της γραμμής 4 στα Εξάρχεια & γιατί πρέπει να ανοίξει η πλατεία Εξαρχείων
content:
Σύνδεσμος δημοσίευσης: 

Προβληματισμοί για τη χάραξη της γραμμής 4 στα Εξάρχεια & γιατί πρέπει να ανοίξει η πλατεία Εξαρχείων










Η εκδήλωση θα μεταδοθεί από το OmniaTV

:







YouTube




PeerTube




Facebook













Η γραμμή 4 του μετρό, το μεγαλύτερο δημόσιο έργο της χώρας, έχει εκτροχιαστεί. Οι σοβαρές ζημιές στα κτίρια της Κυψέλης,  η απόρριψη της μελέτης για τον σταθμό Ριζάρη από το ΣτΕ, οι δικαστικές διαμάχες σε Γουδί, Αλεξάνδρας και Εξάρχεια αποκαλύπτουν ότι ο τρόπος σχεδιασμού του δεν έγινε προς το συμφέρον των ανθρώπων της πόλης, αλλά με γνώμονα τα υπερκέρδη των μεγαλοεργολάβων, θυσιάζοντας την ασφάλεια και την ποιότητα ζωής όλων μας.




Η επιλογή χάραξης της γραμμής – των σημείων που κατασκευάζεται η σήραγγα και που βγαίνουν οι σταθμοί –  οι ελλιπείς και σε κάποιες περιπτώσεις ανύπαρκτες μελέτες για το υπέδαφος, τα κτίρια, το περιβάλλον, η αδιαφορία για τα «θέλω» και τις ανάγκες των ανθρώπων των γειτονιών διαμόρφωσαν εξαρχής ένα ασφυκτικό πλαίσιο. Οι γειτονιές μας έχουν μετατραπεί σε απέραντα εργοτάξια, οι ελεύθεροι χώροι μας καταστρέφονται, τα σπίτια μας, τα σχολεία και τα δημόσια κτίρια κινδυνεύουν. Σε όλα αυτά έρχεται να προστεθεί και η εκτίναξη του κόστους του έργου, που ήδη υπολογίζεται στο μισό δισεκατομμύριο ευρώ, σε συνδυασμό με τις καθυστερήσεις παράδοσής του, αφού πια γίνεται λόγος για το 2036 και αν.




Οι γειτονιές αντιστέκονται και τα Εξάρχεια ήταν από την αρχή μπροστά. Η ανοιχτή συνέλευση «Όχι μετρό στην πλατεία Εξαρχείων» εδώ και 5 χρόνια, με έρευνα και πολλή δουλειά, έχει ξεσκεπάσει με κάθε μέσο που διαθέτει την σκανδαλώδη επιλογή κυβερνήσεων, ΕΛΛΗΝΙΚΟ ΜΕΤΡΟ και αναδόχων του έργου να χρησιμοποιήσουν τη γραμμή 4 ως μέσο αλλαγής φυσιογνωμίας της γειτονιάς μας. Η επιλογή κατασκευής του σταθμού στην πλατεία,  όπου ο σταθμός δε χωράει ακόμα και με τεχνικούς όρους, η υποβάθμιση της ζωής των κατοίκων της με την κοπή των δέντρων, τις λαμαρίνες, το κλείσιμο δρόμων κ.ο.κ., η απομόνωση και πραγματική υποβάθμιση των συνθηκών κατοικίας και δραστηριοποίησης στην περιοχή είναι πλέον εμφανείς ακόμα και στους πιο δύσπιστους. Και βέβαια η απάντηση σε όλα αυτά από την πλευρά της κυβέρνησης είναι η καταστολή.




Η πλατεία Εξαρχείων πρέπει να απελευθερωθεί! Όποιος ακόμα επιμένει ότι το έργο αυτό πρέπει ουσιαστικά συναινεί στην καταστροφή όλων αυτών που ορίζουν τι είναι η γειτονιά.




Την Πέμπτη, 5/11, παρουσιάζουμε και συζητάμε μελέτες που αποδεικνύουν την επικινδυνότητα συνέχισης του έργου με τους υπάρχοντες όρους στα Εξάρχεια, ενημερωνόμαστε και προχωράμε ένα βήμα πιο κοντά στην τελική νίκη! Κανείς πλέον δεν μπορεί να ισχυριστεί ότι δεν ήξερε. Όλοι και όλες μαζί θα σώσουμε την πλατεία Εξαρχείων, την ύπαρξή μας στη γειτονιά όπως εμείς την ορίζουμε.




Ανοιχτή Συνέλευση “Όχι μετρό στην πλατεία Εξαρχείων”




*Στην εκδήλωση θα παρουσιαστούν μεταξύ άλλων στοιχεία που αφορούν το σύνολο των κτιρίων που βρίσκονται επί της χάραξης και της ζώνης επιρροής εργασιών στην περιοχή Νεάπολης – Εξαρχείων, καθώς και η κατάσταση του υπεδάφους στην ίδια περιοχή.Επιπλέον, εκτός των ομιλητών/τριών παρεμβάσεις θα γίνουν από τη δικαστική επιμελήτρια, Ξένη Κεσίνη και τον Νίκο Κρασάκη, δομοστατικό πολιτικό μηχανικό.

author: Freedom Editor
title: Social reheating in Italy: Reflections on Friday’s mass strike
content:
The day was a breath of fresh air, with large turnouts opposing both war and the rising cost of living

30 October was a remarkable day. Not for many years has a strike called solely by grassroots trade unions achieved such success on a national level, with dozens upon dozens of local demonstrations filling streets and public squares. Various accounts highlight several common features: intergenerational participation, a significant role played by students, and a broad turnout of workers—all of which point to the clear success of the strike, even as the specific participation figures await further analysis.

Most striking, however, was the large number of young people—many of them very young, and some even minors—whom the government seeks to chain to school desks or factory benches, or else cast directly into juvenile detention centres. The first, clear outcome of 30 October was the overturning of fear. These major demonstrations reclaimed the public space—in squares, schools, universities, and workplaces. Repression was certainly present, with police charges in Rome, Turin, Vicenza, and Venice, alongside mass identity checks and pre-emptive detentions in many other cities.

Furthermore, news emerged that on 31 October, searches were carried out across the country targeting over 60 individuals—allegedly in connection with the street tensions of previous weeks, though seemingly only on the grounds of so-called “incitement.” Yet, on the day of the strike itself, the government chose not to intervene against the demonstrations; even various symbolic acts—such as blockades (notably at ports) or the occupation of university buildings—largely took place without police interference. Another clear outcome of the strike is that it has sidelined cross-class perspectives, as well as right-wing tendencies—such as those seen in the truckers’ protests—which could otherwise have played a role in the tensions currently brewing in the country.

Certainly, 30 October offers a breath of fresh air: such large turnouts in public squares, opposing both war and the rising cost of living, open up new possibilities at a time when the horizon appears increasingly bleak. Yet, it is worth noting that this day did not come entirely as a surprise. Although organised in a rush—lacking the typical, extensive preparation that usually precedes a general strike—this day of action was specifically crafted to address a social situation that had become increasingly explosive.

In fact, the month of October brought long-standing issues to a head. Over the last few weeks, growing discontent with the consequences of the government’s pro-war policy has spilled out into the streets and public squares—albeit in a fragmented way, and with many limitations and contradictions. Various segments of society, seeking to respond to the rising cost of living, engaged in forms of struggle that were met with government repression. Faced with these unmistakable signs, many grassroots trade union organisations decided to call for a strike on 30 October. The event served as a catalyst for the pressures building within society and for protests that had, in some instances, already been suppressed by the government.

After such a day there is a need for continuity, to avoid 30 October having been just a relief valve, after which the movement disperses with the risk that it could be recovered by the party and union bureaucracies. We should take to the streets every week, every day, against war and high prices, to bring down the new repressive rules, to bring down this fascist government. But we must also question the reality around us and understand what are the times and tools with which we can continue. For example, the anti-strike law, starting from the constraint of objective rarefaction, does not allow using only the strike tool to develop a movement. The student components of schools and universities can play an important role again at this time, in some cities already fully mobilised, but in others still at a standstill.

The phase we are going through could have disruptive outcomes, also creating deep fractures in society. We consider that in addition to an exaggerated use of institutional violence both in the streets and in emergency legislation, for the first time the fascist government is testing on a national scale the use of violent groups and gangs outside the state apparatus. In recent weeks, fascist groups have staged small provocations in many squares, even CasaPound and Forza Nuova, as well as Futuro Nazionale, regardless of their front position towards the government, have gone into action, for now at a low level.

Even the announced mobilisation of some football fan groups historically aligned to the right, against “maranza”, “casseurs” and demonstrators in general, must not be seen as folkloristic curiosity, but as an attempt to organise extralegal violence. It is no coincidence that in this climate, as if in response, ultras groups marched in some strike squares and lined up in support of the demonstrators. The legislative arsenal put in place by the government in recent years, together with other reforms not yet launched, such as that on self-defence, goes in the direction of fuelling political violence by protecting the defenders of privilege.

In such a complex situation we cannot choose to wait or delegate the solution to others. We need to organise ourselves and build the present and future we want.

author: Lance Selfa
title: Trumpism swamped at the ballot box
content:
The US midterm elections were a stunning rebuke to President Trump and the Republican Party.

Votes are still being tallied around the country. But the extent of the Democratic Party’s victory is becoming clear. In Congress, Democrats will take office in January 2027 with majorities in both houses that were at the upper end of expectations before the election.

In fact, the national popular vote margin in favour of the Democrats is the largest since the mid-1970s Watergate era, and Democrats could end up with as many as 56 (of 100) senators, up from their current number of 47. That would be the largest Senate majority of either party since 2009. Media estimates predict a House majority of at least 250 Democrats (of 435 House members). That would be the largest House majority for either party since the early 1990s.

Democrats won Senate seats in longtime conservative Republican strongholds like Kansas (which hadn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1932), Texas and South Carolina. Democrats made gains in every demographic group and region, compared to Kamala Harris’s performance in the 2024 presidential election.

In 2024, Harris lost a close race to Trump largely because, as the incumbent vice president, she carried the can for the Biden administration’s inability to tackle the inflation eroding working-class living standards. Key to Trump’s victory was his ability to add small, but significant, numbers of inflation-strapped voters among young people and people of colour (especially Latinos) to his “base” of white, middle-class Christian conservatives.

But Trump’s policies—from his erratic tariffs to the war against Iran, to huge cuts to medical assistance to fuel tax cuts to the rich—worsened the ability to afford necessities. What’s more, the administration’s unleashing of camouflaged thugs to arrest, imprison and deport hundreds of thousands of immigrants outraged millions. Democrats also tapped into disgust with the open corruption of Trump and his cronies, along with their disdain for the struggles of ordinary people.

The impact of these Trump actions repulsed all the groups who took a chance on Trump in 2024. Going into the 2026 midterms, opinion polls showed Trump to be the most unpopular president since Harry S. Truman in 1946. So, a pro-Democratic “wave” election wasn’t really in doubt. The question was how high the wave would be when it crested.

As has happened historically, Democratic gains rode atop a surge of Black (and more recently, Latino) voters. After the Supreme Court eviscerated the Voting Rights Act last summer, many civil rights advocates feared the return to political Jim Crow and a strengthening of one-party Republican rule in the southern states. But Black voters’ outrage expressed on 3 November had the impact of breaking through Republican domination in states like North Carolina, Georgia, South Carolina and even Mississippi.

In Texas, Latino voters forced a generational change and statewide sweep of the state that had become the cradle of post-civil-rights-era Republican politics. If the Republicans, as they are currently constituted, “lose” Texas, they will lose any sort of national political viability for a generation.

The 3 November results do not undermine the case for new civil rights and voting rights protections to undo the damage Trump and the Supreme Court have inflicted on the gains of the 1960s civil rights movement. But they show that breaking what former AFL-CIO political director Michael Podhorzer calls the “

Greater Confederacy

” is possible.

Trump and the Republicans had nothing positive to offer to voters. And they and their deep-pocketed donors spent billions attempting to excite their base with non-stop anti-trans and racist messaging against their Democratic opponents. Abdul el-Sayed, the Democratic senator-elect from Michigan, took the full brunt of an Islamophobic campaign against him—not only from his Republican opponent, but also from pro-Israel Democratic Party politicians and operatives.

But all of this failed to rescue Republicans, even in their longtime strongholds. The voting majority rejected these “culture war” appeals, seeing them as deliberate attempts to distract from Republican malfeasance and catering to the rich. When all is said and done, Elon Musk will have figuratively lit half a billion dollars on fire.

It’s important to understand the election as a repudiation of Trump and Republican rule, not an endorsement of whatever it is the Democratic Party stands for. In many ways, and in many parts of the country, the electorate voted for progressive ballot measures. Voters in Missouri and Virginia codified abortion as a state constitutional right. Virginia voters ended the lifetime denial of voting rights to convicted felons and upheld same-sex marriage. In almost every locality where a moratorium or regulation on AI data centres—hated symbols of Big Tech oligarchs—was on the ballot, it passed.

But while the progressive tide on ballot measures was undeniable, it wasn’t universal. For example, some anti-trans measures passed, Idaho’s abortion ban remains in place, and Oklahoma elected a governor who wants to jail abortion patients. The proposed “billionaire’s tax” lost in California, mostly because many Democratic politicians opposed it.

And there is no denying the reactionary policies of some Democratic politicians, like Texas senator-elect James Talarico or Iowa senator-elect Josh Turek, who opportunistically threw trans people under the bus, or who insisted that they were for “border security”. That’s a reminder that while the Democrats may be the other option to the GOP on most ballots, 

they are not an opposition party

. The Democratic Party is a corporate-backed entity dedicated to supporting American capitalism and US empire.

Democrats campaigned on vague promises to bring “affordability” to ordinary Americans and “accountability” to the criminals in the Trump administration. But now that they have won congressional majorities, the voters who enabled those majorities will want to see real action. Half-hearted measures crafted to get around a Trump veto won’t suffice.

The corporate Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become speaker of the House in January, is already trying to soft-soap pledges to hold Trump and his minions accountable for corruption and law-breaking. Dems will also come under pressure not to “cut and run” from the Middle East if congressional majorities move to cut off funds for Trump’s war. Already, Big Tech is looking to hire Democrat-connected lobbyists to defend its interests on Capitol Hill.

The voters rejected what they saw as a corrupt status quo rigged in favour of a handful of billionaires and oligarchs. They are not looking for the Democrats to reconstruct that status quo on slightly more polite terms. If Democrats don’t realize that, they are setting themselves up for an even bigger defeat than 2024’s in the future.

One last point. When Trump came into office touting a mandate for a reordering of society along hard-right, ethnonationalist lines, about every major “liberal” institution capitulated to him. Law firms. Universities. Businesses that had touted their commitment to diversity. Even some labour unions, like the Teamsters. A considerable number of Democrats voted to support Trump’s program of mass arrests and deportations. For a few months, Trumpism appeared to be a juggernaut.

But ordinary people weren’t as cowed. Their bravery, particularly in organising to defend immigrants from raids in Los Angeles, Chicago and, most importantly, Minneapolis, gave confidence to millions. Minneapolis unions and activists mounted a mass political strike in January. Without these efforts to fight back against Trump’s depredations, his support would not have collapsed as rapidly or as thoroughly. No politician did that.

That will be an important lesson to remember in what will continue to be a long struggle to send Trumpism into the dustbin of history.

First published at the 

International Socialism Project

.

title: SAVE THE SOUTH SUFFOLK ONE!
content:
Oh, wait… sorry. The Judge already did that in court. 




John ‘Pinocchio’ Henty’s case ends in acquittal

. 




Thank you to

 

South Suffolk Hunt Sabs

 

for this guest article.




A court case brought by former Essex & Suffolk Hunt huntsman John Henty against a hunt saboteur has ended in a resounding victory for the defence, with the saboteur found NOT GUILTY.




John Henty outside court.




Following allegations made to police, former Essex & Suffolk Hunt huntsman John Henty pursued a prosecution alleging abusive and threatening behaviour under Section 5 of the Public Order Act. The case followed an incident on a quiet country lane in which Henty pursued the hunt saboteurs’ vehicle, blocked it in, approached it and attempted to provoke a reaction.




What followed was a lengthy legal process based on Henty’s account of events. However, when his evidence was examined in court, serious questions arose about the credibility of that account and whether the alleged behaviour actually amounted to a criminal offence.




A case that should never have reached court?




The Judge was highly critical of the way the case had been handled by the CPS and the police officers involved, making clear that the alleged actions did not meet the legal threshold required for a criminal offence.




Both the prosecution and the defence barrister sought to discontinue the case on more than one occasion. The case was nevertheless directed to proceed. The circumstances surrounding that decision raise serious questions about why so much time and public money were spent pursuing a prosecution that ultimately failed.




Former Essex & Suffolk Hunt huntsman John Henty is now at The Ludlow Hunt.




The evidence tells a different story




Henty submitted two video clips, recorded by himself, which were played in court. The footage showed Henty pulling his vehicle alongside the hunt saboteurs’ Land Rover, getting out of his own accord and filming the encounter.




Our saboteur told Henty to ‘f*ck off’ before closing the vehicle door. Rather than disengaging, Henty continued filming and engaging with the occupants. Despite claiming under oath that he had been alarmed and distressed, the circumstances captured on his own footage told a different story.




The prosecution was unable to produce further evidence demonstrating that Henty had experienced the alarm or distress alleged.




Henty spun a yarn of lies that should never have made it to court.




The judge’s conclusion




Having heard Henty’s evidence under cross-examination and considered the footage and relevant law, the Judge concluded that:







Henty had parked his vehicle alongside the saboteurs’ vehicle of his own accord.




He had got out of his vehicle voluntarily.




He had chosen to film the encounter.




He had continued the interaction of his own accord.




He had not contacted the police immediately, instead reporting the incident to 101 approximately two hours later.







These circumstances were central to the Judge’s assessment of Henty’s claim that he had experienced fear, alarm and distress. Following Henty’s evidence and cross-examination by the prosecution and defence, the case concluded without our hunt saboteur needing to take the stand.




The verdict

: 

Not guilty. Acquitted.




After all the allegations, the police involvement, the CPS proceedings and the considerable expenditure of public resources, the case ended in an acquittal. A considerable amount of time, money and public resources had been spent pursuing this matter, only for the court to reach a conclusion that raises serious questions about why the prosecution was pursued in the first place.




Hunt saboteurs will not be intimidated out of exposing illegal hunting. And they will not be silenced by allegations that cannot withstand scrutiny in court.




The South Suffolk One stands vindicated.




SAVE THE SOUTH SUFFOLK ONE!




South Suffolk Hunt Sabs remain steadfast and will not be intimidated or silenced.




Show some support to 

South Suffolk Hunt Sabs.



















The post 

SAVE THE SOUTH SUFFOLK ONE!

 appeared first on 

Hunt Saboteurs Association

.

author: Paul Tiyambe Zeleza
title: The End of the Trump Era: The Democratic Sweep of the Midterm Elections
content:
Early this morning, I was woken up by a text from my daughter in Atlanta, nine hours behind Sharjah, UAE, where I’m currently located. Dems are leading, she exclaimed. Can you chat for a quick second? Before I called her, she sent another text, saying, it’s breaking news: Keisha Lance Bottoms is the projected winner as Governor of Georgia. My daughter, who has lived in Atlanta since she went to university there in the early 2000s, was ecstatic beyond measure.




Our celebratory chatter woke up my wife, a political scientist and keen observer of American politics. The ancestors must be smiling, she proclaimed with giddy excitement. We switched on the television and followed the elections on American stations we had access to, including CNN International and Bloomberg, while simultaneously perusing newspapers including The New York Times and The Guardian.




The more we talked and thought about the unfolding election results, I couldn’t help and filtering the elections through Africanist and global lenses, the clearer it became that this stunning blue wave, which polls had been predicting, represented political triumph in five dimensions, what I would the 5Ds: democrats, democracy, diversity, demography, and development.




The Democratic Victory




The Democrats won a resounding victory. Their victories swept the electoral map in Congress and across red states, as they held on to their constituencies. It was a political tsunami that routed President Donald Trump and the Republicans in a stunning rebuke of their failed policies and divisive politics, in which diversionary and inflammatory cultural wars trumped the deteriorating material conditions and interests of the electorate.




Democrats seized both chambers of Congress. Their candidates flipped seven Republican seats in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas, red states some of which had not elected a Democrat in decades. They retained seats in five states, namely, Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, and Virginia.




At the time of writing, the Democrats had flipped 35 seats previously held by Republicans in the House, including multiple seats in states won by Trump by more than 10 points such as Texas, Iowa, Florida, and Pennsylvania, along with key wins in Kentucky, Missouri, Nebraska, Ohio, and Utah. They successfully defended all or nearly all of their incumbent districts , including 22 that were considered vulnerable because Trump carried them by more than 10 points in the 2024 election, and are projected to win 242 to 258 seats when all the votes are counted, 40 more than they need to form a majority.




In a tectonic shift, at the time of writing, with 32 of the 36 seats contested, Democrats had also flipped five state governorships from Republicans in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa, and Nevada, and successfully defended 15 states. They won a total of 29, earning a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010.




So far, with final calls still processing, Democrats have flipped 12 of the 88 state legislative chambers on the ballot from Republican control in Pennsylvania (Senate; they already controlled the House), Wisconsin (both chambers), Arizona (putting Republicans in a legislative minority for the first time in 26 years), North Carolina (House), and drastically broke Republican supermajorities in states like Florida, South Carolina, and Indiana. They successfully defended 25 legislative chambers, including competitive ones in states like Maine, New Mexico, Oregon, and Washington, where they were able to preserve existing Democratic trifectas.




Similarly, Democrats dramatically outperformed Republicans in races for attorney general and secretary of state offices. For the former, the biggest upsets were in Texas and Georgia, while key defensive holds included Nevada and Michigan. Democrats also won the majority of contested secretary of state offices, seizing several from Republicans and holding those they held before.




The Resurgence of Democracy




America’s beleaguered democracy won. Electoral democracy in the United States has always been compromised by gerrymandering, voter suppression, politicization of the judiciary, and the financialization of politics. funding. This is why a conservative outfit like The Economist considers the United States a flawed, rather than a full, democracy compared to its increasingly alienated Western allies such as Canada.




Gerrymandering spectacularly backfired for Republicans. They redrew congressional boundaries across seven states, including Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Alabama, and Louisiana) hoping to flip 15 vulnerable or targeted seats. Democrats succeeded in redrawing maps only in California, seeking 5 pickup opportunities, and Utah an additional seat was created after a court order that struck a Republican map.




Democrats won or held onto at least 10 of the 15 seats targeted by Republican gerrymandering, while successfully defending their own incumbents in heavily redrawn territory. In California and Utah, the Democrats successfully swept all six of their projected pickups, including 3 critical flips in California and won Utah’s court-ordered 1 redistricting seat. This might be one of the most consequential results of the election: the erosion of gerrymandering as a potent political weapon.




Voter suppression involves the imposition of legal, administrative, or logistical measures to discourage or prevent specific segments of the population, mostly racial minorities, from voting. Republicans have become increasingly adept and brazen in trying to use voter purges, strict identification requirements, targeted closure of polling places, restrict mail-in and absentee voting, and raise administrative and psychological barriers through constant and often last-minute changes to voting rules.




Leading to the midterm elections advocacy groups raised the alarm about these tactics, abetted by the erosion of the Voting Rights Act (VRA) by the Supreme Court that in the 2013 Shelby County v. Holder decision gutted pre-clearance provisions of the Act which required states with a demonstrated record of racial discrimination to get federal approval before changing any voting laws or closing polling places, which was reinforced by the 2026 Louisiana v. Callais decision that raised the legal bar for opponents of biased maps to prove intentional malice rather than just discriminatory results.




Cumulatively, these changes to the VRA shifted the burden of fighting voter suppression to more individuals rather than monitoring the state, thereby legalizing voter suppression. However, it backfired as these blatantly anti-democratic measures provoked mass resistance, especially among Black and Latino voters whose early voting turnout surged. The architects of voter suppression were also stalled by defeats in the courts that struck down gerrymandered maps and denied last-minute efforts by the Trump administration to block mail-in ballots and mass purges just before Election Day,




Thus, the highly coordinated voter suppression efforts were neutralized by a combination of historic voter mobilization and decisive judicial interventions, underscoring the fact that popular will and institutional guardrails could withstand the weaponization of voting by anti-democratic forces inspired by the restrictive political covenants of the pre-civil rights era of white supremacy.




Unusual among Western democracies is the scale of the financialization of American politics, which has turned the electoral process into a high-stakes, multi-billion-dollar industry in which megadonors seek to buy political candidates, messaging, and power primarily to serve their interests rather than those of the electorate. They seek to turn elections into empty performative rituals to reproduce state capture and consolidate oligarchic self-enrichment. According to 

OpenSecrets

, the 2026 midterm elections are the most expensive in U.S. history, costing an extraordinary $11.9 billion.




This is the logical consequence of the systematic dismantling of post-Watergate campaign finance laws, in which the Supreme Court ruled that money is a form of constitutionally protected speech. This dates back to the 1976 Buckley v. Valeo decision, which stipulated that while the government could limit direct contributions to candidates to prevent bribery, it could not limit independent spending by individuals or campaigns.




Sanctifying the financialization of elections was the landmark 2010 Citizens United v. FEC decision, which declared that corporations, non-profits, and labor unions have the same First Amendment free speech rights as individual people. Also in the same year, the SpeechNow.org v. FEC and McCutcheon v. FEC decisions facilitated the creation of Super PACs and megadonors as vehicles for massive funding of elections by allowing individuals, corporations, or unions, as long as they didn’t directly coordinate with candidates, to contribute any amount without restriction.




Subsequent Court decisions and election rules legalized pop-up dark money, loosened relations between candidates and Super PACs, and removed restrictions on how much candidates could raise after the elections to pay themselves back for personal loans made to their campaigns. This is the landscape that allowed megadonors such as Elon Musk to donate between $445 and $483 million to Republican candidates and Michael Bloomberg to donate $116 million to Democratic candidates.




Overall, many Republicans relied on large donors while many Democratic candidates boasted about a broader base of small-dollar individual contributions. In the final 10 weeks of the election cycle, Pop-up Super PACs spent a massive $637 million collectively, with Republican-linked late groups outspending Democrats two-to-one while keeping their initial donor identities legally hidden past Election Day.




Financialization undermines American democracy in so far as massive political contributions are increasingly viewed by corporations and billionaires as capital investments that expect a return on investment through targeted tax cuts, regulatory rollbacks, government contracts, or favorable economic policies. This compromises accountability as lawmakers are trapped in a vicious cycle of “permanent fundraising,” shifting their time and accountability away from everyday constituents toward their megadonors.




However, the returns diminish as the media landscape becomes deluged with continuous attack ads, which creates public fatigue, exhaustion, and cynicism about the political process. The results of the election would seem to suggest limits to the financial capture of elections by megadonors. In many cases, their candidates in the primaries of both parties lost, and in the elections the billions spent by the titans of the tech industry and the American Israel Political Action Committee (AIPAC) to support Republicans amounted to a spectacular waste of money, showing the limits of buying democracy for a population fired up by their own economic and existential interests.




The Triumph of Diversity




Disparaged diversity won. There will be more minority governors, senators and representatives in Congress than ever before in American history. Altogether, the lone Black governor, Wes Moore of Maryland who won his re-election, will be joined by four new Black governors: three of them Democrats, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black female governor in U.S. history, David Crowley, who made history as Wisconsin’s first Black governor, Aaron Ford, who flipped the Nevada governorship out of Republican hands, and one Republican, Byron Donalds, who became Florida’s first Black governor.




In addition, two Latinos were elected Democratic governors: Gina Hinojosa, who pulled off a historic upset by defeating three-term incumbent Republican Greg Abbott, becoming the first Latina governor in Texas history, and Xavier Becerra, who became California’s first Latino governor since 1875. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland, a Democrat, made history as the first Native American female governor of a U.S. state.




In the meantime, 12 white women were elected as governors, four for the first time: Amy Acton (D-OH), who defeated the insufferable Vivek Ramaswamy to become the first woman governor in Ohio’s history, Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), who became the first female governor in Minnesota’s history, Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), who also made history as the first female governor of Tennessee, and Kelly Ayotte (R-NH), who retained Republican control in a highly competitive race. Eight other incumbent white women governors retained their seats, six of whom are Democrats and two Republicans.




As for senators, two newly elected African American and African-descended senators, Juliana Stratton (D-IL) and Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) will join five sitting African American senators who were not up for election this cycle: Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD) and Tim Scott (R-SC). As for Latinos, the newly elected Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) and re-elected incumbent Alex Padilla (D-CA) will serve alongside four sitting senators Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Ben Ray Luján (D-NM), Ted Cruz (R-TX), and Bernie Moreno (R-OH). The Senate will also have one new Native American senator, Peggy Flanagan (D-MN), as well as three sitting Asian American Democratic senators, Andy Kim (NJ), Tammy Duckworth (IL), and Mazie Hirono (HI). At the time of writing the election in Alaska has not been declared, and the democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, is Native American.




While we await the release of all House seats, it is more than likely that the number of minority representatives will be historically unprecedented. Among the highlights is the fact that Hakeem Jeffries is slated to become the first Black Speaker of the House. Another Black interesting development is that the number of House members who are African-born immigrants or first-generation children of African immigrants will grow.




Twenty-nine-year-old Melat Kiros, born in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, a Democratic Socialist, will join Ilhan Omar, born in Somalia, as the second African-born woman in the House, and the first Black woman from Colorado and Gen Z. In Maryland, 32-year-old Adrian Boafo, a son of Ghanaian immigrants, won his House seat, where he will join Joe Neguse, a son of Eritrean immigrants who won his reelection in Colorado, and Gabe Amo, a son of Ghanaian and Liberian parents, won his reelection in Rhode Island.




Other remarkable electoral victories include from the Asian American community Pia Dandiya (D-FL), a first-generation Indian-American, who enjoyed one of the most high-profile flips of this election cycle in a gerrymandered Republican district. From the Native American community, there is Claire Valdez (D-NY), who ran on a progressive platform and became the first Native American woman representative from the state of New York. Among the Latino community, Denise Powell (D-NE) flipped a Republican seat to become the first Hispanic representative ever elected to Congress from Nebraska, while Emily Randall (D-WA) made history as the first openly LGBTQ+ Latina ever elected to the United States Congress.




The diversity of the newly elected state governors and members of Congress constitutes a blistering rebuke of Trump’s chaotic, crass, corrupt, and cruel presidency, of resurgent white supremacy, of MAGA’s racist, reactionary and retrograde efforts to turn back to Reconstruction-era America. It also throws a harsh light on companies, institutions, and organizations, including businesses, media houses, universities, and law firms that unashamedly and hurriedly abandon diversity, equity and inclusion, often preemptively obeying executive orders or political pronouncements by Trump and his minions that went beyond the law.




The Power of Demography




Shifting demography won. It is often not well understood or fully appreciated that massive transformation of the American population is a product of the Civil Rights Movement. Three landmark laws were passed in response to civil rights struggles led by African Americans against centuries-long oppression, persecution, and marginalization.




The first was the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, and officially ended legal segregation in public places and schools. Second, the Voting Rights Act was passed in 1965, which banned discriminatory voting practices that had been systematically used in southern states to disenfranchise Black voters. Third, the Immigration and Nationality Act in 1965, which abolished the “national origins” quota system that had severely restricted immigration from non-European countries since the 1920s, opening immigration to people from Africa, Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean.




The backlash against the changes wrought by these laws provoked racist revanchism among some whites unable to compete without the privileges of whiteness. They were cynically mobilized by radical conservatives increasingly coalesced in the Republican Party, whose conservative ideologues were burnished by a network of well-funded right-wing and populist institutions including think tanks, the media, professional associations, and even universities where affirmative action combined with neoliberalism created intense, racialized competition for the symbolic capital of access, certification, and professional status.




This explains why elite universities quickly embraced judicial assaults against affirmative action because they never believed in it; it only served a performative role, which lost its currency with the resurgence of a populist backlash against the Great Recession and the Obama Presidency, which turbocharged fears of white replacement. These fears fueled anti-immigration sentiments, culminating in the militarized brutalities of ICE raids in Democratic-led American cities.




The results of the midterm elections represent a repudiation of the cultural and civic wars of the American right, a powerful indictment of the governance failures of contemporary American right-wing populism, which has failed to address the pressing economic, social, technological, political, and geopolitical challenges facing the nation in a rapidly changing and highly competitive world marked by multilateralism and the relative decline of Euro-America.




America’s populism combines three strands: the age-old reflexes of white supremacy, the anti-immigration crusade of European right-wing movements, and the historic lessons of white minority rule from apartheid South Africa, eagerly financed and popularized by the South African mafia led by Elon Musk that has constructed the perverse myth of white genocide in post-apartheid South Africa that Trump and his MAGA base have fervently embraced.




When comprehensive election data is available, I expect that it will show racial minorities, women and young people, including those who gravitated to Trump in 2024, believing his grandiose lies and false promises, were in the forefront of the political tsunami that has swept the Republican Party from congressional power. Those who voted for Trump in 2024, either out of ideological conviction or in the vain hope that his retrofitted administration would improve their lives and livelihoods, have been rudely disappointed over the past two years.




Among Trump’s supporters in 2024, there were 69 percent of white men without a college degree, 53 percent of white women, 46 to 48 percent of Latinos, 37 to 40 percent of Asian Americans, 20 to 21 percent of Black men. Sequels are rarely better than the original show, so it is with Trump. He returned to power freed from institutional guardrails, eager to exact retribution on his enemies, real and imagined, surrounded by spineless and enabling sycophants, and more erratic and opinionated than ever, basking in his omniscience and omnipresence.




His administration took away reproductive rights from women, emasculated his white male supporters, including young men with diminishing wages and prospects for enjoying the American dream. It also ensnared Latinos with the otherization of draconian immigration crackdowns, and dismantled the promises of the model minority myth for Asian Americans as they faced rising racism. Further, it decimated opportunities for Black men in an economy waging war on Black employment and businesses in the crusade against DEI.




Above all, it raised the cost of living for everyone through his inane tariff policies and unprovoked war with Iran, as he simultaneously enriched his wealthy, feckless cronies and cheerleaders with unconscionable tax cuts and indulged in unprecedented corruption of any president in American history.




The Seductions of Decency




The desire for decency won. As they say, reeled from the shenanigans under the unbelievably inept and self-destructive second Trump administration, more and more Americans yearned for something better. They became exhausted by its relentless assaults to their sense of decency, by the mindlessness of its gratuitous meanness, and the endless embarrassment from the cringeworthy idiocy of their globally despised president. Americans, like other people, derive part of their national pride from the international reputation of their leaders. Trump has brought Americans widespread shame.




The midterm elections gave them an opportunity to exact their revenge, against the despicable misogyny, the wanton racism, the economic incompetence, the daily spectacles of vengefulness, the deepening partisanship and polarization, the public incivility and the sickening abandonment of moral values, the incessant pathological lying. They sought the ennobling possibilities of community, dialogue, and dignity.




The electorate also responded to the quality and conduct of the candidates. Many of the Republican candidates, some of whom were strongly supported by Trump, were not only patently unqualified but also known to be corrupt and engaged in vicious personal attacks mimicking their godfather, Trump, whereas the Democrats were focused on issues.




The Imperatives of Development




The search for development won. As in other parts of the world in both the developed and developing countries, the working and middle classes strive for the well-being and social stability that comes from living wages, access to good education, healthcare, social services and public infrastructure. They resent deepening inequalities, the unelected and unaccountable power of oligopolies and obscenely rich oligarchs, who see themselves as masters of the universe.




Especially unpopular are the tech bros, whose data centers are gobbling up massive water and energy resources, raising the utility bills of local communities, threatening jobs and the future of humanity in a mindless and unregulated chase for super-intelligence whose dangers are poorly understood or appreciated.




In this election, the legacies of more than forty years of neoliberalism, reframed by the Great Recession and Covid-19 pandemic, were on trial, so were cuts to healthcare and other welfare programs. In the meantime, people saw levels of national indebtedness rise, surpassing $40 trillion, and military expenditures on a new forever war in Iran exploded. At the same time, the war brought higher oil and gas prices and for other commodities whose production and flows have been severely disrupted by the war in West Asia. According to The New York Times, every demographic group, including White voters, Hispanic voters, Black voters, and young voters, moved left.




The affordability crisis, emblematic of the broken promises of the neoliberal development model, is evident in many parts of the world. Europe has been engulfed by escalating protests led by Gen Z and working people. This is true in many parts of the Global South as well. The political ramifications vary as some incumbent populist governments fall, for example in Hungary and Serbia, while elsewhere liberal regimes are threatened by rising disaffection and disorder that empowers populist forces as evident in Germany and France. In Brazil, the incumbent left-wing government of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva survived the insurgent crusade of the populist right wing of the Bolsonaros, who fancied themselves as replicas of Trump in Latin America.




With this election, Trump has become the Bolsonaro of North America, his party decisively rejected by the electorate. Trump is now officially a lame duck president, a fate that befalls most presidents after they lose the midterm elections, which is often the case, especially during their second term. But Trump is different from his predecessors in that he is the first president in a century to serve two nonconsecutive terms.




Perhaps even more crucial is that this might portend something much larger: the collapse of the MAGA, the end of the Trump era that has dominated American politics during the past decade ever since he entered the race for the presidency in 2016. Trump has been a consequential president, not because his policies were good for America, let alone the world, but because he fundamentally transformed American politics and institutions, articulating and accelerating trends that long antedated him.




The Challenges and Possibilities of Change




Many analysts are concerned about what a lame duck Trump might mean for the world, in so far as many of his predecessors turned to foreign policy to burnish their legacy. Trump has no international legacy to build on. But he can cause a lot of damage as he lashes out against his political diminution and inquisition of his policies by a Democratic Congress in reckless foreign adventures including restarting the Iran war and embark on regime change in Cuba and elsewhere, or reignite his disputes with Canada and America’s NATO allies, collude with Russia and China to divide the world into three great power spheres.




As to be expected, the Democratic sweep has triggered a blame game among Republicans. For example, Vice President J.D. Vance blames the loss on the Iran war, in a veiled criticism of his boss. This presages the possibility that defiance, or at least disaffection and distancing from Trump’s policies, might grow.




But the victorious Democrats will also be under enormous pressure to check Trump and meet the demands and expectations of impatient voters. The president will wield veto power over their legislative initiatives, which would require them to work with chastened Republicans to override. They need to work on the cost of living crisis by rolling back tariffs, dealing seriously with government debt, which would require both raising taxes and entitlement reform, ending the war in Iran, regulating the AI industry, strengthening job training and improving education, robustly dealing with the climate crisis, and helping provide health care beyond the limited measures of the Affordable Care Act or Obamacare.




I’m not sure if Democrats are up to the task. Not only is their tent in the new Congress more ideologically diverse than ever, but the party establishment is also timid, beholden to large donors and lobbyists, and they seem invested in the myth of the political center as the best political space to occupy. They need to abandon meaningless centrism and embark on bold, popular programs to improve the well-being of ordinary people, and worry less about the rich and their ideologues in the media and academy.




They also need to manage America’s adjustment to one major power among others in a multilateral world. American supremacy, indeed, imperialism, after World War II brought the country great benefits to its economy and standard of living. But it has now become an unsustainable drag on its economy. The party that manages America’s transition and its transformation into a nation that is not permanently embroiled in foreign wars will be good for itself and the world. Imperialism at home and racism at home reinforce each other.




One critical international relationship that is likely to become central in the United States is the relationship with Israel, a country that has an oversized impact on American foreign policy because of the role of the Israeli lobby. The fierce criticisms of America’s subservience to Israeli interests, what some regard as the tail-wagging-the-dog syndrome, by many Democrats, especially the Democratic Socialists, and among younger Americans, will force changes. Preemptively, on the morning of the election, Trump announced that the United States will cease providing its newest $4 billion annual aid to Israel.




It is unlikely that U.S. – Africa relations will change much given that the executive branch controls foreign affairs. However, with long-time Africa policy advocate Senator Chris Coons (D-DE) poised to take over as Chairman of the powerful Senate Foreign Relations Committee, there may be renewed scrutiny on foreign aid and agency cuts, efforts to reset relations with African nations, including South Africa, that have been battered by indifference, transactional diplomacy, and a focus on the extraction of critical minerals, data, and other resources, and a reevaluation of visa restrictions and travel bans.




America must strive to become an inclusive non-racial democracy. All this is a tall order. But Democrats must use their new power strategically and act decisively. If they fail to do so, the voters will punish them in two years, and the musical chairs of political switcharoo will come back to haunt them to the detriment of the American people.
