title: Karasu: The Republic must be democratised according to today's understanding of democracy
content:
Mustafa Karasu, a member of the KCK Executive Council, spoke about current affairs during a special programme broadcast on Medya Haber.




The first part of this interview can be read 

here

.




The AKP government is entering into various alliances, particularly in the region. The benefits and drawbacks of these alliances continue to be debated publicly. Can the AKP secure its own position through such alliances?




After Devlet Bahçeli made his call, what did both Bahçeli and Erdoğan repeatedly say? They said that we needed to strengthen the domestic front. They also described this process as one of strengthening the domestic front. Yes, resolving the Kurdish question means strengthening the domestic front. This is because, from the Ottoman period onward, whenever Turkey has come into conflict with the Kurds, it has lost. Whenever it has maintained positive relations with the Kurds, it has achieved stability and strengthened its position.




Indeed, one of the most important factors in the decline of the Ottoman Empire was its failure to resolve its problems with the Kurds. From the nineteenth century onward, it entered into conflict with them. Once it became hostile to the Kurds, it began to decline rapidly. Had it resolved the Kurdish question and adopted the right approach, the Ottoman Empire might not have disintegrated to the same extent. Now, if the government claims to be pursuing a policy of strengthening the domestic front and repeatedly emphasises this objective, yet then assumes that it can secure its position through alliances formed abroad, I have to say that this is a misconception. No matter what alliances you form abroad, they will not achieve much if you do not first consolidate the domestic front. They may even produce the opposite results. In fact, the anxiety that has led to the formation of so many alliances stems precisely from the failure to strengthen the domestic front. This is preparation for war. The formation of so many alliances in the Middle East, which lies at the centre of ongoing wars, amounts to preparation for such wars—or to taking sides on the various war fronts.




If the domestic front were strong, if Turkey genuinely resolved the Kurdish question and took steps towards democratisation, it would not feel the need—or fall into the misconception—that it could save itself by forming one alliance with this party and another with that one. In this respect, let me be clear: the formation of so many alliances is also taking place under the direction of certain external powers. In his statement, Tom Barrack indirectly indicated that the alliances Turkey is forming are known to us, serve our interests and form part of our policy; they are not separate from it.




Thus, this alliance policy may be an attempt to secure Turkey's position, but it also creates antagonisms. Every alliance is, at the same time, directed against someone else. Of course, a state can form alliances and may need to do so. But because Turkey has failed to consolidate its domestic front, it feels weak. Consequently, it considers entering into various alliances necessary—or, more precisely, it feels compelled to create new enmities.




We do not believe that Turkey can resolve its own problems through alliance policies. The policy of strengthening the domestic front is correct, and this is what the government says it is pursuing. Yet instead of fulfilling the requirements of that policy and strengthening the domestic front, the government prefers to create its own fronts abroad and take sides in existing conflicts. This will not benefit Turkey very much. Turkey will suffer the consequences.




Abdullah Öcalan, the leader of the peoples, has described the process he initiated as one of change and transformation. In this context, efforts to organise a movement for a democratic republic are also on the agenda in the field of political struggle. What would you like to say about these discussions?




A republic was established in Turkey. Yes, a republic is a system of government in which those in power come to office through elections. Of course, a republic does not automatically mean direct democracy. There are many republics in the world that are undemocratic, even dictatorial. Conversely, there are countries without republics, where monarchies still exist, and certain offices are not filled through elections. Sweden, Norway and the Netherlands are examples, yet these countries do have certain democratic institutions, albeit within limits, as well as a democratic outlook.




In this respect, a republic is not inherently a bad thing. Having all institutions filled through elections is a positive development. Indeed, the course of human progress will inevitably move beyond such arrangements one day. There will no longer be kings, queens or similar institutions, nor rulers who inherit their positions from their fathers, through dynasties or family lineages.




In this respect, after the Ottoman Empire, Turkey abandoned that system of government and proclaimed a republic. But it did not become democratic. And because it was not democratic, it could not resolve its problems.




Will Turkey genuinely become democratic? Or will it remain, like many countries in the Middle East, a non-democratic monarchy or authoritarian regime? What will happen to Turkey if it remains that way? Where will it go? Turkey itself needs to consider these questions.




Turkey has its own history and a history of popular struggle. There have been struggles by democratic forces and intellectuals, by working people and by the Kurdish people for freedom. All these struggles make Turkey's democratisation necessary.




Turkey can advance towards its future through democratisation. If it seeks a future, it can secure that future by becoming democratic. Its prospects can then be bright and positive.




For this reason, the Republic must be democratised—but according to today's understanding of democracy. What did democracy mean 200 years ago? It meant little more than elections, with universal and equal suffrage. That understanding has since been surpassed.




We now need a form of democratisation based on an organised society, freedom of thought and organisation, and local democracy. Otherwise, as we see in current debates, people ask what democracy will actually bring. Some still think in terms of the democratic understanding of a hundred years ago, while others speak according to their own particular conceptions of democracy.




That is not what we mean. Today's understanding of democracy—the democratic conception articulated by Leader Apo—is based on freedom of thought and organisation and embraces local democracy.




Democratising the Republic on this basis would resolve all of Turkey's problems. It would resolve not only the Kurdish question but also the Alevi question, the question of women and all the other problems facing society.




Let us make this clear and emphasise it once again: when the Kurdish people, when we, and when Leader Apo speak of democracy, we are not speaking of democracy only for the Kurds. We are speaking of democracy for all of Turkey.




A Republic alone does not guarantee democracy




Some people say that the Kurdish question will be resolved, but ask what will happen to all the other issues. That is not how it works. The Kurdish question cannot be resolved without democratisation in Turkey. And when we speak of democratisation, we mean a process that resolves the Kurdish question, the Alevi question, the question of women and the problems faced by working people. This is what we mean by a democratic republic.




Discussions about a democratic republic have been taking place, with conferences and meetings organised on the subject. These are important because they are helping ideas to mature and take root. Gradually, almost everyone in Turkey who genuinely wants democracy is coming to demand that the Republic be democratised in a meaningful way.




A republic alone does not guarantee democracy. There are certain nationalist circles that think in the rigid terms of the 1920s. They keep talking about the Republic, the Republic, while opposing democracy.




That is not what a republic should be. It is not a defence of the Republic, nor is it genuine republicanism. It is reactionary. It amounts to demanding the continuation of a system founded on hostility towards the Kurds.




Therefore, when we speak of a democratic republic, we mean a republic in which society is organised from the grassroots; freedom of thought and organisation is fully guaranteed; different identities, including Kurdish and Alevi identities, can express themselves freely; and local democracy is established.




We hope these discussions about a democratic republic will help ideas mature throughout society and influence both the state and the government. Turkey has no other path. It must either democratise the Republic or continue to experience the difficulties of the troubled Middle East, facing ever greater risks and dangers.




Attacks on the natural environment in Kurdistan continue unabated. There is some public opposition, but it tends to remain localised. Why is organised resistance to attacks on nature, particularly in Kurdistan, so weak?




Let us make one thing clear. When we speak of nature, we are talking about the very reality that makes human existence possible. Humanity evolved within nature and reached its present state through that process. The evolution of nature gave rise to human beings.




If you disrupt nature, destroy it or eliminate its essential characteristics, you create a danger for all humanity. This threatens all women, all young people, all peoples and all of humanity, regardless of whether they are rich or poor. It is a danger to everyone.




Of course, the wealthy may try to protect themselves from these conditions by promoting environmentalism in their own way, living in pleasant surroundings or using their resources to move away from polluted and damaged areas into more desirable places. That may be their approach. They, too, may talk about environmental protection and seek to live in beautiful natural surroundings. They can use their means to escape degraded environments and settle somewhere better. But the danger remains one that affects all humanity. For this reason, everyone needs to be aware and concerned. Every single person.




Let me put it this way: not everyone possesses a deep level of consciousness. Not everyone can fully understand every issue. Their historical awareness, ideological awareness or other forms of understanding may be limited. But if they are alive, they will defend themselves, as all living beings do. The ecological crisis has now become a matter of self-defence for all living beings. It has become a matter of human self-defence. It is therefore a problem for all humanity. We must make it a priority, bring it to the forefront and keep it constantly on the public agenda.




In Kurdistan, meanwhile, attacks on nature have become part of the genocide against the Kurdish people. The geography of Botan is being devastated. The geography of Dersim is being devastated. Kurdistan is being made almost uninhabitable.




Mesopotamia was described as paradise in the sacred scriptures. Yet today, in the interests of capitalism and as a consequence of the Turkish state's genocidal policies, this paradise is being turned into hell. In this respect, the Kurds must be vigilant. Every Kurd must defend their own village, their water, their streams, their mountains and their forests.




This means honouring their ancestors, who passed these lands down to them. It also means protecting their children and grandchildren, and safeguarding what will be passed on to future generations. There has been some progress in this area, but it is insufficient. Ecologists in Kurdistan must undoubtedly conduct this struggle together with ecologists in Turkey, and the movement must expand across a much broader front.




At present, the efforts are inadequate. Just as the Kurdish people have waged a struggle for freedom for a hundred years—or, more specifically, for fifty years—we need to develop an ecological struggle of comparable determination. This, too, is a form of the Kurdish people's struggle for freedom. It is a struggle for the very existence of the Kurdish people.




For this reason, ecological awareness is extremely important. Ecological organisation is equally important. There must be ecological organisations in every region, every city, every town and even every village. People must defend their natural environment. We see trees being cut down and streams being poisoned. In Amed, villages are defending their land. These are positive developments, but everyone must get involved.




If a particular village is fighting for ecological protection, that struggle must not remain confined to that village. All the surrounding villages should join the struggle alongside it. Every city in Kurdistan must be concerned and involved. It must not be only the people of Botan who take part; all the people of Kurdistan must participate in the ecological struggle. The ecological struggle is not just the struggle of Varto, Dersim or Botan. It is the struggle of Amed and of the entire Kurdish people. In this respect, ecological awareness, organisation and struggle must cease to be the concern of only those places directly under attack. They must become the struggle of the Kurdish people as a whole.




Only then can results be achieved. Otherwise, all our villages will be destroyed, our forests will disappear, and beautiful Botan and Dersim—one of the most beautiful parts of Kurdistan—will be devastated. For this reason, our people must become more conscious of these dangers and intensify their struggle.




An integration agreement has been reached between the Yazidi people in Shengal and the Iraqi state. How do you assess this achievement by the Yazidi people, who have suffered massacres?




We are particularly sensitive when it comes to the Yazidi people. Leader Apo is sensitive to their situation, and so are we, because Yazidism is one of the oldest faiths of the Kurdish people. It is a great cultural and spiritual treasure. Religious beliefs are also part of humanity's accumulated heritage and values. For this reason, preserving the existence of the Êzidî people, ensuring their survival and enabling them to live freely are extremely important. It is especially important that they be able to practise their faith freely.




With the emergence of capitalist modernity, the notion of a single nation gave rise to all kinds of uniformity, and Yazidism was increasingly marginalised. Before capitalism emerged, Yazidism actually had a significant following in the Middle East and Kurdistan. But the homogenising nation-state mentality created by capitalist modernity has subjected all these identities to forms of genocide. This has targeted not only ethnic identities but religious identities as well.




We have always been particularly sensitive to this issue. When ISIS attacked, our movement was among the first to come to the Yazidi people's defence. It was the guerrillas who intervened and saved them from genocide. The ISIS attack was the 74th ferman—the term used for a decree of persecution or massacre against the Yazidis. The guerrillas rescued them from that ferman.




Our movement's role in saving the Yazidis from persecution and genocide was extremely important and decisive. Everyone knows this. Later, our military forces withdrew from the area. Nevertheless, our ideological influence remained. Leader Apo had issued calls in support of the Yazidi people. He stood by them, and because of his support, the Yazidis also listened to his ideas and political approach. In this way, they organised themselves and developed their own self-defence structures.




They have now reached an agreement and are pursuing integration. This has resulted in significant military integration. The YBŞ will remain in its own region as a local component of the Iraqi army. Its members are all Yazidi young people. Had the Yazidis possessed their own self-organised structures and military organisation when ISIS attacked, ISIS would not have been able to enter Shengal. The Yazidis would have resisted, even if it had cost them their lives. But the Iraqi army and the KDP Peshmerga forces withdrew when the attack came. For this reason, the continued presence of a local military force is important.




The Yazidis also have some degree of administrative and political organisation. However, this must be developed into more established legal and political institutions. We hope that progress will also be made in this area. Military integration alone—the integration of the YBŞ into the army—is not enough. The Yazidis also have a distinct religious identity. They need their own administrative and political structures, as well as local democracy. We believe that the organised strength of theYazidi people will enable them to achieve this.




As the youth movement that began in France spreads across Europe, it is also beginning to draw in all sections of society. I would like to ask about the role of left-wing, socialist and democratic forces in ensuring the continuity and effectiveness of these movements. If we turn the critical lens on ourselves as well, what shortcomings have left-wing and socialist movements displayed in these developing mobilisations?




We must acknowledge that capitalist modernity is in crisis. We say that capitalism's crisis is deepening and that the turmoil is intensifying. We argue that capitalism has become an unliveable system and that its end is approaching. This is our assessment as socialists. That assessment is correct. Capitalist modernity has indeed become a system fundamentally at odds with human life, a system that has lost its connection with the way humanity should live.




Yet while we say that the capitalist system is collapsing, that capitalist modernity is profoundly destructive and that it harms all humanity, we must also acknowledge that we, as socialist forces, are ideologically, politically and organisationally unprepared to respond adequately. Our preparations are weak and insufficient. This is clear, and it is a serious problem. Socialism has certain ideological and political shortcomings. As a result, we are unable to provide an adequate response. These shortcomings must be overcome.




Leader Apo has advanced important theses on this question. He has put forward an ideological and theoretical perspective that moves beyond the conventional socialist understanding rooted in a statist mentality. Rather than reproducing that traditional conception of socialism, he proposes a system in which society governs itself democratically without the state, enabling it to overcome capitalism.




It is genuinely only through such an approach that capitalism can be transcended. The crisis of capitalism is profound. Yes, society will overthrow it, but it seems this will no longer happen through extremely violent wars. Once society becomes organised, what use will capitalism be, given that it has already become unnecessary? Organised social forces will overcome capitalism and build democratic socialism in its place. For this reason, democratic socialist forces need to recognise the shortcomings in their ideological and theoretical positions. They must approach the issue critically and engage in self-criticism.




Why are we unable to meet society's needs adequately? Why can we not organise society fully? Why are we failing to respond sufficiently to the needs of young people, women and working people?




We need to ask ourselves these questions. At the same time, we must recognise that these shortcomings have emerged within, and are partly a consequence of, the crisis generated by capitalist modernity. France, meanwhile, has historically been one of the places where revolutions and uprisings have repeatedly begun and erupted, particularly since capitalism entered the historical stage. Consider the French Revolution of 1789. There were also democratic revolutions, often described as bourgeois-democratic revolutions, but the people left their mark on all of them. Popular influence was decisive. The Paris Commune came later, and there were earlier episodes as well. In this respect, French society has historically been inclined towards such uprisings and expressions of resistance.




There is also the crisis of capitalism, the situation of migrants and the hostile attitudes directed towards them. There is the rise of right-wing governments, which societies refuse to accept. These developments, too, provoke resistance. In this context, the uprising of young people in France became an important signal flare, showing what might be possible. Young people in Serbia, for instance, have in a sense made their mark on the country's political leadership. We cannot currently describe Serbia as a democratic socialist country, but the reflection of young people's will in political life is significant. It represents the expression of a democratic will. Similar developments have occurred in Portugal. In fact, this is what will increasingly unfold throughout capitalist countries. They are unable to find solutions.




There are two competing approaches to resolving the crisis. Right-wing governments say that they will come to power, wield the sword and resolve the crisis of capitalist modernity. But whose solution is that? It is not a solution for the people. It is a solution for monopolies and exploiting classes. Social democrats and liberals are also unable to resolve the crisis. They are not genuinely and fully democratic. On the one hand, they appeal to the people; on the other, they protect the interests of the ruling classes. For this reason, social-democratic and liberal policies cannot resolve the crisis of capitalism.




We are therefore passing through a historical period in which genuinely democratic socialist organisations, movements, ideologies and political programmes can offer solutions. If democratic socialists develop the right programme, critically examine the past and formulate a new line of struggle—both ideological and political—they can achieve significant advances under these crisis conditions. In many places, they can establish democratic socialist forms of popular self-government and begin building a new social order. We believe this is possible.

title: Hope lies with young people
content:
Our generation grew up under the influence of the 1968 Youth Revolution. More precisely, we were forged in the fire of that historic revolution. The Revolutionary Youth Movement of 1968 was based primarily on university students. It was the most striking example of conscious, organised youth taking the lead in society as a whole. Through this revolutionary movement, university students proved themselves and passed the test of history.




The 1968 Youth Revolution was the most influential revolutionary wave since the 1917 Soviet Revolution, which emerged during the First World War. It aimed not only to overthrow the system of capitalist modernity, whose crisis was deepening, but also to transcend actually existing socialism, which had moved away from the principles of equality based on freedom and diversity. For various reasons, it undoubtedly failed to overthrow the system of capitalist modernity. However, it played a significant role in the collapse of actually existing socialism, which had proved incapable of correcting or renewing itself. Had actually existing socialism understood the revolution developed by intellectual university youth, and demonstrated the capacity to transform and renew itself on the basis of that revolution's characteristics, perhaps it would not have met the tragic end it did, nor disintegrated in that way.




The 1968 Youth Revolution first developed on the European continent, and its influence gradually spread. From that point onward, Turkish youth, inspired by the forms of organisation and struggle developed by their European peers, reached the peak of their revolutionary activity in 1970–71. The Revolutionary Youth Movement, which also knew how to draw on the Palestinian Resistance in practice, succeeded in leading the democratic revolution that Turkey experienced during the 1970s. New socialist and revolutionary formations in Turkey and Kurdistan also emerged from the fire of this movement. Undoubtedly, the most influential representative of this new wave was the PKK.




Today, under conditions in which the system of capitalist modernity has brought nature and society to the brink of destruction—going beyond even the peak of crisis and chaos—the breakthrough is once again coming from Europe, and once again from the youth. It is the youth who carry hope. This time, however, the spark is being ignited not by university students but by secondary-school students. Scientific and technological advances undoubtedly play an important role in this. It is clear that secondary-school students are using these advances more effectively.




As has so often been the case, the secondary-school youth movement that began in France has, this time too, spread across almost all of Europe in a very short period. It also appears to have succeeded in mobilising different sections of society. In a manner reminiscent of the “sans-culottes” of an earlier era—the so-called “ragged-trousered” masses—the movement of secondary-school students, who were dismissed as “just a few kids”, has already managed to shake the system of capitalist modernity very seriously, and right at its very centre. It is abundantly clear that these “few kids” are achieving extraordinary things and inspiring everyone's admiration. Indeed, the French government has introduced a partial curfew, while it appears that new measures are also being discussed at the European level.




The popular movement led by young people, which continued throughout October and has progressively developed and spread, is undoubtedly extremely intriguing. It demands close attention and a sound assessment. Although its underlying causes are largely understood, it remains difficult to predict how events will unfold, how the movement will progress, and where it will ultimately lead. It is also becoming clear that the movement cannot be easily dismissed or suppressed through simplistic approaches.




One particularly interesting and striking question is why secondary-school students, rather than university students or young people as a whole, are driving this movement. As noted above, secondary-school students appear to be using science and technology more effectively and organising themselves more rapidly. While this is one contributing factor, it cannot, of course, be regarded as the only one. Another possible factor is that a deliberate system of special warfare has been applied to university youth, with the result that this section of the younger generation has, to a considerable extent, been integrated into the system. Just as special warfare policies were implemented against the working class after the 1917 Soviet Revolution, it seems that a similar plan may have been pursued against university students following the 1968 Youth Revolution. If this is the case, university youth can be said to be facing a serious process of criticism and self-criticism.




Clearly, in its current form, this wave of mobilisation appears to be confined to Europe. But that does not mean it cannot spread rapidly. Nor can we claim that precisely the same events of 1968–70 will be repeated. Nevertheless, it is equally impossible to say that the youth-led popular movement in Europe will not spread to Turkey, or that Turkey will remain unaffected. Of course, it will spread to Turkey in one form or another and exert the same influence there. Although nothing definitive can be said about when or how this will happen, it can confidently be stated that such a spread is inevitable. Neither intensified special warfare practices nor the schemes and deceptions developed by the AKP government during what it considers its period of political maturity can prevent this kind of development.




In fact, had the government and the state fulfilled the requirements of the Peace and Democratic Society Process developed by Kurdish people's leader Abdullah Öcalan—that is, had a shift in mentality and politics taken place that would democratise Turkey and resolve the Kurdish question—these developments could have unfolded in a controlled manner, without destructive consequences. The Kurdish side had already defined the process in these terms, describing the Peace and Democratic Society Process as one of change, transformation and restructuring. In order to bring about this change from its own side, both Leader Abdullah Öcalan and the Freedom Movement had undertaken intensive efforts and taken the necessary steps.




A process of change, transformation and restructuring cannot be one-sided; it must involve both sides. Just as the Kurdish side is undergoing the changes in mentality and politics required by the process, the state and the government must also undergo a serious transformation in their outlook and political approach. In other words, they must abandon the mentality and policies that deny the existence of the Kurdish people and subject them to genocide, and instead adopt an approach to democratisation grounded in Kurdish freedom and Turkish-Kurdish fraternity. No such commitment or effort towards change, transformation and restructuring is evident on the Turkish side. There is no talk of legal or political changes to resolve the Kurdish question and democratise Turkey. Indeed, regardless of the purpose behind them, even the statements made by Devlet Bahçeli, leader of the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), at his parliamentary group meeting, along with the promises he made on that basis, are not being implemented. The necessary work to democratise the Republic is not being carried out.




It is abundantly clear that the AKP is obstructing change. For approximately 25 years, it has governed Turkey under the coup-era constitution imposed after 12 September 1980, and at times it has failed even to implement that constitution. Its entire political strategy is directed towards ensuring Tayyip Erdoğan's re-election within the existing legal system and extending his time in power. It does not hesitate to turn everything into an instrument for achieving this goal. It thinks only of maintaining its own rule, while failing to recognise—or deliberately ignoring—the dangers facing Turkey.




Meanwhile, the dangers surrounding Turkey are growing, and the circle of encirclement is tightening. Some striking and dangerous statements have been made in this regard. Following reactions from the Middle East and Europe, the United States has also strongly criticised Turkey's attempt to develop a maritime territorial-waters policy with Libya, describing the initiative as a provocation. It has also been revealed by an Iranian official who participated in talks during the Mecca Alliance's visit to Iran that a Saudi Arabian minister said, “After Iran, Turkey and Saudi Arabia are next on Israel's list of targets for attack.” Clearly, the AKP's submissive and collaborationist policies are not enough to save Turkey either. It is evident that Turkey's salvation lies in the success of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, which would democratise and strengthen the domestic front. To this end, the Leadership and the Movement, which emerged from the 1968 Youth Revolution and continue to place their hopes in the youth today, must no longer be obstructed. One thing is clear: what does not change will be overcome; whoever stands in the way will be consigned to the dustbin of history.




Source: Yeni Özgür Politika

title: Tekirdağ'ın Saray ilçesinde taşkın: Köprü kapatıldı, mahsur kalan 2 kişi kurtarıldı
content:
Tekirdağ'ın Saray ilçesinde Galata Deresi'nde meydana gelen taşkın nedeniyle Kiremithane Köprüsü, güvenlik amacıyla geçici olarak ulaşıma kapatıldı.

Saray Belediye Başkanı Abdül Taşyasan, Fen İşleri Müdürlüğüne bağlı ekiplerin köprüde gerekli güvenlik önlemlerini aldığını bildirdi. Köprü çevresinde polis ekiplerince de güvenlik önlemi alındı.

Mantar toplamak için Kanara Kanyonu'na giden Y.B. ve A.K, derenin debisinin yükselmesi sonucu mahsur kaldı. İhbar üzerine bölgeye AFAD, jandarma ve itfaiye ekipleri sevk edildi. Mahsur kalan 2 kişi, ekiplerin iş makinesiyle yürüttüğü çalışma sonucu kurtarıldı.

Safaalan Mahallesi'nde ise su baskını tehdidi altındaki bir ev ekipler tarafından boşaltıldı. Evde yaşayan 6 kişilik aile, Saray Belediyesi tarafından otele yerleştirildi.

Sağanağın etkili olması beklenen ilçede belediye ekipleri, yaşanabilecek olumsuzluklara karşı tedbir amacıyla hazır bekletiliyor.

author: Unknown
title: Şüpheli şekilde yaşamını yitiren Nurcan Akpirinç’in dosyasında 5 aydır gelişme yok
content:
Diyarbakır'ın Bağlar ilçesinde 20 Haziran’da evinde şüpheli bir şekilde ölü bulunan 23 yaşındaki Nurcan Akpirinç’in ölümüne ilişkin soruşturma sürerken, aradan geçen 5 aya rağmen otopsi raporu hâlâ çıkmadı. Anne Asiye Akpirinç, kızı ve katledilen tüm kadınlar için adalet talebinde bulundu.

Olay günü mahalleye ambulans geldiğini 4 ay sonra öğrendiklerini belirten Asiye Akpirinç, birinin 112'yi arayıp yardım istediğini, ambulanstakilerin mahalleye gelip arayanı bulamayarak geri gittiğini söyledi. Kızının sağlık ekiplerini arayıp yardım istediğine inandığını ifade eden anne Akpirinç, bu durumun ve 112 çağrısının detaylı bir şekilde araştırılmasını istedi.

Kızının ölümünün üzerinden 5 ay geçmesine rağmen otopsi raporunun hâlâ çıkmadığını ve verdikleri dilekçelere her seferinde "incelemede" yanıtı aldıklarını kaydeden Asiye Akpirinç, "Kaç defa dilekçe verdik, otopsi raporunu istiyoruz. Kızımın 112’yi arayıp yardım istediğinin araştırılmasını istiyoruz. Neden hâlâ bize bir cevap verilmiyor?" diye tepki gösterdi.

Kızının alnında ve sağ kulağının arkasında darp izleri gördüğünü belirten anne Akpirinç, M.A. ve annesi C.A. tarafından sürekli şiddete uğradığını ifade etti. Olay günü kendilerine bilgi verilmediğini, kızının evde olmadığının söylenerek köyde aranmasının istendiğini, saatler sonra ise aynı evde yaşamını yitirdiğini öğrendiklerini aktaran Akpirinç, "Kızımın intihar ettiğine inanmıyorum" dedi.

Sorumluların açığa çıkarılmasını ve cezalandırılmasını talep eden Asiye Akpirinç, "Adalet istiyorum. Hükümet sesimizi duysun, savcılar, hâkimler sesimizi duysun. Sadece kızım için değil, katledilen bütün kadınlar için adalet istiyorum. Başka annelerin canı yanmasın. Bu işin peşini bırakmayacağız, sonuna kadar mücadele edeceğiz" ifadelerini kullandı.

Diyarbakır'ın Bağlar ilçesinde 20 Haziran’da dini nikahla evli olduğu aktarılan M.A. ile tartıştıktan sonra annesini arayan Nurcan Akpirinç ailesinin yanına gitmek istemişti. Kızlarından haber alamayan ailenin evine gitmesi üzerine Nurcan’ın evde olmadığı söylenmiş, yaklaşık iki saat sonra ise evin misafir odasında yaşamını yitirdiği ortaya çıkmıştı. Aile, Nurcan’ın daha önce defalarca tehdit edildiğini belirtmesine rağmen 5 aylık süreçte otopsi raporunun çıkmadığı ve yalnızca aile bireylerinin ifadesinin alındığı bildirilmişti.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Dyepeson Martins
title: Brasileiro eleito na Flórida diz que Trump ajuda quem foge da Justiça e deporta domésticas
content:
Mais do que um nome na política, Felipe Sousa-Lazaballet, 40, também quer ser símbolo de representatividade. Ele se tornou o primeiro brasileiro eleito representante (um deputado estadual, para nós) na Flórida, nos Estados Unidos (EUA). O estado é reduto político do Secretário de Estado norte-americano, Marco Rubio, principal responsável pela expansão do movimento nacionalista 

Make America Great Again

 (MAGA) na América Latina. Na Flórida também está localizada a Mar-a-Lago, uma espécie de Casa Branca secundária utilizada por Trump como centro de deliberações políticas.




Filho de empregada doméstica, Felipe nasceu em Duque de Caxias (RJ) e, aos 14 anos, migrou para os EUA. É ativista comunitário, militante do movimento LGBTQIA+ e agora também é o primeiro imigrante abertamente gay a integrar a Florida House of Representatives (a Assembleia Legislativa da Flórida).




Em entrevista à 

Agência Pública

, ele reforçou que teve a campanha pautada pela igualdade de direitos sociais e comentou a controversa política trumpista que, ao mesmo tempo, deporta imigrantes que fortalecem a economia americana, enquanto ajuda figuras como o Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). O senador deixou o Brasil dois dias depois de ser derrotado na eleição à Presidência da República apesar da determinação do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) para que ele entregasse o passaporte à Polícia Federal.




“Primeiro, queria dizer que, pra mim obviamente, o Brasil é um país soberano e a Justiça do Brasil deve ser respeitada. Pra mim não faz sentido nenhum que os Estados Unidos estão aceitando uma pessoa que está literalmente fugindo da Justiça no Brasil e, enquanto isso, está deportando uma empregada doméstica, ou seja, não faz sentido nenhum”, declarou o deputado eleito. Flávio Bolsonaro é investigado, entre outros crimes, por lavagem de dinheiro e organização criminosa.




Além de Felipe, outros seis brasileiros foram eleitos deputados estaduais nos EUA. Em Massachussets, foram quatro: Danillo Sena, Lorena Betts, Priscila Sousa e Rita Mendes. Em Connecticut, foi eleito Farley Santos e, em Nevada, Elaine Marzola.




A eleição americana representou uma grande derrota ao presidente Donald Trump com a vitória avassaladora de candidatos do partido Democrata, que agora tem a maioria no Congresso Nacional americano. Na Câmara, dos 435 membros votantes, haverá 231 democratas, 139 republicanos e 65 nomes ainda em definição devido às disputas acirradas em alguns estados, que podem levar semanas para contabilizar todos votos. Os Democratas também terão 54 das 100 vagas do Senado. Os republicanos garantiram 44. Duas vagas ainda estão em definição.




As eleições de meio de mandato são chamadas de “midterms” e marcam a metade da gestão de Donald Trump. Nos EUA, o sistema de votação e apuração dos votos ocorre de forma descentralizada e cada estado tem autonomia para definir as regras do pleito na região, diferentemente do modelo adotado no Brasil, onde as normas são regidas pelo Superior Tribunal Eleitoral (TSE).




“Por muito tempo, os democratas não estavam tão focados nos assuntos que realmente estão impactando mais a classe trabalhadora aqui, que é o custo de vida, ter oportunidade de poder ter um imóvel próprio, que é o caminho mais comum e tradicional de conseguir chegar ao sonho americano”, frisou Sousa-Lazaballet.




Confira os principais trechos da entrevista:




Como foi a sua inserção na política partidária americana?




Eu fiz parte de uma marcha que foi de Miami até Washington D.C., que foram 1.500 milhas [2,4 mil km] a pé até lá. E foi assim que a gente conseguiu, na época, mudar a maneira que o presidente Obama pensava sobre a instituição da imigração e quem deveria ou não deportar. E dessa maneira conseguimos conquistar grandes coisas para o movimento. Ao mesmo tempo, também batalhei bastante para o movimento LGBT+. E sempre tive essa atuação política mais no sentido do lado de fora.




Não do lado de dentro, não da parte partidária, como você mesmo disse. Mas, mais ou menos uns dois anos atrás, quando o presidente Trump foi reeleito pela segunda vez, eu lembro que eu estava no meu carro pensando “uau, a gente vai acabar vivendo nesse mundo com o presidente Trump e o governador DeSantis”, que é o governador daqui da Flórida – um governador muito anti-imigrante, muito contra a comunidade LGBT +, mas muito de direita, que tem realmente criado vários problemas para as comunidades que vivem aqui. E naquele momento eu pensei: “nossa, a gente tem que realmente se expandir, se sacrificar, fazer coisas que a gente nunca fez antes”.




Políticos de outros países, como na Argentina, estão se baseando na mobilização digital e popular do Brasil para enfrentar candidaturas apoiadas por Donald Trump e Marco Rubio. Diante disso, Você percebeu reflexos da eleição brasileira também nos formatos e estratégias de campanha nos EUA?




Um impacto que teve foi uma maneira de “ver diferente” – que a gente pode ganhar contra a direita e que o voto funciona. Ou seja, as pessoas que não votam, saindo para votar, podem realmente criar uma mudança social e foi dessa maneira que a gente conseguiu tantas conquistas eleitorais pelo país inteiro e aqui na Flórida.




Embora a gente tenha perdido as eleições estaduais para os cargos estaduais, nós conseguimos mudar 16 cadeiras da legislatura da Flórida de republicano para democrata.




Flávio Bolsonaro escolheu a Flórida para viver o seu autoexílio porque tem uma rede de apoio. Paulo Figueiredo, por exemplo, doou US$ 10 mil para Maria Elvira Salazar nas últimas eleições, meses antes de ela propor uma lei para penalizar Alexandre de Moraes. O que um representante como você pode fazer para esclarecer se as autoridades dos EUA ajudam ou acobertam ações golpistas contra o Brasil promovidas por este grupo?




Primeiro, queria dizer que, pra mim, obviamente o Brasil é um país soberano e a Justiça do Brasil deve ser respeitada. Pra mim não faz sentido nenhum que os Estados Unidos estejam aceitando uma pessoa que está literalmente fugindo da Justiça no Brasil e, enquanto isso, está deportando uma empregada doméstica, ou seja, não faz sentido nenhum.




Mas, como deputado estadual, os assuntos de migração são federais. Então, eu não tenho uma linha direta para poder realmente causar uma mudança nesse cenário. Porém, eu ainda assim posso reivindicar que os nossos congressistas, que nos representam aqui na Flórida, principalmente em Orlando, tomem essa bandeira – o que, na verdade, já está acontecendo: o nosso congressista Maxwell Alejandro Frost é um congressista muito progressista, muito a favor da democracia do Brasil e já está atuando nisso.




Alexandre Ramagem, ex-chefe da Abin [Agência Brasileira de Inteligência], fugiu para os EUA com o apoio de um minerador ilegal que o hospedou na Florida. Ramagem foi condenado pela tentativa de Golpe de Estado e tem extradição pedida pelo governo brasileiro. Mesmo assim, quando foi preso pelo ICE, por seus laços criminais, ele foi solto em menos de 24 horas por pressão, segundo vários políticos, da Casa Branca. É possível a casa legislativa buscar esclarecer o que houve?




O ICE é uma entidade federal. Bom, claro que a gente pode fazer perguntas. Mas não é a mesma coisa de falar “não, não, não, estou aqui usando o meu poder como congressista para ver o que você está fazendo”. Porém, voltando ao assunto do ICE, aqui no estado da Flórida passaram várias leis anti-imigrantes que estão fazendo com que a polícia local esteja ajudando o ICE. E essa é a razão principal que está causando a quantidade de deportação na Flórida.




Na verdade, a Flórida lidera em número de pessoas que estão sendo deportadas. Por isso que eu digo: a gente tá aqui deportando um pedreiro, ou seja, mandando uma empregada doméstica para uma detenção, que é uma prisão para imigrantes. E, ao mesmo tempo, tem pessoas que cometeram crimes que estão sendo investigadas no Brasil e em outros países também. Não é só o Brasil, ou seja, essas pessoas estão recebendo, na minha opinião, uma ajuda ou até mesmo uma maneira diferente de trabalhar com eles.




No Brasil, alguns políticos cresceram e se elegeram por visões violentas contra a participação de mulheres na política, por exemplo. Isso lembra muito o discurso propagado por Charlie Kirk, que segue sendo referência para políticos aqui do Brasil. E tem brasileiro nos EUA, como o blogueiro Paulo Figueiredo, que tem a mesma narrativa, e é contra o voto feminino. Embora esse tipo de discurso tenha apoio, ele também causa medo. E isso foi importante na mobilização contra a candidatura de Flávio Bolsonaro. Esse medo da perda de direitos básicos, de perda de espaço político, deve ser usado como munição pelos democratas contra o trumpismo?




Olha só, foi tentado dois anos atrás, quando houve a eleição do Trump, onde teve uma conversa muito grande sobre os direitos civis das pessoas que são parte de minorias. Enfim, e não foi o que realmente fez com que as pessoas fossem votar.




O que realmente está fazendo as pessoas votarem aqui é o custo de vida, essa essa ideia de que o sonho americano cada vez está mais difícil de conseguir. O desemprego entre as pessoas jovens, por exemplo. Antigamente você saía da faculdade, você conseguia um emprego, assim, dessa maneira. Hoje em dia você não consegue emprego – ou seja, está tendo uma revolução econômica que está beneficiando os bilionários e está deixando a classe trabalhadora cada vez mais pobre.




Então, isso é o foco principal. E as pautas que realmente estão criando essa “mudança”, né? Que a gente chama desse “tsunami azul” que aconteceu.




Sua mãe é do Ceará. Bem, o Nordeste foi essencial pro resultado eleitoral aqui no Brasil. Você vê influência nordestina, da política no Nordeste e da vivência de quem é de lá, na sua formação política?




Sem dúvida, sem dúvida. Eu cresci no Rio de Janeiro, porém, a minha mãe é cearense, a minha família inteira é cearense, ou seja, cresci comendo baião de dois. E a minha mãe é uma pessoa muito trabalhadora, humilde, e ela me ensinou a diferença do que é o certo e o errado. É daí que vem essa minha vontade de ajudar o próximo, essa vontade de fazer diferença na vida das pessoas que não estão vivendo uma vida muito difícil, essas injustiças sociais que acontecem muito, com certeza. Eu me chamo de “cearoca”.




Ela mora aqui no Brasil ainda?




Sim.




Ela comentou com você sobre as eleições do Brasil?




Olha, não falou muito, né? Porque ela não fala muito, ela não é tão politizada como eu sou. Mas quando eu decidi me candidatar, eu lembro que liguei pra ela, falei o que eu tava pensando em fazer e ela me disse: “meu filho, você não se esquece que nós viemos da poeira”, que é como dizer “não se esquece das suas raízes”. E claro que eu nunca esquecerei.

1. Defying the zio-global dictatorship

!










by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article 

here




I am sure you don’t need me to tell you that we are heading into a crucial period of history.




Not only is the shadow of a possible world war looming over us, but our freedom is coming under rapidly accelerating assault.




Here in France, for instance, the system started out by simply ignoring schoolkids protesting against the poor condition of their schools and their lives, then went on to 

gas

 and 

beat

 them, 

smear

 their uprising in the media, 

team up

 with far-right street gangs to attack the ever-broadening revolt, 

ban protests

 in city centres, 

pass a law

 to make demonstrators pay for windows they did not break on the basis of some kind of assumed collective responsibility, place protesters under 

house arrest

 as “terrorists”, constantly 

lie

 about the size of the turn-outs, 

manipulate

 social media algorithms so that people did not know about the demos and threaten to pull that communication plug 

altogether

.




I should add that there is also the possibility that at least some of the protesters and looters were 

agents provocateurs

 working for the system to undermine public support for the youngsters’ cause, although I have not yet seen any hard proof of this.
















In an article for 

Le Monde diplomatique

 (November 2026 edition), Benoît Bréville describes how politicians were lining up on TV to demand a fascistic response to the protests, with many blaming the left-wing opposition party 

La France insoumise

 – president of the French senate Gérard Larcher even suggested the party should be dissolved.




“Others suggested creating thousands of new places in prisons on the model of Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, of removing benefits from the trouble-makers’ families or of hardening the law against minors”.




Bréville notes that curfews were imposed in several cities, policed by drones and helicopters. “Gatherings are banned and in certain neighbourhoods it is even forbidden to walk around with a rucksack or hat”.




He adds that the French railways, SNCF, cancelled trains to prevent some people from attending demos and those arriving by road and rail were subject to police checks.




 “In Paris, the army was mobilised to supervise the demonstrators, along with the brigade of regional intervention, the RAID (

Recherche, assistance, intervention, dissuasion

) and the national gendarmerie’s intervention group (GIGN)”.




But in the face of all that, numbers on the protests across France did not drop away and the uprising is still going strong as I write!




All across Europe protests are 

breaking out

 – including against what looks like an attempted 

German-backed

 EU 

coup d’état

 in Poland – and it seems that policing is increasingly being carried out by 

Eurogendfor

 (European Gendarmerie Force), the European mercenary army deployed, as one 

X

 user 

put it

, “by the EUSSR to crush local uprisings, hijack demonstrations, and stage coups. They have no ties whatsoever to the local population (they don’t even speak the language) and will ruthlessly crush any form of civilian resistance with an iron fist”.










Meanwhile, hitherto unthinkable restrictions are being placed on people’s international travel on the basis of them not being appreciated by the zio-imperialist mafia (ZIM).




Take, for example, the way that veteran anarchist and co-founder of Food not Bombs 

Keith McHenry

 was banned from entering Canada essentially on account of the decades of state violence and harassment  he has faced for feeding homeless people (

see below

).




Much of the repression centres, of course, around critics of Israel and its genocidal activities.




Swedish academic Andreas Malm was 

refused entry

 to the UK, where he was due to headline an anti-imperialist and pro-Palestinian conference, on the grounds that his presence in the UK “may not be considered to be conducive to the public good”.




New York journalist Jeremy Loffredo has also 

revealed

: “The UK is refusing to let me enter the country to report on and investigate the ongoing crackdown against elderly Palestine supporters because my ‘presence in the UK is not conducive to the public good’”.




Regarding those protests, 

Council Estate Media

 

relates

 that police in London are now saying that “providing logistical support” for supporters of the supposedly “terrorist” Palestine Action group, which could include passing a bottle of water to a sit-down protester, is an offence.










The blog states: “Not only are grannies and wheelchair users terrorists for expressing opinions the government doesn’t like, but anyone who is nice to those grannies and wheelchair users is also a terrorist”.




And an absurd report was accepted by the Zio-Labour government suggesting a frightening rise in “anti-semitism” which required the banning of Palestine badges in schools and heavy-duty brainwashing of British children to swallow zionist lies.




In fact, as 

Council Estate Media

 

pointed out

: “A key argument for this moral panic is that three out of five Jewish pupils have experienced antisemitism in schools. However, that figure comes from a survey of 5,000 kids, only 92 of whom were Jewish. That’s right, the sample size was just 92!




“Those 92 kids were asked if they’d personally experienced antisemitism at school and only 70 responded. Twenty-nine said yes – that’s less than one in three of those asked! Only 12% of the kids who responded said they felt antisemitism was a problem at their school and only 2% said it was a big problem”.




In Australia, as Caitlin Johnstone has 

laid out

, the country’s so-called “antisemitism envoy” is trying to demonise left-leaning pro-Palestine supporters for daring to challenge the “chosen” people’s God-given right to commit (demonic) genocide.










A new report by Jillian Segal (

pictured

) claims: “Over time, the language of human rights and its greatest crimes  –  apartheid, ethnic cleansing, genocide, etc.  –  has increasingly been appropriated to portray Israel (and, relevantly, members of the Jewish community who support it) as morally evil, often to the point of being equated to Nazis.




“In contemporary Australia, elements of Australia’s historically fringe radical left have sought to appeal to well-meaning mainstream progressive Australians who may perceive the Palestinian cause as a matter of social justice. This ‘gateway’ issue, of sorts, has been used by far-left activists to magnify their appeal and prominence and to attempt to introduce traditionally moderate Australians to radical and anti-Jewish propaganda that would previously have been of little interest”.




What we seem to be seeing everywhere is a desperate attempt by the ruling mafia to smother and crush the great wave of awakening that they have themselves unleashed by their barbarity and lies, as well as by the increasingly obvious reality of their control of governments and global media.




It is no coincidence that the first week of November saw the “The First International Congress of Noahides” staged in Jerusalem. As I previously 

reported

, Jana S Bennun has warned: “The shift from just ‘abstract’ religious ideas to a real, functioning global Noahide legal system is happening right under our noses”.




“They are openly planning to draft a binding universal charter, elect councils across six continents, and officially launch the First International Rabbinic Court, or 

Beit Din

.










“Led by Rabbi Oury Cherki 

(pictured

), this supreme legal body will use regional judges to oversee a strict, three-stage process where non-Jewish people make official legal declarations, locking themselves into a centralized authority based in Jerusalem”.




In other words, because ZIM is now convinced that it wields overwhelming power in the world, it is pushing us into a judeo-supremacist dictatorship in which we 

goyim

 will be no more than slaves.




The enormity of this threat – to 99.8% of humankind and to all our unborn descendants – can hardly be overstated.




Because ZIM has, indeed, stolen most of the world’s wealth and captured most of the world’s institutions, this threat is not something we are going to be able to see off through letter-writing, petitions or voting for the usual political puppets.




I think this is why,  in recent weeks, I have been returning to anarchism as a source of inspiration. It is not only the anarchist 

vision

 of a sane future built on natural order that we need, but its 

vital energy

, its complete and courageous rejection of oppression and domination.




When I see the young generation out on the streets, often 

proudly brandishing Palestinian flags

, I sense that they intuitively 

know

 that what is needed is the 

raw revolt

 I have written about.




The 

life force

 is 

shining

 in them, 

animating their resistance

 – and that is why ZIM and its puppets are so scared.

Winter Oak has focused much in recent years on ZIM – the zio-imperialist mafia.

October 7

In recent weeks there has been an accelerating wave of revelations about zionist involvement in all sorts of monstrosities.




For instance, after the uncovering of a regime

 in Ukraine, run by the neonazi Azov entity, word

3. 

Banned from Canada










by 

Keith McHenry




The salmon and turquoise glow illuminated the Taos Mountains outside the dining room window. Allan Antliff, professor of Art History and Visual Studies at the University of Victoria, glass artist Mary Shaffer, and I enjoyed dinner at her beautiful adobe home in Taos, New Mexico, one evening in 2017. Mary and Allan had just met in Marfa, Texas, during the former ghost town’s annual open studio exhibits.




Allan asked if I would be interested in having my archives at his university, and I accepted his offer. I spent several months organizing my documents in the manner he suggested, and once they were ready, I drove cases of legal documents, flyers, sketchbooks, newsletters, and personal planners up to British Columbia, crossing into Canada on the ferry in my G20 conversion van. This would be one of nearly 40 trips to Canada I had made since I settled my 25-to-life Three Strikes Felony case on February 16, 1995, in Judge Lucy McCabe’s San Francisco court. The criminal case started when I was attacked by Mayor Frank Jordan’s film commissioner, Nick Rommel, in a first-floor City Hall phone booth. The near-daily arrests for felony conspiracy to share food in violation of a court order had not stopped us from feeding the homeless, so it seems that the mayor thought sending me to prison for a quarter of a century might do the trick.




After I made my first delivery for the archives, I periodically shipped more materials, including original paintings and the 750,000-word manuscript of what would become my 150,000-word memoir, 

Soup Street.










I emailed Allan to let him know my first memoir would be published in May 2026 and that I was ready to come up to Victoria as promised. Allan responded, “I propose organizing a Big Celebration of Food Not Bombs at University of Victoria to showcase your Food Not Bombs collection in the Anarchist Archive, plus you can launch your book at the event.” He purchased a round-trip flight from San Francisco and emailed me a link to request a table at the Victoria Anarchist Bookfair. He warned me that some of the local activists were smearing me and to make sure my application focused on my books. These were the same smears that had been used to cancel my presentation at the fifth anniversary of the founding of Food Not Bombs in Waltham, Massachusetts, suggesting there is an intelligence agency effort to silence anarchists who question obedience to government policies.




I was excited to speak at the dedication of the Food Not Bombs archives on Monday, September 21, 2026, and present my latest title, 

Soup Street,

 at the Victoria Anarchist Bookfair.




When I landed at Vancouver International Airport, all went well until I was stopped by Canadian Border and Customs. I have entered Canada at least 40 times since 1995. Each time I entered, I would be questioned about my felony conviction in San Francisco for assault, battery, and strong-arm robbery. I would explain that I had been framed by Mayor Jordan in San Francisco’s campaign to stop Food Not Bombs from protesting war by feeding the hungry.










I would share that I had to plead out in a case in which I was attacked in a phone booth at San Francisco City Hall by the mayor’s film commissioner. As I was telling them about the events of January 4, 1994, I would open a copy of one of my books, such as 

Hungry for Peace,

 and show them the photos of the riot police guarding the food from the homeless at Golden Gate Park. I would tell the story of the arrest, explaining that I was wearing a chef’s coat and a puffy chef’s hat and had been holding a sign saying “Viva Zapatista, No NAFTA” while waiting for the rest of the food to be delivered for that noon’s meal. “Some guy crossed over the street from City Hall and yelled at me.” The deranged man made a call on his flip phone, and before long, a tow truck arrived and towed my truck and its load of bagels from my legal parking spot.




I described how I walked through the City Hall metal detectors to the closest payphone to call parking and traffic to locate my pickup. The guy I would later learn was Nick Rommel cornered me and started attacking me.




I would tell them that while on the call, I told the woman at towing, “I am sorry; someone is smashing against the phone booth, and I have to find another phone to call from.” That often drew a smile from the Canadian officials.




I continued by explaining that I went to a second-floor payphone and, after locating my truck, I headed down that beautiful cascade of stairs in the rotunda. As I was about halfway down the stairs, one of those in the mayor’s police detail called out, “Hey Keith, we want to speak with you.” I described how one of the officers had a little blue book, holding it up and saying I was being arrested under the new California Three Strikes law, suggesting the code was in the publication.




Most of the time, the Canadian border officials would laugh at the insanity of the conviction and wave me through. If they didn’t, I would drive to the next border crossing; I would repeat the story, and they would wave me through.










Not this time.




A tall, lanky officer directed me to place my suitcase and backpack on a long stainless steel counter. His partner removed all my things and spread them out.




I shared the story of my having been arrested for feeding the homeless and gave her a copy of the letter of invitation from the University of Victoria. I opened the books 

Hungry for Peace

 and 

Soup Street

 to show the photos of riot police guarding the food from the homeless, but the young customs official, Jessica Vung, was not interested and told me she had to go to a back room to check things out.




She returned, asked more questions, and went to the back office. When she returned, she asked if I had ever had any problems getting into Canada before. I replied that I am always questioned about this arrest, but I have always been let in. I told her about the time I was crossing over at Niagara, and an officer found two glass vials in my ashtray, unscrewed the cap on one of them, licked her finger, and tasted the powder. When the officer asked what it was, I told her that it was my friend Eric Weinberger’s ashes. The seven border officers searching my vehicle all stepped away from my van and let me into Canada.




While I was sitting and waiting for the border and customs officer to return from the back room, I got a text from Air Canada saying my flight to Victoria was boarding. The official came back and asked more questions. The next time she returned, she asked if I wanted any food or water and showed me a menu. I requested water, coffee, and their vegetarian sandwich without cheese. They also let me charge my phone. I called my girlfriend, Kathleen, in Santa Cruz to tell her what was happening. She called Allan to let him know that I still hadn’t made it through customs.




The officer was growing more sympathetic with each encounter. When she would return from the back office, I started to greet her with “Fantastic, so they are letting me in,” and she would smile, but there were others in the back room who had other ideas. Kathleen suggested I show them the letter from Amnesty International in which they would declare Food Not Bombs activists “prisoners of conscience” and call for our unconditional release if convicted. I found the document on my phone and showed it to them, but they didn’t seem too interested.










At one point, she asked me about the FBI and its interest in Food Not Bombs. I shared that according to a 2009 U.S. State Department lecture on C-SPAN comparing the people who share vegan meals in the parks with al-Qaeda and asking who was more dangerous, the Obama State Department official claimed that the people sharing vegan meals were more dangerous because they were friendly local community members who were advocating that our taxes should be “diverted from the military to fund healthcare, education and other social services.” He claimed that if Americans were to agree with the vegans, there wouldn’t be enough funding to fight al-Qaeda.




I ate the Tim Hortons sandwich with lettuce and a slice of tomato before she led me to the back room. That officer told me that under Canadian law, they couldn’t let me in because in Canada my “conviction” would be penal code —blah, blah, blah. She told me they would not charge me with a criminal violation of Canada’s immigration laws and would just send me back to the United States.




The officer placed two papers in front of me. One was “Allowed to Leave Canada,” and the other said “is a person who is a foreign national who has not been authorized to enter Canada and who in my opinion, is inadmissible pursuant to: Paragraph 36(1)(b) in that there are reasonable grounds to believe is a permanent resident or foreign national who is inadmissible on grounds of serious criminality for having been convicted of an offense outside Canada that, if committed in Canada would constitute an offense under Act of Parliament punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of at least 10 years.”




Below that, in the section titled “This report is based on the following information,” item 4 stated “Sought entry on 2026/09/18 at Vancouver International Airport for the purpose of speaking at a presentation in Victoria.”




Item 5 read, “Was convicted on 1994-10-28 for Force?ADW Not Firearm:GBI Likely (245(A)(1)PC San Francisco.”




It is odd that they claimed I was convicted on October 28, 1994, since I pleaded out, getting credit for 500 days served in jail to avoid life in prison on February 16, 1995, and the only court appearance of mine in October 1994 was on Halloween. It was a very memorable court appearance because those who came to support me took Halloween candy set out at offices throughout the courthouse and shared the treats with the public to mock the law against sharing food that had placed me in this position.




The Notice of Transporter had the checkbox labeled “allowed to withdraw his/her application to enter under section 42IRPR” checked.




I signed the forms.










They had said that they had to put me on the first flight to the United States, which was leaving for Austin, Texas, at 2:00 a.m., because that was Canadian policy. I asked if Air Canada would fly me to San Francisco from Austin, but that was not possible. I would have to buy my own ticket home. Finally, they agreed to send me on the morning flight to San Francisco.




A security team directed me to remove all my belongings, including my wallet, phone, belt, shoes, and pain medication, and ordered me to stand against the wall with my hands spread out. They frisked me, checked under my hair, and placed me in a chilly holding cell with the lights blazing. I tried to sleep on the metal-ribbed bench, but it was impossible. It would turn out that this aggravated the back injury I had been seeking surgery for, and I suffered level-10 pain for the following two weeks.




The distant clanging of doors and muffled conversations filled me with the dread I remembered when locked up during my days in jail facing the Three Strikes sentence.




Finally, they opened the cell and told me to get dressed. A security woman took me to the ticket desk where papers had to be signed. After that, she led me through the TSA-style security check, then took me to U.S. Customs, where the officer asked why I was being removed. I said for feeding the hungry. After that brief interaction, the security officer walked me to the gate. Following a 30-minute wait, the security officer led me to the boarding agent.




While waiting to board, I spoke with another passenger who it turned out was headed to TrueNorth Health in Santa Rosa, California. I let her know I had done several water-only fasts at TrueNorth and found it very helpful. I shared that my first 23-day water-only fast cured me of 20 years of suffering from fibromyalgia. This seemed to give her hope that she could recover from her autoimmune illness. Sadly, after all the “coincidences” in my life that have turned out to be part of an intelligence operation, I worried this might also be the case, but so far there is no evidence of this, and it was likely one of the many non-state-sponsored events of serendipity that have blessed my life.




There were more papers signed at the gate. I boarded, and a white envelope was handed over to an Air Canada employee. I was tired and in so much pain that I found the flight exhausting.




When I was leaving the plane in San Francisco, an airline attendant handed me a white envelope with legal documents and my passport. I phoned Kathleen to let her know I had landed and headed for the area where Ubers do their pickups. A young man was standing outside his car and I asked if he was an Uber driver. He was, and he was willing to drive me home to Santa Cruz.










My girlfriend, Kathleen, had emailed my emergency contacts while I was in the holding cell. Among those who responded was my friend and one of my lawyers, Randy Baker, who had defended me against the attacks by the government in San Francisco and had filed the civil rights lawsuits that included documents in discovery that provided me with the September 27, 1988, wiretap memo by San Francisco Police Department commander Richard Holder that was used to justify the police beating I took outside the Presidio on October 15, 1988, during a protest against the U.S. war in El Salvador. This is the text of his response to Kathleen’s email.




“Keith is indeed an exemplary man. Few people have allowed themselves to be subjected to the scores — perhaps hundreds — of arrests, and numerous beat-ups that Keith has suffered in the cause of advocating for a society in which our abundant resources are devoted to human needs, rather than to unnecessary wars.




In the course of representing Keith and Food Not Bombs in the early 1990s a letter from the San Francisco D.A. to the San Francisco City Attorney that I obtained in discovery in one of Keith’s suits underscored that law enforcement was not the objective underlying the City’s relentless brutality towards Keith and Food Not Bombs. The letter told the City Attorney to stop the arrests, because his office would not prosecute the cases. Yet the arrests and police harassment continued.




Since Food Not Bombs’ dispensing of free bagels, miso soup and anarchist literature was not threatening public safety, and prosecution was off the table, it became rather difficult to conclude anything other than that the point of the City’s persecution of Food Not Bombs was to stop their highly visible and poignant representation of the insanity of our current system, attracting groups of largely unsheltered people standing in line for food in highly visible venues — along with the message that things didn’t have to be this way.




In light of the City’s clearly speech-suppressive objective underlying its relentless persecution of Keith and Food Not Bombs, I think it virtually unbelievable that the prosecution that resulted in Keith’s convictions cited by Canadian officials was not the result of the City’s presentation of a grossly misleading account of an incident, rather than any felonious conduct on Keith’s part.




Insofar as Canada has relied on those convictions in considering the appropriateness of Keith’s entry into the country, it is grossly mistaken. Canada can only benefit from his presence. The government needs to reconsider its decision to exclude him.”




“Randy Baker




Attorney at Law”










During this ordeal, I often thought of how lucky I was, thinking of all those people captured by ICE, often disappeared from their families and held in horrid conditions for weeks and months before being shipped off to countries with which they often have no connection. Stories like that have been shared by a young Food Not Bombs volunteer in Monterrey, Mexico, who had spent his life in San Antonio, only to be dropped off in a remote area of Mexico and forced to search for his friends who had come to the border to meet him.

Why anarchists must confront totalitarian humanism










by 

Keith Preston




It can reasonably be said that the overwhelming majority of liberals, progressives, social democrats, and Marxists would affirm all or most of the following presumptions:







The state is an expression of popular democracy (see Jean-Jacques Rousseau)




The ever increasing centralization of institutions is conducive to economic and technological progress




Ever larger states with an ever greater number of functions are necessary to modern society




The state is a means of advancing the disadvantaged and imposing progressive values on benighted or reactionary local communities and regions




The legitimacy of an eventual world federal government, and the principles of collective security, liberal internationalism, human rights internationalism, or what Noam Chomsky critically calls “military humanism”




The desirability of forging a national and international consensus around “progressive” values with these to be imposed by national governments and international institutions




The desirability of the welfare state, the managerial state, and managed economy




The core principles of the Enlightenment religion of reason, progress, and scientism




The legitimacy and necessity of the public administration state




The desirability of the nanny state and its involvement in such issues as the compulsory use of seat belts, smoking bans, diet regulation, firearms prohibition, compulsory education, far reaching measures aimed at “child protection,” etc.







It goes without saying that the overwhelming majority of these precepts, perhaps all of them, cannot be reconciled with libertarian, anarchist, anti-statist, decentralist, or anti-authoritarian values of ANY kind.




It also goes without saying that since the days of the rivalries between Marx and Engels, and Proudhon, Stirner, and Bakunin, authoritarian leftists, statist socialists, and centralizing progressives have been our enemy. Period.




It is time for anarchists to carve out an entirely new paradigm for themselves that defines the political spectrum not in terms of left and right or reactionary and progressive, but in terms of anti-authoritarian vs authoritarian, anti-statist vs statist, and decentralist vs centralist. This will be among the primary dividing lines of the future.

Peter Marshall: an organic radical inspiration




The latest in our series of profiles from our sister 

organic radicals

 site.
















“Living systems do not form hierarchies but rather networks at different levels”




Peter Marshall (1946-) is an anarchist philosopher, historian, biographer and poet.




His broad and inspiring vision also includes ecology, alchemy and archaeology and he has been described by 

Resurgence

 magazine as one of the 25 ‘visionary voices’ who shaped the new world view in the last quarter of the 20th century.




In the best organic radical tradition, he stresses the importance of holistic thinking as the basis of any authentic philosophy.




He wrote in the 2000 book 

Riding the Wind

: “Ultimately, holistic thinking recognizes that all things come from the One and proceed to the One. All is One and One is All.













“There is unity in diversity throughout the universe; indeed, the greater the diversity, the more overall the harmony. It comes as no surprise that the Greek word 

kosmos

 originally meant both the universe and harmony: they are synonymous”. (1)




Marshall traces the thread of this holistic thinking through Eastern religions to the medieval alchemists’ belief in an 

anima mundi

 or world spirit. (2)




Anarchism very much forms part of this philosophical tradition. In his book 

Demanding the Impossible

, Marshall traces anarchism’s roots back to the Taoists of ancient China. (3)




Explaining the later development of anarchist theory, he described how its thinkers had challenged the idea that order and stability had to be imposed on human communities from above.




He wrote: “The State with its coercive apparatus of law, courts, prisons and army came to be seen not as the remedy for but rather the principal cause of social disorder.













“Such unorthodox thinkers went still further to make the outlandish suggestion that a society without rulers would not fall into a condition of chaotic unruliness, but might produce the most desirable form of ordered human existence”. (4)




From this anarchist perspective, the “state of nature” without government would not be Thomas Hobbes’ nightmare of a permanent war of all against all, but a harmonious and peaceable way of living.




Marshall endorses 

Peter Kropotkin’s

 nature-based understanding of authentic society when he notes: “Living systems, it is now clear, do not form hierarchies but rather networks at different levels.




“An ecosystem is a network of organisms, in which each organism forms a node, with each node itself a network of organs and so on”. (5)
