Türkiye, Pakistan ve Suudi Arabistan arasında imzalanan Mekke Ortak Savunma Anlaşması'nın onaylanmasına ilişkin kanun teklifi Türkiye Büyük Millet Meclisi (TBMM) Genel Kurulu'nda görüşülüyor.




Genel Kurulda, teklifin tümü üzerinde görüşmelerin tamamlanmasının ardından maddelerinin görüşmelerine geçildi.




Teklifin ilk maddesi de gece saatlerinde kabul edildi. Bunun üzerine TBMM Başkanvekili Celal Adan, birleşime ara verdi. Diğer maddeler üzerindeki görüşmeler bugün 14.00’te devam edecek.




Ancak dün akşamki görüşmeler tartışmalı geçti. İktidar ve muhalefet partileri anlaşmanın Türkiye açısından nasıl askeri yükümlülükler doğuracağı ve ülkeyi bölgesel çatışmalara dahil edip etmeyeceği üzerinden tartıştı. 




AKP ve MHP anlaşmanın bölgesel güvenliği ve caydırıcılığı güçlendireceğini savunurken, CHP de barış ve iş birliğine katkı sağlayacağı gerekçesiyle destek vereceğini açıkladı.




YENİ Parti, DEM Parti, İYİ Parti ve Yeni Yol ise Türkiye'nin üstleneceği askeri yükümlülüklerin belirsizliğine ve bölgesel çatışmalara dahil olma riskine dikkat çekti. Askerin yurt dışında görevlendirilmesi ve olası savaş riskleri üzerinden tartışmalar yaşandı.




Genel Kurul görüşmelerinden öne çıkanlar




AKP Kayseri Milletvekili Hulusi Akar, anlaşmanın Pakistan ve Suudi Arabistan'la mevcut askeri iş birliklerini kurumsallaştırmayı amaçladığını belirterek, "Bu anlaşma hiçbir şekilde NATO'ya alternatif vesaire değil; bu tamamlayıcı bir birliktelik ve hiçbir ülkeye de karşı değil" dedi. Akar,  askerin yurt dışında görevlendirilmesinin söz konusu olması halinde bunun "mutlaka Meclisin iznine tabi" olacağını söyledi.




MHP Erzurum Milletvekili Kamil Aydın da anlaşmanın "kolektif caydırıcılığı artıracağını" savunarak MHP grubunun teklife destek vereceğini açıkladı.




CHP Grup Başkanı Faik Öztrak ise anlaşmanın yeni çatışmaların değil, bölgesel barış ve iş birliğinin aracı olması gerektiğini söyledi. Öztrak, "Bu iş birliğinden doğan güç yeni savaşlar açmak için değil savaştan caydırmak, barışı sağlamak, sınırlarımızı korumak ve ticareti geliştirmek için kullanılmalıdır" diyerek CHP'nin anlaşmaya olumlu oy vereceğini açıkladı.




İYİ Parti ise anlaşmanın sınırlarının belirsiz olduğunu savundu. Grup adına konuşan Lütfü Türkkan, "Bizim itirazımız işbirliğine değil, belirsizliğedir, ortak savunmaya değil sınırları çizilmemiş yükümlülükleredir" dedi. Türkkan, Türkiye'nin askeri ve mali yükümlülükleri ile bölgesel çatışmalara taraf olma riskine karşı güvencelerin açıklığa kavuşturulmasını istedi.




DEM Parti Antalya Milletvekili Saruhan Oluç da Türkiye'nin yeni vekalet savaşlarına dahil edilmemesi gerektiğini belirterek, "Türkiye herhangi bir vekalet savaşının parçası olmamalıdır, bunu reddediyoruz" dedi. DEM Parti Diyarbakır Milletvekili Ceylan Akça Cupolo ise partisinin "hayır" oyu vereceğini açıklayarak, "Gözümüz kapalı bir şekilde savaşa gitmeyi reddediyoruz" ifadelerini kullandı.




Yeni Yol Grubu'ndan Hasan Karal, savunma iş birliklerinin güçlendirilmesini desteklediklerini ancak askeri yükümlülüklerin ve Meclis'in denetim yetkisinin açık biçimde belirlenmesi gerektiğini söyledi. Karal, "Bu konulardaki belirsizlikler giderilmediği için kanun teklifine mevcut haliyle olumlu yaklaşamadığımızı ifade ediyorum" dedi. Aynı gruptan Selçuk Özdağ da anlaşmaya ret oyu verdiklerini açıkladı.




YENİ Parti İstanbul Milletvekili Namık Tan ise anlaşmanın Türkiye'yi sınırları belirsiz askeri operasyonlara sürükleyebileceğini savundu. "Mehmetçik'in asli görevi Suudi vatanını değil, kendi vatanımızı korumaktır" diyen Tan, anlaşmaya karşı olduklarını söyledi.




TBMM Dışişleri Komisyonu Başkanı Fuat Oktay ise eleştirilere yanıt verirken anlaşmanın otomatik olarak asker gönderilmesi anlamına gelmediğini savundu. "Anlaşma onaylandığı takdirde, Suud çöllerine Türk askerini, Mehmetçik'i gönderiyoruz... Böyle bir uygulama da söz konusu değil, böyle bir şey de yok" diyen Oktay, olası adımların tarafların değerlendirmesi ve oydaşmasıyla belirleneceğini söyledi. Oktay'a göre destek; istihbarat ve tecrübe paylaşımından ekipman desteğine veya askeri karşılığa kadar farklı biçimler alabilecek.




Oktay ayrıca, anlaşmanın ilk 10 yılında çekilmeye getirilen sınırlamayı savunarak bunun uzun vadeli stratejik anlaşmaların doğasından kaynaklandığını söyledi. "10 yıl süre içerisinde de herhangi bir konuda oydaşma sağlanamazsa [...] Türkiye'nin arzu etmediği bir konunun uygulamaya alınması asla ve asla mümkün değildir" dedi.



















Suudi güvenliği için üçlü askerî ittifak: Mekke Anlaşması komisyondan geçti




27 Ekim 2026













Anlaşma metni şöyle:




Türkiye Cumhuriyeti, Pakistan İslam Cumhuriyeti Ve Suudi Arabistan Krallığı Arasında Ortak Savunma İçin Mekke Anlaşması




Türkiye Cumhuriyeti Hükümeti, Pakistan İslam Cumhuriyeti Hükümeti ve Suudi Arabistan Krallığı Hükümeti (bundan böyle "Taraf", "Taraflar" veya "Çekirdek Taraflar" olarak adlandırılacaktır),




Egemenliğe karşılıklı saygı, Birleşmiş Milletler Şartı ilkeleri, uluslararası hukuk ve ilgili iç hukuk ilkelerini göz önünde bulundurarak; "Taraflar" arasındaki savunma ortaklığına yönelik mevcut işbirliği mekanizmalarını, koordinasyonu ve entegrasyonu bir ortak savunma anlaşmasına taşımak hususunda mutabık kalarak,




"Taraflar" arasındaki ilişkileri, ortak menfaatler doğrultusunda, silahlı kuvvetlerin birlikte çalışabilirliği, hazırlık düzeyi ve etkinliğini de kapsayan işbirliği, koordinasyon ve entegrasyon temelinde daha da geliştirmeye yönelik iradeyi teyit ederek, böylelikle "Taraflar" ve halkları arasında mevcut dostluk ve kardeşlik bağlarını pekiştirerek,




"Tarafların" birbirlerinin iç işlerine karışmama, egemen eşitlik, toprak bütünlüğü ve uluslararası kabul görmüş sınırların ihlal edilemezliği ilkelerinin önemini teyit ederek, bağımsızlıklarına, egemenliklerine ve toprak bütünlüklerine karşı silahlı saldırı durumunda gerekli karşılıklı destek tedbirlerinin uygulanmasının esas olduğunu beyan ederek,




Küresel ve bölgesel barış, istikrar ve güvenliğin temini için uluslararası hukuk ve Birleşmiş Milletler Şartı'na uygun olarak ortak çaba ve eşgüdümün önemini belirterek,




Terörizmle mücadelede "Tarafların" yetkili makamları arasında mevcut işbirliğinin derinleştirilmesi arzusunu kaydederek,




Uluslararası konularda ortak bir duruş sergilemek maksadıyla bölgesel ve uluslararası kuruluşlarda "Taraflar" arasında mevcut işbirliğinin güçlendirilmesinin önemini vurgulayarak,




"Taraflar" arasında savunma ve savunma sanayii işbirliğinin daha da geliştirilmesinin gerekli olduğunu kaydederek,




Müteakip hususlarda anlaşma sağlamıştır:




Madde 1




"Taraflar" birbirlerinin bağımsızlığının, egemenliğinin, toprak bütünlüğünün ve uluslararası alanda tanınan hudutlarının ihlal edilemezliğinin sağlanması ve korunmasını teminen işbirliği yaparlar. "Taraflardan" herhangi birinin toprak bütünlüğünün, egemenliğinin ve uluslararası alanda tanınan sınırlarının tehdit edilmesi veya tehlikeye düşmesi durumunda, "Taraflar" bu tehdit(ler) veya tehlike(ler)i bertaraf etmek maksadıyla gerekli tüm yöntemleri kullanırlar.




Madde 2




"Taraflardan" herhangi birine yönelik dış kaynaklı bir silahlı saldırı, tüm "Taraflara" yönelik bir saldırı olarak kabul edilir. "Taraflardan" birinin başka bir ülke veya ülke grubu tarafından silahlı saldırıya veya askeri saldırganlığa uğraması halinde, "Taraflar" saldırıya uğrayan "Tarafa" birbirlerine sağlayabilecekleri karşılıklı yardım imkanlarının tamamını kullanarak derhal yardım edecektir. Bu amaçla "Taraflar", Birleşmiş Milletler Şartı'nın 51'inci Maddesinin tanıdığı meşru müdafaa hakkının kullanılmasını teminen, ihtiyaç duyulan yardımın objektif değerlendirmesini müteakip sağlanacak desteğin kapsam ve niteliğine karar vererek; askeri imkân ve kabiliyetler de dahil olmak üzere mevcut imkanları çerçevesinde işbirliği yaparlar.




Madde 3




"Taraflar", işbu Anlaşma'nın 2'nci Maddesi gereğince savunma, savunma sanayii ve güvenlik alanlarında yakın işbirliği yapar; Silahlı Kuvvetleri arasındaki ilişkileri geliştirir ve savunma alanındaki işbirliğini güçlendirmeye yönelik mutabık kalınan faaliyetleri uygular.




Madde 4




"Taraflar" uluslararası güvenlik konularında düzenli olarak istişarelerde bulunurlar. "Taraflar" hayati çıkarlarını ve ulusal güvenliklerini korumak ve milli güvenliklerine karşı tehdit ve tehlikeleri bertaraf etmek maksadıyla ortak değerlendirmeler temelinde bireysel ve müşterek tedbirler geliştirmek üzere sürekli ve etkili bir şekilde birbirlerine yardım eder ve işbirliği yaparlar.




Madde 5




"Taraflar", bölgesel ve uluslararası istikrar ve güvenliği olumsuz etkileyen terörizmin tüm çeşit ve tezahürleriyle mücadelede operasyonel seviye de dahil olmak üzere mevcut işbirliğini ve müşterek çabaları güçlendirirler.




Madde 6




Savaşta ve barışta, "Taraflar", savunma yeteneklerini geliştirmek maksadıyla, savunma kurumları arasında karşılıklı personel değişimi, ortak eğitim programları ve tatbikatlar ile "Tarafların" Silahlı Kuvvetlerinin birlikte çalışabilirliğinin artırılmasına yönelik konuşlanma ve faaliyetleri teşvik ederler.




Madde 7




Savunma yeteneklerini güçlendirmek maksadıyla "Taraflar" karşılıklı mutabakat temelinde aşağıdaki alanlarda savunma sanayii kurumları arasında teknoloji paylaşımını, ortak teknoloji geliştirilmesini, ortak üretimi ve savunma sanayii kuruluşları arasındaki işbirliğini desteklerler:




a) Savunma alanında ortak üretimin teşvik edilmesi,




b) Uzmanlık gerektiren teknolojilerde ortak Ar-Ge projeleri ile savunma inovasyonunun hayata geçirilmesi,




c) "Tarafların" topraklarında, herhangi bir "Tarafın" uzmanları vasıtasıyla insan kaynağının yetiştirilmesi ve askeri sanayinin desteklenmesi,




d) Savunma sanayii ile savunma Ar-Ge ve inovasyonu alanlarında uzmanlık ve edinilen derslerin paylaşılması,




e) "Tarafların" karşılıklı mutabakata varacağı diğer işbirliği alanları.




Madde 8










"Çekirdek Taraflar", ortak savunmaya stratejik yön vermek, "Taraflar" arasındaki savunma ve güvenlik işbirliğini geliştirmek ve işbu Anlaşmanın uygulanması sırasında ortaya çıkabilecek engelleri ele almak maksadıyla, "Tarafların" Dışişleri Bakanları, Savunma Bakanları ile Genelkurmay Başkanlarından oluşan "Stratejik Siyasi ve Savunma Komitesi"ni kurar. Komite "Taraflar" arasında dönüşümlü ev sahipliğiyle yılda iki defa toplanır. "Tarafların" liderleri, gerekli görüldüğü takdirde yılda bir kez toplanabilir.










"Stratejik Siyasi ve Savunma Komitesi", gerekli gördüğü takdirde, alt komiteler kurabilir.










İşbu Anlaşmada öngörülen işbirliği alanlarının uygulanması maksadıyla, gerektiğinde "Taraflar" arasında anlaşmalar veya protokoller müzakere edilir.










"Stratejik Siyasi ve Savunma Komitesi", "Çekirdek Tarafların" oydaşmasıyla, bu Anlaşmaya diğer "Tarafların" katılımına ilişkin usul ve esasları belirlemeye ve onaylamaya yetkilidir.










"Stratejik Siyasi ve Savunma Komitesi"ne hizmet vermek üzere, merkezi Suudi Arabistan Krallığı'nda bulunan bir Sekretarya ihdas edilir. Sekretarya, Suudi Arabistan Krallığı ile bir merkez anlaşması akdeder. Sekretaryanın işleyişi, teşkilat yapısı ve kuruluşuna ilişkin usul ve esaslar, "Çekirdek Tarafların" oydaşmasıyla bilahare kararlaştırılır.










Sekretaryaya, "Çekirdek Taraflar" arasında dönüşümlü olarak üç yıllık bir süre için görevlendirilen bir Genel Sekreter başkanlık eder. İlk Genel Sekreter Pakistan İslam Cumhuriyeti vatandaşı olacaktır.










Bu maddenin hükümleri, "Taraflar" arasında mevcut askeri işbirliği komitelerinin çalışmalarına halel getirmez.










Madde 9




İstihbarat alanındaki işbirliğini derinleştirmek ve bu doğrultuda gerekli eşgüdümü sağlamak amacıyla "Taraflar", bilgi güvenliği, verilerin korunması ve gizliliğe riayet ederek, karşılıklı mutabakata varılan güvenli kanallar üzerinden istihbarat paylaşımında bulunacaktır.




Madde 10




"Taraflar", lojistik destek hizmetlerinin mevcudiyeti ve uyumluluğuna bağlı olarak, barışta, savaşta ve diğer olağanüstü durumlarda, silah, mühimmat, yakıt, yedek parça ve diğer teçhizat dahil olmak üzere birbirlerine lojistik destek sağlar.




Madde 11




Uluslararası hukuk ve "Tarafların" ilgili iç hukukları saklı kalmak kaydıyla, "Taraflar", bu Anlaşmanın hükümlerinin uygulanmasında işbu Anlaşmayı hukuki dayanak olarak kabul edecek ve ihtiyaç halinde ilave yasal düzenlemeler önerecektir.




Madde 12




İşbu Anlaşma, "Tarafların" daha önce akdetmiş oldukları uluslararası anlaşmalardan doğan hak ve yükümlülüklerine halel getirmez.




Madde 13










"Taraflar", işbu Anlaşma kapsamında elde edecekleri gizlilik dereceli bilgi ve belgelerin mahremiyetine riayet ederler ve milli mevzuatlara saygı gösterirler.










Gizlilik dereceli bilgi ve belgeler, "Taraflar" dışındaki bir devlet, şirket ya da kişiyle paylaşılmaz.










Gizlilik dereceli bilgi ve belgelere erişimin "bilmesi gereken" prensibiyle ve sadece uygun seviyede güvenlik yetkisine sahip kişilere sağlanması temin edilir.










Madde 14




İşbu Anlaşmanın yorumundan veya uygulanmasından doğacak herhangi bir anlaşmazlık, "Taraflar" arasında istişareler ve görüşmeler vasıtasıyla dostane bir şekilde çözülür.




Madde 15




İşbu Anlaşma "Çekirdek Taraflar" arasında istişareler ve oybirliğiyle tadil edilebilir.




Madde 16










İşbu Anlaşma, her bir "Tarafın" tabi olduğu usuller uyarınca onaylanacak ve son onay belgesinin "Stratejik Siyasi ve Savunma Komitesi" Sekretaryasına tevdi edildiği tarihte yürürlüğe girecektir.










İşbu Anlaşma süresiz olarak yürürlükte kalacaktır.










Herhangi bir "Taraf", işbu Anlaşmanın yürürlüğe giriş tarihinden itibaren on yıl geçmesinin ardından, çekilme niyetini en az üç ay önceden diğer "Taraflara" diplomatik kanallardan yazılı bilgilendirme yapmak suretiyle Anlaşmadan çekilebilecektir.










İşbu Anlaşmanın sonlandırılması ya da Anlaşmadan çekilmesi, sona erme ya da çekilme tarihinden önce "Taraflarca" mutabık kalındığı üzere halihazırda devam etmekte olan hiçbir faaliyet ve projeyi etkilemez.










"Tarafların" gizlilik dereceli bilgi ve belgelerin korunması ve ifşasının önlenmesi konusundaki sorumlulukları, işbu Anlaşmanın sona ermesi ve Anlaşmadan çekilmesinden sonra da devam eder.










İşbu Anlaşma, Türkçe, Arapça ve İngilizce dillerinde, her bir metin aynı derecede geçerli olmak üzere, üç asıl nüsha halinde imzalanmıştır. Metinlerin yorumunda farklılık bulunması halinde İngilizce metin esas alınır.




İşbu Anlaşma 7 Ağustos 2026 Cuma günü Mekke'de imzalanmıştır.







(HA)

author: Menchani Tilendo
title: Women tending the Kasibu barricades against large-scale mining
content:
At the barricade, she has found her place by turning its often-invisible work of care into a collective act of resistance.







KASIBU, Nueva Vizcaya – In this third class municipality some 300 kilometers north of Luzon, land is life. It feeds families, sustains Indigenous communities, and carries generations of history. Yet under Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s banner of “development,” mining expansion threatens to dispossess communities of the very land that keeps them alive. 




In defense of their land, the people of Kasibu set up the people’s barricade against large-scale mining. Their steadfastness was met with force when on 

August 28 

this year, police arrested 11 locals of Barangay Paquet for blocking the entry of North Luzon Mineral Resources Corporation (NLMRC).




They were later released on bail, but the crackdown has not ended because members of the community continue to face 

trumped-up criminal charges

 or what advocates consider as Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation (SLAPP). 




The NLMRC is the seventh company to attempt exploration in the area. It holds a government-issued exploration permit covering 4,456 hectares across parts of Kasibu, where it seeks to explore for gold, copper, and other minerals. 




It is no coincidence that mining companies have their eyes on Kasibu. Beneath its mineral-rich mountains lie the farmlands and watersheds that sustain its people. Known as the Citrus Capital of Luzon, the municipality grows calamansi, other citrus fruits, and vegetables, while the 18,417-hectare Kasibu Watershed forms part of a vital network of watersheds in the Sierra Madre. 




For farmers already struggling with high production costs and potential losses of P25,000 ($392.63) to P150,000 ($2,355.75) per cropping cycle, mining threatens to worsen their hardships. They fear contamination of soil and water, as well as landslides, droughts, and floods. The drive to extract mineral wealth destroys the land that feeds communities and sustains generations. 




But the people of Kasibu have never surrendered their land. Their resistance dates back to 2007, when the Kasibu Inter-Tribal Response for Ecological Development (KIRED) emerged from the community’s struggle against large-scale mining. Alongside the Alyansa ng Novo Vizcayano para sa Kalikasan (ANVIK), they have helped sustain a network of barricades against successive mining ventures. 




There are currently six barricades standing across Kasibu, positioned along routes that mining operations could use to advance into community lands. The main barricade in Barangay Paquet has drawn more than 100 regular members, with more joining when the community calls for reinforcements.




Women play a central role in sustaining this resistance. 




At least 300 women are part of the wider community barricades, taking on leadership roles and helping sustain their operations. As mining threatens their livelihoods and ancestral lands, these women are fighting for their families’ right to remain on, live from, and care for the land they call home.




Nanay Linda: Never giving up




Nanay Linda, 60 years old.




At 60, Linda Kuruko knows the weight of a life spent working the land. Born in Lamot, Ifugao, she grew up in poverty before her family settled in Kasibu in search of a better life. She has spent years as a farmer, making ends meet even when harvest prices fall. 




“I’m still strong—if I don’t work, I won’t have anything to eat,” she told 

Bulatlat

 in Filipino. 




Despite the exhaustion that comes with age, she continues to climb the mountain to join the barricade. She and her son have even built a small hut uphill so they can stay close to the community’s defense line.




Her determination is rooted in what she has witnessed in Didipio, a neighboring village in Kasibu where 

OceanaGold 

operates a large-scale gold and copper mine. She has seen how mining can damage the land and leave slopes vulnerable to erosion and landslides during heavy rains. She fears Kasibu’s communities will suffer the same fate if mining operations continue. 




But fear has never been reason enough for Nanay Linda to surrender. She knows the hardship of living harvest to harvest, and she knows what losing the land would mean for families who depend on it. Despite the harassment and the strain of waiting at the barricade for possible confrontations, she continues to stand with her fellow defenders.




“Sometimes, I feel hurt by what they do to us, but I try to keep my composure so I don’t become stressed. We are fighting for our children’s rights and for what we will pass on to them,” she said. 




She wanted her children to raise their families on their own land and her grandchildren to have the opportunity to study—something poverty denied her generation. She hopes they can build a future in Kasibu without being forced to leave in search of a livelihood elsewhere.




For  Kuruko, growing older is no reason to abandon the struggle. Years of hardship have taught her what is at stake, and the damage she has witnessed elsewhere has only strengthened her resolve.




Stella: Taking a mother’s fight beyond the household




Stella, 50 years old.




For Stella Mari Marquez, 50, being a mother means more than raising her four children. An Ibaloy who has lived in Kasibu all her life, she farms rice, vegetables, and other crops to help sustain her family. But with fertilizer costs rising and crop prices fluctuating, even months of hard work can end in losses. Now, as mining threatens the land and water her family depends on, Stella has taken her fight beyond the household. 




“If we lose our land, what will happen to our children and grandchildren?” she said in Filipino. 




She recalled that when the community barricade against NLMRC began in June 2026, residents were told the company’s entry was just for road clearing, never expecting the confrontation that followed. 




During the August 28 police assault, Marquez and the other women in the barricade were on the frontline, linking arms and preparing to face the advancing police.




“We said the women should be at the front because maybe the police would have a conscience. But it turned out they spared no one,” she told 

Bulatlat.

 




Marquez’s husband was among the 11 residents arrested on August 28. Watching a video of him being dragged by police was painful, she said, especially seeing an elderly woman dragged alongside him. After four days in detention, her husband returned home with pain in his hands and back. 




At the barricade, Marquez’s role as a mother does not end; it expands into collective care and the defense of their shared future. At the barricade, she has found her place by turning its often-invisible work of care into a collective act of resistance. Women in the barricade prepare meals and coffee, welcome visitors, and look after those keeping watch. 




To the mothers standing beside her, she has one message: “Let us continue the struggle until we win.” 




Femadel: Inheriting the fight, defending the future




Femadel, 25 years old and her cousin Cherybeth, 23 years old.




At 25, Femadel Pablo put up a small 

sari-sari 

store to help support her family. She is the second of five siblings. 




Since high school, Pablo has helped her parents in the farm and dreamed of using her education to support their farming. 




She visits the barricade twice a week, where her mother, grandparents, and other residents are also present, ready to defend their land. 




Pablo grew up hearing stories of her grandparents going to the barricade as early as 2007. 




It was her first time joining the barricade in August 2026 and witnessed police handcuffing fellow residents. She and other young people documented the arrests, recording videos that could serve as evidence. 




“I was angry, I wanted to cry, but I was also afraid,” she said, adding that seeing those arrested refuse to give up has inspired her. “They didn’t give up, so we shouldn’t either.”




For Pablo, young people have a vital role to play. They document incidents, share information online, and help ensure that abuses do not go unrecorded. But she believes courage must come with knowledge. 




Young people need to understand mining and their rights so they can face authorities with confidence and stand their ground. “It’s good to be brave, confident, and knowledgeable, so you don’t feel small,” she said. 




Watching the elders defend their land has taught her that the struggle is not theirs alone. It is also about the land and future that her generation will inherit and eventually pass on to their own children. 




It moves her to tears to see elderly residents, some already frail, still standing at the barricade. She hopes more young people will join them, bringing their skills and energy to the struggle.




Pablo dreams of a day when Kasibu will be known not for mining threats and arrests, but for the abundance its land provides. 




“I hope the news will say, ‘Kasibu, Citrus Capital of Luzon’—I hope that’s the kind of news people hear,” she said. “It’s such a waste, because Kasibu is so rich in agriculture. I hope that’s what goes viral, not another story about mining here.” 




For Pablo, defending the land is no longer simply a struggle she grew up hearing about. It is a responsibility she has chosen to carry forward. She hopes that one day, young people in Kasibu can build their lives without having to fight to protect the land that sustains them. 




Nanay Linda, Marquez, and Pablo share one conviction: Kasibu’s future must belong to the people who call it home. 




As mining is increasingly framed as “necessary for a greener future”, their struggle exposes a deeper contradiction: what kind of progress destroys the land, water, and communities that make life possible?




Their message is clear: there can be no genuine progress when communities must lose their land, livelihood, and future to make way for it. 

(AMU, RVO)

author: Vinil Kumar
title: Western Sydney Airport is a gift to business
content:
It’s rare for aviation executives and prime ministers to party in Western Sydney. But the opening of Sydney’s second airport, Western Sydney International (WSI), was an unmissable photo opportunity. Attendees included Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, his predecessors Tony Abbott and Scott Morrison, Jetstar CEO Stephanie Tully and NSW Premier Chris Minns. 

After the first passenger flight departed, the exodus back to the leafy Eastern Suburbs began, leaving behind the roar of turbo-fan engines that will only grow more frequent once the fanfare around the airport subsides.

The new airport is a monument to twenty-first century capitalism: a feat of human ingenuity, subordinated to corporate interests, with working-class people paying the price.

Background

Sections of business have long campaigned for a second major airport in Sydney. 

The established Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport at Mascot is boxed in by residential suburbs and Botany Bay. A third runway was opened in 1994, but community protests won a night-time curfew and hourly flight limits. 

Aviation is central to supply chains and corporate Australia wanted a new airport with minimal restrictions on its use.

After 60 years of 

proposals, disputes and false starts

, the project was revived in 2012, with the release of the Joint Study on Aviation Capacity in the Sydney Region by the federal and New South Wales governments. Its co-authors included the incoming Business Council of Australia head, Jennifer Westacott. 

The 

report

 warned Kingsford Smith airport would reach capacity by 2027 and unmet passenger and freight demand could cost as much as $60 billion by 2060. It argued the curfew “creates impediments for night-time movements of freight”, but that “an opportunity exists for a 24-hour freight facility to be established at a secondary airport”. Proximity to future warehousing and distribution centres made Western Sydney an enticing option.

Although the proposal for an airport at Badgerys Creek was rejected by the state and federal governments at the time, the 

Daily Telegraph

 immediately launched a 

renewed campaign

 for one. It was joined in its 

lobbying

 by the National Australia Bank, Harvey Norman, Crown Resorts, Channel 7 and executives from Western Sydney University. Backing was also 

secured

 from the peak body of local councils in Sydney. 

The Sydney Business Chamber, Western Sydney, led by former Labor state minister and member for Granville David Borger, 

established the Western Sydney Airport Alliance

 to cohere a local campaign for the airport.

In 2014, Liberal Prime Minister Tony Abbott’s federal cabinet approved the proposal for an airport at Badgerys Creek.  

Local residents objected. “Well, it’s going to make Western Sydney a nightmare to live in”, Geoff Brown, a 40-year resident of Penrith and member of the Western Sydney Conservation alliance, 

told the ABC

 at the time. “Growth and a fair go for Western Sydney doesn’t mean trashing the place, doesn't mean turning it into a wasteland of factories and industrial sites”, he said.

Abbott’s successor, Malcolm Turnbull 

manoeuvred

 to make the new airport a government-run project. The state and federal governments provided 

$29 billion in public funding

. Meanwhile Western Sydney’s hospitals, schools and public housing continued to crumble.

Government control enabled a grander development plan, including the construction of a new CBD around the airport, 

Bradfield City

. Part of Bradfield City’s purpose is military support, by “strengthening the defence industrial base through advanced manufacturing and semiconductor packaging”. 

The government ensured businesses had direct input. “It’s not often you get to help design an airport from scratch,” former Qantas CEO Alan Joyce 

celebrated

 in 2019. WSI’s then-CEO 

warmly welcomed

 the freight industry: “Tell us what size facility you need, tell us what technology you want in it and how you want it designed to optimise your productivity”. Construction company Lendlease was another big winner, scoring a 

$644 million contract

 for the airport’s earth works.

Careful messaging trumpeted WSI’s economic benefits to a dubious public, while noise and environmental concerns were addressed through non-binding consultation. Naming the airport after Australia’s youngest female pilot, Nancy Bird Walton, and highlighting Indigenous culture and sustainability in its design, represented an attempt to further head off opposition. 

Today

Cargo operations at WSI commenced on 26 July, and passenger services on 25 October. From November, WSI will also take over Kingsford Smith’s night freight operations. By 2063, the airport is projected to service 82 million passengers annually, and have a second runway. 

Noise was already an issue by August.

Barry Garousse, whose family lives less than two kilometres from the new airport, told the ABC that he gets as little as two hours of 

uninterrupted sleep

 some nights. “[I] drive semi-trailers, heavy vehicles, which we gotta comply with fatigue laws. At the moment I don’t comply with fatigue laws,” he said. 

The government’s promised noise insulation program is limited to adjacent suburbs and won’t process applications until April next year.

In July, 

Sydney’s redesigned airspace

 came into effect, concentrating multiple flightpaths for both airports over Western Sydney, particularly between Parramatta and Penrith. More flights have been routed over the city's poorest areas, while fewer flights will pass over its richest.

Flight paths over Western Sydney after 9 July. Graphic by Vinil Kumar using Inequality Map from 

OpenStats.com.au

, and flight paths from wsiflightpaths.gov.au.

“Since August, it’s been giving us grief,” Gina, a St Mary’s resident, told 

Red Flag

. “[T]rying to sleep with an aeroplane every half hour is cooked.”

Aircraft noise poses numerous health risks. The UK-based Aviation Environmental Federation 

found

 exposure “can lead to short-term responses such as sleep disturbance, annoyance, and impairment of learning in children, and long-term exposure is associated with increased risk of high blood pressure, heart disease, heart attack, stroke and dementia.” 

It also poses a 

risk to nearby wildlife

, including a not-for-profit animal sanctuary.

WSI’s noise abatement procedures “prefer” diverting night-time flights over the less-populated southwest approach—but only if conditions and flight numbers permit.

Traffic is also an issue—the airport’s train line won’t open until late 2027 or 2028. 

Instead, private bus services can charge 

up to $55 one way.

 Ubers cost 

even more

. A free shuttle bus from St Mary’s station runs every half hour, carrying 37 passengers per trip. It would take up to five buses with up to a two-hour wait to transport all 188 passengers on the first sold-out flight, assuming there’s no traffic. 

This was not an oversight: roads were prioritised. 

The initial plan in 2014 

did not include a rail link

, instead allocating $1.2 billion to upgrade major roads. The 2016 Airport Plan 

dismissed the need for rail services

 until “the mid-2040s”. Airport rail was only 

confirmed in 2018

 as part of a line for the new Western Sydney CBD. However, construction only began in 2022.

But 

freight was sorted by 2019

: “The airport’s freight precinct is set to have dedicated road access off the Northern Road, separating heavy vehicles from passenger traffic, which will enter the airport from the M12 on the opposite side of the site”.

Jet fuel will also be brought in by road

, using up to 65 B-double tankers per day at full capacity. A dedicated pipeline was investigated in 2024, but may not be “economically feasible” until the 2030s.

Safety

Capitalism’s drive to cut costs and intensify work also jeopardises industrial safety, including in aviation.

Multiple 

“near misses”

 at Kingsford Smith airport began the day after freight operations commenced at WSI, totalling eleven incidents by 31 August. 

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau’s 

preliminary report

 highlighted staff shortages, excessive workloads and noted controllers were “combining operational roles”, that is, doing two or more jobs at once.

Controllers had made 

anonymous complaints

 “regarding controller training, experience levels and overall preparation for the Sydney Basin airspace changes associated with the opening of the new Western Sydney International Airport”. 

To cut costs during the pandemic, the private operator of air traffic control services, Air Services Australia, offered early retirement to controllers more than 56 years old. This 

eliminated

 the most experienced 15 percent of its workforce. Recruitment has increased, but decades of experience can’t be replaced overnight.

Those holding the system together are working under pressure, with some working 

up to 800 hours of overtime per year, or working ten days straight on a regular basis

 according to the association representing controllers. 

But the bosses making decisions in corporate boardrooms are insulated from these problems. If anything, they’re determined to have fewer humans working in aviation.

WSI will be the first airport in Australia without a conventional control tower. Twenty-five cameras will feed video to a control centre seventeen kilometres away in Eastern Creek. 

Anonymous sources told the 

Sydney Morning Herald

 in August that 

low video quality

 required slowing flight movements as a precaution. Controllers couldn’t just look through binoculars or out the window to confirm aircraft positions. 

Loss of connectivity poses another risk. During 

April

 and 

September

, a remote control facility in Philadelphia lost radar around Newark Airport for more than a minute due to damaged cabling and backup systems failing. 

Some US airports have 

introduced AI systems

 to “advise” human controllers, with workers raising concerns about the reliability of summarised information and their ability to override AI guidance. 

 The politics of air travel

Working class people are locked out of decision making in capitalism. Democracy doesn’t extend to the workplace or the economy, including construction projects like WSI, Sydney’s toll roads, stadiums, countless luxury apartment blocks and data centres. 

The only way we can influence anything is collectively: campaigning, protesting and going on strike. Sydney Airport’s curfew, for example, was won through mass protest in the 1990s, including thousands rallying at Leichhardt oval and 

a 10,000-strong blockade of the airport

. This curfew was an important improvement in living standards for those living near the airport, which are not wealthy areas. 

Blockade of Sydney Airport on 17 December 1994. PHOTO: Photo: Brendan Esposito, Fairfax Archives.

The health and lives of western Sydney residents matter as much as anyone else’s. Demanding a curfew and 

compensation

, as was paid to residents near Kingsford Smith airport in the 1990s, should be the bare minimum. This will take serious public pressure and industrial muscle.

In recent months, 

hundreds of airport ground staff have struck

 to improve wages and conditions, meaning safer skies for everyone. Flight disruptions showed the potential power aviation workers have. 

Aviation has helped make satisfying human need possible by moving resources and people around the world at unprecedented speed. But capitalism’s profit-driven logic limits the possibilities. In a socialist society, where workers democratically control the economy, safety and sustainability would be prioritised over profit. 

Airports could be built away from cities, connected by rapid transit. Planned production could reduce excess flights from competing airlines, 

empty flights

 and unnecessary business travel. Destructive industries that add to travel volume, like the military, could and should be abolished Homes surrounding airports could be designed or upgraded with the best possible noise insulation. 

But capitalism will not forgo profits just so people can live decent lives. To win anything, from a decent night’s sleep to a decent society, we’ll need to fight them together and make a lot of noise of our own.

title: PENa Kurd dê li Amedê konferanseke li dar bixe
content:
PENa Kurd dê li Amedê bi navê, “Di pêvajoyên lihevrûniştin, lihevkirin, aştî û wekheviyê de rola wêje, ziman û rewşenbîriyê” Konferansa Wêje û Aştiyê li dar dixe.




PENa Kurd di 6ê Mijdarê de bi tevlibûna gelek rewşenbîr, nivîskar, helbestvan û siyasetmedaran li Amedê Konferansa Wêje û Aştiyê li dar dixe. Di konferasê de dê li ser gelek mijaran gotûbêj were kirin û konferans wê 2 rojan berdewam bike.




Bername




Roja yekemîn a konferansê bi mijara, “Ziman, Wêje û Mafên Gerdûnî di Pêvajoyên Aştiyê de” dest pê dike û axêver jî wiha ne:




Moderator Dîba Keskîn (Nivîskar), Burhan Sonmez (Serokê Giştî yê PENa Navneteweyî-London), Dr. Bêrîvan Doskî (Seroka Rûmetê ya Navenda PENa Kurd-Silêmanî), Weysî Aktaş (Siyasetmedar-Amed), German Rojas (Serokê Komîteya Nivîskarên ji bo Aştiyê ya PENa Navneteweyî –Santiago/Çîlî)




Beşa 2emîn a konferansê bi mijara, ‘Rola Qada Navneteweyî, Siberoja Wekheviyê û Mafên Mirovan’ û beşdariya; Moderator: Zana Farqînî (Zimannas), Carles Torner (Cîgirê Serokê PENa Navneteweyî – Katalanya), Tanja Tuma (Alîkara Serokê PENa Navneteweyî -Slovenya), Mueyed Teyîb ( Helbestvan- Hewlêr), Şadiye Manap (Nivîskar – Amed) berdewam bike.




Beşa 3emîn a konferansê bi mijara, “Rabûna Bandora Şer û Ragêşiyê ya Li Ser Ziman û Azadiya Xwederbirînê” û bi tevlibûna; Moderator: Mîna Acer (Nivîskar), Urtzî Urrutîkoetxea (Serokê Komîteya Mafê Ziman û Wergerê ya PENa Navneteweyî yê Berê – Bask), Dr. Dilawer Zeraq (Akademîsyen-Nivîskar – Amed), Fîlîz Yildirim (Akademîsyen li Cambridgeê) bi dawî bibe.




Daxuyanî




Di roja duyemîn a Konferansa Wêje û Dîrokê de beşdarvanên konferansê dê li cihên dîrokî yên Amedê bigerin û serdana Komeleya Wêjekarên Kurd, Yekîtiya Weşangerên Kurd (YEW-KURD) Enstîtuya Kurdî ya Amedê, MED-DERê, Komeleya Rojnamegeran a Dîcle Firatê (DFG) û Komeleya Rojnamegeran Jin a Mezopotamyayê (MKG) bikin.




Konferans dê bi daxuyaniya hevpar a li ser navê beşdaran, bi banga ji bo aştiyeke birûmet, wekheviya zimanê Kurdî, azadkirina zindaniyên siyasî, rojnamegeran û pêşxistina çanda demokrasiyê bi dawî bibe.







*Çavkanî: AW

author: Brian Hioe
title: What Does the Taipei Mayoral Debate Tell Us?
content:
THE TAIPEI MAYORAL DEBATE occurred on October 31st, after much discussion ahead of time about whether Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an would be willing to participate. The Shen campaign clamored for a debate, seeing as Shen’s strengths were seen in public speaking and debating, while Chiang is known for sometimes being a stiff public speaker.

The controversy about a police raid on Commander D, a gay bar in Ximending, added to such speculation. Namely, with Chiang stating that he would still attend Pride after the controversy following the raid, the debate was scheduled on the same day as Pride. That Chiang suspended a day of campaigning due to poor health prior to Pride and the debate stoked further speculation. Still, in the end, Chiang appeared at the debate without issue.

Few new policy proposals were made at the debate, which instead was primarily an opportunity for the two candidates to criticize each other and to craft their political images. Shen doubled down on efforts to depict himself as a candidate who is knowledgeable about policy, has a firm grasp of data, and has a vision for Taipei governance. By contrast, Chiang mostly touted the accomplishments of his mayoral administration, and suggested that Shen lacked knowledge of what the Taipei city government was already doing.

Both candidates accused the other of focusing simply on attacks, even as Shen asserted that he has avoided conducting a negative campaign. It is notable that Shen has avoided hyperbolic rhetoric in his campaign to date, even as the overall implication is to suggest that Chiang’s mayoral administration is inept and that he would do better.

On the whole, however, Chiang proved unusually aggressive. Frequent points of criticism alleged that Shen is simply all talk and that his proposals are not rooted in reality, while suggesting that in reality, he does not have the firm grasp of data that he seems to have. Nevertheless, given that Chiang has already accrued an image of not being able to remember facts or produce data off the top of his head, and Shen has built up an image of himself as a nerdy academic, this may not work for Chiang.

To this extent, Chiang’s points of attack on Shen may not be surprising, in appealing to social conservatives. Chiang accused Shen of promoting drug use through his advocacy for harm reduction policies, being weak on crime, and failing to carry out sufficient measures to protect children. This has been a recurring theme for the KMT, in attacking progressive politicians such as Chiang, while calling on them to enact measures to deter crime such as ensuring the continual use of capital punishment. For his part, Shen criticized Chiang for weaponizing the issue at the expense of vulnerable groups such as drug abusers who may need social support to rehabilitate themselves.

Likewise, Chiang attacked Shen on cross-strait policy several times, while also accusing Shen of having orchestrated the Great Recall Movement last year but refusing to admit to it. Shen reaffirmed a stance against mayoral exchanges between Taipei and Shanghai, provided China continues with military threats directed at Taiwan, as well as stating that he would not be against some exchanges such as sports exchanges. At several points, Shen also criticized Chiang for attempting to attack him on issues of national policy, when what is being debated is mayoral policy for Taipei, suggesting that if Chiang was so concerned with national policy, he should return to being a legislator. Shen also attacked Chiang for a poor record in attendance at some government meetings.

On the whole, the debate was what was to be expected, then. Chiang managed a strong enough performance that the debate will probably not impact him as negatively as the Shen campaign would have hoped, which is probably why the Shen campaign has called for further debates to take place, with the view that Chiang might slip up in a future debate in such a fashion as to give the Shen campaign political ammunition that could be used against him. It is unclear whether this debate will take place, with the Chiang campaign remaining reluctant to debate.

At the same time, Chiang was clearly on the defensive, which is what pushed him to a combative attitude against Shen. It is, of course, Shen whose banners are visible throughout Taipei streets, and who commands a substantial share of media attention, such that it is his mayoral campaign that has breathed new life into DPP campaigns across Taiwan. Chiang was hoping to run a conservative campaign where he said as little as possible and touted existing accomplishments in Taipei, which is considered politically safe for the KMT, but the rise of Puma Shen as a tough challenger with a seemingly bold and new vision for Taipei has instead put him on the defensive, and at this late stage in the game, it is too late for Chiang to reinvent his image or pledge to have some competing vision for Taipei in his second term.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Protecting the mangrove paradise in Tacloban
content:
For Gilda Salazar Laag, if it were not for the mangroves, more would have been dead from Yolanda.







By Agatha Canape




CANCABATO BAY, Tacloban City – Gilda Salazar Laag, 69, recalled that she and her fellow volunteers found human bones when they tilled the muddy soil to plant the mangrove seedlings in Paraiso, which literally means paradise, a couple of months after supertyphoon Yolanda (international name: Haiyan) struck. 




On November 8, 2013, the storm surge in Tacloban began at 7:00 a.m. and lasted until 8:30 am, submerging the city in seven meters of water. “Atop their roof, we witnessed the cries of people who could not be rescued as they were swept by the floods,” Laag said. The typhoon left thousands of people dead, millions displaced, and destroyed 90 percent of the city. Twenty-three people of those killed were from Paraiso.




Laag’s home was totally destroyed by the typhoon. Originally from Catarman, Northern Samar before she married, Laag was asked by her extended family to come back to her hometown while the city has yet to recover. She refused as her family feared losing whatever was left of their home. They rebuilt their home on the same lot where it was destroyed using materials that could be salvaged from its ruins.  




Besides, Laag was tasked to deliver relief to households in the barangay. As a barangay health worker, she was knowledgeable about the number of people and needs of every household, and the nooks and crannies of the barangay.







Gilda, 69 years old, served as a barangay health worker in Paraiso for more than half of her life. She is one of the members of the local organization that started the mangrove reforestation in Paraiso in 2014, only a couple of months after Typhoon Yolanda.

 (Photo by Agatha Canape)







Relief and recovery efforts bled into the next year. In February 2014, they were gathered by their barangay captain to look after the mangroves next. 




Yolanda flattened the two-hectare mangrove forest in Paraiso to 0.2 hectares (2000 square meters), or merely 20 percent of the original coverage. The reforestation team started with 25 people, eight of whom were women. 




The barangay, with support from international non-government organizations, procured seedlings which they potted, tended to in a nursery for two years before planting along the land at the edge of Cancabato Bay. Through their hands, they have grown back the mangrove forest and made it denser than before.




Paraiso was brought back to life. Between 2015 and 2018, approximately 30,000 mangrove seedlings were planted. According to a study, the mangrove forest cover in Paraiso increased by 80 percent compared to its pre-disaster state, expanding from two hectares to 5.18 hectares. In 2019, the Paraiso Mangrove Eco-Learning Park was opened to the public.










Satellite image of the mangrove forest in Paraiso, November 10, 2013. (Google Earth image) 




Satellite image of the mangrove forest in Paraiso, November 3, 2026. (Google Earth image) 










Mangrove rehabilitation and reforestation in Paraiso began in early 2014, a couple of months after Yolanda. In 2019, the Paraiso Mangrove Eco-Learning Park was opened to the public.

 (Photo by Agatha Canape)




Today, Paraiso is once again under threat. The multi-billion Tacloban Causeway Project, a 2.55-kilometer road embankment and land reclamation project that will directly connect the Daniel Romualdez Airport to downtown Tacloban, is slowly killing the Cancabato Bay. 




The city government, in the first volume of the Tacloban City Comprehensive Land Use Plan 2017-2025 claimed that the bay is “polluted and dying” to justify the plan to reclaim and convert it into a new central business district. (The plan has since been revised into a third volume where this claim has been removed. It is the only version available on the city government’s website.) 




Rodolfo “Rudy” Delliva, 71, debunked the city government’s claims.




Delliva, a fisher who earns his living by catching blue swimming crabs, was among the volunteers who restored the mangroves along Cancabato Bay.




“Alive. It’s very much alive,” Delliva said about Cancabato Bay. He then enumerated the sea creatures he has known in the bay: 

danggit

 (rabbitfish/spinefoot), 

iito

 (catfish), 

lumong

 (whipfin silverbiddy), 

tamban

 (sardines), 

mangagat

 (mangrove red snapper), 

tingag

 (grouper), 

aguyong

, 

kirawan, punaw

 (clam), and many more. 




The efforts of the community for the past decade have revived the mangrove forest. One could hear the euphony of birds, which is not heard elsewhere in the city. 




The trees are marked by their roots propped aboveground, taking up almost a third or even half of their heights. These are the 

Rhizophora apiculata

, known as 

bakhaw lalaki

, and the 

Avicennia marina

, known as 

apiapi

. 




There are multiple mangrove species in the forest belonging to eight families: Avicennia, Combretaceae, Lythraceae, Meliaceae, Rhizophoraceae, Sonnertiaceae, Rubiaceae, but the bakhaw and apiapi outnumber the rest. The trees are planted too closely against standards but create a beautiful, entangled landscape.



















Inside the forest it feels cooler. One could hear the euphony of birds, which is not heard elsewhere in the city.

 

The trees are marked by their roots propped aboveground, taking up almost a third or even half of their heights. The trees are planted too closely against standards but create a beautiful, entangled landscape.

 

(Photo by Agatha Canape)




What the mangroves keep alive, the Tacloban Causeway Project is killing. 




Delliva shared that fisherfolk’s catch from the bay has decreased since the construction of the causeway began. 




“Before the causeway, when it rains, the saltwater [of the bay], naturally, gets diluted. Some sea creatures die. But it does not take much time for the bay to recover because the rainwater flows off and is replaced by saltwater from the sea,” he explained.




Now, he said, the causeway obstructs and constricts the water flow of the bay. Rainwater does not immediately flow off, and it takes longer for the bay to recover its salinity, killing off marine life.




Stewarding the mangroves




Delliva learned from experience the importance of preserving the mangroves.




Similar to Laag, Delliva built his house with his own hands from the scraps abound after Yolanda. He intended it to be only makeshift, but he has lived in it 13 years since. He was also scouted by their barangay captain to help with the reforestation. He had been living in Paraiso for a while then, but that was the first time that he paid attention to the mangroves and learned about them.




“Mangroves are habitat and spawning grounds for sea creatures. Fishes lay their eggs there. Blue swimming crabs live and also lay their eggs there. They also feed on the leaves of mangroves,” Delliva said.







Rodolfo “Rudy” Delliva, 71 years old, is a fisher who earns his living by catching blue swimming crabs. He was among volunteers who restored the mangroves along Cancabato Bay.

 (Photo by Agatha Canape)







“Now, when tragedy strikes, or extreme weather comes, such as during Yolanda, mangroves help a lot,” Delliva told 

Bulatlat

. 




He added, “The boats and motorboats are carried along by the current. They do not hit the households [in the coastal areas] because of the mangroves. The sea cannot be stopped from rising and flooding the coast. But the waves can be subdued. Before they reach the coast, the waves lose their power. The waves are broken at the mangrove strip. That’s the job of mangroves,” he said. 




For Laag, if it were not for the mangroves, more would have been dead from Yolanda.







Mangroves are habitat and spawning grounds for sea creatures. (Photo by Agatha Canape)







Looming threats




Laag, Delliva and the rest of Paraiso folk are resisting “development projects” which would destroy the mangrove forest.




The Tacloban Causeway Project was among 21 projects in Leyte that were awarded to Sunwest, Inc., which was founded by former Ako Bicol Partylist Representative Elizaldy “Zaldy” Co, between 2020-2025, coinciding with his allyship with the province’s 1st district Representative, Martin Romualdez. They are co-accused for a plunder charge for allegedly receiving kickbacks worth over P7 billion (USD 110.2 million).




Co resigned from congress in September 2025 after being accused of corrupting public funds for flood control projects. He is currently a fugitive abroad facing multiple charges of plunder, graft, and malversation. Some of the criminal charges against him are directly linked to irregularities related to a Sunwest, Inc.-contracted flood control project in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro. 




In September 2026, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) affirmed that it will continue constructing the causeway. Construction halted last year after the corruption issue involving Co, Romualdez, and other high-level public officials was exposed. The Commission on Audit and DPWH will inspect the project to determine which “portions of the project may be continued and subsequently subjected to re-bidding or proposal for future funding.”




The DPWH issued this statement despite outstanding concerns about the impacts of the causeway to Cancabato.  The Environmental Impact Assessment and Environmental Compliance Certificate of the project have not been disclosed despite 

requests

 from local advocates. 




Advocates are planning to file a writ of kalikasan to halt the causeway project and uphold the status of the Cancabato Bay as a marine protected and fishery reservation area. 




“If we were to decide, we do not want to proceed with the project,” Laag said. “The government did not consult us. They just decided on their own.”







Multi-billion Tacloban Causeway Project threatens Cancabato Bay.







Further disruption




It is not only the causeway that has affected the lives of the people in the community but also military exercises. 




Last May 5, the lives of the fisherfolk in the San Jose district were disrupted by the firing of the Tomahawk missile using the Typhon missile system from Tacloban City Airport to a target 600 kilometers away at Fort Magsaysay in Laur, Nueva Ecija. 




The fisherfolk communities near the airport were abruptly barred from sailing in San Pedro Bay a few days before the firing of the missile without ample time to prepare, nor sufficient support to compensate for the loss of income. 




The missile firing was part of the largest US-Philippines Balikatan war exercises involving around 17,000 troops, held between April-May across the country, with Tacloban as one of the host cities. 




Balikatan has normalized military presence in the fisherfolk communities along Cancabato, and the rest of Tacloban. It was followed by the US Navy-led Pacific Partnership held on September 18-29, which deployed military forces across the city and nearby municipalities on the premise of humanitarian and disaster preparedness missions. Besides the US and Philippines, hundreds of armed forces from Canada, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom also joined. 




Military delegates of the Pacific Partnership performed various innocuous tasks such as building and repairing school and water facilities, medical missions, and even playing live music, whitewashing militarization through services that should have been provided by the Philippine government.




These efforts are part of the escalation of US-led militarization in the country and the rest of the Asia Pacific to project its power against China.




Paraiso’s dreams




In a zine-making activity, three elderly women volunteers of the Paraiso Eco-Learning Mangrove Park wrote and talked about their dreams for their community. (Left to right: Nati Pacunla, 64 years old; Gilda; Mila Roca, 74 years old) (Photo by Agatha Canape)







Amid all these threats, the people of Paraiso only yearn for a simple life. 




In a zine-making activity, three elderly women volunteers of the Paraiso Eco-Learning Mangrove Park–Laag, Mila Roca, 74, and Nati Pacunla, 64–wrote and talked about their dreams for their community. All three were barangay health workers who served their community for most of their lives. 




After Yolanda, they were all recruited to clean the mangrove area, prepare the seedlings in a nursery, and finally, plant them. They were proud that many came to visit their park, and worried about the lack of finance to support its maintenance. Roca shared her dream of sprucing up the mangrove park into a tourist spot worthy of Tacloban. 




The fight for our land and resources are led by the likes of the elderly volunteers of Paraiso. With little support, they have managed to restore and grow the mangroves in the city from the devastation of Typhoon Yolanda, and sustain the life of the bay that has fed and sheltered their communities for generations. 




But the precarious state of the park also tells that community-led efforts are unsustainable in the long-term without systematized support. The challenge to the government to redo its priorities remains. 

(AMU, RVO)
