author: Jerome Small
title: Debt angst is class war
content:
A flood of water, meant to symbolise debt, flows from the Victorian parliament, inundating suburban streets and living rooms while a scared child watches on. AI-generated ads like this, sponsored by right-wing outfit Fix Victoria, will be familiar to anyone in the state. 

Overwhelmingly, the media narrative is that Australia in general and Victoria in particular is drowning in debt. We’re told there’s no choice except brutal cuts to health, education, and other government spending. 

This is a powerful narrative, but a false one. 

It is being used by the ruling class to force workers to accept cuts, and to attack Labor governments federally and in Victoria. Labor is already bowing to this pressure by implementing cuts to vital services and implementing sharp cuts to real wages, except where union revolts threaten a crisis. 

Contrary to this right-wing myth, neither Victoria nor Australia is drowning in debt. Total government debt (combining both federal and state) has 

risen

 from 40 percent to 52 percent of gross domestic product over the past decade. But this level of debt is still relatively low by international standards—well below the UK (102 percent of GDP), Spain (97 percent), Canada (115 percent) and plenty of others. According to the International Monetary Fund, the “advanced economies” have an average government debt of 107% of GDP, more than double that of Australia.

Around the world, however, ruling class concern over debt levels—and who will pay that debt—has been sharpened by the sudden spike in global inflation and interest rates since mid-2021. The inflationary surge was fuelled initially by dislocations from the pandemic, and then by a series of “geopolitical shocks”—a euphemistic term for brutal imperialist wars—first Russia invading Ukraine in 2022, and more recently the US and Israel’s attack on Iran. These disrupted energy markets and pushed up the price of oil and gas, causing a global price shock. 

Surging demand for capital to fuel the AI bubble is also pushing global inflation and interest rates higher, as are rapidly expanding US deficits to fund Trump’s tax cuts for the rich and rearmament to prepare for war with China. 

None of these factors driving borrowing costs higher were created by working-class people, let alone by those of us who happen to live in Victoria. But around the world, and in every state, it’s working-class people who are expected to endure the increased cost of finance—through below-inflation wage rises, and by seeing vital services cut. 

In Victoria, Labor’s ambitious infrastructure agenda is at the centre of the right-wing campaign against the government. Initially, though, there was little serious ruling-class concern over this. 

Few disputed the need to update Melbourne’s rail infrastructure, or remove its plentiful level crossings. Melbourne still has nearly 

100

, despite the extensive program of removals, compared to just a 

handful

remaining in Sydney. Notably, removal of level crossings is a boon to road transport of all sorts—including major freight companies and small businesses, as well as commuters of all classes. 

Prior to Melbourne’s Metro Tunnel, the last major expansion of the city’s rail infrastructure was the City Loop, built under the state Liberal governments of the 1960s and 70s and opened by Labor in the early 1980s. And despite the river of anti-union propaganda about the construction unions, it's simply 

not the case

 that cost overruns on Victoria’s Big Build are substantially different to similar projects in New South Wales or elsewhere. 

Victoria is also far from the only state which financed infrastructure by taking out loans during a period of historically low interest rates. Victoria’s debt of $160 billion is 

higher

 than New South Wales at $117 billion, but both states have the same 

debt rating

 from international agencies—along with every Australian state except Western Australia, which enjoys massive royalty flows from iron ore and gas. Liberal and Labor governments in New South Wales in recent years found $65 billion for a series of massive new 

Metro rail projects

, $20 billion for the gigantic WestConnex tunnel, and a few billion here and there to help pay for a new international airport, a city tram system, and sundry other projects.

Former Premier Daniel Andrews’ approach to achieving its ambitious infrastructure agenda did not depend on increased taxes when it was launched. Instead, like similarly neoliberal governments around the world, Victorian Labor financed some of it through privatisations (notably the Port of Melbourne and VicRoads) and the rest from loans. The rail projects were an important part of Labor’s economic strategy, supposedly leading to increased land values and high-rise development, which would ultimately boost state government revenues. Everyone was a winner, it seemed.

This was uncontroversial at first. In 2016, the federal government could raise ten-year loans at interest rates as low as 2 percent, sinking to 1 percent in 2019. Even with the slight premium paid by state governments, a program of “borrow and spend”, as unapologetically advocated by Andrews, seemed a foolproof way to build long-overdue infrastructure and promote economic growth.  

That world is now gone. And the question of “who pays” has become a question of class power. 

By the end of 2022, central banks around the world were hiking interest rates at a rapid pace to combat rising inflation. It was clear from that point that 

a brutal reckoning

 for debtor states and companies was looming. 

Current economic orthodoxy states that any inflation above 2 or 3 percent per year—even if caused by “geopolitical shocks”—has to be countered by central banks raising interest rates. This cuts demand and, eventually, inflation. 

That this policy also risks mass unemployment and mass bankruptcies isn’t some mistake: it’s the point. One example of this brutal logic is the startlingly frank 

declaration

 by Reserve Bank of Australia governor Michele Bullock that one in 20 workers in Australia might have to be unemployed in order to depress demand enough to dent inflation. Interest rate rises also 

protect

 the enormous wealth of international finance at the expense of borrowers. 

Global pressures meant that by early 2022, the interest rate paid by the Australian government on a ten-year loan was over 3 percent: today, this rate is well over 5 percent. States pay slightly more, so refinancing costs for Victoria have jumped from close to 1 percent in 2019 to around 6 percent today.

So who will pay? Australia’s capitalist class wants workers to. 

Australian bosses have already achieved world-beating cuts to real wages, with the OECD 

reporting

 in July this year that though real wages have regained some of the lost ground in virtually all other “advanced” capitalist countries, “real wages are near the trough of the cost-of-living crisis only in New Zealand and Australia”. 

Victoria’s Labor government has done at least its share of the heavy lifting in this area. The string of drawn out, high-profile enterprise bargaining disputes this year—most notably involving school staff, but also tens of thousands of healthcare workers—has been fuelled by cuts to real wages of 11 percent for teachers,12 percent for many local council workers, 13 percent for allied health professionals, 14 percent for hospital orderlies, and 16 percent for medical scientists. These are extraordinary, life-altering cuts to living standards. These figures understate the hit to real wages for those with mortgages, which are not counted in the most common measure of inflation, the Consumer Price Index. 

Labor achieved this by imposing a below-inflation wage cap on public sector workers. Union leaders were initially successful in selling these wage cuts on behalf of their Labor pals, though repeated episodes of rank-and-file revolt since 2022 have led to several important fights. Some of these battles (especially by nurses, ambulance paramedics, school staff, and medical scientists) have resulted in wage rises that might remedy the real wage cut of recent years by 2028 or 2029 if inflation doesn’t keep accelerating. 

But even then, the tens of thousands of dollars lost to inflation over several years represents a substantial involuntary donation by working-class people to Victoria’s creditors—which include the wealthiest entities in the country and the world. Calculating this total vast transfer of wealth with any accuracy is a job that no journalist for the capitalist press seems to have gotten around to (in contrast to various made-up, hyperventilating estimates for the alleged cost of union wages on construction sites). For a very rough calculation, we can use a conservative 

estimate

 of $20,000 in total wages lost to inflation over the past four years by someone on the average wage. Multiplied across 320,000 Victorian public sector employees, we come to a rough figure of $6.4 billion since 2022. 

Labor has also raised money by introducing new taxes small-scale capitalists—for example a tax on Airbnb rentals which is 

reported

 to raise $86 million per year; a 2021 “premium” stamp duty on real estate sales over $2 million, which was 

planned

 to bring in $137 million per year; and a 2023 reduction on the threshold at which land tax becomes payable on second properties, 

stated

 to bring in around $1.2 billion per year. And to howls of protest from big business, the Victorian government also imposed payroll tax surcharges on the biggest companies, lifting the rate in Melbourne from 4.85 percent to 6.85 percent of payroll. These surcharges reportedly raise $2.2 billion per year—less than two percent of the state government’s $130 billion budget for this year. 

For the big capitalists, and the many small fry, these taxes are an offence against all that is holy. Cue AI-generated attack ads, reams of doomsday class war rhetoric in the pages of the 

Australian Financial Review

, and an entirely predictable capitulation from Labor. One part of this is Labor premier Ben Carroll 

announcing

the phased reversal of the changes to the land tax threshold by 2031 at a cost of $230 million over the next five years, part of the pre-election gallop to the right by an already thoroughly neoliberal Victorian Labor government. 

A more consequential move has been Labor’s dramatic and ongoing cuts to public sector jobs and programs, starting in 2023. The well-publicised “Silver Review” released last year, which recommended 1,000 public sector job cuts, is supposed to save $4 billion over the next four years. 

But this is just the tip of the iceberg. The entire Victorian public sector is effectively in the grip of a giant continuous restructuring and downsizing exercise. Most of these cuts fly under the radar, apart from the occasional ones made an issue by workers, unions and concerned others. These include the planned destruction of 

VicHealth

 (Victoria’s only public health promotion agency), cuts to the beloved 

State Library of Victoria,

 and the 

abolition

 of a program which helps new parents learn how to settle their babies. 

This will accelerate under a Liberal government. The Liberals have publicly declared they will not fill vacancies in the public service for four years if elected in November. This will have a devastating effect across every government service.

Labor is paving their way. Every week brings news of fresh cuts, like that to 

disability inclusion funding

 in Victorian schools, or long-term underfunding, such as the 

news

 that a third of the new Footscray hospital is empty because of a lack of funding for staff. Then there are the big announcements which turn out to mean nothing much, such as the recent announcement of a supposed path to so-called “full” funding for Victoria’s government schools. A look at the 

detail

 shows this announcement fails to increase funding in real terms by even one full percentage point over the next four years.

Despite a few minor gestures to cost-of-living relief here and there, and some relatively minor taxes on business, the largest part of Labor’s plan to appease the gods of the financial markets is to impose austerity on those of us least able to afford it. 

Of course, this is not the only course available. 

Victorian Socialists’ policies 

include

 some straightforward measures to raise revenue, such as ending Crown Casino’s one-dollar-per-year peppercorn rent on their massive Southbank site, imposing a 10 percent wealth tax on billionaires’ assets, and further increases on payroll tax for large companies. These and other measures, to quote the VS program, “should be used to push towards a socialised and democratic economy that works in the interests of the majority”. 

A step towards that would be seriously taxing the super-rich. The wealth of the country’s richest 200 people more than tripled in the past decade, from $197 billion in 

2016

 to $707 billion in 

2026

. So there’s no shortage of wealth. There’s just a shortage of a mass working-class movement prepared to fight—industrially and politically—to reclaim the wealth that our labour produces. Our task is to build such a movement. 

Labor, Liberal or One Nation—or whatever toxic combination we end up with in Victoria—will cut vital services for workers and the poor, to supposedly fix the supposed “flood” of debt. Whoever ends up in power, working-class people will have a hell of a fight on our hands.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: The women of Davao Oriental protecting Balete Bay
content:
Amid the warming climate and the looming impacts of large-scale extractive mining projects, women like Peralez, Millomeda, and Decena, from fishing, farming, and religious backgrounds across Mati City have come together to protect one of the most ecologically critical areas in their town. 







By Michelle Mikiko Pagaran




Along the coast of Balete Bay, women farmers, fisherfolk, advocates, and church workers across Mati, Davao Oriental are coming together and turning to collective action and organic farming to protect their coasts, and adapt to extreme weather impacts of climate change.







A small mangrove grows amid thick aerial root networks in Balete Bay, Davao Oriental

. 

(Photo by Michelle Pagaran)







Tucked quietly along the coast of Mati, Davao Oriental is Balete Bay, a small inlet along the southern border of the province. Known as a breeding ground for various fish species, reef species and lobsters, the bay is of great ecological significance. A marine inlet, its cove-like structure hosts seagrass beds, diverse reef fisheries, and abundant mangroves.




A sanctuary of corals, mangroves, and commercially vital fisheries, the bay is important for local fisherfolk who depend on it for their livelihood. It serves as a breeding ground for shellfish and wild lobster fry.




In 1994, it was declared a NIPAS protected area as part of the 20,873.43 hectare Pujada Bay Protected Landscape and Seascape, through Presidential Proclamation 431. It is an inlet of the larger Pujada Bay which was declared one of the Most Beautiful Bays in the World in 2020.




Amidst its ecological importance, locals in Mati near the coast and further upland experience the growing impacts of climate change amid a backdrop of looming impacts from extractive industries surrounding the area.







Low tide at the Balete Bay. (Photo by Michelle Pagaran)







Mangroves and Marine Resources Crucial to Local Fisherfolk




Christine Peralez recalled her fondest memory of the bay.




“My fondest memory of the bay is playing among the mangroves when we were children. We would play amongst its roots. The mangrove was our playground. We would play pretend. We gathered shells that cling to the roots, collected them, and those were what we pretended to sell”, she said in an interview with Bulatlat.




Peralez was born in Bigue. She recounted her childhood growing up in a fishing community in sitio Bigue, one of the communities along Balete Bay. She would help her parents catch fish and play amongst the mangroves in the coast of the bay.

Their house before was right by the sea. Whenever there was high tide, the sea would go under their house.




“As kids we would bathe right under our house every time it was high tide. That’s why my hair was always bleached yellow,” she said.







Peralez, 32, grew up along the coast of Balete Bay, helping her father, a fisherman, catch fish and sea cucumbers. (Photo by Michelle Pagaran)







“Before, we hardly felt how difficult life was, thanks to our parents’ hard work. My father was a fisherman. Mostly gathering shellfish and sea cucumbers. He was the go-to person for people looking to order shellfish and sea cucumbers, or what we call bat. Sometimes when he couldn’t go diving, he would go line fishing or spear fishing. That’s really how we survived. Through his fishing,” Peralez said.




She recounted that her father would catch fish for their own consumption. Her father’s catch was also enough for selling at the market to provide for their daily needs.




She speaks about her childhood with fondness, recalling how the bay, teeming with fish, gave their father a livelihood and provided their family with food on the table.







“Manginhas”. Locals forage for shellfish, sea cucumbers, and seafood during low tide at the bay. (Photo by Michelle Pagaran)







“

I used to join in net fishing back then so that the catch was strictly ours to share, without having to divide it with other people. I heard stories from the old days that before, fish would almost swim up to you. Because they were so abundant, fish back then would reach right up to the shore,” Peralez said.




But times have changed since then. Fishing has been harder, especially amid the rising heat. 




She said that back then, her father did not have to go far to gather shellfish. She recalled how easily her father could get shellfish across their house in Bigue. 




“Today my father can no longer fish right across from our house. He has to go far to get to more abundant areas of shellfish.” Peralez said, adding that other fishers who go net fishing in Bigue have to travel far away for about three to five days before they can return home.




Rising temperatures, dwindling catch




The changes in weather patterns and the warming temperatures have affected the livelihood of fisherfolk in the bay. These days, Peralez’s father has stopped fishing regularly due to fewer and fewer catches.

“With the recent heavy rains, mud has piled up there. The fish are no longer the same. Fishermen have to go farther out and under the extreme heat. It’s already too hot. The catch keeps getting smaller”, Peralez said. 




Fisherfolk have noted the differences in catch amid the warming temperatures over time. Rising global temperatures due to climate change are further exacerbated by the “super” El Niño this year that is seen to stretch out until 2027. 




“It’s really different from before. Like now, we go for long periods without rain and the temperatures are very hot. Fishermen catch less. It’s been two months with no rain here. That’s why the fish really need a cooler area”, says Danny, a senior resident and former fisherman, who says long dry spells have hurt their catch.







Fisherfolk dock their boats during low tide. (Photo by Michelle Pagaran)







The World Meteorological Organization has forecasted that the established El Niño in 2026 will continue to strengthen with and last until February 2027. Driven by exceptionally warm ocean conditions, some climate observers have called it a “Super El Niño” as it is forecasted to be one of the strongest El Niño on record, expected to cause shifts in rainfall patterns, drought, floods, and other weather extremes.




El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phase that brings warmer weather throughout the globe. This increases the risk of extreme weather and global temperatures that are already rising due to human-induced climate change. 




While discussion is ongoing in the scientific community, 

studies

 published by scientific journal Nature suggest that global heating may be leading to stronger El Niño events. Other 

studies predict extreme El Niño events to double over the next century

 because of faster surface warming of the eastern Pacific Ocean due to global temperature rise.

In September, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) issued a similar climate advisory to the public warning of a “Very Strong” El Niño. They highlight that this phenomenon may bring prolonged lack of rainfall and drought along with short-term heavy rainfall, affecting food security, water resources, and water supply along with impacts on public health and the economy.




The impacts of the El Niño are already being felt by locals in Davao Oriental like Danny and Christine Peralez. 




To cope with the warming waters and dwindling catch, sometimes fisherfolk are forced to take on loans during difficult seasons, which they pay off when the fishing season returns. Other fishermen shift to other sources of livelihood, as miners, drivers, or other odd jobs especially during off season. 




The rising temperatures have brought on harder times for women like Peralez. Now a mother with two young children of her own, she carries the added responsibility of making sure that her children’s needs are met. 




Like many mothers, she not only takes on household work, but also finds different ways to make ends meet. 




“I ensure the budget for the household. I really get bothered when I have no money, especially because I have children who depend on me. Daily expenses are intense. My budgeting is strict. I prioritize needs over wants,” Peralez said. 




She also takes some side hustle to gain income to sustain her family’s needs. 




“I make ice candy, I cook peanuts, I sell dried fish (

bulad

) on credit. I book flights, I process passports online, stuff like that. That’s just how it is. It’s hard, but we persevere”, Peralez said. 




Women in the household are among the most affected by climate change. According to estimates by UN Women, by 2030, about 10.8 million adult women in the Philippines could face food insecurity and 1.9 million could live in extreme poverty (below $2.15 a day) if the current climate path continues. 




El Niño Impacts from the coast to the mountains




Fisherfolk in the Balete Bay are not alone in facing the impacts of the El Niño. Many of the farmers of the upland areas surrounding the Bay have been stretching their resources to cope with the impacts of the “super El Niño”. 




For Tina Millomeda, Chairwoman of the local chapter of Farmers Advocates for Sustainable Agriculture and Development (FASAD), the El Niño has proven to be challenging with her crops slowly dying due to extreme heat and lack of water.







Tina Milliomeda, 48, tends to her garden of organic vegetables in Cuabo, Davao Oriental amid the heat and dry weather of the super El Niño. (Photo by Michelle Pagaran)







“Before, when we farmed, there was a routine. There were months for harvesting, and months for planting. Now it’s different. There has been no rain for several months. The corn grows with no kernels. The bananas easily topple over”, Millomeda said.




Coping with the impacts of the El Niño comes at a high cost for farmers like Millomeda who now have to take on additional costs to fetch water from far-off sources along with the cost of gasoline for transportation. 




“It’s costly. I have to scoop water for the plants. It costs P20 (less than $1) per container. Some now use a carwash machine to pump water from the creek, which costs a lot too. In addition, you need at least four rolls of hose. I have many plans for the farm, but there’s no water.”

For her small backyard garden of organic vegetables, Millomeda uses an estimate of 5 containers at P20 per container or about P100 (less than $2) per day just to keep her plants alive. As months go by without rain, the cost of keeping her crops alive adds to the burden of an already limited household budget. 




As a mother of two children, Tina has come up with unique ways to cope with the El Niño while saving up on household costs. For one, she said the water used for laundry is saved up to be used for watering plants in her garden. 




Due to the extremely dry weather and heat, the leaves of her fruit tree seedlings have dried up. To cope, she puts a make-shift  device fashioned from old plastic bottles that drips water slowly all day to make sure her tree seedlings stay alive.







Fruit tree seedling in Millomeda’s garden dried up after two months of little to no rain. (Photo by Michelle Pagaran)







Across Mindanao, an estimated 5,950 people are affected by the El Nino in farming and fishing communities, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) El Niño report.




An estimated P540 million ($8.47 million) in agricultural losses has been recorded, with the highest loss recorded in Davao Region at P410 million ($6.44 million) Nationwide, agricultural losses and damage is estimated at P6.54 billion ($102.62 million USD), according to the report. 




Millomeda, along with other women farmers of FASAD, cope with the changing climate hand-in-hand with the women fisherfolk of Balete Bay through collective efforts like seed-sharing, exchanging of best organic farming practices, and mutual aid in environmental protection efforts through mangrove planting activities by the bay.




A history of resistance 




Winceslao “Wenie” Mapa of the Farmers Advocates for Sustainable Agriculture and Development (FASAD), a local organization of farmers and advocates across different barangays in Mati. said they have been planting mangroves in Sitio Bigue, Balete Bay since the early 2000’s.







Wenie Mapa of FASAD in Davao Oriental, along the coast of Balete Bay. (Photo by Michelle Pagaran)







Maps is a long-time environmental defender and has seen the highs and lows of the bay. He can also trace back the history of resistance and climate action from the coast to the upland farms.




He recounted how, in 1998, local residents successfully came together to halt the operations of Holcim Philippines, Inc. which planned to conduct mining operations in Mati, upstream along the right border of the bay, facing the open sea. 




Davao Oriental is rich in mineral resources including nickel, gold, silver, copper, limestone. Out of 568,000 hectares of the province’s total land area, 449,335.84 hectares or close to 80% of the province’s total land area is covered by mining permit applications, according to data published by the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB). The demand for Nickel, in particular, continues to grow globally,  especially amid the transition to renewable energy technologies. 




Gregoria Decena, a 70 year-old retired school principal and member of the Nagkahiusaing Kababayen-an sa Kalambuan ug Kalinaw (NKKK), bore witness to the historic struggle and triumph of resisting the attempted entry of mining operations in their community in the 1990’s.







Gregoria Decena, 70, is a lay worker and organic farming practitioner in her hometown in Davao Oriental. At 70, she continues to learn and teach through organic farming and herbal medicine training for women in their community

. 

(Photo by Michelle Pagaran)







“Our barangay would have seen the same fate. There are 16 springs. It would have been mined,” Decena said, recalling how their community came together to protect their local water sources. 




“We wondered why the machinery that arrived was so new. They said the machinery was for road widening, which wasn’t really a priority,” Decena said. 




“They were really building a road toward the mining area. And there were springs there. If those were touched, what would become of them? So we called an assembly. We made a resolution addressed to the governor and the mayor, and it was approved: San Isidro says no to mining. Their operation was stopped,” she added.

Until today, residents remember that important victory made by the community, thankful that their mountains continue to stand tall amid news of landslides in neighboring mining areas.  




“That’s why, after the landslide in Davao de Oro, people now say: Ma’am, if you hadn’t acted back then, what would have become of us now? We’d be gone by now,” Decena said. 




In February 2024, a landslide in Barangay Masara, Maco, in the nearby province of Davao de Oro, a gold-mining community, killed at least 98 people. The Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB) attributed it to natural causes, including persistent rain and the area’s long-mapped landslide risk. 




Environmental groups have questioned whether the mining company and regulators did enough to prevent it. For Decena, the disaster showed what could have happened in her barangay. 




While the impacts of upstream mining activities are not immediately felt in Balete Bay today, environmental defenders like Mapa and Decena fear the risk of siltation and heavy metal contamination posed by upstream mining activities if they are allowed to continue. They fear that this in turn would lead to damage to the marine life and ecological integrity of the bay downstream, affecting their lives and livelihood. 




Rivers in neighboring areas have seen such consequences play out. In 2022, siltation seeped into two rivers, the Mapagba and Pintatagan Rivers in Banaybanay town, Davao Oriental. The rivers turned orange after heavy rainfall attributed to mining activities upstream. DENR Davao issued a cease-and-desist order to Riverbend Consolidated Mining Corporation after investigation found that rain pushed overburden materials that contributed to the overflowing of their silt pond that drained into the rivers.




Today at least two mining companies, which include Hallmark Mining Corporation and Austral-Asia Link Mining Corporation, hold Mineral Production Sharing Agreements (MPSA) covering about 10,000 hectares in Barangays Macambol and Cabuaya, according to the MGB. Mati’s environment office puts the site about four kilometers from the Pujada Bay protected seascape boundary. Balete Bay is an inlet of Pujada Bay. 




Hallmark Mining Corporation says nickel ore from its operations in Mati was shipped to China and Indonesia between 2022 and 2025, where it is processed for use in electric vehicle batteries, company spokesperson Jose Butch Sebua said, 

as reported by the Manila Bulletin

 on January 5, 2026.




Locals are not without hope. Learning from experiences of the past and from the mining impacts in neighboring provinces, public sentiment has been translated into policy initiatives.




In 2019, the House Bill 8815, which sought to declare Davao Oriental as a mining-free zone was passed on third and final reading in the 17th Congress of the House of Representative. However, there was no counterpart bill in the Senate to be able to pass into law.




On January 28, 2026, the Sangguniang Panlalawigan issued Resolution No. 18-24-01-2026, which sought to rescind, revoke, and cancel the body’s previous endorsement and declaration of feasibility and tree-cutting permit application of Austral-Asia Link Mining Corporation and Hallmark Mining Corporation.




Beyond policy efforts, locals are taking climate adaptation and mitigation efforts into their own hands. At 70 years, Decena, a retired school principal, continues her environmental protection advocacy through teaching and learning along with other women like Christine Peralez and Tina Millomeda. She keeps herself busy by practicing organic farming in her small lot and by actively participating in the mangrove planting efforts along the bay.







Balete Bay at low tide surrounded by nearby mountains. (Photo by Michelle Pagaran)







Women Nurturing Mangroves for to Adapt to Climate Change




“The aim is really to be protected from typhoons. The seashore won’t be damaged as much. Also, the fish will have a home”. Ma’am Decena explains why she joined in the mangrove planting efforts along the Balete Bay. 




To adapt to the impacts of a changing climate, and continuing effort to continue protecting the environment, FASAD and the Nagkahiusaing Kababayen-an sa Kalambuan ug Kalinaw (NKKK), a women’s organization of farmers, fisherfolk, and advocates in Mati, Davao Oriental, have turned to repopulating mangroves along the bay.







Women fisherfolk, farmers, and youth together with missionary Benedictine Sisters ready to plant mangroves in Balete Bay, Davao Oriental. (Photo courtesy of Masipag-Mindanao).







On March 8, 2026, women farmers, fisherfolk, and advocates planted mangroves along the coast of Balete Bay to mark International Women’s Day, according to organizers from FASAD,  MASIPAG-Mindanao, and the Benedictine Sisters.




The group, led by women farmers, fisherfolk, and organic farming advocates, planted at least 50 mangrove seedlings provided by the DENR, along with more sourced from mature mangroves in the bay, organizers said. Before planting, a short discussion on the importance of mangroves was given by MASIPAG-Mindanao (Magsasaka at Siyentipiko para sa Pag-unlad ng Agrikultura), a farmer-scientist network that works with FASAD.




According to Benedictine nun Sr. Claudia Sampal, one of the co-organizers of the event, the activity is part of a long-time and ongoing effort of local fishers, farmers, and advocates to populate the bay with mangroves. For many of the attendees, the activity also served as a space for learning and cross-sector solidarity for adaptation and mitigation amid the climate crisis.




Farmers and fisherfolk, especially women and youth, who bear the brunt of climate change impacts were brought together to learn about the causes of rising global temperatures and what can be done about it.




After planting, the seedlings are looked after by youth scholars who live by the bay. Part of their community service commitments is to nurture and ensure that the seedlings stay alive. 




Amid the warming climate and the looming impacts of large-scale extractive mining projects, women like Peralez, Millomeda, and Decena, from fishing, farming, and religious backgrounds across Mati City have come together to protect one of the most ecologically critical areas in their town. 




The collective efforts of the local women’s organization in environmental protection not only transform the bay, it also transforms the women as well.




 “Little by little, the culture of silence begins to fade. They grow more courageous,” Sampal said. 




Throughout her work with local farming and fishing communities, she observed that discussions and training help local women find their voice and gain confidence in their leadership.




Across sectors and across generations




For Peralez and Millomeda, the need for immediate support for their livelihoods and families is urgent. Foremost among their calls: livelihood support and access to water amid the super El Niño. 




“It would be good to have livelihood programs, especially for beneficiaries who are women. Because in our community, there is really no livelihood. It would be good to have livelihoods that can be permanent.” 




For Millomeda, support and access to water is crucial for farmers like her: “Farmers should be supported with water. Water sources should be increased, because the water now is slow and not enough for everyone. We really need support for water.” 




Even more importantly, they underscore the need for mutual support between different organizations and among different sectors.




“For me, if we do it alone, it leads nowhere. It’s better to reach out to your community, unite, and make plans for the environment, or work with other organizations that value climate change work. It’s better to communicate, because if it’s just you, it leads nowhere”, says Peralez. Now she joins different women farmers and advocates through the local chapter of their farmers’ organization, FASAD. 




“It’s good for farmers and fisherfolk to work together to protect the environment from abuse by big companies. One way is planting mangroves and cleaning up. Who else will help each other? It’s only us in the community” Millomeda said. 




For the women of Balete Bay, that describes what they say needs to be protected: water, secure livelihoods, and resources in the mountains and the bay. 




Beyond support between farmer and fisherfolk sectors, Ma’am Decena calls on the youth to support the continuing struggle for environmental protection in Balete Bay and in the upland areas of Davao Oriental.




“I hope and pray that the young generation will realize we have an obligation to care for the environment, to produce safe food, to support organic farming, and to help care for the environment.” 

(AMU, RVO)

The women of Davao Oriental protecting Balete Bay

author: Unknown
title: Lois Waisbrooker - A Sex Revolution
content:
Author

: Lois Waisbrooker

Title

: A Sex Revolution

Date

: 1894

Notes

: Second Edition

Source

: <

http://www.pierssen.com/misc/treasures/asr.htm

>




Preface.




 Dear Reader:—The history of the past shows us that nations rise, go through a longer or shorter period of prosperity and then decay. The ruling motive in the life of nations, so far, has always been the same, the aggressive or masculine. Self-aggrandizement, 

our

 nation right or wrong, all to be laid upon the national altar in the name of patriotism, a centralizing of wealth and power in the hands of the few at the expense of the many, and the result has always been what? Go, gather together the human wrecks of any one nation and you have your answer. 




 Now will not this latest and brightest of nations perish also unless methods are changed, unless the social lever is reversed? Already the seeds of decay are taking root; is there not some law through which we may take a new lease of life, and what is that law, if there be such, if it be not that 







 “woman, take the lead?” 







 True, woman is already quite prominent, is becoming more so, but she does not seem as yet to realize that with man’s methods she will succeed no better than man has done. She must formulate her own methods before her true work can appear. Woman must be free, must refuse to be led, must believe in herself, before the evils attendant upon imperfect motherhood can be eliminated, and as I see things, the only hope of our nation lies in this direction. 




 Let us once rise above the necessity of armies, navies, prisons, almshouses, asylums, etc., then the future will stretch out before us with ever increasing brightness. The first step toward this desirable consummation is to believe that it 

can

 be done; the next is that it 

will

 be done, and lastly to determine to do it 

ourselves

. 







 L. W. 







Chapter I.




 First, a little something about myself. I, Margaret Mulgrove, am a childless widow. My husband, Richard Mulgrove, went into the Union army at the beginning of our last war and never came out alive. My only child, little Bessie, took the scarlet fever in the second year of my widowhood, and though employing the most skillful physician in the whole country around, I could not save her. To say that I was desolate does not begin to express the feeling I had. 




 An aunt, my father’s only sister who lived in another State, hearing of my bereavement, decided to come and stay with me awhile and wrote me to that effect. Now my father and mother had in their lifetime (I forgot to say that I was an orphan also) had been good orthodox Christians and had brought me up to walk in the same path, so when Aunt Belinda wrote me she was coming I was a little troubled, for I had been told that she was an Infidel. 




 I believed infidelity to be something awful, and as our community was a very respectable one, to have a woman of that character come among us, and as my relative was an affliction I had not counted on, but it could not be helped; aunt would be there the next day and I must make the best of it. So the next morning I went to work to put things in the best order possible to receive my expected relative. 




 She came about ten o’clock, a pleasant faced, white haired lady toward whom my heart instinctively went out, and in spite of my prejudices I felt that I should love her. She stayed with me several months during which time nothing was said or done which brought up the subject of beliefs. True, I had purposely avoided everything that could lead in that direction, but she did not seem at all inclined to be aggressive. 




 The Sunday, and in fact the day before she left, our minister’s sermon called out some remarks from her that surprised me very much. 




 “Why aunt,” I exclaimed, “I thought you were an Infidel!” 




 “And so I am to church theology.” 




 “And yet you have just affirmed your belief in the underlying principle of all church theology.” 




 “How is that?” she asked. 




 “You said you believe in God manifest in the flesh.” 




 “I said I believed God manifest in the flesh was necessary to the salvation of the race, but I did not say I believed it had already taken place.” 




 “Not taken place! do you then look for a coming Christ?” 




 The old lady smiled. “Before you can understand me,” she said, “you must learn that a narrow personal application of a general principle is, must be false. The universal spirit of life can never be manifest in its fullness through, or be embodied in a person, in any one man or woman. When God is manifest in the flesh as I mean, it will be through the race. Man, as a race will have become God-like, will have arisen above his present condition, will be saved, not from future, but from present hells.” 




 “Well, I really cannot understand you, aunt.” 




 “I mean simply this, my child, when enough of the love, power and wisdom immanent in the deific fountain becomes developed in the race, and in harmonious proportions, then the evils which now afflict humanity will disappear.” 




 “But how is this to be done?” I asked. 




 “By belief in our own power to accomplish, through the God within ourselves, that which the church expects, waits for a God outside of ourselves to do for us. God, the soul or spirit of the universe must be manifest in, and act through us to the overcoming of all difficulties, to the surmounting of every obstacle that lies in the way of the progress of the race.” 




...

author: Leanne Sanders
title: AFN, other defendants delaying lawsuit by former national chief, lawyer says
content:
It has been five months since a judge issued a court order requiring the Assembly of First Nations and the other parties named in a lawsuit by former national chief RoseAnne Archibald to produce their documents by July 31.

Nearly three months later, Archibald’s lawyer says they’re still waiting.

David Shiller said the AFN and the other parties remain in breach of that order, forcing the matter back before the court for another case conference and another delay.

“Oral examination for discovery (was to) occur, between November second and November 9th,” Shiller said in an interview with APTN News. He added that they’ve still not received the required documents. On July 31, 2026, what they delivered to me was what they called a draft affidavit of documents, and it was only purporting to be from the AFN.

“There was nothing delivered on behalf of the individual defendants who were the individual members of the executive committee.”

The affidavit of documents is a form that comes from the court that discloses relevant evidence related to a case.

“What they delivered was a document that says ‘I, blank, of the town of blank, in the county of blank, affirm I am the blank, of the Assembly of First Nations.’ It wasn’t a sworn affidavit of documents. It was a draft,” Shiller said. “And that’s not just a technical difference. The whole point of making each side swear an affidavit is to get them to tell the other side and the court that they have done a diligent search of their records.

APTN reached out to AFN for comment and received a statement that said it can’t comment on a legal case but that the organization ”remains committed to meeting its legal obligations to the courts.”

Archibald launched the lawsuit June 14, 2022, naming the regional chiefs of the AFN at the time of her dismissal. Those regional chiefs include Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, Paul Prosper, Ghislain Picard, Glen Hare, Joanne Bernard, Kluane Adamek, Terry Teegee, Bobby Cameron, Darlene Bernard, Junior Gould and Gerald Antoine.

Woodhouse Nepinak is now the national chief, Prosper is a sitting senator, while Picard and Bernard are retired.

She also named the AFN as a whole, as well as the National Indian Brotherhood and the executive committee comprised of the regional chiefs.

Archibald is seeking damages of $5 million for “breach of contract and oppression; indemnity for the legal fees incurred by the plaintiff from July, 2021 through June, 2022 in connection with the campaign to sideline her and oust her from the Assembly of First Nations,” according to the statement of claim.

She is also seeking the legal fees she incurred in order to respond to her “unlawful suspension of her employment and the unlawful prohibition imposed on her by the Executive Committee of the Assembly of First Nations in connection with the 2022 Annual General Assembly and the Chiefs and Assembly meetings,” according to the statement of claim.

In its statement of defence, filed in Ontario Superior Court on Feb. 6, 2026, the AFN and the other defendants said they “deny each and every allegation contained in the Statement of Claim…” and that “the relief sought in paragraph 1 of the statement of claim is grossly excessive, exaggerated, inflated, and too remote and not commensurate with any losses, damages, or expenses, if any, sustained by the Plaintiff.”

The statement also said the defendants specifically deny that they initiated or engaged in any campaign of retaliation against Archibald and they have “no knowledge of any campaign to sideline and oust” Archibald from the Assembly of First Nations and that she must offer “strict proof” of the allegation.

They also deny that the defendants conspired to trigger workplace-harassment complaints against the plaintiff and also denies that the four complaints themselves were part of any conspiracy and that the Executive Committee exceeded its jurisdiction… or that there was an abuse of power by the Executive Committee as alleged.”

Archibald served as the AFN regional chief for Ontario from 2018 until she ran for national chief and won in 2021. She butted heads with then national chief Perry Bellegarde over “serious issues regarding the way the AFN and the Executive Committee were run,” according to her statement of claim.

Shiller said the fact that the AFN only provided a draft affidavit not signed by anyone means that that Archibald doesn’t have the “comfort of an oath that the proper search has been done. And looking at the documents that they listed in their draft, it supports the assertion that a proper search was not done.”

Just ten documents were produced by the AFN, according to Shiller.

“Doing a quick review of the ten, right away I see that one document is clearly missing. That’s the June 17, 2022 letter from Paul Prosper of the executive committee to the national chief saying that she’s suspended,” Shiller said. “Well, this whole case is about the steps taken by the executive committee to derail the national chief’s agenda. And certainly that suspension is a central part of what we say is a campaign to derail her platform.”

Shiller noted that there are no emails listed between the executive committee members and other people within the AFN regarding the actions taken against the national chief.

“Those things are clearly relevant and have not been produced. (AFN) Counsel has advised me that, she is still reviewing the emails. So, the fact that there’s some review going on now tells me that there are emails that might be relevant, and they haven’t been produced,” Shiller said.

During the November hearings, Shiller said the rules give each side only seven hours of examination.

“So, you know, here we are. We don’t want to be asking questions about documents we don’t have. We don’t want to be going there and saying, can you produce this document and that document? It should have been done already,” Shiller said.

The delay has necessitated another case conference with possible dates provided by the court in November.

Shiller said Archibald remains steadfast.

“And, you know, she’s patient. She’d rather not have these delays, but the delays are not going to make her go away,” Shiller said.

AFN misses deadline as former national chief RoseAnne Archibald’s $5M lawsuit moves into discovery

Former AFN national chief RoseAnne Archibald suing organization for $5M

Vote to oust RoseAnne Archibald ‘not taken lightly,’ AFN interim chief tells leaders

Archibald posted an update on social media on Oct. 21, writing in part:

“…I have nothing to hide. I put my allegations on the public record and shared my court documents for anyone to read. I am prepared to have the evidence examined, and I will see this process through. The AFN should be equally prepared.”

“Over the past year, I’ve heard from community members across many Nations who want the same things: truth, transparency and accountability from those in leadership,” Archibald continued.

“That is not asking too much. It is what our people deserve from anyone entrusted to lead. And when our questions remain unanswered, we keep asking.”

Leanne has a certificate in broadcasting and has more than 12 years of radio news experience, both as an anchor and reporter in Saskatchewan and Alberta. The Métis journalist is a passionate writer and born storyteller and loves to connect with people and learn about their life experiences.

author: Riese
title: Dems Crush Midterm Elections After Republicans Spent Millions on Weird Anti-Trans Ads
content:
we’re putting ms rachel on the $100 bill. you can’t even fathom the pronouns we’re going to invent. pete hegseth wanted people to watch a public execution, well they’re seeing it tonight. we’re making paxton play in girls sports TOMORROW – saddle up bitch. If you’re in line for your free gender reassignment surgery at the elementary school STAY IN LINE. If only Mitch McConnell were alive to see this.

Two things we haven’t had the occasion to say in a while: last night was a glorious night on Twitter, and it was also a glorious night in America. Millennial optimism infused the national mood. Some dared to declare that Woke was back, some suggested we begin transitioning Chick-Fil-As into COVID-conscious lesbian bars. Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers were credited with turning Texas blue and so were — bless their hearts — The Hunting Wives.

Amid the bleakest political era of my lifetime, and mere days after Americans were forced to buy Halloween candy that cost 71% more than it did in 2022, Democrats delivered a decisive, across-the-board victory, flipping the House and the Senate, exceeding every pollster’s wildest expectations. The Democratic majority in the House will be significant.

Many votes are still being counted, but so far most things are looking very good for us — as good as anything can look under capitalism. Kansas elected a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since 1932. Annie Andrews will become the first Democratic senator elected in South Carolina in 30 years. Ohio made Amy Acton the first woman elected governor in Ohio.

Former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms is tge first woman and the first Black person to be elected governor of Georgia and the first Black female governor in U.S. history. She beat Republican Rick Jackson, who was aiming to become the 84th consecutive white man to govern a state with the third-highest Black population share in the country.

In Texas, Gina Hinojosa, who has a stellar voting record on trans-related legislation, beat Gov. Greg Abbott to become her state’s first Latina governor.

Deb Haaland, formerly Joe Biden’s interior secretary, will become the first Native American woman to govern a U.S. State when she assumes office in New Mexico, while Peggy Flanagan will become the first Native American woman elected to the U.S Senate, winning in Minnesota.

These are just some of this election’s notable victories. But this election also was a referendum on political mobilization against trans rights — and the verdict was sometimes good (when it came to candidates targeted by anti-gay ads), and sometimes quite bad (when it comes to ballet measures aimed mostly at trans youth). Let’s get into it, and other crucial LGBTQ+ wins of the 2026 midterms.

This election is serving as a referendum on the violently anti-trans strategy the GOP has been romancing for the past few election cycles. Nearly $200 million Republican dollars were sunk into anti-transgender ads this election cycle by candidates certain that ambiguous fears about trans kids playing soccer or taking medication would mean more to voters than genuine concerns about inflation and gas prices, gangs of lawless ICE agents assaulting and murdering their neighbors, rising healthcare costs, defunding of essential government programs and the state of democracy in general. “What did [anti-trans ads] buy the Republican party?” asked Erin Reed of Erin in the Morning. ” An earth-shattering loss, and a stunning rebuke of anti-transgender politics.”

Texas saw $78 million real dollars thrown away on anti-trans ads, part of an overall package that made it the most expensive non-presidential election on record. Elon Musk dropped $29 million on an ad that warned, “Every mom in Texas should be worried about Senate candidate James Talarico putting parents in jail if they do not support surgically transitioning their children.” Another campaign used AI-generated footage to highlight Talarico saying “God is nonbinary” in 2021. Stephen Miller called Talarico the “first transgender Senate candidate.” This all went on despite Talarico not actually even being a strong advocate for trans rights during his campaign. Still, James Talarico won, the first Democrat to do so in Texas since 1988. And all the noise against him inspired some really good TikToks.

author: Andrés
title: El Gobierno Provincial intenta despojar de sus tierras a la comunidad Tekoa Kuaray Amba
content:
Hostigamiento de la policía de la provincia a la comunidad Mbya Guaraní




El Gobierno de Misiones criminaliza al Pueblo Mbya Guaraní para desconocer sus derechos territoriales. Bajo el argumento de que las tierras habitadas por la comunidad son fiscales, funcionarios provinciales impulsan acciones judiciales por una presunta ocupación irregular, mientras el propio Estado incumple su responsabilidad de reconocer y garantizar la posesión tradicional indígena. Por Clarisa Néztor para 

ANRed

.







La comunidad Mbya Guaraní Kuaray Amba, ubicada en Puerto Iguazú, denuncia una escalada de amenazas de desalojo, hostigamiento policial y criminalización de su recuperación territorial. Las familias reclaman el reconocimiento de sus derechos constitucionales y cuestionan la intervención de organismos provinciales que, en lugar de garantizar su permanencia en el territorio, participan en procedimientos intimidatorios.




El pasado 3 de noviembre, más de 15 efectivos de la Policía de Misiones ingresaron a la Tekoa Kuaray Amba acompañados por representantes del Ministerio de Ecología provincial. Según denunció la comunidad, los agentes llegaron para intimidar a las familias, recopilar sus datos personales y advertirles sobre un posible desalojo.




La intervención se produjo en el marco de un conflicto territorial que involucra a funcionarios de la Secretaría de Tierras de Misiones y que derivó en actuaciones judiciales iniciadas a partir de una denuncia de Rubén Sales, director de la Secretaría de Tierras, según la información aportada. El Gobierno provincial identifica los terrenos como propiedades del Estado, mientras las familias Mbya Guaraní reivindican su posesión tradicional y rechazan ser tratadas como ocupantes ilegales.




Un poco de historia: una comunidad en recuperación de su territorio tradicional




La Tekoa Kuaray Amba habita en la zona conocida como las 600 Hectáreas de Puerto Iguazú.




Durante 2025 se presentó un hombre que aseguró haber comprado las tierras y exigió que las familias abandonaran las tierras. Según el mburuvicha Lidio Rivarola, el supuesto propietario lo amenazó y le otorgó un plazo de 15 días para retirarse. Desde entonces, la comunidad denuncia que las amenazas se intensificaron y que funcionarios provinciales y municipales comenzaron a intervenir para exigirles que abandonaran el territorio que reivindican como tradicional.




Funcionarios provinciales y policías involucrados en las amenazas de desalojo




El 16 de septiembre una comitiva integrada por aproximadamente siete efectivos policiales, dos patrulleros y funcionarios del Gobierno provincial ingresó a la comunidad sin aviso previo. Entre los presentes se encontraba Daniel Behler, subsecretario de Gobierno, Asuntos Registrales y Tierras de Misiones, acompañado por Vanesa Caballero, representante del área municipal de Asuntos Guaraníes de Puerto Iguazú.




Según denunció Rivarola, los funcionarios les comunicaron que debían abandonar el predio porque las tierras serían ocupadas. El mburuvicha rechazó la exigencia y cuestionó que pretendieran expulsarlos del territorio que reivindican como propio.




La intervención de la Secretaría de Tierras, bajo la responsabilidad de Daniel Behler, forma parte de las situaciones de hostigamiento denunciadas por la comunidad. Las autoridades sostienen que se trata de tierras fiscales, mientras las familias afirman que representantes gubernamentales les manifestaron que esos terrenos estarían destinados a emprendimientos hoteleros.




La comunidad cuestiona que funcionarios del Estado provincial intervengan para exigirles que abandonen sus tierras, en lugar de garantizar el reconocimiento de su posesión tradicional, y esclarecer los derechos territoriales reclamados.




Luego de retirarse de Kuaray Amba, la comitiva se habría dirigido a la Tekoa Tekopora Poty, ubicada en el mismo sector territorial, donde se denunciaron nuevas amenazas de desalojo. De acuerdo con los testimonios, el hostigamiento provocó que varias familias abandonaran sus viviendas por temor a una intervención violenta. También se denunciaron desplazamientos de otras dos familias que habitaban en las inmediaciones.




El 21 de octubre se produjo una nueva intervención policial. Según la información aportada, diez efectivos ingresaron a Kuaray Amba y fueron recibidos por el segundo mburuvicha, Francisco Rivarola, a quien solicitaron los nombres y datos personales de las familias, argumentando que debían remitir esa información a la Justicia.




La comunidad cuestionó que los agentes no presentaran documentación que justificara el procedimiento ni identificaran formalmente la autoridad que lo había ordenado. Estos antecedentes fueron denunciados públicamente por el Equipo Misiones de Pastoral Aborigen (EMIPA), que documentó las amenazas de desalojo y las intervenciones policiales registradas durante septiembre y octubre.




 




La intervención de funcionarios de Tierras en la causa judicial




La existencia de actuaciones judiciales quedó confirmada mediante el expediente N.º 187270/2026, tramitado ante el Juzgado de Instrucción N.º 3 de Puerto Iguazú, a cargo del juez Martín Luis Brites, a partir de una denuncia de Rubén Sales.




En la causa también figura Aníbal Gorguez, responsable de la Secretaría de Tierras en Puerto Iguazú, identificado en el oficio judicial como personal de la Dirección de Tierras de la Provincia. El documento, fechado el 23 de octubre de 2026, dispone la citación de Sales y Gorguez para prestar declaración testimonial el 5 de noviembre, y ordena una inspección policial sobre los terrenos identificados en las actuaciones como propiedades del Estado provincial.




Mientras el Estado provincial promueve actuaciones judiciales para investigar la ocupación de las tierras, las familias denuncian que las intervenciones policiales se desarrollan en un contexto de amenazas, intimidación y temor a ser expulsadas de su territorio.




El oficio examinado no contiene una orden judicial de desalojo, pero confirma la intervención de funcionarios provinciales de Tierras y la existencia de diligencias policiales vinculadas al conflicto territorial.




El Estado niega el reconocimiento jurídico y condiciona el acceso a derechos fundamentales




A las amenazas de desalojo se suma otra denuncia de gravedad: la comunidad sostiene que desde 2025 solicita su personería jurídica sin obtener respuestas de las autoridades competentes. Según Lidio Rivarola, hace más de un año presentó la documentación correspondiente ante el área municipal de Asuntos Guaraníes, dirigida por Francisco Rodríguez, pero hasta el momento no recibió una resolución sobre su solicitud.




El mburuvicha denunció que la comunidad solicitó asistencia para acceder al agua y que Vanesa Caballero le respondió verbalmente que no podrían recibir ayuda hasta contar con la personería jurídica.




Las familias reclaman acceso al agua potable, electricidad, viviendas, caminos, atención sanitaria y educación, servicios esenciales cuya garantía no debería quedar condicionada exclusivamente a un trámite administrativo.




La denuncia expone una grave contradicción en el accionar estatal: mientras las autoridades demoran el reconocimiento jurídico de la comunidad, esa misma falta de regularización es utilizada para cuestionar su permanencia territorial y, según sus integrantes, negarles asistencia básica.




La ausencia de personería jurídica no elimina la preexistencia de la comunidad ni los derechos territoriales que la Constitución Nacional reconoce a los pueblos indígenas.




Tierras fiscales, criminalización y despojo territorial




En Misiones, distintas comunidades Mbya Guaraní denuncian que el Gobierno provincial repite un mismo mecanismo de despojo y violencia institucional: desconoce la posesión tradicional indígena, declara fiscales los territorios de las comunidades, promueve denuncias penales y las amenaza con desalojos, mientras sus tierras quedan expuestas a los intereses empresariales.




El Estado, que debería reconocer y garantizar los derechos territoriales indígenas, termina utilizando la falta de regularización como argumento para criminalizar a las comunidades. Bajo la figura de tierras fiscales, los territorios ancestrales quedan a merced de decisiones gubernamentales que pueden favorecer su entrega a emprendimientos privados, convirtiendo tierras que sostienen la vida de los pueblos indígenas en un botín para los negocios empresariales.




En el caso de Kuaray Amba, el mburuvicha sostiene que representantes gubernamentales llegaron a afirmar que las tierras pertenecían a emprendimientos hoteleros, mientras la comunidad asegura que se trata de territorio indígena previamente relevado.




Esta denuncia exige esclarecer la situación dominial del predio, los antecedentes de ocupación tradicional y la posible existencia de intereses privados sobre las tierras reclamadas.




La Constitución Nacional, en su artículo 75, inciso 17, reconoce la preexistencia étnica y cultural de los pueblos indígenas argentinos y la posesión y propiedad comunitarias de las tierras que tradicionalmente ocupan.




Asimismo, el Convenio 169 de la Organización Internacional del Trabajo obliga al Estado a reconocer los derechos de propiedad y posesión de los pueblos indígenas sobre sus tierras tradicionales, adoptar medidas para identificarlas y garantizar su protección efectiva.




La condición de tierra fiscal que invoca el Gobierno provincial no elimina los derechos de posesión tradicional indígena ni convierte a las comunidades en usurpadoras. La ausencia de un título de propiedad o de personería jurídica tampoco puede utilizarse como fundamento suficiente para desconocer derechos territoriales preexistentes.




La responsabilidad del Estado provincial no se limita a administrar tierras o intervenir en conflictos de ocupación. También debe garantizar que los derechos territoriales indígenas sean reconocidos y protegidos frente a posibles desplazamientos y presiones de intereses privados.




Un conflicto que se repite en otras comunidades Mbya Guaraní




Durante 2026, otras comunidades Mbya Guaraní de Misiones también denunciaron operativos policiales, amenazas de desalojo y criminalización de sus autoridades tradicionales.




Uno de los antecedentes más graves ocurrió en la Tekoa Puente Quemado II, donde durante mayo se registraron detenciones de integrantes de la comunidad en el marco de un procedimiento denunciado como un desalojo encubierto. En julio, la comunidad volvió a enfrentar otra intervención de desalojo, según documentó EMIPA.




Estos antecedentes reflejan las denuncias recurrentes de comunidades indígenas sobre el uso de procedimientos policiales y judiciales en conflictos territoriales que requieren respuestas institucionales orientadas al reconocimiento y la protección de derechos.




La comunidad exige reconocimiento territorial y el cese de las amenazas




Frente a esta situación, las familias de Kuaray Amba reclaman que las autoridades provinciales y municipales cesen las amenazas, respeten su permanencia territorial y respondan a las solicitudes de reconocimiento jurídico y respeto de sus derechos fundamentales.




El mburuvicha Lidio Rivarola expresó su preocupación por el temor que atraviesan las familias y cuestionó que los organismos creados para acompañar a los pueblos indígenas sean, según su denuncia, los mismos que participan en las intervenciones que los intimidan.




El Gobierno de Misiones tiene la obligación de esclarecer la situación territorial, garantizar la posesión tradicional cuando corresponda y evitar que la falta de regularización administrativa se convierta en una herramienta para desplazar a las comunidades.




El Pueblo Mbya Guaraní no necesita que el Gobierno le conceda su preexistencia ni sus derechos territoriales. Necesita que el Estado deje de desconocerlos, cumpla sus obligaciones constitucionales, y ponga fin a la criminalización de las comunidades que defienden sus territorios.

author: Kerry Smith
title: Community campaign forces Westpac to end Palantir contract
content:
Two months after Coles announced it would cut ties with surveillance company Palantir, Westpac has announced it will not renew its contract with the company, bending to a powerful community campaign

More than 40 organisations have joined the Dump Palantir Coalition (DPC) to pressure organisations to end contracts with the technology company over its role in supplying Israel’s genocide in Gaza and United States President Donald Trump’s deportation regime.

Palantir, founded by tech billionaire Peter Thiel, signed a strategic partnership with Israel’s Ministry of Defense in January 2024, to supply technology and surveillance to support its genocide in Gaza and occupation of the West Bank.

United Nations Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese named Palantir as being among those companies profiting from an “economy of genocide”.

Palantir supplied a US$30 million system to support Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) identification, tracking and deportation of migrants.

DPC spokesperson Mustafa Saabi said a “global movement” is determined to drive Palantir out of businesses, governments and institutions.

“When a protester told Palantir CEO Alex Karp that his company’s technology kills Palestinians, he replied: ‘Mostly terrorists. That’s true.’

“The UN has found that nearly 70% of the deaths it verified in Gaza were women and children … That’s the company Westpac was doing business with.

“This isn’t a public relations problem Palantir can fix with better messaging.”

The day Westpac reported its decision, Palantir shares fell by 7.3%, temporarily wiping about US$32 billion from its market value.

Westpac’s claim that its decision to end the contract with Palantir came down to “technology simplification” ignores the powerful public pressure campaign.

“Westpac didn’t wake up with a conscience,” Justice for Palestine Magan-djin spokesperson Remah Naji said. “We made its relationship with Palantir a liability. “"GetUp and SIX mobilised thousands of consumers and shareholders. Grassroots Palestine groups organised across the country. Ordinary people stood up, and we won.

"First Coles. Now Westpac. Every company doing business with Palantir should be asking itself one question: are we next?"

DPC spokesperson Subhi Awad said public money is still flowing to Palantir through the Future Fund, which holds $114.6 million in Palantir shares and government agencies continue to purchase Palantir technology.

“We’re coming for those relationships too,” Awad said. “Our message is simple: do business with Palantir and you risk losing customers and wrecking your reputation.

“We organised. We made Westpac dump them. And we’re not finished.”

[Sign up for updates about the next Dump Palantir Coalition campaign.]

Justice for Palestine Magan-djin
