author: Keelan Jacobs
title: Mississaugas of the Credit invests $15M million to become shareholder in First Nations Bank of Canada
content:
Mississaugas of the Credit in Ontario has invested $15 million in First Nations Bank of Canada, becoming one of the bank’s largest shareholders with an ownership stake of approximately 10 per cent.

The $15-million dollar investment for an approximate 10 per cent stake values First Nation Bank of Canada at roughly $150 million

The deal, announced Wednesday at Canadian Club in Toronto, completes a $50 million capital raise by the bank and brings the total number of First Nations and shareholders to 117.

Chief Margaret Sault said the investment is part of the Nation’s long-term economic strategy.

“This investment represents an important step forward in our Nation’s commitment to building a strong and sustainable economic future for our people,” Sault said. “By becoming a major shareholder in First Nations Bank of Canada, we are investing in an opportunity to build long-term wealth for our community with a partner who understands our needs and aspirations.

“Meaningful participation in the Canadian economy includes having ownership in the institutions that help drive and shape its future. We see this investment as an opportunity to create lasting benefits for future generations,” she added.

FNBC president and CEO Bill Lomax said the addition of Mississaugas of the Credit strengthens the bank’s founding vision.

“Today, we are building a growing national bank, supported by First Nations and Indigenous shareholders from across the country, and well positioned to pursue the significant opportunities ahead.”

“For 30 years, First Nations Bank of Canada has been focused on building a strong, successful financial institution dedicated to serving Indigenous communities,” Lomax said. “With the addition of Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation as a major shareholder, that founding vision is stronger than ever.”

According to Lomax, the investment will allow FNBC to loan more money to First Nations businesses for community infrastructure and economic development.

The bank, founded in 1996, is Canada’s only Indigenous-owned chartered bank. It operates 22 branches and service centres across six provinces and three territories, manages more than $1.625 billion in assets.

Fintrac imposes penalty on First Nations Bank of Canada

For First Nations, equity ownership in a federally regulated bank represents a shift from being primarily clients of mainstream financial institutions to being owners.

Lomax has described the institution as doing “the economic part of reconciliation and the financial part of nation-building.”

Other First Nations have said that having a stake in the bank gives them the ability to keep money within the community rather than extracting it.

Mississaugas of the Credit, the sole Treaty holder in the Greater Toronto and Golden Horseshoe region — an area that generates roughly 25 per cent of Canada’s GDP — framed the investment as both “economic and generational.”

The announcement included a fireside discussion with Sault, Coun. Larry Sault, Lomax and was moderated by Bank of Canada senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers.

Keelan is Anishinaabe from Walpole Island First Nation (Bkejwanong Territory). He graduated with an Honours B.A. In Political Science from the University of Toronto and follows the stories where power, money and public policy meet. Keelan has a strong interest in economics and finance, and is a lifelong hockey and sports fan.

author: Unknown
title: At least 25 people executed in Iran within six days
content:
The “No to Executions on Tuesdays” campaign, which is being organised by political prisoners in 66 prisons across Iran and is now in its 145th week, announced that at least 25 people had been executed across Iran and Rojhilatê Kurdistan (Eastern Kurdistan) over the past six days.




It was reported that Şehab Zuhedi, Omran Amani, Emin Pirdal, Arman Merefeti, Şayan Shekibayi and Metin Farinyan, along with numerous other political prisoners whose names have not yet been made public, have been sentenced to death.




The campaign's statement said: “Neither threats nor death sentences will be able to silence the voices raised against inhumane punishments. We demand the immediate abolition of all death sentences and all forms of killing in Iran.”




Two young protesters executed in Isfahan




Iranian judiciary-affiliated Mizan News Agency has announced the execution of two detained individuals, Amir Hossein Maleki and Amir Hossein.







The report stated that the death sentences handed down to Amir Hossein Maleki and Amir Hossein had been upheld by Iran’s Supreme Court.




Shahrzad Shahbazi, one of the lawyers involved in the case, emphasised that none of the defendants had been directly accused of murder and that the trial proceedings had not been fair.




Amir Hossein Maleki and Amir Hossein were arrested by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in January 2026, during popular protests held at Alihan Square in the city of Isfahan.

author: Unknown
title: Ağbayır: Those invoking Dar al-Salam must take responsibility for peace
content:
Muslim feminist Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır, one of the signatories of the "Women Side by Side, Discussing the Future" conference held in Ankara, spoke to ANF about the importance of the conference, what peace means for women and the role of the women's struggle.




Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır, who spoke to ANF on the second day of the conference, expressed her happiness at being among its signatories. She said that the first day had exceeded expectations and that they had placed greater emphasis on forums to enable participants to take a more active role in the discussions.







 







'We have a common aspiration'




Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır said, "We actually have a common aspiration here," and added: "This conference emerged from the question of how we, as women who have been discussing the ongoing process, growing inequality in Turkey, poverty, economic violence and all the problems that come with them separately, can speak with one another despite our different political views, positions and disagreements."




Ağbayır said that the discussions in the forums had demonstrated how useful this approach was, noting that they had come together with many women throughout the day, from Söke in Aydın to Ankara, and from Bodrum to Diyarbakır (Amed).




Ağbayır said that the conference had provided an opportunity to hear about issues they had not known about or previously considered. 




Ağbayır said: "Women are engaged in a political struggle everywhere, from inside their homes to the streets. Sometimes they find themselves confronting the challenges of simply being women, sometimes women's poverty, and sometimes the very reality of child poverty.




That is why we planned today's session around a panel followed by forums, creating a space where we can speak and listen together. What will emerge from this? How can we move forward? We envision a process in which the women here have a say and are the ones speaking today. I hope it will turn out very well."




'We think peace is an issue only certain groups can discuss'




Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır challenged the perception that peace was an issue only certain groups could discuss, emphasizing that peace had not been achieved within society itself. She drew attention to the following problems: "We tend to think that peace is something only a particular group can talk about. But peace does not exist within this society either. We are talking about a society that lacks internal peace. We are talking about a system in which a child can go to school in the morning carrying a pump-action shotgun. We are talking about a world where addiction is increasing and children are left in desperate conditions on the streets because of it. At the same time, we are discussing violence against women. The very existence of male violence often places us under this oppression. The system does not distinguish between Muslim women, secular women or any other women when it does this.




The system does this because it sees you as vulnerable simply because you are a woman. And we really are among the most vulnerable groups. That is another aspect of the issue. Although we are not on the side of the oppressors but among the oppressed, we are women who continue to struggle."




Ağbayır continued: "As a Muslim woman, I believe we live in a society where those who constantly take pride in Islam as a language of peace and repeatedly invoke Dar al-Salam, meaning the abode of peace, should perhaps question why peace does not exist in this society and take responsibility."




She added: "I am still at a point where I cannot call this a peace process. That is something I also want to discuss here. I am among those who believe that peace must be achieved, that we must discuss what kind of peace we want, and that all women must be able to speak freely at that table."




'We will not allow peace to be framed as a story centered on men'




Ağbayır said, "We will not allow peace to be framed as a story centered on men," and emphasized that the issue was not merely about preventing loss of life. She stressed that Muslim women must assume social responsibility in accordance with their faith and help build a peaceful future based on equal citizenship for everyone.




Ağbayır said that faith itself demanded such responsibility: "Faith itself commands this. I say that nothing inhumane can be part of Islam. So where do we stand? What kind of peace do we want? We are the ones who will discuss this. Peace cannot exist where one side is victimized, ignored or subjected to inequality. Democracy cannot exist there, nor can justice be achieved. Peace must also be a process in which we question our own position and what it represents."




'There is no need to debate ECtHR rulings'




Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır criticized the failure to implement the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) ruling concerning the "right to hope" of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan. 




Ağbayır said: "Today, Bahçeli uses the term 'founding leader.' If I had used it, I would probably have been imprisoned long ago. We are therefore talking about Öcalan, who has been imprisoned for many years and is regarded as the leader of a people, of a large community. I approach this from the following perspective: Suppose that, as a sociologist, you do not recognize Öcalan as a leader. But when we discuss legal rights and equality, should he be released in light of the ECtHR rulings? We do not need to turn this into a debate. Can he be released from a legal standpoint? Yes, he can.




I say this to those who have reservations: We must address the independence of the judiciary. We see how the right to hope, a concept that has emerged through the experiences of an entire society, relates to everyone's freedom. Therefore, from a position of defending the right to hope, I believe his freedom must be secured on the basis of judicial independence, setting aside everyone's political views and positions."




Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır also criticized the failure to implement the Istanbul Convention and the "My Family Is Safe" operations, saying that she was not seeking justice from those responsible for these practices but was demanding an independent judiciary. 




Ağbayır said: "In a country where even the Istanbul Convention is not effectively implemented, I certainly have no legal demands to make of those who saw the convention as a threat and abolished it, or those who break up other people's families through the 'My Family Is Safe' operations. My demand is directed at the law itself. We live under a system in which the principle of equality requires an independent judiciary. The law does not, and should not, allow impunity."




'We struggle by breaking through these barriers'




Ağbayır said that women would continue to resist attempts to confine them to their homes through religion or other ideological instruments. She continued: "We struggle by breaking through these barriers. That is why we want a legal system that also puts an end to violence. Perhaps some people think: There is already lawlessness and impunity, so what are we even talking about? But we must not stop speaking out. Until something changes, until we make that change happen, we must not abandon our responsibility to raise our voices and do whatever we can, through whatever forms of struggle are available to us.




The system is already trying to render us passive. Look at all those in power today. For example, Muslim women and religious women should be the first to reject the image of a woman confined to her home in the name of religion. Neither a state, nor a religion, nor an ideology can determine the standards by which a woman is considered acceptable."




Ağbayır emphasized that women should define themselves according to their own moral principles and values. She concluded: "That is why we will continue our struggle from a position of responsibility, criticizing the government's policies of impunity and refusing to contribute to the invisibility of violence."

title: The anatomy of special warfare and paths to youth liberation in the Middle East
content:
Special warfare is not an overt military operation carried out with tanks and artillery. It is a system of psychological and social destruction that directly targets society's consciousness, culture and moral values. Within this system, the most strategic targets of dominant and colonial powers are young people and young women. This is because youth is the dynamic driving force of social transformation, while young women are the founding subjects of a free society. The state mentality and dominant powers seek first and foremost to paralyze this revolutionary and pioneering force in order to permanently establish their hegemony over the will of peoples.




As Abdullah Öcalan, whose ideas have become central to the political and philosophical discussions of the Kurdish people, the Middle East and peoples around the world, has strongly emphasized, unless a radical consciousness of "self-defense" is developed against this systematic process of social degradation, society will be completely severed from its historical and moral foundations.




The following sections examine, point by point, the reality into which young people have been pushed, the social destruction caused by the instruments of degradation described as the "three horsemen of the apocalypse," and the paths to liberation, with the aim of providing every young person with a guide to action.




The situation of young people and young women: What has the system reduced them to?




Warmongering and extremist forces originating from capitalist colonial states, which have now become direct instruments of special warfare, have subjected young people to a system of comprehensive control through systematic policies that are "flexible and soft" on one side and "brutal and militaristic" on the other.




Lack of ideology and spiritual emptiness: 

Young people are being subtly distanced from ambitious aspirations, the pursuit of freedom and the consciousness of assuming social responsibility. Life is reduced to the superficial mentality of "live for today and consume," with the aim of preventing young people from reflecting on the future of their countries.




Hopelessness and pessimism:

 Systematic perception management is employed to undermine young people's belief in their own transformative power. A sense of helplessness, expressed through the idea that "We cannot change anything; the system is too powerful," is instilled in young minds, forcing society's leading force towards submission, passivity and escape through migration abroad.




Loss of identity and alienation:

 Through policies of cultural destruction, young people are pushed into a cycle of shame concerning their own languages, historical roots and social values. A generation isolated from its own culture and alienated from its identity becomes the most loyal servant of the deception of capitalist modernity.




The systematic targeting of young women: 

Young women are systematically portrayed by the system as "commodities" or objects of consumption. Through social media illusions and the fashion industry, their minds are diverted from genuine freedom, particularly intellectual and political freedom. Their potential is confined within a cage of "physical appearance and makeup," depriving them of their pioneering roles.




The three horsemen of the apocalypse (instruments of social destruction)




To achieve these objectives, the dominant system deploys three of its most poisonous instruments, directly undermining the moral foundations of society.




Drugs (all physical and psychological stimulants)




Objective:

 To deliberately and systematically facilitate the spread of drug networks in neighborhoods, schools and spaces where young people live.




Consequence:

 The mind of a young person trapped by drugs becomes paralyzed, their will is broken, and they lose the ability to react against injustice. They are transformed from a politically conscious and active subject into a dependent object focused solely on obtaining substances, becoming a heavy burden on their family and society.




Gambling (and digital games of chance)




Objective:

 To create the illusion of "getting rich quickly and easily without working" among young people through online gambling websites, betting applications and digital games.




Consequence:

 The value of labor and production is undermined. Young people who lose everything through gambling are crushed under heavy debts and lose their dignity. In their desperation to obtain money, they become vulnerable to all forms of criminal activity, corruption and even networks of informant recruitment.




Sexual degeneration and the paralysis of will




Objective:

 To separate sexuality from its natural foundations of love, commitment and mutual respect, creating profound social degeneration through the pornography industry and forms of relationships considered immoral.




Consequence:

 This cultural erosion leads young men and women to view one another merely as instruments of physical gratification. The sacred spirit of comradeship and the consciousness of revolutionary loyalty are destroyed. When intellectual productivity comes to a halt, only instincts remain, and animalistic impulses become the sole governing force of life.




What is the way out of this system of oppression?




As clearly articulated from a philosophical perspective, the way to dismantle this oppressive system is not through passive rejection or complaint, but through radical self-organization and the construction of a new way of life. Young people and young women can reclaim their lives and futures through the following steps:




Establishing academies of enlightenment (a campaign for self-education)




Action:

 Young people must stop relying on institutions and establish their own "Self-Education and Reading Groups" as independent academies in every neighborhood, village and street.




Method:

 Philosophy, the history of peoples' resistance, analyses of special warfare and women's science (Jineolojî) must be studied in depth. Young people who develop intellectual competence will not surrender to the lies and traps of the system.




Developing mechanisms of social self-defense




Action:

 Young people and young women must become the moral and physical protectors of their own living environments.




Method:

 Self-defense and social ethics commissions must be established within people's assemblies. Those who introduce drugs into neighborhoods, operate gambling establishments or harass young women must be identified by young people themselves, publicly exposed and socially ostracized. Social isolation is the strongest sanction.




Reconnecting with historical and cultural roots and building a collective economy




Action:

 Mother tongues, indigenous cultures, revolutionary art and historical memory must be preserved against the consumerist frenzy imposed by capitalist modernity.




Method: 

Alternative theater, music, literature and folklore collectives must be established within assemblies. Young people whose inner worlds are enriched by revolutionary art and historical consciousness will not fall into spiritual emptiness. At the same time, agricultural, craft and production cooperatives must be established to revitalize the collective economy and counter the system's economic blackmail.




The joint leadership of young women and youth




Action: 

The patriarchal mentality (baviksalarî) must be radically dismantled within families, assemblies and social spaces.




Method: 

Young women must educate themselves in political and philosophical fields, particularly through Jineology, and raise the banner of rebellion against traditional and modern forms of oppression. The shared and equal roles of women and young people will give the emerging democratic communal system its true spirit and invincible strength.




The reality of Middle Eastern youth, the Leviathan system and a radical way out




Special warfare is a global system that subjugates society not through the force of arms, but by undermining its moral and intellectual foundations. As conceptualized by Abdullah Öcalan, the philosophical genius of our era, this crisis is not confined to a single people but is a systemic plague collectively produced by the centers of global capitalist modernity. This system has effectively become a global Leviathan, a monstrous force threatening to devour humanity.




The policies of dominant systems towards Middle Eastern youth




The capitalist monster and nation-state mechanisms in the region implement different special warfare strategies according to the sociological characteristics of each people.




Kurdish youth: Assimilation, terror and cultural destruction policies




Oppression and distinctive characteristics: 

Because the Kurdish youth's strong passion for freedom and radical activism are well known, the system employs physical destruction, intense political repression and an increasingly severe economic embargo against them.




Instruments of special warfare:

 Policies of linguistic assimilation are implemented to strip young people of their identity, while drugs are deliberately introduced into neighborhoods. Through pressure to become informants and psychological warfare techniques, bonds of comradeship among young people are undermined, and their energy is redirected towards leaving their homeland through migration and refugee routes.




Arab youth: Trapped by unemployment, sectarianism and radicalism




Oppression and distinctive characteristics: 

Following the Arab Spring, global capital and reactionary forces in the region have turned the Arab world into a laboratory of endless civil war and chaos.




Instruments of special warfare: 

Sectarian divisions, particularly Sunni-Shiite tensions, have been artificially inflamed to prevent the enormous energy of Arab youth from developing into democratic transformation. Young people are trapped in a cycle of deep poverty and unemployment, either driven into the killing fields of false radicalism and armed groups such as ISIS and its offshoots, or left to drown in the Mediterranean while pursuing dreams of reaching Europe.




Turkish youth: Blind nationalism, chauvinism and cultural erosion




Oppression and distinctive characteristics:

 The central state mentality in Turkey raises Turkish youth within an ideology of fanatical nationalism, chauvinism and fascism, positioning them as instruments of repression against the freedom demands of other peoples.




Instruments of special warfare:

 To prevent Turkish young people, who are trapped in a severe economic crisis and a lack of prospects for the future, from rebelling against the system, the digital gambling industry, corrupting television programs and sexual degeneration, described as "porno-nationalism," are used as a form of opium. Young people are conditioned to become guardians of the totalitarian state rather than defenders of freedom.




Persian youth: Theocratic repression, hypocrisy and the gallows




Oppression and distinctive characteristics: 

The theocratic regime in Iran, under the guise of religion, surrounds the lives of young people, particularly young women, with the harshest political and social restrictions.




Instruments of special warfare: 

The regime maintains its empire of fear through the execution of young people sentenced to death. On the other side of the coin, however, the system covertly facilitates the spread of drugs and prostitution in the underground world. This structural hypocrisy drives young people into profound existential nihilism, a loss of belief, and confines them to a hopeless and degraded existence behind closed doors.




This remarkable practice of resistance and self-organization is not merely a local patriotic duty. It is freedom itself, the security of today and the guarantee of tomorrow. Middle Eastern youth, rising with this universal and confederal consciousness, will dismantle the capitalist Leviathan and become the founding architects of a new democratic, ecological world based on women's freedom.

title: Iran attacks Komala base in Balîsan
content:
Iran attacked a base belonging to the Komeleya Şoreşgerên Zehmetkêşên Kurdistanê (Association of Revolutionary Toilers of Kurdistan) in Balîsan, southern Kurdistan, this morning. According to the party, the attack took place at around 8:40 a.m. and involved two explosive-laden drones.




Komala stated that no one was injured or killed in the attack northeast of Hewlêr (Erbil). However, the organization reported that the attack caused significant damage to property at the base.




Since the outbreak of the war between Iran, the United States, and Israel, Tehran has repeatedly attacked targets in various parts of southern Kurdistan. More than 30 people have reportedly been killed in these attacks so far.

title: Students demanding education in mother tongue attacked in Hesekê
content:
A demonstration demanding the right to education in the mother tongue was attacked in the northeastern Syrian city of Hesekê. Students had gathered outside the provincial administration building to demand education in their own language. Forces affiliated with the Syrian transitional government intervened against the gathering and fired shots into the air.




According to information obtained by the ANHA news agency, a group believed to be Arab residents from the Xiwêran neighborhood initially attacked the demonstrators with stones. Meanwhile, security forces of the transitional government attempted to disperse the protest and prevent it from continuing, using firearms.




The students condemned the intervention and emphasized the peaceful nature of their demonstration. “What have we done wrong to be prevented from doing this? We took to the streets peacefully and are demanding our right to our own language,” they told ANHA. The protesters also made it clear that the attacks would not deter them from demanding education in their mother tongue.




Since early September, students and their families in Rojava have been protesting against restrictions on Kurdish-language education. The protests were triggered by the Syrian transitional government’s decision to scale back Kurdish-language instruction and limit Kurdish classes to three hours per week. Previously, Kurdish had been not only a subject but also a language of instruction in schools administered by the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria (DAANES).




The protesters regard the decision as an attack on the linguistic and cultural rights of the Kurdish population. They are demanding that pupils and university students continue to receive education in their mother tongue and that the educational structures established under the autonomous administration be preserved.

title: Hatimoğulları visits Demirtaş, calls for the release of political prisoners
content:
Ten years after the crackdown on the Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP), Tülay Hatimoğulları, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), called for the release of all political prisoners in Turkey. Following a visit to former HDP Co-Chair Selahattin Demirtaş, who has been imprisoned since November 2016, at Edirne Prison, she declared that the struggle would continue until no one remained behind bars for political reasons.




The subsequent rally outside the prison was attended by numerous supporters and representatives of left-wing and socialist parties, including Seyit Aslan, Chair of the Labour Party (EMEP).




The gathering marked the tenth anniversary of November 4, 2016, when the Turkish government launched a sweeping crackdown on the parliamentary representation of the Kurdish population with the arrests of the HDP’s co-chairs and several other members of parliament.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/814f1fab_20261104123621_2026-11-04-edirne-tulay-hatimogullari-dem-parti-es-genel-baskani-edirne-cezaevi-aciklama-1.mp4










Hatimoğulları called for the immediate release of Selahattin Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ and all those imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê trial. She demanded the implementation of the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR).




Hatimoğulları stated that the practice of appointing government trustees had spread across the country since November 4, 2016, and condemned the arrests of elected mayors and the appointment of trustees to replace them.




DEM Party Co-Chair said that Demirtaş would continue to support the Peace and Democratic Society Process despite his imprisonment. “The struggle will continue until all political prisoners are free. Our comrades behind bars are continuing their struggle, and we will continue ours to build a democratic society. Our struggle will continue until not a single political prisoner remains,” she stated.




Labor Party (EMEP) Chair Seyit Aslan also called for the release of political prisoners, an end to the practice of appointing government trustees, and the introduction of a general political amnesty.




“We demand concrete steps to ensure that the Kurdish people can live on equal terms, along with the necessary legal reforms, particularly the recognition of the right to education in the mother tongue. Without these measures, without taking these steps, we cannot achieve or establish peace,” Aslan said.




DEM Party Istanbul MP and Socialist Solidarity Platform (SODAP) spokesperson Kezban Konukçu emphasized the need to strengthen a common platform for collective struggle to advance the peace process. She called on Turkey’s socialist left to unconditionally support the Kurdish people’s demand for peace.




“We must intensify our struggle to improve people’s livelihoods, secure women’s freedom, defend our right to life, and enable the Kurdish people to achieve peace in this country. These demands are inseparably linked,” Konukçu stated.

author: Unknown
title: Kurdistan Region Parliament elects presidency
content:
The first session of the Kurdistan Region Parliament’s sixth term began earlier today after the required quorum was reached with the participation of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and several other parliamentarians.




As Mihemed Silêman of the New Generation Movement and Azad Mihemedemîn of the PUK were absent, KDP member Semîra Hesen, the oldest parliamentarian present, presided over the session.




During the session, held without the participation of the PUK (Patriotic Union of Kurdistan), candidates were nominated for the positions of Speaker, Deputy Speaker, and Parliamentary Secretary.




In a joint statement issued yesterday, the KDP parliamentary group and the Turkmen Reform Party called on all parliamentarians to attend today’s parliamentary session. The Presidency of the Kurdistan Region Parliament announced that only 43 parliamentarians had signed the request for the session and that the meeting could not be held because the required quorum had not been reached.




Responding to the KDP’s call to convene parliament, the PUK stated: “In accordance with our deep commitment to the principles of the rule of law and national consensus, we believe that this meeting is illegal and constitutes an attempt by one side to impose its will.” The PUK also announced that it would not recognize any parliament or government formed following the session unless national consensus was achieved and all elected parties were guaranteed the opportunity to participate in the process under free and democratic conditions.




As the parties had failed to reach an agreement on the allocation of ministerial portfolios, the PUK, the New Generation Movement, the Justice Community (Komela Dadgerî), and several other parties boycotted today’s session of the Kurdistan Region Parliament.




With the participation of 52 parliamentarians, which met the required quorum of 50+1, elections were held for the parliamentary leadership positions. Vala Fardi was elected Speaker of the Kurdistan Region Parliament, Rami Nouri was elected Deputy Speaker, and Mona Qahwachi was elected Parliamentary Secretary.

author: Unknown
title: Call for action on the anniversary of November 4 coup: Comply with ECtHR rulings, release prisoners!
content:
Civil society organizations, professional associations, and bar associations in the Kurdish region gathered outside the Diyarbakır Courthouse on the anniversary of the November 4, 2016 operations targeting the HDP.




During the gathering, participants unfurled a banner featuring photographs of politicians imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê trial. The banner read: “A requirement of the rule of law, a necessity for democracy: Freedom. Implement ECtHR rulings, pave the way for democratic politics.”




Diyarbakır Bar Association President Sertaç Buluttekin recalled that former HDP Co-Chairs Selahattin Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ, along with HDP MPs, had been detained and unlawfully imprisoned in 2016.




Buluttekin said that Turkey had failed to implement the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) despite the Court’s findings of violations. He emphasized that the continued imprisonment of those imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê trial and the failure to enforce judicial decisions undermined public confidence in social peace.




In a joint statement read by Ercan Yılmaz, Co-Chair of the Diyarbakır branch of the Human Rights Association (İHD), the organizations stated that the Kobanê trial was part of broader efforts to undermine democratic politics through judicial means.




Yılmaz recalled that 27 HDP MPs had been detained in the process following the November 4, 2016 operation, with 15 of them subsequently imprisoned. He noted that five politicians had been released under a ruling issued by the Ankara 22nd High Criminal Court on May 16, 2024, while the cases of 72 politicians had been separated from the main proceedings. He added that 108 people were still facing trial in connection with the case, including 14 who remained in detention.




Yılmaz said that the ECtHR rulings concerning Demirtaş, Figen Yüksekdağ, and other politicians indicated that their detention lacked a legal basis and were politically motivated.




Emphasizing that ECtHR rulings are binding under domestic law, Yılmaz called on the 22nd Criminal Chamber of the Ankara Regional Court of Justice to issue release orders for the imprisoned politicians without further delay.




“This decision is not only a requirement under the principle of legal certainty but also one of the most important steps toward establishing lasting peace throughout our region,” Yılmaz stated.




The statement emphasized that the imprisonment of politicians affected not only individual freedoms but also the political will of voters and their right to democratic representation.




Lawyer Erhan Ürküt stated that the rule of law must be restored to achieve peace. He stressed that the release of politicians imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê trial was essential for advancing the democratic resolution process.




Batman Bar Association President Abdulhamit Çakan also called for the implementation of ECtHR rulings and the immediate release of Demirtaş and other imprisoned politicians.




Meral Danış Beştaş, Co-Spokesperson of the Peoples’ Democratic Congress (HDK), described the arrests carried out on November 4, 2016, as a coup against democratic politics.




Beştaş emphasized that the freedom of Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ was crucial to paving the way for democratic politics. “Their freedom is a test of the sincerity of the process,” she stated.




The statement concluded by reiterating calls for the release of politicians imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê trial, the implementation of ECtHR rulings, and the opening of channels for democratic political participation.

author: Unknown
title: Bakırhan visits Figen Yüksekdağ, calls for freedom for political prisoners
content:
Ten years after the wave of arrests targeting the Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP), representatives of several left-wing and democratic parties gathered outside Kandıra Women’s Prison in the western Turkish province of Kocaeli to demand the release of political prisoners. The gathering marked the anniversary of November 4, 2016, when the Turkish government launched a sweeping crackdown on the parliamentary representation of the Kurdish population with the arrests of then-HDP Co-Chairs Figen Yüksekdağ and Selahattin Demirtaş, along with several other members of parliament.




Tuncer Bakırhan, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), had earlier visited Figen Yüksekdağ, who has been imprisoned for ten years, together with a delegation. Following the visit, party representatives and numerous supporters gathered outside the prison. Under the slogan “Freedom for political prisoners – for peace and democracy,” they demanded the release of those imprisoned.







Bakırhan: The political crackdown of 2016 continues to have repercussions today




Bakırhan described the arrests of November 4, 2016, as a “political coup” whose consequences have long since extended beyond the Kurdish opposition. He said the process had begun with the lifting of parliamentary immunity on May 20, 2016, a move that had also been supported by sections of the opposition at the time.




“On that day, a deep wound was inflicted on Turkey’s political history,” Bakırhan stated. He argued that the violations of rights committed at the time had since expanded to affect nearly all opposition forces. “What was done to the HDP back then is now being directed against all institutions and individuals engaged in opposition activities.”










“This is not just a peace process”




Referring to the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process, Bakırhan stated that the continued imprisonment of opposition politicians contradicted the declared objectives of political reconciliation. He stressed that anyone seeking to overcome social polarization must first address past injustices. This includes, in particular, implementing the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) and Turkey’s Constitutional Court, he noted.




“For ten years, we have been standing outside these prisons and making statements. Hasn’t it been enough? In the eleventh year, our friends must once again be able to engage in democratic politics alongside us,” Bakırhan said. He stressed that Figen Yüksekdağ should be able to advocate her political position on peace outside prison. Selahattin Demirtaş, too, should be reunited with his people and his political colleagues, he said.




“This is not just a peace process. It is also a process of democratization,” the DEM Party Co-Chair emphasized. He remarked that prisons must be emptied for Turkey to achieve the rule of law, justice and democracy. Alongside Yüksekdağ and Demirtaş, he named several imprisoned politicians and activists, including Can Atalay, Osman Kavala, Bekir Kaya and Leyla Güven. He stressed that their place was not in prison but in society.




Left-wing parties demand an end to political prosecutions




Representatives of socialist parties also linked their demands for the release of political prisoners to fundamental democratic rights. Sezin Uçar, Deputy Co-Chair of the Socialist Party of the Oppressed (ESP), recalled the decade-long resistance against political persecution.




“Without freedom of expression, protest and organization, we can neither achieve peace nor build democracy,” she stated. Uçar said the ESP was demanding the release of all political prisoners, the repeal of Turkey’s Anti-Terror Law and the removal of all restrictions on freedom of expression, assembly and organization. She specifically highlighted those imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê and Gezi trials.













Levent Tüzel, Deputy Chair of the Labour Party (EMEP), described the Kobanê trial as a politically motivated prosecution. He pointed out that the HDP had been justified in calling for solidarity with the resistance against the siege of Kobanê in 2014. According to Tüzel, however, the protests at the time had been manipulated by paramilitary forces, with responsibility for the violence subsequently attributed to the HDP leadership. Tüzel criticized the lengthy prison sentences imposed as a result. He emphasized that the demand of peoples to live together in equality and freedom was at the heart of the current peace process.













Öztürk demands concrete steps from the government




Hakan Öztürk, Chair of the Labour Movement Party (EHP), called on the Turkish government to follow up its political statements and legislative measures with concrete action. Otherwise, he warned, the peace process risked losing credibility.




“If the reports that have been prepared and the promises that have been made were not merely empty words, they must now be put into practice. Otherwise, seriousness and trust will be lost,” Öztürk said.




Öztürk stated that the Kurdish movement and Abdullah Öcalan had made their contribution to changing the political climate. He said that this development must now also be reflected in Öcalan’s prison conditions and ability to work. In particular, Öztürk called for the establishment of the previously announced body for peace and political participation, which is intended to coordinate the further implementation of the process.




The EHP Chair also demanded the release of the politicians imprisoned in Kandıra, arguing that they had been deprived of their freedom through politically motivated court rulings and should be released immediately.

author: Unknown
title: Peace Mothers: There can be no peace unless Abdullah Öcalan is free!
content:
The Peace Mothers, who traveled to Ankara from various cities across Kurdistan and Turkey, held meetings at the Turkish parliament on Tuesday. As part of their peace initiative, they met with representatives of several parliamentary groups, including the YENI Party, the Yeni Yol parliamentary group, the MHP, and the ruling AKP. The discussions focused on Abdullah Öcalan’s physical freedom, the release of political prisoners, and concrete measures to advance the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




The meetings followed the Peace Mothers’ gathering in the parliamentary park, where women from 24 cities held a peace vigil on Monday and called on political leaders to advance the Peace and Democratic Society Process through concrete measures.




After a press statement about their meetings, the mothers returned home yesterday, while a delegation representing them remained in Ankara for further talks.




As part of their meetings in parliament, the Peace Mothers met with Speaker of Parliament Numan Kurtulmuş on Wednesday. Peace Mothers Hanife Akpolat, Müzeyyen Bütün and Afife Kartal attended the meeting, which took place in the Speaker’s office. Following their meeting with Kurtulmuş, the mothers held a press statement outside parliament’s Dikmen Gate.




Speaking here, Peace Mother Müzeyyen Bütün said: “The meetings went well. We hope this process will reach a successful conclusion. We repeatedly expressed our demand for peace. We came here for peace, and we thank all the political parties and their leaders. We also thank Speaker of Parliament Numan Kurtulmuş for hosting us. They spoke positively to us, and we believe that peace will come to this country and that we will live together. Until peace is achieved, we will raise our voices and demand peace morning and night, everywhere, in the streets and in the cities. We believe our demands will be met. We also call on the mothers of soldiers and police officers to join us so that we can demand peace together.”




Zeynep Çalıhan, a Turkish mother, said: “There are Peace Mothers all around the world, and they all want peace. We want Mr. Abdullah Öcalan to be free. There can be no peace unless he is free. We want him to regain his freedom. Enough blood has been shed on these lands. It is time to plant saplings in this soil, not bury more people. I also appeal to Turkish women: Come, let us build peace together. We want peace, not war.”

author: Jonathan Strauss
title: Qld LNP crushes public sector workers’ right to organise
content:
The Queensland Liberal National Party (LNP) government introduced legislation in October to make it more difficult for state public sector and local council workers to organise and take industrial action. Nearly 400,000 workers in the state who are not covered by the federal Fair Work Act will be impacted.

The legislation raises the threshold for workers’ compensation claims for psychological injury, requiring work to be the “major significant” cause of the injury. This could reduce the number of claims for these injuries, about which workers are now more conscious.

It does not address these injuries’ causes, such as the unsafe conditions, excessive workloads, chronic understaffing and exposure to violence and abuse faced by public sector workers, who are five times more likely than other workers to experience psychological injury, according to Queensland Unions (QU).

The legislation introduces the restrictive provisions already included in federal laws that make it more difficult for workers to take industrial action. This includes restrictions on union organisers' right to enter workplaces with “fit and proper person” tests, a requirement of three working days’ notice before taking industrial action and allowing employers to reduce pay during industrial action partial bans and withhold pay from workers on strike.

The Queensland bill goes further than federal laws in some ways.

It changes the basis for the Queensland Industrial Relations Commission’s (QIRC) orders — which determine which employers and employees will be covered by an agreement.

It adds the criteria that the order must “not adversely affect the business or operational needs of any employer to be covered”. This would allow actions like those taken by Qantas, which split workers across three distinct companies to drive down pay and conditions.

Another change prevents workers from taking industrial action during QIRC’s conciliation of bargaining. This ban is not automatic under federal laws.

The bill gives the industrial relations minister extraordinary power to ban otherwise protected industrial action, even before it begins.

The minister would also be able to ban actions if they “disrupt the delivery of a public service” or “otherwise have a significant effect that is contrary to the public interests”. This severely limits the ability of public sector workers to take industrial action.

If bargaining reaches a deadlock, the legislation would force the QIRC arbitration to consider not only workplace productivity and public interest — provisions included in federal laws — but also the state’s fiscal strategy and the public employer’s financial position.

That means workers will be limited to the pay caps for workers that the government could declare before bargaining begins.

The legislation weakens workplace health and safety by lowering standards and removing codes of practice. Workers’ ability to cease unsafe work will be further limited.

QU said the preventive role of existing codes will be reduced and Queensland specific codes which address local industry risks — such as sugar milling, coal dust exposure and diving — are being replaced with broader national guidelines.

The bill would also allow employers to request a job applicant’s workers compensation claims history.

QU’s response has been to launch its Protect the People Who Protect Queensland campaign. This includes a petition, gathering stories of personal experiences of workplace injuries, and leafleting, letterboxing and other campaigning in workplaces and at transit hubs.

Meetings are planned across regional Queensland in November as well as an online forum.

But workers can consider what else could be done to defend organising rights and fight back against the restrictions on industrial action.

[Jonathan Strauss is a long-time unionist and community organiser.]

Liberal National Party of Queensland (LNP)

author: Dennis Ward
title: SCO grand chief given a ‘reprieve’ from a vote that could have ousted him
content:
The grand chief of an organization that represents 33 Anishinaabe and Dakota Nations in southern Manitoba will carry on in his leadership role until at least June 2027.

This past summer, a former ally of Jerry Daniels brought forward a motion seeking a vote to remove him as leader of the Southern Chiefs Organization (SCO).

“Chiefs have raised numerous concerns regarding governance, leadership, accountability, transparency, organization decision-making and the confidence of member Nations in the current leadership of the Organization,” said a resolution at the time tabled by Lake Manitoba Chief Cornell McLean.

A response, at the time, attributed to the SCO Chiefs Executive Committee, cited the financial cost of a summit, among other reasons, and called for the motion to be brought forward at an ordinary summit

That meeting, SCO’s Chiefs-in-Summit gathering, got underway on Wednesday in Brokenhead Ojibway Nation, where a vote on Daniels’ leadership was expected.

According to an SCO spokesperson, “the Chiefs withdrew the proposed non-confidence motion at today’s SCO Chiefs-in-Summit, and no vote was held.”

McLean told APTN News that “it wasn’t a win for him, it’s more like a reprieve. We decided to wait until his term is over in June.”

Daniels has previously faced two non-confidence votes.

Those came shortly after a fight involving the grand chief outside of a bar in Ottawa in December 2024, on the eve of an Assembly of First Nations gathering.

The SCO Chiefs-in-Summit is closed to the media.

Dennis is Métis from southern Manitoba. After spending a decade working in TV in Alberta and Ontario, Dennis returned to Manitoba to join APTN. In 2016, he won a Canadian Association of Journalists award for his story A Soldier Scorned for APTN Investigates. In 2017, he became a host/producer for APTN National News and Face to Face.

author: LCM-Redaktion
title: The Kids Are All Riot – Gen Z gegen Zeitenwende und Staatsräson
content:
Nachdem die Social Media-Algorithmen wochenlang voll waren von einem Mix aus aufständisch-revolutionär wirkenden Szenen und TikTok-Tänze tanzenden Teenagern vor überforderten Bullen aus Frankreich, Albanien und Co., war es am Samstag endlich so weit: Nachdem zunächst anonyme KI-generierte Aufrufe online den 31. Oktober als Stichtag dafür ausgerufen hatten, den Funken der Revolte endlich auch nach Deutschland überspringen zu lassen, wurden in über 30 Städten Demonstrationen organisiert. Mit Blick auf die Entwicklungen im Ausland wurde dieser Tag von verschiedenen Seiten mit großer Anspannung erwartet. Während die revolutionäre Linke zu großen Teilen damit zu rechnen schien, dass die online entfachte Stimmung auch eher online bleiben würde, warnten Politik und Presse davor, dass der Untergang unserer zivilisierten Ordnung an diesem Halloween eingeleitet werden würde und in den Klassenräumen deutscher Großstädte wurde darüber diskutiert, was man sich zuerst aus den Media-Markt Regalen holen würde, wenn „die Revolution losgeht“.




So ganz scheint sich keine dieser Prognosen bewahrheitet zu haben. Tatsächlich ist es nicht übertrieben davon zu sprechen, dass die „Gen Z regelt“ Proteste die größten organischen Jugenddemonstrationen seit Fridays for Future auf die Straße gebracht haben und der Auftakt für eine relevante neue Bewegung mit wesentlich größerer Bedeutung werden könnten. Und auch wenn nun mit aller Macht versucht wird, die Bilder aus Frankfurt, Hamburg und Köln heranzuziehen, um zu beweisen, dass die vorangegangene Panikmache völlig berechtigt gewesen sei, blieben die völlig unangetasteten Spanholzfassaden, die auf einmal in großen und kleinen Städten überall auftauchten und kleinlaut wieder abgenommen wurden, um den alltäglichen Konsum am Montag wieder freien Lauf zu lassen, mehr Grund für Belustigung im Netz und bei vorbeigehenden Passanten als nötige Schutzmaßnahmen gegen den revolutionären Mob.




Panikmache oder reale Angst?




Doch die Angst, die im Vorhinein angeheizt wurde, ist echt. Es ist nicht die Angst einer Bevölkerung, die um die eigene Sicherheit und Innenstädte bangen muss, auch wenn mit aller Macht versucht wird, das zu behaupten. Es ist die reale Angst einer herrschenden Klasse davor, dass sich tatsächlich eine Stimmung in der deutschen Jugend breitmacht, die sich gegen die Verhältnisse richtet, in denen sie in zunehmend kaputt gesparten Schulen darauf vorbereitet wird, Nachwuchs für die Klasse zu sein, aus der jetzt auch noch der letzte Tropfen Lebens(=Arbeits)kraft ausgepresst wird, um den Krieg zu finanzieren, in dem sie außerdem als Kanonenfutter verheizt werden soll. Denn mit einer solchen Jugend wären Deutschlands aktuellen imperialistischen Bestrebungen tatsächlich nur schwer zu machen. Dementsprechend ist nicht nur die Angst der Herrschenden sehr real, sondern auch ihr Wille, eine solche Bewegung gegen ihre Politik zu verhindern.




Auch die Repression steht erst am Anfang




Diesen Willen bewiesen sämtliche großen Medienhäuser bereits im Vorfeld des Aktionstags, die die Proteste so schnell wie möglich gesellschaftlich zu delegitimieren versuchten. Das massive und aggressiv auftretende Polizeiaufgebot ist ein weiterer Beleg dafür, wie ernst es dem deutschen Staat mit seinem Willen ist, eine echte neue Jugendbewegung nicht aufkommen zu lassen. Bei aller Freude darüber, wie stark sich der Widerwille gegen die Politik dieses Staates am Samstag gezeigt hat, dürfen wir nicht darüber hinwegsehen, dass die Reaktion der herrschenden Klasse noch deutlich stärker werden wird. Historisch waren erstarkende und in Teilen militante Widerstandsbewegungen immer auch Grund für eine eskalierende Reaktion. Das ist kein Argument, als Bewegung die Spaltung, die durch die mediale Hetze erzeugt werden soll, zuzulassen, aber wir müssen ehrlich einschätzen, wie bereit wir dafür sind, die sich zuspitzende Dynamik von wachsender Repression und sich radikalisierenden Protest auszutragen. Andernfalls droht eine weitere Verschärfung des deutschen Repressionsapparats, ohne dass wir als Bewegung unseren Zielen wirklich näherkommen.




Es wäre ein Fehler, zu unterschätzen, wie wirksam die BRD bereits darin ist, radikalen Protest zu unterdrücken. Dass für eine Eskalation oft juristische Konsequenzen drohen, die das gesamte weitere Leben einschränken und nicht nur primär körperliche Gewalt durch die Cops, führt bereits jetzt dazu, dass solche Eskalationen vor allem von denjenigen Jugendlichen ausgehen, die diese Konsequenzen unterschätzen. Als Bewegung dürfen wir nicht einfach abfeiern, wenn Jugendliche völlig unvorbereitet, unmaskiert und öffentlich ohne Weiteres identifizierbar in Geschäfte rennen, um sich mit einem Paar teurer Sneaker zumindest ein kleines bisschen Verbesserung ihrer materiellen Lage zu verschaffen. Es sind gerade diese Jugendlichen, die jetzt zur Zielscheibe medialer und politischer Hetze werden, immer auch verbunden mit den widerlichsten rassistischen Feindbildmarkierungen, die zunehmend von allen Seiten des politischen Establishments zur Zielscheibe Nummer 1 werden. Gerade diesen Jugendlichen muss unsere volle Solidarität sicher sein, ob das heißt, sich der öffentlichen Hetze entgegenzustellen oder den 15-jährigen neben sich zurückzuhalten bevor er völlig unvermummt vor die nächste Überwachungskamera rennt, um eine Straftat zu begehen. Wir dürfen die meistgefährdeten Teile unserer Jugendbewegung nicht einfach ins offene Messer laufen lassen, weder indem wir sie anfeuern, sich Gefahren auszusetzen, denen viele von uns bewusst lieber aus dem Weg gehen, noch indem wir sie der rassistischen Hetze von Staat und Presse zum Fraß vorwerfen.




Hetze und Distanzierung bis zur Bedeutungslosigkeit




Dass jetzt öffentlich immer weiter das Schreckensbild der kriminellen migrantischen Jugendlichen betont wird, ist nicht neu. Aus der politischen Rechten kennen wir das schon lange, mit den Entgleisungen rund um den Genozid in Gaza haben auch wesentlich weitere Kreise bis hinein ins vermeintlich linke Spektrum dieses Feindbild übernommen. Dabei müssen wir uns auch bewusst machen, dass diese „migrantischen Jugendlichen“, welche in Politik und Medien als Schuldige und Feindbild Nummer 1 markiert werden, der Sündenbock der heutigen Zeit für die deutsche herrschende Klasse, den deutschen Imperialismus und die rassistisch aufgehetzten Teile der deutschen Gesellschaft sind. Ein konstruiertes „migrantisches Milieu“ wird immer expliziter für alles schuldig gemacht, was schiefläuft in diesem Land – von Antisemitismus bis zu „es gibt keine Zahnarzttermine“, um die Wut der Bevölkerung über die Verhältnisse und die Sozialkürzungen von ihren eigentlichen Ursachen wegzulenken – die klassische Sündenbockstrategie eben. Damit sind als migrantisch a.k.a „fremd“ markierte Gesellschaftsgruppen aber auch die gefährdetsten Ziele, welche in Zukunft immer expliziter rassistisch angegriffen werden. Pogrome, Morde, Abschiebungen und Feindseligkeit werden mit diesem Diskurs erzeugt und aktiv in Kauf genommen, wie der rassistische Anschlag vom 23. Oktober in Frankreich, bei dem der 26-jährige Pengo Bossio Wangi durch einen Faschisten ermordet wurde, deutlich beweist. Eine Linke im Allgemeinen hat die Aufgabe, diese als Sündenböcke und Feindbilder markierten gesellschaftlichen Gruppen zu unterstützen und zu verteidigen. Das sind unsere migrantischen Jugendlichen, das sind unsere Leute. Das ist der Grund, warum wir uns nicht von den Ausschreitungen distanzieren und nicht, weil die Plünderungen ein politisch revolutionärer Akt waren. Es muss darum gehen, eine Bewegung des politischen Widerstands aufzubauen und dabei die Angriffe und Hetze gegen unsere migrantischen Klassengeschwister abzuwehren.

Ein Zulassen der Spaltung kann dazu zum effektiven Todesstoß einer echten klassenkämpferischen Bewegung werden. Die Stärke unserer Bewegung hängt maßgeblich von ihrer Einheit ab. In Frankreich sieht sich der Staat gerade zu immer mehr marginalen Zugeständnissen und (bisher) hohlen Versprechungen gezwungen, weil es eben nicht gelingt, einen Keil zwischen die Schulblockaden aus den unterschiedlichsten gesellschaftlichen Schichten, die Gewerkschaftsbewegung und die Jugendlichen aus den Banlieues zu treiben. Die Methode dieser Spaltungsversuche ist nicht neu und sie wird von den Herrschenden gegen eine Vielzahl linker Bewegungen von reformistischen bis revolutionären Massenbewegungen eingesetzt.

Nach genug Hetze baut die bürgerliche Öffentlichkeit Druck auf die Bewegung auf, sich von ihren vermeintlich problematischen Teilen zu distanzieren und für die Verletzungen der bürgerlichen Spielregeln zu entschuldigen. Es wird eine Trennung aufgemacht zwischen der vermeintlich akzeptablen Protestbewegung, die – solange sie nach den bürgerlich-demokratischen Regeln spielen würde – auch ernst genommen werden würde, und den „Störern“, den „ausländischen Plünderern“, den „linksextremen Gewalttätern“, den „Terroristen“, „Antisemiten“ etc., die am Ende den brav und friedlich Demonstrierenden am allermeisten schaden würden.

Das greift die gesellschaftliche Akzeptanz sozialer Kämpfe an, wird aber erst richtig effektiv, wenn im zweiten Schritt die Bewegung selbst anfängt, sich in moralisierenden Diskussionen darum zu verlieren, was tragbar ist, auf die bürgerlichen Forderungen eingeht, sich von diesen und jenen zu distanzieren und sich im Endeffekt bis in die Bedeutungslosigkeit zu spalten. Während bis dahin die Stoßrichtung klar gegen die herrschende Ordnung gerichtet ist, die unser aller Leben immer weiter in die Scheiße reitet, drehen sich ab diesem Zeitpunkt die meisten Diskussionen darum, wer jetzt den eigentlichen Zwecken der Bewegung schadet, wer wen verrät und wo genau jetzt eigentlich die Trennungslinie der Distanzierungen verlaufen soll. Damit ist es für den Staat ein leichtes, die besonders unliebsamen und gefährlichen Teile der Protestbewegung mit massiver Repression zu überziehen und den Rest mit kleinsten Zugeständnissen abzuspeisen oder einfach nur zu warten bis sie sich selbst zerlegt, ohne irgendetwas erreicht zu haben. Deshalb wäre es der größte Fehler, wenn die Jugendlichen in der Breite jetzt einknicken und den Forderungen nach Distanzierungen und Verurteilungen nachkommen.







Beginnt die Revolution am Schuhregal hinter der zerschmissenen Scheibe?




Dennoch besteht die Aufgabe revolutionärer Kräfte nicht darin, jetzt nur bedingungslos alles abzufeiern und zu romantisieren, was an Riots und Plünderungen passiert. Wenn ein Haufen Jugendlicher in Frankfurt die Scheiben einiger Läden einschmeißt und sich im Snipes-Store eindeckt, dann ist das kein revolutionärer Akt. Es ist auch kein Schaden, den wir bedauern müssen, aber wir sollten uns auch nicht die Illusion machen, dass dies bei vielen der Jugendlichen aus einem politisch-revolutionären Bewusstsein geschehen ist. Sicher ist es aufregend, gemeinsam so die Regeln zu sprengen, aber im Endeffekt dürfte die Hauptmotivation der meisten einfach sein, sich entweder coole Schuhe zu holen oder ein paar Euros damit auf Kleinanzeigen zu verdienen. Damit haben wir auch kein Problem, aber gleichzeitig sollte eine Linke das richtig verstehen und nicht romantisierend als revolutionär verklären.

Wie sehr diese Taten zum Zentrum des Diskurses gemacht werden, ist am Ende einzig und allein im Interesse der Herrschenden, um weiter Hetze und Spaltung zu betreiben und die für sie wirklich bedrohliche Stimmung in der Jugend gegen Kürzungen, Militarisierung und Polizei zu zerstreuen.

In einer Gesellschaft, in der es für viele Jugendliche essentiell wichtig erscheint, ihre materielle Lage um ein paar Euro oder ein strahlendes Statussymbol zu verbessern, wird es immer zu Ladenplünderungen kommen, wenn eine große Masse von Menschen auf den Straßen ist und sich der Polizei entschieden entgegenstellt. Die sich zuspitzenden Proteste schaffen Möglichkeiten, die Notwendigkeit für diese Taten schafft dieses System aber ganz von selbst. Es ist deshalb zentral, die Diskursverschiebung nicht einfach mitzutragen, indem man sich in langwierigen Diskussionen über die moralische Legitimität von Plünderungen verliert, egal wie genau man sie nun bewertet. Stattdessen muss der Fokus darauf liegen, eine wachsende Bewegung aufzubauen, sich darauf vorzubereiten, dass die Repression dieses Staates noch lange nicht erschöpft ist, tragfähige Organisierung zu schaffen und solidarisch miteinander zu bleiben.




Anzeichen einer neuen Qualität des Kampfes




Denn während sich medial viel um die nächtlichen Ereignisse in Frankfurt dreht, hat sich am 31. Oktober vieles anderes ereignet, was sich gerade mit Blick auf den Vergleich zur letzten großen Jugendbewegung als absolut positive Entwicklung zeigt: In der Jugend wächst ein Bewusstsein, dass es nicht reicht, wenn wir einfach nur nett darum bitten, dass Politiker uns ernst nehmen. Über große und kleine Städte hinweg war am Samstag oft spürbar, dass eine deutlich wütendere Stimmung herrschte, ein Bewusstsein, dass der Widerspruch zu der herrschenden Politik grundlegender ist. Für die Größe der Proteste war auffällig, wie geschlossen eine Haltung gegen die Polizei vorherrschte, egal ob Pyros gezündet, Anweisungen ignoriert, spontane Ausbrüche versucht oder polizeifeindliche Sprüche gerufen wurden. Das ist mit Sicherheit ein Ergebnis davon, mit welcher Reichweite sich Videos von durch nichts zu rechtfertigender Polizeigewalt aus dem Ausland, seit Samstag aber vor allem auch aus Deutschland auf Social Media verbreiten.




Die Bedeutung von Social Media, insbesondere von TikTok bleibt weiterhin auffällig. Vor allem schien es dadurch, als ob ein Großteil der Hetzkampagne in den großen Medien der etablierten Presse an den Jugendlichen selbst vorbeiging. Von der Panikmache blieben vor allem Videos sichtbar, die sich über die verrammelten Ladenfronten lustig machten. Es macht Mut, wie sehr die herrschende Klasse den Zugriff auf die Jugend verliert. Auch wenn die Proteste bei weitem noch nicht das Ausmaß erreicht haben, dass wir brauchen: Sie zeigen eine deutliche Weiterentwicklung im Bewusstsein und im Willen zum Widerstand der Jugend unserer Klasse.

Benjamin Lehmann

The Kids Are All Riot – Gen Z gegen Zeitenwende und Staatsräson

 erschien zuerst auf 

Lower Class Magazine

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Angie Nixon Hints at Another Senate Run in 2028, After Being Heavily Outspent
content:
Nixon, Democrats’ candidate for US Senate in Florida, didn’t receive any funding from the party’s Senate PACs.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Democratic candidate Angie Nixon has suggested she could run again in 2028 after being narrowly defeated in her race for U.S. Senate in Florida on Tuesday, falling to Republican opponent Ashley Moody by roughly 3 points after being massively outspent in the race written off by the Democratic establishment.

Moody received 50.9 percent of the vote to Nixon’s 48 percent, still overcoming a 10-point swing toward Democrats compared to 2024. Nixon got roughly the same proportion of the vote as Florida governor candidate David Jolly, a former Republican member of the House who left that party in 2018 and registered as a Democrat last year.

The race was a special election to fill the Senate seat left vacant by Marco Rubio, who won the seat in 2022 but left to become Secretary of State. Moody was chosen by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis as a temporary replacement, and has now been officially elected to serve the rest of the term.

This means that the seat will be up for grabs again in 2028 — and Nixon, who has already defied the odds in her race, has left the door open for another run.

In her concession speech on Tuesday, Nixon struck a positive tone despite the loss, touting the movement built by her campaign. “When we started this campaign, people told us it could not be done,” she said. “They told us we couldn’t compete with the political establishment.”

“I need y’all to stay in this fight. The war is not over. 2028 is around the corner. So Ashley Moody, you better get it right. Cause we’re coming for you,” Nixon said. Let’s go win y’all.”

Indeed, it is extraordinary that a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) could come so close to a win in the red state. Though Nixon has rejected the socialist label, the DSA has been relentlessly vilified by conservatives and liberals alike, and Nixon has embraced left-wing stances like rejecting assistance to Israel and supporting Medicare for All.

Nixon’s primary race was already historic. She won despite being outspent by roughly 13 to 1, and raised just under $1 million compared to $16 million raised by opponent Alex Vindman, a former national security official in Donald Trump’s first administration.

The Democratic establishment, however, seemingly wrote off her race — or potentially actively opposed her bid. Neither the Senate Majority PAC nor the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) spent any money supporting Nixon’s race, The American Prospect points out.

According to AdImpact data, Republicans spent $28.7 million on TV ads supporting Moody, while Democrats only spent $7.9 million. Nixon’s campaign says that support and fundraising from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) was an enormous help.

“Bernie’s impact on our campaign was immeasurable. He was one of our most important partners, by far,” said Kevin Lata, Nixon’s deputy campaign manager, on X on Tuesday evening. “I can almost guarantee that the democrats who are blaming Bernie did very little themselves to help, and should instead be looking inward, not at him.”

Some politicians chalked the lack of support from the main arms of the Democratic Party as racism as well as pro-centrist bias. Last month, Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Massachusetts) called out the DSCC for this disparity.

“It is shameful that we are not seeing an equitable investment in progressive and diverse candidates like Abdul El-Sayed, like Angie Nixon, like Scott Colom,” said Pressley. Nixon and Colom, whose Senate race in Mississippi is too close to call as of Wednesday afternoon, are Black, while progressive Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed is Arab American.

“They have earned and need the investment so that we can have a majority,” Pressley said, as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) nodded beside her.

Nixon added on Wednesday, after sweeping Democratic wins even across traditionally red states in the South, that Democrats must not write off the region.

“Invest In The South,” Nixon wrote.
