title: Rojhilat Alliance: Member parties in favor of continuing dialogue
content:
The Rojhilat Kurdistan Union Group issued a written statement regarding its meeting with representatives of four member parties of the Alliance of Political Forces of Eastern Kurdistan.




The statement said: “In order to activate the Alliance of Political Forces of Eastern Kurdistan, which was established more than eight months ago, and to identify the obstacles preventing it from functioning effectively, the Rojhilat Kurdistan Union Group invited the Alliance’s six parties to a consultative meeting.




The Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), the Kurdistan Freedom Party (PAK), the Organization of Struggle of Iranian Kurdistan (Sazmana Xebat a Kurdistana Îranê), the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan (KDP-I), and the Association of Kurdistan Toilers attended the meeting.




Only the Komala Party stated that it was not prepared to attend the meeting. In addition, a few days before the meeting, the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan (KDP-I) withdrew without providing any explanation.




On Sunday (1 November 2026), a three-hour meeting was held between the Rojhilat Kurdistan Union Group and representatives of four parties belonging to the Alliance of Political Forces of Eastern Kurdistan.”




The statement noted that the four parties regarded the political alliance as an important and long-term necessity. It added that the Political Alliance could become more active and effective in the near future by adopting a charter, defining roles and responsibilities, and establishing mechanisms for joint work.




Regarding the possibility of dialogue with the Iranian state, the statement said that the parties had agreed that, should an opportunity for dialogue arise and the need for negotiations emerge, no member party of the Alliance should independently enter into negotiations with the Islamic Republic of Iran without the Alliance’s participation and coordination.




The statement described the meeting as a positive step, noting the willingness to discuss directly the challenges facing the Political Alliance—an initiative that deserved support and further development. It added that representatives of all the parties had expressed positive assessments of the meeting.




The statement also emphasized that the parties should refrain from accusing one another in order to avoid undermining trust between them and jeopardizing the continuity of their joint work.

author: Daron Letts
title: ‘Government-wide effort’ needed to fix broken foster system: premier
content:
One day after the federal auditor general’s office published its latest 

report

 on the state of Nunavut’s foster care system, Premier John Main pledged his government will do better.




“This report is upsetting,” Main said during a news conference at the legislative assembly Wednesday. 

“The responsibilities that lie with our government are serious and we need to live up to the duties that have been entrusted to us.”




Deputy auditor general Andrew Hayes tabled the report, 

Foster Care in Nunavut,

 in Nunavut’s legislative assembly on Tuesday. The federal auditor general has the authority to review the effectiveness of Government of Nunavut programs.




The document outlines the Family Services department’s failures to maintain regular contact with children in care, to screen and monitor foster homes, and to maintain reliable information on the number of children in the system and where they had been placed — a problem that was highlighted in the auditor general’s 

2023 report

.




“The Department of Family Services did not provide timely and effective foster care services to protect and support the safety and well-being of children,” Hayes said during a news conference Tuesday afternoon. “It could not consistently demonstrate that basic safeguards intended to protect children and place them in safe environments were being followed.”




The department’s failure to solve the lapse in data stems from the department staff’s lack of training on its 

centralized reporting system

, known as Matrix, Hayes said.




“We saw differences between the manual lists that the department is working with and the information in Matrix. That is a problem,” Hayes said.
















Family Services Minister Gwen Healey Akearok said that is changing.




“The Matrix training has been unrolling throughout the territory,” she said at the news conference. “There’s another one happening this month.”




She said 90 per cent of front-line staff and 80 per cent of other staff have been trained so far.




“We know we need that evidence. We need strong documentation. We need excellent records,” Healey Akearok said. 

“Every foster file is now in one system.”




She said that 

97 per cent of home studies have been completed and, as of October, 82 per cent of annual reviews had been completed.




“There’s still work to be done,” she added.
















The auditor general will release another report in the spring of 2027, on the department’s “quality assurance work,” Hayes said. 




Nunavummiut will see improvements in that report thanks to “a government-wide effort,” Main said. 

“Our sincere hope is that future audits will show real improvement.”




Asked if any staff will lose their jobs over the report’s findings, Main said he will not share that publicly.




“From the upper management on down, there is an expectation that you will fulfill your duties, and if not, you’ll face the consequences,” he said.

author: Katharine Trendacosta
title: Google Summaries Aren't About AI, They're About Lock-In
content:
Whether they call it AI summaries, knowledge panels, or AMP, Google takes actions that are less about functionality and more about locking you into its own ecosystem. Knowing that makes it possible for all of us to choose better services than Google's, defeating their anticompetitive goal. In this case, as it is so often, knowledge is power. 

 




In the old days, when dinosaurs roamed the earth and getting online involved your computer making eldritch shrieking, Google was a website that took whatever you typed in and gave you a list of links that best matched what you were searching for. As it's grown beyond that, however, the core function of Google Search has moved from giving you the best answer to your query to a number of other things, most of them about making money for Google.

 




This is obviously not a new observation. It's at the core of what EFF Special Advisor Cory Doctorow named "

enshittification

." But it's important to remember that whatever shiny new name or technology is wrapped around these tools, it's not about the wrapping, it's about the monetization.

 




In the case of Google Search, the company has a history of rolling out new "features" that are less helpful to the searcher and more designed to keep you and your data within the Google ecosystem. One easy example of enshittification is putting sponsored links and ads at the top of search results, forcing you to scroll down past a bunch of not relevant links to get to your answers. Or, in some cases, accidentally clicking on sponsored links that might be designed to give you the opposite information of what you're looking for or for a competitor to the product you intended to buy. 

 




The other clumsy version of this is Google's self-preferencing, where Google's own services—say YouTube if you're looking for a video—are weighted so that they appear at the top of a search over a competitor's. Similar to this was Google's push for websites, particularly news ones, to be made available via what it called 

"Accelerated Mobile Pages" or AMP

, which in theory stripped out features that might make loading a page on mobile too slow, but also handed over control of how webpages looked on mobile to Google and turned mobile links, often by default, into Google links. 

 




But the other way that Google has historically kept your—and your valuable eyeballs—on its website has been to just obviate the need to even click on a link and leave Google at all. The first version of this was what Google calls "knowledge panels." These are snippets of information shown on the results page of a search that purport to answer your question. Knowledge panels predate the AI push and haven't always been what you could call 

accurate

. 

 




Knowledge panels are extremely similar to the AI summaries we now see at the top of Google Search results, except that instead of pulling quotes from specific linked sources, it's the AI doing the summarizing, though also sometimes with links. They are basically the same thing, mostly changed only in branding, because AI is now the cool kid on the block. The goal is essentially the same—it's less about providing you with the best answer to your query and more about making you think it's unnecessary to click a link and leave Google's ecosystem. And, more importantly, it keeps you on Google's pages longer to read the content. More time on the page is more time exposed to ads and sponsored links and more money for Google. 

 




The biggest irony here is that 

it didn’t even work

. People choosing to use “AI mode”—and possibly made accustomed to getting information as text instead of links through the knowledge panels and the AI summaries at the top—has caused 

“lower monetization”

 via ads. Ads, remember, are Google’s main source of revenue. Like newspapers before them, Google is finding that counting on a monopoly on ad space maybe isn’t the most sound strategy in a shifting technological landscape. And to get out of the hole it has made for itself, it is lighting cash on fire to try to get back on top. Perhaps they should consider pivoting to video. 

 




Every time you see a feature like this, no matter what it is called or what "new" technology they claim fuels it, remember that it is Google's monetary incentives that drive the decisions and not necessarily the tech itself. And you can always choose to ignore it, scroll past, disable it, or even 

go to another service entirely

.

author: Daniel Hunter
title: The Midterms Repudiated Trump. Grassroots Momentum Will Shape What Comes Next.
content:
We can exhale — and celebrate — and then we need to sustain movement energy for the long-haul pressure campaigns ahead.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The broad strokes of the midterms are clear: A massive repudiation of MAGA’s fascist wave has ended the Donald Trump 2.0 era of congressional complicity with his authoritarian takeover. Trump’s lame duck presidency now begins.

This lopsided electoral rejection is historically rare: Flipping control of both the House and Senate in a midterm has only occurred three times since World War II (in 1946, 1994, and 2006). The breakthroughs are astounding: the first Native American governor and senator, five Black governors, the first majority of Democratic governors in 16 years, and critical down-ballot wins like the first Democrat to win as Texan oil regulator since 1990 and the first openly transgender state legislator in Alabama.

Authoritarians do not do well when trapped — and with a famously norm-busting president, anything is possible. But, critically, election deniers like Darline Graham and Greg Abbott are conceding their races. Trump is already saying he’s “absolutely willing” to accept the results and told CBS, “Congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country.”

These midterms have left me, like many, with abundant free-floating anxieties. The “what if” scenarios have been abundant — and while some of the most extreme versions did not happen, the federal government was weaponized against the election system like never before.

Because the times have been so rough, it can be hard to exhale and accept a win, especially since elections are not material changes — they are promissory notes that the future may be different. Until January 3, we live under the same dangerous authoritarian government, even if the atmosphere has changed.

Before I advocate for you to breathe, let’s affirm all the many hard reasons to not exhale. The wins were not universal, as some big losses cut deep. There’s a reality that all of this is ephemeral if Democrats cannot govern a policy of change — if we only manage an economic status quo it will disillusion and likely result in yet another whiplash election in the other direction. And it’s hard to breathe in a dizzying moment.

The country looked at fascism and fully rejected it.

Further, the attacks on elections were treasonous. I won’t list the complete litany of federal assaults — but we have a Department of Justice captured by authoritarian forces using its power nakedly for partisan goals. The far right openly prepared sham legal theories to refuse certification of Democratic representatives. While we did not get systematic federal law enforcement terror at polls, we saw National Guard throughout Washington, D.C. We still have too many election officials committed to the Big Lie. And ongoing structural impediments to a fair election are consequential: In Mississippi, the Senate margin remains tiny while any win may be marred by equipment trouble, poll changes, and voters unexpectedly removed by data purges from the voting rolls.

Notably, the election maps themselves have been gerrymandered by racists to ensure power — though their greed led to multiple losses in these redistricted seats. (Groups like Black Voters Matter deserve a huge shout-out for fighting in the South and in races Democrats had abandoned.)

Despite all that, we managed a pro-democracy win that was too big to rig. The country delivered a shellacking to MAGA politics — an encouraging sign for all of us who are hoping for a better future. Ultimately, the election proceeded with voters refusing to be intimidated.

Buddhists remind me we can take a breath anytime. But this moment seems as good a moment as any, especially when we remind ourselves that exhaling isn’t signaling that things are over. Exhales are how our body gets in tune with this moment and releases the latest tension. Bracing doesn’t make us wiser, just tenser.

So really, take five breaths right now. As you breathe, read in a poem by Jarod Anderson:

You can be still while the world is whirling.

You can be silent while your heart is thundering.

You can be alone while your memory is teeming.

You can live forever in the span of a moment.

You can grow kindness in the soil of hatred.

You can decide purpose. You can decide victory.

As we breathe in — exhale and inhale — it’s worthwhile to remember the overwhelming number of people standing up to authoritarianism right now.

Media have focused on tariffs, affordability, and the Iran war as the defining issues of the midterms. But, as usual, they’ve skipped over the resistance that has taken root in this country. People lost their livelihoods exposing this regime’s corruption and risked their lives resisting ICE.

We got to this moment thanks to many unsung people.

Here we could begin listing thousands upon thousands of names. The list would include top election officials in all 50 states who refused to be cowed by the DOJ’s threats to arrest them for doing their jobs. (Some of them are quite hilarious, like Oregon’s Secretary of State Tobias Read, who mocked the DOJ hacks who misspelled his name: “My name is spelled R-E-A-D, as in ‘read the Constitution.’”) But those names extend deep through the electoral ecosystem, with many officials running extreme training scenarios steeling themselves against federal overreach, like Boulder’s County Clerk and Recorder Molly Fitzpatrick, and others coming up with creative solutions, like Georgia’s Irwin County Election Supervisor Ethan Compton who added “panic buttons” for poll workers to get immediate backup support.

Recognizing how election officials remain under attack, Protect Our Election set up a way to thank them online, and the National Conference on Citizenship created Election Hero Day as a “national celebration recognizing the tremendous contributions” of election officials.

But, of course, credit extends beyond officials. It goes to people like Keith Odom, a 62-year-old forklift driver, who joined over 5,000 at the “All Roads Lead to the South” rally in May, pushing back against the Supreme Court’s Callais decision undoing civil rights legislation. Credit is due to organizers like Chanae Jackson of Florida for All and Bill Hogseth of Grassroots Organizing Western Wisconsin, and Cassandra Welchlin of Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable, which collectively trained thousands of election defenders.

All that worked mattered greatly to avoid the worst scenarios.

When the FBI raided the Ohio Organizing Collaborative — a get-out-the-vote community group in Ohio working primarily with people of color — it could have broken. Instead its director, Prentiss Haney, struck a defiant public stance, naming the raid for what it was: “a political act to try and intimidate people from voting.” The Ohio Organizing Collaborative kept going — and was backed by allies across the nation under the banner of “Hands Off Ohio.”

Despite all the threats, voters voted. And that’s thanks to Tobias, Ethan, Molly, Keith, Chanae, Bill, Cassandra, Prentiss, and the tens of thousands who fought to keep the election fairer despite the authoritarian attempts to subvert them.

Civil resistance researcher Hardy Merriman developed a helpful framework for understanding the full election cycle in authoritarian times. It’s four steps: Fight, Win, Prove, Enforce. Fight for every legal voter to vote. Win pro-democracy electoral victories. Prove what actually happened and expose manipulation. And finally: Enforce the will of the voters — and stop any attempt to overturn it.

We don’t get to where we are right now without successfully moving through these early phases — Fight and Win. Take a moment to consider how you’ll appreciate those unheralded heroes — because you can be guaranteed the punditry class largely won’t do them justice.

The election was decisive, but it’s not over. The current phase of battle includes wrangling over ballot counts — and making sure those counts are understood as significant despite all the shenanigans.

Anyone in or near a closely contested race can help in this phase by volunteering to cure ballots — the process of helping fix ballots with minor imperfections like a missing signature. Rules vary widely, so contact a local election or campaign office or find efforts at We Are Ground Control.

As of Wednesday afternoon, Mississippi is still one of the hottest of these races, with Scott Colom on track to win narrowly if a clean election process unfolds, a challenge given the state’s messy, rickety election verification process. The Colom campaign feels confident that they will win.

Our job remains to be grounded in facts. Turn to trusted, verified reporting, like Votebeat or Brennan Center for Justice. Pause before sharing any election information and try to verify its authenticity. And we must remind ourselves that this win was not inevitable, it was despite — despite DOJ lawsuits, despite ICE threats, despite gerrymandering, despite consistent attacks on voters, and despite the many ways the federal government tried to keep voters from voting.

While Trump, Vance, and MAGA will make up lies, what happens next will depend in part on what their potential accomplices will do. Some groups like May Day Strong are wisely pressuring corporate targets now, knowing that corporate accomplices make disenfranchisement much easier. They’ve notched some important wins: For example, the entire city of Culver City, California, approved the Business for Democracy Pledge, pledging public business opposition to any post-election shenanigans.

Which reminds us that proving the results doesn’t just happen in courtrooms and elections — it happens in the streets, too.

A key lesson here comes from the 2000 presidential contest between George W. Bush and Al Gore. Folks who are old enough will remember that it came down to Florida, which was decided by a margin of a few hundred votes out of the 6 million that were cast. As the recount began, paid Republican operatives screamed and pounded on doors of the Miami-Dade counting office, intimidating staffers and causing a halt to the recount. A history-changing moment unfolded: Democratic operatives told activists to not go into the streets and protest — trust the courts, they said. The courts sided with Bush, cleared the way to never count the ballots, and the legal coup was cemented. (Three members of today’s Supreme Court were part of that Republican effort to halt the recount.)

The No Kings movement just proved the value of going to the streets. Its organizers experimented with gathering folks for Vote Early Day, to help surge turnout. Indications are this was very critical for the win. A TargetSmart analysis compared places with and without the No Kings Early Day mobilizations. The results were remarkable: a 19 percent increase in turnout for early voting occurred where the mobilizations were planned.

So coupling street heat with elections boosted energy and turnout.

The pattern affirms what we learned from Serbia and Brazil — in both countries, an unprecedented number of people voted and overcame huge challenges with a drumbeat of protests leading up to the elections. Serbia experienced a record 70 percent turnout and Brazil’s Lula won the largest number of votes in Brazilian history.

A recent detailed review concludes that anti-ICE and pro-immigrant actions have reached historic levels, even in Trump-won counties. It cites research linking bases of support activated by protests and how they translate into previous midterm outcomes. The authors ask the question: “Will historic protests against ICE shape the midterms?” It appears they did.

So while our election infrastructure appears to be holding, our readiness to take to the streets only strengthens our hand. Local Indivisible and 50501 chapters have plans to hold upbeat “count every vote” rallies (you can find ones in your area on Mobilize). This is wise because it creates a narrative counterweight — especially as MAGA is expected to fill the narrative field with garbage.

Famously, in 2024, Philadelphia responded to Trump’s outrageous threats against the people counting the vote by holding an upbeat dance party outside of the Philadelphia Convention Center — a visible demonstration of countering ugly fear and threats with joy and life.

Trump and Vance have developed a narrative about fraud that they could use to discredit selective election results. We know the DOJ is captured completely by Trump and subject to his whims.

We are not out of the authoritarian woods, and the big-tent attitude that got us here is still required, even as tensions are going to arise over strategy and direction.

We know Trump is too impulsive not to do something. Reading exactly what he’ll do and where is an exercise in reading tea leaves, but it appears more likely he’s following the path of victimhood, attacking Republicans for their lack of loyalty. Alongside telling the New York Times that he “look[s] forward to working with” Democrats, Trump has posted furiously on Truth Social. He has been attacking Greg Abbott for losing because he was a Republican In Name Only, or RINO, writing “FoxNews bears responsibility for these losses,” and asserting that the Republican Party as a whole would have won if he were on the ballot.

Alaska remains another state to watch, given MAGA’s claims that Alaska was stolen. For now the courts have rejected the DOJ’s Alaska gambit to force the state to refuse certification if the Republican candidate for Senate loses. And the drumbeat to stop Alaska’s certification has been dulled underneath the electoral avalanche that has descended on the Republican Party.

Losing appears to be increasing Republican in-fighting. That’s understandable, since Trump is clearly no longer the mighty savior he once appeared to them to be. They, too, need to adjust to the new reality of the end of Trump 2.0 and discover what life under lame-duck Trump is like.

Part of the Enforce phase also means getting the message of the elections right. The most dominant message needs to be that the country looked at fascism and fully rejected it. This door must remain closed — and now we turn our attention to debating how we solve people’s pocketbook issues such that we don’t have a return to fascist populism.

Here are three actions to stay prepared:

Each person in a state with yet-to-be-called races or candidates who have not conceded should find if there are local ways to help with ballot curing and tracking their own state’s certification dates. If you’re not in one of those states, get ready to act in solidarity with other states.

Circle January 3 as a key date to anchor our planning — that’s when Congress is seated and our “end date” of the election cycle.

Get your list of people that you would want to go into the streets with. There likely are local groups you can connect with.

So if you haven’t already: Write down the names of three or four people you would be willing to go into the streets with if something happens. Talk now about how you will contact one another, how you will make decisions, and what kinds of actions you are prepared to take. Agree on basic commitments: stay nonviolent, check information before acting on it, look after one another, and do not let a rumor become the plan.

To help demonstrators get plugged into a national response, No Kings has set up an election pledge for people to join a mass nonviolent action in rapid response to election disruption and subversion if needed. Mass calls are already prepped for nationwide updates and mobilizations: On Nov. 4 there is a No Kings Mass Call and on Nov. 5 there will be a Working Families Party Mass Call. If you’re looking for more guidance on forming election protection groups, Hold the Line and Strike Ready offer trainings and resources.

Activist Nadine Bloch has helpfully added a fifth phase to Hardy’s model: Since the elections are not an endpoint, we must Sustain — which is about sustaining the energy and movement for the long-haul pressure campaigns that come after. We still have a whole body of work in front of us.

One tempting mistake is to waste the bulk of our ammunition against each other. We are not out of the authoritarian woods, and the big-tent attitude that got us here is still required, even as tensions are going to fray over strategy and direction.

Still, some reckonings are overdue. In Florida, mainstream Democrats were shocked by Angie Nixon’s primary win and canceled their planned unity rally. Her loss in the general election stings, especially because her organizing juggernaut defied centrist expectations and lifted turnout and down-ballot wins across the state. Running progressives did not, as some folks worry, result in devastating losses — quite the opposite.

Still it’s unhelpful for anyone to get cocky and claim the American public has embraced their entire platform. This was less a blue wave and more a red repudiation.

This period of lame-duck Trump presidency remains precarious as progressives, centrists, populists, and anyone at all still have the chance to prove they have ideas that help people’s pocketbooks. Regular folks still want practical problem-solving but know the system needs more than tweaks to get there.

With Democrats locked out of the executive branch, some policies remain out of reach. We have to communicate that often — so people do not lose sight of the need for a 2028 win and get needlessly discouraged that this moment does not result in faster change.

That means constantly telling a compelling story about the structural problems we face so that the solutions become more evident, while also showing that government can work. Think of Mamdani’s constant videos about the big challenges we face, paired with solving everyday problems like fixing potholes. We got into this authoritarian mess because of much bigger issues than Trump: The social isolation. The drive of capitalism to pull wealth from the Earth and our own pockets. The way politics drives wedges between communities.

All these problems require big structural fixes and strengthening local civic relationships. There is work everywhere and, as Bloch reminds us, the election is not an end but a beginning.

It’s important that we be ready to advocate for new policies that get us out of the forever gerrymandering wars. Restoring the Voting Rights Act, for a start. Protect Democracy is pushing for proportional representation, both because it provides a pathway to meaningful alternative parties, which we desperately need, and because it also allows states to be more representative of their population. Plus, it can be implemented without a change in the Constitution.

We’ll need these kinds of bootstrapping solutions that move us closer to the democracy we have always deserved. Thankfully a range of groups are trying to help us fill this need: Issue One has been gathering policymakers to create legislation to steer money out of politics and reduce executive overreach — which did not start with the Trump administration. Go From Here is aiming to grow multiracial working-class power using new rights, legal rules, and governing strategies. Democracy Revival Center has been offering trainings called “How to Fix Our Broken System.” They offer a set of options on what we can do to get out of the authoritarian doom loop, echoing ideas like proportional representation, expanding the courts, and subjecting judges to actual ethical guidelines.

It took a lot to end this devastating chapter of Trump 2.0. Now let’s exhale, appreciate the unsung folks behind this historic win, and roll up our sleeves.

These are important structural fixes that need to be joined with policies that directly speak to the “affordability” crisis. This crisis, just newly discovered by the media, has been around for my entire lifetime — folks struggling to get by on wages that are too low amid health care costs that are too high. Pollsters tell us “Medicare for All” and other ways of saying guaranteed health care for everyone in the U.S. keep growing in popularity.

This Sustain work isn’t just big national policies. There is a lot that needs to be done in our local communities to reengage civil society and experiment with new versions of community to rebuild trust and repair. I’ve been inspired by many groups, like Michelle Alexander and Nyle Fort’s Spirit of Justice, which is experimenting with new religious formations, and Common Justice, which is modeling alternatives to incarceration in New York City that are victim-centered and result in a stronger community — not the diminished one offered by the carceral state.

All this to say, it took a lot to end this devastating chapter of Trump 2.0. Now let’s exhale, appreciate the unsung folks behind this historic win, and roll up our sleeves — there’s much work to be done in this next chapter.

This piece was co-published with Waging Nonviolence.

We are fundraising today to fund our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: “Donald … Call Me Senator”: Abdul El-Sayed Wins by 7 in Triumph Over GOP Bigotry
content:
“Donald, I know you struggled with my name. So after JD swears me in … call me senator,” El-Sayed said.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Abdul El-Sayed walloped his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, in Michigan on Tuesday, marking a massive triumph over the strategy of flat-out Islamophobic bigotry that Donald Trump, the GOP, and even many liberals embraced in the months of fierce campaigning against the progressive pro-Palestine senator-elect.

“They went all in on one of the ugliest campaigns we’ve seen in our lifetimes,” said El-Sayed in his victory speech early Wednesday morning. “They weren’t just attacking me. They were targeting and attacking you. They were targeting and attacking the very idea of America.”

With over 95 percent of votes counted, El-Sayed had 52.5 percent of the vote compared to Rogers’s 45.5 percent — matching the exact margin that El-Sayed predicted he would win back in May.

This is despite Trump and Republicans making him one of their primary targets this midterm cycle, with Trump spewing Islamophobic hate and incitement to violence against El-Sayed nearly every time he spoke at a rally or with the media. At a rally in Michigan in late October, Trump said El-Sayed is a “jihadist” and that the Senate should install a metal detector just to screen him.

He and others like Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) suggested that El-Sayed was violent with no evidence, pointing only to his faith. After winning the primary in August, Rogers’s first statement suggested that El-Sayed was a terrorist. “I spent years hunting terrorists and bringing Osama bin Laden to justice,” he said.

Liberal pundits and politicians, too, joined in on the bigoted pile-ons; El-Sayed’s AIPAC-backed primary opponent, Haley Stevens, used hateful tropes against him during the bitter primary race, and she ultimately issued a surprise endorsement of Rogers two days before the election.

El-Sayed often spoke out against the hate, hammering people like Trump and Vice President JD Vance. He also kept a laser-focus on his agenda: Medicare for All, banning corporate money in politics, and opposing further assistance to Israel.

On Wednesday night, El-Sayed said that his win was for “all the parents who struggled to explain why the president openly mocked” people like him.

“Mike, enjoy your retirement…. You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope. May we never have to see the likes of you in this state ever again,” he said.

“JD, habibi. There is this delicious irony that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January,” El-Sayed went on, to raucous cheers from the crowd. “Donald, I know you struggled with my name. So after JD swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me senator.”

El-Sayed also spoke out against the pro-Israel lobby, with AIPAC pouring a record amount into the election to defeat him. He espoused the “love” that he has for the Palestinian people, drawing a sharp contrast to the hatred levied against him.

“To AIPAC who spent $42 million against us: Thank you for giving me the opportunity to beat you twice,” he said. “They try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers, to not be murdered by our tax dollars. If you believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination, that’s not hate, it’s love.”

The corporate media waged an all-out attack on El-Sayed, in part due to his stances on Israel. Outlets like The New York Times ran stories about him losing Jewish voters and accusing him of antisemitism, without evidence. Corporate outlets also spread a narrative that he had “struggled to win over Black voters” in the state, as Politico wrote on Sunday, or that many Democrats were peeling off from him to vote for Rogers.

But Tuesday’s result shows that these narratives were overblown. Exit polls suggested that Jewish people overwhelmingly went for El-Sayed, and data from VoteHub finds that El-Sayed won majority-Black districts by a whopping 81-point margin. The “Democrats for Mike Rogers” PAC, which poured millions into the race, was revealed by Truthout in October to be a Republican front group.

DEARBORN, WE MADE HISTORY!!! 🇺🇸 Over 45,000 votes cast. The highest voter turnout in our city’s history! You showed up, shattered records, and made your voices heard. Thank you, Dearborn!

Progressives in the movement for Palestinian rights also notched several wins across Michigan on Tuesday. Progressive activist William Lawrence, a cofounder of the Sunrise Movement, won his race for U.S. House 51 to 48, unseating the Republican incumbent.

Lawrence won in the face of massive spending by the GOP. According to a progressive booster, AdImpact data shows that Republicans spent $23 million against Lawrence, marking the biggest spend against a Democratic House candidate this cycle.

Democratic Socialist Donavan McKinney, who has called for an arms embargo to Israel, won his race to represent Detroit in the U.S. House by a landslide.

Attorney Amir Makled, who represented pro-Palestine student protesters in their case against University of Michigan, won his election to the university’s Board of Regents in a blowout.

And Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Michigan), the only Palestinian American in Congress, easily won her reelection, 76 to 21 — a 55-point margin.

author: labor4pal
title: A fightback is building as crackdown deepens against civil liberties (Workers’ Voice)
content:
Dozens of activists are accused by the federal government of contributing to bogus “criminal conspiracies.” In Minnesota, two separate conspiracy cases accuse 54 people of participating in illegal conspiracies for participating in protest and journalistic activities. The Minnesota 15, Righteous 39, Michigan 8 (now 12), Spokane 3, and Prairieland Defendants are the most well known cases in the ongoing crackdown. All of these cases are attacks on organized labor.

The California Faculty Association and the Graduate Employee Organization at University of Michigan (GEO-AFT 3550) are facing frontal attacks on their unions by the right-wing press and FBI. Doctored video of a CFA meeting was leaked to Trump booster Bari Weiss’s Free Press in an attempt to scandalize the union with false accusations of antisemitism. The Department of Justice first charged GEO President Hiab Teshome with felonious financial crimes. Those bogus charges were dropped the same day that a grand jury subpoenaed GEO’s books, including all member lists, meeting minutes, and financial records. The union is fighting to retain basic privacy rights.

Fueled by National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, U.S. intelligence and police apparatuses are being explicitly targeted at anyone standing for basic democratic rights, immigrant communities, and racial justice. As the world drifts closer to major inter-imperialist conflict and expanding zones of overt imperialist military occupation takes hold in the semi-colonies, Western imperialisms are tightening restrictions on protest, speech, and organizing for progressive movements.

While there are many additional cases of “lawfare” and anti-protest policing, it is worth taking a moment to review two of the cases mentioned above to understand the tactics and scope of the current crackdown.

Around two dozen protesters held a noise demonstration on July 4, 2025, outside of the Prairieland Detention Center in Texas. As the protest was winding down and many of the participants had left, Alvarado Police Officer Thomas Gross sped onto the scene and almost immediately aimed his gun at a demonstrator moving away from him. Video evidence indicates that Gross discharged his weapon, something that would appear to have been covered up by the judge and prosecutors.

In response to seeing a potentially lethal attack on a protester, Marine Corps veteran Benjamin “Champagne” Song let out a warning shot into the ground away from the officers. Gross went to the hospital for superficial wounds that the government alleges resulted from being shot by Song, but video evidence released after sentencing indicates Gross was likely hit by shrapnel produced from his own weapon’s discharge.

Using the presence of guns and defensive action of Song as pretext, 22 people were ultimately indicted as part of an alleged conspiracy to attack cops and carry out an armed prison break. One person, Daniel “Des” Rolando Sanchez Estrada, was not at the protest at all. Des was convicted for “corruptly concealing a document or record” and sentenced to 30 years for possessing legally protected political materials.

After arrests, pressure and legal sabotage was mounted by the judicial system against the defendants. Many were initially held in solitary confinement, with one reporting that human feces coated their cell. U.S. District Judge Mark Pittman blocked the defendants from retaining a private attorney, meaning they had to use public defenders. Song’s legal team was not allowed to make an argument that the warning shot was taken in self-defense. Eight defendants became cooperating witnesses, providing coerced testimony to validate the government’s made-up conspiracy theories.

Before the trial even began, the deck was stacked against non-cooperating defendants. In an explicit “warning” to the left, Judge Pittman laid down ridiculously high sentences of between 30-100 years to non-cooperating defendants.

From the war on drugs to the war on speech: Minnesota 15

The Minnesota 15 are 15 activists accused of a “conspiracy to impede or attack federal agents.” The majority are current or recent union members and all are community activists. They are not accused of participating in or coordinating any acts of violence. Instead, the original 92-page indictment against them lists “evidence” including participating in rapid response group chats, protests, and mutual aid activities. Any successful convictions on the basis of these charges would be a tremendous blow to freedom of speech and association.

The white supremacist structure of U.S. law and society lays the foundations that are shaping today’s repression. Discovery materials released in connection with the Minnesota 15 case show that a longstanding multi-state ICE undercover program “Operation Keyhole” was effortlessly transformed into a political policing operation. According to court documents, Operation Keyhole has carried out at least 77 investigations into “narcotics trafficking, child sexual abuse, financial investigations, and counter-proliferation” since it began in 2008.

Conspiracy cases, informant networks, and mass surveillance all have deep roots in the “war on drugs.” As large pharmaceutical companies profit off addiction and U.S. police and military operators protect “illicit” drug trafficking at every level, locking up street dealers and mostly Black and Latino users are the major justifications for expanding the surveillance state. Alongside fear-mongering about “Islamist terrorism,” the steady growth of policing technology and methods based on military occupation is made through criminalizing working class people of color.

These methods include the exact “guilt-by-association” dragnet investigations now mobilized against the political left, particularly in the Minnesota 15 and Prairieland “conspiracies.” Journalist Ali Winston shows that Reaper drones, private data brokers, and financial audits are all being used to “investigate” any type of potential organization, including trade unions. Documents connected with the MN15 case show that even SEIU regions have been targeted for federal investigations.

Democratic rights are never guaranteed for the working class. Our ability to speak and organize are constantly under threat. The Trump administration is in continuity with all other U.S. administrations in functioning first and foremost to ensure capitalist class rule. Police state methods are always used against workers and oppressed people whenever the big owners think they can get away with it.

Capitalism utilizes both coercion and consent to continue exploitation and oppression. In normal times in an imperialist democratic republic, the police and military are focused on combating “crime” and claim to be apolitical. Obviously this posture is a fraud, but it serves the role of allowing people to maintain illusions in some “impartial” system.

Trump’s NSPM-7 and the overtly partisan transformation of virtually the entire federal government’s media operations breaks this illusion for many who would otherwise be or have been passive in the face of extreme police terror in Black and Brown communities. The government’s efforts to link all types of political beliefs as broad targets for repression shows that everyone in the U.S. interested in the basic principles of free speech and free thought needs to be marching alongside each other.

Minnesota 15 defendants are bravely showing the way toward a real mass defense of democratic rights. In the face of major conspiracy charges, under constant surveillance by the state, all 15 are committed to speaking out publicly and have been doing just that around the country. Alongside screenings of the documentary “When ICE Melts,” defendants are speaking to faith groups, unions, community organizations, and assemblies of all kinds explaining not only their case, but also the tremendous organizing that pushed ICE out of the Twin Cities. In Connecticut, the persistence of activists raising MN15 everywhere led to Senator Richard Blumenthal publicly calling the charges against the MN15 “bogus” and demanding they be immediately dropped.

These efforts need to be deepened and expanded all over the country and internationally. Every activist organizing for solidarity with victims of repression needs to think about how we can bring this case to the biggest audience possible. And how can the desire for solidarity be turned into mobilizations on the shop floor and in the streets?

title: Eskişehir Tepebaşı Belediyesi davası: 5 kişi tahliye edildi
content:
Tepebaşı Belediye Başkanı Ahmet Ataç | Fotoğraf: DHA

Eskişehir Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı’nca yürütülen soruşturması kapsamında geçen mayıs ayında Tepebaşı Belediyesi’ne operasyon düzenlendi. Gözaltına alınan 22 kişi işlemlerinin ardından adliyeye sevk edilirken, 7’si kamu görevlisi 12 kişi tutuklandı. 10 kişi ise adli kontrol kararıyla serbest bırakıldı.

Eskişehir Cumhuriyet Savcılığı’nda hazırlanan iddianameyle 4’ncü Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi’ne dava açılırken, 15 kamu görevlisi hakkında zimmet suçundan 5 yıldan 12 yıla kadar, diğer 7 kişi hakkında ise ‘suça iştirak veya yardım’ iddiasıyla 2 yıl 6 aydan 6 yıla kadar hapis cezası talep edildi.

İddianamede Tepebaşı Belediyesi’nde aralarında özel kalem müdürü ve başkan yardımcısının da bulunduğu kamu görevlilerinin, organizasyon firma sahipleri D.A.'nın ve T.G.'nin üzerinden belediye bütçesinden yapılan ödemeleri zimmetlerine geçirdikleri öne sürüldü.

Eskişehir 4’ncü Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi’ndeki davanın yaklaşık 11 saat süren ilk duruşmasına mahkeme heyeti tutuklu olan Süleyman U., Celal T., Fatma Begüm A., Ceren Aytaç A. ve Filiz T.’nin tahliyesine karar verirken, tutuksuz yargılanan Murat Ç.’nin ise tutuklanmasına hükmetti.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: La Zarzamora
title: La Chilean Horror Story, nuevas temporadas
content:
El mal sigue aquí. 56 engendros, extorsionadores de mujeres, violadores, pedófilos y torturadores de la DINA-CNI, responsables de marcar a sus víctimas con cuchillos de combate, amarrarlos a rieles y tirarlos vivos al mar, de violar y abusar sexualmente, fueron liberados por la Kasta gobernante y están listos para reincidir.

En este thriller maldito, la Kasta está siendo coherente con sus siniestras convicciones y su maligna esencia blancona. Es la Chilean Horror Story, en la que calzan perfecto: dictadura, “Colonia Dignidad”, Paul Schäfer, Spiniak, “los coroneles” de la derecha, los decretos de libertad a criminales, y el alienado proyecto de ley de la escalofriante Vanessa Kaiser contra las víctimas.

Son crímenes inmortales de la continuación del horror político de “los nuevos padres fundadores” de los años 70 y 80, coordinados por el funesto subsecretario general de Pinochet, Jovino Novoa, el psicópata serial Paul Shäfer y los demonios de la DINA-CNI, que usaban como cuartel general de violaciones y otras torturas, la pedófila “Colonia Dignidad”.

No es casual que 20 años más tarde, en 2002, se inaugurara el siglo XXI con el sacrificio de niños y niñas de clases pobres, una nueva temporada de horror pedófilo por el mismo protagonista de la anterior, Jovino Novoa, esta vez acompañado por los libertinos vejadores Carlos Bombal de la Unión Demócrata Independiente y Nelson Ávila del Partido Radical; y dirigidos por el escatófilo Spiniak (pedófilo invitado).

El sacrificio fue quitada de cartelera informándose que Novoa, Bombal y Avila habrían sido “falsamente” acusados. Sin embargo, fue una generación que también en los años 90 albergó demonios torturadores y pedófilos organizados en el estado, especialmente los perturbados “Amigos de la Colonia Dignidad”. Algunos ya están muertos vivos como el asesinado, pero no menos maligno, ideólogo de la dictadura Jaime Guzmán; también, los “malditos Sergios”: dos ministros del interior de Pinochet, Sergio Onofre Jarpa y Sergio Fernández, y el grotesco delegado en la ONU, Sergio Diez. Y siguen vivos muchos “vampiros amigos” del Paul Schäfer” que traspasan siglos: Hernán Larraín Fernández, ministro de justicia y “derechos humanos” del piñerismo2 junto al conspirador Andrés Chadwick Piñera, ministro del interior de la misma masacre, el piñerismo2, ambos responsables de mutilaciones y violaciones a manifestantes del estallido.

Chadwick además, integra los “coroneles”, pilares del poder de los fundadores de la derecha, junto a Juan Antonio Coloma, quien fuese base “juvenil” de la dictadura, y también junto a Pablo Longueira, el mismo que habla con espectros. No hay que olvidar a las estrellas femeninas como la implacable -ya desaparecida- Mónica Madariaga, ministra de justicia y de educación de la dictadura, que dio el visto bueno a la constitución de Pinochet junto a Guzmán, ni debemos dejar fuera a la ambiciosa -y muy viva- Evelyn Matthei, reciente ex candidata presidencial, candidateándose otra vez, y defensora -solapada- de la criminal junta de gobierno, del golpe de estado y de la dictadura en que participó su padre. Todas y todos son villanos políticos, fríos y calculadores, además de grandes amigos de la pedófila “Colonia Dignidad” de Schäfer.

Nueva temporada: “La liberación”

La línea de la historia chilena del horror que continúan los padres fundadores-Generación Z, es innegable. En este inolvidable octubre 2026 de la Kasta, Fernando Rabat Celis, ministro de Justicia, Luis Silva Irarrazaval, vicepresidente del partido republicano y ahora ex subsecretario de Justicia, y Pablo Mira Hurtado, subsecretario subrogante, firmaron los decretos de liberación de sus engendros y mintieron diciendo que estaban “obligados” por una doctrina inexistente de la Corte Suprema, misma institución judicial que, apurada, mediante un fallo, los desmintió.

Ninguno de los criminales liberados por ellos había presentado individualmente un recurso de amparo porque los pedófilos están informados de sus derechos. La opción de salir en libertad se terminó en 2022 cuando Piñera2, el mismo que gobernó con los “amigos de la Colonia” pedófila, los excluyó, justo a ellos, pero no a los violadores en general, en su Ley N°21.421.

Antes del piñerismo2, habiendo tantas “comisiones de género”en los partidos de la Concertación,los pedófilos no habían sido excluidos de las rebajas de condenas, y los violadores de mujeres, menos. La ley anterior de rebajas de condenas, la N°19.856 de 2003, fue enviada por Lagos en 2001. Aunque sí establecía reducción de condenas, la verdad es que al emperador concertacionista no le importaban las víctimas de los violadores ni los presos (menos las presas). Lo relevante para su gobierno y coalición, era decir que con esto el estado chileno se quitaba de encima el problemón de la sobrepoblación carcelaria y, por lo tanto, el “laguismo” tampoco excluyó a los pedófilos.

En 2024, Monsalve mediante, el progresismo feminista de Boric hizo el decreto N°36 (2024) que actualizó y modificó el reglamento de la Ley de Lagos, y su ministra reemplazante Aisén Amelia Etcheverry Escudero -parisina y chilena- abogada, miembra del Frente Amplio y también ministra de Ciencia y Tecnología, firmó el decreto cuando la vocera oficial Camila Vallejos Dowling, estaba en su postnatal. Pero a ningún progresista, ni Boric, ni Camila, ni Aisén, ni ninguno de sus famosos asesores del segundo piso, pensó -antes o después- en adicionarle a su decreto, la negación de libertad a los violadores de mujeres en general, y de otras personas adultas como homosexuales, trans, hombres; muchos que suelen ser violados cuando están privados de libertad por machos perversos con mayor poder, por sádicos en los cuarteles, y tantas veces por cualquiera de los poderosos de raleas que adoran el equilibrio sagrado del racismo y la misoginia. La cuestión es que a los progres gobernantes, no les alcanzó el feminismo para oponerse al mal patriarcal.

En Chile, no se prohíbe la rebaja de condenas a los agresores sexuales en general, solamente se les restringe la solicitud de libertad condicional a un “informe psicosocial favorable”, y se les podría conceder la salida incondicional luego de cumplir dos tercios de una pena que puede ser de 5 años y un día a un máximo de 15 años.

Aunque se disculpen, den de baja subsecretarios, el daño está hecho. Se lo traían entre manos, y la prueba está en que la Liberación de engendros podría ser ampliamente complementada por el proyecto de ley encabezado por la cínica totalitaria Vanessa Kaiser, senadora del Partido Nacional Libertario, quien, en su defensa reiterada de torturadores y otros agresores, proyecta encarcelar a las mujeres, por denunciar.

Esta guardiana del patriarcado que aspira, seriamente, a un “ministerio del Hombre”, lleva adelante un proyecto de ley sobre “denuncias falsas” que encarcelará a las víctimas que no puedan probar violación y otras agresiones. Abarca contextos de familia, alimentos, violencia intrafamiliar y así mismo, delitos sexuales (Boletín N°18.239-36), es decir, protege a los violadores.

Ficha técnica: la Kaiser y otras desalmadas de Renovación Nacional como Andrea Balladares y María José Gatica, junto a los brutales Enrique Van Rysselberghe de la Unión Demócrata Independiente, Manuel José Ossandon y José Manuel Rojo Edwars Silva, de Renovación Nacional. Son un equipo de culto que fortalece el privilegio de “la presunción de inocencia” que los violadores ya tienen. Y en su empeño de perseguir a las mujeres, estos alienados personajes hacen alusión a la pseudocientífica teoría “SAP”, síndrome de alienación parental, con que los Milei y otros malvados, alimentan su “batalla cultural» para conservar el abuso de poder sobre las mujeres. Si su ley pasa, denunciar a los agresores será imposible, porque como sabemos la violencia machista opera hipócrita y solapada en el secreto familiar, comunitario y sistemáticamente misógino. Se viene una temporada recargada en la Chilean Horror Story antimujeres

author: William D. Hartung
title: The Democrats have a mandate for peace — here are 4 urgent priorities
content:
This article 

The Democrats have a mandate for peace — here are 4 urgent priorities

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







Voters in the midterm elections dealt a decisive blow to Trump’s war agenda and have created new possibilities for challenging militarism and ending the debacle in Iran. The blue tsunami that swept across the country was driven by 

many issues

, including tariffs, corruption and higher prices, but voter discontent was rooted in opposition to the war against Iran and the high fuel costs and inflation that resulted. 




The election outcome presents an opportunity for activists to intensify pressures to end the war, reverse excessive arms spending, restore necessary funding for vital social and environmental priorities, and protect democracy. We need to elect a government that will build the foundations for a forward-looking, progressive foreign policy by expanding essential diplomatic capabilities and restoring U.S. support for global cooperation.




The current electoral realignment can be compared to the dramatic political transformation that occurred in the 2006 midterm elections. That year, the Iraq war was the 

decisive issue

 in helping Democrats pick up 31 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives and six in the Senate. Then as now, affordability and immigration were important issues, but the dominant concern was war in the Middle East. As analysts argued at the time, Iraq was the “

Archimedean lever

” that shifted voters toward Democrats. 




But when the new Congress assembled in 2007, Democratic Party leaders equivocated. Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid proposed a legislative agenda for the new Congress that ignored Iraq. 




Embed from Getty Images




As Tom Hayden wrote in  “Ending the War in Iraq”, antiwar activists were furious. Constituents bombarded Democratic leaders with demands to prioritize withdrawal from Iraq. Protesters gathered outside Pelosi’s San Francisco home. An estimated 100,000 people marched in an antiwar rally in Washington, D.C. 




Democratic leaders quickly got the message and agreed on a legislative strategy to establish a timetable for withdrawal, which Congress subsequently adopted. 




We may need to exert similar pressures now to ensure that the new Congress fulfills its political mandate to end the Iran war and takes action to reverse other elements of Trump’s dangerous foreign policies. 




The threats to peace have grown significantly in recent years, and they are enormous and multifaceted. An unending, illegal war in Iran and related carnage throughout the Middle East; the arming of repressive regimes, up to and including enabling genocide in Gaza and occupation and ethnic cleansing in Lebanon; the skyrocketing of military-related spending (proposed at more than 

$1.5 trillion

 this year) and an accelerating nuclear arms race. All of this is occurring while the Pentagon is 

moving

 rapidly towards the deployment of AI-driven weapons systems that can operate without human pilots or human control.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










The threat or use of force has taken precedence over diplomacy, economic development and peacebuilding programs. The White House has rebuked democratic allies in Canada and Europe while coddling authoritarian regimes in Russia and Saudi Arabia. 




The human, economic and environmental consequences of these militarist policies have been disastrous — 

trillions

 of dollars wasted, 

hundreds of thousands

 of lives lost and 

tens of millions

 of people driven from their homes.      




The pursuit of peace abroad depends on the defense of democracy at home. Legislators must protect democracy by removing obstacles to the exercise of basic rights, including the right to vote, the right of assembly, freedom of speech and an end to discrimination based on race, gender, religion and sexual preference. We need to create an America where every person is cherished, and every person is treated with the dignity they deserve — and then we need to extend that ethos to the rest of the world.




For cooperation, not confrontation




On the foreign policy front, we must demand congressional and executive action on the following major goals:




1. End the Iran war

: Prohibit the use of funds for military hostilities over, in, or off the shores of Iran. Work through the United Nations to reach a comprehensive diplomatic agreement to open the Strait of Hormuz and contain Iran’s nuclear program. Close vulnerable American military bases in the region.  




2. Halt and reverse the arms race

: Enact major reductions in the bloated Pentagon budget, roll back spending on nuclear weapons systems and rein in the rush towards automated warfare based on artificial intelligence. Block funding for renewed nuclear testing and the production and deployment of additional nuclear warheads.




3. Stop arming genocide and repression

: Cut military aid and arms transfers to Israel that violate U.S. human rights law and enable genocidal policies in Gaza, and accelerate dispossession and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and aggression in Lebanon. Stop providing arms and aid to repressive and undemocratic regimes in the region. Terminate the Saudi nuclear deal.




4. Roll back the war at home

: End militarized immigration enforcement, the unlawful detention of immigrants and ICE repression — including murder — of peaceful protesters. ICE should be eliminated as part of a thorough revamping of immigration policy.




Together these points form a peace agenda that lays the foundations for a progressive foreign policy that rebuilds critical diplomatic capacities and U.S. support for multilateralism.




Congress already started to take action on some of these priorities, even under Republican majorities. And the Democrats in Congress have started to take stronger stands against endless war and excess military spending in a way that has not happened in decades. In June of this year, the Senate joined the House of Representatives in 

adopting House Concurrent Resolution 86 

under the War Powers Act, directing the President to end military hostilities in Iran, although the White House ignored the order. 




In July Senate Democrats 

refused to authorize

 the bloated $1.15 trillion request for funding of routine Pentagon operations over concerns about the Iran war. Congress needs to follow through in the lame duck session to oppose any increases in the Pentagon’s topline budget. 
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













Also in July, almost half of the Democratic members of the House voted to eliminate U.S. aid for Israel as part of 

groundswell of opposition

 to Israeli policy in Gaza. Congress must follow through with actions to end U.S. complicity with war crimes. Prospects for success on these and related legislative measures in the new Congress will increase with the arrival of dozens of new representatives and senators elected on a mandate against endless war. But success is not assured.




A new Congress as a new beginning




While the realignment of Congress in the midterm election is a victory for sanity and peace, it is only the beginning of the struggle that lies ahead. To become law, the peace agenda needs the backing of a strong, growing movement of coordinated national and grassroots public action. This will require dialogue and relationship-building across the various movements fighting for justice and peace, a process that is already underway in many places.  




We must demand that the leaders of the new Congress prioritize the proposed peace agenda, as part of a pivot toward developing and reinvesting in an alternative foreign policy for peace. If the newly elected members waffle or refuse, we should protest in Washington, D.C. and assemble at their local offices to demand that they act. 




We will need to undertake coordinated and systematic efforts to brief new members of Congress on the key issues and the legislative options for ending the war in Iran, reversing America’s militarized priorities and preventing oppression and violence in the Middle East. 




Plans are needed in the coming weeks and months to convene community meetings and teach-ins on the proposed peace policy agenda — both at the national level and in dozens of key states and districts. It is essential that members of Congress hear the demand for change not only from lobbyists in Washington, D.C.  but from voters in their home districts.




Embed from Getty Images




We need to be clear that creating a new foreign policy means more than an end to Trumpian policies, as unconscionable as they are and have been. America’s penchant for war without public or congressional consent has persisted under presidents of both parties, as has unstinting support for Israel’s brutal conduct in Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon and Iran, as well as the repression and political machinations of oil rich states like Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. 




To craft a new foreign policy, we need more than the absence of Trump.  We need the presence of an alert, mobilized citizenry committed to radically changing America’s approach to the world. Our mission is to turn our country toward diplomacy and international cooperation rather than war, and to hold officeholders of both parties to that standard.




We need a foreign policy of, by, and for the people — all of us, not just a narrow, self-interested, corrupt elite. Foreign policy should serve the aspirations of everyone for peace, sustenance and basic human rights, regardless of race, religion, place of origin, gender or sexuality. Not just changing America but also joining hands with movements and peoples around the world in struggles for peace and democracy against war and repression.




This article 

The Democrats have a mandate for peace — here are 4 urgent priorities

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.

author: Sasha Abramsky
title: The Egg on Elon Musk’s Face Cost More Than $440 Million
content:
Musk’s astronomical campaign contributions were no match for outraged voters across the US.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Elon Musk, the world’s wealthiest man, went on a spending spree in the weeks leading up to the midterms. By Election Day, he had invested — and I use that word deliberately — more than $440 million into propping up the GOP to try to make its message and its candidates more palatable with voters during an election cycle in which their brand had become increasingly toxic.

Astoundingly, nearly half of that money — more than $190 million — was spent on one campaign: Ken Paxton’s effort to make the leap from an impeached state attorney general to being U.S. senator for Texas. Musk was, in broad daylight, like the gilded age oligarchs of the late-19th century, essentially trying to buy himself a senator.

Many rich candidates have in recent years self-funded their candidacies or intervened in initiative campaigns — Michael Bloomberg put in more than $1 billion into his go-nowhere presidential campaign in 2020, Tom Steyer spent upwards of $200 million in his recent futile attempt to become the California governor, and a cluster of billionaires, led by Google’s Sergei Brin, put obscene amounts of money into opposing the billionaires’ wealth tax initiative before voters in California this election. This year, the Texas race seems to be the first time a single non-candidate donor has put this much money into a particular marquee contest.

Musk — who relocated to Texas during the pandemic in a fit of pique against California’s public health mandates — has a large and growing business footprint in Texas, and a desire to take over more land both for his space launch business and his data centers; he therefore needs political figures from the state not only on his side but in his pocket, as Democrats began gleefully pointing out in the final month of the campaign.

The SpaceX titan isn’t, of course, alone in his mega-donations. The Brennan Center for Justice has reported that in the 2026 election cycle, 40 mega-donors altogether ponied up an astounding $2.5 billion, the large majority for GOP candidates. But the scale of Elon Musk’s financial outlay does put him in a league of his own. Individually, in 2026 Musk gave more than twice as much to candidates as did the entire cryptocurrency industry — which has also not been shy about buying political loyalties as its footprint has increased in size.

Most of Musk’s money was channeled through the Senate Leadership Fund, the coordinating fund the GOP ran for its Senate candidates. This move allowed Paxton, whose entire career has been a pinball exercise caroming from one corruption scandal to the next, to flood the vast Texas media market with attack advertisements in the weeks leading up to the election. The Republican candidate’s campaign promptly used this money to lean ever further into anti-trans messaging, saturating the airwaves with ads accusing Democratic candidate James Talarico of being an extremist for transgender rights.

Then, as the governor’s race in Texas tightened, with Democrat Gina Hinojosa making an unexpectedly strong run to break the GOP stranglehold on the state’s top office, Musk also began injecting millions of dollars into Greg Abbott’s re-election campaign.

But Musk’s ambitions weren’t limited to the Lone Star State. In this election cycle, the oligarch gave tens of millions of dollars to super PACs supporting vulnerable GOP candidates in House races around the country and funneled millions more to gubernatorial and attorneys general campaigns, recognizing that a Democratic victory would likely harm his corporate ventures and reduce the flow of money from government contracts.

In New Hampshire, Musk’s super PAC, America PAC, pumped $1 million into supporting Republican candidate John Sununu for a Senate seat that the GOP identified early in the campaign season as a possible pick-up. In New York, the trillionaire’s PAC put hundreds of thousands of dollars into efforts to salvage GOP Congressman Mike Lawler’s campaign in the competitive 17th congressional district. Singlehandedly, Musk seemed intent on showing, throughout election season, just how much financial sway the oligarchy can have on U.S. politics. And, as he injected more money into the elections, at the same time he warned his opponents — who have been talking about investigations into his business practices and his work at the “Department of Government Efficiency” — that he was preparing to go to war against them. The tycoon also allocated over $100 million for a get-out-the-vote ground operation.

Like Bloomberg and Steyer’s ill-fated campaigns, however, as the election season entered its final weeks, polling suggested Musk’s interventions could actually backfire. In an era of anti-oligarchical, anti-Big Tech fury, Musk has become something of a poster child for all that is wrong in the U.S. economic and political systems. His money is seen as tainted, and his interventions are perceived as little more than an effort to bribe the electorate.

In Texas, Talarico and Hinojosa knew they couldn’t compete dollar for dollar with Musk, but they also knew that voters were souring on his brand. At one campaign rally after the next, they hammered home the point that Musk was trying to buy Texans’ loyalty. Talarico also took to X to denounce Musk’s intervention and repeatedly accused the tycoon of “trying to buy Texas.” It was a skillful move that could only work — as it so clearly did — in a populist moment defined by rage against economic elites. In all the other major races into which Musk poured money — New Hampshire, New York’s 17th congressional district, and others — the Democrats won as well. All told, more than 98 percent of Musk’s dollars led to zero political gain.

Instead of Musk buying a Senate seat in Texas, he helped trigger an absolute political earthquake. Texas electing both a Democratic senator and a Democratic governor — on the back of huge Black and Latinx voter turnout, and making huge inroads into the state legislature — is as significant as California turning blue in the wake of the anti-immigrant campaigns and legislation of Republicans in the 1990s. It may ricochet through the country’s body politic for decades. And, for that, at least in part, Democrats have Musk to thank. His shameless attempt to buy a Senate seat is probably the most self-defeating expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars in U.S. political history.

Musk warned that he would go to war against his opponents if he lost. Now, he has no choice — for Democrats have just been given an overwhelming mandate, and answering it will require them to drive oligarchs out of the political arena.

author: David Swanson
title: Taxpayers Mobilize in Washington, D.C., to Protest $1.5 Trillion Military Budget
content:
Economic Cost, Immorality, Nonviolent Activism, North America, What to do

By CODEPINK and a large coalition of advocacy groups, November 4, 2026

Taxpayers from across the U.S. will gather in Washington, D.C., from November 10 to 12, 2026, to protest the proposed $1.5 trillion 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). Organized by CODEPINK and a large coalition of advocacy groups, the demonstration aims to put the country’s excessive and harmful military spending at the forefront of the national conversation after the midterms.

“The midterm elections were a nationwide condemnation of Trump and Hegseth’s horrible war in Iran. The Taxpayer Uprising is about creatively and beautifully making sure this current Congress doesn’t forget about it – because passing Trump’s war budget would mean green-lighting his reckless wars for the remainder of his presidency,” explained CODEPINK’s national co-director Danaka Katovich.

The three-day event will feature office visits with elected officials and visual demonstrations. Tentative schedule as follows:

Tuesday, November 10: Senate Office Visits from 10 am- 4 pm: The group will kick off the first day of action at the Dirksen Cafeteria at 10 am. They will break off into specific advocacy groups and visit senators’ offices.

Wednesday, November 11: Victims of the War Budget Processional, 10–2 pm, starting at Peace Monument.

Thursday, November 12: House of Representatives office visits, 10 am-4 pm. The group will meet at the Rayburn Cafeteria at 10 am, then break into groups to visit their representatives’ offices. There will also be an Ice Cream Social with Ben & Jerry’s own Ben Cohen at 2pm at the Intersection of First Street SE and Independence Avenue SE.

Constituents from various states, including California and Texas, will join organizations like CODEPINK, World BEYOND War, RootsAction, National Priorities Project at the Institute for Policy Studies, Doctors Against Genocide, Climate Defenders, CAIR National, Eisenhower Media Network, National Iranian American Council, Fellowship of Reconciliation, American Muslims for Palestine, Veterans For Peace, DSA International Committee, and more in demanding a reallocation of funds towards domestic needs.

“We’ve tried voting our way to represent our overwhelming public preference for less war funding and more funding of human and environmental needs. Now let’s add the powerful tool of nonviolent activism. Now let’s make it harder to defy the people of this country than it is to defy the war profiteers.” – David Swanson, Co-Founder and Executive Director, World BEYOND War.

“Americans are increasingly recognizing the connection between funding the genocide in Gaza, the ongoing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, Israel’s escalating aggression across the region, and the illegal war on Iran, and their own struggles to make ends meet and achieve economic mobility. Our lawmakers appear more concerned with appeasing the Israel lobby and war profiteers than listening to the majority of Americans, who do not want endless, unjustified wars and instead support greater investment in social welfare, education, healthcare, and workers’ rights. The Taxpayer Uprising is our way of continuing to build the political power necessary to secure a future that prioritizes people over war and invests in the well-being of our communities.” AMP executive director, Dr. Osama Abu Irshaid

The Trump Administration’s proposal marks the largest increase in military spending in modern history, prioritizing the war budget over human needs like healthcare, education, and housing. The proposed budget allocates about $116.43 million per hour to US warfare, ranging from illegal boat bombings in the Americas to the disastrous war in Iran. Half of that will go directly to contractors in the arms and AI industries. Meanwhile, nearly 45,000 Americans die annually due to lack of health insurance. Shifting even a small share of military spending to healthcare and social programs would save countless lives in the US and worldwide.
