author: Sharon Zhang
title: Pentagon Sued Over Hegseth’s New “Future of Warfare” Committee Led by Musk
content:
The lawsuit comes as Democrats are eyeing impeachment for Hegseth if they win Congress.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth broke the law in establishing an advisory committee, co-led by Elon Musk, to guide the “future of warfare,” a new lawsuit says, citing “major conflict of interest concerns.”

The lawsuit, filed by watchdogs Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), Public Citizen, and Project on Government Oversight (POGO), says that the Pentagon did not go through the proper requirements under the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA) in the creation of “Project Meridian: The Future of Warfare.” This means that the committee is not subject to public disclosures or scrutiny as it should be, the suit says, and is operating illegally, having had two meetings already.

The lawsuit also alleges that Department of Defense leaders failed to ensure there is a proper balance of expertise and viewpoints on the committee, which is being led by Musk, Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey and former GOP Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich. This has led to “enormous” conflict of interest concerns regarding the group’s makeup, CREW’s president noted.

Pentagon officials “have failed to comply with FACA’s procedural and substantive requirements for new federal advisory committees, including FACA transparency requirements that disallow Project Meridian’s closed-door operations,” the lawsuit says. “Compounding the problem, Project Meridian’s private-sector membership raises precisely the type of conflict-of-interest concerns that FACA was designed to address.”

“As a FACA committee, Project Meridian cannot lawfully provide critical military advice to DoD without public participation and balanced membership to counteract the self-interest and biases of its private-sector members,” it goes on.

The lawsuit comes as Hegseth is slated to be under the microscope if Democrats win Congress, with top House Democrats hinting that impeachment of Hegseth will be their top priority.

Hegseth directed that the Pentagon form the committee in a memo dated September 30. “Project Meridian will study the battlefields of the future, identify which weapons and technologies warfighters will need to harness to dominate in these environments, and propose actionable solutions to start developing, testing and fielding these capabilities,” it says. The memo also says that the “Joint Staff and all services” should transfer its research and plans to the group.

Anduril and Musk’s SpaceX have been awarded with tens of billions of dollars’ worth of federal contracts, including from the Department of Defense, in Trump’s second term. Musk was also under scrutiny recently for seemingly unilaterally deciding to harm Ukraine’s military efforts against Russia by throttling their internet service, which is provided by SpaceX’s Starlink.

“The Federal Advisory Committee Act sets clear requirements about transparency and avoiding conflicts of interest, and Project Meridian must either comply or stop operating,” said Donald K. Sherman, CREW’s president, in a statement.

Public Citizen co-president Robert Weissman raised concerns that Musk and Luckey would work to entrench Big Tech’s interests into military operations, pointing out that FACA was written to prevent such strong influence in government committees.

“Project Meridian would outsource design of grand military strategy to two extremist Pentagon contractors, Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey,” said Weissman. “Very predictably, they will recommend more spending, much more spending, on more AI-enabled weaponry. That would simultaneously make the world more dangerous and starve funding for domestic and human needs.”

author: Chris Walker
title: US Continues Strikes on Iran Despite Trump Claims That War Is Over
content:
The White House has not reported on the US’s strikes on Iran over the past several weeks.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

On Monday night, the United States conducted a series of strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, the latest in a number of strikes over the past several weeks that have previously gone unreported.

Qeshm Island reportedly houses a large underground missile site and a naval base. It also has a desalination plant, which may be considered a civilian target rather than a military one.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump dismissed the idea that other previously unreported strikes have been taking place.

“We had a war with Iran. We won,” the president claimed during a speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, adding that the U.S. hasn’t engaged in “any fighting for months.”

However, other officials speaking to The Wall Street Journal said that the U.S. has been launching smaller-scale strikes for several weeks, with one source telling the publication that the administration has been downplaying the attacks to avoid signaling any intention of resuming major combat operations.

Trump has been inconsistent in his remarks regarding the future of the U.S.’s war on Iran. During his speech on Monday, he told reporters that a peace deal with the country “looks like [it’s] coming together very nicely.” That comment came shortly after Trump stated on Truth Social that a deal “could happen,” and that Iran wanted a resolution to the conflict “as soon as possible.”

But for several weeks, the president has been suggesting that major hostilities could resume shortly after the midterm elections, sometimes using explicitly genocidal terms. Less than a day after his speech at the Reflecting Pool in which he said a deal was close, Trump indicated in an appearance on “Fox & Friends” that he may restart major attacks on Iran.

Asked by the Fox News hosts what “the next thing” in the war would be, Trump nonchalantly suggested that he could order the resumption of major combat operations.

“I’m not looking to kill lots of people, but if we have to, we’ll have to,” Trump said.

Notably, Trump spent most of the interview peddling blatant falsehoods — including falsely claiming that “inflation is solved” and that “everything is going good” regarding the economy.

In response to The Wall Street Journal report, the National Iranian American Council (NIAC) expressed alarm at the revelation that the U.S. has been launching strikes without publicly announcing them.

“After eight months of an illegal war, there was finally some hope that a diplomatic agreement might be within reach and this war could end through negotiations rather than spiral into the violent scenarios being threatened after the midterm elections,” NIAC President Jamal Abdi said in a statement. “But these deeply alarming revelations suggest we may be heading in precisely the opposite direction.”

Every day that Congress fails to intervene is another day this administration is allowed to wage an unauthorized war, conceal its military operations, and gamble with millions of lives. Congress must immediately demand answers, oppose further military action, and use its power to cut off funding for this unauthorized war.

author: Aaron Mackey
title: Postal Service Surveilled Protest Activities Online With Little Rules, Oversight
content:
The U.S. Postal Service used social media surveillance to monitor and report on protests across the political spectrum, government records show.

The records, disclosed to EFF and other requesters suing the postal service under the Freedom of Information Act, show that the agency’s internet Covert Operations Program, or iCOP, routinely sifted through social media posts organizing and discussing protests with little records of any oversight or legal justification.

EFF filed suit in 2021 after Yahoo News disclosed the program’s existence and how the agency used it to monitor First Amendment protected activities. After years of delays and technical failures that led the agency to lose access to a trove of emails discussing the program, the postal service disclosed records to EFF and several other requesters this year.

The disclosures include a series of bulletins created from iCOP, which show that the postal service used the program in 2020 and 2021 to monitor and circulate information about a wide range of planned protests. They included a planned “Million MAGA March,” a guns rights advocacy event and counter-protest in Virginia, a nationwide Save the Post Office Saturday protest, and planned protests in front of then-Postmaster General Louis DeJoy’s home in Washington, D.C.

Many of the bulletins provide dry descriptions of the events being planned and reference public discussions or events on major social media services. Others seem to imply or anticipate that the protests would turn violent.

For example, in discussing planned national and international protests scheduled for March 20, 2021, the bulletin references potential violence in light of “online inflammatory material.” Yet the bulletin acknowledges that the agency has “no intelligence to suggest specific threats.” This bulletin was described by Yahoo News when it disclosed iCOP’s existence.

Another bulletin discussing an ongoing Black Lives Matter protests in response to police shooting and killing people styles itself as a “National Civil Unrest Update.” The bulletins also recount and monitor threats sent to then-Postmaster DeJoy.

The Postal Service also disclosed three email chains to EFF that, while heavily redacted, show how the agency queried iCOP and disseminated what it found (Read the emails here, here, and here). The government agreed to release the email messages as part of settling EFF’s FOIA suit this fall. To EFF’s knowledge, they are the only existing materials that reflect how the agency queried iCOP.

According to the agency, after Yahoo News disclosed the program in 2021, the postal service renamed it and publicly said that it had stopped issuing bulletins. But the documents do not say that the agency’s social media surveillance stopped.

At the same time, EFF and several other FOIA requesters sought records detailing how the agency used iCOP and what rules the postal service had for using the program and distributing information it gained from surveilling social media. EFF spent years pushing the agency to disclose email communications about the program, which the agency had stored on an external hard drive. Amid these negotiations, someone dropped the hard drive, rendering it inoperable, agency officials said. By the time that happened, the agency had already deleted the underlying email messages pursuant to the agency’s retention schedule.

EFF’s FOIA request sought internal rules, guidance, and training that would show what safeguard the Postal Service imposed to protect First Amendment rights. The agency disclosed very few documents in response to this part of EFF’s request.

For example, a series of slides give an overview of the program, but do not explain how officials used iCOP. The closest thing to internal guideline that the agency disclosed were talking points the Chief Postal Inspector authored in response to questions about iCOP.

The inspector wrote that, “In reviewing social media postings to gather information we did not single out any particular group and did not base what was reviewed on race, religion, gender, sexual orientation, immigration status, or a person’s exercise of First Amendment freedoms.” The statement echoes language in the bulletin stating that its purpose is not to infringe on First Amendment rights; Other parts of the talking points characterize the surveillance as providing officials with situational awareness.

The postal inspector’s talking points go on to say that “the recent attention on iCOP has highlighted opportunities for improvement, including enhanced executive oversight. We have stopped the distribution of the bulletins like the one you have seen in the media reports.”

Setting aside that it’s unclear whether internal oversight occurred or resulted in any changes, the claim that iCOP did not infringe on First Amendment rights rings hollow. As the records disclosed show, surveilling and reporting on social media users’ efforts to organize rallies and protests was a feature of iCOP.

But more fundamentally, the claims by Postal Service officials fail to recognize that surveillance directly chills First Amendment rights. Further, the government can misuse the information it obtained as part of its social media surveillance to harass or retaliate against those exercising their constitutional rights.

Although EFF’s case seeking records about iCOP has ended, we will continue to bring more transparency to the government’s use of social media surveillance and look for ways to challenge the practice, especially when people are caught in the dragnet for exercising the First Amendment rights.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Federal Agencies Use Internal List to Send Pro-Trump Email Blast Before Election
content:
Experts said the emails likely violate federal law barring use of an official office for election activities.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The Social Security Administration (SSA) and Internal Revenue Service (IRS) sent out mass emails praising President Donald Trump to online account holders just days before the midterm elections, potentially violating federal laws prohibiting the use of official government resources for a campaign.

The emails were sent on Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, with statements from the agencies’ shared director, Frank Bisignano, touting Trump’s supposed achievements during his second term.

“Under President Donald J. Trump, the Social Security Administration (SSA) is transforming into a model of excellence, one that meets and exceeds customer expectations for fast, accurate and secure service,” said one email signed by Bisignano, a Trump nominee. The wording is similar to that of a press release issued by the SSA last month.

Another email seemingly sent to the IRS account holder list touted the 2025 Republican tax cuts, which are estimated to lead to 51,000 early deaths each year while taking money from the poor and handing massive sums to the rich.

“Last year, President Donald J. Trump signed into law the Working Families Tax Cuts, landmark legislation that ushered in a new era of tax relief and prevented the largest tax increase in American history from taking effect,” the email said, per screenshots posted online and news reports. “Hardworking Americans like you are keeping more of what they earn because of President Trump’s historic tax cuts.”

Recipients of the email expressed fury over receiving the emails on social media. It’s unclear how many emails were sent.

Experts said that the emails may be the latest potential violation of the Hatch Act by the Trump administration, which has been desperate to sway elections in Republicans’ favor as pollsters and analysts predict a blue wave. The Hatch Act and other government ethics laws prohibit federal employees from using federal resources to participate in political and election-related activities, partly with the goal of ensuring that federal programs are administered in a nonpartisan fashion.

One expert likened the emails to the TV ad praising Trump that ran on networks in September and was paid for with taxpayer money.

Critics have said that this administration is a frequent violator of the Hatch Act. One recent complaint by Democracy Defenders Fund said that the Trump administration likely violated the Hatch Act in its pre-dawn raid of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minnesota) home last month, just weeks before the election in which she was running.

The Trump administration has also repeatedly seemingly misused personal information for political projects.

For now, courts have blocked the Trump administration’s plan for the IRS to transfer massive amounts of taxpayer data to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in order to facilitate mass deportation. And, earlier this year, the Department of Justice admitted that a member of Elon Musk’s “Department of Government Efficiency” team had signed an agreement to hand over Social Security data to a group that seeks to overturn election results.

title: Auditor general points out ‘fundamental weaknesses’ in Nunavut’s foster care
content:
This story was updated on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at 5:53 p.m. ET.




Nunavut’s Department of Family Services “did not provide timely and effective foster care services to protect and support the safety and well-being of children,” says Canada’s deputy auditor general Andrew Hayes.




Family Services Minister Gwen Healey Akearok sits in the Legislative Assembly last week. On Tuesday, Canada’s auditor general published a report that found her department “did not provide timely and effective foster care services to protect and support the safety and well-being of children.” (File photo by Lilli Akpaleeapik)




He tabled the report, 

Foster Care in Nunavut

, in the legislative assembly Tuesday. Family Services Minister Gwen Healey Akearok had announced in March that the audit was underway.




“Fundamental weaknesses” in the territory’s foster care system includes “failures to maintain regular contact with children in care, weaknesses in the screening and monitoring of foster homes, and unreliable information on children and their placements,” according to a news release issued by the auditor general’s office Tuesday, ahead of Hayes’ tabling of the report.




While it’s estimated that about 400 children are in the foster care system, the department remains unaware of the exact number or where the children are located, the latest report states.




This is despite the department rolling out a

 

centralized reporting framework

 called Matrix three years ago.
















The audit states that the department relied on a manually compiled list instead of using the software.




Additionally, the department failed to keep up monthly in-person contact with children and foster caregivers, “a basic safeguard intended to protect children in care,” the report states.




“In more than 90 per cent of the files we reviewed, there was no evidence that the required monthly contact with children or foster care caregivers had been maintained,” Hayes said at a press conference in the legislative assembly, where he tabled the report earlier in the afternoon.




In five cases, there was no documented contact with a child for more than one year, including one gap of more than 17 months.




The report also found cracks in the department’s screening process. Family services conducted 52 per cent of home studies, which evaluate the safety of a foster home, before it placed a child.




Long-term monitoring also fell short, with annual reviews that confirmed a foster home remained safe were missing or 

incomplete in 62 per cent of examined cases.
















Caregivers were not given important information about a child — such as health, family or trauma history — in 32 of 44 files.




An onboarding process for new caregivers was absent, training for caregivers was infrequent 

and the foster caregiver manual had not been updated in more than 10 years, the report states.




“There’s recruitment and retention issues that the department needs to address,” Hayes said. “In some cases, housing can be a problem.”




Previous audits in

 2011

,

 2014

,

 2023

 and

 2025

 found similar problems, including one finding from 2023 that the department

 could not provide

 an accurate count for the number of children in its care.




Following the October 2023 report, former family services minister Margaret Nakashuk 

apologized

 for the department’s failure to protect children in its care.
















“Ultimately, we need to see more from the department and improve services to these families and children,” Hayes said.




“Hopefully there is an urgency that is being recognized by the department and that the legislative assembly members can use our report and the department’s responses to hold the department accountable for making the improvements that they’ve committed to.”




The auditor general will release another report in the spring of 2027, on the department’s “quality assurance work,” he said.




Akearok thanked the auditor general for the report and its recommendations, saying it validates many of the actions already underway in her department.




“Meaningful change requires accountability, consistent follow-through, and sustained action,” she said in a Government of Nunavut news release issued after the report was tabled.




Akearok said her department is strengthening prevention and family supports, improving oversight, equipping staff with tools and training, and supporting foster caregivers.




Update

: 

This story was updated to include comments from deputy auditor general Andrew Hayes and a comment from Family Services Minister Gwen Healey Akearok.

author: Ryan Devereaux
title: Tribal Members Proven Right as Border Wall Contractors Desecrate Ancestors’ Remains
content:
“​​Who knows what more will come up,” said a Hia-Ced O’odham elder. “They’re going to find remains wherever they dig.”

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Lorraine Eiler stood in the blazing August sun, surrounded by reporters, to offer a warning. The Trump administration was racing to erect a second border wall across Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, southwest of Tucson. If the bulldozers came, she said, they were bound to disturb the final resting places of her family and Hia-Ced O’odham tribal ancestors.

“People used to live here,” the 89-year-old said.

Fifteen days later, her fears were realized.

ProPublica has confirmed that Native American remains were unearthed in Organ Pipe amid soil overturned by border wall contractors.

The discovery, unreported until now, was made on Sept. 8, the National Park Service said in a statement. “Following established protocols, the University of Arizona conducted an assessment and confirmed that the remains are human and align with tribal cremation practices,” the agency said.

The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act governs the steps agencies must take following an inadvertent discovery of Native American remains on federal land. Those steps include halting any activity that contributed to the discovery until tribal communities are consulted.

“The National Park Service is committed to respecting tribal rights and traditions,” the agency went on to say, adding that it was “working diligently to identify the culturally affiliated tribe and ensure the respectful return of the remains, so the tribe may observe their religious and cultural practices.”

Eiler was alerted to the discovery by a cultural affairs specialist with the Tohono O’odham Nation, a larger tribe whose reservation is east of Organ Pipe, and later by the Organ Pipe superintendent’s office. Her family discussed what to do next. Ultimately, they decided to hold off on reburying the newly unearthed remains until construction in the area stops, fearing the work will disturb more sites.

“​​Who knows what more will come up,” Eiler said in an interview. “They’re going to find remains wherever they dig.”

Customs and Border Protection contractors have bulldozed a wide swath of vegetation parallel to the international divide. The agency has fashioned staging areas for heavy equipment by knocking down, uprooting and attempting to transplant select specimens of the monument’s native plants. Eiler was told the remains were found by a park service archaeologist near the base of a saguaro cactus that was still standing.

In a statement, CBP said it was advised of the discovery six days after it was made, that its cultural resource specialists examined the area and found no other remains, and that “no additional construction has occurred at this location to date.”

The discovery comes amid tensions between the Department of Homeland Security and tribal communities in the Sonoran Desert. In April, border wall contractors bulldozed through a large, well-marked earthen etching, known as the Las Playas Intaglio, that was believed to be at least 6,500 years old. (CBP said the incident was accidental.)

Soon after, the department awarded a $1.3 billion contract for construction of a 62-mile border wall across the entirety of the Tohono O’odham Nation. The tribe is fighting the project in federal court and has erected “no trespassing” signs to keep border wall contractors off its land. As ProPublica recently reported, DHS has responded by deploying masked federal agents as escorts for its work crews and conducting aerial surveillance of tribal members. The head of CBP has justified the need for a wall by describing the reservation as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border.”

Verlon M. Jose, the tribe’s chairman, expressed gratitude that the park service had notified his office of the discovery, but mourned the fact that it was necessary.

“When you have mass destruction and disturbance of land taking place where there are clearly sacred sites, cemeteries and other areas of cultural importance, these types of discoveries are bound to happen,” Jose said in a statement. “Every time this happens it is a wound to the heart of all members of the Tohono O’odham Nation — these are our ancestors, our family members — whose remains are being desecrated.”

U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, who appeared with Eiler and the chairman at the August news conference, blasted the government for failing to heed their warnings. “Tribal leaders and elders have warned DHS about the devastating consequences of bulldozing through their ancestral lands, beginning with the destruction of the Las Playas Intaglio,” she said in a statement. “For months, those warnings have fallen on deaf ears. Now, we are seeing exactly what they feared: sacred sites destroyed and ancestral burial grounds desecrated.”

James T. Watson, curator of bioarcheology in the Arizona State Museum at the University of Arizona, analyzed the remains recovered in Organ Pipe in the field.

While he was not authorized to discuss the details of his findings without park service approval, Watson said in an email that he confirmed the remains were human. The evidence suggested they were cremated in a manner consistent with precolonial practices in the region dating back 1,500 years, he wrote.

Under NAGPRA, the graves protection act, Native American remains inadvertently uncovered on park service lands must be immediately secured, Watson explained, and the superintendent of the jurisdiction must notify “all relevant lineal descendants” with “potential cultural affiliation or ancestral ties to the land.”

“Work in the immediate discovery area must remain suspended for at least 30 calendar days,” he wrote, while the park service consults with tribal representatives “to determine the disposition and physical treatment of the remains.”

In a region as rich with archaeological sites as the American Southwest, the inadvertent disturbance of Native American remains occurs with some regularity. What sets the discovery in Organ Pipe apart are the extraordinary powers the Department of Homeland Security wields to expedite wall construction in the borderlands.

Following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Congress passed the Real ID Act, which included a provision empowering the secretary of DHS to waive any law that might slow border wall construction. In the two decades since, DHS has invoked its powers 66 times, with 60 of those instances occurring under President Donald Trump’s two administrations.

When DHS uses this authority, it typically waives dozens of laws at a time. That was the case in 2019 when the department set its sights on Organ Pipe. A waiver issued by then-acting Secretary Kevin K. McAleenan set aside more than 40 of the nation’s most stringent environmental and cultural resource protection laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act and others. Also on that list was the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, the landmark 1990 law that acknowledged the nation’s long history of desecrating Native American burials and required that ancestral remains and cultural objects be returned to tribes.

In an internal 2019 report obtained by The Washington Post, park service officials identified nearly two dozen archaeological sites in Organ Pipe as at risk of damage or total destruction by government contractors.

Of particular significance is a desert oasis known as Quitobaquito Springs. Less than 200 feet from the international border, the springs provide one of the only reliable sources of groundwater and shade for miles around, and they were a longtime gathering place, grazing site and home for O’odham families.

“Archaeological evidence of human presence at Quitobaquito extends back thousands of years, at least to Archaic times,” the survey found, adding that the springs represent the “only known Hia C-ed O’odham village site in the United States.”

A park service report in 2024 noted that a cemetery at Quitobaquito holds the remains of at least two families, including Eiler’s, and 34 graves. Throughout the region, remains of 5,500 ancestors that were displaced have been made available for return to the Tohono O’odham Nation, according to ProPublica’s NAGPRA database.

“This sort of incident has happened numerous times across our homeland, and it’s always alarming to hear about a case from an O’odham point of view,” said David Martínez, a professor of American Indian and transborder studies at the University of Arizona and a member of the Hia-Ced O’odham and Akimel O’odham tribes, as well as the Gila River Indian Community.

“Those remains shouldn’t have been disturbed in the first place,” he said. “While there are protocols existing today to properly care for these remains, ultimately, whatever either the government or the corporate world is pursuing to build, we know that at some juncture that construction will continue, and it always leaves us feeling, I think, a little hollow.”

Today, Quitobaquito lies in the shadow of the border wall erected during Trump’s first term. Its construction required detonating explosives in the national monument, blasting apart an area called Monument Hill and outraging tribal leaders. According to Eiler, the remains recovered in September were not found at the springs, though government work crews are working in close proximity to the site.

This year, DHS hired Sundt Construction, an Arizona-based company, to build a second wall in the monument. The $443 million contract was finalized in May. (Sundt directed questions concerning the discovery of human remains on its job site to CBP.)

According to CBP, the 2019 waiver for Organ Pipe is still in effect, years after completion of the project that prompted it. A second waiver, exempting DHS from many of the same laws and applying to the national monument as well as a wildlife refuge to the west, was issued by Homeland Security’s then-Secretary Kristi Noem last year.

“Unfortunately, there is no end date to the effectiveness of the waivers,” said Dinah Bear, a Tucson-based lawyer who served for 25 years as a senior attorney in the White House’s Council on Environmental Quality under both Democratic and Republican administrations. What’s more, she added, “there’s nothing in the statutory language that ties the waivers to a particular project.”

The Department of Homeland Security’s waiver powers have been central to a high-profile legal fight over the department’s efforts to build a border wall through Big Bend National Park in West Texas, with a federal judge overseeing the case recently ordering a temporary halt to the project.

Borderlands advocates in Arizona are hoping for similar interventions. In Congress, Grijalva is preparing legislation to void existing waivers that have allowed DHS to disregard laws designed to protect tribal sovereignty, sacred sites and environmentally sensitive lands.

In the meantime, construction on the border continues. For Eiler, it’s not just the destruction in Organ Pipe that’s troubling. She sees the disturbance of tribal graves resulting from wall construction as reflective of a wider pattern of destruction across the border.

“It’s sad because it’s not only happening down there,” she said. “It’s happening all over the United States, and nobody’s saying much about it.”

content:
Αφίσα/Κάλεσμα από τον 

Ρουβίκωνα

:




Κάλεσμα σε κινητοποίηση την Τετάρτη 4 Νοεμβρίου και ώρα 08:30 π.μ. στην Τράπεζα της Ελλάδος, για τη στήριξη οικογένειας με γονείς με αναπηρία ενάντια σε απειλή έξωσης.







Απειλή επικείμενης έξωσης οικογένειας με γονείς ΑμεΑ από την πρώτη και μοναδική κατοικία της έλαβε χώρα στις 23/10/2026 από εισπρακτική εταιρεία, η οποία προχώρησε σε χυδαία αμφισβήτηση της κατάστασης της υγείας των γονέων.




Τα αδηφάγα κοράκια επιμένουν ότι η κόρη της οικογένειας πρέπει να αναλάβει τα χρέη των γονιών της, παρ’ όλο που η ίδια αγόρασε πίσω το σπίτι της οικογένειάς της από τον πλειστηριασμό του, καθαρό από οικονομικά βάρη.




Τα κοινωνικά αγαθά της στέγασης, πρόσβασης σε νερό και ενέργεια και των βασικών ανθρώπινων αναγκών είναι και θα παραμείνουν αδιαπραγμάτευτα. Δε θα επιτρέψουμε σε κανέναν να πετάξει έξω από το σπίτι του καμία οικογένεια, πόσο μάλλον ανθρώπους ευάλωτων κοινωνικών ομάδων.




Απέναντι στην τρομοκρατία αυτή το μόνο όπλο μας είναι η αλληλεγγύη και η μόνη ασπίδα προστασίας της λαϊκής κατοικίας είναι οι οργανωμένοι και μαζικοί αγώνες της κοινωνικής βάσης.




Στηρίζουμε την κινητοποίηση στην Τράπεζα της Ελλάδος, οδό Αβέρωφ 2.

title: Συγκέντρωση ενάντια στην απόλυση εργαζόμενου, Τετάρτη 4/11, στις 09.00, στο Δικαστικό Μέγαρο Ιωαννίνων
content:
Κάλεσμα/Αφίσα από την 

αναρχική ομάδα 

A Batalha:




Να σπάσουμε τον τσαμπουκά των αφεντικών







Στις 16 Σεπτεμβρίου του 2025 μία ακόμα απόλυση εργαζόμενου είχαμε στην πόλη των Ιωαννίνων, αυτή τη φορά στη γειτονιά της ΒΙΠΕ. Πιο συγκεκριμένα στο εργοστάσιο Ηπειρωτικές Πρωτεΐνες εργαζόμενος απολύθηκε αιφνιδιαστικά με την αιτιολόγηση της αναδιάρθρωσης της επιχείρησης. Η εκδικητική αυτή απόφαση της εργοδοσίας υπήρξε αποτέλεσμα της συμμετοχής του εργαζόμενου στην απεργία της 28ης Φεβρουαρίου, όπως και της διεκδίκησης, μαζί με άλλους εργαζόμενους, αύξησης των αποδοχών και στελέχωσης του ήδη ελλιπούς προσωπικού. Ένα χρόνο μετά λοιπόν, θα γίνει η αναμενόμενη εκδίκαση της παράνομης και καταχρηστικής απόλυσης του εργαζόμενου, διεκδικώντας τα αυτονόητα. Την επαναπρόσληψή του στο εργοστάσιο




Δεν είναι η πρώτη φορά που βρισκόμαστε αντιμέτωποι-ες με τέτοιες απολύσεις. Πάντοτε το κεφάλαιο καρατομούσε όποιον και όποια διεκδικούσε καλύτερες συνθήκες στο εργασιακό του/της περιβάλλον, αντί να μειώσει κατά ελάχιστο τα υπερκέρδη του. Χώροι εργασίας και εργοστασιακές μονάδες με ανύπαρκτα μέτρα προστασίας, με την εντατικοποίηση να βαράει κόκκινο και όλα αυτά για πενταροδεκάρες. Και αν τολμήσεις και σηκώσεις κεφάλι σε στέλνουν σπίτι σου.




Την ίδια στιγμή το νομοθετικό πλαίσιο τους δίνει τέτοια αβάντα που δεν μπορείς να πιαστείς σχεδόν από πουθενά. Απολύσεις χωρίς αιτιολόγηση, απολύσεις με sms και μία επιθεώρηση εργασίας τόσο ανύπαρκτη και ακίνδυνη που υπάρχει μόνο για να συντηρεί τα γραφεία της υπηρεσίας. Προφανώς λοιπόν με μία τέτοια εργασιακή πραγματικότητα, θα έπρεπε να είναι τελείως φοβικός και μαλάκας όποιος θα άφηνε στην επιχείρησή του εργαζόμενες και εργαζόμενους που διεκδικούν τα αυτονόητα.




Με την εκμετάλλευση και την εντατικοποίηση της εργασίας στο ζενίθ λοιπόν, εκεί που οι εργαζόμενοι-ες παλεύανε κάποτε για 8 ώρες δουλειάς, ξεκούρασης και ύπνου, σήμερα φτάσαμε στο σημείο να δουλεύουνε πολλές φορές από το πρωί μέχρι το βράδυ. Όχι να μιλάμε για αυξήσεις στους μισθούς και πραγματική μείωση των τιμών πρώτης ανάγκης και των ενοικίων, αλλά να καθόμαστε όρθιοι και όρθιες, είτε με ένα δίσκο στο χέρι, είτε μπροστά από μία μηχανή, ένα γραφείο, ένα τιμόνι ή ένα ταμείο 13 από τις 24 ώρες που έχει η μέρα.




Σαν εργαζόμενοι και εργαζόμενες δεν θα μπορούσαμε να μη βρισκόμαστε στο πλευρό κάθε αγωνιζόμενου/-ης που παλεύει στις γαλέρες της βιομηχανικής. Αλληλέγγυοι και αλληλέγγυες σε όποιον και όποια επιλέγουν να μην γίνουν ρουφιάνοι και προσκυνημένοι μπροστά στην εργοδοσία. Και επειδή για να βρεις το δίκιο σου σήμερα πρέπει να περάσεις από 40 κύματα, σε αυτόν τον αγώνα οφείλουμε να οργανωνόμαστε τόσο στους χώρους εργασίας μας, όσο και στα σωματεία μας. Γιατί απέναντί τους το μόνο που έχουμε είναι ο ένας τον άλλον.

author: Clara Saliba
title: O Lula venceu. E agora, haverá ajuste?
content:
O presidente Lula foi reeleito para seu quarto mandato, em meio a uma virada de votos histórica que contou com a participação popular em peso, nas ruas e nas redes. Ufa. 




As brasileiras e os brasileiros avaliaram o que tinham a perder com uma vitória de 

Flávio Bolsonaro

. Para não falar da aproximação do ex-senador com as milícias ou dos escândalos de corrupção, me restrinjo a comentar a promessa de um “tesouraço” de até R$ 200 bilhões nas contas públicas que, 

conforme apuração da Folha de S.Paulo

, poderia incluir congelamento de benefícios, desvinculação das aposentadorias ao salário mínimo e o fim dos pisos constitucionais de educação e saúde (o mínimo que obrigatoriamente tem que ser gastos por estas pastas). 




Por isso, no dia 25 de outubro, o povo escolheu. Na minha visão, 

a vitória de Lula, amparada no que talvez tenha sido a maior mobilização popular desde a redemocratização, não deixou dúvidas sobre o projeto de governo que ganhou as eleições. Os votos foram contra os cortes nos programas sociais. 




Mas, 

já no dia seguinte, os jornais bradavam pela imperativa necessidade de um ajuste fiscal. Sinalizavam que a dívida pública brasileira, hoje no patamar de 82,9% do PIB, é preocupante, e não resta escolha para o governo vindouro a não ser colocar as contas nos eixos. 




Esse movimento, de cobrar a partir “do mercado” uma política econômica diferente daquela que foi eleita, tem sido chamado entre os economistas e analistas políticos de “terceiro turno” da eleição presidencial. Escolhemos o presidente. Agora, precisamos escolher o projeto econômico. 




É nesse contexto que escrevo sobre ajuste fiscal nesta coluna. Antes de mais nada, esclareço que, as eleições só têm dois turnos. 

O projeto econômico já foi escolhido, junto com o presidente – e qualquer movimentação que vá em direção ao corte em programas sociais é estelionato eleitoral. Isso não significa que nenhum corte de gastos possa ser feito

; mas voltaremos a isso mais à frente. 




Primeiro, precisamos entender o que é o tal do ajuste fiscal, e por que ele tem sido vendido como incontornável. Em palavras simples, 

um ajuste fiscal é uma reordenação na política fiscal, ou seja, na forma como o governo arrecada e gasta seus recursos, com vistas a reduzir a diferença entre o gasto e a arrecadação.

 Ele pode ser de várias dimensões e incidir sobre diferentes etapas do grande guarda-chuva do “gasto público”. 




A necessidade de ajuste vem da ideia de que uma relação muito alta entre a dívida do governo e o produto da economia pode causar problemas, como desconfiança no mercado, elevação do risco-país e a inflação. 




Sem entrar no mérito da validade dessa discussão, 

vale lembrar que, se nossa dívida está na casa dos 80%, a dos Estados Unidos está em 123%, a da França em 113% e a do Reino Unido chega a 92%.  




Mais importante que isso é entender o que leva nossa dívida pública para cima. Muito mais do que os gastos com Bolsa Família ou Pé de Meia, 

o que coloca a relação dívida/PIB do Brasil num patamar relativamente alto é a nossa taxa de juros astronômica. 




A maior do mundo, vale lembrar. 




Em 2026, o pagamento dos juros da dívida pública respondeu por 83% da pressão sobre a dívida pública

, como explicou meu colega Lucas Marçal, em 

texto para o jornal Hora do Povo

. O resultado primário, isto é, 

a diferença entre o que o governo arrecada e o que ele gasta, respondeu por menos de 10%. 




Ou seja: dá para fazer ajuste sem cortar programas sociais, e de forma muito mais efetiva.

 Por exemplo, repensando o modelo de metas de inflação, que coloca nossos juros em patamares cronicamente altos e sufoca a possibilidade de estabilização da dívida.




Também dá para fazer ajuste mexendo em outros gastos governamentais, como os supersalários do judiciário ou as emendas parlamentares impositivas, em especial as “emendas pix”, que caem diretamente na conta dos entes federativos sem destinação clara. Ou, ainda, aumentando a arrecadação, elevando a carga tributária sobre os mais ricos e revendo isenções fiscais a grandes empresas.  




E, por último, mas não menos importante: dá para fazer ajuste crescendo. Se o PIB aumenta, a relação dívida/PIB também cai. Através do investimento público, da continuidade das políticas sociais e de um projeto econômico pautado no crescimento – e não no “freio de mão” – é possível manter uma gestão fiscal responsável sem virar as costas para o projeto que elegeu o próximo governo, como o próprio Lula já afirmou. Esse parece ser o único caminho justo, em termos sociais, econômicos e democráticos.

received anonymously via email:




“One of us had driven past and seen signs advertising ‘fresh eggs’, a few big barns were visible from the road further down. A few nights later once we’d lined up good homes we came back as a small group with carriers. We had brought a crowbar and some conveniently sized bolt cutters to assist us with entry but the doors weren’t locked, always check the doors. We were greeted by the standard sight of a filthy barn crammed with thousands of hens looking worse for wear. They were good as gold and stayed quiet on the walk back and seemed happy with their new temporary accommodation when we got them home.




We dedicate this action to the T&S rabbits, the ones that got out and the ones that didn’t. We send our greetings to every human that helped pave the way to their freedom. But the fight goes on until every cage is empty.”

author: Scot Nakagawa
title: The fight after the vote
content:
This article 

The fight after the vote

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







The good news is that the courts closed off most of the routes by which the Trump administration could have impeded, intimidated or purged voters before Election Day. On September 14, the Supreme Court blocked the Postal Service’s restrictions on mail ballots, and in June it 

upheld

 grace periods for ballots postmarked by Election Day. The Justice Department has reportedly lost nearly all of its 30 lawsuits seeking states’ voter files. And federal law already bars armed federal agents from polling places, a protection seven states reinforced this year by advancing bans of their own.




Pressure doesn’t disappear when one door closes. It moves to the next one. With the front end of the election largely protected, the softer targets are now the count, certification and the seating of the new House.




What to expect




The most likely danger is also the most familiar: a fraud story built on slow counts. Fourteen states and the District of Columbia count ballots that arrive after Election Day, so in many places the results will take days. That delay is normal, and it’s a sign the system is working. But it’s also an opening for anyone who wants to claim that votes counted later are suspect, and the ground is already prepared. One 

survey

 found that fewer than half of voters expect a fair election.




The second danger may already be under way. The “

sanctuary surge

” the administration announced in late September is bringing immigration enforcement into 11 states in the days before the vote. The Homeland Security secretary says agents will appear at polling places only in response to “a threat” or with a warrant. Whatever happens at the polls, the surge’s real effect may be to frighten eligible voters in immigrant and mixed-status families into staying home.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










After the votes are cast, the fight shifts to close races. Democrats need a net gain of about six seats to win the House, so a handful of tight contests could decide who controls it. Expect recounts and lawsuits in every one of them. Expect, too, that some county boards will refuse to certify results. Courts have forced certification every time a board has tried this since 2020, but each refusal buys time and headlines for the story that something went wrong.




Two darker scenarios are less likely but would do far more damage. The first is the seizure of ballots or voting machines by federal authorities. That would break the chain of custody that makes results trustworthy, and it isn’t hypothetical: The FBI has already raided election offices in Fulton County, Georgia, and Maricopa County, Arizona. The second would be a fight over seating the new House on January 3, in which a newly installed House clerk could leave contested Democrats off the roll. Scholars call that far-fetched, and it could only work if control of the House rests on a handful of seats. But the fact that it’s being discussed at all tells us how much of our democracy now depends on officials choosing to follow the rules.




The work after the vote




What can grassroots groups and local officials do once the polls close? The honest answer is that the most useful work will be slow and procedural. It isn’t glamorous. It comes down to three things: making sure every valid ballot is counted, making sure certification happens on time, and keeping the public calm while both are under way.




The first 72 hours matter most. The deadlines to fix rejected ballots, known as cure deadlines, run only a few days, so coalitions should be helping voters amend ballot mistakes right away, while trained observers watch the count. Their public message should be simple and repeated until it sinks in: Slow counts are normal. Local election officials have a parallel job. They can give daily public updates on the count, open counting rooms to observers from all sides, secure ballots and machines, and refuse to release any of them without a court order.




Over the following two weeks, the action moves to county canvass and certification meetings. Coalitions should attend every one, document problems and report them to election protection lawyers, and thank election workers in public, because many of them have been threatened for doing their jobs. Officials, for their part, should certify on time and say in advance that they will, with county and city attorneys ready to go to court the same day any board refuses.




From then through January 3, the work is endurance. Coalitions need to stay organized through recounts and lawsuits, keep local reporters supplied with accurate numbers, and hold mass mobilization in reserve for a real trigger rather than spending it early. Local officials can issue joint statements across party lines affirming the results, and coordinate with their state attorney general on any federal demand for ballots or equipment.
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













A few principles hold through the whole period. The first is that losers conceding matters as much as winners winning. A local candidate who loses and says so plainly does more for public trust than any press release, so ask them to do it. The second is to witness, not obstruct. If federal agents try to take ballots or equipment, the grassroots job is to film, call lawyers and alert officials. Physically blocking agents would hand over the pretext for a much wider crackdown. The third is that sheriffs and police chiefs have a particular role to play. They can say publicly that they will protect counting sites and lawful assembly, and that they answer to state law on election materials. The fourth is to use unusual messengers: Republicans, veterans, clergy and business owners vouching for the local count will reach people that advocacy groups never will. And the last is to hold on to the volunteers. Whoever shows up in November should be invited into a standing structure before December, whatever the result.




If the result holds, don’t stand down




That last point matters more than any other, because it’s where the breakthrough trap begins. The breakthrough trap is the pattern in which a movement wins a breakthrough, an election or a transition, and then goes home, while the forces it defeated regroup, wait and come back. It has happened around the world. It happened here. In 2020 we won, exhaled and demobilized. Four years later, the movement we had beaten returned with a plan, a party and a governing agenda we never matched.




A House majority won in November will not spell safety. It will be an opening, and openings close. The people who show up this fall to watch the count and defend the result are the beginning of something we’ve never had enough of: a permanent grassroots demand system that can hold new leaders to account and defend what we win.




Winning is the breakthrough. Holding it is the job.




This story was adapted from The Anti-Authoritarian Playbook, which has

 

a post-election checklist

 

here.

Waging Nonviolence

.

author: Amy Goodman
title: After ICE Terror, Poll Finds 61 Percent of Latino Voters Say They’ll Vote Blue
content:
However, warns the director of the advocacy organization Mijente, Democrats can’t take Latino voters for granted.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

In 2024, Donald Trump won the presidency with the support of 44% of Hispanic voters, suggesting that a major realignment in party preferences might be underway. But just two years later, it appears much of that support has eroded. Sixty-one percent of Hispanic voters say they will now support Democrats in the midterms, including 11% who previously had voted for President Trump.

We get a bird’s-eye view of what to expect from the Latino vote from Marisa Franco, the co-founder and director of the advocacy organization Mijente. While ICE brutality will be at the front of voters’ minds, she says, Democrats cannot continue to take Latino voters for granted. “The vast majority of Latinos are working-class. Quite simply, they voted for Trump because they were looking at issues of economy, cost, inflation,” explains Franco. “And at the end of the day, these same issues have worsened under Trump’s administration, under Republican control. So people, I think, are looking for someone who’s going to explain what’s happening and propose solutions and be dogged about finding them.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org.

We end today’s show looking at how Latino voters could impact today’s midterms. In 2024, President Trump won the presidency with the support of 44% of Latino voters across the country — a significant shift following decades of Democratic advantage among Latinos. Two years later, it appears much of those Republican gains have eroded, and Democratic voters are significantly more motivated to go to the polls. Polling suggests cost of living is the top concern for all voters, including Latinos, who now trust Democrats more than President Trump to manage the economy. But the Trump administration’s violent crackdown on immigrants has also hurt his support among Latinos.

This is a former Trump supporter in Miami, Wayne DeMario, whose wife Yamile, who is Cuban, was recently deported to Mexico.

WAYNE DEMARIO: I am praying that everybody votes these pieces of garbage out. That’s it. Team up, everybody. I don’t care. Don’t be afraid that you voted for this jerk. Don’t be afraid that you voted for this guy. Team up and vote against him. Don’t worry about losing your guns. You’re not going to lose your guns if you vote Democrat. You’re not going to lose anything. Matter of fact, if I would have voted Democrat, I wouldn’t have lost my wife.

AMY GOODMAN: To talk about this and more, we’re joined by Marisa Franco, co-founder and director of Mijente, a national digital organizing hub for Latinx and Chicanx communities, joining us from Houston, Texas.

Thanks so much, Marisa, for being there. The New York Times has said Latinos are the most important swing vote in today’s election, making up 20% of registered voters in two dozen highly competitive House races, from Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Pennsylvania, Texas and other states. Can you talk about the shift that we’re seeing from 2024?

MARISA FRANCO: It’s good to be with you, Amy.

Yeah, it’s going to be a big night. The forecasts show a 15-point swing towards Democrats from Latinos and in heavy Latino districts. Just a quick roll call. You look at Florida, a place that oftentimes people have counted out as gone to the right. I’m really looking at the Boricua vote in Florida. I’m looking at Venezolanos, who were heavily hit by ICE. You just heard the gentleman talking about the impact of ICE and deportations on himself personally, feeling that, that Trump remorse, that MAGA remorse.

Georgia and North Carolina, and just overall in the Southeast, I’m looking at Latinos continuing to advance. I think you’re going to be looking — I’m really paying attention of, like, where are we making advancements and where are we helping break through. Georgia and North Carolina, I think you’ve seen the growth of Latino populations and actually be a flank and, what I would affectionately say, being helpers and not hurters, not only in Georgia and North Carolina, but also in Mississippi in a key race there.

Then we go to the Sun Belt — New Mexico, Colorado, Nevada and my home state of Arizona — where I am hoping that voters in southern Arizona take out “el trumpitas” Juan Ciscomani out of the House.

And then, last but not least, Texas, which I think could be the story of the night for the Latino vote. We have Democratic candidates who are knocking on the door. No Democratic candidate has won statewide in Texas for over 30 years. The early vote nationally is up 44% in comparison to the ’22 midterms. A big chunk of that is young voters, infrequent voters. That is the case here in Texas.

So, the question tonight is going to be: Will these numbers get at presidential levels, or will we surpass the early vote from ’22? Which candidates will voters go for? And what is the message they’re sending to the Trump administration?

AMY GOODMAN: So, talk about, from the deadly immigration raids to the spiraling economy due to Trump’s war on Iran, how those who supported Trump in 2024 shifted their views. And what does it take for Democrats to keep that support, Marisa?

MARISA FRANCO: So, I think it’s important to understand that Latinos, overall, are very, very working-class. The vast majority of Latinos are working-class. Quite simply, they voted for Trump because they were looking at issues of economy, cost, inflation. The people talk about the price of eggs. And, you know, we can talk about Trump’s overreach, but, in essence, what voters are looking at is impact. And at the end of the day, these same issues have worsened under Trump’s administration, under Republican control.

So people, I think, are looking for someone who’s going to explain what’s happening and propose solutions and be dogged about finding them. I think that it is an assumption to believe that whatever happens in this election, that Latinos are back in the Democratic tent for good. I believe that over the last election cycles, Latinos have been showing — declaring, in essence, their independence from partisan politics. And so, I think that the issues that they’re really caring about in this election is the cost of living, the war, opposition to the war, and ICE and what they’ve been doing in communities across this country.

AMY GOODMAN: Now, what are you doing about the possibility of voter suppression? ICE is supposedly not going to be deployed to the polls. We don’t know what’s actually going to happen. But other federal agents, about a thousand, are being sent to the polls across the country. What is Mijente and other Latinx groups doing?

MARISA FRANCO: You know, in some ways, I look at the Trump administration, I follow the moniker in Spanish, ”Más vale pedir perdón que pedir permiso. And that is, it’s easier to ask for forgiveness than permission. I think sometimes they don’t even ask for forgiveness. So, they’re saying they’re not going to be there. Who knows? I think there is a robust operation across the country of election protection. This has been an issue over several cycles. People will be on alert.

In our community, the damage has been done. It’s not only election, but they have been terrorizing our communities. There was incidents in the Central Valley, where you have a race, David Valadao, Republican, versus Randy Villegas, where ICE was in the community, was door knocking, supposedly looking at election fraud. Those are reports we got from the ground weeks ago. People are on alert.

And all we can do is urge people to come out and to have — you know, to utilize the infrastructure and the operations that have been set forth. But we cannot allow them to intimidate us from exercising our democratic right to vote, and ideally to vote them out.

AMY GOODMAN: Marisa Franco, co-founder and director of Mijente, a national digital organizing hub for Latinx and Chicano communities.

Tune in tonight for Democracy Now!’s four-hour live election night special, starting at 8 p.m. Eastern. We’ll be streaming live at democracynow.org, also on our YouTube channel. Check your local Democracy Now! station for listings.

Oh, and Steal This Story, Please!, the documentary about Democracy Now!, is available now in the United States and Canada on many streaming platforms, from Amazon Prime to YouTube to Apple TV. Go to StealThisStory.org, and you can see where you can watch it. And check our website for where it is in theaters still.

Democracy Now! produced with Mike Burke, Deena Guzder, Anjali Kamat, Messiah Rhodes, Nicole Salazar, Nermeen Shaikh, María Taracena, John Hamilton, Sara Nasser, Charina Nadura, Sam Alcoff, Tey-Marie Astudillo, Robby Karran, Hany Massoud, Laura Bustillos and Diego Ramos. Our executive director is Julie Crosby. I’m Amy Goodman.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. As Trump attempts to silence dissenting voices, we have no choice but to ask for your help.

We are fundraising today to fund our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

title: The Michigan 8 Are Now the Michigan 12
content:
A post shared by Michigan 12 Defense (@michigan12defense)

FBI agent stopping and searching a vehicle in Ann Arbor, MI as part of the crackdown on new defendants, October 29, 2026.

The federal government has again escalated its attack on Palestine solidarity movement in Michigan, adding four additional defendants to the Michigan 8 case. The Michigan 8 have now become the Michigan 12.

On October 29, 2026, FBI agents arrested Drin Shapiro as he left the Detroit public school where he teaches. He was stopped by agents pointing rifles at him, with over six FBI cars present. About an hour after his arrest, more than 15 FBI agents searched Drin’s home in Detroit, seizing his car and multiple devices. While Drin was in police custody, the remaining residents, including Zainab Hakim, one of the original eight defendants, were prevented from recording the search despite their legal right to do so.

The same afternoon in Ann Arbor, FBI agents racially profiled, detained, and searched Eric Ming VonBargen, mistaking them for their sibling, Aaron VonBargen. Agents only asked for Eric’s identification after handcuffing them, putting them in a cop car and searching their belongings and vehicle. “As I was walking to my car after class, multiple unmarked vehicles cornered me and about a dozen FBI agents proceeded to search and detain me. It wasn’t until minutes in that they asked for my name, and only then did they realized I was not my sibling, who is several years older,” Eric said. “By the time I was released, my car and backpack were already thrown apart. This was not a simple accident, but a combination of racial profiling and the general incompetence of the FBI, who despite possessing the surveillance needed to track me down in the street were unable to correctly identify me. While the FBI continues to issue political charges to repress my sibling and others fighting for justice in Michigan, the University of Michigan continues to remain complicit in the ongoing genocide in Palestine.” After learning that there was an arrest warrant for them, Eric’s sibling, Aaron VonBargen, turned themselves in to the court on the morning of Friday, October 30, 2026.

The remaining two newly indicted defendants are currently out of the country and seeking legal counsel.

On October 30, 2026, the Justice Department unsealed a superseding indictment laying out charges against the four additional individuals. All are recent University of Michigan graduates. They are charged with the same “conspiracy” charges as the first eight defendants. The new indictment repeats the same bogus rhetoric of “terrorism” as the first indictment. Similarly to the Minnesota 15 and Praireland cases, it considers use of encrypted messaging as evidence for criminal activity.

In the press release announcing the indictment, the Justice Department described their allegations as “a Sprawling Conspiracy Terrorizing [the] Jewish Community” and compared the defendants to the biblical Pharaoh and to Hitler. Judge Judith E. Levy herself has countered such sensational claims from the government in the past, as in Zainab’s September bond hearing where she remarked, “it was said [by US Attorney] at the detention hearing that [Zainab] hates Jewish or Israeli people. There’s nothing that’s happened over the last two months or maybe last year or anytime I’ve seen, there’s nothing in the indictment, there’s nothing in any of this material that would indicate that that’s the case.”

The DOJ’s press release also reiterates that the FBI is receiving assistance from “many local, state, and federal agencies” in the effort to criminalize Palestine solidarity activism. Once again, this confirms that local and state police, including the University of Michigan Police Department, are collaborating with the Trump administration to carry out this repression.

On October 30, friends, family, and community members packed the Detroit federal court for the bond hearing of two of the four new defendants. Both were released on $10,000 unsecured bond, with restrictive conditions similar to those of the Michigan 8. The bond conditions include travel restrictions, being prohibited from communicating with co-defendants or alleged victims in the case, and wearing a GPS ankle monitor. These two co-defendants are scheduled to complete their arraignment on Wednesday in Detroit federal court.

On November 2, 2026, two days after the arrests, US Attorney Maggie Smith filed an emergency motion to revoke Zainab’s bond and hold her in detention based on the claim that she tampered with evidence during the raid on Drin’s home. Zainab will have a hearing on this motion on November 18 in Ann Arbor.

We will not be intimidated. We will hold the line. We will continue to defend Palestine solidarity activists criminalized by this genocidal government. And we will continue to fight for a free Palestine.

Μετά τις μαζικές συγκεντρώσεις και πορείες που πραγματοποιήθηκαν Δευτέρα 2 και Τρίτη 3/11 στην Κάτω Τούμπα προς υπεράσπιση της κατοικίας ηλικιωμένου ζευγαριού που απειλείται με έξωση από τα κοράκια της αγοράς, νέα κινητοποίηση προγραμματίζεται για αύριο το πρωί Τρίτη 4/11 στις 8:00. Σήμερα, Τρίτη 3/11, στις 17:00










Αύριο, Τετάρτη 4/11, στις 08:00

– Να μπεί τέλος στις εξώσεις και τους πλειστηριασμούς που αφήνουν ανθρώπους χωρίς σπίτι.

Η στέγη είναι δικαίωμα!










ΤΑ ΣΠΙΤΙΑ ΤΟΥ ΛΑΟΥ ΤΑ ΣΩΖΕΙ Η ΑΛΛΗΛΕΓΓΥΗ!

ΙΩΑΝΝΙΝΑ – Κινητοποίηση ενάντια σε απειλή έξωσης

Τα κοινωνικά αγαθά της στέγασης, πρόσβασης σε νερό και ενέργεια και των βασικών ανθρώπινων αναγκών είναι και θα παραμείνουν αδιαπραγμάτευτα. Δε θα επιτρέψουμε σε κανέναν να πετάξει έξω από το σπίτι του καμία οικογένεια, πόσο μάλλον ανθρώπους ευάλωτων κοινωνικών ομάδων.




Απέναντι στην τρομοκρατία αυτή το μόνο όπλο μας είναι η αλληλεγγύη και η μόνη ασπίδα προστασίας της λαϊκής κατοικίας είναι οι οργανωμένοι και μαζικοί αγώνες της κοινωνικής βάσης.




Στηρίζουμε την κινητοποίηση στην Τράπεζα της Ελλάδος, οδό Αβέρωφ 2.

author: David Venn
title: Ikur’raq cabin program expands with $500,000 in federal money
content:
The federal government has topped up a cabin program meant to reduce homelessness in Nunavut, Family Services Minister Gwen Healey Akearok announced Oct. 27.




Close to $514,000 will go towards the territory’s Ikur’raq Cabins Initiative, a project meant to give people a temporary place of respite from overcrowding, violence and addiction issues. The money will fund 15 cabins.




“Out-of-shelter homelessness is a major public health and safety issue,” Akearok said in her minister’s statement at the legislative assembly. “The Ikur’raq cabins offer a practical response to this urgent need.”




The GN funded the 

first set of 16 cabins

 in 2022 and the program was revived in 2025 with $1 million in federal money to build 20 additional cabins.




Akearok’s Oct. 27 announcement will bring the total to 51.




Hamlets, non-profits and hunters and trappers organizations can apply for $50,000 grants with the new round of funding.




The original 16 cabins include three Pangnirtung, two each in Arviat and Pond Inlet, and one cabin in each of Coral Harbour, Iqaluit, Clyde River, Naujaat, Baker Lake, Igloolik, Kugaaruk, Taloyoak, and Kugluktuk.
















As of Oct. 20, six cabins from the second round of funding were complete and 14 were under construction, according to Family Services spokesperson Irma Arkus. Sanirajak and Kugaaruk have finished two each, while Sanikiluaq and Iqaluit have finished one each.




Two cabins in Arctic Bay are under construction, while one cabin in Arviat, Baker Lake, Chesterfield Inlet, Gjoa Haven, Igloolik, Kugluktuk, Naujaat, Pangnirtung, Pond Inlet, Qikiqtarjuaq, Rankin Inlet and Taloyoak are under construction.




Akearok said her department is working to build the cabins “in the communities where the need is greatest.”

author: CMI Argentina
title: Cientificidio: en tres meses se destruyeron casi 23 empleos por día
content:
El promedio se ubicaba en 8,5 trabajos perdidos por día desde diciembre. Un informe del grupo Economía Política Ciencia (EPC) del CIICTI explicó que este descenso en velocidad del empleo científico se debe, principalmente, a la reducción de becas en el CONICET, los retiros en el INTA y el recorte de personal en la empresa pública FADEA.







Por Guillermo Lavecchia




El 

cientificidio

 que lleva adelante el Gobierno nacional, cuyas consecuencias se verán en los próximos años (o décadas), tiene efectos concretos, números reales, personas e investigaciones truncas detrás.




Un 

informe del grupo Economía Política Ciencia

 (epc) del Centro Iberoamericano de Investigación en Ciencia, Tecnología e Innovación (CIICTI) da cuenta de cómo la destrucción de los puestos de trabajo en ciencia y tecnología creció drásticamente en el tercer trimestre del año en curso. Mientras que el promedio se ubica en 8,5 empleos perdidos por día desde diciembre de 2023, en los últimos tres meses la cifra se elevó a 22,8 por día.




El Grupo EPC explicó que este descenso en velocidad del empleo científico se debe, principalmente, a la reducción de becas en el CONICET, los retiros en el INTA y el recorte de personal en la empresa pública FADEA.




Foto: Edgardo Gómez @jedgardogomez




El CONICET, principal organismo nacional de investigación científica, perdió 722 investigadores de carrera y personal de apoyo desde diciembre de 2023. Además, disminuyó su cantidad de becas en 2418, lo que recorta drásticamente la formación de profesionales a mediano y largo plazo.




El informe del Grupo EPC detalla la situación del INTA, organismo golpeado por la desarticulación de programas y actividades de ciencia y tecnología, que redujo casi 1.000 trabajadores en el último trimestre: su deterioro alcanza una reducción de personal de 27,3% desde diciembre de 2023.




Un país sin ciencia es un país sin inteligencia colectiva




Ya en julio pasado, trabajadores y trabajadoras de Universidades, Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas (Conicet), Instituto Nacional de Tecnología Agropecuaria (INTA), Instituto Nacional de Tecnología Industrial (INTI), Servicio Meteorológico Nacional (SMN) y Comisión Nacional de Energía Atómica (CNEA) firmaron en conjunto una dura carta contra la política de destrucción del sistema científico del gobierno de Javier Milei. “Alertamos de la crisis terminal que atravesamos y el impacto destructor para la Argentina en el presente y el futuro”, advirtieron.




Definieron al “proceso de destrucción de su sistema científico, tecnológico y universitario” como “absolutamente irracional desde el punto de vista político, social y económico” y recordaron que la 

inversión pública

 en la función ciencia y técnica, por debajo del 0.15% del PBI, es la más baja en la historia de nuestro país, al menos desde los últimos 54 años.




El desfinanciamiento sostenido, los retiros voluntarios, despidos y renuncias de personal altamente calificado forzados por pérdidas salariales cercanas al 40% desde diciembre de 2023, y la paralización total de programas estratégicos “son un proceso planificado por el actual gobierno que busca destruir capacidades construidas durante décadas por generaciones enteras de argentinos y argentinas”.




Científicas y científicos remarcaron que “nunca un país que hizo un esfuerzo sostenido durante más de 200 años para generar capacidades científicas y tecnológicas al servicio de la sociedad las destruyó en tan corto tiempo”.







https://t.co/BCNEqe6iNS




— Jorge Aliaga (@jorgeluisaliaga) 

July 6, 2026







Las y los firmantes consideraron que el desmantelamiento del sistema científico tecnológico puesto en marcha desde diciembre de 2023 “no tiene absolutamente nada que ver con el déficit cero o restricciones presupuestarias”. Por el contrario, “es una decisión política y cultural tomada por un gobierno que ha declarado abiertamente su voluntad de destruir al Estado que conduce”.




Cuestionaron que hoy investigadores, docentes y técnicos altamente calificados se ven forzados a migrar, realizar otros trabajos ajenos a su formación o al pluriempleo. “Argentina invirtió en la formación de estos recursos humanos, una inversión que este gobierno tira a la basura impidiendo que trabajen para el desarrollo de nuestro país (…) Este ataque a las instituciones y a sus trabajadores y trabajadoras es principalmente un ataque feroz a la capacidad colectiva de la sociedad argentina para cuidarse, producir, imaginar y construir futuro”.




“Ningún país se desarrolla destruyendo su inteligencia colectiva –alertaron al conjunto de la sociedad- Lo que está en juego va mucho más allá del doloroso presente, lo que está en juego es el derecho colectivo a tener un futuro”.




Trabajadores y trabajadoras que firmaron lo hicieron de forma anónima, “por la persecución y militarización en algunas de nuestras instituciones”, y recordaron que “el INTA fortalece una agricultura competitiva, federal y con desarrollo territorial; el INTI impulsa una industria nacional con innovación, tecnología y valor agregado; la CNEA sostiene la soberanía energética, tecnológica y nuclear de la Argentina; el SMN protege a la población con información climática estratégica, alertas tempranas y monitoreo meteorológico; el Conicet genera nuevas ideas, produce conocimiento y lo transfiere a la sociedad; las Universidades Nacionales forman profesionales, construyen pensamiento crítico y desarrollan conocimiento estratégico”. En todos estos espacios hay procesos de desfinanciamiento, desmantelamiento y/o vaciamiento por el éxodo que genera la pérdida feroz de poder adquisitivo.




“No lo tenemos registrado como una fuga masiva”




El cientificidio tiene múltiples facetas. No solo despidos y recortes en becas. También, indefiniciones y dilaciones que dejan a gran cantidad de investigadores en un limbo. Son más de mil científicos y científicas quienes tienen sus concursos aprobados para el ingreso al Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas (Conicet). Pero el organismo no confirma sus altas, lo que les impide ocupar sus puestos. Hoy están cumpliendo “tres años de amarga espera”.




Así lo difundieron a través de un comunicado. Denunciaron que el organismo nacional de ciencia y técnica adeuda desde fines de 2023 alrededor de 600 altas de personal con sus concursos aprobados. En 2024 se sumaron 400 personas más a esa lista. En su tercer aniversario de espera, en septiembre pasado, movilizaron al Polo Científico-Tecnológico en CABA. El reclamo tuvo sus réplicas en distintos puntos del país.




“Aproximadamente hay cien miembros que dejan Conicet por año de una comunidad de más de doce mil. Eso no lo tenemos registrado como una fuga masiva”, declaró días atrás el presidente del Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones, Científicas y Técnicas, Daniel Salamone. También afirmó que “el hecho de irse del país tiene otros componentes que van muchísimo más allá de estar mal o bien” y destacó que el organismo “ha continuado dando becas”. Sus palabras generaron indignación en una comunidad que viene batallando contra el cientificidio implementado desde la asunción de Javier Milei.




“El Conicet ha continuado dando becas, se han mantenido activas más de 1.800 becas por año”, dijo Salamone a Infobae. Resaltó que entre el 2024 y el 2025 ingresaron 400 personas a la carrera de investigador y que el monto destinado a proyectos pasó de dos millones a diez millones de pesos. “Por supuesto que no es mucho eso para una comunidad de más de 12 mil investigadores y nueve mil becarios, pero se ha hecho un esfuerzo”, aclaró.







Miembros de Conicet nucleados en ATE salieron a responderle. Con datos: “La planta de Conicet se redujo en casi un 10% desde que asumió. El organismo perdió 2.365 trabajadores desde el 2023 y acaba de expulsar a 400 becarios posdoctorales. Además anuló 500 concursos de la Carrera de Personal de Apoyo y aún está pendiente la efectivización de más de 1.000 altas a las carreras, postergadas desde hace 3 años. El desfinanciamiento se muestra en el presupuesto del sistema científico, que se redujo casi un 50% entre 2023 y 2026”.




A través de un comunicado, desde ATE Conicet explicaron que la pérdida de recursos humanos no sólo se debe a los despidos, los recortes en los cupos de becas e ingresos a las carreras y la demora en las altas, sino sobre todo a las renuncias, que aumentaron significativamente desde que Salamone asumió. “Estas renuncias están principalmente motivadas por la falta de perspectivas, y sobre todo, por una reducción del salario real cercana al 50%”, precisó Gonzalo Sanz Cerbino, secretario general adjunto ATE Conicet Capital.




Uno de los 400 despedidos del Conicet, por ejemplo, realizó un hallazgo en enfermedades neurológicas. Facundo Chrestia y Cecilia Bouzat, científicos de la 

Universidad Nacional del Sur

, analizaron los efectos del cannabidiol (CBD, una sustancia derivada del cannabis pero sin efectos psicoactivos) en una molécula denomina alfa-7, que interviene en procesos cognitivos y juega un rol clave en patologías relacionadas con problemas de memoria. Además, los especialistas hallaron en qué parte de alfa-7 se une el CBD. Si bien ya existen compuestos que potencian la actividad de esta molécula, el trabajo de los investigadores abre la puerta al diseño de fármacos más eficientes para enfermedades neurodegenerativas y trastornos neurológicos.




El trabajo fue publicado en la 

revista PNAS

 junto a colegas de la Universidad de Oxford y podría transformar las estrategias terapéuticas en todo el mundo. En medio de la alegría por la difusión de la investigación, Chrestia se transformó en uno de los 400 becarios posdoctorales despedidos por el Conicet.




“Ahora me quedé sin la beca y no me puedo dedicar todo el tiempo a la investigación porque tengo que hacer otras cosas para poder seguir subsistiendo. Me siento muy triste y muy defraudado, me duelen todas las palabras de este gobierno. Encima, nadie nos dice cómo seguir y el silencio es más doloroso. Mientras tanto, muchos investigadores tienen que abandonar la ciencia porque no les queda otra”, señaló el bahiense a la Agencia de la UNQ.







Fuente: 

https://www.tiempoar.com.ar/ta_article/cientificidio-23-empleos/

Cientificidio: en tres meses se destruyeron casi 23 empleos por día

 se publicó primero en
