title: Landmark Collective Agreement for Migrant Workers
content:
Article from Znetwork. More articles by the author here. Photo above: migrant workers after the agreement was signed. Photographer: Valeriia Eltarenko.

Workers at the construction of a Microsoft data center in Sweden secured a collective agreement under threat of strike action through the syndicalist union SAC.

A trade union victory at a Microsoft construction site has attracted attention from a large number of European media outlets. The workplace is situated outside the city of Gävle in Sweden.

The Guardian has published a five-month investigation into conditions for migrant workers on data center sites across Sweden, Norway, Belgium and the Netherlands. The investigation uncovers evidence of dangerous conditions and unpaid wages, including at the Microsoft site outside Gävle.

“Days before publication of this investigation, the syndicalist union, representing 70 Romanian workers at Microsoft’s site in Gävle, brokered a settlement with BenBau, which it says will give workers back pay and allow unions access to sites,” reports the Guardian. The back pay amounts to 15 million Swedish kronor (roughly 1, 5 million US dollars).

On October 25, this group of workers voted unanimously for a collective agreement with BenBau AB, one of the companies building Microsoft’s server halls, reports the Swedish newspaper Arbetaren. The deal raises wages to 260 kronor an hour (26,46 US dollars), includes a time bank for longer leave periods in the workers’ home countries, and allows the workers to elect health-and-safety delegates from their own ranks.

The agreement opens with the statement: “This collective agreement is the first Swedish collective agreement written by and for migrant workers.” Since the deal was struck, even more workers have joined the union at the construction site.

This outcome is the latest result of the syndicalist union’s years of organizing among migrant construction workers, particularly those from post-Soviet countries who use Russian as a common language. Freelance journalist Volodya Vagner has reported extensively on these efforts. “By confronting exploitative employers with aggressive litigation and long-forgotten methods of struggle, like blockading the construction sites of contractors with wage debts, the union has managed to redistribute millions of dollars in unpaid wages and damages,” writes Volodya Vagner.

The collective agreement at the Microsoft site is consistent with SAC’s new collective agreement-strategy articulated in 2020. This strategy is a response to a Swedish anti-strike law that entered into force in 2019. The strategy was presented on the Counterpunch news site: “According to our assessment syndicalists can still fight lawfully for both collective agreements and alternatives to such agreements”, SAC representatives stated.

Yet collective agreements are nothing new for Swedish syndicalists. During the 20th century, Swedish syndicalists entered into hundreds of collective agreements.

SAC was founded in 1910. Fittingly, the vote on the 2026 collective agreement took place in the childhood home of the legendary Joe Hill.

This rewrite was made by Rasmus Hästbacka, labor lawyer and member of SAC

author: Amy Goodman
title: Raskin Urges Kushner to Recuse Himself From Negotiations Amid Book’s Allegations
content:
Author Matthew Cole discusses the findings of his new book, Princes and Thieves, that prompted the move.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Vanity Fair recently published an excerpt from longtime investigative reporter Matthew Cole’s new book, Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East.

The excerpt alleged that during President Trump’s first term, Saudi and Emirati leaders secretly put at least $2 billion into bank accounts and gave access to Kushner. At the time, Jared Kushner was serving as senior adviser to President Trump, his father-in-law. He is now Trump’s special envoy. Kushner’s lawyers responded by demanding that Vanity Fair retract the article and threatening legal action against the book publisher, Simon & Schuster.

Jared Kushner denied the report, saying, “The allegations made by this author are completely insane, categorically false, and never happened. We denied every one of these claims on the record, yet the author failed to provide a single shred of evidence to substantiate any of them.” His lawyers say no such bank accounts existed and that the allegations are unsupported by the verifiable evidence.

In an extended interview with Democracy Now!, author Matthew Cole stood by his reporting. “This book is a result of more than 50 sources. There was an enormous amount of fact-checking and legal vetting that went into this book,” says Cole. “There’s plenty of information and reporting in the book that lets us establish and understand that there was … an unholy alliance between Jared Kushner and the leader of the UAE, the leader of Saudi Arabia and, at the time, Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister of Israel.”

On Friday, Congressmember Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, called on Kushner to recuse himself from Middle East and Ukraine negotiations and to produce a “comprehensive list of bank accounts or other financial instruments” that he had access to during his time in government.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.

With the midterms a day away, polls show corruption has emerged as one of the top issues for many voters. A new Harris poll for The Guardian found 76% of voters said elected officials care more about enriching themselves than improving the economy for ordinary people.

We turn now to the new book Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East. It’s written by longtime investigative reporter Matthew Cole.

Vanity Fair recently published an excerpt headlined “The Art of the Deal: Jared Kushner’s Hacked Phone Revealed His Secret Negotiations — Including More Than $700 Million in Transfers.” The excerpt alleges that during President Trump’s first term, Saudi and Emirati leaders secretly put at least $2 billion into bank accounts and gave access to Jared Kushner. At the time, he was serving as a senior adviser to President Trump, his father-in-law. Kushner is now Trump’s special envoy.

Jared Kushner’s lawyers responded by demanding Vanity Fair retract the article and threatening legal action against the book publisher, Simon & Schuster.

Jared Kushner denied Cole’s reporting, saying, quote, “The allegations made by this author are completely insane, categorically false, and never happened. We denied every one of these claims on the record, yet the author failed to provide a single shred of evidence to substantiate any of them,” unquote.

Kushner’s lawyers say no such bank accounts existed and that the allegations are unsupported by the verifiable evidence.

In a book review in The New York Times, Fintan O’Toole writes, quote, “If Cole’s claims are accurate, Kushner’s political and financial relationship with the UAE’s president Mohammed bin Zayed constitutes what must surely be the worst case of U.S. foreign policy being conducted outside the law and democratic oversight since the Iran-Contra scandal during the Reagan administration in the 1980s,” unquote.

On Friday, Congressmember Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, called on Kushner to recuse himself from Middle East and Ukraine negotiations and to produce a, quote, “comprehensive list of bank accounts or other financial instruments,” unquote, that he had access to during his time in government.

Well, I last week sat down with Matthew Cole and interviewed him about his new book.

AMY GOODMAN: Why don’t you lay out your explosive allegations that Jared Kushner’s lawyers categorically deny? MATTHEW COLE: Yeah. Well, let’s first by reiterating that Mr. Kushner emphatically and entirely denies everything that’s in the book. I obviously still stand by my reporting. I will continue to stand by my reporting, because it’s accurate, and it will ultimately bear out. The first thing I want to do, Amy, for your audience is to just give you an overview and sort of start at the beginning, which is that what the book lays out is at the beginning of Trump’s time, start in office the first time, in 2017, he gave his son-in-law the most consequential job in foreign policy that the American government has, which is running, essentially, the Middle East foreign policy, and tapped him with trying to solve the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. And when they came into office, we had — he had, essentially, two important players from the Middle East rush to the scene, you know, intentionally and very specifically, to New York, before he even got into the White House, to meet with the Trump transition team. And that was MBZ, Mohamed bin Zayed, the ruler of the UAE, and Mohammed bin Salman, known as MBS, who was at the time the deputy crown prince of Saudi Arabia. And what these two Arab rulers, leaders wanted were, as it happened, the same thing that Kushner and Trump wanted in terms of what they were going to do in the Middle East, which was to remake the map altogether, completely change what was going on in the Middle East. And so, what they had in common were they wanted to thwart Iran, they wanted to undo the last remnants of the Arab Spring, they wanted to potentially make a deal for — in Israel’s favor in a Palestinian-Israeli settlement, and they were willing to marginalize the Palestinians in doing so. And MBZ and MBS had other asks. MBS wanted to become the crown prince. He wanted to jump up a rung so that he could become the future king of Saudi Arabia. And the question was going to be: How are they going to manage all of that? And that was Jared Kushner’s task when he came into the White House. OK? And so, in that setting, they move forward. And quickly one of the things that the three of them start to negotiate or discuss is the idea of a foreign policy fund that would be used — that would be paid for by the Saudis and the Emiratis overtly, not secretly necessarily, for several billion dollars that would support Trump’s initiatives around the world, because you have to remember that America First at that time, and to some extent today, meant no more spending U.S. tax dollars on defense and policies in the Middle East, that Trump wanted to pull soldiers out. He wanted to get rid of — no more wars. I mean, it seems laughable now saying it, but that was what it was. And so, these two guys, MBS and MBZ, were offering to essentially bankroll that. And one of the ideas that they had was building the wall in Mexico that Trump had been pushing on. And the idea was that when he was going to run for election in 2020, he would have these accomplishments, and they would have supported it. And it was — you know, it’s not — it would not have been illegal necessarily, although it would have been complicated. And so, that was the original idea. That idea, in part, I believe, because it was complicated and tricky to do in terms of how you spend — Congress, there are laws about spending, outside spending, on things that Congress has not authorized, or especially if they have authorized. So, it faded. What comes next is a secret arrangement between Kushner, MBS and MBZ for a similar idea: a foreign policy fund, if you will, a secret pool of money that Kushner could help manage. And the pool of money — one part of the pool of money was going to be for the efforts of the UAE and Saudi Arabia to remake the Middle East. Some of the ways that they were trying to remake the Middle East: They wanted to end the war to their favor in Yemen; they wanted to get rid of the ruler of Qatar; they wanted to support Khalifa Haftar in eastern Libya to overthrow the government in Tripoli. So, you had these pieces on the puzzle, if you will — I mean, the chess board. They wanted to move pieces around. And this money, originally, that’s part of the idea. And so, Kushner starts to get — he agrees. There is some movement of money in the mid — in mid-2017. What happens at the same time is MBS and MBZ declare a blockade on Qatar in June of 2017. The book lays out and my — AMY GOODMAN: This is during the first Trump administration. MATTHEW COLE: First Trump administration. It’s sort of the first big foreign policy issue that Trump confronts. You have — just to back up for a second, the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, all very wealthy Gulf Arab states, all have U.S. troops and bases on them. They’re all allies. author: Kiara Green
title: What Rights Are at Stake in the Supreme Court’s 2026-27 Term?
content:
The US Supreme Court reconvened on October 5 for its 2026-27 term which concludes in June of 2027. Cases involving the rights of immigrants, rules governing elections, LGBTQIA rights, and more, stand at the forefront this term. The Court’s decisions could have significant consequences for how federal and state laws protect individual rights.

The Court begins this term with a 6–3 conservative majority. Three of the nine justices, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett, were nominated by President Donald Trump. Recent decisions, including the overturning of Dobbs and rulings affecting the enforcement of the Voting Rights Act, have already reshaped the legal landscape. This term, the justices will consider additional disputes over voting regulations and the rights of young people.

Among these cases is Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota, which is scheduled to be heard on December 8. The Court will decide whether Arizona can require proof of citizenship to register to vote and if the National Voter Registration Act prohibits Arizona from canceling the registrations of non-citizens within 90 days of a federal election.

Despite the lack of evidence of noncitizen voting, concerns about voter eligibility have led to policies that can create additional hurdles for eligible voters in Arizona, especially indigenous people. Arizona is home to one of the largest Indigenous reservations in the US, but was one of the last states to allow Indigenous people to vote.

Indigenous votes play a vital role in deciding the outcome of state and federal elections. In 2020, Indigenous voters from the Hopi and Navajo reservation cast nearly 60,000 votes.

The Supreme Court’s decision could affect how Arizona and other states administer voter registration and verify citizenship. It will also determine how federal law limits states’ authority to change voter registration records close to an election.

The Court will also hear International Partners for Ethical Care, Inc. v. Ferguson on December 7. The Administration has vilified the queer community spewing anti-trans and homophobic rhetoric in the name of religious freedom. The decision of this case will impact the livelihood of queer adolescents that struggle with their gender identity.

The case is challenging a Washington State law on whether runaway minors can seek access to gender-affirming care without parental permission. Ending gender-affirming care has been a top priority for the Trump administration pushing for hospitals to discriminate against patients based on gender orientation and identity. This pressure has led at least six hospitals to agree to refuse gender-affirming hormones and surgery for transgender young people and agreed to make payments to the federal government.

As the term continues, the Court’s decisions will shape how federal protections and state laws apply to voting access, family rights and LGBTQIA+ communities. Oral arguments will offer insight into the justices’ questions, but final rulings are expected later in the term.

The Supreme Court’s work affects people across the country, often in ways that reach beyond the specific parties involved in a case. As the midterm elections approach on November 3, make a plan to vote, bring friends, spread the word. For nonpartisan voter registration information, election dates and voting resources, visit Vote411.org/feminist.

author: Dan DiMaggio
title: Book Review: A Model for U.S.-Mexico Cross-Border Solidarity
content:
Labor law reform in Mexico has opened up a major opportunity for workers fighting for genuine, independent unions. What can U.S. unions do to support our brothers and sisters there? And how can we build cross-border campaigns to confront our common employers?




Unions asking these questions will find valuable ideas in the e-book 

International Solidarity in Action: The Relationship Between the United Electrical Workers (UE) and Frente Auténtico del Trabajo (FAT)

, available for free download 

here

. 




Author Robin Alexander, retired director of international affairs for UE, led her union’s partnership with the FAT, which began in 1992, during the campaign to oppose the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).




UE members were seeing their employers cut manufacturing jobs in the U.S. and shift production to Mexico. “The UE leadership became convinced that the union needed to find a labor organization it could work with in Mexico,” Alexander writes, “and also that it was essential to connect international work more directly with UE members and with organizing.”




In a meeting in Mexico to discuss the campaign against NAFTA, the UE found the FAT—the only Mexican labor organization to oppose NAFTA.




Here was a union that had a lot in common with the left-led UE: fiercely independent, with radical roots and leadership. The FAT had long stood out against Mexico's state-dominated unions and fought for workers’ right to form genuine, independent unions.




Both unions were concerned about the growing number of jobs that corporations had moved to assembly plants near Mexico’s northern border with the United States, where unions were either nonexistent or a tool of the government’s development strategy of low wages and long hours.




“The UE,” Alexander writes, “was interested in seeing the plants organized by a union that would serve as a partner and ally in Mexico and believed that it could provide solidarity, including some leverage, where it continued to represent workers employed by those companies in the U.S… The FAT was eager to organize the plants that were moving across the border, but lacked the resources to do so.”




LIKE-MINDED UNIONS




Thus kicked off a partnership that has now lasted 30 years. The book contains several case studies of how the UE and the FAT worked together to back each other’s campaigns against employers such as General Electric and Echlin (a transnational auto parts maker later bought by Dana).




For U.S. unionists unfamiliar with the obstacles that Mexican workers are facing as they struggle to oust protection unions and replace them with genuine unions, these sections will be particularly valuable.




At Echlin, for example, workers attempting to confront dangerous exposure to asbestos and solvents and form a democratic union were met with a barrage of tactics often deployed by employers, official unions, and Mexican labor boards.




For instance, workers were refused a copy of their own collective bargaining agreement. The company fired dozens of independent union supporters, and stalled the union election by claiming the independent metal workers union did not have the proper paperwork to represent auto parts workers.




Worse, it allowed the official union to deploy 170 thugs, “some wielding metal rods, clubs, and guns,” into the plant on the eve of the election. And workers were forced to vote out loud in front of the company, official union, and labor board officials.




TWO-WAY SOLIDARITY




The UE supported the FAT’s organizing by filing complaints under NAFTA’s labor side agreement (NAALC), as well as by providing funds, pressuring shareholders, and organizing speaking tours to draw attention to workers’ rights in Mexico.




The relationship went both ways, with the FAT providing important material support to UE’s organizing efforts and fight for labor law reforms in the United States. During a UE organizing drive at a Milwaukee foundry, the FAT provided a Mexican organizer—an activist who had been fired from a GE plant in Ciudad Juarez—to help campaign among a predominantly Mexican immigrant workforce. The organizer spread the word that the UE was not like the official unions in Mexico which so many had had bad experiences with.




The FAT has also helped draw attention to the severe limitations on labor rights in states like North Carolina—home of UE Local 150, the North Carolina Public Service Workers Union—where many public sector workers are banned from collective bargaining. Mexican unions filed complaints at the International Labor Organization challenging the ban, and the ILO issued a decision that called on North Carolina to repeal it. The FAT also filed a charge under NAALC, and the Mexican government issued a favorable report in response.




While North Carolina’s ban still persists, this work has helped legitimize the union and chip away at the law’s aura of invincibility. Alexander writes, “This was tremendously energizing for the low-wage, primarily African-American workers in North Carolina’s public sector because it turned the long-held belief that public sector workers ‘just don’t have that right’ on its head: from the perspective of international human rights law, it is the state’s ban on collective bargaining that is ‘illegal,’ not workers’ attempts to assert their rights.”




WORKER TO WORKER




Part 3 of the book details worker-to-worker exchanges, which the UE and the FAT used to deepen the solidarity and “undercut the stereotypes that existed” among members on both sides of the border.




The UE-FAT exchanges happened in both the U.S. and Mexico, with an emphasis on rank-and-file participation. Members of both unions “toured plants, exchanged experiences, walked picket lines, attended meetings, assisted with organizing drives, taught high school and university classes, and participated in radio and television programs in an effort to share information, learn about each other, and take the information back to their locals and communities.”




UE Local 150 members were part of one set of exchanges where they met public sector unionists from Mexico and Quebec (the exchanges were not always just binational). The experience raised their confidence and expectations, and led to the campaign on international law.




There have also been exchanges between co-op members of both unions, organizing institutes, and cultural exchanges, including a cross-border mural project.




It showed that “the most effective way to educate workers in the United States and in Mexico—and to motivate them to educate others—was through direct contact with each other,” writes Alexander. “I still have a vivid recollection of workers bonding over their mutual outrage that instead of bonuses the company rewarded both groups by buying them pizza.”




Although social media and Zoom have made it easier to meet with people around the world, they’re no substitute for the extended, face-to-face interactions that such exchanges allow. Yet there are remarkably few such programs in place—and our labor movements are worse off because of it. Setting up more such programs should be an urgent task—and Alexander’s book provides practical advice to help.




EXPANDING OUR VISION




There’s also a glaring need for more education for U.S. unionists about what is happening in the labor movement south of the border (not to mention all over the world)—now more important than ever, as our billionaire-backed president whips up hostility against immigrants and workers abroad.




One part of UE’s solidarity work was “Mexican Labor News and Analysis,” a monthly summary that lasted from 1996 to 2016. Reviving such a project would be a real contribution to promoting an international perspective among U.S. union members. Although the UE and the FAT are both small, they have played significant roles in expanding the vision of their countries’ labor movements. 




In Mexico, where, as Alexander writes, “the FAT and their lawyers... were dismissed as dreamers who were a little crazy when they spoke of the need for secret-ballot elections, the elimination of protection contracts, independent labor judges, or registries of unions and contracts,” the 2019 labor law reform included all of those elements. 




In the U.S., the UE played a significant role in helping a then-obscure socialist candidate named Bernie Sanders win his first election to Congress in 1990, which decades later helped pave the way for Sanders to popularize an unapologetically pro-worker politics in his two presidential campaigns.




Similarly, these two unions have set out a path for international solidarity. Could more unions follow their example, and lay the foundation for a growing sense of shared struggle by U.S. and Mexican workers as a counter to the rising forces of right-wing nationalism? Alexander’s book is a great guide for anyone looking to push their unions along that path.			     




A longer version of this article first appeared in 

New Labor Forum

.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: First Nations in B.C., environmental group call out foreign investment in liquid natural gas
content:
An announcement by the Mitsubishi Corporation (MC) Monday, which says it will partner with Blackstone Credit & Insurance in its liquefaction infrastructure holding company for the LNG Canada project in British Columbia, isn’t sitting well with some First Nations and environmental groups.

The transaction is valued at approximately US$1.6 billion.

“By investing billions in LNG Canada through American private equity funds, four of Canada’s largest pension funds have ignored their core obligations to their contributors and beneficiaries,” said Shift Action for Pension Wealth and Planet Health. The charitable organization works to protect pensions and the climate by bringing together beneficiaries and their pension funds to engage on the climate crisis.

“These pension funds are gambling their own members’ retirement savings on a high-risk, highly-polluting LNG facility that’s harming local residents and contributing to catastrophic climate change,” a news release from the group said.

On Monday, an investor consortium led by Blackstone, in partnership with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPPIB), Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System (OMERS), Investment Management Corporation of Ontario (IMCO) and Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP), announced that it would invest billions to acquire a 49.9% stake in a Mitsubishi Corporation (MC) subsidiary that holds MC’s stake in LNG Canada – a giant liquefied natural gas (LNG) export terminal near Kitimat, British Columbia (BC).

Shift said the LNG industry is “already propped up by generous public subsidies and tax shields in Canada, (and) is now relying on billions of dollars invested from Canadian workers and their retirement savings” to support the project.

The group said LNG Canada is a “high-carbon project that has been plagued by severe and ongoing operating issues. It is estimated that LNG Canada flared more gas in 2025 than any other facility in the world.”

Natural gas flaring is the controlled burning of waste or excess natural gas through a flare stack or boom at oil and gas extraction sites, refineries, and processing plants.

Among the environmental affects, it produces black carbon particles that settle on ice and snow, accelerating Arctic melt and regional warming.

The group also stated that New York-based Blackstone Inc has likely expanded its ownership into LNG Canada, and already holds existing ownership in Ksi Lisims LNG, Canada’s two largest liquefied natural gas projects.

Ksi Lisims LNG is a proposed floating natural gas liquefaction production, storage, and offloading facility with a marine terminal located on the north coast of British Columbia. Prime Minister Mark Carney referred Ksi Lisims LNG to the Major Projects Office on Nov. 13, 2025.

The project referral also includes the 800-kilometre Prince Rupert Gas Transmission Project to supply feed gas for liquefaction, and a 95-kilometre electrical transmission line to supply electricity to the facility.

“As Indigenous Peoples, we follow our LAW to protect Land, Air, Water, all humans depend on these. These projects destroy our law – yet our pension funds are choosing to ignore our laws and our rights when investing in LNG Canada,” said Chief Na’Moks, Hereditary Chief of the Tsayu (Beaver Clan) of the Wet’suwet’en Nation.

“Just last month, I spoke to the CPP executives about the lack of consent for major parts of this project, and they heard overwhelmingly from other pension members and beneficiaries that we do not want our hard-earned dollars to be invested in oil and gas projects that are destroying our climate,” Chief Na’Moks said.

“Why are they choosing to ignore Indigenous leaders and a clear chorus of voices who are opposed to this move. Why would we allow this?”

On October 6, Indigenous leaders and health and environmental groups also hold a news conference on Parliament Hill to announce a challenge over Export Development Canada’s financing of maritime liquefied natural gas (LNG) infrastructure.

In April 2026, it was revealed that LNG Canada has been excessively flaring up to an average of 40 times more gas than its permits allow and continues to experience ongoing operational issues due to a defect in the main flare stack.

The groups also emphasize that LNG Canada’s expansion modules will be built in China, and Ksi Lisims LNG’s modules by Samsung Heavy Industries in South Korea, and claim both projects’ primary economic benefits will not remain in Canada.

Protest outside First Nations–First Ministers Meeting decry closed doors and ‘economic coercion’

Prime minister announces 5 major ‘national’ projects that include LNG, mining and nuclear energy

Blackstone holds ownership in Ksi Lisims LNG through a private equity placement into Texas-based Western LNG, which is “the entity that will construct, own and operate the assets of the Project,” according to the province of B.C.

The groups further noted that Blackstone founder, Chairman and CEO is multi-billionaire Stephen Schwarzman, who is an informal advisor and close ally to United States President Donald Trump.

Leanne has a certificate in broadcasting and has more than 12 years of radio news experience, both as an anchor and reporter in Saskatchewan and Alberta. The Métis journalist is a passionate writer and born storyteller and loves to connect with people and learn about their life experiences.

author: Victoria Valenzuela
title: Incarcerated Los Angeles Youth Fought for the Right to Hug Their Parents — and Won
content:
This story was co-published with

 

Truthout

.




Mercedes Maradiaga sat across from her 19-year-old son in the Los Padrinos Juvenile Hall in Los Angeles in complete devastation. Her son had at that point been incarcerated at the prison for two years and she had visited him every weekend. But that day in September 2024 was especially hard because it was their first visit since he had been beaten by officers earlier that week in a space in the jail where there were no cameras. The guards had jumped on and kicked him, and he needed surgery for a torn ACL. All she wanted was to give him a hug and reassure him that she was there. However, because of the no-contact visit policies at Los Padrinos, she was unable to give him that comfort.




Even during birthdays and holidays, they weren’t allowed to embrace. The boy endured the jail’s horrible living conditions — including rat infestations and flooded toilets — but couldn’t hug his mom for a moment of escape.




“I couldn’t even let him know I’m here just with the little hug,” Maradiaga said. “It would have meant everything to him. It was sad, and I did that for four years.”




Los Padrinos had 

reopened a year earlier

 in 2023, after being shut down in 2019 due to conditions that violated the Board of State and Community Corrections (BSCC) standards, including abuses by staff. Six officers were criminally charged with 

assault and child abuse

 for using pepper spray on several teenage girls. Reports 

also cited a decreasing youth population

 as a factor for closure, yet staff 

claimed to feel “outnumbered.”

 When Los Padrinos closed, youth were shuffled to another facility called Central Juvenile Hall — and then in 2023, that facility was closed down due to similar issues. Los Padrinos reopened, and just months later, the abuses restarted. In 2025, 

30 officers were criminally charged

 by the California Attorney General with child endangerment and abuse, conspiracy, and battery for encouraging “gladiator fights” that pit youth against each other.




Olivia Shields, a justice transformation policy coordinator at Urban Peace Institute, described the constant closing and reopening of BSCC facilities as a “cycle of noncompliance.” Shields said the Los Angeles County Probation Department has ultimately failed with these maneuvers to address the core issue: unmet youth needs — which won’t be addressed through incarceration but through coordinated care in the form of individualized, robust support systems and resources.




“Rather than decarcerate these populations of young people and find community-based alternatives or step-downs for as many of them as possible, they basically shift the youth around from facility to facility to avoid noncompliance,” Shields said.




Long before the closing of Los Padrinos in 2019, the facility had a bad reputation among Angelenos. Maradiaga recalled hearing disturbing stories about the facility in the ’80s when she was a kid.




“I think it needs to be shut down,” Maradiaga said. “I think that there needs to be a better way for the youth. I don’t think locking them away from their family is the answer.”













The Appeal in Your Inbox




Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.
































          Sign Up
        
















Barred From Basic Human Contact




When Ilana Parach, executive director and co-founder of 

Hoops 4 Justice

, went inside Los Padrinos with a basketball and mentorship program, she quickly learned about what youth were facing inside. She felt it was important to give them a platform to express their needs directly, so she pivoted to working with them on legislation.




“They made a list of specific programs they wanted — resources for their families, reentry support,” Parach said. “At the bottom of that list, they wrote, ‘We want to hug our moms.’”




Incarcerated youth directly told her that one parent who hugged her son during a visit on his birthday then had her visit terminated and future visits suspended for two weeks. She said another youth was incarcerated for three years and had no choice but to watch his mother cry during the visits because she couldn’t hug him.




Contact visitation policies vary across California and are often left at the discretion of correctional officers. Parach said youth and staff both told her that Los Padrinos stopped allowing contact visits after the pandemic. Parach said that during meetings of the board of supervisors, she heard officers citing staffing shortages, financial issues, and concerns about drugs as reasons for disallowing contact visits. Still, visitors have to go through extensive screening when they come through a facility, including going through body scanners, sniffing by drug dogs, and X-ray scanners for their belongings.




“How could a young person’s parent bring in those drugs into a facility when they cannot even hug their loved one,” said Emily Zamora, policy and campaign coordinator at Youth Justice Coalition, an abolitionist organization that empowers impacted youth to dismantle the system.




Parach knew it wasn’t right that the youth weren’t allowed to embrace their family members, so she brought elected officials in to hear their stories. One of the elected officials who visited was California Assemblymember Isaac Bryan, who later introduced the 

Hug

 

Act

, the bill authored by the youth. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed it into law on September 27. The newly passed law will make it a right for all youth in juvenile detention centers to hug their parents, no longer leaving it at the discretion of the probation department that oversees the youth facilities.




Parach said it is important to center young people and amplify their voices.




“I think that they have to keep the kids at the center of the decisions,” Parach said. “Not just figuratively, but I think youth literally have to continue to provide direct input because they’re the ones that understand their needs the most, and making decisions about them without them is a detriment to all of us.”




Abolishing Youth Incarceration




Many youth advocates, youth, and families say the Hug Act was long overdue.




“It’s really devastating that it has taken up to this point towards this becoming legislation … for young people to be able to hug their loved ones,” Zamora said. “But the fact that this has been like something that hasn’t been around is honestly inhumane.”




Now, some of the organizers who had pushed to make the Hug Act a reality are continuing their longer struggle: shutting down dangerous facilities like Los Padrinos, and decarcerating youth out of the system altogether.




Shields said it’s inhumane not to allow young people who are going through the worst experience in their lives to hug their loved ones and experience the kind of comfort that they and their loved ones desperately need in these moments. And beyond that, incarcerated youth have been shuffled around various facilities as they have opened and closed and reopened.




“Detention is not a place where young people will have their needs met … It’s not something that we can reform our way out of.”




Shields said that after Los Padrinos reopened in 2023, “It was just pure chaos. Because this was like a dilapidated facility that hadn’t been used in years, and it hadn’t been updated in any way, shape, or form, and then you’re just putting a bunch of young people there.”




“Detention is not a place where young people will have their needs met,” Shields said. “The culture of probation and the culture of the way that they’re treating young people … is so deeply entrenched. It’s not something that we can reform our way out of.”




Justice advocates in Los Angeles have been calling out the youth incarceration system for years. In 2022, their campaign to put pressure on the Los Angeles Board of Supervisors resulted in the creation of the 

Department of Youth Development

 (DYD) to transition to a care-first approach. Shields said DYD is a county-run entity, which involves navigating tough bureaucratic barriers. The department and the work that they are building is new, requiring constant tending and resources from the board, as well as work to stay rooted in the vision and strategy of youth and community advocates.




Shields and Zamora believe in community-based care and alternatives to incarceration, rather than youth detention. They are also proponents of credible messenger programs in which someone from an organization connects youth to resources and opportunities both while they are incarcerated and after they return home so they have a support system when they leave, with the ultimate aim of decarceration.




“A lot of the young people that we work with will talk about why a credible messenger was so much more impactful for them than a probation officer and being incarcerated,” Shields said.




Zamora said detained youth have told her about many cases of medical neglect in Los Padrinos. In one case that her organization highlighted at the time, she says a 

young person drank bleach

 to get the attention of staff and finally get seen by a nurse. She said she also heard about a teenager in Los Padrinos who didn’t get to hug their parent before the parent passed away because of the no-contact visiting policy. Additionally, she has heard 

a lot about overdoses

 in the facility. She said Los Padrinos should have stayed closed given its huge track record of corruption and abuse.




The Youth Justice Coalition operates in a space that previously operated as the David V. Kenyon Juvenile Justice Center courthouse, where youth were detained and often given long sentences. Zamora said the transformation of the building from a punitive space into a place where youth find community and empowerment, as well as a garden and high school for system-impacted youth, gives her hope for what abolition can look like.




“This space is such a testament to what it looks like to shut down facilities that do not serve our communities and do not serve our young people … so that we could support these young people in being who they can be under the conditions that they deserve,” Zamora said.




Shields said there is a coalition of youth justice organizations in Los Angeles that will continue drawing attention to the conditions inside, showing up to the BSCC and board of supervisors’ meetings, and amplifying what they have been hearing from young people about how egregious those conditions are.




“We can’t incarcerate our way out of lack of safety,” Shields said, adding that instead we must find “a way to not reform but transform the youth justice system so that it really is rooted in love, care, healing, and a different form of accountability.”




The post 

Incarcerated Los Angeles Youth Fought for the Right to Hug Their Parents — and Won

 appeared first on 

The Appeal

author: Sharon Zhang
title: House Democrats Want Stevens Out of Their Caucus After Her “Despicable Betrayal”
content:
The Michigan Democratic Party’s chair removed Haley Stevens from the party for endorsing Abdul El-Sayed’s opponent.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

A growing number of House Democrats are calling for Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Michigan) to be expelled from their caucus after she seemingly broke rules in her surprise endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers in the tight Senate race in Michigan on Sunday, marked by some as a “despicable betrayal.”

According to Politico, at least eight Democrats were supportive of some form of punishment by Democratic leaders as of Sunday afternoon, with likely many more also quietly on board. Top progressive Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), the former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said that Stevens “has shown her true colors.”

“She is supporting a candidate for Senate that is a rubber stamp for Trump’s disastrous and dangerous administration,” said Jayapal. “She has no place in our party. This is exactly why she lost the primary despite tens of millions of dollars and why she is of no relevance to the future of this country.”

Rep. Marc Veasey (D-Texas), who supported Stevens in the primary, told outlets he backs her ousting. “I was the first Caucus member to host a fundraiser for her Senate bid. And, I’d be the first to make the motion to remove her,” he said, per Politico.

“Capitulating to fascism, Islamophobia, racism and the policies hurting everyday Americans makes you unfit to serve with the Democratic caucus,” said Rep. Delia C. Ramirez (D-Illinois) in a post on social media. “Shame on Haley Stevens. She must be removed from the caucus.”

Democratic caucus rules specify that members can’t “participate in campaign activities for any candidate in a partisan federal election who is not a Member of the Democratic Party.” Members can be expelled by a two-thirds vote.

Stevens has already faced some retribution. As of Sunday, Stevens was removed from the House Democrats’ text chains. Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel Jr. also said that Stevens “is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.” And a huge proportion of her staff have resigned, including her former communications director, expressing disgust with the lawmaker.

Stevens, whose political career has been marked by her vehement support of Israel, put out a shock endorsement of Rogers after appearing at a Black church service with the GOP candidate on Sunday. This came just days after saying that she was going to do a campaign event at a Black church with primary opponent Abdul El-Sayed, and after she evidently swore in private conversations with several Democrats that she wouldn’t back Rogers.

The decision set off a political earthquake just two days before the general election on Tuesday, with Stevens swearing that she is still a Democrat and backs the party in other races.

Numerous Black politicians and commentators have noted that it was especially cynical for Stevens to use Black voters — who overwhelmingly back El-Sayed in the race — and a Black church to debut her support for Rogers.

Progressive Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Massachusetts) said that Stevens used Black people as a “prop.” Pressley said that Stevens personally swore in a conversation that she would back El-Sayed.

“Well, Haley, I guess in this instance you’ve chosen a white supremacist order and then have the audacity to use Black people as a prop and as a shield for your ignorance,” Pressley said.

“She used Black people as a prop to pursue an agenda of sore loser-ness,” said political organizer Stacey Abrams in an interview with MS NOW. “Her personal animus has now overtaken her respect for the Black people with whom she worshipped and for every Michigander from whom she has requested a vote.”

Stevens’s defection is a major test for Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), who is slated to become the next House speaker if the party retakes the House.

The Democratic leader hinted at punishment for Stevens in remarks to Politico. “Haley Stevens made a terrible decision, blindsided everyone and isolated herself from the House Democratic caucus. We will have a discussion about appropriate next steps upon our return,” Jeffries said.

But Jeffries has faced criticism over his failure to rein in other defectors before. In September, Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine), a fellow staunch pro-Israel Democrat, broke with the party to endorse Republican Rep. Mike Lawler (R-New York) in his tight race for reelection against Democrat Cait Conley. Jeffries has had harsh words for Lawler after that endorsement, but has barely mentioned Golden’s defection.

title: Dockers Shut Down Over 100 Ports Worldwide Against Genocide, Wars; Brazil’s Mass Mobilization for Lula Offers Lessons For US Workers; Prairieland “Antifa” Convictions Threaten Political Speech (Pacific Radio’s Capitalism, Race & Democracy)
content:
By Capitalism, Race & Democracy

Following Flávio Bolsonaro’s strong showing in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election, millions of young people, workers, and retirees took to the streets in a massive mobilization against the far right. The protests shifted the dynamics of the election, helping bring an additional 10 million voters to the polls and contributing to Lula’s victory. The message from the streets was clear: the Brazilian people did not want a far-right government backed by Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu.

Fabio Bosco, a transit worker in São Paulo and a supporter of Conlutas, Brazil’s national labor federation, spoke to Pacifica’s Steve Zeltzer about the mass mobilization.

How Millions Rallied In Brazil For Lula & Lessons For US Working Class With Fabio Bosco

On October 30, dockworkers in more than 100 ports around the world took part in a coordinated day of action. Workers shut down port operations and joined tens of thousands of other workers and young people in demonstrations against the genocide in Gaza and imperialist wars. In the United States, the only labor action took place at the Port of Oakland, where members of ILWU Locals 10 and 34 joined community supporters for a rally in solidarity with Palestine and against militarism.

Clarence Thomas, retired secretary-treasurer of ILWU Local 10, spoke about the significance of this international mobilization.

The current ILWU local 10 President Mike Villeggiante spoke to Pacifica’s Steve Zeltzer about how his union connected with the global day of action.

Next, April, a member of Gabriela, a Filipino women’s organization, and the Defend Negros Island Campaign of Northern California, spoke about the connections between struggles here and in the Philippines. She discussed their shared fight against C & H Sugar Company in Crockett, California, and the importance of building solidarity across labor and community movements.

Global Day Of Action & Docks In Trieste As Action Against Genocide,Wars & Attacks On Working Class

ILWU 10 Leaders Speak Out On Dockers International Day Of Action At Port of Oakland On Oct 30, 2026

ILWU 10 & 34, Supporters Rally Against Genocide, Wars & Attacks On Working Class At Oakland Port

At 10/30 Action At Port Of Oakland, ILWU10 Retired Sec of Treas. Clarence Thomas On Genocide & War

Back on March 25th we aired an interview of Amber Lowrey, sister of one of the Prairieland defendants in north Texas. All nine of those charged with federal crimes had just been convicted of at least one terrorism-related charge stemming from a “noise” and fireworks demonstration in support of detained immigrants at an ICE prison in Alvarado, Texas on July 4, 2025. Today we air a portion of a panel discussion hosted by Chip Gibbons, Policy Director at Defending Rights & Dissent. The moderator is the National Lawyers Guild’s “Mass Defense Initiative” attorney Xavier de Janon. Dario Sanchez, a state-level defendant in the case and Seth Stern of the Freedom of the Press Foundation make up the rest of the panel exploring the implications of these ramped up “terrorism” convictions for political speech and action in Trump’s America.

In our July 7th show of this year, we reported on the outlandish sentences imposed on the eight federal Prairieland defendants by two federal judges — a combined 450 years imprisonment with sentences ranging from 30 to 100 years! All of those cases are currently on appeal. For updates on their cases, appeals, and to support their defense efforts, see the website https://prairielanddefendants.com/.

We thank all of Pacifica’s sister stations and affiliates that contribute to the production of this show. Today’s program was produced by the Capitalism, Race & Democracy collective, with contributions from Steve Zeltzer, Ann Garrison, Polina Vasiliev, and Thomas O’Rourke.

You can find this and all previous episodes at our website “capitalism race and democracy dot ORG”. Don’t forget to subscribe. Follow us on X, formerly Twitter, @PacificaCRD.

title: Hitting the mark: “Grand Theft Capital”, by Fred Magdoff and John Bellamy Foster
content:
REVIEWS




The Guardian

: “Trump’s billionaire-blue collar coalition has been smashed by class politics” by 

Aditya Chakrabortty




“…Over decades – through Reagan and Clinton, Bush and Obama – Republicans and Democrats have changed the tax code to reward ownership rather than earning, so the richest 400 households 

now pay lower rates of tax

 than the bottom 50% of Americans. As the radical economists Fred Magdoff and John Bellamy Foster show in their new book,

 Grand Theft Capital: What Workers Should Know About the Affordability Crisis

, the share of national income going to ordinary workers has slumped from 30% in the 1960s to 20% today. This is the destruction of working-class lives and dreams in which Republicans and Democrats colluded. This is the American carnage that in 2016 helped propel Trump into the White House. But the most glaring feature of this era of Trumponomics has been its shameless inequality….” 

Read more

…. 

And you can see the A

dam Smith Institute’s miffed response

 to his piece, here…if you are interested in how weak it is.







Red Pepper

 picks: “

Botany, welfare, friendships, work and housing. 

David Matthews

 picks six of the best new books for leftists

“




“Capitalism has been stagnating for decades, characterized by sluggish growth. Yet the wealthy continue to grow richer while the rest of us face declining wages and eroding living standards. Focusing on the United States yet deeply relevant to Britain and other capitalist countries, Magdoff and Bellamy Foster make clear that in a climate of economic decline, big business has deliberately and strategically targeted workers as a primary source of wealth extraction. Their conclusion is a call for mass action, from below…”




People’s Voice 

(Canada): 

“Succinct and accessible, this economic primer hits the mark for working people today”

, by Stéphane Doucet




“Magdoff and Foster have truly hit the mark with this short book…Interesting figures include the precipitous drop of work stoppages involving over 1000 workers, from over 330 per year in 1975 to less than 20 since the 2010’s; the corporate tax rate being more than halved since 1950; the CEO-to-worker pay ratio being multiplied by more than 10 times in 60 years; labour’s share of GDP dropping more than 10 percent since the 1960’s; and private sector workers with defined-benefit pensions dropping for 60 percent to 10 percent of the workforce. All these are very broad, clear, decisive and very powerful figures. The book provides many more, along with the necessary context…” 

Read more

…




Counterpunch

: “

Why Working People Got the Blues

“, by Ron Jacobs




“The lack of affordability is the curse of the working class, whether its individual members are working or not. Politicians talk about it and some might even propose legislation to moderate it, but the cost of almost everything keeps going up more than wages and retirement benefits. The domination of the economy by monopolies and cartels–many of which are invested in the business of war and resource extraction–and by politicians at their service means the bills they rack up are going to be paid by us. When the ruling class tells us they can’t afford to continue providing social services, they’re lying. It’s not that they can’t, it’s that their priorities lie elsewhere, with consistently higher profits being near or at the forefront.” 

Read more…

here

author: Erica Chenoweth
title: Will historic protests against ICE shape the midterms?
content:
This article 

Will historic protests against ICE shape the midterms?

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







Tomorrow’s midterm elections are widely viewed as a referendum on Trump’s second presidency. 

Prior studies

 have found strong associations between protest and U.S. election outcomes, including the 

2010

 and 

2018

 midterm elections. Protests can influence popular 

opinion

 on policy issues, boost turnout among eligible voters, and shape how candidates 

set policy priorities

.




At the Crowd Counting Consortium, or CCC, we have tallied an 

extraordinary number of protests

 since Donald Trump’s second inauguration in January 2025. The majority of protests in Trump’s second term so far have named democracy or the presidency itself as a primary claim — think the nationwide Hands Off and No Kings protests in 2025 and 2026. 




But among protests focused on more specific policy domains, one key theme stands out. The administration’s anti-immigration policies and expansive, violent crackdown on immigrants have generated active, grassroots support 

networks

 in neighborhoods across the country and fueled a wave of protests in support of immigrants’ rights. During Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis and St. Paul, protests took place in over 30 percent of counties containing 80 percent of the nation’s population. March 2026 may have been the month with the highest number of pro-immigrant protests in U.S. history. A significant proportion of these protests occurred in counties that Trump won in 2024. 




Trends in immigration-related protests since January 20, 2017




Of course, the current wave of protest builds on a longer-term foundation of pro-immigrant demonstrations. Since the CCC started collecting data on protest in the United States in 2017, we’ve seen that protests against the federal government’s immigration policies have been a constant feature of the protest landscape across all three presidential administrations — Trump 1, Biden and Trump 2 (see Table 1). 




Table 1: Immigration protest events as a share of all left/liberal protests







Little more than a week after Trump’s first inauguration in January 2017, numerous protests took place around the country in response to his Jan. 27 signing of Executive Order 13769, sometimes called the “Muslim Ban,” which restricted citizens of seven majority-Muslim countries from entering the U.S. On Jan. 28 and 29, mass protests occurred in and around airports, where immigrant rights groups and community members assembled to ensure the safe arrival of citizens of those countries who were in transit when the executive order went into effect. Protests against the executive order continued in February 2017 under the slogan “No Ban No Wall.” The Trump administration ultimately revised the executive order to a narrower version that the U.S. Supreme Court upheld as lawful; multiple protests followed on June 26, 2018. 




But the biggest jumps in protest participation came on coordinated, nationwide days of action related to the administration’s immigration policies. The first, on June 30, 2018, was a national day of action declaring that “Families Belong Together.” These protests demanded an end to the administration’s “child separation policy” — the practice of separating migrant children from parents and caretakers upon arrival at the U.S.-Mexico border — which was in effect under the Obama administration but escalated under Trump. This protest campaign was highly effective: The pressure placed on the administration led the White House to end the policy through an 

executive order

, though loopholes remained.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










On Jan. 19, 2019, the third annual Women’s March on Washington represented an additional increase in coordinated nationwide protests in which immigrants’ rights were a core issue. And July 12, 2019 saw the 

Lights for Liberty

 day of action, which attempted to pressure elected officials (particularly in the newly Democratic Congress) to close detention centers and adopt more humane immigration policies. Ultimately, congressional Democrats introduced legislation in 2021 to reunite immigrant children with their families. In sum, the first Trump administration saw an impressive range of protests on behalf of immigrants’ rights, some of which had powerful impacts. 




Overall, the Biden administration saw a decline in such protests, with about 60 percent fewer than during the first Trump administration (seven percent to 11 percent as a share of overall left/liberal protests, respectively). Notable days of action during the Biden administration included continued protests calling for closure of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, detention centers, as well as protests against ongoing family detention and separation practices, and protests against asylum restrictions during a major surge in deportations in 2024. 




During the second Trump administration, such protests have seen a breathtaking rise. 




Figure 1 provides a comparative view of the number of immigration-related protests under the second Trump administration, compared to the first. The y-axis, showing the cumulative number of immigration-related protests since Trump’s two inaugurations, demonstrates the massive scale and steady climb of protests during his second term so far.




Figure 1: Counts of pro-immigrant protest events during Trump’s first and second terms







Figure 2 shows the frequency of such events on a monthly basis. There have been more protests in support of immigrants in seven of the months since January 2025 than in any of the 48 months of Trump’s first term. In 10 of the first 17 months of the current term, protests against Trump’s immigration policies made up over 20 percent of total protests. Few other protest claims have animated the public with such enduring salience over time.




Figure 2: Pro-immigrant protests in the U.S., January 20, 2017 – May 31, 2026







Figure 2 also shows clear increases in the number of immigration-related protests during nationwide anti-Trump protests. Spikes in activity occurred on April 19, 2025 during the Hands Off protests; on October 18, 2025, when many No Kings protests adopted opposition to ICE and Trump’s mass deportation agenda as a central claim; and on March 28, 2026, when the third No Kings protests again made immigration a primary claim. Our tallies have also documented 170 repeater events (protests that are scheduled to take place daily, weekly or monthly) that specifically mention immigrant rights or opposition to ICE in their stated claims.




In Illinois and Minnesota, protests started local and went national




Trump’s immigration policies have produced particularly intense local mobilizations in areas that saw escalated ICE deployments, which then diffused to solidarity protests nationwide. For example, from early September to mid-November 2025, ICE launched Operation Midway Blitz targeting immigrants in Chicago. During that period, the CCC documented 3,491 protest events in opposition to Trump’s immigration policies, starting in Chicago and spreading across the country during the No Kings mobilization on Oct. 18, 2025, which named immigration as a central issue.




Operation Metro Surge

, the federal immigration enforcement operation in the Minneapolis-St. Paul region, also provoked powerful opposition locally and beyond, with over 4,400 protests taking place between Dec. 2, 2025 and Jan. 31, 2026. Significant numbers of protests responded to specific, publicized government abuses, such as aggressive law enforcement actions against immigrants, the killings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti, and the detention of a 5-year-old child of a Colombian immigrant. Three waves of action stood out: the ICE Out For Good weekend of action on Jan. 10-11; the Day of Truth & Freedom on Jan. 23, which was concentrated in Minnesota; and the National Shutdown and ICE Out of Everywhere actions, which mainly spanned Jan. 30-31, with some events lasting into Feb. 1. 




Figure 3 shows the number of counties that saw pro-immigrant protests in Illinois and Minnesota, respectively, after Operation Midway began in Chicago and Operation Metro Surge began in Minneapolis-St. Paul. Overall, these two states saw higher-than-average numbers of counties featuring protests, including among counties far afield from the major cities in which ICE focused its deployments. 




Figure 3. Pro-immigrant protests in Illinois and Minnesota during and after ICE operations in Chicago and Minneapolis-St. Paul







Nationwide, the total volume of protest produced during early 2026 is extraordinary. 




January 2026 alone featured the fourth-most protest events recorded in all 10 years of CCC data, owing to the massive number of protests in Minnesota and around the country in opposition to Operation Metro Surge and its impacts, and to Trump’s immigration agenda in general. 




And the events in Minnesota seem to have been a flashpoint. Anti-ICE protests continued in February and March 2026, and anti-ICE claims were central to the nationwide No Kings mobilization on March 28. March 2026 may have been the month with the highest number of pro-immigrant protests in U.S. history (see Table 2).




Table 2: Top 10 months by total protest events, January 20, 2017 – May 31, 2026







Protests opposing Trump’s immigration policies were reported in 933 counties during Operation Metro Surge, between Dec. 2, 2025 and Feb. 1, 2026 — about 30 percent of all counties in the U.S. These counties were densely populated: Together, they contain more than 80 percent of the U.S. population (see Figure 4). From March 2026 through May 2026, the CCC continued to record thousands of events protesting ICE, with hundreds of distinct civic organizations and hundreds of thousands of people participating. 




Figure 4: U.S. immigration protests following ICE deployments to Minneapolis







Nor are protests against ICE operations an exclusively liberal phenomenon. Instead, there has been a stark increase over time in the number of pro-immigrant protests in counties that Trump won in 2024 by at least a 5-point margin (see Figure 5). Among the pro-immigrant protests that occurred in March 2026, about 40 percent of them occurred in such counties. 




Figure 5: Pro-immigrant protests in counties Trump won by >5 Points in the 2024 Presidential Election, January 20, 2017 – May 31, 2026







Across the country, a broad range of constituencies using a variety of means have expressed opposition to Trump’s immigration policy. Demonstrations have just been one method. Those activating on behalf of and in support of immigrants include people forming human chains to 

protect

 immigrant workers; neighborhoods organizing support networks for affected immigrant families; students engaging in 

walkouts

 from schools and protests at college 

career fairs

; people engaging in 

hunger strikes

 in support of international and undocumented students; 

knitters

 engaging in “craftivism”; people holding 

encampments

 outside of ICE facilities or 

noise demonstrations

 outside of hotels in which ICE agents were housed; consumers engaging in boycotts and sell-backs at 

Target 

and 

Home Depot

; clergy engaging in 

civil disobedience

; communities holding 

vigils 

for slain immigrants or those killed while advocating for them; community members building 

raised beds

 across thoroughfares to prevent ICE vehicles from accessing facilities, and more. Institutions and employers have raised their voices: Local businesses and business associations have called for the end of ICE operations in their towns, ranchers and farmers have decried treatment of their immigrant employees, and the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops has condemned mistreatment of immigrants as well.




Counter-protest was minimal




Trump’s immigration policies 

have supporters

 in the country, particularly among Republicans. But few people have rallied or marched in defense of them. Right-leaning protests made up fewer than two percent of all immigration-related protests during the first 14 months of the first Trump administration, and less than 0.7 percent of immigration-related protests during the same stretch of his second administration. 




The frequency of pro-immigrant protests during Trump’s second term has eclipsed that of anti-immigration protests by 145 to 1. The vast majority of anti-immigration protests have been counter-protests occurring at demonstrations in support of immigrants and their rights. 




However, right-leaning protests have been increasingly characterized by anti-immigrant claims over the past three presidencies. Whereas anti-immigrant protests constituted 1.68 percent of all right-learning protests during Trump’s first term, that proportion has increased sevenfold so far during his second, to 12.43 percent. 




Table 3: Anti-immigration protest events as a share of all right/conservative protests







A powerful and growing pro-immigrant constituency




Today’s mass protests in support of immigrants’ rights build on a durable pattern of pro-immigrant and anti-ICE protest in the U.S. To wit, the CCC has documented a prayer 

protest

 outside an ICE facility in Broadview, Illinois that has been held every Friday for the past 20 years. 




But the recent increase in pro-immigrant protests and their intensity is notable. The breadth and volume of pro-immigrant protests show that committed activists and organizations have succeeded in rallying huge numbers in favor of justice and dignity for immigrants, indicating a durable underlying infrastructure. In this essay, we focused on street protest as one indicator in the overall picture. But community mobilization on behalf of immigrants has meant far more than demonstrations. Mutual aid and neighborly support, observing and documenting ICE operations, litigation, support to immigrants in detention, and direct appeals to public officials have all been central to America’s response to Trump’s immigration policies. The growth of pro-immigrant protests reflects a (potentially growing) constituency willing to take risks to defend a multicultural vision of America, potentially widening its appeal. 
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













In short, we see capable organizers and the mass public pushing hard for humane treatment of immigrants for the foreseeable future. Neither political party has figured out how to address immigration in a way that resolves the need for safe and secure borders and the need to treat everyone on U.S. soil with dignity, decency and due process. But the impacts of Trump’s policies on immigrants, their families and their broader communities provide a galvanizing issue for Americans who otherwise agree on little else. For example, some 

conservative faith communities

 and various progressive groups increasingly find themselves on the same side when it comes to immigration. 




Policymakers often resist turning to activists, civil society organizations and community groups for policy solutions. But the persistence of multi-sectoral immigration activism, as seen through protest alone, also reflects a powerful and growing constituency in favor of just and humane approaches to immigration. Protests reflect and shape the existing moral consensus but also can reorient constituencies in favor of a new consensus. We hope the members of the next Congress pay attention.

Will historic protests against ICE shape the midterms?

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence
