title: Peace Mothers: There will be no peace until our leader reunites with his people
content:
Peace Mothers from 24 cities gathered in Ankara to demand the physical freedom of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan and concrete steps within the framework of the peace and democratic society process. The mothers, who are set to hold a “Peace Vigil,” issued a statement at Parliament Park. Carrying a banner reading “Take steps for peace, Parliament must act,” the mothers chanted slogans including “A thousand greetings to Imralı,” “Long live the resistance in the prisons,” and “Women do not want war, they want peace.”




Speaking on behalf of the group, Peace Mother Meryem Korkmaz stated that Öcalan’s legal status had still not been recognized. “The architect of peace is still on Imralı. We demand that the promises made be fulfilled and that steps be taken toward peace. We have always stood for peace. We do not accept any interruption of this process. Steps must be taken without delay. Our leader’s status must be secured, and the prisoners must be released. Only then can peace be achieved,” she said.




Peace Mother Mürvet Demir stated: “We will not stop until peace is achieved. There will be no peace until our leader’s status is secured and those in prison and in the mountains return. There will be no peace until our leader reunites with his people. That is why we are here.”




Kezban Kalın, the mother of an army lieutenant, also addressed the gathering, saying: “I wholeheartedly share the suffering of these mothers. If they are calling for peace, we cannot remain indifferent after so much suffering. Justice is necessary for all of us. Everyone must take responsibility and do their part.”

title: Aygül Yağış: Save our young people from drugs
content:
Alongside special warfare policies, drug use, betting, gambling, gang activity and incidents of individual violence are among the major social problems in Kurdistan. Field studies conducted by civil society organisations and bar associations indicate that addiction is becoming increasingly widespread, particularly among young people, while families continue to call for solutions. According to available data, the age at which children begin using drugs has fallen to as low as nine, while a significant proportion of users are first introduced to drugs through their friends.




Reports published in the media indicate that 71.2 percent of drug users were first introduced to drugs between the ages of 15 and 24, while 74.4 percent first obtained drugs from friends or people in their immediate social circles. The Turkish Green Crescent's 2025 Gambling Report also highlighted that the age at which people begin gambling has fallen to 15.




According to data from the Diyarbakır (Amed) Bar Association, lawyers were appointed to represent 2,173 people prosecuted for drug production and trafficking between 1 January and 9 September 2023. Lawyers were also appointed to represent 291 people accused of drug use or purchasing, accepting or possessing drugs for personal use.




Growing concerns include young people being drawn into addiction, the weakening of social ties and the increasing economic vulnerability of families, while special warfare policies continue to be systematically implemented in the region.




Aygül Yağış, who said that many families around her were struggling with similar problems, has been fighting for years to free her son from drug addiction. Yağış stated that young people were being drawn into drug use very quickly and found it difficult to overcome addiction. She drew particular attention to the targeting of young people and children from patriotic families.




‘We did everything we could, but we could not save him’




Aygül Yağış described the difficult experiences her son had endured because of drug addiction. She said that the family had searched for a solution for a long time but had been unable to achieve any results. Yağış, whose son struggled with addiction for six years, said: "Recently, almost everyone around us and in our families has been affected by these policies. The person closest to me who was affected was my son. Unfortunately, he went through a long and difficult period because of drug addiction and was eventually arrested.




My son was working in another city. When he returned here, he started using drugs. He began taking drugs while spending time with his friends. We did everything we could and tried every possible intervention, but we could not save him from addiction. Eventually, he completely lost control of himself. When he was under the influence of drugs, he was not himself and was constantly aggressive. When he came to his senses, he apologised to everyone. He was suddenly drawn into this situation, and before we could understand what was happening, he had become addicted."




‘Even his arrest did not free him from addiction’




Aygül Yağış said that her son sometimes told her about what he was experiencing. She explained: "Sometimes he would tell me, 'Mum, the police come and see us, then take notes and leave.' I repeatedly told him that this was not happening for no reason. Many investigations were opened against him after his arrest. From the day he started using drugs, I never once saw him in a good condition. We tried everything, but we could not persuade him to stop. He remained in this situation for six years and was eventually arrested.




I thought he might get better after his arrest. Even he used to say, 'Maybe I can overcome this if I go to prison.' But despite being imprisoned, nothing has changed in his condition. Moreover, it is not only my son. Many people around him are struggling with the same problem. All these people live here. We also see people coming here from other provinces to use drugs."




‘Everyone, from children to the elderly, is gambling’




Aygül Yağış pointed out that betting and gambling, as well as drug use, were becoming increasingly widespread among young people, placing families under economic and social strain. She said that families were worried about protecting their children and were being forced to send them elsewhere.




Yağış continued: "All mothers and families are now complaining about this situation. People are extremely afraid that their young people will be led down the wrong path. They do everything they can to protect them. Out of fear, they send their children to other places. Our young people need to be freed from this situation. It is not just drug use. Betting and gambling among young people are also spiralling out of control. Someone introduced my son to drugs by telling him, 'Take this to someone else.' Once he started using drugs, he could not give them up."




Yağış also described the difficulties faced by people who had accumulated gambling debts. She said, "I saw an elderly man crying because of his gambling debts. This is what people have been reduced to, and the situation is driving both families and young people into poverty."




‘Children from patriotic families are being targeted’




Aygül Yağış described these developments as part of special warfare policies, stating that young people, particularly children from patriotic families, were being targeted. She pointed out that young people were being pushed away from social relationships.




Yağış said: "Our young people need to be freed from this situation. Young people, particularly children from patriotic families, are being targeted. It is not only young people; mothers and fathers are also being targeted. The attitude is that young people should not throw stones, but they can do whatever else they want. That is why young people are being targeted. They do not even allow two young people to come together."







 







‘Necessary steps must be taken to find a solution’




Aygül Yağış appealed to all sections of society to take action against addiction, emphasising that political parties and public institutions must assume responsibility. She called for young people to be freed from addiction.




Yağış said: "Everyone must do whatever they can. Whether political parties or the state, everyone must make an effort to put an end to this situation. This is the only demand of our families: save these young people from this poison. We have had enough. Almost every family has a son or a child caught up in this poison. Save our young people from this poison. We do not want any mother or any young person to suffer."

title: ‘No independent investigations conducted into murders of journalist in the Kurdistan Region’
content:
The Metro Center for Journalists’ Rights and Advocacy issued a statement on the occasion of November 2, the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists, designated by the United Nations (UN) in 2013.




The statement read: “In the Kurdistan Region, no independent investigations into the murders of journalists have been conducted because the judiciary is under the influence of the ruling political parties. Cases that have sparked widespread public outrage, such as the murders of Soran Mame Heme, Serdeşt Osman, Kawa Germiyani, Vedat Hüseyin, and Abdülstar Tahir Şerif, remain unsolved. Neither those who carried out the murders nor those who ordered them have been identified or brought to justice.”




Calling for the investigations into these cases to be reopened, the Metro Center drew attention to statements issued by UNESCO, stating: “Impunity for crimes leads to an increase in murders and violence and undermines the legal and justice systems. UNESCO warns that such impunity allows serious human rights violations and corruption to be concealed, causing harm to society as a whole. For this reason, the government, civil society organizations, and media outlets are being urged to uphold the rule of law and support international initiatives aimed at putting an end to such practices.”

title: DEM Party co-chairs visit Peace Mothers holding a vigil in Ankara
content:
Members of the Peace Mothers Assembly from 24 cities continue their vigil in Ankara, demanding freedom for Abdullah Öcalan, the release of political prisoners, and concrete steps in the peace process.




Accompanied by members of the Central Executive Board (MYK) and members of parliament, co-chairs of the DEM Party visited the Peace Mothers.













Speaking here, Tülay Hatimoğulları said, “You are the ones who deserve peace the most and have struggled the hardest for it.”




Hatimoğulları noted that the Peace Mothers have consistently fought for peace in public spaces and squares to put an end to suffering. She said, “At the current stage of the peace and democratic society process, you have taken to the roads and come to Ankara to help accelerate the process and enable us to achieve peace sooner.”













The DEM Party co-chair added, “Our visit today is, of course, intended to express both our solidarity with the Peace Mothers, with whom we have walked this path together, and our commitment to our shared struggle. We will most certainly bring peace to this country and these lands. Peace will be established in this land as pure as your white headscarves, with the same dignity and integrity they represent. This is our promise.”













Tuncer Bakırhan, for his part, said, “We have gathered here for a very special cause,” adding, “Our Peace Mothers, who have lost their children and loved ones, have traveled from all corners of Turkey to Ankara today.”




Emphasizing that the Peace Mothers had embarked on a journey for a sacred cause and were engaged in a struggle for something sacred, Bakırhan said, “Once again, we make a promise to the Peace Mothers. Your sacred struggle is immensely valuable.”













Bakırhan added: “Your decision to come to Ankara to make sure that our young people do not lose their lives is extremely valuable. The process is moving somewhat slowly, but we promise to accelerate it. We pledge to speed up the peace process in a manner worthy of the honorable struggle you have demonstrated today, so that no mother in this country will ever lose her child again. We will act in a way that ensures war, bloodshed and conflict never return to the agenda in this country.”













Underlining that peace is in the interests of the country, Bakırhan said, “We will intensify our struggle to fulfill the demands of our mothers so that, hopefully, we can live in this diverse land of 86 million people in an environment free from fighting and conflict. We call on all authorities to heed this honorable voice and respond with sensitivity.”













The Peace Mothers, speaking in both Turkish and Kurdish, stressed that the government must take steps to advance the process.




Meanwhile, the Peace Mothers will attend tomorrow’s DEM Party parliamentary group meeting. They will also visit other political parties represented in parliament and submit documents outlining their demands.

title: Activists Destroy Military Equipment at ‘Death Factory Supplying Israel’
content:
Activists opposing Israel’s genocide in Gaza broke into a factory in Tring, Hertfordshire, on Monday morning, before smashing equipment there with hammers. 




Three members of the group People Against Genocide (PAG) were arrested after the break-in at the facility, which is owned by military technology firm Ultra Intelligence & Communications (I&C).




The activists say Ultra I&C is a key supplier of UAV Tactical Systems, which is owned by Israeli weapons firm Elbit Systems. Novara Media contacted Ultra I&C for comment but had not received a reply at the time of publication.




Ultra I&C makes military satellite and cybersecurity technology. Video posted by PAG on social media showed people destroying what appeared to be large parabolic antennas.   




Monday’s break-in was timed to coincide with the 109th anniversary of the Balfour Declaration, a statement issued by the British government in 1917 that is widely seen as laying the foundation for the colonisation and ethnic cleansing of Palestine. 




“Not only did the British government sign away a country that was not theirs to give, they have continued to assist in the Zionist occupation of Palestine, and in the murder of its native population, right up to the present day,” the group said in a statement. “Chief among the other foreign actors actively assisting the genocide is, of course, Britain’s unruly offspring, the US, where Ultra I&C is headquartered.”




It added: “By shutting down the Tring death factory today, and dismantling the weapons inside, our action-takers are aiming to save lives in Palestine, and uphold international law. 




“The Labour governments of both Burnham and Starmer have not only failed to do anything to stop the genocide, abandoning their commitments to international law, and to simple human decency, they have actively assisted the Israeli military with spy flights and arms shipments.”




The group has targeted Ultra I&C on several occasions. During a previous raid on the Tring facility on 9 July, its activists allegedly caused £1.3m of damage. Its members have also staged actions at sites in Cambridge, Aberdeen and Maidenhead this year.

author: Jillian C. York
title: Independent Digital Media Is Not a Privilege Governments Can Revoke: The Fight to Save Egypt’s Mada Masr
content:
On November 11, Lina Attalah, founder and editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet 

Mada Masr

, will face trial for the second time in just two weeks. This time, she faces charges of spreading false news, an accusation that has become one of the Egyptian government's most frequently used tools for prosecuting journalists.

 




The trial follows a conviction on October 27, when Attalah was 

found guilty

 of managing an unlicensed news website. The Mada Masr team had repeatedly applied for a license, but their attempts went unacknowledged. The proceedings took place in a single hearing, which Mada Masr 

states

 included serious violations of her right to a fair trial. She was sentenced to the maximum fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (approximately 55,000 USD), forcibly removed from the courtroom, and held for seven hours until the fine was paid. The court also ordered Mada Masr's closure and the confiscation of all equipment belonging to the organization.

 




The current wave of repression has also targeted 

Matsada2sh

, a fact-checking and open-source intelligence initiative. Its entire six-person newsroom was 

violently arrested

, illegally detained, and interrogated under torture before being charged with terrorism-related offenses and spreading false news. The team remains in pretrial detention.

 




According to CPJ, at least 

25 other journalists

 are currently incarcerated in Egypt.

 




Governments seeking to control the flow of information increasingly rely on a combination of legal harassment, financial pressure, criminal prosecution, and restrictions on the infrastructure that makes independent publishing possible. Egypt's media licensing regime is a particularly troubling example. Requiring news organizations to obtain government authorization to operate creates an obvious mechanism for restricting who gets to publish and whose voices are allowed to reach the public. 

 




The charge of spreading false news is similarly dangerous. Governments around the world have increasingly invoked the language of misinformation to justify restrictions on speech, often without meaningful safeguards against political abuse, as we laid out in our 

recent submission

 to the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Governments should never be the arbiters of which reporting is permissible, particularly when that reporting concerns their own conduct.

 




Why Mada Masr matters

 




Founded in 2013, Mada Masr has spent more than a decade doing the kind of journalism that authoritarian governments find most threatening: documenting abuses, amplifying marginalized voices, and reporting on issues that powerful institutions would prefer remain hidden.

 




Its reporting has given torture survivors and the families of political prisoners a platform. It has opened space for debate about reproductive rights. It has brought frontline reporting from Sudan and Gaza, and stood alongside refugees facing xenophobic attacks and security crackdowns.

 




Emerging as a digital-first publication, in a media environment where traditional outlets were increasingly constrained, being purely digital allowed Mada Masr’s founders to build an independent publication outside the structures of legacy media. 

 




At a time when 

only 43% of Egyptians had access to the internet

, going fully digital meant taking a big risk, but it was one that has been rewarding: Despite being blocked by the Egyptian government since 2017, Mada Masr has continued to reach Egyptian and global audiences, and Attalah has received numerous accolades, including the 

Knight International Journalism Award

, the 

Ordre des Arts et des Lettres

, and a spot in 

TIME Magazine’s 100 most influential people

 (2020).

 




Mada Masr has also consistently engaged with technology and advocated for a free and independent internet for the global majority. It has covered dozens of hot-button tech stories in recent years, from 

Egypt’s Cybercrime Bill

 and 

Israel’s use of AI weaponry in Gaza

, to stories about the “

privacy chaos

” caused by biometrics to more 

personal essays

 about the importance of the internet and tech. In August, they launched an 

open call for proposals

 on original critical reporting on artificial intelligence.

 




Mada Masr may be thoroughly Egyptian, but it doesn’t belong just to Egypt. Its team has made into a publication that represents the kind of independent, local, grounded journalism that international audiences need, particularly at a time when international reporting on state repression is lacking. They built on-the-ground networks to center local voices in Sudan (publishing in both 

English

 and 

Arabic

 on the conflict) and Gaza out of a sense of cross-border responsibility and solidarity.

 




This is precisely why its potential closure should concern everyone who cares about a free press. The ability to publish independently, investigate powerful institutions, and to share information without government interference is fundamental to the exercise of free expression. 

 




From solidarity to action

 




The international community has repeatedly expressed concern about restrictions on 

press

 and 

internet

 freedom in Egypt. More than 100 organizations have now joined 

statements

 of 

solidarity

 with Mada Masr, and with 

Matsada2sh

. 

 




These expressions of support matter, particularly when journalists are increasingly isolated and under threat—but solidarity must also translate into sustained political and institutional pressure.

 




The international governments and institutions that maintain relationships with Egypt—including those in the European Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States—should make clear that the prosecution of journalists and the forced closure of independent media outlets are unacceptable. 

 




The cases against Lina Attalah, Mada Masr, and Matsada2sh must be dropped. The journalists who remain in detention must be released. And Egypt's licensing regime, with its profound chilling effects on access to information and independent knowledge production, must be brought to an end.

 




There is a particular urgency to defending independent media at a moment when governments are finding ever more ways to restrict the circulation of information. Whether through internet shutdowns, platform restrictions, surveillance, or the criminalization of reporting, the result is often the same: fewer opportunities for people to understand what is happening around them, to challenge official narratives, and to hold power accountable.

 




We cannot allow the closure of one of Egypt's most important independent newsrooms and the prosecution of its editor-in-chief to become another routine episode in the global erosion of press freedom. Nor should we wait until the last independent journalists have been silenced before recognizing what has been lost.

 




To learn more about Lina Attalah in her own reads, you can read our 

Speaking Freely interview

 from January 2026.

author: Doha Ali
title: There are no apolitical girls in war
content:
“Doha, come sit with us. We need to talk to you.”

I was 15 years old, had just finished high school, and was getting ready to start university in Sudan. My mother knocked on my bedroom door and asked me to come into the living room. My parents were waiting for me.

“We need you to understand something important,” my father began. “When you go to university, don’t talk about politics.”

I remember asking the only question that made sense to me. “What is politics?”

My father paused for a moment before answering. “Politics is the art of what is possible,” he said. “It’s how people pursue what they believe can be achieved.”

I stared at him, trying to make sense of words that felt much too big for a 15-year-old. Before he could explain any further, my mother interrupted him.

“No,” she said quickly. “Politics is what old people talk about.”

She looked directly at me. “You shouldn’t talk about it. Bad things can happen if you do.”

That was the lesson I understood.

Politics was dangerous.

Looking back, I realize that my parents were not trying to teach me politics. They were trying to teach me how to survive.

The conversation was not unique to me. My older brother had already had it. So had my sister. When I arrived at university, I discovered that almost all of my friends had grown up with some version of the same warning.

We learned where not to stand on campus. We learned to walk past the “political corners” without slowing down. We learned that curiosity could be mistaken for affiliation, and that sometimes the safest opinion was no opinion at all.

I became very good at being what I thought was an apolitical girl.

Even when I began working in human rights and activism, I carefully separated my work from politics. I spoke about dignity, equality, and justice, while convincing myself that these belonged to a different conversation altogether.

Looking back now, I smile at the contradiction.

What are human rights in a country where people are taught not to have opinions?

The 2019 revolution unsettled the belief I held all my life about avoiding politics.

Suddenly, politics escaped our living room.

For the first time in my life, I witnessed people debating it in cafés, on buses, in university hallways, and in the streets. Conversations that had once been whispered became public. My political realization was clearly shaped: politics does not belong to politicians; it belongs to all of us, and we can shape it together.

The streets became classrooms. Neighborhoods became places of organizing. Around me, people argued, dreamed, volunteered, fed each other, protected each other, and imagined a country that felt possible.

For the first time, I felt as though I had permission to talk politics without immediately looking over my shoulder.

But permission is not the same as understanding.

People often say that understanding the past helps us understand the future. Yet Sudan’s history felt less like a straight line than a circle: military rule, uprisings, coups, moments of hope, and promises that always seemed to collapse back into the familiar.

But the revolution changed something deeper than the government. It changed what those outside of institutional power believed they were capable of. I had never thought of myself as a political actor, but suddenly questions of how my neighborhood was organized, protected, and cared for felt like questions I could participate in answering. We were not simply demanding that someone else build a different Sudan; we were beginning to practice it ourselves.

Later, I came across the “Revolutionary Charter for Establishing People’s Power.” What stayed with me was not simply the language of a political document, but the idea behind it: that the people who had filled the streets could also become the people who shaped what came next.

Looking back, I wonder if that was what frightened those in power most: not simply that people were demanding change, but that they had discovered their own power to organize without waiting for permission — to build networks, provide care, protect their neighborhoods, and imagine political alternatives from below.

And perhaps this is what makes popular movements so threatening to systems built on concentrated power.

You can suppress a protest.

You can arrest a leader.

You can overthrow a government.

But what happens when people have already discovered that they have power together?

Then came the coup of 2021.

But the coup did not erase what had happened in 2019. If anything, it deepened the determination of many people to resist. The streets filled again. The organizing continued. The language of resistance changed, but the belief that another Sudan was possible did not disappear.

And then came the war.

During the first weeks of the war in April 2023, time stopped making sense.

Our lives became organized around survival.

We waited for water that only came for a short time before dawn. My mother and I played Ludo on a board we had drawn by hand to make the endless hours pass. Whenever the electricity returned, everything else stopped. We rushed to charge our phones, download messages, and discover who had managed to leave Khartoum, who was still trapped, and who had disappeared from our screens.

Those moments became our connection to the outside world.

Somewhere between waiting for water, rolling dice across a handmade board, and searching for familiar names online, one question settled into my mind and refused to leave.

How did we get here?

At first, I thought I was asking how a war had started. But I was not an outsider looking in; I had spent years on the ground, organizing, listening, and navigating the realities of Sudan myself. Yet, so much of what was happening did not make sense. The more I searched for the missing pieces in the history I thought I knew, the more I realized I was asking different questions.

How could a militia become powerful enough to wage war against Sudan’s national army? Why is the story of this war being told as though one side represented the nation and the other simply threatened it? And why did we stop asking what both sides have done to the people they claim to represent?

Every article I opened answered one question and created another.

The story clearly had not begun in April 2023. It stretched back years.

My father once quoted a saying often attributed to Imam Al-Shafi’i:

“My opinion is correct with the possibility of being wrong, and the opinion of others is wrong with the possibility of being correct.”

He told me that the moment someone believes their opinion is the only truth, dictatorship begins.

Sudan knows dictatorships well. One of them was Omar al-Bashir, who seized power in a 1989 military coup. Under his rule, the Janjaweed militia was used to fight rebel groups in Darfur. Over time, those forces evolved into what would later become the Rapid Support Forces.

Yet even this history did not fully answer my question.

I expected the answers to be found inside Sudan. Instead, every path I followed seemed to lead somewhere else.

The deeper I read, the more often Europe appeared in a story I had always believed belonged only to Sudan.

I wasn’t looking for European migration policy. Yet somehow, it kept appearing in the story.

That was how I stumbled across something called the Khartoum Process, also known as the EU-Horn of Africa Migration Route Initiative, a political dialogue launched in 2014 between European and African states to cooperate on migration along the route between the Horn of Africa and Europe.

What followed was a growing European investment in managing migration in Sudan. Through programs such as Better Migration Management, European funding supported capacity-building, training, information-sharing, investigations into trafficking and smuggling, and efforts to strengthen border management. Sudan had become important not only because people were leaving it, but because people were passing through it.

And this is where the story became uncomfortable.

The people being asked to help Europe control its borders were not operating in some neutral security system. They were part of a state security apparatus with a long history of violence and repression. The RSF was itself deployed along Sudan’s borders to stop irregular migration and combat trafficking. European policymakers knew the risks. In 2016, members of the European Parliament were already questioning how EU migration cooperation could prevent equipment and training intended for border control from being diverted toward repression.

The EU has repeatedly insisted that it did not fund the RSF. That distinction matters, and I am not arguing that Europe created the RSF. But I began to ask a different question: what happens when the desire to keep migrants away from European borders turns a violent security system into an international partner?

What happens when governments that are willing to use violence against their own people are nevertheless treated as necessary partners because they can stop people from moving?

This became harder to ignore when I looked at Omar al-Bashir. The ICC had issued a warrant against him, including charges of genocide, yet European cooperation with Sudan continued. At what point did stopping migration become important enough to make cooperation with a regime accused of genocide acceptable?

I am not arguing that migration policy alone sustained Sudan’s security system. Rather, migration control is one example of how international actors continue to engage with, build the capacity of, and legitimize Sudan’s security institutions, helping create the conditions in which this war became possible. Sudan’s political and military elites bear their own responsibilities. But they did not operate in isolation from the international systems that helped make their power possible.

Power is rarely built through a single cheque, an agreement, or a foreign government. Sometimes it is built through years of political relationships that make certain actors more powerful, more legitimate, and more useful to the outside world.

I thought I was researching Sudan.

I didn’t realize I was beginning to uncover how decisions made far beyond Sudan had become part of the conditions that made this war possible.

Eventually, I crossed the border into Egypt.

The road out of Sudan was marked by checkpoints. At some, it was the RSF. At others, it was the military. The faces and uniforms changed, but the feeling did not.

I did not feel safe at either checkpoint.

It wasn’t because I believed the two forces were the same. They weren’t. The Sudanese Armed Forces are a national institution, and I know that there can be no future Sudan without a national army. But at that moment, I could not bring myself to choose between the two sides because, for me, choosing either side meant accepting a war that I did not believe should define Sudan’s future.

I didn’t want Sudan to be ruled by the RSF. I didn’t want Sudan to return to military rule either. I wanted something else.

I wanted the Sudan I had seen become possible in 2019: a Sudan where civilians could determine their own future, where people could organize themselves, resist military rule, and believe that the country belonged to them.

And then I crossed the border.

I believed I had reached safety. Instead, I found myself confronting a different kind of confinement.

Before the war, I never dreamed of leaving Sudan. Many people my age did. They spoke about scholarships, jobs abroad, and better opportunities elsewhere. I understood why. Sudan was never an easy place to build a future. But I never shared that dream.

I wanted to stay. I wanted to become rooted in that place.

Home, to me, was never a house. It was the one place where belonging required no explanation. I didn’t have to earn it. I didn’t have to prove I deserved to be there. I could fail, begin again, change my mind, and still know I belonged.

I didn’t realize then that belonging itself could become political.

Crossing the border wasn’t only the loss of a country. It was the loss of that effortless belonging.

I was no longer trapped by shelling and checkpoints, but by visas, residency requirements, shrinking opportunities for movement, and the knowledge that my future depended on decisions made in distant capitals.

For the first time, I understood that migration policies are not experienced as documents. They are experienced as the limits placed on an ordinary life.

At first, I didn’t have the language for what I was feeling.

I only knew that something had shifted.

A few years earlier, I had a flight connection through Egypt. I left the airport for a few hours, wandered around the city, bought a few things, and returned in time for my next flight. I entered the country in less than 10 minutes. No one asked how long I intended to stay. No one questioned why I was there.

After the war, the same border felt almost unrecognizable.

It took me a week of daily visits to obtain residency. Every morning I woke before dawn and joined hundreds of other Sudanese people already waiting outside the immigration office. We arrived around four in the morning and often stayed until late afternoon, only to be told to return the next day and begin again.

What struck me most was what we were waiting for. Not citizenship. Not permanent protection. Not even freedom of movement.

We were waiting for a document that would allow us to remain without fearing another forced displacement. A document that would allow us to keep a functioning phone line that would reconnect us with family scattered across different countries, for the chance to exist legally for a few more months.

Even after I received it, I never left the house without checking several times that my passport was in my bag.

What if I forgot it? What if I was stopped? What if one missing document was enough to uproot me all over again?

That was when I understood something I had never considered before: crossing a border does not always end displacement; sometimes it simply changes its shape.

For generations, Sudanese people moved between Sudan and Egypt with a familiarity that reflected the long history connecting the two countries. Suddenly, we were being spoken about through a different vocabulary: numbers, quotas, security, migration management.

Somewhere along the way, I stopped being a neighbor.

I became a migrant.

A refugee.

A potential burden.

The conversations around us increasingly revolved around pressure on jobs, pressure on housing, pressure on public services. I found myself wondering how quickly a person could become a problem simply by crossing a border they never wanted to cross in the first place.

I want to be careful here. This is not a story about Egypt rejecting Sudanese people. My experience in Egypt was also shaped by kindness, generosity, and people who welcomed us. Ordinary Egyptians were often navigating their own economic hardships while extending compassion to strangers.

The story is bigger than Egypt.

And that is where my personal experience began to lead me back to the question I had been asking in Khartoum.

How did we get here?

The more I tried to understand why displacement still felt like confinement, the more I found myself reading about migration policies again and the relationship between Europe and countries such as Egypt, Sudan, Libya, and Niger.

That was when I came across a term I had never heard before. Border externalization.

At its simplest, border externalization is the practice of moving migration control beyond a country’s own borders. Rather than preventing migration only at European frontiers, European governments increasingly invest in stopping migration much earlier, through partnerships with countries that people pass through long before they ever reach Europe.

The border, I realized, no longer begins at the Mediterranean. It begins in places like Khartoum. It continues through Cairo. It stretches across deserts, checkpoints, visa offices, and residency queues.

What surprised me most was not only that these policies shaped the journeys of people hoping to reach Europe, but also shaped the lives of people like me, who were not trying to reach Europe at all.

I had escaped one war only to discover that I was now living inside another political system — one that quietly determined where I could move, how long I could stay, and whether I could build a life again.

The more I learned, the more another concept emerged alongside border externalization: the securitization of migration.

Migration was increasingly discussed not as a human experience, but as a security problem.

Refugees became statistics.

Migrants became risks.

Movement became something to contain.

I found myself wondering what happens when people begin to see you first as a category and only later, if at all, as a person.

The irony was impossible to ignore.

The very policies designed to manage migration had become part of the story that uprooted so many of us in the first place.

Without ever intending to, I had gone searching for the politics of Sudan. Instead, I found myself studying the politics of borders.

For years, I believed that understanding Sudan required understanding Sudanese politics.

The war taught me otherwise.

To understand why I was trapped inside my home in Khartoum, I had to understand decisions made far beyond Sudan. To understand why I felt trapped again after crossing the border, I had to understand migration policies designed far beyond Egypt.

The deeper I looked, the more I realized that migration policy was only one thread.

Sudan’s war is often described as a civil war, or as a humanitarian crisis. I struggle with both descriptions. Calling it a civil war makes the conflict sound internal, as though Sudan’s future is being decided only by the two armed forces fighting on its soil. But this is also a proxy war: a war sustained by regional and international actors pursuing their own interests through Sudanese territory, resources, and armed actors. The war is being fought in Sudan, but its conditions do not exist only within Sudan.

Yet, the danger of describing Sudan only through its external actors can make Sudanese people disappear from the political story altogether. Because what is at stake is not simply which armed force wins, or which foreign power gains influence.

The people who filled the streets in 2019 were not fighting simply to replace one ruler with another. They were fighting to break a cycle: the cycle in which military power repeatedly interrupts civilian politics, takes control of the state, and decides the country’s future for its people.

That is why I struggle with the idea that this is simply a war between two generals. What about the Sudanese people who wanted neither? What about the Sudan they were trying to build?

A Sudan governed by civilians. A Sudan where sovereignty means more than the ability of armed institutions to control territory. A Sudan where people who had spent decades being told that politics belonged to generals discovered that politics could belong to them too.

The war is not only destroying lives. It is threatening the possibility of breaking the cycle.

When we call Sudan “the world’s largest humanitarian crisis,” the focus naturally shifts to aid, displacement, food insecurity, and emergency response. These realities demand attention. But humanitarian language can also flatten history. It can make war appear as though it erupted on its own, disconnected from the political choices, international partnerships, economic interests, and regional power struggles that helped shape it.

It can shift the question from why are we at war, and how do we stop it? to how do we continue responding to the consequences of war? And there is a danger in that distinction. Because if we only manage the humanitarian consequences, we can end up managing an endless war.

Wars do not simply happen; they are built. Sometimes they are built through weapons. Sometimes through money. Sometimes through diplomatic agreements signed years before the first shot is fired. Sometimes through migration policies that reward stability at any cost, even when that stability depends on empowering those willing to use violence.

That does not mean Sudanese people are passive victims of decisions made elsewhere. Sudan has its own political history, its own actors, and its own responsibilities. But refusing to look beyond Sudan means refusing to see the whole picture.

The more I searched for answers, the more countries entered the story. Each revealed another thread connecting Sudan to a much larger political landscape.

And I finally understood why the question I had asked while sitting in my dark house in Khartoum — “How did we get here?” — could never be answered by looking at Sudan alone.

I spent years believing that politics was something I could choose not to discuss. I now understand that it was never something I stood outside of. It shaped the country I called home, the war that forced me to leave it, and the borders I encountered afterwards.

Perhaps that is another part of what I had been searching for all along. Not only how Sudan arrived at war, but how the story of Sudan itself is told. What we choose to remember, what we choose to leave out, and whose voices we choose to hear are all political choices.

When I was 15, my mother told me that politics was what old people talked about. She was trying to protect me from the consequences of speaking.

But perhaps that is what I misunderstood.

Politics was never simply something people talked about. It was something that determined who could speak, who could belong, who could move, who could stay, and ultimately who could decide what Sudan would become.

I became political not because I chose politics, but because war made it impossible to remain outside of it.

There are no apolitical girls in war.

Only girls who eventually discover that politics has been shaping their lives all along.

author: The Elephant
title: Wandia Njoya – The Politics of Work: Kenya’s Unspoken Political Agenda
content:
Work must be central to any serious political agenda because it is where citizens experience the state most directly: through wages, security, opportunity, and dignity. In Kenya, where most new jobs are informal and decent-work deficits remain widespread, a politics that ignores work ignores the daily realities of the majority. The Elephant in conversation with Prof. Wandia Njoya.




The post 

Wandia Njoya – The Politics of Work: Kenya’s Unspoken Political Agenda

 first appeared on 

The Elephant

.

title: Trino Vercellese: un caso simbolo del tandem data center, nucleare e bolla speculativa
content:
Riportiamo parte degli interventi della serata informativa organizzata da

 

Legambiente del Vercellese e della Valsesia – gruppo di Trino

 

il 16 ottobre 2026 a Trino alla quale abbiamo partecipato, in modo da fissare alcuni concetti chiave nell’approcciarsi a questo terreno. 







I PARTE Domanda energetica fuori dalla realtà 




1.1 Dal reattore al Data Center 




Ad aprire l’incontro è stato Fausto Cognasso, già membro del 

comitato TriNO

 contro l’installazione del Deposito nucleare nazionale nella pianura risicola vercellese. Il suo intervento è servito a confrontare la narrativa istituzionale sul 

Cavour Hyperscale Campus

 (CHC) con i rischi reali per il territorio legati alla realizzazione del progetto.




Del CHC si parla infatti solo in termini entusiastici. 400 MW di potenza di calcolo, 4 miliardi di euro di investimento, importanti ricadute occupazionali: un rilancio economico a tutto campo. Ma né dentro né fuori dalle sale comunali si è ancora avuto un vero confronto politico sul progetto.




Il silenzio ufficiale lascia al momento sospese questioni decisive per la valutazione del CHC da parte del territorio. Ad esempio, il 

campus

 potrà affidarsi a fonti rinnovabili per le sue esigenze energetiche? O si dovrà piuttosto ricorrere al nucleare, come ha lasciato intendere l’assessore all’Ambiente della Regione Piemonte Marnati? C’è il rischio che i costi di adeguamento della rete elettrica alla proliferazione di data center in Lombardia e Piemonte vengano scaricati sui cittadini attraverso un aumento in bolletta? L’insediamento di un data center potrebbe dare luogo o esasperare fenomeni di isole di calore? E se, come dovrebbe avvenire nel caso del CHC a Trino, i 

server

 non saranno raffreddati ad acqua, si userà allora un liquido refrigerante a base di PFAS? I rischi legati a questi “inquinanti eterni” sono stati opportunamente valutati?




Colmare il vuoto d’informazione




In merito a questa ondata di data center che si sta abbattendo sul nord Italia, l’opacità rilevata anche a Trino in merito al progetto del CHC è la regola: comitati, associazioni, stampa indipendente e cittadini si stanno mobilitando per “coprire il deficit di informazione e democrazia”.




Ad esempio, il nesso tra crescita della produzione di PFAS e accelerazione sui data center per le necessità dell’intelligenza artificiale è un fatto assodato. In un 

report

 pubblicato dalla ONG svedese ChemSec viene illustrato come dai piani industriali dei primi dieci grandi produttori mondiali di PFAS emerga l’intento di espandere la produzione dei composti in risposta alla crescita esponenziale del settore 

tech

. Come abbiamo accennato, nel caso dei data center i PFAS entrano in gioco per il raffreddamento in quanto necessari ai liquidi refrigeranti alternativi all’uso di acqua o aria fredda. Queste moderne tecnologie di raffreddamento dipendenti dai PFAS vengono tipicamente impiegate negli 

hyperscaler

 come il CHC. Il colosso francese dei materiali Arkema, ad esempio, ha inaugurato in Kentucky uno stabilimento da circa 60 milioni di dollari per la produzione del gas HFO R1233Z, refrigerante di largo impiego e utilizzato anche nei data center per il raffreddamento dei server.




Quanto alle ricadute occupazionali, resta da capire se artigiani e imprese locali abbiano effettivamente le competenze per lavorare a una struttura come il CHC. Nel caso della centrale Galileo Ferraris, ad esempio, gran parte dell’imprenditoria locale dovette accontentarsi di subappalti marginali.




Sul piano amministrativo il coinvolgimento del territorio è completamente assente. La dichiarazione di interesse strategico nazionale approvata recentemente dal Consiglio dei Ministri per il CHC comporta la nomina di un Commissario straordinario di governo, incaricato di garantire la “tempestiva realizzazione dell’investimento”. L’iter ordinario, che pur essendo più laborioso offre maggiori tutele per il territorio e le comunità che lo abitano, qui dovrebbe lasciare il posto a un’autorizzazione unica, pensata per accelerare i tempi e offrire certezze a chi muove i capitali. Come in altri casi di grandi opere imposte dall’alto, il rischio è che la pianificazione urbanistica locale ne esca subordinata a interessi di mercato e politica di palazzo. Tanto più grave risulterebbe in questo quadro l’assenza di dibattito pubblico fin dalle fasi preliminari del progetto.




La concentrazione di data center, di vecchie centrali atomiche non ancora dismesse e depositi nucleari su aree relativamente ridotte risulterà inoltre in una militarizzazione dei territori. Questo, per due ordini di motivi. Primo, si renderà necessaria per impedire a cittadini e comitati di monitorare e contrastare il progetto. Secondo, una volta in funzione, questi impianti diventerebbero bersagli in una guerra globale le cui forme più distruttive sono sempre più vicine anche alle nostre latitudini: la stessa che motiva i massicci investimenti piemontesi in intelligenza artificiale e data center e che favorisce l’

establishment

 finanziario-industriale.




Altrettanto concreto appare, nel quadro delineato, il ritorno dell’atomo nel vercellese. La legge 169, appena approvata, delega al Governo la disciplina del nucleare “sostenibile” e pone in prima fila come candidati per l’insediamento di futuri reattori i siti ex nucleari, Trino compreso. Indicativa del processo di riapertura all’atomo la metamorfosi dell’azienda Sogin: nata per smantellare le vecchie centrali e restituirle libere da ogni vincolo radiologico, è oggi tra i protagonisti del suo rilancio. Secondo l’ex amministratore delegato Artizzu, i siti da lei gestiti sono già pronti ad accogliere i nuovi reattori.




Nel frattempo la Commissione consultiva comunale di Trino sullo smantellamento della centrale Enrico Fermi non si riunisce da due anni, nonostante le richieste dei membri designati dalle associazioni ambientaliste. Restano inevase anche le domande a Sogin sul Programma Vita Intera (PVI), il cronoprogramma che dovrebbe documentare avanzamento e costi dei lavori. Atteso per il 2023, è arrivato solo nel 2025 e attende ancora il vaglio dell’ARERA. Dal documento emerge che i costi del solo 

decommissioning

 superano di 2,8 miliardi le stime del 2020-2021 e che la chiusura della commessa slitta di dieci anni, dal 2029 al 2039.




Il 7 ottobre, infine, il Sindaco di Trino ha partecipato a Roma a un incontro negli uffici di Inrete, società di 

lobbying

 che mette in relazione il mondo politico-istituzionale con quello imprenditoriale. L’evento, intitolato “Il nucleare per lo sviluppo energetico dell’Italia”, era promosso da Nuclitalia, società partecipata da Enel, Ansaldo Energia e Leonardo, e nata per guidare il ritorno dell’atomo in Italia. Nessuno ne ha dato notizia, né prima né dopo: cittadini e comitati l’hanno scoperto da una determina che stanziava i fondi per la trasferta.







1.2 Data center e nucleare: a che punto siamo? 




Gianpiero Godio, referente dell’Osservatorio dei Cittadini sul nucleare, ha approfondito il gigantismo energetico dei data center, analizzando più da vicino la possibile interazione di queste strutture col nucleare, con le rinnovabili e con i paradigmi energetici impliciti alla corsa agli 

hyperscaler

. Nel corso della sua vita professionale Godio è stato per vent’anni responsabile dell’unità di automazione e calcolo scientifico dell’impianto nucleare Eurex di Saluggia (CNEN), dirigendo quindi un “piccolo data center” per l’impianto di riprocessamento. 




Le osservazioni di Pro Natura alla consultazione sul disegno di legge regionale




Il 15 luglio la Regione Piemonte, tramite l’assessorato Ambiente, Intelligenza Artificiale ed Energia, ha aperto una consultazione pubblica sul disegno di legge regionale “Disciplina per l’insediamento di data center”. Pro Natura ha presentato quattro pagine di osservazioni, i cui punti principali elaborati possono così essere riassunti:







L’AI va considerata un bene comune, quindi sottratta a usi bellici, speculativi e antidemocratici, con uno sviluppo aperto e graduale.




L’addestramento nei data center deve adattarsi alla disponibilità oraria e stagionale delle rinnovabili. Queste devono essere l’unica fonte da subito e provenire da nuovi impianti e nuovi accumuli dedicati, senza accentrare tutta l’energia rinnovabile già prodotta sul territorio sottraendola ad altri ambiti.




Lo sviluppo va pianificato a livello statale e regionale, stabilendo potenza, collocazione e finalità dei data center prima di realizzarli.




I territori ospitanti vanno protetti da interruzioni di fornitura e, aggiunge Godio, anche da aumenti dei prezzi locali. Le popolazioni devono essere consultate con un’inchiesta pubblica preventiva.




Sul piano etico, ci si chiede a chi serva davvero un’AI “totalizzante”: se arricchisca il pensiero o lo sostituisca, e se serva percorsi di emancipazione collettiva o speculazione e guerra.







I numeri dei consumi dell’AI – intelligenza artificiale




Un data center da 400 MW consumerebbe circa 3,5 miliardi di kWh l’anno, cioè il triplo dei consumi di tutti i settori della provincia di Vercelli e più di tutta la produzione fotovoltaica installata in Piemonte, che si aggira sui 3 miliardi di kWh. A meno che l’addestramento dei modelli di 

machine learning

 e 

deep learning

 non venga pianificato in modo flessibile, alimentarlo continuativamente (come queste strutture normalmente richiedono) con l’agrivoltaico richiederebbe circa 35 km² (3.500 ettari) e una quantità impressionante di batterie.




Inoltre, un approccio che ponga come imprescindibile a una riappropriazione popolare dell’AI la sua sincronizzazione con le FER (Fonti Energia Rinnovabili), escluderebbe a priori i data center 

hyperscale

. Per dare un’idea della scala delle necessità energetiche di queste strutture rispetto alle possibilità e ai costi delle rinnovabili, il grande impianto fotovoltaico di Enel di Leri Cavour produce meno del 5% di quanto servirebbe a un data center da 400 MW come il CHC. Per permettere le modalità di insediamento massiccio di queste strutture che stanno via via facendosi sempre più ingombranti, il ricorso alle fonti fossili è inevitabile, anche se questa invasione in atto sembra debba fare da volano a forme energetiche anche più problematiche.




La svolta sull’atomo: vecchi siti per il nuovo nucleare




Rieccoci, dunque, allo spettro del ritorno al nucleare in Italia. Quello fra data center 

hyperscale

 e nucleare è un “matrimonio di interesse e di potere” che non s’ha da fare, né a Trino né altrove. Dopo la pausa di agosto, a settembre è emerso che la nuova legge delega sul nucleare fortemente voluta dal Governo e già approvata dalla Camera, sarebbe stata approvata anche dal Senato. L’approvazione formale infatti è avvenuta il 23 settembre.




La legge delega 169, come abbiamo già avuto modo di accennare, all’articolo 2 amplia la destinazione d’uso dei vecchi siti nucleari. Le finalità comprendono nuovi impianti di produzione, impianti di fabbricazione e riprocessamento del combustibile, stoccaggio temporaneo e smaltimento definitivo. Nella pratica una loro riattivazione, legittimata dalla corsa ai data center, senza che sia mai avvenuta una vera disattivazione.




Ad andare incontro a questa  riattivazione potrebbero essere il centro Euratom a Ispra, sul Lago Maggiore; Bosco Marengo, dove si fabbricavano le barre di combustibile; il deposito di Tortona, e addirittura le miniere di uranio di Peveragno e dell’Alta Val di Susa.

Sufficienza e bene comune: ripensare il progresso




Se data center, AI e nucleare sono il progresso, emerge con forza la necessità di ripensare il concetto stesso di progresso. Per abbandonare le fonti fossili servono sufficienza, efficienza, flessibilità e rinnovabili “fatte bene”, cioè motivate organicamente dalle necessità e aspirazioni dei territori e non dalla speculazione finanziaria.




I data center 

hyperscale

 sono, invece, l’antitesi della sufficienza: raggiungerla implicherebbe infatti chiedersi quali usi digitali siano davvero necessari al benessere umano e sociale e quali siano invece forme di sovraconsumo ed estrattivismo.




Non basta puntare sull’efficienza, perché questa genera un effetto rimbalzo: una maggiore efficienza, portando a un aumento della produzione, porta a uno sfruttamento complessivo maggiore delle risorse. La sfida è invece quella di un cambio di paradigma, di una sovversione dei rapporti di forza: l’AI deve essere un bene comune, di uso limitato e per fini quali la ricerca scientifica o le applicazioni mediche, e sincronizzata con la disponibilità giornaliera e stagionale delle rinnovabili, conclude Godio.

1.3 I consumi elettrici




Interviene Umberto Lorini (Pro Natura Vercellese, Valsesia e VCO), con una riflessione sulle conseguenze dell’avvento dei data center sul consumo di energia elettrica. Lorini guarda alla scala nazionale e contestualizza storicamente quanto sta avvenendo.




Cosa è accaduto riguardo al fabbisogno di energia elettrica negli ultimi 100 anni?

 




Nella prima metà del XX secolo in Italia non si superò mai la soglia dei 25 TWh e l’energia era prodotta principalmente attraverso centrali idroelettriche. Nel dopoguerra, gli anni del 

boom

 economico e dell’industrializzazione, il fabbisogno triplicò. Nel 1968 vennero superati i 100 TWh annui grazie anche all’uso di altre fonti: all’idroelettrico si affiancò soprattutto il petrolio. Nel 1973, alla vigilia della prima grande crisi petrolifera, due terzi del fabbisogno nazionale di energia elettrica erano coperti da centrali a olio combustibile. Negli anni ’70-’80 ci fu il momento del nucleare; quattro centrali che anche quando funzionavano tutte e contemporaneamente non coprirono mai più del 4-4,5% del fabbisogno elettrico nazionale, che in quel periodo era tra i 150 e i 200 TWh annui (e che lasciarono strascichi che si paghiamo ancora). Negli ultimi 20 anni del XX secolo la domanda di energia elettrica in Italia crebbe fino a sfiorare i 300 TWh annui. Rispetto alle fonti, Lorini mostra dati che indicano come il petrolio sia stato in gran parte progressivamente sostituito dal gas naturale, con cui nel 2000 in Italia si produceva più della metà dell’energia elettrica.




Il picco dei consumi elettrici in Italia venne raggiunto 20 anni fa, nel 2007, con 340 TWh annui: da quel momento – gli ultimi 20 anni – il fabbisogno di energia elettrica è rimasto stabile fra i 300 e i 320 TWh. Di questi, il 40% è attualmente coperto con fonti rinnovabili: fotovoltaico soprattutto, ma anche idroelettrico, un po’ di eolico, un po’ di geotermico. La crescita costante di consumo che ha caratterizzato tutto il XX secolo, con il XXI si è sostanzialmente arrestata, se non leggermente calata.




Quali sono i motivi di questo calo di consumi nell’ultimo ventennio?




–        L’efficientamento: per fare le stesse cose che facevamo 20 o 25 anni fa, oggi, grazie al miglioramento tecnologico, consumiamo meno energia elettrica.




–        L’autoproduzione e l’autoconsumo, che non rientrano nei dati ufficiali, per cui chi avesse pannelli solari sul proprio tetto per i propri consumi, non rientra nel conteggio ufficiale a livello nazionale (si stima sia tra i 5 e i 10 TWh annui).




Se i consumi restassero stabili, entro il 2030 si potrebbe arrivare al 50% del fabbisogno elettrico coperto da fonti rinnovabili (oggi siamo intorno al 41%) e quindi progressivamente aumentare la quota di rinnovabili per sostituire progressivamente le fonti fossili nella transizione energetica. Il professor Angelo Tartaglia ha calcolato che con gli attuali pannelli fotovoltaici in commercio il fabbisogno complessivo annuo nazionale (315 TWh) potrebbe essere coperto con pannelli installati sullo 0,52% della superficie del territorio nazionale (Lorini cita esplicitamente tetti e coperture, non suoli agricoli). Tra l’altro, così facendo e con consumi stabili, entro il 2030 l’Italia non avrebbe più bisogno di importare energia elettrica dalla rete europea, di cui, per inciso, meno della metà arriva dalla Francia nucleare. Va infatti sottolineato che gli acquisti dall’estero dipendono per lo più dalla convenienza del prezzo in certi periodi, più che dalla capacità di produzione.




A partire da questo quadro di informazioni, Lorini propone due possibili scenari per la transizione energetica:




–        se la domanda si stabilizzasse a 300 TWh all’anno, per arrivare al 63,4% da rinnovabili (obiettivo PNIEC) servirebbe  produrre 190 TW, che è un obiettivo fattibile.




–        Se però la domanda crescesse fino a 400 TWh all’anno, diventerebbe difficilissimo coprire questo fabbisogno con le rinnovabili.




È qui che Lorini inserisce un discorso sui consumi che potrebbero portare il fabbisogno da 300 a 400 TWh all’anno, e che identifica nei seguenti tre:




–        i condizionatori. L’aumento delle temperature comporta una crescita stimata di circa 7 TWh all’anno entro il 2030.




–        Le auto elettriche. Previsioni dicono che si passerà dall’1% attuale al 5% nel 2030 e 10% nel 2035, con un consumo di circa 15 TWh all’anno in più.




–        I data center. A livello nazionale si prevede che arriveranno a consumare ulteriori 30-35 TWh all’anno.




Sono quindi soprattutto i data center a far saltare il banco con una richiesta di energia abnorme, per cui le uniche strade sembrerebbero quella del continuo consumo di combustibili fossili o la costruzione di nuove centrali nucleari. La proliferazione dei data center altamente energivori porterebbe inevitabilmente con sé il ritorno alla produzione di energia con il nucleare, perché non basterebbero i pannelli fotovoltaici sugli edifici o sui campi per coprire questi ordini di grandezza.

 dei clienti, nonché una crisi di liquidità delle imprese del settore, dovuta tra l’altro alla crescita dei ritiri dei finanziamenti da parte del mercato.”




Da un lato quindi si verifica una mole di investimenti gigantesca accumulata nel corso del tempo e, dall’altro lato, a fronte dell’indebitamento c’è forte incertezza rispetto ai risultati reali in termini di margine operativo lordo. 




Un altro elemento importante è il seguente: per effetto di un indebitamento così marcato e per i massicci investimenti di grandi aziende (Nvidia, Microsoft, OpenAi, Antropic) si sono venuti a creare multipli azionari con un rapporto tra prezzo e utile attestatosi intorno a numeri altissimi. Ciò significa che c’è una grande attribuzione di valore alle società legate al mondo dell’AI a fronte di un indebitamento che sostiene grandi aspettative ma che cova incertezze sulla sua tenuta e sulla realizzazione reale degli investimenti. 




Questo processo sta però mostrando i suoi primi segnali di incrinatura e del rischio bolla finanziaria, ossia una forte contrazione del valore azionario di alcune di queste società. Ciò che ne si può dedurre è un dato generalizzato di un parziale rallentamento. Perché ? L’AI dovrà fare i conti con il progressivo aumento dei tassi di interesse. Infatti per  effetto dell’indebitamento complessivo negli USA i tassi si stanno gonfiando, il Paese è  alle prese con la ricomparsa dell’inflazione (4%) e, quindi, per situazioni così indebitate poter far fronte al mantenimento del valore del proprio titolo con ulteriore ricorso al debito, se i tassi di interesse crescono, diventa un meccanismo sempre più oneroso e complicato. Non è un caso, aggiunge Volpi, che OpenAi e Antropic hanno ritardato la loro iscrizione in borsa, questo perché la quotazione oggi è pericolosa. 




Infine, una parte significativa delle risorse viene dai grandi gestori internazionali del risparmio (BlackRock e altri): realtà che inizialmente hanno sostenuto questo sforzo comprando i titoli di Alphabet INC e Nvidia, grazie alla capacità di assorbire azioni a livello internazionale. Ma in questo momento anche i grandi fondi, che dispongono del risparmio mondiale, devono indirizzarlo verso prodotti sul mercato globale che duplicano gli indici con una maggiore certezza. Bisognerà dunque vedere se questi fondi di investimento continueranno a indirizzare le loro iniezioni di capitale nel settore dell’intelligenza artificiale. Questo perché se scende il valore delle azioni dell’AI saranno costretti a venderle  in modo da ricomporre il paniere dei fondi di investimento dei risparmiatori, al cui interno infatti sono presenti anche fondi pensione, inclusi quelli di gran parte degli italiani. Il meccanismo descritto implica un fattore di rischio su settori fortemente iniettati di capitale privato, strettamente legati all’andamento della borsa mondiale e, dunque, immersi nella possibilità di sgonfiarsi completamente svalutando così pezzi di stato sociale che dovrebbe invece essere garantito. 




La bolla dunque è costruita su questa simmetria: risultati non sufficienti a giustificare multipli azionari di questo tipo e, parallelamente, aumento dei tassi di interesse. Oltre al contesto americano va tenuto in conto il debito europeo e il processo che alimenta la bolla legata agli investimenti nel riarmo (anch’esso legato all’intelligenza artificiale) oltre che alla spesa a esso dedicata. 




La bolla dell’AI è una bolla finanziarizzata: l’interrogativo riguarda il fatto se le vendite future riusciranno a coprire gli enormi costi già in atto oppure no e l’esempio dei progetti di data center è un fattore concreto di questo processo che si materializza sui nostri territori. 







2.4 Dibattito sul

 

ruolo della politica




L’intervento di Alberto Deambrogio pone alcuni interrogativi importanti sull’atteggiamento e sul ruolo della politica nei confronti del dilagare di data center in atto. Il quadro che ne emerge è preoccupante e desolante allo stesso tempo: una politica che pare aver smarrito il proprio reale compito, insufficiente nel suo agire e continuamente alla rincorsa nel tentativo di normare qualcosa che nella sostanza le sfugge di mano.




Una riflessione questa che si rispecchia su livelli diversi, a partire dal regolamento europeo che prevede una rendicontazione annuale per una serie di dati riguardanti queste megastrutture, uno schema di 

rating

 per classificare i data center e un tentativo di stabilire standard minimi vincolanti di prestazione energetica. Al di là della dubbia efficacia delle prime due misure dovuta alla grande opacità dei proponenti dei progetti (come riportato da diversi studi), nella sostanza si palesa un orientamento stabilito in maniera non autonoma, che semplicemente insegue il progredire del fenomeno.




Anche a livello nazionale però le norme denotano un atteggiamento di insufficienza, tra l’altro votate bipartisan. Il quadro normativo, sostanzialmente riconducibile al Decreto legge semplificazioni e bollette dell’anno corrente, si focalizza sul procedimento unico e sui tempi di realizzazione delle strutture, sulla semplificazione dei nodi di connessione e sul ricorso a un commissario di governo per investimenti strategici superiori a 1 miliardo di euro, senza neanche menzionare l’interlocuzione e il dialogo con i territori interessati. Una pericolosa dinamica quest’ultima, che ripropone lo stesso schema utilizzato per il nucleare: tutto viene centralizzato, le decisioni sono prese dalle alte sfere in autonomia e il coinvolgimento delle comunità locali è assente (si ripresenta anche sotto questo aspetto dunque il legame fin qui più volte sottolineato tra data center e atomo).




Per quanto concerne la regione Piemonte invece un testo di legge a oggi non c’è ancora, esistono però delle proposte che lasciano intravedere un orientamento di massima: si accetta il fenomeno data center in maniera acritica impegnandosi a stabilire dei paletti per limitare gli inconvenienti. Si ripropone dunque anche a livello locale l’atteggiamento politico di cui sopra: la volontà di attrarre sul territorio capitali e strutture per poi agire di rimando. Gli stessi “paletti” auspicati nelle proposte appaiono comunque deboli, in particolar modo in merito al consumo di suolo e acqua, all’inquinamento acustico e al tema delle monetizzazioni; i riferimenti sono troppo morbidi e non contengono limiti cogenti.




Il testo di legge finale della regione Piemonte sta probabilmente attendendo di valutare quel che sta accadendo in Lombardia, dove una legge esiste già, poco efficace, ma dove esiste anche un fermento e un movimento di protesta importante che richiede a gran voce una moratoria che si può riassumere così: è necessario fermarsi per comprendere e valutare attentamente la natura del fenomeno (utilità, fattibilità, impatti di varia natura, a chi torna utile…) e in un secondo momento scrivere la normativa, senza rincorrere il proponente di turno. 




Di fronte a questo tipo di atteggiamento normativo passivo urge dunque fare pressioni affinché la politica costruisca un proprio punto di vista critico autonomo, al fine di contrastare il comando di scienza e tecnologia (prendendo coscienza che esse non sono mai neutre), il cui potere pretende sempre più di essere considerato indiscusso.




Occorre si prendano posizioni critiche a monte, senza avere alcun timore di essere considerati retrogradi o “quelli del No”. Non si tratta di volersi fermare per guardare indietro, bensì di porsi interrogativi seri al fine di scegliere un modello diverso. Il relatore si pone poi una serie di interrogativi che riproponiamo qui per sviluppare dibattito in merito: questi mega impianti, questi 

hyperscaler

, sono davvero la priorità e lo sviluppo futuro che vogliamo pianificare? E’ in grado la politica di farsi proponente di un’alternativa reale per poter cogliere le vere opportunità del progresso tecnologico senza prostrarsi ai proponenti portatori di interessi di profitto? Perché nessuno considera il principio di “calcolo diffuso” (o distribuito) con cui sviluppare l’AI che può realmente servirci mediante il potenziamento dei nostri computer? E ancora, le aziende alle spalle di queste mega strutture lavorano e accumulano ricchezza con i dati che produciamo noi tutti e forniamo loro gratuitamente: vogliamo parlare di come distribuire i proventi?




C’è poi un ulteriore elemento che la discussione politica elude trasversalmente: l’effetto cumulativo dei data center. Come descritto precedentemente è in atto una bolla finanziaria enorme nel settore dell’AI e varrebbe la pena porsi un interrogativo: nel momento in cui scoppierà questa bolla, quale sarà l’effetto sui territori occupati da queste strutture? Chi pagherà il conto? La risposta è chiara fin da ora: il dominio della finanza lascia dietro di sé macerie che paga la collettività.




Conclusioni




A fronte di queste riflessioni concludiamo quindi con un nostro punto di vista. Il punto per noi sta nella proprietà e nella contesa del potere dell’energia in senso generale, unica possibilità per stabilire a chi serve e per cosa. Soltanto nella possibilità di riappropriarsi della produzione, gestione e consumo dell’energia si potrebbe aprire uno scenario di sostenibilità e uguaglianza. Per fare questo è evidente che non basti enunciarlo ma che occorra porsi il problema dei rapporti di forza e della riorganizzazione generale dei rapporti nella società. Detto questo, se pensiamo a un certo tipo di fonte energetica come le rinnovabili, uno scenario simile non sarebbe così fuori dalla realtà. Il primo problema dunque, quando ci si vuole approcciare al tema dei data center e dell’AI nei termini di una possibile loro riforma, riguarda il fatto che il loro sviluppo è materialmente inscindibile dall’utilizzo di energia nucleare. Questo quindi impone un serio bagno di realtà: l’energia atomica è l’energia padrona per eccellenza e uno scenario di controllo popolare su di essa è escluso, come la stessa storia del movimento antinucleare ci insegna. In secondo luogo, l’intelligenza artificiale sviluppata oggi non può prevedere un suo impiego che escluda il dual use per il militare: è impossibile dunque pensare di scindere una AI “buona” da una AI “cattiva”. Il punto quindi non è per noi doversi porre il problema di trovare loro una soluzione per risolvere la crisi in atto quanto più di porre con fermezza un NO chiaro e netto alla messa a disposizione dei territori e di chi li abita per una rivoluzione industriale che è contro gli interessi collettivi ma insitamente in favore degli interessi di chi deve oggi garantire un’egemonia globale tramite la guerra. Lo abbiamo detto sin dal primo momento con il 

Manifesto

 di Confluenza: dire NO è il primo atto costitutivo di un processo democratico reale e ricompositivo e dietro il nostro NO c’è già di fatto una proposta autonoma del vivere il territorio e le relazioni in e con esso.

title: PETA Vegan Award 2027 – jetzt bewerben für den Bereich Food
content:
Immer mehr Menschen entscheiden sich für eine 

vegane Lebens-

 und 

Ernährungsweise

. Zudem greifen auch vermehrt Menschen auf vegane Alternativen zurück, die sich 

vegetarisch

, 

pescetarisch

 oder omnivor ernähren. Um der wachsenden Nachfrage in dieser Branche gerecht zu werden, bieten mittlerweile zahlreiche Marken und Unternehmen vegane Produkte an.




Um diese bemerkenswerte Entwicklung hin zu mehr Tierschutz durch ein zunehmendes veganes Produktangebot in der Ernährungsindustrie zu würdigen, verleihen wir von PETA Deutschland jährlich den 

PETA Vegan Award im Bereich Food

.




Der PETA Vegan Award im Bereich Food




Mit unserer jährlichen Auszeichnung werden tierfreundliche vegane Lebensmittel wie Alternativen zu verschiedensten Milch-, Eier- und Fleischprodukten sowie Snacks und Fertiggerichte prämiert.Wir zeichnen zudem Produktreihen, Sortimente und Supermärkte für ihren Beitrag aus, eine vegane Ernährung in der Gesellschaft zu etablieren.




Der PETA Vegan Award ermöglicht den Gewinnern eine deutschlandweite, reichweitenstarke Plattform, um ihre herausragenden Produkte zu präsentieren, die vegan und tierfreundlich sind.




„Mit dem PETA Vegan Award im Bereich Food 2027 wollen wir zeigen,, dass tierfreie Innovationen nicht nur die Zukunft der Ernährung prägen, sondern auch Spaß machen, inspirieren und positive Veränderungen für Tiere, Menschen und unseren Planeten bewirken können. Jetzt ist die Zeit, eure Ideen sichtbar zu machen!“

Tobias Schalyo, Senior Corporate Engagement Manager bei PETA Deutschland




In den vergangenen Jahren wurden bereits Unternehmen und Marken wie LIDL mit der Eigenmarke VEMONDO, die Fleischalternativen von GREEN MOUNTAIN, Fischalternativen von UNFISHED, der Haferblock von THE VEGAN COW als Butteralternative und MAGNUM für sein veganes Angebot an Eis mit der heißbegehrten Auszeichnung gewürdigt.








		Jetzt bewerben	







In diesen Kategorien werden Awards vergeben




Für den PETA Vegan Award 2027 im Bereich Food gibt es zwölf klar definierte Hauptkategorien. Pro Kategorie wird grundsätzlich maximal ein Award vergeben. So schaffen wir mehr Exklusivität der eingereichten Produkte.




Die Kategorien umfassen:







Beste vegane Innovation




Beste vegane Fleisch- oder Wurstalternative




Beste vegane Fisch- oder Meeresfrüchtealternative




Beste vegane Käsealternative




Beste vegane Milch- oder Joghurtalternative




Bestes veganes Frühstücksprodukt oder bester Aufstrich




Bestes veganes Convenience-Produkt




Bester veganer herzhafter Snack




Beste vegane Süßigkeit oder bestes Dessert




Beste vegane Sauce, bester Dip oder beste Würze




Bestes veganes Getränk




Bestes veganes Protein- oder Functional-Food-Produkt







Zusätzlich können bis zu zwei jährlich wechselnde Kategorien hinzukommen, sofern ausreichend qualifizierte Einreichungen vorliegen.




Unser Auswahl- und Bewertungsverfahren




Sie möchten ein Produkt für den PETA Vegan Award einreichen? Dann füllen Sie zunächst unser 

Bewerbungsformular

 aus. Voraussetzung für die Teilnahme ist, dass das Produkt vollständig vegan ist und die Teilnahmebedingungen erfüllt.




Die eingereichten Produkte werden anschließend anhand dieser einheitlichen Bewertungsmatrix von unserer Jury beurteilt:







Geschmack, Textur und sensorische Qualität:

 30 %




Innovationsgrad:

 20 %




Potenzial, tierische Produkte zu ersetzen:

 20 %




Alltagstauglichkeit und Marktzugang:

 15 %




Nachhaltigkeit:

 10 %




Transparente und glaubwürdige Kommunikation:

 5 %







Für die Bewertung sind standardisierte Produkttests vorgesehen. Ein Produkt sollte dabei mindestens 75 von 100 Punkten erreichen, um für einen Award infrage zu kommen. Wenn kein Produkt die Qualitätsansprüche erfüllt, bleibt die Kategorie unbesetzt.




Während der Auswahl werden pro Kategorie drei Produkte für eine Shortlist nominiert. So erhalten diese bereits vor der Bekanntgabe der Gewinner zusätzliche Sichtbarkeit. Abschließend werden die ausgezeichneten Produkte in einer Award-Übersicht mit hochwertigen Grafiken und individuellen Jurybegründungen vorgestellt. Pro Marke wird grundsätzlich maximal ein Award vergeben.




So geht es nach der Verleihung des Awards weiter




Als ausgezeichnetes Unternehmen können Sie Ihren Award nutzen, um Ihr Produkt zu bewerben. Dazu können Sie das Award-Logo auf Ihrem Produkt einsetzen und die Auszeichnung gemeinsam mit uns kommunizieren.




Zudem bleiben wir mit allen teilnehmenden Unternehmen im Austausch. Dadurch möchten wir neue Kooperationen schaffen und langfristige Partnerschaften aufbauen.



















































































































































































































Bewerben Sie sich jetzt für den PETA Vegan Award 2027




Sie bieten ein innovatives, veganes Food- oder Beverage-Produkt an, haben eine vegane Eigenmarke oder ein herausragendes veganes Sortiment?




Dann bewerben Sie sich jetzt für den PETA Vegan Award 2027 im Bereich Food!

Wir zeichnen die vielversprechendsten Einsendungen aus.

Der Bewerbungszeitraum erstreckt sich von Montag, 02.11.2026, bis einschließlich Montag, 30.11.2026.




Wir freuen uns über Ihre Teilnahme!








		Jetzt bewerben
