title: YJA Star guerrillas: We gained our identity as resisting women through Bêrîtan
content:
Commander Bêrîtan (Gülnaz Karataş) was commemorated by her comrades in the guerrilla areas on the 34th anniversary of her martyrdom. Commander Bêrîtan was martyred in 1992 after carrying out a self-sacrificial action in Xakurkê during the war against the Turkish state and its collaborators. Bêrîtan, who became a symbol of women who refused to submit in the face of calls for surrender, established a new path of struggle. Guerrillas of the Free Women's Units (YJA Star) shared their feelings and thoughts on the anniversary of Martyr Bêrîtan's death.




YJA Star guerrilla Avaşîn Efrîn

 







 







"First of all, on the anniversary of Comrade Bêrîtan's martyrdom, we respectfully commemorate all the martyrs of freedom. We have reached this stage thanks to the efforts and truth of our pioneering martyrs. We will never forget the efforts of these heroes. Through her stance, Comrade Bêrîtan showed us the path of self-sacrifice. Bêrîtan's path is the path of freedom, and it is also the path of all martyrs. We unite around this path and educate ourselves on this basis. Particularly in this period, establishing genuine comradeship with Abdullah Öcalan is possible through a proper understanding of the martyrs. Thanks to Comrade Bêrîtan, we learned how to struggle as YJA Star guerrillas, came to know ourselves and developed an identity. On this basis, we renew our promise to uphold the legacy of the martyrs."




YJA Star guerrilla Azê Azad 







 







"On the anniversary of Comrade Bêrîtan's martyrdom, I respectfully commemorate all our martyred comrades. Upholding the dreams of our martyred comrades is a fundamental duty for us. Words may be inadequate to express our feelings about Martyr Bêrîtan. However, today we follow in Comrade Bêrîtan's footsteps and want to wage a genuine struggle worthy of the martyrs of freedom. Through her efforts and knowledge, Bêrîtan reached the highest level of self-sacrifice, and the women's army was established through her example. We have reached this point today thanks to Comrade Bêrîtan's sacrifice. As YJA Star guerrillas, we will uphold the dreams of our martyred comrades who sought to secure Abdullah Öcalan's freedom and strengthen our struggle."




YJA Star guerrilla Bêrîtan Zagros 







 







"As YJA Star guerrillas, we commemorate all our comrades who were martyred in October through the example of Comrade Bêrîtan, and we promise to fulfil their dreams. As YJA Star, we are carrying out such a strong struggle today particularly thanks to the legacy of the martyrs. Through Bêrîtan, we gained our identity as women of resistance. Martyr Bêrîtan's stance did not remain confined to the past; it is kept alive at every moment.




Just as Comrade Bêrîtan took the path of Besê and Zarîfe as her guiding principle and resisted, we also uphold the path of free women on the basis of the truth of those martyrs. Comrade Bêrîtan constantly strove to understand the reality of Abdullah Öcalan's leadership. She had developed a clear commitment to this path and therefore adopted radical and organised positions. This stance formed the foundation of our freedom struggle. Our aim is to secure the physical freedom of Abdullah Öcalan and uphold the struggle and dreams of the martyrs."

title: Shengal is at a historic turning point
content:
Shengal is now at a historic turning point. Shengal’s existence and integration bring with them a comprehensive unity with Iraq. The integration of the collective will and the genuine integration of people’s everyday lives represent the first concrete step towards bringing the two communities together in a shared life, while preserving their mother tongues and native cultures. The political reality and future represent a historic stage in which this social unity is translated into a political reality.




The coming together of the two communities through their respective cultural values and their ability to live in their mother tongues forms the cornerstone of this process. This political and cultural integration carries a force that connects with the reality of Abdullah Öcalan’s life and unites the entire society around this collective will.




This historic process expresses the will of the people of Shengal to determine their own future and live on an equal footing with Iraqi society, while also laying the foundations for building a shared future, peace and stability.




A shared political future aims to strengthen the political and social status of the Shengal region within Iraq as a whole and to permanently enshrine the people’s right to self-determination on a constitutional basis.




The integration process enables people of different faiths and identities to develop practices of coexistence based on social peace and tolerance. It is clear that the harmony fostered by integration will contribute to preserving regional stability and establishing lasting peace in Shengal and the surrounding areas.




The integration of security and administrative structures also involves reorganising the region’s security and administrative mechanisms so that they are aligned with the collective will of the people.




Socio-economic development and the integration of services will also improve people’s living standards by strengthening the region’s infrastructure, healthcare and education services.




Historical memory and recognition of identity




This process also entails preserving historical memory and acknowledging the truth, demonstrating respect for the region’s past and enabling its people to look towards the future with confidence in their own identity.




Shengal’s legal status and administrative structure within Iraq as a whole are being balanced within a framework of mutual respect and shared interests with other communities in the region. The key to the success of this process lies in the people’s will and their ability to shape their own future through their own collective decisions, across every area, from infrastructure to education.




Democratic Participation and Representation:

 The process is based on a participatory model of democracy that ensures different segments of society are represented equally and effectively within governing institutions.




Pluralistic Representation and Participatory Politics:

 The integration process has been designed to ensure that the will of all social groups, religious communities and women’s councils living throughout Shengal is reflected at the highest level in governing institutions. Rather than a narrow structure of power, this approach demonstrates a commitment to implementing an egalitarian, participatory political model that develops from the grassroots upwards. In this way, every individual’s voice can be represented in the process of governance.




The Principles of Justice and Equal Citizenship:

 The integration process is based on establishing justice in the region and fully safeguarding the constitutional rights of all ethnic and religious groups. This is intended to guarantee equality before the law for every segment of society and peaceful coexistence within a democratic legal order.




Distinctive Education and Cultural Preservation:

 The integration process guarantees the restructuring of the region’s education system in accordance with the principle of education in the mother tongue, as well as the transmission of cultural heritage to future generations. This is a critical step towards protecting and strengthening local identity.




Socio-Cultural Development and Social Welfare:

 The integration process also encompasses development programmes designed to strengthen the region’s social fabric and improve people’s well-being. Raising standards in education and healthcare and improving infrastructure are essential to establishing the foundations for a stable life.




Historical Memory and the 2014 massacre:

 The people of Shengal continue to carry the profound pain of the massacre and atrocities they endured in 2014. The systematic violence inflicted on women and children has been etched into the community’s collective memory. The steps being taken today demonstrate that this process is part of the struggle to confront that historical trauma. This struggle is being carried forward in dedication to the memory of the heroic martyrs, with the aim of safeguarding the community’s future through this resolute stance.




This process reflects a historic reality in which the suffering experienced, and the struggle waged in Shengal are intertwined with the cherished memory of those who lost their lives. The continuation of the struggle and its achievements symbolise how these sacrifices have strengthened the collective will of the people and helped lay solid foundations for the future.




Constitutional guarantees and legal status




Securing an autonomous and legally recognised status for Shengal within Iraq would ensure that the people’s democratic rights are protected within a constitutional framework and that Shengal can integrate with Iraq through its own administrative institutions.




Democratic Governance:

 Removing all administrative and legal obstacles to governing Shengal through its own councils and autonomous structures would enable the collective will of the people to be reflected in political decisions.




The Functioning of Local Government:

 Local councils and committees in Shengal make decisions through the direct participation of the people and carry out their administrative functions in accordance with democratic principles. This structure aims to ensure that the needs of the community are met as effectively as possible.




Historical Justice and Social Healing:

 The steps being taken for Shengal are vital not only for establishing its political status but also for recognising what happened in 2014 and achieving historical justice. Being able to look towards the future with confidence requires confronting the painful truths of the past and drawing strength from them to reinforce the collective will of the people.




Democratic Autonomy and Rights:

 This process also represents the people’s determination to secure their own governing institutions and rights within a framework of democratic autonomy, with constitutional guarantees.




Self-Governance and Social Organisation:

 The model of social organisation initiates a process through which Shengal can establish its own administrative structures and popular assemblies, putting political and administrative autonomy into practice.

title: Iran sentences three protest detainees to death, whereabouts unknown
content:
Branch 23 of the Islamic Revolutionary Court in Tehran has sentenced three men arrested during the December 2025–January 2026 protests to death on charges of “espionage.”




An informed source who spoke to the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) said that the men, named Mehdi, Amir-Reza and Vahid, were notified of their sentences in Greater Tehran Central Penitentiary on 26 October.




The source added that on 28 October, the three political prisoners were summoned to the prison’s guard office on the pretext of being transferred to Ghezel Hesar Prison in Karaj, but were taken to an undisclosed location.




Security forces arrested the three men during the protests in Tehran and transferred them to the Greater Tehran Central Penitentiary after a period in detention. Their case was referred to Branch 23 following their indictment on charges of “espionage”, the source said.




At the time of the report, their transfer to Ghezel Hesar Prison remained unconfirmed, with no precise information available about the trial proceedings or the latest status of their cases.

title: Kurdish Peace Mothers to launch a vigil in Ankara
content:
The Peace Mothers Initiative aims to increase pressure for concrete steps in the peace and democratic society process through a multi-day vigil in the Turkish capital, Ankara. Representatives of the Peace Mothers’ Councils from 24 cities will gather on November 1, hold talks with political parties, and set up a protest tent. Their central demands include freedom for Abdullah Öcalan, action to address the situation of political prisoners, and accountability from the Turkish state for advancing the peace process.




At a press conference held at the branch of the Human Rights Association (IHD) in the province of Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır), Nezahat Teke recalled that Öcalan’s call on February 27, 2025, had raised great hopes. “However, for these hopes to develop into a genuine peace process, the state must also take action. If Öcalan is not free, any laws that are passed will be meaningless,” Teke said.




Demands for Öcalan’s freedom and improved prison conditions




The Peace Mothers are demanding that Öcalan be granted a legally and politically recognized status that would enable him to participate actively in the peace process. According to Teke, his inclusion in existing or planned commissions could make a significant contribution to advancing the process. “Our most important demand is the freedom and recognition of our leader’s status. Talks are held only once every two months, and that is not enough. The person who can bring about a solution is Abdullah Öcalan,” Teke said.




She also drew attention to conditions in Turkish prisons, saying: “Numerous prisoners are seriously ill, while others are being denied release despite having served their sentences. The Peace Mothers no longer want to see prisoners returning from detention facilities only after their deaths.”




Talks with political parties planned through Tuesday




The delegations plan to present their demands in Ankara. In addition to meetings with political parties, they intend to hold a vigil and submit documents outlining the Peace Mothers’ concerns. “We will go to Ankara and convey our demands to the political parties. We will stay there until Tuesday,” Teke stated. She also called on civil society organizations in the capital to show solidarity: “Today, everyone has something to say about peace. They should support the mothers as well.”




The Peace Mothers hope that political leaders will respond to their demands. “We will present our documents, demands, and concerns in Ankara. We hope they will receive us and not send us back empty-handed,” Teke said. In closing, she appealed to the media to refrain from using language that fuels hostility and obstructs peace.

title: Seit Mai 2023 blockiertes Arbeitsgerichtsverfahren in Lissabon: Teleperformance Portugal, Google-Integration und die Frage nach wirksamem Rechtsschutz
content:
Dossier




„

Im Mai 2023 reichte Marc S. Weidner beim Arbeitsgericht Lissabon Klage gegen Teleperformance Portugal ein. Er klagt, weil nach seiner Darstellung erhebliche Vergütungs- und Differenzansprüche, Bonuszahlungen, Erstattungen, Prämien, Gratifikationen sowie Ansprüche aus Aufgaben- und Rollenentwicklung offen sind. Zudem geht es um die rechtliche Einordnung seiner Tätigkeit: Nach Darstellung des Klägers war er nicht bloss in einem üblichen Call-Center-Beschäftigungsverhältnis tätig, sondern funktional weitgehend in Strukturen der Google Germany GmbH und Google LLC eingebunden, während die arbeitsrechtliche Führung formal über Teleperformance Portugal lief.

 (…) Nach einer ersten Anhörung im Juni 2023 kam das Verfahren nach Darstellung des Klägers weitgehend zum Stillstand (…) Der Fall hat inzwischen existenzielle Folgen

…“ Siehe die vollständige Darstellung durch Marc S. Weidner seines Falls an der Schnittstelle von Big Tech, ausgelagerter Beschäftigung, prekärer Rechtsdurchsetzung und institutionellem Versagen – sowie eine Spendenkampagne zur Existenzsicherung und Rechtsverteidigung des Betroffenen:







Teleperformance/Google: 19 Zeugen zugelassen – Hauptverhandlung erst am 7. Oktober 2027 – Unterstützung des Klägers bleibt notwendig 

 


„

In meinem Verfahren gegen Teleperformance Portugal gibt es endlich einen konkreten Fortschritt: Das Arbeitsgericht Lissabon hat die benannten Zeugen und sämtliche Beweismittel und Anlagenkonvolute zugelassen und inzwischen die Hauptverhandlung terminiert. Damit kommt ein Fall voran, dessen Bedeutung über meine persönlichen Ansprüche hinausreicht. Es geht darum, europäische Arbeitnehmerrechte auch dort durchzusetzen, wo Beschäftigte vertraglich einem Dienstleister zugeordnet sind, tatsächlich aber in der Arbeitsorganisation eines Technologiekonzerns arbeiten. Ein Erfolg könnte andere Beschäftigte in vergleichbaren Konstellationen ermutigen, ihre Ansprüche ebenfalls geltend zu machen.




Dennoch wird weiter die zeitliche Karte gespielt, um Druck auf den Kläger auszuüben und aufrechtzuerhalten: Die Hauptverhandlung soll erst am 7. Oktober 2027 beginnen.




Seit dem 22. Mai 2023 liegt meine Klage gegen Teleperformance Portugal beim Gericht. Sie umfasst 96 nummerierte Beweispositionen, teilweise umfangreiche Anlagenkonvolute, und benennt 19 Zeugen. Wesentliche Unterlagen sind Originalartefakte aus den Google-Systemen, in denen ich gearbeitet habe. Damit will ich konkret nachweisen, wer Aufgaben vorgab, Weisungen erteilte, Leistungen kontrollierte und meine Arbeit tatsächlich organisierte.


Mit Beschluss vom 17. Juli 2026, mitgeteilt am 24. Juli, ließ das Gericht die benannten Zeugen und die eingereichten Dokumente zu. Alle 19 benannten Zeugen waren damit von der Zulassung erfasst.


Am 18. September 2026 wurde eine Sitzung zur Vorbereitung der Hauptverhandlung für den 26. Oktober 2026 angesetzt. Bereits diese Terminierung beanstande ich als verspätet: Zwischen Anberaumung und Sitzung lagen 38 Kalendertage, während Art. 62 Abs. 2 des portugiesischen Arbeitsprozessgesetzes für eine audiência prévia eine Frist von 20 Tagen vorsieht.


Beim Termin am 26. Oktobern 2026 sollte ich mich zudem auf zehn Zeugen beschränken. Auch dabei kam ich dem Gericht entgegen. Noch in derselben Sitzung wurde der erste Hauptverhandlungstermin auf den 7. Oktober 2027 festgelegt. Weitere 346 Tage. Seit Einreichung der Klage werden dann mehr als vier Jahre und vier Monate vergangen sein.


Kooperationsbereitschaft war also vorhanden. Ein zeitnaher Hauptverhandlungstermin leider nicht.




Europäische Rechtsprechung stärkt die Grundlage des Verfahrens




Während mein Verfahren wartete, hat der EuGH am 24. Oktober 2024 in der Rechtssache C-441/23, Omnitel Comunicaciones und andere, unter Beteiligung von Microsoft Ibérica, wesentliche Fragen zur Arbeitnehmerüberlassung geklärt. Das Urteil konkretisiert gerade die unionsrechtlichen Maßstäbe, auf die ich meine Klage stütze.


Entscheidend sind unter anderem die tatsächliche Aufsicht und Leitung im Einsatzunternehmen. Eine fehlende behördliche Zulassung als Leiharbeitsunternehmen schließt den Schutz der Richtlinie 2008/104/EG nicht allein deshalb aus. Liegt Arbeitnehmerüberlassung im Sinne der Richtlinie vor, muss die Vergütung während des Einsatzes mindestens dem entsprechen, was der Arbeitnehmer bei unmittelbarer Einstellung durch das Einsatzunternehmen erhalten hätte.


Zusammen mit den vorgelegten Unterlagen und den zugelassenen Zeugen sehe ich darin eine deutlich gestärkte Grundlage, meine Ansprüche durchzusetzen. Die tatsächliche Einbindung in die Google-Arbeitsorganisation muss nun endlich anhand dieser Beweise verhandelt werden.


Auch zur Verfahrensdauer gibt es einschlägige Rechtsprechung. Im Urteil Ferreira da Silva e Brito und andere gegen Portugal vom 22. Mai 2012, Beschwerde Nr. 46273/09, stellte der EGMR wegen eines überlangen Verfahrens am Arbeitsgericht Lissabon eine Verletzung von Art. 6 Abs. 1 EMRK fest. Er betonte ausdrücklich die besondere Sorgfalt, die Arbeitsstreitigkeiten verlangen. Die Verpflichtung zu wirksamem und rechtzeitigem Rechtsschutz ist längst formuliert.




Unterstützung bleibt notwendig




Weiterhin brauche ich Mittel für eine verlässliche anwaltliche Vertretung. Besonders wichtig wäre mir, meinen erst befassten Rechtsanwalt als Wahlanwalt erneut beauftragen zu können, der bereits mit der Sache befasst war. Die Dokumentation und rechtliche Aufarbeitung habe ich über Jahre selbst vorangetrieben. Diese Arbeit weiterzuführen und die rechtlichen Möglichkeiten konsequent zu nutzen, erfordert jetzt auch finanzielle Unterstützung.


Deshalb bitte ich um Solidarität für die Fortführung des Verfahrens und den Wiederaufbau meiner Lebensgrundlage. Ein Erfolg könnte zeigen, dass Beschäftigte auch gegenüber einem großen Dienstleister ihre tatsächliche Einbindung in einen Konzern offenlegen und daraus folgende Rechte durchsetzen können. Genau dafür lohnt es sich, diesen Fall weiterzutragen.




Spenden für Rechtsverteidigung und Existenzsicherung:

 

https://www.gofundme.com/f/rechtsverteidigung-existenzsicherung-arbeitsgericht-lisbon




Auch der Kauf meiner Bücher hilft. Wer noch ein Weihnachtsgeschenk sucht, kann mich auf diesem Weg unterstützen. Wer selbst nichts beitragen kann, hilft durch Weiterleiten dieses Berichts und des Spendenaufrufs.

Seit Mai 2023 blockiertes Arbeitsgerichtsverfahren in Lissabon: Teleperformance Portugal, Google-Integration und die Frage nach wirksamem Rechtsschutz




„

Im Mai 2023 reichte Marc S. Weidner beim Arbeitsgericht Lissabon Klage gegen Teleperformance Portugal ein. Er klagt, weil nach seiner Darstellung erhebliche Vergütungs- und Differenzansprüche, Bonuszahlungen, Erstattungen, Prämien, Gratifikationen sowie Ansprüche aus Aufgaben- und Rollenentwicklung offen sind. Zudem geht es um die rechtliche Einordnung seiner Tätigkeit: Nach Darstellung des Klägers war er nicht bloss in einem üblichen Call-Center-Beschäftigungsverhältnis tätig, sondern funktional weitgehend in Strukturen der Google Germany GmbH und Google LLC eingebunden, während die arbeitsrechtliche Führung formal über Teleperformance Portugal lief. Dazu zählt unter anderem eine dokumentierte Quiet Period mit Tradingverbot für Google-Aktien, wie sie typischerweise auf eine besondere Nähe zu konzernrelevanten Informationen und internen Compliance-Strukturen verweist.




Auch die ausgeübte Tätigkeit ging nach Darstellung des Klägers deutlich über klassische Call-Center-Arbeit hinaus. Sie umfasste spezialisierte Aufgaben, Qualitäts- und Prozessverantwortung sowie Personalentscheidungskompetenz. Der Fall wirft damit eine grundsätzlichere Frage auf: Wenn selbst hochqualifizierte Spezialisten mit faktischer Verantwortung in Konzernabläufe eingebunden, aber arbeitsrechtlich über externe Dienstleisterstrukturen geführt werden, wie belastbar ist dann der Schutz vor ausgelagerter Verantwortung überhaupt noch?




Der Umfang des Verfahrens zeigt zudem, dass es sich nicht um eine Petitesse handelt. Die Klageschrift umfasst 63 Seiten mit 319 Absätzen. Dazu kommen 96 Beweiskonvolute, teilweise mit mehr als 30 Seiten je Konvolut, darunter Unterlagen aus internen Google-Systemen beziehungsweise internen Unternehmenssystemen, sowie 20 benannte Zeugen u.a. der Google Ireland Ltd., die die Europa Geschäfte koordiniert. Dieser Umfang macht Aktenzugang, strukturierte Aufbereitung und prozessuale Interventionen zwingend und zugleich kostenintensiv.




Nach einer ersten Anhörung im Juni 2023 kam das Verfahren nach Darstellung des Klägers weitgehend zum Stillstand: keine Beweisaufnahme, keine Entscheidung, keine wirksame Verfahrensförderung. Hinzu kommt ein weiteres Problem, das für Beschäftigte ohne eigene Mittel besonders schwer wiegt: die wiederholt instabile Pflichtvertretung. Mehrere beigeordnete Anwälte schieden aus oder blieben aus Sicht des Klägers untätig. Damit wird aus einem arbeitsrechtlichen Verfahren auch eine Frage des Zugangs zum Recht: Was nützt ein formal eröffneter Rechtsweg, wenn er über Jahre nicht praktisch durchgesetzt werden kann?




Der Fall hat inzwischen existenzielle Folgen. Nach Angaben des Klägers führten Verfahrensdauer, ausbleibende Klärung und fehlende stabile Vertretung zum Verlust von Wohnung, Haushalt und zuletzt auch zur Sperrung wesentlicher Infrastruktur. Die ursprüngliche Falldokumentation ist deshalb derzeit nicht mehr auf der eigenen Seite erreichbar, aber über das Web Archive abrufbar. Eine S

pendenkampagne zur Existenzsicherung und Rechtsverteidigung besteht ebenfalls; sie ist Folge der Situation, nicht ihr Ausgangspunkt

.“ Darstellung durch Marc S. Weidner seines Falls







Siehe zum Fall:







Arbeitsgerichtsverfahren Lissabon




Umfangreiche 

Archivierte Falldarstellung von Marc Weidner

 

 zuletzt updated am 9. Mai 2026  




Rechtsverteidigung, Existenzsicherung: Arbeitsgericht Lisbon




„… 

Die Klage ist eine klassische arbeitsrechtliche Streitigkeit vor dem Arbeitsgericht Lissabon und beruht auf einem schriftlich dokumentierten Arbeitsverhältnis mit Teleperformance Portugal S.A. Entsprechend geht es nicht um Sonderrecht, sondern um arbeitsvertragliche Vergütung und die Rechtsfolgen einer streitigen Beendigung des Arbeitsverhältnisses. Der Streitgegenstand lässt sich in drei Blöcke fassen:




Vergütungs- und Differenzansprüche: aus der tatsächlichen Aufgaben- und Rollenentwicklung, faktische Höhergruppierung, verdeckte Promotionen, variable Bestandteile und damit zusammenhängende Abrechnungsfragen.




Rechtsfolgen der Beendigung: Streit darüber, ob und wie das Arbeitsverhältnis beendet wurde, und welche gesetzlichen Zahlungsfolgen daraus bis zur gerichtlichen Klärung resultieren.




Schadenpositionen: materiell: entgangener Verdienst; immateriell: persönliche Beeinträchtigung.




Dass bislang wenig spruchreif wirkt, liegt nicht an fehlender Anspruchsgrundlage, sondern daran, dass zentrale Punkte tatsachen- und beweisgetrieben sind und ohne konsequente Terminierung und ohne bisherige Beweisaufnahme faktisch in der Schwebe bleiben. Der Streitwert der Klage ist auf 137’938,20 EUR festgesetzt

title: Silivri açıklarında bulunan cansız bedenin batan geminin 2'nci kaptanına ait olduğu belirlendi
content:
İstanbul – Silivri açıklarında Alsu isimli gemiyle çarpıştıktan sonra batan Tuğberk İmamoğlu isimli gemide bulunan 9 mürettebatı arama çalışmaları sırasında dün bulunan cansız bedenin geminin 2'nci kaptanı Rahmi Temel’e ait olduğu belirlendi. Cenazesi ailesi tarafından Adli Tıp Kurumu'ndan alınan Temel'in 31 Ekim'de İzmir'de toprağa verileceği öğrenildi.

Silivri açıklarında 2 Eylül'de Alsu isimli gemiyle çarpıştıktan sonra batan Tuğberk İmamoğlu isimli gemide bulunan 9 mürettebatı arama çalışmaları sürüyor. Çalışmalar sırasında suda, kimliği henüz belirlenemeyen erkek cesedi bulundu. Ceset, kesin ölüm nedeni ve kimliğinin belirlenmesi için Adli Tıp Kurumu'na götürüldü.

Cansız beden geminin 2'nci kaptanına ait çıktı

Adli Tıp Kurumu'nda yapılan incelemelerde, suda bulunan cesedin Tuğberk İmamoğlu isimli geminin 2'nci kaptanı Rahmi Temel'e ait olduğu belirlendi. Cenazesi ailesi tarafından Adli Tıp Kurumu'ndan alınan Temel'in 31 Ekim'de İzmir Karşıyaka’da Hacı Mustafa Beşikçioğlu Camii’nde öğle saati kılınacak namazın ardından toprağa verileceği öğrenildi.

Rahmi Temel’in abisi Remzi Temel, "Çok elim bir deniz kazası sonucu 10 denizcimiz Marmara’da sulara gömüldü. Bugün 57’nci günde bir naaş çıkarıldı. Bugün çıkarılan ikinci naaş benim kardeşimin. Diğer 8 kişi aranıyor. Aileler çadırlarda bekliyor. Zor şartlarda, ümitsizce, çaresizce bekliyorlar. Herkes bir yakınına ulaşmak için canla başla bütün duruma katlanıyor, bütün güçlükler ve zorluklar içinde bekliyorlar. Bizim için sevindirici olmadı, üzücü oldu. Ben bugün haberi aldıktan sonra başımdan aşağı kaynar su dökülmüş gibi oldu. Ama en azından bir naaşa kavuşmanın da bir rahatlığı olacak, bir mezarımız olacak. Onun için buradayız, cenazemizin verilmesini bekliyoruz. Dün gemide bulunduğunu söylediler. Biz akşam haber aldık. Kimlik tespiti bugün yapılıp haber verildi. 1 gün sonrada kimliğini öğrendik. Silivri açıklarında 35 kilometre uzağında bu olay olmuş. Marmara çukuru denilen derin bir yerde. Diğer kazazedelerin de kurtarılmasını, çıkarılmasını diliyorum, inşallah çıkarılır. Ailesi ve 2 kızı var perişan. İzmir'de oturuyorlar. Şimdi buradan bir süre sonra İzmir'e gideceğiz. Perişan olmamak elde değil. Bin de bir de olsa bir ümitle bekliyorsunuz ama bugün kayıp bulundu denmesi sevinç yerine daha büyük bir üzüntü yaratıyor" ifadelerini kullandı.

Gemide aranan mürettebattan Abdulbaki Mirzaoğlu’nun dayısı Recai Yılmaz, "Tuğberk İmamoğlu gemisinde çalışan aşçıbaşı Abdulbaki Mirzaoğlu’nun dayısıyım. 4 senedir bu şirkette gemilerde aşçıbaşı olarak çalışıyordu. 7 ay sonra 48 yaşında son emekli olacaktı. 8 çocuk babası. Ailesi de gemide çalışmasına razı değildi. Çünkü çocukları babalarını görmeden büyüyordu ve haklı da çıktılar. Deniz işçileri böyle bir yaşamı hak etmiyor. Bunların hak ve hukukları daha çok korunmalı, sahip çıkılmalı diye düşünüyorum. Denizde, gemide veya geminin yan tarafında deniz dibinde arama yapılıyor. Biz aile olarak da kısa zamanda 10 aileydik, 9'a düştük. 9 aile de çadırda Silivri'de bekliyoruz. Bu hava şartlarında orada bekliyoruz" dedi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: 15 gazeteci anlattı: Çatışmasızlık Kürt gazeteciliğini nasıl değiştiriyor?
content:
Medya ombudsmanı Faruk Bildirici, 29 Ekim'de yayımladığı “Çatışmasızlık hali ‘bölge’deki gazeteciliği nasıl dönüştürüyor?” başlıklı yazısında, Kürt meselesi etrafında gelişen çatışmasızlık sürecinin bölgedeki gazeteciliğe etkilerini ele aldı.



















22 NİSAN KÜRT GAZETECİLER GÜNÜ




"Kürt gazeteciler baskılara rağmen hakikatin izinde"




22 Nisan 2026










Diyarbakır, Van ve bölgenin farklı kentlerinde çalışan 15 gazetecinin görüşlerine yer veren Bildirici, çatışmaların azalmasının gazetecilere yeni çalışma alanları açtığını, ancak basın özgürlüğüne yönelik sorunların devam ettiğini aktardı.




Çatışma haberlerinden toplumsal sorunlara




Bildirici, 1990'lı yıllarda gazetecilerin hedef alındığı dönemi hatırlatarak bölgedeki gazeteciliğin uzun yıllar çatışmaların, operasyonların ve hak ihlallerinin gölgesinde geliştiğini belirtti.




PKK'nin silahlı güçlerini çekmesiyle oluşan çatışmasızlık ortamının özellikle Kürt gazeteciler açısından yeni olanaklar yaratabileceğini ifade etti.



















Faruk Bildirici: Tutuklu Kürt gazetecilere çifte standart uygulanıyor




27 Kasım 2023










Gazeteci Abdurrahman Gök, çatışmasızlığın kalıcılaşması durumunda gazeteciliğin güvenlik odaklı gündemden toplumsal hafızaya, haklara ve yaşam koşullarına daha fazla yönelebileceğini söyledi.




ANKA Diyarbakır Temsilcisi Ahmet Ün ise çatışmaların sona ermesiyle kırsal alanlarda haber yapmanın kolaylaşabileceğine; çiftçilerin, işsizlerin, emeklilerin ve yoksul kesimlerin sorunlarının daha görünür olabileceğine dikkat çekti.



















Kürt gazetecilerin öldürülmesi İstanbul'da protesto edildi




26 Ağustos 2024










Güneydoğu Gazeteciler Cemiyeti Başkanı Felat Bozarslan da yeni dönemin göç, ekolojik tahribat, kadınların sorunları ve gençlerin gelecek kaygısı gibi konuların daha kapsamlı işlenmesi için fırsat sunduğunu belirtti.




“Çatışmasızlık basın özgürlüğü anlamına gelmiyor”




Gazeteci Hatice Kamer, bilgiye erişim olanaklarının artmasına rağmen doğru ve güvenilir bilgiye ulaşmanın zorlaştığını, ekonomik koşullar ve mesleki risklerin gençlerin gazetecilikten uzaklaşmasına neden olduğunu anlattı.




İrfan Aktan ise Kürt meselesine ilişkin haberlerde bazı engellerin kısmen aşılmasına karşın eleştirel gazetecilik üzerindeki siyasi ve hukuki baskıların devam ettiğini vurguladı.



















Bakırhan MA ve JINNEWS'i ziyaret etti: Kürt gazeteciler büyük bedeller ödedi




22 Nisan 2024










Sürece yönelik eleştiriler de baskı altında




Gazeteci Mahmut Oral, barış sürecinin geleceğine ilişkin belirsizliğin gazeteciliği etkilediğini belirtti.




Oral'a göre hem iktidara hem de sürecin diğer siyasi aktörlerine yöneltilebilecek eleştiriler, gazetecilerin “süreç bozgunculuğu” suçlamasıyla karşılaşma kaygısını artırıyor.




Mezopotamya Ajansı muhabiri Zeynep Durgut da barış gazeteciliğinin güçlenmesi için öncelikle basın üzerindeki engellerin kaldırılması gerektiğini ifade etti.




Yazının tamamını 

buradan

 okuyabilirsiniz.

title: İspanya’da can kaybı 69’a yükseldi, makinistler grevde: Demir yolu işçilerinin sesi duyulmadı, özelleştirme çarptı
content:
İspanya’nın Toledo bölgesinde iki hızlı trenin çarpışması sonucu hayatını kaybedenlerin sayısı 69 yükseldi. Kaza, özelleştirme tartışmalarını yeniden gündeme taşıdı. Geçtiğimiz 18 Ocak’ta bir başka tren kazasında 46 kişi ölmüş, demir yolu işçileri özelleştirmeyi ve yarattığı güvenlik risklerini protesto etmek için grev yapmıştı. Hükümetin taahhütleri üzerine grev tamamlanmamış ancak vaatler yerine getirilmediği için makinist sendikası Semaf, “demir yollarında güvenlik” koşullarının sağlanması talebiyle 29 Ekim için yeni grev kararı açıklamıştı. Kaza, grevden bir gün önce gerçekleşti. Sanchez Hükümeti kazanın hemen ardından “insan hatası” diyerek demir yolu işçilerini hedef gösterirken, Samef grevi iptal etmedi ve makinistler dün 24 saat iş bıraktı.

Toledo’nın Urda bölgesindeki kazada devlete ait Renfe şirketine ait bir AVE treni (hızlı tren), Madrid-Endülüs yüksek hızlı demir yolu hattının 118. kilometresinde durmakta olan Iryo şirketine ait trene arkadan çarptı. Çarpışmanın etkisiyle Iryo treninin en arkadaki iki vagonu raydan çıkarak yuvarlandı.

Kazadan birkaç saat sonra İspanya Ulaştırma Bakanlığı “insan hatası” açıklaması yaparak suçu işçileri yıkmanın yolunu açtı. Sendikalar ise özelleştirme sonrası arızalı sistemler, azaltılmış personel ve taşeronlara devredilmiş, finansmanı kesilmiş bakım hizmetleriyle ayakta durmaya çalışan demir yolu sistemine dikkat çekiyor.

18 Ocak 2026’da da Adamuz bölgesinde de yine bir Iryo treni raydan çıkarak yan hattın üzerine girmiş ve bu hattaki bir trenle çarpışmıştı. Iryo, kasım 2022’de hizmet vermeye başlayan İspanya’nın ilk özel hızlı tren operatörü. Bu kazada 46 kişi hayatını kaybetti, 126 kişi yaralandı. İspanyol Lokomotif Makinistleri ve Demiryolu Yardımcıları Sendikasının (Semaf), ağustos 2025’te demir yolu altyapısından sorumlu devlet kurumu Adif’e, daha sonra raydan çıkma olayının meydana geldiği bölgedeki rayların aşırı aşınması konusunda uyarıda bulunduğu, ancak herhangi bir önlem alınmadığı ortaya çıktı. Adamuz kazasından iki gün sonra, Barselona’da bir setin çökmesi sonucu stajyer bir makinist hayatını kaybetti.

Demir yolu işçileri o dönemde de taşeron şirketlere devredilen ve kaynak ayrılmayan bakım hizmetleri sorununa dikkat çekmiş ve 9, 10 ve 11 Şubat tarihlerinde grev ilan etmişti. İlk gününde greve, ülke genelinde 34 binden fazla demir yolu işçisi katıldı ve 350 trenin seferleri durduruldu. Grev çağrısını yapan CCOO, UGT, CGT ve Semaf sendikaları, hükümetin “sektörün yapısal sorunlarını” ele almasını talep etti. Bu dört sendikadan üçü olan CCOO, UGT ve Semaf, Ulaştırma Bakanlığı ile bakım harcamalarının artırılması konusunda anlaşmaya vardıktan sonra grevin diğer günlerini iptal etti.

Ancak bu taahhütler yerine getirilmediği gerekçesiyle İspanya’daki tren makinistlerinin yüzde 85’inin örgütlü olduğu Semaf sendikası 16 Ekim’de yaptığı açıklama ile 29 Ekim için 24 saatlik grev ilan etmişti. Grevin talepleri arasında “Raylar üzerindeki risklere karşı önlemlerin alınması” ve “Demir yolu araçlarında süregelen güvenlik ve güvenilirlik sorunlarına yönelik gerçek ve kalıcı teknik çözümler” yer alıyordu.

Semaf, Toledo’da meydana gelen kazadan sonra yaptığı açıklamada da, güvenlik konusunda yapısal iyileştirmeler ve verilen taahhütlerin yerine getirilmesi talebiyle çağrısını yaptıkları 24 saatlik grevden geri adım atmadıklarını duyurdu. Grev gece yarısı başladı ve dün gerçekleştirildi.

Ayrıca, önümüzdeki cuma gününden itibaren Ouigo’da altı günlük grev çağrısını da sürdürme kararı alındı. Ouigo, Fransa Devlet Demiryolları (SNCF) bünyesinde faaliyet gösteren, 2021’den itibaren İspanya’da da düşük maliyetli hızlı tren hizmeti sunan bir ulaşım şirketi.

Bu arada Genel Emek Sendikası (CGT) da Toledo kazasında bağımsız bir inceleme yapılmadan makinistlerin suçlanmasına tepki gösterdi. CGT Konfederasyon Komitesi Daimi Sekreterliği, “Demir yolu güvenliği için yatırım, bakım ve yeterli personel gereklidir. Bu on yıllardır talep ettiğimiz bir konudur” açıklaması yaptı.

Demir yollarının özelleştirilmesi sadece bir hükümet politikası değil, Avrupa Birliği’nin de üyelerine bir dayatması.

İspanya basınında demir yollarındaki güvenlik sorununun başlangıcı olarak 1991 yılı gösteriliyor. O yıl 91/440/CEE sayılı Avrupa Direktifi, demir yolu altyapısı ve tren işletmeciliğinin birbirinden ayrılmasını zorunlu kıldı. İspanyol demir yolu sistemi Adif ve Renfe olarak iki şirkete ayrıldı. AB’nin çok sayıdaki demir yolu direktifleri trenlerin işletilmesi ve taşımacılık hizmetinin yaygınlaşmasını dayattı.

İspanya’da ayrıca 2000’li yılların başında yeni yasa ile bakım, güvenlik ve inşaat gibi demir yolu hizmetlerini taşeronlaştırmasının yolu açıldı. 2020 yılında İspanyol demir yolu sistemine yeni operatörlerin girmesine izin verildi. Bunlar arasında Fransız Ouigo ve İtalyan Iryo yer alıyor.

Basındaki verilere göre, 2024 yılında yüksek hızlı tren ağındaki trafik, 2019’a kıyasla yüzde 46 oranında arttı.

Ayrıca 2019’dan bu yana hem Renfe hem de Adif’te yüzlerce işçi işten çıkarıldı. Sadece Renfe’de son yedi yıl içinde zorunlu emeklilik veya görev yeri değişikliği yoluyla 500’den fazla işçinin çıkarıldığı belirtiliyor. Bu sayının artması Çalışma Bakanlığı tarafından engellendi. Bakanlık 2025 yılında yüzlerce zorunlu emekliliği “Haksız toplu işten çıkarma” olarak değerlendirerek iptal etti.

Tren kazası İspanya’daki seçim kampanyasına da çarpmış durumda. Başbakan Pedro Sanchez, Maricarmen Abascal isimli 87 yaşındaki bir Madridlinin 70 yıllık evinden kira zammı sonrası atılmasıyla başlayan konut krizi protestolarının ardından erken seçim ilan etmişti. Karar, Sanchez Hükümetinin krizi çözmek üzere hazırladığı kararnamelerin meclisten geçmesi, sağ Halk Partisi (PP) ve anketlere göre oyları giderek arkan neofaşist Vox partisinin öncülüğünde engellenmesi üzerine alınmıştı. Ülkedeki sağ yükseliş protestolarla birlikte tersine dönmüştü. Ancak tren kazası, 2018’den bu yana iktidarda olan Sanchez Hükümetinin de neoliberal politikaların suç ortağı olduğunu hatırlatmış oldu. Kazanın ardından Vox üyeleri hükümeti protesto için sokağa çıktı.

Aceleyle yapılmış “insan hatası” açıklamasıyla ilk adımı yanlış atan Sanchez ve hükümetinin bu süreci nasıl yöneteceği ve seçim sürecinin bundan nasıl etkileneceği önümüzdeki günlerde netleşecek.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Adıyaman'da su dolu çukura düşen 7 yaşındaki çocuk yaşamını yitirdi
content:
Adıyaman'ın Besni ilçesinde, bir inşaatın asansör boşluğu için kazılan su dolu çukura düşen çocuk, kaldırıldığı hastanede yaşamını yitirdi.

Erdemoğlu Mahallesi'ndeki bir inşaatın asansör boşluğu için kazılan çukur, ilçede etkili olan yağış nedeniyle suyla doldu. Bu sırada inşaatın çevresinde oyun oynayan 7 yaşındaki Yunus Emre Mutlu, dengesini kaybederek su dolu çukura düştü.

Çevredeki vatandaşların müdahalesiyle sudan çıkarılan çocuk, olay yerine çağrılan sağlık ekiplerince Besni Devlet Hastanesine kaldırıldı. Yunus, burada yapılan müdahalelere rağmen kurtarılamadı.

Ekipler olayla ilgili inceleme başlattı.

author: Kelly Hayes
title: AI Is Class Warfare. Workers Are Fighting Back.
content:
“AI is leveraged as a cudgel against the working class,” says writer and sociologist Alex Hanna.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Big Tech is selling us a future in which workers are increasingly disposable, human expertise is devalued, and corporate power is more concentrated than ever. But is that future inevitable? In this episode of Movement Memos, host Kelly Hayes talks with Alex Hanna, co-author of The AI Con, about AI as a tool of class warfare, the hype that obscures its real-world harms, and how workers are organizing to resist Big Tech’s agenda and win meaningful protections in the workplace.

Music: Son Monarcas and Guustavv

Note: This a rush transcript and has been lightly edited for clarity. Copy may not be in its final form.

Kelly Hayes: Welcome to “Movement Memos,” a Truthout podcast about organizing, solidarity, and the work of making change. I’m your host, writer and organizer Kelly Hayes. Today we are talking about how workers can resist automation and AI in the workplace. We’ll be hearing from Alex Hanna, co-author of the book, The AI Con: How to Fight Big Tech’s Hype and Create the Future We Want. Alex is a writer and a sociologist of technology, labor, and politics. Alex is also the director of research at the Distributed AI Research Institute, and leads the organization’s Luddite Lab project. Kelly Hayes: Which is such a great name for a podcast. Alex Hanna: Yeah, I mean, I have a lot of thoughts on this. I mean, I have thoughts on the claims of singularity or AGI, which is artificial general intelligence. Jack Clark is kind of an interesting figure because he used to be a policy person at OpenAI. And then I actually have been reading [or have at least been attentive to] his newsletter for years now. And it’s kind of interesting the ways in which he has gone from someone who had some interesting things to say about AI and interesting things to say about policy, to someone who’s very much bought into the narrative of things like the singularity, this hypothetical event in which human beings all merge into a singular kind of consciousness with the machine.

This is an idea that’s been proffered by someone named Ray Kurzweil, who is a futurist who has worked at Google for the last number of years. And it’s this fantastical idea that comes from science fiction. And what’s not new is that there’s claims about the singularity is already here, the same thing with artificial general intelligence. Oh, it’s already here. This is something that [OpenAI CEO] Sam Altman has said. And so you have this thing where there is this model of the world that at one point, is eschatological, like it’s: We’re going to have the rapture, we’re going to have the end times. And now as an economic move, these people within these companies have said, “Well, it’s already happening. We’re starting to be raptured. We’re starting to be moving into this space.”

And you’re like, “Ah, okay.” So your model of the world has changed from kind of an end times type of Christian, everybody’s going to merge into this one thing and there’ll be this tipping point to, well, it’s actually already happening and this is very important. And it just gives the game away that Jack Clark is giving the speech to the IMF, this neoliberal organization that has done so much damage in the majority of the world through structural adjustment programs and the ways that they are forcing austerity spending by their client governments. It’s effectively saying we need to revamp this element of trade policy or whatever the IMF is funding to accommodate for this kind of fantastical thinking. And so that’s definitely one thing that that signals.

The element of the model welfare thing, the idea that the models could just feel pain, I mean that’s this kind of thing which is — this has been around for quite a bit of time. And there was this thing that happened a few weeks ago where there was this GitHub repository … So GitHub is a code-hosting platform that is currently owned by Microsoft. And there was these sets of experiments that were created when this person who read this paper that said, “Well, if we were going to simulate pain in a language model, this is what it would look like.” And so this person developed this repository, this bunch of code where they were simulating intense amounts of pain that would be afflicted to a model. And then it was just an incredibly ridiculous event because there were many people — many users on the platform were then targeting this person saying, This person is literally torturing models and they’re putting the code on the web. And what an inane timeline because now there’s this focus on this idea that models are aware and they’re conscious and they can feel pain.

And to what degree are we — what evidence is given that a model can do that? These are big piles of linear algebra, that is effectively, I mean, that is not what is happening. And what really gives it away to me too is these are people who are more defensive of big piles of linear algebra than they are of real human beings, of Black and Brown people, of people in poverty. And this has been said by a lot of people in many different guises, but it’s effectively like people in this field seem to care a lot more about hypothetical, maybe conscious piles of linear algebra, rather than people in actual pain in the world right now. And that just tells you all you need to know about their ideology and how they view the humanity of people who are in the margins.

Kelly Hayes: Absolutely. And I think all of this goes back to how we have to think about AI conceptually, because we’re being pulled in a lot of imaginary directions. So it’s important to stay really grounded. You’ve argued in your work that AI isn’t even a coherent set of products and services; it’s a marketing term. It’s used to describe not just chatbots, but a wide range of computational services, including things that existed well before the era of chatbot hype. And AI, in addition to being a sort of product genre, should also be understood as a political project. The devaluation of human beings, our thinking, our well-being, and our labor is the crux of that project. And this weird, fashy, sci-fi fantasy really adds up to the devaluation of most living people, here and now. And so, in some ways, that’s the most important thing to understand about any aspect of AI as a marketing effort, and as a political project, is really that it’s about our devaluation. That’s what every one of these talking points comes down to: how much AI is worth, even if it’s not turning a profit, and how little each of us matters, in the new scheme of things.

Alex Hanna: Yeah, absolutely. I mean, I think that’s really hitting it on the nose. If you envision a few different elements of AI as a political project, you can see this devaluation of the human in a lot of different incarnations. And so I focus a lot on work and understanding that the primary economic rationale behind AI is obviating the need for labor. If there is some kind of way in which you can get rid of or automate so much of the work of human beings, then that means that you can just do massive layoffs and you don’t have to have folks who are real skilled laborers involved in the work process. And we’re seeing this in so many different industries, whether that’s health care, whether that’s education, whether that’s software engineering, whether that’s public service, whether that’s in social welfare. I mean, the list kind of goes on and on.

And there’s so many people who are salivating at this, especially venture capitalists who are willing to fund these projects to the tune of millions of dollars in their first funding rounds. And so we see this in labor. We see this as people who are living in the shadow of data centers. We see so much of the contention — not only in the U.S. but around the world — about how everybody needs to kowtow to the “greater good” of data center development in the U.S. We’ve seen it very sharply in the fight in Memphis, in Boxtown, which is a majority-Black neighborhood that is experiencing just a renewed round of environmental racism based on the build-out of the xAI data centers. We’re seeing this fight in the Philippines. We’re under this program, which Jacob Helberg [Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs] has headed this program called Pax Silica, which is intended to be this anti-China AI supply-chain securitization scheme.

And so it’s this whole arrangement and it’s causing this reconfiguration of who is fighting who. And so it’s wholly this political project on reconfiguring the centralization of political and economic power … [and] most people are stridently against this.

Kelly Hayes: It feels like a kind of full-spectrum class warfare, as a political project. Alex Hanna: Yeah. I mean, I think that seems like that’s what the desire is. I mean, we’re in a space now where the kind of class arrangements are very much set. And I mean, the kind of political realignment that’s happening is very interesting to witness in real time, where so much of capitalist desire is becoming made just abundantly clear in the ways that AI is leveraged as a cudgel against the working class and a cudgel against really anybody that’s holding land as well. I mean, that’s not just people who are land defenders that we see for spaces that have been traditionally held by the rightful Indigenous owners, or rather caretakers, but also the ways in which it’s also kind of a target of people in the U.S. who own lands or who are more conservative or farmers. And so I don’t have a good theorization of it to put a point on it, but you can very easily see how it’s just kind of a full-scale assault on anybody who’s not fulfilling the AI project of just kind of intense centralization.

And so what that means is these coalitions they’re developing are really novel and a little bit tricky, but some have been just very successful. And I mean the kind of rearrangements we’ve seen in places like New York State, where it’s this kind of combination of environmental groups and land defenders and First Nations and labor and democratic socialists have constructed in such a way that they’ve passed a moratorium in New York State for at least, I think it’s a year-long one.

And we’re seeing more and more of that tension coming to the fore as so many different groups are being opposed to data center build-out. And so yeah, I mean, we’re at this moment where AI is this manifestation of so much of the tech oligarchy and tech fascism where I’ve been in this area for 10 years and it’s just kind of an intense kind of thing seeing that, Oh, this thing I’ve been studying for 10 (I mean actually probably closer to 15) years is just now coming to hit us in the face by really presenting how much this has become a full-throated tool or full-throated incarnation of class warfare.

Kelly Hayes: Yes, it’s absolutely a class war offensive, and I think it’s so important to discuss it in those terms, whether it’s being wrapped up in these eschatological predictions about the end of the world, or talk of abundance, or the singularity. Whatever fantasies or talking points they’re throwing at us, that’s all wrapping paper for a project where capitalism is sort of redistilled — or, as Ruth Wilson Gilmore would say, the next round of capitalism saving capitalism from capitalism. In an era of catastrophic change, AI is being positioned as the basis for a reorganization of social and economic relations, using particular platforms and products to make human beings easier to isolate, control, disorient, and swap in and out of various labor roles.

So, we know that in the business world, there’s been a lot of excitement at the top about AI products because of the potential to eliminate jobs. But job elimination isn’t the only way workers are being affected. Can you talk about the changes you’re seeing, both in terms of job losses, and how people’s working conditions are being affected?

Alex Hanna: So we see jobs being eliminated because of at least the purported promise of AI tools in a lot of the creative classes. So we have seen a bit of a decimation of stable jobs in things like freelance graphic design, concept art. We see it a lot in translation as there’s been more of a move to use automated tools to do translation, even though these tools are not actually approximating good translations of anything. And we’ve seen this at places like Meta and Oracle. I think Oracle has been one of the places, and this is an organization that is supporting so much of the data center build-out, and they’ve just absolutely thinned out their senior developer pool. And I have some friends at Oracle who have mentioned that and they’re doing it in a ruthless way, people who are actually somewhat close to retirement or having retirement savings, actually just having those wiped out. And so yeah, I mean, those places are very, very worrisome. I mean, these are also places which have some of the worst union density, either because most of the fields are freelance or they work on a bit of a guild system. And so you’re only in the guild during the duration of a job.

And so we’ve seen a lot of that. And mind you, it is not necessary for the tools to actually work well for jobs to be decimated there. They effectively have to be thought to work well, and that may be just good enough for corporate managers there. They can then hire or rehire the same people at a fraction of the cost to fix those outputs, the sloppy AI outputs. And so we’ve seen another bit of a cottage industry even in fixing the outputs of those tools.

Kelly Hayes: I really appreciate what you were saying about turning people into fixers. And again, so much of what actually gets discussed around this, in popular discourse, is just the packaging. It’s the sci-fi narratives, the fantasies, the promises, or the threats. Alex Hanna: Yeah, absolutely. And we’ve seen this gigification happening in higher ed, in nursing for quite some time now. And so if we understand AI as an intensification of those processes rather than something that’s kind of brand new, I mean, I think that helps our analysis quite a bit.

Kelly Hayes: So there is a ubiquitous message that resisting AI is futile, and workers simply need to upskill and learn how to use it. Can you talk about what this rhetoric of reskilling gets wrong about what’s happening to skill, expertise, and professional knowledge?

Alex Hanna: Yeah. I mean, that’s a thing that I think is a bit worrisome. I mean, it’s not just worrisome in the workplace, but it’s also worrisome as we’re encountering students as educators. I haven’t been in a formalized classroom in a couple of years, but I’ve been an educator since I was an undergraduate about 20 years ago. Now I’m aging myself a little bit. And so the preliminary studies that we’ve seen on things like cognition, on retention when using these technologies is pretty upsetting. We’ve seen at least one study that suggests that cognitive ability, when measured by different cognitive imaging tools, seems to go down. There’s a study of a lot of Chinese students where I think they showed that, I think it was an experiment, students that used LLMs [large language models] to complete homework had higher homework grades, but had much lower test scores, which seems to signify that retention is going down.

And there is a study that was done by Anthropic themselves that showed that using AI-assisted coding tools, when people were learning how to use a new software library, they basically had no knowledge of how it worked or how you could execute with it. And so that could lead to things like cybersecurity attacks or not being able to check the code, not being able to understand what it’s doing in a way that is careful and thorough. And so this kind of thing is also okay with a lot of the tech executives. I haven’t read the whole of this interview, but it came out today. But if we’re thinking about calculators doing something of that nature versus doing any critical thinking, I mean, that’s very, very concerning as an educator. That’s concerning to me as a writer, as a reader, I’m very worried about that. And so, even if this is not the intention of tech leaders or corporate execs or corporate managers, but it does look like this is an intentional strategy to de-skill people and make them wholly reliant on the technology.

And so I’m very concerned that that is the future that is, that we are being sold. And on some degree, it is an intentional strategy to remove agency and to remove a certain kind of specialization of work, that we have gained these skills through hard-earned education and trial and error and through long years of education and experience. Now, can they do that in many fields where the automation isn’t quite there yet? Well, maybe it doesn’t work very well, but corporate managers may still argue that these are sufficient replacements and then that does lead to a further de-skilling.

Kelly Hayes: Absolutely, and this is something our listeners may be tired of hearing me rant about, but I really want it burned into people’s brains that Sam Altman thinks intelligence should be a utility that we have to pay tech companies to access. And you know, I think Marc Andreessen saying that he doesn’t believe in introspection is maybe also a bit relevant here. As a populace, we are being strategically simplified. And I don’t think you can really fight that unless you acknowledge that it’s happening. One of the objectives of that simplification, in addition to, I would argue, pacifying the populace more easily, is making us more interchangeable as workers. So we have to consider what that means in the context of the gigification of our work lives. I know some people who aren’t tech bros or billionaires who say things like, Well, this is just what capitalism has always done, or what’s the difference between this and a calculator, and I think we really need to reckon with the extremes we’re dealing with, in terms of how the harms of capitalism can be multiplied and amplified with this technology.

Alex Hanna: Yeah. No, completely agreed. And I think this is helpful to also think through because when we hear somebody like Altman saying, “Well, we need to make intelligence a utility” — or the latest incarnation I’ve heard of this is Mark Zuckerberg saying that we need to democratize superintelligence. And what he means by that is now we have this news agent that pops up when you use WhatsApp or Instagram. It doesn’t really mean anything. It means that there’s a product that’s now on your other product, now on your other Meta products. But this trajectory of gigification is something that we’ve seen for … I mean, we’ve seen it for years. I mean, it has been popularized by Uber and Lyft, but the kind of history of the gig is temporary work, it’s contract work. Now that work is mediated by an app, it’s mediated by the platform. And so one of the things that we can see is a way that gigification and casualization is intensified.

I can speak specifically to the way that we see that in, let’s say, education. We already have this trajectory in education in which universities have really leaned into the casualization of teaching. I mean, the last time I was a professor, over half the classes in my department were taught by contingent faculty, by adjuncts. And that’s just increasing. I mean, tenure-track jobs are becoming more and more scarce, and more of this labor is being done by people who are being paid piecemeal. We see this intensely in higher education, in a place that already suffers from what the economist [William] Baumol called cost disease. But the marginal cost of your violin player does not go down because people go to the symphony and that is something that requires a huge amount of training, but universities feel like they might be able to solve this cost disease with the usage of AI tools. I owe this analysis a lot to Dan Green, who has a great essay that I shout out every time I can, which is What Does AI Do? Kelly Hayes: You know, speaking of academia, I was actually chatting with a professor recently who was talking about the complexities around students using AI, and how they had a lot of sympathy for students who felt drawn to it. Real writing is valued less, or looked at as suspect, in a world awash in slop. And, under capitalism, producing slop doesn’t ultimately make a person more valuable — it just makes them more interchangeable with other people, who are also being devalued. And as we’ve discussed, it also cuts people off, in terms of their actual potential to gain ground with their skills. There are things I didn’t learn when I was in junior high and high school, because I didn’t go to the best public schools, and there’s so much I learned in my first year of college, from my favorite philosophy professor, about how to think critically, and how to scrutinize the values that were being normalized around me. So, I am really with that professor, in terms of not being judgmental about why individuals would gravitate toward these tools, or punitive about those things, but I am deeply concerned about what people are being robbed of, and about how we’re all being devalued, collectively, in ways that I think are going to have really ugly consequences in the long and short term, unless we fight.

Alex Hanna: Yeah, absolutely. So a few different wins that we’ve seen. Let me start with journalism. We’ve seen several wins in journalism. One of the organizations that we profile is the Ziff Davis Creators Guild. So this is writers and editors that are affiliated with the company Ziff Davis. So that includes publications like Mashable, CNET, ZDNET, these are online only, online first news sites. And so they have contract language that allows them to have control of any AI-generated content, any synthetically generated content that would go on their site and to have them have editorial control as well as establishing an AI committee in which they can discuss these changes. Another example within journalism is a recent arbitration win that we saw with the PEN Guild. The PEN Guild is the union that represents about 225 writers and non-supervisory editors at Politico and E&E News. In the latest contract that PEN Guild had bargained over, it required that any new technology be brought to discussion with the union within 60 days. Politico ran afoul of those rules, did not advise the union and implemented this AI tool, which they called Capitol AI for Politico Pro members, which is a paid product that Politico has. And they also had a number of different AI summaries that they used during presidential debates. And this was not brought to the union’s attention. The union filed a grievance. Politico disagreed. They took it to arbitration and PEN Guild won. And they basically said this runs afoul of the contract.

These things need to be bargained over with the union. You need to have some kind of oversight over this if this new technology comes into play. So that’s in journalism. I talked a little bit about the New York Times Tech Guild and about the kind of layoff protections, the just cause protections. You brought those up, Kelly, and the establishment of the AI subcommittee in their contract that they eventually won with a short strike. And then one we haven’t brought up in this conversation is around National Nurses United. National Nurses United is a union that’s a super union of many different state and local associations. I live in California, so here it’s California Nurses Associations. In New York, it’s the New York State Nurses Association.

Their wins have had some contract provisions, but what really impressed us in speaking with National Nurses United is the depth of political education that they engage in. You see an upskilling of people within that union that educates their members about what AI is and the way that it shows up in their job. Because, Kelly, one of the things that we find is that when you talk about AI, you have to set table stakes. We have to have that conversation we had earlier, which is: What do we even mean when we say AI? And that’s something that needs to be discussed from the jump, because how do you even spot what’s happening in the workplace? So in nursing, that looks like automated transcription. It looks like automated charting. It looks like automated scheduling. It looks like patient monitoring. It looks like all these little pieces that are often built into health care.

It looks also like platformization that nursing is going through as well, the kind of ways in which there’s these platforms in which nurses operate more like Uber drivers. And so what National Nurses United does really well is that they established a political education program from the ground up. They have a really robust political education department that presents materials and also gives those materials to local leaders to train up their membership. And they also use the machinery of professionalization committees that nurses have to go through as a condition of maintaining their licenses, and they use that as a mechanism to also deliver political education. National Nurses United is really unique in the sense that they not only [don’t] stop at talking about these issues of productivity culture, of layoffs, of the use of AI as a cudgel against workers, but they’re connecting the data infrastructure and the political economy of these companies to so many other areas.

Right now, National Nurses United has been doing actions against Palantir because they know that the data harvesting that’s being done, some of those systems have to be outsourced to be built by someone else. Sometimes it’s Palantir. In England, in the U.K., the NHS [National Health Service], their data warehousing system was run by Palantir. As you and I know, Palantir is wholly implicated in ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] raids, in border terror, in terrorism brought upon our undocumented neighbors and friends and family, in wars throughout the world. They’re just implicated in so much. And so their political education program doesn’t just stop at discussion of AI in the workplace, but the ways in which the organizations are building this kind of surveillance regime that is implicated with state violence.

Kelly Hayes: So what lessons do you think we can take away from these campaigns about what workers should be doing and demanding?

Alex Hanna: I mean, these are very inspiring campaigns and what I take away from them is understanding that anybody can fight AI. You don’t have to understand how something works to understand that it’s hurting you. You don’t have to understand how a gun works to know that you can get shot by one. You don’t have to understand how a synthetic text extrusion machine could say that you are not fit to receive health benefits and know that you are not going to get health benefits that month or that year. And so one of the things that we can take away is that anybody can join this fight.

The second is that the most powerful way that we really are able to fight these is if we’re in a collective, if we are in a group of people. Of course, I’m channeling Mariame Kaba, thinking about anything worthwhile is done with other people. And I think that’s something that is very helpful. I think one of the things that we think about in any of these tech justice struggles is understanding who around you is already doing this work. Where can you plug in? Where does it make sense to? Is there a way that you can lend your own expertise or skill set?

And then I think with worker struggles specifically, one of the things I think is really heartening is that in the U.S., in an era of rising fascism where the government — the federal government, and more in many places, the state government — is absolving any responsibilities or ignoring any checks that can be put on these tools. Workers’ organizations are one of the strongest types of counter-governance structures that we have. So workplace democracy means real life democracy too. I mean, not that workers, workplaces are not real life, but workplace democracy reflects state governance, and in a vacuum, state governance as well. And so in that case, that means governance over technology, governance over what technology is doing in our lives and in our workplaces.

Kelly Hayes: The Luddite Lab also stresses that these fights begin long before bargaining and continue after a contract is signed. You’ve been talking about examples of strong political education, inoculating workers against the idea that adoption is inevitable. What does good political education around AI look like and what resources should people be tapping into?

Alex Hanna: Yeah. Good political education around technology and AI looks like one, doing a little bit of denaturalization of what we mean when we say AI. What does it mean to talk about these technologies? In that case, we often rely on sets of questions, like in a particular type of tool, what goes in and what comes out? Does it make sense to connect the inputs and the outputs? Who benefits when the system goes well? Who benefits when it actually goes not as well? What are the companies that are building these tools? What other contracts do the companies have? Where does the data go? Is there any way to protect the data? Is there a way to remove the data? Is there any kind of meaningful opt-out? What does consent look like in these cases? And then what is the supply chain in the development of this? I mean, what are the other data practices or what are the other labor practices that these companies are implicated in?

And so it is rarely about the technology. You don’t need to know a lick about machine learning or neural networks to understand the connections between inputs or outputs, whether that even makes sense on the face of it, but you can understand the kind of network of organizations and the ways that they are implicated in the workplace. So the most successful political education programs have been the ones that do that. And so again, I want to continue to point to National Nurses United that does a great job of talking about that, developing those tools, connecting it with other kinds of pieces of political economy that talks about the data infrastructure and the ways that these companies are implicated in border terror and war making.

Kelly Hayes: The word “democratization” gets thrown around a lot when people talk about AI and its outputs, which is actually really ironic, given the fascist environment we’re living in, and the ways this technology is being weaponized toward fascist ends. But if we took worker control seriously, what would a genuinely democratic politics of technology look like — not simply thinking about workers getting to say no to a bad system, but workers and communities having the power to decide what technologies are worth building, and what problems are worth solving?

Alex Hanna: I think it would look dramatically different. I mean, first, there’s some good discussion to be had about thinking about work more generally and to think about what kind of work that we want to do in life. And if we think work can be worthwhile, then what would it mean to have technology that actually facilitates people’s jobs? It can look like a number of different things. I don’t purport to have any kind of solution ready-made as I shouldn’t because I think so much of this solution is much more local and is much more bound in what local conditions are. So for instance, what could be other conditions of worker organization that are more cooperative in nature? If they’re more cooperative in nature, what might be types of technologies that facilitate democratic decision-making in the workplace? What are ways that people can actionably change those pieces of it?

There’s many different experiments in democratic decision-making in technology. What would it look like for, let’s say, people who are non-technical to contribute to technology projects? What would it look like to encourage people who don’t have, let’s say, coding skills to contribute in such a way in which their needs are taken into consideration, rather than that kind of knowledge being generated or produced by some benevolent tech dictator?

And I think we need a lot of experiments in this. There’s a person, Rafael Grohmann, he’s written a bit about platform cooperativism and the idea that there’s joint platforms where individuals are in tech worker collectives. And so that might be an alternative model for control over one’s workplace, which I think then extends to control over the technology. And so that’s one thing that comes to mind. But I really think that one of the things that I have an armchair theory about, which I think is correct because it hasn’t failed me yet, is that technology really reflects the organizations in which it is embedded.

This is not a new idea perhaps, and when I say it, it’s rather simple-sounding. But effectively, one argument that’s a mainstay of science and technology studies is that a weapon like the atomic bomb could not exist if it was not for a huge organization that had to manage all the accesses or do all the building of such a thing. And it requires a bit of an authoritarian structure of organization to maintain. And this is a point that Langdon Winner makes in some of his texts. The same could possibly be said of technology where if you have a collective, then it might look like your technological development is much more communal or collective. If you have something that’s wholly top-down, then it is fine to buy ChatGPT Pro as a service and to give it to all your employees, especially if ChatGPT allows an administrator to see everybody’s prompts and outputs. I mean, that’s a full panopticon of boss access. So I do think there’s that kind of reflection, that technological world we want to see also depends on what kind of organizations that we make and build as alternatives to capitalism and fascism.

Kelly Hayes: I appreciate these insights so much. As we wrap things up here, is there anything else you would like to share with or ask of the audience today?

Alex Hanna: My only ask or my only request of people is to know that you, no matter where you are with regards to how much you know about technology, have the ability to direct where technology should go. And it can be as easy as getting with other people in your community and understanding and trying to get a sense of what your needs are, and then articulating that in a way that you could possibly build something different and newer and better and more communal. So that’s probably my last optimistic thought.

Kelly Hayes: Well, Alex, I want to thank you so much for joining me today. And where are all the places people can find your work?

Alex Hanna: So you can learn more about the Luddite Lab at labor.dair-institute.org. And then you can follow me on Instagram at AI_Killjoy as well as on TikTok. And then I’m on Bluesky @alexhanna.bsky.social. And then you can just find me around. I’m fluttering around the interwebs.

Kelly Hayes: Wonderful. Well, I really appreciate you making time to join me, while you’re still recovering from not feeling well, and I really hope we can do this again sometime.

Alex Hanna: Absolutely. Thank you so much for having me, Kelly.

Kelly Hayes: I also want to thank our listeners for joining us today, and remember, our best defense against cynicism is to do good, and to remember that the good we do matters. Until next time, I’ll see you in the streets.

Don’t forget to check out Alex’s book with Emily Bender, The AI Con: How to Fight Big Tech’s Hype and Create the Future We Want

You can learn more about the Luddite Lab and check out their resource hub here.

To learn more about what AI can and can’t do, check out the Distributed AI Research Institute’s website.
