title: "Women, Justice and Memory" vigil in Amed: “Rojda is not alone”
content:
Women’s organizations have once again protested against patriarchal violence, femicides, and impunity for perpetrators outside the courthouse in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır). The “Women, Justice and Memory,” organized by the Network Against Violence, entered its fourth week on Tuesday. Alongside representatives of political parties and civil society organizations, Rojda Odabaşı also took part in today’s demonstration. She had survived an attack in late August when a neighbor shot at her with a shotgun in her apartment.




The participants carried photographs of murdered women and a banner reading “Women hold vigil for justice and memory,” chanting “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî,” “Femicide is political,” and “Long live women’s struggle.”




ÖHD: Rojda’s safety must be ensured immediately




The demonstration focused on demands for protection and justice for Rojda Odabaşı. The suspect had been released late last week following the armed attack on her. Aycan Diril, from the Women’s Commission of the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD), criticized the decision and called for a thorough investigation into the case. “We demand that Rojda’s safety be ensured immediately, that the decision to release the suspect be subjected to effective judicial review, and that every aspect of the attack, including possible intent to kill, be investigated. We will continue to follow this case. Rojda is not alone,” Diril declared.




The lawyer emphasized that the vigil was intended not only to commemorate women who had been killed but also to highlight the responsibility of state institutions. This week, the focus was on seven women who were killed or died under unclear circumstances between October 18 and 26. Representatives of the participating organizations shared their stories.
















Killed despite protection orders




Criticism of the state’s failure to protect women from violence was particularly evident in the cases of Sevda Dinler and Perihan Akbulut. Both women were killed despite having already obtained protection orders against the suspected or eventual perpetrators. Sevda Dinler, a 22-year-old graduate of a vocational school of health sciences, was shot dead with a hunting rifle on October 21 in the Kozan district of Adana. According to media reports, she had rejected Gamber Fidan’s advances and had subsequently been threatened and stalked by him. A protection order had been issued against the man. Following the killing, he was arrested and placed in pretrial detention.




Perihan Akbulut, a 61-year-old mother of five, was stabbed to death in the street the following day in Yeşilyurt, in Malatya. She sustained eight stab wounds. A protection order had also been issued against her husband, Hasan Akbulut. The perpetrator died in hospital after attempting suicide while being pursued by police.




“Femicide is not an unforeseeable event. Previous violence, threats, persistent stalking, and applications for protection orders are often warning signs. When a woman is killed despite a known risk to her life, it must also be investigated whether state authorities fulfilled their duty to protect her,” the statement said. The activists linked this criticism to the economic conditions that can prevent women from leaving abusive relationships. They opposed political attacks on alimony rights and highlighted the lack of security regarding housing, income, and caregiving responsibilities.




Femicides and unexplained deaths




The vigil also commemorated Melek Altınboğa and Aliye Aker. Melek Altınboğa, a 30-year-old mother of one, was killed with a hunting rifle by her husband, Murat Altınboğa, on October 18 in the Akören district of Konya. The couple had been married for just four months. The perpetrator subsequently injured himself with the same weapon. Women’s organizations criticized media reports that reduced the murder to a domestic dispute, thereby downplaying the patriarchal violence involved.













Aliye Aker, 27, was shot dead on October 21 in Osmaniye by Salih Aker, whom she had married just 20 days earlier. The man subsequently took his own life. The activists emphasized that a perpetrator’s death following a femicide did not absolve the authorities of their duty to investigate possible failures to protect the victim and the circumstances surrounding the crime.




Particular attention was also paid to 26-year-old lawyer Özge Penbegül, who was shot dead on October 22 in her apartment in Menemen, near Izmir, by her fiancé, Aykut Erol. The man, who worked as a police officer in Hakkari, subsequently took his own life. The network emphasized the particular responsibility of state institutions when armed public officials commit violence against women. They underlined that wearing a uniform must not shield anyone from scrutiny or accountability for such acts.




Alongside these femicides, the women highlighted two unexplained deaths. Remziye Damar, 61, was found dead in her apartment on October 20 in Kızıltepe district of Mardin. The activists warned against prematurely classifying her death as suicide. They demanded that possible circumstances involving violence and coercion also be investigated.




Kazakh national Aisulu Bekmakhanova (26) died after falling from a great height in Istanbul’s Şişli district. The exact circumstances remain unclear. The network called for a thorough investigation and emphasized that women’s protection and access to justice must not depend on their nationality or residence status. In this context, the activists once again criticized Turkey’s withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention.




Bucak: Rojda demands justice for herself and other women




Following the commemoration of the seven women, Rojda Odabaşı herself addressed the gathering. She demanded justice and appealed to the media and women’s organizations to support her struggle. Amed co-mayor Serra Bucak praised Odabaşı’s courage: “Rojda has stated with great courage and clarity that she wants justice. She is demanding this justice not only for herself but also for other women.”




Bucak called on the women of the city to join the vigil and maintain pressure on the judiciary. “I appeal to all women in Amed: Come here every Tuesday, to stand before the institution that fails to hold the perpetrators accountable.”




The fourth vigil ended with a minute of silence in memory of the women who had been killed.

title: Trial begins in Leipzig over knife attack on Kurdish woman
content:
Proceedings began today, 27 October, at the Leipzig Regional Court in a case concerning the stabbing and serious injury of a 31-year-old Kurdish woman on a tram on 26 January 2026. The 21-year-old Syrian defendant, Ahmed A., faces charges including aggravated assault, threats, robbery and insult.




According to the indictment, the defendant, Ahmad A., and another person who is being investigated separately insulted and attacked the Kurdish woman aboard tram line 16. The attackers reportedly threatened Kurds, saying, “We will kill all Kurds.”




During the incident, the woman was injured by knife blows and her thumb was severed. It was later surgically reattached at a hospital. She reportedly sustained permanent restrictions in movement and loss of sensation in her hands and fingers, and continues to receive psychological treatment.




Defendant denies anti-Kurdish motive




Speaking in court, the defendant, Ahmed A., admitted to attacking and robbing the victim but claimed that he had no personal issue with Kurds or with the woman he attacked. He said he had consumed alcohol on the night of the incident and had become involved in a knife fight on the tram.




The victim previously told the German newspaper 

Taz

 that she believed she had been attacked because of her Kurdish identity. “Their problem was that I was Kurdish. They didn’t need my money,” she said.




Defendant faces up to eight years in prison




Ahmed A. has been held in pretrial detention since May. He is also facing charges relating to another robbery that took place in Leipzig in February and resisting police officers.




The presiding judge stated that, under certain circumstances, the defendant could face up to eight years in prison for the attack on the tram. The trial is scheduled to continue with four further hearings through 24 November.

title: I’m fine with anyone using ‘dead naming’ for themselves. People have many reasons to have a painful…
content:
runicdesk

:

Trans sensitivity question!

Is the term ‘dead naming’ reserved for trans people, or can it be used for people who changed their name for other reasons? Thank you in advance.




I’m fine with anyone using 'dead naming’ for themselves. People have many reasons to have a painful association with their past name and if having a term that says ’

do not fucking use this name

’ is convenient for you: go for it. 

But also, I may be an outlier, as I am trans and I hate the term 'dead naming’ and would never use it for myself. 

I’m not dead. Nothing about me died. My past name isn’t a horrible memory that must never be uttered, it’s just a name I once used. It’s as mundane as my pre-transition pictures, which are still on my wall because my transness is not a dirty secret to be hidden. 

Someone who uses my past name for me deliberately is being a transphobic asshole, but they don’t hold any power over me. I will not cry myself to sleep because they used the secret spell of trans pain. I’ll just think they’re a transphobic asshole and I’ll move on.

title: Virtual Press Conference RE BAAJA
content:
Jordan Harmon, policy analyst and legislative advocate at the Indigenous Environmental Network. Growing up in the oil and gas hub of Tulsa, Oklahoma, once dubbed the “Oil and Gas Capital of the World,” Jordan witnessed firsthand the negative environmental and economic impacts of the fossil fuels industry and currently focuses on influencing public policy that will benefit Indigenous peoples, open spaces, and the environment while ensuring Tribal sovereignty and free, prior and informed consent is upheld.

Rashida Tlaib, member of Congress, U.S. House of Representatives. Democratic Representative Tlaib has served the people of Michigan since 2019 representing the 12th Congressional district. As a lawyer and the first Palestinian American woman to serve in Congress she has consistently supported environmental and economic policies that prioritize community health and well-being, especially in the face of corporate interests. She sits on the House Environmental Justice Caucus that she founded with Representatives Summer L. Lee (PA-12) and Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07).

Daisy Maldonado, organizer with Fight Chihuahuan Desert Xtraction in New Mexico. Daisy is a trained economist and has been a community organizer in the area for twenty years. She works alongside working-class and colonia communities in southern New Mexico that have long faced environmental neglect, inadequate infrastructure, and barriers to political participation. She is currently focused on stopping the data center campus, Project Jupiter. In 2021, she was appointed by the Governor to the Sustainable Economy Advisory Council (SEAC), advising the state’s Sustainable Economy Task Force on strategies to diversify New Mexico’s economy away from reliance on natural resource extraction.

KeShaun Pearson, Director of the Memphis Community Against Pollution (MCAP). For years, KeShaun has organized South Memphis residents to stop toxic air pollution and safeguard community health from big business and their often anti-democratic practices. He is a Boxtown resident who has most recently been organizing communities to fight the air pollution spewing from Elon Musk’s xAI facility near Memphis, Tennessee. Before that he mobilized grassroots support to oppose the Byhalia Connection Pipeline, attempting to build through predominantly Black neighborhoods.

Erik Schlenker-Goodrich, executive director of Western Environmental Law Center. Erik joined WELC as a staff attorney in 2003 and became executive director in 2012. He has fought in court to safeguard the climate from dirty fossil fuels, promote a transition to a clean energy future, and protect the West’s rivers and wildlands. An expert in issues related to oil and gas development, Erik leads WELC’s campaigns to phase out fossil fuels and build climate resilience. Prior to joining WELC, he worked as a public lands attorney for The Wilderness Society.

Good morning everyone and thanks for joining us today. My name is Joshua Detman and I am the Executive Director of the Labor Network for Sustainability. We connect trade unions, worker centers, and climate and environmental justice groups to build a just transition to an ecologically sustainable and economically just economy and we are opposed to the bipartisan Affordability and Jobs Act for many reasons.

Primarily, we know that temporary and short-term jobs do not support families and should never come to the cost of the entire community’s health and well-being. Faster project approvals alone do not guarantee good jobs, lower energy costs, or healthy communities. Today, you’ll hear from a group of environmental policy experts, climate justice leaders, community leaders, and elected officials who represent thousands of communities across the United States, territories throughout Indian country.

What they have in common is their profound belief that people and the land, air, and water that we survive on is worth protecting. This bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act ensures the opposite and is the most egregious attempt yet to give big oil, gas, and tech a free pass to pollute and lock in harm for generations. Permitting reform is necessary.

Our speakers are here to tell you why and what their communities and constituencies think about it. We’ll hear from the following, John Beard Jr., founder and CEO of Port Arthur Community Action Network in Texas. We appreciate him for joining us last minute and claiming the Southwest.

On short notice, Kashawn Pearson had an unexpected travel come up and won’t be with us today. We’ll also hear from Daisy Maldonado, community organizer with Fight Tichuan Desert Extraction in New Mexico. Eric Schenker Goodrich, executive director of Western Environmental Law Center.

John Harmon, policy analyst and legislative advocate at the Indigenous Environmental Network. And finally, U.S. Representative Rashida Tlaib, who has served the people of Michigan since 2019, representing the 12th Congressional District. Each speaker will have about five to seven minutes, so we have time for Q&A at the end.

Please put your name, organization, and any questions you have for the speakers in the chat, and we’ll try to get to as many as we can count, as many as we can at the end of the press conference. Without further ado, I’ll pass it over to John to get us started. Mr. Beard.

John Beard Jr. Thank you, Mr. Dedron. Good morning, everyone. I hope you’re doing well, or wherever you are this morning here.

Hopefully we have an international audience on this because it’s a very critical matter for the entire nation, as well as for those of us here in the Gulf South, as we call it in Texas. And I am John Beard, the founder and CEO of the Port Arthur Community Action Network, an environmental, social justice, and community development organization located in the corner of Southeast Texas, near Louisiana, in the Gulf of Mexico. Mr. Beard, I’m so sorry to interrupt, but the Congresswoman will need to leave very shortly, so I think we need to let her speak first.

I’m so sorry to interrupt. That’s fine. Yeah, I’m so sorry.

I have to head to Southwest Detroit, just getting calls and stuff. It looks like I might have gotten the director of ICE to remove them, but I really apologize. But I hope I helped set the tone and everything, because I’m really angry right now, John.

So I’m gonna be able to go. Thank you so much for always inviting me to this space. I know you all have been so unified, so loudly in saying no to this horrible permitting reform bill.

And we are not getting fooled by the titles. I have been in Congress and unbelievable in seeing so-called big, beautiful bill and all of the different titles that they have that they add to the bill, but all it is is poison. The bipartisan, so-called bipartisan—I hate even calling it—the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

The fact that they even can call it bipartisan breaks my heart. We all know it’s a gift to big oil and big tech. Our communities will be left paying the price.

We’ve seen this already from my community, where I thought that smell was normal. I thought that many folks having asthma and respiratory issues, and even Sierra Club Detroit doing a White Cross campaign of people with cancer or survived cancer or died of cancer, suffering—all of them watching all the crosses on people’s front of their lawns, small crosses, again, symbolizing the fact that we are sacrifice zones. We know the bill is 417 pages of empty promises.

We’ve got to get that out to our community, written in secrecy with no public input. The thing is, we can’t get too technical with our residents. One of the things I always tell folks, you know, they’re building these structures and these policies so that we can’t understand it easily.

Even as a lawyer, as an advocate that worked in nonprofit sector, I still literally struggle in understanding these permitting processes. Again, it’s done in a way, to me, as one resident said, Rashida, just call it permission to pollute process, because that’s what it feels like. We know it’s a shame that we have to fight so hard for our elected officials to do the right thing—Democrats and Republicans—to stand up for their residents and vote this down.

Even in our own backyard, I watch our governor literally roll out the red carpet in Michigan for data centers. The permitting reform deal, we know, would speed up those construction of those data centers. Right now, communities all across the country—I mean, what’s incredible is seeing the different backgrounds of people.

You know, they all think this is a Democratic issue. I said, no, this is an American issue. I don’t care if you up north in Michigan, where it’s a little, you know, probably leaning more Republican, to over here in Wayne County.

You see a unified message. We don’t want this in our community. I am so proud in my own backyard, a city of Inkster.

Residents came together and successfully defeated a data center proposal by flooding the city council meeting. I’ve never seen anything like it. And people came together in a unified message.

We don’t want this in our backyard. We also know that this bill also make it easier for fracked gas pipeline projects. We know that the fossil fuels, fuel damage, damages our environment are accelerating the climate crisis.

I just did an op-ed about how our children are suffering so much because we actually have to have days because it’s so hot out that our kids can’t even go to school because they don’t have HVAC and we don’t have the resources. So our kids are staying home because the heat is so high and they could, again, it’s harmful to have them go to school like that. Again, the impact of the climate crisis is already here.

So that’s why, so why is our government making it easier for big polluters? We all know why, right? This is corporate money into politics and corrupting our democracy. We know the bill strips away what little tools our communities have to defend ourselves from corporate polluters. It threatens tribal nations, sacred sites and cultural resources.

We should be strengthening these environmental protections, not tearing them down. And please don’t settle for the crumbs. I remember under the Biden administration, the Biden administration licensed more fossil fuel projects than any previous president.

And it’s something he actually touted about and then gave us a little bit of funding and grants for addressing the climate crisis. But I just don’t understand how do you do both? So what good are laws like the Clean Water Act if Congress allows polluting companies to exploit and extract our water, right? So enforcement matters. We’re facing a public health crisis.

Neighborhoods are suffering from toxins in their air and water. I’m tired of hearing our families say, Rashida, I can’t even afford, you know, I can’t afford my water bill. But on top of that, they’re paying for poisoned water.

Our families are struggling to keep up with the energy cost. Every single time I turn around, we have our monopoly utility companies here in Michigan raising the cost on all of us. And, you know, again, these are the consequences of our government’s own action.

I am so proud that Congresswoman Summer Lee and Adelita Garjava and I in March started the People’s Environmental Justice Caucus. This is your caucus. Use us.

Use this caucus to make sure that our voices are heard all throughout the halls of Congress. So I’m standing strong with all of the groups, 200 community labor environmental justice groups, many of whom are on this call today. Thank you.

Thank you for rejecting this power grab. Thank you for speaking the truth. It is a growing movement that I know will push Congress to do the right thing.

But again, it is important for you all to know how incredibly bipartisan this is, which means when the Democrats, if they do get the gavel, John, Joshua, Jordan, all of you on the call, I’m looking at all of you, when they get the gavel, I hope you understand that doesn’t mean we’re safer. That doesn’t mean they’re going to address the issue. Because one of the things I’ve noticed, and we had a trifecta, we still were seeing, again, the lack of urgency in addressing some of these issues.

And I’m sad to say that we’re going to have to make sure that as they are trying to repeal all the bad things that Trump has done, that they also include this. This is where we all come in and push back against, again, this narrative that, oh, this is not the time. It has been the time.

And so please don’t settle for crumbs. Do not settle for the press conferences. Settle for real action.

We’re not going to be putting these folks in power and advocating and showing people why we have more dirtier water now. It’s not just lead anymore. You guys know this.

It’s plastic. It’s everything. And so let’s just really, really work together.

So let me go out there and beat up on ICE, but thank you all so much for coming together. And thank you. Thank you for squeezing me in and early because this is the neighborhood I grew up in and I’m devastated.

Thank you, Congresswoman Tlaib. Just to return to, we appreciate the sentiments that were given and the encouragement. We encourage you to go and challenge ICE to the best of your capability.

And we want to return to our initial schedule and we want to return to Mr. Beard. Thank you, Joshua. Appreciate it.

Appreciate the words from the Congresswoman with regard to that. And once again, good morning to all of you that are here today. A lot has been said already.

It really covers a lot of this, but I want to bring you a snapshot of what this bill is going to do closer to home here. Port Arthur, Texas is in what I call the belly of the beast. And if you don’t know what that term means, it means the worst and direst of situations that you could ever be in.

Why do I say that? Because I’m looking out of my window right here on my patio and I can see less than a quarter mile away, the largest refinery in the country. And to my, what would be your right, which would be my left, less than a half mile away is another major refinery, Valero, which had a major explosion and fire back in March of this year that shook my home. I thought initially a plane had crashed into my house.

The wall danced like it had legs. And then subsequently just this past September, we had the tropical storm Eduardo. And that storm caused major releases from these plants that were so severe that you could see the chemicals in the rain that were falling on your house, on your car, and on the streets and driveways.

That leaves that iridescent sheen that you know when there’s the presence of oil or some hydrocarbon. Well, yes, we experienced that. The cost of electricity and utilities has gone up substantially. Some of the highest in the country are right here in Texas, where I live. It is going to also mute our voices by taking away the ability to utilize the court system, and also to utilize the laws that are currently already on the books that force the companies to take due diligence to notify and inform the public in a timely fashion, so that we can look at, examine their proposals, and respond in ways that protect our communities.

It will shorten that statute of limitation from six years to 150 days. As you well know, with a lot of the regulatory agencies and political government bodies signing NDAs, and also signing confidentiality agreements, that these things are used to keep the information from us. And as I was just told recently by a government body here that, oh, we’re going to bring in an open session in our meeting and discuss it, and you can come then.

Well, this bill will help do that. It will also harm us, because it strips away the protections of NEPA, the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Air and Clean Water Act.

And already, we have some of the worst conditions here, environmentally speaking. A U.N. study attests to that. And also other studies that were done, that this is some of the most contaminated air in the country, with formaldehyde, nitrous oxides, and others that are present here.

And how do we know that? Because we see in Port Arthur twice the state and national average for cancer, and that people of color have a 40 percent higher chance of dying from cancer who live in close proximity to these plants within 25 miles than people who live further away. This bill is not about affordability. It is about giving a blank check to the oil and gas industry.

It is about giving a blank check and free rein to the data centers and all these other businesses that are trying to come into our communities without our consent, without our voices being heard. It is undemocratic because it takes away our ability to speak to the things that help us. So I’m here to speak on behalf not of just Port Arthur, but of Lake Charles, Louisiana, of Brazoria, Brazoria County, of Corpus Christi, Brownsville, of my friends and brothers and sisters in Appalachia, and all who are affected by pipelines, by transmission lines, by all of these things that are going to hurt and harm our communities without our having a say in the matter.

Suffice it to say that if this bill passes, it will be the end of environmental justice if we know it in this country. Our voices have been muted, neutered, neutralized, and snuffed out if this bill is allowed to pass. So we say no to the BAAJA.

We say no to muting our voices. We say no to hurting and harming our friends, relatives, neighbors, and our very own families. I have family members too that have been affected by the releases and all of this.

So I’m going to end here and pass this on to my colleagues, but I want it to be known and said that we say no, we stand against this bill because of the harms it would create, and we urge you to talk to your senators and congressmen and tell them to do the same. This bill must be DOA. The BAAJA must be DOA.

Thank you so much, Daisy. And thank you, John. Previously, Eric, we’d like to call you in.

Hey, folks, it is very lovely to follow on Daisy, my neighbor down in County Eric Schlenker Goodrich. I am the executive director of the Western Environmental Law Center. I’m based up in Taos.

We wholeheartedly oppose the Baha, the permitting deal negotiated behind closed doors in the Senate. We don’t think that this is a close call. But it is a terrible bill. And trust and credibility is earned. And this bill betrays that trust to the climate community, to the environmental community, to the environmental justice community.

Now, I want to talk about some of the details on this bill. And I’m glad Daisy mentioned the Desert Southwest Pipeline, because that factors into what this bill’s harms would do. Now, first point I want to make is that when you take a look at the permitting deals provisions, you have to map it onto what has been happening in the Trump administration through its deregulatory actions, much of which was articulated in the Project 2025 playbook that they have been executing ruthlessly and relentlessly for the past 18 months or so.

We have witnessed over 550 deregulatory actions by the Trump administration. So the notion that we are going to move forward in a lame duck session, a 417-page bill that further erodes bedrock statutory protections under the Clean Water Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, this seems, this is flat out absurd. Now, with the Desert Southwest Pipeline, keep in mind that this bill in Section 1102 would exclude the vast majority of natural gas pipelines from any environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act.

No more environmental review for those pipelines. So those laterals that Daisy is talking about really depends on the facts, but around the country, what we’re going to see is many of those pipelines just get bulldozed through without any environmental review and without any public participation in those decision-making processes. Even worse, even if they weren’t excluded from review, because there are certain projects that will still be subject to review, the public has no recourse in federal court.

Sure, they can file litigation and go to court. However, as John Beard mentioned before, the statute of limitations has been cut down to 150 days. Set that aside, if you go to court, and even if you are able to prove a violation of either the National Environmental Policy Act or the National Historic Preservation Act, a court is deprived of its longstanding authority to vacate that underlying federal permit or license.

And further, they’re deprived of their equitable authority to impose an injunction to prevent irreparable harm. That’s unacceptable. That’s just flat-out unacceptable.

And relative to the deregulatory agenda, keep in mind too that just yesterday, the Trump administration announced that it was going to roll back Environmental Protection Agency methane protections from oil and gas. So you have a highly polluting upstream oil and gas industry no longer subject to methane safeguards. Then you have midstream natural gas pipelines that are excluded from federal environmental review, with the public deprived of its ability to participate in those decision-making processes.

And for what? With the Southwest Desert Pipeline, we know they’re taking natural gas from the Permian Basin, punching that west across New Mexico and into Arizona to power AI data centers. We know this for a fact. Now let’s talk about the permit certainty provisions in the bill, because these are arguably even more troubling than the erosion of those bedrock environmental protections, which is wild to even say.

Now there are two provisions here that are deeply troubling in particular. Section 1401 creates an incentive for fossil fuel industry data centers to stockpile permits and authorization during dependency of the Trump administration while they are able to enjoy a highly deregulated state where many of the federal regulations have been rescinded or watered down. A future president would find it very, very difficult, but maybe not impossible, but extraordinarily difficult to unwind those permits.

What is perhaps even more alarming is that Section 1401 would prohibit the ability of a future president to repair those public health and environmental safeguards, and then to apply and enforce them against Trump-era permits. So it would freeze in place the regulatory state as the Trump administration understands it. Section 1402.

So Section 1401 looks back, really freezes in that deregulatory state, incentivizes AI data centers, fossil fuel companies, other extractive interests to stockpile permits. Section 1402 looks forward, and it looks forward by taking power away from people and from future presidents to unwind the harm that this current administration has caused. It would chill and hobble the ability of a future president to put in place a robust climate agenda and conservation agenda and environmental justice agenda.

And it does that by allowing fossil fuel and other energy interests to claim that they are in effect a protected class, and 1402 prohibits disparate treatment against those particular energy sources. This is noxious because this protective standard for those interests, it’s pulled from civil rights and anti-discrimination law. And it’s applying that anti-discrimination law, putting it into statute, and then applying it to corporate energy and data center interests.

That is astounding. And so if a future president decided we need to transition away from fossil fuels to renewables, that could be used per the statute as evidence that the president is disparately treating fossil fuels, and that will be a weaponized against the administration’s efforts to put in place strong rules and a strong agenda to transition from fossil fuels to renewables. Now, let’s move forward and think about this bill in a broader context.

What I think this bill reflects is a withering of climate ambition, in particular by the energy wonk crowd. We’re now narrowly fixating just on infrastructure and technology as the solution to what we need to do about the climate and suspect thinking about how the markets will play out. There is no carbon signal in this bill.

There is nothing that limits climate pollution. It is all based on wishful thinking about how the markets will play out. Now, I do want to acknowledge that we know that Rhodium, as well as Resources for the Future, that they’re looking at the greenhouse gas emissions estimates for this bill, and that our understanding is that they have found and will publish hopefully soon.

I mean, we have a vote coming up on November 9th. It’d be nice to have this analytical data in advance so that we could actually scrutinize it. I mean, I trust Rhodium and Resources for the Future.

But then at the same time, it is an assumption laid in process to move forward with a model. It is not a prediction. It is a data point.

Now, that data point can be useful for making an informed case for this bill, but it is not a substitute for wisdom and judgment and the values that we care about relative to the communities and places that we love, that we live in, that we call our home. Now, what we think Rhodium and Resources for the Future are going to find is that this may reduce greenhouse gas emissions relative to the status quo. That is not a reassuring finding, and it’s not a reassuring finding, and let me put this in colloquial terms.

It’s akin to acknowledging that, let’s say you have a credit card and you’re putting more and more money on your credit card every single month. Really difficult to pay that down. We’re still adding with this bill more and more debt to our credit card, our carbon credit card, every single month, even with this bill.

It just makes it a little, little less than what we were doing before. So as we run up continuing that carbon credit card, it’s better than nothing, but it’s not exactly a compelling argument for a deal that would nonetheless still add vast quantities of greenhouse gas emissions to the atmosphere, and because of that Section 1402 provision and Section 1401 provision, erode the optionality of a future president to unwind the harm that President Trump is causing and to put us on a pathway to true climate action. The other key point I want to make here is greenhouse gas emissions are one component of this deal.

This deal has massive implications to communities and people and public lands, wildlife and watersheds, cultural resource protections, all across the country, in all of our communities. And there is no analysis of what this bill’s impacts would be. And in fact, this is one of the reasons we think that Senator Heinrich—and I say this as a New Mexican who has voted for Senator Heinrich, who has worked with Senator Heinrich for 20 some odd years—that we feel betrayed, because they are not having an honest conversation with us about those trade-offs.

They just talk in very generalized terms. Well, there are trade-offs. We need trade-offs.

What are those trade-offs? In New Mexico, we’re talking about the Southwest Desert Pipeline. We’re talking about Greater Chaco, a place that Senator Heinrich has purported to defend, that this bill would, with the Trump administration revoking protections for Greater Chaco, allow oil and gas companies to really hit Greater Chaco and bulldoze over it. So this bill, this bill isn’t about good policy.

It’s about power. And it shifts power from the public and from future presidents to capital and markets. That is why we oppose this bill tooth and nail, and we will fight it till it’s dead.

Hi. My name is Jordan Harmon. My clan is the Deer Clan.

My tribal town is Chiaha. I’m a Muskogee Creek citizen based in Oklahoma in the Muskogee Reservation. And it is with the interests of Indigenous peoples’ sovereignty and the well-being of Mother Earth in mind that we must urge Congress to oppose this poison pill bill, vote no on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, stand up for tribal consultation, and stand up for the health of all of our communities within every congressional district.

The sweeping and unnerving changes proposed specifically to the tribal consultation process under the National Historic Preservation Act, Section 106, can be seen as no less than an outright attack on tribal sovereign rights and Indigenous peoples. The NHPA Section 106 is the only codified standard for government-to-government tribal consultation that is a mandated duty under the legal trust and treaty obligations. And this is an incredibly important law for tribes and for our communities.

And in 1835, when my people were forcibly removed from our homelands and forced to make the long walk from Georgia to Oklahoma, now it is thanks to the Section 106 consultation process that our sacred mound sites still exist in our homelands, and I have been able to make the journey home and pray with our ancestors at our sacred sites. That might not have been possible without this process. And rather than bringing tribal nations, Indigenous communities, and traditional knowledge holders to the table for meaningful consultation regarding one of the most important laws that exists in Indian law, Senators Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse chose to betray the trust of Indian country and used our sacred sites as a backroom negotiating deal.

Instead of listening to the tribal nations in his state who reached out in good faith, Senator Heinrich turned his back on prayer and ceremony and walked out of a meeting with Pueblo leaders. That is unacceptable behavior and it really reflects his lack of regard for our lands and rights as sovereign peoples. You cannot support his bill.

If the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is passed as is, tribal voices will effectively be shut out of the process with regard to our own sacred and cultural sites. With this bill, the federal government is seeking an authoritarian control over determining whether a tribe’s historical site is important enough to count and whether it deserves protection. This would inevitably lead to the unnecessary destruction of important Native American sacred sites.

Most of this country does not support doing that. Most voters don’t want to destroy Native American sacred sites. This would have lasting generational impacts akin to assimilation era policies.

It’s an extension of a genocide. Once our sacred sites are gone, they’re gone. We don’t get a second chance at getting those back.

You have to include tribal voices. Congress members must understand that Section 106 is non-negotiable. It must be off the table, period.

All of Indian country is united on this. Voting to take away tribal consultation in this way would be an unforgivable act for a Congress member to do. There are a handful of very wealthy greenwashed organizations investing a lot of PR money into the narrative that, as John says, the BAAJA is a necessary measure for clean energy.

But the reality is that taking the public voice out of decision-making actually paves the way for more unwanted polluting industries like hyperscale data centers and fossil fuels. Our voice was never the red tape in the way of permitting. Public input, thorough environmental assessment, and meaningful tribal consultation was never what was causing permitting delays.

Most permitting delays under the NEPA and NHPA process are not caused by public input or tribal consultation. They’re caused by staff shortages, communication delays between project developers and permitting agencies, and the facts show that it is a lack of public engagement that frequently causes permitting delays for clean energy projects. When you shut out the people and communities from decisions impacting their homes, their health, their livelihoods, and sacred sites, opposition to a project should not be surprising to you.

In fact, it should be expected at that point. Early stakeholder engagement, meaningful tribal consultation leads to better decision-making, and ultimately faster project completion. And we do have ideas about how to improve permitting, actually.

Early and meaningful tribal consultation and look at the Environmental Justice for All Act that we’ve been working on. The justifications for this bill are simply not sound. Trust me that Indian country is by and large on board with clean energy transition.

Most tribal nations want clean energy, actually. And trust me when I say that we as Indian people want and need lower utility bills. I’m literally just about priced out of my house and home over here with these high utility bills.

I’m not even joking. But this bill, the BAAJA, is not a magic fix for that. In fact, the opposite is true in that it contains a lot of harms against the most vulnerable among us and is a blank check for fossil fuels.

We need our champions and allies in Congress to publicly stand with us. We need our so-called progressive allies to stop selling the lies that we as Indigenous people are worth sacrificing for the sake of transmission lines. It’s not worth the sacrifice, and we’re not going to just lay down and let it happen.

We need our Congress members to vote with the best interests of the people in mind, not the interests of billion-dollar industry and not the interests of their own campaign fundraising. This will be a legacy vote. You will have to ask yourselves what you want your legacy in Congress to be.

Do you want to be the one who voted against tribal sovereignty? Do you want to be the one who voted to revive genocidal assimilation-era tactics against Indigenous peoples and destroying our ancient cultural sites? Or do you want to be the one who stood with us and protected our sacred sites? It is that deep. Protect the NEPA. Protect the Clean Water Act.

Protect the Endangered Species Act. And please, whatever you do, protect the tribal consultation process under the NHP Section 106. That is all we have.

Do the right thing and vote no on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Job Act. It’s a crap bill. Thank you, Mado.

Thank you, Jordan. I would love to just take a moment to thank all of our speakers, Congressman Tlaib, Mr. Beard, Eric, Jordan, and of course, Daisy, for your time and your efforts and for your committed challenge to challenging this Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which pits always corporations and prioritizes corporations, prioritizes oil and gas over the lives of people and over the life of our planet. The permitting bills that we’ve been getting ever since the IRA, the Inflation Reduction Act, the big beautiful bill, the bipartisan Infrastructure and Jobs Act, and now this, those are dirty bathroom deals.

They are all bad, actually, because you have Republicans and far right people and people in the fossil fuels industry pushing for these reforms. I’ll happily address this question as well, that the permitting reform debate is a fundamental misdiagnosis of many of the problems. It fixates in on the point when a permit is issued. It does not look upstream at what the mission of the agencies who are moving through the permitting process, what they are charged with actually doing in terms of delivering on the public interest, because it doesn’t.

It’s based on this all of the above or tech neutral agenda that essentially cedes power from the government to determine what kind of technologies and energy sources we should be using, where they should be located and how, and then it cedes that to capital and markets. The second thing you need to do is you need to actually invest in those agencies, that you need to provide them with the resources to assess permit applications, to figure out what should get priority, and then to move deliberatively through those decision-making processes.

So really focus upstream on mission and agency capacity. And that is essential. And that is what the literature says.

I know that everybody’s inundated with all these PDFs and reports from all these billionaire funded think tanks that, oh, the problem is NEPA or the NHPA or the Clean Water Act or whatever. Like, that’s bogus. Look to the law professors, the academics, the domain experts like the folks here who have worked with these processes, and you know that that is not the problem, but there are solutions out there, and we are open to that conversation.

Let me also chime in on that. There’s what permitting reform looks like. It looks transparent.

It looks inclusive of the parties and people who are being effectively locked out. It looks engaging to be able to bring all of those parties to the table to make these decisions and to talk about this. And Eric is correct that this is really a misnomer because it’s not really about permitting reform.

It’s about giving free reign to the oil and gas industry to push their projects through unheeded and unimpeded. And that is not reform. That is simply wiping out the democratic process that gives people such as BIPOC communities and also indigenous communities a voice in these matters.

They deserve to be heard because they are being effective, and they’re willing to sit at the table. Environmental justice in terms of this, as well as this bill, looks like the EJ for All Act that is inclusive, comprehensive. It lies in the delays and the things that are done that are trying to be done in a way which goes against the needs of people who are going to be affected and who also are end users of all of these things that we call affordability-based. Thank you. We’re getting a few questions in the chat, and so I want to kind of continue to move the needle a bit.

We will kill this bill. This bill will be dead on arrival because we’re going to do everything in our power to make sure we are heard, seen, and felt. This shall not come to pass.

We will do everything in our power to make sure that it doesn’t. Senator Whitehouse, if he’s here or anybody knows how to get in touch with him besides me, which I’m going to do, I want to remind him of the fact he came here and he saw this. Once again, how dare you give a slap in the face to not just my community, but to me, who invited you here to see this up close and personal, and you will put this kind of bill before the people.

Thank you, Mr. Beard, for your profound power and enthusiasm. I think we may have time for one more question, and I do want to address the idea of the fact that we can’t just count jobs. We have to measure job quality, and this act really strikes the ability to measure and know what are safe and clean jobs.

I think the last and final question is what powers would this bill give the Trump administration to further his war on renewables? We’ll start with Daisy and for anyone else who wants to answer. This will be our final question. Yeah, thank you for that, and I think that Eric had mentioned about Senator Heinrich and the propaganda machine around how this is about renewable energy is just false, because in fact, it’s the opposite, right? Senator Heinrich has been making the rounds talking about how this would be good for New Mexico, this would be good for our country, and this would move forward energy plans that have been bucked up against roadblocks.

In fact, those are pipelines, those are gas plants that are seeking approval without permits so that they don’t have to construct renewable energy. In fact, that they can, again, pollute and make as much money as they want off the backs of working everyday people. But I think also some more technical stuff could be shared by other folks who can answer that in a more comprehensive way.

Thank you. Any other panelists want to approach that question? I would just say that there’s a couple of provisions, the project certainty and disparate treatment provisions that are going to basically guarantee that the Trump administration’s priorities with regard to the data center and AI build out as well as natural gas and fossil fuel build out are pretty much locked in stone. And it’s not something that, let’s just say hypothetically, a progressive president comes back into office, they can’t just undo that if they even would want to.

Yeah, I’ll just mention, with the project certainty provisions in this bill, they’re truly troubling because it essentially allows capital markets to take over the direction of how energy is developed in the United States. That doesn’t make it impossible, but what it will do when you layer it onto all the erosion of the bedrock environmental laws is it creates what may be generations long harms to communities and generations long work that we will then need to put in motion to try to remedy much of the harm that this bill will cause on the ground. And that’s what the problem is.

We don’t have that kind of time. I mean, people keep claiming that, oh, there’s urgency to move this bill over the lame duck session as if Democrats aren’t about to win at least the House and perhaps the Senate next week on November 3rd, where they’ll have more leverage. And the notion that somehow that there is no possibility of moving forward with something better than, frankly, this really terrible bill just seems absurd to me.

The timing issue actually plays in favor of opposing Baha because we need to maximize the opportunity for our communities and for future presidents to unwind the harm that this administration has caused and to put us on a true path to progress. Thank you, Eric. And thank you everyone for joining us today.

Please feel free to reach out to us for any follow-up questions or anything else you would like to know pertaining to this press conference and our position against the bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, not affectionately known as Baha. And we’ll send this recording out shortly after this call. And if you’d like to talk more, please feel free to respond to the speakers as we send out the emails and information of the speakers and the panelists.

We’ll do our best to connect you with the panelists. And please have a great rest of your day. And thank you.

Dear Leaders Thune and Schumer, and Senators Lee, Capito, Heinrich, and Whitehouse,

On behalf of the undersigned Tribal organizations, we write to express our strong opposition to Title III of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act BAAJA), concerning changes to the Section 106 review process of the National Historic Preservation Act. While we object to other provisions in BAAJA, this letter will focus on Title III’s proposed changes, which are in deep conflict with federal trust and treaty obligations to engage sovereign Tribal Nations in government-to-government Tribal consultation and to protect our irreplaceable cultural heritage. They fail to respect our inherent sovereignty, self-determination, and Indigenous Knowledge. We urge the immediate rescission of this language from the proposal and ask that you instead consult with Tribal Nations on permitting reform that will bring Tribal Nations to the federal decision-making table earlier so that together we may guard against further destruction of our sacred sites and cultural resources.

The reviews required under section 106 are vital to the continuity of Native cultures, the practice of our spiritual traditions, and the protection of our sacred sites from irreparable degradation and ruin. After centuries of federal action designed to strip us of these fundamental rights,1 the Section 106 review process, though imperfectly implemented, provides Tribal Nations with a mechanism and resources to help the federal government make better decisions that avoid the ongoing loss of our identities, ceremonies, and

1 Federal Indian law is and always has been a reflection of international norms, recognised by the very first U.S. Supreme Court cases in the Marshall Trilogy. As international norms evolve, including to better recognize Indigenous peoples’ cultural rights, see Articles 11 and 12, U.N. Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, federal Indian law must not be left behind.

Ancestors in the name of progress.” Now, with the introduction of BAAJA, the federal government is proposing to facilitate the demolition of our heritage, a regressive action that ignores the progress made in the Tribal-U.S. relationship during the self-determination era and returns us to a place of U.S.-sanctioned encroachment and dispossession.

Permitting reform does not involve a binary choice between the pursuit of infrastructure projects and the protection of sacred sites through the Section 106 review process. Together, we can craft federal policy that accomplishes both aims. When Tribal Nations are brought into federal decision making at its earliest stages, we can help guide project design to avoid irreparable harm and legal violations—allowing for faster and more durable decisions. Indeed, without our Tribal experts, there is no way for a federal agency or project proponent—even with the help of archaeologists—to accurately identify our historic properties and the effects we may feel on them. We must be part of the solution, not pushed away from the table. While we acknowledge that Title III contains some positive provisions, including the codification of Tribal consultation and an increase in the Historic Preservation Fund, these are far overshadowed by provisions that would undermine our ability to participate in federal decision making and protect against cultural loss, including:

• Narrowed definitions and increased exemptions limiting scope of Section 106: By limiting and creating exemptions for important definitions, such as “undertaking,” “effect,” and “area of potential effects,” the bill greatly reduces when the Section 106 review process is triggered, thereby reducing opportunities for Tribal Nations to be involved in federal decision making to assist in cultural reviews. Each of these changes may affect our ability to even have knowledge that an infrastructure project is occurring, all but guaranteeing that construction through sacred places will proceed without the involvement of Tribal Nations.

• Reduced Tribal Nation articipation and increased federal deference: Under the bill, Tribal Nations need not be consulted as federal agencies designate an area of potential effect, identify historic properties, and assess potential effects—requiring only that federal agencies consult after they issue a report containing their pre-determined conclusions. The federal agency could be the sole entity in determining whether a Tribal cultural property exists, despite Tribal Nations, our designated officials, and cultural experts being the only entities qualified to make these determinations on our behalf. Moreover, the bill would give federal agencies the authority to determine that “other considerations” outweigh adverse effects on our sacred places.

• Inappropriate federal oversight of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers: The capacity issues facing Tribal Historic Preservation Officers (THPOs) are well known and can be attributed to chronic federal underfunding and neglect. However, in response to a problem of the federal government’s own making, this bill proposes to penalize Tribal Nations, contravening policies of self-determination and self-governance. For example, under this bill, missed review deadlines will result in the loss of THPO status and funding, as well as the deeply paternalistic assumption of THPO functions by the Department of the Interior, which is wholly unqualified and lacks the necessary expertise to perform these sacred duties.

• Limitations on judicial review: As the leadership of the Committees of Jurisdiction over permitting processes, you are well aware of federal agency shortcomings in the Section 106 process as it currently exists. These shortcomings often result in failures to properly consult with Tribal Nations and to act upon our guidance. In the case of these failures, Tribal Nations are frequently left without recourse or options beyond the judicial system, if we are to protect our heritage and seat at the table. We do not seek to engage in litigation, nor are these ‘nuisance’ lawsuits. Any litigation represents our last attempt at preserving our cultural identities. Instead of acknowledging and mitigating federal failures, this bill attempts to shut Tribal Nations out of the court room. Most glaringly, it provides certainty in the face of federal ineptitude and nearly eliminates any real remedies available to Tribal Nations by stipulating remand without vacatur as a baseline, thus allowing projects to proceed while remand to address inadequate Section 106 review is ongoing. This bill also institutes a 150-day statute of limitations, attempts to limit standing, forces a Tribal Nation to assert substantive objections to a federal agency’s Section 106 report within a mere 30 days of receipt, and creates additional burdens for litigating Tribal Nations.

Tribal Nations should not be forced to bear the brunt of these cultural and spiritual harms so the nation can further develop and transport its energy resources. We have already sacrificed the majority of our lands and natural resources—oftentimes through force or coercion—upon which the United States has become the world power it is today.

As Indian Country has noted repeatedly, early, robust, and meaningful consultation with Tribal Nations (that includes mitigation and avoidance requirements) and meaningful increases in funding owed for Tribal historic preservation will result in faster infrastructure deployment and greater certainty in the permitting process. While we strongly support robust and strengthened national infrastructure, any infrastructure build-out, in Indian Country and beyond, must not occur at the expense of Tribal consultation, sovereignty, sacred sites, or public health.

It is with this in mind that we register our strong opposition to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act as written. We urge you, in the strongest possible terms, to withdraw this language and work in collaboration with Indian Country on a more honourable alternative.

Sincerely, Affiliated Tribes of Northwest Indians Association on American Indian Affairs Midwest Alliance of Sovereign Tribes National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers National Congress of American Indians Native American Rights Fund Rocky Mountain Tribal Leaders Council Tribal Self-Governance United South and Eastern Tribes Sovereignty Protec

author: Mada Masr
title: Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was fined LE3 million by the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, which convicted her on charges of managing an unlicensed website, issuing an order for the website’s closure. Attalah was taken into custody after the issue of the ruling.




Tuesday’s session at the ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, presided over by judge Mohamed Mubarak, was temporarily suspended for deliberations after Attalah’s defense counsel requested time to review the case file.




After the court returned from deliberations, the judge ordered the courtroom cleared of everyone except Attalah and her defense counsel, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ executive director Hossam Bahgat, who was also present, told Mada Masr. The room then filled with plainclothes officers and guards, with a National Security Agency officer in attendance, he added.




The presiding judge and a Supreme State Security Prosecution representative returned to the session and the judge announced that the court has decided to stand by its rejection of all the procedural arguments presented by the defense, including requests to bring in any documentation or hear any witnesses.




The judge then asked the defense team to present its plea. The counsel insisted that it would not submit a plea as long as its requests were unanswered by the court.




The judge then abruptly asked for a lawyer unknown to any member of the defense counsel to be brought in, “in a move that astonished all those present,” said Bahgat, and announced that the court decided to appoint a lawyer for Attalah.




At that point, all members of the defense counsel cried out to reject the court’s appointment of a lawyer when the eight chosen lawyers were present. Attalah herself spoke to say she did not accept the court-appointed lawyer acting on her behalf, an objection the judge refused to have recorded in the session’s minutes.




“In an even more shocking move,” said Bahgat, the judge himself began to log down the requests of the court-appointed lawyer, without the lawyer having said a word. The judge then read out the conviction amid shouts and protests from the defense counsel.




The judge sentenced Attalah to the maximum possible penalty: a LE3 million fine, the closure of Mada Masr’s website and the confiscation of its property.




Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse.

author: Tam Saavedra
title: WEI and UN Women Co-Launches Guide for Disability-Inclusive
content:
Across Asia and the Pacific, 350 million women and girls with disabilities navigate conflict, crisis, and climate instability. While they are frontline peacebuilders, community leaders, and human rights defenders, they remain systematically excluded from formal peace and security decision-making.

To break down these barriers, Women Enabled International (WEI) and the UN Women Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific have officially launched a landmark publication today: the Guidance Note on Disability-Inclusive National Action Plans on Women, Peace and Security in Asia and the Pacific. Released ahead of the annual UN Security Council high-level debate in New York, this first-of-its-kind guide provides a practical, policy-oriented blueprint for governments, policymakers, and civil society.

Read the full Guidance Note on Disability-Inclusive NAPs on WPS in Asia and the Pacific

Historically, women with disabilities in peace policies have been viewed narrowly as victims or passive recipients of protection. Co-drafted through consultations with 26 women and gender-diverse people with disabilities, in collaboration with Women Enabled International and the UN Women Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific, this guide directly challenges that narrative. It grounds its framework in a human rights model of disability and the core movement principle: “Nothing about us without us”.

As WEI Executive Director Maryangel García-Ramos Guadiana stated during the launch:

“The true value of this Guidance Note is that it exists, not as a siloed document, but as a means to ensure we, as feminist disabled change-makers, are not left out of the agenda, but we are the ones who get to set the agenda.”

UN Women Regional Director for Asia and the Pacific, Christine Arab, added:

“National Action Plans on WPS that include everyone lead to peace that lasts.”

The publication was shaped by participatory research, drawing on focus groups and surveys with 26 grassroots leaders with diverse disabilities across the region. It addresses critical ground-level hurdles—including digital exclusion, inaccessible evacuation infrastructure, and ableism in mainstream spaces—ensuring that the voices of women, girls and gender-diverse people with disabilities form the foundation of the guidance.

The publication urges stakeholders to align National Action Plans (NAPs) with international standards—including the CRPD, CEDAW, and UN Security Council Resolution 2475—across all four WPS pillars:

Participation: Reserve seats for organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs)—especially women-led OPDs—on NAP steering committees with full accessibility support.

Participation: Reserve seats for organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs)—especially women-led OPDs—on NAP steering committees with full accessibility support.

Prevention: Recognize women and gender-diverse people with disabilities as active peacebuilders and integrate intersectional early-warning indicators.

Prevention: Recognize women and gender-diverse people with disabilities as active peacebuilders and integrate intersectional early-warning indicators.

Protection: Address unique forms of violence (such as caregiver abuse or institutionalization) and guarantee accessible shelters and evacuation procedures.

Protection: Address unique forms of violence (such as caregiver abuse or institutionalization) and guarantee accessible shelters and evacuation procedures.

Relief & Recovery: Ensure transitional justice mechanisms, reparations, and post-conflict upskilling actively include women with disabilities.

Relief & Recovery: Ensure transitional justice mechanisms, reparations, and post-conflict upskilling actively include women with disabilities.

The guide also features a practical Disability-Inclusive WPS NAP Checklist to help stakeholders evaluate progress at every stage of policy implementation.

This Guidance Note was made possible with the generous support of the Government of the Republic of Korea (through the Ministry of Gender Equality and Family) as part of the project “Promoting Leadership of Future Generation Peacebuilders and Change-makers in Asia and the Pacific”, and of the Australian Government under the Regional Framework Towards Peaceful, Inclusive Societies (2023–2027).

title: Navigieren auf einer neuen Welle von Unruhen
content:
Jetzt ist es wieder soweit, europäische Regierungen zucken zusammen vor Tausenden Randalierer*innen die in den Metropolen auf die Straße gehen, ohne das sie von den Polizeikräften in Schach zu halten sind.




Macron tönt, nicht zum ersten Mal in seiner Amtszeit: 

"Wer zerstört hat, muss dafür bezahlen. Wer geplündert hat, muss den Schaden ersetzen. Wer versucht hat, die Republik zu stürzen, wird dafür zur Rechenschaft gezogen." 

 


Die Papageien der Medien schäumen vor Wut, wie immer wenn die Ohnmacht die Seiten wechselt, und auch die freiwilligen Putzkräfte, die im Sommer 2017 beim G20 in Hamburg mit Bürsten die Bordsteine des Schanzenviertels von Krawallspuren beseitigten sind am Start. Jetzt kratzen sie in Paris geschmolzene Leihräder aus dem Asphalt oder sortieren Mülltonnen in Mailand.




Aber wo sind wir? Überrascht von diesen Wutexplosionen, zu deren entstehen wir wie so oft, nicht viel beitragen konnten. Um nicht den Überblick zu verlieren, eine unvollständige Zusammenfassung der letzten Events,




Brüssel


Am 9. Oktober folgten 30.000 Menschen den Aufrufen von Gewerkschaften gegen die antisozialen Maßnahmen der Regierung. Schüler*innen und Student*innen blockierten Bildungseinrichtungen. Von morgens bis abends kam es im Zentrum, im Bereich der Bahnhöfe zu Zusammenstößen mit den Bullen. Unterbrechung des Konsums, statt die wie eine Pest verbreiteten E-Scooter für eine leicht zu trackende Fortbewegung zu nutzen, werden sie heute von Jugendlichen massenhaft ins Feuer geworfen. Die Spannungen hatten sich schon an den Vortagen und auch in anderen Städten angekündigt.


Am 17. Oktober weitere Krawalle in Brüssel und Lüttich, 195 Festnahmen bei einer Demo gegen die Sparmaßnahmen im frankophonen Bildungswesen, gegen die Polizei und gegen die aktuelle belgische Regierung.




Paris


Nachdem letztes Jahr eine Alles Blockieren Bewegung im September an vielen Orten eskaliert war, wurde deren vermeintliches Ende mit einer lahmen Stimmung eines müden Generalstreiks Anfang Oktober 2025 besiegelt. Um plötzlich mit den diesjährigen Bildungsprotesten und Schulblockaden in eine neue Runde zu gehen. Seit Wochen tut die CRS das, was sie immer macht, sie schießen Demonstrant*innen mit Flash-balls die Augen raus und sprengen Jugendlichen mit Granaten die Hände weg. Aber offenbar war am 17. Oktober die Wut größer als die Angst und Frankreichweit wurden Bullen angegriffen, Geschäfte geplündert, Symbole des Staats zerstört. Trotz jahrzehntelanger Erfahrung mit Aufstandsbekämpfung, gelingt es Politik und Verwaltung bisher nicht, die Allianzen von Schüler*innen, Überresten der Gelb Westen, Banlieue Bewohner*innen, Linken und anderweitig Angepissten zu spalten. Macron, der seine Truppen von Kanaky bis Erbil kämpfen lässt und momentan besonders die Golf Monarchien verteidigen will, kündigt Verhaftungswellen und Ausgangssperren an.




Barcelona


Lange blieb es ruhig in Barcelona aber am 5. Oktober kam es wegen der Wohnungsproblematik zu Riots im Zentrum. 100.000 Menschen beteiligten sich an einer Demo, zu der die Sindicat de Llogateres tenants' union aufgerufen hatte, danach Unruhen im Bereich Plaça Catalunya und La Rambla. Bullen setzten wie immer Gummigeschosse ein, 30 Mossos wurden verletzt, Stadtmobiliar lieferte an 28 Stellen das Barrikadenmaterial. Die Sprecherin des Sindicat erklärte als Ziel, das Land zu paralyzieren. Die Regierung hat nach dem Tod von Maricarmen Abascal aufgrund der Zwangsräumung und ihrem Scheitern in der Wohnungspolitik Neuwahlen für den 29. November angekündigt. Anarchist*innen verteilen ein Flugblatt während der disturbios:




"Möge die Wut über alle hinwegfegen. Politische Parteien, Gewerkschaften, Parlamente, alle Organisationen links von der PSOE, Polizei, Richter, Journalisten, Faschisten, jeder einzelne von ihnen ist Teil desselben Apparats zur Kontrolle und Bewältigung unseres Elends. ... Unser einziges Ziel ist es, Bündnisse im Kampf und auf der Straße zwischen Gleichen zu knüpfen, unsere Klassenfeinde zu identifizieren und sie mit allen Mitteln anzugreifen."




Mailand


Am 17. und 18. Oktober erlebte Mailand in seinem kommerziellen Zentrum die Ausschreitungen, die es verdient. Dort drehte sich die Demonstration um die für viele nicht mehr zahlbaren Lebenshaltungskosten. Wie in den anderen Städten auch wurden Bullen angegriffen, Geschäfte geplündert, Banken zerstört und überflüssiges Zeug den Flammen übergeben. Der Bürgermeister Giuseppe Sala befand:




"I'm very worried because it's a new phenomenon, which also originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself."

 Mehr als 200 Festnahmen in Mailand, Ausschreitungen auch in Bologna und Turin.




Tirana


Albanien sah den Sommer über monatelangen Widerstand gegen den Plan der Trump Familie, ein Naturschutzgebiet in ein Luxus Tourismusressort zu verwandeln. Die sogenannten Flamingo Proteste waren Ausdruck der Spaltung der Gesellschaft in die ohnmächtigen und überflüssigen Segmente und die Clique um den korrupten Regierungschef Edi Rama. Seit Anfang Okober verschärften sich auch die Aktionen von Schüler*innen und Studierenden, inzwischen mit Riots an acht Tagen in Folge. Das Bildungsministerium ging in Flammen auf. Edi Rama dazu bei einem Treffen mit Lehrer*innen und Direktoren: 

“A wave of stones, an attempt to overthrow the government and change those in power through the imposition of violence — something that will never be allowed to happen, in any form or for any reason.”




Lissabon


Der Rossio verwandelt sich in ein Zeltlager als Ausdruck der Verzweiflung über eine Stadt, die sich in wenigen Jahren zur am meisten gentrifizierten Metropole Europas gewandelt hat. Airbnb und Luxus Lofts für Internetnomaden und liberale kalifornische Millionäre haben die soziale Basis der Stadt zerstört. Als die Polícia de Segurança Pública am Morgen des 20. Oktober knüppelschwingend zur Räumung schreitet, wird sie mit Gegenständen beworfen, 55 Verhaftungen.




Und in Deutschland? Die Gesellschaft verbleibt noch passiv, wie fast immer. Konfliktscheue Pseudo-Gewerkschaften waren hier nie bereit Arbeitskämpfe auf die Straße zu tragen, das Mietenproblem seit einiger Zeit durch sinnfreie Enteignungsdebatten entschärft. Doch Spannungen an den Schulen beunruhigen die Herrschenden, Hetze in den Medien und vorauseilende Distanzierungen von Gewalt reichen sich bereits die Hand. 

https://www.tagesschau.de/inland/aufruf-demos-sicherheitsbehoerden-100.html


Barrikadenzündler*innen und Steinewerfer*innen stehen vor mehreren Problemen. Hier bleiben oder reisen? Die Informationslage aus den Krawall Hotspots ist dürftig, die Berichte und Mobilisierungen aus erster Hand auf Indymedia gehören der Vergangenheit an, die noblogs Seiten abgeschaltet, die neue Bewegung kommuniziert nicht mehr über eigene Medien sondern die des Feindes. Wer auf Insta und Co verzichtet kann den Dynamiken schwer folgen.




Zudem scheinen manche strategischen Grundlagen in Frage gestellt. Als Anarchist*innen stellen wir keine Forderungen an den Staat um diesen nicht als Dialogpartner zu legitimieren. Jedoch resultieren die aktuellen Unruhen aus der Weigerung von Regierungen, auf die Forderungen von Schüler*innen, Mieter*innen und von hohen Preisen Geplagten, einzugehen. Ohne abgelehnte Forderung keine Wut, ohne Wut kein Krawall?




Auch das appelistische Milieu in Frankreich stellt sich auf einem blog Fragen und beantwortet sie gleich mit einem Vergleich zu den Gelb Westen:




"How should we make sense of repeated defeats, even despite the persistence of conflictual forms of action? What conclusions are we to draw from this? How are we to “survive” the present moment? How do our enemies continue to prosper? How can we confront capital with seriousness and strategy and truly reinvigorate revolutionary ethics and perspectives?"

 Um diesen interessanten Text aus einer problematischen Ecke nicht verkürzt wiederzugeben, liest Du selbst "Becoming Alive, Autonomous, and Explosive - The Invisible Committee" auf 

https://illwill.com/becoming-alive




Aus einer anarchistischen Perspektive fällt auf, dass zwar nicht mehr eine Beteiligung an den gegenwärtigen Unruhen in Frage gestellt wird, weil dort dumme Symbole gezeigt werden, wie die französische Fahne, aber das Zusammenfinden auf der Straße erscheint schwer. Wir agieren zu selbstreferentiell und konnten weder große Menschenmengen bei AfD Parteitagen zum Angriff nutzen, noch die Demonstrationen gegen den Genozid in Gaza bei Überfällen der Polizei verteidigen. Vor knapp 10 Jahren zur Eröffnung der EZB in Frankfurt, brannten die Streifen vor der Bullenwache, eine Mobilisierung Gleichgesinnter weit über die Region hinaus machte es möglich. Während dieser Periode wurden wichtige Momente der Konfrontation in den vielen Städten Europas weit im voraus bekannt gemacht, diskutiert, und als Möglichkeit des sich findens wahrgenommen. Mittlerweile hat sich direkte Kommunikation und Anteilsnahme verschoben in den digitalen Ether. Mögliche Momente der gemeinsamen Konfrontation und geteilte Erfahrungen auf der Strasse werden zum nebeligen Teil des nächtlichen Doomscrolling. Warum wir nicht mehr ausrasten beschäftigt sogar das Feuilleton der Zeit. Laura Cwiertnia stellt dort fest:




"Beobachtet man die Protestkultur in Deutschland in den vergangenen Jahren, kann man sich fühlen wie in einer düsteren Variante von Samuel Becketts Warten auf Godot."

 

https://archive.ph/20261022092258/https://www.zeit.de/feuilleton/2026-10/proteste-europa-deutschland-frankreich-lebenshaltungskosten-jugendliche




Jetzt die Apathie durchbrechen, ritualisierten Spektakelkonsum in Frage stellen - damit am 31. Oktober die mögliche Ausweitung der Jugendproteste nicht durch Organisationen wie "Initiative Gen Z regelt" abgewürgt werden kann.




Und danach am 20. November auf die Straße! 

https://youthstrike.org/

 Jetzt gibts keine Ausreden mehr von wegen nichts gewusst.
